The second section of the Separate Preface through the tenth section is completed.

From the conclusion of the "Chapter on Stating the Fundamental Tenets" to the beginning of the "Chapter on Receiving the Consent (Chanda)," Sixth Scroll.
From the conclusion of the *Karmavastu* chapter, through the *Sīmābandhana* chapter, Volume Seven;
from the conclusion of the *Saṃghagrantha* chapter, through the *Ācāryopādhyāya* chapter.
Volume Eight concludes with the Section on the Confession of Precepts; Volume Nine begins with the Section on the Invitation at the End of the Rains Retreat.
The section on the Exposition of Names concludes. The sixth section, the Exposition of Characteristics, ends here. Volume Ten: The Sounds of the Six Realms.
The chapter on the Ordination of the Seven Classes of Practitioners concludes. The Two Indeterminate Offenses conclude.

From the completion of the thirty precepts up to the ninety precepts;

From the thirty-one precepts out of the ninety precepts, the Section on Following the Precepts (Suíjípiān),

Fascicle Seventeen:

From the end of the *Śrāmaṇera* Section, the Table of Contents for the *Jianzheng Ji* (Record of Verification and Correction) of the *Xingshi Chao* (Manual of Monastic Practice) based on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya), Part Two: The Section on Transmission (*Chuantongfen*). (End.)
*Jianzhengji* (A Record of the Simplification and Rectification of the *Sifenlü Chao*), Scroll One.
Compiled by the Great Master Qingliang Jingxiao, who was granted the purple robe for his long lectures on the Vinaya and his presiding over ordination platforms during the Wu-Yue Kingdom.

I have heard that the *Shisao* (The Essentials of the Vinaya) is profound and abstruse, and its practical application is truly deep. It serves as the pivotal opening of the treasury of the Vinaya and is the very foundation for practice and observance.
Regarding the *Qianjian* (The Tongs and Keys): from the Zhenguan era of the Great Tang onwards, more than forty families have produced commentaries and records;
their systems are extremely numerous and their volumes are vast. Should one wish to examine them all, it would be difficult to fathom their origins and lineages.

However, as I, Jingxiao, have long been nurtured by the conditions of transformation and have inherited the teachings of my masters, I have taken the liberty of selecting various correct principles and compiled them into this work, so that future students may [benefit].
This is intended solely for the purpose of their merit and utility.

I shall now explain the commentary on one section of the text, which is divided into two major parts. First, I shall establish the chapters and provide a preliminary analysis so that one may have a general understanding of where the teaching leads.
Second, I shall provide a critical interpretation of the topical outlines and extensively distinguish between the text and its meaning. Regarding the first part, there are four further sections.
This is divided into four parts. First, it clarifies the Teacher who expounds the doctrine, distinguishing the three bodies (trikāya) according to the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

Second, it clarifies the treasury of the teachings expounded, namely the distinctions between Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma. Third, it concerns the compilation, preservation, and separation into various schools.
The fourth section, concerning the reasons for the production [of this work] during the era of translation, consists of four parts.
First, regarding the Teacher who is able to preach it: this refers to our own Master, Śākyamuni Buddha. This section is divided into two parts.
First, the general name is explained; next, the specific names are interpreted. This is the beginning of both sections. In its complete Sanskrit form, it is Śākyamuni-buddha.
This is translated as "The Able Benevolent One, the Silent Awakened One. The two characters "Śākya" constitute his clan name; this is translated as "Able Benevolent.
It originated from Nila due to his father the king’s threefold praise, and the clan name was established based on his virtue, as will be described in detail below.
"Siddhārtha" is a name; it is a corruption of the Sanskrit sound. In full, it should be *sarvārthasiddha*.

In the language of Tang (Chinese), this means "One Who Has Accomplished All Meanings. This refers to having achieved the meanings of both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Alternatively, one may achieve the noble paths of the Three Vehicles; thus, he is called "Accomplisher of Meaning" (*Arthasiddha*). "Muni," or alternatively "Maunī," is a term that here translates as "Silent One" (*Śānta*)."
Hei. To clarify the meaning of "contention" (*raṇa*): it refers to the fact that within the bodies of all sentient beings, there are each fundamental ten afflictions. These are:

attachment, aversion, ignorance, pride, doubt, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the misapprehension of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and the misapprehension of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Because the essential natures of these ten afflictions are mutually contradictory, they are termed "contention. For instance, attachment arises by taking an agreeable object as its condition, while aversion is directed toward an disagreeable one.

They arise from their respective objects. Delusion (*moha*) is the failure to comprehend cause and effect. Pride (*māna*) has the nature of haughty self-exaltation. Doubt (*vicikitsā*) is hesitation and indecisiveness.

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) clings to "I" and "mine. The view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) clings to either annihilationism or eternalism. False view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) denies cause and effect. Adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) clings to what is inferior as being superior.
Adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) reckons what is not a cause to be a cause. These ten afflictions exist within the bodies of sentient beings.

It provokes unwholesome states, brings harm to oneself and others, serves as a condition for karma that draws in rebirth, and is constantly characterized by clamor and contention. Now, the Buddha is not like us;
after his passing, upon the Vajra Seat, he completely severed and exhausted [all afflictions] through thirty-four moments of mind.
Therefore, he is called "silent and still. Furthermore, among these thirty-four moments of mind, the first thirty-three do not yet receive this title; it is only upon reaching...
It is only upon reaching the thirty-fourth moment of mind that one first obtains this name. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:

"The bodily and vocal actions of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as the mental [action], are the three *vīryas* (powers/virtues)... *Buddha* is a title (*nāmadheya*). There are ten such titles;

for now, we shall discuss only one, which is the ninth among them: the title of Perfectly Awakened Clarity (*saṃbuddha*). This is translated here as "Awakening" (*bodhi*). Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* says...
It is said: "Awakening" (*jue*) refers to discernment (*juéchá*). Discerning afflictions is like awakening from a dream. "Awakening" also refers to the realization of what is known (*suozhi*);

its manifestation is like the blooming of a lotus flower. Furthermore, awakening possesses three meanings: first, self-awakening (*zijué*), which distinguishes the awakened mind from that of ordinary beings (*fánfū*), for ordinary beings have not yet attained self-awakening;
second, awakening others (*juétā*), which means awakening others in a way distinct from the two vehicles (*èrshèng*), for the two vehicles are only capable of self-awakening.
Since this awakened mind does not awaken others, it has not yet awakened others; thus, the three aspects of awakening are fulfilled. For a Bodhisattva, both form and mind have subsided.
Next, although a Bodhisattva awakens to form and awakens to mind, form and mind have not yet been simultaneously extinguished.

Because only the Buddha possesses the three meanings fully, he still manifests awakening. Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "Because he has awakened to the characteristics of all dharmas. Furthermore:
All sentient beings have long been submerged within the three realms. Once the eye of the Way has opened, one awakens oneself and awakens others, and the practice of awakening becomes perfected;
therefore, one is called a Buddha. (The preceding section concludes the explanation of the general name.)
Next, regarding the specific names: it is said that the Buddha has three bodies (*kāya*), distinguished as the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body.

For now, to explain according to the Hīnayāna, these are likewise divided into three (and so forth). First, concerning the "Dharmakāya consisting of five parts": "five" indicates the number; "parts" (*bhāga*) means segments; "dharma" means that which serves as a norm and sustains;
and "body" (*kāya*) refers to substance, basis, or accumulation. This is because the five constituent elements of dharma (*dharmaskandha*) are accumulated therein.

Within the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it is therefore called the "fivefold aggregate" (*pañcāṅga*). First is the aggregate of morality (*śīlaskandha*). To prevent what is improper and cease evil is called morality. Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:
"The discipline of body and speech, as well as right livelihood, of one beyond training, are termed the aggregate of morality.

This means that the bodily action of one beyond training is right action; the vocal action of one beyond training is right speech; and the begging for sustenance of one beyond training is right livelihood. [It is] free from...

Regarding the four types of wrong views, the five types of wrong views, and so forth, among the eightfold noble path, these three are called the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*). This refers to the non-informative (*avijñapti*) discipline that co-exists with the path;

specifically, it is untainted pure wisdom (*anāsrava-śuddha-prajñā*) which, when functioning simultaneously with volition (*cetanā*), possesses the capacity to prevent [unwholesome states] and to initiate [wholesome ones], and is therefore termed "discipline.

Second is the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*): the cessation of mental attention toward external objects is called "concentration. Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* states: "The wishless samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*)."
Regarding the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*): among the three liberations (*vimokṣa*), there is the liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa*).

This arises based upon the untainted meditative absorptions (*anāsrava-samādhi*) of the eight stages. While in that state of concentration, one performs the aspect of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-ākāra*) as an antidote to objective phenomena;

this is called the wishless samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*). Since its essence is concentration itself, it is included within the aggregate of concentration. This [state] also consists of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) together with the concomitant volition (*cetanā*).

Manifest activity possesses the functional capacity to prevent [afflictions] from arising. Regarding the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*): the discernment that penetrates existence and non-existence is called wisdom.

Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* states: "Right view and right knowledge are called the aggregate of wisdom. Seeking [the truth] is termed "view" (*dṛṣṭi*), while definitive resolution is termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*).

Although view and knowledge differ, their essence is both the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) among the specific objects of cognition; therefore, they are taken as the aggregate of wisdom. Fourth, liberation.
When the aggregates (*skandha*) are exhausted and purified, and one does not stagnate in being or non-being, this is called liberation (*vimukti*). Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:

"The resolute confidence (*adhimokṣa*) associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is called the aggregate of liberation. This refers to the resolute confidence within the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).

This resolute confidence can immediately sustain the objects of the Four Noble Truths, such as: "Suffering has been known by me; its origin has been abandoned by me; its cessation has been realized by me..."
Realization: Having cultivated the Path, because one has attained mastery within the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), it is called "liberation" (*vimukti*).
Question: What is the difference between liberation and resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*)? Answer: In the causal state, when the object is predominant, it is called resolute conviction;

in the resultant state, when afflictions are severed, it is called liberation (based on this, there is a distinction between cause and effect). The fifth aggregate is that of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha*), which refers to [the realization] regarding oneself and others.

Liberation (*vimukti*) and its full manifestation are termed the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha*). Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"That which is associated with and present before the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) is called the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.

This is explained as referring to the wisdom within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) following the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*). [The practitioner thinks: "I have known suffering; I shall know it no more. I have abandoned the origin; I shall abandon it no more. I...

"Cessation has already been realized; it shall not be realized again. The Path has already been cultivated; it shall not be cultivated again. These two types of knowledge are collectively termed the "knowledge and vision of liberation" (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*).
Question: What is the distinction between liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation? Answer: There is a difference in terms of superiority and inferiority.
Liberation takes the four noble truths as its object through the arising of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*); the knowledge and vision of liberation takes nirvana as its object.

These aforementioned five factors of the dharma-body are accumulated within the person; furthermore, they possess the quality of universally perfuming [all things], and are thus also called the "fragrance of the fivefold dharma-body.
(The preceding concludes the explanation of the fivefold dharma-body.)

Second, regarding the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body): it is called "recompense" (*pāka*) because the arising of the fruit serves as a requital for past causes. The meaning of "body" (*kāya*) is as explained previously;
that is to say, by requiting former causes, one invites the present fruit—namely, the majestic marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), and a physical form of purple-golden hue.

Abiding in the world for exactly eighty years, he extensively expounds the teachings of the Three Vehicles. To explain these distinctions, they are briefly analyzed through six gates. First, the clarification of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
This consists of six sections: first, the Buddhas encountered; second, the period of time for the complete cultivation of the six *pāramitās*;

third, the cultivation of the causes for the [thirty-two] marks of excellence over one hundred eons; fourth, the intention to attain Buddhahood while born among humans; fifth, taking the final birth, leaving the household life, and severing delusions by practicing the path with outflows (*sāsrava*);
and sixth, severing delusions by practicing untainted contemplation (*anāsrava*) beneath the Bodhi tree. This is the first section.
The Sanskrit term *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* is fully expressed as "an incalculable eon. This translates into Chinese as "innumerable time-periods" (*wúshù shífēn*).

For brevity, it is now simply called *asaṃkhyeya*, which translates as "incalculable" (*wúshù*). Question: Since it is said to be "incalculable," why speak of "three"? Answer: The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "This refers to the name of the eon;
it does not mean that its numerical quantity is unknown. Question again: I do not yet understand what numerical quantity is accumulated [to constitute one asaṃkhyeya].
Regarding "one incalculable eon" (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*): according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, among durations of time, the shortest possible does not exceed a single *kṣaṇa*.
The longest is an *asaṃkhyeya*. Specifically, one hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* constitute one *tatkṣaṇa*;
sixty *tatkṣaṇas* constitute one *lava*; thirty *lavas* constitute one *muhūrta*; and thirty *muhūrtas* constitute one day and night.

Thirty days and nights constitute one month; twelve months constitute one year. When these years are accumulated to eighty-four thousand years, thereafter, for every hundred years, the lifespan decreases by one year.
In this manner, it decreases until the lifespan reaches ten years. Then, for every hundred years, the lifespan increases by one year, returning to eighty-four thousand years.
This is called one cycle of increase and decrease (*vivarta-saṃvarta*). Twenty such cycles of increase and decrease are called...
The first is the kalpa of abiding. Since the kalpa of abiding lasts for twenty kalpas, the kalpas of formation, destruction, and emptiness each likewise last twenty;
together they constitute eighty kalpas. These eighty kalpas constitute one great kalpa (*mahākalpa*).

From this, ten becomes ten, ten times ten becomes a hundred, ten times a hundred becomes a thousand, ten times a thousand becomes ten thousand, and ten times ten thousand becomes a *lakṣa*. Ten *lakṣas* become one *atula-lakṣa*. Ten...
One *du-lo-cha* (nayuta) constitutes one *ku-ti* (koṭi). Ten *ku-ti* constitute one *mo-to* (madhya). Ten *mo-to* constitute an *a-yu-to* (ayuta).
Ten *a-yu-to* constitute one great *a-yu-to*. Ten great *a-yu-to* constitute one *po-na-yu-to* (prabhedāyuta).
Continuing in this manner up to the fifty-second numerical position, it is named *a-seng-qi* (asaṃkhyeya), which is cited as "innumerable. This is repeated three times.
Therefore, it is said to be "incalculable eons" (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*). Regarding the Buddhas encountered therein, this refers to the period spanning the three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;

it remains uncertain exactly how many Buddhas were met during that time. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "During the three incalculable eons, one successively makes offerings to seventy thousand [Buddhas], then fifty, sixty, and seventy thousand Buddhas.
As for the phrase "successively making offerings to seventy thousand," this refers to the first and second [eons].
In each of the three [kalpas], there were seventy thousand [Buddhas]. Furthermore, he successively made offerings to five, six, and seven thousand Buddhas;

as in the first kalpa when he made offerings to seventy thousand Buddhas, so too did he make offerings to five thousand. Having completed the offerings to seventy thousand in the second kalpa, he again made offerings to seven thousand.
Having completed the offerings to seventy thousand in the third kalpa, he again made offerings to seven thousand. If one calculates these numbers:
This amounts to twenty-one thousand in three sevens; furthermore, five, six, and seven thousands add up to eighteen thousand.
Together with those above, there are twenty-two thousand eight hundred Buddhas. This is also stated merely according to the fundamental tenets of the Hīnayāna.
According to the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) of the Mahāyāna, as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, one makes offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of twenty-six Ganges Rivers;

practicing the six perfections in a disordered manner constitutes the first reliance, pertaining to the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi. One makes offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of five Ganges Rivers from the first bhūmi through the seventh bhūmi;
this constitutes the second reliance. One makes offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of six Ganges Rivers during the eighth and ninth bhumis; this constitutes the third reliance.

Relying on [the Buddhas], one makes offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of seven Ganges Rivers; having attained the Ten Grounds and Equal Enlightenment, this constitutes the fourth reliance.
One makes offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of eight Ganges Rivers. Furthermore, according to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"At the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I encountered eight hundred and forty million *nayuta* Buddhas, all of whom I made offerings to, none of whom were passed by in vain. Question Three.

The number of Buddhas encountered during the three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) and the extent of the offerings made to them have already been established. However, it remains uncertain what the names of those Buddhas were. In response:
since the number of Buddhas is so great, they cannot be described in full detail. Now, following the treatises, we shall cite only the first and the last. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* verse states:

"When the three incalculable eons are completed, one encounters, in reverse order, the Victorious Vision (*Vipaśyin*), the Lamp-Lighter (*Dīpaṅkara*), and the Jewel-Crested (*Ratnaśikhin*). This is the first [eons]."
*Kāśyapa* and *Munī*. This refers to the Buddhas who appear after the completion of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; hence it says "the completion of the three incalculable eons.
"In reverse order" indicates that it is not in the regular sequence. For example, during the third incalculable eon, one makes offerings to seventy-seven thousand Buddhas.
At the end of the most recent kalpa, the Buddha was named Vipaśyin; during the second incalculable eon, he made offerings to seventy-six thousand Buddhas.
At the end of that [same] most recent kalpa, the Buddha was named Dīpaṃkara; during the first incalculable eon, he made offerings to seventy-five thousand Buddhas.

At the end of the final *kalpa*, the Buddha’s name will be Ratnaśikhin. As for the first Śākyamuni, this refers to the Buddha named Śākyamuni encountered at the beginning of the first *kalpa*; he is the ancient Śākya Buddha.

It is said that while the Bodhisattva was still in the stage of causes, having been the son of a potter, he encountered this Tathāgata Śākyamuni and consequently gave rise to a virtuous mind, making a solemn vow and a great aspiration. He vowed:
"When I attain Buddhahood in the future, I shall be exactly like the World-Honored One of the present.
Therefore, the sentient beings whom I deliver now shall all be equal to those of the past sages. (The above concludes the account of the Buddhas encountered throughout the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.)
Second, regarding the period during which the cultivation of the six *pāramitās* is brought to completion, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"Merely through compassion, he gave universally; He offered his body without anger upon the wooden frame; He praised Buddha Tiṣya; And thereafter, [he attained] unsurpassed bodhi. (The above is the verse.)
Furthermore, regarding the first *pāramitā*, that of generosity (*dāna*): it refers to the Buddha’s constant bestowal of external wealth, such as gold and silver, during his time as a bodhisattva;

furthermore, it refers to his relinquishing internal wealth, such as his head, eyes, marrow, and brain—as exemplified by the verse concerning his self-sacrifice and his compassionate feeding of the tigress.
Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "When the Bodhisattva, through mere compassion alone, is able to give away his entire body and life."

Up to the point where there is not even the slightest trace of attachment or craving, and one does not seek the distinction of a superior rebirth out of fear—this is defined as the stage when the cultivation of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) is complete. Second is the stage of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*).
This refers to when the Bodhisattva, while still in the stage of a causal practitioner, was once a rishi dwelling alone in the mountains practicing the Way.

At that time, there was a king named Kali (alternatively spelled Kāli; in the Tang language, this means "strife"). The king, together with his consorts and attendants, entered the mountains for recreation.
The king became slightly fatigued and rested for a short while, while the women continued on ahead. By chance, they arrived at...
At the place where the seers resided, the seers preached the Dharma extensively to them. Because they were so intent on hearing the Dharma, they forgot to return home.
When the king later realized this and ordered a search, he discovered that they were inside the seers' huts.
The king became enraged, thinking that the seers had lured away his retinue, and immediately cut the seers with sharp knives.

His limbs and joints were severed and scattered. Having performed this deed, he returned to the palace. On the way back, he suddenly encountered a phenomenon where heaven and earth turned dark, stones rolled, and sand flew;
he was unable to proceed further. The King thought to himself, "This must surely be the work of the rishi. I should have him repent.
He then turned back to that place and sought his grace to atone for his transgression. Suddenly, he heard a voice from the air proclaim:
"Great King, you should know that I am one who seeks great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
Even as Your Majesty strikes and cuts my body, I harbor not even a single thought of resentment. The king then asked, "Who would believe these words of yours? The seer replied to the king:
"O King, if you do not believe my words, listen as I make this vow: if I harbor any feeling of resentment or malice, may this body of mine never be restored to its former state;
but since I am certainly free from any heart of hatred, I pray that this body be restored to its original condition. Having spoken these words, his body returned to its former state.
This is called the two *pāramitās* of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*), through the absence of anger and resentment.
...the mind. Furthermore, one does not contemplate seeking a reward for it. Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"If at that time a bodhisattva has their limbs and joints severed until nothing remains, even though they have not yet abandoned desire and greed, their mind is free from anger and resentment.
Up to this point, it is called the period when the two pāramitās of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*) are fully cultivated. Third, regarding diligence (*vīrya*), the *Vibhāṣā*...
Śāriputra said: "At the time when the Bodhisattva was practicing with courageous diligence, the Tathāgata Tiṣya had two disciples:
one named Śākya and the other named Maitreya. Among these two disciples, it was according to principle that Maitreya should have been the first to attain Buddhahood."
Śākyamuni is a bodhisattva in whom compassion predominates; he delights in practicing deeds for the benefit of others, and those among his disciples to be converted have already reached maturity.

Maitreya is a bodhisattva in whom wisdom predominates; he delights in practicing deeds for his own benefit, and those among his disciples to be converted have not yet reached maturity. Thus that Buddha reflected.
Although Śākyamuni was destined to attain Buddhahood later, how could his sphere of influence—which had already ripened—be suppressed or forced back to a later time?
Although Maitreya was destined to attain Buddhahood first, since his sphere of influence had not yet ripened, what benefit would there be even if he were to achieve the Way?
"It would be better for him to turn back now," [Śākyamuni thought]. Furthermore, it is better that many turn back than one. Thus, he devised a skillful means.
He then addressed the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, saying, "I wish to enter the mountains; you should go as well.
At that time, the Bodhisattva received his command and took the Buddha’s sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), placing it upon his shoulder, and followed him.

When the Buddha had reached the mountains, he suddenly manifested himself and then concealed his body, entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*) within a cave of *vaiḍūrya* gemstone, sitting cross-legged.
He sat cross-legged and entered the fire-element samādhi. Śākyamuni Bodhisattva suddenly lost sight of his teacher and searched for him everywhere, but could not find him anywhere.
Later, he suddenly saw him within a jeweled niche, absorbed in meditative concentration, with a majestic radiance far more intense than usual.
He then stood on one foot for seven days and seven nights, giving rise to a pure mind free from indolence, and [recited] with wondrous gāthās...
He praised that Buddha, saying: "In the heavens above and the earth below, there is none equal to the Buddha," and so forth. The new *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:

"In the heavens, on earth, in this world, in the abode of the learned (Mañjuśrī), in the palaces of the departed, or in any place throughout the ten directions—nowhere is there an equal to the Great Śramaṇa, the Bull among Men, who has searched the mountains and forests.
The commentary explains: "Heaven and earth" refers to the celestial realm above and the terrestrial realm below; "this world" refers to...
This refers to the three thousandfold world system. To the north is the palace of Vaiśravaṇa, which in this language is called the "Hall of Much Hearing" (Tuowenshi).
Because his fame for faith and reverence fills the ten directions, it is so named. The "Palace of Departure" (Shigong) is the palace of the Great Brahmā King;

non-Buddhists cling to it as being eternal, but the Buddha refuted this by calling it the "Palace of Departure" (shì meaning "to go away"). These celestial abodes include not only the Palace of Departure and others, but are not limited to them.

There is no one resembling the Buddha even throughout the worlds of the ten directions. One who possesses the marks and signs of wisdom and is adorned with them is called a "Great Man" (*mahāpuruṣa*).
Because his gait is dignified and auspicious and he possesses great power, he is titled a "Bull King" (*ṛṣabha*). From the perspective of the meaning of subduing evil, he is named a "Śramaṇa.
Searching everywhere through mountains and forests, there is none equal to the Buddha. In the treatise, it is asked: "Regarding those near the Buddha and Bodhisattvas..."
The names and phrases were skillful. Why did he recite only one verse for seven days and seven nights? Answer: Because his resolve was supreme.
Had he used elaborate names and phrases, there would have been a fear that his mind might not remain focused; therefore, there was only one verse.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva had spoken this verse, he instantly bypassed nine kalpas and attained Buddhahood first. This stage is termed the cultivation of the *vīrya-pāramitā* (Perfection of Diligence).

Regarding the period of the perfection of cultivation, the *Vibhāṣā* states that when a bodhisattva sits upon the Vajrāsana and dwells in the Vajropama-samādhi, this marks the completion of the cultivation of both the pāramitās of concentration and wisdom.
These six pāramitās are thus accomplished through cultivation across four stages; as the *Abhidharmakośa* says regarding the six pāramitās:
These four stages are each composed of one and two. Furthermore, they are cultivated to perfection in this manner of one and two.

Moreover, according to various sūtras, these six pāramitās are clarified as being for the purpose of counteracting six opposing obstacles: first, because of excessive greed, one practices *dāna* (generosity); second, because of violating prohibitions, one practices *śīla* (ethical discipline);
third, because of excessive greed and anger, one practices *kṣānti* (patience); fourth, because of laziness, one practices *vīrya* (diligence); fifth, because of excessive... [text truncated]
Contemplation is established for the sake of inducing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Delusion is established for the sake of cultivating wisdom (*prajñā*). Thus, there are six [perfections].
Furthermore, what is the reason for the sequential order of these six? The answer is that, according to the Mahāyāna treatises, there are six reasons:

first, each preceding one induces the subsequent one; second, each subsequent one sustains and purifies the preceding one; third, the preceding ones are coarse while the subsequent ones are subtle; and fourth, they follow the sequence of ease and difficulty in cultivation.
It is thus. A detailed explanation is as follows (some provide an extensive account of the six perfections of the Mahāyāna, though this is neither a core tenet nor a fresh inquiry).

Regarding the third point, "cultivating the causes for the marks of excellence over one hundred kalpas": this refers to the fulfillment and perfection of the cultivation of the six perfections throughout the three preceding asaṃkhyeya-kalpas.
As one is about to ascend to perfect enlightenment, one must rely upon these marks of excellence; for this reason, they are explained next. As for what is called "one hundred kalpas":
One interpretation states that this refers to the *alukula* kalpa; another states it refers to the kalpa of water and fire.

This means that when a Bodhisattva has completed the cultivation of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, according to the underlying principle, they must spend a hundred kalpas cultivating the causes for the marks of excellence (*lakṣaṇa*).
However, because he previously stood on one foot and praised the Tathāgata Tiṣya for seven days with diligent effort, he surpassed nine kalpas. Now...
It was merely ninety-one kalpas [until] his marks and signs were perfected. This is stated according to the Hīnayāna;

however, if one follows the Mahāyāna teaching, he transcended forty kalpas. By spreading his hair to cover the mud, he transcended eight kalpas (the causal origin is as described in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*).

By standing on one foot to praise the Buddha, he transcended nine kalpas (as recounted in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*). By the Prince Sattva sacrificing his body, he transcended eleven kalpas (the causal origin is as follows).
[From the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*]: Seeking half a verse on Mount Himavat, he transcended twelve kalpas (as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*). The above applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

In total, this amounts to forty *kalpas*. Question: The Mahāyāna teachings speak of transcending forty *kalpas*; I do not yet know how many more *kalpas* must be used to cultivate the causes for the excellent marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
Answer: One interpretation states that if one considers only the *Abhidharmakośa*’s account of transcending nine *kalpas*, then ninety-one *kalpas* must be spent to complete the cultivation.
However, if one takes into account the texts of all the various teachings, since forty *kalpas* are transcended, only sixty *kalpas* are required here.

This refers to the cultivation of the marks. Now, I say this is not so. Even granting that what is said regarding the "transcending" of forty kalpas is true, one must still spend ninety-one kalpas in total to cultivate the excellent marks.
The reason for this is that standing on one foot to praise the Buddha for nine kalpas is admitted by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles;
these fall within the hundred kalpas. Furthermore, the remaining thirty-one kalpas of arduous practice are transcended according to the Mahāyāna.

The original agreement was that within the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one would transcend the kalpas of water and fire; it is not appropriate to add to this by including the number of the hundred kalpas outside the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
Consider the explanation of Master Ci'en Ji as his authoritative source. Question: What are the characteristics and forms of these wondrous marks?
Answer: The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "They are accomplished through the Buddha’s contemplation, each adorned and embellished by a hundred merits."
Regarding the term "hundred blessings" (*śata-puṇya*): the virtuous thoughts of a hundred people are designated as "a hundred blessings.

These consist of the three bodily, four verbal, and thirty mental paths of action (*karmapatha*). Now, concerning the three bodily and four verbal actions, if we take only the act of killing as an illustration, there are five [aspects].
First, there is the thought of practicing non-killing oneself; second, not only practicing it oneself but also exhorting others to practice non-killing together—this is called "exhortation."
The volition of guidance: seeing another not killing, one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy; this is called the volition of sympathetic joy.
Seeing another not killing, one speaks words of praise; this is called the volition of praise. Directing these four types [of volitions] toward enlightenment is called the volition of dedication.

Since these five volitions are present within a single path of action, they combine to form fifty when applied across the ten paths of action. This is like cultivating the white [tuft] between the eyebrows.
At the time of [producing] a single hair-mark (*loma-vyañjana*), fifty volitions (*cetanā*) first arise to purify the vessel of the body;
next, one volition arises to project that sublime mark; finally, fifty volitions arise to adorn it. In reality, there are one hundred and one volitions.
As this is the case for a single mark, the same principle applies to the others. It is like a farmer who first prepares the furrows and ridges, then sows the seeds, and afterwards...
He irrigates it with water. Furthermore, a sutra states: "The bodies of all Buddhas are golden in color, adorned with the marks of a hundred merits.

At that time, having cultivated these marks, the Bodhisattva next enters the stage of the path of cultivation, which is called "abiding in meditative concentration. Therein, the Bodhisattva abandons six inferior matters.

He is designated as one who has attained six superior states; he is called one who has reached the six equalities (*ṣaḍ-samāpatti*). First, he abandons all evil destinies and is always born in the good destinies of humans or devas.
If he had not yet cultivated these marks, he might have been born in an unfavorable destiny (and so forth). Second, he abandons lowly families and is always born into noble lineages.
If he had not yet cultivated these marks, he might have been born into a base family; now that he has cultivated these marks, he is always born into a [noble] realm.
Third, he abandons being born into a Brahmin family; though previously his faculties were incomplete, he now constantly possesses complete faculties.

If, prior to attaining the signs of cultivation, his six faculties had been deficient, now that the signs of cultivation have been attained, they are certainly no longer deficient. Fourth, he abandons the non-male body.

One constantly obtains a male body. Prior to cultivating these marks, one may possess female organs, both sexual organs, or the like; now that the marks have been cultivated, one definitively and constantly possesses the male organ.
Fifth, abandoning the loss of mindfulness, one constantly attains natural mindfulness. Prior to cultivating these marks...
Regarding the tasks one undertakes, there was previously the possibility of much forgetfulness; now that these marks have been cultivated, there is certainly no forgetting.

Sixth, one abandons all forms of despondency and constantly attains firm concentration. Prior to cultivating these marks, when performing virtuous deeds, there was the possibility of falling into despondency;

now that these marks have been cultivated, they are certain to be firm and stable (the first four [marks] eliminate the four evils, while the latter two attain the two merits). Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "From the cultivation of the excellent marks..."

When a Bodhisattva attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called "being born into a noble family in a happy realm" and "possessing a male body with firm mindfulness. (This verse reverses the order of the preceding points.
Because of these six kinds of concentration, one obtains the designation of a "Bodhisattva abiding in true concentration.

If one has not yet cultivated the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), because that would be contrary to concentration, one cannot be called a Bodhisattva abiding in concentration. [Question: What is the meaning of "marks"? Regarding what the Bodhisattva...

[The questioner] asks: What is the meaning of "marks" (*lakṣaṇa*)? [The respondent] answers: They signify the sense of blazing radiance and the sense of auspicious omens. [The questioner] asks: For what reason must the Buddha’s body possess the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*)?
[The respondent] answers: Because one desires to provide a vessel as the basis for unsurpassed *bodhi*.
Since supreme merit necessarily relies upon a supreme body, it is necessary that the thirty-two marks be fully and perfectly complete. (The third section above is concluded.)

Regarding the meaning of attaining Buddhahood among humans as the fourth place of birth: it means that once a Bodhisattva has cultivated the marks [of a Great Man], he must manifest the attainment of Perfect Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) within the human realm; thus, he comes through the gate. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"At that time, at the beginning of the Bhadrakalpa when the lifespan of humans was twenty thousand years, the Bodhisattva was named Mahāpratibhāna (Huming). In the country of Vārāṇasī, at the Deer Park..."
In a forest grove, he received the prophecy from Kāśyapa Tathāgata: "In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.
Having been thus prophesied, he was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven as a Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood.
In that heaven, a lifespan lasts four thousand years, which corresponds to four hundred years in the human world; this constitutes one day for the gods of that realm.
By day and night, this state is calculated to be five billion eight hundred million years [in duration]. He dwelt in that heaven preaching the Dharma and transforming beings through instruction.
Subsequently, during the ninth eon of decrease within the Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was one hundred years, he descended from that heaven.
Manifesting the auspicious sign of a white elephant, he was born in the region of Central India, in the city of Kapilavastu in the kingdom of Kāśī, to King Śuddhodana.

In the royal palace, he was conceived in the womb of Queen Māyā. This occurred on the fifteenth day of the seventh month in the twenty-third year of King Zhao, the fourth sovereign of the Zhou dynasty in this land.
Once he had taken up residence in the womb, he likewise followed the manner of us ordinary beings;
when the ten months were complete, he was born. This was in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao, the year of Jiayin (the first year of the sexagenary cycle).
On the eighth day of the month, he was born from the right side beneath an *aśoka* tree within the Lumbinī grove.

Upon his birth, Brahmā and Śakra rained down fragrances, and nine dragons emitted water to bathe his body. Seven stalks of lotus flowers sprang up from the earth beneath his feet to represent the seven factors of enlightenment.
He then took seven steps in each of the four directions to demonstrate that the heterodox teachers who pride themselves on their own status would inevitably fall.
The evil realms. [The Prince] manifested signs with his hands, pointing toward heaven and earth to signify his unique supremacy. His father, the King, doted on him; the ministers all revered him.
He was immediately installed as Crown Prince to succeed to the Eastern Palace. While wandering through the four gates, he realized the truths of old age, sickness, and death.

Later, beholding the deportment and appearance of a śramaṇa, his heart of joyful admiration grew deep. This occurred precisely in the forty-second year of King Zhao’s reign; such was the age of the Crown Prince at that time.
(19) Thereupon, at midnight on the eighth day of the second month, he leaped over the city walls to leave the household life.

He went to Mount Gayā and practiced asceticism with diligent effort, vowing to seek the path of Buddhahood. (The above concludes the primary intent of the main section. Next follows the questions and answers to remove obstacles. Question:
Why does a Bodhisattva in his final birth (the *upapadya-bodhisattva*) choose to be born among the six heavens of the desire realm—specifically in Tuṣita Heaven—and not in the two higher realms?
Regarding the Bodhisattva descending to the three lower heavens, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Whether ascending or descending, in both cases doubt arises.

Nevertheless, being born in those heavens does not contradict the nature of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). As for the phrase "whether ascending or descending": "ascending" refers to the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*) and the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*Paranirmitavaśavartin*);
"descending" refers to the Yāma, Trāyastriṃśa, and the Four Heavenly Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*) heavens. Regarding the statement that "doubt arises in both cases," it means as follows:
That is to say, if he were reborn in the two higher heavens, people would harbor doubts, asking: "Why does the Bodhisattva not take birth in the three lower heavens?
If he were reborn in the three lower heavens, people would again harbor doubts, asking: "Why does the Bodhisattva not take birth in the two higher heavens?"
Thus, both the higher and lower [theories] inevitably give rise to doubt in people. However, being born in Tuṣita Heaven does not contradict the constant law of all Buddhas;
for according to the constant law of past Buddhas, those who are Honored Ones in their final stage of rebirth (*caramabhavika*) are all born in Tuṣita Heaven.

Furthermore, it is said that this heaven is among the celestial realms within a small chiliocosm (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*), serving as its very center, just like the navel. This is because it occupies the correct position.
Because they are middling. Furthermore, the gods above have dull faculties, while those in the three lower heavens are negligent; only the Tuṣita heaven is free from these two faults.
Moreover, that heaven is called "Contented," because during the course of day and night, its inhabitants know contentment regarding sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, if one is born in the Nirmāṇarati heaven, the lifespan is sixteen thousand years; in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven, the lifespan is eight [thousand years].

"O Thousand-Year One, if you wait until this heavenly lifespan is exhausted before descending to be born among humans, the time when the faculties of sentient beings have matured will have already passed;

lacking anyone to teach them, they will instead fall into the three miserable realms. If you descend to be born among humans when your lifespan in the lower three heavens has ended, the spiritual capacities of sentient beings will not yet be matured, and your emergence would be in vain and of no benefit. Only in the Tuṣita Heaven does the lifespan end [at the proper time]."

At that time, when he was to descend and be born among humans, the faculties and capacities of sentient beings were fully matured; their weariness with suffering was acute, and they already understood the suffering and pleasure of birth and death.

Because he possessed these many aforementioned qualities, he was born only in the Tuṣita Heaven. Furthermore, it was asked: "For what reason was he not born in the Form or Formless Realms? The answer was:
"The Formless Realm lacks form, and thus the Dharma cannot be taught there. Although the Form Realm possesses form,"
Because they are attached to the flavor of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-rasa*) and do not benefit sentient beings, they are not reborn in the two higher realms. Question:

For what reason does a bodhisattva pass away only from the heavenly realm and not come from the human realm? The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: Among the various destinies (*gati*), the heavenly destiny is superior;

furthermore, those who come from the heavens are held in high esteem by humans, and those who come from the heavens possess supernormal transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*). [If they were to] come from the human destiny...
Such a thing does not exist. For this reason, the Bodhisattva came from the heavens. If that were so, why did he not attain enlightenment in the heavens and then come to the human realm?
The *Vibhāṣā* answers: "Because it accords with the constant law of all Buddhas.
That is to say, all the World-Honored Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all attained perfect enlightenment among humans; and it is likewise for the present. Furthermore...
Furthermore, the celestial body is not a vessel capable of serving as the basis for unsurpassed bodhi.

The human realm possesses faculties and dispositions that are sharp and keen, and for the most part is able to receive the Tathāgata’s teachings. Moreover, there are two conditions within the human realm by which a Buddha appears in the world:
first, the presence of a mind of renunciation; second, the presence of a sharp and keen mind. Although the various devas possess a sharp and keen mind, they lack the mind of renunciation.
"Mind" refers to being attached to pleasure. Although there is a mind of weary detachment toward the three miserable realms, it is not yet sharp or intense;

only in the human realm do these two conditions exist, which is why Buddhas appear in the world. Question: The human realm consists of four continents; for what reason are Bodhisattvas born only in the southern continent? Answer:
Because the people of the southern continent possess sharp faculties of awakening and wisdom, whereas those of the other continents do not. Question:
Humans are subject to all four modes of birth (*yoni*), yet the miraculous birth (*upapāduka*) is the most excellent. Why, then, did the Bodhisattva accept only the womb-birth (*jarāyu-ja*)? Answer:

As stated in the *Abhidharmakośa*, he saw that accepting the womb-birth brings great benefit. First, it was to guide his kinsmen of the Śākya clan by providing them with a point of connection, thereby leading them into the True Dharma.
Second, he wished to lead various classes of beings to recognize that the Bodhisattva is of the lineage of a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*). For these reasons...
First, it enables one to abandon what is deviant and return to the True Dharma. Second, it causes those to be converted to give rise to a superior resolve (*adhimukti*), thinking:

"Since he was already a human being yet could accomplish such a great task, we too are likewise capable; why should we not do the same? Thereby, they initiate right effort and single-mindedly cultivate the True Dharma.
Were it otherwise, their noble lineage would be difficult to discern. Third, it serves to prevent doubt and slander, for there might be fear that he was a phantom or a celestial being.
He was born as a ghost. Furthermore, non-Buddhists slandered him, saying: "After more than a hundred kalpas have passed, a great illusionist shall appear in the world.

Therefore, he accepted birth from a womb to quell such doubts and slanders; or perhaps he accepted birth from a womb in order to leave behind his physical remains (śarīra), so that immeasurable humans and various other species, by making a single offering, might be reborn in heaven a thousand times and realize liberation. If he were to undergo such a birth...
Because there are no external seeds, as soon as the body perishes, nothing remains; it is like the extinguishing of a lamp's light, where nothing more is seen.
(The fourth section above is concluded.)
Regarding those in their fifth and final birth who leave the household life and cultivate the path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*) to sever the afflictions:

the *Abhidharmakośa* states, "Born in a royal palace, they abide in their final existence (*antya-bhava*). Furthermore, a Sūtra says, "My births in the womb are exhausted; this is called my very last body," and so forth.

The "path with outflows" (*sāsrava-mārga*) distinguishes it from the path without outflows (*anāsrava*). "Severing delusions" refers to the suppression and abandonment of the delusions of the lower eight stages.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva reached the age of nineteen, on the night of the eighth day of the second month in the forty-second year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, corresponding to this period, [he sat beneath the Bodhi tree].
Having left the city to become a renunciant, he entered the forest of asceticism on Mount Gayā to cultivate the path of the Buddha.
There, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven presented him with a blade to shave his hair and bestowed upon him the dharma robes. When the King, his father, learned of this, he was deeply displeased.
He then summoned three members of the inner clan: first, Āśva; second, Mahānāman (both sons of King Śuklodana); and third, Bhadrika (the son of King Amṛtodana). He further summoned...
There were two kinsmen from outside the royal clan: one was Kauṇḍinya and the other was Vīrya-Kāśyapa (both being maternal uncles of the Buddha’s two aunts).
The King said to these five men, "My son has left home to practice the Way and dwells in the deep mountains; now you all must constantly follow after him."
The five men, having received their charge, did not dare to refuse or disobey. They entered the mountains and attended upon the Prince (as described).
Together with those five men and various non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*), they sustained their lives by consuming hemp and wheat daily. Thereupon, the five men deliberated among themselves:
"Is the Way realized through pleasure, or is it realized through suffering? Three of the inner group said: "We have long dwelt in these deep mountains..."
The palace constantly experiences happiness. If the Way is realized through happiness, one knows that happiness is employed as the true path;

there is no need to cling to suffering. This is according to the interpretation of Master Jiji. However, according to the records compiled by later generations and the traditions passed down among various schools, it is said: [text continues].
The statement that "the inner clan clings to pleasure while the outer clan clings to suffering" is an error. It means that these five people’s views and understandings naturally differ;

because their calculations are not the same, they give rise to discord and contention. At that time, since the two members of the outer clan maintained that pleasure was the Way, [the others opposed them].
Seeing the Prince, he said, "Consuming hemp and wheat is considered an unorthodox path. He then departed and went to the Deer Park.

At that time, the Prince first went to the hermitage of Ārāḍa Kālāma and practiced the meditative concentration of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*). Next, he went to the hermitage of Udraka Rāmaputra and studied the meditative concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi*).
By means of the path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*), he severed the afflictions of the lower eight stages pertaining to both the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
As for delusions, since ordinary beings do not distinguish between principle and phenomena, they are to be severed all at once.

Now, regarding the severance of delusions through the path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*), one performs the contemplation of the six aspects of practice (*ṣaḍ-ākāra-pratipatti*). "Six" refers to the number. "Practice" refers to the various characteristics of cultivation; "phenomena" (*vastu*) refers to that which is coarse and superficial.
"Contemplation" (vipaśyanā) means observation; that is, rejoicing in the superior, pure, and sublime while feeling aversion toward the inferior, painful, coarse, and obstructive.
Furthermore, at the time of such rejoicing and aversion, for each category [of affliction], there is one path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) and one path of liberation (vimukti-mārga).

All paths of uninterrupted transition take the various contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma) of the lower stages as their objects, applying the three aspects (ākāra) of "coarse," "painful," and "obstructive. "Coarse" is so called because it is not tranquil; "painful" is so called because it is not exquisite or beautiful.

Therefore, because the hindrances are not the path of deliverance, the various paths of liberation take the contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the higher stages as their objects, forming the three aspects of "pure," "sublime," and "detached.
"Pure" is so called because of its tranquility; "sublime" because of its excellence; and "detached" because it is the path of deliverance.
When forming these aspects, one must necessarily contrast the upper and lower realms, just as when one practices revulsion toward the lower realm.

When one contemplates the coarse aspects [of the lower realm], the path of liberation takes delight in the higher realm; at that time, when one contemplates the pure aspect, one must take delight in the higher realm by forming the aspect of "sublime.
When one feels aversion toward the lower [realm] and forms the aspect of "obstructive," one must take delight in the higher realm by forming the aspect of "detachment."

The inferior [stages] cannot be intermingled. Thus, by delighting in what is superior and loathing what is inferior, one proceeds through the successive rungs of the ladder to sever the afflictions of the eight lower stages, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Only the single stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) remains; because its outflowing power is weak, it cannot be severed.
Therefore, the treatise states: "The Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*); it does not extend to the tainted (*sāsrava*).
When reaching this stage, because there is no higher stage to be delighted in, the lower stages are to be loathed. (The fifth section above is hereby concluded.)
Regarding the sixth point, those who cultivate untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-bhāvanā*) beneath the Bodhi tree to sever delusions: this refers to the aforementioned bodhisattvas.

Although they may sever the afflictions of the lower eight stages by means of worldly paths (*laukika-mārga*), they remain ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and have not yet escaped saṃsāra; how then could they realize sainthood?

Therefore, one must give rise to the sixth consciousness to initiate the untainted (*anāsrava*) contemplation. Regarding what is called "under the Bodhi tree," the *Record of the Western Regions* states:
more than two hundred *li* west of Rājagṛha in the kingdom of Magadha within the borders of Central India, there is a Pippala tree.
All Buddhas have realized Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) at this very spot; thus it is called the Bodhi tree. [End of fragment]
"Contemplating the outflows" (*āsrava*) means distinguishing them from that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*). "Severing delusions" means permanently severing all afflictions (*kleśa*).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "At that time, the Bodhisattva’s ascetic practices were complete, and his physical appearance was emaciated and withered.

Fearing he would be accused by the self-mortifying non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and wishing to verify that suffering was not the ultimate truth, he then accepted the milk-rice to demonstrate that he was not a mere starving man. This is based on the *Mahāvyūha-sūtra*.

The Sūtra states that the devaputras of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven informed the two sisters of a cowherd’s family—one named Nanda and the other named Bhadrā—that Prince Siddhārtha was about to attain enlightenment and asked, "Why do you not prepare fragrant honeyed milk-rice to offer him?
Upon hearing this, the women were filled with joy; they then prepared the fragrant milk and boiled the rice, using a golden...
He placed it in the bowl and went in person to where the Bodhisattva was. Kneeling, he presented it to him.

Having accepted it, the Bodhisattva took it to the soft grass on the banks of the Nairañjanā River and sat down cross-legged. He reflected upon the constant practice of past Buddhas when receiving food:
that they eat while sitting on a clean cloth skirt. The rest is as described therein (*etc.*). At that time, three members of the inner clan...
The men, who had previously held suffering to be the Way, now saw the Bodhisattva partaking of the milk-rice meal;
their hearts were filled with despondency and they said to one another, "This man has lost his mind and is acting recklessly; this is not the true Way. They then abandoned the Prince and departed.
Returning to the Deer Park, they encountered two members of the royal clan who were discussing the Prince’s failure. Thereupon, they made a pact together regarding Siddhārtha.
"Now that you have sold the Way and defiled your resolve, you will surely come here later. If you see those five men, do not go to welcome or honor them.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, having extensively cultivated the causes and certain to pray for the great fruit, proceeded to bathe in the Nairañjanā River.
He moved the branches of a precious tree so they bent low; as the Bodhisattva stepped onto the bank from the branch, the earth shook and trembled. At that moment, Śuddhodana...

The place where the Son of Heaven resides is also the site where the Bodhisattva attained enlightenment; it is not far from here. There is a precious throne made of vajra, measuring over a hundred paces in circumference.
It reaches from the surface of the earth down to the Golden Wheel. When the world was first formed, it arose together with heaven and earth.
The thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa have all ascended this throne to attain enlightenment. The Bodhisattva went there and arrived as well.
He reflected upon the method by which the Buddhas of the past attained enlightenment. "Where can I now obtain pure fragrant grass?

At that time, there was a householder named Śrī who offered him fragrant grass. According to some accounts, the gods of the Pure Abodes, in response to the Bodhisattva’s thought, manifested as a man carrying grass and passed before the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva approached him and requested it; he personally delivered the pure grass to him.

The World-Honored One, having received the grass from the bodhisattva, spread it out and sat upon it. With thirty-four moments of mind, he attained equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

First, he severed the delusions of view through sixteen moments of mind—eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and eight knowledges (*jñāna*). Next, he gave rise to eighteen moments of mind for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

The nine paths of uninterrupted activity (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) together comprise thirty-four moments of mind across the three [preparatory] stages. Furthermore, regarding the sixteen moments of the afflictions of seeing (*darśana-heya*):

this count of "mind" is stated according to the realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*). If one were to calculate based on the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*) alone, there would be only fifteen moments—namely, the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and seven knowledges (*jñāna*).

This is because the sixteenth moment belongs to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). For now, we shall distinguish the sixteen moments within the realization of the truths during the path of seeing.

Regarding the mind of one who practices to sever delusions, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "Immediately following the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), one produces the untainted dharma-patience (*anāsrava-dharma-kṣānti*) taking the suffering of the desire realm as its object;

next, one proceeds to the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*). This means that from the stage of the fourth wholesome root of application (*prayoga-mūla-kuśala-mūla*), one is separated from the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
That is to say, the Supreme Mundane Dharma is tainted (*sāsrava*); if it were a tainted similar cause, it would be able to produce further existence.

The outflows (*āsrava*) and their resultant flow (*niṣyanda-phala*). Now, having entered the principle of the untainted truths (*anāsrava-satya*), one must therefore depart from the preceding tainted (*sāsrava*) moments.

Regarding that which acts as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*): it means that mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) arise from four conditions, while material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) arise from two conditions.

"Equal" (*sama*) means identical; "immediate" (*antara*) means without interval. This refers to the fact that the equal-and-immediate condition for the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) extends across the three time periods. The preceding moment... [is] without... [interruption].
The outflowing mind and mental factors are equal and serve as conditions for the subsequent moments of mind and mental factors.

If the preceding moment is past, the succeeding moment is future, and the intermediate one is present; yet the preceding moment does not cease, the present does not arise, and the present does not cease while the future does not arise.
Thus, the three periods of time are without interval, except that one enters [the state] free from the causes of outflows.
Regarding the Path of Seeing (hence the expression "immediately following the Supreme Mundane Dharma"), that which takes the suffering of the desire realm as its object means:

when there arises a cognition capable of taking the objective sphere of the Noble Truth of Suffering in the desire realm as its object, an untainted (*anāsrava*) dharma is produced; this is called "Dharma-patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*). Therefore, the verse says: "The untainted dharma-patience arises.

As for the term "Dharma-patience regarding suffering," "suffering-dharma" refers to the dharmas belonging to the category of the Truth of Suffering, such as the three types of suffering or the five types of suffering.

This is correct. "Patience" (kṣānti) means to accept or acknowledge. It refers to the fact that since beginningless time, one has been shrouded by the afflictions such as the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), failing to understand these four noble truths and falsely reckoning them as pleasure.

Now, having perfected the practice, one brings forth the untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna) of the path of seeing (darśanamārga) before oneself, thereby accepting the severance of this suffering. One reckons with the ten underlying afflictions (anuśaya) [of the desire realm]—this is the first moment.

That mind is called the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), because it abandons the afflictions. Regarding "the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) arising immediately after receptivity": this refers to that which, following the receptivity to phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*), again takes the suffering of the desire realm as its object.

There arises an untainted dharma called the "dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*). This means that when knowledge arises taking the dharma of suffering as its object, it is termed the "dharma-knowledge of suffering.

It realizes the principle of the lower *tathatā* (this second moment of mind is called the "path of liberation," because it realizes [and explains] cessation). Next, there arises an untainted dharma taking the upper realms as its object;

this is called "subsequent knowledge" (*anvaya-jñāna*) (the third moment of mind, because it simultaneously severs the afflictions underlying the truth of suffering in the upper realms). The subsequent single moment is called "suffering" (*duḥkha*).

Subsequent Knowledge (the fourth momentary mind; because it realizes the principle of the True Suchness of suffering in the lower realms). Furthermore, when one again contemplates the Truth of Origination in the Desire Realm, there arises an untainted dharma called the Receptivity to the Dharma of Origination (the fifth momentary mind;
because it abandons the afflictions pertaining to this Truth). Immediately following, in the next momentary instant, there is the Knowledge of the Dharma of Origination (the sixth momentary mind;

because it realizes the principle of the True Suchness of analytical cessation). Next, when one contemplates the Truth of Origination in the higher realms, there arises an untainted dharma called the Receptivity to the Subsequent Knowledge of Origination.

(The seventh moment of mind: because it abandons the afflictions belonging to this truth. Next, one moment is called the "subsequent knowledge of origin" (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*) (the eighth mind; because it realizes the principle of *tathatā*).

Furthermore, when one again contemplates the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) of the desire realm and an untainted dharma arises, it is called the "patience regarding the dharma of cessation" (*nirodha-dharma-kṣānti*) (the ninth moment of mind;

it abandons the afflictions belonging to this truth). Next, one moment is called the "dharma of cessation" (*nirodha-dharma*) (the tenth mind; because it realizes the *tathatā* principle belonging to this truth). Next, one contemplates the truth of cessation of the higher realms.

There is an untainted dharma called the patience regarding the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-kṣānti*), [occurring at] the eleventh moment, because it abandons the afflictions belonging to this truth.

The subsequent moment is called the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), [occurring at] the twelfth mind, because it realizes the principle of *tathatā*. Furthermore, one again contemplates the path-truth (*mārga-satya*) of the desire realm;

there arises an untainted dharma called the patience regarding the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*), [occurring at] the thirteenth moment of mind, because it abandons the afflictions belonging to this truth. The subsequent moment is called the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*), [occurring at] the fourteenth moment, because it realizes the principle of *tathatā* of this truth.

Next, one contemplates the path of the higher realms (*ūrdhvadhātu*). There arises an untainted dharma called the "patience of the subsequent knowledge of the path" (*mārgānvayakṣānti*)—this is the fifteenth moment of mind.

Upon reaching this moment of mind, all conceptualizations and delusions regarding the principles are completely exhausted. Immediately following that, in the next moment, there is the "subsequent knowledge of the path" (*mārgānvayajñāna*)—this is the sixteenth moment of mind. At the time of this mind, one realizes the third fruit (*phala*).

Thus, the aforementioned sixteen moments of mind consist of eight patiences (*kṣānti*), which are termed "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) because they all sever the afflictions; and eight knowledges (*jñāna*), which are termed "liberation" (*vimukti*). All...
This is because they realize the principle; the detailed explanation is found in the treatise. Question:

When a bodhisattva reaches the sixteenth moment of mind, why do they not realize the first or second fruits, but instead directly realize the third fruit? Answer: There are nine grades of delusions regarding phenomena within the desire realm.
The first six stages obstruct the second fruit; the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages—these three stages—can obstruct the third fruit.
Now, when the Bodhisattva was at the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), he gave rise to the path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*) and has now severed the lower eight stages.

Since both delusions regarding principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) have been exhausted, these [stages] cannot act as obstructions to the second or third fruits; therefore, he truly realizes the third fruit. Furthermore, one must know these ten...

Regarding the six minds and eight knowledges (*jñāna*): fundamentally, they do not sever afflictions (*kleśa*). They exclusively realize cessation (*nirodha*). Only the eight forbearances (*kṣānti*) sever afflictions.

Furthermore, among these eight forbearances, the four dharma-forbearances (*dharmakṣānti*) likewise have no afflictions to be severed, because at the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one had already previously employed the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) to sever them.
Now, one merely re-arouses them as a path of confirmation (*anvayajñāna*) and traverses them once more; only the four subsequent forbearances (*anvayakṣānti*) sever afflictions.
These four types of patience (*kṣānti*), according to their underlying principle, generally involve the severance of afflictions across eight stages (*bhūmi*).

However, speaking now in terms of their essential nature, they sever only the view-delusions (*dṛṣṭi-heya*) of the single stage of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). As for the seven lower stages, these have already been severed previously; for the time being, we shall speak of them collectively.

The eight patiences (*kṣānti*) eliminate the delusions [of the path of seeing] (the preceding section concludes the explanation of the characteristics of the practice of realization and elimination during the path of seeing). Next, we distinguish the eighteen moments of mind regarding the delusions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

According to the Sarvāstivāda school, at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), having already realized the third fruit, one does not emerge from the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) but remains in a single sitting.
Furthermore, there are three types of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the single stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception: attachment, delusion, and pride.

These three afflictions are divided into nine grades, namely from the highest-of-the-high (adhimātra-adhimātra) down to the lowest-of-the-low (mṛdu-mṛdu), and so forth. Upon abandoning each grade, there occurs one path of uninterrupted activity (ānantarya-mārga) and one path of liberation (vimukti-mārga).
First, by means of a mind of the lowest-of-the-low grade, one abandons the highest-of-the-high grade [of affliction] that has existed since beginningless time.
Delusions are severed by the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and realized by the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

In this manner, up until the ninth stage, when the highest-of-the-high grade of mind arises, it severs the lowest-of-the-low grade of delusions that have existed since beginningless time. At the moment of the path of uninterrupted transition, it corresponds to the seventeenth moment of mind;
at this time, it is associated with the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), whereby all subtle afflictions are completely and utterly severed. This is the...

During the single moment of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) immediately following the four stages of approach (*pratipannaka*), one is conjoined with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.
This is the eighteenth moment of mind; together with the preceding sixteen, they constitute thirty-three moments of mind that belong to those still in training (*śaikṣa*).

The thirty-fourth moment of mind is the first moment of the Buddha’s state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Thus, nineteen [days] were spent in renunciation, and in the thirtieth, he attained enlightenment.
This corresponds precisely to the eighth day of the second month in the second year after King Mu of Zhou ascended the throne.

At that time, the earth spirits informed the air spirits, and the air spirits informed the celestial spirits; in an instant, all throughout the triple world knew that the Tathāgata had attained enlightenment.

At that moment, the World-Honored One observed that the multitudes in the triple world were oppressed by various sufferings and could not endure them for long, and thus he resolved upon *nirvāṇa*. At that time—
Brahmā descended and requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma, speaking in verse: "In Magadha, amidst various defilements and impurities, the Buddha has been born therein.
We pray that you open the gate of ambrosia and preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings. The Tathāgata silently granted his consent.
He then surveyed all sentient beings to see whose faculties were mature enough to be delivered, and he thought to himself: "In the past, I once [taught] at Udraka..."
"At the abode of Ārāḍa Kālāma, I studied the concentration of the sphere of nothingness (*asaṃjñāyatana-samādhi*). Since he has been kind to me, I should go there first to deliver him.
A *Śuddhāvāsa* devaputra announced from mid-air: "His life has ended; seven days have already passed. The Tathāgata laments that he lacked merit and did not meet [the Buddha] in time.
Furthermore, [the Buddha] thought: "Ārāḍa Kālāma, it was with him that I once studied the concentration of the sphere of nothingness. Now..."
"You may go and deliver them. The deva of the void replied, "He has been dead for five days. The Buddha again sighed deeply.

He then reflected upon the five men, both from his inner and outer clans, who had formerly attended him: "I should now go and deliver them. Thereupon, he rose from beneath the Bodhi tree and proceeded toward the Deer Park.
His deportment was serene and tranquil; his divine radiance shone brilliantly, and the white hair-tuft between his brows contained the luster of jade.

His body was as radiant as gold. As he proceeded forward with serene composure, the five men saw the Buddha from afar and said to one another, "That Sarvārthasiddha who is coming here has been gone for many months and years, yet he has achieved no fruit or realization; our minds have repeatedly turned toward him."
"Therefore, let us search for our own [interests]. We ought to remain silent together and have no need to go out to welcome him.

However, as the Tathāgata drew near and they were overwhelmed by his majestic radiance, the five men unconsciously went forward to receive the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One addressed them, saying: "You foolish men! You have established your own regulations."
They were unable to maintain their resolve and instead turned back to destroy it. The five men asked, "Where has Siddhārtha attained enlightenment?
