The Buddha replied, "I have attained perfect awakening beneath the Bodhi tree upon the Vajrāsana; I have already obtained the flavor of the nectar of the Dharma.
It is for the sake of delivering you that I have come here. Yet, the five men still had not given rise to faith in their hearts, and so [time] passed for one—

In the summer, he disciplined his faculties. First, for Ājñātakauṇḍinya, he turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths in twelve aspects through three revolutions. Regarding the "three revolutions," this refers to three cycles of turning.
The first is the revolution that demonstrates the characteristics: "This is suffering," meaning the oppression of the three realms, which pertains to the aspect of the fruit.

It is called "suffering" (*duḥkha*). The three sufferings, the five sufferings, and the eight sufferings—even up to the bliss of the various heavens where the five signs of decay appear—are all suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
This is "origination" (*samudaya*); it is the cause that produces birth and death, and is thus named origination. This is "cessation" (*nirodha*);

the state where afflictions are exhausted and the Nirvāṇa realized is named cessation. This is the "path" (*mārga*); the cause of noble wisdom is named the path. (At this point in the turning of the wheel, Ājñātakauṇḍinya...)

[This refers to] entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). Second, the turning toward cultivation (*bhāvanā-parivṛtti*), which states: "This is suffering; you should know it. This is its origin; you should abandon it.
This is its cessation; you should realize it. This is the path; you should cultivate it. (At this point of turning, Ājñātakauṇḍinya enters the Path of Cultivation).
Third, the turning toward realization (*sākṣātkriyā-parivṛtti*), which states: "This is suffering; I have known it. This is its origin; I have abandoned it. This...
"This cessation has been realized by me; this path has been cultivated by me. (At the time of this turning, Ājñātakauṇḍinya entered the path of no-more-learning.
Thus, because it was turned three times, it is called the "three turnings of the Four Truths. Regarding the term "the wheel of twelve aspects": "twelve" refers to the number.
At each turning, all four factors are present—namely, vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening. Therefore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "In [the stage of] seeing..."

Within the Path, the Dharma-patience (*dharma-kṣānti*) is called the "eye" (*cakṣus*); the Dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*); the subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) is the "clarity" (*vidyā*);

and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is "awakening" (*buddhi*). The eye that can clearly perceive is the "eye"; decisive discernment is "wisdom"; illuminating comprehension is "clarity"; and alerting and exhorting is "awakening.

Furthermore, beneath each [Truth] such as Suffering, there are three turnings: the demonstration of characteristics, the exhortation to practice, and the citation of evidence. These constitute the twelve [aspects]. The same applies to the remaining Truths of Origin, Cessation, and the Path.
That is so. To speak according to the actual principle, there are thirty-eight aspects; however, for the sake of numerical correspondence, twelve are provisionally indicated here.

This does not mean that the three turnings of the Four Noble Truths consist exclusively of twelve aspects. As for the term "wheel" (*cakra*): if one follows the calculations of the Sarvāstivāda school, these very teachings on the Four Noble Truths constitute the true wheel.
Now, according to the Sautrāntika school, the Four Noble Truths are not the true wheel; rather, they are merely a skillful means of the [Buddha’s] household.
Now, taking up the Noble Eightfold Path, this is the true Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). As for what is called the Noble Eightfold Path, it consists of eight factors:

right speech, right action, right livelihood, right view, right intention, right mindfulness, right effort, and right concentration. Question: For what reason is this Noble Eightfold Path established as a "wheel"?
Answer: It is established by way of analogy. Just as a worldly chariot wheel is complete with spokes, a rim, and a hub, so too is this path.

Third, there is the sense of "crushing and turning. First, the central hub (*nābhi*) is like the core of grain. Next, the eighteen spokes (*ara*) that converge upon the wheel from the outside are called "spokes.
The rim (*nemi*) encircles the wheel from the outside. The six segments are able to contain the eighteen spokes; each segment governs three spokes, and three times six makes eighteen.
If there were no rim to hold the hub and the spokes together, there would be no way for the wheel to be formed. Thus, the hub has the sense of being that which provides support.

The spokes possess the meaning of having something upon which to rely; the rim possesses the meaning of gathering and binding. These three together constitute the whole, only then being able to support the load.
Now, these eight branches of the Noble Path are likewise so: the three consisting of verbal action and livelihood serve as the grain, acting as the basis.

If ethical discipline (*śīla*) is not pure, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) will not manifest, for all myriad practices depend upon precepts. Right view, right thought, right effort, and right mindfulness constitute wisdom (*prajñā*).

The spokes are the basis, meaning that they arise in dependence upon ethical discipline (*śīla*). Right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) is the wheel-rim; the rim has the sense of gathering and encompassing, which is able to collect the scattered and restore the true [nature].
These eight branches of the Noble Path were originally present within the body of Ājñātakauṇḍinya, much like the Mahāyāna teaching of *tathatā* (suchness), because it does not come from the outside.
However, it was merely obscured by the coverings of afflictions (*kleśa*) and thus did not manifest. Now that...

Having been taught the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths by the Tathāgata, after hearing that Dharma, one is able to spontaneously give rise to wisdom, crush and grind away the afflictions within one's own body, and realize the fruit of sainthood;
this is called "turning the wheel of Dharma. The wheel has three meanings: first, the meaning of completeness, as it possesses the three parts of spokes, rim, and hub;
second, the meaning of indeterminacy, as it proceeds from the Path of Seeing to the Path of Meditation, and from the Path of Meditation to the Path of No-More-Learning.
The Path. Having personally attained this, one turns it over to explain it to others, establishing the Noble Path within the bodies of others (this is according to the Sautrāntika school).

If one follows the definition of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) as conceived by the Sarvāstivāda school, it is restricted solely to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). They ask: "How is it known that the Wheel of Dharma is restricted solely to the Path of Seeing? The answer is:
When the Path of Seeing arose in Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others, the deities of the earth and sky proclaimed: "The Tathāgata has turned [the Wheel of Dharma]."

Regarding the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*): since it is said to have "already been turned," it is clear that this refers exclusively to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). [The Sautrāntika school] does not hold this view; for all three paths are accessible to the mental continua of others, and at the moment the Path of Seeing arises...
Having already reached the initial turning, it is therefore called "already turned. Third, the meaning of crushing and grinding:

just as a wheel can crush a cicada resisting its path, so too the Noble Path, when held within one's heart, can crush afflictions and the like (and so forth). "Turning" (*vartana*) means to move, to manifest, to transport, and to arise.
Master Ji said: "To move is to proclaim the teachings; to manifest is to extol the subtle principles; to transport is to bring the Noble Path forward; and to arise is true wisdom."

Following these words, he completely crushed all obstacles and afflictions; this is called "turning the wheel of the Dharma" (if one distinguishes the wheels according to the Mahāyāna, there are the wheel of self-nature, the wheel of cause, the wheel of fruit, and the expedient retinue, as explained therein).
At that time, after the World-Honored One had turned the Dharma of the Four Truths for Ājñātakauṇḍinya, he then asked Kauṇḍinya whether he had understood it.
When Ājñātakauṇḍinya first answered with understanding, the earth deities also testified that Ājñātakauṇḍinya had understood; therefore he was named Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
His realization of the Way was unsurpassed by any other. At that time, having realized the fruit, Ājñātakauṇḍinya—
He sought ordination as a monk under the Buddha. The Buddha, with his golden mouth, personally addressed him by name, saying: "Welcome, bhikṣu!
Within my Dharma, you shall joyfully cultivate the pure conduct (brahmacarya) and swiftly reach the end of the source of suffering. At these words, he felt the precepts enter his being;

his hair and beard fell away naturally, and the kāṣāya robe draped upon his body, no different from a bhikṣu of five summers. Having thus acquired the full monastic appearance, he took leave of the Buddha and entered the city.
He went begging for alms. At that time, the other four were still in the stage of the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*).
Next, he taught the two, Aśvajit and Mahānāman, regarding matters such as the merit and bliss of rebirth in heaven through giving; the two immediately realized the first fruit (*srotāpatti-phala*).
Later, he taught the Dharma to the two, Bhadrika and Bāṣpa, who also realized the first fruit. He then addressed them with the words "Come hither" (*ehi-bhikṣu*), and each received the precepts.
While still in their physical bodies, they perfected the marks of the Saṃgha and entered the city to beg for alms. Now these five men are commemorated as the Pañcavaggiya (the Group of Five).

"Vagga" means "class" (lun); it refers to the fact that they attained the Way according to the sequence of this group of five. Alternatively, they are called Pañcavaggiya because "vaggiya" means "kinsmen" (lin), signifying their close affinity.
Because these five were all kinsmen of the King, at that time, once the Tathāgata had turned the Wheel of the True Dharma, the earth deities informed the air deities,
the air deities informed the celestial deities, and so on, until it was known throughout the Brahma palace that the Tathāgata’s Wheel of Dharma had been turned.
Above, [the Buddha] attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree; this was the beginning of the Jewel of the Buddha. At the Deer Park, he turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths;

this was the first instance of the Jewel of the Dharma. He delivered the five bhikṣus; this was the commencement of the Jewel of the Saṃgha. Thus, the transformational Three Jewels were fully perfected.
It was precisely on the eighth day of the eighth month in the second year of King Mu’s reign during the Zhou dynasty that he turned the Wheel of Dharma.

[The section on] the wheel is concluded. The sixth gate above is finished. There were six topical summaries (yǒu liù shōu kē) previously mentioned [as indicated by "etc."]. This concludes the second [section], the exposition of the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

Regarding the third, the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*): "Transformation" (*huà*) refers to transformative manifestation. The conversion of the fundamental essence is called "change" (*biàn*). That which was non-existent suddenly comes into being; that which exists...

That which has already returned to non-existence is called "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*). Only that born within the royal palace of this Southern Continent [Jambudvīpa], who attains enlightenment through thirty-four moments of mind, is the true body (*dharmakāya*).
As for those who manifest forms and preach the Dharma throughout the ten directions, reaching even the six realms of existence, these are either small or entirely transformations.
Question: Within the three bodies (*trikāya*), which body is it that speaks the present Vinaya Piṭaka? Answer: It is the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) that speaks.

The preceding [sections] have three parts (as detailed). Thus concludes the analysis of the three bodies according to the Hīnayāna school. From here on, the analysis will be brief according to the Mahāyāna.
If one follows the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise in One Hundred Dharmas) and other such works, they mostly employ twelve gates of classification, as is the case therein.

This is self-evident. This is not the primary thesis here; rather, one must simply understand the similarities and differences. There are three general distinctions: first, the explanation of names; second, the determination of the essence (*svabhāva*);
and third, the teaching and non-teaching of the Dharma. This is the first of the three sections. Regarding the phrase "the Pure Dharmakāya Vairocana Buddha":
*Pure Dharmakāya* is the Chinese term (*táng-yán*), while *Vairocana* is the Sanskrit term (*fàn-yǔ*). As for "pure" (*qīngjìng*), it means—

These two [terms] clarify that which is defiled. Regarding the *dharmakāya*: "dharma" refers to the sense of "guiding and sustaining. "Guiding" means providing a model that causes sentient beings to give rise to understanding;
thus, the *dharmakāya* is the object of focus (*ālambana*) that causes fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*) to arise and realize it. "Sustaining" means maintaining and not abandoning one's own essence;
thus, the essence itself is able to sustain itself, remaining unmoving and unchanging—this is the meaning of "quiescence" (*śānti*). This is the "body" (*kāya*).
The term "essence" (*tattva*) has the meaning of accumulation. Its essence is stainless *tathatā* (suchness); this is the sense of "essence.

It serves as the basis for the myriad virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as the two bodies of recompense and transformation; thus, it has the sense of "basis. It possesses the qualities of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, as well as names, phrases, and phonemes;
this is the sense of "accumulation. Although it is not an accumulation of physical substance, it nonetheless constitutes an accumulation of meaning. This refers to Vairocana.

This is a term from the Sanskrit language; here it is translated as "Pervading All Quiescence" (*sarvatraga-śānti*). "Pervading" (*sarvatra*) means all-encompassing, distinguishing it from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), whose specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are not such [as to be pervasive], such as earth, water, fire, and wind, which each adhere to their own respective substrates and are therefore not called "pervasive. "Quiescence" (*śānti*) means tranquility.

This distinguishes [the dharmakāya] from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). Its common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—are not like it; their characteristics are turbid and clamorous.
Although the dharmakāya has always been pervasive, eternally abiding, and profoundly tranquil from the outset, "Buddha" means "awakening," as explained extensively above (*etc.*).

To explain the analysis by way of abbreviation: the *kāya* (body) is stainless, having *tathatā* (suchness) as its essence; *dharma* (phenomenon/principle) is the function that gives rise to understanding in sentient beings.

Here, "Dharmakāya" (Dharma-body) refers to the essence subsequent to the absence of function, wherein function is subsumed back into the essence; thus, "Dharma is itself the body" (*dharmasvabhāvakāya*, a *karmadhāraya* compound).
Second is the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body), Vairocana Buddha. "Saṃbhogakāya" is the Chinese term, while "Vairocana" is the Sanskrit term. "Complete" (*yuan*)...

"Universal" (*paryanta*) means that one has already universally cultivated all dharmas; it is used to distinguish this from those who perform the two types of karma, as they have not yet cultivated them universally.

"Fulfilled" (*paripūrṇa*) means complete; it is used because one's cultivation is already complete, thereby distinguishing this from Bodhisattvas, who, although they cultivate universally, have not yet reached fulfillment.
"Retribution" (*vipāka*) is a term for repaying a cause; first, there is the retribution received by oneself, which is the repayment for the three incalculable eons of self-benefit.
Benefiting others, with all virtues perfectly complete and the two obstacles forever exhausted, there is the "wondrous pure cloud" that transcends the mundane world.
Abiding therein, one manifests the great dharma-joy, which is constantly enjoyed for oneself. As for "body" (*kāya*), it also carries the meanings of essence, support, and accumulation.
It takes the actual untainted five aggregates as its essence—this is the meaning of "essence. It takes the inconceivable, sand-grain-like merits as its support.
This meaning is based on the sense of "body" (*kāya*). Since it possesses the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), its essence is the sense of a "collection.

Regarding the analysis of its interpretation, "self-enjoyment reward" refers either to the body itself as the reward, or to the body of self-enjoyment reward; thus, both the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) and *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compounds apply.

Second, regarding "other-enjoyment": it is called "other" because it corresponds to Bodhisattvas of the ten stages. Because it preaches the Dharma for them and cuts through their doubts, it is termed "enjoyment."

The body is as explained previously. Since it takes the transformation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as its essence, this constitutes the meaning of "an accumulation of essence. To explain through analysis:

the "body of others" (*parabhoga-kāya*) is the "body that maintains [the essence]" (a *karmadhāraya* compound). *Vairocana* is a Sanskrit term; here it means "Universal Radiance. There are two aspects to this universal radiance:
if, within the body of self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga-kāya*), fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) arises and internally illuminates the ultimate truth, it is called "internal radiance."

Illumination. After the attainment of the wisdom of subsequent realization (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), three kinds of transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) and ten grades of enjoyment bodies for others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) arise;
these are called the "Universal Illumination of the Exterior. Regarding the "Śākyamuni Buddha of three thousand billion transformation bodies":
"thousand billion" is the Chinese term, while "Śākyamuni" is the Sanskrit term. To say "hundred thousand billion" is to cite the number. This refers to those who are transformed.

This is the realm [of transformation]. The Buddha is the body capable of transformation, manifesting in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings. What was originally non-existent now exists. "Body" (*kāya*) also carries the meaning of a collection based on a substance.

Within the five aggregates (*skandha*) of transformation, the actual five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) constitute the substance. In terms of its function, it serves as the basis for the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

Thus, it has the sense of being a "basis. The provisional marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are based on the actual five sense-objects; this is the sense of being a "collection. Question: Regarding the previously mentioned "body received by others" (*parakāya-parigṛhīta-kāya*)...

Regarding the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*): it takes the transformation of the five aggregates as its essence. Now, the transformation body likewise takes the transformation of the five aggregates as its essence.

If one asks how it is distinguished [from the other bodies], the answer is that there are three distinct meanings: first, the distinction between coarse and subtle; the transformation body is coarse, whereas the enjoyment body for others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) is subtle.

Second, the distinction regarding their location and establishment; the enjoyment body for others resides in a purely pure land and manifests great supernormal powers for Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*).

The manifestation of the marks of bliss and the preaching of the Dharma: if a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) dwells in an impure land, it manifests matters such as having a wife, slaves, suffering, and pleasure for the sake of transforming those of the two vehicles and ordinary beings.
Third, regarding the distinctions in what is transformed: the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya) is transformed upon the Wisdom of Equality (samatājñāna) of the seventh consciousness;

the Transformation Body is transformed upon the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is To Be Done (kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna) of the first five consciousnesses. It is due to these three points that there are differences.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*): first, the great transformation body, which is a thousand *zhang* in height;
second, the manifested transformation body, such as Śākyamuni, who was one *zhang* and six *chi* tall, while the future Maitreya will be one thousand *chi* tall;

third, those that conform to various types, which are not fixed—for instance, the householder Ghoṣila was three *chi* tall when he first resolved his mind toward enlightenment, and five hundred Brahmins gave rise to faith upon seeing their own bodies reduced to ashes.
The Bodhisattva Anantagātra, who has exhausted existence within the higher realms, and ordinary beings at various minor stages, perceive the sixteen-foot form as inexhaustible and so forth.

Although these three aforementioned types are distinct, they are all subsumed under the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body). Regarding their analysis according to the *vyadhikaraṇa-karmadhāraya* (locative determinative compound):
"abiding in the emanation" refers to the body itself; this is a *karmadhāraya* compound. *Śākyamuni* is a Sanskrit term, which has been explained extensively as before (*etc.*). Three.

Regarding the clarification of whether the three bodies (*trikāya*) teach the Dharma or do not teach it, there are two differing schools of thought. The first follows the tradition of Nāgārjuna and Asvabhāva, who maintain that the three bodies do not teach at all.

They state: "The Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall into the three extremes; it is not subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or bases (*āyatana*). Furthermore, they say:

"Having long since transcended conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), he has never taught the Dharma. That which appears from time to time is the Buddha’s fundamental activity for the benefit of others."

Through the power of the conditions of aspiration, the appearance of words and meanings arises upon the consciousness of sentient beings; at the time when these words and meanings aggregate, it is conventionally designated as "the Buddha’s teaching.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "From my sitting upon the Vajrāsana until [my arrival at] the Śāla Grove, not a single word was spoken in the interval.
Also, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "If anyone were to say that the Tathāgata has taught any dharma, then..."
This would constitute slandering the Buddha. Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "As for those who preach the Dharma, there is no preaching and no demonstration;

as for those who listen to the Dharma, there is no hearing and no attainment. Second, regarding the protection of the Dharma and the glorification of the school: all three bodies preach the Dharma. Now, concerning the preaching of the Dharma by the Dharmakāya:
To grasp the meaning of the aspect of arising and understanding it is called "preaching the Dharma," which refers to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

When realizing *tathatā* (suchness), forming the understanding that it is neither born nor extinguished is what is meant by "the body preaching the Dharma. During this process, the mental factors (*caitta*) serve as the audience.

Furthermore, when the four knowledges realize the principle of *nirvāṇa*, they enable the mental factors governed by the three knowledges to reach a unified understanding; at that time, there are sixty mental factors.
In this regard, it is just like the audience; according to this principle, it is the Dharma-body that preaches the Dharma.
If it is the self-enjoyment body, it preaches the Dharma for all Buddhas; if it is the other-enjoyment body, it preaches the Dharma of the ten pāramitās for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages.
Regarding the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), there are four great types: those that teach the Mahāyāna dharma for the sake of bodhisattvas in their stage of application;
those that teach the Triyāna dharma; those that manifest according to the various classes of beings; and those that teach the dharma according to their respective faculties.
Thus, in a sūtra, when the World-Honored One entered the Śiṃśapā grove, he took a few leaves from a tree and asked Kāśyapa: "Are there more leaves in my hand, or more in the forest?"
Kāśyapa said, "The leaves in my hand are few; the leaves in the forest are many. The Buddha said, "The Dharma I have already taught is like the leaves in my hand;
the Dharma not yet taught is like the leaves in the forest. Furthermore, a sutra says:

"Recalling the power of skillful means practiced by the Buddhas of the past, although the path I have now attained should likewise be taught as the Three Vehicles," [the question arises: why is it that in this present Vinaya-piṭaka...
Regarding the body [of the Buddha]: by which body was it spoken? Answer: It was spoken by the small transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Although the doctrinal tenets of the Great and Small Vehicles differ, both take the six-foot-tall body born in the royal palace as the teacher who preached the Vinaya Piṭaka. Thus far, there have been two [sections].
The first part relies on the Hīnayāna; the second relies on the Mahāyāna. These two passages together conclude the first section: the Teacher who is capable of preaching.

Second, regarding the "Teachings and Scriptural Repositories" (*śāsana-piṭaka*) that are preached: since there is already a person capable of preaching who has descended into the world, it cannot be in vain;

there must necessarily be the teachings preached by that Teacher. Therefore, this is discussed next. This section is divided into two parts. First, a general presentation of the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*).

Second, regarding the specific explanation of the two passages according to the teachings, the first part is further divided into two: first, distinguishing the names and essences of the three piṭakas;

second, clarifying the sequence of the three piṭakas. Within the first of these, there are again two sections: first, explaining the names; second, identifying the essence. Within the first [section], there are two parts: first, explaining the three distinct names;
second, discussing the general designation of "piṭaka" for both texts. Now, regarding the first, as for the explanation of the names: originally...

Although the Buddha appeared in the world and taught more than eighty thousand Dharma-gates according to the capacities of sentient beings, when these are summarized against the obstacles of afflictions (*kleśa*), their essential purport does not exceed three names; namely, the *Vinaya* and so forth.

Regarding the first, *vinaya*, it is also called *vinaya* or *vinaya*; these are variations of the Sanskrit pronunciation. Translated generally, this is rendered as "Law" (*lü*). The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

*Vinaya* means "dharma. It weighs the gravity of offenses, adjudicates right and wrong, and renders the distinction between observance and violation crystal clear; thus, there is necessarily no room for doubt or confusion. Second, the meaning of the "pen" (*bi*):

Generally, when one speaks of decisive judgment, it is not settled without a pen. The pen is the symbol of the legal school (the *fajia*). [As stated in the source... Third, the meaning of the "three divisions":

This resembles how the Yin and Yang divide the *lü* and *lü* musical scales; likewise, in the present context, the distinctions between compliance and opposition, and between observance and violation, are also established in this manner.
This is explained in detail as set forth in the commentary. Second is the *sūtra*. Formerly it was called *xiūduluó* (修多羅) or *xiūdùlù* (修妬露);
this is translated as "thread" (*sūtra*). A thread has the meaning of threading together and holding fast;

just as a thread threads flowers so they do not scatter or be lost, so too the Buddha’s holy teaching threads together the principles it elucidates, holding them fast so they do not disperse. If translated according to the old usage, it is rendered as "sūtra" (*jīng* [經]).
"Sūtra" (jīng) means "to pass through" (qùhū). It is like the warp in weaving; it also carries the sense of "pervading" and "encompassing.

Alternatively, it may refer to a distant path that can show people the essential way. Furthermore, it carries the meaning of "constant" (cháng); as the ancients held it in common reverence, that which is not altered by a hundred kings is called "constant.
Moreover, the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* explains the sūtra through five meanings, such as "a spring of water," which can be understood in detail as being "constant."
[It is said: If *sūtra* is a term from a foreign language, it is translated here as *kīngyōn* (契經). "Kī" (契) means to accord with; it refers to the teaching that expresses [the meaning].

"Kyōn" (經) means to accord with the principles that can be expressed and to harmonize with the capacities of sentient beings; thus, it is called "kī. It strings together and sustains the meanings that ought to be known.
Regarding the term *mukha* (gate/entry): the third is *Abhidharma*. Formerly it was called *Pitan*;

here it means "Incomparable Dharma" (*anuttara-dharma*), because it is the most excellent among forms of wisdom (*prajñā*). Since there is no other dharma that surpasses this dharma, it is called "Incomparable Dharma.

Now, according to the new [translation], it is called *Abhidharma*, which means "Dharma in Opposition" (*prati-dharma*). This "opposition" has two meanings: first, "orientation toward," meaning the untainted (*anāsrava*)...
Wisdom is directed toward *nirvāṇa*. Second is "contemplation" (*prativedha*): this refers to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) contemplating the Four Noble Truths.

The previous mention of "directed toward" (*abhimukha*) describes the cause in relation to the fruit; the cause is pure wisdom, and the fruit is *nirvāṇa*. The subsequent mention of "contemplation" (*prativedha*) describes the mind in relation to its object;
the mind is pure wisdom, and the object is the Four Noble Truths. Because it possesses these two aspects, it is termed "directed" (*prati*). It is that which maintains the path and serves as a guide.
Because it possesses meaning, it is called a *dharma*. "Norm" (*niyama*) refers to a standard or rule that causes beings to produce understanding.

For example, the *rūpa-dharma* (form-aggregate) can serve as a norm and a standard, enabling the production of an understanding of its characteristic of resistance; the same applies to sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth. Second, because it can maintain its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
For example, the *rūpa-dharma* has transformation and resistance as its nature; because it can maintain this nature, it is called a *dharma*. The same applies to the others.

Furthermore, there are two kinds of phenomena (*dharma*): first, the ultimate phenomenon (*paramārtha-dharma*); second, the phenomenal characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-dharma*). Regarding the ultimate phenomenon: it refers to all that is *nirvāṇa*.

Because it is virtuous and eternal, it is called "ultimate" (*parama*). Because it possesses substantial reality, it is called "meaning" (*artha*). Thus, "ultimate meaning" is itself the phenomenon (this is a *karmadhāraya* compound).

Second, the phenomenal characteristic phenomenon: this encompasses the four noble truths. "Characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) means nature (*svabhāva*). It is so named in reference to its own essence. This is called... [text fragment ends]

It is the nature [of things]. From the perspective of other conditions, it is called a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*). Because these Four Noble Truths are the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), they are termed "phenomena characterized by their marks.

Since the characteristic is itself the phenomenon (this is a *karmadhāraya* compound), there are further six types of oppositions, such as self-nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth, as explained extensively elsewhere.
Question: Since this is a translation of the *Abhidharma*, why is it now designated as a "śāstra"? Answer: It is a regional designation. In Sanskrit, it is called *śāstra*.
*Śāstra* means "treatise" (*lun*). In the Sanskrit language, it is *mātṛkā*, which means "matrix" (*benmu*). A "mother" is that which can give birth to sublime wisdom;
since sublime wisdom arises in dependence upon a treatise, the meaning of *mātṛkā* is called a "treatise. Regarding this Abhidharma Piṭaka of treatises, there are different classifications.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, there are two kinds: first, the ultimate (*paramārtha*), and second, the...
Regarding the conventional [explanation]: as for the term "Abhidharma of the ultimate" (*paramārtha-abhidharma*), that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) is called "ultimate" (*parama*);
because it possesses a profound and preeminent meaning, it is termed "ultimate" (*artha*). Thus, untainted pure wisdom (*anāsrava-śuddha-prajñā*) is the Abhidharma of the ultimate.

Being free from bondage is called "pure" (*śuddha*); discernment is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*). Furthermore, the coarser factors associated with pure wisdom—namely, the mind associated with wisdom, as well as feeling, perception, and so forth—are its retinue.
All mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), up to the unmanifest form concomitant with the Path (*mārga-sahabhū-avijñapti*), are the retinue of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Thus, this pure wisdom together with its retinue, which collectively subsumes the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), is called the Abhidharma of ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-abhidharma*). As for the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), it refers first to all forms of wisdom.

"Second, the various treatises (*śāstra*). Regarding "various wisdoms" (*prajñā*), these refer to the four types of wisdom associated with outflows (*sāsrava*): first, innate wisdom (*upapatti-pratilambhikā prajñā*), so called because it is acquired at birth;

second, wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*); third, wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*); and fourth, wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*), as is commonly understood.

Regarding "the various treatises," these refer to the six *pāda-śāstras*: first, the *Saṃgītiparyāya-pāda-śāstra*; second, the *Dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra*; and third, the *Prajñapti-pāda-śāstra*. (These three...)

These were composed by the great Arhats during the Buddha’s lifetime: (1) the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, (2) the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, and (3) the *Dhātukāya-śāstra*. These three treatises were composed after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa at the request of the Arhats.

This "Wisdom Treatise" (*Prajñā-śāstra*) concerns contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*); because its principles are coarse and shallow and easily understood, it is termed "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*).
The aforementioned pure uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-śuddha-prajñā*) is attained by relying upon the various forms of wisdom derived from these treatises.
As it is with the Abhidharma, so it is with the other two Piṭakas. That is to say, those meditative concentrations that are capable of conforming to the ultimate reality are the *paramārtha-sūtra*;
contaminated concentrations and various scriptural teachings are the *saṃvṛti-sūtra*.

Uncontaminated restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) is the true Vinaya-piṭaka, termed the *paramārtha-vinaya*; whereas the various rules of discipline and contaminated ethical conduct (*śīla*) are the *saṃvṛti-vinaya*.

*Niye* (the above concludes the total explanation of the three distinct names). Next, the general explanation of the title of the *Piṭaka*. In Sanskrit it is called *piṭaka-kośa*; this is translated here as "piṭaka" (*zàng*).

This is because it takes on the meanings of "encompassing," "containing," and "upholding. It is like a storehouse or chest, which is able to encompass, contain, uphold, and serve as a support for what is held within.
Furthermore, the *Saṃgrahaṇī* states: "For what reason is it called a 'piṭaka'? Because it is able to encompass and uphold all [teachings]."

It should be understood according to the meaning. One must not allow it to be lost or scattered; [this refers to] the Venerable [Master]’s (the *ārya* being the principal member of the compound in a *tatpuruṣa* analysis) compilation and preservation [of the teachings] within the Tripiṭaka. The two preceding sections have been thus categorized (and so forth).
Second, regarding the determination of the essential nature (*svabhāva*): since the preceding section explained the names in order to summon the essence, it is now analyzed in succession.

Within this, following the precedent of the previous explanation of names, it is likewise divided into two parts: first, the ultimate (*paramārtha*), and second, the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). Regarding the determination of the essential nature of the first, the ultimate, it is further divided into three sections.

First, regarding the ultimate discipline (*paramārtha-vinaya*), if we discuss it in terms of its essential nature: from the initial moment of the patience toward suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) up until the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), it takes as its substance the sevenfold untainted form (*anāsrava-rūpa*).

Among the eightfold noble path, it is designated by three factors: verbal action, livelihood, and [right speech]; among the five aggregates, it is subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*);

and among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), it is included within the base of mental objects (*dharma-āyatana*); and among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), it is [included within] the element of mental objects.

Regarding its inclusion within the *dhātus*: if taken together with its retinue as a single aggregate, it consists of wholesome mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that arise simultaneously in association;

thus, it also encompasses the five aggregates (*skandhas*). Within the twelve bases (*āyatanas*), it is included in the base of phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*) and the mind base (*mano-āyatana*); within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), it is subsumed under the element of mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna-dhātu*).

According to the *Paramārtha-sūtra*, its essential nature is untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*); among the mental factors, it has the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) belonging to the universal ground (*mahābhūmika*) as its substance.

Among the five aggregates (*skandha*), it is subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), it is included within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*); and among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), it is subsumed under the element of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*).

If its attendants are included, it is largely the same as previously described. Regarding the third, the ultimate Abhidharma (*paramārthābhidharma*): by defining its essential nature, it has untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) as its substance;

that is, it is a mental factor (*caitta-dharma*), specifically the wisdom included within the universal ground (*mahābhūmika*) factors, which belongs exclusively to the aggregate of formations, the base of mental objects, and the element of mental objects.

[Included]. If including the retinue, there is no difference from what precedes (the above concludes the determination of the essence according to the ultimate truth). Second, the determination of the essence according to the conventional truth.

This is divided into two parts: first, regarding the signifier (*vācaka*); second, regarding the signified (*vācya*). Within the first part, concerning the essence of the signifier, the twenty schools of the Hīnayāna differ;
yet, searching for their general outline, they do not exceed six types of conceptual attachments. Now, among these six, [we shall discuss] the remaining five...
As clarified elsewhere, we shall now rely on the orthodox position of the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. Regarding this, there are two masters’ explanations:
first, the master who holds that vocal action (*vākkarman*) is its essence; second, the master who holds that names (*nāma*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*) are its essence.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* asks: "What is the essence of such Buddhist teachings? Is it vocal action, or is it names and phrases? It should be answered as follows:

There are those who hold that the essence [of speech] consists in vocal action (*vāg-karman*), for speech is simply sound. Since the treatise explicitly employs the phrase "there are some who," it is clear that this position is not yet accepted as definitive.
Second, the masters of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*) challenge the masters of vocal action:

"If that were so, how would you account for the mention of names, phrases, and syllables; prose and verse; their sequential arrangement; and even their successive conjunctions? How would you explain 'speech'?"
The master of karma replied: "The subsequent passage is intended to clarify the Buddha's functional activity. The masters of names and phrases (*nāma-pada*) do not accept this explanation.
Why is that? Sound itself is non-expressive and lacks any capacity for signification; how could it serve as the essence [of speech]?
It must rely upon names and phrases for the meaning and principle to be revealed. Question: Which of these two masters is correct? Answer: According to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, both...
The Master accepted both [positions]. Thus, the *Zhengli chao* states: "Now, examining these two interpretations, each has its own intended conclusion.

All treatises present both masters, and I have never heard of a definitive adjudication between them. If one seeks the underlying intent through the means of expression, there is no way to manifest it without names, phrases, and syllables."

If one hopes to harmonize the teaching with the capacity of the recipient, there is nothing but sound by which it can be manifested; if one hopes to harmonize the teaching with the capacity of the recipient, there is nothing but sound by which it can be heard.
Regarding the two heavens transmitting the Dharma, there were originally two masters: if both are complete, it is perfect; if even one is lacking, it is insufficient.
The reason for this is that sound constitutes the substance (*bhāva*) of the teaching, while names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*) constitute its function (*kāritra*).
Only when both substance and function coexist is the substance of the teaching fully complete; if even one of these were lacking, the process of signification would not be accomplished.

Therefore, herein, the four factors—sound, name, phrase, and syllable—are collectively taken as the substance [of the teaching] (having concluded the preceding analysis of the substance of the teaching as the signifier). Next, the substance of the principle (the signified) is analyzed as being threefold (as follows): first, the *Prātimokṣa*...

Regarding the precepts (*śīla*), there are two schools with differing views. According to the Sarvāstivāda, both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) take matter (*rūpa*) as their essence.

According to the Sautrāntika, the precept of action (*karmapatha-śīla*) takes both matter and mind (*citta*) as its essence, whereas the unmanifest does not take mind as its essence. As for the precept of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-śīla*), it takes matter as its essence.

Second, the contaminated concentrations (*sāsrava-samādhi*), which have *samādhi* as their essential nature. Third, the contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*), which has the four types of wisdom as its essential nature.

(The above concludes the exposition on the essential nature of the principles [the objects signified]. As previously stated, etc., the general explanation of the names and essential natures of the Three Piṭakas is now complete.)
The second section, "Discriminating the Sequence of the Three Piṭakas," is divided into two parts: first, the actual explanation of the sequence; second, the explanation of the reasons for it.

Within the first part, there are three [subsections] (as detailed below). Regarding the first, which discriminates according to the common tradition: the Sūtras come first, followed by the Vinaya, and finally the Śāstras. The reason for this is as follows:
There are four reasons for this. First, regarding the sequence as explained based on the narrative:
after the Buddha attained enlightenment, he proceeded to the Deer Park and expounded the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths to Kauṇḍinya. Thus, the Sūtra constitutes the first.

Having heard the Dharma, [Kauṇḍinya] was summoned with the words "Welcome," his hair and beard fell away naturally, and he received the precepts within himself; he then followed the Middle Way. This is the Vinaya as the second.
Once the practice has been undertaken, the five aggregates are extensively analyzed as being without self; this is the Abhidharma, which stands last.
Second, regarding the sequence established according to conversion: the *Vibhāṣā* states that for those who have not yet planted roots of goodness, causing them to plant them is the Sūtra;

for those who have already planted roots of goodness, causing them to achieve maturity is the Vinaya; and for those who have already achieved maturity, causing them to attain [liberation] is the Abhidharma.

Liberation—this is the Abhidharma. Regarding the determination of the sequence based on the three [collections], there are two explanations according to the teachings, as clarified elsewhere in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Samantapāsādikā*. For now, this shall follow the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-sūtra*.

According to the *Jñānaprasthāna*, it was initially intended for internal classification; first, the *Sūtrapiṭaka* was compiled. Regarding the determination of the sequence based on four fundamental principles:
since the Sūtras are the foundation, they are clarified first; the precepts arise from them, and wisdom subsequently emerges. Thus, these four meanings are established.
For this reason, the Sūtra Piṭaka is placed at the very beginning. Regarding the second point, the presentation of the Vinaya for clarification:
placing the Sūtras first and the Śāstras last likewise possesses four meanings. First, concerning the preservation of the Dharma: the Vinaya is the life-force of the Buddha’s teachings;

it is through the Vinaya Piṭaka that the Buddha’s teachings abide. Therefore, the Vinaya is placed at the very beginning. Second, concerning the initiation of practice: as for all instances of initiating practice...
The source [of all practice] has the precepts as its foremost element. Since one initiates conduct based on the teachings, the Vinaya Piṭaka stands at the beginning. Thus, a sutra says:

"Precepts are the root of conduct, the face and head, and the collection of all wholesome dharmas. Regarding the three points of establishment, the Vinaya Piṭaka is superior, for the Buddha personally exemplified it.

The other two [Abhidharma and Vinaya] lack this capacity; therefore, they are placed last. Furthermore, the Vinaya states: "To disparage the Abhidharma constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; to disparage the other two constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Fourthly, regarding the internal community to whom they are addressed: the Abhidharma is explained first because the other two do not apply in this same way;

thus, they follow later. Thirdly, as for establishing the sequence by way of superiority and inferiority: this refers to the Abhidharma being discussed first, followed by the Sūtras, and finally the Vinaya. This refers to the Abhidharma.

It elucidates the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*), the source of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Concentration (*samādhi*) can clarify the mind; it arises by means of wisdom. Precepts (*śīla*) subdue body and speech;

they are able to provide protection through concentration. Since these [trainings] differ in terms of superiority and inferiority, [wisdom] is placed first. (The preceding three points, etc., constitute the first section: the clarification of the sequence of the Three Baskets is hereby concluded).
Next, the reason for the Three Piṭakas is explained. This section is divided into two parts: first, the direct explanation of the reason;

second, the analytical discussion through questions and answers. The following passage constitutes the first part: "All Buddhas, upon their appearance, teach the Three Piṭakas without addition or subtraction.

Within this very context, they are distinguished into three categories because, among those to be converted, there are differences in the arising of faith, the initiation of practice, and the realization of the Dharma; therefore, the three are established."
This refers to those who have not yet entered the Dharma; they are led to enter it so that they do not give rise to hesitation regarding the teachings therein.
To counteract this, the Sūtra Piṭaka was established. For those who have already entered the Dharma, it exhorts them to reject the two extremes:

namely, the householders' craving for sensual pleasures and the ascetics' self-inflicted mortification of the body. These two extremes deviate from the Middle Way and cannot give rise to the Noble [Path]. To depart from these...

Because of these two extremes, the Vinaya Piṭaka was established. Once the path has been manifested and all views have been permanently severed, one eliminates the sixty-two views of heterodox persons;
to eliminate these two types of views, the Abhidharma Piṭaka was established. Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"Furthermore, for what reason were the three piṭakas established? To counteract a mind of doubt, the Sūtra Piṭaka was established."
To counteract the two extremes, there are the five *vinayas*. To counteract the attachment to one's own views, the *abhidharma* was established (as has already been explained above).
Next, regarding the analysis through question and answer: it is asked whether these three baskets (*piṭakas*) have distinctions between them.

The answer, as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, is that they may have distinctions or they may not. First, regarding those without distinction: when the Buddha observes the capacities of sentient beings and expounds the teaching, that teaching is...
It is extremely vast; it cannot be fully subsumed within the Three Piṭakas. Therefore, that treatise states:
"When the Buddhas appear in the world, they all teach the Three Piṭakas and so forth without distinction.

The reason for this is that all dharmas are born from the ocean of omniscience, and because they flow forth from the single awakening of others and are encompassed by the ten powers and four fearlessnesses. It is the same.
Because they arise from great compassion, as evidenced by these texts, there is no difference between them. Next, regarding their differences:

although there are three according to their meaning, there are four points of distinction. First, there is a difference in the designating names, namely that the three names—Sūtra and so forth—are distinct.
Second, there is a difference in the designated meanings; that is, the Sūtra designates the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*), while the Vinaya...
Yes. The *Sūtra* (sūtrānta) elucidates the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*), while the *Abhidharma* elucidates the training in higher wisdom (*adhijñāna-śikṣā*).
There is a distinction in what is revealed by these three: within the *Sūtra*, they are revealed according to sequential pursuit; that is to say, one category is taught immediately following another.

This chapter and others like it are proclaimed immediately following that [previous] chapter. In the Vinaya, they are revealed through the *nidāna* (origin stories), meaning the specific circumstances under which the Buddha established the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) and so forth. In the Abhidharma, they are revealed through essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), meaning for the purpose of seeking the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*). There are four types of outflow (*niṣyanda*) with their respective distinctions: the Sūtras depend on the outflow of power; the Vinaya depends on... [the outflow of maturation]; the Abhidharma depends on the outflow of similarity; and the Mātṛkās depend on the outflow of liberation. Furthermore, there are three types of outflow: the outflow of cause, the outflow of fruit, and the outflow of concordance. Among these, the Sūtras are the outflow of power because they reveal the power of the Tathāgata. The Vinaya is the outflow of maturation because it reveals the maturation of karma. The Abhidharma is the outflow of similarity because it reveals the similarities among phenomena. The Mātṛkās are the outflow of liberation because they reveal the path of liberation. Moreover, there are two types of outflow: the outflow of the teaching and the outflow of the realization. The Sūtras are the outflow of the teaching because they reveal the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata. The Vinaya is the outflow of the teaching because it reveals the training rules taught by the Tathāgata. The Abhidharma is the outflow of the teaching because it reveals the characteristics of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata. The Mātṛkās are the outflow of the teaching because they reveal the categories of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata. The Sūtras are the outflow of realization because they reveal the realization of the Tathāgata. The Vinaya is the outflow of realization because it reveals the realization of the Tathāgata regarding the training rules. The Abhidharma is the outflow of realization because it reveals the realization of the Tathāgata regarding the characteristics of phenomena. The Mātṛkās are the outflow of realization because they reveal the realization of the Tathāgata regarding the categories of phenomena. Furthermore, there are two types of outflow: the outflow of the basis and the outflow of the supported. The Sūtras are the outflow of the basis because they are the basis for the Vinaya and the Abhidharma. The Vinaya is the outflow of the basis because it is the basis for the Abhidharma and the Mātṛkās. The Abhidharma is the outflow of the basis because it is the basis for the Mātṛkās. The Mātṛkās are the outflow of the basis because they are the basis for the realization of the path. The Sūtras are the outflow of the supported because they are supported by the Vinaya and the Abhidharma. The Vinaya is the outflow of the supported because it is supported by the Abhidharma and the Mātṛkās. The Abhidharma is the outflow of the supported because it is supported by the Mātṛkās. The Mātṛkās are the outflow of the supported because they are supported by the realization of the path. Furthermore, there are two types of outflow: the outflow of the primary and the outflow of the secondary. The Sūtras are the outflow of the primary because they are the primary source for the Vinaya and the Abhidharma. The Vinaya is the outflow of the primary because it is the primary source for the Abhidharma and the Mātṛkās. The Abhidharma is the outflow of the primary because it is the primary source for the Mātṛkās. The Mātṛkās are the outflow of the primary because they are the primary source for the realization of the path. The Sūtras are the outflow of the secondary because they are secondary to the Vinaya and the Abhidharma. The Vinaya is the outflow of the secondary because it is secondary to the Abhidharma and the Mātṛkās. The Abhidharma is the outflow of the secondary because it is secondary to the Mātṛkās. The Mātṛkās are the outflow of the secondary because they are secondary to the realization of the path. Furthermore, there are two types of outflow: the outflow of the extensive and the outflow of the concise. The Sūtras are the outflow of the extensive because they extensively explain the meaning of the Dharma. The Vinaya is the outflow of the concise because it concisely explains the training rules. The Abhidharma is the outflow of the concise because it concisely explains the characteristics of phenomena. The Mātṛkās are the outflow of the concise because they concisely explain the categories of phenomena. Furthermore, there are two types of outflow: the outflow of the literal and the outflow of the interpretive. The Sūtras are the outflow of the literal because they primarily teach the literal meaning. The Vinaya is the outflow of the interpretive because it primarily teaches the interpretation of the training rules. The Abhidharma is the outflow of the interpretive because it primarily teaches the interpretation of the characteristics of phenomena. The Mātṛkās are the outflow of the interpretive because they primarily teach the interpretation of the categories of phenomena. Furthermore, there are two types of outflow: the outflow of the definitive and the outflow of the provisional. The Sūtras are the outflow of the definitive because they definitively establish the ultimate truth. The Vinaya is the outflow of the provisional because it provisionally establishes the training rules according to circumstances. The Abhidharma is the outflow of the definitive because it definitively establishes the true characteristics of phenomena. The Mātṛkās are the outflow of the definitive because they definitively establish the categories of phenomena. Furthermore, there are two types of outflow: the outflow of the cause and the outflow of the fruit. The Sūtras are the outflow of the cause because they are the cause for generating faith and understanding. The Vinaya is the outflow of the fruit because it is the fruit of having practiced the training rules. The Abhidharma is the outflow of the cause because it is the cause for generating wisdom and discernment. The Mātṛkās are the outflow of the fruit because they are the fruit of having realized the path. Furthermore, there are two types of outflow: the outflow of the internal and the outflow of the external. The Sūtras are the outflow of the internal because they primarily concern the internal mind. The Vinaya is the outflow of the external because it primarily concerns external conduct. The Abhidharma is the outflow of the internal because it primarily concerns the internal characteristics of phenomena. The Mātṛkās are the outflow of the external because they primarily concern the external categories of phenomena. Furthermore, there are two types of outflow: the outflow of the mundane and the outflow of the supramundane. The Sūtras are the outflow of the mundane because they primarily teach mundane dharmas. The Vinaya is the outflow of the supramundane because it primarily teaches the supramundane training rules. The Abhidharma is the outflow of the mundane because it primarily teaches mundane characteristics of phenomena. The Mātṛkās are the outflow of the supramundane because they primarily teach the supramundane categories of phenomena. Furthermore, there are two types of outflow: the outflow of the listener and the outflow of the teacher. The Sūtras are the outflow of the listener because they are what is heard from the Teacher. The Vinaya is the outflow of the teacher because it is what the Teacher has established. The Abhidharma is the outflow of the listener because it is what the listeners have analyzed. The Mātṛkās are the outflow of the teacher because they are what the Teacher has condensed. Furthermore, there are two types of outflow: the outflow of the root and the outflow of the branch. The Sūtras are the outflow of the root because they are the root of the entire Dharma. The Vinaya is the outflow of the branch because it is a branch of the Sūtras. The Abhidharma is the outflow of the root because it is the root of wisdom. The Mātṛkās are the outflow of the branch because they are a branch of the Abhidharma. Furthermore, there are two types of outflow: the outflow of the beginning and the outflow of the end. The Sūtras are the outflow of the beginning because they introduce the Dharma. The Vinaya is the outflow of the end because it concludes the training rules. The Abhidharma is the outflow of the beginning because it begins the analysis of phenomena. The Mātṛkās are the outflow of the end because they conclude the categories of phenomena. Furthermore, there are two types of outflow: the outflow of the general and the outflow
The Abhidharma is the outflow of great compassion; it is based on the outflow of fearlessness. Question:

According to these three piṭakas, since the expressive words and the expressed meanings differ, the three piṭakas do not mutually subsume one another. Yet, within the various Vinayas, there are mixed explanations of concentration and wisdom.
Is it not because the other two *piṭakas* [are concerned with] those [other matters]? Furthermore, in the Sūtras, one section among the three explains both precepts (*śīla*) and wisdom (*prajñā*);

in the Śāstras, one section among the three explains both precepts (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*). How then can there be a distinction as stated previously? Answer: This is based on the primary subject matter (*abhidheya*) of each school. It is restricted solely to precepts;

however, concentration and wisdom are explained here because they follow along [with precepts]. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "It is spoken of according to what is predominant: the Vinaya explains precepts."

It is superior. Even if it were clear that concentration and wisdom were inferior rather than superior, this principle may be understood by analogy with the two collections of Sūtra and Śāstra. Furthermore, it is asked:
since it is said that the three [collections] encompass all meanings exhaustively, why do various texts speak of a "Miscellaneous Collection" (Kṣudraka-piṭaka)?
Thus, the *Pinfen gongde lun* states: "Some were spoken by the Buddha, some by his disciples, some by non-humans, or they are hymns of praise by devas, or they are..."

The causes and conditions of past lives are manifold in both their phrasing and meaning; because they expound both principle and phenomena, it is called the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka* (Miscellaneous Collection). Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"Whether spoken by Pratyekabuddhas or spoken by Arhats, those accounts that describe one's own past conduct and causes and conditions are termed the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka*."

Regarding this *Kṣudraka-piṭaka* (Miscellaneous Collection), it is uncertain whether it is subsumed within the Three Piṭakas. If one says that it is indeed subsumed within the layers of the Three Piṭakas, then it would be inconsistent for there to still be a separate name "Miscellaneous Collection.

If one says that this Miscellaneous Collection is preserved separately and does not fall under the aforementioned three Piṭakas, then why did the previous statement say that the meaning of the Three Piṭakas is exhaustive?

Answer: From the perspective of being restricted to the specific meanings they convey (*saṃgīta-artha*), it cannot be called a "Piṭaka" (Basket). In reality, however, it is included within the Three Piṭakas.
The *Kṣudrakapiṭaka* (Miscellaneous Collection) is not included [within the three baskets]. If it were explained in a general sense, how could it not be subsumed?

It is only because both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) are elucidated together that it is designated as "miscellaneous. To speak according to reality, however, it does not depart from the three baskets. Furthermore, it was asked:

"Since it does not depart from the three baskets, in which basket is it subsumed? The answer is: Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states, "Various miscellaneous explanations are called *Sūtra*. Furthermore, the Vinaya states, "The four Āgamas..."

The *Kṣudrakapiṭaka* (Miscellaneous Collection) is also subsumed within the *Sūtrapiṭaka*. Regarding the "Four Āgamas," these refer to the *Dīrghāgama*, *Madhyamāgama*, *Ekottarikāgama*, and *Saṃyuktāgama*;
thus they are called the "Four Āgamas. As for the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka*, because it collects various other sūtras and so forth, it is termed the "Miscellaneous Collection";

therefore, it is included within the [other] three [collections], such that one speaks only of the Three Piṭakas. Alternatively, to discuss the matter more broadly, according to various sūtras and śāstras, the Three [Piṭakas] are also taught.
The Pitakas consist of two: first, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka; second, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. Furthermore, the *Vibhaṅga-guṇa-sūtra* states that there are four piṭakas:
first, the Sūtra; second, the Vinaya; third, the Abhidharma; and fourth, the Kṣudraka-piṭaka. Moreover, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* lists five piṭakas:

the four as mentioned above, with the addition of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* contains six piṭakas, which include the aforementioned Śrāvaka and Bodhisattva...
Within the Tripiṭaka, each—Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma—is further divided into six, thus forming the Six Piṭakas. Furthermore, the *Garbha-tantra* (Tāizàng jīng) speaks of eight piṭakas;
these also consist of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma within the Śrāvaka and Bodhisattva Piṭakas, with the addition of a Miscellaneous Piṭaka (*Kṣudraka-piṭaka*) to each, thereby forming eight.
Moreover, the *Lalitavistara-sūtra* (Pǔyào jīng) speaks of nine piṭakas, meaning that within each of the three piṭakas, there are again Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma. The above is general.

According to various teachings, they may be few or many; yet when discussed from the perspective of the ultimate, they do not transcend the Three Piṭakas, differing only in their expansion or contraction (the preceding discussion on the two [categories], etc., has concluded with the general enumeration of the Three Piṭakas).

Second, regarding the specific explanation according to the teachings: while the preceding section provided a general overview of the Buddha’s Dharma throughout his entire career, the present section excludes two of the aforementioned three categories and provides a specific explanation solely based on the Vinaya-piṭaka. Within this text, there are two distinct parts: first, clarifying its inclusion within the Piṭakas;

second, distinguishing its categorization within the Vehicles (Yānas). Regarding the first of these two parts, there are again two sections: the first clarifies the *Vinaya-mūla* (the root of the Vinaya).
Regarding the origins of the arising [of the Vinaya]: secondly, categorized by what is included within the Piṭakas. First, as for the origins of the arising of the Vinaya itself:

this refers to the period after the Buddha attained enlightenment and before twelve years had passed, during which he did not yet expound the profound causes, but spoke only of the concise teachings (*saṃkṣipta-śāsana*). It was only after twelve years that the extensive teachings (*vistara-śāsana*) arose.

As for what is called the "concise teaching," it refers to the single verse from the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* beginning with: "Well-guarded are one's verbal utterances," and so forth. As for what is called the "extensive teaching,"...
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: At that time, when the World-Honored One was staying at the Pīlaṇḍa hermitage in the kingdom of Kusumapura, Śāriputra was dwelling in a quiet place and reflected:
"Which Buddhas, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, cause the practice of the holy life to endure for a long time?
Which Buddhas, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, cause the practice of the holy life not to endure for a long time? Having had this thought, he rose from his quiet place and adjusted his robes.

Having donned his robes, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Tathāgata regarding the matters he had contemplated while dwelling in seclusion, requesting that the Buddha would grant him an exposition. The Buddha told Śāriputra: “Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Krakucchanda, and Kāśyapa...”
"The Dharma of these four Buddhas shall endure for a long time. Vipaśyin and Kanakamuni—these two Buddhas' Dharmas shall not endure for long.

Śāriputra asked: "For what reason did the Buddha say this? Why is it that under these two Buddhas, the disciples were taught the extensive teachings externally, while only the concise teachings were spoken [internally]?
When those Buddhas were in the world, the Dharma remained and was practiced; after their parinirvāṇa, various faults arose and it quickly perished."
The True Dharma is like various beautiful flowers scattered upon a table; when the wind blows, they are dispersed.

Because they are not strung together with a thread, [the teachings] of the four preceding Buddhas are understood by contrast. Śāriputra then requested the Tathāgata, who then [taught] for the sake of the bhikṣus.

Regarding the formulation of the extensive teaching, the Buddha said, "Cease for now; I myself know the proper time. He meant that as long as the bhikṣus have not yet obtained gain or fame, and no taints or faults have arisen, they remain pure;
however, once they obtain gain and fame, taints and faults will arise. Once these taints and faults have arisen, [the teaching must be established].

It was then that the precepts were established. At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Vaiśālī. Sudinna, the son of a Śākya, returned to his native village and committed an act of sexual misconduct with his former wife.
At that time, there were those who practiced *dhūta* austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse, who informed the Buddha.
The Buddha assembled the bhikṣus and, after rebuking him in various ways, asked: "For what reason did you commit this first offense? and so forth. (As detailed in the full account. Then...
Ten categories of offenses were established and the first precept was enacted. Subsequently, when Dhanika stole the king’s timber, the second precept was enacted.

Thus, as each offense occurred, a corresponding rule was established until the Vinaya was complete. This is like a garment whose seams have not yet been sewn, or medicine awaiting the onset of illness;

only when transgressions arose did the various sections (pārājika, saṃghāvaśeṣa, etc. become manifest. Based on this, the gravity of the offenses was determined, and the maintenance or violation of the precepts was thereby regulated.

The formal classification has already been established; thus, the Great Canon of the Vinaya arose as its scriptural teaching (the preceding section on the origins of the fundamental Vinaya is concluded).

Next, regarding its inclusion within the Pitakas: there are three distinct types of Pitaka, as already clarified above and need not be recounted again here. That which is our primary subject of study is as follows.
This is included within the Vinaya Piṭaka. Next, regarding the classification by vehicle (*yāna*): there are three vehicles. For now, they shall be explained generally;
next, their inclusion will be discussed. First, the individual names of these three types are explained; second, the general designation "vehicle" is interpreted. Regarding the first term, *śrāvaka*:

"voice" (*śabda*) refers to sound, and "hearing" (*śravaṇa*) refers to listening. This refers to the sentient beings to be converted who, having generated consciousness, listen and receive [the teaching]. By virtue of this—

Hearing the Buddha’s teaching, they believe, accept, and practice it, thereby departing from the three realms of existence. This refers to the time when the World-Honored One first turned the Dharma wheel of the Four Noble Truths;
at the sound of those truths, Śāriputra and others immediately realized the supreme fruit. This is called "awakening to the Way through sound," and thus they are termed *śrāvaka* (Voice-hearers).

This name is established based on their initial condition. If considered in relation to the present day, it refers to those who merely rely on the teachings of sound to practice and realize the [Four Noble Truths].

The fruit of the śramaṇa is also called a śrāvaka. Second, regarding the pratyekabuddha: in Sanskrit they are called *pratyekabuddha*, which here is translated as "enlightened by conditions" (*yuanjue*).

"Conditions" (*yuan*) refers to that which is taken as an object, namely the objective realm of contemplation, which is the twelve links of dependent origination. "Enlightened" (*jue*) refers to the wisdom capable of contemplating.

Because such a person can realize the Way by taking these conditions as their essence, they are called a pratyekabuddha. For brevity, the Sanskrit term is now abbreviated, and they are simply called *pratyeka*.
There are two types of these. The first is the solitary *pratyekabuddha*, who appears in an age when no Buddha exists.
Merely observing that the grasses and trees of the world sprout in spring, grow in summer, wither in autumn, and fall in winter, they naturally awaken to the Way without relying on instruction.

Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "They always delight in tranquility and do not wish to dwell in a crowd; merely by fulfilling their preparatory practices (*prayoga*), they awaken of themselves in the absence of a Buddha. Therefore...

They are called Pratyekabuddhas, or alternatively "Rhinoceros-like" (Khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa). This is designated by way of analogy, meaning that like the single horn of a rhinoceros, they do not arise in pairs.
Now, if one calls them *Pratyekabuddha*, it refers to the sense of "awakening" (*buddha*); if one calls them "Rhinoceros-like," it refers to the "horn" (*viṣāṇa*) of the head.
