he feared they might equal those of King Bimbisāra, so he removed one set. There were sixty chests of golden grain; each chest contained two hundred and thirty *hú* of gold.
Even the lowest quality of fine cloth was worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold, for it was fastened with gold nails.

They buried it seven feet deep; the woolen cloth was not pierced or torn, remaining exactly as it was before. Such was the wealth resulting from the power of their merit. However, they had no children.
Beside their house stood a tree of the *puṇya-deva* (merit-god). The husband and wife went there to pray and offer sacrifices, entreating that they might have a child.
When there was no response for two years, they spoke with anger and resentment, saying: "Now, for another seven days, we shall serve you with all our hearts."
If there is no sign of success later, he will surely burn and cut it down. The spirit tree, filled with grief and fear, then informed the Four Great Kings.
The Kings, in turn, reported this to Śakra. Śakra surveyed all the people of Jambudvīpa and found none capable of becoming that son;
he then reported these matters to Brahmā. With his divine eye, Brahmā beheld a Brahmā-son deity who was about to pass away.
Rejoicing at his rebirth in the Brahma realm, the King of that Heaven said, "The dharma of the brahmins is full of evil and wrong views;
I do not dare to become their son. The Brahma King spoke to him, saying, "This brahmin possesses great majesty and virtue.
The people of Jambudvīpa have little merit and are unworthy to be his sons. You must certainly be born there; I shall embrace you."
"I shall protect you; I will never allow you to give rise to wrong views. Brahmā said, "So be it. I respectfully accept your holy command and dare not transgress it.
Thereupon, the Brahmā King informed Śakra, and Śakra related these matters in detail to the tree spirit.
The tree spirit was filled with joy and went to the brahmin’s house, saying to him, "Do not harbor resentment toward me any longer. He then turned back.
"Seven days from now, your wish shall be fulfilled. When the seven days had passed, the wife realized she was pregnant.
Upon reaching the completion of ten months, she gave birth to a son whose countenance was upright and handsome, his body the color of pure gold, and his radiance blazing for forty *li*.
A physiognomist divined and said, "This child’s merit from past lives is profound; he will certainly renounce the world. When his parents heard this, they were overcome with grief and distress.
The husband and wife said to one another, "What plan should we devise to sever his intent?
They further reflected, "That which the world is most attached to is nothing but beautiful form; we shall betroth him to a maiden of exquisite beauty to cut off his passion.
When he reached the age of fifteen, they wished to take a wife for him. Having learned of this, he felt deep displeasure and said to his parents, "My aspiration is for purity."

"It is not necessary. His parents would not permit it. Knowing he could not escape their will, he devised a stratagem and said to his parents, "If there were in this world a woman with a purple-gold complexion just like mine, I must have her. His parents immediately prepared a banquet.
He widely summoned his kinsmen, Brahmins, and others, and traveled everywhere seeking a bride. The Brahmins collectively devised a plan:
they cast a golden deity of exquisite and extraordinary beauty and paraded it through the village. They proclaimed aloud:

"If there is a girl who beholds this golden deity and pays homage to it, when she later comes of age for marriage, she will surely obtain a husband of excellent appearance with a body the color of gold. Thus they spoke.

Upon hearing this, the women all rushed out of the house; however, there was one girl whose body was golden in color, upright and exceptionally beautiful—she was the very person who had been the poor woman during her causal stage.
Due to her past superior conditions, she had attained such a physical form and, being devoted to purity, alone refused to go out.
The other women forcibly led her along to see the Golden Deity. Once the girl arrived, her golden radiance shone forth.
Drolanglen. The Brahmin immediately arranged for her to be married. Once she arrived at her husband’s home, the couple faced one another;
both were pure and entirely free from carnal desire. They made a solemn agreement to each occupy a separate room.

When their parents learned of this, they demolished one of the rooms so that they might share a dwelling, providing them with a single bed. The husband said to his wife: "When I am sleeping, you then..."
[The husband] practiced walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). "If you fall asleep," he thought, "I shall practice the path. Later, his wife lay down with her hand hanging over the edge of the bed.
A venomous snake entered the room and bit her hand. When her husband saw this, he wrapped his garment around her hand and lifted it onto the bed.
His wife then woke up and reproached her husband, saying: "How can you, my husband, lack such integrity as to secretly lift my arm? Her husband pointed [at the snake].
Regarding the matter of the venomous snake before the bed, his wife finally attained awakening. The husband and wife both grew weary of the world and subsequently sought to renounce their homes.
Their parents gave their permission, and they became śramaṇas. Pure and true, they maintained their simple nature;
free from action and free from desire, they dwelt in seclusion, diligently practicing asceticism. Thereupon, Kāśyapa made this vow: "Whatever exists in the world shall become [an Arhat]."

"I take refuge in all the Arhats. Having spoken these words, he was fully endowed with the deportment of a renunciant and all the precepts (according to this, one obtains the precepts through this self-vow to the supreme Dharma).
The World-Honored One then preached the Dharma for him, whereby he attained the three insights, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.
Later, his wife, the woman Suvarṇavarṇā, paid homage to the Tathāgata and likewise attained the fruit of sainthood. Furthermore, Kāśyapa...
He constantly sat facing the Tathāgata to hear the Dharma being preached. He will attain Buddhahood in the future, and his name shall be Prabhāsa (Light).
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Buddha bestowed this prediction upon him. When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted all his teachings to Kāśyapa.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, once the compilation of the Tripiṭaka was completed, [Kāśyapa] entered the Samādhi of Vow-Knowledge (*praṇidhijñāna-samādhi*). Observing that nothing was lacking, he then led his disciples...
The assembly went to offer their condolences to King Ajātaśatru. King Ajātaśatru said to the Venerable One, "The Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, yet I did not have the opportunity to see him.
When you, Venerable One, enter nirvana in the future, I pray that you will grant me notice. Kātyāyana replied, "Very well.

Thereupon, in the city of Rājagṛha, he extensively proclaimed and disseminated the teachings to transform and deliver sentient beings, performing great Buddha-works. As his time for converting others was drawing to a close, he reflected to himself: "Now..."
"I am advanced in years; my body is decrepit. Who would delight in such a body? The time for my parinirvāṇa has now arrived.
He then went to where Ānanda was and spoke these words: "Venerable one, you should know that in the past the Buddha, the World-Honored One, entrusted the Dharma to me.
Now that I am advanced in years and am about to enter parinirvāṇa, the supreme eye of the world is now to be entrusted to you. You must diligently guard and protect it. Furthermore—
Fearing that Ānanda might have no one to whom to entrust the Dharma in the future, Kāśyapa recorded for him:
"In the city of Rājagṛha, there is an elder named Śāṇakavāsin; you should ordain him and entrust the Eye of the Dharma to him. Ānanda replied, "So be it.
Kāśyapa then circumambulated and paid homage to all the Tathāgata’s relics and stūpas, just as a king of geese flies toward the great ocean to reach the Bhagīratha Dragon.
In the palace, he paid homage to the Buddha’s tooth relic. Then, as swiftly as a strong man might bend and extend his arm, he reached the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to make offerings to the Buddha’s hair.
Descending from that heaven, he returned to the royal city, with Ānanda constantly following him, never leaving his side, fearing that he would not see him again after his parinirvāṇa.
Later, on one occasion, Kāśyapa said to Ānanda: "You should enter the city first to beg for alms..."

"I shall also go to eat. Ānanda, having received these instructions, went on ahead. Kāśyapa thought to himself, "King Ajātaśatru has a prior engagement with me," and so he took leave of the king and arrived at the gate.
The gatekeeper said, "The king is currently asleep. If you startle him from his sleep..."

"The laws of the kingdom are not lenient; I did not dare to inform him. Kāśyapa said to the gatekeeper, "If the King awakens, tell him that when Kāśyapa wished to enter *parinirvāṇa*, he came to take leave of the King but did not see him.
At that time, the Venerable One donned the noble robes of the Buddha, took his own bowl, and after begging for food and eating, he entered Mount Kukkuṭapāda (Kuccha in the Sanskrit language).
Paṇḍava; in the language of Tang, it is called Kukkuṭapāda (Chicken Foot). This is because the mountain has three peaks that resemble the upturned feet of a chicken.

The Venerable One entered therein and sat cross-legged, making three vows: first, he vowed that his body, along with his robes and bowl, would remain for a long time without decaying until Maitreya’s descent, at which time they would perform great Buddhist deeds;
second, he vowed that the three peaks of this mountain would merge into one to conceal him...

[The Buddha] said, "I wish that Ānanda and King Ajātaśatru might come together; when they arrive, this mountain shall open of its own accord to allow them entry, and once they have departed, it shall close again.
Once the vow was made, the three peaks merged into one, enveloping the Venerable One. The great earth shook, and the devas were moved with longing.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru dreamed in his sleep that a rafter had broken, which signified that the rafters and ridgepole of the Buddha-dharma were breaking.
The king was then struck with terror; sweat flowed from his entire body, and he was filled with profound dread.
The gatekeeper said, "Kāśyapa entered nirvāṇa just now; he came to take leave of the king but was not seen. Upon hearing these words, the king fainted for a long while before regaining consciousness.
He then went to where Ānanda was, wailing and weeping bitterly. Together with Ānanda, he proceeded to Kukkuṭapāda Mountain. When the king arrived at the mountain, the mountain opened.
The gate was opened. The King and Ānanda entered within and beheld Kāśyapa sitting cross-legged; his entire body remained intact and undispersed.

They also saw celestial flowers covering his body. After the King had prostrated himself in worship, he wailed aloud with a raised voice and made various offerings before returning to his own country.

The mountains closed together as they were before. The *Record of the Western Regions* states that this mountain is located in the kingdom of Magadha. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*) states that Kāśyapa did not enter parinirvāṇa directly;
rather, he entered the samādhi of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), sustaining his body through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bala*) until the descent of Maitreya.

If one follows the *Vibhāṣā*, other masters say that he leaves behind his skeletal remains or his body; however, according to the school of the *Abhidharmakośa*, he enters directly into parinirvāṇa, merely sustaining his body through the power of his vow.

Examining the purport of the teachings now, since he previously made a vow and subsequently entered a state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), it is not contradictory to conclude that he must be sustained by the combined power of both concentration and his vow, remaining until the descent of Maitreya from here.
Having crossed the mountain, he saw Kāśyapa presiding over the assembly for the compilation of the Dharma-piṭaka concerning few desires. At that time, the disciples thought to themselves:
"If Kāśyapa is so humble and lowly, what must the physical stature of Śākyamuni Tathāgata have been? Maitreya said:
"Kāśyapa’s saṃghāṭī was woven by the maternal aunt of Śākyamuni Buddha; it is the golden-threaded kāṣāya now entrusted to me. Now, [he] crosses over.
The disciples who had inherited the Dharma of the four assemblies approached Maitreya and received it from him.

At that time, after Kāśyapa had delivered the robe, he leaped into the air and performed the eighteen miraculous transformations. Having completely eliminated all pride, the Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they all attained the fruits of sainthood.

At that moment, Kāśyapa transformed his *pariccheda-kāya* (segmented body) and manifested its cremation by fire, entering the realm of *nirupadhi-śeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder). Those who witnessed this—
There was none who did not give rise to feelings of sorrow and transformation. (The first master has concluded above.
Second is Ānanda, here translated as "Joyful Celebration. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that he was born on the night the Buddha attained enlightenment; at that time, Māra...
Seeing that the Buddha had attained enlightenment, they felt hatred and jealousy and came to harass and disturb him; however, they were all surpassed by the Buddha’s divine power and transformations.
They then went to the king and said, "Siddhārtha died upon the Vajrāsana last night. When the Great King heard this, he was filled with incessant grief.
After a short while, Māra withdrew, and the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven announced from the sky: "Prince Siddhārtha, at the Vajrāsana..."
Just as he sat upon the seat of enlightenment and attained perfect awakening, the Great King heard of this and was instantly filled with joy;
his celebration and consolation were boundless. Furthermore, at that same hour, the King’s younger brother, Śuklodana, addressed the King, saying: "Last night, a son was born to me."
The King said, "My noble younger brother has fathered a son; my heart is filled with joy. Today is most auspicious. As for this newborn son, he should be named Ānanda (meaning 'Joy' or 'Rejoicing').

Alternatively, he may be called 'Huanxi' (Joy). This is because his family has cultivated patience through successive lifetimes, and furthermore, because he was born with a handsome and upright appearance, causing his father, the King, great delight;
it is for these reasons that he is given this name. Furthermore, the *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhi Sūtra* states that the Buddha told [the assembly]:
"Ānanda, your name is 'Joy' (*ānanda*), yet it is based on that which is not fixed or real. Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Ānanda possesses four rare qualities:
first, when he enters the great assembly in silence, those who see him rejoice; second, whatever he speaks, those who hear it rejoice;
third, the members of the fourfold assembly give rise to a heart of reverence and admiration, gazing upon him without weariness; fourth, whatever he speaks..."

He never grew weary of listening. For these reasons, he was named "Joyful" (Nanda). As the years passed and he gradually grew up, he followed the Buddha into the homeless life and became an attendant.

This man was foremost among the wise and the learned; he maintained the treasury of the Dharma and could recite eighty-four thousand [teachings], as well as everything spoken by the various Arhats, receiving and upholding them all without ever forgetting. Furthermore, there was a beggar...
Regarding the causal conditions for eating: I have heard of these repeatedly, but fearing prolixity, I shall not recount them here.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, at the time of the First Council, the *Śīlakaṇḍasūtra* states that Kāśyapa posed three thousand eight hundred questions, to each of which [Ānanda] replied; his answers were no different from those of the Buddha.

Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptavinaya-dharmakośa-śāstra* (or *Dharmatrāta-pūrvaprayoga*) states that after receiving Kāśyapa’s entrustment and having finished paying his respects and accepting the Dharma, he went to see King Ajātaśatru.
King Ajātaśatru said to Ānanda, "Venerable sir, I did not witness the passing into parinirvāṇa of either you or Kāśyapa.
When you, Venerable sir, enter parinirvāṇa hereafter, I pray that you will inform me. Ānanda replied accordingly.
Thereupon, he proclaimed the sublime Dharma and transformed sentient beings for twenty years in this world. Later, on a certain day, he saw a bhikṣu in the forest.
He heard those verses on the Contemplation of the Dharma, which say:
"If a person lives for a hundred years without seeing an old white crane in the water, it would be better to live for but a single day and behold one.
Ānanda, hearing this, was displeased and sighed deeply, saying: "The eye of the world is extinguished; how swift is this! He departed.
Refuting the holy words and lacking wisdom, he said to him: "What you have contemplated was not spoken by the Buddha; it must not be practiced.
Furthermore, according to the *Dharmatrāta-avadāna* (The Transmission of the Dharma-treasury), Ānanda further told him: "There are two types of evil people..."

This is called slandering the Dharma. First, though one may possess great learning, one gives rise to false views; second, failing to understand the profound meaning, one explains it erroneously and perversely.
Possessing these two qualities, one brings about self-destruction and cannot cause others to leave the three evil realms. You should now listen as I recite the Buddha’s verses:
"If a person lives for a hundred years, understanding the dharma of arising and ceasing for a hundred times, it is not equal to living for a single day [understanding it once]."
He attained understanding and mastery of it. This bhikṣu then relied upon it and recited it. Later, he spoke of it to his original teacher.
The teacher said, "Ānanda is aged and decrepit; his wisdom has declined and his speech is full of errors. He is not to be trusted.
You should continue as before and merely recite the previous verse. Later, when Ānanda heard that the bhikṣu in the forest was still reciting the previous verse, he asked him for the reason.
He answered Ānanda with the words of his original teacher. When Ānanda had finished, he reflected to himself: "Does he slight me?
He then entered into *samādhi* and examined the eternal, holy virtue [of the Buddha], seeing that there was not another person capable of turning back the mind of that bhikṣu’s original teacher.
He then thought: "How strange! Impermanence is exceedingly fierce and powerful; false views are blazing and unobstructed."

[Their] growth [is hindered]. They slander the Tathāgata and sever their mindfulness of the True Dharma. Now, regarding this bhikṣu, although I have preached the Dharma for him, he has instead accepted perverse words.
The various sufferings of the world make it difficult to remain long; today, it is fitting that I should quickly enter parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, according to the *Aśoka-rāja-sūtra*, Ānanda first went to Śāṇakavāsin and informed him, saying: "The Buddha has entrusted the Dharma..."
He entrusted it to Kāśyapa. Kāśyapa entrusted it to me. Now that I am about to enter parinirvāṇa, I entrust it to you; you must guard and protect it.
Furthermore, fearing that after the time of Upagupta there would be no one for the White Dharma, he then addressed him, saying:

"In the past, when the World-Honored One traveled through the kingdom of Mathurā, he declared that within that country there was the son of a householder named Upagupta, who is the foremost among those in the dharma of dhyāna."
First: Although he lacks the primary and secondary marks of a Buddha, he can transform and deliver beings such as myself; thus, he may be entrusted with the Dharma-treasury. Upagupta spoke thus.
Furthermore, the *Dharmatrāta-dharmaparyāya-śāstra* (Fu fazang zhuan) states: When Ānanda was about to enter nirvāṇa, he thought to himself that King Ajātaśatru had a prior connection with him.
He then went to take his leave of the king. The gatekeeper said, "The king is currently asleep; I dare not disturb him. Ānanda—
He said, "If you wake up, report this to him: 'Ānanda has entered parinirvāṇa; he came specifically to bid the King farewell, but was not seen.
At that time, while the King was asleep, he dreamed that the handle of his parasol snapped, yet it did not fall. He then suddenly woke up and informed the gatekeeper of what had occurred.
Upon hearing this, the King fainted for a long while before regaining consciousness, whereupon he lamented: "The Tathāgata..."
After his entry into parinirvāṇa, the senior disciple Kāśyapa, who possessed great renown, succeeded him in the place of the Buddha;
yet he too entered parinirvāṇa, and the Dharma gradually declined. Next was Ānanda, who upheld the treasury of the Dharma and was venerated with reverence like the sun and the moon;
now he too has entered nirvāṇa—what more can we rely upon? Indeed, as the Dharma is nearing its end and all manner of evils flourish, he then asked:
The gatekeeper said, "Where is Ānanda now? The *Zonglun shu* (Commentary on the *Samayabhedoparacanacakra*) states:

At that time, a guardian deity of the kingdom addressed the king, saying, "Ānanda has already gone to the kingdom of Vaiśālī to enter parinirvāṇa. The king then prepared his carriage and the fourfold army and went to the banks of the Ganges.
There he saw Ānanda riding in a boat in the middle of the Ganges; the king prostrated himself and said, "O Bright Lamp of the Three Realms!"
"He has already abandoned me and departed. Now I rely upon you; do not enter nirvana. Even if you do enter nirvana, return to my kingdom.
At that time, a deva in the city of Vaiśālī further informed the king: "Ānanda is in the middle of the Ganges River and intends to enter nirvana.
The king again prepared his chariot and the fourfold army and went to the banks of the Ganges to once more entreat Ānanda to come to his kingdom.
He entered parinirvāṇa. The devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven further requested that he return to the palace of Śakra; he entered the city and passed away.

The Nāga King Sāgara further requested that he return to the nāga palace; he entered it and passed away. Since he had been invited from all four places, he could not favor one location over the others.
Consequently, he attained parinirvāṇa in the middle of the Ganges River. At that time, the great earth shook, and snow fell.
In the mountains, there were five hundred rishis. Upon witnessing these signs, they reflected to themselves:
"The Tathāgata appeared in the world, yet we remained attached to the flavor of dhyāna and did not seek liberation. When Kāśyapa entered parinirvāṇa, I was unaware;
now Ānanda is entering parinirvāṇa—if we do not further seek liberation, it will be impossible [to attain it]. Thereupon, they exhorted one another and requested ordination.

They were liberated. Thereupon, they all flew through the air at once and arrived at the place where Ānanda was. They earnestly entreated him with compassion to allow them to leave the household life. Ānanda silently consented.
He immediately transformed the waters of the Ganges into golden ground and preached the Dharma for the sages. According to the *Kriyāsaṃgraha* (付藏傳), it says: [as follows].
Ānanda preached the Dharma to them according to their needs, and their hair and beards fell off naturally as they became arhats;

it is not said that they received the precepts through him. According to the *Śātavāhana-rāja-sūtra*, Ānanda presided over the *karmavācanā* for their ordination: upon the *jñapti* (the motion), they attained the first fruit; upon the first *jñapti-caturtha* (the motion followed by one proclamation), they attained the second fruit;
upon the second *jñapti-caturtha*, they attained the third fruit; and at the time of the fourth *jñapti-caturtha*, they attained the fourth fruit. Having thus attained the fruits, they all...

Desiring to enter *nirvāṇa*, there was one last person named Madhyāntika. Ānanda alone did not permit him to enter *nirvāṇa*, but commanded him to uphold the treasury of the Dharma and go to the kingdom of Kaśmīra to propagate and transform beings. He replied accordingly.
Thereupon, Ānanda leaped into the void and performed the eighteen transformations; he entered the *vega-samādhi* and divided his body into four parts, giving one part to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
One portion was given to the devas; one portion to Sāgara, the Dragon King of the great ocean; one portion to King Viśālī; and one portion to King Ajātaśatru.
Stūpas were erected in each of these four locations for their veneration. (The second master’s account concludes here.)
The third was Madhyāntika (also known as Madhyantika or Kimila), who was the very last among the five hundred rishis mentioned previously;
he received the transmission of the Dharma from Ānanda. According to his biography, at that time Ānanda said to him:
"Formerly, when the Buddha traveled through the country of Uddiyāna and returned after subduing malevolent deities, [he stayed] by the dragon pond of that country."
The Master ascended and, looking back, said to me: "After my parinirvāṇa, Madhyāntika will establish a monastery by this pond and perform great deeds of the Buddha.
When Madhyāntika heard the Buddha’s prophetic declaration, his heart was filled with joy.
He then proceeded to the kingdom of Jibin (Kashmir), which is variously called Kaśmīra. When he first arrived in that country, there was no population at all;

there was only a great dragon lake. According to the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions), the circumference of this lake is over seven thousand *li*, and its four borders are backed by mountains that are extremely steep and precipitous.
When Madhyāntika reached that place, he went first to the summit of a great mountain to rest.

He sat down and performed a great supernatural manifestation, shaking the dragon pool. The Dragon King developed deep faith; he transformed himself into a human being with white hair and beard, his countenance compassionate.
The Venerable One also recognized him as a dragon and preached the Dharma for him. Subsequently, the Dragon King experienced the flavor of the Dharma.
Wishing to repay his kindness, he then asked Maudgalyāyana what he required. Maudgalyāyana replied, "I require only a place to dwell.
The Dragon King asked again, "I do not know exactly how much land you require for that dwelling. Maudgalyāyana said, "I only hope for the space of a single sitting mat (*kaṭhina*).
The Dragon King said, "More than that would be impossible; [this] one sitting mat’s worth of land, Ānanda, is sufficient."
"Venerable One, do you see this pond of mine? It is my dwelling place. At that time, the Dragon King, by means of his supernormal power of karma, contracted the waters of the pond for Madhyāntika.
As the Dragon King gradually withdrew the water, Madhyāntika gradually spread out his sitting mat.

In this way, he contracted the water for one thousand *li*, yet the sitting mat was not yet fully covered; he continued until seven thousand *li* had been contracted, until the water was entirely withdrawn and vanished.
Before the seating area was fully prepared, the dragon thought to himself, "I have truly promised another one *paryaṅka* (seating mat) of land; how could I go back on my word?
Thereupon, all the dragon subjects ascended onto the shore, and the Dragon King returned to Mṛttika to beg for the land. Mṛttika then... [granted it].
In the western corner, he left behind a small pond, one hundred *li* in circumference, and resided there.
The Nāga King further addressed the Venerable One, saying, "Although I have provisionally granted you this pond for now, it shall be reclaimed once the Dharma perishes.

At that time, Madhyāntika, having obtained the land, exercised his supernormal powers to construct five hundred monasteries. He purchased cooking pots from various foreign lands and provided them to the low-born.

The monastic emissaries followed these instructions and extensively propagated the teachings through such means as conversion and guidance. When the conditions for Maitreya’s (Madhyāntika) ministry were exhausted, he passed away in this country.
Since Śāṇakavāsin was still alive, the Dharma was not entrusted to him separately; rather, it was after the Venerable One had passed away [that the succession was finalized].
Many people of low caste established their own rulers; neighboring countries despised them for their low birth and would not engage in intercourse with them.

In Sanskrit they are called *kṛtaka*, which here means "placed" or "obtained," and is also called the "Country of the Low-born. During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, the Tripitaka Master went there.
Seeing that water is abundant while dry land is scarce, one knows that the teaching will soon decline. Question:
Previously, Ānanda first entrusted the Dharma to Upagupta and later to Madhyāntika; why is it now that Madhyāntika is placed before him? Answer:

According to the *Aśoka-rāja-sūtra*, Upagupta is in the third position and Madhyāntika occupies the fourth. In this case, for the sake of the circumstances, Upagupta’s transmission of the Dharma has been taken up [and placed first].
Because of Kuṭadanta, Madhyāntika is placed third. According to the records of their missionary activities, there was no chronological priority between them;
this is because Madhyāntika entered parinirvāṇa without separately transmitting the Dharma [to a successor]. (The account of the third master concludes above.)

The fourth is Śaṇavāsa (or Śaṇakavāsa). This is an abbreviation; if rendered in the correct Sanskrit as Śaṇakavāsa, it translates as "Cloth-of-Śaṇa" or "Fiber-Cloth. It refers to this Venerable One who, in the past, was once a merchant.

The *Saṃnipāta-sūtra* originally contained six schools; however, according to various biographical records, there are only five extant divisions.
Regarding the first, based on the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, the six schools are as follows: First, the Dharmaguptaka school. The sūtra states:

"After my parinirvāṇa, there will be disciples who receive, uphold, transcribe, read, and recite the Tathāgata’s twelvefold scriptures, yet they will misinterpret their meaning and preach the Dharma erroneously."
Because he taught in reverse order, he concealed the Dharma-treasury. His name was Dharmagupta, which means "Dharma-secrecy" (曇摩鞠多) or also "Dharma-store" (法藏).

Regarding the term "reverse order": it refers to the sequence of the transformative ritual; furthermore, he taught without following the standard order, always placing the stars before the sun. Moreover, when intending to speak of names, he did so in reverse. He established his name based on the Dharma, namely the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Second, regarding the Sarvāstivāda:
the Sūtra says, "Even if one recites, copies, or studies external texts, there are three types of recipients."
He refuted both internal and external [views], destroyed the non-Buddhists, and was highly skilled in debate. He taught that all natures (*sarvabhāva*) are capable of receiving the precepts;

whatever questions or challenges were posed, he was able to answer them all. For this reason, he is named Vātsīputra (the meaning of "Vātsī" being that one who holds that the three times possess substantial reality is called a Sarvāstivādin;
as for "all natures," it is because he allows that precepts can be received by those of good, evil, and neutral natures). His name was derived from his doctrine, namely the tenth...

This refers to the recitation of the Vinaya. Regarding the third, the Mahīśāsaka: the Sūtra says, "One does not construct the marks of earth, water, fire, or wind, nor the marks of space or consciousness;
therefore, it is called Mahīśāsaka. (Earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—these six elements are all empty; thus, one does not construct [marks of] earth, water, and so forth.

This refers to the contemplation of non-attachment to existence and non-existence. It is named after its Dharma, namely the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*. Regarding the fourth, the Kāśyapīya school: the Sūtra says... [it explains].
There is no self (*ātman*) nor any experiencer (*bhoktṛ*). One turns away from all afflictions (*kleśa*) as if they were a corpse;
therefore, he is named Kāśyapa, or alternatively Kāśyapīya. (This refers to the non-Buddhists who cling to the existence of a real self that experiences sensory objects, calling it the "experiencer.

This teacher now asserts that there is neither self nor sensory objects, thereby distinguishing his view from what people falsely grasp. "Turning away" means abandoning. Because one abandons the afflictions like a corpse, this is cited as an illustration. This is translated as the "contemplation of repeated emptiness," and so forth. From the Dharma...
The establishment of their name is precisely the *Vimokṣa-vāda* (School of Liberation). Regarding the *Pañca-sthavira-vāda* (Five Elders' School), the Sūtra states:

"They all teach that there is a self (*ātman*) and do not speak of the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*); they are like small children. For this reason, they are called *Bāhuśrutīya* (or *Vatsīputrīya*). They are also called *Vajjiputtaka*.

These masters maintain that the substantial entity (*dravya*) of all sentient beings is neither identical to nor different from the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and is neither annihilated nor eternal. If one were to say the aggregates and the self are identical, then when the aggregates perish, the self would also perish, thereby resulting in the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). If one were to say the aggregates and the self are different...

If the aggregates were to cease and the self remained, it would constitute the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). Therefore, one knows that this self and the phenomena of the five aggregates are neither identical nor different, neither annihilated nor eternal. Thus it is said: "In all cases, they speak of the existence of a self; they do not speak of the characteristic of emptiness.

As for the phrase "like a small child," this describes the appearance of ignorance. This refers to the *Vātsīputrīya* (literally "Calf"). In antiquity, there was a non-Buddhist who was born from a cow; the founder of this school was his descendant. Since the original Vinaya texts have not yet arrived, it is unknown what their specific doctrinal names are, and so forth.

The above concludes the five schools of the Staff-Branch (*daṇḍa-varga*). Regarding the sixth root school, the Mahāsāṃghika: the Sūtra says, "Extensive and comprehensive, they have mastered the five classes of scriptures."
The Scripture states: "For this reason, it is called the Mahāsāṃghika; this is translated as 'The Great Assembly' (the above is from the Scripture). Next, the exhortation for the compilation says:
'Good son, although these five schools differ, they do not obstruct the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas and the Great Nirvāṇa' (and so forth).

Question: The scriptural text lists six schools; for what reason does the exhortation for the compilation mention only five? Answer: As the *Shoushu* (Initial Commentary) states: 'General and specific.'"

There are six [schools]. The *Saṃghāṭī* (Mahāsāṃghika) is the general [school], for it leads the multitude of monastics so that their practice and understanding may be vast and unobstructed, preventing the arising of biased attachments.

Because it universally illuminates the five views through its universal application, it is clearly known that the preceding five are the specific [schools], each of which refutes divergent views and flows forth from that [general school].
If the *Saṃghāṭī* were the fundamental school and everyone would have accepted and believed it, yet the latter five are the specific schools, one fears that people might not believe them.
Therefore, I specifically encourage [the study] of this. Thus, in the separate preface below, the *Chao* (the *Shishi yaolan*) provides its own commentary, stating:
"The *Mahāsāṃghika* is the root; the others are the five branches. This is precisely based on the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*. Furthermore, it is asked:

"Since the *Mahāsāṃghika* is the root, why are there currently so many fascicles, yet [this version] consists of only forty fascicles? The answer is: "The five masters collected texts according to their own perspectives and biases, each..."
It constitutes a single vision. Because other external phenomena and dharmas are gathered together in one place and are not numerous, it consists of only forty fascicles.
Nevertheless, as this is the fundamental [text], it is like a tree from which five branches extend;

although the trunk itself may be small, it is still called the "body," while the four sides, even if large, are merely termed "branches. Furthermore, these forty fascicles of the *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya] have no other refuge to which they should return.

Introduction. It is established that this [text] is the fundamental [Vinaya]. Furthermore, the Commentator (Chaozhu) explains: "The Mahāsāṃghika is the fundamental [tradition], transmitted by the Great Assembly;
it was not produced by the five schools over the course of a hundred years. This is the correct interpretation.

Alternatively, to rely on narrow claims and assert that these forty fascicles of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* belong to the Mahāsāṃghika school of Mahādeva is incorrect. A detailed refutation of this is found elsewhere (*yún yún*). Next, according to the *Buddha-mūla-...*.
[This concerns] the *Caryā-saṃgha* and the *Mahāsāṃghika*. A private note by the later translator states that there were only five schools. It says:
"One hundred years after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, following the fifth patriarch Kukkuta, five [teachers] simultaneously arose within the Sthavira school and established five distinct sects.
Four of these are as previously described; the fifth, the Bāhuśrutīya, is the *Mahīśāsaka* Vinaya."
"How are they divided now? The answer is: "I do not dare to divide them arbitrarily. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* clarifies their differences.

If one were to follow the current *Bao cu jing*, one should not say that [the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*] surveys all five divisions. (The above is from the commentary; for now, we rely solely on the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* to establish the correct principle. Even today there are those who hold erroneous views, likely because they have failed to investigate the source.
The division into five sections is hereby concluded.
Next, regarding the clarification of the division into two schools: these are the Mahāsāṃghika and the Sthavira. Question:
When discussing the schisms of the schools, it would logically follow from the fewest to the most; why now proceed from the many back to the few? Answer:

Although the previous division into five schools appears numerous, they were still in accord with the principles of the sages and remained within the single tradition of the Sthaviras. Now, however, we are contrasting them against the ordinary followers of Mahādeva.

Regarding the three divisions of the Dharma-vastu, there were two [schools] due to differences in time periods. If previously there were only five sections, they were not yet designated by the name "Sthavira" (Elder).
It was only upon reaching the period of the two schools that the Sthavira school first emerged. Question:
By what causes and conditions did it split into these two schools? Answer: It was due to Mahādeva—translated here as "Great God"—who, before he had left the household life, committed [the following]:

Regarding the third [category of] transgressions: after he had already left the household life, he further created five conditions that resulted in such contradictions; therefore, it is divided into two parts.
Now, based on the *Commentary on the Saṃmitīya-nikāya-śāstra* (*Zonglun lun shu*), I shall briefly describe the origin of these events.
Formerly, in the kingdom of Mathurā, there was a merchant leader who took a young wife and fathered a son of handsome and upright countenance, named Mahādeva. Not long after, his father...
He took a vast amount of wealth and traveled to other countries; however, due to obstructing circumstances, he did not return for a long time.
Consequently, Mahādeva gradually grew up and became intimate with his mother. Later, when he heard that his father was returning, he became terrified and devised a plan together with his mother.
He then killed his father. Having committed this one *ānantarya* crime, the matter gradually became public knowledge;
he lived in constant anxiety and, taking his mother with him, fled from place to place until they reached the city of Pāṭaliputra.

Upon arriving there, he suddenly encountered the very same *aśaikṣa* bhikṣu whom he had previously supported. Fearing that his crimes would be exposed, he devised a scheme to kill that *aśaikṣa*. Having committed...

After committing the second immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*), he was overcome with grief and fear. Later, seeing his mother in an illicit liaison with another man, he gave rise to anger and resentment, saying:
"It is for this reason that I have committed two grave offenses; I shall migrate to another country, wandering restlessly and ill at ease."
"Now once again I have committed such a foul and impure act together with another; how can I possibly endure it? Thereupon, employing a skillful means, he killed his mother once more.
Having thus committed the third *ānantarya* karma, because he had not severed his roots of goodness, he was deeply filled with remorse.
He then reflected to himself: "By what means can I extinguish this sin? I have heard that the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, possess a method for extinguishing sins.
He then went to the Kukkuṭārāma monastery and saw a bhikṣu outside its gate walking slowly in meditation.
He recited a verse, saying: "If one commits a grave offense, yet cultivates goodness to extinguish it, that person can illuminate the world, like the sun rising over the veil of snow.
When Mahādeva heard this, he was filled with joy and exultation; knowing that by taking refuge in the Buddha's teaching his sins would surely be extinguished, he went to a certain bhikṣu.
Originally an outsider monk, he sought ordination under him without undergoing any formal examination.

He was subsequently ordained. After receiving the precepts, he retained his name Mahādeva. Before long, being intelligent and wise, he was able to recite and uphold both the texts and meanings of the Tripiṭaka.
His speech was clear and refined, and he was skilled at preaching the Dharma; there was no one in the city of Pāṭaliputra who did not look up to him in reverence.
When King Aśoka heard of this, he repeatedly invited him into the palace to provide offerings and requested that he preach the Dharma. Thereupon, [Mahādeva] deceived him...
The King said, "I am an Arhat. Having entered the royal palace, he frequently saw the ladies-in-waiting;

at night, upon leaving the monastery, he experienced a nocturnal emission of impurity and had his disciple wash the soiled garment. The disciple said, "I have heard that for an Arhat, all outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted.
Why, then, does my teacher still experience such a thing? Mahādeva replied, "This was the work of a celestial Māra; it was not something I did intentionally. You..."
One should not find this strange. Thus, there are briefly two kinds of leakage (*āsrava*): first, the leakage of afflictions (*kleśa-āsrava*);
second, the leakage of impurities (*aśuci-āsrava*). If it is the leakage of afflictions, Arhats have already eliminated it; if it is the leakage of impurities, Arhats still possess it.
For example, during the Buddha’s lifetime, although the Arhats had exhausted their afflictions, did they not still have excrement, urine, mucus, and saliva?
Furthermore, various devas and māras constantly give rise to hatred and envy toward the Buddha-dharma; upon seeing those who cultivate goodness, they immediately seek to destroy them.
Even Arhats are disturbed by them. Question: What fault is there in such a statement? Answer: There are truly two kinds of outflows (*āsrava*).
If they are the outflows of afflictions (*kleśa*), these consist of the five categories of lower afflictions, such as craving and so forth. Not...
The leakage of impurity is like passing excrement. Now, Mahādeva dreamed of discharging impurity; this was clearly a manifestation of his afflictions (*kleśa*).
His disciple intended to ask about this, but instead received an answer concerning the leakage of impurity. This constitutes a deceptive delusion (concluding the first instance of false speech).
Furthermore, that Mahādeva, wishing to have his disciple joyfully approach him, devised a crafty stratagem and sequentially bestowed upon him the four [revelations].
Regarding the fruits of the śramaṇa, at a later time his disciples, having examined the various holy teachings, said:
"An arhat should know [these things] for himself; why is it that we do not know them at all? Mahādeva told them: "Indeed, even those of great stature may have ignorance;
you should not find this strange. Now, there are briefly two kinds of ignorance: first, afflicted ignorance; second, non-afflicted ignorance."
[The interlocutor] says: "I understand. If it is defiled ignorance (*kliṣṭājñāna*), the Arhat does not possess it; however, if it is impure defiled ignorance, the Arhat still possesses it.

Therefore, you yourselves have not realized this through personal knowledge. [The opponent] asks: "What fault is there in saying this? [The respondent] answers: "In that case, [you would be admitting that] there is ignorance [even in an Arhat]."
There are two kinds of ignorance (*ajñāna*). Ignorance that is defiled (*kliṣṭa*) refers to the lack of affliction regarding the Four Noble Truths.
Ignorance that is impure and defiled has inferior wisdom (*hīnaprajñā*) as its essence; according to principle, it exists in all beings prior to the attainment of Buddhahood.
However, what your disciple has now asked concerns precisely defiled ignorance, yet you have answered by referring instead to impure ignorance. This is called deception.
(Concluding the second causal connection). Later, a disciple harbored doubts regarding the Four Noble Truths and addressed his teacher, saying:

"I have heard that Arhats have already severed their afflictions (*kleśa*) and that doubt, arising from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), is eliminated upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

How is it, then, that we still harbor such profound doubts concerning the Four Noble Truths? Mahādeva replied: "There are two kinds of doubt: first, latent doubt (*anuśaya-saṃśaya*); second, [doubt regarding] the focal point (*sthāna-...*)."
Doubt. If it is latent doubt (*anuśaya*), it does not exist in an Arhat; if it is doubt regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*), it exists in an Arhat.

Question: What fault is there in saying this? Answer: Indeed, doubt is truly of two kinds. If, among the Four Truths, one does not clearly understand suffering, its origin, and so forth, that is latent doubt.
To speak in a way that does not accord with reality is called "impossible" (*asthāna*); to speak in accordance with reality is called "possible" (*sthāna*). Regarding this...
"Doubt regarding two points is called 'uncertainty. Now, my intention as a disciple was to inquire specifically about the latent tendency of doubt;
yet you have instead answered by addressing doubt concerning what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*). This constitutes deception. (This concludes the third condition.
Later, when the disciples read the sacred teachings, they said: "The Arhat should realize this for himself; we, however, rely merely on the words of our teacher and do not possess self-awareness."
He attained awakening. Mahādeva told him: "Indeed, there are Arhats who also attain awakening through others and do not realize it for themselves.

Do you not see what is said in the sūtras regarding Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others—that if the Buddha had not bestowed upon them the prediction that they would become Buddhas in the future, [they would not have known it]?"
He himself did not know it at that time; it was only after the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) that he came to know it for himself.

You should not now interrogate him on this matter by asking what fault there is in his statement. [The Buddha] replied: "When the disciple asked precisely about the untainted noble dharmas (*anāsrava-āryadharma*), he was entirely unaware of them himself.

Now, instead, you have answered by citing the capacities, practices, and realizations belonging to another person's body. This constitutes deception and falsehood" (this concludes the fourth ground for false speech).
However, although that Mahādeva had committed various evils, he had not yet severed his roots of goodness. During the middle watch of the night, he suddenly reflected:
"Before I left the household life, I committed three of the heinous crimes (*ānantarya*). The original purpose of receiving the Buddha-dharma was to eliminate such transgressions;

yet now, after having gone forth, I have again created false conditions, violating the net of the teachings. I do not know where I shall receive retribution after death. Thus he was filled with anxiety.
Overwhelmed by terror, he repeatedly cried out, "Alas, what suffering! At that time, a close disciple heard him and was deeply shocked;
rising early to pay his respects, he asked, "Master, were you at peace last night? Mahādeva replied, "I was very well. The disciple said to the Master:
"Why did you repeatedly cry out 'Suffering' last night? Mahādeva replied, "I was calling for the Noble Path;

you should not find this strange. It refers to the Noble Truth of Suffering. If one does not earnestly invoke it, it will never arise, just as a child will not be taken into his mother's arms unless he cries.
He asked, "What fault is there in saying this? He answered, "Generally speaking, to speak of realizing the Noble Truths, one must practice them oneself."

One maintains the precepts and cultivates wisdom, enters into the stage of application (*prayoga*), and gradually contemplates the principles of the truths (*satya*). It is only upon realizing cessation (*nirodha*)—after having abandoned the afflictions to be eliminated through seeing and cultivation—that one truly perceives the truths.
Now, this Mahādeva is fully possessed of afflictions and has not yet severed them at all; how can he be called "suffering"?
Thereupon, the Noble Path arose within him; thus he committed a falsehood (this constitutes the fifth instance of lying). Later, Mahādeva, having formed this habitual view, composed a verse, saying:
"Led astray by others and lacking wisdom, He was made to enter the Noble Path through the hesitation of another.
No false voice was uttered; This is the Tathāgata’s true and pure teaching. (The phrasing differs slightly, but the meaning is no different. [This occurred] at the Kukkutārāma Monastery. Above...
Most of the bhikṣus seated there had already attained parinirvāṇa. During the fortnightly recitation of the Prātimokṣa, it was next the turn of Mahādeva.
He then took the verses he himself had composed and inserted them after the section on the seven methods for settling disputes.

At that time, those among the assembly who were beyond training (aśaikṣa), possessed of great learning, and practiced meditative concentration, heard these verses and were all struck with astonishment and alarm. They immediately rebuked him, saying: "Alas, you foolish man! How could you speak such words? This...
Regarding the Tripiṭaka, he had never heard such a thing before. He either confronted him directly or translated that verse back, saying:

"The first three lines are as above... (and so forth). At the end of the section, it said: "These words are not the Buddha's teaching. Thereupon, they engaged in a tumultuous dispute throughout the entire night.

By the end of the morning, their faction had grown increasingly powerful. Upon hearing this, the King himself also became suspicious and immediately addressed Mahādeva, asking, "Regarding this matter of right and wrong, which side should I now rely upon?
Mahādeva told the King, "The teachings contain a clear text: if one wishes to terminate a dispute, one must follow the 'majority vote' (*yadbhūyasikīya*).

[This is a misapplication of the Vinaya text; for in that text, there are three ways of casting ballots. If the Upādhyāya or elders are among the side acting according to the Dharma, they cast their ballots openly. If the Upādhyāya..."* (text continues).

Venerable elder, while you were among those who follow what is not the Dharma, you acted by whispering. Now that those who follow what is not the Dharma are numerous, it is necessary to initiate a formal procedure for causing a schism. Since there are now many who follow what is not the Dharma, we should proceed to cause a schism. Therefore, I shall now have voting sticks distributed according to the majority decision.
Was this not because they used the Vinaya in a perverse manner? At that time, King Aśoka ordered the two factions of the Saṃgha to live separately and cast voting sticks (*śalākā*).

Thus, within the faction of the Noble Assembly (*āryasaṃgha*), although there were many elders, the number of monks was somewhat small; whereas within the faction of Mahādeva, although there were few elders, the number of people was still greater.
Since the voting sticks representing the illegal position were numerous, the King followed the majority and, relying on Mahādeva’s words, rebuked and subdued the rest of the assembly.
When the task was completed, they returned to the palace. At that time, the disputes at the Kukkuṭārāma had not yet subsided;

subsequently, following divergent views, the community split into two schools: first, the Sthaviras (the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states these were the five hundred who held the council within the cave; they took the name of their leader, the Sthavira Kāśyapa, to designate their school); second, the Mahāsāṃghikas (this refers to the followers of Mahādeva, whose original teacher was a monk outside the cave;

his descendants gathered for a council in the Great Forest where both ordinary and noble ones assembled together, hence the name "Great Assembly"; here, the names of these three [sub-sects] are taken). Although the community was divided into two schools at that time, it was also...
Furthermore, while they were together at Kukkuṭārāma, the assembly of noble ones wished to leave Kukkuṭārāma and travel to another country.
When King Aśoka heard this, he became enraged; he placed them on a broken barge and set out for the Gaṅgā River, intending to drown the assembly of noble ones.
The assembly of noble ones learned of this in secret and immediately informed one another. "This is a peril to our lives; we must each employ our supernatural powers.

Those who had not yet attained such powers were also enabled to act with mastery, just like a king of geese soaring through the air toward the western lands. They proceeded until they reached the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
He dwelt in the mountains and hid in the valleys. When the king heard of this, he felt deep remorse and sent messengers to summon him, ordering him to return to his own country.
However, the assembly of holy ones did not comply with his command. Later, in that kingdom, he extensively constructed five hundred monasteries and made various kinds of offerings.
By the king’s decree, the *Mahādeva-piṇḍada-sūtra* was no longer as it had been originally, yet it did not depart from Kukkutārāma. As for that Mahādeva...
Later, he encountered a physiognomist who said, "This son of the Śākyas will surely meet his end in seven days. The disciple informed the Master, who replied, "I know my own lot.

He then ordered that the news be proclaimed throughout the realm to the king and his ministers. After seven days had passed, he entered parinirvāṇa. Those who heard this were filled with grief and longing.
Beyond the seven days, his life indeed came to an end. The commoners and officials prepared fragrant oil and firewood in abundance.
They wished to cremate [the remains] together as an offering, but as soon as the fire was applied, it would go out as soon as it reached them.
Furthermore, they encountered someone who possessed these same signs, who said to the people: "This is not fit to consume such things as fragrant oils;
you should use filth and excrement to cover it. They followed his words, and at that time, the blazing flames were completely extinguished. A violent wind immediately arose, scattering [the ashes].

There is nothing further. The reasons for the division of the schools are now set forth. The two schools of India remain both flourishing to this day. (The preceding section explaining the division into two schools is hereby concluded.)

Regarding the division into twenty schools in the third period: this refers to the further subdivision of the aforementioned two major schools. Within the Mahāsāṃghika school, nine branches were formed;

within the Sthavira school, eleven branches were formed. Furthermore, among these twenty, each contains the names of five sub-sects, though these may vary due to partial attachments and other factors.
Now, wishing to categorize them, I first compose a verse: "One hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa..."

The remainder (the *Zhenbu* states it was one hundred and ten years). The two original schools split (namely, the Sthavira and Mahāsāṃghika schools). Four hundred years elapsed before they received the scriptures.

The division into twenty schools is concluded (The Mahāsāṃghika for two hundred years; the Sthavira for three hundred years; the first schism occurred at four hundred years; all twenty schools are now complete).

Among these, first is the Mahāsāṃghika (the first division among the two major sects). Four schisms led to the formation of eight (the Mahāsāṃghika underwent four successive divisions, resulting in eight branches).

Three schools each arose at the beginning and at the end (the first [schism] constitutes the beginning, and the fourth [schism] constitutes the end; thus, at both the beginning and the end, three schools each were separately established). The second and third [schisms] each resulted in only one.

(The second and third times [are mentioned] because in each case only one branch was separated). The primary school became nine (meaning the fundamental Mahāsāṃghika school together with its eight branches, totaling nine).

The division occurred at the end of the two hundredth year (meaning the end of the second century and the beginning of the third). During the period of the Sthaviras, there were seven divisions (seven successive divisions of the preceding and following schools).

From the fourth and third divisions (meaning four schools were simultaneously and suddenly separated from within the third, Vātsīputrīya school). The remaining single schools are five or six sects (excluding the aforementioned...).

The three Vatsīputrīya schools were divided all at once into four sections; outside of these, there were six further divisions occurring sequentially, with only one new school emerging from each successive division—hence the term "remaining single" (the rest being independent).

Including the root and the branches, this totals eleven schools (the Sthavira school is the root; the others are its branches, termed "ends"; thus, there are eleven in total, as explained below). Once the initial schisms had occurred, each school specialized in its own region.
(The above concludes the brief citation of the verse text. Furthermore, the *Zonglun shu* states: "According to tradition, one hundred years after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Bhagavat..."

In the subsequent years (as Paramārtha says, this refers to the period one hundred thousand years later), the time since the Sage had departed was as long as days; he had been submerged for ages (this is said because while the Buddha was present, he was like the blazing sun whose light illumined no dark corner;
once he had entered Parinirvāṇa, he was like the sun hidden behind the western mountains). In the kingdom of Magadha, at the city of Kusumapura, there was a king named Aśoka.

Hardly had he taken control of the region when he received a white parasol, through which he unified both humans and spirits (there are also versions where "化" is written as "治"). At that time, the Buddha-dharma...
The first schism among the Great Assembly occurred during the hundred years following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, under a king named Aśoka.

Possessing the power of an iron wheel—though no actual wheel appeared—he was moved by a single white parasol that remained constantly suspended in the sky, manifesting the virtue of his governance and transformation.
At this time, regarding the first division, it was asked: "For what reason did the Mahāsāṃghika split first? Master Ki replied:
"Within the Mahāsāṃghika, ordinary people are many and noble ones are few; within the Sthavira, ordinary people are few and noble ones are many.

For this reason, between the two, the Mahāsāṃghika was the first to break away. The treatise states: "By the beginning of the second century, the Mahāsāṃghika first split, flowing out into three [schools]."
1. The Sautrāntika school (This school’s master asserts that all phenomena lack substantial reality and exist only as provisional designations. "Name" here refers to the teaching itself;

nor does he distinguish between contaminated and other phenomena, as all lack substantial reality and possess only the provisional designations that express them. Within these expressions, there is no duality of signifier and signified; since substantial reality contradicts what is inherently existent, one forgets these names). 2.

The Lokottaravāda school (The master of this school asserts that mundane, contaminated phenomena all arise from inversion and, being unreal, exist only as provisional designations. However, supramundane phenomena do not arise from inversion and thus possess substantial reality; hence it is called the Lokottaravāda school). 3. The Kaurukullaka school.
