Commentary: The three methods of explanation are subsumed within the six modes of interpretation (*ṣaḍvyākhyāna*). Regarding the initial section, which provides a detailed analysis of the general and the specific:

the two characters "four parts" (*sifen*) are the specific, being the name of one among the five divisions. The single character "vinaya" (*lü*) is the general, being the collective title for all five divisions.
Neither of these two names may be omitted; for if the specific name were absent, it would be difficult to manifest its universal application. Thus begins the opening.

The character "four" (四) is placed first to indicate the *Dharmaguptaka* school. Opening the scroll and recognizing the core tenet, one immediately knows this to be the Vinaya of the *Dharmaguptaka* tradition, and not other systems such as the *Mahīśāsaka* (*Wufen*) or the *Sarvāstivāda* (*Shisong*).
If the general designation of "Vinaya" were omitted, there would be no means to encompass its specific names; therefore, the character for "Vinaya" (律) is placed last.

If abbreviated as simply "Four Parts" (四分), the name "Four Parts" is applied flexibly and indifferently to refer to the *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*, as well as to various sutras, śāstras, records, and biographies.

In these cases, the character "Vinaya" (律) is marked below to distinguish it from others. Furthermore, if one were to follow the chronological order of their appearance, the Vinaya ought to come first;
yet, while the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) existed during the Buddha’s lifetime, it was only a century later that the [Mūlasarvāstivāda] Vinaya arose, which logically should follow it.

Now, the four parts (*caturvarga*) are placed first, solely to distinguish them from other schools (the preceding general and specific analysis is thus concluded). Second, the detailed analysis is divided into two sections:
first, an explanation of the two characters *sifen* (four parts); second, an explanation of the single character *lü* (vinaya). Regarding the first, as for "four parts":
In Sanskrit, it is called *Caturvargika* (or *Caiturdiśika*). This translates as "four" (*catur*), meaning the number four;
and "division" (*varga*), meaning a section or a cause. Because the master of this school divided the great treasury of the *Vinaya* into four sections, it is called the *Caturvargika*.
Specifically, the twenty fascicles of the *Mahābhikṣu-prātimokṣa-sūtra* constitute the first division, while the fifteen fascicles of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* constitute the [subsequent] divisions.
The second part consists of fourteen fascicles on the *Varṣā* (Rainy Season Retreat).
The third part consists of eleven fascicles on *Vihāra* (Dwellings). Regarding the origin of these titles for the four parts, there are two interpretations.

First, the correct explanation; second, the refutation of errors. Regarding the correct explanation: it begins with the distant record from the golden mouth of the Tathāgata, followed by the proximate division of schools by the masters of the sections.
As for the distant record from the golden mouth of the Tathāgata, according to the "Śrāvaka Chapter" of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, the Buddha told Kauṇḍinya:
"After my parinirvāṇa, there will be disciples who receive and uphold the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s scriptures."

They will copy, read, and recite [the scriptures], yet they will misunderstand their meaning and preach them erroneously. Because they preach erroneously, they will conceal and obscure the treasury of the Dharma;
this is called Dharmagupta (as stated in the sutra). This is the Buddha’s prediction made during his lifetime that, after his passing, this Vinaya would necessarily come into existence.
It circulated throughout the world. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa convened the council, and the five holy ones upheld it, passing it down like water being poured from one vessel to another.

At the end of the first century, on the day the fifth master, Kuṭadanta, transmitted the Dharma, it coincided with King Aśoka’s reign over the world and a great assembly where they deliberated upon the Buddha-dharma;
due to disagreements, the Vinaya of the Great Canon was subsequently divided into five treatises. Among them—
There is one school named Dharmaguptaka. Recalling the words of the Tathāgata’s distant prophecy, they uphold the designation of the "Four Divisions" (Caturvarga).

The founder of this school himself said: "If one wishes to speak of non-existence, one must first speak of existence; if one wishes to discuss existence, to speak of it first is a perverted interpretation of the meaning.
Furthermore, my name is Dharmaguptaka; since our names are identical, the doctrine I uphold should be clearly elucidated."
"Four Parts. Thus, he transmitted the text four times, exhausting all the characteristics explained therein;

he recalled the text in four sections, corresponding to that teaching of the "Four Parts" (the above briefly presents the correct interpretation). Next, regarding the refutation: according to the *Nanhai Jiguī Neifǎ Zhuan*, the Tripiṭaka Master Yìjìng stated as follows:
"The name 'Four Parts' was established based on the Sanskrit manuscript. That is to say, the Sanskrit manuscript..."
4. Each fascicle was divided into one part; four fascicles were thus divided into four parts. He then raised an objection to the previous explanation, saying:
"If you claim that the name was established based on recitation, that principle is not correct. For instance, when Mahākaśyapa, the Great Arhat, first presided over the compilation [of the canon]..."

Furthermore, there were eighty scrolls; it was impossible to recite them all from beginning to end while seated upon the platform. The Dharmaguptaka school transmitted the text in four parts, and by the time they had finished reciting the Vinaya-piṭaka, [the tradition] was established.

Now, relying on the *Fazheng ji* (Record of the Rectification of the Dharma), it is refuted as follows: "Even if the Sanskrit manuscript consisted of four fascicles, each fascicle was translated as one 'part' (*bhāga*), thereby resulting in the name 'Four-Part' (*Caturvarga*).
If this were the case, the designation 'Four-Part' would have no basis in the original source; its origin must be sought here in our own land, though this remains uncertain."
During the first millennium of the Western Regions, by what title was it designated?

As for the subsequent "Seizing and Destroying," it refers to this Vinaya text, which originally had no Indian manuscript (Sanskrit folios). When this period arrived, the Tripiṭaka Master Jue-ming orally recited the text from memory.
Fearing that the recited text might be erroneous or corrupted, the Qin ruler then verified it against more than fifty thousand words from the Qiang script and the *Yao* [script].
The daily recitation was completed. He held the text and covered it over, not omitting a single character. Only when the Ruler of Qin showed deep faith did he grant permission for the translation.

Initially, when the Sanskrit manuscript first arrived in this land, why did the commentary state that the title was established based on the manuscript? (Regarding the previous mention of "relying on the register": the Ruler of Qin, Yao Chang, was originally a Xiongnu from the West.

Having led his army to surrender to Fu Jian, he was appointed General Longxi; later, he made Chang’an his capital and founded Later Qin. As most of his followers were Qiang people, it is called a "register" [ji]. Medical prescriptions are easily understood, etc.). That...
Shi Nan said: "If Upāli could still recite it eighty times, how could Dharmagupta have finished reciting it only four times?

At the time of the first council, the texts and phrases were scattered; therefore, it was difficult to reach eighty recitations. By the time of the schism, the upper sections had already been codified in writing, making it easy;
thus, he recited it only four times. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Vinaya of the country of Mathurā..."
There were eighty sections (*aṣṭaka-bhāga*). The *Kashmir Vinaya* was condensed by taking only its essential parts to form ten sections.

As for what is called "eighty sections," that [text] itself explains it as "eighty recitations" (*aśīti-saṃgīti*). The "ten sections" refers to the *Daśabhāṇavāra*. The same applies to the *Pañcavargika*.

By citing this as evidence, we know that the names were established based on the number of fascicles; thus, the entire title is fully formed. (The two characters for *Sifen*, or "Four Parts," are concluded above.)

Next, the explanation of the single character "lü" (律) is divided into two parts: first, the translation of the name; second, the explanation of its meaning. Regarding the translation of the name, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:
"Based on the subject and the object, there are three names in total. First, the Sanskrit term *vinaya*, *vinya*, or *vinika*, all of which are translated as 'lü' (vinaya).
This refers to the teaching that expresses [the precepts]. Second, the Sanskrit term *śīla*, which is translated here as 'jie' (戒, śīla), meaning..."
That which is explained is practice (*caryā*). Third, the Sanskrit term *pratimokṣa* translates here as "individual liberation" (*bie jie tuo*).

This is the fruit realized. Because practice arises based on the teaching, such practice is not in vain; it must necessarily realize its fruit. Therefore, liberation from bondage stands at the very end [of the process].

In the *Jie shu* (Commentary on the Precepts), it further asks: "Since there are three names, why was 'the scale of the Vinaya' (*lü cheng*) designated first? The answer is that the *Vinaya* is based upon...
The teaching is able to give rise to practice and understanding; because the five aggregates rely upon this to uphold its virtues, it is called the "cause of precepts" (*śīla-hetu*).

Precepts sever and prune karma, and because they may lead to the cessation [of suffering], they are called "liberation" (*vimukti*). Thus, these two aspects of the fruit both arise from the teaching; therefore, the function of the teaching is first cited to encompass these two.
Alternatively, all three may be a single transformation, as it is not necessary to require them all at once from beginning to end; hence, they are fully designated.

Regarding the *Vinaya*, it is now called the *Four-Part Vinaya* (*Caturvargika-vinaya*), rather than the *Four-Part Precepts of Liberation*. Question: Is the translation of *vinaya* as "law" (*lü*) a literal translation of the term or a translation of its meaning?

Answer: It is a translation of the meaning, not a literal transliteration. Therefore, according to the tradition passed down by various schools, when the Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty translated the scriptures, there were instances where he translated the term and instances where he did not.
Furthermore, there are five reasons for not translating it: first, because it gives rise to wholesome states.
There are cases where [Sanskrit terms] are not translated. For example, *buddha* is rendered as "Awakened" (*jue*), and *bodhisattva* is rendered as "Sentient Being of the Path" (*daoyouqing*).

In such instances, the Sanskrit names are retained with the intention of generating wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*) in the practitioner. Second, there are cases of "secret non-translation," such as *dhāraṇī* and other teachings on total retention (*saṃgraha*).

If one recites and invokes these according to their Sanskrit sounds, they possess a subtle power of efficacy; however, if they were translated into the vernacular of this land, that power would be entirely lost.
Because it lacks spiritual efficacy, and because it contains multiple meanings, it is not translated [into Chinese].

For example, *Bhagavat* contains six meanings in a single name: first, sovereignty (because he is not permanently bound by the two kinds of birth-and-death); second, brilliance (the fierce flames of the fire of wisdom burn the fuel of afflictions); third, majesty (adorned with the perfection of the primary and secondary marks);

fourth, renown (possessing great fame that pervades the ten directions); fifth, auspiciousness (constantly bringing benefit and fortune at all times); sixth, glory... [as in the case of the two dragon-kings of water]... seven.

1) Lotus-born (as in the case of the Buddha’s footprints producing lotuses). 2) Noble (because they are honored by those who have transcended the world). If one were now to translate any one of these, the remaining five would be lost; therefore, their Sanskrit names are retained.

4) Following ancient precedent, some are not translated, such as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment), which has remained untranslated from the Han through the Tang dynasties.
5) Not translated for lack of equivalent, such as the story of the shadow of the Jambū tree penetrating the moon and conceiving children as large as eight-pitcher jars; [this is] here...

Since they do not exist [in the source language], they cannot be translated. Apart from these exceptions, all others have been translated. Within the category of translations, there are again two types:

first, literal translation (zhèngfān); second, semantic translation (yìfān). This is because in both the Eastern and Western lands, there are instances where the abbreviated forms of names or terms differ.
One should thus use these terms to translate those Sanskrit words. For example, the Sanskrit word *mṛdālika* is translated here as "white lotus.
Similarly, the Sanskrit word *cakṣu* is translated as "eye," and so forth; these are all termed "correct translations" (*zhèngfān*).
If there is an object that exists in the Western land [India] but is entirely absent from this land [China], yet there is a certain class of objects that slightly resembles that object, then—

This method involves using one term to translate the meaning of another. For example, the Sanskrit word *nyagrodha* refers to a tree in the Western lands that is exceptionally large, capable of shading five hundred chariots, and whose seeds are like one-quarter the size of a sesame seed.

Although this tree does not exist here [in China], the willow tree somewhat resembles it in its growth habit; therefore, "willow" is used as a translation for it. Furthermore, the term *tricīvara* (three robes) is translated as "bedding."
The various [terms] such as "equipped" and so forth are all like this (as detailed above). Now, this *vinaya* is translated from that *vinaya*. This is a translation based on meaning (*arthānuvāda*).

Since the Buddha appeared and arose in the Western Land and preached this *vinaya* scripture, and since this region originally lacked the Buddha’s transformation of the world, there was no direct translation.

Subsequently, when that Buddha preached the *vinaya*, it expounded the five groups of offenses (*pañcāpatti-skandha*) to restrain the five assemblies (*pañca-saṃgha*), not permitting any transgression.
In this land, the five types of physical forms are conventionally designated by these names; they are also used to govern the myriad people so that no transgressions arise.

Since their meanings are similar and their functions in preventing wrongdoing are the same, the names for the Vinaya of that [Indian] land have been translated using the terminology of this land’s legal codes.

Although there have been many such translations in antiquity, I refrain from recording them here for fear of being too prolix. (The section on translating the names is concluded. Next, regarding the explanation of the meaning, it is divided into three parts: first, *vinaya* (律); second, *śīla* (戒).

The three expositions clarify the meaning of *vinaya*. As explained in the following text, *vinaya* means "dharma. It refers to the dharma that defines and weighs the gravity of offenses and non-offenses;

all such matters are elucidated by the *vinaya*, which is thus its definitive exposition. Furthermore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "*Vinaya* means 'dharma. It derives its name from the teachings.

It distinguishes between the light and the heavy, and determines what is permitted or prohibited, and what constitutes observance or violation. Since it is not a dharma that is indeterminate, there are nine supplementary [categories] in common usage."
The Dharma constitutes one of these [categories]. Therefore, worldly legal systems regarding the transmission of the Dharma all categorize matters based on physical form.
The Way differs from the secular; thus, their names and designations are distinct. Yet, when it comes to adjudication, both rely upon the established laws (the above is from the commentary).

This means that while the dwellings of the clergy and the laity, as well as the appearance of their penal codes, are each different, those among the clergy who commit offenses must have their cases adjudicated according to the established laws of physical form. Furthermore, as for the *vinaya*...

This is the character for "pen" (bi). This character for "law" (lü) has the radical *zhí* (walking) with *yù* attached to it. *Yù* takes its sound from "pen," and it is also explained as meaning "pen.
Thus, the original form was created by Meng Tian of Qin. In the *Shuowen*, it is used in the sense of "writing. During the Chu period it was called *yù*; during the Wu period it was called *lǜ*;
during the Yan period it was called *fú*; and during the Qin period it was called *bǐ*. Now, "law" (*lǜ*) interferes with its original meaning.

The term "bi" (筆) carries the meaning of taking, cutting, and measuring. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states that it refers to the act of "judging" (*chu*)—the *Tangyun* glosses this as the manner in which a criminal is interrogated and investigated.

If the judgment is not fixed by the "pen," then the pen is not fixed; the "pen" is precisely the assembly of the Legalists (*fajia*). Furthermore, "lü" (律) means division, like the division of the breaths in the musical scales (*lülü*).
Moreover, among common parlance there are three kinds of "lü": first, the Yin-lü; second, [the Yang-lü]; third, [the Zhong-lü]. (Note: The text appears to be incomplete at this point.)
This accords with the *Lü* (Laws/Regulations). Regarding the three categories of *Lü*, the last one will be clarified below; for now, I shall clarify the first two.
That is to say, among the twelve months, those with an odd number of days are *Lü* and belong to Yang, while those with an even number are *Lǚ* and belong to Yin.
These are: the first month, Gūxiǎn and Tàicòu; the third month, Gūxiǎn; the fifth month, Zhìbīn; the seventh month, Yízé; the ninth month, Wúshè; and the eleventh month, Huángzhōng.
(These six are called *lü*). The second month is *Jiāzhōng*; the fourth month is *Zhònglǜ*; the sixth month is *Línzhōng*; the eighth month is *Nányǔ*; the tenth month is *Yìngzhōng*;
and the twelfth month is *Dàlǜ*. (These six are called *lǜ*. These are the two sets of *yīnyáng* and *lǜ*, which correspond to the musical scales.)

The *Monthly Ordinances* (*Yueling*) states: "Use the inch-measure to determine the pitch-pipes (*lüguǎn*). Each pipe has its own number of inches; fearing prolixity, I shall not cite them here [etc.].

It further states that one fills the pipes with the ashes of *jiā* (pronounced *jiā*) plants (i.e., *lùhuā*) during the twelve months; when the seasonal qi arrives, the ashes move, corresponding to the seasonal nodes (*jiéhòu*) with exact precision and without deviation.
Thus it is said they "correspond to the pitch. Therefore, the *Commentary on the Precepts* (*Jieshu*) says: "Although Yin and Yang have no form..."

By means of the pitch-pipes (*śaṅkhu*), one uses bamboo ashes to distinguish the seasonal nodes; by relying on these divisions, the internal teaching is likewise ordered. In accordance with the essential nature, two types of observance (*dhāraṇī*) are established;
in opposition to that nature, two types of transgression are established. Without the Vinaya, these would not be clear; it is also like the vital breaths of the musical pipes.
Furthermore, the *Śīla-viniścaya-ṭīkā* asks: "The Vinaya is taught as the Dharma; its application and performance possess ritual propriety. How does it differ from the other two Piṭakas?"

What is the distinction? The answer is that they are not the same. The other collections clarify the principles inherent in spiritual penetration; by attaining proficiency in any one gate, one accords with the contemplation of the Way.
The causes for his five hundred bodies are nothing but the correct teaching. When Śāṇakavāsin manifested through meditative power, Kumāralāta could not fathom its limits.

The intent lies in removing obstructions; why restrict oneself to the literal words? The Vinaya is not like this. Regarding the gravity of offenses, their allowance or prohibition, and the standards for judgment, these are not fixed.

To disrupt the constant order and ruin the continuity of the *kōgyaku* (meritorious achievements) and necessarily rely on the formal rules for punishment—speaking from this perspective, the meaning of the Dharma becomes even more manifest. (The above is from the commentary.)

Based on this meaning, it is said that among the three categories of the teachings, only the Vinaya possesses the function of providing definitive judgment and establishing standards; the other two lack this capacity. Therefore, it alone is defined as "Dharma" (the teaching).

The *Shu* (Commentary) further states: "Although the Vinaya is concise in its principles and decisive in its forms, it entirely deviates from [mere] prescriptions and lacks the systematic methods for refuting 'similarities' (pseudo-similarity).
Thus, for the time being, we shall translate it according to the intended meaning as presented above" (the above is the text of the *Shu*). Regarding the phrase "refuting similarities," it refers to—

Regarding the five types of disciplinary punishments (*pañca-prāyaścittika*), there is no difference in their hierarchical gradation; those that are grave are punished severely, and those that are light are punished lightly, with no distinction made otherwise.
The *Śū* (Commentary) further states: "The term *vinaya* means 'dharma' (law). It possesses ritual protocols from beginning to end, and this principle can be established within the Buddha's teaching.

Thus, the establishment of the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* categories is observed equally by all three periods of time. However, while the specific methods of conversion (*upāya*) differ, the nature-precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) remain constant. The *vinaya* rules, however, are not so; they vary according to the era."

There has been an evolution [in this practice]. In antiquity, the actual form of the flesh was used; "form" (*xing*) here refers to the precept (*śīla*). Once that flesh is destroyed, it remains permanently so for the rest of one's life and cannot be restored.
Judging by this principle, it is like the secular legal codes which have both new and old versions, depending on whether they were based on the specific regulations of a particular era.
The five ancient punishments were those established by the Qin Chancellor Gongsun Yang (pronounced *yú* with the second tone), who was enfeoffed as Lord Shang.
These are the punishments: First, branding with ink, which means using a knife to carve the character for "thief" on the forehead and then dyeing it black with ink.

Second, *ni* (pronounced *yùqì*), which is the excision of the nose. Third, *gōng*: for those who engage in sexual intercourse without following the rites—men have their generative organs removed, while women are confined in the palace.
Fourth, *gé*, which refers to the cutting off of the ears. Fifth, *zé*, which refers to the feet; this is the most severe offense.

In general, one is dealt with according to the preceding offense, as determined by the regulations above. During the Later Han dynasty, the Chancellor Xiao He established the *Zetuo* (pronounced "cuo-he") and, based on the *Xin* (New), formulated the five forms of punishment to codify the Three Thousand Articles. The golden statutes and jade articles replaced the ancient laws. Regarding the first type, the *tai* (pronounced "ren-zhi"):

[The text continues with the specific punishments for each of the five forms. ...the *tai* (pronounced "ren-zhi") [is applied]. (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a legal commentary, likely from the *Xinlü* (New Code) or related Tang dynasty legal materials, discussing the transition from ancient law to the codified statutes of the Later Han.)
A small cane is called a *chāi*. *Chāi* means "shame" (*chǐ*), as it brings shame like that of being whipped with a whip or the like. This has five grades: ten, twenty, thirty, forty, and fifty.
One is flogged until the skin turns blue, symbolizing the color of wood belonging to the East, the branches *jiǎ* and *yǐ*.

As for the two types of canes: a large cane is called a *zhàng*. A *zhàng* is a long wooden staff. It also has five grades: sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety, and one hundred. One is flogged until the color of the flesh is visible.
Red. This represents the south, where *bing* and *ding* correspond to fire, which is red. "Three *tu*" refers to slaves (*nu*). In these places of suffering, they are driven like cattle;
by night they are confined, and by day they labor until dusk. Their color is white, representing the west, where *geng* and *xin* correspond to metal, which is white.
"Four *liu*" means dispersion. The three grades [of distance]—two thousand li, two thousand five hundred li, and three thousand li—resemble water flowing eastward.
There is no returning westward again. Its color is black, representing the North, where the *geng* and *gui* trunks belong to the element Water, which is black.

"The five deaths" signifies exhaustion. Second, [the two methods are] strangulation and decapitation; when a person dies, their soul and spirit (*hunpo*) return to the heavens above, while their flesh and bones are buried in the earth below.

This represents the Center, where the *wu* and *ji* trunks belong to the element Earth, which is yellow. Although the five punishments—new and old—differ from one another, there is none that does not turn its back [on life], serving as a restraint.
To govern the myriad people so that they do not give rise to transgressions, one fears the punishments of the law. The laws of the Dharma-kings of the Western lands are likewise thus;
they constantly construct embankments to ensure that what is improper does not arise. (The explanation of the meaning of *vinaya* is hereby concluded.)

Second, regarding the explanation of the meaning of *śīla* (precepts): The *Śīla-ṭīkā* states, "Precepts mean 'to warn' (*jìng*). They warn and spur the three karmas [of body, speech, and mind], distancing one from non-objective conditions;

this clarifies their cause. Furthermore, precepts mean 'to prohibit' (*jìn*). By means of the good, they prohibit the evil, and so forth... Third, regarding the explanation of the meaning of *vimukti* (liberation):

Having already abandoned obstructive defilements and forever emerged from worldly toil (*saṃsāra*), it is called "liberation" because karma and delusion have been exhausted. Liberation is not... [text ends].
It is the same. There are two kinds: first, liberation at the time of the cause; second, liberation at the time of the fruit. Regarding "liberation at the time of the cause":

this refers to guarding against evil when encountering objects and temporarily subduing transgressions and faults; it attains liberation from the side of non-arising defilement. Second, liberation at the time of the fruit also has two types:
first, individual liberation (*prātimokṣa*); second, ultimate liberation. Regarding "individual liberation," it pertains to humans and devas.
Regarding the fruit: if it refers to the fruits of humans and devas, one has not yet escaped saṃsāra, nor has liberation been fully manifested.

For now, however, by merely avoiding the three miserable realms (durgati), it is designated as "liberation. Second, regarding ultimate liberation: the cause refers to the arising of either pure concentration or wisdom.
As a sutra says: "If one possesses pure wisdom, one shall attain the foremost path. Furthermore, according to the commentary:

It is said: "The Way is sometimes called liberation (*vimukti*). In terms of the practice of precepts, it is called individual liberation (*prātimokṣa*). It is further said: "There are two kinds of hindrances: first, the hindrance of karma; second, the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśa*).
To purify the hindrance of karma, one relies on wisdom; because this is distinguished by its expectation of severance, it is called liberation.
Subsequently, when wisdom eliminates the hindrances, it is termed ultimate [liberation]. (The meaning of liberation above is concluded.)

The preceding section has correctly established the causes for the meaning of the *vinaya* as the expressive medium (*vācaka*), and has thereby clarified the meaning of the expressed content (*vācya*), namely the precepts (*śīla*) and liberation (*vimukti*).

This concludes the explanation of the translated meanings. As noted above, there are two points summarizing this section (etc.). Third, regarding the conclusion that returns solely to the explanation:
[The question is asked: Why does this inquiry arise? [The answer is: That which was clarified above—the four parts (*catur-bhāga*)—is the text consisting of four sections; "vinaya" is...

[This] ritual manual proceeds from the four sections of the text below. Within these, because there are distinctions regarding essence and function, the supported and the support, superiority and inferiority, difference and identity, and to avoid confusion with the "non-conceptual" (asaṃjñika), it is necessary to differentiate them; therefore, they must be clarified.

Furthermore, in all Indic texts, whenever there are two characters above [a term] that possess essence and function, they must be explained and differentiated accordingly; even when there are two characters, [if they do not meet these criteria, they need not be so treated].
Furthermore, as they lack both essence and function, they cannot be treated by a single rule. Within the cited text, it is divided into two parts: first, a general explanation;
second, a conclusion that returns to their specific affiliation. Regarding the first: in Sanskrit, *ṣaṭ* (translated here as "six") and *samāsa* (translated as "compound" or "combination").

"Six" refers to the enumeration; "separating first and then combining" refers to the method of explanation (*vyākhyāna*). The above constitutes the general name. Next, the individual items are listed in verse:

It is said that there are six types of compounds: *karmadhāraya* (appositional), *tatpuruṣa* (dependent), *bahuvrīhi* (possessive), *dvigu* (numeral), *avyayībhāva* (indeclinable), and *dvandva* (copulative).

Regarding the first, the *karmadhāraya*, Master Bao says: "Holding" (*dharana*) means to sustain; "activity" (*karman*) means functional operation. Because the essence is able to sustain its function, it is called *karmadhāraya*.

For example, in the phrase "the eye-faculty is pure," the four great elements and the form derived from them constitute the essence. The "faculty" (*indriya*) refers to the capacity to exercise sovereignty over the production of consciousness.

"Shān" (刪), according to the *Shēnglèi* (聲類), means "to fix" (*dìng*). According to the *Guǎngyá* (廣雅), it means "to pare down" (*xiāo*). According to the *Sāncāng* (三蒼), it means "to eliminate" (*chú*).
Confucius "pared down" the Odes and fixed the Rites; now our Master has pared down and fixed [this work]. Alternatively, this character "shān" may be used as a verb.

The character "pángdāo" (旁刀) is a *huìyì* (compound ideographic) character. Generally, there are six types of characters commonly understood in the world: first, *xiàngxíng* (pictographic), which imitates the form of an object, such as the characters for "sun" and "moon";
second, *huìyì* (compound ideographic), such as "peace through the halting of weapons" for "military prowess" (*wǔ*), or "human speech" for "trustworthiness" (*xìn*);

third, *xíngshēng* (phonetic-associative), where either the left side is the semantic component and the right is the phonetic, or as in characters like "bǔ," "quē," "lǜ," and so on; fourth, *zhǐshì* (indicative), such as...
The first six categories among the characters deleted today are associative (huiyi) characters. This is because in ancient times there was no paper;
whenever one composed literary works, they were all written on slips of bamboo or wooden tablets bound together with strips of seasoned leather.
Thus, when Confucius read the *Yi*, he had already worn through three sets of such leather bindings.
"Severing" (jue) is precisely its intended meaning. Therefore, the four ends of the characters were carved on the tablets to represent them;

the two horizontal ends were fashioned like seasoned leather to resemble the ancient knife and brush. That which was correct was retained, while that which was incorrect was scraped away with a knife.
Thus, the character for "severing" (删) is placed with a knife, which is the very appearance of excising a section. Later, in the Eastern Han, Cai Lun invented paper to replace the bamboo tablets.

The character *wen* (文) likewise now follows the precedent of placing the "knife" radical beneath the "casket" radical; this is still intended to synthesize the meanings of the ancient forms. *Cháng* (長), *lán* (濫), and *è* (惡) follow suit.

*Mǐn* (敏) has the "tie" radical placed below it (pronounced *mò*); this too is a synthesis of meaning. The brief explanations of these characters above are now expanded upon. These extensive interpretations were established by those of Eastern Wu and are not considered orthodox, so they are not recorded here.

The various records and bequeathed instructions left by former masters are twofold: prolixity and length. "Prolixity" refers to matters that are entirely irrelevant to the present purpose;

Only the single path of the *karmavācanā* remains; this is the method that flourished in the world at that time.

however, it was intended solely for the practical application of the *Vinaya* texts in three lines of conduct. Therefore, it is said that "practical conduct" (*xing-shi*) refers to the functional application of the text of the *Chao*.

Regarding the first character of the *Sijian chao* (Commentary on the Fourfold Discrimination), there are two interpretations. If it is derived from the radical for "hand" (手), it is simply glossed as "abbreviated," meaning that while the text is concise, its meaning is abundant.

Now, following the radical for "metal" (金), it possesses three meanings. The meaning of "abbreviated" is as explained above. According to the subsequent text, which states, "It is firmly intended to be a compendium," this means the main text encompasses all essential points.
Second is the meaning of "firmly enduring" (*jiugù*). This is like how true gold in the world does not change even when subjected to pressure or refinement.
It remains unchanged even after being refined a hundred times; though buried for a long time, it does not decay.
Furthermore, it is like a subject who has rendered great service to the state in this world, who is granted an iron bond (*tièquàn*) to signify that his descendants shall enjoy honor without end.

This scrip is likewise: it is to be used forever, with no time of its abolition. Third, regarding the meaning of its utility: just as gold has the function of relieving poverty, so too does this scrip.

To apply this to specific matters and thereby respond to the exigencies of the occasion is precisely what is meant. Thus, the subsequent text says: "I hope that it may be of practical use when facing such occasions, so that one may act immediately according to the matter at hand," and so forth.

Fifth, regarding the explanation of the single character *xu* (序) in the title: the *Kaogong ji* states that it means "to unfold" (*shu*). It refers to unfolding the general meaning of the entire work.
Furthermore, the *Mao Shi* says it describes the origins and causes of a single section. The *Guang Ya* states that it clarifies the sequence of the text within a section.
Moreover, regarding the *Li* [Classic of Rites], which mentions "the *xiáng* in the east and the *xù* in the west," Guo Pu comments: "The *xù* demarcates the interior from the exterior;
that is, the eastern and western walls are called the *xù*. These walls stand in the middle of the inner gate. When a guest wishes to enter, they first adjust and gather their cap at this location."
Since one enters to see the honored master only after arranging the ritual implements on the ground, this wall is designated as the *xu* (preface/introduction).

Now, the intention in placing this preface at the beginning of the scroll is so that those who consult it shall not lose the meaning within the text; thus, it is called a "preface" (*xu*). Furthermore, "preface" (*xu*) means "thread" (*xu*).
It refers to a starting point, just as the head of a response is called the "thread. Since this stands at the head of this entire work, it is called a preface.
Furthermore, "preface" (*xu*) means "to narrate. To narrate the text of a single division [of a scripture], tracing it back to the point of its initial inception, is called a preface.
(The three characters above [“又序者敘也”] summarize the eight characters; this concludes the general explanation of the title of the Dharma.)
Next, the marginal note clarifies the difference, stating that there is no author. Regarding the title that indicates a distinct identity, there are two interpretations for each of these.
This [title] distinguishes itself from the preceding title of the Dharma-text. If one wishes to explain this passage, one should first ask me why it was produced.

Now, the Master, relying on what he had studied, could have simply compiled the *Sifenlü shan* (Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya); why then did he specifically include the name "Nabha"? The reason for the marginal note is that it answers by stating the author.
(As stated above). The meaning is that regarding the school’s own tradition (*sva-siddhānta*) which he studied, there were many commentaries and sub-commentaries composed by predecessors;
thus it says, "the authors are not lacking. Now, by designating the title *Shanbu* (Deleted and Supplemented), he distinguishes it from those of old, as such a title has never existed before.

Therefore, it says, "he designates the name to manifest its distinction. The note in the middle fascicle states: "The author uses multiple names; he establishes these names to mark his distinction. The lower fascicle says:
Regarding the commentary: it was not long ago that the title was established to manifest these three fascicles.

Although the phrasing of the commentary differs, the meaning and intent are no different (according to this point of interpretation, the introductory notes at the beginning of the three fascicles are all the master’s own annotations). The second interpretation states:

"To distinguish it from the title of the work, these are the words of praise and exposition from the *Śāstra* of the Xiangbu school. At the time this *Chao* was first composed, the name of the author was not revealed. Later...
There was one copy that reached Master Xiang [Xuanzang], the author of the *Shu* (Commentary), who truly cherished it and considered it definitive.
However, it was not known for certain who had originally composed it. During the Zhenguan era, the author of the *Chao* (Excerpts) traveled four times in search of rare texts;

upon arriving at the residence of Master Xiang, they met him and discussed matters concerning the Vinaya school. Thereupon, [Master Xiang] said: "Recently, I have obtained a copy of the *Yixing Shichao* (The Ten-Scroll Excerpts)."

This is extremely timely. However, it was not yet known who had composed it. Master Nanshan remarked, "It was written by someone else. The author of the *Śāstra* (the *Sūtra Commentary*) was struck with wonder and requested that the title be inscribed.
Consequently, the author of the *Vyākhyā* (the *Sub-commentary*) wrote "Chongyi Temple in Jingzhao" and so forth at the beginning of each of the three fascicles (and so on).
Thereupon, the author of the *Śāstra* filled in the empty space between the title of the Dharma (*dharmapada*) and the title of the author’s name, writing [his own name] upon the back.
The eight characters [of the title] are words of praise. This is the case at the beginning of all three fascicles. The two preceding interpretations each represent a different path;

however, based on my received tradition, I have definitively adopted the first interpretation. Even if the original manuscript were indeed without the author’s name, it still could not serve as a reliable proof (consider this).
Next, the author distinguishes the personal name of the author. Regarding the passage from "Jingzhao" to "shu," there is first a brief clarification, followed by a detailed explanation.
In the former, "Jingzhao" refers to the territory under the jurisdiction of the Son of Heaven. "Chongyi Temple" is a specific designation for a monastic residence (*saṃghārāma*).
"Śramaṇa" is a general designation for those who have left the household life. "Śākya" refers to the clan of capable people.
"So-and-so" is a specific dharma-name extracted from [the original]. "Compiled" (zhuàn) means to select ancient surviving texts; "narrated" (shù) means to recount without creating anew.
Next, the section on detailed explanation has six parts. First, regarding the term "Jingzhao": "Jing" means great; "Zhao" means city.

Furthermore, it is a numerical designation: ten billion is called a *zhao*, and ten *zhao* is called a *jing*. As for the current term "Jingzhao": *(Note: The provided source text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion of the commentary.)*
This is the land where the Son of Heaven resides; it is also called the "Capital" (*jīngshī*). *Shī* means "multitude. The *Baihūtong* states:

The *Shiji* states: "The Han Founder established his capital at Chang'an, where the population was vast and the territory of Qin was extensive."

The Grand Treasury (responsible for tribute, personnel, offerings, and the two markets). When Kāśyapa Mātanga arrived during the Later Han dynasty, as he was a monk from a foreign land, he was temporarily accommodated at the Court of State Ceremonial.
Subsequently, a separate monastic complex was constructed outside the Yong Gate, where he took up residence with his white horse that carried the scriptures.

Third, regarding the analysis of the two characters for *śramaṇa*: it is also called *sāmen* (桑門), both of which are abbreviated forms.

When combined, they form *śramaṇa*, which is translated here as "pacifying the mind" (*xīxīn*). Thus, the *Ruiying jing* states: "The three realms are designated as 'disturbance,' and the six destinies are designated as 'obscurity.

One who pacifies the mind and reaches the fundamental source is therefore called a *śramana*. Alternatively, it is said that it means "pacifying evil," being able to pacify [the afflictions] through the wisdom of the emptiness of arising. That which is pacified...
These are the afflictions. Therefore, the Treatise says: "The accumulation of merit abandons all that is non-virtuous; in this world and the next, one possesses wisdom and is free from affliction.
Because all of birth and death is eliminated, one who realizes this is called a śramaṇa. The commentary explains:

The wisdom and insight (*jñāna-prajñā*) regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is termed "merit" (*puṇya*). This wisdom and insight is not attained in a short time; at the fastest, it takes three births, and at the slowest, sixty.
*Kalpa* means accumulation. *Tyāga* (abandonment) has the sense of casting off and turning away. These are not merely the root afflictions (*kleśa*) or the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
"This world" refers to the body of fragmented birth-and-death (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*). "The other world" refers to the body of transformation birth-and-death (*pariṇāma-jāti-maraṇa*).

Regarding the "extinction of all birth-and-death," this is discussed for the time being in terms of the fragmented type, without yet addressing the transformation type. One who realizes this is called [an Arhat].

The term *śramaṇa* is an abbreviation (the preceding [section] on the explanation of the name is concluded). Question: It is not yet clear what the nature (*svabhāva*) of a *śramaṇa* is, what the essence of the fruit (*phala*) is, and how many distinct types of fruit-stages there are.
Answer: As stated in a verse of the *Abhidharmakośa*: "The nature of a *śramaṇa* is the pure path;
its fruits are conditioned and unconditioned. These consist of eighty-nine: the paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*). Commentary: All untainted (*anāsrava*)...

The Path. The wisdom that realizes the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the wisdom that realizes the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), which is free from defiled afflictions, is called the "Pure Path.
This Pure Path is the essential nature of a *śramaṇa*. One who harbors this path is called a *śramaṇa*. Regarding the conditioned and unconditioned fruits:

the conditioned and unconditioned constitute the essence of the fruits of *śramaṇaship*. The conditioned refers to liberation (*vimukti*); the unconditioned refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). These consist of eight [types].
Nineteen. Regarding "the paths of liberation and cessation": this enumerates them according to the stages of abandoning afflictions (*kleśa*).

There are eighty-nine paths of liberation, which are conditioned fruits (*saṃskṛta-phala*); furthermore, there are eighty-nine types of analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) that are realized.

This is the unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛta-phala*). That is to say, in abandoning the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*), there are eight paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*)—namely, the eight volitions (*cetanā*)—and eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)—namely, the eight knowledges (*jñāna*).

In abandoning the afflictions of the nine stages belonging to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there are eighty-one paths of uninterrupted transition and eighty-one paths of liberation. When the paths of seeing and cultivation are combined, there are eighty-nine.
Furthermore, the path of uninterrupted transition is exclusively the nature of *śrāmaṇya* (the state of being a recluse); the path of liberation is both that nature and its fruit.

From the perspective of the meaning of "stopping evil," this is the nature of a śramaṇa (*śrāmaṇya*). From the perspective of being an outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), it is the fruit of the śramaṇa (*śrāmaṇya-phala*).
A single analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is exclusively unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and constitutes the essence of the fruit of the śramaṇa.

That is to say, the absence of the path is the nature of the śramaṇa, and analytical cessation is its realization; thus it is called the fruit of the śramaṇa. It is also the result of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*) and the result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala* [the latter being the external master’s effort]). If one follows this interpretation:
In principle, one who has truly realized the state of a sage is designated as a *śramaṇa*. At present, those in the ordinary ranks of Tang China possess all afflictions (*kleśa*) in their entirety;
they do not yet merit the title of *śramaṇa*. Nevertheless, because it is permissible to discuss the fruit based on the cause, the term may still be applied.

Furthermore, since ancient times there has also been the "universal characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) [which applies even to ordinary people]; the present case refers to this universal characteristic *śramaṇa*.
Fourth, the explanation of the single character. In full, it should be stated as "Śākya," which refers to the clan and lineage of those who have left the household life.

Because the abbreviated form is retained here, only the designated character is explained. Question: Above, the term *śramaṇa* was mentioned; below, it is again selected and explained. Is this not redundant? Answer: It is for the sake of eliminating confusion.
There are also those who have left the household life and are *śramaṇas* by nature, yet do not belong to the Śākya clan. Therefore, the term "clan" (*gotra*) is used as a qualification.
Regarding this, only Dharma Master Jiji of the Mahāyāna school analyzed it using the fourfold categorization (*catuskoṭi*):
first, those who are śramaṇas but not Śākyas, referring to the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) of the Western Regions; as the Vinaya states: "When a śramaṇa receives food," and so forth.

Second, those who are Śākyas but not śramaṇas, namely the various members of the Śākya clan in the Western Regions. Third, those who are both śramaṇas and Śākyas, namely those who have now left the household life. Fourth, those who are neither.

These are simply the secular lineages. Furthermore, after the transmission of this [teaching] by the immortals and before it reached the regions of Qin and Jin, all were referred to by their secular surnames, or sometimes by the surnames of their teachers.
For example, Master Sheng’s original surname was Wei, yet after he left the household life, he followed his teacher’s surname.

Master Zhu Fahu’s original surname was Zhi, while Master Mudu Zhu followed his teacher’s surname, and so forth. It was only from the time of Master An of the Eastern Jin that [the practice of using dharma names] became established.
This changes the course [of the argument]. An said: "I have never held Śākyamuni in such high esteem; all [members of the four castes] should equally be given the surname 'Śākya'.
Later, when the *Ekottarika Āgama* arrived from the West, it indeed confirmed this point. Thus it says: "The four rivers flow into the sea and no longer retain their original names;
likewise, those of the four castes who leave the household life all take the surname Śākya. Furthermore, the *Kaṭhina-vastu* of the *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* states: "It is just as the four..."
"All rivers flow back to the sea. Likewise, Maudgalyāyana, those who have left the household life to study the Way within my Dharma are all called sons of Śākya;
they all now follow the Buddha’s clan name. Since I and the monastics of today honor the lineage of Śākya, one must know that the source from which their nature was obtained cannot be ignored.
To fail to understand this is like a grandson who does not know his grandfather’s name, or a son who does not know his father’s taboo name. This, too, is the Way."
The common people share this sense of shame. This is based on the customs of this region: in the Southern Dynasties, there were the four clans of Wei, Zhang, Gu, and Lu;
in the Northern Dynasties, there were the four clans of Ji, Zheng, Cui, and Lu. Furthermore, there are many others who acquired surnames due to their residence or their noble titles and enfeoffments.

These are recorded extensively in the *Kaibian Dingpu Lu* (Register of Surnames Fixed in the Kaiyuan Era), but fearing prolixity, they are not cited here. Now, according to the four clans of the Western Regions, these too are distinct; thus, the Western Regions...
The record states: Now, as for the distinctness of lineages, there are four classes. First, the *kṣatriya*, which refers to the royal caste;
they have presided over the throne for generations, taking benevolence and forbearance as their ideal. Second, the *brāhmaṇa*, here translated as "Pure Resolve";

they maintain the Way with steadfast devotion and keep their conduct pure and white. Third, the *vaiśya*, here translated as "Merchant"; they trade goods according to supply and demand, pursuing profit far and near. Fourth, the *śūdra*... [text ends]
