Their purity and impurity follow distinct paths, and they do not intermarry. As for the remaining three castes, whose ways of flight and concealment differ, they are discussed elsewhere.
Here, I shall only describe those of the *kṣatriya* nature, because the Śākya clan originated from them; therefore, this—

Their lineage is the most noble. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "At the beginning of the kalpa, they were like the gods of the Rūpadhātu; later, they gradually increased their craving for flavors. Due to indolence and hoarding, thieves arose;
they were hired to guard the fields. The *Śāstra* (Commentary) says: "At the time of the kalpa's beginning, the people of this Jambudvīpa were all like the various gods of the Rūpadhātu:
their physical forms were upright and majestic, their bodies were suffused with radiance, and they could soar through the air."
They were autonomous, enjoying food and pleasure, and lived long lives. Thus, from this earth-essence (*pṛthivī-rasa*), a sweet substance spontaneously arose, its fragrance being most fragrant.
At that time, there was a man whose nature was addicted to flavors; he took some and ate it. The other people followed his example.
In the end, they all took this to eat (this is called the first solid food at the beginning of the kalpa). Once they had eaten it, their bodies consequently became solid and heavy;

their radiance vanished and darkness arose. From that point on, the sun, moon, and various stars appeared. As they gradually became addicted to its flavor, the "earth-flavor" (pṛthivī-rasa) then disappeared.
From this point on, *pṛthivī-parpaṭaka* (earth-cakes) appeared. They vied with one another to consume them, and the earth-cakes vanished.
Thereupon, *vanalatā* (forest-vines) appeared; these too vanished, and fragrant rice grew spontaneously. The multitude gathered it together and ate it until it was exhausted.

The first three [types of food] were subtle morsel-food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), which permeated the limbs and body like oil poured onto sand, leaving behind only impurities and sweat. The fourth was coarse; therefore, it left behind residual filth.

While still within the body, with the desire to eliminate [the impurities], they divided into two paths; from this, the male and female organs arose. Due to the difference between these two organs, their physical forms also became distinct.

By the power of past habitual tendencies, they began to gaze at one another. Consequently, improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) arose, and the demon of lustful craving deluded and disturbed their bodies and minds.
Losing their composure and becoming deranged, they engaged in unchaste conduct (*abrahmacarya*). (Among humans, there was a desire to see...)
At the time of its initial emergence), the people there took the fragrant rice but did not initially store any away. Later, there was one person whose nature was indolent;
he took a large amount of the fragrant rice at once, storing it for future consumption. The others imitated him, and they gradually began to stockpile more.

Because of this, the rice gave rise to the notion of "mine," and they harvested it without satiety. Subsequently, wherever the rice was harvested, it no longer sprouted again. Thereupon, they [gathered together...]
The fields were divided. With foresight for the distant future, each person exerted their efforts; they plowed, sowed, and cultivated.

Regarding their own allotted plots, they developed a sense of protective cherishing; yet regarding the plots of others, they harbored intentions of encroachment and seizure (the transgression of robbery and theft began at this time).

Desiring to prevent such interference, they collectively deliberated and unanimously appointed a virtuous man from within the community. Each person was to provide one-sixth of their harvest to hire him [to oversee the fields].
He protected [the land] and was appointed as the Lord of the Fields; for this reason, he was given the name *Kṣatriya*.

Because the great masses revered him and his grace flowed throughout the land, he was further named *Mahā-sammata*, which means "Commonly Agreed Upon. Among all subsequent kings, this king was the first.
Later, there was a king who, being greedy and stingy regarding wealth and treasures, was unable to distribute them equitably among the people of the realm, so that some were poor...
Regarding those who were destitute, they frequently committed theft, which the king prohibited by inflicting light and heavy punishments (the karma of killing and harming originated from this time).

Later, when a person with a guilty conscience was terrified and sought to conceal their crime, the authorities investigated thoroughly to extract the truth; thus, speaking with a deceptive intent (the words of falsehood) first appeared at this time.
That King Mahāsammata’s descendants succeeded one another, and there were nineteen universal monarchs (*cakravartin*). The last was named...
King Mahāmeru. From this king, his descendants succeeded one another, producing one hundred and seventy-three thousand two hundred and eighty-four minor universal monarchs (*cakravartin*).
Among them, the number of minor kings (*kṣudraka-rāja*) is unknown. The last was named Matsyarāja (Fish King).
The descendants of this prince succeeded one another for one hundred and forty-three generations of minor kings (*kṣudrarāja*).
The last was named King Mahā-tṛṇa. This king had no son; he therefore entrusted the sovereignty to his great ministers. According to the law of the Western lands, succession follows two lines:
first, the royal lineage; second, the lineage of sages (*ṛṣi*). The king reflected: "Since I have no son, it would be improper to allow the royal lineage to be severed."

The lineage of the Buddha was severed, so he entered the mountains to practice the Way. At that time, there was an attendant who followed the king to the mountains, desiring to seek what he had learned.
Fearing that later on someone might insult or harm him, [the attendant] placed him in a bamboo basket and hung it from a tree. A hunter observed this;
seeing the basket, he thought it was fruit, and seeing the king, he suddenly saw the king’s head—pale and white—inside, thinking it was a crane. He then drew his bow...

He drew his bow and aimed; the arrow struck the king’s heart, and his life ended therefrom. At the moment of the shooting, two drops of blood fell to the ground, from which grew two stalks of sugarcane.
When the sun scorched them and they were split open, one grew on the left, becoming a young boy, and one grew on the right, becoming a young girl.
The boy was named Sujāta and the girl was named Sujātā. The elder ministers then established Sujāta as king and Sujātā as queen. [End of section.]

Regarding the station of governing the kingdom (in the Western lands, one does not marry outside of one's own clan): King Śaṃjaya had a son named King Udayana (the *Pañcavargika* states he was King Drumāyana).
There were two queens. The first queen had a son named Jīvaka (Long-sheng), who was dull-witted, foolish, and ugly;

everyone loathed and despised him. The second queen had four sons: the first was named Ālokacakṣus (Zhào-mù), the second Śravaṇacakṣus (Tīng-mù), the third Hastivinita (Tiáofúxiàng), and the fourth Nila (Nílóu).
These four sons were intelligent, sagacious, and martial, possessing great majesty and virtue. Their...
The queen secretly thought to herself: "Although my son has grown up, he lacks the capacity for state affairs.

Should he inherit the great enterprise, it will surely be usurped. Those four sons possess both majesty and virtue; the destiny of the kingdom will surely fall to them. I must plant their seeds [in his stead].
What plan should I devise to secure my son's foundation? Thus, she first sought him with her feelings and subsequently moved him with reason. Later, on one occasion, the King arrived."
The Queen was staying in her quarters. She addressed the King, saying: "I have eliminated craving and so forth (as detailed at length). I pray that Your Majesty will inter and banish me;
only then shall my mind find peace. The King said: "Your four sons are filial and fraternal; they have committed no offense against the state. Why should you be interred and cast out?

Since the Queen’s heartfelt request was not granted, she used a sequence of reasoned appeals (some versions read *gan* [感], which may mean "to move" or "to affect"; it may also be interpreted as "to cause disorder," which is acceptable). The Queen said: "I have now eliminated craving."
In truth, this concerns both the state and the family, and not merely for the sake of this son. His four sons are all divinely martial; the people each long to return to them.

After Your Majesty’s ten-thousand-year reign, they will all desire to be sovereigns—who would be willing to serve as ministers? They will surely destroy one another and bring about the ruin of the great state.
That which was once my refuge has now turned into the possession of another; I pray you, follow him from this moment on and do not think of me, your only son. My words are as they are:
if there is any remaining joy in your original precepts, it shall cease from now on. The King said, "Your words are correct; I myself know the proper time."
Later, on a certain day, he commanded his four sons, saying: "You have committed offenses against me. I cannot bear to see you die;
you must now leave the kingdom and seek your livelihood through self-discipline. Be most careful not to look back upon Yu, lest you incur regret that is difficult to remedy.

The four sons, knowing they were themselves without fault, then packed their travel gear and set out together with their biological mother, their elder sisters, and the senior ministers, all of whom wished to accompany them.
The King granted him permission in its entirety. Thereupon, he departed through the northern gate of the city. The path was perilous and obstructed;
crossing the Vāgīśī River, he reached the north of the Snowy Mountains, near the Naḍa-śai forest, where he beheld that land. It was narrow from east to west but broad and long from south to north;
it was said that the ground was abundant with fertile soil and frequented by various birds. He then took up residence there and established a camp at that very spot.
Those who returned to the city were like clouds; those who followed him were like a marketplace. Before long, it flourished into a great kingdom.
He installed the youngest son, Nīthu, as king, while his three elder brothers served as ministers. As they attended to their sovereign, they recalled the past and questioned the various ministers.

One who knew the matter reported it to the king, recounting the events in detail. The king summoned those sons back to the palace, but the four brothers resolutely refused to obey their father’s command. The father-king...
He then sighed three times from afar, saying: "My son Śākya! My son Śākya! From this, the clan name Śākya (translated as "Capable Man") was established.
Nīlo had a son named Aśvamukha; Aśvamukha had a son named Niṣadha;
Niṣadha had four sons: first, Śuddhodana; second, Śuklodana; third, Droṇodana; and fourth, Amṛtodana.
Regarding food: King Śuddhodana had one son named Siddhārtha. King Śuklodana had two sons: the first was named Ānanda and the second was named Devadatta.
King Droṇodana had two sons: the first was named Mahānāman and the second was named Aniruddha.
King Amṛtodana had two sons: the first was named Bāhula, and the second was named Bhadrika. Siddhārtha had a son named Rāhula.
From King Nīlodaka down to the Buddha’s own person, the lineage was extended through six generations. The present-day monks and nuns are the fellow students of Rāhula;
the nuns are the seventh-generation descendants of King Nīlodaka. (The explanation of the characters is hereby concluded.)

Regarding the fifth point, the explanation of names and taboos (*ming-hui*): in the tradition of oral transmission and exegesis, there are instances where names are explained and instances where they are not. If one follows secular etiquette, names are tabooed;
however, there are also exceptions, such as "not tabooing [names] when facing the text," "not tabooing [names] in the *Shi* and *Shu*," and "not tabooing [names] within the ancestral temple.

If we follow the internal teachings (Buddhism), we are encouraged to recite the names of the Buddhas of the past; therefore, we must now emulate this practice. The name of the author of the *Chao* is Dao.

"Proclaiming" means the Way, which is the Dharma. "Proclaiming" means pervasiveness; it refers to manifesting, exalting, widely expounding, and universally demonstrating [the Dharma] to sentient beings.

The Great Master was a man of three lifetimes who was foremost in upholding the Vinaya. He was born during the Qi dynasty; his dharma name was Saṃgharakṣita. He resided at Yinyue Temple on Mount Shicheng in Shan County, Yuezhou.
The stone cliffs of that mountain were steep and precipitous, rising several tens of zhang high, and within them was a figure resembling a Buddha.
The form of the Radiant Light (Jvalanaprabha) constantly heard celestial music whenever he was walking in meditation (caṅkrama).

Following this auspicious omen of extraordinary fragrance, he made a vow to construct a ten-zhang Maitreya statue to correspond to the future thousand-fathom body of the Buddha, so that all who have a karmic connection might together ascend to the three assemblies.
Construction began during the Jianwu era; it was completed in barely one year. However, he subsequently suffered from a severe illness.
He passed away at the age of one hundred and twenty. On his deathbed, he made a vow, saying: "I did not expect to live out this life; I pray that in my second birth, I shall surely succeed.
In the sixth year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, Lu Xian, the Magistrate of Shifeng County in Taizhou (now renamed Tangxing), returned to the capital after completing his term.
While traveling through Shan and Han, he stopped there for the night. During the night, he dreamed of three *brahmacārin* monks who said: "Jian'an..."
"Your Highness, your illness has not yet been cured. If you could construct the Holy Stone City and complete the holy image, you would surely recover.
Lu Ling was sent back to the capital, and everyone forgot this matter. Years later, a monk came to stay at the residence.

During conversation, he said, 'Why have you not carried out what was entrusted to you after [the visit to] Shan? Lu Ling, having already clung to his former dream, [acted accordingly] after the monk had departed."
He reflected carefully before finally speaking to him. This monk was precisely the third person seen in the midst of the dream.

He immediately reported the matter to Prince Jian'an and submitted it to the imperial court. An edict was issued for its construction, and the monk Sengyou, who was skilled and devoted, was appointed exclusively to oversee the carving of the statue.
Construction began in the twelfth year of the Tianjian era and was completed after fifteen years. The seated figure stood five *zhang* high.
A statue ten *zhang* in height was erected, and it was renamed Shicheng Temple. Vinaya Master Sengyou was its second incarnation;

his secular surname was Yu. His ancestors were from Xiajiang in Pengcheng (the "pi" in "Xiajiang" has the pronunciation "pí"). Furthermore, because his forebears had served in office in Tang, they settled in Jianye.
At the age of seven, Sengyou entered Jianchu Temple and refused to return home.

When he grew up and his parents wished to arrange a marriage for him, he subsequently evaded them and sought refuge at Dinglin Temple on Mount Zhong, where he requested full ordination from Master Fada. He studied the Vinaya with great precision.
Because Sengyou’s surname was elegant and refined, whenever there were matters of statecraft or refinement within the realm, he was invariably entrusted by imperial decree to handle them.
In the seventeenth year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, he passed away at his home temple. The details are as extensive as recorded in the *Sengzhuan* (Biographies of Monks) [and so forth].

His third birth was this present life; he was born during the Sui dynasty, originally belonging to the Qian clan. In various records, it is stated that he was a native of Changcheng in Huzhou (the same is true for his biographical inscription).
The memorial states: "According to the genealogies of the Qian clan, his grandfather was a native of Changcheng. When the Great Master was...
He was a native of Jingzhao. He stated that his great-great-grandfather was a *fu-ma-du-wei* (Imperial Son-in-law) during the Chen dynasty;
his grandfather served as the Governor of Chenliu; and his father’s name was Shi Shen (the variant reading "Shi You" is erroneous), who was the Minister of Personnel (*li-bu-shang-shu*).

When the Chen dynasty was annexed by Sui, this Shi Shen, along with the Chen Emperor Houzhu, was simultaneously captured and brought to Chang’an. Subsequently, the Prince of Chen met his end at the hands of the Sui.
The bandits’ chariot turned back, sparing him from harm. It was not until the sixteenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty that the Great Master was born.
The Master had two sons, of whom the elder was named Shen. (Based on this account, it is clear that the Great Master was born in Jingzhao. His mother’s surname was Yao;
she dreamed that a moon pierced her womb, and again she dreamed of a foreign monk who said, "What you carry, O virtuous lady, is the Vinaya Master Sengyou of the Liang dynasty; you should..."
Even after he entered the monastic order and widely propagated the Buddha’s teachings, he remained in the womb for twelve months.

He was born on the eighth day of the fourth month in the Bingchen year, the sixteenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. From the day he wore his youth’s hair-knot, he was distinguished from ordinary children;

at ten years of age, he had thoroughly read all manner of books, and by twelve, he was proficient in literary composition. At fifteen, he sighed deeply and said: "The honors and emoluments of this world cannot endure forever."
Baoyu then cast aside his bamboo horse and his "Sleeping Dragon" sword, turning his heart toward the Śākya school. He served Dharma Master Huījūn of Riyán Monastery.
Within twenty days, he had recited the *Sutra of Mindfulness* sixteen times; during that fortnight, he recited the *Flower Garland Sutra* seventeen times.

In the eleventh year of the Dayè era, having reached the age of twenty, he received the great favor of heaven and, following Preceptor Shǒu, received full ordination. He placed [the precept bowl] upon his head...

Wearing a jeweled casket, he circumambulated the stupa while walking in meditation; moved by this, the śarīra relics descended into the casket. As he was about to perform the Dharma rites, after having received full ordination, he followed the Great Master Shou to study the Vinaya-piṭaka.
Having mastered it with a single recitation, he attained spiritual penetration; he then desired to return to the mountains to dwell in tranquil seclusion.

His preceptor rebuked him, saying: "Since you have set out for distant lands, you must first seek to understand the essential chapters. Your cultivation and renunciation shall have their appointed time; your merit must be fulfilled.
It is not fitting that you depart while violating the rules of discipline. You must remain and continue your studies. Consequently, he acted as his predecessor’s substitute in all monastic affairs.

He followed the text according to its sequence and recited it twenty times. At that time, during the transition between the Sui and Tang dynasties, when the practice of lecturing was temporarily suspended, this occurred in the fourth year of Wude.

In his later years, he was finally permitted to listen again. When the Great Master Shou ordered him to lecture on the text once more, he realized that his understanding of the words and phrases was deficient and that it was not yet a realization of the mind;
thus, he refused to accept the task. Only when his refusal was met with insistent refusal did he finally proceed to lecture on the text.

In the ninth year of the Wude era, during the purge of monks and nuns by Emperor Gaozu of the Tang, he went into hiding at Mount Zhongnan and composed this *Commentary on the Vimalakīrti*. This was in the eighth year of the Zhenguan era.

He manifested great benefit for the continent; his literary works and commentaries were re-edited, and he composed both the *Karmavācanā* and the *Śīlacittabhāṣya*. There was none among whom the dragons and devas did not pay homage, offering incense and flowers.

Whenever monastics or laypeople consulted him on matters of dharma, they all received his prophetic responses in advance. His three robes followed the prescribed measurements, never mixing silk with cotton or wool.

He maintained the practice of constant sitting and eating only once a day, never altering these from beginning to end. When traveling, he moved with such urgency that lice and nits were left behind to roam at will. Such was his virtue.

His aspirations were lofty and his fame resounded throughout India; thus, he was able to converse with the Arhat Piṇḍola. A long-eyebrowed Brahman monk praised and recounted the matters concerning the expansion of the altar.

During the Tang Dynasty, when the Tripiṭaka Master translated various scriptures, he commanded the Great Master to personally assist in the administration of the teachings and to compose the *Wenji* (Records) on the *Mifamen* (The Gate of Entering the Dharma).
These works comprise more than two hundred and thirty fascicles in total and have been circulated throughout the ages.

In the second month of spring, in the second year of the Qianfeng era of Emperor Gaozong, he experienced a profound spiritual resonance with a celestial being. This being conversed with the Master, saying:

"This year, your spirit shall be transferred; you will be born in the palace of Maitreya. He further presented a packet of incense, saying, "This is 'thorn-forest incense' (jílín xiāng), which the heavenly hosts constantly burn.
Having spoken, the being departed. On the third day of the tenth month, a Great Unrestricted Assembly (wúzhē dàhuì) was convened. At noon, the Master...

The common people all heard celestial music and extraordinary fragrances; thereupon, he composed his countenance and passed away. He was seventy-two years of age and fifty-two years since his ordination (*saṃghāraka*).
He had initially been settled at Shangu Valley. In the third year [of the reign], an imperial edict inquired about his whereabouts; at that time, there was Fengde Temple.

The temple head, the Sōjō Ryūn, reported the matter in full to the throne and requested that, according to the customs of the Western Regions, the body be cremated to obtain *śarīra* relics, and that three pagodas be erected—one at Fūdoku-ji, one at Anpū-bō, and one at Rin’gan-ji.
In the fourth year of the Xiántóng era, the *śarīra* from Anpū-bō were combined with those at Rin’gan-ji, and a single pagoda was constructed for them both. Although many years have passed...

The remains were moved, yet his enduring legacy did not perish. In the fifteenth year of the Xiantong era, Emperor Zizong, desiring to show his favor, honored him by posthumously bestowing the title Chengzhao (Pure Illumination) in recognition of his sagacious counsel from days past, and inscribed his lifelong virtues upon a stele; his stupa was named Jingguang (Pure Light).

The clarity of his illumination makes the mirror of the Vinaya manifest without dimming; the purity of his radiance causes the excellence of the precepts to shine forth brilliantly. That the teachings and the patriarchal lineage flourish and prosper is truly due to this.
(The explanation of the two characters for his name and title is hereby concluded.)

Regarding the two characters "zhuan-shu" (compiled and authored), there are many interpretations; here, we shall preserve the correct explanation. "Zhuan" means to record, specifically referring to the recorded writings (*yiwen*).
This pertains to the arrangement [of the text], such as the two prefaces, the thirty chapters, the sequence of practices, and the national language [of the commentary].
This author belongs to the category of those who cite the scriptural texts of the Tripiṭaka; it is not a work of personal invention based on one's own mind.

Just as Confucius "recited but did not compose," this author merely recounts ancient matters. The present case is likewise: he simply recounts the writings of antiquity, as well as the various holy teachings and so forth.

Question: What is the difference between "reciting" (shu) and "composing" (zuo)? Answer: Paramārtha says: For example, the Buddha’s sūtras are "composed" (the Buddha being the author), whereas the treatises composed by Bodhisattvas are "recited" (based on the Buddha’s word).
This directly expresses the Buddha’s intent; it merely serves to describe and recount it. If this is so, for what reason did the previous commentary state that the author is not non-existent?
Answer: When a Bodhisattva composes a treatise to explain the Buddha’s words, arranging them into the textual form of the treatise, they may also be called the "author.

The composition and compilation of commentaries and sub-commentaries on the sacred teachings by masters of the past and present, which likewise arrange the material into written form, follows this same principle. What prevents these too from being called "composed"? Question:
Why are both "compiled" (*zhuàn*) and "composed" (*shù*) used as headings? Answer: If one were to compose without compiling, it would mean that the *chāo* lacks talent;

if one were to compile without composing, it would be like following one's own whims without consulting the ancients. Thus, Confucius said: "Excessive refinement leads to the style of a court historian; excessive plainness leads to the rusticity of the common folk.

Only when refinement and plainness are harmoniously blended does one become a gentleman. Based on this principle, the term "authorship" (*zhùshù*) is employed. If one were to completely abandon literary composition, then...
This follows the conventions of historical writing; it embellishes the facts and their underlying meanings. If it were too plain, it would become crude and rustic, making it unfit for careful study.

Now, it is half-plain and half-literate, refined and harmonious, yet not overly ornate—this is the style of a gentleman. Therefore, in this composition, both plainness and ornamentation are essential; one cannot be omitted.
The preceding section concludes the identification of the names of those who authored [the work]. The above constitutes the general explanation of the preface.
The general title is hereby concluded.
*Jianzhengji* (A Record of the Selection and Rectification) of the *Sifenlü Chao* (Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya), Scroll Two.
Compiled by the Vinaya-transmitting Śramaṇa Jing’an Zhaoyuan of Zhenshen Temple in the Wu-Yue region, during the Ding-si year. Re-edited and finalized.

On the twenty-eighth day of the fourth month in the year of Wuxu (4583), during the Tianfu era, at Zisheng Temple in Huzhou, the bhikṣu [Mǎi] (the character for his name is written as 邁-禺+(口/口)) recorded this posthumously while listening to the *Jianzheng ji* on the third fascicle of the *Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya* (Shicao).
This concludes the General Preface; now begins the first section of the Specific Preface.
Compiled by Jingxiao, the Great Master Qingliang, who lectured on the Vinaya for many years under the Wu-Yue Kingdom and was granted the purple robe while presiding over ordination platforms;

this second volume is compiled separately according to the text and divides the two orders (*liǎngxù*). Fearing that the major sections (*dàkē*) would be too cumbersome, they are not cited here (and so forth).

Regarding the two orders: according to various sacred teachings, they are sometimes complete and sometimes incomplete. For instance, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vibhāṣā* states that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, [the following was established]...

The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* lacks both introductory sections entirely. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* contains only the "Arousing" (*utthāna*) section and lacks the "Certainty of Faith" (*śraddhā-prasāda*).

Additionally, the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* contains only the "Certainty of Faith" and lacks the "Arousing. Now, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* possesses both introductory sections in their entirety.

Since this *Vinayavibhāṣā* takes the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* as its primary authority, it likewise possesses both sections. Nevertheless, the arrangement differs from that of the Vinaya; this is when considering them in terms of the general and the specific.

Regarding the explanation: the five-character verses of the Vinaya text constitute the general preface (*sūtra-piṭaka*), while the section beginning from "At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Kusumapura" constitutes the specific preface (*vibhaṅga*).
This present *Chao* (Excerpts) is likewise: the first part clarifies the general preface, and the subsequent part clarifies the ten sections individually.

However, if one considers the establishment of the teaching through the testimony of faith (*śraddhā-prasāda*), the *Chao* differs from the Vinaya; for although the Vinaya first clarifies the general [preface], [the *Chao* proceeds differently].

Preface. Generally speaking, the "General Preface" (zǒngxù) is termed "Verification" (zhèng), meaning that when the founder of the school establishes his doctrine, he first pays homage to the Triple Gem to verify it so as to inspire faith, and only afterwards clarifies the "Specific Preface" (biéxù).
The "Specific Preface," in turn, is termed "Initiation" (fājī). However, this present commentary does not follow that pattern; it first clarifies the General Preface.
The first part is named "Initiation" (*pravartana*). The subsequent ten sections constitute the "Sequence of Certification and Faith" (*saddhā-pratyaya*).

The reason for this distinction is that when the founder of a school intends to propagate the original meaning of the Vinaya so that it may endure for a long time, he must first provide certification to inspire faith;

only then does he proceed with the initiation. Now, the Master [Daoxuan], in composing his *Commentary* (*Chao*), first analyzes the causes for the initiation, fearing that those who perform the rites...

There is an obstacle. Later, ten sections were composed, wherein the "Testimony of Faith" (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra) was established as having its own origins and causes [and so forth]. From this point onward, the narrative follows the text;
the various minor sub-sections are not listed in full [and so forth].

The initial statement, "As for the ultimate image," is a general praise encompassing both the Dharma and its metaphors. Question: Although the compositions of past and present have extensively propagated the Holy Teaching, there is concern that demonic activities (*māra-karman*) may arise;
thus, all [authors] first take refuge in the Triple Gem and request their protective empowerment, desiring that the teaching endure and circulate for a long time.
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "I bow my head to the one who is perfectly pure in the nature of consciousness. Furthermore, as the *Abhidharmakośa* says:
"Homage to such teachers of the Dharma as they truly are," and so forth. Furthermore, the *Commentary on the Hundred Dharmas* (*Bai fa shu*) says:

"Now, the ultimate principle is profound and mysterious. And the *Ci'en Commentary* (*Ci'en shu*) says: "We have heard that the ultimate awakening [is both] provisional and real," and so on; these are all expressions of reverent homage.

Why, then, does this present *Yao* (Excerpts) not offer refuge, but instead directly extols the virtue of the precepts? Answer: There are many interpretations. The first states: "Generally, there are two kinds of reverent homage: first, the implicit (*ming*)."

Therefore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The reason why the Sangha precedes the Buddha is that the Way relies on individuals for its propagation; this is the natural course of worldly affairs.

When Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna first arrived, they manifested the outward forms and deportment of the Sangha, describing the five vehicles as the causes of goodness and clarifying the three miserable realms as the results of evil."
This is the manifestation of the Buddha’s majestic form (*buddha-vigraha*). This Dharma is profound and vast; it is not something that can be opened up by ordinary or inferior beings.

Therefore, an image was depicted upon the cool terrace. Inferring from what has been taught, this is the manifestation of the Buddha’s majestic form. (The preceding section contains four points, etc.; this collectively clarifies the Chapter on the Triple Gem.)
"Relying on the teachings to establish the practice of concentration and wisdom—its merit is peerless. This clarifies the excellence of practice. "Relying" means to depend upon.

"Teachings" refers to the Vinaya teachings (also called the Three Piṭakas). "Establishing" means to institute. "Practice" refers to progressive cultivation. "Concentration" is that which is elucidated by the Sūtras.
Regarding the elucidation of the meaning of "wisdom" (*prajñā*): "merit" (*guṇa*) refers to functional efficacy.

The phrase "none can equal it" intends to clarify that the monastic community of monks and nuns, by relying upon the Vinaya teachings to establish their practice, achieve a merit superior to that of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom; thus, it is said that none can equal them. Question: Why are they not equal? Answer:

This is explained according to their relative superiority and inferiority. Concentration is able to realize the mind, while wisdom is able to sever delusions. [The character] "qu" (from the *Song* edition) is taken as...

It is particularly excellent. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "If one were apart from the discernment of phenomena (*pravicaya-dharma*), there would certainly be no superior means capable of extinguishing the various afflictions.

Based on this, it follows that ethical discipline (*śīla*) is not equal to wisdom (*prajñā*). When we say they are "not equal," this is said provisionally with respect to those who have newly entered the Buddha-dharma and practice according to the teachings;

among the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*), ethical discipline occupies the foremost position. The severing of delusions and the realization of the path arise through both discipline and wisdom, just as birth arises from being bound [to the womb].
Therefore, the *Śīla-sūtra* says: "When precepts are pure and wisdom is present, one attains the foremost path. Furthermore, when *śīla* is purified, *samādhi* manifests before one.
Moreover, the *Tattvasiddhi* states: "Precepts are like seizing a thief; concentration and wisdom are like killing the thief.

Since the precepts must first seize the thief, just as they do now, this work extensively propagates the teachings of the Vinaya; therefore, it specifically rejoices in *śīla*, desiring that it be put into practice.
People revere and honor this teaching. The phrase "above, relying on the teaching" refers to the *vinaya*, which serves as the expressive medium (*vācaka*);
the phrase "below, concentration and wisdom" refers to the two things expressed (*vācya*). This is intended as a concise abbreviation (unlike the confused explanations of various other schools).
That the abiding and maintaining of the Buddha’s various scriptures occurs here where the chanting ceases—this clarifies the excellence of the teaching (*jiao*).

That the multitude of dharmas abide and are maintained within the various scriptures—this refers to the fact that abiding and maintaining arises from practice, while the teaching clarifies practice. Since [the teaching] abides within [practice], the textual expressions it clarifies are naturally preeminent.
Previously, the teaching was raised to manifest what is clarified by the teaching; now, practice is raised to manifest the teaching that clarifies practice.

Regarding this teaching, both aspects are mentioned interchangeably, as the agent and the object are distinct. According to the *Jiaochao* (Explanatory Commentary): "Abiding" (*zhu*) means to dwell for a long time; "sustaining" (*chi*) means to maintain.
Because one dwells for a long time and maintains the World-Honored One’s teachings, it is called "abiding in and sustaining the Buddha-dharma.

As for the phrase "the various texts cease their chanting": "various" (*qun*) means many; "texts" (*ji*) refers to scriptures and treatises. Since the sūtras and śāstras are numerous, they are called "various texts. "Cease" (*xi*)...

"Zhe" (者) means "to cease"; "chang" (唱) means "to explain. The Vinaya remains for a long time to sustain the Dharma. During the age of the Semblance Dharma, monasteries were established to instruct the laity and the fourfold assembly of monks;
through the *karmavācanā* procedures, they administered punishments, banishment, and the seven types of grave and light transgressions.
For twelve thousand years, the true regulations did not fall into ruin—all of this was implemented by means of the Vinaya. As for the other two [collections], at that time—
For now, let us cease further discussion; thus it is said, "At this point, the chanting is suspended" (with the double heading as indicated).
Next, we shall distinguish its rise and decline by examining the Dharma in relation to the times.

Since the preceding section praised the precepts—the signified meaning—and revealed the excellence of the texts that signify them, we have not yet translated these texts for their widespread propagation. Therefore, based on this teaching, we shall now examine its application in relation to the times.
Regarding its flourishing and, by extension, its decline and cessation: because this reveals the profound intent behind its composition, it is divided into two sections (as follows).

As for the phrase "from the time [the Buddha] personally [taught] the scriptures," this passage has two meanings: first, that the Buddha specifically propagated the precepts because they possess superior virtue;
second, one must understand that the scriptural teachings are the Buddha’s own direct pronouncements. Regarding the phrase "since the Great Master was in the world":
"Freedom" means liberation. "Great" means that it simplifies the small. It is the most honored within the three realms, and its virtue is unsurpassed.
Therefore, the treatise fully explains four meanings: first, greatness of cause, which is the vow to deliver all sentient beings; second, greatness of fruit, which is the realization of great bodhi;

third, greatness of the principle realized, which is True Suchness (tathatā) pervading the entire dharma-realm; and fourth, greatness of the realizing wisdom, which consists of the four wisdoms, such as the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom. III.
One who receives the two fruits of the realms is called a "Teacher" (*śāstṛ*). *Sati* means "to abide"; *loka* means "interval.

In common parlance, it is said that "generations" (*lokas*) refer to one generation being the succession of a son following his father, or thirty years constituting a generation. In the internal teaching (Buddhism), it is said that *loka* refers to the "world" (*loka-dhātu*).

The term *loka* (world) signifies that which is subject to destruction, impermanence, and lacks long-term stability; because one dwells within it, it is called a "world" (*loka*). There are two types of worlds:

first, the world of matter (*bhājana-loka*), which has atoms as its substance. Because it is subject to flux and destruction, it is called a "world," and because one dwells within it, it is termed a "world.

Second, the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), which has the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as its substance. As these too are subject to flux, they are called a "world," and because one dwells within them, it is so named.

[The explanation of the names is concluded. Now, to briefly clarify the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of their manifestation: regarding the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), its formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness cycle without end.
Once it has been formed, it abides; once it has abided, it is destroyed; once it has been destroyed, it becomes empty. In this manner, twenty kalpas elapse, totaling eighty kalpas.
There are many such variations as clarified in other places; what is discussed here is the period of increase (*vivarta*).
The *apacayakalpa* (aeon of decrease). This refers to the destruction of this world by the three calamities: the fire calamity destroys the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first dhyāna;

the water calamity destroys the second dhyāna; and the wind calamity destroys the third dhyāna. The fourth dhyāna is not subject to destruction by these calamities; the other two calamities are as explained elsewhere.
Now, let us first discuss how fire destroys the desire realm and the first dhyāna. At what specific time does this destruction occur?

For now, within the twenty intermediate kalpas of this current abiding kalpa, we are currently in the ninth *apakarṣa-kalpa* (decreasing eon). When the human lifespan is one hundred years, a Muni appears;
after his parinirvāṇa, the lifespan decreases by one year every hundred years. As it thus decreases down to ten years, a minor triad of calamities (*trikalpa*) arises. That is to say:
Warfare, pestilence, forced labor, and famine afflict sentient beings. Following the period when the human lifespan is ten years, the world enters the *utsarpiṇī-kalpa* (the aeon of increase).
It increases by one year every hundred years. As stated in the *Kalpa-śāstra*: "The son’s age doubles that of his father" (*Aśoka-sūtra* also says this).

Thus it increases until the lifespan reaches eighty-four thousand years; at that point, the ninth *avasarpinī-kalpa* (aeon of decrease) begins. Furthermore, when the lifespan decreases back down to eighty thousand years, Maitreya will appear in the world.
There is further decrease and increase. When the fifteenth aeon of decrease arrives, ninety-five Buddhas appear one after another.
This continues until the twentieth aeon, which consists of increase only, without decrease. When this increase reaches eighty-four thousand years, the kalpa of abiding is complete.
Within this process, one must employ three propositions for analysis: the first aeon involves only decrease and no increase; the last...
In one kalpa there is only increase; in the final kalpa there is only increase and no decrease. During the eighteen intermediate kalpas, there is one increase followed by one decrease.
At present, the world is about to be destroyed. There are two modes of destruction: first, nineteen kalpas of destroying sentient beings; second, one kalpa of destroying the non-sentient environment.
Regarding sentient beings, the three lower realms are destroyed first, followed by humans and devas. As for the lower [realms]...
Among the three [types of destruction], the hells are destroyed first. Thus the treatise says: "Destruction begins with the non-arising [of beings] in hell.
This means that when this world is about to be destroyed, no new sentient beings are born in the Avīci and other hells; at that point, the kalpa of destruction (saṃvarta-kalpa) truly begins.

Those whose karmic retribution for offenses has been fully exhausted transmigrate to the Second Dhyāna heaven. As for those whose karma is not yet complete, as well as those who have newly incurred such karma, they remain [in the lower realms] for the time being.

They are transferred to the hells within other world-systems (accordingly, first the Avīci hell is destroyed, then the seven upper hot hells, and further the eight cold hells and their sentient beings).
Next, the asuras, hungry ghosts, animals, and so forth are destroyed, and they are all reborn among human beings. Subsequently, humans and devas are destroyed;
among the four continents of Jambudvīpa, the southern continent is destroyed first. When it is about to be destroyed, ten billion flying yakṣas patrol the sky.
He proclaimed: "At the end of this kalpa, there will be ten billion people who, upon hearing these words, will feel revulsion and fear.

First, one person—without a teacher and by the natural law of things—will sit and attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Upon arising from that concentration, he will proclaim: 'The bliss of concentration is exceedingly tranquil.
The others will all follow his example, sitting and attaining the first dhyāna. From this point on, when they pass away, they will all be reborn in the first dhyāna heaven. East and West.

The continents are likewise. First, those in the Northern Continent are born among the gods of the six heavens of the desire realm (this marks the destruction of the human realm). Subsequently, the six heavens of the desire realm are destroyed.
The sons of heaven therein are all reborn in the first dhyāna (the destruction of sentient beings in the desire realm is complete). Next, the first dhyāna is destroyed.

At that time, there remains a single sentient being in the first dhyāna who, without a teacher, sits and attains the concentration of the second dhyāna. Having arisen from that concentration, he proclaims: "The joy and bliss born of concentration are most delightful and most tranquil. The others...
They all followed his example. Upon emerging from concentration, he proclaimed: "The joy and bliss born of concentration are peaceful. The others all followed his example.
Having emerged from concentration, they passed away and were all reborn in the Second Dhyāna. Thus far, this has been based on the great calamities that destroy the realm of desire.
This is explained up to the first dhyāna of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). As for the destruction by water, it affects the second dhyāna;
as for the destruction by wind, it affects the third dhyāna. All sentient beings are born in the fourth dhyāna, because the fourth dhyāna is not destroyed by the three calamities.

Therefore, the Buddha taught that the fourth dhyāna is called the "Unshakable Ground" (*aniñjya-bhūmi*), comparable to a lamp in a sealed room (as described at length in the treatise). Thus, from the destruction of sentient beings in the hells up to the existence in the first dhyāna—
In this manner, it takes nineteen kalpas for the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) to be destroyed; this is called the destruction of the world of sentient beings.

Next, during the one kalpa in which the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) is destroyed, although sentient beings have perished and the world is empty of people, the places where they once dwelt remain like an empty house.
Now, when this [receptacle world] is about to be destroyed, the intensity of the sun increases fourfold, and the rivers and ponds dry up.
The grasses, trees, and firewood are consumed and destroyed. Next, two or three suns appear, whereby all rivers and streams completely dry up, and the waters of the great ocean decrease by one-third.
Furthermore, four or five suns appear, causing the waters of the ocean to suddenly vanish. After this, for six or seven days, [six suns] manifest.
All mountains and rocks melt away; the great ocean and Mount Sumeru simultaneously burst into flames, like burning resin wood, leaving nothing behind.
Regarding this, the masters of the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* offer two interpretations. The first says: when this world is being formed, seven suns appear beneath the Yugandhara Mountains;
one is emitted at a time to illuminate the world until the end of the kalpa, after which another is emitted.
The other six [elements] emerge. Second, it is said that on this single day alone, the intensity is double that of the usual seven days;

the rivers and seas dry up, the various mountains burn with intense flames, and all three wheels of the continents are completely incinerated. Therefore, the treatise says: "Destruction proceeds from the hells, not from their non-arising."

When the receptacle world has been completely exhausted, a question is asked: "Since both are equally subject to destruction, why do sentient beings take nineteen kalpas [to be destroyed], while non-sentient things require only one kalpa?

The answer states that the *Śāstra* says: "Sentient beings involve individual karma (*pratyeka-karman*) which is difficult to transform, and thus their duration is long; non-sentient things involve collective karma (*sādhāraṇa-karman*) which is easy to transform, and thus their duration is short.
(The above explains the destruction of the sixfold world-system by fire over twenty kalpas). Next, for twenty kalpas, the upper and lower realms remain as they were.
[Black (this emptiness lasts for twenty kalpas). Next, the twenty kalpas are distinguished. In the first kalpa, the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) is formed;

in the subsequent nineteen kalpas, the sentient world (*sattva-loka*) is formed. Regarding the formation of the receptacle world in the first kalpa, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The eon of formation begins from the arising of wind.
This means that subtle winds arise beneath the second dhyāna, passing down through the first dhyāna, where they reach the former abode of the Brahmā King.
Thereupon, he established the palaces of the Brahmā Kings along with the gods of the Brahma-purohita assembly (thus concluding the three heavens of the first dhyāna).

Furthermore, a subtle wind reached the desire realm, establishing the abodes for the four heavens of the space-dwellers. Next, a fierce wind arose, swirling down to the lower part of the desire realm.
At the location of the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), a wind-circle is formed to serve as the foundation of the world-system. The dimensions of this wheel’s four sides total six thousand worlds;
it is one hundred and sixty billion *yojanas* in height and breadth. Its shape is like a shallow basin with its rim turned upward, surrounding and supporting the water so that it does not disperse.
This wheel is so solid and hard that even if the god Nārāyaṇa were to strike it with a vajra-pestle, it would suffer no damage.

Once the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) has been formed, there is the Ābhāsvara Heaven (*Ābhāsvara-deva*) in the Second Dhyāna. A "Golden-Treasury Cloud" (*suvarṇa-kośa-abhra*) spreads forth—its density being like that of gold in a treasury, hence it is called the "Golden-Treasury.
Once this cloud has spread throughout the trichiliocosm (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*), it sends down rain with drops as large as chariot axles.
Resting upon the wind-circle, it forms the water-circle (*jala-maṇḍala*), with a thickness of one billion one hundred and twenty thousand *yojanas*. Furthermore, within this water-circle...

Internally, it measures thirty-two million *yojanas*. Just as when a single dish of milk is boiled down until it solidifies into a golden wheel (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*), the remaining eighty million *yojanas* constitute the water wheel (*abbhakūṭa*).
Once the golden wheel has formed, the Ābhāsvara gods again rain down upon the golden wheel to form the ocean waters.
Through the ripening of the karma of sentient beings, skillful winds strike and agitate [the waters], forming Mount Sumeru by means of its four secret locations.

It is said that [Mount Meru] is composed of silver in the east, crystal (sphatika) in the west, lapis lazuli (vaiḍūrya) in the south, and gold in the north. It rises eighty thousand yojanas above the water, and its depth below the water is likewise.
At its summit are situated the palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; furthermore, at the four tiers halfway up its slopes, the abodes of the Four Great Kings are located.

2. Mount Axle-Holder (the mountain has various peaks shaped like carriage axles); 3. Mount Rafter-Wood (the mountain has hollowed trees shaped like rafters); 4.

That mountain resembles the nose of that deity; thus it is so named). Seventh is Matsya-mukha Mountain (the shape of the mountain is like the mouth of a fish). Furthermore, within each of these seven mountains, there is a fragrant sea.
Moreover, outside the seven golden mountains, the Great Cakravāḍa Mountains are placed encircling them. Within the Iron Ring Mountains, there is a salt sea.

Within the salt ocean, the four great continents are situated as the dwelling places for the human realm (*manuṣya-gati*), formed from earth and stone through the karmic retribution of sentient beings.
First is Jambudvīpa (so named after the *jambu* tree); second is Aparagoyānī (translated as "Cow-Trade," for there cattle serve as the medium of exchange);

third is Pūrvavideha (translated as "Eastern Superior Body," because the physical forms there are superior to those of the southern continent); and fourth is Uttarakuru (translated as "Northern Abode," or alternatively "Superior Birth"). The above constitute the human beings.
Having completed the formation of the four continents, he further established the abodes of asuras, hungry ghosts, and animals along the shores of the great ocean.
Moreover, beneath the southern continent (Jambudvīpa), he placed the palace of King Yama and the locations of the eighteen hells.

In this manner, during one kalpa, the receptacle world (bhājanaloka) was formed; although its structural components were present, no sentient beings yet inhabited it—just as a house may be finished today, yet remains empty.
It remains uninhabited. Thus, one cycle of increase and decrease has passed (the explanation of the receptacle world is now complete).
Next, regarding the formation of the sentient world over nineteen kalpas, the treatise states:

At that time, a certain devaputra from the second dhyāna, due to the ripening of subsequent karma, was reborn in the first dhyāna as the Great Brahmā King. Although he was the Brahmā King, he had no retinue; he remained entirely alone.
Because he remained [there]. The Sūtra says: "After one cycle of increase and one cycle of decrease, a thought arose in him: 'There is not a single person who shares my lot.

As soon as the Brahmā King had this thought, various sons of gods from the higher realms—possessing karma to be reborn in a subsequent existence—descended to be born in the First Dhyāna as his retinue;
these were the Brahmapurohitas and the Brahmapārṣadyas. The King said: 'I first gave rise to this thought, and you have already been born.'"
"He is my son. He also said, "I have come here because of the Brahmā King's thought; he is my father.

At that time, the kalpa of formation was completed. Thus the treatise says: "Formation proceeds from the arising of wind until the first birth in the hells" (the above constitutes twenty intermediate kalpas;
the completion of the two types of worlds in the kalpa of formation is finished). After formation, there is further abiding; subsequently, after destruction, it returns to emptiness.

It is like a waterwheel, ultimately without end. Now, we are precisely at the beginning of the kalpa of abiding; this clarifies that within the ninth period of decline, the Muni appeared in the world.

[This] interval was for the sake of transforming sentient beings; therefore, it is said that the Great Master was in the world (one should know that the account of the eightfold manifestation of enlightenment here does not fully accord with the meaning of the text).

"Good son, there are four kinds of persons who can protect the True Dharma, establish the True Dharma, and bring great benefit and compassion to the world. For...

From this, one may attain the second fruit.
The second reliance is the fruit of the non-returner (*anāgāmin*). The third reliance is the fruit of the arhat. The fourth reliance is the fruit of the arhat. Question:

If this is the Mahāyāna, for what reason has the four fruits of the Hīnayāna and so forth been correlated with it above? Answer:
