Now, since those who transcend the world rely upon the four reliances (*catvāri pratiśaraṇāni*) and must practice the correct conduct of these four reliances, the next section distinguishes the practice of the four reliances.
Thus, the Vinaya states: "The practitioners of the Three Vehicles universally rely upon these for their sustenance: first, rag-robes (to cover the body); second, alms-food (to avoid hunger);

third, sitting at the foot of a tree (to provide shelter from the elements); and fourth, medicinal dregs (to treat ailments). This explanation is provided here primarily in terms of the prohibitions (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*). However—

Each has its own distinct opening, which is not similar to what Deva established. Regarding the "Three Dharmas and Four Reliances," according to the *Guijing yi* (Ritual of Taking Refuge and Reverence), it begins with the initial worthy and culminates in the ultimate sage.
Humans rely on the untainted (*anāsrava*), while the essence of dharmas is emptiness. Based on this, by relying on the eternal principle, one is free from error and inversion;
therefore, they establish the reliance on Dharma to manifest the definitive standard. First, rely on the Dharma and not on the person (meaning the Dharma...).

1) The dharma of intrinsic nirvāṇa does not rely on the dharma of the śrāvakas. 2) Rely on the meaning, not on the words (that is, rely on the meaning that is realized, and do not depend on words that are merely ornamental).
Third, relying on wisdom (*jñāna*) and not on consciousness (*vijñāna*); this means that while the nature of consciousness ceases, wisdom should abide.

Fourth, relying on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and not on sūtras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*); this means that the scriptures of the unsurpassed Mahāyāna are of definitive meaning, whereas the textual teachings of the two vehicles are called provisional.

Although these three types of reliances are distinct, they are all the practice of a single person; one must possess these three to be fit for propagating the teaching. Now, there are twenty-four members.
The Bodhisattvas, one by one, successively transmitted the lamp so that it shone brightly without interruption. Thus it is said: "Extending even to the Four Reliances, their legacy remains unaltered.

"Legacy" (yí) refers to what remains; "wind" (fēng) refers to the teachings. "Unaltered" (wù) is a name established in contrast to "existence" (yǒu); "altered" (tì) means to abolish or fall into ruin.
Question: Why is the wind used as a metaphor for teaching? Answer: It is because, in the world, the wind possesses the power to cause beautiful grasses to bend.
Thus, a Confucian text says: "The wind is formed by the mutual striking of the vessels of yin and yang. It further states that it arises from the tiger’s roar.

The east wind is called *gufeng* (the valley wind; spring wind). "Valley" (*gu*) means to nourish; because it nourishes the myriad things, it is so named. The south wind is called *kaifeng* (the joyful wind).

The summer wind is called *kai-feng* (the "auspicious wind"). *Kai* means "to grow long"; it is so named because it nurtures all things to full maturity. The western wind is called *liang-feng* (the "cooling wind")—it is the autumn wind. *Liang* means "to thin out"; it is so named because it causes all things to wither and diminish.

The north wind is called *feng* (the winter wind that rolls up things; when all things have reached maturity, it is called "completion"). The reason these winds of the four directions differ from one another is as follows.
In the east, the qi of clamor first arises; in the south, it beats upon the myriad things to bring them to completion; in the west, the golden wind ripens the things;

in the north, the yin qi cools and distinguishes, causing the myriad things to wither and dry. Since the four seasons are thus distinct, there is growth in spring, development in summer, withering in autumn, and falling in winter.
The winds of the world proceed in this manner, and the teaching is likewise so: it is able to cause the practitioner to be divided into five groups of five.
The Dharma-body first arises and subsequently grows, described as the flowering and fruition [of the teachings]. At no time do these fail to arise from the instruction;
therefore, it is said that while the Buddha was in the world, his influence spread widely. After his *parinirvāṇa*, the Bodhisattvas of the Four Reliances continued the scriptures.
Although they were divided into the five distinct Nikāyas and so forth, they were not called "corruptions" or "substitutions," because the Four Reliances served as their sustaining support. And...
When the Buddha was present, there were no differences [in the Dharma]; therefore, it is said that "the legacy remains unaltered" (the commentary notes this as the conclusion of the section).

Second, regarding the errors and substitutions in the maintenance of the teachings during the Semblance and Final Ages, this is divided into three parts: first, a general clarification of the shifting of times and the substitution of teachings;

second, a specific clarification of the gains and losses in the transmission and maintenance of the teachings in this land; third, the phrase "reaching unto the matter," which refers generally to the Western [Heaven].

During the age of the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka*), the teachings became corrupted and declined; because they were taught predominantly in this region, [the period] was moved to precede the three losses (which differs from the *Xianzheng lun*).

*Dai* means "to reach"; *you* means "to arise from"; *xiangsi* means "semblance. *Ji* refers to the end. This means it generally clarifies that the Buddha-dharma, as a whole, consists of three periods:
first, the Period of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), lasting one thousand years. *Zheng* means "sage" or "holy," and it possesses [all qualities].

The four dharmas of doctrine, principle, practice, and fruition are the very essence of *tathatā* (suchness), the basis for both ordinary beings and sages. From this, the twelve divisions of the teachings flow forth;

all these contain the practices that are to be expounded. By practicing in accordance with the teachings, one will certainly attain the realization of the fruit, no different from when the Buddha was alive;
therefore, it is called the "True Dharma" (*saddharma*). Second is the period of the "Semblance Dharma" (*pratirūpa-dharma*), which also lasts for one thousand years, though there is only...

Third, the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*) lasts for ten thousand years. Because there is little fruit or realization and it resembles—though does not truly embody—the discernment of the correct Dharma, it is called the "Semblance Dharma. Third, the Final Dharma (*paścima-dharma*) lasts for ten thousand years.

As the time since the Sage has passed becomes remote and sentient beings lack wisdom, they possess the scriptural teachings yet are unwilling to practice them; compared to the periods of the Correct and Semblance Dharmas, this is the case here.

This will serve as a gradual introduction; however, there are only the first two [stages], and because the practice and its fruit are entirely absent, it is called the Dharma of the Final Age (*mofa*).

Furthermore, during the second millennium of the Semblance Dharma (*xiangfa*), the first five hundred years still possessed the realization of the fruit, while the latter five hundred years possessed only the first three.
Now, when this *Chao* (Excerpts) was composed, one thousand five hundred and seventy-four years had passed since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; that is, the Semblance Dharma.

It is the end of the Middle [Period]. Hence it is called the "Semblance Age" (*xiàngjì*). (The common interpretation of old times, which explains this solely by means of the Final Dharma Period [*mòfǎ*], is incorrect.

Regarding the phrase "the times have become increasingly debased and erroneous": "times" refers to the era; "become increasingly" (*zhuǎn*) refers to shifting and changing. The Semblance Age is not like the True Dharma Age; the end of the Semblance Age is not like the beginning of the Semblance Age.

Thus it is said that "the times have become increasingly [debased]. "Debased" (*jiāo*) means thin or meager; "erroneous" (*é*) means delusive and spurious. It is like having objects in the world that are neither square nor...
"Round. Furthermore, that which lacks sharp edges is called "corrupt" (*wò*). People propagating the Dharma today are not equal to those of the True and Semblance Dharma periods;
hence it is said to be "corrupt. Regarding the phrase "those who contend at the tips of their lips and tongues": "contend" means to compete; "tip" (*fēng*) means a blade.

The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it refers to the edge of a knife. It is said that there are three "tips" in the world: the tip of the tongue for the eloquent debater, the tip of the brush for the literary scholar, and the tip of the blade for the warrior. Of these—
The three [extremes] are extremely sharp like blades. Of the two blades—the pen and the brush—they only harm the physical body.
As for the blade of the tongue, it harms both the physical body and the Dharma-body; that is, when one speaks words that injure others, it is like a blade. Liu Zi said: "The mouth contains a blade."

To move [the tongue] is to harm others. This present contention of blades is the blade of the tongue. Furthermore, because the matters involved are shallow and superficial, it is said to be "between the lips and the tongue.
Regarding the phrase "stirring up discursive arguments about formless matters": "stirring" (*gǔ*) means to agitate; "discursive argument" (*lùn*) means to measure or deliberate.

Both such agitation and deliberation lack canonical authority. "Form" (*xíng*) means completion or manifestation. All such deliberations and measurements originate solely from the depths of one's own breast.

[This] discussion does not constitute an authoritative source (the first interpretation). Furthermore, another interpretation: "Form" (*xing*) refers to physical form, meaning the rules and rituals of the *vinaya*.
These are the actions performed by the body of a bhikṣu, and are thus called "formal matters. Now, [the present case] establishes its own regulations contrary to the Dharma;

lacking canonical precedents, these are not actions performed by the body of a bhikṣu. Therefore, it is called "a matter that is not formal. Thus, the subsequent text states: "In all instances of transformation..."
The *Zhishuocheng* (止出應) contains no exposition whatsoever regarding that orthodox teaching; when matters arise, it employs non-Dharmic language that results in distortion and confusion.

(This interpretation in the *Souxuanji* is also tenable, though there are other interpretations which are not correct). This [text] is concise; approximately five hundred years later, those in the Western Regions did not rely on the characteristics of the teachings but instead relied solely on their own fabrications.
This is an example of the mutual refutation between the characteristics of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles (etc.).

Second, a specific clarification: it is said that there are errors in the transmission of this [text]. [The author] sets forth the topical divisions (*kāṇḍa*) as follows... Regarding the phrase "the reason why" up to "only":

the two characters "so-yi" (the reason why) function as a prepositional particle referring back to what precedes. This means that the preceding section clarified that in the Western Land during the Age of Semblance (*pratirūpaka-yuga*), the four reliances were lacking and the flourishing succession of Bodhisattva scriptures had been interrupted;
this was precisely at a time of corruption and decline. As for this [Eastern] land, [the teaching] has long been heard of. Therefore, he marks the "reason why."

This is based on the characters. "Zhen" (震) is the name of a country; "Ling" (嶺) is the designation for a mountain range. In Sanskrit, it is called *Cīna*, or sometimes *Cindana*, *Tandan*, *Jinana*, or *Jinan*.
These are variations in the weight of the Sanskrit pronunciation. Collectively, this is translated as the Land of Han. According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*:

Two transcriptions for this name are established. The first is *Jina*, which here means "Country of Renowned Objects" (meaning that this country produces many extraordinary things and is thus renowned among all nations;

alternatively, it is written with the character for "heaven," or it is said to mean "Martial Country," though this is likely incorrect). This is a term of praise. The second is *Jian*, which here means "Frontier or Barbarian Country.
This is a term of disparagement. Furthermore, the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: *Mahājina*, which here means "Great Han Country. Now, regarding the present [term]...
"Zhen" (震) is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term. Ancient records all state "Zhen," referring to the kingdom of Zhenxi (東震以西國) to the west;

this is regarded as the Palace of Zhen (the East). "Dan" (旦) refers to dawn; because when the sun first rises it illuminates the eastern corner like cinnabar (dan), it is also called "Qidan" (其丹) and so forth.
This is not the original meaning. It is likely because the sound of "Zhen" is identical to the pronunciation of the Palace of Zhen in this region; having already been translated, it was not changed.

The name is not [phonetically] consistent; this is an explanation of the meaning according to the Sanskrit pronunciation. As for "Ling" (嶺), it refers to the Pamir Mountains (蔥嶺). It is so named because the mountains abound in onions (*gṛñjana*).

The reason both [the eastern and western] Ling regions are designated here is to avoid confusion. To the east of the Pamir Mountains lie the six kingdoms of the Hu people, where the Buddha once traveled and the Dharma was propagated.
What is transmitted here, however, pertains entirely to the territories west of the mountains, from which the Buddha-dharma has come to us. It passed...

This is because of this mountain ridge; it distinguishes [this tradition] from the non-Buddhist customs of the Hu kingdoms of the Six States. Regarding the term "transmission of the teaching" (*chuánjiào*): "transmission" (*chuán*) refers to the dissemination [of the Dharma], and "teaching" (*jiào*) refers to the doctrinal system.

In the fifth year of the Yongping era, during the reign of Emperor Ming, the second sovereign of the Later Han, he was moved by a dream of a golden man (the origins of which are recorded in the fortieth fascicle of the *Yuanqi*;

the details of its arrival and the narrative thereof may be learned from that source). In the seventh year, he dispatched envoys; in the tenth year, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna entered Luoyang; and in the eleventh year—
He founded monasteries. He sincerely awakened to the Buddha-dharma. At that time, the teachings of Śākyamuni flourished greatly, and those who left the household life were exceedingly numerous;
hence it is called the "Transmission of the Teachings. Regarding the phrase "heard by nine generations": "nine" refers to a number, and "generation" (*dai*) refers to a sovereign dynasty.

If one calculates the sovereign dynasties of this land from the beginning of creation through the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, down to the intercalary Qin and the Former Han, from this point onward—
Prior to this, as the Buddha-dharma had not yet spread, these matters were not discussed at all in this land;

rather, the account begins from the time of Emperor Ming of the Later Han dynasty until the present, spanning nine successive dynasties: 1. **Later Han** (Liu dynasty, capital at Luoyang; fourteen sovereigns for a total of one hundred fifteen years).

2. **Wei** (Cao dynasty, capital at Luoyang; five sovereigns for a total of forty-five years). 3. **Western Jin** (Sima dynasty, capital at Luoyang; four sovereigns for a total of fifty-two years. It was subsequently destroyed by the Former Zhao. Five of its princes crossed the Yangtze River southward to the region of Ling [Jiangnan]).

1. The Wang of Langya (Liang): He assumed the mandate and established himself as the sovereign of Eastern Jin, with the capital at Jianye; together they lasted for one hundred and thirty years. 2. The four Song dynasties (the Liu family): They took the capital at Jianye;

there were eight rulers, totaling fifty-nine years. 3. The five Qi dynasties (the Xiao family): They took the capital at Jianye; there were seven rulers, totaling two hundred and thirteen years. 4. The six Liang dynasties (also the Xiao family): They likewise took the capital at Jianye;

there were four rulers, totaling fifty-four years. 5. The seven Chen dynasties (the Chen family): They also took the capital at Jianye; there were four rulers, totaling thirty-three years. 6. The eight Sui dynasty (the Yang family): There were three rulers. The first, Emperor Wen, resided in Chang’an; the next, the capital was at Yangdu (in present-day Jiangsu); finally, Emperor Gong also resided in Chang’an; together they lasted for three... [years].

The eighteen dynasties (spanning nineteen years to the present day). Their reigns began with the Wu [Zetian] period and continued until the beginning of the Jingfu era, totaling approximately one hundred and seventy years.

Nevertheless, among these nine dynasties, there were also inconsistencies in their reckoning: the South took the Chen dynasty as the starting point for its count, while the North took the Zhou dynasty.

Thus, after the four great figures such as Yuwen Jue of the Later Zhou received the mandate from the Yuanwei (the Wei being the successor to the Kuoba [Quba] lineage, and Yuan being derived from the name of the founder), they succeeded to the positions of the Chen and Liang dynasties.
Now, these nine dynasties must necessarily be enumerated. This refers to the fact that the Zhou and Chen were contemporaneous, though distinguished as North and South.

Since the Zhou dynasty began two years after the Chen, and as the Chen’s commencement was earlier, it is appropriate to include the Chen and exclude the Zhou (those who argue for the inclusion of the Zhou have likely failed to investigate its inner significance).
Now, the nine cycles of transformation do not exceed five principles: first, the mutual generation of the Five Elements, such as [the sequence] from Han (Fire) to Wei (Earth).

Earth: Jin; Metal: Song; Water: Qi; Wood: Liang (the above follow the sequence of mutual generation). Chen subsequently returned to Sui. Sui is the King of Great Virtue (the ruler is addressed as such); Earth does not generate it.
After the Great Sui, the Zhou dynasty received the abdication [of power]; this is Wood. Wood generates Fire. Zhou received the position from Yuan Wei;

Wei is Water. Water is able to generate Wood. Tang received the abdicated position from Sui; Tang is the King of Earth Virtue (the word "king" is pronounced with an departing tone); Fire generates it.

Because it was made of earth. Second, the King of Chu transmitted it to [Cai] (pronounced *cong*). This was the First Emperor of Qin. He obtained a jade from Lan-tian, four inches square with one corner slightly missing.
The *jiao* and *chi* dragons were carved in fine detail. Upon it was a coiled dragon and a hidden phoenix; he sought out Li Si to examine its markings.

On both sides of the small green jade were eight characters each. The inscription read: "Heaven has conferred the mandate upon him; may his life be long and his prosperity eternal. Furthermore, on the upper side was a coiled dragon.
The inscription reads: "Receiving the Mandate of Heaven, the Emperor’s longevity shall flourish. From Qin it was transmitted to Han; from Han to Wei, Jin, Song, and Qi;
reaching the Liang dynasty, it was usurped by the rebel Hou Jing. At Xiqia Temple, it was recovered by the monk Yong.

After Yong, he entrusted it to his disciples, all of whom had the character "Zhi" in their names. Zhi subsequently presented it to the Chen dynasty. From Chen, it was transmitted to Tang. These three dynasties succeeded one another through abdication.

"Position" refers to the abdication of the throne, such as when the Tang dynasty received the mandate of succession from the Sui. "Four" refers to occupying the Central Land, such as Luoyang being the center of the nine provinces.
"Five" refers to children's rhymes, such as those from the Jin period which say: "Five horses float across the river; the smallest ones transform into dragons."

Furthermore, it is said that during the Tang period, "mi mi" (mimmi) and "tang tang" (tanggeng) were all used interchangeably. Moreover, among these five [dynasties], they did not necessarily all exist together;

there were instances of only four, three, or two. Beyond these, there were further peripheral regimes not included within this classification, such as Nanwu and Xishu during the Cao Wei period, Qian Zhao, Houshu, and Qian Liang during the Western Jin, and [the various states] during the Eastern Jin.
The Later Zhao, Former Qin, Later Qin, Later Liang, and other such states were all contemporaneous but did not endure for long;

they were all designated as hegemon rulers. These matters are explained extensively elsewhere, so I shall not elaborate further here. Regarding the phrase "standing out from the masses" (*bà cuì chū lèi*): "standing out from the masses" (*bà cuì*) means to stand out preeminently.
*Cù* (pronounced *bìng zuì fǎn*) means to gather together. When grass grows in a thicket within a hollow, it is called a *cù*. Among them, there may be a single stalk that rises above the rest.
It stands far above others; hence it is said to "pluck out the excellence" (*bà cuì*). To "stand out from one's kind" (*chū lèi*) refers to a person.

"Out" (*chū*) means to transcend; "kind" (*lèi*) refers to a category or class. A gathering of people is called a "class. Among a multitude of people, if one individual’s wisdom and virtue surpass those of the crowd, it is therefore called "standing out from one's kind.
Here, "person" (*rén*) and "grass" (*cǎo*) are discussed in contrast. Regarding "wisdom merely recounts": this refers to the recounting of dharmas through both emotion and wisdom. This section...
Regarding the land of Han: among the nine dynasties, the ancients did not rely on the Vinaya texts, but instead followed secular precedents in their practice.

Their dwelling in emotional intellect and ritual arts was entirely based on personal conjecture and empty speculation. Thus, when there were those who committed transgressions, punishments such as forced labor outside the monastery, the provision of rice, and the use of hoes for harvesting lasted for an entire year;
all of these were matters of arbitrary judgment. Because they practiced such ritual arts according to their own minds, it is said that they merely "described their wisdom."
Furthermore, another commentary states: "The term 'arts' (shu) refers to divine arts. This means that great wisdom is leisurely and expansive, while small wisdom is laborious and constrained.

Great wisdom is like the Way (Dao), whereas small wisdom is like an art (shu). For example, there have been those in antiquity who swallowed needles, ate iron, climbed up onto swords, or ascended blade-ladders."

All of these are provisional designations for the duration of a single lifetime. If one were to take this ritual procedure to convert others, it would not be [the same as] the explanation found in the *Huainanzi* record.
Regarding the statement "desiring to reach the evaluation," there are six phrases in total. The first five are specific, while the final one is general.
When explaining, the single character *yù* (desiring) is applied to the beginning of each of the five phrases, and the single character *zhě* (who/that which) is likewise applied.
Below the five phrases of "Pervasive and Universal Attachment," one may further examine and evaluate them in detail. Each phrase is to be concluded under each of the five phrases (and so forth).
First, regarding the statement "desiring to clarify and manifest the conduct": this may be examined and evaluated in detail. "Desiring" (*yu*) means to hope for or require.
"Clarifying" (*ming*) means to reveal or make manifest. "Manifesting" (*yang*) means to propagate. "Conduct" (*xing*) refers to the [practice] of the assembly...
This refers to the practice throughout the three periods of time. "Ritual" (*yi*) means ritual procedure (*yigui*).

The meaning is that if one wishes to manifest and extol the three modes of conduct and their horizontal patterns and models, one must be one who clearly understands the Vinaya and is proficient in its characteristics; only then can one examine and evaluate them in detail.

This demonstrates that those who possess outstanding wisdom and skillful means are not found within the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* (the treatise on the Middle Way). [Those] who can [attain this] are those who clearly understand the Vinaya. "In detail" (*xiang*) means to scrutinize.

"Commentary" (ping): "Ping" means to discuss. The same applies to all four subsequent phrases. This serves as a counter-illustration that wisdom and skillful means cannot be [objectively] grasped. Second, regarding those who wish to rectify and uphold the teachings of the Buddha: "Kuang" (匡) means to correct.

Upholding. Regarding the semblance-dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*), "teaching" refers to the verbal expression. This means that during the final age of the semblance-dharma, there must be those who provide correction and uphold it.
If one is a person of refined intelligence and mastery of the characteristics of the Vinaya, they may examine and evaluate this in detail;

however, those of mere clever artifice cannot be counted among such ranks. Third, wishing to transmit these models and instructions for the sake of those who have not yet studied... [the text continues].

"Zhe" (者) is a term denoting the appearance of something covering from above down to below; thus, in the scriptures, we find such expressions as "cloud-like and hanging down. "Xun" (尋) means constant or regular.
*Vinaya* is the eternal canon transmitted by the thousand Buddhas. "Fan" (範) means dharma or law. Because the *vinaya*-dharma is the constant law of all Buddhas, it is so designated.
"Xun" (訓) means instruction. It is formed from the character for "speech" with the radical for "river"; that is, speech is like a great river that nourishes the land.

Commentary on the Meaning: Those of later generations are called "unlearned. This implies that if one now wishes to take these teachings and instruct those of the later stream, one must clearly understand and be well-versed in the characteristics of the doctrine; only then can one evaluate it in detail.

As for those like the practitioners of intellectual artifice mentioned above who fall within the scope of critique, they seek to tie together the profound guiding cord that has already been severed—"cord" here meaning to reconnect.
This being so: "Severed" means cut off; "mysterious" (xuan) means wondrous. "Gang" refers to a main rope or net. The *Vinaya* is the main rope of the mysterious and wondrous.
Now that it has been severed, who will continue its flourishing in this age of the Semblance Dharma? Those with clear understanding may examine and evaluate this in detail;
however, those of superior intelligence who recount [the truth] do not fall within the scope of these words. The tree of the five desires has already toppled.

A "great pillar" (*daihyō*) refers to something erected upright. "To topple" (*ten*) means to fall or to overturn. The "great pillar" is a metaphor; it is like the bridges, fords, mountains, rivers, and perilous paths of this world.

When one erects a pillar or a *kṣetra* (stupa/pagoda), it is intended so that those traveling on land may see the pillar and know there is a bridge or road ahead, and those traveling by water may see the pillar and know there is a ford, a ferry, or a place to anchor. Now, this edict [addresses] this...
The Vinaya is taken as the great standard. Its intent is to manifest and show the correct path of the five karmas, so that practitioners, looking toward this standard, shall not become confused.
Now, in this age of the Dharma’s decline, that standard has already fallen. I do not know who might re-establish it. If one possesses clear understanding, they may evaluate it;
those of outstanding talent are not restricted by the requirement for exhaustive scrutiny. Thus ends the first of the five points.
"First, all these [arguments] merely reveal that those who rely on empty voids cannot [be trusted], and so forth.
To say 'is it not so? is to ask 'how could it be? It is not that it is not so. Those who rely on empty voids do not rely on the Teaching.

That which is easily expressed through form and sound—'form' refers to the body and 'sound' refers to the Teaching—does not distinguish between the sufficiency of one's capacity; therefore, form does not discern [it]."
The seven characteristics of what is not [the Dharma] are as follows: "That which is easy by way of sound and difficult by way of practice is for the sake of manifesting purity.

Here, "track" (軌) refers to the rules; "matter" (事) refers to the characteristics of phenomena. "Difficult to perform" means it is not easy. Regarding "manifesting purity": when referring to heaven, it is the sun amidst mist and dew; when referring to earth, it is the source of springs.
This means that if dew descends from heaven, how could it not be pure? Thus, the rules of the Vinaya and the characteristics of phenomena are established by means of these six [points].

Regarding the ten dharmas that distinguish individuals during the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure): the primary basis consists of the first three and the last five, with the second and fourth in between.
From beginning to end, not a single word may be added or omitted. Such ritual procedures are as pure as morning dew; they are truly not easy to master. Thus, the *Zhanguo Ce* says:
"If all people in the world were ghosts and demons, it would be easy to employ cleverness [to deceive them]. (The phrase from the *Shangchao* text, "relying on emptiness is easy," follows here.)

"To depict dogs and horses is difficult to master" (corresponding to the *Heshang chao* [Tiao-zhao + Sheng] section on "the difficulty of the matter and the text"). Next, it clarifies the errors committed by the seven dynasties from the Jin and Song onwards (as indicated by the topical outline). Regarding the passage from "Now, however... to "excessive license":

...it is said that from the time of the Jin and Song onwards, throughout the seven successive dynasties, there were instances of transgressing the principles of adherence and falling into error. This refers to the fact that while the former masters had already established the rules for the *shu* (commentary) and *zhu* (sub-commentary), later generations failed to observe these regulations, resulting in a proliferation of errors and a lack of restraint. Thus, the text states: "Now, however, [the practice] has become excessive. This indicates that although the foundational principles were clear, subsequent scholars neglected them, leading to a state where the boundaries between the primary text and the commentary became blurred and confused. This is what is meant by "excessive license."
This text refers to the Eastern Jin period. Although the Later Qin dynasty possessed the Vinaya, the ancient masters of that time had not refined their study and practice;

thus, there were errors in their teachings, and no commentaries or sub-commentaries were produced. Nevertheless, the two characters [“ran ze”] serve as a transition from the preceding to the following section, meaning "however" or "but.

A former scholar offered one interpretation, stating that those "ancient masters prior to Nanshan" refers to the various virtuous elders who followed the Vinaya for their spiritual cultivation before the time of Master Daoxuan (Nanshan). This...

I fear my understanding may be somewhat superficial and diffuse. For now, I shall simply take one class of ancient masters from the end of the Northern Qi dynasty who composed commentaries; these are those whose names precede the current practitioners.

As for those who "spread [their teachings] across the Vinaya-piṭaka," such ancient masters held firm convictions regarding the Vinaya texts, which do not permit addition or subtraction, but rather require one to apply them by referring directly to the specific matters described.
To "apply" means to refer to a preceding matter and read the relevant passage of the Vinaya text. This is like, for example, when performing the duty of nursing the sick.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* for rewarding labor: one does not inquire about the three robes or the six requisites; rather, all reports are recorded in full. The wording concerning the six requisites is found in the text.
Those who place faith in authentic records maintain that this *karmavācanā* method was taught by the ancient masters as the actual words spoken from the golden mouth of the Buddha.

This is certainly not an arbitrary claim; its transmission to this land is a direct translation. One should simply recite it according to the text, for it is a reliable record that must not be expanded upon or abbreviated.
As for those who rely on external conditions (*paratantra*), their current practice is incorrect. "Entrusting" (*yituo*) means to entrust oneself;

"conditions" (*yuan*) refers to the conditions for what is being performed, namely the intermediate state between two or three [moments]. This is indeed abundant. To recite strictly according to the text is considered prolix, yet when applied to actual matters, it is not so.
This becomes an abuse (the first part; by citing this explanation, the rest can be understood as examples).
The second section states "furthermore, up to the maximum," which refers to the *saṃgha*. This is because of the aforementioned reliance on attachment.
This is already one layer of error; now there is further the addition of speculative assertions, which is why it is said "furthermore.
When a student studies, it is not that they do not study; "refinement" means thorough mastery, and "broadness" means vast learning. Thus, the *Lìqǐngzhòng yí* states:
"One who is broadly versed in all sections and refined in discerning right from wrong, yet cannot be refined in their own school or broad in other traditions, is merely an ancient..."

It is a matter of human beings. Both [masters] opened up the capacity for the two conditions. "Ō" (臆) refers to "guesswork" (臆度). The ancient virtuous ones were neither refined nor broad in their learning;
whenever they discussed these two matters and adjudicated right from wrong, they did so entirely according to their own subjective minds (*shixin*), without opening up scriptural authorities.

If one explains this specifically according to the Vinaya teachings, it refers to the provision of the eighty recitation *vinaya* as a medicinal remedy, tailored to the capacities of the six groups and seventeen groups of monks.
Generally, when wishing to preach the Dharma to suit the capacities of beings, one must avoid three faults.

Regarding the three faults: first, not knowing the nature of medicines; second, knowing the Dharma but failing to recognize the capacity of the recipient, being merely conversant with the teachings while lacking the skill to observe the faculties of others—like a person who knows medicines but is unskilled in diagnosing pulses;
third, failing to recognize both the capacity of the recipient and the Dharma—this can be understood. Now, when the Buddha preaches the Dharma, he is free from these three faults;
he knows that the root-natures of beings are manifold and diverse, just as a great king of physicians is skilled in treatment.
Regarding the various illnesses, one should provide medicine according to the ailment so that they may take it and practice; there is nothing seen or heard that does not receive benefit.
