Distinguishing between permissions and prohibitions: according to the scriptural texts, these permissions and prohibitions apply not only while the Buddha was in the world, but also extend to the future;
thus, there are permissions and prohibitions for both periods, which differs from what was stated previously. That the teachings "pervade two eras" refers to the present and the future.
The permissions established during the reign of King Prasenajit are precisely the original expositions. That is to say, while the Buddha was alive, these were all one and the same matter;
yet at the same time, what was prohibited in one place was permitted in another. This is called the teaching for the present age.

Alternatively, what was prohibited in the same location this year was permitted the following year, or prohibited again the year after that; this is called the teaching for the future. Thus it should be known.
The teachings regarding permissions and prohibitions within the Vinaya apply not only to the Western lands and other regions, nor are they restricted to the period when the Buddha was in the world;

rather, they are intended for the flexible application of the final age. Now, by taking this precedent and applying it to the Vinaya, we seek to understand the underlying intent behind the establishment of these teachings.
Regarding the phrase "the text states 'hence the arrival of the words,'" this cites the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (The Collection of Five Hundred) to clarify the teachings for future generations.
This passage occurs in the fourth division of the text; therefore, it is referred to as "the following text. It says: "After Kāśyapa had completed the council, there was an elder named Pūrṇa."
Accompanied by five hundred bhikṣus, he went to Rājagṛha to the place where Kāśyapa was and said:
"I have heard that the Venerable One, together with the various arhats, is compiling the Dharma and the Vinaya; I also wish to participate. At that time, Kāśyapa had Upāli ascend the seat.
For the sake of the bhikṣu Pūrṇa, who was reflecting deeply, he said: "Regarding all matters, whether prior or subsequent, they are all permissible, with the sole exception of this one matter."

The relatives followed the Buddha and remembered his instructions without forgetting them; thus, even when the eight restrictive rules were relaxed, they were all able to obtain food. Kāśyapa said, "It is exactly as you have said.

During times of famine, when people were devouring one another, the Buddha, out of compassion, temporarily relaxed these rules. However, this was for the time of scarcity; once the harvest is abundant again, [the rules must be observed]."
Furthermore, because there was a subsequent prohibition, the Elder saw only the prior allowance and did not hear of the later prohibition.
Pūrṇa said, "The Buddha is omniscient; how could he prohibit something and then allow it again, or allow it and then prohibit it once more?

Kāśyapa replied, "It is precisely because the Buddha is omniscient that he prohibited something and then allowed it again, or allowed it and then prohibited it once more. In this passage, it is Kāśyapa who speaks.
Answer: I shall now cite the relevant passage to demonstrate that the Buddha’s establishment of the teachings while standing was not intended solely for the bhikṣus of the present;

rather, it applies equally to the prohibitions and permissions from the period of the Semblance Dharma down to the Final Dharma. Therefore, it is called the "teaching for the future. This constitutes the vertical exposition of the higher and lower [realms].
This is called the *Vinaya* teaching of time (*kāla-vinaya*). Within this [teaching], there is also the *Vinaya* teaching of place (*deśa-vinaya*), which means:

if this year a certain location has an abundant harvest, eight matters are restricted; if next year that location is abundant while here it is scarce, those restrictions are again relaxed. This is called the *Vinaya* teaching of place.
Although there is textual evidence for this in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, as it is not skillfully or excellently formulated, I cite the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* to corroborate it.
The phrase "as stated in the *Pañcavargika* [Vinaya]" clarifies that this refers to the present teaching. This merely cites the *Pañcavargika* to establish the *Bhikṣu-vinaya* (the Vinaya for monks);
it does not mean that the teaching of the *Pañcavargika* itself was being promulgated, which is why the character "ru" (as) is used.

According to the text of the *Bhojana-khandaka* in the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Pañcavargika*, regarding the passage "although what I have prescribed," the *Pañcavargika-vinaya-śū* (Commentary on the Pañcavargika) states: "Although..."
Regarding the practice of eating by hand that I have prescribed: if it does not produce wholesome results when practiced in other regions, then it should not be employed.

Now, as for the claim that eating by hand is a local custom of the Western lands (India) and thus should not be followed because it was not ordained by the Buddha—this is another interpretation, but it is also not to be accepted.

Furthermore, there are those who attempt to resolve this by distinguishing between "large morsels" and "small morsels," but this too is not to be used. For now, I shall briefly cite the three periods for the distribution of rooms.

This is explained as follows: In the Buddha’s principle, there is equality and no distinction between host and guest. Dividing the rooms according to the three periods was originally a regulation established by the Buddha.

If in this land one relies on secular law to permanently assign names and titles for the maintenance of the monastery, and does not follow the division according to the three periods, then such a regulation would be improper.
Although these are not established by me, such as the use of spoons, straws, or socks, which were originally not ordained by the Buddha, they must now be practiced in accordance with this region;
therefore it is said that one "cannot but practice" them (all such examples). This refers to the time and has no specific location;

it differs from the "transverse" [directions] and is called the Vinaya of the Directions (*dig-vinaya*). It is also called the Teaching of the Present Age (*pratyutpanna-kāla-śāsana*). This refers to the present.
"Existing" refers generally to the present; it is not restricted solely to the time when the Buddha was alive.

This means that throughout the twelve thousand years [of the Dharma's duration], all moments within a single day and a single time are designated as "present. Next, we shall harmonize these two perspectives.

Regarding the statement that "the two teachings are mutually integrated and encompass one another": at the time of the *Vinaya*, there were two *vinayas*; this does not refer to the *Dharmaguptaka* and *Mahīśāsaka* schools.
"Mutually integrated" means they are harmoniously unified. This implies that within the temporal [teaching] there is the spatial, and within the spatial there is the temporal.
Now, concerning the presence of the spatial within the temporal, although there are many interpretations, they are not without confusion; therefore, we now rely upon...

Jing said: "The eight matters permitted during times of scarcity were originally taught as vertical [principles] for the Vinaya of the time. Now, we shall discuss them horizontally according to regional regulations and prohibitions.
For instance, in the Western Land (India), these eight matters are strictly prohibited; yet in the Eastern Land (China), during times of scarcity, they are permitted.
Since the East and West differ, is it not the case that there are regional distinctions within the context of time? Conversely, within the two regions, there are temporal distinctions."
Explanation: Take one instance as an illustration; all others are to be treated accordingly.

The statement "from three up to the same" refers to the third analogy. Although it was understood above that the teachings regarding permissions and prohibitions apply to future generations, there are distinctions between male and female among those beings to whom they apply; thus, the establishment of the teachings for them also [varies].

There are many aspects. Since the preceding [section] has not yet clarified this, it shall now be examined. Regarding the explanation of the names: "retribution" (*pāpa*) refers to the ripening of causes.
Male retribution is superior and strong; female retribution is inferior and weak. This means that the male’s disposition is firm and robust, while the female’s nature is compliant and submissive.

Thus, strength and weakness are not fixed. Furthermore, regarding the gravity of the teaching: "teaching" refers to the Buddha preaching according to the capacities of sentient beings. As for "female retribution":...

Because [the offense] is weak, the teaching that explains it allows for restoration; this is like the case where one who has abandoned the precepts is not permitted to return. During the summer retreat, if there is a necessary reason, one is merely permitted to accept the seven-day period;

as for the sixteen types of vessels, one must declare their possession and so forth. Because the power of the Saṃgha’s report is strong, one must undergo purification by formally abandoning the precepts.
The opening of the sevenfold repetition [of the *poṣadha*] and returning during the summer retreat;

all these open the three types of receiving the day, the sixteen vessels, and the requirement for great *śuddhi-viśuddhi* (purification)—this is the intended meaning of the teaching, which is to permit them. In the text, the character "chóng" (repetition/layered) may be pronounced in the level tone (*píngshēng*).

It also applies to the *saṃgha*, as it refers to repeated permission granted because of their strength. For the *bhikṣuṇīs*, repeated permission is not permitted because of their weakness. (The above presents the correct interpretation.)

[End]. In the *Xianzheng ji* (Collection for Manifesting the Correct), it is stated that the four *pārājika* rules were established because the karmic retribution (*vipāka*) of monks is strong, whereas the eight *pārājika* rules were established because nuns are weak.
Furthermore, regarding the claim that those of superior faculties have strong retribution while those of middling or inferior faculties do not—this is likely incorrect.

If the precepts are established based on the distinction between monks and nuns, this is an explanation based on formal regulation (*prajñapti*), which does not correspond with this text. If, however, they are established based on superior, middling, and inferior faculties...

[This is] an explanation. Furthermore, the differing levels of spiritual capacity and awakening are the intended meaning within the categories [of the Vinaya], though they are not explicitly taken up here. Regarding the establishment of deep prohibitions to delimit specific portions, Xuán says:
"For example, in the precept against touching women, it is established within the category of deep prohibitions as a *pārājika* offense because it accords with heavy afflictions (*kleśa*).

Since one has already experienced physical contact, there is fear that a great evil will be committed; therefore, for the Saṃgha, it is merely established within the category of limited portions (*sthūlātyaya*) as a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, because the general framework of the Great Dharma is strong."

Since it does not necessarily constitute a grave offense, the eight rules for *bhikṣuṇīs* are established as a "deep prevention" (*shenfang*), while those for *bhikṣus* are established as a "limitation" (*xianfen*).
Alternatively, some explain that the rules concerning drinking water containing insects and the prohibition against striking others are classified as "deep prevention" and "limitation," respectively;

however, this is incorrect. Regarding the distinction between "mountain" and "worldly" practices, Xuán says: "This refers to the specific conduct practiced [in different contexts]. "Mountain" [refers to the monastic community].
That is to say, "mountain" refers to an araṇya (wilderness), while in the world it refers to a village, city, or town. The Saṃgha permits residence in an araṇya;

there, one is permitted to be separated from one's robes for six nights, to be separated from them without a fixed limit of days, and to possess robes of excessive size. Furthermore, one may construct a dwelling without begging for materials, and so forth.

However, nuns are not permitted to reside in an araṇya, as they do not have the aforementioned precepts; should they nevertheless act contrary to these rules, they incur only a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) offense, because their karmic retribution differs [from that of monks].
Because they are the same (the above constitutes the conclusion of the formal explanation). According to the *Jizong ji* (Record of the Succession of the School), it says:

"For those of superior faculties dwelling in an araṇya, the Buddha taught the dhūtas such as dwelling among tombs or at the foot of trees; for those of inferior faculties dwelling in a village, the Buddha taught the construction of dwellings" (the above is the text from the record).

At first glance, this appears to be so, but upon closer examination of the textual flow, it actually falls under the second section: the Gate of the Relative Weight of the Instituted Teachings, number seven.
Regarding the section on "distinguishing differences through practice" (*xing*) and "noisy versus quiet," that is not the intended meaning of this passage.
Fourth, "taking the awakening of the capacity (*ki*) as primary" indicates that the awakening of the capacity is the fundamental basis of the exposition.

This means that although the preceding discussion used the examples of male and female, strong and weak, to include all cases, within the Vinaya, one must consider the capacities of those being addressed (*beiji*), which vary according to whether their faculties are sharp or dull. Regarding these...

The establishment of the teachings also varies; since this was not clarified previously, it is discussed next. "Faculties" (*ki*) refers to the spiritual capacities (*indriya*); "awakening" (*go*) refers to entering into realization.
Regarding "acting first," it means that the Buddha first observes the faculties and only thereafter preaches the Dharma in accordance with those faculties.

As for the resulting separation between the lightness and heaviness of the teaching gates, it is because the faculties to whom they were addressed were largely diverse; thus, the teachings that express them also vary in their lightness and heaviness.
There are many varieties. As asked in the Vinaya, these matters differ in degree of gravity. For instance, among the requisites for sustaining the body, there are six distinct categories.

Thus, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "As with the Bhikṣu Mianwang (Simha), who wore his fetal membrane upon entering the Dharma and vowed never to wear other garments—this was the first regulation established by the Tathāgata according to the capacities of those to be taught. Second is the ability to endure..."

It was cold and bitter. Because the Great Sage assessed the capacities of his disciples, he prescribed the three robes (*tricīvara*). Although the possession of these three was prescribed, the hands and feet were still exposed.
Therefore, the Tathāgata, assessing their capacities, permitted the keeping of the "one hundred and one" items for identification and maintenance.

Fourth, because mental application is not beneficial if it waits for the right time or place, or requires smoke or specific conditions before one can advance in practice, he permitted the keeping of extra robes (*atirekacīvara*) to be accepted according to what is offered.

Fifth, because one must rely upon substantial material goods to settle the body and advance on the Path, the Buddha permitted bedding and quilts and did not require them to be given away as pure gifts (*śuddhadāna*).

Sixth, it was necessary for the community to have actual funds before one’s mind could find peace; thus, the Buddha permitted their use for a single night to attain the Path (the above is from the *Śāstra*).

Among these six points, each preceding item is more serious than the following, while each succeeding item is lighter than the preceding. Since there are already these six types regarding the requisites for sustaining the body, is this not [the case]?
The distinctions between heavy and light lead to separation. The Buddha first observes the capacities of sentient beings (*indriya*) and establishes his teachings accordingly.

For some whose capacity finds the teaching of the "heavy" to be effective, the thought of wearying detachment (*nirveda*) arises, and they awaken to and enter the gateway of the Path; for these, the Buddha teaches the "heavy. For others whose capacity finds the teaching of the "light" to be effective, weary detachment arises;
for these, the Buddha teaches the "light. Because capacities differ, the teachings are largely distinct. Regarding the "different tenets of the five schools" and so forth:

The citation of evidence establishes the aforementioned meaning. However, the intent of this is that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the period beyond one hundred years, the community split into various sects because the capacities for awakening and understanding differed among practitioners.

For example, the masters of the Mahīśāsaka school maintained that the ground should be purified through ritual knots, that the *prātimokṣa* should be recited with melodic chanting, that five *māṣaka* coins constituted a grave offense, and that they observed the three grades of the *rakṣā-vidyā-mantra* and the reception of the sun, and so forth. The Mahīśāsaka...

The Sautrāntika masters maintain that the mindfulness of the precepts is based on literal sound; the Sarvāstivāda masters maintain that the purification of the ground (pradeśa-śuddhi) constitutes a grave offense when eighty small coins are involved, and so forth.

These differences all arise from the varying capacities for awakening of their respective adherents. By this, it is proven that the capacities for awakening regarding the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) are likewise distinct;
it does not mean that the teachings of the five schools were promulgated with universal clarity for all.

Regarding the statement "the five [topics] up to the loss": although the preceding four categories have already been used to distinguish the arising of the teaching, within the Vinaya there are *karmavācanā* (formal procedures) along with the matters they apply to;
these constitute the "leaves" of the Bhikṣu. Since these were not previously mentioned, they are clarified here.
As for "matters," this refers to the matters to which [the procedures] apply. As for "methods," this refers to the methods that apply them. Now, by pairing the matter with the method, and...

This concerns the distinction between the general and the specific. Regarding the fact that the *dharma* serves solely as a formal model: for example, the "single white" (*ekoddiṣṭa*) motion consists of fourteen characters:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen; if the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; the motion is as follows. The *karmavācanā* (formal act) consists of thirty-one characters:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen; which elders among you consent, let them remain silent; those who do not consent, let them speak," and so forth. Thus [the motion] consists of fourteen characters.

One must establish these with precision; if they are deficient or redundant, they are not valid. If one deviates from the meaning of the text, then even the matters addressed in the interim will not be accomplished.

Regarding matters that pertain to both the emotional (sentient) and the non-emotional (insentient): this refers to the matters addressed in the second, fourth, and third [sections] of the interim, which encompass both sentient and insentient things, as well as the unified matters of confession, treatment, formal acts (*karma*), the observance of days, and so forth. These are the two types of dwellings for sentient beings, which establish all [matters].

The elements (*dhātu*) and so forth are insentient matters; being separated from robes, staffs, and the like constitutes a matter of conjunction. Regarding the attainment or loss [of merit] based on the object:

it depends solely upon the preceding object. One should instruct [the practitioner] according to the Dharma. For example, when a *śrāmaṇera* establishes a boundary (*sīmābandha*) without obstacles or impediments, proclaims the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and demarcates two rooms, there is no hindrance or difficulty.
Terms such as "robes," "heavy," or "illness" are used as names for that which is in accordance with the Dharma. Conversely, if one obtains a name, it is a loss.
Alternatively, regarding those that record the conditions of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*): within the affairs of sentient beings, these are further distinguished according to the three natures.

For example, receiving the precepts, repenting of offenses, and determining the days for the *poṣadha* are of a wholesome nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*). Actions such as formal treatment, suspension, rebuking, and admonishing are of an unwholesome nature (*akuśala-svabhāva*).

Ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) for those who are insane or delirious are of a neutral nature (*avyākṛta-svabhāva*). Alternatively, there are those that arise following worldly censure, such as the ritual procedure for a family under discipline (*śikṣādattaka-karman*).
The monk Cūḍapanthaka went to the homes of laypeople to receive alms, causing them to be completely exhausted and inviting public reproach.

Consequently, a *karmavācanā* was performed to prohibit him from going there. This rule arose because of the reproach of worldly people; it is likewise a rule for prohibiting entry into the homes of white-robed [laypeople].
To clarify this as a precedent, the subsequent text states: "From beginning to end, not a single word may be added or subtracted."
The practice of donning the robes and upholding the Dharma must first be established for the ritual matters to be perfected.

This serves as the general outline. Regarding the phrase "merely citing briefly," etc., this concludes the five preceding examples. "Merely" (*qie*) is a term indicating incompleteness. "Bundling" (*shu*) refers to the five brief examples;

"various articles" (*zhutiao*) refers to their collective name. "Superficial knowledge" (*boku-chi*) conveys a sense of rudimentary understanding. "Direction" (*fang*) means the locus or destination. "To arrive at" (*yi*) means to reach. For now, we shall summarize...
In general, by citing these five examples, one may gain a slight understanding of the intent behind the emergence of the teaching.

To summarize and encompass them all, they consist simply in the seeking of Bodhi (the above constitutes the correct explanation). Alternatively, some commentaries explain that these five are to be categorized within the Vinaya Piṭaka as representing the intent for the emergence of the teaching.
However, among these five, there are varying degrees of gravity; this is because [the text] has not yet clarified "the ultimate" and so forth. (2)

The seven examples were previously set forth for analytical explanation; now, for the time being, they shall be clarified by means of five examples, so that one may have a slight understanding of their general principles.
However, my current intention is not so. If one were to provide such an interpretation, it would seem to give rise to the second section on "Light and Heavy" (the *qīngzhòng mén*) below.

This would involve casting aside the three and five types of mental intentions (*yìniàn*) and seeking instead the gateway to the "Mud and Sun" (*nírì*). Thus, while discarding [the former], one does not grasp [the latter]; this is the essential summary.

As for the term "yi" (already): it refers to the fact that while the preceding sections have clarified the arising of the threefold and fivefold teachings, it remains uncertain what the ultimate purpose of producing these scriptural texts is, or what they seek to alleviate through fear.
Therefore, this section is established to comprehensively clarify the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) of their production. "Zong" (total) means comprehensive; it means to summarize.

"Bao" (encompassing) means to include within its scope; "ju" (raising) means to initiate. Having surveyed the arising of the threefold and fivefold teachings above, this is termed a "comprehensive summary," as there is no other way to do so.

It is "non-existence" (wu). It is not "not by means of" (fei you bu ye). It is ultimate salvation (ji ji). It is guidance and reception (jie yin). "Ordinary" (fan) refers to the common, mundane person;

"constant" (chang) refers to the everyday. Herein, the intent of encompassing and raising up the teachings to flourish is entirely for the sake of ultimately saving and guiding the common, mundane, and ordinary classes, causing them to rely on the teachings to advance in practice, sever delusions, and realize the principle. This is the fundamental purpose. "Ni" (mud) refers to Nirvana (ni yuan nie pan).
"Brahman" (梵) is entirely a term from the Sanskrit language; here it means "neither going nor coming, neither arising nor ceasing. The new [translation] renders it as *parinirvāṇam*.
Here, "pari" means "universal pervasion," which distinguishes it from the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
It is not like earth, water, fire, or wind, which each adhere to their own substantial bodies. "Quiescent" means tranquil;

this distinguishes it from the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), such as arising, abiding, change, and cessation, which, though pervasive, are not quiescent. Regarding this, four analytical distinctions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are made:

first, that which is pervasive but not quiescent refers to the subtle four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*); second, that which is quiescent but not pervasive refers to the five previously mentioned unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*); third, that which is both pervasive and... [text fragment ends].
"Quiescence" (*śānti*) refers to this very *nirvāṇa*. "Neither complete nor quiescent" refers to the form and mind (*rūpa-citta*) of the causal stage.

Now, this commentary preserves the traditional terminology and simply calls it "mud" (*paṅka*). This [topic] is explained through three distinct sections: first, enumerating the numbers and explaining the names; second, identifying the essential nature (*svabhāva*);
third, determining who attains them. First, regarding the enumeration, there are four: first, intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*); second, with remainder (*sopadhi-śeṣa*); third...
The nirvāṇa without remainder; the four abodes. Regarding the explanation of the names: first, the self-nature purity. "Nirvāṇa" refers to the meaning of the fundamental essence (*svabhāva*).
"Purity" means the sense of being unstained. This means that from its original nature, this nirvāṇa has never been stained by the two obstacles.
All that exists possesses the nature of a cloud; like the moon within a cloud, it is free from all defilements.

Therefore, it is called "pure. Possessing the function of perfect, eternal quiescence, it is termed *nirvāṇa*. When these functions are subsumed back into the essence, there is the intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*);
this is a *dharmadhāraṇa-karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) where *nirvāṇa* is the attribute. Second, regarding *nirvāṇa with remainder*:

the term "remainder" is established in contrast to "non-remainder," referring specifically to the five-aggregate body of those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) among the two vehicles. This means that from time immemorial, they have been [afflicted] by afflictions...

It obstructs the remaining basis. Now, for those of the Two Vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), although the afflictions that serve as the supported [phenomena] are absent, they nonetheless abide within this body while realizing *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is called "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*).

Regarding "existence with remainder" (*upadhi-śeṣa-nirvāṇa*): within the very substance of existence, there remains a further function; thus, "existence with remainder" is the sustaining of *nirvāṇa*.

Explanation of the compound: *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with a remainder) is explained by the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. Question: For one who has attained the fourth fruit in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no physical body;
how, then, can it be called "with a remainder"? Answer: Although there is no physical body, the four aggregates (*skandha*) still remain; thus, it may also be designated as "with a remainder.

Furthermore, there are other "remainders" such as the three [remaining] aggregates and the eight bases (*āyatana*). This is explained in detail in the treatise. Regarding *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without a remainder):

"Without remainder" (anupadhiśeṣa) is a designation established in contrast to "with remainder. This refers to the fact that after an Arhat has transformed his body by fire, these five aggregates no longer remain as a residual basis.
Because one realizes this nirvana upon the cessation of that remaining support, it is called "without remainder."

"Without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*) is explained by the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound; "the basis of what is without remainder" is explained by the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. This refers to the nirvāṇa without abode (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*).

That is to say, when awakening realizes the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), one does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa. Ordinary beings, lacking wisdom, delight in abiding in nirvāṇa;

however, at the time of realizing the principle of the emptiness of phenomena through awakening, there is great wisdom. Thus, it distinguishes [this state] from that of ordinary beings. It is not [the case that they do not abide].
Because they abide within saṃsāra out of compassion, they are distinguished from those of the two vehicles who do not abide in nirvāṇa.
Due to these two benefits—compassion and wisdom—the two wheels [of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa] have no fixed point of rest; therefore, it is called "nirvāṇa without abode" (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*).

"Without abode" is a *karmadhāraya* compound (the first member modifies the second). (The explanation of names by numerical analogy is concluded. Second, regarding the essential nature (*svabhāva*): first, self-nature pure nirvāṇa has true suchness (*tathatā*) as its essence.

Among the six kinds of *tathatā* (suchness), this refers specifically to the *tathatā* of ultimate reality (*dharmatā-tathatā*). There are ten meanings that explain *tathatā*; I shall not seek to describe them here at length, as they are explained extensively in the treatises.
Second is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder). It takes the emergence from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) as its function and *tathatā* as its essence.

Thus, the treatise says: "That is to say, it is *tathatā* itself emerging from the obstacle of afflictions. Question: Is the *tathatā* realized by those who have attained the first three fruits [of the śrāvaka path] also...

If one has emerged from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), should it not be called *nirvāṇa with remainder* (*sopadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*)? Answer: Because [afflictions] have been exhausted, that body which serves as their basis is no longer designated as "remainder. Question:
Since the body that is the basis of suffering remains while the "remainder" has not yet been extinguished, how can one be said to have realized *nirvāṇa*? Answer:
Although the body that is the basis of suffering still exists, because all afflictions are absent, the true reality that is realized is designated by the name *nirvāṇa*. Thus says the treatise.
It is said: although subtle suffering has not yet been extinguished, because it manifests eternal quiescence, it is called *nirvāṇa*. Third is *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (Nirvāṇa without remainder).

It takes true suchness (*tathatā*), which transcends the suffering of birth and death, as its essence. Therefore, the treatise says: "That is, true suchness itself transcends the suffering of birth and death.
Since afflictions have been exhausted and the remaining substratum no longer exists, all sufferings are eternally stilled; hence it is called *nirvāṇa*. Fourth...
The fourth is non-abiding nirvana (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*), which takes as its essence the suchness (*tathatā*) that emerges from the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

This means that by realizing the suchness of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-tathatā*), the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) severs the obstructions and does not abide in saṃsāra; subsequently, the subsequently-attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) gives rise to compassion to benefit sentient beings and does not abide in nirvāṇa.
Thus, the treatise says: "That is to say, suchness itself, emerging from the cognitive obstructions, is [the union of] great compassion and prajñā."
That which provides support and protection. Because of this, one does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa; until the end of the future, one acts while remaining eternally quiescent.

(The section on "Transcending the Realms" concludes. Third, regarding those who have attained [the fruit]: the meaning is that among both ordinary beings and sages, do all fully possess [these qualities], or are there some who do not?

Therefore, the treatise says: "All sentient beings possess them. Regarding the first [category]—those of the two vehicles who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—it is possible for them to possess the first three.

Only I, the Tathāgata, can be said to possess all four [nirvāṇas]. As for the statement that "all sentient beings possess the first," this refers to all those of the three vehicles and five natures, both before and after the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), as well as those who have attained the first three fruits;

they all possess only the nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddha-nirvāṇa*). Regarding the possibility that those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) of the two vehicles may possess the first three, this is not a fixed rule. This is explained from the perspective of...

This is divided into two categories: first, those of fixed nature; second, those of unfixed nature. Regarding those of fixed nature, they possess the first three [natures], excluding the "without-abode" (anupadhiśeṣa).
Those of unfixed nature possess two natures, as well as the "with-remainder" (sopadhiśeṣa). Question:

Since the body and wisdom of one of fixed nature already exist, how does such a person realize the "without-remainder" state? Answer: They realize the "with-remainder" state. In essence, there is no difference.
They are distinct. This is because both are the *tathatā* (suchness) of the emptiness of one birth. If this is so, since these two nirvāṇas are of the same essence, how are they distinguished?

Answer: Although their essence is one, there is a distinction based on what is manifested. When viewed in relation to the emergence from the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), that which is manifested is designated as "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*).

When viewed in relation to the emergence from the suffering of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), that which is manifested is named "without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*). Question: Does one of indeterminate lineage realize the nirvāṇa with remainder?
At that time, they also attain *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. Based on what [criterion] do we say they do not possess all three? The answer is:
if those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) later undergo the great cremation of the body (*mahā-dhātu-parinirvāṇa*), they definitely manifest it.

However, those of indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*), although they realize *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, turn their minds toward the transformation body (*pariṇāmi-kāya*) and do not undergo cremation by fire; therefore, it is not manifested, and they possess only two. Since this is the case for Śrāvakas, [the same applies to] Pratyekabuddhas.
One may know this by applying the same principle. Next, regarding the Mahāyāna: for those who attain sudden enlightenment prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), the Bodhisattva has only the first [type].

For those who attain gradual enlightenment, if they are *śaikṣa* (still in training) and have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], there is the addition of the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder). If one has already ascended the stages and attained sudden enlightenment, there are three periods;

for the *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder), it is gradual. If one is a *śaikṣa* who has turned their mind, there are two [periods] with the addition of the *sopadhiśeṣa*. If one is an *aśaikṣa*...
Regarding the training in the turning of the mind (*cittavivarta*), there are three stages of application (*prayoga*) but no abiding place. Only I, the Tathāgata, can be said to possess all four;

for their essence is the naturally pure (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*) mind. Having attained the state of self-experiencing wisdom (*svasaṃvedana-jñāna*), this is the state with remaining support (*sopadhiśeṣa*). It is the relinquishing of the death-and-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*).

One attains the nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) and severs the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), thereby attaining the non-abiding [nirvana]. Question: How can the Sugata attain nirvana with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*)?

The intent of this question is to say: if the Buddha-stage possesses nirvana with remainder, then it would follow that the Tathāgata could possess a physical body as the basis for fragmented suffering.
Answer: There are two explanations. First, an interpretation based on the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*); second, [an interpretation based on the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*)].

Regarding the interpretation based on the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body): first, concerning the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), the treatise states: "Although there is no actual support (*niśraya*), it is manifested as if there were.

This differs from the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, who possess a body of suffering (*duḥkha-śarīra*) as their support. If one speaks of an actual body of fragmented existence (*bheda-bhāga*) at the stage of Buddhahood, it is termed 'having a remainder of support' (*sopadhiśeṣa*);
yet in reality, such a thing does not exist. If considered from the perspective of manifestation, how could it be that there is also a manifestation identical to that of the two vehicles?"

Regarding the body of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), because one severs the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and realizes *nirvāṇa* with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*), the next [section] distinguishes it according to the Body of Real Reward (*sambhogakāya*).
The treatise states: "Alternatively, 'remainder' refers to the exhaustion of the basis of suffering; it is not that the basis of non-suffering remains and is called 'with remainder.'"

This refers to the moment of attaining the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). At that time, one abandons the basis of suffering consisting of the changing five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) with outflows (*sāsrava*), and attains the basis of bliss consisting of the actual retribution of the five aggregates without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Abandoning impermanent form, one obtains the permanent. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
This very basis of bliss is called *nirvāṇa with remainder* (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*). There are further meanings, which are explained extensively in the treatises.
[Commentary: If one were to elaborate further, it might not be the most essential point. The intent of this present compilation is as follows:

although the aforementioned motivations for the arising [of the teaching] differ in three or five ways, they all converge on the fact that the minds of practitioners have become corrupted; this is precisely the underlying purpose for the emergence of the teaching.
Next, the following citation is introduced. Regarding the phrase "Therefore, the text says... up to 'therefore,'" this refers to three passages from the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*.

It states: "The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: 'The training in higher morality, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom—by training in these three trainings, one attains the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, and arhat.
Therefore, you should train. At that time, Ānanda was in the city of Vārāṇasī at Kukuṭārāma..."

In the garden, there was a brahmin named Mayūra-śikha who went to where Ānanda was and asked: "O Gautama śramaṇa, for what reason have you established the training in the higher precepts (adhiśīla-śikṣā) for the bhikṣus?

Ānanda replied: "It is for the sake of taming those who have entered into greed, hatred, and delusion so that they may be brought to exhaustion that the training in the higher precepts has been established.
He asked again: "What is meant by 'training'? He replied: "It is for the purpose of seeking the stage of stream-enterer (srotāpanna), and so forth."

Regarding the "four fruits": in the present *Chao* (Excerpts), the phrasing of the Vinaya text has been revised. Question: Since the severing of afflictions (*kleśa*) depends upon wisdom (*prajñā*), why speak of precepts (*śīla*)?
Answer: Because they serve as a remote cause (*dūre-hetu*). One must first take precepts as primary; only then will concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom arise. Thus, the treatise says:

The precepts guard against coarse transgressions, while meditative concentration eliminates subtle distractions. Wisdom cuts through the fetters of inherent nature. Wisdom does not arise in isolation; it must rely upon concentration.

Concentration has its source, and its efficacy stems from pure precepts. Based on this fundamental principle, it is said that the precepts are capable of "taming. Within the text of the *Chao* (the *Shan-jian-pi-po-sha*), there are four instances of the character for "fruit" (*phala*).
Although these are cited as scriptural evidence, they pertain to the Hīnayāna. Furthermore, regarding the gradual cultivation of practice, [the text] is necessarily brief and omissions.
[This] clarifies that, on the contrary, it becomes a loose and superficial treatment. The details are as shown in the *Yitu* (Diagram of Meanings);

they are entrusted to the relevant passages as they arise in the text, with separate commentaries provided for explanation (*et cetera*). Regarding the phrase "among the various sections below," Xuán says: "The 'various sections' refers to the nine sections that follow.
"The intended meaning of the composition" refers to the underlying purpose behind the arrangement of these nine sections. "Merely following the preceding matter" means...
The nine matters, beginning with "light and heavy" and so forth, will not be recounted again here. As for the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, it is intended for those of later generations to cultivate.

By following the [preceding] nine items below, one will know that [the fruit] is never absent; the meaning is that one seeks *nirvāṇa* (mudiyu). (This interpretation is restricted and not universally accepted.)
Now, according to the *Xianzheng* (Exposition of the Correct), this refers to the "Thirty Chapters" (Sāṃdhinirmocana-sūtra). This is the original intent here. One should first raise the objection:
Does this chapter fully clarify the purpose for the arising of the subsequent chapters? If it does not, it cannot be called a "Great Outline" (*dàgāng*).

If it does fully encompass them, why do the subsequent chapters still have their own distinct purposes that can be cited from the *Chao* (Commentary)? The answer is: "Within the various subsequent sections, regarding the monastery... and so forth. All [subsequent points].

The "Gates" consist of thirty chapters. This refers to the subsequent chapters which clarify the underlying intent [of the preceding sections]. They merely describe the specific purpose of each respective chapter and do not comprehensively elucidate the reasons for the arising of all teachings.

For example, the "Proclaiming the Tenets" chapter merely describes the intent behind proclaiming the tenets, and the "Assembling the Sangha" chapter merely describes the intent behind assembling the Sangha;
thus, it is said they "merely follow the immediate matter. Now, this present section comprehensively elucidates the reasons for the arising of all teachings, thereby...
Later students, by investigating the principles of this first gate, will know that the fundamental basis for the arising of the teachings in all subsequent chapters lies entirely within this gate;
it is the very root. (The first gate concludes above.)

Compiled by the Qingliang Dashi Jingxiao, who was granted the purple robe for his long-term lecturing on the Vinaya and presiding over ordination platforms during the Wu-Yue Kingdom.

The second section is divided into two parts. First, the title and its explanation: the phrase "The second" up to "the meaning" indicates the title of the section. First, the purpose for its inclusion is clarified.
Above, the emergence of the teaching was analyzed through five examples that negate [inherent] nature. Now, a teaching does not arise in isolation; it must necessarily have degrees of gravity.
Therefore, the preceding text states: "Teachings do not arise in isolation; their arising must depend on persons. Since persons differ, the teachings are likewise not uniform."

First: Since there are many types [of offenses] according to circumstances, how could there not be distinctions of light and heavy? If these were not clarified now, by what standard would one judge them?

Therefore, they are distinguished next. Regarding the explanation of the names: *di* (first) means "position"; *er* (second) is a numerical increment; and *zhi* (prescribed) refers to that which is regulated.

"Teaching" (*śāsana*) refers to that which expresses [the meaning]. "Light" means slight; "heavy" means coarse and heavy. This refers to the teachings established by these four parts, which possess degrees of lightness and heaviness.
"Intent" (*abhiprāya*) refers to the underlying purpose; thus it is said, "The second [point], etc. (and so forth).
Regarding the most difficult aspects within the "Explanations" (*śāstra*), they concern the weighing and measuring of gravity, and the determination— which means cutting through—

the texts of the formulated precepts. It is difficult to weigh, determine, and cut through the gravity within these texts because, while the five categories of offenses generally follow a progression from heavy to light,
there are also instances where, regarding a single matter, the intent behind the formulated precept may be light while the offense is grave, or conversely, the intent may be grave.

The intent of the teaching may be grave while the offense is light; or both may be grave or both light, being indeterminate. For example, among the natural precepts (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), killing a human incurs a *pārājika*—the most serious offense;

killing a non-human incurs a *sthūlātyaya*, which is progressively lighter; and killing an animal incurs a *pāyattika*, the lightest. Among the proscribed precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), building a hut that exceeds the prescribed dimensions incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, which is grave;

cutting grass or digging the earth incurs a *pāyattika*, which is progressively lighter. All of these were established by the Buddha during his lifetime according to the specific needs of those to be trained.

"Zhang. Now, because ordinary sentiments find it difficult to measure and judge, it is said to be "difficult. As for the phrase "what leads to the ultimate," these two characters constitute a challenge (*pūrvapakṣa*).

This means that although the preceding section has already praised the teachings on lightness and gravity as being difficult to measure, the underlying principles of this difficulty have not yet been explained.
In order to expound the following text, he first raises this challenge to initiate the inquiry; thus he asks, "What is the reason? to investigate the capacity of that [teaching].
The teaching of bestowal (*śī*) is the original source. Furthermore, the mind’s anger toward the "source" (*yuan*) is as follows. Regarding that, the *Zongji* states:
"From this land looking toward the Western Land, it is said that when the Buddha was in the world, the established teachings were located in the Western Country.

One may interpret "this" and "that" by viewing the person in light of the teaching; thus, one can consider this teaching as "this" and that [Western] teaching as "that. As for "the teaching of bestowal," "bestowal" (*shi*) refers to—
Regarding "provision" (*prajñapti*): if one considers the principle, the Buddha is the one capable of establishing the teaching, yet the teaching itself is that which is bestowed.

To speak now of the "one capable of bestowing" refers merely to the Buddha in relation to the sentient beings who are the objects of his instruction (and so forth). Regarding the phrase "the Master of the Teaching who exhausts the capacities of beings":
the Master of the Teaching is the Buddha; as a Buddha among humans, or within the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), he is able to perceive all faculties and capacities.
This is the foundation. Hence it is said, "exhausting the subtle mechanism" (and so forth). Inferring from this, the persons for whom [the teaching] was intended are likewise significant.
"Inferring" means to investigate. Those for whom [it was intended] are the six groups, the ten groups, and so forth. These individuals are precisely vessels who respond to the medicinal application.

Master Xuanyun says that "tui" (推) means "to conceive" (*xiang*). This refers to conceiving those such as the group of six (*ṣaḍvargika*) who, through the conditions of dependent origination, are all vessels for the medicinal teachings of the Tathāgata.
Alternatively, one may take the character "wei" (惟) to mean "to cherish," which is also acceptable (and so forth). For this reason, the medicine and the illness strike one another;
thus the two characters arise by following upon the previous [term]. Because the former Teacher thoroughly understood the capacities of sentient beings, there was nothing in vain.

The impairment of receiving [the teaching] is like medicine: the medicine is the teaching and the illness is the faculty (*indriya*). "Correspondence" (*xiang*) means being mutually appropriate; "striking" (*kou*) refers to striking, like a great bell waiting to be struck.
The categories of meaning are constant, yet they follow the specific conditions of the illness, which constitutes their differentiation. Their benefit and grace are without fixed direction.

This refers to the benefit of the "intercalary" (li-rùn) [teachings] and their application through analogy. Since there is nothing further to compare it to, it is like the case of the group of six monks and others;
from the time the regulations were established, they have followed the teachings as medicine, not daring to transgress them. The gateway of this benefit is beyond comparison. Thus the Sūtra says:
"Administer medicine according to the illness so that it may be taken and practiced; even those who merely see or hear it shall all receive benefit. This section...

The commentary consists of six phrases in total. The first two phrases show that the original teaching exhaustively accommodates the capacities [of sentient beings]. The following four phrases infer that these capacities respond to the teaching.

The phrase "how could it be possible" concludes with the intent of the difficulty of severing [afflictions]. This means that the aforementioned distinctions of heavy and light were all made by the Great Sage while he was in the world;
observing capacities and extending the Dharma, he proclaimed what was heavy or light according to his Buddha-wisdom. How could an ordinary person...
Based on the sentiments expressed in these discourses, one can infer the original intent behind the established teachings; hence it is said, "How could one possibly... (and so forth).
Regarding the phrase "even though" (*yōu-rán*) used in the expression "even though [the teaching] has reached its completion": the two characters are terms used for both concession and refutation.

If one concedes, it would be difficult to discern the relative gravity of the doctrinal principles; yet even through refutation, there remains a principle by which they may be understood. Question: According to what teaching can this be known?

Regarding the principle, the *Shuochao* (Commentary) explains its own text as follows: "To re-examine and verify [the teachings] together and to manifest the reality for distant posterity—this refers to 'reiteration' (*chong*).
'Examination' (*he*) means to investigate and scrutinize; it also implies 'reality. 'Distant' (*yuan*) refers to the distant exposition; 'manifestation' (*biao*) means to indicate.

The Vinaya teachings serve as the model for monks and nuns for twelve thousand years, and all shall have their share therein. The author of the *Chao* has perused, investigated, scrutinized, and sought them out."

The meaning of the text is as follows; thus it says, "re-examining," and so forth (*etcetera*). (This is based on the *Wenji* [Textual Record] for interpretation). Furthermore, the thesis states: "To 'indicate' (*biao*) means to 'show' (*shi*).
The intent is to say that this Vinaya teaching is not confined to the period when the Buddha was present; in truth, there was an intentional indication that this teaching would reach the present day.
"Truly reaching the descendants" (*shibei yizhe*): "Reaching" (*bei*) means to extend to; "later" (*lai*) refers to those who come later, and "descendants" (*yi*) refers to...

"Descendants. Furthermore, it is said that the downward-draping of a garment's lapels signifies "descendants" (*yi*). It is also said that the continuous succession of descendants is called "descendants" (*miao-yi*).
Now, since the Master has thus investigated the meaning of the text, we know that this teaching extends to the future;

therefore, one can also understand the principle regarding the relative gravity of the prescribed regulations. If this is so, please cite the scriptural evidence for it; the *Chao* (Commentary) may be cited.
The answer states that this is self-evident from the text itself; why then rely on further proof to understand the principles governing the gravity of the prescribed teachings?
If that were so, I would request you to cite the scriptural evidence. Thus, the Preface to the Vinaya says:

"At a time of famine, when it was difficult to obtain alms, Maudgalyāyana used his supernatural powers to travel to the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru) and fetch naturally grown non-glutinous rice. The Buddha rebuked him, saying: 'You possess supernatural powers; such an act may indeed be permissible.'"
Regarding the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*), how else might this be? Maudgalyāyana said, "I shall use my supernormal powers to receive them and lead them there.
The Buddha said, "That may be so while you are in the world; however, future bhikṣus will possess no supernormal powers themselves, nor will they have others to receive them.
They will incur the world's censure, saying: 'They are not like the bhikṣus when the Buddha was in the world,' and so forth. Furthermore, this is listed in the Vinaya texts.
Regarding the ten benefits, the very last one states, "to cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time," and so forth. All of these are clearly evident within the Vinaya texts of this very school;
there is no need for the trouble of further citing proofs from other teachings. Second, regarding the proof based on the stages, it says, "now reaching the seventh.
This means that the previous text—which was twice examined and re-examined—applies universally to the monastics of the final age. Since today’s monks and nuns...
All possess their respective portions, and may likewise be sequentially described and weighed. It is further said: "I now introduce this general outline.

"Great" (da) takes simplicity as its meaning, while "outline" (lue) refers to the essential framework; these discussions do not exceed seven categories of gravity and lightness, within which everything is fully encompassed.

Regarding the gradual and sudden arising of the mind of revulsion (*udvega*), there are many types. First, the arising of the mind is explained in terms of receiving and relinquishing precepts. Within the category of receiving, there is the gradual and the sudden:

merely receiving the five precepts or the ten precepts is termed "gradual," whereas receiving all of them is of the other class [the sudden]. Furthermore, within the mind of revulsion that leads to relinquishing, there is both the gradual and the sudden.
Relinquishing the full precepts (*upasampadā*) to become a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) is gradual; relinquishing the full precepts to become a layperson (*avadātavasana*) is [sudden].
Next, regarding the four modes of conduct concerning observance and transgression, as clarified by the arising of the mind:

when one gives rise to a mind that accomplishes the two types of observance (*dharana*)—severing all evils and cultivating all virtues—it is called the "sudden" (or instantaneous) state of the two observant minds.

When one only partially severs evil and cultivates virtue, this is the "gradual" state of the two observant minds. When one commits all evils and halts all virtues, this is called the "sudden" state of the two transgressing minds.

To perform a small amount of evil and cease from good is called the "two-fold transgression of the mind. "Gradual" refers to the teacher’s intention being light; "sudden" refers to the teacher’s intention being heavy.

All instances of generating weariness toward [transgressions], whether gradual or sudden, are clarified herein (the previous citation from the *Fù* states: "The interpretation provided is exceedingly elegant and appropriate"). According to the *Jìzōng jì*, this is distinguished by means of the established precepts (*śikṣāpada*):
it is based on those who take pleasure in committing offenses as "generating [weariness]," and those who rarely commit them as "wearing out [transgressions]"; the offense is grave.

The offenses categorized as "sudden" (*tun*) involve heavy penalties, while those categorized as "gradual" (*jian*) involve light penalties, and so forth; a detailed explanation is provided therein (*et cetera*).

Now, upon careful examination, this explanation actually serves as the second section for establishing the formal categories of karma (*karmavastu*), and thus slightly deviates from the present context. Regarding the second section on establishing the formal categories of karma:

it refers to the five classes of offenses (*pañcāpatti*) for both monks and nuns, which are termed "formal karma" (*samyakkarma*) to distinguish them from "causal karma" (*hetukarma*). Among these, each preceding category is more serious than the one following it.
For example, killing a human being constitutes a *pārājika* as its primary offense; killing a non-human (*amanuṣya*) constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* as its fifth category of offense.

Although this *sthūlātyaya* is not included among the enumerated five categories [of offenses], it is nonetheless a fundamental sin. Killing an animal constitutes a *pāyattika* as its primary offense. Furthermore, regarding the case of a female object:

There are five categories of light and heavy *samyak-karman* (correct actions). For example: engaging in sexual intercourse constitutes a *pārājika* offense as a *samyak-karman*; touching [a woman] constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense as a *samyak-karman*;

sitting or walking together [with a nun] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense as a *samyak-karman*; receiving food in a forest hermitage or a difficult location constitutes a *pratideśanīya* offense as a *samyak-karman*;

and performing work together in an improper manner or with deficient conduct constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense as a *samyak-karman*. In all these cases, the preceding is heavy and the subsequent is light.

Furthermore, regarding the three types of retributive fruits (*vipākaphala*) being different: this refers to causes cultivated in the past that result in a fruit in the past, which is termed a "retributive fruit.
In terms of male and female retribution, there are already differences such as being a monk or a nun; consequently, the establishment of the teachings results in varying degrees of gravity.

For example, because the retribution of a monk is stronger, within his own division alone, he is permitted to receive the precepts, repent of offenses, and even to re-ordain up to seven times after having relinquished the precepts.

Regarding the return [of a nun]: during the summer retreat (*varṣā*), if there is a specific cause, the opening of the three-day *dharma-śikṣamāṇā* period is permitted; however, the intent of the teaching is that this is considered light.

Because nuns are physically weak, they must receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*) and perform the confession of offenses within the assembly of both Sanghas (*ubhayato-saṃgha*). After renouncing the precepts, they are not permitted to return. During the summer retreat, if there is a specific cause, only the seven-day *parivāsa* (probation) is permitted;

however, the intent of the teaching is that this is considered grave. Furthermore, as in the case where a monk incurs a *thullaccaya* offense due to a lapse, the intent of the teaching is grave; the same applies when a nun incurs such an offense.

The *pāyattika* (offense requiring confession) for a monk who touches a nun is taught as light because the underlying intention is light; for a nun [who touches a monk], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense involving suspension from the community), taught as heavy because the underlying intention is heavy, and so forth.
Regarding the superiority or inferiority of the four destinies (*gati*), this clarifies the gravity of the offense based on the object encountered. For example, the human realm is superior;

thus, killing or stealing results in a *pārājika* (defeat), and the underlying intention is correspondingly grave. Non-humans are next in inferiority; thus, killing or stealing results in a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), and the underlying intention is correspondingly lighter. Animals... [and so forth].

The destination [of the offense] is most inferior. Killing, stealing, and taking the tongue [are grave], while the intent of the instruction is the lightest. Regarding the fifth point, "the reality or unreality of the recipient's disposition":

this refers to whether the disposition of the person toward whom the act is directed is real or unreal. If it is real, the offense is light; if unreal, it is heavy. For example, if one knows for oneself that one has attained sainthood (āryatva) and this is true, then promising to tell a like-minded bhikṣu about it constitutes no offense;
however, if one tells someone who has not received full ordination (upasaṃpad), one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation). This is the instruction.

The intention is light. If one has actually attained nothing, yet falsely claims to have attained superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) to deceive others, this is a *pārājika* offense because the mind is insincere;

thus, the intent is grave. Furthermore, when Devadatta committed the five wrongs and caused schism in the Triple Gem, he was guilty of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense because his mind was insincere in defying the admonitions; thus, it is grave.

In the case of the bhikṣu Liṭha, who claimed that sensual desire does not obstruct the Path, he was guilty of a *sthūlātyaya* offense for defying the admonitions because his mind was sincere; thus, it is light.

Therefore, regarding the mutual establishment of the six categories of opening and restriction: this is based on the arising of the four types of delusion and non-delusion. The establishment of the teachings also possesses degrees of gravity.

For example, in the five propositions concerning the perception of an object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), the first proposition involves a correspondence between the mind and the object, resulting in the commission of a root offense of the five categories;

thus, it is grave. The remaining four propositions involve the mind not corresponding to the object and the object not matching the mind; these result only in the commission of preparatory offenses (*upakrama*). This is the intended meaning of the teaching.
Regarding the light offenses (*laghu*), within the latter four phrases, let us first explain them in terms of the precept against killing.
For example, the two phrases concerning the "perception of a human or a non-human" involve an object that is open (*anāpatti*). The "perception of a non-human" constitutes an open case (*mukha*).

In the latter two phrases, "perception of a human" and "doubt regarding a non-human," the non-human is the open object, while the perception of a human constitutes the prohibited mind (*pratiṣiddha-citta*). All phrases concerning objects and perceptions follow this pattern (and so forth). Furthermore, as in...

Regarding the precept against destroying living beings: when no *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to prepare food) is available, one may personally purify fruit; this is an allowance (*anujñā*) and not a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). When a *kappiya-kāraka* is present, it is not permitted; this is a prohibition and not an allowance.
Furthermore, regarding the precept on being separated from one's robes: if one enters a boundary after meeting with a wife from outside, one is not permitted to relinquish the robe;

this is an allowance for a minor matter where there is no prohibition for a major one. If one enters the boundary and [the conditions] are met, it is not permitted to relinquish the robe from afar; this is a major prohibition.

Regarding "no leniency" (all instances of permission and prohibition follow this pattern). Regarding "mutually established": they are established by being mutually contrasted. Within the category of "leniency for light offenses," there is no "prohibition for heavy offenses" (and so forth);
within it, there is no "leniency for light offenses" and so on—this is what is meant by "mutually established. Seventh, "distinguishing differences based on practice":

while the preceding six [points] all clarify the matter by contrasting a single case with the teaching, here the capacities of those being addressed and the practices performed differ; thus, the lightness [of the offense] is distinguished.

This concerns gravity. For instance, regarding the single rule concerning noise and stillness: this is an explanation of the matter of the breath (vital energy). "Noise" refers to a village; "stillness" refers to an araṇya (forest hermitage).
If a superior practitioner dwells in an araṇya, being permitted to remain separated from his robe for six nights, the intent of the teaching is light.

If those of middle or inferior capacity dwell in a village, where there is no difficulty [to be away], being separated from one's robe for even a single night constitutes an offense; the intent of the teaching is thus grave. Furthermore, as with a superior practitioner...
When people are restricted to dwelling among tombs or under trees, possessing only the three robes as their sole benefit, the intent of the teaching is grave.

For those of middling or inferior faculties, however, long-term residence in housing was permitted, along with the possession of the "one hundred and one" items and the authorization to establish kitchen facilities; thus, the intent of the teaching is comparatively light.

If explained in terms of transgressions: for those of superior practice, the offense is light; for those of middling or inferior faculties who violate the rules, the offense is heavy. (The above seven examples must be understood according to this principle of relative gravity.)
The third conclusion states: "In all these examples, 'all' (fan) implies more than one; it refers back to the seven preceding examples.

'Conceived' (huai) refers to the underlying sentiment—that is, within the Buddha’s own sentiment, there are no instances where the original prescriptions for the teachings vary in weight beyond these seven.

Regarding the principle and substance of the judgment: 'principle' (zong) refers to the central tenet, and 'substance' (ti) refers to the structural framework. Now, the Master, having thoroughly investigated the Vinaya-piṭaka, knows..."
This teaching was intended for the future; thus, seven categories were established so that one might understand the fundamental intent behind the Buddha’s regulations.

Now, in evaluating the current situation, we rely on these as our primary authority. Fearing that the details may not yet be fully understood, I have specially established this introductory section as a general framework.
The Third Gate. First the heading, then the explanation. Regarding the initial statement "the third" up to "the intention": first, I shall clarify the purpose for its inclusion.

This means that what was explained above—namely, the two intentions of lightness and gravity—constitutes the core principle for the adjudication of the four categories of offenses. However, one must recognize this core principle and apply it to the adjudication of specific cases.

Therefore, it is called "discrimination" (biàn). Regarding the explanation of the term "correspondence" (duì): "corresponding person" refers to the individual capable of responding; "judging matter" refers to the presiding official who adjudicates;
and "corresponding practice" refers to the specific matters being addressed. Since both the subject and object are manifested together by the assembly, it is termed "corresponding to matters.

(In various commentaries, this is generally contrasted with the preceding seven categories; however, this particular explanation may be considered overly restrictive. Regarding the explanation according to the teachings (jiào), there are two interpretations. The *Sou xuán* [commentary] interprets this according to its own school...

Regarding the fundamental tenets of the Vinaya teachings, the commentaries distinguish them according to the five different schools. For my part, I take the former interpretation as correct. Why is this?

Because in the first gate [of the preceding discussion], it was stated that the analysis was conducted solely from the perspective of our own school; furthermore, the seven examples in the second gate likewise relied exclusively upon our own school.
Although this present gate provides a general analysis of all five schools, when investigating the underlying principles of their differences, [the former view remains authoritative].

The commentary also relies on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* for the rules regarding receiving [the precepts] and their corresponding characteristics. Even when explaining external traditions, these are merely mentioned incidentally.
Therefore, one should know that [the measurements] are strictly confined to the dimensions and demarcations of one's own school. Reflect on this.
In the commentary, the phrase "since the Buddha-dharma flowed eastward for nearly six hundred years" means "from" (zì). "Nearly" (jǐ; pronouned as qí) means "approximate.

From the tenth year of the Yongping era of the Later Han (the Dingmao year) until the ninth year of the Wude era of the Tang, five hundred and fifty-nine years have already passed, which is close to six hundred.
This is calculated by arranging the sexagenary cycle (*jiǎzǐ*). [Some sources state that five hundred and sixty-four years have passed, short by thirty-six years.]

"Six hundred full. (The meaning is not detailed. "Carries" (*zài*): in the eras of Tang and Yu, it was called a "carrying" (*zài*). Tang refers to the lineage of Yao, the Pottery Tang; Yu refers to the lineage of Shun, the Youyu.

Furthermore, they both mark the end of a period, as they were all recorded upon bamboo slips (*jiǎn*). Thus, explaining the end of the number ten as "carrying" (*zài*) makes manifest that numbers have a beginning and an end.

Moreover, in the Zhou era, it was called a "year" (*nián*). "Year" (*nián*) means the character for "thousand" (*qiān*) beneath the character for "grain" (*hé*); it signifies that the thousand [stalks] have grown tall. It is said that...
Because the grain ripens once [per year], it is called the "summer year. "Year" (*sui*) is the name of a star. Thus, the Confucian texts state: "In the east, Jia and Yi correspond to Wood;

the planet *Sui-xing* (Jupiter) revolves one degree every twelve months. In the south, Bing and Ding correspond to Fire; the planet *Kui-xing* (Venus) revolves once every sixty days. In the west, Geng and Xin correspond to Metal;
the planet *Tai-bai-xing* (Venus) revolves once every thirty days. In the north, [it corresponds to] the Water planet (*Shen-xing*)."
It does not revolve. The central position is Earth (Wu-ji). The Star of Stability (Venus) revolves once every three years. This refers to the summer season;

taking the Star of the Year (Jupiter), it completes one circuit around the heavens, and as the climatic seasons change, it is called a "year" (*sui*). When it is high, the days lengthen. "Lengthening" (*yi*) refers to the time for sacrifices being altered once;
descendants follow their ancestors, establishing this as the seasonal rhythm for sacrifice. This is the current text.
Regarding the phrase "carried" (*zài*) in the middle [of the text], it is used for the sake of convenience in expression; there is no other underlying principle.

As for the passage from "the various masters" to "said," this clarifies the errors made by ancient virtuous teachers in their delusions regarding the tenets and their judgments at the time when the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* was circulating. Thus, the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states:

"Since the time after the Golden River [the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa], the various teachings have been promulgated in succession. Yet, the various lecturers have vied with one another in a biased and inconsistent manner, each holding their own views..."

The *Qizong* (Dharmaguptaka) school rarely possessed a broad understanding of the Vinaya, yet the *Mahāsāṃghika* flourished greatly. Within the Guanzhong region, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong lü) was prevalent, while in the regions south of the Yangtze River, it spread widely.
Although there was the śramaṇa Tandi, who mastered the *Karmavācanā* of the *Dharmaguptaka*, the original texts of that Vinaya had not yet reached the regions south of the Yangtze.

Consequently, within Guanzhong, the *Dharmaguptaka* *Karmavācanā* was practiced; each followed their own respective traditions, such as the *Mahāsāṃghika* or the *Sarvāstivāda*, rather than adhering to the fundamental principles of their own schools.

This is an inversion. It is also due to being driven by haste; following one’s own sentiments and allowing them to lead, while deviating from the actual characteristics of the teaching, is called "punning and forced interpretation" (*chuàn-záo*).

To claim that one's own judgment is correct and to disparage the teachings of others as incorrect is what is meant by "judging right and wrong. Regarding "vying to seal [their views on] identity and difference": "vying" (*jìng*) means to contend; "sealing" (*fēng*) means to cling to or hold fast to.

They contend and cling to the view that receiving the precepts through the *caturvargika-karman* (the ritual of the fourfold assembly) is identical [to other methods], which is termed "clinging to the minor recitation" (*xíng xiǎo sòng*).
Alternatively, the *Saṃghāṭa* [Vinaya] considers these to be distinct as they follow [the rules]. Their number is quite large; hence it is said they are "incalculable.

The phrase "excellent ultimate destination" (*liáng zhì qù*) explains the reason for departing from divergent attachments. This refers to the preceding judgment and demarcation of right and wrong, where people vied to seal their own positions regarding similarities and differences—asking, "What should one adopt?
One may cite the text of the *Shuochao* (Commentary on the Vinaya), which states generally: "It is truly because... and so forth.

"Good" means abundant. "Real" means actual. "By" (*yóu*) refers to the cause or source; "seeking" (*xún*) refers to investigation; "tenet" (*zōng*) refers to the path of the school; and "purport" (*zhì*) refers to the underlying meaning. Xuán says:
"Because they do not recognize the purport of the five schools, they act according to their own whims. Their practice is dark and confused, deviating from the essence of the precepts.

They rely on the *Dharmaguptaka* for obtaining the precepts, but follow the *Mahāsāṃghika* regarding robes—both the general rules for robes and the specific protection of robes—and they do not permit the shifting of respect."

Having completed the formal act (*karmavācanā*), one goes beyond the boundary. Four *kārsāpaṇas* and three *tri-koṭis* constitute a heavy offense. Alternatively, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, eighty small coins constitute a heavy offense.
One may accept [the robe] for seven nights and thirty-nine nights. At the time of receiving the precepts, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) has broken the precepts.
Or [the preceptor] may not be present; for instance, if a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch) acts as the *upādhyāya*, and so forth. Those who stand outside the group of ten may all perform the duties.

Or, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, one may directly recite the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and so on. All such cases are instances of being confused regarding the fundamental purpose [of the rite]. (There is an interpretation which claims:

"Not recognizing that the *Mahīśāsaka-śāstra* is the fundamental doctrine of the Dharmaguptaka school, and that the *Mahāsāṃghika-śāstra* is the fundamental doctrine of the Sarvāstivāda school, leading to confusion in ritual practice—this is incorrect.")

Regarding the phrase "therefore, reaching the point of reprimand," this is an exhortation for Master Ji to receive formal transmission. Because previously he was muddled and did not follow the path of the school, he must now be clear and proficient in order to recognize the fundamental intent;
thus, the two characters [for learning and transmission] are necessary. These words build upon what precedes and lead into what follows. "Learning" (*xué*) refers to practice and study;
