"transmission" (*shī*) refers to receiving formal instruction from a master. Thus, the Confucian texts state that in antiquity there was Dong Yu, who truly loved learning the characters and often spoke of the "three surpluses."
The winter is the remainder of the year; the night is the remainder of the day; the rain is the remainder of the administration. These three avenues may serve as subjects for study.
Furthermore, it is superior to know through the observation of the stars; to know through study is next best. It is also said: "Jade is not made into a vessel unless it is carved;
a person does not come to know the Way unless they study. Even if one does not eat all day and does not sleep all night...
[To penetrate and master]. To think about it is of no benefit; it is better to study. Furthermore, Xiang Tuo was seven years old when he became the teacher of Confucius.
He once gathered the scholars of the four schools at the Shu River to serve as teachers for the Master (and so forth).

This must refer to a long-term commitment, meaning not merely a single session or half a day (the character *xiang* is pronounced "diao," meaning twenty sessions), but rather requires the accumulation of days and the pursuit of merit. Therefore, the Confucian has...
Three winters. The Buddha permitted five summers [of training]. For example, during the Han dynasty, there was Dongfang Shuo, whose courtesy name was Mengman. He borrowed three winters to study;
his learning encompassed ten thousand scrolls of books, the five musical tones and six pitch-pipes, and the various arts of yin and yang—all were thoroughly mastered.
Within the Buddhist teachings, one relies on a teacher for five summers, just as the Great Master Nanshan listened to the *Shoushu* twenty times and mastered the five sections [of the Vinaya].
Only when one has not mastered the Vinaya teachings, as well as the various sūtras and śāstras, can one truly uphold the Vinaya texts and wear the authentic scriptures upon oneself.

Since the tenets of different schools differ, one must act according to the specific school one relies upon; only then will there be no doubt or stagnation. To revile, to scold, or to disparage—how could such things be permissible?
To sink into ruin is "lunmo" (淪沒). To mock with a slight smile is "chi" (嗤). To criticize through words and appearance is "ze" (責). May you be spared from these [faults].
It is neither subject to censure, disparagement, or reproach, nor is it submerged in ridicule or blame.

Regarding the statement, "Now, as for the judgment up to the 'consequent' (anuvartana)": this precisely distinguishes the determination based on the established doctrine. As for the phrase, "Returning to its essential nature (āśraya-svabhāva)":

one must rely upon the original undertaking (upasaṃpad) to clarify the subsequent practice. Regarding the statement, "Since the essence is already divided into four parts, and so forth": this refers, for the time being, to this...

Regarding the monks and nuns of this land during the Cao Wei period: because the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmatrata intended to translate the *Caturvarga-karman* (Four-Part Vinaya Karma), those who received the precepts and practiced accordingly ought to rely solely upon the *Caturvarga*.

It was improper to use the *Daśabhāṇavāra*, the *Mahāsāṃghika*, or the *Mahīśāsaka* to judge the transgressions and observances of the *Caturvarga* school. Therefore it is said: "How could one clearly follow [other schools]? (This is stated from one perspective).

If one provides a further general explanation: just as one receives the precepts based on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one must also rely on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* itself to determine the conduct that follows them.
The same applies to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. It is sufficient simply to follow the path of the school to which one belongs; one need only ensure that there is no confusion. (And so forth.)
The phrase "fearing that even those who are dull-witted" means "still more so. This refers to the previous general explanation based on the facts;
it was necessary to clarify the following of the original precepts. Fearing further that later students might not yet understand clearly, he again provides this instruction.

The term "general outline" (*dàgāng*) refers to the essential meaning of the judgment regarding the cases. The phrase "to take [the matter] up" (*zhé jiāng xià*) correctly indicates the boundaries of the classification. As for "takes up":

This refers to monopolizing authority. In ancient times, those who took the *Saṃghāṭi* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* as their own field of study would judge the essence of ordination, the observance, and the transgression of others according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
This was during the Cao Wei period; although monks and nuns received the precepts by relying on the *Dharmaguptaka-karman* translated by Fandi, the full Vinaya texts had not yet circulated.
It was not until the sixth year of the Hongshi era of Later Qin during the Eastern Jin that [the full texts appeared].

Puṇyatāra first translated the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which became widely prevalent throughout the region south of the Yangtze River. It was not until the twelfth year [of the Jianyuan era] that he translated the *Caturvargika-vinaya*;
at that time, however, it had not yet been circulated at all. During the Xihuan era of the Eastern Jin dynasty, he further translated the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

The ancient masters within the Guanzhong region all studied both the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, and regarding what they themselves studied, they relied upon the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* for their judicial determinations.

Regarding the four *qián* and three *jiǎo* (4.3) as a heavy offense, it was permitted to keep the robe through the night; however, during the summer retreat (*varṣā*), receiving formal authorization (*karmavācanā*) and departing the boundary at sunrise were prohibited.
Alternatively, according to the *Śāriputra Vinaya*, the severance of theft is determined by eighty *wén* (coins), based on the seven-night and thirty-nine-night periods.

From the Yuan-Wei period onwards, precedents were all like this. Later, because of Master Fachong, who suddenly examined the essence of the precepts (*śīlaskandha*), it became known that [the limit] originated from the four [coins].
"Only by attaining the precepts can one rectify former delusions, as if returning to one's original destination.

Master Nanshan, fearing that there may still be those of a similar nature in the present day, has therefore demonstrated this once more (etc.). 'Should one happen to incur transgressions,' it refers only to those who are ignorant for failing to study.
'Happen' (tuō) means suddenly; 'incur' (lí) means to encounter; 'transgression' (qiān) means sin. The meaning is: if there should be such erroneous judgments, they all arise from..."

Regarding the teachings, they have not yet been clarified or understood. The fundamental differences between the two schools, their relative urgency, the intent behind right and wrong, and the offenses incurred—all these stem from a lack of study and ignorance.

Question: Suppose there is someone who studies the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) and judges that using a copper vessel belonging to another according to the *Caturvarga-vinaya* constitutes a minor offense.

From the perspective of the principle of damaging the permanent property of the Sangha (*saṃghika-sthāvara*), would this not constitute a grave offense? Answer: There are two interpretations. One says it does not constitute an offense.
This is important. It means that one should not use biased Confucian perspectives to judge [the matter] or revert to [erroneous views], but should rely upon the Vinaya teachings as authority.

One incurs only the minor offenses of "lack of learning" (*aśikṣita*) and "ignorance" (*ajñāna*). (The above follows the interpretation in the *Souxuan*). Second, some say it constitutes an offense against the root [precepts], with the additional factor of lack of learning and ignorance.
Now, examining these two interpretations, the first explanation is superior; the latter meaning contradicts the *Chao* and is therefore not accepted.

The phrase "now arriving at the contemplation" establishes the general principle. "Now" distinguishes the present from the past; "principle" (*tōng*) refers to the comprehensive rule, while "standard" (*gé*) refers to the correct norm.

Within this single section of the text, two types of fixed standards are established: the first twenty-nine chapters constitute the standard for the Vinaya Master of the *Dharmaguptaka* (Four-Part) school when performing the affairs of that school;
the thirtieth chapter constitutes the standard for the Vinaya Master of the *Dharmaguptaka* school when performing the affairs of other schools.
This is the established standard for comparison. Baoyun states: "The horizontal bar at the rear of a carriage is called a jiào; jiào means 'to correct' or 'to rectify.
Zhǔn means 'to take as a standard' or 'to level,' and it also refers to a target. It is understood that scholars of the five Vinaya schools all use this to adjudicate cases.

If one school collectively establishes a clear standard, then one must rely on the original transmission of that school to determine whether an offense has been committed or avoided. As for "one who discards [the precepts]," this reveals that...

This section is unfolded once more. It provides both the detailed articles and the governing principles. By examining the articles of this single section, one comes to know the practices of the subsequent chapters;
though their origins differ and their schools are distinct, they are like the hair of a fur coat. This section is like the collar of that coat. "Shi" (釋) means to explain and to unravel.
This is indeed so. Great observation arises from clarity. In the *Yījīng*, there is the hexagram of Guān (Observation), which corresponds to the image of great brightness.
If one examines the principles of this single gateway, one will see the general purport of the practices in the subsequent chapters;

it is like a bright mirror suspended upon a high terrace, or like ascending a lofty mountain to behold all things—nothing remains unclear. Bao further explains that "guān" (observation) is read as "àn guān" (to press and observe).
As for the term "contemplation" (*guan*) used for the dwelling place of the Way-streamers, it also takes up the sense of ascending and reaching toward a goal. As he described it (and so forth).
The text of the fourth section has two parts. First is the heading followed by the explanation. The phrase "the fifth meaning" is the heading.

This means that while the previous section has already clarified the determination of the *āyatana* (bases), it must take the original reception (*mūla-samādāna*) as its primary tenet. Now, within the tenets of the original reception, there may be instances where the textual meaning is not exhaustive;
thus, one must rely upon other schools (*nikāya*). However, since there are established criteria for what to cite and what to reject when doing so, this section is established to serve as [a guide].

This is done for the sake of establishing a standard. Question: Since you have already refuted the ancient misconceptions regarding the criteria for judgment, and since you intend to clarify this by following other schools, why establish this specific gate as a model? Why is it distinguished [from others]? Answer: It is not so.
The former approach abandoned the root for the branches; according to the Vinaya itself, there are cases where one does not rely on that. First, let us examine the precedent.
The primary tenet should serve as the basis for judgment. Only if the primary tenet is deficient should one cite another school;

furthermore, these must be taken because their thematic force is related and their urgency is comparable, so as to provide supplementation. Regarding the explanation of the term: "various" (*zhū*) means not being one.

"Section" (*bu*) means "category. Excluding the four external divisions, it comprises the five sections and ten *nikāyas*, as well as the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras, śāstras, records, and biographies.
Whenever there is an exposition of the Vinaya that corresponds with the Vinaya, it is all subsumed within these various characters.
Since the categories are equal, they may be cited universally.

Regarding the statement in the commentary, "The term 'comprehensive' (*tǒng*) refers to the textual exposition": "Comprehensive" (*tǒng*) derives from "pervasive" (*tōng*). It pervasively clarifies the single great *vinaya* scriptural treasury (*piṇḍa-piṭaka*), which was established by the Buddha in person according to the capacities of his disciples.
Although it had not yet been fully expressed in written characters, it was nonetheless the *vinaya* of one of the [three] scriptural treasuries.

At the time of the compilation (*saṃgīti*) after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it was fully articulated in written form; thus, it is also the teaching of the great scriptural treasury. This is subsequent to the completion of the compilation.
During the period of one hundred years, the five sagely rulers maintained the Dharma no differently than the former; thus it is said that the fundamental reality is but a single principle.

As for the phrase "merely reaching the establishment," "merely" (*dan*) is a term denoting exclusivity or limitation. "Awakening" (*wu*) refers to penetrating realization. Since the capacities and dispositions (*indriya*) of beings differ, [the teachings vary accordingly].
Their realization and entry [into the path] are also distinct; this is what makes them different. These are the various calculations of the five masters.
Following Upagupta, there were five disciples whose views and inclinations differed, and for this reason they split into five schools. "Mountains standing like peaks" refers to mountain ranges.

According to the interpretation of the characters, "mountain" (*shan*) refers to a place where prisons are established beneath it, serving as a site for governing and restraining ghosts and spirits. There are one hundred and twenty river valleys and plains;
those whose cliffs and crags are particularly steep and precipitous are enfeoffed as "peaks" (*yue*). Thus, in this region, there are five peaks: Mount Tai, the Eastern Peak, is in Yanzhou;
Mount Heng, the Southern Peak, is in Hengzhou; Mount Hua, the Western Peak, is in Huazhou; and Mount Huan, the Northern Peak... [is in]... (the text here is incomplete).
Huanzhou (now changed to Zhenyou Dingzhou to avoid [the imperial] taboo). Mount Song, the Central Peak, is located in Luozhou. Baoyun said:

Someone raised an objection, saying, "The Five Peaks are in this region, while the Five Masters divided the teachings in the Western Land. Since they have no Five Peaks there, why do you speak of establishing 'Peaks'?
Now it is said that this is not so; although the division of the teachings took place there, the compilation of the *Chao* was conducted here in this land at that time.
Citing these five mountains of this land as a parallel to the five masters of the Western Regions, it may be that the number five is intended to be identical;

thus they are cited as an analogy. This means that just as those five masters suddenly arose, each competing with the others and differing in their emotional views, so too do these five mountains of this land vie for height, jostling one another as they soar upward (and so forth).

The statement "the reason for reaching the authoritative texts" explains the basis for their individual distinctions. "Desire and inclination" refers to the five masters' minds of seeking and longing for pleasure.
"Establishing one's own school" means establishing the respective schools of the five masters themselves. Question:
Since they establish their own schools according to their desires and inclinations, from where do they take their textual sources? Answer (in the *Chao*): They compete in weighing [the evidence].
Regarding the passage "The text of the Mahāsāṃghika," etc.: "Jing" (競) means to contend, to gather, or to examine. *Mahāsāṃghika* translates as "Great Assembly";
it refers to the *Aṣṭaka-bhāṣya* (Eighty Recitations), which is named according to its doctrine (and does not refer to the Mahāsāṃghika of the Mahāyāna).

As for using [texts] to compile the scriptures of a single school: for example, within the Great Canon (*Tripitaka*), one takes passages reflecting the specific views of the Sarvāstivāda and compiles them into ten [sections].
To recite the scriptures of only one school while the others follow this same pattern (and so forth; there is no need to cite specific examples for clarification).
The phrase "therefore it reaches the manifest" concludes the point that they are mutually deficient. "Therefore there are" carries the sense of causal basis (*hetu*).

Because, as mentioned previously, each has selectively adopted portions of the Vinaya texts according to their own subjective views and established five schools, there are consequently four types of deficiencies. This is [the meaning].

Because of attachment, there are these two characters [of "heavy" and "light"]. To say that "the weight and lightness differ in their force" means that regarding the actions performed, although they belong to the same category within the five groups of precepts (*pañca-nikāya*), they mutually possess varying degrees of gravity.

For example, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, violating the precept against causing a dispute among nuns results in a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), which is heavy; whereas according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense), which is light.

According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, stealing five coins results in a *pārājika* (defeat), which is heavy; whereas according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (grave transgression), which is light. In the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, there is also the case of doubt...

If one commits a *pārājika* offense in the presence of another person, it is grave; whereas in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is merely a *sthūlātyaya*, which is light. Since the gravity of the offenses differs, they represent distinct systems, and there is no other underlying principle [to reconcile them].

Regarding the divergence between observance and violation: the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* first prescribes purification, followed by the making of the three robes at the beginning and end [of the rainy season retreat].

It is not necessary to relinquish [the purity] to achieve observance (*dhāraṇa*). According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one incurs an offense (*āpatti*) by obtaining [an object] without relinquishing the purity, which constitutes a transgression.

Furthermore, in the sections on the precepts of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, all [rules] conclude that the offenses of the three lower assemblies constitute a transgression; in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, they do not conclude that it constitutes observance (hence the saying: "observance and transgression follow separate paths"). Regarding those [precepts] that appear alternately as existing or non-existing:

the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* contains many rules concerning the veneration of stupas that are absent from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*; conversely, there are rules present in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* that are subject to differentiation [and thus absent elsewhere].

Regarding the *grāmavastu* (the section on village boundaries): the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) lacks [certain rules], while the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Five-Part Vinaya) contains them, including those concerning the three *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and the water boundary (*udakavastu*).

These are absent in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. They emerge alternately from one another (hence the phrase "and so forth"). As for the alternating manifestation of what is discarded and what is established: the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* establishes the practice of reciting the precepts with melodic chanting (*gāthā*), whereas the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* discards it.

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* establishes the purification of the site (*śuddha-sthāna*), while the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (the *Daśabhāṇavāra*) sets them aside to clarify their mutual relationship; they merely differ in terminology.

(Regarding the upper robe, the formal explanation relies solely on the *Kaṭhina-sūtra*; this is analyzed by comparing the five schools [excluding the *Mahāsāṃghika*, which is a root school and not to be conflated with the explanations found in the *Śāṭhyasūtra*]).
Second, within the specific [section], I establish the fundamental assembly by drawing upon various texts. The initial statement, "Now I establish...

up to "...not the same," means that based on the preceding standard, during the time before the division, it was uniformly one great treasury of the *Vinaya*. Toward the end of the hundred-year period, as the divisions followed their respective paths, it resulted in the incomplete nature of the ritual procedures and the Dharma.
Now, because the practice and maintenance according to the four divisions are not comprehensive, it is necessary to cite other schools to supplement the deficiencies. Just as...

Just as before the division [of the schools], there was no single unified body. Regarding the *Dharmaguptaka* (Four-Part) school being the foundation, it accords with what is stated in the tenth section below:
"The *Dharmaguptaka* school is that which the *Sifenlü chao* (Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya) takes as its primary authority; thus, this Vinaya is taken as the foundation.

Alternatively, within the foundation itself, matters both with and without precedent are cited from other schools; therefore, one must not fail to utilize them. This is not like the narrow-mindedness of those in ancient times."
This is the core tenet.
Second, citing [this treatise] as authoritative. Regarding the phrase "therefore, up to 'knowing,'" this is the general heading cited from the treatise.

As for what is called the *Sudarsana* (Good Vision), it was composed by five hundred arhats; this treatise explains the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, being able to analyze it skillfully so that its meaning is easy to understand.

Because it is seen [clearly], it is called "Good Vision" (Sudarśana). Now, regarding the composition of treatises (*śāstra*), there are two distinct types in the Western Regions: first, commentaries (*vyākhyā*); second, thematic treatises (*siddhānta*).
If it is a commentary, it follows the text of a single foundational scripture from beginning to end, explaining it point by point.

For example, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna composed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* to explain the six hundred fascicles of the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. Likewise, Vasubandhu composed the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* to explain the *Golden* [Prajñāpāramitā].

In works such as the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāraṃitā Sūtra*, if it concerns a treatise (*śāstra*), one does not provide an exegesis; rather, one takes a single authoritative scripture as the primary source (*mūla*).

Where the primary source is prolix, one deletes it; where it is deficient, one supplements it by citing passages from various scriptures, as is done in the *Mahāvyutpatti* (or *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* is also such a work. This current *Sudarsana-śāstra* was originally a commentary (*vyākhyā*), but was later revised into a treatise (*śāstra*).
The *Śāstra-sāra* follows the structural model of this [latter] work, resembling the *śāstras* of the Western Regions (India). Within that treatise, it refers to various Arhats.

Originally, I intended to compose a treatise that would explain the text of the four divisions (*caturvarga*) in sequential order. However, by the time we reached the precept against sexual misconduct, it had already reached six fascicles.
Fearing that the text would become overly prolix if I were to complete the entire work, I deliberated and changed my approach to a topical commentary (*mūla-śāstra*).

Thus, he said: "The Master said, 'The Vinaya text is already complete; I shall now provide a detailed explanation. The Master said, 'Within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, within the meaning of each phrase...'"

Regarding the difficult questions: if one wishes to know [the answer], there are four divisions of the Vinaya (*caturvarga-vinaya*). Those of great virtue who possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) have extracted [the essentials] to enable others to understand (this concludes the treatise).
Now, I shall briefly explain it. As for the term "Dharma Master" (*dharmācārya*), it refers to a Vinaya Master (*vinayadhara*).
The five hundred Arhats, being those who understand the Dharma, are titled "Dharma Masters. The word "called" (*yue*) is a term of the treatise. The root text of the Vinaya is already complete.
This refers to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, which is already complete in itself; there is no need to further compose a commentary to explain it point by point.
When I say "I shall provide a detailed explanation," this is intended here as a treatise on the essential principles (*zonglun*). As for what is called "possessing supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*):

One interpretation states: [it refers to] the three knowledges (trividyā) and the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā). A second interpretation states: it refers to the supernormal power of the mind endowed with divine wisdom (divyaprajñā-cetasaḥ-abhijñā).

Regarding the phrase "extracted so that people may know," this means that the assembly deliberated and selected one treatise from the fundamental canon (mūla-śāstra) to enable others to study and understand it.

Second, the four dharmas are explained separately based on the treatise. Regarding the phrase "one fundamental [text] up to... [it means] first to present the text of the fundamental treatise; thus he addressed the assembly and asked.
He asked, "What are the four aspects of the Dharma? He replied, "First, the root; second, that which follows the root; third, the words of the Dharma-master; and fourth, the application of the mind.

These are the four. He asked, "What is meant by the 'root'? He replied, "The entire Vinaya Piṭaka. He asked again, "What is meant by 'that which follows the root'? He replied, "The four great bases (*mahā-vastu*).
He asked again, "What is meant by 'the words of the Dharma-master'? He replied, "The five [procedures] for assembling the community."
When there were one hundred arhats, the seer first spoke the root text; when there were five hundred arhats, they extensively analyzed and propagated it—this is the speech of the Dharma Master.

Furthermore, he asked: "What is meant by 'application through intention'? He replied: "Setting aside the root text, setting aside that which follows the root text, and setting aside the speech of the Dharma Master, one crosses over by means of application through the skillful means of the mind;
one crosses over by means of the extensive exposition of the Sūtras; and one crosses over by means of the extensive exposition of the Abhidharma. By means of the *Vibhaṅga*...

The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* (or *Vinaya-mātṛkā*) explains this in detail; this is what is called "the application of the mind" (above, from the main treatise). The citations in the *Chao* (Commentary) exist for the purpose of brevity; they are explained immediately following their headings.
As for the phrase "all the Vinaya Piṭaka," it refers to the twenty *khandakas* of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Its text is not small.

Therefore, it is said "all"; this does not mean that "all" refers to the eighty recitations of the Vinaya. Second, following the original [text]: according to the treatise (*śāstra*), these are the four great bases (*mahāsthāna*).

However, the explanations of these four great bases differ; according to the treatise, they are clarified within the first precept, but here, based on their meaning, they apply universally to all precepts.
For now, we shall discuss them within the context of the natural precepts (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) by contrasting them with what is non-preceptual, as for the remaining precepts.
To illustrate this: these four phrases consist of two general conditions for the precept (the first two phrases) and two specific conditions for the precept (the latter two phrases).
The first and third are instances of transgression; the second and fourth are instances of non-transgression. First, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"I have declared [certain actions] to be impure (because their intrinsic nature as *śīla* is evil), yet I do not prohibit them (for they are permitted when committed during states of insanity or mental derangement). However...

This is "impure" because it follows entry [into the act], even though there is a textual allowance for a single moment of mindfulness (wherein the bhikṣu enters while performing the preliminary action).

Because it falls within the stage of transgression, one does not enter the pure state; this is called impure. (There is a single moment of mindfulness regarding the body, yet this bhikṣu does not enter the textual allowance; this is called impure. Second, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I have spoken of the impure" (as above), yet he did not prohibit it. However, this following entry into the pure state is called pure. (While performing the preceding action...)

If there is not even a single thought that knows this bhikṣu is complying with the opening text, it is therefore called "pure. Third, regarding the Buddha’s instruction to the bhikṣus: "I declare that purity is permitted and not prohibited" (this refers to the first precept;

when encountering circumstances of hostile compulsion, union with the object is permitted, which is termed "not prohibited"). However, this does not mean one enters into impurity (if during the three periods [of the act] a single thought of defiled pleasure arises, it is immediately termed "impure").

Regarding "not entering into what is pure": for you, this refers to not entering into what is impure (meaning that when one enters into the permitted category with a mind of defiled pleasure, it is called "not entering into what is pure").
Fourth, he addressed the bhikṣus: "I have declared what is pure and permitted, and have not prohibited it" (as above).

However, this "entering into what is pure" means that for you, it is pure (when performing the aforementioned act without a mind of defiled pleasure, one enters into the permitted category without offense; therefore, it is called "pure"). As for the remaining natural precepts (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), the first two lines apply universally and are identical; the latter...

The second category, distinct conditions (*viśeṣa-pratyaya*), refers to differences in the specific circumstances. For example, regarding the precept against stealing, forming the perception that there is no owner or the perception that the object belongs to a close friend;

regarding the precept against killing, forming the perception that it is a wooden post, and so forth—these are distinct conditions. Prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepa-śikṣā*) are likewise as above; for instance, cutting grass or burning a temple with a wild fire constitutes a distinct condition.
Regarding the precept against intoxicants, if a medical treatment fails to cure an illness and a physician says that wine must be drunk, this is a distinct condition. If...

If one swallows once, the illness is cured; if one swallows a second time, it violates the text of the allowance. This is called "impure," as it does not enter into the state of purity and constitutes an offense of *pāyattika*.
If the illness is not yet cured, swallowing a second time is permitted; this follows into the state of purity and is non-offensive. This is called "pure. This applies to all precepts.

The present text is concise, merely indicating the two phrases of "following" (*anuvartana*) and "original" (*mūla*), rather than listing them as separate items. Third, regarding the words of the Dharma Master:
This refers to the words of the five hundred arhats. In the present text, the phrase "the one who says" (*yun yun*) refers to the author of the treatise (*lun-zhu*).

The commentator of the *Jiyi jiao* (Excerpts on Meaning) points to the aforementioned arhats as being the principal authors of the treatise. Fourth, regarding "using the Tripiṭaka by means of inference," the text is also abbreviated;

it simply states generally that "the Tripiṭaka is as previously mentioned. One may consult the extensive citations from the treatises for details (the above interpretation follows the *Lunji* [Record of the Treatise]).

Regarding the application of the threefold interpretation of meaning, the phrase "first arriving at the Dharma" refers, according to the treatise, to a re-explanation of the fourth application of meaning.

Thus, that treatise states: "How is the meaning to be cited? Do not hastily adopt the literal text and proceed; one should first examine the root and contemplate the meaning of the phrases, analyzing each part individually and weighing them together.
Only thereafter should one examine the words of the Dharma Master. If the literal text and [the teacher's explanation] are consistent..."
[One] should accept [it]. If one observes that it is inconsistent, one must not accept it. This is called "using according to one's own intention" (the above is from the treatise).

Now, this *Chao* merely quotes briefly, saying: First, observe the root text (which is the Vinaya); second, examine the phrasing and meaning (which refers to the "Great Sections"); and finally, observe the words of the Dharma Master (which are the words of the five hundred Arhats).
That is to say, one should measure whether what is spoken in the Tripiṭaka corresponds with the meaning of these texts; if it does, it may be used. Otherwise, it should not.

Correspondence [to the teaching] is precisely cessation; therefore, it says, "do not grasp. Regarding the detailed explanation of the Vinaya Master’s dharma in the commentary, the sixth fascicle of that treatise states:
"A Vinaya Master possesses three dharmas and only then achieves accomplishment: first, reciting and mastering the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*; second, upholding it firmly without departing from it;
third, receiving and upholding it sequentially from a teacher without allowing it to be forgotten. One who possesses these three dharmas is called [a Vinaya Master]."
The Master of Vinaya says, "The main text is as follows," which indicates the conclusion of the main text. This refers to the main text of the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing).

Therefore, the *Hechao* (Combined Commentary) imitates the four methods of that treatise. Although the preceding [section] relies on what is analyzed in the treatise, it has not yet clarified which four methods belong to the commentator (*chaojia*).
Now, their names must be briefly stated; that is, when Nanshan intended to compose his commentary (*shu*), he explained these four.

Regarding the *Vibhāṣā-vinaya* (Analysis of the Vinaya): he then deliberated with himself both mentally and verbally. "If I were to compose a commentary (*śāstra*), I would have to explain it point by point in sequential order;

such a text would be voluminous and extensive—how would it differ from the ancient [commentaries]? Now, I shall revise it into a digest (*piṇḍīkṛta*). I shall simply take the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* as my primary authority. As for the "one basic text":

this refers to the single *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, which is the fundamental text upon which the composition of the digest is based. As for the "secondary texts following the basic one": this refers to...

In the Vinaya, regarding the explanation of the meanings of the various precept phrases (in the *Yǒujì*, it is stated that the four [sections] are subsumed under the "following the original"; this is likely incorrect). As for the words of the three Dharma masters:
This refers to the present master [Jizang]. He established two sequences and thirty chapters, explaining them in successive order. His commentary on the Vinaya clarifies the procedures for practice;
it is known that five hundred arhats distinguished and circulated this work (the phrase "Jizong will lead" or "the original manuscript was by the Dharma Master" refers to the words of the Master).

As for the application of the four intentions (*caturabhiprāya*), it means selecting corresponding passages from within the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*) according to one's intent and using them to supplement this particular school.

This fills the omission so that the ritual practice is sufficient, thereby avoiding any points of stagnation or doubt. Next, the section clarifies the discernment of right and wrong (the *ke* states: "as follows," etc.).

Regarding the phrase "Indeed, it is most perplexing": this means that when one wishes to discern and grasp the general meaning of the text, one first laments that the intent behind what is to be adopted and what is to be rejected is difficult to fathom. The word "Indeed" (*ran*)—

The "Xuanji" (Mysterious Record) explains this correctly: "To practice" means to employ; "to store" means to set aside. Thus, the *Lunyu* says: "When used, it is practiced; when discarded, it is stored.
This means that within the texts, what is essential is brought forth into the *Chao* (the compendium)—this is "practice";

what is not essential is set aside and discussed—this is "storing. It is cited as being "not easily [achieved]," hence it is said to be truly difficult (this refers to the difficulty of the rigid and the prolix).

That "accepting and rejecting is not easy" means that regarding the four-part *Dharmaguptaka* school as the fundamental tradition, if one finds it insufficient and must supplement its deficiencies with texts from other schools, this is even more difficult.
For example, while the *Dharmaguptaka* lacks a text concerning the holding of robes (*cīvara*), such a text exists in both the *Mahāsāṃghika* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra*.

One does not yet know what to accept and what to reject; thus it is said to be "not easy. (This refers to the difficulty of supplementation. For now, I shall set forth the general principles to ensure there is no confusion.

"Moreover" (*chʼieh*) refers to that which has not yet been fully exhausted in discussion. "To describe" (*shu*) means to narrate. "That" (*chi*) is a particle used as an auxiliary. "Great" (*ta*) refers to the discourse on the fundamental framework.
"To explain" (*chʼüan*) refers to the meaning being explained. "Briefly" (*chʼieh*) means to take up [the essence]; it means to grasp the general outline. "By means of" (*yi*) means to employ.
"To demonstrate" (*chʼeng*) means to show. "Delusion" (*huo*) means doubt and confusion. By employing this demonstration, one enables students to avoid giving rise to doubt and confusion.
The statement "this refers to those who seek [ordination]" indicates that this school is the Dharmaguptaka school. Regarding the phrase "both text and meaning are complete":

for example, when ten people in the Central Kingdom or five people in the borderlands receive the precepts, this constitutes completeness of the text (*vyañjana*). That all must be pure and in harmony constitutes completeness of the meaning (*artha*).
In terms of the ritual act of receiving the precepts, there is nothing lacking; the *Pravrajyāvastu* (Chapter on Ordination) of this specific school is itself fully sufficient.

Why need one further seek the *Daśabhāṇavāra* within other schools? [In our tradition,] there are cases where the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) is outside the group of ten, or where a layperson serves as preceptor, or where the preceptor is not present before the assembly.

Furthermore, regarding the various formal acts (*karmavācanā*)—the single announcement (*jñapti*), the two-fold announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), and the three-fold announcement (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*)—the essential framework and the underlying conditions are sufficient in themselves;
these texts are complete. One performs the announcement exactly as prescribed for an announcement, and one performs the formal act exactly as prescribed for a formal act.

Regarding the *karmavācanā*: if it is increased or decreased, it is not accomplished. This is "perfection of meaning" (*artha-paripūri*), as it lacks no deficiency concerning the matter to be addressed;

it is self-sufficient within its own section. Why then rely on the non-standard texts of other sections, such as the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*? Furthermore, regarding the matter of receiving [the *poṣadha*] for a day:

one receives it in three grades according to the length of the occasion. This is "perfection of text" (*vyañjana-paripūri*). It must not be confused or inverted; this is "perfection of meaning. This refers to the reception of the day.

Since these matters are complete within the ritual for receiving the *uposatha* day according to this specific school, why should one seek external texts such as the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*’s account of the thirty-nine nights or the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*’s passage on the completion of the ceremony? (The above constitutes a general refutation of those passages that should not be adopted.)
Regarding the statement, "There are others that reach one section," this passage specifically clarifies the complete extraction of the text.

"There are others" refers to those external [to the current context]. Aside from the previously mentioned textual meanings that are already complete, there are further four categories which require the extraction of other texts.

These four categories are: first, a Vinaya text that is incomplete; second, a matter that has been superseded by a prior rule; third, where there is a meaning but no text, yet there is a factual precedent; and now...

The first point states: "Regarding the unclear points in the Vinaya texts: for instance, in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*’s section on the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) ceremony, while the procedure for selecting those endowed with the five virtues is explained, it merely mentions appointing individuals to receive the *pravāraṇā*, without specifying their number (this is the first unclear point).

Furthermore, in the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual text), it simply says, 'The Saṃgha appoints Bhikṣu So-and-so,' without designating two persons (this is the second unclear point). The following text cites the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, both of which require that two persons be appointed."

The ritual procedure is now definitively settled. Furthermore, as clarified in the *Anvaya-vastu* (Section on the Monastic Year) regarding the rules for the summer retreat (*varṣā*), it is stated that during the summer, boatmen, woodcutters, cowherds, and oil-pressers may invite bhikṣus to observe the retreat; the Buddha declared this permissible.

[If] Śīlaskandha says that one must first form the intention to reside [there], this is not definitive. Moreover, during the summer, if one divides the period into the rainy season and moves away, the Buddha declared this permissible.

"Go. This does not at all mention the place where one has faith and joy, nor where food, clothing, and bedding are abundant (these two points remain unresolved). The following text quotes the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, which says:
"Those who rely on such persons as mentioned above, having first formed the intention to go, may obtain the basis for the rainy season retreat (*vassa*).

If they subsequently move elsewhere, it is permitted to follow the place where there is faith and joy and where food and clothing are abundant; only then is it considered a definitive resolution. Furthermore, this is as stated in the *Anuśaya-nirdeśa* (or *Svalakṣaṇa-nirdeśa*). With... [text continues].
Regarding those who have not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*), when reciting together from within the *Vinaya*, they merely say, "Spoken by the devas and ṛṣis.

If they recite together in this manner, all incur an offense. It is entirely incomplete if they do not state that [the teaching] has been approved by the Buddha (this is the "indefinite" case). The following passage cites the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*:

"If what was spoken by others has received the approval of the Buddha, then reciting it together constitutes an offense. Only then does it become a "definitive" case (there are many such examples, but fearing prolixity, they are not recorded in full).
Regarding the second point, "the matter being superseded by what precedes it": as in the Vinaya sections, fish and meat are all permitted as staple foods (*bhojana*).
However, according to various sutras such as the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, these are all prohibited. Those scriptures state: "One who eats meat severs the seed of great compassion;

it creates enmity among all living beings of water, land, and air. Therefore, one must not eat meat. By citing such teachings that supersede [the previous rule], they set aside the earlier Vinaya texts.
Regarding the third point, "having the meaning but lacking the text": this refers to the section on the method for relinquishing the precepts in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, which states:

"One who relinquishes the precepts must necessarily understand and be conscious [of the act]. If one does so before those who are insane, mute, deaf, or those suffering from both forms of sleep (i.e., deep sleep and drowsiness), the relinquishment is not accomplished.
(This constitutes the "meaning"). However, in the *Campā-sūtra* regarding those ineligible to be counted, only twenty-eight persons are enumerated; beyond these, all others...

There is no textual passage concerning deficiencies such as being mute or deaf (i.e., there is no such text). The *Chao* (Commentary) cites the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* below, stating that those who are asleep, mute, deaf, and so forth, are not included among those who constitute a quorum.
This is because the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* lacks certain supplementary details.

Regarding the fourth phrase, "there is no text but there is the matter," this means that within the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, while there is the matter of establishing boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*), there is no text concerning the six ways of assembling the Saṃgha or the distances [of those present].

Below, six scriptural texts are cited regarding the performance of the four types of acts (*caturvidha-karma*). As for these six texts: those that can be specifically identified should be relied upon from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), while those that cannot be specifically identified should be relied upon from the *Saṃghabhedaka-vastu*.

A forest hermitage free from difficulties follows the *Saṃyukta-ratnapiṭaka*; one with difficulties follows the *Sudarśana-śāstra*. The practice of the path follows the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*; the water element follows the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*. These shall be distinguished by comparing the respective texts as shown below.

Regarding the phrase "furthermore, it also occurs in the *Upādāna*": the word "furthermore" (*yòu*) indicates repetition. This means that the preceding four lines have been modified and repeated within the text of the *Upādāna*.
Although it is permitted to cite texts from other sources when there are omissions in the *Caturvarga-vinaya*, nevertheless, among the categories of texts being cited:

One must carefully discern and cite only those passages that are consistent; those that are inconsistent should not be cited (hence the phrase "the categories of texts cited"). Regarding those whose meaning and context are interrelated, the *Biao* states:

for example, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*’s rules on wearing robes and protecting the boundary markers (*sīmā*) are identical to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* regarding the protection of the boundary markers;
likewise, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*’s rule that those who are mute or deaf are not counted in the quorum corresponds to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
In that case, the renunciation of the precepts is not valid; this is because their underlying principles and implications are interconnected.

Furthermore, the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* permits the transfer of one’s consent (*chanda*) up to seven times, which is likewise connected in its principles and implications to the permission for the transfer of consent found in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. This may be cited to supplement what is lacking (hence it is said that it can be used as proof).
As for matters of urgency or gravity, while there is no explicit text in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, although other schools possess such rules, they do not accord with the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

The principles and their applications are not mutually related; thus, one must not arbitrarily adopt them. Now, I shall divide the preceding matters of urgency and gravity into four sections for analysis and judgment.
Regarding the first section on those that are "relaxed" (less urgent): for instance, the *Daśabhāṇavāra* contains texts concerning the wearing of robes;

the *Daśabhāṇavāra* and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* both protect the "bright sign" (*prabhāta-lakṣaṇa*). These principles and applications are mutually related, and thus the Tathāgata may employ them as corroborative proof. If...

In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the rule for protecting robes throughout the night is very lenient; therefore, it is not adopted [here]. (The remaining cases are all to be treated according to this principle). Regarding the two "strict" [rules]:

as distinguished in the section on the purification of *parivāsa* (assignment) in the *Bhaiṣajyavastu*, although the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* contains a text permitting such assignment, it lacks the restriction limiting the proximity of the monastery's residence.
Both the *Mahāsāṃghika* and the *Mūlasarvāstivāda* vinayas each contain texts with specific limitations. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "If the monastery has previously..."

The *Sūtra* clarifies that once the dawn has appeared, the formal assignment [of duties] is no longer valid. This point is consistent with the general principle of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) and may be used as corroborating evidence.

If one were to follow the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Shisong lü), which states that monks must not remain past the first watch of the night, this would be too restrictive; therefore, it is not adopted (other cases should be judged by this same principle).

Regarding the "threefold" [rule]: the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) merely states that if one accepts and maintains the three robes without performing the formal rite (*anujñā*), one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense;

however, it lacks a passage concerning the offense incurred by staying overnight apart from them. Yet, in many instances, both Vinayas contain the relevant texts, frequently stating that one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense for both "deficient clothing" and "impaired dignified demeanor.
This is consistent with the general meaning and intent of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and can be used to corroborate it. If one relies upon...

Regarding the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Views): apart from the "not yet added" [category], staying overnight with the three robes also constitutes a *pāyattika*. Because this would be too severe, it is not adopted (the remainder is to be judged by this precedent). Regarding the four light cases:
as in the *Theft Precept*, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) does not distinguish between the gravity of the offenses for stealing across the six boundaries.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā* (Liao lun) and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Shi song) both contain such texts. In the *Liao lun*, stealing across the six boundaries is uniformly classified as a grave *pārājika*; this is identical to the case of burning [property] in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
The meanings and implications of "burying" and "ruined color" are interrelated and can be used as corroboration.

If the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that both constitute a *sthūlātyaya*, this is too light and is therefore not accepted (all such cases follow this precedent). Regarding the statement that certain articles are excluded based on the treatise (*śāstra*), Baoyun says:
This refers to the aforementioned variations in laxity and urgency, heaviness and lightness. If one considers these from the perspective of that school's own tenets, they are deemed correct;

however, if compared to my own fourfold system, their logical force and significance are unequal, and thus they are called "incorrect. Since these differ from the present [system], their specific attachments and calculations are likewise distinct.

According to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, that which does not correspond with the words and phrases is not accepted. (According to the *Souxuan*, if the meaning and the force of the function are equivalent, it may be cited as being correct.)

If one does not cite [the scriptures] when the matter is urgent or grave, it is entirely unreasonable (consider this). Third, the citation of evidence: regarding the phrase "therefore, it reaches [this point]," this refers to the text from the *Caturvargika-vinaya* (The Vinaya in Four Parts), the fourth section, the *Upāli-paripṛcchā*.
That text states: The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "There are four kinds of 'extensive explanations. First, if a bhikṣu speaks thus:
'Venerable sirs, in such-and-such a village or such-and-such a city, I personally heard and received [the teaching] from the Buddha.'"
"This is the Dharma; this is the Vinaya; this was spoken by the Buddha. Upon hearing such a statement, one should neither praise it nor disparage it.
Rather, having carefully determined the words and phrases, one should examine and investigate the Sūtras and the Vinaya, and scrutinize the legal codes.
If [the teaching] is inconsistent and contradicts the Dharma, one should say to that person: "What you have spoken was not spoken by the Buddha."
What has been spoken [by him] may be that the Elder did not carefully grasp the Buddha’s words; there is no need to recite it further, nor should you teach it to the bhikṣus.
You should now abandon it. However, if upon hearing what he says, you find it accords with the Teaching and he says, "What the Elder has spoken is indeed what was spoken;

this is the word of the Buddha," and you ascertain that he has correctly grasped the Buddha’s words, then you should read and recite it yourself and teach it to the bhikṣus, so as not to let it be lost.

One should avoid losing [this teaching] (this is the first detailed exposition). Second, hear it from the senior monk (*sthavira*) among the Saṃgha. Third, hear it from many monks who know the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Mātikā.
Fourth, hear it from a single monk who knows the Dharma; it is the same for these four methods. Taking these four dharmas [as one's basis]:
To examine whether a person is heterodox or orthodox and to discern right from wrong, many matters are discussed; therefore, it is called "extensive exposition" (*vaipulya*).

Although there are no four [distinct categories] within the extensive exposition itself, the name is established based on what is heard from the perspective of four types of persons. The intent of citing this passage is to corroborate the previous reliance on the *Śāstra* regarding the correspondence or non-correspondence of receiving [the precepts].
As for the mention of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the "ink seal," and so forth, the meaning is that it is not only the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* that contains them.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Wén) states that the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Shí-sòng) also explains it in this same way; therefore, it says, "the meaning is also the same. That [text] states:

"Why did the Buddha teach the four seals of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*)? Answer: Because he wished to explain the true characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), so that future bhikṣus might thoroughly understand what is the word of the Buddha and what is not the word of the Buddha, and so forth.
The first four are explained extensively from the perspective of the person who teaches them; the latter four...

"Seal of ink. This designation is established based on the scriptural texts as they are explained [in the Vinaya]. (In ancient times, many interpreted this as "words and ink," which contradicts the textual accounts of other Vinayas. Therefore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
If one says, "I heard this from the Buddha," or even "I heard it from a single bhikṣu," one should not immediately praise or condemn it;

rather, one must verify it against the noble teachings of the Tripiṭaka. Since these are called the "noble teachings of the Tripiṭaka," and "teachings" (śāsana) are that which express [the meaning], when they are recorded upon paper and ink, one must apply the principle of verification through the teachings, just as in the case of the fourfold statements.
Regarding the statement "if it is thus, up to 'perishing,'" this establishes that there is benefit. "If" (若) means "as" (如) or "by means of" (以用).

If one takes the meaning according to the text as previously relied upon in the *Sudarsana*, such that the sense and the force of the argument correspond before it is grasped, then this is the mind capable of grasping.

It illuminates the objects of perception, which are the realms of the apprehended; it further illuminates the mind that perceives, which is the apprehender. Thus, it is said that "mind and object illuminate one another.

"Mind" refers to the mind of the author of the *Chao* (the *Shishi Yaolan*), who skillfully grasps [the truth]. "Object" refers to the phenomena within the Tripiṭaka teachings that correspond to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
All movements and actions are made visible; as for the discussion of "standards and patterns," these are the rules and models.

This is the principle of the Dharma. Regarding the adoption of a middle path between prolixity and brevity: for instance, while the *Caturvarga-vinaya* lacks a passage concerning the place from which the assembled monks have come, the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* (the *Chao*) extensively cites texts from six versions of the Vinaya to supplement it;
though prolix, it remains balanced. Furthermore, the *Caturvarga-vinaya* omits the rules for carrying robes.
Both [versions] cite a single passage from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. Although it is brief, it is also moderate (hence the phrase "taking the middle between the prolix and the concise").

Why would the principle be obscured? "Principle" refers to doctrinal meaning (*artha*). "Obscured" means dark; "submerged" means sunk or lost. Since both mind and objects are each empty, the doctrinal meaning can never be dark or obscured.
Thus, what is reckoned in the mundane world as the moon being deficient—its waxing and then its waning—is called the "moon. The moon...

The first day of the month is called *shuò* (朔). *Shuò* means "to give birth" (*shēng*) or "to revive" (*sū*). When the moon is full, it is called *wàng* (望). The period before the full moon and after the full moon, at the end of the month, is called *huì* (晦).

*Huì* derives from "darkness" (*àn*). This is intended to clarify that the texts cited above must not be obscure or ambiguous. Regarding the phrase "if it were the ultimate teaching" (*ruò zhì jiào*), this modifies the meaning of the preceding text;
it is used for fear that someone might doubt or forget, as it was previously stated that one may not cite other sections [of the canon] based on the authority of ancient masters.

[The Master] says: Now, as this Master composes these writings, he further cites external (non-Buddhist) sources. Is there no contradiction? For this reason, I have written this text to refute the biased attachments of narrow-minded views.
If they are not equal, it is because the mirror is clear; "lan cai" (覽採) means to observe and gather. "Yu" (隅) refers to a corner or angle.

This means that if one is not clear and proficient in observing and gathering from other sections, but relies solely on a single passage from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, this is merely the narrow view of one who is ignorant and stuck in a single corner—just like the first of the six teachers mentioned below, who did not distinguish [between them].
Regarding "shen shi deng" (涉事等), "she" (涉) means to involve or relate to; if one does not take up [the teachings of] others...

The textual passage concerning the matter of holding robes (*cīvara*) is incomplete, as it does not fully cover matters such as the assembly of the *saṃgha*, because no such text is found within the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (*Sifen lü*).
Regarding the collation of the text, there is nothing in the text to rely upon; "collation" (*jiaokan*) refers to the act of comparing and verifying.

For instance, if one possesses robes but does not perform the formal procedure of acceptance (*parigraha-dharma*), or if the *saṃgha* is not assembled at the time of establishing a boundary (*sīmā-bandha*), when one examines these points against the scriptural texts, the texts provide no basis for verification. Consequently, [the author] proceeded according to his own subjective views.

"臆" (yì) refers to the breast or chest; it signifies superficial views. Whatever matter is explained without relying on scriptural texts, but instead trusting one's own sentiments, is called "臆見" (yìjiàn—arbitrary views).
Thus, regarding those who compete with one another over right and wrong, the *Jìzōngjì* states:

One master made three robes, but merely held them in his hands, asserting directly that there was no need to perform the ritual of "adding the dharma" (*kṣepa*). Another master asked, "Why not stay overnight [with them]? That is to say...

This is what it means to uphold [the teaching]. It does not mean holding it in one's hand. To hold it in one's hand means to consider oneself right and to regard those who do not hold it in their hands as wrong.
Not holding it in one's hand means to consider oneself right and to regard those who hold it in their hands as wrong (hence it is said that each vies over right and wrong).
As for "mutually pointing out the other as deluded": the one who holds it in his hand points to the one who does not hold it in his hand as being deluded; the one who does not hold it in his hand...
To point out those who hold [this view] as being deluded is an interpretation that may be relied upon and inherited.

If one follows the *Souxuan* (Investigating the Profundities), which correlates the person who guards their robe throughout the night according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* with one who does not apply the ritual method at all, it deviates from the meaning of the text.

"Truly due to the absence of instruction" (*chengyou wujiao zhe*) means "it is indeed true. The *Zongji* (Record of the School) states: "This refers to the two masters mentioned above, each pointing out the other as being deluded. Suddenly...
As for those who do not reject [the practice], it is truly because they rely on the absence of scriptural evidence.

If one understands that this must be based on the teachings, one can cite the text from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which states that [a bowl] is neither held in hand nor separated overnight (all commentaries claim that there is no mention of this in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* teachings;
to cause mutual adherence based on such a claim is not a correct understanding).

Regarding the phrase "if it reaches the actual matter," this is a textual emendation. It means that within the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, there may be a certain matter for which the Vinaya text, despite its established limitations, lacks a specific passage concerning the performance of the ritual procedure.
Now, we cite a passage from another school (*nikāya*) to supplement it; however, these limitations were originally based upon the *Caturvargika*.
If one were to rely instead on the text of another school, it would then become a matter belonging to that other school. Furthermore, according to the Vinaya:
There may be a certain matter that, although it involves specific limitations, lacks a textual passage concerning those limitations.

If one were now to bring in a passage from another school’s canon, since that other school’s canon does not contain these limitations, one would likewise have to add these fourfold limitations to the cited text (and so forth).

To explain this by way of a concrete example, the *Biao* states: as in the section on "Assembling the Sangha," where a passage from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is cited, which can be divided [accordingly].
"A separate village" refers to the boundary of the village; this is the boundary of the Saṃgha-ratna. Regarding the "fourfold division of activities," the sub-commentary states:
"Up to the place where they come and go. This refers to the passage in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* which adds a demarcation of thirteen steps outside the village.

Within these thirteen paces, people are gathered by command. Now, if one relies on the *caturbhāga-grāma-sīmā* (the boundary of a village-quarter), it is limited solely to the interior of the courtyard enclosure.
Even if there are bhikṣus outside the courtyard wall, there is no fault if they do not assemble.

Although the author of the *Chao* (Commentary) cites the passage from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* regarding the "distinguishable assembly of the Saṃgha," his limitation lacks a basis in our own [tradition].

[The assembly] shall gather within the boundaries of the monastery precincts. However, according to other texts, if there are persons within a distance of thirteen paces outside the monastery precincts, they must also be gathered;
in this case, one must again employ the texts of those other schools to accomplish the matters pertaining to those other schools.

Furthermore, as in the *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* on the separation from robes, four types of "natural robe-protecting boundaries" (*prakṛti-sīmā*) from other traditions are cited to supplement what is lacking in the *Dharmaguptaka* school.
If one were to follow that school’s doctrine, protection would extend only as far as the physical boundary itself, because their outer garment boundary lacks a zone of influence (*prabhāva*).

Now, according to the *Dharmaguptaka* school, it is necessary to add this zone of influence; thus the text below states: "By this measure of fifteen [cubits], it naturally extends to where it may be worn.
If one were now to cite that passage while failing to add the thirteen-step zone of influence, one would simply be adopting the system of another school.
[This is] the textual [explanation]. It is for the purpose of establishing the matters of other schools (*nikāya*).
Regarding the phrase "or reaching its application," Xuán says: This revision of the text differs from the preceding section.

The previous section was based on the *Dharmaguptaka* (Four-Part Vinaya), which has its fixed divisions but lacks a text specifically addressing this particular matter; consequently, it cited another school. Nevertheless, although it was cited, one must understand how to apply it to the present situation.
At that time, [the compilers] added or subtracted [details] in accordance with the *Dharmaguptaka* school.

As for the texts cited here, while the *Dharmaguptaka* contains only the facts, when it comes to the point of actual practice, the Vinaya is merely textual; not only is there no text, but there is also no underlying meaning (31).
Within the texts of other schools, both versions are present, and both are sufficient for practice; one cannot simply adopt one and discard the other.

Now, these must all be cited together for later generations to examine and apply as they see fit. Regarding the "two Vinayas," this refers to explaining two distinct Vinayas apart from the four divisions (*caturvarga*).
One must not take the *Dharmaguptaka* (Four-Part) Vinaya and treat it as one of the two in contrast to another school.

For example, in the section on receiving the precepts, when clarifying the time of receiving the robes and bowl, the *Dharmaguptaka* does not specify the season; however, according to other schools, there is...

Regarding the two types of instructional texts, each has its own locus for exposition. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the instructor is to receive the precepts first on behalf of the candidate, and only thereafter does the candidate proceed to full ordination (*upasampadā*).
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the *karmavācanā* master is to receive them on behalf of the candidate after [the robes have been prepared].

Since it is said that these two are like the wings of a bird and must necessarily accompany one another, and fearing there might be a deficiency regarding the robes, it is logically necessary to receive them on behalf of the candidate. Thus, both Vinayas clearly elucidate this point.
Now, these [passages] are cited all at once for your practical application. Therefore, the text below states:
"If one follows the various schools, this point constitutes the formal reception of the robe and bowl; or, within the assembly, the preceptor receives them on one's behalf.

There is no such text in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, yet it is preserved accordingly" (the character "or" above indicates an indefinite discussion). Or, within two scriptures, where both the text and the meaning are clearly elucidated, as in the section on the "Monastic Net" (*Sengwang pian*).

Regarding the section on punishing wicked bhikṣus during the Meiji era: while the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) clarifies only the seven and nine rules [for disciplinary measures], it does not explicitly state that kings or ministers are permitted to impose penalties.
However, within the sūtras, it is taught that these matters are all indeterminate. First, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the punishment of kings or ministers is not permitted;
thus, the subsequent text states: "If a bhikṣu possesses virtuous qualities both internally and externally, is widely learned and renowned, and inspires great faith in many..."

Regarding the analogies of ox-gallstone and incense, it was initially forbidden for kings and ministers to administer punishment. Subsequently, according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, punishment was permitted.

This means that those who are shrouded in the darkness of ignorance and fail to discern right from wrong—specifically those who transgress the three gates of the clergy and the laity—are permitted to be punished.

Therefore, the following section of the *Chao* (Excerpts) cites both [texts] together for one to adopt as appropriate. Alternatively, when the meaning of the two treatises clarifies both points, as in the section on the Two Robes (*Ēr yī piān*) concerning mending and washing:
the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya) merely states, "If the three robes are torn, they should be mended early," but it does not specify the dimensions of the tear.
If one follows the *Shanjian lü piposha* (Samantapāsādikā), it says: "The length is one span (*vitasti*), and the width..."

If the edge is eight finger-widths [in width], it does not constitute a loss of the boundary; however, if it is pierced internally, it is lost. In other places, even a breach as small as a fingernail constitutes a loss.

If there is a cross-thread [sewing it back together], it is not lost. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duolun), if the boundary conditions are not severed, it is not lost. Thus, both treatises clarify this point.

Now, in this commentary (*Caoyao*), both positions are cited within the established text to demonstrate that if the boundary conditions are severed, one follows the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*; if there is a break in the middle, one follows [the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā*].

This is the delimitation of the *Dṛṣṭivāda* (or the various views). Within a single Vinaya or a single treatise (*śāstra*), both the text and its meaning may be clearly elucidated, as in the section on the two types of robes (*dvicīvara-varga*) concerning the master of medicine and the alms bowl (*bhaiṣajya-pātra*).

Regarding whether one must request [permission] or not, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (*Caturvargika*) does not state it explicitly. However, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (*Mahā-saṃghika-vinaya*), one must request it;
thus the text says: "One should seek out those who are learned," and so forth. Furthermore, in the event of death or upon reaching another country, one should again seek out those who are pure. If...

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, among the five groups [of monastics], one may simply grant [the invitation] according to one’s own discretion. Judging by the flow of this text, it appears that at that time [the procedure] was indicated in a general manner;

it does not require that one must first make a formal, predetermined request. Is this not a case where both the phrasing and the meaning are clear? I have cited it here in its entirety so that one may exercise discretion according to the specific occasion. Therefore, the subsequent text states:

"If [a person's] virtue and reputation are lofty and far-reaching, one cannot [simply] attach [the invitation] to them, but must instead follow the practice of the *Pañcavargika*. If [it is] possible..."
Regarding the invocation: one must certainly invoke it beforehand; this is a matter of adopting [the practice] according to one's preference.

Alternatively, within two Vinayas or one Śāstra, both the text and its meaning may be clearly elucidated, as in the case of the "Chapter on the Two Robes," which distinguishes the pure donor remaining in their own place—a point for which there is no textual record in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü).

If one follows the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, [the precepts are lost] within three *yojanas* of the deceased’s location. If one follows the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, they are not lost as long as one knows the person is still alive or on the road.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If death occurs in another country, one may perform the rite again to seek purification.
Now, this manual (*chao*) cites both the texts of Dao'an; it is left to later practitioners to apply them according to the circumstances of the time.
Next, the conclusion is formed to prevent confusion. Regarding the phrase "Thus it reaches [the point]," the meaning of this section is as follows:
although the preceding portion has already been analyzed, if the textual framework corresponds to the thematic force of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya), it is adopted.

However, if there are discrepancies in the pacing, emphasis, or relative weight, one should follow the treatise (*śāstra*) and not adopt [the Vinaya], as this has already been explained in detail. Furthermore, there is yet another reason that has never been set forth.

Commentary: This means that whenever I cite texts from external sources, I have first personally searched through the scriptural writings of the Tripiṭaka and verified them myself before recording them within this sub-commentary (*chao*).
These are not words transmitted secondhand from others; fearing that such doubts might arise, I have recorded this statement once again.
This is indeed so. He personally consulted and examined the sacred teachings of the Tripiṭaka with his own eyes and hands.
It is said that before the author of the *Chao* intended to compose his work, he first read through the Tripiṭaka three times (some accounts say seven times).

He cited over one hundred and seventy texts from the scriptures, having meticulously verified and standardized every word and phrase. One might ask: even if these were based on hearsay, what fault would there be?
The Commentary answers: "It is because there is a fear that hearsay may be confused with the authentic; thus, one fears doubt.

Since one hears from others, there is a suspicion of exaggeration or perversion, which would cause the true and correct [teaching] to become muddled. This is an example of how it defiles the True Doctrine. Question:

This passage states, "I have personally consulted and read the sacred teachings when citing them," whereas the tenth section below says, "Every time a citation is made, I first conduct a verification. What is the difference between these two?

Answer: This is clarified by supplementing the text based on the cited passages; below, it is explained according to our own school (*bendō*) by eliminating redundancies (this differs from the *Sōgen* commentary, as the roles of interlocutor and respondent are not distinguished in these two preceding sections).
Furthermore, it is asked: In this section, it says that "transmission is confused with the real," which intends to eliminate what is spurious.

How does this differ from the intention of the tenth section, which is to "eliminate the spurious and transmit the real"? Answer: This [present] elimination is not a matter of transmission from a person.
The confusion regarding the lower classification of the Tripiṭaka teachings as mere literary elaborations is entirely distinct from this principle.
Second, concerning the differences in the tenets and assertions of those who uphold the Dharma based on specific persons:

as for the phrase "furthermore," it refers to the period from the initial emergence of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) during the early Northern Wei dynasty until the present; within this interval, there are instances where other texts are cited and instances where they are not. Therefore, regarding...

This distinguishes between the universal and the restricted. Furthermore, although the number of ancient masters has been great, none of their differing views and interpretations exceed these six perspectives.
To speak of the "one ultimate," six masters are enumerated. The first is the most restricted; the commentary provides examples such as the case of holding one's robe.
This refers to the fact that the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) lacks textual passages concerning the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) of robes and medicine;

this is clearly a deficiency. Seeing that these texts are absent from the Vinaya, this master asserts: "If a bhikṣu makes a robe for himself, it is perfected simply by wearing it on his head or holding it in his hand;

there is no necessity for specific verbal formulas and so forth. Second, regarding "deficiencies in the texts of one's own school" (*sva-nikāya*): this master observes that the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "If... [and so on].
Having abandoned what was doubted, one should receive it again; thus one knows that there were deficiencies in the text of the *Caturvargika-vinaya*.

One then understands and extracts the text regarding the addition of the ritual procedures from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* to supplement the matters concerning the fourfold division (*caturvarga*). The *Jizong ji* states:

"However, this master, when there was a matter in the *Caturvargika-vinaya* for which there was no explicit text, extracted corresponding passages from other schools (*nikāya*). Compared to the first master, he is somewhat more comprehensive; yet, if there were [explicit] texts in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*..."
