The meaning exists but there is no textual passage. This means that he has not yet understood how to take textual passages from other schools to supplement what is missing; furthermore, it appears narrow and restrictive. Some commentators explain:
"Although this master understands how to cite textual passages, he has not yet understood how to take the meaning from external schools" (this interpretation is highly incorrect;

they must not be repeated. Once one person has spoken one section, another person speaks. Furthermore, if this is not possible, one may simply preach the Dharma and recite the sūtras.

Thus it is said. Judging by this, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* itself does not permit recitation [of spells]. Furthermore, in the secular world today, those who employ incantations and recite texts for specific purposes find that none of their undertakings succeed.
This is simply because the Dharma is revered; one must be exclusively diligent and careful, ensuring that all texts are properly recited and so forth.

Moreover, within the Buddha-dharma, those who recite incantations achieve success in their monasteries; I have never heard of anyone being able to accomplish a task through the mere reading of a spell. Therefore, please raise [this point] for consideration.

This is the principle. When performing the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), it is absolutely necessary to cite [the relevant text]—some say that one should cite a single passage from the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* as a model for all subsequent *karmans*, hence the phrase "modeling upon these," but this is not a correct interpretation.
Furthermore, during the summer retreat (*varṣā*), there may be an intercalary month; as to whether one should rely on it or not, the texts and meanings are both lacking within the Tripiṭaka.
Therefore, one must cite the practice of receiving rain-clothing according to other schools as a model, which clearly demonstrates that an intercalary month definitely exists.

One must rely upon these [principles] (all cases are of this type; they are not recorded one by one here). Alternatively, there are instances where a matter is accomplished by relying on principle (*li*). "Relying on principle" means to reach a definitive resolution.

The general purport of this text also consists of three or five points of practice that are currently in use. These are entirely absent—both in text and in meaning—from our own school’s other sections.
The Master [Daoshi] has therefore utilized principles to provide a definitive selection and resolution so as to eliminate doubts and obstructions.

Therefore, if that were so, the preceding statement says, "both text and meaning are lacking. Since this present statement belongs to our own school while it is absent from other schools, it too would constitute a lack of both meaning and text.

To distinguish between them, the answer is: "both text and meaning are lacking" applies slightly to cases where the logical principles are similar, whereas "decisively excluding" applies to cases where they are entirely different.

The former establishes the point by using a specific instance as an analogy; the latter relies on the principle that something ought to exist in its entirety. This is the doctrine of the present master.

Furthermore, as in the section on those who do not count [toward the quorum], it clarifies the principles that a drunken person does not understand others and that one must remain free from physical obstructions and the like;
these points are then integrated into the section on the quorum. However, neither the text nor the meaning of this exists within the Tripiṭaka.

The reason for this is that the Buddha prohibited ordained monks and nuns from drinking alcohol, and thus there were no drunken persons among them; moreover, he mandated that from the moment one receives the precepts, one must immediately practice [abstinence].

Because they have studied, there are none among them who do not understand. Nowadays, there may be those of pure precepts who temporarily consume medicinal wine, as well as those among the class of students who are yet ignorant.
Even if there are obstructions or enclosures on open ground, are these sufficient? According to the doctrine of the present masters, they are all insufficient.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "One who speaks without understanding, whose words are inverted and discordant—such an ignorant person is insufficient."

"Subsumption," and so forth—all of these are definitive judgments based on principle (*li*). (In some editions of the *Chao*, the character "previous" [前] is superfluous; this would then constitute the preceding text. This is because both the meaning and the matter are lacking; that is to say, regarding the Three Baskets [Tripitaka], neither the text nor the meaning exists.)

However, as for the principle that there ought to be [a term], it is no different from the preceding passage where both the word and its meaning are missing; therefore, it is referred back to the previous case. Hence it is said, "thereby completing the preceding matter. [The commentary] states: "In the base of the *hāo* plant, there is nothing that does not conform to the *zhōn*; this is not yet considered elegant or appropriate.
Regarding the phrase "or although present in the text," this means that although it is complete in the text, there may be a deficiency in the meaning.

When the text lacks the meaning, one determines it by means of the meaning; that is, one brings the meaning forward to resolve the text. Next, an example is cited to explain it: "as in the case of 'having no master.'"

Regarding the precept on the dimensions of a dwelling: it simply states that the length shall be within twelve *vitasti* (spans) of the Buddha and the width seven *vitasti*, without specifying the exact measurements for length and breadth.
However, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, one *vitasti* of the Buddha is equal to two feet and four inches; the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* agrees with this.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Two chi. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Three spans (*vitasti*) of an average person constitute one span of the Buddha.

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣikā* states: "One and a half cubits (*hasta*) of an ordinary person," and so forth. Although these textual accounts are complete, it is not known upon what basis they rely for measurement.

Since the standard unit [of the Buddha] is double that of an ordinary person, the *vitasti* remains the same; therefore, according to the underlying principle, one should simply adopt the "two chi" from the *Pañcavargika*. Although the number of *chi* is thus fixed, as for the *chi* itself...
Furthermore, there are five kinds of differences; as for which one should be used, otherwise the meaning would be deficient.

Now, regarding the measure of the bowl according to the Vinaya, it is based on the *dou* (bushel) of the Jizhou (Western Zhou) period. As for the current measurement in *chi* (feet), one should likewise take the standard *chi* of the Jizhou period as the definitive rule.
This is precisely using the underlying principle to resolve the textual ambiguity. Thus, when the treatise says "as stated," it refers to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. This is the reasoning.

This refers to "principle" (*yukti*). As explained above, regarding the principle that a Buddha is twice the height of a human, one *vitasti* (span) is equivalent to two *ratni* (cubits), which is precisely taking principle as the standard for correctness.

Furthermore, the explanation regarding the dimensions of the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary) within the context of establishing boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*) may also be cited (fearing prolixity, it is not recorded here).

Regarding the phrase "although the meaning must necessarily be established," this is like the case in the Vinaya where the meaning of receiving [the precepts] repeatedly must necessarily be established; thus, having listed all these...

Regarding the many occasions for receiving the precepts, it is permitted on every day. Furthermore, depending on whether one's parents have faith and joy or lack faith and joy, there are naturally the four grave offenses (*catur-guru-dharma*) and so forth;
this constitutes the meaning of "grave. However, there is no explicit textual authorization for receiving them repeatedly.

Because the ancients saw no such text in the Vinaya, they established that during the summer retreat only three methods were permitted, as they did not allow for repeated reception. Now, our Master has therefore unified...
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the *Pañcaśata-praśna-śāstra*, and the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* all permit the re-reception [of the *poṣadha*]. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"Whether there are [other monks] or not, invite everyone to listen and receive [the *poṣadha*] for seven days. Since it says "everyone," it is clear that re-reception is permitted. Furthermore, the *Pañcaśata-praśna-śāstra* states:
"If one has previously requested seven days to go out of the boundary, one need not receive [the *poṣadha*] again while traveling; once the seven days are completed..."

He then received it once more. Furthermore, he cited the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (the *Prakaraṇābhidharma-vyākhyā*) treatise, stating that if an obstacle arises within seven days, one may act according to one’s inclination;
by practicing the three types of liberation and the nine grades of categories, one can finally cease the criticisms of the ancients. Question:

Regarding the previous statement that "it universally opens up all sections," does this refer to the text (*vyañjana*) or the meaning (*artha*)? Answer: It is acceptable to call it the text, and it is also acceptable to call it the meaning. Question: If one calls it...
This is for the sake of the meaning. That principle may be so; however, if it were called a "textual passage" (*vyañjana*), it would not be established.
Does the fourth [section] employ the textual passages and meanings of various schools? Answer: It does not. Within the fourth section, it relies on the precise and appropriate textual passages.

The *Pañcavastuka-vibhāṣā-śāstra* and other works cited above do not, for the time being, constitute explicit textual passages regarding repeated ordination; rather, they merely extract the sense of multiple layers from other texts.
Thus, there is no confusion. If, among the various commentaries, one were to take this phrase as using the text to resolve the meaning, the principle would likewise not be lost.

Now, following the *Zongji*, I have directly taken the text; the subsequent meaning will be categorized accordingly. It would also be excellent to take the meaning to resolve the meaning (consider this).

Regarding the phrase "the text is thus, reaching the object": "thus" (ran) means it is already established as truthful; "abandoning" (hei) means to discard; and "establishing and adopting" (ryūshu) means to set forth and accept. This refers to resolving difficult points through the four preceding propositions:

abandoning the ancient interpretations to establish and adopt the present text. Specifically, one abandons the ancient practice of reciting the *karmavācanā* for oneself and establishes the present requirement of mindfulness (*smṛti*), and so forth.
One abandons the ancient reliance on encountering the scriptural texts (*śāsana*) and instead establishes the present standard of five parts and two cubits (*vitasti*).

Moreover, to abolish the ancient practice of receiving the *jiezhi* (precept-renewal) three times during a single summer retreat, and instead establish the present system of receiving it repeatedly—such an abolition and establishment is truly difficult.

Regarding those who "do not understand" (*bái fēi zhě*): this is a definition based on meaning; it refers to those who do not comprehend the fundamental principles of observing and violating the precepts, yet claim to have a profound understanding of the characteristics of the Vinaya and the original intent behind the regulations for lifting prohibitions.
This indicates they are not well-versed in what is permitted and what is prohibited. Therefore, if one does not belong to either of these two aforementioned categories...

This is not so. For example, as when one recites the *Karmavācanā* (ritual formulas) but fails to establish the boundary (*sīmābandha*), thereby incurring the offense of failing to perform what ought to be done;
this is a burden upon one’s own mind. Consequently, one cannot perform such tasks as bestowing the precepts or conducting formal procedures for others, which is of no benefit to the sphere of others.

Furthermore, even regarding the summer retreat (*varṣā*), although only three days are permitted for requesting [the end of the retreat], if one does not clarify the characteristics of the teaching (*śikṣā-lakṣaṇa*), it likewise constitutes a failure to train.
Ignorance is a burden to one's own mind; without a mind, one cannot discern the conditions for generating goodness or extinguishing evil in others.
Therefore, it is of no benefit to the realm of others.

Regarding the phrase "The original Vinaya, when it reaches the commentary": this is a citation of scriptural evidence. It refers to the *Dvādaśa-vivāda-arthaviniścaya* (Treatise on the Resolution of the Twelve Disputes) in the sixtieth fascicle of the *Vinaya* of that school.

It states: The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "When the Elder speaks, there are four cases: where both the phrasing and the meaning are identical; where the phrasing differs but the meaning is the same;

where the phrasing is the same but the meaning differs; and where both the phrasing and the meaning differ. In all these instances, he says: 'Do not engage in mutual strife. If one is virtuous, one should not..."

Regarding "dispute": those that are unwholesome lead to contention (whereas those that are wholesome do not contend; those that are understood do not contend, while those that are not understood do contend; this is because they provide excellent instruction for understanding).

Regarding the first point, where both the text and the meaning are identical: the proponent of the thesis (*yujia*) says that the *Prātimokṣa* for the two communities of monks and nuns each has five sections—this is textual identity—and both prevent the seven types of transgressions—this is semantic identity. Regarding the discussion of the meaning: it is said that since the two genders are distinct, they are already divided.

These two types [of interpretations] should be known as both inconsistent with the text and the meaning, and they give rise to disputes. If one were to argue for the "good" [position], one should say:

although the text and meaning are the same, there is a distinction between the physical forms and retributions of monks and nuns; furthermore, it is feared that speaking together would involve others in suspicion and resentment.

Therefore, it is necessary to establish a separate *śīla-mūla* (precept root). As for the case where the text is the same but the meaning differs, the *Vinaya* corresponds to the third phrase, while the *Śāstra* (Commentary) adopts the phrasing for its consistency.

Therefore, it is moved to form the second sentence. Regarding the difference in the established propositions (*pratijñā*): it is said that while the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (or *Vinaya-ksudraka*) permits receiving the precepts by counting the months of the womb and intercalary months as years—just as one might calculate a reduced age—the *Upasampadā-karmavācanā* (the ordination manual) likewise permits counting the womb and intercalary months; thus, the text is the same. However, the meaning differs:

in the *Upasampadā-karmavācanā*, the teacher (*upādhyāya*) is permitted [to count them], whereas in the *Śrāmaṇera-karmavācanā*, it is the disciple who obtains the precepts [by such counting]. As for the discussion of the meaning: since the texts are identical, how can the meanings differ?
From this, a dispute arose. Regarding cases where the three texts differ in wording but agree in meaning:

the proponent of the Vinaya’s second position states that although the prohibitions are distinct in wording—specifically regarding the consumption of water—they are identical in meaning because both are intended to protect life. Regarding the proponents of the Abhidharma (Lun-yi), they state that since the wording is different, how can the meaning be the same?
From this, a dispute arose. Regarding cases where both the wording and the meaning differ: the proponent of the [Vinaya]... [establishes the position].

Regarding this: some say that rules such as those concerning spinning and weaving, and rules such as those concerning the evening instruction, are distinct between the ranks of monks and nuns, with each set of rules being different.
Those who debate the meaning argue that monks should also possess rules regarding spinning and so forth, and nuns should also possess rules regarding the evening and so forth;
how can these not be mutually applicable? If one were to argue skillfully, one might say: although monks may spin and weave, they simply do not take pleasure in doing so.

The Bhikṣuṇī is the primary subject of these regulations; thus, they are formulated specifically for her. Although the Bhikṣuṇīs possess precepts and instructions, because they do not encounter circumstances that give rise to public censure or slander, [the rules] were not formulated [for them here].
Regarding "fully detailing the movements": this is fully present in the Vinaya texts as a detailed exposition of the movements.

Now, this commentary (chao) cites the text of Dao'an merely to provide evidence for what precedes it, to resolve and clarify difficult points of meaning, and to avoid further laborious writing and explanation.

This concerns the textual passages on arising and ceasing. Now, I shall extract these texts and categorize them according to the four types of *dharmas* found in the Vinaya. First, those where both the text and the meaning are identical:

for example, the three minor boundaries (*kṣudrasīmā*) and the boundary of the precept platform (*śīlacaṅkramaṇa-sīmā*), both of which are prescribed to be established and dissolved; thus, the text is identical. Furthermore, the three minor boundaries are established by reversing the procedure for dissolution.
The *śīmaṇḍala* (precept field) is an example of this; it should likewise be treated in the same manner, for the principle is identical.

Now, the Master cites the three minor boundaries (*kṣudra-sīmā*) as being formed by reversing the procedure of binding, whereas the text definitively establishes that the *śīmaṇḍala* is formed by reversing the procedure of binding. In truth, this is not easily altered. As for the two texts having the same wording but different meanings:

it is like "protecting" and "further protecting" the robes, where both generally regulate the appearance of dawn (*āloka-lakṣaṇa*). Thus, the wording is the same. "Protecting the robes" prevents the fault of losing a robe, while "protecting the summer [retreat]"...

The principle of preventing harm to life and inviting karmic conditions is distinct [from other rules]. Now, I cite the text on protecting robes to resolve the matter of protecting the summer retreat.

Unless one has profound insight, this cannot be understood. As for the three texts where the wording differs but the meaning is the same—such as the measurements for the dwelling and the alms bowl—the wording is indeed different.

Since the capacity of the *dou* measure from the Ji-Zhou period was adopted, it is appropriate that the dimensions of the dwelling likewise adopt the *chi* measure of the Ji-Zhou period. By means of these differing texts, the underlying meaning is resolved and made clear.
The same applies here. Unless one is thoroughly proficient, it is difficult to understand at a glance. Regarding those cases where both the text and the meaning differ:

for example, when a *bhikṣuṇī* receives the precepts or performs the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* confession, the texts for the "receiving" (*upasaṃpad*) and the "following" (*anuvartana*) differ. Receiving the precepts results in benefit, while confessing the offense removes transgression; this constitutes a difference in meaning.

Since one must separately establish the boundary (*sīmā*) during the confession of offenses within the "following," it is determined that at the time of the initial reception, one must likewise establish them separately. Thus, since the receiving and the following...

[The text continues with] "etc. Why was this not included [in the previous section]? One must penetrate deeply to understand it; it is difficult to comprehend through ordinary means. If it accords [with the principle], one must proceed;
if it differs, one must desist. This is found in the subsequent text. Fearing that it would result in prolixity, I have not troubled myself to provide a detailed explanation here.
Regarding the phrase "to reach the ultimate traces": the character *rán* (then/so) is a term for certainty, decisive comparison, and judgment.
This means that among the four preceding lines, each has its own right and wrong; what is wrong is to be eliminated, while what is right is to be relied upon and applied.

To engage in such selection and rejection, one must clearly understand the intent of the Vinaya texts of the five schools and be proficient in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras that follow the Vinaya, as previously stated in the fourth section.
[This is] the Gate. Only after [studying] the six masters can one thoroughly investigate this teaching of decisive penetration. Regarding "traces" (jì):
Lǎozǐ said that the *Shī*, *Shū*, *Lǐ*, *Yuè*, and *Chūnqiū*—the Six Classics—are the arrayed traces (*cén-jì*) of the former kings.
Now, I have secretly adopted their intent to take the teachings as the traces of principle and to seek principle through these [traces], and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "therefore, it reaches the Vinaya," this refers to the authoritative proof (*pramāṇa*). First, "the origin" (*nidāna*) refers to the place where a transgression was committed and so forth.

Second, "the formulation of the precept" (*śikṣāpada-prajñapti*) refers to the initial establishment of the rule in response to specific circumstances. Third, "subsequent formulations" (*anuprajñapti*) has two aspects: first, subsequent formulations arising from a change in intention (*citta-vaiṣamya*), such as the case of Bhañja.
Vatsīputra thought to himself: "Sudinnaputra delighted in the Buddha-dharma; because his precepts were flourishing, he committed an offense through his actions.

Now I do not delight in the Buddha-dharma; since my precepts are weak, I should not commit an offense through my actions. The Buddha, following this, established the rule: "If one's precepts are weak and one does not repent, it is likewise an offense.
Regarding the distinction between the two forest regions and the subsequent establishment of the rule: a bhikṣu thought to himself, "Because the human realm is superior..."
"One should incur an offense. [The opponent argues: "Since animals are inferior, one should not incur an offense. Consequently, he engaged in unwholesome conduct with an animal in the forest.

The Buddha then established the rule accordingly, saying: "Even engaging with an animal constitutes an offense. Because the rule was established according to the specific act, it is said that among the three types of "establishment according to the case" (anuvyañjana-samāpatti), each individual precept contains both types.
Within these, whether an "establishment according to the case" occurs or not is not fixed. As for the phrase "and including" (bing zhi): this is the interpretation of its meaning.
This refers to the *Vinaya*. Regarding the commentary on the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, it states: "As for 'if a bhikṣu,' this refers to the eight types of bhikṣus and so forth.

As for 'vinaya' (discipline), it refers to the sevenfold vinaya and the councils of five hundred and seven hundred [monks], which are able to determine right from wrong, giving rise to the wholesome and extinguishing the unwholesome.
As for 'Ekottarika' (Incremental), this refers to the incremental texts within the Vinaya, ranging from one to twenty-two, each increasing by one."

Therefore, regarding "permissible and prohibited" (*kai-sha*): "permissible" (*kai*) means to allow or authorize; "prohibited" (*sha*) means to restrain or forbid. Regarding "the gravity of the sutras":

achieving the fruit is grave, while remaining in the cause is light. As for the "five primary colors," this explains the permissible and prohibited: east is blue, south is red, west is white, north is black, and center is yellow.
Furthermore, there are five secondary colors: east is green, south is purple, west is pale blue (*pyō*), north is... [softly dyed azure-yellow]. North... [text fragment].
Among the [permissible] colors, red is included. Such colors as these are not permitted to be worn; this excludes the three—blue, black, and wooden lacquer—which are termed "non-colors.
What is permitted is called "pure" (śuddhaka); this refers to the preliminary deliberation and reflection, which are essentially the first three matters.
One has not yet reached the interpretive understanding of the Vinaya and so forth, but acts in reliance upon them.

Regarding the statement "clearly explained up to the exposition," this is also the same as the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations). First, the origin (*nidāna*), such as being caused by famine and so forth; second, the person, namely Sudinna;
third, the establishment of the precept, which is the formal enactment of the rule; fourth, the detailed classification of the established precept, which refers to the exegesis of its meaning;
fifth, the determination of right and wrong, which clarifies the characteristics of the gravity or lightness of offenses committed in three circumstances. Within these five aspects—
"Proficient" means that those who each understand the Vinaya have no fear in their hearts and no longer depend on the facial expressions of others.
"The text is abbreviated as above" means that the first two [sections] are like the *Vinayamātṛkā*, while the third is like the establishment of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*) in the Vinaya;

the fourth and fifth differ somewhat from the sequential establishment of precepts in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. Therefore, it is said that "the text is abbreviated as above. The details are as explained in the *Viniścaya-uttaravihāra-śāstra* itself.
Therefore, it is said that this expands upon that explanation (the preceding topical outline, etc., concludes the fifth section).
As for the sixth section: first, regarding the heading "The Meaning of the Chapters," one first clarifies the purpose of its introduction.

This means that while the five preceding sections have fully elucidated the teaching as the expressive medium (*vyañjana*), it has not yet been examined what specific content is expressed by those scriptural texts; therefore, the following section is presented to clarify this.
Regarding the "Explanation of Terms" (*Shiming*): "Teaching" (*jiao*) refers to the teaching that is capable of expressing [the meaning]; the underlying intent (*zhiqu*) is that which is expressed.

In the commentary, the phrase "the expression reaches the offenses" first provides an interpretation based on the *vinaya* text that is the primary subject. This refers to the textual passages of the teaching.
Although these texts are vast and extensive, they comprise the entirety of one *vinaya* collection. "Vast" (*hao*) means great; "extensive" (*bo*) means broad and comprehensive. [Sixty...]
The twentieth fascicle, the *Khandaka*, is indeed vast. If one summarizes its essential purport, it does not depart from the observance and transgression of the precepts;

that is to say, the two sections of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* extensively clarify the observance [of the precepts] across twenty *khandakas*. By extensively clarifying the performance of observance, the two types of observance are inverted to form the two types of transgression.

Therefore, it is said that it "merely clarifies observance and transgression. Next, as for the commentator of the *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu-śīla-śāstra* (the *Shan-chien-lü-p'i-p'o-sha*), it refers to the thirty chapters. If one considers them collectively...

I shall clarify this. Following the practices of this one section constitutes observance (*dhāraṇa*); violating them constitutes an offense (*āpatti*). If explained individually, the characteristics of the *pien-chu* (sections and clusters) are defined;

the three preceding sections extensively clarify observance and violation. As for the remaining twenty-seven sections, they extensively clarify "active observance" (*zuo-chi*), wherein the reversal of observance constitutes an offense.
Regarding the "intent" (*qu*), the underlying purpose does not exceed these four points. If we rely on ancient traditions, this was merely intended as a summary according to the Vinaya.

Explanation of the Text: It is not incorrect that [certain matters] are not clarified in the *Shuochao* (Commentary). Some people maintain that these should be explained solely according to the *Shuochao* and do not permit them to be explained based on the root Vinaya texts.
Their reasoning is that the root text and the *Shuochao* clarify the general outline of the thirty chapters within;

if one were to explain them directly from the Vinaya text, it would seem to involve extraneous matters, as the ancients took "observance and violation" (*shichan*) as the primary subject matter (*suochuan*). However, my current view is not so. Generally...

In discussing any single matter, one must first establish the fundamental tenets (*siddhānta*) upon which it rests, then investigate the principles and examine the texts; none surpasses the topics of observance and transgression (*dhāraṇa* and *āpatti*).

These are, indeed, the practices of conformity and opposition within the school. However, as the following passage states: "The Vinaya school consists solely of observance and transgression. One might ask:

since observance and transgression are taken as the very tenets, why not fear that this would lead to confusion regarding what is actually expressed? Upon careful and detailed examination, there is no logic whatsoever in such a claim. Please rely on [the following]:
The preceding passage presents two interpretations together, as it is necessary to do so for completeness;

reflect upon this. Regarding the statement "it is thus, extending even to the external": "thus" means that it is indeed so. As for the phrase "the object extends to both the internal and the external": "internal" refers to the internal mind, while "external" refers to external phenomena. Question:

An "object" (ālambana) is a name applied specifically to the mind in its subtle aspect. How, then, can this internal mind itself function as an object? Answer: [The mind can serve as an object when it takes itself as its own focus.]

In the *Souxuan ji* (Record of Searching the Profundities), there are two interpretations. The first maintains that internal mental states which serve as conditions can also function as objects (*ālambana*).

That is to say, when the Dharma is received within the body, it is termed the "precept-substance" (*śīla-tattva*). Based on the teachings, one guards against transgressions and gives rise to a mind of non-negligence (*apramāda*), which possesses the three types of wholesome mental conduct, such as non-greed.
Subsequently, the mind of non-negligence arises in relation to these; thus, these three types of wholesome mental conduct can serve as the object. If...
Violating the teachings, one gives rise to a mind of heedlessness, which causes the three poisons—greed and so forth—to arise. Subsequently, one gives rise to a mind that opposes this heedlessness;

it is precisely these three poisons that are designated as the "object" (*ālambana*). Heedlessness and non-heedlessness act as the "arising agents," while the three poisons and the three wholesome states are the "arisen.

Because the agent and the object are mutually dependent, they are designated as an "object. (Now, upon careful examination, I fear this interpretation may be conflated with the Mahāyāna and thus do not adopt it). Now, relying on [the following]:

The second explanation concerns another person’s internal mind as being the object of my transgression. According to the section on "Observance and Transgression" (*dhāraṇa-āpatti*) below, there are cases where one's own mind serves as the object, such as when one perceives food or clothing with a defiled mind while thinking they have been permitted. This refers to the mind of another person serving as the object for oneself.

An example is knowing that a pond has been well-inspected and thus preventing a dispute; yet, by now initiating [the act again], one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense in relation to that prior "well-inspection."

The mind itself constitutes the object-field (*viṣaya*) of my own mind. Furthermore, having known that another person has already consented [to give], if one takes what was intended for the Saṃgha and incorporates it into one's own possession, one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense;
taking that which was consented to for the Saṃgha as a whole constitutes the object-field corresponding to "what belongs to me.

Moreover, when a nun receives food or clothing from one with a defiled mind, knowing that their mind is defiled, if one accepts the food or clothing and takes it as a remnant, taking that defiled mind constitutes the object-field (the above is a provisional explanation of how the object-field is common).
Regarding the internal [objects]: if an object extends to the external, it refers to matters such as killing and stealing, or matters such as robes and bowls—these are external objects.
Since the text of the *Chao* (Commentary) specifies that objects extend to both the internal and external, when providing an explanation, it is logically necessary to distinguish them:
first clarifying internal objects, and subsequently clarifying external objects. Furthermore, the records of Wei Nan and the modern-day Ji Zong and others all rely upon the practitioner themselves.
Regarding the statement that "the mind is internal," this merely explains that one can attain the mind capable of maintaining either precepts or transgressions.

Since it does not take the internal mind as its object, it would greatly contradict the text of the *Chao* (Commentary). Nowadays, many rely on this interpretation to clarify the underlying intent (*yì*). Next, the locus where karma is completed is explained.
Regarding the phrase "from internal up to contrary," in order to explain this passage, one should first raise an objection:

since it was stated above that objects (viṣaya) pertain to both the internal and external, it remains to be clarified what kind of mind constitutes the internal and what kind of phenomena constitute the external object. One may cite the *Chao* (Commentary) for the explanation:

"Internal refers to the karmic bonds of the active mind; external refers to the favorable and unfavorable conditions of sensory objects. (The text of the *Chao* explains the terms "internal" and "external" at this point, precisely clarifying the locus where karma is formed.)

"Active mind" (*citta*) refers to the exclusion of the three minds of perception (*saṃjñā*), feeling (*vedanā*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). The first three are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and cannot constitute karma;
it must flow to the fourth, the active mind, before it can migrate and create the two types of karmic results—those of commission and those of omission.

Regarding the school that follows the Mahāyāna, the formation of karma is extremely rapid, requiring four moments (*kṣaṇa*); that is to say, apart from the mind-king (*cittarāja*), there is nothing else.

Regarding what the mind contemplates: if the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) arises, it does not do so simultaneously [with its functions]. Just as in the first moment of consciousness, this mind-king merely cognizes the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

Second, perception (*saṃjñā*) arises to grasp the specific image; third, sensation (*vedanā*) arises to experience it. With respect to these three entities, they are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and are not yet capable of forming karma.

Only when proceeding directly to the fourth [function], volition (*cetanā*), is karma established. This differs from the Sarvāstivāda school, which maintains that apart from the mind-king, there exist separate...

When a mental state arises, it necessarily occurs simultaneously [with its object]. (In the preceding text, the minds of others were treated as internal objects; here, in explaining time, one must again include the fourth mental state of another person before concluding with my own mind regarding the karmic fruits of upholding or violating precepts.

One must not treat these cases as identical. Regarding the phrase "external," this refers to the conformity or opposition of emotional circumstances. "Emotional circumstances" comprehensively includes both sentient and insentient matters, as well as matters that are a combination of the sentient and the insentient.
With respect to these three types of matters, there are three types of conforming mental states and three types of mental states involving opposition through the three poisons.
When the mind maintains [the precept], it constitutes observance; conversely, it constitutes an offense. This is as in cases such as digging the earth, harming living beings, or constructing houses.
Regarding these matters, compliance with the teaching constitutes observance, while violation constitutes an offense. As for the phrase "merely causing [it] to reach," "merely" (但) means exclusively;

"teaching" (教) refers to that which expresses, while "practice" (行) is that which is expressed. Regarding the term "following" (循), there are many various interpretations by different scholars; here, I follow the definition in the *Shuowen Jiezi*.
"Following" refers to the correspondence between the teaching and its practice. One follows the locus of practice by verifying it against the teaching, just as a mirror reflects the face.
Since practice must be concise and restrained, one must verify that practice with the teaching; hence it is called "mutually cultivating.

Regarding "beginning and end," this is spoken according to the beginning and end of a single period: the initial day of receiving [the precepts] is the beginning, and the fourth abandonment is the end. To remain diligent and unoffending throughout this interval is—
This refers to maintaining [the precept]. Alternatively, among the [ten] precepts, each individual precept is explained as follows:

for example, regarding the object of the precept against killing, if one perceives a human being as a piece of timber, and at the moment of severing their life, one continues to perceive them as a piece of timber until the end, without further shifting that perception in the interim.

Since this constitutes a lapse through delusion and forgetfulness, it does not constitute a prior offense; thus, one is effectively maintaining the precept (the same applies to other precepts). Regarding the phrase "if one is born [to it]," this distinguishes the characteristics of the offense.
"Born" refers to the initial moment of obtaining the precept, when one is born through transformation by means of the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the four-part motion).

It refers to the arising of the thought not to train oneself; it does not mean that being born from the womb is called "born. Therefore, the Preface to the Vinaya says: "From the Buddha’s precepts..."
To be born thus is to be truly born. It is like Aṅgulimāla, concerning whom the Tathāgata gave this prophecy:

"Aṅgulimāla"—this means 'Finger-Garland'—was originally a non-Buddhist who followed the teachings of a false teacher, being commanded to kill a thousand people and take their fingers to make a garland.
Having attained the fruit of Arhatship, he had already killed nine hundred and ninety-nine people, lacking only one. He then intended to harm his mother.
The Buddha, observing that his faculties were ripe for conversion, went before him. As the executioner sought to kill the Buddha, the latter said, "Stop!
I am the Great Śramaṇa, the Prince of King Śuddhodana. I am Aṅgulimāla; now I shall pay you the tax of a finger. The Buddha told him, "You foolish man!"

He himself did not abide [in permanence], yet he realized that the Tathāgata abides eternally. Having been thus questioned, he attained awakening and sought to leave the household life as a monk under the Buddha.
King Prasenajit, seeking him out with the intent to kill, went to the Buddha’s location to search for him. The Buddha said, "Aṅgulimāla has never committed a transgression since birth."
The King said, "This man has committed many killings; how can you say he has never committed a crime? The Buddha said, "Because since entering my Dharma, he has never committed one.
Citing this passage as proof, it shows that once the precepts have been received, one is considered to have been [virtuous] from birth.

As for those who have not heard the Dharma, although they have restrained their minds since birth, they do not study the laws regarding what constitutes an offense, its gravity, or its lightness; thus, they lack the cause for understanding and realization.

Regarding the principle that merit may coexist with punishment, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: Upāli asked the Buddha whether an offense is committed through a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*), an unwholesome mind (*akuśala-citta*), or a neutral mind (*avyākṛta-citta*).
The Buddha replied: "There are indeed offenses committed through a wholesome mind. For example, when a newly ordained person removes weeds from atop a stūpa, this is based on such a wholesome mind;
thus, merit and punishment coexist. While it is wholesome to purify the stūpa and thereby gain merit, harboring the intent to harm [the sentient beings within] constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense."

This is punishment. Furthermore, there is the cultivation of evil; this principle encompasses both merit and punishment. Seeking profit through trade is evil; using acquired wealth to create images is good.
With a virtuous mind, one gains a small portion of merit, yet because one fails to avoid violating the teachings, one incurs sin—this is punishment.

Good and evil minds serve as the cause; merit and punishment are the result. (There are many other interpretations, but they are not correct and are therefore not recorded here. Now, if one wishes to adjudicate punishments and the like, one need only examine:
Regarding the actions previously performed that correspond to the Buddha’s prohibitions, one incurs an offense regardless of whether the facts of the matter are true or false.

"The matter" refers to the act committed; "the person" refers to the one who committed it. Whether the intention is false or true, both constitute an offense. Even if one performs meritorious acts such as cleaning a stupa with a virtuous mind, it is still an offense [if it violates a rule];

likewise, if one sells goods with a malicious intent, it is an offense because of the falsity of the intent. (There is also a view that if one knows there is an offense, it is considered true; if one does not know there is an offense...)

To claim that offenses are unreal is not an understanding [of the Dharma]. This "general designation of upholding and violating" is the conclusion (*nigamana*). By means of a single mental state (*citta*) directed toward the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, all the precepts it encompasses are subsumed.
As these aspects of the practice of the precepts proceed in succession, if the mental state corresponds with the teaching on violation, it constitutes an offense;

if it corresponds with the teaching on upholding, it constitutes upholding. Now, the phrasing should be adjusted to say: "This is called the general designation for upholding and violating," meaning it is a general explanation of the one [mental state].
The "Precepts on the Mindset Regarding Upholding and Violating" constitutes the general outline of this section on Methods.

As for the statement regarding "reaching the ultimate result," this refers to a specific clarification: it means that when the fundamental primary offenses of the five categories are committed, one must thoroughly investigate the various disciplinary measures.

For an offense in the first category, if the offender is unwilling to repent, the punishment of *nihsargika* (expulsion) must be applied; if they are willing to repent, the punishment of *śikṣādattaka* (probationary training) is applied.

Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses involving concealment (*sāvadya-praticchādana*): first, one undergoes discipline for the concealment, which involves the forfeiture of thirty-five matters and so forth. These preparatory acts (*prayoga*) are grouped together as in the case of the primary precepts (*mūla-śikṣā*).
Before reaching the fundamental offense (*maula*), there is one *dukkaṭa* and two *sthūlātyaya*s; at that point, the fundamental offense is fully accomplished.

If one reaches the stage of the fruit (*phala-avasthā*), since the cause has already been established, the fruit is realized accordingly; this follows the principle of the fundamental offense and differs from other schools. Once the fruit is accomplished through the cause, [the process] continues further...

Regarding the statement that "there are original [rules] and skillful means, and that words may easily lead to confusion," this indicates the method for determining the specific case. "Measuring" (*liang*) refers to careful evaluation;

"relying upon" (*ju*) refers to having a basis; and "investigating" (*he*) refers to thorough examination. This means carefully evaluating the offense committed, relying upon the act performed, and investigating to ascertain the actual facts.
For example, in the case of the precept against stealing, one carefully evaluates the offense of theft, relies upon the fact of the theft, and investigates to determine the truth of the matter.

One must investigate the actual circumstances of the offender one by one—whether they acted with a specific intention, whether they advanced for their own benefit, whether they moved an object from its original place, whether they took it with a mind of unrestrained desire, whether they perceived it as a close friend's property, or whether they perceived it as ownerless—and only then may they be punished.
This ensures that the punishment does not contradict the principles of the teachings (the teachings which explain both phenomena and principle). Furthermore, one must...

One must carefully examine the circumstances of the offender. If one intentionally violates the teachings, whether they are experienced or unlearned, both are bound by the fundamental offenses of the five categories;

this judgment of gravity accords with both principle and teaching. If a student, being unable to learn or confused, commits the aforementioned acts, they are exempted according to their perception of the object;
this also accords with principle and teaching. "Jiaozhao" (皎照) means clarity and distinctness, as described above.

From the initial arousal of the thought of merit, up until taking what is not given with the perception that there is no owner—such distinctions are clearly discernible, as vivid as the sun illuminating objects;
hence it is said, "brightly shining. Weeds disordering a fertile field are called *wú* (overgrowth); turbid water mixing with a clear stream is called *làn* (contamination).
If one does not distinguish between the light and the heavy, it is like a fertile field being overrun by tares and weeds, or a flowing stream becoming muddied.

They are not distinguished. Now, by clarifying this through the teachings, one may avoid such errors. Regarding this separate clarification of observance and transgression (*dhāraṇa-āpatti*), the phrasing may also be adjusted to read:

"This is called the separate clarification of observance and transgression; it is explained individually in contrast to the five categories [of offenses], such as non-stealing, non-killing, and so forth."
The Section on Not Following Characteristics. This alone serves as the general outline (the sixth gate above is concluded).
The seventh gate is divided into two parts. First, regarding the heading from "The Seventh" to "The Meaning": this first clarifies the purpose for its introduction.

That is to say, while the preceding five gates have distinguished the expressive text (*vyañjana*) and the sixth gate has further distinguished the expressed meaning (*artha*), such that the principles of maintaining and violating [the precepts] are already known, its subsequent application...

Although the scriptural texts are numerous, they do not transcend the two teachings of transformation (*hua*) and regulation (*zhi*). As for the distinction between their practices, essential bodies, and boundaries, these are currently conflated.

Therefore, the following section analyzes what is common and what is specific regarding the capacities of those for whom they are intended. Regarding the explanation of the name: that which penetrates all things is called the "Path" (*dao*).

Because the mind penetrates the Bodhicitta of the Three Vehicles, this mind is itself the Path. This name is established based on cultivation (with the departing tone). It refers specifically to the five groups of the ordained.
Furthermore, there are three types of "worldly" (su): first, the worldly of daily customs (*fengsu*), so called because they change with the times and are not constant;

second, the worldly of the deaf (*longsu*), so called because they are obstructed by affairs and deluded regarding principle; third, the worldly of dust (*chensu*), so called because they are constrained by the six sense objects (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Alternatively, their affairs and entanglements are like dust. These refer to the two groups of lay followers. In the old Sanskrit, they are called *upāsaka*, which translates here as "pure."

"Faithful man" (*śraddhā-puruṣa*) and "upāsikā" (the *yǐnyún* [alternative reading] for "pure-faith woman"). The new Sanskrit term is *upāsaka*. *Upa* is translated as "near" (*jìn*), and *āsaka* means "to attend to" (*shì*).
Since *saka* is a masculine sound, it is translated as "male attendant" (*jìnshì nán*), referring to the precepts for the five classes of persons and so forth.
They are capable of approaching, attending upon, and serving the bhikṣus who are great arhats. If one says *upāsikā*, the suffix *-kā* is feminine;
it is translated as "female lay follower" (*jìnshì nǚ*). They likewise receive the precepts, their conduct is pure, and they are capable of serving the great bhikṣuṇīs who are arhats.
Regarding the seven groups: there are two categories of the laity and five categories of the ordained. This applies universally.

"Local" (*ju*) refers to the fact that the *Huàjiào* (Transformation Teaching) is universal, whereas the *Zhìjiào* (Regulation Teaching) is specific; this is the intended meaning of what is expounded by the "Gate," hence it is so called (and so forth).

In the commentary, the statement "revealing the principle up to the second" is a general heading for all the teachings. To speak in terms of their general characteristics, it is for the purpose of revealing...
*Bodhi* reveals the teaching of the truth of *nirvāṇa*; hence it is called "revealing the principle. Because it adapts to the capacities of beings without exception, it is said to have "many paths.
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The Dharma-aggregates taught by the Muni number eighty thousand," and so forth. If explained according to their specific characteristics:

for those with the capacity of humans and devas, it reveals the principle of the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions; for those with the capacity of *śrāvakas*, it reveals the four [truths]... [and so on].

The principle of the Truths (*satya*) is revealed for those with the capacity of Pratyekabuddhas; the principle of the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is revealed for those with the capacity of Bodhisattvas;

and the principle of the threefold pure precepts (*tri-koṭi-śīla*) is revealed for those with the capacity of Bodhisattvas. Although these teachings that reveal the principles are numerous, if one seeks them through the underlying intent, they do not exceed the practice of transformation (*pariṇāmanā*).

When gathered together, they are fully encompassed; therefore, it is said that "generally there are two. Regarding the seven groups of followers (*sapta-parṣad*), this refers to the appearance of the Buddha.

The "method of transformation" (*huayi*) is termed the "teaching of transformation" (*huajiao*). That which is restricted to the internal assembly refers specifically to the three types of practice performed; because these are designated as the "teaching of practice" (*xingjiao*), it is so called.

Regarding the phrase "one [type] refers to those up to the 'narrative'": that which "penetrates both the monastic and the laity" indicates the capacity of the recipients. This merely provides a general clarification of the causes.
The "fruit" (*phala*) refers to the classification of teachings (*yàojiào*). The term "but" (*dàn*) is a word denoting partiality or restriction.

"Vastly" (*fàn*) is one way of saying it is not fixed or determined; alternatively, both interpretations may be taken to mean "broad. As the Confucian texts say, "Vastly love the multitude of gentlemen," referring to the operation of a broad heart of love.

Here, we adopt the latter interpretation: that is, to broadly clarify the causes and effects, as well as the heterodox and orthodox, so that one's practices and deeds may be known for their excellence.

Because wholesome karma leads to birth among humans and devas, while evil karma causes one to fall into the three miserable realms, the eighty-four thousand gates of *pāramitā*—all wholesome dharmas—act as the cause for obtaining the fruits of humans and devas, such as the three types of virtuous action.

Conversely, all afflictions and evil karma act as the cause that invites the fruits of evil karma in the three miserable realms. For one who discerns the false and the correct, the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths is the correct path. Twenty-five.
The [four] truths are the false; right view is the correct. The sixty-two views are the false; the four reliances are the correct.
The five perversions are the false; the noble eightfold path is the correct. Denying cause and effect is the false; analytical cessation and nirvāṇa are the correct.

The *pradhāna* (primordial essence) as nirvāṇa is the false. Taking the mother as the object of reliance is the correct; taking spontaneity (*svabhāva*) as the principle is the false. Regarding the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses...

The precepts of the Buddha are correct; the precepts of chickens, dogs, and the like are deviant. This is intended to cause people to recognize and thoroughly understand them, so that they may abandon the deviant and follow the correct.
Regarding the phrase "classifying their practices and deeds," *ke* (科) means to categorize. That is, to distinguish the practices one performs and the karmic actions one commits.
For example, the layman Vimalakīrti entered various brothels to demonstrate the faults of desire, and likewise...

King Anala ruled his kingdom by transforming people through slaughter. When Sudhana felt doubt, the king took Sudhana’s hand and showed him a palace of hundreds of thousands of lights, saying, "I have attained the Illusion-like Samādhi;

toward even insects and ants I harbor no thought of killing, much less toward human beings. Furthermore, it is like the case of the woman Vasumitrā, who manifested forms and transformations (and so forth).
This is simply like the period of the Qi and Liang dynasties in this land, when figures such as Master Zhi, Beidu, and She-shun all acted in opposition to the norms of their time;

they manifested traces among ordinary people, making them difficult to fathom. Although these matters are not explicitly clarified in the formal teachings, they are cited here as examples to demonstrate the nature of their karmic retributions.
"Retribution" refers to both good and evil; as recorded in the sutras, it concerns the various disciples.
"Attaining Buddhahood in the future" and so forth are the results of wholesome karma (*kuśala-vipāka*). To clarify the results of unwholesome karma, the Sūtra states:

"The net of killing causes one to fall into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the animal realm, where one undergoes various bitter retributions. Such are the two kinds of karmic fruits: the wholesome and the unwholesome.
It is clearly understood and easy to perceive; therefore, it is said that it is "clearly comprehended and easily explained.

Regarding the phrase "the two ultimate transgressions," this distinguishes the function of the Vinaya (the teaching of prohibitions). Since the phenomena of the *vinaya* cannot be accomplished without practice, the teaching is able to express them;

thus, it is called the "teaching of practice" (*xingjiao*) and also the "teaching of prohibition" (*zhijiao*), because the teaching restrains and prohibits one, causing the cessation of evil and the cultivation of good.

Therefore, the phrase "restricted solely to the internal community" clarifies the specific capacity of those to whom [the teaching] is addressed. Regarding the determination of what is to be adopted and what is to be rejected:

at the time of initial ordination, if one’s person is free from obstacles and impediments (*antarāya*), one may receive the precepts—this is "adoption. Conversely, if these conditions are not met, it is "rejection.

Furthermore, among the two types of conduct in practice, that which conforms to the observance of the precepts must be relied upon as "adoption," while that which constitutes a dual transgression must be abandoned as "rejection. If one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense...

That which remains after the removal of the most serious offenses is called "taking" (upādāna); committing the four grave offenses (pārājika) constitutes "abandoning" (prahāṇa), as such individuals are to be permanently discarded.

Furthermore, among the disciplinary measures, the seven methods are termed "taking," while the nine methods involving temporary suspension are termed "abandoning. Regarding the establishment of the governing framework: "framework" (jālaka) serves as a metaphor;
just as a net is held together by its main ropes, so too, by establishing the framework of the five sections and seven groups, one raises the net of the two hundred and fifty precepts.

This is the section on "The Eyes. Regarding the manifestation of upholding and violating the precepts: beneath each individual precept, there are two types of conditions—the general and the specific. When these conditions are fulfilled, the precept is upheld;

conversely, in cases such as insanity, the conditions for violation are absent, and so forth. Regarding the resolution of doubts and obstructions: failing to comprehend the verbal teachings is termed "doubt."

Regarding the application of these matters, one must not allow them to become obstructed by ignorance. Once the extensive teachings on what is maintained and what is transgressed, as well as the texts concerning the differentiation of light and heavy offenses, are clearly understood, one will be free from the arising of doubt and stagnation. Furthermore, as seen in the *Śaikṣa* section, Upāli questioned the Buddha about each matter he doubted;
the Buddha resolved his doubts for him so that there would be no further impediment. Moreover, as indicated below following the section on the precepts, all [the rules] are likewise provided.
The passages concerning the four and five categories of objective conditions (*ālambana-saṃjñā*) are all intended to resolve doubts and obstructions.

"Pointing to specific matters and explaining them in detail" means that, following each specific case, one explains it exhaustively. For example, regarding the first precept on violating another's territory, there are three types of beings:

humans, non-humans, and animals. Within the category of humans, there are two kinds: males and eunuchs; the same applies to non-humans and animals (as Cheng states). This is done for each respective object.

Regarding the locations (*sthāna*), there are two [types], which together form twelve. Furthermore, among humans, there are three types: girls, women, and those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*); the same applies to animals (forming nine).
For each object (*viṣaya*), there are three non-locations (*asthāna*), totaling twenty-seven. Combined with the previous twelve, this makes forty-nine.

When contrasted with the objects of awakening, sleep, recent death, and limited objects—discussed in terms of four objects—this results in one hundred and fifty-six phrases. These are further applied to the categories of "enveloping" (*paryavasthāna*) and "obstructive" (*vibandha*).

The four phrases [of each category] (forming six hundred and twenty-four phrases in total, all of which are transgressions). If there are circumstances such as being coerced by an enemy, these are applied to the six phrases of defiled pleasure (totaling three thousand seven hundred and forty-four phrases, all of which are transgressions;
other examples of violating remaining precepts are similar). Thus, for a single finger-ring, one instance of donning it suffices to know that it does not require repeated application;
hence it is said that the text contains no principle of "repeated grasping. Regarding the determination of the offense: as if one were about to perform the aforementioned...

Regarding the time of the act: when first initiating this karma, the mind forms a distant preparatory effort (*dūre-prayoga*). When desiring to grasp the object, it is called the intermediate preparatory effort (*antike-prayoga*).

At the point of accomplishing the fundamental [act], one forms the proximate preparatory effort (*sāmantaka-prayoga*). If, facing the resultant state, one forms the fundamental [act] and further gives rise to a mind of jubilation, [this constitutes the completion].
Furthermore, the subsequent mind constitutes the formal offense (*āpatti*). According to the time at which it is committed, all are established as transgressions.

Because such offenses are thus formally established and clearly adjudicated, it is said that "the establishment of the offense is clear and decisive. Regarding matters where a fault is subject to a double penalty:

for instance, among the two hundred and fifty precepts of the Great Bhikṣus, if one violates a natural precept (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) within the seven categories, there is an additional path of action (*karmapatha*) on top of the formal offense.
This results in the fault of a double imposition; hence it is called "a second charge" (this does not mean that one is exempt from the offense of ignorance regarding the secondary branches).

The phrase "it is thus ultimate" is a term used for both concession and refutation. The "two teachings" refer to the transformative (*hua*) and the regulatory (*zhi*). Regarding the character *xiū* (to cultivate/practice), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states: [it means to nourish].

It is so. "Huan" (環) means circular. This refers to the fact that within both teachings, there are scriptural passages concerning lust, theft, killing, and falsehood; as these are arranged in a circular sequence, they are not without mutual overlap.

For example, while the Sūtras and Śāstras of the *Huàjiào* (Transformative Teaching) primarily elucidate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), they also clarify the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*);

whereas the Vinaya Piṭaka of the *Lǜzàng* (Discipline Storehouse) primarily elucidates ethical discipline, it also clarifies meditative concentration and wisdom. Thus, the two teachings are intermingled regarding offenses and transgressions.
The cycles [of the teachings] overlap with one another; how now may they be distinguished so that no such confusion occurs? One may cite the *Chao* (Commentary), which states in general:
"If one judges by citing the fundamental principle, the truth will naturally become manifest. This passage has two interpretations. The first, according to the *Shunzhengji*, states:

Even though the texts of the Vinaya and other collections are explained, they also serve as auxiliary supports. Furthermore, within the practice of the teachings found in the Vinaya texts, although concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are clarified, they appear to overlap with the teachings of other schools;
nevertheless, the Vinaya Piṭaka takes precepts (*śīla*) as its primary tenet, and thus even where there are passages concerning concentration and wisdom, [they remain subordinate].

This also serves as a supplementary aid. Now, by citing only the two orthodox teachings (*zhengzong*), the inclusion of the ancillary expositions (*bangquan*) is naturally clarified (as recorded in the text above).
The intention [of the author] is not [what you suggest]. This passage is a heading (*biao*), while the following sentence provides its own explanation.

"The preceding statement cited the essential tenets (*zong*) as if they were a definitive judgment, and their principle is naturally manifest; however, it is not yet clear how these cited tenets are to be distinguished. This should be clarified in the *Chao* (Excerpts)."

The commentary states: "This refers to the internal mind’s compliance or resistance, taking principle as its thesis, and so forth. Since the *Chao* (the sub-commentary) explains this itself, why labor to provide a preliminary interpretation?
