"Gate Gautama possesses many kinds of merit. The King asked, "From what is such a Dharma-body obtained? The Nirgrantha replied, "This precept is the beginning.
Great King, you should know that because the precepts are pure, one does not sever the lineage of the Triple Gem; because the precepts are pure, one's merit is immeasurable.
If one does not uphold the precepts, one may even fail to obtain the body of a dog or a jackal. How much less so for others?
How much more so when one attains a body of merit! When the King heard these words of Yi, he gave rise to the bodhicitta.
Regarding the phrase "the moon-lamp man": although there may be those with physical beauty, noble lineage, and great learning—where "beauty" refers to a handsome countenance—[he surpasses them].
"Lineage" refers to high-ranking families and great clans. "Much learning" refers to being skilled in the four Vedas, the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), and so forth.

If one lacks both precepts and wisdom, they are like birds or beasts; as a sutra says by way of analogy: "It is like a corpse adorned with golden necklaces. Thus it is for one who is learned but violates the precepts.
It is also like this: it is just as distinct species are not differentiated [from one another].

Although one may occupy a lowly position and possess little learning or insight—this reverses the preceding passage—it may be that such a person is lowly, meaning poor, destitute, and base, yet is nonetheless able to maintain the precepts. The concluding phrase of the following line states:
"One who purely maintains the precepts is called a superior person (*satpuruṣa*)."
Regarding the phrase "Nirvana is like... and so forth: it means that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, yet it is not manifest because it is shrouded by the veil of afflictions and delusions.
If one now wishes to see this nature, one must first eliminate the afflictions. To eliminate the afflictions, one must first maintain the precepts.
When afflictions and delusions are exhausted, [the nature] will naturally be seen. If one sees this [nature], it is called realizing Great Nirvana. If one maintains...
"To disparage this sutra while violating the pure precepts" means to break these very precepts. The subsequent phrase states: "They are followers of Māra, not sons of the Buddha.
The Buddha does not permit them to receive and uphold this sutra because they contradict the Buddha’s emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and their upholding of it would be without benefit.
Regarding the verses from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and so forth: what is cited here clarifies that the precepts are the foundation of a bodhisattva, encouraging one to uphold them.
It is the Buddha’s praise of the benefits for the future, stating that because the precepts are pure, one shall attain Bodhi.

These are cited again because they appear three times throughout the preceding and following sections; this is the repeated citation of the passage concerning the Sangha Jewel. One should cause these to be recited from the heart.
This means: one is exhorted to constantly remember and maintain [the teachings], hence it is called "reciting" (*song*). The mind is the sovereign of the body and the most preeminent;
one is exhorted to keep it in memory so that it is always present in the mind, hence it is called "the head of the mind" (*xinshou*).
The phrase "The Treatise on the Four Great Vehicles" is the heading. Regarding the passage from "The Treatise on Wisdom" to "fear":
if one seeks the great benefit—the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi is called the great benefit—those who seek this fruit must first maintain pure precepts;
this marks the first meaning. "The root of all virtues" marks the second meaning. "The essential requirement for leaving the household life" is the third meaning. As it says:
Having briefly explained the meaning of the second faculty regarding "cherishing the abode of the precious and sublime Dharma," it is as follows:
Just as worldly treasures are cherished by all people, so too is the protection of the precepts. It is like protecting one's own life;

for all sentient beings cherish their own lives, and now they are made to protect the precepts accordingly. As for the statement that the precepts are the abode of all wholesome dharmas, all unwholesome [dharmas]...

"Abiding by the precepts" is the meaning of its being the root. Furthermore, regarding the previous third essential point—that one who is without feet cannot walk, up to the point where nothing at all can be attained—it is known that the feet are essential.
As for one who desires to fly but has no wings: when various birds ascend into the sky, they must rely upon their wings; without wings, they cannot take flight. Thus it is known.
The wings are essential. For one who wishes to cross without a boat: indeed, those who wish to traverse rivers and seas to reach the other shore must rely upon a boat for transport;
if there is no boat, they cannot cross. Thus, we know that the boat is of vital importance. The principle of the subsequent verse should be stated thus:
if one lacks the precepts and yet seeks excellent fruits, they likewise cannot be attained. This is because one lacks the feet of the precepts, and so forth.
There is no crossing over without precepts; this cannot be attained. "If one abandons these precepts" means that "abandoning" refers to relinquishing them.

Even if one dwells in the mountains practicing austerities, it is like the non-Buddhist practitioners or those who starve themselves; such acts are merely called "perverse conduct" because they are empty and yield nothing.
Although one may be poor, lowly, or even illiterate—this explains the previously cited statement regarding the meaning of "benefit," namely that "whatever one wishes for shall be obtained."

This refers to humans, devas, and those of the three vehicles; according to their respective aspirations, they obtain these benefits. Regarding the "wind-blade dismembering the body," the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"The human body has one hundred distinct locations called *marmans*, which are translated here as 'vital joints' (*si jie*).

At the time of death, the three great elements dismember the body. When the fire element dismembers it, the fire burns the tendons and joints, causing the mind to become restless and distressed before long."

When life ends and the water element dissolves, it first causes the tendons to rot; before long, one passes away. When the wind element dissolves, it causes the tendons to shatter and perish, such that one is neither conscious nor aware [of it].
Question: Why does the earth element not dissolve the body? Answer: The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

Because there are three external calamities—water, fire, and wind—and while these exist externally, internally there is only water, fire, and wind. Since the earth element is absent externally, there is no corresponding calamity of the earth element within. Thus, [the earth element does not dissolve the body].
There is no affliction of the earth element here; this is based on what exists among humans. When one dies in the heavenly realms, there are only the five signs of decay (*pañca-vyasanāni*):
first, the clothes become soiled with sweat; second, the flowers upon the head wither; third, sweat breaks out from the armpits; fourth, a foul odor enters the body;
fifth, one finds no pleasure in one’s own seat. If these five appear, death is certain. Now, for a person who maintains the precepts, at the time of their end, the "wind-sword" (*vātāsi*)...

Regarding the dissolution of the body: even if the sinews and veins were to be severed, the mind would be free from fear. The commentary explains that this is because one may perceive auspicious signs and know for oneself that one’s observance of the precepts is pure;
thus, there is no fear in the heart. It is by virtue of maintaining the precepts in this way that such benefits are obtained.
Regarding the statement "from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* to the *Vyākhyāna*," the thirty-two marks are now listed according to the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:

the soles of the feet are level with auspicious wheels; the toes are slender; the hands and feet are rounded and soft; the ankles are like those of a royal goose; the calves are like those of a deer king; the male organ is retracted within a sheath; the body is full and upright;
each hair grows individually from its own pore and curls to the right with a golden hue; there is a constant aura of light; the skin is fine and smooth; and seven parts of the body are well-filled.
His body is tall and straight; his shoulders are rounded and broad, reaching down to his knees; he possesses the lion-like vow of forty even teeth, which are closely set, fresh, and most excellent;

his tongue is long and his eyes are clear and blue-black; he bears the marks of the *ūrṇā-kośa*, the white tuft of hair between the brows, and the Brahma-voice (the explanation of this verse is omitted for fear of being too prolix, but it is cited here merely as evidence of his virtuous discipline).
Furthermore, he himself maintains the precepts with firmness and does not allow others to violate them; thus he attains the first mark: the soles of his feet are level.
The mark of level palms and soles is like the bottom of a cosmetic box (*lián*). Furthermore, by refraining from double-tongued speech, one attains the mark of forty teeth.

Question: What is the meaning of the term *lakṣaṇa* (mark)? Answer: The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that it signifies the meanings of being manifest, blazing, preeminent, and auspicious. Question:

How do the marks and minor characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-anuvyañjana*) of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) differ from those of a Buddha? Answer: The verse in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says: "Because their marks are not perfectly round and luminous, they are not equal to those of a Buddha."
This means they are incorrect, incomplete, and unclear. Although the thirty-two marks enumerated above are distinct, they all have the observance of the precepts as their cause;
there is no further differentiation between them. Therefore, it is said that "the causes are without distinction" and so forth. If one does not observe the precepts, [these marks cannot be attained].

This is as stated in the text (and so forth). Regarding the "Ten Abodes" and so on: in that [work], the fourteenth [chapter] consists of two sections. The first, the "Praise of Morality" (*Śīla-praśaṃsā*), states:
"A brief praise of a small portion of *śīla*. *Śīla* is the root of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

*Śīla* is an accumulation of the jewels of merit; it is also the dwelling place of merit. It enables one to cross the ocean of birth and death," and so forth. Next is the "Fruit of the Reward of Morality" (*Śīla-vipāka*).
It says: "A Bodhisattva who is able to purely uphold the *śīla* attains freedom from defilement (which is the Second Bhūmi).

He shall become a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), transforming people through the ten wholesome paths of action and enjoying the seven treasures at will. Such is the retribution he receives, as explained in detail therein."
The second section, the *Zhìjiào* (Teachings on Discipline), is divided into two parts. "Discipline" (*zhì*) refers to the Vinaya teachings. The first is the *Lǜběn* (Root Text of the Vinaya);
the second is based on the Vinaya commentaries (*lùn*). The statement "First, clarifying the *Lǜběn*" serves as the heading. Regarding the passage from "The *Sēngqí*" to "the five benefits":

[it concerns] the three points where one does not wish to harbor doubt or regret and thus seeks instruction from others. Xuán says: "Since he upholds and maintains [the precepts], his understanding penetrates the sacred teachings."

Regarding "if one asks another": some commentaries explain that this means one does not personally harbor doubt or regret; even if there is uncertainty, one simply consults another. This is inferior to the former [method].
Regarding "wandering and transforming in the five directions" and so forth: the teachings and principles of the Buddhadharma throughout the ten directions are no different.

If one does not clearly understand that the Teacher (the Buddha) is present in many places, one may feel fear. However, if one acts in accordance with the teaching, having a mind free from dread, this constitutes sincere faith.
The following is the conclusion.
Regarding the passage from "The Four-Part [Vinaya]" onwards, although there are five phrases, they are divided into three according to their meaning. The first concerns one's own practice;

the subsequent three concern the conduct of governing the community. If this practice is perfected, one is then able to uphold the Dharma, ensuring it does not fall into ruin for a thousand years. Therefore...

Finally, there is the practice of establishing the True Dharma. First, "the precept-category is firm and solid" means that mindfulness, wisdom, and equanimity—the three—cause the precepts to be pure and prevent them from being destroyed by external conditions;
hence they are called "firm and solid. Second, "excellently overcoming all enemies": Xuán says:

1. Upholding and breaking [the precepts] are two meanings that are as contradictory as enemies; now, with a pure inner mind, one proceeds toward them. 2. Regarding the third, being fearless in making definitive judgments among the assembly:

since one has already eliminated flaws when making determinations within the community, there is logically no cause for fear or hesitation. 3. Regarding the fourth, being able to resolve doubts and regrets:
having a clear understanding of what constitutes upholding or violating the precepts, one can resolve the doubts and anxieties of others. 4. Fifth, being skilled in upholding the *vinaya*.
Regarding the term "nuns and others": it means to uphold the Vinaya so that the Dharma does not decline, which is called "long endurance.

Furthermore, ten benefits are obtained, as in the passage concerning "gathering the Saṃgha," where only the first point is briefly mentioned: (1) gathering the Saṃgha; (2) causing the Saṃgha to rejoice;
(3) causing the Saṃgha to dwell in peace and happiness; (4) causing those who have not yet had faith to believe; (5) increasing the faith of those who already believe; (6) [difficulties...]
1. To bring about tranquility; 2. to inspire shame and remorse; 3. to bring peace and happiness; 4. to sever present outflows (*āsrava*); 5. to sever future outflows; 6.
to cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time. Regarding the statement "the same applies up to ten," that Vinaya contains thirty-seven [questions].
It asks: "How long will the Buddha-dharma remain in the world? The Buddha answers: "It shall remain as long as pure bhikṣus recite the precepts without breaking them."
This is called the "Dharma Abiding in the World. Buddhas of the present and future also speak in this way; therefore, it is said that the same applies to the three periods of time.

Regarding the phrase "second, based on the Vinaya and Śāstras," this is the heading. Question: Since the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) treatises have already been cited previously, why is this explained again here?
Answer: The former were treatises representing the one-sided dogmatic tenets of the Small Vehicle, whereas those cited here are based upon the Vinaya.

The *Mūla* (Root) [Vinaya] either takes the *Caturvargika-vinaya* as its basis, such as the *Samantapāsādikā* and others; or it explains the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, such as the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* and others;
or it explains the Vinaya among the twenty schools, namely clarifying the *Sāmmitīya-vinaya* and so forth. All of these belong to the category of the Prescriptive Teaching (*prajñapti-śāsana*).
This is distinguished from what preceded.
Regarding the phrase "clearly reaching that [state]," the original term is *vinaya*; this word *vinī* is an abbreviated form of *vinaya*.
First, as for "being able to bring about various benefits," the *Chao* text itself explains: it induces both mundane and supramundane [attainments].
It is good. There are two ways in which it induces: first, it can induce forty-two thousand merits of the True Dharma;
second, it can induce a mind that does not harbor resentment, leading even to liberation. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "If one attains the fruits of humans or devas, it is mundane goodness;
if one attains the fruits of the Three Vehicles, it is supramundane goodness. Regarding the phrase "second, it can teach," the commentary explains: "it can obstruct..."
Not allowing evil to arise through body and speech is precisely the meaning of "being able to teach. Because one does not become turbid or defiled, it is called "purity of body and speech.
Because one is not defiled by the turbidity of views, it is named "straightforward purity. Thus, it is directed toward the right path; thus, it leads toward *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the third point, "the ability to extinguish transgressions," the commentary explains that there are two kinds of extinction: [extinction through] skillful means and... [two].

"Extinction of actual transgressions" refers to attaining *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (nirvāṇa). Because ethical discipline (*śīla*) can obstruct all obstacles of transgression, it is called the "means of extinction.
Because obstacles do not arise, the extinction of transgressions is attained; these two together are respectfully termed *vinaya*. Regarding the phrase "capable of leading," the commentary states:
"It is capable of leading householders and those who have gone forth but have not yet abandoned desire, causing them to attain the Brahma-abodes (*brahmavihāra*). From...
The Noble One attains *nirvāṇa* with remainder. Because it subsequently becomes superior, it is called "leading to the ultimate meaning" (*paramārtha-nayanīya*).

Regarding the phrase "even reaching the Brahma-abodes," the treatise states there are eight types of abiding: first, abiding in the objective field (*ālambana-vihāra*), which refers to the Tathāgata relying upon the sixteen great kingdoms;

second, abiding in the basis (*niśraya-vihāra*), which refers to dwelling in the Jetavana monastery; third, abiding in the four modes of conduct (*īryāpatha-vihāra*), namely walking, standing, sitting, and reclining; fourth, [abiding in] the non-... [text fragment].
Abiding by relinquishing the life-span refers to the period prior to eighty years [of the Buddha’s life]. Abiding in the fivefold Dharma-body refers to the five heavens.
Abiding in the Great Brahma refers to cultivating the four immeasurable concentrations (*apramāṇa*) and opening the path to the Brahma realm.

Abiding in the seven noble ones refers to abiding in the three samādhis—namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—which constitute the three samādhis. Abiding in the eighth non-abiding refers to abiding in...
One enters parinirvāṇa through the precepts of the nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa. The *Chao* (Excerpts) omits the first five [categories], hence the inclusion of the phrase "up to" (*zhì*).

Regarding the "five superior persons" (*pañca-uttama-pudgala*): "superior" (*shèng*) means preeminent; "person" (*rén*) refers to the Buddha, followed by the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas. That which they all practice therein is precisely the precepts.
If an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) understands and practices them, they are also called a "superior enterer. If one is not a superior or sublime person, [they do not].
How can one maintain the precepts? Now that they are maintained, what is not excellent about them?
As for those such as the Sarvāstivādins who say that all sentient beings possess the fruits of gods, humans, and so forth, which arise by means of the precepts: [this is so].
This is because all [virtues] exist by virtue of upholding the precepts. This refers exclusively to the wholesome paths as being "all. Therefore, the Record states:
"Breaking the precepts leads to entry into the three evil realms; that these too exist by virtue of the precepts" is included within the section on violating the precepts. Reflect upon this.
Regarding the phrase "merit therein," this refers to both the sūtras and the śāstras. Therein, the sūtra represents meditative concentration (samādhi) and the śāstra represents wisdom (prajñā).
Since concentration and wisdom lack this specific function, they are excluded; the preceding and following contexts make this clear (and so forth).
Regarding the phrase "it is well-arrived": this refers to the five persons who uphold the Vinaya, speaking in terms of the Sangha Jewel as the presiding authority. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:

"In a village or a forest, if five Dharma masters assemble the Saṃgha from the four directions, this is called the 'Community of Monks. They abide according to the Dharma within a great ocean of merit.
Even if immeasurable people have broken the precepts, provided that these five persons remain pure and maintain the Dharma through their governance, [the community remains established]."
This causes the Dharma to perish. Regarding the fourth point, "from four up to twenty people purifying themselves of offenses":

starting from the confession of one person and proceeding to the confession of other offenses, it is said that "until the body is purified. When those who uphold the Dharma maintain the rites, it ensures that the Dharma remains long and does not perish.
As for the statement "remaining in the world for five thousand years," according to the eighteenth fascicle of that treatise, there are two periods of five thousand years; the first...

Five thousand years. During the first thousand years, one attains the three types of supernormal knowledge (*traividya*). During the next thousand years, one attains the fourth fruit [of arhatship], but lacks the three types of supernormal knowledge.

During the next thousand years, one attains the third fruit [of non-returning], but lacks the fourth fruit. During the next thousand years, one attains the second fruit [of once-returning], but lacks the third.
During the final thousand years, one attains the first fruit [of stream-entry], but lacks the second. (This constitutes the first five thousand years). Hereafter...

Five thousand years. [During the first period,] one may study and attain the fruits of the Way; after ten thousand years, the Dharma will be exhausted and vanish, leaving nothing but the shaving of hair and the wearing of dyed robes.
If one follows the standard of the Buddha’s teaching remaining in the world, the attainment of the fruits constitutes the first five thousand years.

If one speaks only of the existence of the Buddha’s Dharma in the world without the realization of its fruits, this refers to the latter five thousand years. The citations listed here in this excerpt pertain to the latter five thousand years.

Regarding the phrase "five hundred, etc.," according to the underlying principle, it should state: "If the Buddha were in the world, one would take the Buddha as teacher," and so forth. Since these words are now omitted, the term "up to" (乃至) is used.
As for the statement that "if one upholds the five precepts, one immediately perceives the Dharma-body": upholding the precepts is the very cause for the purity of morality;

from morality arise concentration and wisdom, through which one attains knowledge and vision. Therefore, by upholding the five precepts, one immediately perceives the Dharma-body. If one protects the Dharma...
"Below" refers to the dual illustration. This means that apart from the Dharma there is no Buddha, and apart from water there are no insects.
Thus, to protect the Dharma is to protect the Buddha, and to protect the water is to protect the insects. To drink the water is to kill the insects; to break the precepts is to harm the Buddha.
Therefore, it is called "the analogy of drinking water and killing insects. The details of this causal origin are as explained in the following text.
Regarding the statement, "The Sarvāstivādins say [it was taught] at [the time of the council]," this is initially based on what was said during the first council:
within the stone chamber, five hundred arhats spoke with one voice, all saying that the Vinaya should be collected first, because the Vinaya is the root of the Buddha-dharma.

As for the phrase, "The sūtras do not select specific times or places," this is an inverse explanation of the aforementioned secret meaning; it means that [the sūtras] do not necessarily have to be preached every half-month. It does not.

There is no selection of time, because [the Dharma] abides within the *dharmadhātu*. There is no selection of place; it is said that Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, celestial seers (*ṛṣi*), and others may speak, provided they are authorized by the Buddha, for then it is called a *sūtra*.
Regarding the selection of persons, the Vinaya is not like this; this is the opposite of the aforementioned [case], and so forth.
As for the *Pinfen gongde lun* (Treatise on the Analysis of Merit), it says: "The two assemblies of monks and nuns recite the two hundred and fifty precepts."
This matter is not the concern of external officials; it is something practiced by worldly people, not something for śrāmaṇeras, laymen, or laywomen to hear or see.

Furthermore, the citation from the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* serves to further explain the preceding passage, clarifying that it is not for worldly people to witness or hear this, because they are ignorant, inferior, and of meager capacity.

One is unable to guard and maintain these precepts. Xuan says: Because the noble ones of the Three Vehicles possess wisdom, they honor and revere the precepts with excellence, thereby attaining the three types of bodhisattvas.
Conversely, the base and ignorant, being both deluded and inferior, treat the precepts lightly and thus fall into the three evil realms.
If one follows the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra*, which is a Mahāyāna treatise, this should properly have been explained within the preceding section on the "Transformative Teaching" (*huàjiào*). Now...
However, because the textual momentum follows [the previous section], it is cited here. Those of old failed to grasp this and falsely claimed it was not the text of the *Śāstra* (Commentary).

It says, "The two contradictions regarding the precepts" and so forth; this refers to the combined explanation of the two teachings, namely, the *Hua* (Transformation) and *Zhi* (Regulatory) teachings.
It is not as previously categorized, where Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as the *Zhi* (Regulatory) teachings and the sūtras and śāstras, each have their own distinct categories and sequential order.

Although we now again cite both the texts on transformation (*nirmāṇa*) and discipline (*vinaya*), whether they appear earlier or later, we simply cite them wherever the flow of the text naturally leads, without establishing a formal sequence of headings;
therefore, it is said that they are "explained in a miscellaneous manner."

Regarding the statement in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* concerning those who have "slightly attained [realization] and become confused": having slightly attained [realization], they immediately claim to be noble ones (*ārya*).

Merely understanding the five *smṛtyupasthānas* (foundations of mindfulness), such as the contemplation of general and specific characteristics, is called "slight attainment. Because their minds have been stilled through *śamatha*, they then claim that those who have attained the four fruits of the path are no different from themselves;
thus, they say, "I am a noble one. Regarding the second point, "laypeople being born in heaven," etc., this is from the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā).
It is said: "Laypeople have no [monastic] discipline upon their persons; they merely possess devoted faith, and thus they are able to be reborn in the heavens.
Those who have left the household life possess the Dharma and serve as fields of merit for the world, yet they instead violate it, unworthily accepting the offerings of the faithful.

By opening the gates to all transgressions, they cause many sentient beings to follow their example and thereby enter the evil realms. Third, regarding those who abandon worldly activities and so forth, it is as stated in the *Kṛkī-rāja-sūtra*.

The King said, "In my dream, a great elephant was inside a single room. By means of its skillful means, it managed to extend its body through a window, yet its tail remained obstructed so that it could not emerge.
The Buddha said, "This symbolizes the disciples of Śākyamuni’s bequeathed Dharma who have left home to become renunciants, yet they are greedy for fame and pursue profit.
They violate the Buddha's precepts; such are those who break the precepts, and many people assist them, just as [the elephant's tail]."
The Sūtra says: "In the king’s dream, he saw a monkey that lacked majesty and virtue. The sentient beings of the four great oceans bathed its head with water and established it as king.
This signifies that among the disciples of Śākyamuni’s bequeathed Dharma, those who have broken the precepts are established as the leaders of the Saṃgha, and they assist one another;
this is precisely the meaning. As for even Arhats being beaten and reviled, Xuán says:
The Vinaya text is in the *Dazang* (Great Canon).
Regarding the passage "not cultivating one's own body, precepts, mind, and wisdom," it is identical to the twenty-ninth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Now, I shall provide an interpretation based on its essential meaning. The Sūtra says: "If a bhikṣu does not contemplate the body as impermanent and impure, this is called 'not cultivating the body. If...
Not examining the precepts—since the precepts are the ladder for all wholesome dharmas—is called not cultivating the precepts.

If one does not examine the mind and its wisdom flickers and wavers, then restraining and subduing it is called cultivating the mind. If one does not examine wisdom, even if one possesses great power and influence, this is called not cultivating wisdom.
Second, keeping śrāmaṇeras; third, providing dependence to others—these two types concern a teacher who fails to instruct.

Instruction: Regarding these śrāmaṇeras and those who have newly received the precepts, because they commit evil deeds and do not understand the three characteristics [of impermanence, suffering, and non-self], they dispatch other *karmadāna* (lay attendants) to handle the earth.
Failing to use pure speech, they say, "Know this! Look at this! or directly command, "Dig the earth for me.

This is impure speech. It is the same when cutting grass. As for watering (the character *gai* is pronounced *gu-ai*; at the time of irrigation), if one does not use a straining cloth, it is now simply done [in this manner].
The pronunciation of "gài" (溉) is [as indicated]. The remaining text is easy to understand.
Regarding the passage from "The Four-Part [Vinaya]" to "the True Dharma": those who uphold the Dharma are the masters of the Sūtras; those who uphold the Vinaya are the masters of the Vinaya;
those who uphold the Mātr̥kā are the masters of the Abhidharma. "Mātr̥kā" is likely a phonetic corruption; it should be pronounced "mó" (摩).
*Taḷika*. This is translated as "Mātṛkā" (Mother). It is a synonym for *Abhidharma*.

It means that if one does not instruct the five groups of renunciants, as well as laypeople and others, and the succession of this Dharma is not maintained by anyone, then it is said that the Dharma has perished.

Regarding the statement "according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*": that text’s thirty-fourth fascicle states that some bhikṣus neglected the study of the *vinaya* and instead devoted themselves to reciting the sūtras and śāstras.
The World-Honored One rebuked them and, in their presence, praised those who maintained both [the sūtras and] the *vinaya* as being the most excellent, supreme, and foremost.
The bhikṣus then thought, "The Buddha praises the *vinaya*; why should we not study the precepts? At that time, there was an elder...
"Elder, you have indeed departed from that training in the Vinaya.
Quoting the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, the Sūtra states: "Elders, senior monks (*sthavira*), and those of middle age are collectively categorized into four stages:
those from one summer-retreat up to nine summers are called 'junior'; those from ten summers up to nineteen summers are called 'middle-aged'; those from twenty summers up to forty..."

Those with nineteen years of *varṣa* are called *sthavira*. Those from fifty years of *varṣa* upwards are called *vṛddha*. Regarding "elder" (*sthavira*), it refers to one who initially did not delight in the precepts.

As for "one who initially saw [the value of] delighting in the precepts," it means that when others praised what was not right, he did not join in the praise; that is, he did not study at all at first, but later returned to practice and study them.
Regarding "I do not praise him," he subsequently provides his own explanation: "For what reason? Because other people share his same views. Long... (text fragment ends).
Because one suffers at night. That is to say, in the Vinaya, it was first prescribed that for five years one must focus exclusively on the Vinaya rules;

having received [the precepts], if one subsequently experiences pleasure and violates the Buddha’s regulation, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. Like those in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, one will fall into hell for a vast number of kalpas and undergo the suffering of disadvantage.
In the preceding section of the text, regarding the total abandonment of study, it says "reproach" (*ākrośa*), which shifts the topic. This is based on...
At first, one does not study; later, one continues to study as before. The only difference from what preceded is that it says "one does not praise. Reflect on this.
Regarding the phrase "containing the ultimate mark" (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*) within it: according to the subsequent precept on possessing jewels, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is cited, which says:

"If my disciples have no one to provide for them, in order to protect the True Dharma, I shall permit them to possess [jewels] and allow them to be entrusted to faithful donors (*dānapati*). Now it says...
"Those who do not listen" refers to those who do not uphold the precepts. Regarding the *Māyā-sūtra* and other texts, they state:
"After eight hundred years, the bhikṣus will delight in fine clothing and engage in frivolous play. After nine hundred years, slave-bhikṣus will have bhikṣuṇīs as their servants.
After one thousand years, they will take no pleasure in the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). After one thousand one hundred years, they will disparage..."
They will slander the Vinaya. After twelve hundred years, they will engage in unchaste conduct; sons born will become bhikṣus and daughters born will become bhikṣuṇīs.
[The text] omits this phrase. After thirteen hundred years, the saffron robes will turn white and no longer take dye.

One thousand four hundred years later, people will take pleasure in killing and greedily sell the property of the Triple Gem (as cited above from the sutra). Now, our Master has composed this *Jiyao* (Essential Extracts) during the ninth year of the Wude era at the beginning of the Tang dynasty;
more than one thousand four hundred years have already passed. If one examines the various transgressions mentioned before and after [the cited passage], they are all clearly visible therein;
however, among them, the white *kāṣāya* has never been seen with my own eyes. The purport of the Master’s commentary is that there are matters concerning India, and he poses a counter-question.

That Brahmin monk further stated that since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he had never seen anything turn white. There are differences in the explanations provided by various records of antiquity and modern times.
The first interpretation states: "To not uphold the precepts while being defiled by the flavor of the Dharma is called 'turning white. Now, this is refuted:

since the scriptural text refers to a physical transformation, it is inappropriate to apply it to the Dharma. The *Jie xuan ji* (Record Explaining the Profundities), based on the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, [provides the following]...
The Sūtra says: After the King had made a great offering to the bhikṣus, he addressed the bhikṣu Dharmarāja, saying: "Venerable masters, you dwell here; we shall provide for your sustenance.
Please preach the Dharma for me, and I shall listen with a sincere heart. The bhikṣus remained silent, and there was no one to speak.
The King repeated his request twice more, yet still there was no one to speak. The King said to the bhikṣus, "I do not know the Dharma."
He spoke to them, and their *kāṣāya* robes turned white; the dye no longer appeared, and they all fell from their beds, rolling about upon the ground.
Now, the commentary states: although this describes a physical transformation into white based on a specific event, there is scriptural authority to support it.

However, the *Māyā-sūtra* speaks of a period one thousand three hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, whereas the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* cited above still pertains to the time when the Buddha was alive.
This appears to be contradictory. The *Junzheng ji* (Record of Correcting the Norm) states: "In the present day, monks and nuns do not dye according to the Dharma;

they merely produce a shallow, onion-colored hue, which is roughly a transformation of white. Now, I refute this: since they dye it a shallow color, it completely contradicts the meaning of the scriptural passage stating that one does not accept dyed colors.
Now, relying on the Dharma-treasure, I shall set forth the correct interpretation. It is only [the following] that is entrusted...
The Ritual for Entrustment (Zhuyi), also known as the Ritual for the Buddha’s Entrustment of the Dharma.

In the second year of the Longshuo era, the Tripiṭaka Master Nadi brought this to the capital and translated it together with the editor; it was completed in six fascicles. The latter part of the text states:

When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he commanded Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva to take the Buddha’s saṃghāṭī robe and reside upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, where he was to erect a stūpa and make offerings. Furthermore, he commanded...

Śakra, the Lord of Devas, caused the various devas to rain down flowers that scattered upon his robes. He further commanded the King of the Wind Spirits to blow away the withered flowers and rain down fresh ones.
He also commanded the Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Samantabhadra to collect the withered flowers in Jambudvīpa and erect stūpas over them.

At that time, those in the assembly gave rise to doubt. Then a minor Śāriputra asked the Buddha: "After my parinirvāṇa, when one thousand three hundred years have passed, the *kāṣāya* will turn white.

Now, relying on this [teaching], I have preemptively countered it so that it shall not turn white until the very end of the Dharma. This was established as a definitive teaching. [The interlocutor] asked:
"Why does the *Chao* (the *Fozu tongji*) not clarify this? The answer is: The *Chao* was compiled during the Wude era; it records the ritual for the entrustment of the Dharma.
"This was after the year Longshuo (662). Furthermore, he asked why the *Gantong zhuan* (Biographies of Spiritual Resonance) was not recorded [in the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*]. He replied:
'The *Gantong zhuan* was compiled by Xian-du; since it was also produced later, [it was not included]' (and so forth)."

Regarding the passage in the *Yunzhilun* (Cloud Wisdom Treatise) concerning "upholding the precepts," this refers to the text from the fifteenth fascicle of that treatise. Master Baoyun remarked: "That treatise consistently employs metaphors to illustrate the corresponding principles.

Now, [the current text] frequently places the metaphors above [the principles], resulting in the error of breaking the syntactic structure. I request that you carefully examine the intent of my transcription.
For example, 'a tomb' (*zhǒng*) is a place where corpses reside; likewise, within the body of one who has broken the precepts, the life-force of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) has already perished."
Therefore, a "withered tree" refers to one that lacks branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit; a person who has broken the precepts does not produce the flowers and fruits of the myriad virtues.
Though they possess a stately body of six feet in height, they are no different from a withered tree.

A "rākṣasa" is one who eats human flesh and whose evil intent grows ever more fierce; a person who has broken the precepts harms their own Dharma-body and never ceases their evil intent, just like a rākṣasa.
The "greatly ill person" refers to one who is foul and filthy; because they do not refrain from associating with those who violate the precepts, they commit two kinds of offenses that are foul.
Pure sages do not delight in being near such persons. The "poisonous snake" harms a person's physical flesh, whereas violating the precepts can harm the Dharma-body.

"Even though [they are equal]" means that although one wears the Dharma-robes, if one practices what is contrary to the Dharma, one will inevitably experience the retribution of having one’s body wrapped in iron sheets for using things in an unrighteous manner.

When eating the food and drink of others, one’s heart feels as if it were a vessel of molten copper. Furthermore, since one who has broken the precepts cannot digest the clothing, food, and other goods of others, they receive such offerings like a thief;
after death, they will certainly enter hell. The admonitions and exhortations following this are easy to understand.
Regarding the phrase "the question occurring in the middle": this question arises within the fifteenth fascicle of the *Treatise* (*Śāstra*), in the context of explaining the meaning of *prajñā*.
As for the statement "sin cannot be apprehended" and so forth: if a person abandons evil and practices good, this constitutes the observance of precepts (*śīla*).

Why, then, is it said that neither sin nor non-sin can be apprehended? There are three points in the answer: first, the difficulty of conforming to the contemplation of principle; second, [the passage beginning with] "If one's flesh... which provides an illustration.
The analogy clarifies that this is not so. Third, the commentary below the current recitation distinguishes against such confusion. The treatise states: "Not" refers to wrong views and coarse minds.

To speak of practicing the samādhi of emptiness where nothing can be apprehended means that the mind is merged with principle and its nature and characteristics are quiescent; thus, both sin and merit are equally non-existent.
Therefore, the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* says: "Since my mind is already devoid of a master for either sin or merit, one may say that sin is unattainable;

otherwise, it would be no different from that of oxen or sheep. Oxen and sheep have eyes, yet they see only signs (*nimitta*) and do not see the signless (*animitta*). Now, humans lack the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*), seeing only with the physical eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*).
Since the physical eye sees only the difference between form and emptiness, and does not see that form and emptiness are non-different, [it is] like...
"Cows and sheep are no different. Xuán says: "That [text] merely states that what is seen by the fleshly eye is called 'not seeing,' such as the absence of cows, sheep, and so forth.

This phrasing is cited from the *Xiàchão* (Lower Excerpts) to distinguish against confusion. Regarding "the commentary (*shū*) extracts": *shū* means "sparse" or "to loosen. Its meaning is to resolve and clarify, and to open up and facilitate understanding.

Regarding the statement that "the four parts reach the Path," this refers to the purity of bodily precepts (*kāya-śīla-viśuddhi*). This is identical to the *Poṣadha-karman* (recitation of the precepts). There are two ways for the Saṃgha to abide;

yet, if one breaks even a single precept, one is cast out from the assembly. Is this not self-destruction? Whenever one breaks a single precept, one becomes subject to the reproach of the laity regarding the Saṃgha.
They rebuke and expose their transgressions against the Buddha, further reviling and scolding them in various ways; thus it is said that they are censured by the wise.
Fourth is the regret of not upholding the precepts, which refers to one's own violation of the precepts.
Regarding the statement "The *Daśabhāṇavāra* reaches the 'fearful'": that refers to the twenty-eighth [chapter], with five additional lines.

By combining two sets of five, they form ten dharmas. That section omits the question: "How many dharmas does the Buddha possess that cause the Dharma to perish? The Buddha replied: "There are five. What are the five?
First, there is a bhikṣu who has attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). Second, he is further unable to cause others to understand. Third, he is unable to..."
Regarding "up to proper deportment": fourth, there are those who preach the Dharma but cannot instruct according to the Dharma; they engage in strife and mutual recrimination.

The *Chao* (the *Yogācārabhūmi-bhāṣya*) omits this phrase, hence it says "up to fifth, not delighting in forest hermitages (*araṇya*)," where the *Chao* has altered the character for "Dharma" (*fa*) [to "hermitage"].
Furthermore, the section beginning with "not following the instructions of the Dharma" constitutes the next five items. First, the *Chao* omits the phrase "following unlawful instructions. Second...
The *Fushuirinbōshō* (Excerpts on the Dharma of Non-Compliance) omits this phrase. Third, "not respecting the elders" (*san fukyō jōza*).

The manuscript lacks the character "having" (*u*), and the commentary on the character "sufficient" (*soku*) explains: "Not respecting is itself the absence of dignified deportment (*mui-i*); it does not mean that the elders lack dignified deportment."
Furthermore, one may deeply guard against the fear that those who lack respect and proper decorum might treat an elder with contempt.

Fourth, if the four elders do not instruct according to the Dharma, or if when an elder preaches the Dharma he is sorrowful and stingy, causing later generations to be unable to receive instruction in the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma;
the *Śāstra* omits the Sūtras and Abhidharma because its focus lies in the Vinaya. Fifth, the elder commands [the disciple] to practice...
Thereafter, monks become negligent, accumulate what is not the Dharma, and lose all wholesome qualities; this is called the destruction of the Dharma. The opposite of this is non-destruction.

The following section on "delighting in composing literary verses" is a separate text and is not related to the five [categories]. Now, for the purpose of abridging, the second [category] is removed, and this [section] is used to fulfill the number five.
That is to say, in the final age, people delight in worldly dharmas; such as these are not the way of those who have left the home life.

The practices [of the three vehicles] follow the principle of non-deliberation (*acintya-dharma*); they are the holy dharmas of the Three Vehicles and the conduct of those who have left the household life. To now refuse to cultivate and study them is to not follow the principle of non-deliberation.
The *Vinaya-mātṛkā* clarifies this through general characteristics, while the *Śāstra* (the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan*) explains it by pointing to specific instances.

The Section on Assembling the Sangha is divided into two parts: first, the designation of the title; second, the explanation. Regarding "Assembling the Sangha," there are two sections: first, the intent of its introduction; second, the explanation of the title.

Within the first section, the preceding part designated the Precepts as the primary principle, pointing toward the essential nature and the modes of practice of the Dharma. Having already understood that one personally bears the sacred Dharma, [the following] establishes and promotes it.

There is a basis for this: one must invariably uphold the Dharma through formal ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*). These procedures require reliance upon specific rites; the essentials of such rites are as follows: first, one must assemble the Saṃgha. Since there are differences regarding whether the assembly is distant or proximate, the following section distinguishes between their universal and restricted applications. Second, the explanation of names. First, regarding "assembling the Saṃgha": [The text continues with the explanation of the term *saṃgha*: The word *saṃgha* is derived from the root *gha*, meaning "to strike" or "to destroy. With the prefix *sam*, it signifies "to gather together. Thus, it refers to those who have gathered together to destroy afflictions (*kleśa*) and the like. Furthermore, because they have gathered together to destroy the various types of suffering, they are called the Saṃgha. "Accumulation" (*saṃgha*) refers to that which accumulates, namely the seven types beginning with "acting as a group. "The Saṃgha" refers to that which is accumulated, namely those gathered throughout the entire realm and so forth.

According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are five kinds of Saṃgha: first, the "sheep-like Saṃgha," consisting of the ignorant; second, the "shameless Saṃgha," consisting of those who violate the precepts;
third, the "separate Saṃgha," consisting of those who are discordant; fourth, the "pure Saṃgha," consisting of those who uphold the precepts; and fifth, the "ultimate Saṃgha."

The Noble Sangha consists of sages. Furthermore, the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing) identifies four types: first, those with a sense of shame who maintain the precepts; second, those without shame who violate the precepts;

third, the ignorant like a flock of sheep; and fourth, the truly noble sages. Moreover, the *Shilun jing* (Sūtra on the Ten Treatises) speaks of four kinds of Sangha that encompass both ordinary persons and sages, distinguishing between the monastic and the lay.
The sages range from the four fruits to the four stages of approach (*pratipannaka*). The lay are those who...
Those who have realized the fruit within the household are also called the Saṃgha of the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya). Regarding the term "assemblage" (*jì*) used here, the *Fǎbǎo* states:

"The five kinds and four kinds are all gathered and brought forward; it is only in the subsequent section that they are distinguished. In Xuán's commentary, there are two interpretations. The first is identical to the one above.

The second interpretation states: "Among the five [assemblies], only the latter two are collected; among the four, the first and last are collected accordingly. For now, we shall rely on the former interpretation.

Next, regarding the distinction between the general and the specific: *Baoyun* says that the assembly in a village for nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*) when it can be distinguished is general, whereas the sixty-three paces when it cannot be distinguished is specific.
In a forest hermitage (*araṇya*), the assembly within a five-li radius when there is no danger is general, while the seven turns [of the hand] when there is danger is specific.

Gathering at the *dharmaparyāya* (boundary markers) constitutes a restricted [gathering]. Walking six hundred paces along the path constitutes a universal [gathering]. The area reached by the sprinkling of water from the water-element constitutes a restricted [gathering] (this is distinguished as universal or restricted based on the natural [limits]).

Where there is a *sīmāmaṇḍala* (precept-field) within a *mahāsīmā* (great boundary), gathering at four locations constitutes a dissolution [of the boundary]; where there is no *sīmāmaṇḍala* within a *mahāsīmā*, gathering at two locations constitutes a restriction.

For the three small boundaries (*kṣudrasīmā*), one does not establish boundary marks but points directly to the seating places; this conforms to a restriction (this is distinguished based on the non-Dharmic boundary). Or...

There is an interpretation which states: "The natural ritual action (svayambhū-karman) establishes the boundaries; those who gather within these boundaries are all [considered] extinguished [of the offense].
Those outside the boundaries need not come, as there is no fault of a separate assembly (nānāsaṃgha). This is a restrictive rule (to be considered according to one's judgment).

If speaking in terms of the Saṃgha, four persons constitute the essence of the Saṃgha. Performing the three *karmans* is the general rule; being differentiated according to the specific matter is the restrictive rule. For instance, regarding the four..."

If people perform only ritual acts such as formal proclamations (*jñapti*), this is universal (*sāmānya*). If they receive the precepts in a border region (*pratyantaka*), this is restricted (*prādeśika*).

Receiving the precepts with five persons in a border region is universal; being unable to do so in the Central Land (*madhyadeśa*) is restricted. Being able to confer the precepts with ten persons in the Central Land is universal;
being unable to perform the confession of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense is restricted. Confessing offenses with twenty persons and so forth are all permissible and thus universal.

It is consistently for the purpose of providing a thorough explanation. In the preceding [text], "madness" was expected to have both cessation and limitation. "Pian" (chapter) refers to a title for a section or division;
"di" (number) is a term denoting non-confusion; and "er" (two) is a numerical increment. Therefore, it is collectively indicated as "[...]".
In the second part, the "Exegesis by Section," the various minor sub-sections will not be listed again.

Regarding the initial statement, "The Saṃgha arrives at its place," the phrase "the Saṃgha takes harmony as its meaning" is also intended to refute the views of ancient scholars. They claim that the Sanskrit term *saṃghāya* is translated as "harmonious assembly.

This refers to the formal procedures for performing acts such as the *karmavācanā* (formal announcements) and the *jñapti* (motions), which are distinguished based on a body of four or more persons; hence it is called a "harmonious assembly."

Now it is said that the term "assembly" (saṃgha) is subject to ambiguity. For instance, three people may also be called an "assembly," yet they are unable to perform rituals such as the *karmavācanā* and thus should not be termed an assembly.

If one were to say that four people who can perform the *poṣadha* and other rites constitute a "harmonious assembly," then those groups of one, two, or three people would fundamentally lack the function of the six harmonies (*ṣaḍ-samaya*), resulting in the fault of double-counting. Therefore, the *Chao-wen* explicitly uses the term "monastic community" (*seng*).

"Harmony" is its essential meaning. The mere designation of the term "Saṃgha" (Sangha) is an abbreviation; in the Sanskrit original, it already encompasses three people, two people, or even one person, collectively termed "Saṃgha.
Since it is said that harmony is its meaning, even a single individual must possess the six kinds of harmony."

How could it be that only four people are called a "harmonious assembly"? This present harmony is merely a functional application within the Sangha; thus it is said that "harmony constitutes its meaning. As for the six harmonies (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*):

precepts, views, and livelihood, as well as body, speech, and mind, can be understood accordingly. To briefly distinguish the essence of the Sangha in contrast to this, the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states:

"According to the Vinaya and in accordance with the Śāstras, the actual intent established is that [the Sangha] is formed by gathering the fingers to constitute a 'lifting' (an act), and by gathering the aggregates (*skandha*)."
Regarding the formation of a person: a person takes the four elements as their body; now, it is likewise by means of the four primary elements that the body is constituted.

Furthermore, it is said that the essence of the Sangha Jewel must depend upon the Dharma to be established. As for the eternal Dharma, even if there are hundreds or thousands, they do not function as a single entity.

If they do not assemble together and their characteristics are in discord, then among the six harmonies, the latter three are not in harmony. That is to say, the persons are not integrated, and the four modes of conduct are all separate.
"Separated. Being hidden, obscured, or partitioned constitutes "separation" (*vibhakta*). Because people do not assemble, the performance of the ritual (*dharmakarma*) is not accomplished;
the matter at hand is likewise invalid. Thus, it possesses three kinds of invalidity. As for the phrase "hence, regarding the universal and the specific," this opens two chapters.

Regarding the phrase "from the four [directions] to striking [the gong]," this corresponds to the text on the thirty-four methods for reciting the *Poṣadha* (confession) found in the Vinaya. The *Jie-mo-su* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states:
"The reason why the seats are first laid out and the *gandī* (wooden gong) is subsequently struck is that when the announcement by sound is made, the assembly gathers immediately;

however, before the beds and seats have been spread, the attendants remain in a state of anxious hesitation, which would hinder the performance of the ritual duties. The establishment of the seating order is precisely for this purpose. This passage generally clarifies the gathering of the *saṃgha*.

This refers to the standard procedure. Regarding the "fivefold division" and so forth: in that twenty-second [section], it says that at the time of the *poṣadha*, some were unwilling to assemble, thereby neglecting seated meditation and the practice of the Path.

They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "One should announce that the time has arrived. As for striking the *gandī* drum or other instruments, they did not know whether one should strike them;
the Buddha said, "Have the novices (*śrāmaṇera*) or the gardeners strike them. Initially, the visiting novices struck them, but they did not know [how].
[The monks] missed the proper timing. The Buddha said, "Let the resident *śrāmaṇeras* and *karmadānas* strike it. [Consequently, they struck it too many times.
The Buddha said, "It should be struck three times. The three strikes are as described below. They did not know what kind of wood to use for it.

With the exception of lacquer trees and poisonous trees—which bite people's hands and are unfit for this purpose—one may use other woods, or have it made of copper, iron, or clay, provided it rings out clearly. Baoyun says that in the text, the character used is "clay" (*wa*).
Examining that Vinaya text, it says: "Other items made of clay, wood, copper, or iron that produce sound are permitted. Here, the character for "clay" (瓦) is placed above;

the characters for "dividing," "a pinch," and "interchangeable" (分抄迴互) are below it. There are instances where the character for "ordinary" (凡) is erroneously written instead; this is incorrect. Regarding the "two times," these refer to the two meal times: the morning and the afternoon.

Regarding the statement "The *Daśabhāṇavāra* says...": this refers to the *pratideśanīya* (offenses requiring confession) concerning a bhikṣu who accepts food from a woman while staying in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*).
This citation serves as proof that laypeople may employ gestures [to communicate]. As for the *Ekottarika Āgama* and other texts...
When the summer retreat had concluded, he wished to receive the *varṣā* (the communal confession), and thus ordered Ānanda to strike the *gandī* to assemble the Saṃgha.
Ānanda went to the lecture hall, took the *gandī* in his hand, and spoke these words: "I now strike this drum of the Tathāgata’s faith;
may all disciples gather together. Thus, the striking of the bell to summon the assembly is called "faith" (*śraddhā*). That which moves the hearts of sentient beings is called a "drum" (*dundubhi*).
Citing this passage also serves as proof that the aforementioned bhikṣu may perform [the duties]. Regarding the phrase "as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*," this text has two intentions:

first, the primary exposition; second, the subsequent explanation of the meaning of the *karmadāna* (Venerable Officer) according to the *Śabda-śāstra*. This citation of the original text reflects its fundamental purpose.
He orders the *karmadāna* (vina) to announce that the time has arrived and to strike the *gandī* (wooden gong). Regarding "sweeping and plastering":
this refers to the practice in the Western Regions (India) where, at mealtime, many earthen mounds (*stūpa*) are erected; one is for sitting upon, and the other is for placing the food.

When seated, one sits on the skirt of the garment with the feet hanging down, treading them upon the ground; they must not be suspended. This is also like sitting on a corded bed in this land (China) with the feet hanging down.
The ground is level as if stepped upon. Directly in front is a mound of earth called the "food-press" (*bhojana-pīṭha*). One spreads clean *mārga* grass upon it and then places the food thereon.
In this way, one sits with the hem of the robe purified to prevent contact with impurity. Such is the nature of that earthen mound.

One must still perform repairs, plastering, and other such treatments. Although this region lacks earthen platforms and one does not sit on the floor, there are nevertheless beds, stools, cushions, and mats;
these should likewise be swept, cleaned, and maintained according to the Dharma. Regarding pure fruits and vegetables:

According to that text, it was reported to the Buddha that no one was purifying the fruits and vegetables; no one was inspecting for insects in the fermented rice wine; no one was distributing water during meals;
and no one was snapping their fingers when the assembly spoke in disorder. Consequently, the Buddha ordered the establishment of the *karmadāna*.
(The term may also be called *karmadāna*; the Sanskrit pronunciation is not fixed. If one uses the term *karmadāna*, according to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (*Chizhi lun*), it is as follows:

It is translated as *sīghra* (temple guardian). If one says *karmadāna*, this is translated as "officiant" (*śu shi*). Furthermore, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), fascicle 34, it is appointed by means of a formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*);

nowadays, however, it is simply appointed by a verbal announcement to the assembly. Regarding the translation of *anupūrvi* as "sequence," it refers to one of the categories within the five sciences (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*).
As for what are called the five sciences: first, the inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*), which refers to the [teachings of] all Buddhas...

1. Grammar (śabdavidyā) reveals the characteristics of correct causes and effects. 2. Logic (hetuvidyā): "cause" refers to the words of the proponent, and "logic" refers to the wisdom of the opponent.
3. Phonetics (śabdavidyā): skillfully understanding all languages, sounds, and so forth. 4. Medicine (cikitsāvidyā):
thoroughly investigating the roots of illness and knowing the origins of disease. 5. Arts and Crafts (śilpakarmasthānavidyā): being well-versed in all crafts, fine arts, and the like.
This is now the third *śabda-vidyā* (science of grammar). The remaining text is easily understood.

As for the phrase "if it reaches the bell," if one follows the seven methods of assembly mentioned in the text, this refers to the procedure for summoning the *saṃgha* according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Regarding "measuring the shadow": take the shadow of a one-foot wooden staff at midday as the standard. Regarding "splitting bamboo to make a sound," this means:
Take a bamboo pole about one *zhang* in length and split it so that one end remains whole while the other is hollowed out;

holding it by the solid end and shaking it produces smoke, which is no different from the beacon fires used by military camps today. As for the blowing of the conch (*śaṅkha*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states:

"The *haijie* (sea-shell) can produce sound when blown"; it is also called a *li* (conch-shell horn) today. Regarding the beating of the drum and the striking of the *gandī*, these will be explained below.
When the proclamation is made, "Venerable sirs, the time for the Poṣadha has arrived," this originally does not fall within the enumeration of the four types or seven aspects.

This is because among the seven, the single aspect of "striking the ground" (bhūmi-ghāta) is somewhat prone to confusion or error; therefore, the *Chao* (the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan*) excludes it and replaces it with this proclamation, thereby restoring the number to seven.
The *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: "The seven aspects for summoning the Saṃgha do not depart from color and sound; one measures the shadows and looks toward [the assembly]."
Smoke is visible form (*rūpa*); the other five are sound (*śabda*). Furthermore, these seven characteristics must all be known in advance by the entire monastic community;
only when such an agreement exists is it considered a formal assembly of the Dharma.

It is also not stated that a *bhikṣu* alone performs this, for the aforementioned various sections of the Sūtras and Vinaya all state that a *bhikṣu* may also perform it, as seen in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the *Ānanda-ghaṇṭā*, and so forth. (10)
The recitation instructs the *karmadāna* (Venerable) to strike the gong, and so forth. It is not stated here that a *bhikṣu* performs this task for this boundary;
rather, the intention of the Master is to show that it may be performed by a *bhikṣu* based on various teachings. The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states:

"As prescribed by the Vinaya, if a resident *śrāmaṇera* or a low-ranking lay attendant (*upāsaka*) strikes [the gong], this is a regulation of the monastic community (*saṃgha-dharma*), not something performed by one who possesses the Way. Unless there are necessarily two persons, assistance is not permitted. This is cited as an example.
He has verified this; it is sufficient to know that the preceding sections of the *Chao* (Excerpts) cite various schools, while the subsequent sections conform to the specific Vinaya in use.

One should apply them in detail according to the occasion. These excerpts draw out the essential *vinaya*. Regarding the translation of the term for the *gandī* (wooden gong): the character *gān* (犍) has a sound but no corresponding character;

one must borrow this character, pronounced with the *jù* (巨) and *hán* (寒) finals. *Chuī* (搥) is the original local pronunciation; it is also called *jiànzhi* (犍稚) in the sūtras, as the characters *zhì* (稚) and *di* (地) are phonetically close.
The character "cuò" (錯) is written as "chuí" (搥); both are errors resulting from transcription mistakes. The rest is as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "from 'above' up to 'toward'":

this concludes the preceding section and introduces the following one. Regarding the phrase "from 'generally' up to 'in the center,' and then according to the text, strike the bell, as detailed in the *Sengfa* (Method for Assembling the Sangha)":
this refers to what is clearly explained in the *Guīdù tújīng* (Diagram Sutra on Rules and Measurements). According to the *Dàtáng*...

The *Qūzōngjì* states: After Emperor Wu of the Later Zhou abolished the two teachings [Buddhism and Daoism], he selected renowned practitioners from among the monks and Daoists and established them within the Tōngdàoguān (Palace of the Penetrating Way).
He cast a bell for the monastery and hung it within the observatory. Every time after the court session concluded, he would assemble the monks and Daoists to debate their relative merits.
Following the death of the Later Zhou Emperor, Emperor Wén succeeded to the throne and moved [the institution].
In the old city of Chang’an, on the Longshou (Dragon Head) Plateau, the Chang’an City was established with one hundred and twenty wards (*fang*) across its eastern and western markets.
Consequently, one ward was set aside for a monastery named Xingshan, and another ward was set aside for a temple (*guan*) titled Xuandu.

A bell, granted by imperial decree to facilitate the transmission of the Way, was bestowed upon the Xuandu Temple; however, it was subsequently requested by the monk Puguang of Xingshan Monastery and returned to Xingshan. Later...

Because the lay attendants did not understand the striking of the bell, they struck it indiscriminately. Consequently, the Great Master was requested to compose these rules for the ritual procedure. He said:
"One should recollect the Triple Gem and maintain the five assemblies, each consisting of eight members; by means of forty strikes, one mounts the three paths.

Thus, one hundred and twenty strikes constitute a single cycle. Now, however, the time is measured according to the assembly, with a minimum of twenty-seven strikes as the standard, divided into eight cycles.

Each set of three makes twenty-four; adding another three at the bottom, they are collectively gathered into the Three Vehicles. In the middle case there are forty; in the maximum case, one hundred and twenty.
These fully enumerate the three dharmas; since this [text] now refers back to them, it is said to be "within the *yiqun sengfa*" (the Dharma for the Assembly of Monks).
Regarding the statement, "Although it has reached its practical application, although people all perform it, for the most part there are no models or standards":

this means that while everyone performs the striking of the bell, for the most part there is no pattern or standard to follow. There are many commentaries on the essential points regarding the various sections and pauses;

"sections" (kē) refers to divisions, and "essentials" (yào) refers to summaries. "Various sections and pauses" means that the number of strikes is not fixed. Thus says the *Jíjí* (Collection of Clouds).
A bhikṣu strikes four times; when gathering śrāmaṇeras, he strikes three times; for an upāsaka, twice; and when gathering karmadānas (pure men), once.
Regarding the phrase "but now, as it has been abandoned by common practice": this refers to the current ritual methods of striking, which for the most part do not rely on the original sūtra texts;

hence it is said they have been "abandoned by common practice. As for the phrase "though easy, it is difficult": one interpretation states that while the aforementioned sūtra text is easy to understand, establishing the current method of striking is difficult.

This is difficult to resolve. A second interpretation states: it means that although the Sūtra prescribes striking four times down to one time for the assembled great Saṃgha, this is easy [to carry out] because the boundary (sīmā) is vast and [the sound] is difficult to hear.
For now, we shall rely on the first interpretation. Regarding the statement, "Now, by establishing a single rule of cessation, a general standard is fully established":
this marks the difference between the present and the past. "Establishing a single rule of cessation" means establishing one hundred and twenty strokes as constituting a single [unit].

The Dharma: To establish the general outline according to the formal regulations, this serves as the gradual basis for the sequence of three strikes, thirty long beats, forty *lian-chui*, and another forty—totaling one hundred and twenty beats—as set forth in the following text; it differs from the explanations found in various commentaries.

Consider this. The phrase "regarding the number of monks, etc. explains the meaning of "the above standard. Within a boundary (*sīmā*), one hundred thousand or even ten million people constitutes the maximum;
down to three or five people is the absolute minimum. This is determined by the urgency of the matter at hand, as it depends on whether the preceding circumstances are urgent or relaxed.
Regarding the phrase "measuring according to the time," this refers to gauging the timing—whether early or late—as there may be obstacles or difficulties due to external conditions.
