This present text concerning the separate assembly (*bhinna-saṃgha*) comes from the *Campa* chapter of the Vinaya;
it applies generally within the boundary of the assembly and subsequently encompasses all three types of action (*trividha-karma*). It is not in accordance with [the previous rule].

This is a summary by way of analogy. Furthermore, the precept regarding eating in a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇa-bhakṣaṇa*) is likewise a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that concludes with the delimitation of the transgression.

Since none of the various commentaries evaluate this point, a detailed exposition is of great necessity. The first two characters, "chu zhong" (beginning and middle), cite the characteristics of eating in a separate group;
this constitutes the first section of the text.

Regarding the statement "the four parts lead to the assembly," this refers to the analysis based on the three types of action (trikarma). "Those who ought to come" distinguishes them from those who ought not to come, namely those with the thirteen *ānantarya* offenses and so forth.
If those who are pure and dwell together are required to assemble but do not come now, this constitutes a failure of the body to assemble.

Since the body does not come, one cannot participate in the formal ritual (karmavācanā). This constitutes the non-assembly of the mouth; since the mind does not consent, this constitutes the non-assembly of the mind.

Regarding the two cases of those who should have given their consent (*chanda*) but did not, or those who came [without it]: if one is pure but has a reason for absence and transmits the consent through another, this is called the non-assembly of both body and mind.
When the body does not come, this is the non-assembly of the body. When the mind is not sent along, this is the non-assembly of the mind. An objection is raised:
"Even if one transmits their consent (*chanda*), if the person does not come in person, why is it said that 'the body has not assembled'?

Answer: "If one transmits consent and comes in person while remaining within the hall, there is no fault. However, if one does not send forth the mind [of consent] while remaining in the courtyard, there is the fault of being apart from the assembly (*nānāsaṃvāsika*).

Therefore, it is said that 'the body has not assembled. [The opponent] further challenges: "Since they do not transmit consent, their speech also has not assembled. Why is this not [considered a valid assembly]?"

He replied: "Even if one transmits the *chanda* (consent), if the mouth [of the messenger] remains within the monastery, it cannot serve as a valid witness for the *karmavācanā*. Therefore, the presence of the mouth is not considered.

Even if the mouth were within the monastery, if the *chanda* has not been conveyed, the household [of the messenger] likewise incurs no fault of being a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*). Why, then, should this be debated?"

The preceding section concludes the "Correct Interpretation for Searching the Profundities. Some commentators explain that the mouth is governed by the mind; since the mind cannot endure [the offense], the mouth is not autonomous.
This is analogous to the case of the "fire-prohibiting son," and it is feared that this would fall short of the previous ritual. Consider this.

Regarding the third point, "one may not scold those who have already been scolded," etc., this distinguishes such cases from the previous instances of reprimand. Regarding the fourth point, "one must not scold; now, this is the mind of one who is pure," etc.
When one speaks words of reproach that do not accord with the Dharma, it is called the non-convergence of mind and speech.

As for the phrase "and as for 'arriving,'" it refers to being in accordance with the signs of harmony. First, those who ought to come must come; when the three karmas converge, this is precisely what is meant by "now arising in the hall.
Second, those who ought to give their consent (*chanda*) must give their consent; this is the convergence of mind and speech, wherein the mind is sent forth to reach the Sangha.
"Mind-gathering" (citta-saṃnipāta). "Verbal expression entrusting this to another" is "speech-gathering" (vāk-saṃnipāta). An objection is raised:

In the previous section on "contrary characteristics," the second point—where consent (*chanda*) was not given—constituted a lack of gathering of body and mind, yet speech was not mentioned. Now, in the case of "concordant characteristics" where there is harmony, this is the reverse of the preceding statement;
why then is there specifically "speech-gathering"? The answer is: The reason speech was not mentioned in the preceding section is that it serves as proof for the formal ritual act (*karmavācanā*).

As for the mouth: since the body does not come [to the assembly], there is no accumulation of meaning through the mouth; therefore, it is not discussed separately. This mention of the "accumulation of the mouth" is merely a conventional expression. Reflect on this:

the previous discussion of verbal karma (*vākkarman*) did not concern the "correct mouth" that requires external testimony. Furthermore, regarding those who do not rebuke [the offender] while present:

this refers to the accumulation of both body and mouth, such as when the body is present in the *saṃgha* but the mouth does not rebuke, and so forth. Again, as for the mention of Śāriputra and others: this...

This refers to the first phrase among the fifteen points, which will be clarified below. That is to say, when one observes the Saṃgha performing a formal act (karmavācanā) according to the Dharma, yet because one considers it to be contrary to the Dharma, one does not mentally approve of it and does not voice a protest; this is also called being "in harmony and according to the Dharma."
Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, as for the 'persons who have arrived'": the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (or *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*) states that the group of six consists of:

first, Nanda; second, Upananda; third, Kālodāyin; fourth, Channa; fifth, Aśvaka; and sixth, Punarvasu. When they arrive at the place where the precepts are recited and the assembly of monks is seated, they remain standing.

This discrepancy in the four modes of deportment constitutes a separate assembly (*pṛthag-saṃgha*), which is contrary to the Dharma. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, all [of them] sit or lie down during the recitation of the precepts.

Regarding the term "and so forth" (*ādi*): Xuánzàng says that two people—one sitting with their back turned and one lying down with their back turned—are referred to as "and so forth. The Dàdé says that this merely discusses having one's back turned;
whether one is sitting or lying down, both are subsumed under "turning one's back," and it is improper to arbitrarily divide them into two separate persons.

If there were a discrepancy regarding the four modes of deportment (sitting and lying), the text from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* cited below will clarify this itself. Regarding the twelve types of persons in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, each of the four modes of deportment...
This completes the twelve [categories]. This is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "separately reaching the number," this refers to the distinct assembly of pure monks (*viśuddha-saṃgha*).

In contrast to the aforementioned "insufficiency" (*aparyāpta*), these cases involve mutual entanglement and overlapping, forming four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). For now, we shall divide them into two: if one does not join the assembly of monks, it is called a "distinct assembly" (*pṛthag-jana*);
if one joins the assembly of monks but the ritual form (*vidhi*) is in violation, it is called "insufficient in number. Therefore, it says "for now" (*tāvat*).

Regarding the statement "as for what is called 'separate' (bie) up to this point," Baoyun says: this is a classification based on breadth and narrowness. If discussed in terms of essence (*tǐ*), it is insufficient to encompass both pure and impure realms;
"separate" assemblies pertain only to pure objects. If clarified in terms of location, "separate" assemblies encompass both the interior and exterior of the assembly, and are thus broad;

"sufficient" assemblies exist only within the assembly itself and are insufficient to encompass both the interior and exterior. Regarding the four propositions (*si jù*) as explained separately, the *Jiemo shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states:

Although the preceding section lists names comprehensively, including both the correct and the incorrect, these are merely conflated due to differences in conditions and thus indiscriminately applied to pure practices;

therefore, they must be distinguished by means of the Dharma to avoid confusion. This is divided into two pairs. Regarding the first four lines: one is the distinct "non-sufficient" [category] consisting of sixteen persons.

First, those who should come but do not; second, those who come without having granted their consent (*chanda*). Within the first category, there are five types: the obscured, the departed from sight, the separated by hearing, the obstructed, and so forth.
Within the fourth category, there are seven persons regarding the legal procedures for those undergoing *saṃghāvaśeṣa* penance; two of these are sufficient and do not require a separate individual.
The virtuous bhikṣu himself is included among the assembly; as his moral conduct is manifest, he is counted in two positions. Three [categories] are both distinct and sufficient.

Six persons include those who have been censured, those who censure others, and those who sit with their backs turned, as well as those whose four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*) are transgressive. Four are neither sufficient nor distinct: thirty-nine persons.
Within the first section, there are eleven persons according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and three according to the *Karmavibhaṅga-śāstra*; these are added based on the underlying meaning.
These three groups together make sixteen people. Together with the twenty-three mentioned in the second section, there are thirty-nine. An objection is raised:
regarding those among them who are ignorant, drowsy, intoxicated, or insane—do they possess the substance of the precepts (*śīla-dravya*) or not?

If one says they lack the substance, then they would be subsumed under the "thirteen difficulties" (*trayodaśa-antarāya*), and their precepts would be those of a layperson (*avadātavasana*). If one says they do possess the substance of the precepts, that may be acceptable; why then [is it said otherwise]?
"Not separately. The answer is: some explain that one does not perform it separately because one is among the assembly;
furthermore, due to lack of understanding, sleep, or intoxication, one cannot realize the Dharma, and thus this [situation] is insufficient. The Venerable Jingshui said:

according to the *Jietan jing* (Sutra on the Ordination Platform), within the section on the success or failure of performing the ritual acts, Nanshan himself explains: "Now, one who upholds the Dharma does not merely recite it alone as a single monk."
Furthermore, one must be in communion with the assembly; those who do not understand this are neither sufficient nor distinct.

Because they are ignorant and do not know the conditions for harmony and patience, nor are they familiar with the characteristics of sameness and difference, they are not included within the two [categories]. There is no fault in their not assembling [in such cases]. (Based on this, it is provisionally explained that those who do not understand are not included within the three categories.

Regarding those who are asleep, intoxicated, or insane: the *Kē jì* states, "Sleep and intoxication lead to a lack of awareness and the loss of the functions of a bhikṣu"; this serves as the precedent.

The same applies to those who have lost their mental faculties, such as the insane; one should reflect on this by analogy with the previous case of those who do not understand, as it is like a clear mirror.

Second, regarding the insufficiency [of the quorum], there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) in relation to a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*): first, being insufficient but not a separate assembly, such as the person for whom the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is being performed;

second, being a separate assembly but not insufficient in number, as in the third permutation above concerning the six persons; third, being both a separate assembly and [insufficient]... [text ends].

Sufficient. This is the same as the first phrase regarding the sixteen persons. Four cases are neither distinct nor insufficient: three persons possessing the power of psychic travel (*ṛddhi*) reside separately upon a boundary (*sīmā*) or a ritual ground (*karmabhūmi*) in mid-air;
these are all included within different territories (*anyadeśa*).
Regarding the phrase "as for discussing the ultimate": there must be no method of interpretation, nor any opening up of its practice. Xuán says:

"The two methods of 'opening' (discussing) and 'self-indulgence' (恣) mean that in all *karmavācanā* rituals, one may not act separately; furthermore, there is no fault if those who should assemble do not come at the time of performing the ritual."
There is no fault of forming a separate assembly. As for those who are "in between," they do not reach the level of the Great Sangha above, nor are they the same as the ten-precept śrāmaṇeras below;
hence they are called "those in between."

Regarding the phrase "the two interpretations or the 'not'": Xuán explains that this refers to whether the monastic community being distinguished (*bībié*)—or the community performing the ritual (*néngbǐngfǎ sēng*)—is constituted as distinct or not;

hence the expression "constituted or not. To provide another interpretation: although the preceding discussion has distinguished right from wrong based on the four modes of deportment and the three types of action (*trikarma*), it has never yet examined in detail the gravity or lightness of offenses according to the five categories (*pañcāpatti*), nor whether they were committed knowingly or unknowingly.

Therefore, it is distinguished next. As for the statement "if one reaches the opening," this refers to offenses of the latter four categories (*pārājika* excluded) that are subsumed under the category of "separate assemblies" (*betsshū*).

This is because their characteristics are minor. Even if one commits an offense of the first category (*pārājika*), as long as the three roots [of the offense] have not yet been manifested, others will say that the person is pure.
Furthermore, there is no separate assembly; this is because the transgression is grave, rendering one unfit to dwell together, such that they remain indistinguishable from others.

The following passage serves as proof that, although the formal substance [of the *saṃgha*] has been destroyed, it does not obstruct the performance of legal acts (*dharmakarma*) within the meaning of being a separate assembly. This includes both scriptural authority and an analogy. The original text states:

"Within the boundary, there are in fact no bhikṣus, yet one falsely conceives the notion that there are. Because they do not actually exist, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is successfully accomplished."

If one already harbors pure thoughts [toward her], one should indeed summon her; however, because the mind does not desire to practice the Dharma together with her, it constitutes an offense of *aniyata* (undetermined).

(The analogy concluded. As for the application of the rule (*dharmayoga*), it is as previously stated regarding the destruction of the substance of a grave offense (*pārājika*): it is like a non-monk (*abhikṣu*), in that the person is not recognized as such.
Now, suppose there is the perception that a monk is pure; one should immediately summon him. However, because the mind is not in accord, it will not be auspicious. The *Chao* text states:

"Even if one maintains the perception of purity, the ritual act is still accomplished. Previously, one acted with the perception [of impurity] out of ignorance; now that it is known, one may act according to one's own preference."
The "thirteen difficult cases" refers to thirteen types of persons, such as those who have committed boundary offenses or been defeated by thieves.

Regarding the four types of *ni* (nuns), they are: the *bhikṣuṇī*, the *śikṣamāṇā*, the *śrāmaṇera*, and the *śrāmaṇerī*. Some count the *śikṣādattaka* (one undergoing penance) among them, but this is not correct;

since the intermediate persons (*antarapudgala*) were already discussed previously, they need not be recounted here. The "three formal accusations" (*tri-udghāta*) refer to the [accusations] of "not seeing," etc. The "three forms of insanity" (*tri-unmāda*) refer to madness.

A human being; one with a distracted mind; one whose mind is impaired by illness; one who is mute, deaf, or deficient in cognition; or one who was not originally a monk—these explain the thirteen types of persons who are ineligible for ordination (*anantarāyika*).
Or one who has been punished midway through the process—this explains the three types of persons subject to formal censure (*tshad-pa*). Those with a defective physical form.

This refers to the four classes of persons, beginning with the bhikṣuṇīs. Regarding the three [classes], there is a distinction based on male and female physical forms. Regarding the śrāmaṇeras, there is a distinction based on the rules for the great saṃgha.

Those who are exempted due to the retribution of illness refer to the three types, including the insane. Those who are exempted due to obstacles caused by circumstances refer to the two types, the mute and the deaf.
It is incorrect to claim that those who cite the characters "jiàn" (obstruct) and "shēng" (sound) as conditions are referring back to the aforementioned individuals.

To say, "All who reach the middle," the word "fán" (all/ordinary) means "various. These two characters refer to the various types of people mentioned previously. This does not yet discuss those who are distinct.
This refers to the extensive discussion previously concerning whether the quorum is met or not; all of that was based on the number of four monks being sufficient.

Since it had not yet been discussed whether, at the time of performing a rite through face-to-face procedure (*pratimukha-karman*), one has already obtained the dharma for an individual (*pudgala*), this section now clarifies that point;

hence it says, "it has not yet been discussed whether the quorum for an individual is met. An objection is raised: "Since this concerns the dharma for a separate assembly (*bhinna-saṃgha*), why [is it discussed here]?"
The method for determining the quorum is explained again. The answer is that it is clarified because they follow one another by way of convenience (*prasaṅga*).

Just as in the section on the "Method of the Quorum," the meaning of a "separate assembly" (*pṛthag-saṃgha*) is also explained by way of convenience; thus the preceding text states: "Even if one is inside a room, the principle allows it to be accomplished"—this too is by way of convenience.
Regarding the "face-to-face" (*pratimukha*) ritual procedure where the object before one is confused with the real: this refers to two persons performing the rite face-to-face;
the person being faced is termed the "object before one. "Confused with the real" means that while the substance is an obstructive condition (*pratyaya-vibandha*), it is termed "confused";
if the substance accords with the Dharma, it is termed "real. To take the example of those within the *saṃgha*: if such persons number four or more, they constitute a *saṃgha*.

Regarding the Dharma: it is sufficient when performed before another individual face-to-face. However, if within the assembly the three roots [of the offense] are manifest externally, they cannot be employed because they are insufficient for the monastic rite (*saṃghadharma*).

Now, coming here, it is likewise insufficient for me to perform it before an individual face-to-face; therefore, it is said that one should take the case from the midst of the *saṃgha*. An objection is raised:
The *pratimokṣa* (face-to-face) procedure is a dharma for two persons. Why, then, discuss the requirement of a quorum? Answer: Originally, this was intended for a *saṃgha* (community) dharma;

however, because there were no people within the boundary (*sīmā*), the *pratimokṣa* was permitted as an exception. Although such persons exist today, they are not fit to complete the quorum and do not participate in the formal ritual acts (*karmavācanā*).

Because there is no separate assembly [of monks]. Furthermore, regarding such acts as the formal holding of robes (*cīvara-dhāraṇa*) or the declaration of purity (*śuddhi-ārocana*) performed in the presence of another (*pratyekam-mukha*), although there may be such individuals present, they are incapable of serving as the counterpart for the rite;

one does not perform it together with them, but performs the *pratyekam-mukha* rite oneself. In this way, even when performing the mental recitation (*manasikāra*), there is no fault of having a separate assembly.
Furthermore, there are other points that are not consistent with justice; fearing prolixity, they are not set forth here.

As for the statement, "Now, as for those who have attained compliance," many possess distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), which refers to the specific manifestations of the assembly. To further clarify this:
"Furthermore, 'heavy' (zhòng) means to manifest and clearly bring forth. From 'the deportment is identical' (*weiyi xiangtóng*) onwards, two chapters are opened.

Regarding the statement from 'it is said' (*yún yán*) up to 'only' (*zhǐ*): as for 'the *saṃghāṭī* robe, performing ritual acts,' this refers to instances where there is a discrepancy within the formal characteristics (*xiàng*).

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* regarding the 'back of a sick person' means that one is facing away from the person presiding over the rite; therefore, this constitutes a separate assembly (*bié zhòng*). This passage discusses only the matter of turning one's back."
Know that this applies regardless of the four modes of deportment (*iryāpatha*). The fact that the group of six monks did not sit is likewise a discrepancy in these modes of deportment.
As stated in the *Vinaya* regarding eating while walking among the "separate assemblies," once one has abandoned the formal deportment, one commits the offense of eating from a full bowl.

Regarding the statement that "the monastic community shares the same defilement": this refers to the food according to the Dharma. Although the Dharma and the food differ, the four modes of deportment do not; therefore, they are the same.

Regarding the phrase "as for the two, reaching the limit and being enumerated," and the phrase "the two minds, the empty and the real": Xuán (Xuánzàng) says that compliance is the real mind (*saccitta*) and opposition is the empty mind (*tuccha-citta*). Based on this, it merely explains the attainment of the empty and real minds, yet it does not state the source from which the two characters "attainment" (*de*) originate. Various schools of interpretation explain that "empty" constitutes one and "real" constitutes two; thus they say "the two minds, the empty and the real. I fear this may not accord with the intent of the text. Now, following the *Zhōunán* [commentary]: [The text continues: "The two minds, the empty and the real, refer to the two types of mental states: first, the empty mind, which is the mind of non-attainment; second, the real mind, which is the mind of attainment. 'Reaching the limit' refers to the limit of the path; 'being enumerated' refers to the enumeration of the stages. As for 'compliance is the real mind,' this means that when the practitioner complies with the Dharma, their mind is substantial and true.

As for 'opposition is the empty mind,' this means that when the practitioner opposes the Dharma, their mind is hollow and false. Thus, by complying with the Dharma, one attains the real mind; by opposing the Dharma, one falls into the empty mind. This is why it is said that 'the two minds, the empty and the real, reach the limit and are enumerated.'"* *I have provided the reconstructed commentary based on the context and the preceding analysis.*
The *Jì* (Record) states: "The preceding section opened two chapter headings. The *Chāo* (Excerpts) states: "The assembly takes up the majestic appearance;

these constitute a single chapter. Not acting in accordance with the mind constitutes one hindrance. Within the first section, the commentary explains: "Regarding 'majestic deportment' (*vīryāpatha*), according to the principle it should be stated as 'initially, majestic deportment.
The character 'initially' (*chū*) was omitted because it was considered too few in its composition. The current mention of 'two minds' refers to the two characters 'false' (*xū*) and 'real' (*shí*)."

Regarding the citation of the text: when the mind is contrary, it becomes empty; when the mind is compliant, it is real. One must not see two characters within the text and immediately claim they represent the "mind.
The remainder of the text is easily understood.
Regarding the phrase "if one reaches the middle": the general meaning of this passage concerns the time for the recitation of the *Poṣadha* (confession of offenses).

When the *Karmadāna* (the ritual master) performs the formal announcement (*jñapti*), it is logically appropriate for him to spread his sitting mat and kneel with lowered body on the edge of the quiet side of the hall. He should respond to the ritual formula by saying, "The *Poṣadha* *Karma* is being recited.

The preceptor (*śīla-ācārya*) must not yet proceed to perform the simple announcement (*ekajñapti*); rather, he should wait until the *Karmadāna* has returned to his original seat on the platform and sat down, at which point the procedure may be performed. If...
He then makes the formal announcement (*jñapti*). If he performs this while remaining within the assembly of monks, it constitutes a separate gathering (*bhinnasaṃgha*).
If, however, he sits by the side of the mortar, or if nowadays he simply remains in his original position, the method of answering does not fall under this restriction.

Regarding the abolition or establishment [of rules] as explained in the *Yìchāo* (Excerpts on Meaning), this will also be discussed further below in the fifth chapter, within the section on the ten conditions. A detailed analysis is provided in the *Karmavācanā* (Ritual Procedures).
The Commentary states:
"Regarding the phrase 'as far as the explanation goes,' the general meaning of this section of the *Chao* (Excerpts) is as follows:

it refers to the fact that the previously detailed descriptions of ritual procedures were inconsistent—for instance, while the presiding official sat, all others were required to sit; even a single discrepancy constituted a separate assembly (*biezong*). This is based primarily on the majority case."

It is stated that although there are those who stand while among the seated monks during the performance of a ritual (*karmavācanā*), even though their physical demeanor deviates from the norm, it does not constitute a separate assembly (*bhinna-saṃgha*).
When asked who these people are, the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*) explains:

"Excluding the person being disciplined, because they are the object of the *karman* being performed, they do not count toward the quorum of the Saṃgha; this means that today the community of monks is specifically performing a ritual for that person."
Since he does not count toward the quorum of the Saṃgha, although he does not sit [with them], there is no "separate assembly" (biezòng). Even though this is so, one must further examine the case.
The person against whom the act is directed must possess two conditions for his standing to be permitted as being outside the boundary of a separate assembly:
first, he is the object of the action; second, he does not count toward the quorum. This applies to cases such as Devadatta, where a false assembly acts.
It is to be administered by the Saṃgha. Furthermore, those who do not count toward the quorum, as well as those who have committed a grave offense (pārājika) and have been expelled, are excluded.

Regarding the three types of persons subject to formal accusation (*karmavācanā*): they are like a "bad horse" (*māri*). When two or more such persons are present, one may sit or stand at will; this does not obstruct the Dharma-activity, nor is there the fault of a separate assembly (*nānāsaṃvāsika*).

If, however, it concerns acts such as censure (*tarjanīya-karman*), since these require the possession of the essence of the precepts (*śīla-samvara*), one must sit to perform them; standing would not be valid. This means that [the person] is qualified for all [other] matters.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual action), one must not follow others blindly and parrot them. Many are confused by this section and claim that all disciplinary punishments (*daṇḍakarma*) are permitted to be established [by a single person];

such a view is entirely reckless. As for other matters where one sits and requests [a formal act] in accordance with the Dharma, the nine classes of persons (*navavidha-pudgala*) explain it according to their own inclinations;
however, three requests (*tri-yācana*) are strictly required, otherwise the act is not valid. Furthermore, it must be performed together with the Saṃgha.

One must sit. Otherwise, performing the *pārivāsika* (probation) or *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (formal acts of expiation involving forfeiture) separately from the assembly would be contrary to the spirit of the rules;

these too must be requested while seated. For a *bhikṣuṇī*, the confession for a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense also requires three requests, performed while kneeling on the long knees. Examples such as those concerning the elderly, the sick, being separated from one’s robes, or the two types of rooms should be understood according to each specific category;

this is the general principle. Regarding the clear explanation of the text and its meaning, Xuán states: "The Vinaya clarifies that the method for entering the assembly to request [expiation] must first involve the five barbarian tribes (*hu*)."
"Kneeling with palms joined, etc."—this refers to those who "hold the rite until it is accomplished. The general meaning of this passage is as follows:

previously, it was clarified that the person performing the rite must necessarily be seated, while for others there are cases where it is permitted and cases where it is not. This has already been understood;

however, it remains to be examined whether, when the person holding the rite stands to perform the *karmavācanā* (formal act), the other members of the assembly would thereby constitute a "separate group" (*bhedasaṃgha*) by sitting down. The *Shu-chao* (Commentary) explains: "With the exception of two types of persons: first, the *vinayadhara* (Master of Discipline)."
This is the appointment by the Saṃgha; one must not sit down arbitrarily. If one maintains the Dharma while standing, it is valid; if one sits, it is not accomplished.

Second, regarding the allowance for reciting the Prātimokṣa while standing: this refers to cases where the assembly is large and the voices are too low. Although sitting was originally prescribed, there is an allowance to stand due to specific circumstances, and yet there is no fault of a "separate assembly" (*pṛthag-saṃgha*).
As for all other matters that must be maintained while sitting, "the rest" refers to those outside these two aforementioned methods. From here on, [these apply] to the two Dharmas.

Regarding the various *karmavācanā* (formal acts) outside [of the formal assembly], such as those for establishing boundaries (*sīmābandha*) or the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), they must necessarily be performed while sitting;

they are not accomplished while walking, standing, or lying down. A marginal note states: "If there are other circumstances, it is also permissible to perform them while walking or lying down. Xuánzàng explains: "In cases of difficulties caused by kings or bandits, the performance of the ritual while walking is also permitted.
Thus, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Jìlù), fascicle 28, records: "The bhikṣus asked the Buddha: 'Is it permissible to perform a *karmavācanā* while standing?'"
The Buddha said: "One may perform the *poṣadha* while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down" (this note is for provisional clarification). This must be further examined and distinguished:

first with respect to the person presiding over the rite, and second with respect to the assembly of monks. It is just like merchants on a journey; since today is the *poṣadha* day, the merchants do not stop, fearing bandits.
The bhikṣus then pointed to a mountain rock from afar and established the boundary according to that marker, reciting the precepts while walking.
One performs the *jñapti* (the formal motion). This is also permissible as a procedure for one who is acting on behalf of the Saṃgha due to specific circumstances.

Alternatively, there may be a person of great virtue who is learned and well-versed in the characteristics of the teachings, and who is habitually occupied with affairs while presiding over the Dharma for others.

Now, the assembly wishes to have that person preside over this sacred Dharma, yet he is currently unable to sit long due to illness. If such is the case, it is permitted for another single person to preside over the rite while lying down.

[The previous action] has passed. The others may then sit down. This is the case for lying down due to physical obstruction; it is also permissible [to remain so]. Next, regarding the explanation based on the assembly of monks:

at the time of performing the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*), if there is one, two, or even many sick persons within the *saṃgha*, they are permitted to give their consent (*chanda*) during ordinary ritual matters.
This rule does not apply to the transmission of consent across a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*); in that case, one must necessarily attend the gathering. However, if the text...
He sat down. His illness grew more severe. It was not clear how to proceed; initially, one relied on Xuán’s interpretation, which stated:
"If the patient is too ill to sit, then one should lie down according to the patient. The presiding official (*dharmapālaka*) and all the monks must likewise lie down as a single group.
If only the patient lies down while the others remain seated, it constitutes a separate assembly (*nānāsaṃgha*). This interpretation is incorrect. Now, according to Fǎbǎo, regarding the patient...
Ordinary people may lie down as they please. Those who uphold the Dharma and other monks must remain seated unless they are ill; this provision for lying down is granted only to those who are ill.
Others, lacking such a reason, are not permitted to do so. Furthermore, one must face toward the Buddha image and the person upholding the Dharma.

If one turns one's back [to the assembly], it is not permitted. Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "When a sick person sits or lies down with their back turned while the precepts are being recited, the Buddha declared this to be contrary to the Dharma.

Since there is currently no such turning of the back, lying down is permitted due to extenuating circumstances; this principle is thus established, differing from the erroneous traditions of various other schools.

Contemplate the meaning of these passages. Furthermore, calculate in total the number of individuals in the separate assembly: those who ought to come but do not; those who ought to give their consent (*chanda*) but do not;
those who may be censured in person; and the twelve persons according to the *Mahāsāṃghika* rules regarding the four postures.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the minimum number is fixed at sixteen persons, including those who are absent from behind. Master Xuán’s record divides the "those who are absent from behind" into two categories, adding six more to the total.
The group does not sit together. It is incorrect for there to be eighteen people in total. The above concludes the selection of the assembly.

○ The fourth section, the Chapter on Receiving the Consent (受欲), is divided into two parts (as detailed). Regarding the phrase "from receiving the consent up to four," first the purpose of its inclusion is clarified. Previously, the impurity of the substance was explained.
It is not encompassed by the calculation of the full quorum. Since they are called "pure monks" (*śuddhasaṃgha*), they ought to assemble in their entirety according to the principle.

If there are sudden impediments due to circumstances, the regulations require that one's intention be communicated; thus, both the capacity [of the recipient] and the teaching have a basis, and both self and other are equally benefited. To clarify this principle, it is explained next. Regarding the definition of the term:

*pratigraha* (receiving) is named for its function of accepting; *icchā* (desire) has the meaning of longing or need. Because one accepts that [which is offered] while having a need for it, it is called "receiving."
Desire. That which accords with the Dharma is right; that which does not accord with the Dharma is wrong. Because it follows after the third [category], it is called the fourth.
In the commentary, it says: "Now, as for ultimate discernment," this is the general purport. Regarding the character *fú* (夫), it is explained as usual. As for the "matter" (*shì*), Xuán says:

"The matter of the Three Jewels being afflicted by illness comes from without and is not something the mind can fathom; hence it is called 'unexpected' (*bùyì*). The Dharma transcends ordinary sentiment."
The *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, and so forth are the dharmas that constitute the constant duties of the Saṃgha.

Because they were established by the Buddha, the Buddhadharma is constantly proclaimed every half-month and endures without perishing. Furthermore, there is the *pravāraṇā*, the formal accusation of offenses, and the purification through the seven branches.
Because one is not left alone, this is performed once every year; as it is always carried out when the time arrives, it is called "the constant practice" (*jōjō*).

Thus, regarding the phrase "facing the *jō* (sentiment/practice) and complying with the mind," this refers to the method of *zai* (self-indulgence) according to one's habitual disposition, which was explained previously. Since my own body possesses the necessary conditions...

One must not attend the assembly. Instead, one should send a messenger to convey one's intention (*citta*) to the monks, expressing that there is no transgression. This is "conformity of intention" (*cittānuvartana*).

As for "the intention being in accord with the Dharma without fault": since there is a formal basis for transmitting the *chanda*, it expresses the absence of discordance and avoids the offense of forming a separate faction (*pṛthaggaṇa*).
Since the ritual duties of the Hall Head (Dangtou) have been accomplished, it is said that because there is no loss regarding the Dharma, it is called "desire" (*yù*).

Now, as for the point where sentiment and the formal matter are contrary, one interpretation states: "The objection should have arisen first. Since it is permitted to transmit the *yù* in accordance with sentiment, what need is there for this chapter?

One may cite the *Chao* (the *Shishi Yaolan Chao*) which says: "Now then" and so forth (*yúnyún*). The meaning is: when discussing the usual sentiment of the *zì* (invitation for criticism), it is necessary to assemble [the assembly].

Regarding the matter of the mind: to suddenly give rise to seeking [external things] when one ought not to do so is what is meant by "contradiction" (according to this interpretation, the full meaning of the text has not yet been exhausted).
Now, let me offer another explanation of the sentiment: this refers to speaking according to ordinary worldly feelings and various *karmavācanā* (ritual procedures) and the like.

It means that I did not anticipate such matters as illness affecting the Triple Gem. Because there are mutual points of right and wrong regarding both the Dharma and specific events, it is called "contradiction."
The practice performed by the Head of the Hall today—such as the recitation of the *zizhi* (the invitation for criticism) and other such rites—is a dharma that accords with the Dharma.
Matters concerning the quarters and the person are indeed the primary conditions; thus, this [practice] is commensurate with the ritual procedures for fulfilling one's desires.

Why, then, is it necessary to further expound upon this commentary? Although the current occasion involves the Head of the Hall’s ritual duties, which include the recitation of the *zizhi*, these are merely the common practices of the quarters.
Regarding internal conditions: if one is not ill and is engaged in duties consistent with the Dharma, yet fails to grant consent, one incurs an offense;

this constitutes a matter that contradicts the Dharma. Alternatively, there may be occasions when matters within the quarters are actually the primary condition, whereas the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) performed by the Head of the Hall is not the primary condition; in such cases, it is improper [to proceed].

"Granting consent (*chandadāna*). This refers to a case where the formal rule (*dharma*) contradicts the actual matter (*vastu*). When such a rule and the matter conflict, there are mutual points of right and wrong;
hence, they are said to be "contrary. Therefore, regarding the phrase "establishing rules to examine them": "therefore" (*gu*) has the meaning of "due to" or "by reason of.

Because of the aforementioned contradictions, it is necessary to establish formal regulations to investigate and encompass [the situation]. Regarding "examining so that the matter may be clarified": this means to search [for the truth].
Upon examining the various Vinayas, there are textual passages concerning the acceptance of desire (*kāma*). This must certainly be clarified.

If it is to be explained by contrasting it with the "gates" (*dvāra*) because it is so explicit, one cannot do so in a single location; rather, it must be understood through an extended discourse. Below, two gates—the "conditions" (*pratyaya*) and the "dharma"—are established to clarify this in contrast.

As for the statement that "first the conditions are clarified, and subsequently the dharma of desire," according to the standard practice, the headings of all sections throughout the various chapters (the *pārājika*, etc. state: "Proceeding to..."

The middle section is divided into five parts; some say it is divided into three grades. Now, this should also be stated as being divided into two within that [middle section]. Why is the outline (ke) established in such a direct manner?
The Venerable One replied: "The composition is not fixed; it is adapted according to the occasion. This refers to what was previously stated in the general introduction:
"If one explains by means of the 'Gate of Correspondence' (duìmén), then it corresponds to the character 'within' (zhōng) here. This section follows from what has come above.
Regarding the phrasing: "First, clarify its conditions, etc. (and so forth).
From "First" to "is not," the structural outline (*ke*) may be understood. From "First" to "desire," this explains the intent of the regulation.
"All" (*fan*) means "many. As for the various ritual procedures of the *karmavācanā*, those who must have both body and mind fully assembled are all required to attend.

This refers to the hall. Regarding the phrase "if there should be conditions," it means that if suddenly circumstances arise concerning the Triple Gem and so forth, and one seeks [the presence of] those objects but does not succeed, the Buddha did not permit others to send them [to the Sangha] with the intention that they reach the community;
this demonstrates an absence of transgression. Therefore, it is said: "one does not permit the collection [of items] without opening [the formal procedure]."

Regarding the phrase "the capacities and the teachings are not the same": "capacities" refers to those with the karmic affinity; "monks' teachings" refers to the teachings established by the Tathāgata.

Since the teachings do not reach the capacities, and the capacities do not correspond to the teachings, it is said that they are "not the same. Because [the situation] is so urgent, where would the meaning of "deliverance" lie?

Therefore, regarding the instruction to "listen to the oral and mental transmission," Hōun (Hōnen) says: one may transpose the characters to extract the meaning as "hence, listen to the oral transmission."
The mind should attend to the affairs before the Saṃgha; only when it can thus manage both sides simultaneously is it "able to settle both. This refers to the principle (*yīzé*).

That is to say, when the affairs of the Saṃgha are accomplished without the fault of a separate assembly (*biézhòng*), this constitutes a private matter. A private matter is also a condition (*yuán*);
furthermore, one who can preside over both parties achieves success in both places. Is this not a condition for settling both? For this reason, the granting of consent (*yù*) is permitted.

Regarding the phrase "explaining up to the point of 'back'": as for explaining the name, the previous statement that the single character *yu* (desire) is already its name was intended only to ensure one understands the meaning underlying that name.
Generally speaking, when the term *yu* is used, it is mostly taken to mean "that which is feared and required. "Generally" (*fan*) means "variously";
it does not refer solely to the transmitted terminology, but rather, all things that are cherished and enjoyed are collectively termed *yu*. Most...

Regarding the statement that *chanda* (desire) has the meaning of *abhilāṣa* (longing): in many passages throughout the Vinaya, Sūtras, and Śāstras, it is consistently stated that *chanda* has the meaning of *abhilāṣa*.
If one consults the Sanskrit term *icchā*, it is translated as "desire. The character for *abhilāṣa* (悕望)—derived from the radical for the mind—specifically signifies "to seek" (*yāc*).
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Desire (*chanda*) is the longing for the undertaking of an action. This is also [the view of] the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
It says: "What is desire? It is the expectation that a desired object will be as one wishes. This refers to the section following the explanation of the formal procedures for the Saṃgha;
it is the commentary's own explanation. That is to say, when the Abbot performs a formal rite, my mind is resolved and I intend to go and hear the *karmavācanā* and the recitation of the precepts.
Now, an unexpected matter suddenly arises that contradicts my intention; therefore, I communicate this from my mouth to my mind.
Regarding the matter of seeking, it is so called "desire" (*chanda*) because it causes the multitude to understand thoroughly and without contradiction.

As for the phrase "therefore, reaching the Dharma," this is cited from two passages in the Vinaya and the Śāstra to provide further corroboration; it can be understood that previously, "necessity" (*bhū*) was most often taken as the primary meaning.

Regarding the phrase "explaining the determination of the essence": as for determining the essence, since the names were previously explained—whereby a name is used to summon its corresponding essence—it was not yet known how the *yù* (desire) dharma constitutes that essence;

therefore, it is clarified next. According to the *Jiemo shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā), there are many kinds of essences, categorized by *dharmalakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics) and by *vastu* (concrete events).
First, regarding the determination of the essence based on *dharmalakṣaṇa*: specifically, the single dharma of *yù* is taken as the essence. This...

Desire (*chanda*) is a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*). It is included among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), such as sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and desire itself;
thus, it takes this single dharma of desire as its essence. Next, regarding its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): form (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*) constitute its essence.

Prostrating, joining the palms in homage, and so forth are wholesome forms (*kuśala-rūpa*). Uttering words [of prayer] is wholesome sound (*kuśala-śabda*). As for what is received [in instruction], if one has already transmitted it to another, it is neither form nor [sound].

The mind is its substance. This means that there is an acquisition (*prāpti*) which maintains continuity upon that mental consciousness. If this is so, how does it differ from unmanifest precept (*avijñapti-śīla*)?
The answer is that there are two points of difference: first, although this [acquisition] is neither matter nor mind, it is still subsumed under the category of the expressive substance (*vyañjana*);

second, although its substance is not matter, it enables the mind to maintain continuity, such that when suddenly encountering a powerful condition, it does not require the assistance of an acquisition (*prāpti*).
It vanishes into obscurity. If the unmanifest precept (*avijñapti-śīla*) were the essential substance being explained, it would be obtained once and never lost;

therefore, they are distinct. Third, distinguishing the substance by way of the matter: this refers to the text of the present *Chao* (Commentary), which describes its own requirements. There are two things required, meaning there are two kinds of substantial matters:
first, communal matters; second, individual matters. Regarding the first, communal matters, the *Chao* states: "There are both public and private [matters] for the Saṃgha."

The same applies to the *su* (the invitation for criticism). This continues until: "If one rebels [against the duty], there is an offense. The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "As it is said, when the time for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation) arrives, one must certainly perform the recitation;

the recitation must take place within the *saṃgha*. If one is not within the boundary (*sīmā*), one must be investigated and sought out; otherwise, the *saṃgha* incurs an offense. If one intentionally avoids it by staying outside in private," so it is said.
To go beyond the boundary also constitutes an offense; this shows that the rules for the Saṃgha and for individuals must be the same (the former being the general principle).

As for those who act as "single monks" (*dānasaṃgha*) and so forth, this clarifies the specific application. A "single monk" refers to a monk who, at that particular time and occasion, presides over the ritual and is engaged in the specific task.

This is illustrated by the examples cited in the *Xiàochāo* (Excerpts) regarding the reception of precepts. As for the phrase "the Sangha requires my harmony, but I do not necessarily require it," the intended meaning is as follows:
regarding those monks who conduct the formal proceedings—whether they be ten or five in number—they must obtain my harmony (*sāmīcī*) when entering the hall to transmit their intentions (*chanda*).

However, I myself do not necessarily require [their harmony]. The subsequent sentence explains this by stating: "The Buddha did not strictly mandate it," referring to the regular practice of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; the Buddha mandated it for all [other matters].
We follow the same rules. Whether internal or external, if even one person does not come, all are subject to the prescribed offense.
If we were to discuss the acceptance of repentance for offenses, that would be a ritual performed for an individual; the Buddha did not originally prescribe such a rule. I, too, must attend the hall.
Since there is no formal regulation mandating attendance, there is no fault in not going. Thus, it is known that while they require me, I do not necessarily require them.

Regarding the phrase "because it reaches two [limits]": Xuán (Xuánzàng) says that one must first understand the regulations; thus, within the *Śīlaskandhaka* (Secting the Precepts), regarding the formal act of establishing the *saṃgha-sīmā* (monastic boundary), the text states:

"One may not receive *chanda* (consent). This is an explicit statement in this Vinaya, prohibiting the acceptance of *chanda*. Therefore, it says: "Except for the establishment of the boundary. The following passage, beginning with "Although it is not...
and so forth, explains the aforementioned excerpted text, stating that all other matters are permitted. Question: The Vinaya text only mentions the *śīla* (precepts).

Regarding the two methods for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults), there is a textual passage permitting the granting of consent (*chanda*). However, for other *karmavācanā* (formal acts), there is no such passage permitting it.

Why, then, is it said here that all others are permitted? This is answered by the following: although there is no explicit text in the Vinaya, it is permitted for all other [acts]. The *Karmavācanā* states: "In all cases, one may grant consent.
Yet, regarding the six groups of monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) who announced the specific matter while granting consent, the Buddha said: "From this day forward..."

This has already been addressed. It simply states "monastic affairs that are in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmika-saṃghakārya*). Based on this expression "in accordance with the Dharma," the meaning appears to be implicitly opened up;
thus, one should know that all *karmans* are in accordance with the Dharma and it is appropriate to grant consent (*chanda*) for them. Regarding the phrase "because it is not prescribed":

according to the Vinaya, only the single method of establishing a boundary (*sīmā-bandha*) is specifically prohibited from receiving consent; apart from this, there is no prohibition regarding all other *karmans*.
Since it is not permitted to grant one's consent (*chanda*) in such a case, we know that all other instances are permitted.
The statement, "The three concentrations take what is right or wrong as their object," is the heading. Taking what is in accordance with the Dharma as the object is "right";

taking what is not in accordance with the Dharma as the object is "wrong. Regarding the phrase, "If it reaches completion": if there is an act of violating the precepts where the object is not in accordance with the Dharma, the violation of the precepts itself constitutes an unrighteous act. And...

"One who gives consent" (yǔyù zhě) refers to one who falsely manifests purity while forcibly transmitting their intention. Regarding the phrase "because the matter is improper, it is neither valid nor accomplished," Master Baoyun says:
"This can now be interpreted flexibly according to the flow of the text. It should rather say: 'Because the matter is improper, it is not appropriate to transmit consent.

Although it is transmitted by force, even such a transmission is not accomplished. If we follow the passage leading to the "manifestation" (xiǎn), this refers to the section concerning the transfer of consent.

There are three types of occasions [for the *pravāraṇā*]: the occasion concerning the Three Jewels; the occasion concerning the matter of a stūpa during the observance of the precepts when one departs without having given consent; and the occasion concerning the care of the sick at a monastery.

These are explained within the two *khandakas* on the *pravāraṇā*. Since there is also the occasion of illness, the text of the *Poṣadha* (Precept-Recitation) rite states that there are variations depending on the time of the recitation.
A bhikṣu informed the Buddha, saying, "There is a sick bhikṣu who has not come. The Buddha said, "From now on, let him bring his *chanda* (consent).

The above constitutes six matters; these are the items formally listed in the Vinaya text. Regarding the case of the group of six (*ṣaḍvargika*) making robes while expressing their *chanda*, it is to be judged according to the precept on "regretting after having given consent," which states:
At that time, the group of six were constantly following one another as a faction, fearing that the Saṃgha would discipline them.
[The Buddha] prescribed the *daṇḍakarma* (punishment). The Saṃgha intended to discipline him, but had not yet found a means to do so.

Later, at one time, they saw him making a robe and called him to come. He said, "I cannot come while making my robe. The monks said, "Simply have someone bring your *chanda* (consent) here for the sake of making the robe.
He then had one person bring the *chanda* of five people. When asked by those within the Saṃgha regarding the monk [who sent the consent], they immediately performed the *karmavācanā*.

The *karmavācanā* for treating this bhikṣu is established within the Vinaya. Although it was not formally prescribed that one may announce one’s consent (*chanda*) while making robes, at that time the Saṃgha accepted and practiced it.

If one follows this text, it is likewise something not formally prescribed. Now, if one makes robes according to this principle of announcing consent as found in the *Mahāsāṃghika* and other schools, then regarding those who do not come for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the *Vinaya* states that for those in an araṇya...

There are circumstances involving robes and alms bowls, kings, thieves, prohibitions, and the guarding of rooms; these constitute the opening of desire. These are all as clearly explained elsewhere. One interpretation states:
as in that *Ji-wen* (Text on the Jetavana), such causes and conditions are explicitly shown in the external sections. A second interpretation states:

as in the *Yi-chao* (Explanatory Notes on Meaning), the characteristics of these conditions are specifically clarified there, stating: "Regarding 'comparable' (*bi*) up to 'negligence' (*tai*): 'comparable' (*bi*) means near; 'negligence' (*man*) means to slight."

This is an act of contempt. It arises from this: regarding the Dharma as the method for reciting the precepts, one who does not contemplate future karma fails to reflect upon the evil karma of the future.
They perversely practice the Noble Dharma and falsely perform these acts of desire. While truly knowing they are free from illness, they claim to be ill;
while knowing themselves to be impure, they say with their mouths, "I am pure. Their minds have no longing, yet they must speak with their mouths of "desire" and "pleasure," causing others to...
He transmits these false words and speaks them before the Saṃgha; thus, it constitutes entirely deceptive speech.

Regarding the three *pāyattika* offenses according to the number of monks present, they are established as crimes based on the specific circumstances: (1) when one is not ill, (2) when the food is impure, and (3) when one does not desire [the meal].
One should inform the person to whom the transmission is entrusted, so that they may know and report it. Regarding each of the three offenses:

the person before whom one confesses is designated as the "person to whom it is transmitted and who knows. If one fails to inform each individual [of the offense], the three offenses are applied according to the above principle.

By extension, this applies to cases where one lies with the intent to deceive the Saṃgha. Question: How are the boundaries for assigning the offenses determined for both the agent and the recipient? Answer: Both are determined in relation to the Saṃgha.

[The formal act] is concluded at the time of the actual proclamation. If the person to whom it is transmitted does not understand that it is merely the conclusion [of the procedure], it is the fault of the bhikṣu within the room.
If one sympathetically understands it as a false cognition, then it is concluded simultaneously. Some say that as soon as the words are transmitted to the bhikṣu within the room...

"To have already completed [the offense] with him and then immediately form the bond" does not constitute a release. From "evil karma" onwards, the text of the *Chao* (Excerpts) provides admonitions and exhortations.

(In the *Xuánjì*, up to this point, there is a citation regarding how Master [Zhi]yǐn’s composition of the commentary was rebuked by Vinaya Master Yù; fearing it would be too prolix, it is not recorded here.)
Regarding the second section, "The Procedure for Granting Consent" (*chanda-dāna-vidhi*): the phrase "dividing it into two" serves as the topical outline (*śīrṣaka*).

The phrase "concerning the procedure for granting consent" indicates that within the aforementioned procedure for granting consent, there is further division into two parts. First, "the procedure for granting" refers to the method of transmitting consent through a private, face-to-face encounter (*raho-vijñapti*).
Second, "the procedure for declaring" refers to the formal procedure at the time when the person who has received another's consent makes a formal declaration before the Saṃgha.
This is the rule. Regarding the phrase "at the beginning and in the middle": this refers to the middle of the Dharma. Regarding the phrase "from the fourth [category] up to 'correctly'":
according to the *Catuṣpariṣat-sūtra* (Four-Part Vinaya), in the section on the thirty-fourth method for reciting the precepts (*poṣadha*), it simply says:

"Give me your *chanda*," or "I shall speak your *chanda*," or "Speak your *chanda* for me. This applies whether one manifests bodily gestures, speaks at length, or neither manifests bodily gestures nor speaks with the mouth.

"Contradictory speech is the fourth. In the Vinaya texts, there are only these five types; four are abbreviated and one is extensive. Although it is called "extensive speech," it lacks textual passages;
therefore, it is said that the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) is incomplete in its wording. Regarding the phrase "if one posits according to the meaning" (*yi she yun*):

"meaning" (*yi*) refers to the meaning of the present master, and "posits" (*she*) means to establish. The phrasing is as in the *Shu-chao*. If one follows the commentary (*shu*), it is divided into four propositions, the first of which is: [text missing].

1. "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind"—this is the announcement for the one standing before [the assembly] to bear it in mind. 2. "I, [Name], [stating one's own name]"—this is the third. 3.

"In accordance with the Dharma," etc.—this is the formal recitation of the matter to be performed within the *saṃgha*. 4. "Desiring," etc.—this is the actual expression of one’s own intention. Question: It was stated previously that...
If the meaning is not yet clear, upon what basis is it established? The answer is found in the passage concerning the transmission of consent (*chanda*), which states:

"One may transmit consent and purity (*śuddhi*), but later one is not permitted to refer to the specific matter [of the offense]. It further states: "The textual passages regarding 'Dharma-conforming monastic affairs' (*dharmika saṃghakārya*) are severed in two places;

the present Master connects them through their underlying meaning. Since it says "Dharma-conforming monastic affairs," this refers to the context within the Saṃgha; since it says "transmitting consent and purity," this refers to oneself.
"Stops after one recitation" means it excludes the case of three recitations.
As for the phrase "according to [the rule] up to 'thus it is said,'" in the Mahāsāṃghika school, the formal act is accomplished through three recitations; one recitation is not permitted.
This is a matter of an external tradition and must not be adopted. Now, regarding the Dharmaguptaka school and others, this refers to what exists within our own school.
Regarding the formal acts for the proclamation (*saṃghakarma*): there is no text that either elaborates or summarizes them. Generally, there are three ways of proclaiming these formal acts;
once they have been fully recited one time, a note is added below stating, "The second and third [proclamations] are likewise.

Since the currently transmitted *kāma-dharma* (the rules for sexual misconduct) lacks both an extensive text and a summary, we know that a single proclamation is definitive. The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "The Vinaya does not specify the number of proclamations."

Regarding the expression "three recitations" (*tri-vācanā*): once it has been stated, it stops. As for the phrase "to be determined according to the section," this refers to cases such as the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement) and the ritual of *śuddhi-vidhāna* (purification).

The *Karman-sūtra* states: "One recitation suffices to complete [the act]; there is no further need for a formal conclusion. Now, we likewise wish to follow this principle and do not require a formal conclusion.
The practice of former times mostly followed the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika*, taking "three recitations" as the standard; however, that is a matter belonging to other schools (*bāhya-nikāya*).
This is now exhorted to be relinquished. As for the phrase "inquiring as far as the root," the intent of this question is as follows:
At that time, within the words of the transmission of the *yad-bhikṣu-karaṇīya* (consent), it is simply stated, "I grant consent for a matter of the Saṃgha that is in accordance with the Dharma.

Now, while such a "matter of the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma" belongs to the Head of the Hall (*karmadāna*), since this is one's own private room and there are circumstances such as the Three Jewels, illness, or other emergencies, why is it not formally recorded by saying: "The bhikṣu [Name], for the sake of the Buddha..."?
Regarding matters such as illness or other causes and conditions: the commentary explains that "sheng" (稱) refers to human speech, specifically that of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty.

In his *Vyutpatti-vinaya* (出要律儀), within the section clarifying the terminology for sexual desire, there are instances of personal bias; thus, it is insufficient to rely upon. As for not conforming to the original text:

in the body of the Vinaya, one does not see any mention of recording personal matters. If the character "sheng" (稱) appears in the preceding clause [of the text], [it should be understood accordingly].
The first character must be pronounced with the level tone (ping shēng). For the following phrase, both the level and departing tones (qù) are acceptable.

If it is interpreted as the character *chēng* (departing tone), it means that [the current practice] does not conform to the formal teachings of the Vinaya texts, thereby revealing that the speech of those claiming to be superior persons is erroneous. If it is pronounced with the level tone, it means:

"Nowadays, it does not conform," which instead accords with the original text of the Vinaya. Regarding the phrase "Question: As for 'to' (*zhì*) and so forth," this explains the term "not conforming to the *kṣānti* (desire/intention)."

Regarding the phrase "does the ritual for the formal proposal (*karmavācanā*) succeed or not": the meaning is that originally the proposal was intended solely because there was a karmic affinity (*pratyaya*).

Now, since this private and primary affinity has not been formally recorded (*nirdiṣṭa*), it is uncertain whether the ritual for the proposal will succeed. To answer, "It succeeds" means that it is definitively established as successful.

The upper [text] simply provides a direct answer, but it is not clear by what principle this can be established. The lower section of the *Chao* (Excerpts) explains: "Because within the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act), the reason for stating the *chanda* (consent) is not set forth;

that is to say, when one addresses another person before the assembly to state the *chanda*, it is called a *chanda-karman* (act of consent), and it is not called a *karman* [in the strict sense], such as a simple *jñapti* (motion) or a *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion with one proclamation).

This means that when the person before conveys [the consent] to the assembly, they simply say: [...]* *(Note: The source text appears to be an excerpt from a Vinaya commentary discussing the distinction between a formal ritual act (*karman*) and a specific act of conveying consent (*chanda-karman*).)*

Regarding monastic affairs conducted according to the Dharma, one should not include private matters within these formal statements (*vāda*). This implicitly indicates that when performing the *pratimukha* (face-to-face) rite in a secluded place, such matters need not be included in the statement.
One may ask: how is it known that the Three Jewels are not to be included within the *jñapti-karman* (formal motion)?
Regarding such matters, the *Vinaya* texts are cited as follows: if one does not record the names and other particulars, the procedure is nonetheless established.

This refers to a case in the *Vinaya* where a single person receives the consent (*chanda*) of many; if their surnames are not recorded, the intention is conveyed to the Sangha without the need for detailed recitation, just as one avoids mentioning specific names.

This merely describes the large assembly. However, although these two successive question-and-answer sessions seem similar in meaning, the text is entirely different from the preceding single question.
If one follows the commentary (*shu*), they should have been combined into a single excerpt, yet they have been divided into two successive questions.
As for the phrase "asking about the Tathāgata of the ultimate teaching," this refers to what is cited in the *Chao* (Excerpts): "The desire..."

The *jñapti-karman* should be performed with purity, and the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*) should likewise follow the ancient tradition. According to the *Jie-mo-shu* (Commentary on the Karma-vastu), the current master explains it as follows:

"Desire" (*chanda*) signifies that the mind is free from duality; "purity" (*pariśuddhi*) signifies that one's conduct is without flaw. When these are recited together during the formal procedure, they signify both aspects simultaneously.

Regarding the practice of those who have followed this tradition since antiquity: when intending to give consent (*yù*) at the *karmadhāna* hall, if one is not performing the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) but is merely conducting other ritual affairs, the transmission of the words consists simply of saying "I give my consent" (*yǔ yù*), without including the two characters for "purity" (*qīngjìng*).

However, when it is time for the *poṣadha*, both [consent and purity] are formally recorded. The Master now says: "Consent expresses that one’s intention is not different [from the community], while purity expresses that one’s conduct is free from fault. Purity...
One immediately obtains the *karmavācanā* (formal act); however, one does not obtain it if it is impure (*aśuddha*).

If this is the case, then regardless of whether it concerns the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* or any other ordinary monastic affairs, one must invariably state that one has granted consent (*chanda*) and is pure (*śuddha*). Regarding the phrase "because the text explicitly prescribes" and so forth:

Xuánzàng says that according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, when the assembly convenes at the proper time, one grants consent and declares purity; when the assembly convenes at an improper time, one merely grants consent. The Sangha...
It was exactly the same. Later, because disputes arose among the bhikṣus and they were not in harmony, the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) was suspended.

Subsequently, when the disputes subsided and harmony was restored, although it was not the regular fortnightly time for the cessation of disputes, they performed what was called an "untimely communal recitation of the precepts" (*akāla-saṃgha-poṣadha*).

The bhikṣus followed the established regulations, merely stating that they were granting their consent (*chanda*) regarding the matter of obstructing the recitation of the precepts. They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
From this day forward, regardless of whether it is the proper time or not, one must always submit both documents; hence it is said, "The regulation is established by the text.

As for the phrase "not the same as the *Mahāsāṃghika*," this means that when comparing the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika* with our own *Dharmaguptaka*, the second section of the *Dharmaguptaka* regulation is the "abolisher" (*heya*), while the *Mahāsāṃghika* is the "abolished" (*heya*).
Question: If this is so, why is it that in many places throughout the various sections of the lower volume of the *Shu-chao*...

The textual passage states: "If one simply says 'I do not come,' it is the giving of the *chanda*; or it says, 'Has the *chanda* been declared? The answer is that the author of the treatise has abbreviated this text.
Since the exposition is already extensive, those who have studied it will already know it upon reaching the subsequent section.

Although it is not explicitly restated there, one must rely on this extensive text as the definitive rule. This is clearly so; yet nowadays, there are still those with false attachments who [do not accept this]."
This is based on the later interpretation of the "words regarding the mistaken jewel. Regarding the phrase "from 'according to the Dharma' up to 'obstruction':

'if it is not according to the Dharma, there is no need for the *chanda* (consent),' this means that the monastic affairs of the Hall Master are not according to the Dharma, whereas my own quarters are according to the Dharma.

According to principle, one should transmit one's feelings; however, because the monastic affairs have become improper, I simply do not wish to grant the *chanda*. This is due to the conditions of what is not according to the Dharma."

Regarding the phrase "like those within a net": when the Sangha mediates marriages through lay attendants (*upāsaka*), uses communal property to establish unlawful regulations, or imposes shackles, confinement, and fines—such as money and rice—all of these are unlawful.
Question: The procedures performed by the Abbot are indefinite; they may involve the recitation of precepts, the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, or the reception of repentance.
Why, then, in this formal statement (*vākya*), is the Abbot’s specific action not recorded?

Regarding this condition: if one speaks of it in general terms as "a *dharmic* matter of the Saṃgha," there would be no distinction made between what is and is not valid. The commentary on the *Vinayavibhāṣā* explains:
"By stating simply that it is 'in accordance with the Dharma' (*yathādharma*), it allows all legal affairs of the Saṃgha to proceed without obstruction.

The intent is that if it is a *dharmic* matter of the Saṃgha for which a formal consent (*chanda*) is given—provided it is entirely in accord with the teachings and constitutes a valid ritual act (*karmavācanā*)—then such a *dharmic* bestowal of consent is universally valid and effective. If...
To cite only the specific matter handled by the Abbot on that day would not encompass all monastic affairs, resulting instead in a narrow and limited scope;
therefore, this is unacceptable. Furthermore, as the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If an illegal regulation is enacted, one should reprimand it and cause it to cease."

When it is said, "I give my consent (*chanda*) for the legal matter of the Saṃgha," one should depart once the matter is concluded according to the Dharma. If, however, one says, "The business of the Saṃgha is being conducted according to the Dharma, but what is being done today is not according to the Dharma;
my mind does not agree," then one should not grant consent, thereby avoiding the fault of participating in a discordant assembly. An ancient said:

"Since it is not permitted to state the specific details of the matter, how is it that granting consent during the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) ceremony is not stating the details of the matter? The answer to this is as follows: [The text continues: ...the former... [The response concludes by clarifying that while the *pravāraṇā* involves specific details, the formal act of granting consent is a general authorization for the proceeding.]
Regarding the prohibition against mentioning specific matters: this refers to the specific matter for which the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed.
Now, the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) is the proclamation of forgotten transgressions by the entire assembly of monks; it is certainly not a matter concerning a particular individual.
Regarding the phrase "as explained above": this refers to having received another’s *chanda* (consent) and, having completed the deliberation, being about to transmit it to the assembly.
Now, if some unexpected circumstance should suddenly arise for oneself, one must still seek someone else to convey one's own words; how then could one further speak the *chanda* on behalf of another?
Therefore, both my own person and the previous person’s *chanda* are now transmitted simultaneously by me to another to speak. This is according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

Although the transfer of consent (*chanda*) is permitted, it is not specified in the text as to how many times this may be repeated. The *Shuochao* (Commentary) cites the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, which states that seven repetitions are allowed.

Thus, according to that treatise, regarding the "sevenfold corresponding dharma": having received consent from others and transferred it, one may then transfer it to another person; repeating this up to seven times, all such instances constitute pure consent.
This differs from the text of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, where the transfer of consent results in its immediate loss; these differences stem from the distinct traditions of their respective schools.
The wording is as in the *Śāstra* (and so forth).
Regarding the phrase "asking whether it has reached [the assembly] or not": this is a general inquiry into the characteristics of whether the *chanda* (consent) has been successfully conveyed.

Regarding the phrase "the four [parts]... all used": in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there is only the method for a sick person to declare their *chanda*; this serves to distinguish it from the extensive [procedures] where no such declaration of *chanda* exists.

This refers to the *wen* (phrasing). Regarding these *wen*, there are those that are complete and those that are abbreviated; the first [of the four categories] is complete in its elaboration, while the fourth is abbreviated and thus incomplete.
Why is there this completeness and incompleteness? The *Chao* (Excerpts) explains: "It is truly because illnesses vary in severity. When light, one employs the elaborate version."
