Regarding "the offender commits an offense": "recollection" (*smṛti*) refers to causing another to recall past events—such as at a certain place, at a certain time, with a certain person, and for a certain offense—and thus it is called recollection.
Regarding "testimony" (*sākṣin*): it requires a person who knows the Dharma to verify the offense correctly;
they must testify before the person concerned so that their mind does not entertain other transgressions, such as those committed while insane or lacking mental presence.
Regarding the "receiving of the Dharma": bringing [the matter] before the Saṃgha to establish it as a formal witness. Regarding the "three initial establishments of the Saṃgha," etc.:

this refers to the proclamation of the boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*) and the declaration of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-kīrtana*), which constitutes the presentation of the intent. Regarding the "four regular [procedures]," etc.: the fortnightly recitation of the Prātimokṣa and the formal announcement (*jñapti*), which constitutes the presentation of the intent.

Regarding the four types mentioned above: the first is begging, the second is lifting up, and the third is erecting. The heading "proclamation and announcement" indicates that the original intent is being set forth.
Among these four, the former two pertain to individuals, while the latter two pertain to the Saṃgha. As for the phrase "reaching nine," the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states:
The great assembly gathered in detail and said: "There must be a reason for this; the circumstances and the underlying principles must be made clear.

As for the phrase "the tenth [day] has arrived," it necessarily involves a dual citation of both the matter (*vastu*) and the ritual procedure (*dharma*). Now, the *poṣadha*—the admonition and the recitation of the precepts—is solely a matter governed by *karmavācanā*.
Since *karma* is a ritual procedure, one must respond by saying, "The *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the precepts. However, there are both general and specific responses. (End of excerpt)

The *Jiké mósù* (Record of the Karma-vibhāṣā) states in response to this: "Sometimes, when many matters are addressed by a single procedure, it is considered distinct, as in the case of the three 'white' motions and one formal motion (*karmavācanā*) for receiving the precepts, where there are separate inquiries and responses for each.
Or, when many matters are answered with a single response, it is considered general, as in the case of the forfeiture and transgression (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

Or, when many matters are treated separately, it is considered distinct, as in the case of confessing various individual downfalls. Or, it may be that a single matter is answered with a single response."
[This applies] universally, as in the case of the single act of receiving the precepts. While it concerns many individuals, regarding the dharma there are four [types].
A single response from a pure and sufficient [monk] that lasts until the end of the night achieves full accomplishment. Alternatively, one may respond to multiple matters collectively;

for instance, if one intends to perform several rites at a single sitting, one should immediately respond by saying, "The *karmavācanā* for robes subsumes the *karmavācanā* for food. Although the response is given at once, the principle is that they are subsequently performed individually.
There is no hindrance. As for other ritual procedures (*karmas*), one may infer them by applying the same principles as explained in the single response.
Regarding the phrase "up to the *dharma* mentioned above," this refers generally to all those who perform *karmas*;
it indicates that the ten conditions listed above apply universally to all *karmas*. As for what is meant by "all," Xuán says: "This is based on the *saṃgha-dharma*."
The one hundred and thirty-four dharmas are comprised of these ten conditions; thus they constitute the totality.

If one follows the comprehensive collection of the Jiangxi school, they speak of one hundred and eighty-four dharmas by including those performed before the assembly, those performed face-to-face, and those performed mentally. Now, this present interpretation is taken as correct.

As for those that possess nine conditions and so forth—for example, the formal act of boundary-establishment (*sīmā-bandha*)—it lacks the procedure for granting consent (*chanda*), the determination of the day, and the request for permission (*yācanā*); it simply possesses [the remaining factors].
Nine. One may understand other cases by analogy with this. Regarding the statement "as detailed in the separate *dharmas*," this refers to the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā), which states:
"Of the one hundred and eighty-four *dharmas*, all must fully possess the ten conditions (*daśa-pratyaya*). In the texts cited above, some possess only nine conditions;

this still follows the partial interpretation of the ancients. Now, we follow what was transmitted by Tiantai. If one follows our current master, all must fully possess the ten [conditions]. For example, although in the case of establishing a boundary (*sīmā-bandha*)..."

Regarding the absence of the formal motion (*karmavācanā*): at this time, the presiding officer must also inquire whether the formal act has been performed or dissolved, as the transmission of the *chanda* (consent) is not permitted.
Even if the entire Saṃgha is not gathered—having marked out the boundary and assembled within it—one may substitute for them, and this still constitutes the required quorum of ten.

Furthermore, although there is no formal request for the *jñapti* (motion), the Elder, perhaps during the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, may wait until the Preceptor has finished soliciting the *chanda*, and then temporarily restrain [the offender] and command him to remain.
He then said to him: "I have invited you for a day; why do you not arise? This, too, should be understood as a request [for a formal act].
Is this not sufficient to establish more than ten precedents? An external objection asks: "The *saṃgha-karman* of the monastic law possesses ten [requirements];

how can the *cittānuvartana* (mental reflection) and *pratyakṣa* (face-to-face) methods possibly possess them all? The answer is: they also possess the ten. Now, let us take the *deśanā* (confession) as an example: first, the method; second, the seat.
1. One must know that the disclosure of various transgressions may be performed. 2. One must know the proper location; it applies to all places. 3.
One must know the rules regarding whether to proceed with the contemplation at the appropriate time. 4. One must assemble the Sangha, even if only a single person is present. 5.

One must know how to achieve harmony, ensuring that body, speech, and mind are in accord. 6. One must know how to distinguish the assembly, such that one does not face a different group but is sufficient unto oneself. 7. One must know the aspiration required.

Regarding the matter of confession (*pratikarman*): the eighth is the exposition of the original intent; the ninth is the inquiry of the mind; the tenth is the response. Since the procedure for confession is thus, the others are all analogous.
Even down to the *pratimukha* (confession before another), why would they not be complete? They are all as explained in the commentary (*śāstra*).

Therefore, it says, "Extensively as in the separate methods," which differs from the *Xuánjì* (Mysterious Record) that points to the *Jīemóshū* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā). That [text] analyzes it by means of five gates: first, mutual inclusion; second, presence or absence; third...
The sequence of first and last, the four aspects of formation and destruction, and the five points of abolition and establishment do not accord with reason; know this.

Regarding the statement "from two up to destruction," the phrase "the establishment of dharmas, their general and specific applications" refers generally to the fourfold categories of general and specific applications:

namely, dharma, matter (vastu), realm (dhātu), and person (pudgala). First, concerning dharma: Baoyun says that when there are no people present for the formal procedures (*saṃghakarma*), one is permitted to perform the rite in the presence of another (*pratyekamukha*).

Mental intention is termed "universal" (*sāmānya*). When there is a person present, it cannot be termed "restricted" (*pratyeka*). Second, regarding matters: as Baoyun says, for instance, when one must perform a formal reprimand (*tarjanīya-karman*), this is universal;

not permitting mutual performance of such acts is restricted (this refers to mental states and affairs). Second, regarding two dwellings where there is no hindrance or difficulty, both locations are universal;

the existence of prohibitions is restricted (this refers to non-sentient matters). When a person is ill and their robes are heavy, permission to separate from them is universal; mutual [separation]... [is restricted].
"Deficient" means not hearing this procedure (this situation is not a formal act). Xuán says: "When a person is ill, their clothing must be double;

the distinction between sentient and insentient things serves as a general principle. For all other matters, one must not combine them; they are clear in that they are restricted to specific cases (it is not said otherwise). Third, regarding the boundaries (*sīmā*): Bǎo says:

"The formal acts (*karmavācanā*), the mental intimation (*manasikāra*), and the face-to-face monastic procedures (*saṃghadharma*) are general principles. Regarding the aforementioned re-establishment of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) and the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept field)..."

It is not restricted to this alone. The natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*) is limited solely to mental recollection (*citta-manasikāra*), face-to-face confession (*pratyakṣa-vinaya*), and the formal establishment of a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) and a *śīmaṇḍala* (precept platform).
All others are not restricted to this. The *Xuánjì* states: "The ritual-boundary (*karmabhūmi-sīmā*) is common to all three dharmas; thus, it is a common boundary."

Naturally, only those performed through face-to-face address (*pratimukha*) or mental recollection (*manasikāra*) are restricted by boundary (*sīmā*). (According to this principle, it is incorrect to explain [the matter] based on only one side.
Fourth, regarding persons: while the performance of all *karmavācanā* (formal acts) by four persons is general, the specific individuals employed for a given matter differ;

there are seven such distinctions, which constitute the restriction. First, to clarify the scope of mutual inclusion: this refers to the legal proceedings (*dharmakriyā*) currently being undertaken, involving persons and boundaries.
The four names collectively encompass everything; therefore, it is said that they "mutually support one another" and define their respective limits (*pramāṇa*).

In the section on explanation, this is further divided into two parts: first, the mutual support; second, the definition of limits. Regarding the first, which is explained in terms of the dharmas themselves:

as for what is called "dharmas," there are many types. Vertically, there are three: mental recitation (*manasikāra*), face-to-face (*saṃmukha*), and communal (*sāṃghika*) rites. Horizontally, however—

There are eight [categories]. These include: those mental acts (*manasikāra*) performed regarding the *saṃgha-karma*; those performed in the presence of another (*pratyekamukha*); the single announcement (*jñapti*); the two-announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya*); and the four-announcement (*jñapti-caturtha*).
When categorized according to their specific conditions and characteristics, there are as many as one hundred and eighty-four dharmas; however, they are now collectively subsumed into one.

Because these are now unified under the term "dharma" (the ritual act), it is said that they are "subsumed by characteristic. As for their boundaries: mental acts are not [performed] in the presence of another, and those in the presence of another are not [mental acts].

Regarding the various dharmas: there are those that are merely mental (cittotpāda) and not performed before a group; those that are mental and not performed before a group; those that are mental and performed before a single person (pratyekamukha) but not before a group;

and those performed before a single person but not by a single formal motion (jñapti), and so forth—neither by a motion followed by one proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya) nor by a motion followed by three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha).

When categorized according to their conditions and characteristics, there are one hundred and eighty-four such types, each of which is mutually exclusive from the others; hence they are called "delimitations" (sīmā). Second, regarding the matters themselves: in general, there are...

Matters are of many kinds. Vertically, there are three: matters involving sentient beings, matters involving non-sentient things, and matters involving both sentient and non-sentient things combined. Horizontally, there are eight:

matters of mere mental recitation (*cetanā*), matters of mental recitation before another person (*pratimukha-cetanā*), matters of mental recitation according to the formal procedures of the Saṃgha (*saṃghakarma-cetanā*), matters of mere face-to-face communication (*pratimukha-karma*), matters of face-to-face communication according to the formal procedures of the Saṃgha, matters of a single motion (*jñapti*), matters of a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya*), and matters of a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha*). When categorized by their conditions and characteristics, there are one hundred and eighty-four matters.
At most. Now, all are collectively brought under the single character "One Matter" (一箇事). Therefore, it is said they are "mutually supported.

As for "delimitations" (分齊), they do not interpenetrate one another; this constitutes their delimitation. Third, regarding persons: there are many kinds of persons, and vertically, there are two types.
There are two types: individual (*pṛthag*) and communal (*saṃgha*). Transversally, there are three: first, the individual monk; second, the group of many monks;

and third, the community of monks (*saṃghasaṃgha*), categorized according to the specific matter. Regarding the distinct clarifications, there are seven types, beginning from one person and ending with twenty.

All these are collectively subsumed under the single character "one" (*eka*); therefore, it is called the "demarcation of mutual inclusion. One person is not two persons; two persons are not... [the text continues].
From three people up to twenty people, each group being distinct from the others, is termed a "delimitation" (*sīmā*). Fourth, regarding the boundaries (*dhātu*):

there are many types of boundaries. Vertically, there are two: first, natural (*prakṛti*) boundaries; second, constructed (*kṛtaka*) boundaries. Horizontally, there are seven. Within the natural boundaries, there are four:

the village, the forest hermitage (*araṇya*), the road, and the water boundary. Within the constructed boundaries, there are three: the human great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) and the *śīla* (precept) boundary.

There are three types of small boundaries (*sīmā*). In terms of their conditions and characteristics, there are thirteen; in terms of ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*), there are seven. [The first] is a single site; the second is where both persons and the Dharma are identical;

the third is where the Dharma and the food are identical; the fourth is where the Dharma is identical but the food is separate; the fifth is the small boundary for receiving the precepts; the sixth is the small boundary for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*);
and the seventh is the small boundary for the invitation to confession (*pravāraṇā*). There are six that exist naturally: the first is the distinguishable village; the second...
It cannot be differentiated. Third, the aranya free from difficulties; fourth, with difficulties; fifth, traveling on a road; sixth, the water realm (*āpa-dhātu*).
Now, these are collectively subsumed under a single "realm" (*dhātu*) character; thus, it is called "mutual inclusion of characteristics.

As for "delimitation" (*sīmā*), each is distinct and does not interpenetrate, as explained in the preceding examples. The above is the explanation of the mutual inclusion of characteristics and delimitations. Second, separately citing formation and destruction:

This means that phenomena do not arise in isolation; they must ultimately depend on the four conditions, which will be clarified according to their respective meanings. Furthermore, they do not exceed seven types of formation and disintegration, as will be explained in detail below;
thus, they are not elaborated upon here.
Next, regarding the opening of the topical outline (*ko*), the phrase "as for reaching the explanation" serves as a heading. The phrase "firstly...

to the position" indicates that while a detailed expansion would be extensive, we shall now roughly divide them into three positions; thus, it says "for now" (*qie*). The phrase "the three names" is the heading. These are:

mental recitation (*xin-nian*), face-to-face confession (*dui-shou*), and communal rites (*zhong-fa*). According to principle, they should all be listed; however, because the composition might become overly cumbersome, they are merely indicated here without being fully enumerated.

Regarding the phrase "mental recollection" (*cittamanasikāra*): I shall first set forth its names and categories in order to explain its meaning. Within the explanation, the phrase "when a matter arises" refers to minor matters;
this explains what is meant by "mere mental recollection," namely the six recollections and the confession of light offenses (*duṣkṛta*).

Alternatively, regarding cases such as when there is no one present within the boundary (*sīmā*), it is understood that these apply generally to the *saṃghakarma* (formal acts of the community) as well as the two types of mental recollection performed before an individual (*pratyekapudgala*). This is as explained in the *Pravāraṇā* (the ceremony of invitation).
Originally, this was a communal rite for the Saṃgha; now that there is no Saṃgha and only oneself, one must likewise maintain a mind as if holding the robe.
Originally, the declaration of purity (*śuddhi*) was performed face-to-face; now that there is no one to face, one should also perform it as a mental act.

Regarding the phrase "causing one's own practice to be accomplished," this means causing the bhikṣu’s own conduct to be perfected so as to avoid transgressing the teachings. Since various offenses would otherwise arise, it is said that there is no violation.
This concerns the matter of the precepts. Regarding "the arousal of the mind" and so forth, it is first difficult to initiate.

Since it was stated above that this is "mental recollection," it should be a mental recollection arising within the heart, not verbal expression. If one were to verbally articulate it at present, it would inevitably contradict the teachings;

one must not cite the *Chao* (Commentary) as a response [to this objection] (as discussed). In conclusion, it says that the arousal occurs within the inner mind, clearly recording the object before one, yet one must still personally transmit it by mouth.

Regarding internal matters, it means causing the ears to hear; this does not mean that one entirely fails to speak the Dharma words, but rather that when thoughts arise in the mind, it is called "mental recollection" (cittasmṛti).

As for the statement that the *vinaya* procedure is not accomplished, this serves as proof for the preceding text. If even when the explanation is not clear the formal act (*karmavācanā*) is not accomplished, how much more so when there is no explanation at all?
The phrase "reaching [the point]" (*zhì*) explains "in the presence of another" (*duìshǒu*). This means that it does not refer to minor matters that are merely mental recollections;
rather, it refers to cases where two people may perform the ritual procedure face-to-face. This directly clarifies the meaning of "only in the presence of another.

Furthermore, regarding the rule that when there are no monks within the boundary, one must act "in the presence of another," this refers to following the sequence to explain the communal procedures performed in the presence of others, such as the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism).

This is originally the monastic dharma. Now, even when there are only two persons, one must still perform the ritual; this constitutes the *saṃgha-dharma-pratimukha* (the face-to-face procedure for a group).
This applies to groups of two or three persons: for two persons, it is the *pratimukha* procedure without the formalities of a *saṃgha*;

for three persons, it is the *saṃgha-dharma* procedure of mutual *pratimukha*. When it reaches four persons—or perhaps "four" refers to a small quorum—then for many ritual matters, four persons constitute a *saṃgha*. If...

The *pravāraṇā* (self-exhortation) proceeds by successive transmission. When there is one person facing another who possesses the five virtues, this is not a *saṃgha* (monastic community), as will be explained below;
this clarifies that it is spoken with respect to persons. Alternatively, some point to what is said in the *Pravāraṇā-vastu*, namely that they face one another individually, and so forth.
Regarding the derivation of the term *pratimukha* (face-to-face): first, one may raise the question, "Why is it called face-to-face? This can be explained by citing the relevant texts.
When two individuals perform a single ritual act together, it must necessarily be done in the presence of one another; it cannot be accomplished if they are turned away from each other.

According to ancient commentaries, however, it is said that because the two persons join their palms facing one another, it is called "face-to-face" (*pratimukha*). If that were the case, it would logically follow that [the term] should be translated as "joining palms."
These are characters for the hands and feet; reflect upon this. Regarding the phrase "the various assemblies arrive at the Dharma," it can be explained as follows:

from the eight types above, the upper clause concludes what precedes, while the lower clause introduces what follows. That is to say, there are three [types] of mental recollection (*manasikāra*), two [types] of face-to-face (*saṃmukha*) methods, and three [types] of assembly methods (*gaṇadharma*), which are easy to understand.
If one follows the *Jie-mo-su* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā), within the face-to-face methods, a further category of "smaller assemblies" is opened up.
This refers to what people call the *pāṭidesanīya* (confession of offenses) and so forth.

Regarding the term "mindful recollection" (*cetanā*): it is a designation for that which is merely a mental thought. According to this principle, even if one confesses to oneself, the act is still accomplished.
This is an explanation of the names. Regarding the enumeration of the *huṇ* (fragrant herbs/vegetables): this refers to citing specific matters and listing the numerical categories of their names.

The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "Since matters must constantly be enumerated, it would be laborious and distracting; therefore, it is permitted to perform the ritual alone, without requiring the assistance of others" (the aforementioned text from the commentary). Consequently, someone asked:

Since the five contemplations (*pañca-anudhārmika*) are mental recitations (*manasikāra*), they can be included within the *pudgala-karman* (individual ritual action). Regarding the number [of recitations], it does not conform to the Southern tradition.
The Preceptor said: "They may also be included within the category of *manasikāra-karman*. The Venerable One said: "This is not so. Ritual actions must be heard by one's own ears.
As in the case of the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), if the recitation is not clearly articulated, it results in an illegitimate act (*adharma*). Now, these five contemplations are merely..."

Regarding the "single period" (*ika-jiki*): as for the method of contemplative practice (*kan-gyō hō-hō*), it is like a person of sharp faculties who, with every morsel of food, brings it to mind, and with every garment he puts on, brings it to mind.
Why would he need to utter words orally or listen to explanations? This is merely called the method of mental-recitation contemplation (*shin-nen kan-gyō hō*);

it is truly not counted among the formal ritual acts (*karma*). As for the phrase "from two to ten," according to the *Kusha-ron meigi* (Explanations of Terms in the Abhidharmakośa), one should first...

Question: Since these four are called "mental intimation" (*cittānujñā*), how can they also be referred to as "in the presence of another" (*sammukhībhūta*)? The *Chao* [Commentary] states: "This means that they were originally 'in the presence of another'. Thus, the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) says:

"Originally, there was only the 'presence of another,' before the 'mental intimation' was established; the name is given according to the original form, hence it is called 'presence-of-another mental intimation.
Furthermore, the enumeration following this clarifies the number, as in the text. Regarding the phrase "from three up to the robe," this is the first explanation.
Regarding the title "Among [the Rituals]": one should also ask, since it is already called "mental recollection" (*cittānuvartana*), why does it further mention "various dharmas"?

The *Chao* states that the following passage beginning with "it is originally... is the explanation. The *Jie-mo-su* says: "Although this is performed by the Saṃgha, it applies specifically to individuals; fearing confusion with other rituals, [the term 'various dharmas'] is used."

One must still rely upon the established tenets; therefore, it is said: "The mental recitation regarding the communal dharma. Regarding the matter at hand, concerning the acceptance of gifts from outside [the community], the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), fascicle 28, states:
"There was a bhikṣu who resided alone in a certain place during the spring. He received a large portion of property to be distributed among the *saṃgha* present before him.

Regarding the items to be divided, he formed this thought: 'I have obtained property that is to be shared by the *saṃgha*. Now, as I am but a single person and not part of a *saṃgha*, these robes [belong to me alone].'"
Regarding the object: how should it be received? The Buddha said: "When such causes and conditions exist, one should give rise to this thought and speak these words:

'This robe and cloth are to be obtained by the Saṃgha and should be divided; now they belong to me, I guard them, and I shall use them. To form such a mental resolve is called the formal act (karmavācanā)."
If other bhikṣus arrive, one must not give [it] to them. If one does not speak in this manner, one should not accept it as a gift; having accepted it, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
It should be shared with the other bhikṣus. If two bhikṣus perform a reciprocal division, and even if three or four do so, it is likewise.
Regarding "the robes of a deceased person," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle three, states: There was a bhikṣu who had received a robe in trust while traveling along a road.
He saw another bhikṣu coming from the direction ahead and asked, "Where have you come from? The other replied, "I have come from such-and-such a place.
He asked again, "Do you know a certain bhikṣu? The other replied, "I do. He asked once more, "Is he well? The other replied, "He has already died; these are his robes..."
Regarding "objects belonging to one present": if a bhikṣu who knows the Dharma receives an entrusted item, he should form this thought:
"Why should I give this back to this bhikṣu? Then, as that other bhikṣu departs and moves beyond the range of sight and hearing, he should receive it through mental intention (*manasā*).

Once received, because he has formed this thought, he acquires it; however, there are four *vinaya*-transgressions [for failing to do so], which, together with the previous fourteen types, constitute the total.

Regarding the phrase "from 'it is said' to 'the beginning,'" the headings and listings are self-evident. Regarding the phrase "from 'the first' to 'thus,'" "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to both the constructed (*kṛtaka*) and the natural (*svabhāva*);

in all cases, there is no separate location. Therefore, the *Karmasūtra-vyākhyā* states: "Since the matter is restricted to the middle and lower [realms], there is no need for the arduous efforts of the monastic community."

Citing these proofs establishes the performance of the ritual actions. In total, based on the various schools, there are twenty-nine [items]: receiving three (triads) and relinquishing three (triads); receiving and relinquishing ten for the alms bowl;

receiving and relinquishing [the sitting mat]—[this is determined by whether it is permissible to give it as pure-gift (śuddhika-dāna), with the addition of receiving it]; and receiving and relinquishing ten for the "one hundred and one" items.

Renouncing invitations, renouncing the precepts, and renouncing reliance; [the rules on] bowls, medicine, robes, and the ritual of purification (*pāriśuddhi*) (from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*); receiving medicine (with added meaning); receiving the seven-day medicine (from the *Daśabhāṇavāra*);

the rain-retreat (*varṣā*) up to the formal confession (from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*); renouncing the practice of walking and the practice of announcing (from the *Daśabhāṇavāra*); announcing the various practices regarding *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses (from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*);

announcing entry into a village; for a nun, announcing entry into a monastery for monks (from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*); the instruction for nuns and the performance of the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* rite (from the *Caturvargika-vinaya*). [End of] the table of contents for the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*.
29. Regarding the enumeration, there are thirty-three, thirty-one, or sometimes twenty-eight; why is it not fixed? The answer is that Xuán stated:
"Each has its own underlying intent. If there are twenty-eight, this refers to those who categorize based on the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the two schools."

Regarding the statement that [the number] is twenty-eight: this excludes the formal announcement (*jñapti*) for nuns entering the monastery and the like, as well as the invitation for instruction and the *kṛtya* (method) regarding leftover food for nuns.
If it is twenty-nine, this excludes the nuns' announcement for entering the monastery and the instruction.

If it is thirty, this combines the formal announcement for the various procedures regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and the formal announcement for the performance of the penance (*parivāsa*) into one; thus, there are thirty. If [it is] thirty...
First, adding two more nuns is called "overflowing the position" (*yili*). When the two assemblies are discussed together, they total thirty-one.

(Also seven phrases). Third, truly not having committed a *sthūlātyaya* as the heading (also seven phrases). Fourth, truly not having committed a *pāyattika* as the heading (also seven phrases).
