As for the phrase "not reaching the full [requirements]": regarding the two types of rooms that constitute obstacles or difficulties, whether the room has an owner or is ownerless, it must be free of hindrances; one should act according to this standard.

The formal act of authorization (*jñapti-karman*) is accomplished [only under specific conditions]. If either one or both [of the two requirements] are absent, even if the formal act of authorization is performed, it is not accomplished.

Regarding the requirement that "the person and the staff must both be present": the person is sentient, while the robe and the staff are insentient. It is necessary that the person be ill and the robe heavy for the ritual procedure to be validly accomplished;
this constitutes the "two-fold presence. If the robe is light and the person is ill, or if the robe is heavy and the person is not ill, the addition of the ritual formula is not accomplished.
Furthermore, for those who are both old and ill, the use of two sets of staffs is permitted. However, if one is old but not ill, or if one is ill but not old, it is likewise not permitted.
The phrase "this is the ultimate" serves as a concluding exhortation. All that has been described above is the sincere and authentic text of the Vinaya-mūla;
when the time comes to perform these actions, one must not act with ignorance, negligence, or superficiality.
Next, regarding the classification by persons. As for the phrase "the three types of persons": the matters and dharmas discussed in the preceding text are all likewise so;
however, they must rely on persons to uphold the dharmas and adjudicate the matters. If there is a deficiency in persons, the dharmas and matters cannot be accomplished.

Therefore, they are discussed next to show how they collectively achieve the objective. First, regarding "there being three persons": the *saṃgha* constitutes two [categories], and the three persons constitute the latter two. One person constitutes the third. Thus it is said.
Upon first arriving, one cannot yet distinguish the *saṃgha*. Within the *saṃgha*, there are four types: namely, groups of four, five, ten, and twenty persons.
As previously stated, this refers to the explanation of these four kinds of *saṃgha* and so forth found in the "Section on the Quorum of the Saṃgha" within the "Chapter on the Assembly of the Saṃgha.
Only those who preside over the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts)—such as those performed through mental recitation and so forth—exist within the *dharmadhātu*.

Regarding the requirement that all persons must assemble: the text states that within the boundary (*sīmā*), not only those formally designated by ritual action (*karmavācanā*) are included, but those who are naturally encompassed are also gathered.
This refers to the internal limits of the two boundaries; if there are people who have assembled in total, yet even one person fails to come, it is termed a "separate assembly" (*pṛthaggaṇa*).

Such points have been explained repeatedly in the third section, the "Chapter on Distinguishing the Assembly," specifically within the "Sub-section on the Rules for Separate Assemblies" appended to the formal divisions. One need only master the rules for governing the assembly.

The term "person" (*pudgala*) refers merely to a specific, limited meaning. "Controller" (*yantu*) refers to one who holds the reins. The *saṃgha* is the Dharma. Apart from this, regarding mental recollection (*manasikāra*), it does not depend on [the presence of] a person.
If four people were now to perform the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) or the holding of robes (*cīvara-dhāraṇa*) and so forth, it would instead constitute an illegal act.
Therefore, it is said that one must absolutely not do so.
Regarding the phrase "the second [category] changes the method": this distinguishes the cases for two or three people. "Fully establishing two methods" refers to the two types:

the formal assembly method (*saṃghakarma*) and the face-to-face method (*pratyekamukha*). "Both boundaries have no monks, so they assemble together to perform it" explains the aforementioned formal assembly method;
although it is originally a formal assembly method, because there are no monks present, it is performed as a face-to-face method. Now, if one naturally performs the rite [in this way], [it is valid].
If there are monks within the boundary, one must not summon others [from elsewhere] and act privately with only two people; in such a case, it would constitute a separate assembly (*pṛthag-saṃgha*).
If there are no monks in either of the two boundaries, then the *pratideśanīya* (confession) formula is permitted. As for the statement "the two boundaries are not fully assembled," it means this.

This is explained according to the general characteristics. Sometimes it is performed by a naturally assembled *saṃgha*; if there is no *saṃgha*, one performs it in the presence of another (*pratimukha*).
Sometimes it is performed through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), wherein one summons all within the *dharmadhātu*; if that is not possible, one opens the allowance for the presence-of-another method.

When there are guests whose numbers are indefinite, it mostly refers to the intention [of the resident monks]. If the number reaches four, one changes the procedure; this means that what was originally a communal rite (*gaṇadharma*), such as the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* and so forth, now...

Once the status of a *saṃgha* has been established, the *saṃgha*-dharma is immediately resolved. Although the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) may be completed by four, it still constitutes a successive *pratimukha* (face-to-face) procedure.
Until the *saṃgha*-dharma is established, one must have five or more persons before one may perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*) or the *pravāraṇā*.

As for the phrase "if one arrives," or "if one performs the *pratimukha* dharma," this refers simply to the face-to-face procedure. That two people each perform [the rite] without obstructing one another means:

Two bhikṣus may face each other individually to perform the rite of non-assembly; as long as the community of monks within the boundary (*sīmā*) does not suffer from the fault of a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*), it does not obstruct the Dharma-affairs.
If there are necessarily people on the periphery who must be consulted, they are to be examined and determined based on their inquiries.

Regarding the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses that require consultation with people on the periphery, the *Karmavibhāga-vyākhyā* states: "From the *naiḥsargika* down to the four [parājika] dharmas, the forfeiture applies to both the community (*saṃgha*) and the individual (*pṛthak*)."
When returning the property to the Saṃgha with the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), one must repent for the original offense; thus, it is necessary to question the three [offenses] at the boundary.

Regarding the ninety *pācittika* offenses that may be settled by facing [the offender] alone, the Commentary (*Śū*) states: "Since the offense is not removed by the Saṃgha, there is no questioning. However, there are also cases where questioning is universally required;

this is a further explanation for the sake of distinction. The Ancient Record (*Kuki*) states: "The thirty-ninth and the eleventh [rules] are distinguished in their application. This is the general summary.
Questioning those from the borderlands, the character "tong" (通) is used [incorrectly]. The *Xuánjì* states: "The re-explanation of the thirty [rules] is based on the borderlands.

If there are people who must ask, then it is made manifest; if there are no such people, there is no need to ask this text. Within the section concerning 'people,' because the locations are mutually connected, one must ask;

if they were necessarily distinct, there would be no need to ask" (as stated in the preceding text). The Venerable Jingshui refuted this, saying: "This is a repentance for the forfeiture of an article (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*)."

The Dharma of this practice is fundamentally for the sake of the *saṃgha*. Now, it is only because the number of monks is insufficient that the "confession before another" (*pratimukha*) is permitted.

Suppose there were a person from the borderlands present in a covered area outside the enclosure, or standing on the open ground beyond; since they are already within the boundary, they do not need to assemble others.

This is inherently a separate assembly (*pṛthag-saṃgha*). What does it matter whether one asks or does not ask? Now, according to the *Dharmaratna*, I shall again clarify the ninety [offenses]. As for what was just mentioned...
Generally speaking, regarding the ninety *pāyantika* offenses, they are incurred immediately upon the act and do not require questioning.

However, in the present case, even if one is on the edge [of the boundary], searching inside an open space, or within a concealed area that constitutes an obstruction, one must still question them. Therefore, it is said that "there are also cases where questioning is universally required.
The *Shu-chao* (Commentary) subsequently explains this as referring to those who are in the same concealed area, searching inside, and so forth. This necessarily applies when they are outside.
If an obstruction does not exist regarding the inquiry, it must be external; that is to say, one is searching for something outside in an open space.

If there is an obstruction, there is a partition in a covered place. In these two locations, those at the edge are not eligible to inquire. (This interpretation exhaustively reaches the root of the matter; reflect upon it.

As for the phrase "if the mental intention is consistently improper," etc., this excludes the case of being consistently [ineligible]; the inquiry does not depend on whether the obstruction is internal or external, nor on searching inside or outside.
There must also necessarily be that which acts in accordance with conditions (*pratyaya*). It is produced by the mind following every thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) in accordance with circumstances.
Regarding what is called "common" and "distinct": when a single person’s mental intention exists alone within the realm, this is called merely a mental intention.

If there are both *saṃgha-dharma-manasikāra* (formal mental recitation for the community) and *pratyekaka-manasikāra* (mental recitation for an individual), and no one else is present within the boundary (*sīmā*), these two constitute the fundamental types:

one is a *saṃgha-dharma* and the other is a *pratyekaka*. Now, because one is alone, one performs the *manasikāra* for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*); this thus becomes a *saṃgha-dharma-manasikāra*.
Now, since one is alone and performs the *manasikāra* for matters such as the holding of robes (*cīvara*), this is precisely a *pratyekaka-manasikāra*. Both are [valid].
It must be spontaneous. When performing the ritual action, only when there is no other person within the two boundaries does this mental dharma become established.

If there is even one person who acts contrary to the Dharma or constitutes a separate assembly, then a *saṃgha* is formed within the boundary; yet if one now proceeds to recite the precepts through mental intimation (*cittamanasikāra*), it fails to assemble others and thus constitutes a separate assembly.
Alternatively, if there is another person within the boundary who was not summoned and they come to face one another, it likewise constitutes a separate assembly by acting alone.

Regarding the phrase "because it concerns the assembly": there are four types of procedures for the assembly (*saṃgha-karma*) and seven for those addressed to an individual (*pratyekam-śiras*). These are listed as before in the section on the rules.

If one acts solely through mental recollection (*manasikāra*), it does not matter whether the location is shared or separate, because one is merely performing the act oneself. Regarding the distinction between "shared" (*sādhāraṇa*) and "separate" (*asādhāraṇa*):

when seeking the interior, a covered place is considered "shared" with the open ground, whereas a covered place obstructed from the outside is considered "separate" from the open ground; neither of these [distinctions] applies here.
It is the same as the measurement (*pramāṇa*) discussed in this treatise.

Next, regarding the [classification] by way of the realms (*dhātu*): "The fourfold classification by way of the realms" is the citation of the title. Although the three categories of person (*pudgala*), dharma, and matter (*vastu*) have been fully set forth above, [the following is now addressed].
Since it must arise from the *dhātu* (element), it is explained next. To demonstrate that it is not a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the commentary states:

"Regarding the four up to the three types," the four natural ones are: the village, the forest hermitage (*araṇya*), the path, and the water-element; these are found within the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) procedures, and so forth.

This means that among these four [categories], within the one hundred and thirty-four instances of *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts), one may only perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation) for the purpose of establishing a boundary (*sīmā-bandha*).
This constitutes the governance of the Saṃgha. As for "those outside of this" and so forth, they refer to the two types of rituals:

those performed through face-to-face communication (*saṃmukha*) and those performed through mental recollection (*manasikāra*). Furthermore, regarding the "mixed rituals" performed among groups of one, two, or three persons, commentators of both ancient and modern times have taken...

Both [interpretations] are incorrect. Now, according to the *Xuánjì* (Record of Mysteries), it says: "This dharma originally belongs to the Saṃgha to administer; therefore, it is said to be 'within the assembly.

Its application extends to mental intimation (*manasikāra*), face-to-face confession (*pratimukha-vinaya*), and the names for multiple individuals and the administration by the assembly. It is called a 'miscellaneous dharma' because it modifies [the standard rules];

other dharmas do not apply here, as they are not miscellaneous dharmas. For example, [this applies to] the invitation (*pravāraṇā*), receiving [offerings], the Saṃgha’s acquisition of gifts, and [dealing with] the deceased."

Regarding the *pudgala-vastra* (robe belonging to an individual), the *Karman-vibhāṣā* further adds that one may perform the confession through renunciation (*pratyākhyāna*) starting from a single person, or even up to two or three. Thus, it is known that this is not erroneous.

It permits a single person to perform the rite by mental reflection (*manasikāra*), permits two persons to perform it face-to-face (*saṃmukha*), and permits a group of many people to perform it through mutual face-to-face confession (*paraspara-saṃmukha*).
The *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) performed by four persons is not yet the formal rule of the Saṃgha; all must assemble. Regarding the statement "from two up to five persons":

when one employs a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) to gather the Saṃgha, because the ground is naturally weak and the performance of the rite is not yet complete, it is necessary to establish a formal boundary for the Saṃgha;

therefore, this is explained next. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "it also applies to two persons": the Saṃgha constitutes one [category], the individual constitutes two, and the ritual procedure (*dharma*) applies to three—namely, the mental reflection (*manasikāra*), the face-to-face (*saṃmukha*), and...
Regarding the ritual for the assembly of leaders:
as for "proceeding to the designated positions," one divides this area within the dharma-boundary (karmabhūmi) into five stages. Furthermore, these five are briefly divided into three categories:
first, the small boundary (sīmā); second, the ordination platform (sīmāmukha); and third, the great boundary (mahāsīmā). As for "the first arrival": [this refers to reaching the initial stage].
Regarding the "small boundary" (*kṣudrasīmā*) for receiving ordination based on specific circumstances: it refers to a situation where wicked bhikṣus create obstacles by forming a separate assembly.

The origin story (*nidāna*) for this is as described in the section on establishing boundaries (*sīmābandha*); it need not be recounted here. Second, the same applies to performing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony due to difficulties.

Third, the "recitation of the precepts by a limited number of people": this means knowing the exact number of persons currently assembled, as stated in the following text: "so many bhikṣus have gathered," and so forth. This...
"Small and below" explains the meaning of the preceding opening and closing [of the rules]. "To perform only one dharma" refers to the dharma of a single session.
First, it applies only to the present and does not extend to the future; second, it applies only to a temporary period and does not extend to a long duration; hence it is called "a single session.
The subsequent phrase "must be at leisure" means that it is not permitted during times of difficult circumstances; this is what follows to provide proof.

The preceding section was not intended to be permanent or fixed. Regarding the phrase "the four boundaries" (*sīma*) and so forth: "four *karmavastu* sites" (*catur-sīmā*) is the designation of the name.

The explanation of its meaning is as found in the subsequent chapter. Regarding the phrase "originally for... and so forth, this briefly describes the causal conditions for opening and closing [the boundary].

As for the exclusion of the *poṣadha* (confession ceremony): since the original purpose of the *karmavastu* site was for an untimely assembly to perform the *poṣadha*, now that it is for a timely assembly, how could such an opening be permitted?

Regarding this, Xuán says: "In cases of inevitable difficulties, one may also open [the practice] for the aforementioned *śīla-uddiśana* (recitation of the precepts), with the exception of the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish).

The *pravāraṇā* is originally performed at the site of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat). Since the *sīmā-maṇḍala* (precept platform) does not permit people to dwell there, and it is therefore not a place for the *varṣā*, how could one perform the *pravāraṇā* therein?

Xuán says: "In cases of difficulty, one should follow the aforementioned provision to open [the practice]. With the exception of the begging for a bowl and the relinquishment of offenses through confession: this refers to the practice of begging for a bowl.
Regarding the punishment for confession: one was required to use the old bowl and forfeit the new, fine bowl to the monastic kitchen (*saṃgha-kūṭi*).

There, it would be passed around among the monks until the very lowest-quality one was selected and given back to the offender to use. Since there is currently no monastic kitchen at the site of the *sīmā* (precept field), this practice is not permitted.

Regarding the distribution of the property of the deceased: there are six types of light items that benefit the ten directions. When the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) is gathered together, it is now permitted at Yang.

Now, to avoid [conflict] with one's own portion, would this not constitute theft? As for those who receive the *jīvitādhiṣṭhāna* (authorization for the day): the original agreement for receiving [the authorization] was based on the place of retreat (*an-śuk*).
Since the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept platform) does not permit retreat, one cannot maintain the authorization upon it. Regarding the dissolution of the boundary (*sīmā-bandha-vimokṣa*): originally...

It is resolved within the body of the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). Now, since the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept field) is separated by eight *chi* (approx. one meter), it is naturally impossible to resolve [the robe boundary] from afar.

As for the binding of the robe boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*), it was originally intended to designate the robe as belonging to a specific person; therefore, it must be bound. Furthermore, the *śīmaṇḍala* is not originally a place where monks reside;
how could one falsely bind a robe boundary there? Moreover, the resolution of the robe boundary depends upon the arising of the Great Boundary; now, the *śīmaṇḍala* is separated [by eight *chi*].

8. Because it is natural, there is no formal conjunction (*saṃghaṭana*). Regarding the exclusion of the pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*): the pure ground was originally intended to prevent overnight cooking.

Since there are no monks on the threshing floor, what would there be to cook overnight? How could one arbitrarily establish [the boundary] there? Furthermore, the pure ground arises in dependence upon the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*); since its establishment is not permitted above, how could there be a method for its dissolution?

Regarding the exclusion of the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* robe: this was originally for the sake of the summer labor; the site for accepting the robe is not [the place for establishing the boundary].
The place where one sits during the summer retreat is not the place where one guards one's robes; therefore, it must be removed.
Regarding what are called the "five great boundaries" (*pañca-mahā-sīmā*), this is merely a heading here without explanation, as they have already been explained previously.

Thus, the preceding text states: "It also applies to two types of persons, and the Dharma applies to three kinds; this is no different from what came before and need not be stated again. (This is the correct interpretation.)
Some have raised doubts, saying: "The *Chao* merely lists [the terms] but does not explain them; could it be that a section of the commentary was omitted due to haste?

Others cite a passage from a later section regarding the explanation of the *dajie* (great boundary). Neither of these has understood the intent of the *Chao*. Regarding the phrase "Within this... up to "...knows":
the two characters "within" (*jiuzhong*) refer to the previously mentioned *zuofajie* (boundary of ritual action). When opened, it becomes five; when closed...

This constitutes the third [point]. Regarding "permeability" (*tong*) and "obstruction" (*se*): for example, in the case of the three kinds of small boundaries (*sīmā*), it is permeable to perform the conferral of precepts, the *pravāraṇā*, and other such acts;

however, it is obstructive regarding anything outside of these. On the *śīla-kṣetra* (precept-field), it is permeable to permit the conferral of precepts and the performance of repentance (*pratikarmman*);

it is obstructive regarding the ten types of formal acts (*karmas*) that are not permitted upon arrival or departure. On the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), all ritual matters (*dharmakriyā*) may be performed collectively; this is permeability. [The text here repeats: "heavy... [end of fragment].

When establishing the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā) and the Precept Platform (śīla-maṇḍala), these three small boundaries must not be obstructed by them. Regarding "knowable according to their characteristics":
this means they can be understood without difficulty based on the characteristics previously enumerated.
The second major section concerns the gate of formation and destruction. Regarding the phrase "from 'two' up to 'destruction,'" Baoyun says:

Previously, the four categories of phenomena, persons, lands, and realms were explained individually. Now, within this section, we again correlate them with the eight horizontal [categories] of the *Dharmadhātu* to distinguish the characteristics of formation and destruction;
that which is called "formation" is not the same as what is called "destruction. Regarding the phrase "from 'phenomena' up to 'understanding,'" it refers to phenomena...
"Not arising in isolation" means that when one faces the assembly with mindfulness directed toward the higher mind, a ritual (*dharma*) does not arise spontaneously on its own;

it must ultimately rely upon four conditions—namely, the ritual itself, the matter, the person, and the boundary. Since there is a ritual being performed, there must necessarily be a matter to which it applies;

it requires the person who performs it and relies upon the naturally established boundary created by the performance of the rite. It is impossible for even one of these to be missing. This is clarified according to their respective meanings.

Regarding "not exceeding seven types": this refers to the three categories of person (*pudgala*), dharma, and matter (*vastu*). These are combined through various permutations to form seven—namely, the three single instances, the three pairs, and one aggregate, making seven in total.
These seven do not originate from the text of the Vinaya itself; however, if one wishes to provide a comprehensive explanation, they are as follows.

One must first distinguish this; the *Vinaya* text states that the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* (Jie-mo-su) cites the principle of the seven non-validities (*asādhū*) of the *Campā-dharma*, dividing them into four sections:
first, enumerating the number; second, explaining the names; third, discerning the essence; and fourth, the general and the specific. Of these four, the latter two are clarified as in the commentary.
For now, regarding the enumeration of the number and the explanation of the names: first, the enumeration. One: that which is non-Dharma and non-Vinaya.
The *bhikṣuṇī-karman* (formal act of nuns). 1. Illegitimate and performed separately; 2. Illegitimate and performed in unison; 3. Legitimate and performed by a separate assembly; 4.

Legitimate-like and performed by a separate assembly; 5. Legitimate-like and performed in unison. 7. Not ceasing despite being censured for what is improper. (The enumeration of the items is complete. Next, the names are explained.

Regarding the phrase "a *karmavācanā* that is neither *dharma* nor *vinaya*," the commentary explains: When an action lacks a proper procedure (*an-ācāra*), it does not accord with the principles of the teachings and is thus called "non-*dharma*.
Because it cannot produce goodness or eliminate evil, it is called "non-*vinaya*. At the time the matter is being addressed, it may still be termed a "*karmavācanā*.
Within this single case, all three—person, *dharma*, and matter—are non-existent; it is a total invalidity. This refers to one person accusing another.

Even when the Saṃgha is formally charged by the Saṃgha, this person does not perform a single *jñapti* (motion) before a multitude, nor does he perform a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (one motion and three proclamations) before a multitude;
such a *karman* is contrary to the Dharma. It is like having a disease but no medicine, or giving a gift that is inappropriate for one who is healthy; such a matter is invalid.

Second, the "unlawful separate assembly" (*adharma-vibhakta-gaṇa*) refers to performing a *jñapti* for one specific matter, yet performing the *karman* for another matter; this refers to the act itself.

Regarding "dharma-disparity" (*dharmavisaṃvāda*): these are mutually termed "non-dharma. When residing within the same boundary (*sīmā*), those who ought to be present do not come; those who ought to grant their consent (*chanda*) do not grant it;

and there are persons present who are entitled to censure, yet they proceed with the censure as a separate assembly (*pṛthag-saṃgha*). This constitutes both types of non-person (*apudgala*) and non-dharma (*adharmika*).
Third, "non-dharma in harmony" (*adharmasāmagrī*): the meaning of "non-dharma" is as explained previously. "In harmony" (*sāmagrī*) means that those who ought to come have come.
Regarding those who should give their consent (*chanda*): if they have given consent and are not present, they are not to be censured;

however, this constitutes only an illegal (*adharma*) procedure and is not of a single kind. Fourth, regarding the "legal but with a separate assembly" (*dharmika-vibhakta-gaṇa*): where a *jñapti-mātra* (single motion) should be performed, now a *jñapti-mātra* is performed; where a *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion and one proclamation) should be performed, now a *jñapti-dvitīya* is performed;

where a *jñapti-caturtha* (motion and three proclamations) should be performed, now a *jñapti* is performed separately. Regarding the "separate assembly": those who should come do not come; those who should give [consent]... [text ends].
Regarding "desiring what others do not desire": this refers merely to people, not to a single type. As for the five factors of "resemblance while being a separate assembly" (*bhinnasaṃgha*):
first the *karmavācanā* (formal act) is performed, and subsequently the *jñapti* (motion) is made; because the sequence of the ritual procedure is inverted, it is called "resemblance.

"Separate assembly" is as previously explained. This constitutes a case of people who are both non-Dharmic and of two types. Regarding the six factors of "resemblance while being in harmony" (*saṃghasāmagrī*): [it is] resemblance...
As explained previously: regarding "the assembly should come," the coming and so forth are also as before; this refers merely to the presence of the requisite factors, not to a single individual.

Regarding "if one does not cease after being rebuked seven times": because those who should be rebuked share the same intention, if one rebukes the person according to the Dharma and they do not cease, it constitutes an offense;

this refers merely to the fulfillment of the requisite factors, not to a single individual. This is because their minds are not discordant. When the person present before one is rebuked, that is precisely...

It is not that people do not intentionally consider this. An external objection states: "The previous commentary said that phenomena do not arise in isolation and must ultimately depend on four conditions—namely, dharma, rite, person, and realm (dharmā-vastu-pudgala-dhātu).

Now, in the analysis of what is 'not [proper],' why is the non-validity regarding the *dhātu* (realm) not mentioned? Answer: It is hidden within the analysis of the non-validity of the *vastu* (rite/affair).

Alternatively, it may be that the non-validity regarding the *dhātu* was omitted because it is considered minor. Furthermore, there is an objection regarding the four [conditions] in relation to the aforementioned three.

[Question: It is not the middle [category]. Why is it that the two "non-[proper]" categories regarding persons and dharmas are neither numerous matters nor entirely few? [Answer: Regarding the "non-[proper] arising," this pertains to the person because it depends on subjective sentiment (*citta*).

Since the administration of the dharma rests with the person, many instances of falsehood and abuse arise; thus, matters concerning persons and dharmas are manifold. (The preceding two sets of question and answer are both from the *Jie-mo-shu*).
According to principle, the characteristics of the seven types of "non-[proper]" should be established in accordance with the Vinaya. The author of the *Chao* clarifies them in this sequential order.

Furthermore, according to the *Sudarśana-śāstra*, [the procedure] begins with mere mental intimation (*cetanā*) and concludes with the formal motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) to distinguish the non-characteristics.
However, their fundamental lineages do not exceed what has been described above. First, regarding mere mental intimation and so forth, among the eight transverse categories:
Furthermore, it clarifies that this concerns only mental recollection of the dharma and fully distinguishes the characteristics of the seven types of non-transgression (*asādhū*).

This is based precisely on the seventeenth chapter of the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Views), which explains that these are performed within the context of the ritual for administering the precepts (*śīla-dharma*), extending even through the eight stages of the formal motion and resolution (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). Within each of these stages, all seven [factors] are present.

As for the phrase "for those who come first," it means that when one performs this rite in relation to another person, it constitutes a minor offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta-vinaya*), provided that [the intent] is merely...
One should suppress it by reproaching oneself. Now, repenting before another person constitutes a formal offense (*pārājika*); it is not merely a matter of holding the bowl.

Regarding "not speaking with the mouth" or "not having a clear understanding," this requires verbal expression so that one may hear it for oneself; if one does not act according to this method, failing to conform to the teaching, such as when the sequence is confused or inverted, these are instances of an improper method.
As for the "heavy *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) to be suppressed by reproaching oneself," this refers to resolving the error of the action. Baoyun said:
The gravity of a formal confession (*pratideśanīya*) is a matter that must be confessed before another person; it is not merely a mental recollection (*manasikāra*).

Now, to treat a matter requiring confession before another as a mere mental recollection, or to apply the procedure for internal self-reproach to a grave offense committed against another—this is incorrect.

Regarding the various items such as the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), to cite them erroneously one by one is like, for example, taking a large month as a small month, or a bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*) as a dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣa*).

Regarding the date: to state that it is the second day when it is the first, and so on up to the sixth thought-moment; or to claim one is ill when one is not—each such instance of falsely recording [the facts] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (light offense) for violating the teachings.
Regarding the four types of legal procedures (*dharmas*), those that are "in accordance with the matter" (*yathārtha*) are as follows:

a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (heavy offense) is countered by a formal confession (*pratyekamukha*), while a *duṣkṛta* (light offense) is settled through self-reproach (*cittapratyaya*). The other two types may be understood accordingly. Fifth, regarding "matters of persons" (*pudgala-vastu*), they are not [in accordance with the matter].
"Not obstructing the suchness of dharmas" means that one's speech clearly elucidates this suchness of dharmas; the other two [types of non-obstruction] are not so easily known.
Regarding "the six matters of dharmas do not obstruct the person," this refers to things such as forming mental intentions oneself;

the other two are easy to understand. Regarding "possessing the three non-[obstructions]," it is as previously explained in their totality. As for the remaining cases, they are to be understood by analogy. Thus far, these have been discussed in terms of minor *duṣkṛta* offenses.

The six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) are explained by way of clarification. The remaining cases, such as the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and the disclosure of transgressions (*āviṣkaraṇa*), are to be understood by analogy.
Regarding the phrase "from two up to [the number] can be known": this refers to the aforementioned number of seven non-offenses (*saptāpatti*) based on mental recollection alone.

"Applying the practice to the dharma" means that, as previously distinguished according to the dharma, there are seven types within the category of mental recollection performed in the presence of another (*pratyekam-śiras*). That is to say, *an-śānti*... [text fragment ends].

Regarding matters such as wearing robes and performing the *śuddhi* (purification) ritual, one employs the methods of "confession before another" (*pratimukha*) and "mental recollection" (*manasikāra*). Thus, it is said that "each matter has its corresponding dharma with distinct characteristics.
This means that among these seven [categories], each individual case possesses its own non-dharmic (or specific) characteristics. To take the example of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat):
the word "and so forth" (*ca*) indicates that the list is not exhaustive. There are seven types of confession before another and mental recollection; they cannot all be enumerated here at once.
Clarification of Errors: Now, I shall extract one method regarding the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) to fully elucidate the characteristics of the seven types of errors.

The remaining six cases may be understood by analogy with this. Regarding the error of the "superior person" (*upari-pudgala*): if there are people within the boundary (*sīmā*) who perform the rite as a separate assembly (*pṛthag-saṃgha*), they commit this error.

This means that while this was originally a rite performed through face-to-face communication (*pratyakṣa-vinaya*), it was only because no one was present that the mental resolve (*manasikāra*) was permitted. Now, since pure monks (*bhikṣu*) are present, one must not fail to summon them.

"Come. This refers exclusively to the act of performing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony while separated from the assembly. "Not relying on another" means that during the summer retreat (*varṣā*), failing to rely on a fifth *vinayadhara* constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense;
this is likewise an invalidity of the person. As for "verbal utterances being erroneous, omissions, or the text not being clear," and so forth:
"Resolving the prior matter" refers to errors such as mistakes or omissions made during the formal proclamation. "The time is not within the summer limit" means that the prior matter is invalid;
the sixteenth day of the fourth month is the first day of the summer retreat, yet today is the fifteenth.

Regarding the phrase "due to belonging to the retinue, the summer retreat is not established; there are difficult conditions at the location," this means that there may be difficulties caused by fierce beasts such as tigers, wolves, and lions, or there may be spiritual obstacles (*brahmacarya-vighna*) such as eunuchs or prostitutes. The Buddha prohibited residing in such places for the summer retreat.

Now that this has been intentionally contravened, it does not conform to the Buddha’s regulations. Regarding the four "non-[dharmas]" and those following, the *Chao* (Excerpts) provides a brief indication;
these are to be understood by taking the three pairs and one combination as a model, as can be seen from the preceding text.
Regarding the statement "three cases that fall under this precedent": as for those who claim that a separate assembly within the boundary (*sīmā*) is invalid, they misunderstand the point.

The foundation of the *Poṣadha* (confession of precepts) is a communal dharma; it is only when no one else is present that one may perform the mental recitation (*manasikāra*). Now, since there are people present, to act alone in this manner constitutes a separate assembly (*pṛthag-varga*).

To do so is to commit the sixth category of offense (*ṣaḍ-āpatti*). Furthermore, those who have committed an offense are not permitted to participate in the *Poṣadha*. Since you yourself have committed an offense, you are ineligible.

Regarding the combined recitation: as for not presenting the three proclamations, this is an error in understanding the Dharma. It means that although the formal announcement (*jñapti*) is not physically performed during the mental recitation of the precepts, it is logically required to verbally present the three proclamations, saying:
"Today, on the fifteenth day, the Saṃgha recites the precepts; I, so-and-so, am pure"—this being stated three times.
If one does not present these now, or if there is someone who has forgotten or omitted them, even if the words are spoken, the recitation of the precepts will be incomplete.

Regarding the characters "pure" (*śuddha*) and so forth: when there is a deficiency in the communal requisites (*pariṣkāra*), one understands this as an error in the matter. Items such as *śalākā* (voting sticks), lamps, and fire are communal requisites;

because these are currently lacking, it is not the True Dharma. As for "not yet having reached half a month," or even if it is half a month, rising at dawn without waiting for guests and so forth—these four types of "non-[proper conduct]" and those that follow are easy to understand.

Regarding the phrase "from four up to those who know": this refers only to the *pratideśanīya* (confession before another). It is performed solely in the presence of two persons. There are many such examples;

for instance, the case of holding onto an extra robe (*cīvara*) is one. If the person being confronted has violated the precepts or acts contrary to the Dharma, they are not considered a competent witness.
As for the aforementioned *pratideśanīya*, one who has broken the precepts does not count toward the required number for my specific rules, even if they are otherwise pure.

Regarding pure precepts: if there is a discrepancy between one person’s sitting and another’s standing during the ritual, it is called "unlawful" (*adharma*). As for those who criticize, "criticism" refers to criticizing because their minds are discordant;

such criticism constitutes a separate assembly (*nānāsaṃgha*), and this person is not one who upholds the Dharma. To say that the reception [of the precepts] is not correct means that the understanding of the Dharma is erroneous.

This refers to [the robe] having fifteen strips with three long and one short; now it is said to have two long and one short. Since the phrasing of the explanation does not correspond to this robe, it is called "not correct.
Regarding "if the rebuke does not cease": this means that when the person before sees the error, they subsequently utter "ha ha" and do not stop; thus, the formal ritual is invalid.
As for the aforementioned instances where there was a rebuke, "rebuke" refers to a discrepancy in the mind; therefore, it is called a rebuke.
Such a person will not cease their misconduct even when rebuked now; this is a violation of the Dharma, not merely a failure of decorum.
Regarding "the five great primary colors and superior dyes," this explains the nature of the offense: blue, yellow, red, white, and black are the five great primary colors.

True crimson, deep purple, azure, and emerald green are the superior dyes. The four types of improper [dyeing] and the five types of improper [dyeing] constitute impurity. These four [categories] below...

This is to be understood as explained previously. Regarding the phrase "the five cases as examples": among the various formal procedures (*karmas*), those performed through face-to-face consultation (*pratimukha*) are fundamentally legal acts conducted by the Saṃgha. Since the Saṃgha is currently absent, the practice of consultation is permitted as an exception;

such instances are numerous. To provide a brief illustration, consider the single case of the invitation for self-reflection (*pravāraṇā*): four persons conduct the formal act, while the fifth receives the consent (*chanda*).

This refers to understanding that it is not a person [who constitutes the assembly]. It means that within the *dhātu* there are five persons who together constitute the legal assembly (*saṃgha-dharma*). Now, one person gives their consent (*chanda*) while four persons act as mutual counterparts (*parivarta-pratidvandva*).
If the leader is either one whose precepts are impure or one who knows [the situation] yet acts as a fellow practitioner of the Dharma—this former case refers to a person who has broken the precepts.
If one clearly understands the details [of the offense], it is improper to perform the *pravāraṇā* with those of the same dharma; if one does not know, there is no fault.

Regarding the phrase "not mutually declaring," this is an incorrect understanding of the method. For the *pravāraṇā* performed in the presence of others (*pratyekamukha*), it is logically appropriate for each to declare their words to one another.

This is as in the ritual procedure for four persons, where one person speaks separately, saying: "Venerable sirs, please attend to me with one mind. Today, the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā*. I, [Name]..."

"May I be purified. This is recited three times; it is not as when they address one another. Regarding "if the speech is not clear": this refers to cases where, although words are uttered, the phrasing is unintelligible.
The Vinaya states: "One must not perform the *pravāraṇā* in a whisper," and so forth. Regarding "the time is not the end of summer": this explains that the matter is incorrect.
That is to say, the Buddha commanded that the *pravāraṇā* be performed after the *varṣā* retreat is completed; to perform this rite now, before the end of summer, is incorrect.

Regarding "the various difficulties not being complete": if an evil bhikṣu should come, one should immediately know that if he arrives on the fourteenth day, the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) shall be held on the thirteenth;
if he arrives on the fifteenth day, the *pravāraṇā* shall be held on the fourteenth. Although this is not the end of the summer retreat, it is permitted;
conversely, the opposite case is not permitted. The four "non-[cases]" and those below them are easy to understand.
It is said that the six points regarding what can be resolved are as follows: the types of individuals subject to the *śuddhaka-śukla* (pure white) [procedures] are manifold.

In this text, we shall provisionally cite the single dharma of the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) to clarify what constitutes an invalidity; the remaining cases should be understood by analogy. As for their respective differences, these refer to the variations in the individuals previously mentioned.

However, when it comes to what constitutes an invalidity, there is no difference. Regarding "a separate assembly within the boundary" (*sīmāntara-gaṇa*): this refers to a situation where, within a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), there are people...

It is not so when one does not assemble at the site of the precept-platform (*śīlā-maṇḍala*). Regarding those who are not pure: the presiding master of the confession (*pratideśaka*) must fundamentally [be pure];

even for a layperson, they must not have violated the five precepts, and as for one who has gone forth, they must not have violated the heavy prohibitions (*gurudharma*) before they may accept their confession. Now, to do the opposite of this constitutes a human error.
As for the claim that "light and heavy offenses are equal in dharma," this is an error in understanding the dharma; for example, it is like the confession for an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*).

Binding [the robe] according to the prescribed measure constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), which is heavy. Binding it when not according to the measure—according to the treatise—is a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing), which is light. Now, these are treated identically as a single forfeiture and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).

Regarding the distinction between observance and violation: this explains the meaning of the aforementioned gravity and lightness. Binding it according to the measure but exceeding the limit is a violation according to the Vinaya text.

Although binding it below the measure exceeds the limit, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (or *Mahā-saṃghika-vinaya-śāstra*) classifies it as a *dukkaṭa*; according to the Vinaya, it is not a violation and, conversely, is validly established.

"Maintain [the precepts]. If one now performs repentance in conjunction with them, then there is no longer a distinction between 'maintaining' and 'violating. As for those who falsely set forth such statements, they commit the offense of 'prolonged discourse,' following the precedent of the rules regarding being separated from one's robes and so forth.
Regarding the claim that 'wealth is not to be relinquished,' this is an error in the interpretation of the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*). The *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states:"
The robes and materials were scattered, and the defiled and the pure were not distinguished; they were all brought in for relinquishment because the matter was improper (the above is the commentary).
Dharmabhadra further explained: "It is not so. It is like silk floss that is merely ruined by itself; it does not merit being relinquished. Regarding those who do not confess their transgressions:

this refers to categories such as the *ātyaya* (excessive) offenses, the *dīrgha-vipravāsa* (prolonged separation), the *cīvara-nāśana* (ruining of robes), the *vikraya* (selling), and taking the robes of a nun who is not a relative, as well as exceeding the time limit. In principle, these ought to be...

Each of these has been explained individually; they are not all discussed here at once. Regarding the fact that the boundary (*sīmā*) is not a formal act (*kṛta-dharma*): although this *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense logically applies to both types of boundaries, for now we rely on what is governed by the single motion (*jñapti*).
This must necessarily be an established monastic legal procedure (*saṃgha-dharma*), and it must naturally pertain to the Dharma-boundary (*dharma-sīmā*).

As for "the clothing and requisites not being assembled": this refers to when, at the time of performing the formal act, one collects and discards the clothing and requisites within the monastery courtyard. They are not... [assembled].

[The robe] must be relinquished [in its entirety]. It is not permissible to gather [the parts] at different times and present them in the midst of the Saṃgha. Nor should one recklessly entrust it to another;

for instance, having already relinquished the robe and returned to one's room, if one suddenly sees the original object and fears it might become defiled [by further attachment], saying, "I have relinquished this to so-and-so," is likewise impermissible.
As the text below states: "Once it has been made one's own through prior possession, to later relinquish it out of fear of defilement is not pure."
Regarding "giving" (*dāna*), the Buddha judged that it does not constitute [a valid act], and so forth. The four types of "non-[formal acts]" (*asammatā*) and below can be understood accordingly.
As for the phrase "from seven up to knowing," this refers to the two types of *jñapti-dvitīya* (one motion and one proclamation) found in various commentaries;

these are distinguished based on the single dharma of establishing boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*). The claim that "the characteristics are not fully indicated" is an error made by those who interpret [the texts]. [The term] "natural boundary" (*prakṛti-sīmā*) refers to a small area.
Because the markers of the ritual boundary (*karmabhūmi*) are distant, it is necessary to gather all those marked within. Regarding "those who are called by their characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*):

because the markers of the ritual boundary are narrow and the natural boundaries (*prakṛtisthāna*) are distant, one must gather all those within the boundary according to their characteristics. Regarding "the separate assembly within the boundary": within the four locations and six characteristics of the natural boundary, if there are people who do not come, they may be censured;
as for the person who censures, they censure because their mind is discordant. Regarding "the proclamation of the characteristics is unclear," etc.: this is the explanation.

This is not in accordance with the Dharma. It refers to when a bhikṣu who is reciting the boundary markers does not clearly understand the limits of those designated signs, or when he recites incorrectly and so forth, performing the ritual procedure in a manner that is obscure and ungrounded.
Since the recitation of the markers is not clear, even if one maintains the formal rite to establish the boundary, it remains darkly indistinct and fails to be accomplished;
thus, no wholesome dharma arises. Because he lacks clarity and has nothing upon which to rely, it is called "dark" (míng).

"Supporting" (玄云: "As for 'supporting' like an object in the dark, this is incorrect"). "Rebuke when one does not stop" means that because those who know the Dharma fear that the Dharma will not be established and their minds are of one accord, they rebuke [the offender];
yet the other does not cease or abide [in the correct state]. This Dharma is incorrect. "The sign and the essence, etc. refers to the incorrectness of the matter (*vastu*).

The place where the boundary markers (*sīmā*) are proclaimed is called the *karmavācanā* (the formal ritual); the location where they are inscribed is called the *nimitta* (the marker); and the physical site where the ritual is performed is called the *vastu* (the locus).
Because one does not recognize these three distinct boundaries, confusion arises. As for not knowing how the two boundaries—the internal and the external—intermingle:

one fails to recognize that the internal markers of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) constitute "this," while the external markers of the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept field) constitute "that. [The intermediate space between them is...]
There is no intervening space of natural separation; hence it is said that one does not know "this" from "that. Since there are no two realms separated by nature, they spontaneously interpenetrate.
Regarding the repeated formation of mutual interaction: what was previously established by one person is not recognized by the subsequent person.
Furthermore, because it is tied again on top, it constitutes a "double knot. When two boundaries meet, it is called "interlacing.

Regarding the category of "tying from afar," this refers to sitting within the boundary enclosure (*sīmāmaṇḍala*) and chanting from a distance to establish the formal procedure for the internal and external marks of the Great Boundary (*mahāsīmā*).

The latter phrase states that all the aforementioned [procedures] are invalid; hence it says, "none are accomplished. As for "the other cases are known by analogy," this refers to the three pairs and one combination as examples.

This is the explanation. As for the statement "eight [categories] reach the front": although there are many subjects to whom the *jñapti-caturtha* (four-part motion) applies, here only one type—the reception of the precepts—is being distinguished.

Regarding the phrase "the receiver and the obstacles": this is an explanation that clarifies what is not a person. There is another explanation which says: the *śrāmaṇera* is the receiver; on his body...

Because light obstacles and grave difficulties [render it impossible], one cannot receive the precepts. Now, the objection is raised: if this refers to a śrāmaṇera who has difficulties and so forth, it pertains merely to the matter at hand and is not what was being indicated.
Now, according to the *Xuánjì* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), regarding the preceptor (*śikṣācārya*):

if he does not clarify the characteristics of the teachings, does not recognize the characteristics of obstacles and difficulties, and does not understand how to distinguish them, it is not that he causes the candidate to receive the precepts while carrying these [defects]; rather, the essence of the precepts is not obtained. This...
It does not arise from the person of the preceptor; rather, it is that the person is not one who receives [the precepts]. Therefore, the subsequent text says:

"If one asks but does not understand, in the end it is not a valid question," and so forth. Regarding those who do not assemble within the boundary (*sīmā*): this refers for now to the time of receiving [the precepts] within a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*).
As for the deficiency in the number of monks: in the center there are fewer than ten, and at the periphery fewer than five. Even if there are five hundred people... this...
Furthermore, setting aside the terminology for a moment, I shall briefly cite five hundred and fifty dharmas to examine them.
Those that do not qualify are those mentioned in the preceding sections on the "sufficiency of the count," where more than sixty individuals were analyzed across various categories.

Now, excluding those who fall short in even a small measure within the fourth category, the number of persons listed in the first two preceding categories is slightly over fifty. As for those who are generally not part of the formal count, they are as follows:

The aforementioned individuals are all insufficient to constitute the quorum of the *saṃgha*. To claim that those who have received the preliminary [procedures] may proceed with the formal ordination is an erroneous interpretation of the Dharma.

Regarding the eightfold sequence of steps: it refers to the eight requirements for receiving the full precepts (*upasampadā*). First, requesting a preceptor; second, establishing the location where the candidate shall stand;

third, appointing an instructor (*śikṣamāṇācārya*); fourth, emerging from the assembly to question [the candidate]; fifth, summoning the candidate into the assembly; sixth, begging for the precepts; seventh, the preceptor...

The "White Harmony" (Baihe) section concerns the interrogations posed by the Eight Precept Master (*aṣṭāṅga-upāsaka-ācārya*). These eight [questions] all pertain to the period prior to the formal reception [of the precepts];

therefore, it says, "prior to the reception, one proceeds with [the inquiries on] conduct, etc. (and so forth). As for the actual reception itself, there are two persons involved within the rite of reception: first, one instructs the candidate to establish the mind upon the object of focus;

second, one performs the formal ritual of the essence of the reception. These two stages do not involve the eight matters mentioned previously. Regarding the phrase "adhering to the text without error," this is based on...

Wenjin recited the words of [so-and-so] exactly as they were, without making any alterations. Regarding the phrase "the boundaries of the precinct are not clear," this refers to an error in the procedure (*karmavācanā*).
The explanation of the boundaries is identical to that found in the two preceding sections on the formal announcement (*jñapti*).

Regarding the phrase "the robe and bowl are not one's own" and the statement "borrowed from another person," these are similar cases; they are all errors in the procedure and are subsumed here. The remaining cases follow this same principle.
The former may be left aside.
As for the phrase "the rest follows," it serves as a general conclusion indicating the point of reference. "The rest" means the remainder;

that is, excluding what has just been mentioned—the single *jñapti*, the *jñapti-dvitīya*, and the *jñapti-caturtha*—the word "rest" (*śeṣa*) is used. "The True Dharma" refers precisely to the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure). This continues up to... [the mind].

"Mindfulness" means bypassing the intermediate face-to-face [ordination]. "The Dharma is self-sufficient for each respective case and there is no mutual proficiency" means that, setting aside the eight positions [of the ordination lineage] in the horizontal arrangement, one considers the objects of perception and their characteristics;

because the one hundred and eighty-four persons, the legal procedures (*dharmakarma*), and so forth are each distinct from one another, it is said that "the Dharma is self-sufficient for each respective case.
Interchangeability is not permitted, which means there is no mutual proficiency. In a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*), a single Dharma applies to many.
As for those who interpret this broadly, many say it refers to "most cases" (*bhūyastvena*). Alternatively, the title may be indefinite;

that is, among the eight positions, excluding the single position of "mere mental recollection," if there is a person within the remaining seven positions, it constitutes a "separate assembly" (*pṛthaggaṇa*) and is extensively categorized as such.

Regarding the *Yìchāo* (Explanatory Notes), the characteristics of the seven types of non-proper [assemblies] in the Vinaya text are interwoven with both text and meaning. The *Jīmō Sū* (Karmavācanā Commentary) cites that extensive exposition from the *Chāo* (Notes).

The reception of guests has been omitted here and will not be discussed in detail. Regarding the eight types of improper conduct (*asat-saṃvāsa*) mentioned previously, their non-validity is clarified according to their respective meanings.

Furthermore, based on the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Views), it states: "The wording and the intent of the Vinaya are not different. (Note: This refers to the seven types of non-validity which were previously listed separately; they have now been moved to the beginning of this section for explanation.)
Regarding the subsequent explanation of the main text of the *Karmavācanā*: The Venerable Jingshui said, "In the previous sectioning, it was stated, 'By means of understanding the *karmavācanā*.
Now, this merely says, 'Next, explaining the main text. What is the difference between these two statements? The answer is: It is merely a matter of employing a different stylistic phrasing;
there is no other underlying principle. The Venerable further said: "Even so, one must still briefly resolve the preceding [text] in relation to this."

Section. Regarding what is called "interpreting the *karmavācanā* through indirect analysis" (*qujie jiemo*), this refers to meanings that extend beyond the standard [procedural] framework. Among the one hundred and eighty-four types of procedures, these are collectively termed "dharmas.
Since the mental recitation (*cittānuvartana*) and the face-to-face (*pratyakṣa*) methods have easily discernible textual forms, they will not be discussed further here.

However, as for the *karmavācanā* procedures of the Saṃgha, their underlying principles and fundamental conditions are difficult to clarify; therefore, an indirect analysis is provided beyond the standard framework so that people may understand them thoroughly. Hence, it is called "indirect" (*qu*).

[This concludes] the explanation of the preceding section. As for the phrase "next, the explanation" (*kṣe*): "next" (*ci*) refers to sequence; "explanation" (*śe*) refers to explication. Regarding the "main text": this refers to the text consisting solely of the four *jñapti-caturtha* [procedures].
Within this text, each item is treated according to its proper order, such as the number of *jñaptis*, and so forth. As for the phrase "causing it to reach redundancy":

regarding the section "to cause one to know the essential framework" (*kāṅyāo*), an ancient commentary states: "The 'framework' (*kāṅ*) is precisely the 'essential' (*yāo*); it is not something improper."

Also, Xuán says: "The *karmavācanā* (羯磨) has 'bones' (*asthi*) which are called the 'framework' (*jīng*). The intermediate sections that record the specific circumstances (*nidāna*) are called the 'essentials' (*yào*).

This is just as in the case of the single-announcement (*ekajñapti*), where the first three [parts] constitute the framework, while the fifty-four characters are the essentials. Now, the characters serve as the framework, while the two sets of four phrases—the circumstances and the basis—serve as the essentials.

Within the thirty-one characters of the *karmavācanā*, these are the framework; the middle section constitutes the essentials. From the words 'Venerable Saṃgha, listen,' downwards, who are the elders?"

The first "elder" (sthavira) before the word "consent" (*kṣānti*) constitutes one intermediate stage. Who requests the elder's consent? The subsequent silence constitutes the second intermediate stage.

The word "completed" (*kṛta*) at the end of the phrase "the Saṃgha has consented" constitutes the third intermediate stage. This means that if the basis of conditions (*pratyaya-mūla*) is absent, it is inherently useless.
Even if the basis of conditions exists, if there is no characteristic of essential substance (*tattva-asthi-lakṣaṇa*), the matter will not be accomplished. Therefore, one should know [this].
The fourteen characters and thirty-one characters constitute the essential foundation of the conditions; they are the "mainstay" (gang) of the text.

Although the intermediate conditions differ, these are nonetheless the essentials of the mainstay. Some say that the mainstay and the skeletal structure (ku) are distinct, but this is not so; the mainstay is itself the skeletal structure.

The head’s edge along its base is the "tendon" (*jō*). Within the substance of the Dharma-body, it is called "bone" (*kotsu*). These two names do not differ. Regarding the penetration and obstruction of consciousness and understanding:
that which discerns without doubt is called "consciousness" (*shiki*); that which clearly illuminates principles is called "understanding" (*ge*).

The one hundred and thirty-four white tendons and bones are all collectively "penetrated. Among these one hundred and thirty-four, the specific conditions of the intermediate matters each have their own differences.

This is a prohibition. As it is with the *śuddhaka-jñapti* (the formal motion consisting of a single announcement), so it should be understood for the *karmavācanā* (the formal act). "If one does not fully understand" means to be thoroughly and clearly enlightened [regarding the matter].
That is to say, if one does not fully and clearly understand the essential points, the causal basis, and the original response;
