Therefore, their titles are largely identical. By relying on this, that which can be understood may be explained; once scholars have analyzed this single instance, they will be able to comprehend the pattern, for all other cases are likewise so.
"Next, regarding 'the aforementioned text': this refers to the sequential explanation. Within this, it is divided into two parts;

that is, within the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) for receiving the precepts, the major sections are divided into two based on essence and function. First, 'correctly resolving the fundamental' clarifies the seventeen characters of the core framework of the primary essence.
Second, from 'the Saṃgha has already consented' onwards, it establishes the fourteen characters of the core framework of the preceding text."
Regarding the statement "the preceding section has three parts": this refers to the primary resolution of the fundamental [matter].
The term "preceding" refers to the preliminary stage, which is broadly divided into three sections. If categorized by sentence, it would also comprise five segments.
The first segment extends from the initial character up to the character "yuan" (緣). "First" refers to the head of the three sentences. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen" constitutes the skeletal framework.
The *Shao-wen* (Commentary) explains: "Announcing to the assembly to listen again" receives the designation "repeated" (*chóng*) because it follows the preceding single announcement (*dānbái*).
Since the matter is not a minor one—the rite of receiving the precepts is not like ordinary matters; this is the root of the Noble Path for the fourfold assembly—how could it be considered small?
As for "carefully attending to the sounds and characteristics," it means causing the assembly to examine the reality and listen attentively to this presentation of their suffering.
This is the condition for making a definitive judgment. From the second section, from the two characters up to the character "not" (不), it says:

"This [person], so-and-so, from the preceptor so-and-so. The Venerable One said: "One should simply call this a 'close condition' (親緣). There are also those who say it is the 'root among conditions' (緣中之本)."
This person, so-and-so, now requests the Saṃgha for the full ordination (*upasampadā*). So-and-so acts as the preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
He declares himself pure and free from all obstacles; he is twenty-three years of age and possesses the robes and bowl.
The Saṃgha now confers the full ordination upon so-and-so, with so-and-so as preceptor. "Venerable sirs, this is the formal basis (*nidāna*). [The names are] recited twice.
The preceding phrase is the remote condition (*pratyaya*). From "The Saṃgha now bestows" (*saṃgho 'dya dadāti*) onwards is the root text (*mūla*).

Some say that the preceding phrase is the condition within the middle phrase, while "The Saṃgha now" and below is the root within the middle phrase; however, this does not contradict the principle, as the general meaning remains intact.

"Whoever among the elders consents" (*ye āyuṣmanto kṣāntam*) is the skeletal sentence (*asthi-pada*). If, according to the Dongta commentary, the word "consent" (*kṣāntam*) belongs to the following phrase, it constitutes the condition.
In the *Benzhong* (Original Text), there are only thirty characters as the skeletal framework (*ganggu*).

Furthermore, according to the *Huainan Shunzheng Ji*, the character "Seng" (Monk) from the second phrase is moved up to serve as the skeletal framework for the first phrase; thus it should read: "Who requests that the Elder endure the Sangha?

In this way, there are thirty-two characters as the skeletal framework. The Great Virtuous One said, "Neither of these is reasonable. Zhizhou said, "The above has been a preliminary, provisional analysis."

The explanation of the fundamental phrases is concluded. Although these are written in a straightforward manner, the *karmavācanā* texts are somewhat extensive; their value lies in their meticulous detail.

In various commentaries, only the preceding and succeeding sections are cited, which makes them difficult for beginners to understand. Although the present work is verbose, it is nonetheless essential.

Next, regarding the explanation of the analysis: the *Chao bai shi* (Excerpts from the White Commentary) states that "the formal determination of the conditions and the root" refers to the preceding *karmavācanā* text, from "Now, so-and-so...
up until "...having completed the three robes and bowl. This constitutes the formal determination of the conditions.

"Causing [the candidate] to request ordination from the Saṃgha and so forth" constitutes the root. "Measuring whether it is permissible or not" means causing the Saṃgha to carefully deliberate on its acceptability.
Because it is an acceptance that cannot be accepted, it is said "it may be" (*kannō*).
In the third section, the phrase "The Saṃgha now grants full ordination to [Name], with [Name] as preceptor" is the formal basis; then follows, "Whoever among you approves, let him remain silent."
This is stated to clarify that the skeletal framework is white. Regarding the "single citation of the root" for the definitive judgment of accomplishment:

this refers to stating only that "the Saṃgha now confers the precepts upon [Name]," without further recounting the conditions such as the robes, bowl, or obstacles. Hence, it is called a "single citation," and so forth.
The statement that "the second and third [recitations] are also spoken in this manner" is a summary of the text, which is easily understood. [End of] External Objection.
It is said: "In this context, the three rounds together with the formal motion (jñapti) are termed 'the fourfold white' (jñapti-caturtha).
Why is it not increased to five by adding other matters such as receiving the precepts? Why is it not decreased to one? One may cite the *Chao* (Excerpts) to answer:

"If there were only one, the matter would not be successfully accomplished; if there were many, the ritual would be confused and improper. The meaning is that if only one round is performed, the preceding matter has not yet been completed.
If one were to establish five, six, seven, or eight, it would again overlap with other systems.

Since the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* provides no standard for this, stating that such a practice is not the correct rule (*agati*), establishing a fixed limit at this point is precisely to establish the principle of neither too many nor too few.

Just as a seal or official document must always follow a fixed protocol and be strictly determined without deviation, these three dharmas are established out of a mind of profound reverence. Therefore, the three dharmas are established.
This is because it accords with the established rules.
The second section concludes with an exhortation. Regarding the phrase "From 'the two' to 'the essence': "The Sangha has already consented" refers to the bone [of the lineage].
"I confer the full ordination upon so-and-so, with so-and-so as the preceptor" is also a summary of the conditions; it simply sets forth the fundamental basis. [The Sangha] has consented.

Because it is *lìrán* (likewise). It extends up to the character *chí* (hold), which is the skeletal framework (*gǔ*). From *sēngyǐrěn* (the Saṃgha has already granted its consent) downwards, there are fourteen characters in total; these constitute the skeletal framework.

There is also the practice of using the character *jìng* (completed) to form the phrase *jiè'ān* (precept established). Below this, one should say: "The full ordination (*upasampadā*) for [Name] has been completed."

If one acts according to the spirit of the rules, both [the literal and the functional] can be maintained without violating the Great Principle (大理). Nowadays, those who do not understand the Dharma often rebuke and stop such practices;

however, they instead end up committing an offense themselves. The *Chao* (Excerpts) states: "The commentary says: 'This refers to matters directly assigned for settlement that do not pertain to the essential body [of the ritual].

Question: The seventeen characters mentioned earlier constitute the skeletal framework of the *Karmavācanā* (羯磨); how can you say they do not pertain to the essential body? Answer: Great... [text ends]

Dechen: This is stated merely in contrast to the preceding three stages. That is to say, by the time the word "shuo" (say) is uttered during the third stage, the novice’s attainment of the essence [of ordination] is fully accomplished.
Since this is not the concluding summary, how could the receiving of the precepts within the text not pertain to the essential body [of the rite]?

It is not for the purpose of concluding the fourteen characters; it is not included within the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure). Alternatively, some may respond to this by citing the analogy of a seal and the term "darkness."
The analogy of being equal to all things can be understood.

The phrase "as for reaching the non-... is the opening of the topical section (*kāṇḍa*). The phrase "the first... up to 'according to'..."—the two characters "first" (*chu*) and "middle" (*zhong*)—are used to distinguish between addition and subtraction.
Baoyun says: "This is explained solely in reference to the *śuddhaka-jñapti* (simple motion); if there is a second sentence within the motion, then..."
This is an "increase" (*vṛddhi*). Excluding this single phrase is called a "decrease" (*hāni*). An "increase" receives its name in contrast to a "decrease";

it does not mean that new words or phrases have been added. Regarding "light, minor, and lacking the *nidāna*," etc.: as in the *Adhikaraṇa-śamatha-dharma*, which excludes the gathering of wise persons for a simple motion (*jñapti*).
The third phrase, "The Saṃgha now gathers those who possess wisdom," refers to the impartial adjudication of matters; such a motion lacks the second phrase. There is [this].

Regarding the *pratītyasamutpāda* (the causal basis): as it is said, the day and month for the *poṣadha* constitute the *pratyaya* (condition). The proclamation regarding the duration of the observance constitutes the *vastu-pratyaya* (the factual condition).

This serves to record the time-condition and the matter of the *poṣadha*. Since this fundamentally subsumes the great teaching of the Saṃgha and the matter is not trivial, there are five phrases in the formal motion (*jñapti*).

As for the phrase "even unto the *jñapti-dvitīya* [formal acts] and so forth, excluding those of similar category": this refers to bypassing the single-motion (*jñapti*) which possesses five phrases. Thus.
It is said, "up to and including. This applies by analogy to the *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion with one proclamation).

Within the category of *jñapti-mātra* (simple motion), if the matter is minor and lacks a formal request or a narrative background (*nidāna*), it is still constituted by four phrases, such as the *jñapti-dvitīya* for requesting a day-off or for appointing all officials. However, if the matter is not trivial, [it requires the full procedure].

If there is a *nidāna* (introductory narrative) and a motion (*jñapti*), consisting of five phrases, such as the fundamental basis for the assembly in the delimitation of boundaries (*sīmābandha*), the matter is not trivial;

the proclamation of the boundary marks (*cihna*) constitutes the *nidāna*, and the motion likewise consists of five phrases. As for the phrase "the rest is to be applied accordingly" (*śeṣaṃ tathaiva yojyam*), the *Xuánjì* calls these "the remaining [procedures of] the fourfold motion" (*jñapticaturtha*).

This means that what was discussed above is to be applied according to the single motion (*jñaptimātra*), the motion with one proclamation (*jñaptidvitīya*), and the motion with three proclamations (*jñapticaturtha*); the remainder not yet discussed is [to be understood by this principle].

This refers to the *jñapti-caturtha* (the motion followed by three proclamations). Within the *jñapti-caturtha*, although the matters involved pertain to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, all possess a formal origin (*nidāna*) and a request (*yācanā-vākya*).

Since these are invariably composed of five phrases without alteration, it is said that "one is standardized" (*yi zhun*). (This interpretation remains somewhat limited. According to the interpretation of Fǎbǎo, there are three types of "standardized ones":
first, apart from the simple motion (*jñapti-mātra*) which lacks a formal origin, those with a formal origin are all established through five phrases.

As stated regarding the *śīla* (precepts) and so forth, among the two types of *jñapti* (motion), if there is a causal basis (*nidāna*) and so on, all *jñaptis* are constituted by five phrases, such as the *jñapti* for establishing a boundary (*sīmābandha*).
Thirdly, all *jñapticaturtha* (motions followed by one proclamation) involve matters that are not minor or trivial; they must rely on the original five-phrase *jñapti*.
This is precisely what applies to the third [category] as well. This interpretation is most elegant and appropriate.
Regarding the second point, clarifying what is open and what is obstructed: the fourteen characters and thirty-one characters constitute the "open" (tong);

the matters concerning the conditions of the basis constitute the "obstructed" (se). Regarding the phrase "from single up to all": the first is the initial clause, namely the four characters "Venerable Saṃgha, listen";
the third is the seven characters beginning with "If it is time for the Saṃgha"; and the fifth refers to the final five characters of the announcement (*śrāvaṇā*).
These are the three characters. The textual meaning encompasses one hundred and thirty-four [characters], with no more and no less;
this explains the aforementioned general principle. That is to say, the structural framework of the preceding fourteen characters is identical for all single-character "white" (bai) [syllables];
they cannot be increased or decreased. If one does not strictly adhere to this fixed standard, the ritual function will fail to be realized. As for the second and fourth phrases:

"Namely, 'May the Venerable Saṃgha listen' and thereafter, up until 'If the time has come for the Saṃgha'—this refers to the second root of the formal motion (*jñapti*), which is the dual citation of the basis.
From 'If the time has come for the Saṃgha' and thereafter, up until 'The motion is thus'—this refers to the fourth abbreviated citation of the basis of the motion.
The phrase 'each according to the matter' and so forth explains the meaning of the aforementioned obstruction; that is, it follows the specific formulation."

Regarding the explanation of the matters: when each item is cited according to its specific conditions, it refers back to the preceding conditions and is included within these two sets of four intermediate categories.
Because the text clarifies the matters accordingly, they are thus delimited. For example, as stated in the *Prātimokṣa*: "Today is the fifteenth day of the waxing moon;
this is the basis and the original occasion for receiving the precepts," followed by: "This person [the candidate] requests full ordination from [Master] So-and-so."

The *Jiayi chao* (Manual on Robes) is complete. From the passage "Now the Saṃgha confers the full precepts upon so-and-so" onwards, the basis of the formal motion (*nidāna*) and the main body of the procedure (*karma*) are both recited together.
This principle applies universally to all *karmas*; the same holds true for the basis and the main body. In the fourth section, the cases where the basis is recited alone are briefly omitted.
The original text cannot be cited; rather, both the basis and the conditions must be cited together. How is this known?
Because the matters addressed reveal each to be distinct, which constitutes a limitation. As for the principle that exists to inform the assembly and apply universally:

although the wording is limited, because the meaning of informing the assembly and the subsequent logic of the accomplishment of the decision are no different, it applies universally as a single formal announcement (*ekoddeśa*).

Regarding the phrase "as far as it can be understood," this distinguishes the meaning of the accessibility and obstruction of *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts). The phrase "the Saṃgha has already consented and further accepted the entrustment" concludes by returning to the thirty-one characters;
its textual meaning applies to both types of *karmavācanā*: the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (motion with one proclamation) and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (motion with three proclamations).
As for the "intermediate recording of conditions and matters," there is the formula "Let the virtuous monks listen" in the middle, followed by "Who among the elders consents? at the end.
The preceding constitutes the first phrase. "The intermediate 'Elders, do you consent? and the subsequent 'So be it'" constitute the second.
The preceding constitutes the third. Regarding the intermediate section, which restates the conditions and the matter according to the differing capacities of those addressed:

this means that in accordance with the specific requirements of the individuals being addressed, the phrasing may vary while the underlying meaning remains universal; thus, the restatement of the conditions and the matter follows each particular circumstance.
This is merely a textual restriction. Furthermore, although it is restricted, when announcing it to the assembly, the appropriate measure is applied;

because the definitive judgment establishes its meaning as universal, there are fifty-seven *jñapti-dvitīya* (one motion and one announcement) and thirty-eight *jñapti-caturtha* (one motion and three announcements), totaling ninety-five instances.

Thus, it is said that "the meaning is universal. This can be understood by analogy with the preceding *ekajñapti* (single announcement); since the distinction between universal and restricted is no different, it is said to be easily understood. (In the *Souxuan*, a separate commentary was provided here to clarify the conditions for various *karmavācanas*, but I fear it would be too prolix.)

An external objection: In the text of the *karmavācanā*, both the beginning and the end state, "May the Saṃgha listen; may the Saṃgha grant its consent. Why, then, is it said only "Venerable Sir" (*sthavira*) in the middle?
These two words, "Venerable Sir," belong to an individual. Why is there this distinction between the Saṃgha and the individual? Xuan says:
The matter is ultimately accomplished within the *saṃgha* and not in individual instances. One must address the *saṃgha* in accordance with the six points of harmony (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*).

Although provisional names are employed for the sake of designation, they are still raised individually; therefore, it says, "Venerable sirs, please grant your consent. As for the phrase "if [the time] has passed, it is also lost," this is because a mirror reflects by means of its clarity.

Having understood the meaning of these fundamental principles, one obtains what was previously bestowed. When performing a *karmavācanā* based on the conditions received, there is no need to do so again.
This is the text of the *karmavācanā*. If one recites this dharma from memory without understanding it, even if one applies it to the situation at hand, it is still a failure.
Regarding the phrase "the three are correct and the others are incorrect": if one acts in accordance with this, there is no fault and the four [requirements] are fulfilled;

conversely, it is called "incorrect. This will be explained extensively below. Regarding the phrase "from the *jñapti* to 'not accomplished'": as for the three phrases in which both the wording and the meaning of the *jñapti* are fully present, I shall now explain them.
It should be stated that the three phrases within the *jñapti* (formal motion) are common to both the literal text and its underlying meaning. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen" constitutes the first phrase;

"if the time is right for the Saṃgha" constitutes the third and fifth phrases. Thus, there are three such phrases. The total number is one hundred and thirty-four, all of which are not distinct [in their application].

This is because the text universally announces to the assembly and commands them to listen, extending even to the formal announcements (*jñapti*) and so forth; thus, the meaning applies to the *karmavācanā* (ritual procedure).
Regarding the "Middle" [section]: "The text is comprehensive; O Virtuous Sangha, listen! Which elders, if you do not approve, speak forth... and so on, up until the character *chi* (持).
The text and meaning are fully explained across ninety-five translations, yet from beginning to end, not a single word may be added or subtracted.

Xuán states: "In the *dān-bai* (single-announcement) formula, the character *da* (大) is the beginning, and this character [at the end] is the conclusion. In the *jiemo* (karmavācanā) formula, the character *da* is the beginning."

The character *chi* (to hold) is the end. Some say that within a single phrase there is naturally a beginning and an end; for example, in the phrase "white" (*bai*), the character *zhong* (middle/big) is the beginning, and the character *ting* (to listen) is the end.
One should understand subsequent *karmavācanā* procedures by this analogy. Both interpretations are acceptable. Regarding the term "a single word" (*yiyán*): Xuán says:

It is a single utterance. Within these fourteen characters of the *shandai* (single-announcement) formula, one must not increase them to fifteen characters, nor decrease them to thirteen characters and so forth.
They must be recited in their entirety; if there is a deficiency or an excess, it is invalid. An excess is an addition, and a deficiency is a subtraction;
consequently, the preceding rite will not be accomplished. This interpretation is correct. Alternatively, one may follow the tradition of Ganso-sha.
"Li. [The Master] explained one sentence as one word, just as the Confucian texts say: "The three hundred pieces of the *Shi* can be summarized in one word: 'Let your thoughts be without depravity.
This means that because there are three hundred pieces in the *Mao Shi*, it says "the three hundred pieces of the *Shi*.

Regarding "summarized in one word," "summarize" (*bi*) should be read with the departing tone (*qùshēng*). "One word" refers to "let your thoughts be without depravity," which constitutes that single word. This means to manifest...
Zhengyi said: "The thoughts of a gentleman are all correct. Since it is said that 'his thoughts are without deviance,' these three characters constitute a single phrase;
now they may be paired with the phrase 'pure as suchness' (bai ruoshi), which is likewise a single phrase. Dade said: "The three characters form one phrase; you may pair them as you wish."
Or [sentences] may consist of four or five characters. How could one fail to understand this, or misinterpret it? A secular text says "yi" (義, meaning);

that [scriptural passage] says "si wu xie" (思無邪, "thought is without depravity"). Although this consists of three characters forming a single sentence, it is intended solely to clarify the single character "zheng" (正, "correctness").
Is this not, in effect, using a single character as a single word? Furthermore, when composing poetry nowadays, people speak of "five-character" or "seven-character" [lines].

These are also five-character and seven-character [lines]. It cannot be that there are five or seven phrases simply because there are five or seven characters; thus, one should know that this is not an understanding.
Fearing that there may be those who follow such an error in the present day, I have recorded this here.

Regarding the phrase "the rest up to the True Dharma": "the rest" refers to that which is external. Excluding the fourteen characters and thirty-one characters of the skeletal framework of the *jñapti-karman* (the formal motion consisting of a single announcement), everything else is called "the rest.
As for the phrase "the text is restricted while the meaning is universal": the text is restricted because it is not fixed according to the specific capacities of beings.

Although the phrasing is specific, the underlying meaning—concerning the proper proclamation of the circumstances, the assessment of propriety, and so forth—is not distinct; rather, it is universally applicable.

In short, anything that accords with the facts and is appropriate is termed a "matter" (*vastu*). For example, when receiving the precepts, having no physical impediments or disqualifications and possessing a complete set of robes and bowl—all such instances are called matters.

This matter accords with the precepts and the Dharma; therefore, it is called "accordant matters" (*śun-shi*). When there is a person who seeks the precepts and the Sangha possesses the intention to bestow them, this is precisely what is appropriate.

"Not even a fragment" (*pien wu kuai-hsiang*)—where "fragment" (*pien*) means a small amount—"contrary" (*kuai*) refers to being at odds, and "descending" (*xiang*) refers to a deficiency or inferiority.
Since everything is performed exactly according to the Dharma, there is not even the slightest contrariety, deficiency, or inferiority; thus, the matter is successfully accomplished. Moreover...

To cite the case of receiving the precepts, all other instances may be understood by analogy (and so forth). Regarding "increasing" and "abbreviating": "increasing" refers to expansion (*prapañca*), while "abbreviating" refers to brevity (*saṃkṣepa*).

For example, saying "one seeks to receive full ordination" (*upasaṃpadā*) constitutes an expansion; whereas if one says simply "full precepts" (*upasaṃpada*), although the word "full" (*pūrṇa*) is not explicitly attached, [the meaning remains the same].

This results in abbreviation. Furthermore, as with the term "Saṃgha" (the community of monks), it may also be expanded; conversely, to speak of it simply as "Saṃgha" is to abbreviate it. Regarding the difference between *gu* (gloss) and *xun* (exegesis):
these explain the aforementioned terms "expanded" (*fan*) and "abbreviated" (*lüe*). *Gu* refers to brevity of expression, while *xun* refers to elaboration of expression.

For example, in the first volume of the *Erya*, there are two chapters, "Gu" and "Xun," each explaining the single character "zhong" (multitude). In the chapter on "Gu," it says: "The teacher is the multitude."
The phrasing is thus concise. In the *Xunzhang* (Explanatory Chapters), it says: "Bengbeng" means "the multitude. When phrasing is repetitive, it is prolix;
therefore, we know that when one is about to explain the prolix, one will speak to clarify the concise. As stated in the aforementioned *Karmavācanā*: "The Sangha is fully ordained."
Excessive wording results in prolixity; conversely, to say merely that a monk possesses the precepts is a reduction of the phrasing.

Regarding the phrase "without losing the meaning of the text," whether it be elaborate or concise, although there may be differences in addition or subtraction, the correct principle within the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is not lost, and thus it constitutes the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
The True Dharma is precisely the *karmavācanā*. As for the phrase "the term 'category' (*jāti*) means 'to reach,'" this is intended as an explanation.

The Preface raises an objection: "How can it be known that there are variations in expansion and abbreviation, and that the glosses and explanations differ, yet all together establish the True Dharma?

To answer this by citing the *Chao* (Excerpts), it says: "By analogy with the various schools, etc. This means that one should apply the same logic as found in the *Karmavācanā* (ritual procedures) of the various schools regarding the expansion or abbreviation of the formal announcement (*natti*) of a matter.
For example, in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the fourth item is not included in the formal announcement (*jñapti*) for establishing a boundary (*sīmābandha*); the original text contains only the third.

In the three formal motions (*jñapti*), both the basis and the purpose are stated together. Furthermore, within the *karmavācanā*, even if the second intermediate section is omitted, the matter still succeeds.

Now, in this single proclamation (*jñapti*), both the basis and the purpose are presented together; the second intermediate section briefly restates the basis, and both the intermediate sections of the *karmavācanā* are fully complete.
Even if one character were reduced, it would not be among the essential bones [of the text], nor would it harm the meaning of the phrasing.
What logical error is there in this? Therefore, it is said that even regarding the meaning of the treatise, there is not the slightest discrepancy.

As for cases where the phonetic meanings of the Sanskrit and Chinese translations are entirely divergent: "Sanskrit" refers to the language of India, while "Han" refers to the speech of this land [China].

Regarding the divergence of phonetics and meaning, for example, the Sanskrit term *poṣadha* is also called *pōsuǒtuó*; translated into Chinese, it is rendered as "reciting the precepts" (*shuōjiè*). This is...

The term "sound" (*yin*) diverges from "Uposatha. Once the confession is completed, the offenses have arisen; whereas "reciting the precepts" (*shuojie*) serves to prevent those not yet arisen—thus, these two meanings are entirely different.
Furthermore, this semantic discrepancy persists even in the present day. If one adopts the Sanskrit terminology, it is stated in the *Jñapti-caturtha* formula:

"Today is the fourteenth day; the Saṃgha performs the Uposatha," or it is called *Po-sai-tuo* (Pāṭimokkha). If one adopts the Chinese terminology, it is simply called "the Saṃgha recites the precepts" (*zhong seng shuojie*). Up to this point...

The same applies to the fourth single citation of the root text. Thus, although the Sanskrit and Chinese phonology and meanings are entirely divergent, the *Chao* (Commentary) permits that the ritual procedures (*dharmas*) may still be successfully accomplished.

It states in reference to the preceding sentence: "What is transmitted through glosses and explanations is not without dual attainment; therefore, it is established by precedent. The meaning is as follows:
In the text of my current *karmavācanā*, there may be omissions or additions; based on the two preceding examples, both approaches are permissible, and thus the procedure is established.
(The text concerning these two examples from the first two sections of the *Souxuanji* is quite extensive; it is not recorded here in full.)

Regarding the question "Has it reached you?"—the intention here is as follows: although the monastic legal procedures (*saṃghakarma*) in the Vinaya texts consist of one hundred and thirty-four sections, complete in both phrasing and meaning, when it comes to performing these rites in accordance with specific occasions, one does not know which ones are essential or universally applicable.
This means that one continues to hold onto the text and read it. However, there is no scriptural basis for this anywhere within the Tripiṭaka teachings;

thus, both the text and its meaning are deficient. When the ancients observed such practices, they found neither textual authority nor doctrinal justification, yet they still clung to the text and read it while attending to their prior duties.
Whether there are those today who act similarly, I do not know if their affairs can actually be accomplished by doing so. [The response concludes: "As for the answer..."

Regarding those who claim that this does not constitute *niyata* (a formal determination): let the Master answer directly. If one merely adheres to the literal text and reads it aloud, one will certainly not find it;

thus they say it does not constitute *niyata*. The questioner asks: "In principle, for a prior matter to be judged as *aniyata* (undetermined), there must be scriptural authority stating that the action violates the teachings;

therefore, one establishes the *aniyata* by evaluating the act of staying [in the community]. Now, within the Tripiṭaka, there is no such textual or doctrinal basis at all. How does the author of the *Chao* [the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*]..."
What authority is there for claiming that this is not established as a fixed rule? One may cite the *Chao* (Excerpts) to answer:
"Although there is no explicit decision, it may be sought through the underlying meaning," and so forth.
Regarding the similarity in the ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) of the *Śīla-mātṛkā*: this is the principle for correctly interpreting the meaning established above.

That is to say, according to the Vinaya, if one does not recite the precepts during the ritual procedure, one must not be separated from one's formal reliance (*niśraya*) for as long as one lives; this is because both are methods of "active observance" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*).

"How could it be appropriate not to recite? This refers, for now, to the similarity in the requirement to recite. Furthermore, when performing the *Poṣadha* (confession of precepts) or conducting *Karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts), it is necessary in both cases to strike the bell to assemble the Saṃgha, to distinguish between those present and those who have sent their consent (*chanda*), and to perform the inquiries and responses for concord.

Since these ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) are similar, they are said to be "similar in ritual procedure. Below, the formal announcement (*jñapti*) regarding the actual breaking [of the assembly] states: "The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* must necessarily be recited."

Regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedures), how could it be permissible to merely recite the precept texts of one’s own school or those of other schools? It is not permitted to recite them at all;

however, if there is a rule mandating that they must be recited, this principle should apply to the *karmavācanā* as well—it too must be recited. Question: How can one know which precept texts of one’s own school or other schools are mandated for recitation so that they may be put into practice?

Answer: The *Shuochao* (Commentary) serves as proof. Thus, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if no one recites [the precepts] during the half-monthly assembly, [the procedure is deemed incomplete].
Regarding the phrase "the precepts, etc. (and so forth), concerning the prohibition against redundant recitation, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

"The patterns and models of the True Dharma possess constant standards. To recite and explain them repeatedly causes the listeners to become superficial and dull; therefore, it is not permitted" (the above is from the commentary). Question: What if there are instances where one recites redundantly? Answer:

Violating these regulations naturally constitutes an unrighteous act (*adharma*). Since this is the case for the text of the precepts (*śīla*), the same principle applies by extension to the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedures).
Furthermore, one must not perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) twice. To perform it a second time constitutes a "double performance," which is improper.

Some say that double performance is currently not permitted, as it is nowhere mentioned within the thirty chapters [of the *Karmavācanā*]. This, however, does not fully grasp the underlying intent of the teachings.
It is merely a matter of preaching the Dharma and reciting the sutras. [The questioner asks: Originally, the fortnightly recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) was established; now...
Since there was no one capable of preaching, [the assembly] ceased; why then trouble oneself with preaching the Dharma or reciting the sutras? The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) answers:

"Because the three trainings support a person, and the precepts are the foundation of the teaching, they are established first. Only when it is certain that no one can recite [the texts] should one listen to the preaching of the Dharma;

otherwise, one merely recites the sutras. (The aforementioned *Shu*). Based on this, the Master [Yuanzhao] now relies on the text to further criticize the aforementioned practice of reading the *Karmavācanā* aloud.

This is not so. The intention is this: if it were permitted for those who recite the precepts to all be able to distinguish the characters, then it would suffice simply to unroll the scroll and read it in sequence;

why then would such numerous methods be required? This is because their recitation is not permitted. Since the text of the precepts is thus, and the *karmavācanā* (ritual formulas) are likewise matters of performance and maintenance, when they are chanted according to the rules of the school, the manner of performance is similar and the assembly is identical.
"How can one read [this] aloud?"—this is the meaning of its manifestation.

Regarding the phrase "furthermore, as for those who have attained the Way": this refers to secular incantations and the like; that is to say, secular talismans and worldly arts, distinguishing them from the mantras maintained by the Buddha.
As for "the text not being accomplished through recitation," it is like the empowerment of secular methods, wherein one chants it with the mouth.
By forming mudrās with the hands, one can eliminate malevolent influences. The phrase "but only" (*tan-shih*) serves to explain the meaning of "not reciting" mentioned above.
It means that according to worldly principles, what is valued lies within the mind; this is equivalent to maintaining correct and deliberate visualization.
If one maintains undistracted empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the preceding matters will be easily attained, and sincere verification will surely arrive. Regarding "a few words of the text" and so forth:

if one clings to the literal text and reads it with the mind [as mere words], one cannot attain oneness; much distraction will arise, and the matter will not be accomplished. The above has merely cited worldly examples.

Therefore, those who recite mantras within the Buddha-dharma—such as the practice of reciting the *dhāraṇīs* of the five families (*pañcakula*) at present—all of these are dhāraṇī-techniques of the Buddha-dharma.

When holding these mantras, it is only after passing through a number of recitations in the billions that spiritual wonders manifest. If one recites them for only a single period, even if one attains some benefit, it is not yet profound;
I have never heard of anyone being able to receive the empowerment of the preceding *karmavācanā* rites merely by reading the mantras.
The Buddha taught that even the recitation and maintenance [of the precepts] is difficult to accomplish, let alone the practice of incantations (*dhāraṇī*). This implies that incantations are easy;
yet if one cannot even master what is easy, how could one succeed in what is difficult? The *Vinaya* introduction clarifies this:

it states that while the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) of the rishis were created by comparison with the Buddha, the establishment of incantations was established by comparison with the Buddha’s own teaching of the Dharma. Furthermore, incantations belong to the rishis.
Even those who have merely composed [the texts] are made to recite them; since the *karmavācanā* was personally proclaimed by the Buddha, how could it be read silently?

Regarding those who remain dependent on others for their entire lives, the rules for upholding the Dharma state that if one does not recite the precepts for five years, they shall be dealt with according to the law. If one recites first and then forgets [the text], [the same penalty applies].
If one's faculties are dull and one cannot memorize the teachings, one shall not be exempt from the requirement of relying on a preceptor for as long as one lives.
As for the phrase "I have arrived at this Dharma": "I" refers to myself; "Middle" is a specific designation for the Five Indias;

and "Country" is a general term for a settlement or community. By using the Dharma to distinguish the person, the Three Piṭakas are thereby manifested. "Capital" refers to the place where the Son of Heaven resides.
A *lǎn* (pronounced *jū*) is a precious carriage used by emperors and kings. For example, Senghui ascended the carriage of the Ruler of Wu, and Dao’an ascended the *lǎn* of the Ruler of Qin;
those who have transmitted the teachings are not few. Therefore, they are called the "Masters who translated the scriptures.
Since the passing of the Buddha, we have never seen this method of reciting the *karmavācanā* aloud.

Regarding the question on "reaching the thorough understanding" (*yìtōng*): as for the various methods by which monks and nuns perform rituals for one another—namely, the *yìfǎ* (procedural rules) performed by monks for nuns and the *fǎ* (rituals) performed by nuns for monks—how is it that both are texts of *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts)? For this reason, this section must be explained in detail. Answer:

Regarding the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) mentioned in the *Vinaya*: this refers to the combined heading of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇaka-vinaya*. First, I shall explain the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. As Xuánzàng says:

In this Vinaya for Bhikṣuṇīs, because Kālodāyin addressed deceptive words to the bhikṣuṇīs and thereby disturbed the community of nuns, the Buddha ordered that the *karman* of "non-prostration" (*anavaṇdanīya*) be performed against him by the Saṃgha.
The *Karman-vibhāṣā* states: "In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there is only this single [case]; however, according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, there are three types:
the bhikṣuṇī performing the 'non-prostration,' 'no-conversation,' and 'no-respect' [karman] against the bhikṣu. This refers to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

There are three [types]; the four-part [karmavācanā] is only one. These are all *jñapti-caturtha* (white-four) procedures. Regarding these *karmans*, it is not necessary for the person concerned to be present and make a personal statement;
that is to say, they may be performed at a distance without requiring the presence of the bhikṣu before whom the act is done, nor is it necessary to take his personal statement or the like.

As for the Sangha performing [procedures] for a bhikṣuṇī, there are also three methods. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), fascicle 40, states: "At that time, there was a bhikṣu who acted on behalf of a bhikṣuṇī..."

Regarding the *karmavācanā*: the bhikṣuṇīs were displeased and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "A bhikṣu should not perform a *karmavācanā* for a bhikṣuṇī, except for the procedures of receiving the precepts (*upasaṃpadā*), the *mānatva* penance, and the rehabilitation from offenses (*āpattivyutthāna*).
As for other matters, they do not apply reciprocally. The *Karmasūtra-vyākhyā* states: "The three rounds of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations)."
Beyond this, they do not practice it. Their teaching diminishes the practice of *prātimokṣa* (self-indulgence). It is not that there is no mutual variation or mutual interaction;

rather, each performs its own communal rites (*saṃghakarma*). These two divisions do not perform them face-to-face, unlike the previous three or two divisions which collectively preside over the rites.

Regarding the question concerning "arriving at [the proper time]": the intent of the question is as follows. It asks whether, according to current ritual procedures, one may perform the *naivāsika* (non-resident) ordination in the presence of a *bhikṣuṇī*, a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, a *śrāmaṇerī*, or lay men and women. The answer is: it is not permitted. Next, the scriptural evidence is cited.
The Vinaya rules state that one may perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) only when the location is beyond the range of sight or hearing [of others]. An external objection states:

"One must not perform it in the presence of laypeople (*avadātavasana*), because the matter is secret and superior; they should not hear it, as they are ignorant and inferior and incapable of upholding the precepts.

Furthermore, it must not be seen by those of the three lower assemblies, for fear of the difficulty of 'thieving residence' (*caura-vāsa*) which would prevent the reception of full ordination (*upasampadā*). Moreover, Mahāśramaṇīs have already received the Great Precepts."

[The Buddha said: "It is understood. Why was it not permitted? He replied: "In the original context of the Vinaya text, it was indeed permitted. Furthermore, because the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) committed an offense, they told the nuns of the group of six:

'If you see the Saṃgha raise a formal charge against us, you must intervene on our behalf. Later, during the time for the recitation of the Prātimokṣa, the Saṃgha raised a charge against the group of six;
the nun then intervened on behalf of the bhikṣus. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha established the rule that [a nun] is not permitted to stand before the bhikṣus."

If one performs the rite while facing [the person], it is not auspicious for the formal act of confession (*pāyattika*). This excludes the case of the person for whom the rite is performed, namely those receiving the fundamental precepts (*upasaṃpadā*) and nuns undergoing purification from offenses (*āpatti-vinodana*).
Apart from these, it is strictly improper to exclude the person for whom the rite is performed by means of such a statement.

At present, when performing the ritual of receiving the precepts, the presiding master asks the one who has not yet received full ordination, and the respondent provides the answer according to the rule. Within this context, there is no [exclusion].
Regarding those who have not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*), someone rebuked them, saying:

"Since it is said that there are currently no śrāmaṇeras or *dharmabhikṣuṇīs* here, how can this be the Great Precepts? Since you have not yet received full ordination, you must leave; these are simply ignorant people."
This is merely empty talk. Recently, when performing the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), one has held it to apply specifically to this person;
thus, that which was intended [for others] has already been clearly excluded by the text. Why, then, should further doubt arise?

Those who ask this question now do so only out of fear that, apart from this person, there may be others who have not yet received the precepts. Therefore, the preceding text states: "The Dharma does not arise in isolation."
There must have been a specific purpose [for this]. If it were further in the past, then performing the rite at a distance would have been established as valid;

however, regarding the practice of the present time, if one wishes to consult the ancient records and answer according to the Dharma, people simply state that, with the exception of the person for whom the rite is being performed, there are no others who have not yet received full ordination. Furthermore, this also accords with the literal text.

Second, regarding the removal of doubts and obstacles: when the *bhikṣuṇī* community undergoes the rite for the expiation of offenses (*āpatti-vyutthāna*), some maintain that this does not apply, stating that the person for whom the rite is being performed must be excluded.

However, the original ritual procedure was established specifically for the sake of this very person; if one were now to exclude them, for whom would the rite be performed? One should simply answer directly:

"There is no one here who has not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*). While one might consider breaking the rule based on this [argument], reflect deeply and carefully; the previous explanation alone should be regarded as correct.

Previously, it was stipulated that the four types of *śrāmaṇerikās* and others were the persons for whom [the procedure] was intended; beyond these, there are further individuals who have not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*), for whom it is strictly improper.

Nowadays, however, one frequently observes that when nuns receive ordination, it is not necessarily ten nuns; rather, the number of venerable monks (*bhadanta*) is also present nearby to witness the conferral of ordination.
Or, when the nuns perform the primary rite (*mūla-karman*), the great assembly of monks goes there to observe them presiding over the ritual. Both of these cases are...
The foolish teachings of the commoners are already incomprehensible; they do not realize that those who understand the ritual methods upon the altar must likewise be in accord.

Often, there are many great virtuous ones on the altar who themselves do not understand this matter at all. This is largely because these rites were established in their raw, initial form, and they have never studied under an enlightened master, resulting in such ignorance and obscurity.
Since these are matters of immediate necessity during a single ritual session, one must be extremely careful.

This is to clarify the taking [of life]; therefore, it is explained at length. Reflect on this. Regarding the exclusion of King Piṇḍola and others: previously, for the time being, it was stated according to the general rule that one must not face a layperson.
Now, in this subsequent opening, there is permission for those mentioned above. As the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vibhaṅga* states: "The bhikṣus always assemble in one place every half-month.
The king wondered in his mind what they were doing; he did not permit [the assembly] of laypeople. The Buddha then ordered that an opening be made."

To preach the precepts before the king and thereby dispel his doubts is itself the purification of the mind. This is like Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty composing the *Chuyao lüyi* (The Vinaya Ritual for Essential Deliverance), which likewise opened the way for the king to examine and read the monastic codes; this may be taken as an analogy.

Regarding the question "up to the middle": the intent of the question is as follows. In cases such as the *jñapti-dvitīya* (one motion and one announcement) or *jñapti-caturtha* (one motion and three announcements), or in procedures such as receiving a day’s grace (*āpatti-śuddhi*), receiving ordination (*upasampadā*), or disciplinary penalties—within a single *karmavācanā*, how many people can be admitted?

If they are not the same, it means that depending on the specific matter at hand, the number of those involved is also indeterminate; thus, there are four different cases. If it concerns an admonition, a parable, or a conciliatory admonition, [the number] may be obtained.
"Adding how much" correctly explains the meaning of the aforementioned differences.

For example, in the case of Devadatta, when he did not lead his own followers, five hundred people who had split the Saṃgha were all successfully admonished by the Saṃgha acting according to a single Dharma.

Likewise, if a group of monks is disputing—whether numbering one hundred, fifty, or more—it is also permissible for four people to act according to the Dharma and admonish them. Therefore, it is said that "adding is permissible."

"To some extent. Regarding "as for the administration of *karma*, the *jñapti*, and so forth": "administration" refers to the four types of *karma*, such as *tarjanīya* (reprimand) and *pravāsanīya* (expulsion).

"Proposal" (*jñapti*) refers to the three types of proposals, such as the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations). "Request" (*jñapti*) refers to requesting the undertaking of a practice or requesting the confession of an offense.

"For the sake of" (*arthāya*) refers to the transgression of receiving a day’s leave. It shall not exceed four people; at most it may be three, and at least it may be two or one. If it reaches four, the administration and the proposal together constitute a *saṃgha*.
If one proposes [an action] and requests that the *saṃgha* perform it, it immediately constitutes the *saṃgha* acting as the *saṃgha*. Question:

When other fully ordained (*upasaṃpanna*) bhikṣus perform a legal act (*dharmakarma*), even if there are only four of them, at the very moment they perform the act, is this not the *saṃgha* acting as the *saṃgha* beyond doubt?

Furthermore, for instance, when granting the precepts to a śrāmaṇera, since he is not yet a full monk (*bhikṣu*), on what basis can it also be said that the *saṃgha* acts as the *saṃgha*? (Mirror Water Great)

Deyun said: "At the initial administration of the *dharma*, the assembly has not yet become a *saṃgha*. It is only upon reaching the third *karmavācanā* and arriving at the word 'say' (*śā*), when the fourteen characters ending with 'the *saṃgha* has already consented' (*saṃghena kṣāntam*) have been reached, that the four-part *śrāmaṇera* finally attains the essence of a *bhikṣu*.

At the moment of the formal conclusion, it is precisely the *saṃgha* administering the *saṃgha*. This is even more difficult; one fears the status of *saṃgha* might not be established. Now, since the essence has been received and established..."
The monk asked, "Why do you not permit it? He replied, "Because it violates the regulations; the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of binding the boundary will not be accomplished.

Now, the tradition merely says, "I fear there may be the fault of a monk performing [the rite] for a sangha," yet no one fully understands the underlying principles or the proper limits therein. One should reflect upon this.

Regarding the "two or three persons" in the context of the fourfold difficult matters (*caturvargika-karman*): when there is no difficulty, one person serves as the leader; it is only when there is a difficulty that two or three persons are permitted.
As for the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and other texts, they apply to all formal acts (*karmas*) and generally do not allow for a fourth person;

there is no textual opening [in those sources] permitting four members. Regarding the *Vinayamātṛkā* and others: if there are four or five companions who can offer admonition, this indicates that the quorum of the Saṃgha is fulfilled within one's own division (*nikāya*). That...
If one is punished when they do not deserve it, or if one is alone and has no need [for companions], yet falls victim to calamity and harm, is this not suffering?
One should act with *līna* (resignation). Although the heart cannot bear it, one should at least not speak of it, and so forth. Fifteen types of *līna* are largely similar to this.
Regarding "among the nets of the multitude," according to the forty-third fascicle of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, within the *Kṣudraka-vastu*, fifteen [types] are clarified.
This is the seed. The *Xiāngpǔ* (Phases Section) states: "The reason for requiring the *sūri* (preceptor/teacher) is that, in discussing all monastic laws, harmony is paramount.

If the Saṃgha acts improperly—meaning contrary to principle and so forth—one must cause them to be rebuked and interrogated. However, one who is capable of rebuking must necessarily know whether [the offender] will proceed or not."

Now, fifteen types are enumerated, explained in groups of five. Regarding the first five, they are called *adharmavādin* (those who speak what is not Dharma). 1. Seeing a formal act (*karmavācanā*) performed according to the Dharma, one declares it to be contrary to the Dharma;

this is termed *kārya-vādin* (one who speaks of what ought to be done), yet it is fit for censure. 2. Seeing a formal act performed according to the Dharma, one declares it to be contrary to the Dharma while seeking to gain good companions;
this is termed *ākrośa-vādin* (one who speaks with reproach), yet it is fit for censure. 3. Seeing a minor offense, one applies a formal act [of punishment] to it.

1. *Heharī*: To see that there are those within the boundary who have not assembled. 2. *Heharī*: To see that there are those on the boundary platform (*sīmāmaṇḍala*) who perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults).
Next, the five [cases] where it is *dharmī* (in accordance with the Dharma): 1. *Lī*: Seeing an act performed as non-Dharmic;
it is called *lī* because one does not discern the object. 2. *Lī*: Seeing what is non-Dharmic; it is called *lī* because there is no virtuous companion. 3. *Lī*: Seeing a grave offense.
1. Because it is extinguished by means of a *karmavācanā* (formal act of the Saṃgha). 2. Because there is no one within the fourfold assembly who has not gathered [for the purpose]. 3.

Because the views exist within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) and the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) is performed. 4. The latter five are in accordance with the Dharma: i. Being in accordance with the Dharma, they should be in harmony. ii. They should remain thus. iii.
Being in accordance with the Dharma, they should grant their consent (*chanda*). iv. They have heard from a trustworthy person. v. They were previously present among the assembly.
"Li-zhu. Regarding those within the legal assembly's net, it is said: 'If one sees the assembly gathered performing what is illegal, they should be rebuked.
If there are no virtuous companions, one may depart after declaring one's intent (*chanda*). If that is not possible, one should speak to both sides. A person says:
'Lead away from the illegal [area] by sixty-three paces or more. Whether there be a great mountain or earth/salt and the like—outside the mountain or outside the salt—even [if...]"
This [distance] is sixty-three paces. Since there are intervening obstacles, should one gather [the boundary] or not?

Furthermore, within those sixty-three paces, if there is a path or a boundary for walking, should one gather that as well? Moreover, within those sixty-three paces, if there is a water boundary, must it be gathered?

One should observe whether there are mountains, large walls, and so forth. Master Huain says: "It need not be gathered because they constitute intervening obstructions. The Venerable [Master] says: "It must be gathered. First.
Thus, these are both on land; furthermore, as they are within their respective boundaries, they do not combine to form a separate unit.

If it is a path traversing a village boundary (*grāmaka-avadhi*), it must also be combined, because the village boundary is powerful enough to encompass it. If it is a water boundary (*udaka-avadhi*) within sixty-three paces, it ceases upon reaching the water;
each does not encompass the other, as there is no principle of relative strength or weakness. Beyond this, for the forest (*araṇya*) boundary, the path boundary, and the water boundary, all are...
They do not mutually encompass one another; all of this is established according to the *Karmavibhāṣā-śāstra*.

Alternatively, even if both parties are not virtuous persons, it is sufficient that they possess a mind of restraint (*ārakṣa-citta*), as in the analogy of a house being consumed by fire (and so forth). It is as stated therein.
Regarding the question, "As for the phrase 'the text reaches the *caoshu* (extract),' what does this mean? the intent is as follows:

When the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) establishes that a preceding matter has been successfully accomplished, at what point in the text does it reach its conclusion? This refers to the timing of its completion. In response, it is explained that there are many approaches.
The *Karmasūtra-vyākhyā* cites three interpretations from the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*. One master says: "The point where the word 'said' (*shuo*) appears is the place of completion. [The mind...]
The treatise states: "In a single kṣaṇa, both the manifest action (vijñapti) and the non-manifest action (avijñapti) constitute the fundamental karma.

The second master says: "The character 'to reach' (zhì) is the locus where the precept is obtained. The third master says: "Only upon reaching the character 'to maintain' (chí) does it become ultimate.

Among these three interpretations, the interpretation of the third master is largely rejected as being excessive. Regarding the first point concerning the character 'to explain' (shuō), the present master now refutes it.
It says: "Compared to the previous two instances, this appears to be the place of residence. If one were to cite the subsequent [instance] to encompass the preceding ones, it would not yet be final.

Upon reaching the point where one cannot bear to speak, someone immediately rebukes them, and thus it is not accomplished. Now, taking a single method as definitive is identical to the second interpretation.

The *Chao* itself explains: "That is, after the third statement has been made... (and so forth). As for why it differs from the previous interpretation, it is because that [previous view] is not adopted.
This is the interpretation of the first master. The Vinaya states: "As for 'patience,' it extends even to those who revile and break [the precepts]. This is cited as scriptural proof.
Since one has already instructed another to speak, if that person suddenly speaks of matters regarding which one lacks patience, how could this not constitute a breach? Fabao says:

The first master countered and rescued [the argument], saying: "If one has not yet reached the word 'to speak,' the dharma is fundamentally unformed; if one has reached the word 'to speak,' that dharma is already formed; thus, even if one rebukes it, it will ultimately not be destroyed.
He then caused the master to refute [this] by saying: "One names it 'endurance' (kṣānti); if there is no endurance, one speaks immediately upon hearing the sound."

An immediately stated that there is the accomplishment of a dharma. Baoyun said: "This refers to the fact that at the very moment the sound of the reprimand and the sound of the word 'state' (shuo) coincide, it is thereby reprimanded and destroyed.
Fabao said: "Regarding this collection of dharmas, it means that the characteristic of the village is large, while the characteristic of the monastic quarters (saṃghārāma) is small."

This constitutes the "narrow boundary" (*sīmā*) and the "broad assembly" (*saṃgha*) based on the boundary. Regardless of whether the physical characteristics of the monastery (*vihāra*) are established or not, one must always assemble according to the village (*grāma*).

This is because the stronger designation takes precedence over the weaker. Alternatively, if there is a waterway piercing through this village, those crossing from the interior should assemble at the water's edge if there is no bridge;
if there is a bridge, they should assemble together across it. Or, if there are monks upon the water...

Nor is it necessary to assemble [the community], for water differs from dry land; the two realms are distinct. If there were a path traversing the realm, that would be subsumed under the category of a village.
As for "if one's patience fails" (ni-li-xia), the Master here may rely on the first interpretation:

that at the moment the word "to speak" (shuo) is uttered, even if the assembly has not yet reached the point of formal censure, the attainment of the precepts is not hindered. This is the place where the precepts are acquired. Regarding the phrase "attaining both at will," this refers to a mirror and water.

The Venerable One said: "If one utters the sound of a syllable and then, upon reaching the moment of pronouncing the character, someone objects, this is logically untenable; only when one has finished taking up the character is it truly correct.
If the sound of the syllable has ceased and only then does the other party object, or if there is no objection at all, then the ritual act is accomplished at the very moment the character is spoken.
Since both cases apply depending on the circumstances, it is said that 'either way is acceptable.'"

Regarding the *Guangyi chao* (Extensive Commentary): it clarifies that among the interpretations and judgments of the three masters, there are mutual points of correctness and error, as well as the principles for resolving difficult points.

Regarding the *Xuanji* (Mysterious Record), its attempt to analyze [the text] by means of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) is incorrect; one should reflect upon the meaning of the text. [The same applies to] the section headings and so forth.
This is the first [section]. The above concludes the "Chapter on the Dharma to be Upheld.
Next, the "Chapter on the Delimitation of Boundaries for the Place of Upholding the Dharma" is explained in two major divisions:
