As for "if it reaches the ultimate characteristics," the text also has three sections: first, a brief indication of the preceding conditions; second, the formal explanation of the chanting method; third, from "If there are...

onwards, the demonstration of the chanting method with intervening obstructions. Regarding the preceding conditions as mentioned above: the one appointed [to chant] shall immediately assume the ritual deportment and arise.

Ritual: Having performed three prostrations, one stands and chants: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! I, the bhikṣu [name], for the sake of the Saṃgha, announce the boundaries and characteristics of the great boundary of the four directions," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the method for summoning the Saṃgha by means of a formal motion (*jñapti*)," since the procedure for summoning the Saṃgha by means of a formal motion has already been completed previously, why is it repeated now?
Treatise: There is an interpretation which states that this was clarified for the sake of convenience, but it likely lacks scriptural basis.

Now, following the *Wanling* [commentary], the preceding section merely clarifies the four locations and six characteristics for gathering the Saṃgha based on natural boundaries (*dharmatā-sīmā*). If the designated boundary is wide while the actual boundary is narrow, one should gather the people based on the designated boundary.
This has never been clearly explained; therefore, it is analyzed here. Regarding the one who conveys the *chanda* (consent), this refers to the time of establishing the boundary (*sīmābandha*).

It does not permit the transmission of *chanda*, for its meaning is not analogous to the detailed exposition of the causal rules found in the preceding section. From the words "First... up to "according to...":

"One must first [ensure they are] entirely within the natural boundary" means that while the demarcated area established by ritual action (*karmavācanā*) is narrow, the natural boundary is broad. When monks from various boundaries assemble, it is all calculated based on this.

[The boundary] is naturally established by assembly. If the marker (*liṅga*) and the boundary (*sīma*) are equal, it is also established according to the boundary (the two types of assembly mentioned above do not differ between ancient and modern traditions).

If the marker is wide and the boundary is narrow, and [the boundary] is established according to the marker, this is what the present master establishes; the ancient masters did not permit it. Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and other texts:

following the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika*, when a bhikṣu has completed his summer retreat (*varṣā*), there may be trouble from officials or kings, or many insects on land and water, such that he cannot come and go freely.

Fearing that [the rains retreat] might be broken, it is permitted to establish a boundary of three *yojanas* (one hundred and twenty *li*). At the time of the initial establishment, the Sangha must assemble;
they must gather at all the designated markers. Otherwise, one may have another person temporarily go outside the three *yojana* limit to establish it.
Therefore, that text says: "Have them all called in, or they may go beyond the boundary. Now, in this case, since it is intended for two days, it is not necessary for everyone to assemble.
The above is the interpretation of the present master (*jinsī*). From "There is a master" onwards, the ancient views are recounted; there are three points. The first point says:
"But [the rule] ends with 'naturally' (*zìrán*) and so forth. The ancients said: "Even if the designated area is broad, within that designated area, 'naturally' refers to my sixty [li]."

"Three steps away. Therefore, it is not required in the *Wuyao ji* (Collection on What is Not Required). Furthermore, "those for whom the ritual procedures (*dharmas*) have not yet been performed" refers to the second meaning. The ancients said:

"Since the ritual procedure of formal motion (*jñapti*) has not yet been performed, and the time for the formal announcement (*jñapti-caturtha*) has not yet occurred, it is by nature not yet established as the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Even if the ritual procedure (*karman*) is being performed, as long as one has not yet reached the utterance of the words [of the motion], it is likewise not yet the ground where the ritual act is accomplished. Once the words have been uttered..."
The ritual procedure for establishing the *dharmadhātu* has already been completed; why then discuss "spontaneity"? Therefore, a formal assembly is not required.

If the *karma* is performed through formal resolution (*jñapti*), it is only when there is subsequently a gathering of the Saṃgha that [the requirement] arises. If they do not assemble, it will certainly constitute a separate community (*nānāsaṃgha*).

Regarding what is clarified in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, this refers to the third point. The ancients said: "One must not cite other passages from the *Mahāsāṃghika* as precedents. Furthermore, regarding what is clarified in the *Mahāsāṃghika*:
Because there were difficult points [in the ancient commentaries], they were all cited and collected. Since this is not a difficult circumstance, it is not permissible [to do the same here].
The Venerable Master said: "The new chapter is identical to the ancient interpretation; the *Chao* (Commentary) follows the text of the original *Shu* (Sub-commentary).

Regarding the phrase "According to principle, this is not so," etc., the present master refutes the ancients. Since they established three points to refute him, we must now likewise collect and refute them one by one using three methods.

Furthermore, an ancient master previously stated: "As long as one remains entirely within the boundary (*sīmā*), there is no need for a formal assembly. Now, this is refuted by saying that this necessarily constitutes a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*).

Therefore, the Commentary states: "The general binding [of the boundary] within the marked area is intended to establish two types; at the time of the simultaneous chanting, the binding of a separate assembly occurs within" (the first point of the ancient view is thus refuted).
Previously, an ancient master said: "That which is within the marked area is not 'natural' (*svabhāva*); moreover, because the ritual has not yet been performed, there is no separation."

Regarding the term "the assembly" (*saṃgha*): Now, the refutation states: For example, when performing the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, at the moment the word is recited, the boundary for the ritual action (*karmabhūmi*) is established as a whole within the marked area.

Yet, when subsequently performing the formal act of binding [the boundary] back into the fourteen characters, if there are monks upon the ground within that marked area, would this not constitute a separate assembly?

(The refutation of the three ancient interpretations is complete. As for what the ancients previously said—that according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, if there are difficult circumstances, one must immediately gather people according to the markers—this...
Regarding the statement, "After this period of leisure, there are no difficult circumstances; therefore, it is not necessary to assemble," we now refute it as follows:

Even during those times of difficulty, when the circumstances are urgent, one still assembles according to the designated schedule. How much more so during this time of leisure when there are no difficulties—how could one possibly fail to assemble?

Even in cases of urgency, one must still gather [the assembly]; it is not permissible not to gather them. There is no such principle [to support the ancient three-fold interpretation]. Therefore, it is said that according to reason, this is not so;

rather, gathering everyone together is essential. Regarding the lack of authoritative scripture to rely upon: this means that the present master relies on the designated gathering, which accords with the text of the *Cīvara-vastu*.
The ancient masters merely exhausted the natural course [of events], and there was no scriptural basis for their position. (The preceding textual analysis is concluded. Ancient and modern...
There are many explanations. The previous *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* passage regarding "obstacles" (*vighna*) is an error concerning the obstacles posed by wicked bhikṣus. The Venerable [Master] said:

"I have previously examined that text, which states: 'If a bhikṣu has already completed the earlier retreat (*pūrvavārṣika*) and a difficult situation arises—whether it be bandits, a king, threats to life, violations of the precepts, or an abundance of insects in the water such that it cannot be strained and purified—and he wishes to go to another monastery to avoid these circumstances... "

Within a distance of three *yojanas*, if there is a bhikṣu there, he should be summoned. If [the boundary] has already been exited, one should perform the formal ritual (*saṃgha-karma*) [of binding the boundary].
(The above is the original text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*). If one refers to them as "evil bhikṣus," then even if they are within [the boundary], they will ultimately refuse to come when summoned;

how much less would one have them exit the boundary and then perform the ritual? Fearing that people might misunderstand the intent, I now explain it again: when lecturing, it is also permissible to cite the preceding text.
Regarding the phrase "if it is within the boundary" (*sīmāntara*) up to "the example," this refers to the current assembly of the Saṃgha.
Baoyun says: "There are two types within the boundary: first, those naturally within the village; second, those naturally outside the village.
If the monks within the village inside the boundary must assemble, then for the sake of thorough protection, the monks within the village outside the boundary must also assemble. This is because...

Regarding the boundary marker (*sīmā*): "Always naturally" means that for a village located within sixty-three paces of the natural boundary, the monks inside the village do not need to assemble from outside;
this refers to what is said after the formal establishment of the boundary (the correct exposition of the principle is now concluded). Next, the various commentaries explain:

if there is a village within sixty-three paces of the natural boundary inside the marker, the monks within the village must necessarily assemble, because the performance of the ritual requires urgency.
If the boundary markers are inside [the village] while the village itself is outside, the bhikṣus within the village need not assemble.

Although they are situated within the same natural boundary (*prakṛtisthaka-sīmā*), because the proclamation has been made and because the characteristics of the village are identical, there is no fault of a separate assembly (*nānāsaṃgha*). The *Fǎbǎo* (Treasury of the Dharma) says:

"If that were so, consider for a moment a place where the markers are narrow but the boundary is wide; since the area outside the markers is also a natural boundary, they still assemble there. Now, in this case..."

Where the boundary markers are wide and the area they enclose is narrow, or where there is a village within the boundary but outside the markers, these are also naturally included; how could they not assemble?
Furthermore, if they did not assemble at the time of the initial establishment of the boundary, how could it be said that "the current teacher assembles the Sangha according to the markers"?

Therefore, one knows that when the initial proclamation of the boundary is made, everyone must come together; once the proclamation around the village is finished, the rite is completed by the formal act (*karmavācanā*). This demonstrates that at the moment the dharma arises, the village [is encompassed].
This is because it was not within the boundary at that time. If, after that, there were further legal matters (*dharmakārya*), the monks within the village would not need to assemble from outside.
However, the various households did not grasp this meaning, assuming that at the time of the original establishment of the rule, anyone within the village was exempt from the requirement to assemble.
Now, according to the current practitioners of the Jianghuai region who lecture on this [text], they mostly rely on this interpretation; therefore, I have recorded it in detail.

Furthermore, there are two locations in Jiangxi where villages surround one another. At these two sites, when first establishing the community, there was no requirement for everyone to assemble, as the villages were strong and self-sufficient.

If there are two villages with four boundary markers (*catur-lakṣaṇa*), and these were not established at the time of the formal ritual (*saṃgha-karman*), then all persons must assemble together, because the boundaries of the village are weak.

Now, this excerpt concerns only the natural boundaries within the marked area and the village outside; since the boundaries of these two areas are already fully encompassed, it is said that there is no need to assemble those from the outside.
The full details are contained in this text, so there is no need to labor over further searching. I fear some might rely on this explanation.

This is intended to dispel public confusion; therefore, I have briefly pointed this out so that you may understand it. If there are nuns or others within the boundary (sīmā), they shall serve as the presiding heads for the monks and nuns respectively, but they shall not participate in the formal ritual (saṃgha-karma).
It is no fault if they do not assemble. If there is a formally established monastic boundary (saṃgha-sīmā) and so forth...
Even though [the other monks] are within my sixty-three paces, or within the boundary markers when performing the rite of binding the boundary, there is no need to assemble them;
for that is a ritual boundary (*karmabhūmi*), and one cannot naturally assemble those from another ritual boundary. The superior assembly need only remain inside the monastery;
they may enter my natural boundary (*prakṛtistha-sīmā*) immediately. First, circumambulate that boundary and proclaim its internal characteristics.

This concludes the section. To summarize the connection [between the examples and the principle], it says: "As with those dwelling separately within the Cakravāḍa mountains. This is stated by way of illustration for fear that people might not understand.

It is like the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) encircling the four great continents; taking the three-yojana Great Boundary as an example for the Iron Ring Mountains, and taking the four great continents as an example for the four separate dwellings where rituals are performed, the meaning becomes clear.

Regarding the statement "the assembly does not gather": this means that those who share the same fundamental basis refer to the fact that first there was the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) and subsequently there were the various *karmavācanā* (formal acts).

The *poṣadha* is the root; everything beyond it is the branches. Therefore, it is said that "the assembly shares the same fundamental basis. Regarding "not being able to withstand the *karmavācanā*," Baoyun says:
"The ground is naturally weak and cannot withstand the desire for formal acts (*kāma-karma*); this does not refer to the *jñapti-dvitīya* or *jñapti-caturtha* [procedures]."
As the phrasing for the time of transmitting the *chanda* (consent) states: "Venerable Sangha, listen!

Since this is now a natural occurrence and not an act performed according to the formal procedures (*saṃgha-dharma*) of the Sangha, how could there still be a formula for transmitting consent? Therefore, it is not superior. How is this known? According to the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the Karmas), it asks:
"The previous statement that receiving consent is subsumed under the *pratyekamukha* (individual) procedure—since that *pratyekamukha* applies to both realms depending on the location—now..."

Question: Why is it that the *svabhāva* (natural) method does not apply? Answer: Because dharmas have both permeability and obstruction, they are called "models" (*kāimō*). The *sīmā-bandha* (boundary-binding) with the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (one motion and one announcement) is restricted solely to the *svabhāva* method;

the proclamation of *chanda* (consent) and the *pratyekamukha* (face-to-face) method are exclusively performed through formal ritual action (*vidhi*). Although the former is initially termed "face-to-face," this is based on its causal designation;

when analyzed according to its ultimate conclusion, it results in a communal monastic act (*saṃghakarma*), and thus the *svabhāva* method is not applicable [to these]. (The preceding is from the *Shūwén*).

Regarding the phrase "second, the addition of the noble dharma (*āryadharma*)," since the preceding section has already completed the formal proclamation based on the designation, we now add the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the legal procedure consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation).
This rite was formulated by the Noble Ones (*ārya*), and is therefore called the "noble dharma. Regarding this, the *Xuánjì* provides a brief analysis:

the person who proclaims the boundaries (*sīmā*) may not preside over the *karman*, and the person who presides over the *karman* may not proclaim the boundaries; this is because at the time of performing the rite...

Regarding the procedure for designating the boundaries (*sīmā*) for entry into the Dharma: although the individual's name is not explicitly stated, it is said, "The bhikṣus of this residence shall proclaim the fourfold boundaries for the Saṃgha.
Is it not improper to designate oneself? Furthermore, when proclaiming the boundaries, one must not mention the name; likewise, in the *karmavācanā*, the name is not recorded.
This indicates that there is no separate action performed for an individual, but rather for the Saṃgha as a whole. If, however, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* does mention the name...

In the *Sifen* and *Wufen* Vinayas, names are generally not mentioned. Master Baoyun states that although names are occasionally cited in the *Shuochao*, these were likely added during the ritual proceedings and were subsequently removed;
one must not cling to such textual variations. Regarding the phrase "up to the person who marks the boundary": this refers to the person chanting the boundary markers.

Once they have returned to their original positions, they inquire about the essential matters of the rite and proceed according to the standard protocol (etc.). Regarding the phrase "it should reach the formal announcement (*jñapti*)."
This matter has been extensively analyzed in its essential points in the preceding section; it need not be described here in further detail.
Regarding the phrase "from two to [many]," this clarifies the method for establishing a *sīmā* (boundary) with a *śīmaṇḍala* (precept-field).

As for the term "precept-field" (*śīmaṇḍala*), first let us explain its name. The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "Precept" (*śī*) generally encompasses correct practice, while "field" (*maṇḍala*) refers to the process of discernment and refinement."

Coarse. It seems that all worldly sites are nothing but accumulations and knots. Next, regarding the examination of the original texts: the Venerable Jing-shui cites the *Biézhuàn* (Separate Tradition), which says:
"When the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove, the bhikṣu Louti [Ratna] established altars for the various Buddhas to perform the *sīmā-bandha* (delimitation of the boundary) and confer ordination.
The Buddha permitted him to establish three altars within the Jetavana itself: to the east of the gate of the Buddha’s courtyard, he named the first 'The Buddha as a Bhikṣu'."
The ordination platform (*sīmā-maṇḍala*) was established to the west of the main gate of the Buddha Hall; this was named the Ordination Platform for Bhikṣuṇīs, with the Buddha presiding.
To the south of the eastern gate of the outer enclosure, the Saṃgha was stationed to serve as the Ordination Platform for receiving the precepts for bhikṣuṇīs.

The eastern altar was constructed by Mahābrahmā, and the western altar was constructed by Māra Pāpīyas (the above is according to the records of the origins of the ritual sites in the Western Regions). As for the establishment of the ordination platform in the Eastern Monastery:

Regarding the term "Yuan" (Origin/Source): the *Biographies of Buddhist Monks of the Liang* states that in the seventh year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, the śramaṇa Guṇavarman from Shanyin established an altar at Nanlin Temple in the capital of Yangdu, ordering those receiving the precepts to receive them while departing from the altar. This was the dharma-method of Taisi of the Eastern Jin.
Furthermore, an altar was established at Waguan Temple. During the Liang dynasty, Sengyou established four altars:

the first at Yunju Temple, the second at Xiqia Temple, the third at Guishan Temple, and the fourth at Jing’ai Temple. Beyond these, there were others in the eastern mountains, the north of the river, and Jian-nan.
In total, there were more than three hundred such sites; even to this day, their legacy has not declined.

Thus, it was by means of these ordination platforms that the Buddha-dharma in the region south of the Yangtze River has continued without interruption and the scriptures of the Triple Gem have flourished (the above is recorded briefly according to the *Jietan jing*; the full text is as found therein).

Regarding the statement "as for those who arrive first," concerning the boundary markers (*lakṣaṇa*) outside the *śīla-maṇḍala*: some say that if the *śīla-maṇḍala* has internal boundary markers, one must apply the word "external" (*bāhya*) to distinguish them.
Since there are currently no internal markers, it is inappropriate to speak of "external. One may simply refer to them as the "boundary markers of the *śīla-maṇḍala*.
This is a detailed refutation found in the *Chao-wen*; its original intent is not yet known, so please reflect upon it. There is no need to labor over the rest. Thus it is said.

Regarding the actual matter, there are two points in the text: first, to demonstrate that the diagrammatic illustration is beneficial; second, to cite examples of what is not [proper] as a warning. The first is as stated in the text;

the details of the diagram’s appearance can be understood from the illustrations. The Great Virtuous One said: "First, one should indicate the four directions; next, distinguish the outer circle, the central square, the small squares, and so forth.

This will be briefly pointed out during the lecture. Next, the commentary explains the gathering of those near and far. Question: Since the assembly of the Sangha has already been mentioned previously, why is it mentioned again?
"Chapter. Now, why does he clarify this further? Baoyun said: "It is merely because of the profusion of text that he clarifies the practical application of the matter.
He was asked again: "Why does he not write it in prose, but instead compose it as a commentary? Wanling said: "It is for the sake of avoiding prolixity; there is no other principle [behind it]."
Regarding the phrase "this is the external limit": this refers to the circular natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*) outside, which is like the halo around the moon.
This is the sixty-three paces that naturally extend beyond when establishing the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*).

If the monks are to assemble within the *sīmā*-enclosure (*śīmaṇḍala*), they must also assemble from all four sides; this refers to the location of the small red square, the body of the *śīmaṇḍala*, as shown in the diagram. First...
At the time of concluding the boundary, one first assembles the Saṃgha at this location;
it is likewise sixty-three paces, no different from the assembly for the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā). One then instructs them to draw another circular mark. Why is it not seen now?

One may cite the relevant passage. The answer states: "Those listed in the diagram," and so forth. This refers to the concealment of the *śīma* (boundary) and the gathering within the increased natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*).
Question: According to the preceding text, the *śīla-maṇḍala* (precept altar) accommodates twenty-one persons, or according to other schools, forty-one persons.
Now, when various regions establish a *śīma* for ordination, they all follow this precedent. Since it has already been stated that within this [boundary], first—
When the assembly gathers, there may be two hundred people who come into the hall and find there is insufficient seating. How should this be adjudicated?
There are two explanations. First, according to the Ācārya of Ruizhou: if the number of gathered monks is large and the seating is already insufficient...
Furthermore, if one causes others to go beyond sixty-three paces, one is exempt from the offense of being apart from the assembly (*bhedasaṃgha*). Second, according to Master Huainan:
"Let as many as possible sit together; if the *dharmakarma* (formal ritual) is performed, it suffices to follow the minor announcement (*kṣudrakavācana*).

As for the other monks, even if they are outside the arena but within sixty-three paces, there is no violation of being apart from the assembly, provided they have not all come for the purpose of gathering. Fabao says: "The two..."

Each interpretation has its own reasoning. Even if one were to proceed with the practice now according to the first explanation, it would still be impossible to suppress or override it; reflect upon this.

As for the statement that "having reached this point," it is because this monastery (ārāma) is narrow while the natural boundary (jñapti-kṣetra) is wide. Now, the Master says that one cannot distinguish between a village and a small monastery, nor between a [small] monastery and a natural boundary.
According to the *Cīvara-vastu*, sixty-three paces constitute a monastic community (saṃgha-ārāma), which is wider than the natural boundary; thus, it is employed.

The passage concerning "merely avoiding difficulties" exhaustively indicates the collection [of the text]. As for the monks outside the North Zhu (Red) Courtyard, this precisely refers to the distinct groups of people who head toward the central monastic community.
Their heads are positioned sixtieth-three paces apart from north to south; the distance from the center of the north to the center of the south is one hundred twenty-six paces.
The text arranges the three assemblies together within a single diagram, measuring one hundred twenty-six paces in both length and breadth.
Regarding "reaching as far as the distant or near": as for "marking according to the characteristics," this refers to the formal ritual procedure;

it means that one should assemble [the monks] at a distance or nearness based on the markers of the boundary's characteristics. It does not depend on the natural state of the area at the time of the original binding. This can be understood from what follows in the text.

Next, regarding the distinctions in the diagram: as for the statement "this [boundary] must necessarily have a distinct boundary," it refers to the *dharmakarma* (formal ritual) *saṃgha*-boundaries, water-boundaries, and so forth, which cease precisely at that point. These may also be crooked or irregular;

however, for now, we shall rely on the four sides where there is no distinct boundary at all, each extending to sixty-three paces. Thus, the substance of the boundary is simply circular. As for its...

Regarding the "Ultimate Characteristics" (Zhìxiàng): from the passage in the *Chāo* beginning with "From within the vermilion square" up to "is called spontaneous" (*zìrán*), it generally indicates spontaneity as a whole.
From the two sides of the northeast down to the "spontaneous realm" (*zìrán jiè*), there are six lines of the *Chāo* text.
This explains the characteristics of the natural state. Regarding "below and above the small wall": this refers to the area directly below the small wall and upward toward the ground;
both are considered part of the natural state. There is an interpretation which states: because it is "below" the small wall and "above" the top of the wall, the term "below and above" is used;
however, this is not the correct explanation. Regarding "slanting away for about two chi": Fabao states that this is two chi, two cun, and two fen, according to the standard measurement.
This is determined by calculation; thus, the character "xu" (allowance) refers to the remainder. Regarding the phrase "having struck three stakes":
this refers to the stake at the southeast corner, the stake at the southwest corner, and the stake at the northwest corner of the ordination platform (*sīmā*) mentioned earlier.
Since these are all counted together, it is said that "the three stakes have been struck. Some say: "At the due west, eight feet from the great wall, one may strike [a stake] oneself."

Regarding the three stakes (*trayaḥ kīlakāḥ*), one should carefully examine and transcribe them; do not hastily offer conjectures when practicing. If two dharmas are performed, the *sīmāmaṇḍala* (precept site) constitutes one, and the *mahāsīmā* (great boundary) constitutes the second.

Xuán says: This refers to the space measuring approximately eight *cun* (inches) between the southern and western edges, situated within the wall of the *mahāsīmā* and outside the cord of the *sīmāmaṇḍala*.
This naturally vacant space contains monks, yet it does not obstruct either the *mahāsīmā* or the interior of the *sīmāmaṇḍala*.

Regarding the handling of affairs, it is therefore said that there is no obstruction in either location. As for the phrase "because it reaches [the limit]": if one clarifies the external boundaries (*bāhya-lakṣaṇa*), they must necessarily be proclaimed from outside.

This means that since the boundary marker (*sīmā-cihna*) is affixed to the great wall, when now proclaiming the external boundaries of the Great Boundary (*mahāsīman*), one must proclaim them starting from outside the wall.
If one were to proclaim them from within, they would coincide with the internal boundaries of the Great Boundary; furthermore, one may not enter [the interior].
Regarding the phrase "singing [the boundary] at the great enclosure wall" (*da-yuan-qiang*), this refers to an earthen wall that is extremely wide, perhaps six or seven feet or more.

Fearing that people might employ clever stratagems—such as being inside the wall so as to merge with the inner boundary—[it is asked]: "Since the wall is now thick, would it not be possible for [a tunnel] to pass through the very center?

The *Chao* (Commentary) refutes this by stating: "Because the boundary-mark (*xiang*) is not seen. Generally speaking, for something to be called a "boundary-mark," it must possess [visible characteristics].
[The Master] praised [this]. Now that it is situated in the middle of the wall, how could it be seen? This is truly not possible. Regarding the statement "upward one cannot reach":

the term *jie* (界) is a word used for something that is approximate and not yet exhaustive; it is a matter of entrustment. There are many instances of the four locations and six characteristics (*xiang*).
For now, we shall cite those that cannot be distinguished. The southwest corner is one instance regarding the boundary field (*sīmā*). Not yet...

Regarding the necessity of relying on diagrams: it is not necessarily the case that the *śīma-āyatana* (ordination platform) must be situated in the southwest, nor that there must be small walls on the northeast sides, or stakes driven into the ground on the southwest sides.
Alternatively, it may be like the construction of lecture halls or Buddha halls nowadays, located in the center of the monastery.
All such arrangements are determined by the circumstances of the time; for now, I shall set forth the rules so that people may understand how they arise. If one does not rely [on these principles]...
This investigation of other locations is likewise not yet clear or refined.

As for the statement, "Now, the method for establishing the boundaries is explained in three parts," this refers to the actual explanation of the procedure for establishing the *sīmā-kṣetra* (precept field). There are three methods for the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary).
First and last constitute one; the proclamation of characteristics constitutes two; and the performance of the legal procedure constitutes three. Regarding the "initial conditions of first and last":
this refers to first establishing the *śīma-kaṇḍa* (precept-field) and subsequently the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary). Regarding the phrase "according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*":

that Vinaya’s method for receiving the precepts states that if a monk receives the precepts within the boundary as a separate assembly (*pṛthag-jana*), the Buddha declared it contrary to the Dharma. From this time forward, [it was permitted] to proceed toward...
Outside the boundary, one may establish a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) to receive [the precepts]; this is the *śīlākṣetra* (precept platform).

Later, because various bhikṣus were taking those who were to receive the precepts there and encountered bandits on the way who robbed them of their robes, bowls, and other belongings, the Buddha said that they should perform it within the monastery grounds (*saṃghārāma*).

If the large boundary (*mahāsīmā*) has already been established within the monastery grounds, how can one separately establish a *śīlākṣetra* on natural ground? The *Chao* (Commentary) quotes the *Vinaya*, saying:

If a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) was previously established, one must first relinquish it and then re-establish it at the former location; thereafter, one should proclaim the boundary markers to establish the great boundary.
Fa Bao states: "When it says 'one must first relinquish it,' this means that the old great boundary is dissolved, whereby the entire area becomes naturally open ground (*prakṛti-sthita-bhūmi*).

'Then re-establish it at the former location' refers to establishing the boundary for the *sīmāmaṇḍala* (precept site) at the previous spot. First, instruct one bhikṣu to proclaim the boundary for the *sīmāmaṇḍala*."

Regarding the boundary markers: one bhikṣu establishes the sequence by announcing the internal and external markers of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). One bhikṣu then performs the formal act of motion and resolution (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to establish it.

However, fearing that if one were to establish a *karmavastu* (ordination site) directly upon the existing substance of the original boundary, it would constitute a "double establishment" (*punar-bandha*), the rule was therefore enacted requiring that the former be dissolved.

The responsibility lies in tying it on the ground naturally; this is merely to avoid the fault of double-tying. (The interpretations of various schools regarding this section are all incorrect. Regarding "the *vinaya*," etc.:
in that second method of establishing boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*), one is likewise instructed to proceed from small to large.

As for the phrase "even now there are people," etc., this refutes the errors of the ancients. The ancients said: "There is no explicit text in this Vinaya [to support this]; at present, when performing the binding, one simply first..."

If the large boundary is established first, the small one will necessarily be obtained. The reason for this is threefold: first, the Buddha permitted the establishment of a *sīmā-maṇḍala* (ordination platform) within a large boundary;

second, the text for the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of establishing a *maṇḍala* states, "this dwelling place"; and third, the *maṇḍala* is specifically exempted [from the requirements of the larger boundary]. Possessing these three meanings, it is established.
Therefore, the *dhātu* (elements) come first and the *sthāna* (sites) come later. As for the claim that "this does not accord with the holy teachings," this is a refutation by the present Master.

If one says, "The Vinaya contains no explicit text [to that effect]," this person has never read the text of the *Pañcavargika-mātṛkā-śāstra*, for therein the Buddha prescribed the minor rules first and the major rules later.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "residence" (*āvāsa*) within the wording, it refers to the dwelling of the four modes of conduct at one time.
It is not that there was no prior establishment of a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) before it is said to be "this residence.

Regarding the question as to whether it is permissible: the inquiry, "Is the prior binding of the great boundary and the *karmavastu* (precept field) established? is a counter-question regarding the preceding text. It asks:

even if one were to newly bind a boundary at this present time, relying upon another ancient site where a great boundary was previously bound, would it be possible to subsequently establish the *karmavastu*?
Regarding the response concerning the clarification of what should be relinquished and then re-bound, etc.: this refers to the procedure within the fivefold text (*pañcavastuka*).

When the boundary outside the *sīmā* (monastic zone) and the *karmavastu* (ordination platform) are abandoned and one is made to move back to bind [the boundary] within the *sīmā*, does this not prohibit the relinquishing of the old great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) and instead require that one first establish a platform on natural ground and subsequently encircle it with a great boundary? However, the original intention was merely to fear that...

Regarding the fault of "re-binding" (double-binding): according to the method of establishing boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*) used by the ancients mentioned above, at the time of performing the rite, one first reserves a natural ground in advance.
Once the establishment of the Great Boundary (*mahāsīmā*) is completed, one then establishes the boundary for the ritual site (*karmabhūmi*).

Although this involves a discrepancy between the earlier and later stages, since it is established upon a natural ground, it does not incur the fault of re-binding. The subsequent phrase is thus settled, stating: "Therefore, it is known that [the boundary] is formed."

This means that it is established by way of the absence of subsequent bonds (*punarbandhana*). If so, why did [the author] previously criticize the ancients for relying solely on mental verbalization (*manojalpa*)?
Below, he immediately refutes this, saying: "However, it does not establish the subsequent dharmas, and so forth. Fabao says:

Because this contradicts the teachings regarding the point of binding, and because the ritual performed above—such as receiving the confession—is not in accordance with the Dharma, there is fear that it will not be accomplished; therefore, it must be resolved. This is the interpretation based on this passage.
He accepted the confession and took it as a precedent for subsequent practice, citing the *Pañcaśata-praśna-śāstra* (*Wubai wen lun*) to corroborate this.

Since the text states, "fearing that there will be no attainment," the word "fear" (*kong*) denotes uncertainty. This implies a doubt that attainment will not occur; "attainment" (*huo*) here refers to the act of obtaining. Furthermore, the *sīmā* (precept field) is the foundation of ritual performance (*dharmakriyā*).

If the time of its establishment violates the teachings, then regarding the rituals performed upon it, one must fear that they will not be valid. The text further states: "Below, [the offense is] grave."

The explanation is thus established. Although the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* prescribes that the small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*) be established first and the large boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) afterwards, we currently see only the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, which first establishes the large boundary and only subsequently permits the establishment of the *śīma-kaṇḍaka* (the restricted area for the *poṣadha*).

It is not known whether this was a later regulation of the *Pañcavargika*. Now, it may be permissible to perform the ritual procedures upon this site as if it were during the period when the rule "first the small, then the large" had not yet been established;
thus, [the rite] should be successfully accomplished. As for those who rely on mere chance, they encounter [this opportunity] by fortune rather than through their own merit.
This is meritorious. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* has already established the rules. If one now intentionally violates these established regulations, the ritual act will certainly not be valid.

However, if one truly did not know [the rule], it is equivalent to the period before the rules were established; in this case, performing the ritual on this site will certainly be successful (the correct principle is hereby concluded).

According to the *Yunji*, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* is treated as the "subsequent dharma" (*paścātkalpa*), meaning that the sequence of first small and then large [rules] established in the *Pañcavargika* is not considered invalid.

This is the Dharma. Alternatively, according to the interpretation of Rui Sheng in the capital, the *śīma-avasthāpana* (the marking out of the boundary) is treated as a subsequent rite (*paścāt-dharma*).

His explanation states: "The question refers to the *śīma-avasthāpana*, while the answer responds by means of the *mahā-sīmā*. Since the preceding text says 'therefore it is known that it is established,' this citation establishes that the *mahā-sīmā* is successfully formed;
however, the subsequent rite is not accomplished, and the *śīma-avasthāpana* is not finalized. This is illustrated by the analogy of relinquishing [the boundary].

Regarding the *Śīla* (Precepts), it is appended to the section on the *Dharmas*. In the response to the question of why the *bhikṣuṇīs* are not permitted to come again, the answer reverses the previous point by bringing in the *bhikṣus* once more;
this case is likewise so. The Venerable Jing-shui said: "The two interpretations above are both incorrect.
If one takes the *śīlākṣetra* (precept platform) and the five divisions as the subsequent *dharmas*, then the passage from the *Pañcaśata-praśna-śāstra* cited below is entirely [inapplicable]."
This would result in futility; I earnestly request that you examine this in detail. If you do not believe it, consider it further.
As for the statement, "Now, arriving at the site," this is incorrect as it is set forth extensively. It is said that the procedure is divided into four parts:

first, not assembling [the monks] but proclaiming the faults of the additions; second, proclaiming the faults throughout the boundary; third, from above the great boundary, proclaiming the faults of the *karmavācanā* site from afar; fourth, not proclaiming the great [boundary].
The characteristics within the boundary are incorrect. Regarding those who do not assemble within the boundary: this refers to the *śīma-kuṇḍa* (precept platform);
it is a fault regarding the persons if one does not gather all those within the natural sixty-three paces. To chant the three phases collectively is a fault regarding the matter.

To perform both types of *karmavācanā*—for the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) and the precept platform—is a fault regarding the ritual method. "Chanting the three phases collectively" means that five or six people go to the platform.

Regarding the middle [boundary]: concerning the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) and the ordination platform (*sīmā-maṇḍala*), one chants the characteristics of both the interior and exterior of the great boundary all at once;

this is called "challenging collectively" (*saṃgha-ghoṣa*). First, chant the exterior characteristics of the ordination platform once; next, chant the interior characteristics of the great boundary once;

then, chant the exterior characteristics of the great boundary once. Thereafter, issue the collective command: "This is the exterior characteristic of the ordination platform; that is the great boundary."
Having completed one circuit both inside and outside [the boundary], this constitutes the general proclamation of the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Alternatively, regarding the "general proclamation of the three characteristics within the boundary," this differs from the previous case where they did not assemble; it follows the specific addition of the boundary, which is distinct from the former. As for the full procedure of the general proclamation:

first, proclaim the characteristics of the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept-platform) three times; next, proclaim the internal characteristics of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) three times; and finally, proclaim the external characteristics of the great boundary.
The three recitations are called the "Universal Proclamation" (*tongchang*). This refers to the principle that the Dharma follows the person, even when the circumstances differ.
"Three" means: first, one establishes the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*); then, within the Great Boundary, one establishes the *karmavastu* site (*sīmā-maṇḍala*) by proclamation from afar;

subsequently, when proclaiming the Great Boundary within the Great Boundary, one proclaims only the outer limits and not the inner limits, leaving no empty space between them—thus the two boundaries meet. These matters have already been [explained].

[The previous] section concludes. Now, the Master’s [previous] summary does not constitute a valid formal act (*karmavācanā*). Only when the boundary is formally established through the proclamation of the *sīmā* is it considered in accordance with the Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "from 'two' to 'having finished,'" the method of the proclamation is clear. Regarding the phrase "from 'the *karman*' to 'the Dharma,'" there is no further *karman* to be resolved.

The remainder is also easy to understand according to the text. Regarding the phrase "next, the method for the Great Boundary (*mahāsīmā*)," this is the heading. Regarding the phrase "first, to the one who arrives," etc.
In the previous separate recitation, one should say: "This is the internal boundary marker; that is the external boundary marker.

Once these three rounds of the internal and external markers for the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) are completed, they are then combined as a whole. Regarding the phrase "the text reaches the end": this means the text for reciting the markers has been read through.

As for the phrase "the place where the assembly arrives," it refers specifically to including only the single character "internal" (*antaḥ*). Question: According to the text, does it include both "internal" and "external"?

Regarding the character "zu" (foot/inside). Why is it said that there is only the single character "zu" within? One interpretation states: the single character "zu" internally excludes the character "wai" (outside) [though this is not correct].
Next, according to the interpretation of Master Xuán, following the Vinaya Master Guāng, the *karmavācanā* fully recites the boundary marks as the formal condition (*pratyaya*).

When establishing a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) without a designated precinct (*maṇḍala*), the recitation of the boundary marks says: "This is the perimeter of the great boundary outside; one circuit completed. Thus ends the *karmavācanā*.

The text states: "The Saṃgha now, within these outer marks of the four directions, internally demarcates a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). Upon reaching the second demarcation, there is a *karmavastu* site with a great boundary;
the ritual procedure (*karma*) likewise cites the proclamation of the marks as its basis. It is proclaimed: 'This is the complete circuit of the inner and outer marks of the great boundary.
In the text of the ritual procedure, it says: 'The Saṃgha now, within these inner and outer marks, internally demarcates a great boundary,' and so forth."
From now on, even if one proceeds as before, is it not sufficient with the single word "but" (*dan*)?
If one were to rely strictly upon the scriptural text (*vinaya*), the logic of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) actually requires adding two characters.

If, according to the scriptural text, one does not add any characters and so forth, the Master’s intention here is that by relying solely on the root text (*mūla-vinaya*) without any additions, the principle is nonetheless not lost. Nowadays, there are those who establish the boundary of the ordination platform (*sīmā*).

This is the location of the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). Regarding the fact that the *karmavācanā* text lacks the word "inner" (*antaḥ*) and yet one immediately censures [the proponent]: this is the behavior of those who lack knowledge.

In the case of the previously mentioned "unenclosed" (*anāvāsita*) Great Boundary, one proceeds directly to the proclamation of the boundary marks (*sīmā-lakṣaṇa*). In the case of the subsequently mentioned "enclosed" (*sāvāsita*) Great Boundary, it is stated that one must first formally announce and indicate the specific site.

This is because there is a fear that someone might transcribe the *karmavācanā* onto a wooden board [and thus omit the essential details]. Why, then, is this section placed after the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) in the case of this enclosed Great Boundary?
Yes. Xuanyue says: "In this context, there is no *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure). The subsequent reference is as stated above. Or, it may be objected:

"Although it is said that there is no *karmavācanā* for the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), was the preceding *śīmaṇḍala* (ordination site) not a *karmavācanā*? Now, one should simply understand that by performing the act of taking [possession], it is analogous to what came before."

Regarding the statement that "the three small boundaries (*kṣudrasīmā*) are divided into three parts": gathering the Saṃgha as one is the first; not erecting the boundary markers (*sīmālakṣaṇa*) is the second;
and the method of formalizing the boundary (*sīmābandhana*) is the third. Regarding the passage from "the initial" to "is seen": this is no different from the fourfold division [of the *Prātimokṣa*].

The *Vinaya* explains the method of reciting the precepts (*poṣadha*). Regarding the phrase "one who does not agree": it refers to one who has not yet left the original boundary (*mūlasīmā*). Those within the original boundary who should agree must leave the boundary quickly.
[The author] quickly resolves this. The *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Those who do not agree [with us] have not yet entered my seven *pañcavastu* realms.
Outside of twenty-eight cubits (*hasta*), the ritual procedures (*vidhi*) are no different from these; therefore, it says they are "without distinction. The *Fǎbǎo* states:

"The Vinaya is based on the discussion of not having exited another's original boundary, whereas the [present] treatise concerns not yet having entered one's own boundary. Since the conditions for entering and exiting are distinct, it is inappropriate to say they are the same. Now...

Although these are both instances of obstacles, they are not different. Regarding the phrase "in an araṇya, etc.," according to the *Vinaya* text on the small boundary for receiving ordination, it says:
"In an araṇya where there is no village. The text on the small boundary for the *poṣadha* says: "In the midst of a wilderness where there is no village.
And the text on the small boundary for self-protection says: "Not in a village, but in an āraṇya. Thus, one knows that it must certainly be an araṇya; it must be located [there].

"Villages that are not open" refers to those where one is hidden by walls and enclosures; thus, when wicked bhikṣus suddenly arrive, they are not perceived. Now, in an araṇya there are no walls or courtyards;

being concealed within the empty and remote expanse, it is easy to see them when they come. In the text, the character "difficult" (nán) is interpreted in one way as being pronounced with the level tone (píngshēng), meaning:
it is extremely difficult for wicked bhikṣus to come from there, and even if they do come, they are easily seen.
The second interpretation states: "A person who does not agree [with the practice] comes and creates obstacles for me by singing [a song].
Since it is a *viveka-pada* (an open space) that has come, it is easy to see at that time" (both interpretations are acceptable).
Regarding the statement, "Why are the four directional markers not erected?": this refers to the reason why the four boundary markers are not established.

Regarding the statement, "The Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā) and the site (kṣetra) reach the essence": this explains the principle for not establishing the square boundary markers. The Great Boundary and the site are enduring and stable dharmas;

the Great Boundary is where the Saṃgha constantly resides, while the site is where various acts such as receiving precepts and performing repentance are performed. It is necessary that each knows its own domain; therefore, they are established.
The threefold marking of boundaries serves to distinguish between host and guest, so that they may know these three minor realms and so forth.

Since they can be opened by means of difficult-to-bend [flexible] materials, and because this section on "temporary" [boundaries] is understood as soon as it is finished, why establish formal marks? It is sufficient that the body of the boundary simply follows the number of people present.

Regarding what is called "establishing the boundary" (*sīmā-bandha*): Dharma-wish Vinaya Master (*Dharmavrata-vinayadhara*) established the boundary when receiving the precepts. He stated that when receiving the precepts, one must inquire about obstructing conditions (*antarāyika-dharma*).
Therefore, he established the boundary on one side, like the handle of an iron brazier. For the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, one sits directly upright;

there is no opening for ritual implements, and the *Karmadāna* does not perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Since the formal procedures are not carried out, one simply sits upright; outside of this sitting, there is nothing else.
They sit in a circular formation for the *pravāraṇā*. Five virtuous monks are positioned in the center because they are to receive the invitation.
If they were to sit in a straight line or in a cluster, it would be inconvenient for conducting the ritual.

Regarding the phrase "as for this 'ultimate characteristic' (*zhìxiàng*)," the Master now refutes it as a whole. Since all three [types of boundaries] are opened up in response to difficulties and constraints, why is the "characteristic" (*xiàng*) alone retained for the reception of the precepts?
If the characteristic were retained, one would not avoid being censured for others. Now the Master says: there are no external characteristics at all;

rather, the seats occupied by the *saṃgha* are taken as the internal characteristics of the boundary. Regarding the phrase "thus, as for the ultimate characteristic," it serves as proof that [external characteristics] do not exist.

This refers to the external formalities. "The first part" refers to the text for receiving the precepts (*upasampadā*). "The middle part" refers to the text for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).
By these, one knows the number of people present; at that time, one must state whether there are ten, twenty, or more persons according to the prescribed rule.

For now, let us consider this number. "The latter part" refers to the text for the invitation to point out faults (*pravāraṇā*). The rest can be understood from the words. As for the phrase "if it reaches," it refers simply to the sequence.
The eighth [section] says: "If a bhikṣu possesses a robe that has been kept for more than ten days, he should invite the other bhikṣus to go outside the boundary.

If there is no designated *śīmaṇḍala* (precept-field), he should establish a small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*). The text of the *karman* states: 'The Saṃgha now, within one fathom outside this place where we are seated together...
This is a clear textual provision for an exception. It is the same method as the previous *śīmaṇḍala*; it is not an opening for a small boundary. That Vinaya is based on this.
Because it was difficult to assemble the Sangha within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), they went outside and established a *kṣetra* (boundary), which is called a "small boundary" (*kṣudra-sīmā*).
This arose because evil bhikṣus created obstacles so that [the assembly] could not go outside; in other cases where there were no such obstacles, this was not done.

However, ancient masters were confused by the single character "small" (*xiǎo*) and mistakenly identified it as the name [of the rite], leading to this error. Now, the Master says: if one does not believe [this], simply call the *kṣetra* a "small boundary."

As for this, within the *Caturvargika Vinaya* method for the *śīmaṇḍala*, the *śīmaṇḍala* is also designated as a "small boundary" (*kṣudrasīmā*). Is it not possible to establish the boundary marks within such a small boundary?

As for what was said regarding "reaching the center," when the ancients of old were receiving the precepts, they established the boundary marks on one side of the small boundary and conducted the inquiry within those marks.

[Objection: Difficult. Now, our Master has abolished [this practice] and does not permit it. It is unknown when this ritual procedure was established; where did our Master inquire about the obstacles (*paripṛcchā*)?
The *Shan-chao* (Commentary) quotes the Vinaya text, saying: "According to the Vinaya, the inquiry takes place outside the boundary (*sīmā*). Fabao says:

"Even though the text states that one should have the obstacles inquired about outside the boundary, the śrāmaṇera is actually behind the assembly of monks, which constitutes being 'outside the boundary. Therefore, the instructor does not employ [this method]."
Regarding "merely turning the body slightly when outside the boundary": this means that if one calls a śrāmaṇera from outside to come closer, it is permissible;

it does not mean that one must always leave the saṃgha and go entirely outside—know this. As for "when it comes to the time of requesting [the precepts]," etc.: this refers to the time before the śrāmaṇera has entered the assembly.
When ten people are currently present and sitting in a cluster, the priority is to be in front of them; there is no vacant space at all. If it reaches...

At the time of requesting and receiving the precepts, everyone simultaneously draws their knees together to open up the space between them, allowing one guest with bare feet to enter and receive the ritual.
Thus, they are able to perform the divisions of prostration and kneeling. Therefore, the *Karmavācanā-vṛtti* states: "Ten people harmoniously open the space to receive [the candidate]. Question:

Why, in cases of two or three people, is it not possible to harmonize the space because of the narrowness of the area in front of them? Answer: It is because of the narrowness of the space directly before them.
Furthermore, Baoyun said: "The monks may all move together to the rear half [of the boundary]; it is also permissible to do so on natural ground (*svabhāva-bhūmi*).

If that is the case, what scriptural authority can be cited from the *Vinayavibhāṣā*? If one says that one must necessarily occupy half of the external boundary, this is also based on the texts of the *Daśādhyāya-vinaya* and the *Samantapāsādikā*, which state that the quorum of the Saṃgha is fulfilled.
According to the *Daśādhyāya-vinaya* and the *Samantapāsādikā*, if a single bhikṣu is at one location..."
"Sitting. Regarding the number of monks required for the four positions of the feet, it is already established that [the requirement] may be fulfilled.

Now, with half my body outside, what is there that is improper? This is the principle. The *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: "Internally, it accords with the Buddha’s teachings; externally, it approximates what is permissible for the Saṃgha.

Because there is the merit of receiving the Dharma, and because there was no prior vow to receive it in vain—this is the definitive meaning. The phrase "must rely on former usage" and so forth clarifies this.

Regarding the ancients’ practice of leaving behind signs (*nimitta*): at the very moment they first form [the intention], it is not yet established; furthermore, one need not deliberate upon whether it is unrighteous or right.
As for the *Yichao* (Explanatory Notes), there are extensive question-and-answer discussions within the commentary (*śāstra*), which I shall not recount here as they are not essential points.
Regarding what is said about "adjusting" (*kāṅzhāng*): our current Master clarifies this according to the Vinaya. The *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) is a practice of the ancients.
As for the claim that this person’s additional application is not necessarily like that, our current Master says: the *pravāraṇā* is not necessarily fixed;

the sitting for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) is not necessarily always sitting upright. One may also adjust according to circumstances—whether the ground has many thorns or [the location is otherwise unsuitable].
The ground is often damp and uneven, making it impossible to sit cross-legged; one may only sit upright or sit in a cluster while reciting the precepts.

All such matters as adjusting the seating arrangements and establishing ritual protocols according to the specific circumstances should be handled in this manner. The *Record of Mount Ling* states: "For the recitation of the precepts, there is no requirement for elaborate furnishings."
It can be adjusted at that time. As for the five virtuous ones (pañcavarga) who sit upright during the *pravāraṇā*, where could they possibly perform their duties?
Since they are all situated outside the boundary (*sīmā*) in front of and behind those sitting upright, it is impossible to receive the *pravāraṇā* from those outside the boundary.

If one leaves a physical mark in front of oneself, it will again incur reproach; therefore, one must sit according to the ancient circular arrangement. However, this is not the case with the present-day robes.
As for the two groups of five virtuous ones (pañcavarga), they sit alternating with one another. When performing the ritual, there is no need to rise again;
one simply turns slightly to the left or right to approach and take the *prātimokṣa* (self-restraint) [vows]. What could be wrong with this?

Regarding the phrase "next, it arrives": this refers to the principle that the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual text) is now being recorded; however, because such occasions are rare, I have omitted details for fear of overburdening the paper and ink.
The formal announcement (*jñapti*) is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! The Saṃgha has assembled here to establish a small boundary (*sīmā*).

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of forbearance, grant permission to establish this small boundary. The *karmavācanā* is to be understood according to the same pattern [as the *jñapti*] (and so forth). Question: Regarding the establishment of the three...
Regarding the small boundary (*kṣudrasīman*): is it established by simply performing the *karmavācanā*, or must the boundaries also be proclaimed?

The *Nanshan Jie mosu* (Nanshan Commentary on the Karmavācanā) does not discuss this matter. According to the Xiangbu school, however, the boundaries must be proclaimed; although they do not separately establish four markers.
This is also based on the location where the bhikṣus assemble; one should regularly recite [the boundaries] starting from the outer edge of the body, beginning with the southeast, and so forth.
Alternatively, according to the East Pagoda, it is said that there is no need for this, as the rite is successfully completed simply by adding the ritual formula (*vidhi*).

The Preceptor from whom Tiantai received his lineage stated that the East Pagoda’s version represents the correct Vinaya text, and it does not require the recitation of boundary markers (*saṃketa*). Furthermore, within the *Karmavācanā* text itself, there is no mention of reciting such markers.
This is a false and forced interpretation; consider it carefully.

Regarding the statement, "As for the 'others' who are not permitted to leave the boundary," the "others" refers to the three types of distinct boundaries. Excluding the two common boundaries of persons and dharmas, the remainder is called "others.
As for the "three types," they are listed in the text of the *Chao* itself: first, the distinct boundary of separate explanation (*bie-shuo bie*).
Regarding "those who share both benefit and desire": the *Fǎbǎo* says this refers to a passage in the Vinaya where there were two monastic residences.
In one residence, there was only the Dharma but no food; in the other residence, there was food but no Dharma.
As each side lacked what the other possessed—those with food hoping for the Dharma to nourish the spirit, and those with the Dharma desiring food to sustain the body—the Buddha spoke as follows.

Each person, having understood their own realm, assembles in one place. The formal act (*jñapti-dvitīya*) is performed by first announcing the boundary marks (*sīmā*) and subsequently applying the ritual procedure.

(The above is from the Vinaya text; the commentary does not require further elaboration, as its explanation of the principles does not go beyond this. The *Xuánjì* states that the underlying meaning is no different [from what has been explained].

This merely cites the commentary; how can it lead those who come later to understand? Second, regarding the separate explanation of distinct benefits versus the collective explanation of distinct benefits:
the Vinaya also speaks in terms of two types of residences. One residence possesses both the Dharma and material sustenance; the other residence...
"There is only the practice of eating, but no [formal] dharma. Regarding this state of non-dharma, I wish to join this realm and discuss it together.

The Buddha said, "Each should understand and jointly perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) to bind [them]. The *Karmasūtra-vṛtti* states: "When both parties reside in one place, there is no formal ordination (*pravrajyā*) according to the Dharma; [this was] received by Huiming."
The principles of the Dharma are established based on this (the preceding memorial). Third, regarding the specific explanation of distinct benefits and common benefits:

the Vinaya states that there are two types of residences—first, those where both the Dharma and food are present; second, those where the Dharma exists but food is absent. Now, if one requires food to sustain the body and the Dharma already exists within one's own boundary, the Buddha said:
"I permit you to perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) to establish it. Thus, for both parties...

Regarding "common food" (*samabhojana*): some say that when establishing the boundaries (*sīmā*), one must also separately dissolve them and then collectively re-establish them; this is called the "dharma of common food and separate boundaries. This interpretation is reckless;

it must be that [the proponents] have never investigated the Vinaya texts. In the Vinaya, the Buddha stated: "I permit the establishment [of a boundary] by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation)."

It does not state that each [boundary] is separately dissolved while the same boundary is tied; nor does it mention chanting the characteristics [of the boundary]. It merely adds the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act with a motion and one proclamation) to tie two residences.

How could one falsely interpret this? Since the sacred word establishes two distinct realms, each separately encompassing its own assembly, performing the *poṣadha* separately does not constitute the offense of breaking the *saṃgha* through a *karman* or the offense of a separate assembly.
Only the shared consumption of offerings is prohibited; therefore, one cannot say that the original boundaries are separately dissolved. Thus.
In the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* (羯磨疏), this is termed "single meal in common" (*dānabhojana-sādhāraṇa*). Furthermore, the commentary states: "This is a monastic regulation (*saṃgha-vidhi*);

it is not originally for the purpose of establishing a boundary (*sīmā-bandha*). Because of the prior distinction between 'common' and 'separate,' when matters arise regarding the requisites of the Saṃgha from the four directions, the location to which they belong has already been determined.

If one were to perform a formal act of the Saṃgha (*saṃgha-karman*) [to authorize their use], it would be as stated in the preceding commentary. The *Vinayakośopāyikā* (鈔) explains this itself: "It is a method of chanting and responding for the purpose of guarding and maintaining the dwelling place."
The meaning of the *Dongta* (Eastern Pagoda) and the *Chaosu* (Commentary) does not differ; reflect upon this. "The Buddha has already... and so forth is the concluding text. *Dai* means perilous.

Zheng Xuan says it refers to the *ji* (the royal domain). *Ji* arises from proximity. Regarding "if there are conditions for the entire monastery," "entire monastery" means the assembly of monks from one temple.

If there are conditions to provide relief for those in need, one must also perform the ritual procedure; it may not be done directly. If one gives without such a communal consultation, it is improper.
The Sangha is distinct [from the individual], yet both cases are subsumed under the category of theft. The *Xuánjì* provides another interpretation:
that "the entire monastery" refers to the former two cases, while "relieving a lack due to specific circumstances" refers to the latter one; this [latter case] is inferior to the former.

The phrase "Next, explaining the method of understanding" serves as the heading. This means that although it has already been understood through the preceding analysis of how the four stages are established through conditions, the general method for understanding these four stages has not yet been detailed;
therefore, it is explained next. It is clearly known that prior to this point, where the chapter was not yet opened, the *Chao* (the *Zongjing Lu Chao*) states:

Within this, there are two divisions; that is, within the four stages (*catur-avasthā*), there are two parts. First, the formation of the conditions for the four stages is clarified; subsequently, the binding and liberation of the four stages are explained.
Is this not, indeed, the second section concerning the method of liberation? This is a point where the textual lineage of the *Yao* (Commentary) remains uninterrupted;
it must be understood in such detail. Regarding the phrase "first... to the practitioner," it may be understood according to the text. Regarding the word "if":

Regarding "those who have reached the site": first, as for "releasing the great boundary" (*mahā-sīmā*), the *Xuánjì* (Mysterious Record) provides an analogy that can be understood in detail: it compares the act to taking off and putting on clothes.
As for the statement "this reaches the release," in each case where there is a separate document, one uses it to release the great boundary and the *kṣetra* (ordination site).

One must not answer both questions simultaneously; rather, one should wait for the answers to each question individually. Subsequently, one proceeds to the boundary of the precept-field (*sīmāmaṇḍala*) to engage in fresh questioning and answering once more.

This is because, although the formal act of receiving the precepts differs, they belong to the same boundary (*ekasīmā*); thus, a single ritual action may accomplish multiple procedures. In this case, there is a natural interval between them.

The same as the previous [case]. Regarding the method for performing the *karmavācanā*, it refers back to what was stated above; the textual phrasing for the procedure of dissolving the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) without a formal site follows the same standard.

As for the phrase "next, reaching the *Shun*": the old *karmavācanā* refers to Master Guang of the Wei Dynasty, who suppressed the *karmavācanā*. — *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā).

Master Guang’s *Karmavācanā* text contains a separate annotation stating that this single *karmavācanā* applies universally to both boundaries (*sīmā*), regardless of their size, without any partial restriction.

Regarding the statement that "the *śīlākṣetra* (precept field) does not permit the recitation of the *Poṣadha*," this refers to ancient masters using the text for resolving the *mahāsīmā* (great boundary) to explain the *śīlākṣetra*.
Furthermore, the text for the *mahāsīmā* states: "Maintain a single residential site. Now, the [current] field does not permit the Saṃgha [to perform the ritual there].

Regarding the dwelling and the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), how can one interpret them according to that text? Now, the Master takes the "small boundary" (*kṣudrasīmā*) and transforms it into a "formally established boundary" (*sīmābandha*).

Here, the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept platform) follows this precedent, also being transformed and formally established as a boundary; therefore, it is said that the principle is universally applicable. Furthermore, there is no mention of a "dwelling place" (*āvāsa*).
"Conforming to the text of the *karmavācanā* (ordination site ritual)" means that the text is followed accordingly. "The text reaches 'holding [the precepts]' (*dhāraṇa*)" refers to the text itself.

"From 'good' up to 'only then may one obtain'"—regarding the prohibition against erecting a dwelling on the *sīmāmaṇḍala* (ordination site)—this refers to the realization of the aforementioned *sīmāmaṇḍala*.

He did not permit the monks to remain. Even if the King were to establish them—meaning that the bhikṣus were those held in high esteem by the royal preceptors—he would have them reside at the East and West Temples, granting them courtyards and buildings on the former field site. There were those who felt shame and destroyed [the structures].
The character *yì* (易) is pronounced *tālì* (他歷反); it means "to change" or "to alter. [The text states that] when they knew the bhikṣu refused despite three admonitions, they informed the King.
When the King again did not permit it, they immediately began the separate destruction of the kalpa. As for the remaining timber and grass, they were sent to the bhikṣus residing at the monastery.

Fǎbǎo says: "To explain the reversed phrasing, one should respond as follows: 'The bhikṣus were sent to reside at the monastery; or, they resided at the Eastern Monastery. This implies that they then returned to that Western Monastery, and the principle is the same."
...is also the case. Only the Buddha-hall and such structures are excluded. The Venerable [Master] cites the *Jietan jing* (Sūtra on the Ordination Platform), which states:

"This is a place where the Dharma abides; it is not a dwelling for one's personal residence. Thus, the two positions are distinct. Baoyun says: "The ordination platform should be situated within the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).
Why was it just now, regarding the monks of the Eastern and Western Monasteries, that they built rooms upon it and then stripped away the timber and grass? The monks [responded].
"Is it the temple where one resides? You may cite the *Chao* (Excerpts). The answer says: 'Externally, the *jiechang* (precept field) is mostly in open spaces, and so forth.
In India, the *jiechang* was mostly in wild, open places, beneath no roof or covering. To provide an example:"
It is like the sacrificial altars used for suburban sacrifices. The *Hou Han Shu* (Later Discourses on the Spring and Autumn Annals) states:
"Seven li outside the city is called the *jiao* (suburb); fourteen li is called the *shang*; twenty-one li is called the *lin*;

and twenty-eight li is the altar south of the city wall for sacrificing to the celestial deities (*tian-shen*), and the altar north of the city wall for sacrificing to the terrestrial spirits (*di-qi*). Because this resembles that, it is taken as a precedent. Therefore, in the Vinaya, it is sometimes termed a "precept" (*śīla*).

Regarding the *tán* (altar/platform): A question is asked as to what distinguishes a *tán* from a *chǎng* (field/pavilion). Bǎo says: That which is level is called a *chǎng*, such as a battlefield or a ball court;

that which is elevated is called a *tán*. It is constructed by raising a foundation upon the ground surface, similar to where practitioners of the Way perform rituals today within the palaces and monasteries.
The *Wǔbǎiwèn lùn* (Treatise on Five Hundred Questions) and other texts provide evidence that the aforementioned *jiè chǎng* (precept field) was mostly located in the open air. Because...

Thus they followed one another; the sequence of their bonds is clear and can be understood. As for the statement "from three up to the realms," it is as the text states (*Souxuan* [Investigating the Profound] provides a detailed analysis here of the forms and characteristics of the altar of spiritual response, but fearing prolixity, I have not recorded them).

Regarding the statement, "As for the arising or non-arising of the dharma of the three knowledges (*trividyā*)," "dharma" refers to the inconceivable, virtuous non-informative matter (*avijñapti*). "Arising" means to be produced.
It is not yet clear whether, when the formal proclamation of the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*) is concluded, there exists the arising and manifestation of this non-informative dharma;
or if it does not arise, then it is non-existent. The explanations of the two masters are inconsistent. For now, we shall merely set forth the point, and thus it is said, "the dharma arises."
There is both existence and non-existence. Regarding the statement "there is that which reaches [the recipient]," some say this refers to the arising of the formal act (*dharma*);

this is the interpretation of Master Shou. Our current Master’s primary position—that it arises from the performance of the wholesome formal act—is the correct explanation. This means that because one upholds and proclaims the formal acts of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the motion and one proclamation), it is called a "wholesome formal act.

That is to say, one brings forth wholesome non-informative action (*avijñapti*); this means that from within the minds of the assembly of monks, one produces and obtains wholesome non-informative action. Question:

There are four types of mind. Now, when one generates a wholesome non-informative (avijñapti) [action], by which mind is it subsumed? The text explains that it belongs to the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
This is because it is a wholesome mind of formation, possessing the sense of volitional activity (abhisamskāra).

Regarding the phrase "this wholesome dharma corresponds with the place," it means that the Saṅgha gives rise to a wholesome mind of formation capable of cognition, taking the external sign as its object; the "place" refers to the objective sphere, and the "mind of the assembly" refers to the minds of the multitude.
