Taking that sign as the object, it is clearly articulated word by word within the mouth of the proclaimer; it is then mentally recited, and furthermore, one takes the entire procedure of the legal act as the object.
When the procedure is completed, wholesome non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) arises throughout all those signs. Question:

According to the treatises, the arising of non-informative matter must depend upon the informative action (*vijñapti-karma*) of sentient beings. Now, this earth is insentient; how can there be non-informative matter here?
It arises based on this. The *Fǎbǎo Shì* (Commentary on the Jewel of the Dharma) states: "A person is a sentient being who upholds the Dharma;

their single-minded intent is solely to apply [the ritual] to these insentient objects. Although the location is insentient, it is truly because I possess a sentient mind that I can, as prescribed by the Dharma, initiate [the rite] regarding the robes.
The robes themselves are also insentient, yet the bhikṣu achieves the application of the Dharma specifically for these three robes through the procedure of *pratimokṣa*."
From the moment it was first received until the end of one's life, this robe constantly possesses the wholesome unmanifest dharma (*avijñapti*), which subsequently continues in succession;
this case is likewise so. Is this not a high precedent? An external objection states: "Furthermore, regarding the rule for holding robes, when a person dies, the rule for the robe also ceases.
Now, since the method for establishing a boundary (*sīmā-bandha*) is identical to that, if a bhikṣu were to pass away, would the boundary rule [also cease]?"
"Should one also need to offer an apology? The answer is: "No. The holding of the robe is for oneself alone; once the person has passed away, that specific legal act (dharma) no longer exists.
However, the boundary established for the Saṃgha pervades the entire Dharma-realm and is inexhaustible. Thus, although the person who performed the ritual may have perished,"
The meaning of being a member of the Saṃgha is not without its basis; this is recorded in various commentaries on the profound mysteries of the Dharma, all of which share the same intent.

Although such an interpretation exists, it cannot avoid certain difficulties. For instance, when the kalpa-fire arises and destroys the world of sentient beings, at that time, since everything within the dharma-realm has already perished, does the unmanifest (avijñapti) at the site of the boundary-delineation (sīmā-bandha) also cease? If one says the dharma ceases, it would contradict what follows.
[The author] says: If one claims there is no need for gratitude, this would contradict the preceding meaning. Some attempt to defend [the position] by saying:

"Although there are no people in this realm, because the sages of other directions maintain it from afar, it is not lost. This interpretation lacks reason. Now it is said that at the time the boundary was originally established, the intention was directed toward the *saṃgha*.

Since the *saṃgha* encompasses both the present and the future, even when reaching the point where the great kalpa is destroyed and exhausted, although the currently visible *saṃgha* may lack continuity, [the boundary remains].

The principle of the future Saṃgha is not non-existent. Since no formal ritual (*dharma-karman*) has been performed nor any intention of relinquishment (*utsarga-citta*) produced, that dharma remains obscurely unexpired.

Reflect upon this: the school of [Master] Shou takes "receiving [the precepts]" as its primary tenet (which involves the loss of either gradual or sudden attainment). The school of Master San Guang takes "stopping evil" as its primary tenet (if there is an intention to bind [the mind], there is evil; is it possible to stop good?).

1. Master Si (Four-Distance) takes the practice of conduct as his primary tenet (because it would overlap with the other two Piṭakas). 2. Master Shou (Head) takes cause and effect as his primary tenet (because it is also contradictory). 3.

Master Tong (Comprehensive) does not establish any primary tenet at all (because there is nothing to which he can be assigned). 4. Master Li (Whetstone) takes the training in morality (*śīla*) as his primary tenet.

5. Nanshan takes morality as his primary tenet. 6. Master Su (Plain) takes the practice of moral conduct as his primary tenet. Question: Previously, it was stated that wholesome dharmas correspond to their respective bases.
Regarding the statement that "within the universally characterized [ground], there arises a dharma": for instance, the ground (*bhūmi*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Thus, wholesome dharmas are fundamentally connected to the indeterminate ground and can be drawn forth from it. The answer explains: this does not mean that wholesome dharmas are connected to another, the indeterminate [ground].

It is like when one removes the soil from a *li-jin* (a type of vessel); the boundaries of the dharma remain distinct, and thus one knows that [the wholesome dharma] is not connected to the indeterminate ground. To further challenge this: if...
If this dharma were not connected [to the earth], it would not reach the ground. The *Chao* (Commentary) answers: "It is not that they do not reach one another.

It is like when soil is dug up and then refilled; the boundary is established. The Venerable One provides an analogy: "It is like the moon in a clear hole [in the ground]; its reflection appears on the surface of the earth.

If a person digs and continues digging until the soil is removed, that dharma is then lost. If one says it does not reach the ground, then once the soil has been filled back in, [the boundary] would not be valid."
Furthermore, it remains; thus we know that it cannot be definitively determined.

Regarding the statement "from 'good' to 'doubtful': based on the characteristics" means relying on the defining marks (*nimitta*). "Losing the characteristics" means not knowing the boundaries or locations.

For example, regarding places where boundaries were established in the past, people today do not know them because there are no boundary markers, records, or the like; such is the nature of these characteristics.
Even if it is lost, the *dharmapada* (boundary) is not destroyed. Even if one digs down to the water’s edge, it is still not lost. One may construct a three-story building upon it;
although this is a multi-storied pavilion, it is all included within the same *karmapada* (action-boundary).

In the texts, it is merely referred to as "three stories," but according to the underlying principle, there is no limit to the number of stories, as they all constitute a single boundary. If there is a rocky mountain that is broad at the top and narrow at the base, this is—
Mountains and cliffs constitute the boundary. Various interpretations by the Śākyas differ; for now, I shall set forth the correct understanding according to the Dharma-treasury.

Regarding the principle that the top is broad and the bottom is narrow—just as the top might be five *zhang* wide while the bottom is only two *zhang* wide—if the monks establish a ritual boundary (*dharmakṣetra*) at the broad upper part of the mountain, all dimensions must be determined according to the specific occasion. At the broad upper part, one must generally demarcate a space of five [units].

Thirty *zhang* is also permissible; alternatively, merely tying [the cord] at three *zhang* is equally acceptable. If the lower two *zhang* are narrow, one must conform to this standard and not encroach upon the mountain crags below.
Regarding the monks above: even if the upper area is wide, if there are no obstructing monks below, there is no fault of forming a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*).
This constitutes being outside the boundary. Since the boundary is a physical phenomenon (*rūpadharma*), it conforms to the dimensions of the space, whether broad or narrow.
One might fear that people would doubt this, saying: "Since the mountain is five *zhang* wide, its shape is like a birth-dish (*prasava-paṭṭikā*).

Its base is two *zhang* narrow, resembling the pillar of a birth-platform (*prasava-maṇḍapa*). Now, since the bhikṣus are at the foot of the mountain and the upper surface is broad enough to cover the ground, there must be a separate assembly below.
Therefore, he explains: "The boundary (*sīmā*) is a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*). It follows the physical form; it does not [arise] from above."
Descending while suspended in mid-air—how could this constitute a separate assembly (*pṛthag-saṃgha*)? As for descending into the earth: if it is two *zhang* (approx.

6 meters) deep, then from that point of descent, one enters directly into the earth-stratum for another two *zhang*. This is entirely ground that possesses the Dharma. Furthermore, the *Yìchão* (Explanatory Commentary) poses a question regarding the nature of the Dharma:

"Suppose there is an empty space within a mountain crag; if a bhikṣu were inside it, would he be part of a separate assembly? The answer is: "This constitutes a separate assembly, yet it is not sufficient. Furthermore...

Question: Even if one is within [the structure], if one moves through the air, does this constitute a separate assembly? Answer: It also constitutes a separate assembly (the above is the formal explanation;

following this, questions and answers arise). Alternatively, according to the *Huainanzi* record: three sides are suspended and one side is attached. At the top of the mountain it is three *zhang* wide;
from the top three *zhang*, it gradually narrows toward the bottom. One also enters the earth at the narrowest point below (this interpretation is also acceptable). Master Gansu.
[The questioner] said: "The upper width is three *zhang*, and the lower is two *zhang*. Even at the upper wide portion, one must take only the two *zhang* from below so that the bottom is level.
If one follows the upper wide portion, the ritual boundary (*sīmā*) cannot descend while suspended in mid-air;
if one follows the lower part of the mountain, it would reach the ground and thus become the great earth. The Venerable One said: "Based on this explanation, I fear it has not been fully understood."

The meaning of the text is as follows: When one chants the dharma, it follows the mind of the person. Wherever one travels—whether in large or small places—it is maintained through the conditions of that mind.

To claim that it reaches everywhere upon the ground, pervading the entire earth, is logically untenable; reflect on this. Therefore, the word "equal" (等) serves as a general proof for the arising of the dharma.
If there were no arising of the dharma, then constructing a pavilion suspended in mid-air and performing the rite within that pavilion would not be possible, would it?

(As stated above). Regarding the phrase "from the past until now," and the statement "in the past, no dharma arose": the ancient masters said that once the boundary has been established and marked, within that area upon the ground, no wholesome [dharma] can arise.
The text states that the ancient masters themselves cite this as proof that [such dharmas] do not exist. This is from the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (Section on the Settlement of Disputes).
What is meant by "the manifestation of the boundary" (*sīmā-pratyakṣa*)? It refers to performing the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) within [the precinct] and proclaiming the limits.
The intent is this: when one merely upholds the Dharma and proclaims it as the place of these limits, what dharma arises based upon the ground?
As for the phrase "this reaches," the Master now says: although the preceding citation of the Vinaya was used as a basis to state that no dharma arises, that is simply...
I have only had two days to study the text. This passage from the Vinaya merely explains the location for performing the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*);

it does not discuss whether the formal act of measurement (*māna-karman*) arises or not. Therefore, this cannot be cited as proof. Even citing the intention of the Sarvāstivādins serves as proof that the formal act does arise.
If one were to say there are no benevolent deities, then there would likewise be no protection.

As for the "fivefold clarity," this refers to the preceding passage concerning a layperson who has newly constructed a hall and invites the Sangha for the *poṣadha*, or when troubled by non-human spirits (*amanuṣya*); these serve as evidence for the existence of the Dharma.
Regarding the *Xiǎofǎmièjìnjīng* (Sūtra on the Extinction of Minor Dharmas), Xuánzàng stated that it is included among the doubtful and spurious texts. The Great Virtuous One said this is not so;

if it were indeed a doubtful or spurious work, the author of the *Chāo* (Excerpts) would not have cited it. As for the "earth platform" (*tǔtái*), these are terrestrial yakṣas who travel upon the earth as freely as birds fly through the sky without obstruction.
However, when they reach a place where a boundary has previously been established, they are unable to proceed, just as they are hindered by a broken wall. Thus...
[The interlocutor] says: "I understand. Up to the limit of the diamond (vajra), there are dharmas and the arising of dharmas. Or someone may object, saying:

"If minor dharmas were to perish, heaven and earth would not yet have ceased to exist; but when the great kalpa is destroyed, heaven and earth are both exhausted—how then could there be a platform of earth?

Xuanji Tong explains: "The sutra refers to a 'minor kalpa' while describing the events of a 'great kalpa. Even if a great fire breaks out and heaven and earth wither away, the ground where the boundary is established is not consumed by the flames."

What is there to wonder at? According to the *Huainanzi*, it is explained that the Diamond Realm (Vajradhātu) arises through a gradual process. If the earthen platform has not yet been destroyed, it may remain;

if the diamond [foundation] is destroyed, the earthen platform is also destroyed. Even if the earthen platform is destroyed, the unmanifest (avijñapti) remains in space and cannot be said to be destroyed.
Therefore, the *Śīlamaṇḍala-sūtra* states that throughout India and the land of the *Tianzhu*, there are holy traces that have endured through many kalpas and remain present to this day.
Such is the site where [the Bodhisattva] sacrificed his body by means of eight characters, and the legacy of spreading his hair to cover the mud;
even at the site of Jetavana in Śrāvastī, Buddhas have constantly traveled for ninety-one kalpas. When Śāriputra beheld an anthill, he took charge of its affairs with compassion.
This can be understood.

Regarding the phrase "the four ultimate characteristics," this opens two chapters. Regarding the phrase "from the beginning to the realm," the two characters "beginning" (chu) and "middle" (zhong) are used here merely for the purpose of concluding the section;
they do not refer to the actual middle of the formal structure. The rest is explained outside of the characteristics and is fully contained in the preceding text; it is not being raised again here.
To explain this more extensively, it is as stated in brief. Regarding the phrase "losing [the boundary]": "losing" refers to losing the *dharma*; "not" means not losing it.
Regarding the phrase "from one up to the realm of existence": in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, chapter thirty-seven, Upāli asks the Buddha:

"If various bhikṣus abandon a monastery and depart, thinking they will never return, is this called 'abandoning the boundary'? The Buddha says: "This is indeed called abandoning the boundary. However, it must be done within...
If one forms the intention while within the boundary (*sīmā*), but then thinks of relinquishing it while outside the boundary, the relinquishment is not achieved;

this is similar to the case of the *jñapti-dvitīya* (one motion and one announcement), where the relinquishment of the boundary while outside is likewise not achieved—this should be understood by analogy. Regarding the "discarding after one night" mentioned in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, chapter twenty-six:

Śāriputra was traveling with five hundred bhikṣus and stayed overnight at an empty temple. On the day of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), they did not know the distinction between the interior and exterior of the boundary.
He informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "If it is discarded after one night, then [the offense] no longer exists. The Venerable One said:

"Although the preceding Vinaya text states that if one discards [the object] with the intention to do so, it is not lost if it is returned on the same day, one must follow this treatise (*śāstra*) and discard it after it has spent the night until the dawn light appears.

According to this, three conditions must be met: first, the intention to discard; second, the awareness that the object remains within the boundary (*sīmā*); and third, the appearance of the dawn light. This is the meaning of the *Chao*.
The introduction and the main body are explained together, whereby the exposition becomes complete and sufficient.

Regarding the phrase "As for the question reaching the point": this refers collectively to the preceding section on the realization of the Dharma through good evidence, as well as the *Catuṣpariṣat-sūtra* (the Sūtra on the Fourfold Assembly) and the minor disciplinary texts (*Vinaya-kṣudraka*).
Therefore, it is said that they are simultaneous. When digging down to the water’s edge, the water washes away everything, so that the diamond-hard earth platform and the rest are entirely gone.

Yet the bhikṣu still does not lose [the merit]; now, however, by being empty for but a single night, he immediately loses it. Why is there such a contradiction? This is the intended meaning of the answer.

The *Chao* (Commentary) is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "because the *Sifen* [Vinaya] treats the *gāra* and so forth," Xuánzàng says: According to the *Bhaiṣajyavastu*, there are two sections. The text states:
"If a bhikṣu does not know where the pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*) is, the Buddha said: 'If you have doubts, you should abandon it and then perform the formal act of demarcation (*sīmābandha*').'"

Section Two: Regarding the treatment of old sites. May a *kālāma* (monastery) establish a pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*)? The Buddha said: "It may be established; it is simply so that [the purity] is not lost. One may bind a large boundary (*mahāsīma*) and, based upon that large boundary, establish a pure ground. The passage below states: "Citing the Vinaya extensively... This refers to the *Fuchao* (Commentary on the Essentials), which rearranges the sequence of the Vinaya texts. Consequently, there have been no few who have developed erroneous interpretations. It says: [...text omitted... Regarding the phrase "it is simply so that [the purity] is not lost": this means that even if one establishes a pure ground within a *kālāma*, if one subsequently abandons the *kālāma*, the pure ground is lost. However, if one establishes a pure ground within a *mahāsīma*, even if one later abandons the *mahāsīma*, the pure ground is not lost. This is because it relies upon the *mahāsīma*. Furthermore, the text continues: "As for the following... and so forth. This refers to the *Fuchao*, which has rearranged the sequence of the Vinaya passages. Because of this, there have been no few who have produced false understandings. It says: [...text omitted... Regarding the statement: "If one establishes a pure ground within a *kālāma*, and then abandons the *kālāma*, the pure ground is lost. If one establishes a pure ground within a *mahāsīma*, and then abandons the *mahāsīma*, the pure ground is not lost. This is because it relies upon the *mahāsīma*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the text continues: "As for the following... and so forth. This refers to the *Fuchao*, which has rearranged the sequence of the Vinaya passages. Because of this, there have been no few who have produced false understandings. It says: [...text omitted... Regarding the statement: "If one establishes a pure ground within a *kālāma*, and then abandons the *kālāma*, the pure ground is lost. If one establishes a pure ground within a *mahāsīma*, and then abandons the *mahāsīma*, the pure ground is not lost. This is because it relies upon the *mahāsīma*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the text continues: "As for the following... and so forth. This refers to the *Fuchao*, which has rearranged the sequence of the Vinaya passages. Because of this, there have been no few who have produced false understandings. It says: [...text omitted... Regarding the statement: "If one establishes a pure ground within a *kālāma*, and then abandons the *kālāma*, the pure ground is lost. If one reaches the stage of "abandonment" (*śe*), then within the two realms of food and clothing, they arise based upon the human realm; when the root no longer exists, where can the branches remain?

As for reaching the stage of "seeding" (*bīja*), according to the *Jiemo shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā), one adds the mutual binding of divergent views and the mutual binding of the heterodox and the orthodox;
combining these four or five [factors] results in six. Here, there is no [application of] the two [rules], and by opening up the four, five are formed.
Regarding the statement "the first is not reaching the destination" and "not the unrighteous mind of ill-will," this accords with the *Bhaiṣajyavastu* (Medicine Rules), which states:
At one time there was a bhikṣu who, out of ill-will toward another, released a pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*) so that the other would obtain impure food. The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:

"One who releases it does not succeed [in making it impure] and incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; one who does not release it remains pure. Second, according to the *Vinayavibhaṅga* (Commentary on Discipline) 17: "If a bhikṣu..."

Regarding the establishment of boundaries (*sīmābandha*): for a bhikṣuṇī, it is not a boundary for a bhikṣu; however, for a bhikṣu, one may establish boundaries and so forth upon a higher boundary. Question:

When a bhikṣuṇī establishes a boundary upon the boundary of the *saṃgha*, what is the harm in saying that [the previous boundary] is not lost? If the bhikṣuṇī wishes to establish [her own boundary]...

Regarding the preliminary dissolution of boundaries (*sīmā-vimocana*): although the *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules address this, they only permit the dissolution of one’s own boundary (*sva-sīmā*) and do not permit the dissolution of the *saṃgha-sīmā*.
This is as explained in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* (Shanjian-lun). Even if one digs down to the water level, the boundary is not lost. The *Pañcaśata-praśna* states:

"Because it is treated according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the monastery (*ārāma*) does not lose its status as a pure site (*śuddha-sthāna*), for it is entirely devoid of people and serves as the original locus of emptiness. Regarding the phrase "fifth to 'again'": this permits repetition.

Regarding the characteristics of the formal undertaking (*saṃvara*): it must not involve impurity or overlap; otherwise, there is a fear that one will exit the monastic boundary (*sīmā*), and the principle of being of the same Dharma (*samāna-dharma*) will not be established.

This means that when a nun receives a confession (*pratideśanā*), it must be within both assemblies (*ubhayasaṃgha*). Even if they are within the same boundary, there is a mutual concern that the recipient might be within the monks' boundary but not within the nuns' boundary.

Because they are not designated as two separate assemblies. Some say that if nuns come to a *sīmā* (monastic boundary) where monks are performing a ritual, the *sīmā* must also be demarcated for them;
then, relying on the monks' assembly, a larger boundary (*mahāsīmā*) must be re-established by chanting the internal and external markers, and the ritual act is thereby accomplished.

If nuns come to a *sīmā* where monks are performing a ritual and one merely establishes a [separate] large boundary, it is not permitted; this is because the boundaries would intersect (one should reflect upon this ignorance). *Śāstra-śīlataḥ* (The Commentary).

**Seventh: The Section on the Monastic Hierarchy** (*Senggang-pian*)

Regarding the matters to be addressed hereafter, there are six sections in total. The first three concern persons; the next one concerns the Dharma; the next one concerns the *dhātu* (realms) in relation to persons;

and the final one concerns the Dharma as applied to persons. For now, we shall address the section concerning persons. Within the legal framework for the monastic community (*saṃgha*), the primary system is largely divided into two parts:

first, the enumeration of names; second, the explanation. Regarding the initial statement, "The *saṃgha*... up to seven," this first presents the underlying intent, which was clarified in the preceding section on the formal establishment of the community.

The realms and their bases have already been explained. However, regarding the function of governing and directing, it must rely upon sentient beings. As for the basis for determining the status of these sentient beings, one must rely on the teachings;
since this was not discussed previously, it is listed next. To explain the terminology: *saṃgha* refers to those who follow the Dharma, and *kāraṇā* refers to the methods for governing the *saṃgha*.
Because it upholds only the essential principles, it is called the "Great Outline" (*mahākāraṇā*). It is able to discipline those who are difficult to discipline, as [follows]:
The bridle of a wicked horse can subdue those things difficult to subdue; the hook of a wild dream controls that which grows upon the skin. It brings peace to this wondrous assembly.
Just as the hundred rivers converge into a single flavor, it equalizes the severing of the three roots of delusion and karma, gradually realizing the four virtues of the eternal and true.
"Pian" (卷) refers to the name of a chapter or section; the seventh is as explained in the usual manner (etc.). If one follows the *Soushen*...
Xuán: Taking the "Seven Nines" method as the main framework seems too restrictive; I shall now follow the approach of the Venerable Jingshui.
The five gates listed in this chapter constitute the main framework, encompassing the full range of meanings. Reflect upon this.
In the initial section on the general intent of the commentary, it says: "First, regarding 'to the day': 'one direction' refers to one distinct residence.

'Establishing the dharma' means instituting regulations based upon the teachings. Because gentlemen share the same customs even at a distance of a thousand *li*, this is called 'pervasive. Regarding 'dwelling among the multitude' and so forth:

'dwelling' means residing. 'Deciding' (*duàn*) means to sever or determine; 'measuring' (*liàng*) means to assess or regulate. Since these matters cannot be fully encompassed by the scriptures and treatises, it is said: 'Necessarily...'"

Regarding those who, relying on the teachings of the Vinaya, direct their aspirations toward distant regions and foreign lands: "distant regions" refers to borderlands, while "foreign lands" refers to neighboring prefectures.
Because they raise their thoughts and look up toward this [central] direction, it is said that "their hearts aspire toward something.

As for those who practice within the boundaries and advance in their cultivation, they do not worry about punishments for violating the Dharma; thus, they achieve tranquility of mind. The Three Studies state:
The new name is "Advancing in Practice. For those such as these, they will be like grass bent by the wind, such that there shall be none who do not practice.
As for those who have already practiced, they are like the straightening of a crooked line; since no one can resist or stop it, they are encouraged to advance below and commanded to uphold it.
"Far from merely [stopping]" means that there are further benefits such that it is appropriate to stop [the practice] as described above.
"Serenely settling the mind and advancing in the observance of the precepts" refers to the solemn and austere appearance of the monastic community in its purity.

Not implementing vulgar customs or regulations regarding fines and prohibitions is called "resting from the secular. Relying solely on the Vinaya teachings is called "returning to the truth. Only then can one support the withered [monks], and so forth.

This is the standard of the square. Furthermore, it can cause the flowers of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) to bloom, which is the spreading and flourishing of the tree of the Path (*mārga-vṛkṣa*).

This constitutes the enhancement of the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*). Regarding "radiantly exalting the sun of wisdom": the sun of wisdom that sweeps away and eradicates the afflictions within the mind naturally shines forth.
This is the source for severing delusions and the enhancement of the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).
As for what is called "the confusion of dharmas," it refers to those who follow worldly customs and habitual conventions, allowing their own minds to dictate the rules of dharma.

Such dharmas deviate from the common understanding and do not accord with the scriptural teachings; therefore, they lack any authoritative basis. As for "vulgar and base people," this refers to those who are attached to wealth despite their poverty.

If there are now transgressors who are punished by fines, this is identical to the vulgar and evil ways of the common folk. Should there be further offenses, they shall instead be subjected to the cangue and the staff.
"Categories" (*lei*) refers here to the common masses. Regarding "those who can bestow [punishments] equally," these are the individuals established by the regulations;

since they transcend ordinary sentiment and do not rely on canonical authority, their actions are inherently non-virtuous. Regarding "those who are subject [to punishment]," those who have committed offenses and received penalties feel resentment in their hearts, which leads to the arising of disputes.
Is this not included within the category of clamor and disorder? The phrase "therefore, as for the Dharma" serves to cite scriptural evidence.
This is the increase of three phrases in the Vinaya. The Vinaya text consists of four sentences in total. The first sentence says:
"If a bhikṣu [accuses] one who is not a person of the Dharma. The second sentence says: "[To] establish what was not established" means to speak erroneously and deviate from the correct.

The third sentence says: "That which was established is then severed," manifesting error and obstructing the correct. The fourth sentence begins with "In this way... (and so forth). This is analogous to a metaphor.

This refers to those who lack knowledge of the Dharma; fearing that associating with the ignorant is of no benefit—just as it is said in worldly parlance, "Do not dwell with the foolish"—one fears that even if one is born together with them, there will be no growth in benefit.
Therefore, from the words "Thus we know" (*guozhi*) onwards, the Master now offers an exhortation. He uses "Thus we know" to confirm the preceding statement.
What has been cited thus far is the teaching: those whose common sentiments do not rely upon the scriptural canons must not be lived with.
One must surely follow the sacred Dharma.
Regarding what was previously explained: the deletion of the ancient regulations concerning monetary fines and the punishment of shackling and imprisonment is indeed a grave error.
By drawing from the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-parivarta* of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, one should supplement these omissions and deficiencies, so that the regulations accord with the teachings.
Regarding "correspondence" (*saṃprayukta*): The *Fǎbǎo* states that the established regulations must correspond with the teachings of the Vinaya.

As in the following five gates where the establishment of regulations all cite the sacred words (*āptavacana*), they do not contradict the meaning of the teachings. Regarding "concurrent timing" (*sahakāla*):
this refers to when the principles established in the text accord with the timing. For example, when a layperson requests food, one should inquire whether they can partake of the meal or not.
This indicates that one should speak of cause and effect so as not to increase resentment; this meaning accords with the timing [of the teaching].

If one were to follow the *Xuánjì* (Records of the Profound) and provide both extensive and abbreviated explanations, they would inevitably become cumbersome and disordered. Therefore, reflect upon this. Regarding the phrase "the Vinaya says, etc.," this serves as proof.

The text of the Five Hundred Recitations (*pañcaśata-saṃgīti*) was not an original prohibition, such as the fine for money and the like. Since these have now been deleted, they are no longer prohibitions. As for those that are indeed prohibitions, there are seven.
The ninefold dharmas are to be practiced now; this does not harm the Buddha-dharma and is the meaning of its long endurance.

Conversely, those who produce illness, misinterpret the four matters, and so forth, are clearly those who cause diminution. Such people are not trusted by the laity, they cause others to retreat from their pure resolve, they rob sentient beings of their vision, and they sever the seeds of the Triple Gem, as explained in the five gates below.

"Regarding 'proceeding to the characteristics' (*lakṣaṇa*)," this is the opening of the chapter and the arrangement of its sections. "In the first [section], there are two divisions" means that within the first gate, two parts are established:

the initial and the subsequent. "First, clarifying the *Hua-jiao* (Transformation Teachings)" uses the word "first" (*qie*) because it has not yet discussed the *Zhi-jiao* (Regulatory Teachings) below.
"The teachings apply to both monastics and laity": "teachings" here refers to the *Hua-jiao*, which are the written texts that serve as the means of expression (*sūcana*).

Those who have left the household life do so for the sake of the Way (dharma), while kings and ministers belong to the secular world. Regarding the statement that "the Great Assembly reaches extinction," in that sutra the Buddha asks King Bimbisāra:
"If in a future age there should be my disciples who possess abundant wealth and many treasures, and who have great power—of which 'wealth' there are two kinds:
first, internal wealth, referring to sentient beings; second, external wealth, referring to [non-sentient things]..."
The category of sentient beings includes such things as gold and silk. As for "power," it refers to all those who are personally favored by the king;
the entire populace dares not bury or abandon them. You must govern these classes—the Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
If you do not govern them, these four castes will be severed, and the lineage of my Three Jewels will be extinguished, causing the torch of the Dharma to perish and be destroyed.
"The Dharma-ship robs sentient beings of their eyes; it is as if one person were to rob everyone of their sight. Is this sin not very great?
"It is immeasurably great, World-Honored One. The Buddha said: "Suppose there are members of the four castes who possess great power and see my Dharma coming to an end."
"Abandoning [the precepts] and failing to guard them is likewise so. Although one has cultivated morality, generosity, and wisdom for immeasurable eons, it results in the loss of those virtues.
When the king heard these words, he did not weep or sob; instead, he wiped away his tears and said, "I have encountered the Tathāgata, yet I am still thus."

They are unable to perpetuate the lineage of the Triple Gem. While such kings constantly wander through the three evil realms for a long night, if a king makes a vow to protect and uphold [the Dharma], the Buddha said that if he can establish this matter, it constitutes making offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The merit is immeasurable, as explained in the "Chapter on Protecting the Dharma. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "one month or two months," this is distinguished by way of time.
Regarding the phrase "beyond this it is not the Dharma, from one country up to four countries," this is distinguished by way of place.

This transcends what is not the Dharma. "Where there is the Buddha-Dharma" refers to the Dharma itself. This is because, where the Buddha-Dharma is absent, one’s indulgence and self-indulgence increase all the more.
The rest of the text may be understood in detail.

Regarding the phrase "the place where the Ten Wheels reach": because those of dull faculties are unwilling to travel abroad to study, urging them to attend to their duties and so forth constitutes a "meritorious punishment" (fú).
Regarding the phrase "if they reach sentient beings": as for "regretting in one's heart," once evil has been committed, it causes the arising of a mind that repents its transgressions.
Regarding "punishment" (zhé-fá): "zhé" (讁), according to the *Zílín*, means "reproach"; "fá" (罰), according to the *Guǎngyǎ*, means "to break" or "to inflict."
It is so. Regarding the direction toward which the mind inclines, the Buddha knows that this person should be reformed from evil to goodness through the occasion of this reprimand;
for the sake of their benefit, he now speaks of this matter to subdue them.
Regarding the phrase "if one reaches the [appropriate] division": these bhikṣus merely maintain the precepts;
they may have violated royal regulations and, moreover, possess little learning (*alpa-śruta*). When questioned or challenged, they are unable to provide a thorough explanation.

Such individuals are not subject to punishment, with the exception of those who are both widely learned and maintain the precepts. Xuán says: "Being both widely learned and maintaining the precepts is not what is being clarified here."

Therefore, it is said that [the former] is excluded. This serves as a counter-illustration to show that merely observing the precepts without extensive learning is not [sufficient]—this meaning is primary and must not be interpreted erroneously.
There is also a fourfold classification based on these points: first, one who is both extensively learned and observes the precepts is not what is being discussed here;

second, one who observes the precepts but is not extensively learned is likewise never permitted to be punished; third, one who is extensively learned but does not observe the precepts may be punished by the monastic community; fourth...
Those who are ignorant and violate the precepts are subject to punishment by both the monastic and the lay authorities.

As for the "eight classes of devas and nāgas," these consist of eight groups beginning with devas and nāgas, and extending through yakṣas up to mahoragas. Regarding the "precious hidden treasures," this refers to the fruit of nirvāṇa;

because it is concealed and not manifest, it is called a "hidden treasure" (nidhi). Furthermore, the three vehicles (*triyāna*) and so forth are all likewise hidden treasures, which this [teaching] is now able to reveal.

Regarding the ten kinds of superior conceptions (*daśa-viśiṣṭa-saṃjñā*) and so forth: first, when seeing sentient beings who have gone forth under one’s guidance, one should conceive of them as Buddhas.

Second, one should give rise to a mind of generosity. Third, seeing those who violate the precepts, one should conceive of them as upholders of the precepts. Fourth, seeing those who are indolent, one should conceive of them as being diligent.

Fifth, regarding those who are angry and resentful, one should conceive of them as possessing patience. Sixth, seeing those who are distracted, one should conceive of them as being in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Seventh...
1. Seeing those who are deluded, one conceives of them as possessing wisdom. 2. Seeing those who are deceitful and crooked, one conceives of them as being upright and honest.

3. Seeing those who are coarse and harsh, one conceives of them as being gentle and soft. 4. Seeing those who are stingy and greedy, one conceives of them as being generous. In the present text, the first two [of these four] are omitted.

The intended meaning is that although such people may have broken the precepts, they are able to reveal hidden treasures; because they are no different from the Buddha, [they should be regarded as such].

One should cause them to form the perception of a Buddha. Even if they are stingy and greedy, one can show them hidden treasures; one should simply maintain the perception of practicing giving. The eight intermediate phrases are all like this.
Regarding "one should speak with gentle words" up to "prostrating at their feet": even if the person before one has broken the precepts, one must not revile or disparage them with harshness;
rather, one must employ soft and gentle speech and offer respectful prostrations. [The text continues: "...in future lives, one will be born into a noble family..."
"Noble" means that those who attain *nirvāṇa* obtain nobility in the near term and *nirvāṇa* in the distant term. "Therefore, they are equal" refers to those who have broken the precepts;
although they have transgressed the Buddha's rules, at the time they first received the precepts they maintained them according to the Buddha’s words and were thus disciples of the Buddha.
For this reason, laypeople are not permitted to punish them, much less for minor or slight offenses. [This applies even to] cow bezoar.
This refers to the yellow [substance] within a cow's horns. The Venerable One said: "This must be found among a herd of yellow cows—perhaps among three or five hundred.
It is rare to encounter even one head that possesses it; certainly not all do. When taking it, how can one know whether it is present or not?
One must wait for a night of the bright moon; if it is there, the yellow will immediately emerge from the horn-handles. Or...
He emerged from within the horn. While the bull was in the midst of its display, the man stealthily hid beside it, taking care not to be noticed.
He waited until the bull’s head was perfectly upright upon its horns; then, suddenly springing up, he clapped his hands to startle it.

The bull immediately fell to the ground, and thus he captured it. Within three or five days, the bull would surely die. Although the bull dies, the gall (pitta) is fit for use in medicinal compounds. It is fragrant.
It emerges from the navel of a beast; it is what is now called musk and so forth. Regarding incense: although its substance is merely vapor, it can nonetheless permeate all things.

Regarding eye medicine: the Sūtra says it is like a merchant who enters the great ocean, takes the lives of immeasurable sentient beings, plucks out their eyes, and holds *amra* fruit, praying and making offerings to compound it.
Precious Medicine: If there are sentient beings born blind and without eyes, by applying this medicine to them, their disease is cured and their eyes become clear and pure like the *campaka* flower.
Although immeasurable sentient beings may be dead, it can still be administered and treated.
From the passage "Bhikṣus who have broken the precepts" onwards, the scriptural text has been excerpted; the application of the Dharma may be understood [therefrom]. (etc.)
Regarding the phrase "reaching the middle": there are ten types of unlawful acts that incur great offenses.
First, when the Saṃgha is not in harmony, to reprimand [the offender] before the king is called unlawful; the subsequent cases are all to be treated accordingly. Second, among the Brahmins...
Third, before the king’s retinue and great ministers; fourth, among laypeople; fifth, among women and children; sixth, before the monastery attendants (*śrāmaṇera*); seventh, among bhikṣuṇīs;
eighth, before those who were originally one's enemies or with whom one harbors resentment; ninth, to mock or rebuke them with a mind of anger;
tenth, to do so in a manner that is contrary to the Dharma and improper for rebuke. Among these ten points, the second and the [fourth] are missing from the *Chao*.

Regarding the omission of the ninth and tenth [categories]: it is because there are no Brahmins here. As for "the ninth, those who harbor anger," this is a general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), meaning that all such persons possess a mind of anger;
therefore, one rebukes these ten types of people. The tenth, being fully possessed of unrighteousness (adharma), should not be rebuked.
The intent of the *Chao* (Commentary) states that this is also a general characteristic, which then opens up the inclusion of women, children, and original enemies.
This constitutes the tenth [offense]. A "small child" refers to a person who has not yet attained knowledge. A "person originally resentful or hateful" is one who previously committed an offense.
Regarding a monk who is "originally resentful or hateful," the remaining text is easy to understand; thus, it is not explained in detail point by point.
Regarding the statement that "Nirvana has arrived," there are three intended meanings in the text. First, it clarifies the retribution for evil conduct through seven factors.

Second, it reveals the benefits gained by upholding [the precepts]. Third, it praises the ability to remedy and disparages the harm caused by [neglecting] them. This is intended to demonstrate that those who engage in various evil actions will experience karmic results;
specifically, it clarifies that performing evil in the present with a transformative intent constitutes cause and effect in relation to these seven factors, thereby remedying the retribution.
To discipline and punish now so as to quell future great terrors is precisely the bestowing of fearlessness. Regarding the phrase "if it were a virtuous bhikṣu" and so forth:

if one does not discipline him, it will cause this bhikṣu to increase in unwholesome dharmas, leading others to follow his example and destroy the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body, thereby diminishing the Buddha-dharma.
Because such a person is left unpunished, it is now revealed that he is an enemy of the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, if one can expel [the defilements] as described below, it may be known that such a person is a true son of the Buddha according to the Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "from the second" (*yún èr zhì zhě*), this is explained in terms of the Vinaya teachings. Regarding the phrase "from the Sangha" (*yún sāng zhì děng*), as for the "superior grade":

within the Great Dharma—the Dharma of the Buddha—there are three grades of persons, namely superior, middling, and inferior. The superior grade consists of those who are single-mindedly diligent and do not transgress, like a sea of grass.
Regarding the category of jewels: it is like the precious horse of a Wheel-Turning King, which can traverse the four continents in a single day without the need for laborious punishment.

As for those of middling quality, having committed an offense they are able to repent; like a fine thoroughbred that perceives the shadow of a whip and follows the path, there is likewise no necessity for punishment.
As for those of inferior quality, they lack shame and dread of blame; they commit offenses and do not reform. Unless they are disciplined through punishment, how could they ever be brought to rest?
Yes. Just as a slow donkey cannot be made to follow the road without the application of a painful whip, we now excerpt the latter two [categories] and take the middle one as the superior.

As for not taking the first [category], since there is no transgression therein, why bother further to discuss the reason for its exclusion? Regarding "the manifestation of insight," this takes the teaching as the manifestation;
it means that upon seeing the teaching, one is able to reform. To say "this has reached the ultimate" refers to one whose mind has not yet been transformed.

Regarding the term "革" (ge): both characters are glossed as "to reform. As for the phrase "now reaching the Dharma," this reform has three meanings: first, the heading indicating the intent of employing the teaching;
second, from "dividing into four parts" onwards, citing the teaching to provide an explanation; third, from "it must be complete" onwards, the conclusion. Regarding the two kinds of fivefold virtues:

not being partial, not being biased, not being fearful, not being deluded, and knowing how to bring forth charges—these are the first five virtues. Next, "also knowing the proper time" [is the second set].
Not at an improper time; according to reality and not through falsehood; for the sake of benefit and not for harm; with gentleness and not with harshness;
with a compassionate mind and not with anger—these are the five virtues of the first set. [This refers to] the first five among the two sets of five.

This applies to all prohibitive rules (*pratiṣedha-dharma*). The citation from the Vinaya text in the *Śāstra* (Commentary) is precisely correct. Because the *Śāstra* abridges the extensive Vinaya, it states, "As fully detailed in the original Vinaya texts," and so forth;
the remaining text is easy to understand and need not be explained.

It is said that "now, the methods for governing are explained. This refers to the methods of disciplinary punishment. Regarding the phrase "seven kinds... up to," there are nine items listed in the enumeration;

in the explanation, *jiamin* (reduction and burial) is added, making ten when the categories of governance are opened out. Since the heading already states "methods of governance," it is uncertain whether there are seven or nine kinds.
What are the names of these seven and nine? The subsequent text explains this itself, saying: "As for what are called the 'seven kinds,' etc."

(As stated above). Regarding the term "perfect governance" (*zhìzhì*), the *Jiemo shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states: "The three principles of precepts, views, and livelihood must be followed in accordance with reason.

To now speak of them in reverse order is to defile the ranks of the Saṃgha; therefore, one is rebuked and ordered to follow the teaching. This refers precisely to the initial circumstances (*yúan*) at the beginning of the present Vinaya text.
The two, Prajñā and Rohiṇa, engaged in mutual strife with mouths like swords and blades.
Because the Saṃgha used harsh words to strictly restrain them, it is called "reproach" (*pratikṣepa*). As for the phrase "the arrival of words," this clarifies the faults of reproach.
Taking the *Dharmaguptaka*, *Mahīśāsaka*, *Mahāsāṃghika*, and other Vinayas as a whole, all instances of the fault of reproach are brought together in this single location to be explained.
Regarding the phrase "if it reaches the category of seeds": "Sangha" refers to four or more persons;
"bhikṣu" refers to three, two, or one person. The "four matters" are: precepts, views, conduct, and wrong livelihood.

"Speaking perversely" means claiming what is an offense is not an offense (and so forth), or claiming that what is an offense is right, and what is right is an offense. The "first three groups" refer to the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.
Regarding the "sixty-two views" (*dvāṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭi-gata*): the text says "to destroy views," which some take to mean destroying the sixty-two views. This is not so.
Rather, it means that when the sixty-two views arise, they are destroyed by a single right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*).

As for how these sixty-two are to be categorized, the interpretations found in the sutras, śāstras, and the Tiantai school each differ. I shall not elaborate on their specific conditions here; for now, I will follow the Southern [tradition].

The *Shan-jie-mo-shu* (Commentary on the Mountain *Karmavācanā*) explains this in terms of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). For example, taking the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) as the head, there are four permutations [of the other aggregates].

First: form is the cave-dwelling, and feeling (*vedanā*) dwells within it. Second: form is the cave-dwelling, and perception (*saṃjñā*) dwells within it. Third: form is the cave-dwelling... [and so forth].

The formations (*saṃskāra*) dwell within it; the four colors constitute its cave-dwelling, and consciousness (*vijñāna*) dwells therein. Next, taking consciousness, perception (*saṃjñā*), formations, and perception as heads in turn, each forms four propositions.
Four times five makes twenty. Next, these are assigned to the three periods of time: twenty for the past, and likewise for the future and the present, totaling sixty.
Adding further the two fundamental views of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) and eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*), are they not the sixty-two [views]?
The four groups mentioned below are *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, *dukkaṭa*, and *dubbhāsita*. It is easy to understand that the others are also known [by these names].

Regarding the statement from "five" up to "calamity," the treatise asks: "What are the five types of wrong livelihood? The answer is as found in the commentary (*śāstra*) cited in the *Chao* (Excerpts).

Each of these points regarding the pursuit of gain and offerings has been excerpted and abbreviated. "Feigning extraordinary appearances" refers to wearing raw garments in winter and processed ones in summer, or wearing fine robes while pretending they are tattered, and so forth.

"Proclaiming one's own virtues" means claiming for oneself, "I am a practitioner of the foremost ascetic practices (dhūta-guṇa)," or "I recite the sutras and practice the Way, never sleeping," and so on. "Displaying an air of authority" refers to scolding junior disciples, novices, and the like.
The diagram states that this person possesses majestic power (*tejas*). To "arouse" means to incite and stir the donor. Facing the person who has spread the cloth, one says:
"Mr. Wang So-and-so obtained an object yesterday; he intends to give it to me. The person who has spread the cloth then acts like Mr. Wang and also forcibly takes possession of the object.
Regarding those who divined his fortune or misfortune: according to principle, a *śramaṇa* should not practice divination of fortune or misfortune, for even an Arhat [does not do so].
The practice of archery is not yet established [as a standard], as it may be performed in various ways; since the Buddha-dharma is also universal, the Sūtra states:

"Through the various branches of craftsmanship and arts, one benefits sentient beings. Therefore, if one does not act for the sake of benefiting others, there is no offense even if one does not seek the proper application with earnest diligence.

Since the text states that "forcibly occupying signs" refers to taking advantage of others who have not invited one to inquire about their birth year (*jiazi*) and so forth as a means of seeking profit;
and regarding the phrase "the four directions," it refers to those who travel everywhere in search of food and clothing,
such as intermediaries who act on behalf of others, or those who carry official documents to various places to beg for favors and the like.

These are all forms of heterodox practice. Regarding matters such as the waxing and waning of celestial bodies, as well as wind, clouds, vapors, mists, thunder, and lightning, to then predict that this year will be one of abundance or famine, or of military conflict and disease—these are all forms of heterodox reliance. As for those who engage in planting and cultivation:

To sow seeds is called "planting" (*zhǒng*); to transplant them is called "cultivating" (*zhí*). That plants, trees, and grasses grow from the soil by means of roots and so forth—this is the lower form of heterodoxy.

Such minor incantations as treating swellings with spittle or curing insanity and the like are examples of this "cultivation. To encompass the four intermediate directions within the four cardinal directions is itself an unjust principle.
Regarding the explanation in this *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the third fascicle states: "A bhikṣu is one who begs."
A *śramaṇa* is one who maintains a pure livelihood; because he sustains himself by begging, he is called a "beggar" (*bhikṣu*).
At that time, Śāriputra entered the city, and having obtained alms-food, sat against a wall to eat. There was a daughter of a brahmin named Viśākhā who came upon him as he was eating.
She asked, "Śramaṇa, are you eating? Śāriputra replied, "I am eating. The brahmin girl said:

"Are you not one who eats from a square mouth? Śāriputra replied, "I am not. He asked again, "Are you not one who eats from an upward-turned mouth? He replied, "I am not one who eats from an upward-turned mouth.
This continued until he asked, "Are you not one who eats from the four intermediate directions? Śāriputra did not answer each time that he was not so.
Then Vimalanetra asked again, "Although I have just asked these questions, I do not yet understand the meaning and principle behind them. Please explain for me."
Explanation: At that time, Śāriputra explained it one by one for Viśuddhanetra. This is precisely as listed previously (the note says this was clarified earlier;

according to this current explanation, it seems more convenient). Regarding the phrase "the Vinaya reaches the Dharma": this means that even if the aforementioned faults exist, one must have the three roots (*trīṇi mūlāni*) manifest before one may raise a charge against another.
If one commits that very offense, the answer is: "This offense is [immediately] named and [immediately] exists; there is no difference."
To perform the *kṣepaṇīya-karman* (act of censure) is, in fact, an illegal (*adharma*) formal act (*karman*). If one commits this offense, the response is "this offense is equal [to that].
If it is performed according to the Dharma, it is the reverse of the above; thus, an illegal act becomes a legal one. As for the phrase "until the reprimand":

this refers to the path of resolving the offense. This person neither recognizes nor knows it; because they are confused regarding the characteristics of this offense, they commit a *pārājika* or perhaps a *sthūlātyaya*, and thus it is said "not knowing."
"Not seen. One must perform the rite of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*).

Regarding the phrase "the five [cases] leading to robes": "one who quarrels with oneself" means, according to Xuán, that one's affairs do not succeed and one constantly scolds oneself in anger, as if in a state of internal strife (this is one interpretation).
Wánlíng says: "Quarreling with oneself" refers to engaging in verbal dispute with another based on one’s own perspective.
Regarding "causing dissension between others": this refers to not engaging in conversation oneself, but rather speaking to both parties separately so as to cause enmity between them;
thus it is called "causing dissension. If one follows Xuanzang’s commentary on the preceding phrase, here the term is specifically applied to those who dispute with others.
However, that interpretation seems slightly inferior in terms of logical consistency; the latter explanation is preferable. "Not once causing dissension" means [doing so] repeatedly.
To practice such deeds is not a one-time occurrence. To associate with evil friends is to one's own detriment; to have wicked people as companions does not foster wholesome dharmas.

This is identical in meaning to what was stated above. However, "evil friends" refers specifically to those who act as companions for a temporary duration, whereas this refers to those who do so for a long and enduring period.
"Delighting in evil oneself" means that one’s base nature desires to commit evil at every moment of thought.
The first three refer to the violation of the precepts. The violation of views refers to the arising of the sixty-two types of false views, which destroys the single right view.
"Laypeople" (baiyi) refers to householders; one should not allow them to associate with one too frequently, for fear that they might become infected by evil practices.

"Those who approach and submit" refers to those who associate with and become habituated to [unwholesome conduct]. "With eunuchs, males, and so forth" explains the aforementioned physical association.
"Mutually harboring defiled minds" refers to verbal association. These two types together constitute both physical and verbal association.
Regarding "fruits and gourds": those produced from trees are called fruits (*phala*); those produced from vines are called gourds (*ālābu*). The five classes of precepts (*pañca-śīla*).
"Those" refers to the five categories [of offenses], which are called the "five groups. "Thieves" refers to those who commit minor acts of pilfering;
because they fear their owners, they are collectively termed "thieves. "Bandits" refers to those who seize property openly and face-to-face.
"Dice" were created by Laozi for divination, but today they are cast as a game. There are five [types of disputes], following from the fourth category above regarding litigation and contention.
Regarding the four further [faults], there are these five. "Self-exalting" means disregarding others. "Cane-like depravity" refers to a violent nature.

"Meaningless speech" refers to speech that is not in accordance with the Dharma. "Awakening at the wrong time" means that even if it is speech in accordance with the Dharma, one does not know the proper timing;
because it follows upon decline and affliction, it is called "un-Dharmic. "Not associating with virtuous people" means that virtuous people are one's spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
"He is teaching me the Dharma. The Buddha said, "In the past, I encountered the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, who granted me the prediction that I would become a Buddha due to my accumulated merit.
I shall not now associate closely with this man. Regarding the fifth, "one who is respectfully treated by juniors," it means one who is inherently entitled to receive respect from others.

Now, "instead honoring him" means that just as a disciple properly provides service and respect to a teacher according to the Dharma—whereby it is logically appropriate for the teacher to receive such honor and attendance—one instead shows reverence to the other;
this is a reversal of the proper order. Regarding "three admonitions in private": first, an individual should admonish the person to desist.
Regarding "the Saṃgha performing the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*": if the individual admonition is not accepted, one must apply the disciplinary measures (*dharma*) accordingly.
Regarding "those who are renowned for their brilliance": "those who do not respect others" refers to those who rely on their own superiority and do not even count others as human beings.

"Those who treat the great assembly with contempt" means they look down upon, insult, and treat the Sangha with such indifference that they act as if no one were present (this passage frequently appears in the *Pòchāo*).
Regarding "those who fear the *karmavācanā*," the *Chāo* itself explains: "This is another name for *tāḍana* (reproach). The Venerable Master said:
"Fear" refers to the fruit [of action]. "Reproach," established above, refers to the designation based on the cause;
for by means of this reproach, the fear of hell in the future will be stilled.
Regarding the phrase "the superior [cases] reaching the ultimate": this clarifies that those who have transgressed are collectively enumerated and rebuked for the excessive nature of their actions.
"In the presence of the Saṃgha" refers to four or more persons; "a bhikṣu" refers to one or more persons. "All are subject to the formal act of censure" (sarve karmavācanāyām patanti):

"all" means together and exhaustively; it signifies that they all enter into the disciplinary treatment of censure. In the *Yǒujì* (Record of Existence), the character "bǐ" (比) is used as a phonetic gloss for "bǐ" (比).

Category: The initial case concerns the conflict between Wisdom (Prajñā) and Luhe (Rohiṇī), which serves as the origin for the formal reprimand (*tajjaniya-kamma*). Now, this is not merely a single transgression;
rather, all those previously enumerated cases, when compared to the initial case, are collectively subject to the disciplinary penalty of the formal reprimand.
The Venerable One said: "In the manuscript, it was erroneously written as 'bi' (比); however, following the previous 'jie' (皆) is correct. Regarding the phrase "from 'two' to 'understanding'":

as the text states, "establishing the disciplinary measures at the beginning" refers to the first of the four sections; it is the first among the four. This establishes the rules for disciplinary punishment.
Regarding the phrase "this... to 'maintain'": this rule differs from other *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts).
Therefore, that which was explained previously is found in the *Jiangxi Houtang Ji* (Record of the Rear Hall of Jiangxi), which states: "If one wishes to discern this text, one should first ask:

'These seven types [of *karman*] are all methods for disciplinary punishment (*daṇḍa*) by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*; why then is the *tarjanīya-karman* (reprimand) explained at the very beginning?

Immediately following this, the *Chao* (the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*) is cited, answering: 'This differs from the others,' and so forth. Here, "this method" refers to the *tarjanīya-dharma* (the rite of reprimand).

The remainder refers to external matters. Apart from these reprimands, there are six further [categories], for which formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*) serves as the remainder. As for those that differ:
in each of the six subsequent cases, the rule applies to only a single matter; for example, the rite of "carrying out" applies only to those who defile the household through evil conduct.
Matters that obstruct [the path] prevent one from reaching it; such matters as merely reviling or slandering laypeople are but one type. Now, this censure does not apply to only one kind;
rather, all unlawful acts without exception are included within this *karmavācanā* (formal act) for their governance. As the preceding text states, "transgressions are of many kinds," and so forth.

Since these transgressions vary in degree—some being minor and some major—the most significant ones are explained first; thus, it is said they are "explained previously. This is to be understood accordingly.
[The commentator] explains: This appears to be a rebuke arising from the intent of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual). At first glance, it seems reasonable;

however, if one discards the five lines that follow, the text of the *Chao* (the sub-commentary) would become an isolated fragment. Consider this. Now, following the *Xuanji* (the Explanatory Record), it says: "This dharma" refers to these seven types of *karmavācanā*.
"Other *karmas*" refers to those such as the conferral of precepts, the repentance of offenses, and the receiving of days [of retreat]. "There are differences" refers to this...

This is a *karmavācanā* (formal act) that contradicts human sentiment; it was rarely practiced in the present age. The others are *karmavācanās* that accord with human sentiment and were widely prevalent during that era.

Since this one contradicts human sentiment, at the time of performing the ritual, the Saṃgha must verify and rectify the offense. Furthermore, there must first be a formal accusation, followed by the administration of a reminder and the imposition of the penalty.

Moreover, according to the rules for prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), one must conduct a full interrogation regarding the assembly of fellow practitioners who jointly raised the accusation. This constitutes the bestowal of repentance (*pratideśanā*).

...and so forth. Because the dharmas that accord with one's inclinations are entirely different [from those previously mentioned], the meaning clarified above applies to the current practice; this refers to "discrimination" (*viniścaya*).

This interpretation does not contradict the text of the *Śāstra* (the *Jīkǎnmò shū*), and accords with the *Jīkǎnmò shū*. I humbly request your detailed examination. Regarding the fourfold classification used to distinguish [the cases] as cited from the Vinaya by Wǎn Lín, I shall briefly explain them here:
first, these are methods of governance (*dharma-vinaya*) and not methods for extinguishing offenses (*pāpa-praśamana-dharma*). That is to say, these seven types and nine...

The first is the method of treatment (*yukti*), such as the *pratideśanīya* (confession of offenses). The second is the method for extinguishing offenses (*pāpa-śamana*) but not a method of treatment, such as the confession of offenses before the white-robed Saṃgha.

The third is both a method of treatment and a method for extinguishing offenses, such as the expiation of the *śeṣaka* (residual) offenses. The fourth is neither, such as the observance of the *poṣadha* day, and so forth.
Regarding the ten types of causal conditions (*nidāna*) mentioned above: whenever one performs a formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*), one must possess these ten conditions, namely:
This proceeds gradually. The weighing of the preceding matters and so forth—ten in total—are fully explained at the beginning of the fifth chapter.
"Having fulfilled the seven dharmas" means that among the ten conditions, one has reached the seventh condition. Regarding "all matters being presented in the midst of the formal announcement":

all ritual procedures for the Dharma have a presentation of intent, such as the formal acts of binding, reciting, receiving, holding, announcing, designating boundaries, and requesting precepts; however, this is not the case here.

The *Chao* (Commentary) says: He himself explains that this is because it contradicts the mind [of the offender]. How so? It means that one must cause the person who committed the offense to state their intent once more, so that the Saṃgha may verify and rectify their transgression.
"Obtaining the submission of the former offender" means that once the former offender has submitted, they are then accorded with the Dharma.
"One should first perform the *jǔ*" (formal accusation) is explained by the sub-commentary itself. "A person of virtue" refers to the *zhēfǎ* (one who restrains the Dharma). The text states:
If a bhikṣu is to accuse another, there are five internal qualities [he must possess], as previously explained. Regarding "one who causes recollection," the commentary explains it for itself.

Regarding "one to whom an offense should be assigned," the commentary also explains it. As for "the elders and so forth," according to the method of obstruction, when one is to question them fully, that person goes before the elders and says:
"I wish to obstruct such-and-such a bhikṣu. The assembly should listen; having been granted permission by the elders, they should then ask: "You..."
Are there five internal qualities? If he says "no," one should instruct him: "Do not be negligent. If he says "yes," one should ask: "Which ones? If he can answer, one asks again:
"Have you questioned the bhikṣus of middle rank? If he has not yet done so, one should instruct him to do so.

If he says he has finished questioning them, one says: "Have you also questioned the bhikṣus of lower rank? This is to be conducted according to the same method as above; hence the inclusion of the word "complete" (具).
Regarding those who can "lift" (formally charge) a group of followers, whether they be senior (*upādhyāya*) or junior (*antevāsika*), it means that at that time, the assembly must be of one mind.
As for the person being lifted, this refers to a bhikṣu who has committed an offense. Only when each step conforms to the Dharma does it constitute a formal act of the Dharma (*dharmakarma*).

When the Vinaya texts mention the lifting of those involved in disputes, this is a method established for a specific occasion. In the present day, matters should be handled according to the circumstances; one may not adhere strictly to the literal text alone.
(As stated above). Once the *karmavācanā* text has been recited, there is nothing further to explain (as stated above).

As for what constitutes an offense, twenty-seven types of non-proper conduct (*anāpatti*) are enumerated. Regarding those offenses that do not require formal confession, these refer to minor transgressions (*duṣkṛta*).

If one intentionally commits such an offense and realizes it immediately, one should perform a mental reprimand (*cittotpāda-vinaya*), whereby the offense is extinguished and does not enter [the formal category]. Within the section on "Rebuke" (*tarjanīya-karman*), there are seven items to be considered.

The six preceding phrases constitute two [categories]. The three "non-[faults]" (*asaddharma*) do not subsume the person or the method; rather, these two "non-[faults]" follow beneath the seven single phrases mentioned above.
By applying them across those [seven], they form seven sets of three "non-[faults]," thereby establishing twenty-seven "non-[faults]" that distinguish the aforementioned two and three "non-[faults].

Question: In the list of single [phrases] within the Vinaya, why is the "present fault" (*pratyakṣa-āpatti*) not mentioned? Answer: The previously listed phrases concerning the two and three "non-[faults]" are based on the fact that the offender has not yet...

Regarding the ritual procedure (*vidhi*): the preceding section has already explained the presentation of the formal motion (*jñapti*). As for the latter seven points concerning the "three non-presences" (*asammukhībhāva*), these refer to the characteristics of failure when performing the ritual.
If the formal motion is presented but [the accused] is not present, on whose account would one discuss the offense and impose punishment? Therefore, they must be present among the assembly.
If, at the time of the subsequent ritual, the Sangha does not summon them but instead applies the sacred dharma from afar, this constitutes a failure due to non-presence. Reflect upon this.
Regarding "second, explaining the deprivation of practice": this refers to depriving [the offender] of the defiled conduct they have committed. Regarding "granting the destination":

the *Fǎbǎo* (Treasury of the Dharma) states that *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and those mentioned here are collectively termed "deprivation of practice. One must understand their similarities and differences: in the first category (*pārājika*), it is permanently deprived;

in the second category (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), once the confession is completed, one remains as before. Here, if one conforms [to the rule], then according to the traditional reading of the text, this is cited.
This is the meaning. As for "how it reaches equality," this refers to the thirty-fifth inquiry. Regarding "the seven fives are not equal," this is the response and explanation.

From "first" up to "going," it states that one should not confer the full precepts (*upasampadā*) upon others; this is based on the previous section concerning the quorum (*pūrṇa-saṃkhyā*) and the censure [of those who do so].
Because the four limbs have not yet decayed, one may receive the full precepts (upasampadā) from others. That one cannot do so now refers to the period of provisional restriction (*prajñapti*).

Xuan says: "If we follow the practice, when a person is undergoing the *parivāsa* penance, if there is a śrāmaṇera who wishes to take this person as his upādhyāya, the Buddha permitted him to remain [in that position] and act as the upādhyāya. This is according to the method of permission. As for 'now depriving' [him of this status],..."

This is simply a restriction, such as when one undergoes *parivāsa* (probation). Since the thirty-five [days] were previously revoked and the ordination has now been conferred, there is both an allowance and a restriction, and thus they do not contradict one another.
The remaining text may be understood in detail. Regarding the passage from "The two" to "the author," it states that one should not recite the *Poṣadha*.
One may not personally perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of the Dharma-precepts. Regarding those who should not respond: even if one is learned and proficient, one must not do so;
this applies even if one errs in performing the *karmavācanā* or if one is commanded to perform what should not be done.

If it is asked, "Since this is an appointment by the Saṃgha, shall I not now accept it and disobey the Saṃgha's command?"—the answer is that one simply need state one’s own circumstances. As for the phrase "reaching three times in speech," it refers to a wicked bhikṣu.
It is feared that they might become habituated to unwholesome dharmas and further increase their transgressions of the precepts; laypeople fear they might be enticed to abandon the path;

and non-Buddhists fear that wrong views might arise. For these reasons, approaching them is not permitted in any case. "Speaking with heterodox words" refers precisely to being obstinate, defiant, and contrary.
Regarding the statement "as for the four types of 'persons who have reached [the limit]': now, having committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, one points to the lower category as the remainder;

later, having committed a *pāyattika* offense, one points to the upper category as the remainder. All commentaries base this on the arising of the intention (*citta*). To claim that pointing to the upper category as the remainder is incorrect is not right.

One should not resent the person performing the *karmavācanā* or the one who rebukes; rather, it means that originally, before the Saṃgha and the bhikṣus, one committed a transgression and was subjected to censure. Now, furthermore...

Regarding the *kamma* of censure (*paṭisāraṇīyakamma*): having returned together with [the accused], one commits a transgression before the monks of the Saṃgha; this constitutes a continuous subsequent offense.

That is to say, in the presence of the monks of the Saṃgha, one speaks erroneously regarding the four matters, now censuring this *kamma*, claiming it is contrary to the Dharma, and censuring the person and so forth—all these are continuous acts that do not cease, and thus constitute a continuous offense. As for "reaching the fifth person," it means:

Since their provisions have been confiscated, they are unable to do so. Regarding the phrase "the six [items] up to... and so forth: (2) joining the palms to inquire after one's health; (4) the four robes; (5) the alms bowl.
Regarding the phrase "the seven [items] up to... and so forth: "to testify to another's matter" means to provide testimony regarding a legal case involving another person.
Regarding the suspension of the *poṣadha*, it follows the procedure of the *Pratiṣedha-khandhaka*. One says, "Venerable sir, I suspend [the recitation].

This is because the monk who recites the precepts may be one who has broken the precepts, or even one who lacks proper decorum (*īryāpatha*). If it is said that he has broken the precepts, one must specify which precept was broken—such as a *pārājika* or a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Since the purpose is the same—to establish the truth regarding another's offense—one should not suspend the *pravāraṇā*; the principle is likewise applied there. If the other person has not actually committed an offense, then it is a dispute.
