Regarding the term "offense" (*āpatti*): this refers to contending with a virtuous bhikṣu. Since it involves seizing the testimony of one who is correct, it is not appropriate [to do so].
As for the passage from "the three" to "receiving": Xuán says that this is also a text from the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (Section on Reprimands). It is easy to understand and need not be explained further.

Regarding the explanation of the four methods for resolving legal issues (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*) by the Shiming school: if one asks why, among the four—reproach (*tarjanīya*) and so forth—the confession (*pratideśanā*) comes first and the resolution (*samaya*) comes later;

whereas among the three—formal acts of suspension (*ukṣepaṇīya-karman*) and so forth—the resolution comes first and the confession comes later—is this the arrangement of the Vinaya texts? The answer is that the Xiangbu school states:

because the faults of reproach and the like lack any element of compliance (*anuvartana*), confession precedes the resolution. As for the faults of the three formal acts of suspension and the like, because there is a fear that the offense might recur (*punar-āpatti*), the resolution precedes the confession.

"Conformity. This is why one first practices understanding and subsequently performs repentance. The Dongta (East Pagoda) school refutes this, saying: "These seven types [of offenses] are all for the purpose of disciplining a person.

Even though the repentance is completed, the disciplinary method does not cease. Since they were originally intended for repentance to eliminate depravity, how could there be an offense of 'conformity'?
This agrees with the intention of Nanshan; he does not accept the initial interpretation.
Regarding the phrase "The Vinaya says it is so": the expression "the Vinaya says" refers to the text of the *Pratimokṣa-vastu* (the *Khandhaka*).

The intervening words and phrases therein are without further meaning to be explained [and so forth]. Regarding the note stating "those two bhikṣus are also like this": this is based on the case where two individuals have committed the offense together;
since one person has been punished and requests release from the *pāyattika*, the second person must likewise request release. Thus it says, "those two."
It is also thus. If one were to take the phrasing literally, it should say, "The second bhikṣu is also thus. There is another interpretation, but as it is not correct, it is not recorded here.
Question: Suppose two people have committed the same offense. One person complies and requests absolution, while the second person has not yet complied and has not yet requested absolution.
Does that single bhikṣu alone incur the full offense? Someone says: He does indeed incur it. Now...

According to the Vinaya texts, [the formal act] is not accomplished unless two persons perform it simultaneously and request the lifting of the restriction in accordance with the procedure, each reciting the appropriate words;

only then is it accomplished. Regarding the phrase "up to those who hold [the office]," as the text says, those who have arrived [for the assembly] sit below; this does not depend on seniority by *varṣa*.

Regarding "using according to the name on the roster," this refers to cases where the offenses committed are identical; one must not exceed four people in the recitation, for fear that [the quorum] would be exceeded.

"Sangha" refers to the community of monks. "When the time comes, one should measure it" means that when the time for performing the formal act (*karmavācanā*) arrives, one should calculate and deliberate accordingly.
Regarding the phrase "there were two resident masters," according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, in the village of Kālīdāsa near Śrāvastī, there were two resident bhikṣus.
One was named Punnasena and the other was named Assaji. They were corrupters of families and practitioners of evil conduct who destroyed the pure and wholesome minds of others.

The detailed account of their origins is found extensively in the *Anupada*. Therefore, the Buddha ordered the Sangha to act according to the Dharma and go to that place to expel them from the village.

In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, this is called the *niḥsaraṇa-karman* (act of expulsion); it is also termed *nissāraṇa* (sending away). While the terminology differs, the meaning is the same; they are categorized together.

The "Original Teacher" refers to the person being disciplined. Should there be a matter requiring deliberation that cannot be discussed with others—fearing that if others were to answer, it might constitute a *anuvāda* (reproach)—the seven dharmas concerning the *upādhyāya* are established to provide a common means for such cases.
Regarding the phrase "the third [category] reaches the middle": the term "third" refers to those who rely [on others]. The *Jiewen su* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states:

"Although one has long entered the Path, if one's wisdom is dull and one's spirit is clouded, one will commit offenses as soon as one performs repentance; thus, transgressions ceaselessly recur. Since such a person lacks resolve and integrity, they must be governed by relying on a person of eminent virtue.

If one follows the *Nidāna* (Origins), it was because the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita was elderly and ignorant, repeatedly committing offenses despite performing repentance, that the Buddha established this rule to govern him.
One relies upon those who possess virtue. However, if the initial place of reliance later falls into ruin, the Buddha instructed that one rely upon a person;
yet if that person later dies, he therefore instructed that one must rely solely upon those who possess virtue. The rest is as explained in the *Dharmas of Teacher and Disciple*.
Reliance on a group is largely the same, with only slight differences; below this, one relies upon an individual.

Regarding those who come from afar: as for those who revile and slander laypeople and then immediately depart, this accords with the case in the Vinaya of the bhikṣu Kalyāṇadharma, who harassed the householder Citta. This householder had attained the second fruit [of the path];

he had faith in the Triple Gem, honored and supported his parents and śramaṇas, and strictly maintained the precepts he was bound to observe without breaking them. The bhikṣu Kalyāṇadharma had previously accepted...
After making offerings, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana later came to visit. The householder prepared the offerings, but they were tasteless and lacking in quality.
Sudarśana (Śubha) conceived a mind of jealousy and said to the householder, "The food you have prepared today is tasteless and poor;
there is nothing but a little sesame dregs. He thus reviled the householder. The householder’s grandfather had made his living by pressing oil; having heard this, he became enraged.
He was displeased and said to Sādhudharma, "Venerable sir, you have destroyed such [virtues as] the treasures, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and meditative concentration.
He spoke these words by way of illustration, saying, "One should make this a metaphor. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states:

"In a past age, there was a merchant who obtained a pair of chickens, a male and a female, and came to this country to dwell in a *naḍa* forest. The male was eaten by a wildcat; only the female remained behind."
A crow covered [her], and she subsequently gave birth to a son. When the son made a sound, the father spoke this verse:
"This child is not mine; The father is from the wild, the mother is from the village.
Born from their union, the son is neither crow nor chicken. If you wish to learn the father’s voice, Then you are born from the chicken."

"If one wishes to learn the cry of a mother bird, yet its father is also a crow—to learn the crow’s call as a cock’s cry, or to learn the cock’s sound as a crow’s—learning both crow and cock together, neither will succeed.
The Buddha said: "This householder has attained the power of recollecting past lives; he saw that in a previous existence, this bhikṣu was a crow-cock."
"Son," he said, "you mock me in this way. Furthermore, though you have left the household life, your mind and conduct remain worldly; you are like that black hen—resembling nothing at all.

Because of this, wholesome dharmas gave rise to anger in me, and I consequently departed. He reported these matters to the Buddha. The Buddha ordered that a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) be performed to treat him, restricting him from entering the homes of laypeople (*avadātavasana*).

As for the appointment of those to carry out the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation), it should be conducted according to the thirty-fourth rule of the Vinaya. The Sangha...
One is appointed by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*. Ānanda, possessing eight qualities, shall act as the messenger to lead that person undergoing punishment to the householder’s home.
He shall speak thus to the householder regarding the confession: "The Saṃgha has already completed the disciplinary penalty for this bhikṣu. If he accepts the confession, it is well;
if he does not accept it, one should station a bhikṣu authorized by *karman* in a place where he is within sight but beyond hearing, and instruct him as follows..."

He performs a Dharma-confession. He then returns and speaks to the layperson regarding the confession. That bhikṣu previously committed an offense; now he has already performed the confession, and the offense is removed.
If the one receiving the confession accepts it, that is well. If he does not accept it, the person who committed the offense should go in person to confess.
If he still does not accept it, one should perform the "turned-down bowl" (pātra-nyubja) rite, which means that all bhikṣus are prohibited from going there altogether.
He received offerings from this monastic friend, thereby benefiting that lay devotee. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The Saṃgha should say to that offending bhikṣu:
'This lay devotee possesses great power; whether as an official or a bandit, he is capable of committing evil deeds and harassing the community of monks.
You should abandon this dwelling place. If the bhikṣu should insist on remaining, the Saṃgha commits no offense."

Regarding these four types of *karmavācanā*, there are roughly two categories: *tarjanīya* (reproach) and *niśraya* (dependence) constitute internal protection; *pravāsanīya* (banishment) and *apratisaṃkramaṇīya* (prohibition from approaching laypeople) constitute external protection.

Regarding "furthermore, as for the differences": the four refer to the censure and so forth; the three refer to the three types of formal accusations (*tshangs pa mtshungs par spyod pa'i khrims gcod pa*). As for the similarities and differences, they are distinguished within the text itself.

Regarding "as for the preceding... up to 'accusation'": one who ruins their conduct does not rely [on the precepts], but practices while maintaining two types of observance; this is called ruining one's conduct.
"Those who still possess faith in the mind" refers to people who believe that the two causes of good and evil evoke the two fruits of suffering and happiness.
Regarding "those who arrive later," their faith and practice have both degenerated; generally speaking, there are two types:

first, those who believe in the two causes of good and evil evoking the two fruits of suffering and happiness, which is the initial gateway for entering the Path; second, those who rely on faith to initiate practice. There are four kinds of practicing evil, the first of which is...

The practice of restraint through observance (*śīla-saṃvara*) refers to confessing one's transgressions with faith. Second is the practice of restraint through performance (*kriyā-saṃvara*), which refers to seeing that desire is an obstacle to cultivation;
it is the practice of purity through detachment from defilement. These are the three cultivations. When these three cultivations are corrupted, they become the three perversions (*mithyā*).

To counteract these three perversions, the three types of formal accusation (*ukṣepaṇīya-karman*) are established. What is called "accusation" means that after the accusation has been made, there is no longer any leisure for a bhikṣu, just as in the world... [text fragment].

Regarding the use of objects: they are lifted up and set aside. As for "entering the group of monks" (*ju seng*), this refers to a person who, while alive, did not share in the benefits of the *saṃgha*.

After death, their clothing and belongings are not subject to distribution among the *saṃgha*; rather, they are to be bestowed only upon those monks who were with them at that time. The rest of the text is intelligible.
"Now, as for 'the present ruler' (*jin zhì zhì*)," this refers to the current master’s intention. Because the mind has not yet entered the Way, it is due to a lack of faith in the mind. Faith is...
This refers to the mother of Dao-yuan. "Conduct that violates both the great and the small" indicates the corruption of conduct.

"To say with the mouth that there is no sin and no repentance, and that lust is the Way," indicates the corruption of faith. "The person also practices evil and so forth" explains the corruption of conduct.
From "both combined" onwards is the concluding judgment.

Regarding the phrase "next comes the explanation": Xuán (玄) states that within the *Vinaya-nidāna* (origins of the precepts), because of Canda’s state of mind, his false views were destroyed, which immediately obstructed the path of learning the Right Way (*samyag-mārga*).

As for the phrase "or failing to comprehend the teaching" and so forth: if one does not understand the characteristics of the teaching, they will fail to distinguish between what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, and thus will not believe in cause and effect;
or, even if they know [the truth], they act intentionally [against it]. When the Saṃgha questions them regarding this, they either do not comprehend or [refuse to acknowledge it].
To this, he replies that he did not see it; or, knowing [the truth], he deliberately answers that he did not see it, or he refuses to acknowledge it.

Because he persistently claims he did not see it, he is brought before the assembly for discipline. As for those who are expelled from the community: although they remain within the monastery, they do not participate in the monastic laws (*saṃghadharma*) and lack the qualifications for membership.

The rest is understandable. As for the statement "from six up to 'liberation,'" this also takes Cunda as the causal basis, just as in the Vinaya, where purification occurs only through the confession of an offense.
To say that there is nothing to be confessed is a false assertion; it is a superficial proliferation of Mahāyāna teachings regarding the sutras on the emptiness of the nature of offenses.
This is *nirvāṇa*. The rest is as in the text. Regarding the statement "the seven cases of arrival," this was spoken by the Bhikṣu Ariṣṭa concerning the causes and conditions;
it was established because desire does not obstruct the Path. Question: These three types of formal accusation (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) were not seen in the preceding text on accusations.
It is said that one does not believe in the two causes—good and evil—which evoke the two fruits of suffering and pleasure. With false views harbored within, they obstruct the path of training.
Later in the text, it further states: "A decisive and penetrating perverted mind is called 'view' (*dṛṣṭi*)," and so forth. Since this is produced from a mind of false view, [it is so designated].

According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, among the four types of wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), it is the loss of precepts through wrong view that renders one exempt from disciplinary punishment. Huainan says:

"As for what is called wrong view—severing the roots of goodness and losing the precepts—it requires the arousal of a complete mind of the nine grades to constitute a perfect wrong view; only then does one certainly lose the precepts.

Since the substance of the vows no longer exists, one is identical to a layperson (*avadātavasana*) and need not undergo disciplinary punishment. This is the case with the three types of monks who have been formally accused."
Although one may not believe in cause and effect and possess a thoroughly perverse mind, as long as the nine grades of the mind have not yet been fully exhausted, one does not lose the precepts.
However, the Vinaya bases its discourse on coarse appearances; when explained according to subtle details, there are instances of both losing and not losing them.
Although this interpretation is clear in its logic, if one investigates the ultimate source, it cannot entirely avoid difficulties. For instance, in the case of [the offense of] *utthāpana*...
The nine grades of the deviant mind—whether exhausted or not exhausted—all belong to the internal mind of another. How, then, can the Saṃgha now know the affairs of that mind?
Now, following what was received from Tiantai, I shall provide one explanation to assist [in understanding] this:

it is said that because the Saṃgha commands the reforming of evil, they subject the individual to formal disciplinary action (*karma*). When that person undergoes the suffering of the Saṃgha’s punishment, they immediately develop faith; thus, one knows the nine grades.
If the perverse mind has not yet reached its full development, it will invariably resist and oppose, refusing to accept punishment;

this serves as proof that the perverse mind is resolute and thorough, for it has already severed the roots of goodness and thus cannot be disciplined (this interpretation is the most subtle among the subtle).
Regarding the phrase "this is the ultimate measure": it refers to the realization of the preceding seven dharmas which are beneficial for the treatment of persons.

As for the term "a single meaning" (*ekārtha*), according to an additional passage in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "The Tathāgata appears in the world for the sake of a single meaning, for the sake of all bhikṣus."
The *karman* of censure was enacted. Upon hearing this, all the bhikṣus rejoiced, believed with gladness, and practiced accordingly.
The meaning of "gathering [the members] into the Saṃgha" up to the tenth point, "the long-term preservation of the True Dharma," is entirely one and the same meaning. The *Chao* (Commentary) states:

"Up to 'evil mind' and so forth" refers to the various clauses found below in the Vinaya text, such as: "performing the funeral rites," "relying on [another for] dependence," "prohibiting [someone] from going to the homes of laypeople," and "not..."
Regarding the cases of not confessing or not relinquishing [faults], as well as the three formal acts (karmas) such as the *jñapti* for the *Poṣadha* and the *Pravāraṇā*,

the concealment of offenses, the *mūlāpakarṣa*, and the removal of guilt (*āpattivyutthāna*), from the four grave offenses up to the seven methods for settling disputes— in each and every one of these phrases,
it is stated that the Tathāgata appeared in the world and, for a single purpose, established the *tāḍana-karman* (the formal act of censure). The rest may be understood accordingly.

Regarding "the great [calamity] reaching the person," that sutra states: There was a precept-observing bhikṣu named Jue-de (Jñānaguṇa) who prohibited the other bhikṣus from keeping slaves, cattle, sheep, or oxen—things that are contrary to the Dharma.
A learned but precept-breaking [bhikṣu], upon hearing this, conceived an evil mind;
he took up sword and staff and threatened this Dharma-preacher. At that time, King Youde (Guṇavat), in order to protect the Dharma, [intervened].
Therefore, he fought against the wicked bhikṣus to ensure that the preacher was spared from calamity. The king’s body was covered by swords and blades such that no part of him could be seen.
Jue-de (Jñānagupta) praised the king, saying, "Excellent, excellent! You are now truly a king who protects the Dharma.
The king was filled with great joy and soon passed away, being reborn in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha as his foremost disciple.
Regarding the question, "What is meant by 'reaching this point'? Xuán says: The purport of the *Chāo* (the Sub-commentary) lies in allowing for repeated deliberation on whether to advance or retreat.

There are four sections in the response. The first explains the two passages and the dual intent of inclusion and exclusion. The second section, beginning with "Furthermore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*," takes the end and does not take the beginning.
The third section, beginning with "Both are preserved," reverses and stops [the previous argument], because it takes both the beginning and the end; thus, it is said to be "demonstrative."
The fourth section refutes the preceding [position]. It is also a text that reverses and stops [the previous argument]. It takes the conclusion and does not take the beginning or middle;
hence it says "is used. Regarding "both may be retained": this refers to taking the passages where faith is generated, which mostly rely on the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*.

The passage "certainly for those who are ignorant and dark" and below relies on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, which refute the preceding [position]. Furthermore, the phrase "or composed as written characters" is an error.
Regarding the phrase "the arrival of evil leading to expulsion," interpretations of this passage have varied greatly throughout the ages.

Some say that once a grave offense (*pārājika*) has been committed, it is like dealing with a "bad horse" because it manifests an unwillingness to submit; others say it refers to one who has committed an offense from the first category of precepts but has not yet sought repentance.

One should immediately perform the *nigarhaṇīya-karman* (act of censure). Or, it is said that for those who commit offenses of the six classes (*ṣaḍ-varga*) and do not submit, one should perform the *tāla-vitta-karman* (act of striking with the palm).

If one commits an offense of the six classes and acts as a minister toward one who does not act as a minister, this is the third type of formal procedure (*tri-udghāta-karman*). The intent of the present excerpt is as follows:

regardless of whether the offense is light or heavy, if one refuses to acknowledge it by claiming "I did not see it," then this procedure is appropriate. In the previous section on *tarjanīya-karman* (act of reprimand), it was stated: "If they subsequently again engage in mutual abuse... [the remainder of the sentence follows].

Regarding the treatment for increased offenses (*āpatti-vardhana*): this refers to the "treatment of a wicked horse" (*aśva-duṣṭa-vidhi*). By citing this common phrase of mutual reproach, it is shown that this constitutes a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).

As for the phrase "the place where you are going": if this person refuses to accept the treatment and wishes to go to another monastery, the Saṃgha shall immediately dispatch someone to inform [the other community].
This bhikṣu has committed an offense. If he is seen later and it is necessary to discipline him, one acts by making a formal declaration (*svavacana*) before the Saṃgha;

in this case, it is performed through a public announcement, and a personal confession is not required. Once he has heard that he has committed an offense, he must be made to confess it himself before the discipline can be applied.
Regarding such a person, one should not seek their permission [to proceed]. The *Xiāngpù* (School of the Xiang Region) states: "It is performed by making a public announcement before the assembly."
"It is not false. This has the same meaning as "speaking for oneself" and the same meaning as "coming to listen. To expel one according to the Dharma is therefore improper.
Regarding the phrase "remaining silent until [the end]": the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that the bhikṣu Chanda was in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī;
during one summer retreat, he troubled the Saṃgha and did not live in harmony with them. At the conclusion of the summer retreat, a certain bhikṣu went to Kāśyapa and...
He reported the matter to Kāśyapa. Kāśyapa instructed Ānanda: "Go to that country and, in the name of the Buddha and the Saṃgha, perform the Brahma-maṇḍala rite to treat him.
Accepting these instructions, Ānanda went to that place together with five hundred bhikṣus.
When Chandaka heard that Ānanda was coming, he went outside to meet him and asked, "For what reason have you come? He replied, "I wish to benefit you. Chandaka asked, "In what way?"
"It will benefit me. He replied, "I shall punish you by means of the *brahmadaṇḍa* rite according to the Buddha’s word. He asked, "What is this *brahmadaṇḍa*?
He answered, "None of the seven classes of followers shall come and go with you or engage in conversation with you.
Upon hearing this, he fainted and fell to the ground. He said to Ānanda, "This is my execution! How can you say it will benefit me? This is what is called the *brahmadaṇḍa*."

First, discussing it in terms of the Dharma: "Brahma" (*brahman*) means purity; "altar" (*maṇḍala*) means the Dharma. It is governed by the Dharma of non-speech, which is the Dharma of purification that obstructs impure dharmas.
Second, explaining it according to the facts: as the *Chao* (Excerpts) states, "He was governed by the Brahmā-heaven Dharma. Wanling says:
"According to what is taught in the sutras, there is an altar before the palace of King Brahmā. Within the assembly of the Brahmā-hosts..."
Those who do not conform to the Dharma are led by the Brahmās and placed upon the altar. The remaining assembly of Brahmās recites a verse, saying:
"If the Dharma existed from the beginning, it should not now be non-existent; since it is not non-existent now, we clearly know that it was originally existent.
Having finished reciting this verse, they lead them down to the place of the altar. Other devas may no longer speak with them. This is also the same when they are later released.
The preceding ritual: [The offender] is led up onto the altar. The various devas then recite a verse, saying: "If the Dharma was originally non-existent, it should not exist now;

since it does not exist now, it is clear that it was originally non-existent. [The offender] is then led down from the altar. The remaining devas resume their usual comings and goings and engage in conversation as before.
Since it is thus for them, it is the same for this case: when a bhikṣu commits an offense, the seven classes of followers [are likewise affected].
He was not permitted to engage in discussion; later, by following [the instructions] to their conclusion, he attained it. A question is asked:

"For what reason is this method of silence employed to discipline a bhikṣu? The commentary answers and explains: "Because the ground of speech in the desire realm also extends to the form realm (and so forth)."
This means that the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is the locus of speech. As for the statement that it also extends to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the *Fǎbǎo* (Treasury of Dharma) says:

"This speech does not belong solely to the desire realm; it also extends to the form realm. According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, bodily, verbal, and mental actions all involve preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Inhalation and exhalation are the preparatory application of the body; feeling and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā*) are the preparatory application of the mind; and vitarka and vicāra are the [preparatory application] of speech.

Regarding preparatory application (*prayoga*): whenever one wishes to speak, one must first engage in vitarka (initial inquiry) and vicāra (sustained investigation). *Vitarka* means seeking; *vicāra* means examining.

It is also said that coarse deliberation is *vitarka*, while the speech resulting from it is *vicāra*. These are both factors belonging to the category of mental concomitants (*caitta*). However, *vitarka* is coarse and *vicāra* is subtle.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "Vitarka and vicāra are the coarseness and subtlety of the mind. Regarding the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one asks:

do they all generally possess vitarka, vicāra, and speech, or are there some that lack them? Ratnabhadra says: According to the treatise, based on these vitarka and vicāra, three stages are distinguished.
First, the stage with both vitarka and vicāra; this refers to the first dhyāna, namely the Brahmakāyika and Brahmapurohita heavens. Second, the stage with [only] vicāra...
The stage without vitarka (applied thought) is the Great Brahmā Heaven of the first dhyāna; this is what is called the intermediate dhyāna.

The stage without both vitarka and vicāra (sustained thought) begins from the second dhyāna onwards. Although mental states and their concomitants (citta-caitta) exist there, because they are extremely subtle, they do not manifest as active functions (pravṛtti).
Question: For what reason is the Great Brahmā Heaven called the intermediate dhyāna? Answer: This is with respect to vitarka and vicāra.
This is for the purpose of establishing its name. It refers to the mind and mental factors of the Brahmā-kāyika devas, which are neither coarse nor subtle.

Because they exist after the stage with vitarka and vicāra and before the stage without vitarka and vicāra, and thus possess vicāra but lack vitarka in that interval, they are designated by the term "Intermediate" (dhyānāntara).

[The *Xuánjì* contains a false explanation, stating: "That which transcends the first dhyāna but has not yet reached it is called 'dhyāna'; because it exists in the interval between these, it is named 'Intermediate Dhyāna'. Regarding the phrase "showing that there is," there is a sūtra...

Regarding the addition of the *asaṃbhāṣaṇa-karman* (the formal act of not speaking together): the *Karmasūtra-śāstra* states that he once saw this *karman* within a sutra, but having forgotten the name of that sutra, he was unable to find it despite his search.
Xuánzàng says that the twenty-fourth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* contains the *asaṃbhāṣaṇa-karman*.
According to the *Dōtō-sho*, it is simply because a bhikṣu has committed an offense and refuses [to acknowledge it] that one says:

If one does not see the Saṃgha, one should carry out the disciplinary measure of "not seeing" (*adarśana-utkṣepa*). If the mind remains stubborn and unruly, one further applies this method of "not speaking" (*asaṃbhāṣaṇa*);

this constitutes an intensified disciplinary measure for increased offenses. One simply informs the seven classes of followers that they must not speak with him, and thus he shall no longer perform *karman*.
Regarding the *Saṃyukta Āgama* and other texts, the context concerns how the *Mahallaka*, despite repeatedly committing offenses, remained compliant.
Because the conduct of the *saṃgha* is not yet complete, three further penalties are added: first, gentle subduing, which consists of the four methods beginning with censure (*tarjanīya*);

second, harsh subduing, which consists of the three methods beginning with formal suspension (*utkṣepanīya*); if these two do not reform him, third, one must "slay" him, meaning one does not speak with him.
This means that the teachings such as instruction are lacking, and the fivefold Dharma-body (pañcadharmakāya) is about to perish; in meaning, this is equivalent to death.

Regarding the phrase "extinguishing and enshrouding" (mie bin), it serves as the title. The *Fǎbǎo* states: "Generally, the act of titling (biaomíng) and the act of citing the name (diémíng) are distinct.
Nowadays, many fail to distinguish between titling and citing. If the names and numbers have already been listed in the preceding text, they are now to be explained in sequence."

At that time, he raises the name once more and calls out the recorded name. If the preceding text has not yet mentioned it in its entirety, and it stands here in isolation, this is called "stating the name.
Now, regarding this single dharma of "extinguishing the funeral bier," although it is listed among the nine *karmas*, it was never discussed within them.
Therefore, it is said to be "outside" those nine, which is why it is called "stating the name. As for the phrase "reaching the dharma," it is as follows:
The text states, "From the fifth [category] up to 'holding'. This rule has no textual basis in this Vinaya; it is derived from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.

Regarding the statement in the text that "one must not engage in joint affairs," Xuánzàng says: "This refers to the fear of shared business; it means that one may not now participate in the same affairs as them."
Regarding "that which is known by the mind": the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states that *karma* is a Western [Sanskrit] term; here it means "to accomplish a matter.
Generally, all that is subject to *karmavācanā* constitutes a "matter. The remaining text is understandable. Regarding the statement "from pure to defiled," concerning Maudgalyāyana and others:

Xuánzàng says that both the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* contain the introductory narratives (*nidāna*). The present account follows the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* in full because, in the past, the Buddha...
During the time of the recitation of the precepts, a king fashioned a golden lotus throne for the Buddha. On the day of the poṣadha, the Buddha sat upon it.
When the assembly had gathered and he was about to recite the precepts, a petal of the golden lotus fell to the ground. At that moment, there was a bhikṣu...
The thief hid it under his armpit and remained silent, not participating in the *poṣadha*. Ānanda said, "The first watch of the night has passed; I pray that the Buddha will recite the precepts.
He continued to inform the Buddha during the middle and last watches of the night. The Buddha said, "The assembly is not pure. At that time, Maudgalyāyana thought to himself, "Who is impure?
He then used his divine eye to observe and saw a bhikṣu who had stolen a golden lotus leaf. Thereupon, he...
He rose from his seat and led [the offender] outside. Returning, he informed the Buddha that the assembly was now pure and requested that the Buddha recite the precepts.
The Buddha rebuked Maudgalyāyana: "Did I not tell you to wait for things to become manifest of themselves? How can you use your divine eye and ear to see and hear the offenses of others?

Thereupon, he entrusted the recitation of the precepts to the bhikṣus. (The above narrates the origin of the event. Xuán says: This refers to the fact that the three faculties have not yet been manifested; therefore, it must be self-evident.

The statement: "The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun) establishes three bases through public announcement. Since this clearly shows that the preceding [passage] is the same as the previous text, this is the "listening" (*śravaṇa*).
This Vinaya prohibits [the act] unless it is performed in the presence [of the accused]. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states that it may also be done without being present.

If, however, one who possesses the five virtues is brought forward and refuses [to comply], then according to the *bhāṣya*, even if not present, it is also permissible to simply suppress and settle the matter. Regarding "self and others," this refers to the citation concerning the Great [Community].

In the assembly, as each person regards the others, they mutually constitute both self and other; thus, when reciting the precepts together or performing the two types of *karmavācanā*, if one remains [in a state of impurity] without having discussed the matter, the ritual act is not accomplished, and all are guilty of an offense. How is this not a shared defilement?

The phrase "As for the two points regarding the discussion" (*yun er zhi lun zhe*) is the heading of the chapter. The phrase "As for the prior point regarding the establishment" (*yun xian zhi cheng zhe*) opens up the two chapters.

The two characters "beginning" (*chu*) and "middle" (*zhong*) refer back to the preceding section on what is not the Dharma. The phrase "From 'temple' (*si*) to 'the intent of the second day'" (*zi er ri zhi zhe*):

"This" (*ci*) is a Chinese designation; in Sanskrit it is *saṃghārāma*, which in Chinese means "Garden of the Community. Alternatively, it is called *vihāra*, which in Chinese... [text fragment ends].
"Cloud-wandering" (*yún yóu*) refers to traveling to superior places. As for the term "temple" (*sì*) used here, it is based on what was established during the Han dynasty (and so forth).
"Goods" (*huò*) means that which is sold. Apart from money, everything capable of being sold is termed "goods"; in common parlance, this is referred to as "bribes and goods" (*huì huò*).
Regarding "bribery" (*jīu*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To seek justice through wealth," meaning to entrust all manner of bribes and goods in order to solicit a legal judgment, and so forth.
Regarding "loss" (*shī*), it refers to accidental misplacement or loss. Regarding "seizure" (*duó*), it refers to that which is taken by force;

even if the custodian of the property refuses to repay it, how much more so when, upon encountering such an event, one is punished by being made to drink alcohol or other penalties while being required to pay double? All such instances are illegal. Because...
"Imprisonment" refers to a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense being confined in an empty room while awaiting the arrival of state rescue, at which point he is released (and so forth).
"Bribery" refers to one who has committed a grave offense and has been imprisoned for a long time, yet the state offers no amnesty;

he consequently takes his own wealth and presents it to the prison authorities to seek release (and so forth). "Seizing the goods of thieves" refers to one who has committed a grave offense... [and so forth].

A person has been imprisoned for a long time under national prohibitions, and the state offers no amnesty. Having no wealth of one’s own, there is no means by which to request release; yet, because of certain causes, liberation is attained.
When bandits come to plunder a monastery and command a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense to seize their property, they then release him, saying, "Go forth.

As for those who seek profit through profit, it is according to the rule that when a monk loses an object, this act constitutes a loss of mind on his part and a gain of mind on the part of the other; thus, the item definitively belongs to the latter.
To now seize [the property] is already an extraordinary gain; because of this gain, to demand twice as much more is called "seeking profit.
This is like the worldly custom where, having returned the principal object, one further demands double the thief's own property.
Is this not in accord with worldly custom? Regarding "standing naked among the monks": it means standing bare-bodied within that assembly of monks; thus, it is called "standing naked."
Furthermore, some say: "Standing in an open space wearing robes that are not properly adjusted, or blowing away dust and the like, is easy to perceive," and so forth.
As for the phrase "Liang-zhi shuo" (The Explanation by Liang), "Liang" means "actual" and "much. "Gangwei" (綱維) means "the guiding principles and maintenance.

"Fa" (法) refers to the teachings; "wang" (網) refers to the mesh of a net. Because one does not rely on the guiding principles of the teachings, it is as cited below. This refers to the following section.
[The text] says: "It should be explained that this refers to the desire for the Dharma and the arising of going and so forth. Regarding the statement "only three people are permitted," Xuán says:
"Since they are called 'bystanders,' these are people from both sides; together with oneself, how could this not be three? Therefore, one cannot reach four.
As for the reason why it cannot reach four, one interpretation states: "It is for fear of the fault of infinite regress. This is incorrect. Now, following Ējì, it says: [the text continues].

There are those who share the same views; this constitutes being endowed with good companions. Why then need it be stated? When stating "one who does not desire [the view]," it means: "I cannot bear to associate with such a person who does not desire [it].

Thus one speaks three times. Regarding "corresponding to a mind that guards": the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* explains that there are three types of guarding—mindfulness (*smṛti*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Regarding "the mindfulness that constitutes the essence of the original undertaking": this refers to the clear recollection, which is the very first act of mental attention (*manasikāra*). Regarding "the wisdom concerning prior matters": it arises...
"Wisdom that makes a decisive judgment" regarding "abandoning the non-right and following the right" means discarding what is wrong and adopting what is right.

Since it is now stated that one does not desire [wrong views], this corresponds to abandoning the non-right and following the right, which accords with the mind that guards the precepts. Regarding "the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* and so forth," this serves as proof for the preceding passage.

"As explained above" refers to the section on *karmavācanā*, specifically the fifteen types of silent conduct (*tūṣṇīmbhāva*). As for the phrase "asking until the offense is reached," this is the text.
The character "zhōng" (中) should be pronounced either in the level tone (*ping*) or the departing tone (*qù*). Either way, it does not accord with the established rules;

the offense is a *jì* (吉). Regarding the phrase "next, as for 'etcetera'": that which is "in accordance with the Dharma and the Saṃgha’s regulations" is the opposite of the aforementioned "not in accordance with the Dharma.
"Must follow accordingly" refers to the text of the Five Hundred [Elders]’ Council. This was spoken again by Pūrṇa regarding the Vinaya Piṭaka; the subsequent text says, "As the Buddha..."
"Train in accordance with what has been prescribed," and so forth, as explained at length therein (*etc.*). The commentary states:

"Not relying on the original sūtra" refers to such matters as the Buddha’s prohibition against traveling after the summer retreat, the secular king’s prohibition against traveling when there is no business, and the rule that departing from the monastery for ten days results in being judged as having returned to lay life.
The phrase "harsh labor does not exceed two months" clarifies that the aforementioned harsh labor performed over the course of a year constitutes a transgression.
Regarding the "Ten Wheels" and so forth: the preceding text cited those of dull faculties and had them cultivate merit as a form of punishment;
this, too, is in accordance with the Dharma. As for the punishment of standing during the Śarīra festival, the *Ji* (Sengqi lü) states:

when the sitting mat was first prescribed to be one span wide and three spans long, many bhikṣus were discussing it in the lecture hall and complained that the mat was too narrow and small, etc., [claiming it] did not provide sufficient space.
[The assembly was] in disorder. The Buddha asked the senior elder, "Who is this person? Śāriputra replied.
The Buddha rebuked him, saying, "While many fellow practitioners of the holy life are making such a discussion, why did you remain silent?

You shall now be punished: stand upright throughout the day. Śāriputra accepted the punishment and stood. The bhikṣus each repented before the Buddha, saying, "Śāriputra’s body is delicate; please forgive his transgression."
"Do not cause him distress. The Buddha said, "Śāriputra has a wind-cold ailment; it will only be relieved by the sun.
However, while the sun, moon, and stars may revolve within the sky, Śāriputra’s mind cannot be turned back once he has accepted the Tathāgata’s punishment.
This is precisely the legal regulation of the Saṃgha, and one must comply with it. Regarding the fasting: tell the administrator not to give him food, and this applies only for a temporary period.

Regarding the "timely speech": even the confiscation of robes is not permanent; once the [offender] has been subdued, they are returned with harmony. Regarding "making one stand": this means standing within the Saṃgha;
it does not mean standing naked. Regarding "governing among śrāmaṇeras": this refers to the textual passages concerning the teacher’s disciplinary measures for śrāmaṇeras.
Regarding "punishments such as grass-cutting" and so forth: these are likewise in accordance with the Dharma. If one relies on the Vinaya texts, this is the definitive conclusion.
"Depriving of food, depriving of robes, and clearing away weeds, etc., are all methods of penalizing *śrāmaṇeras*. Now, the *Chao* (the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan*) states:

'The main intent is that the aforementioned penalties regarding food and clothing apply to *bhikṣus* as well. However, when it comes to performing these disciplinary measures by means of verbal commands, one may employ *śrāmaṇeras* for this purpose.

Among these, the task of clearing weeds specifically pertains to *śrāmaṇeras*, which is in accordance with the Dharma; if applied to the Great Assembly (*mahāsāṃghika*), it would constitute an illegal act. This is the intended meaning; many people have misunderstood it."

This is incorrect; it is a false claim that this is not the text of the *Yao* (Commentary), and so forth. Regarding "one's own power" (*zili*) and "the power of others" (*tali*): "one's own power" refers to when one possesses the power of virtue and morality such that kings and ministers recognize and respect one’s worth.
Otherwise, one may also obtain [this status] by relying on another who possesses power. This is explained according to the categories of what is contrary to the law.

In the present time, when fines are collected for the monastery’s permanent endowment (*sāṃghika-sthiti*)—such as flour for small snacks and the like—those who receive them must do so in accordance with the Dharma.
This is because these established restrictions must not be abolished. Regarding the prior mention of the ritual method: it was intended to prevent others from violating the monastic regulations;
it serves as a testimony to the principle that, as stated above, one must accept such things in accordance with the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "as for the two ultimate words," it is as explained in the commentary on the text. Regarding the phrase "thus, as for the ultimate obstruction":

if one asks why food is considered a great affliction, the Great Virtue Jing-shui said: "Food is indeed a minor matter; how can it be called a great affliction? If one considers its substance (*tǐ*), it is small;
however, if one relies upon its function (*yòng*), it is absolutely great. Thus, a Confucian text says: "Food can fill the void and connect the vital breaths. It further says: "The body..."
"It is not like a bitter melon. How could one possibly not eat it? Thus, this food is also said to come first.
The internal teachings also state that "food and clothing sustain the body and life," and so forth. Who among men does not require it? Living in the world, one must obtain this food every day.
Among the many things the World-Honored One prioritized during his ministry, the Buddha taught that all sentient beings depend upon and rely on food and drink.

"Abiding. Thus, the section beginning with "comforting those below" serves as a commentary on the preceding text (and so forth). Regarding "those who eat alone": when the bell is struck, it acts as a sign to summon the Sangha from the ten directions;
since there is now such a prohibition, is this not a violation? Regarding "obstructing the Great Dharma": if eating is not permitted, the monastic discipline will be blocked;
is this not an obstruction (and so forth)? Regarding "the cause of hunger": by examining the cause, one knows the fruit; [it arises from] stinginess and parsimony.

To dare [commit such acts] alone will inevitably invite evil retribution; this is the cause thereof. Regarding "intense suffering" (*jùkǔ*): Cāngjié says that suffering experienced exclusively is called "intense.
After one has fully undergone the retribution of hellish suffering in a future life, one further undergoes the retribution of the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Regarding the ancient masters who transmitted the various Dharmas: during the Sui dynasty, at Daci Temple in Xiangzhou, there was the Vinaya Master Lingyu.
Encountering the suppression of Buddhism by the Later Zhou, he concealed his traces on Mount Zhongnan. Wearing lay clothing, he led his disciples in the mountains;

every day he went out into the marketplace to practice divination for money, using the proceeds to purchase rice for his disciples. Later, when the Sui dynasty’s governance was firmly established, an imperial edict appointed him [to the position of State Preceptor].

He served as the Sangha-Controller (Sengtong) and subsequently established Zhixiang Monastery at his residence. The Dharma Master personally composed the "Ten Articles of the Monastery Charter" (*Sijie*) and other works (as detailed in the text).

The remainder is as stated in the source. Regarding the phrase "those who have reached the Dharma," it refers to laypeople (*baiyi*) capable of observing the fasts (*zhai*). The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, fascicle 26, states:
When a layperson came to beg food from a bhikṣu, the bhikṣu did not dare to give it to him, which led to criticism and reproach. This is [the case].

He reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Give it to one who is able to observe the fast. Xuán (玄) says that the phrase "able to observe the fast" refers to the intent of the later temple regulations as cited [in the *Chāo*].
The following text explains this in detail (*yúnyún*). "One who acts in accordance with the Way" means to rely upon it. "Way" refers to the principle;
it simply means to act in accordance with the principles of the sacred teachings, such as giving when it is appropriate to give. "One who likewise protects the Dharma."
This means that one collectively protects the Buddha-dharma. Regarding "not damaging the affairs of the *dānapati*": "affairs" refers to the four types of material support.

By now receiving and using these in accordance with the proper principles, one does not damage the merit of the *dānapati*’s fourfold offerings. *Dānapati* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "donor.
This will be explained further below (as indicated by *yún yún*).

"One who has truly and sincerely left the household life" means that they are genuine and honest; it reveals that they are not false or spurious, but have departed from the home of the three realms (*tridhātu*) to avoid forced labor, hunger, and the like.

"One who fears the many sufferings of the four enemies" refers to dread; the practitioner is the one who fears, while the four enemies are the objects of fear. "Enemies" (*vairin*) refers to those who cause harm;
they are also called the four *māras*. "*Māra*" is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term. According to the correct principle, it should be stated as follows:
*Māra* (pronounced as "Shazai" [殺賊]—slayer of thieves). He is so named because he obstructs the Noble Path and destroys the roots of goodness. Fourth, there are four types:

first, the *kleśamāra* (affliction-māra), referring to the root and secondary afflictions that can harm the body and mind of the practitioner; second, the *skandhamāra* (aggregate-māra), being shrouded by the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) such that one does not perceive the True Reality;
third, the *mṛtyumāra* (death-māra), which destroys the life-faculty of human beings; and fourth, the *devaputramāra* (heavenly-māra), who dwells in the sixth heaven.
"O Heavenly One! This is the excellence of a person's virtue. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "By cultivating the samādhi of emptiness, one destroys the demon of afflictions (*kleśamāra*).

By cultivating the immeasurable concentration of loving-kindness, one destroys the celestial demon (*devaputramāra*). By realizing nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), one destroys the demon of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*).

By remaining for three months [before passing away], one destroys the demon of death (*mṛtyumāra*). Therefore, at the stage of Buddhahood, these can be severed forever. Now, as ordinary beings who have not yet attained this, it is only logical that we should fear them. Thus it is said: 'This is the emergence...'"

"Family" (*jia-ren*) refers to the meaning of "household. The "three realms" (*tridhātu*) are the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; each has its own boundaries, hence they are called "realms. Regarding "impermanence" (*anitya*):

it is a name established in contrast to "permanence" (*nitya*). "Permanence" means abiding and eternity. [In the cycle of] birth and death, things perish after arising, and after perishing, they arise again;
because these two states are not fixed, there are four kinds of impermanence. Regarding the two types of impermanence, the "great period" refers to when the retribution is exhausted and the spirit...

"Shifting and so forth" refers to this. Second, "moment-to-moment": this means that within one day and night there are six million four hundred and eighty thousand *kṣaṇas*, and it is the fact that these *kṣaṇas* do not abide that is meant.
Regarding the "six close relatives": among those held dear outside of one's own person, none exceed the six close relatives.

As the Duke Shang’s commentary on the *Laozi* says: "Father, mother, elder brother, younger brother, wife, and husband constitute the six. Because these six are immediate kin, they are loved and valued. Therefore—
It is said that these are the ultimate objects of affection. As for the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), they are form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. The *Fǎbǎo* says:
"Because ordinary beings give rise to thoughts of pleasure toward these five, they are called 'desires' (*kāma*). Desire actually originates from the mind, taking external objects as its conditions.

They are also termed the "five māras," because the māras defile pure consciousness. They are also referred to as "dust" (*rajas*) and so forth (as explained at length). That which is empty and false is the mundane world.
Conditioned phenomena and the objects of craving and defilement are all unreal; they are called false and illusory, and thus should be abandoned.
The true path is unconditioned, untainted, and eternally abiding; it is ultimately constant bliss, and is therefore named the True Path.
Regarding "fearing narrowness": in Sanskrit, that which is feared is called *śaṅkā* (忌). This refers to fearing a multitude of guests; hence it is called "narrow. Regarding "perilous and fragile":

the lack of peace within the three realms is called "perilous. The essence of the mind is empty and quiescent, fundamentally lacking a body; because the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is merely a provisional mass, it is termed "fragile.
Regarding "floating and provisional": the *ālayavijñāna* maintains continuity through provisional existence; thus it is termed "floating and provisional."

This is the decree of the Buddha. To contravene the various teachings of the Buddha: the Buddha established monasteries (*saṃghārāma*) where both ordinary people and those following the Dharma alike would strike the bell for a virtuous summons, regardless of whether they were mundane or holy beings.

Since you have now imposed restrictions, this is indeed a transgression. Regarding the loss of the donor’s merit: the donor originally provided these offerings for the sake of the Saṃgha, who are the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Now, because [the donors] look toward this [monastery] and do not receive their share of food, it diminishes their non-manifesting merit (*avijñapti*).
Because of this merit. The rest is as in the text (*etc.*).

Regarding the phrase "perhaps some [ask]" (*huò zhì shǎo zhě*): some commentators say that it refers to a foolish person asking this question; others say it may refer to someone [specific] asking this question.
Here, the second interpretation is retained. Alternatively, "or" (*huò*) may function as an indefinite particle, not necessarily implying a total [absence].
Regarding such a view: "shallow degree" (shāndù) refers to a shallow perspective or estimation. "Locking people" (suǒrén): the *Erya* states this refers to "small people" (xiǎorén);

alternatively, it may refer to those who are fragmented or base, a class of individuals whose limited vision has corrupted their nature. Regarding the "four classes" (sìbèi): the *Fǎbǎo* states these are humans, devas, nāgas, and ghosts.
Furthermore, within the human realm itself there are four: the poor, the wealthy, the noble, and the lowly. These were born from Heaven and Earth.

Elder, Heaven gives birth and Earth nurtures; throughout the four seasons of spring and summer, the myriad things are inexhaustible. It is the same with making offerings. As for those who utilize the mountains and seas:
though the hundred rivers return to the sea day after day, the sea receives them without increasing; all species depend upon the sea, yet its use remains inexhaustible.

Though the hundred grasses cling to the mountain, the mountain receives them without increasing; ten thousand trees rely upon the mountain, yet its use remains inexhaustible. Such is the nature of merit.
The field is likewise; the recipient does not increase, and the utility is inexhaustible. Thus, at the end of the *Buddhapiṭaka*, one may know the scriptural citations that prove this.
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, as for 'extensive giving'": extensive giving is not restricted to ordinary persons or sages, nor does it discriminate between host and guest.

As soon as the bell is struck, they come and are given their share of food; this is called extensive giving. "The temple is poor for the sake of guests" means that because there are many guests on the road...

They trample upon and destroy the monasteries, thereby causing our temples to become impoverished and desolate. Regarding the character 作 (pronounced with a departing tone), it is explained as "to do" or "to act.

This refers to how those in this temple, being impoverished and destitute, all go elsewhere to serve as guests [of others]—this is not correct. As for the character 供 (pronounced with a departing tone), it means "to provide offerings."

There are those who pronounce [the character] with the level tone; this is an error. Regarding "box and lid" (*hángài*): the *dānapati* bestows [offerings] for the sake of the Way, and thus it is likened to the box.
The Sangha receives them and returns them to provide for the assembly of the Way, which is like the lid; they correspond to their original purpose. This is the meaning of the balance.

As for the note stating "one takes [the gift] after first considering the principle," since the former person already possesses the principle of universal offering, they are further able to evoke that principle. There is [this].

Furthermore, this refers to those who provide provisions. "To bring forth" means to lead by way of what is appropriate. Because they seek merit for the future, they are concerned with the Path rather than poverty;
they belong to the class of virtuous persons within secular society. Like the son of Cao Shi Piao Yin, he displayed his meal without using more than two flavors.

"Regarding 'not using double mats for bedding' (and so forth): what is meant by 'suffering' (*huan*)? The character *huan* is glossed as 'anxiety. A person who suffers from anxiety harbors a base and stingy disposition.
As for the note stating 'the world holds this in contempt,' the common saying is that a miserly person throws away refuse, and so forth.

'Accumulating affairs while not being anxious for the Way' means merely amassing wealth and property while being preoccupied with food, clothing, and the like; this is what is meant by 'accumulating affairs.'"
Regarding the cultivation of the supramundane path and so forth: one has not yet seen the opening of the Way, nor the obstruction of worldly affairs.

One has not yet seen anyone who, solely concerned with the work of the Path, exerts themselves with diligent perseverance day and night—this is the opening of the Way. Wearing coarse clothing and eating meager food, sufficient merely to sustain life and body—this is the obstruction of worldly affairs.

Regarding the phrase "because the Buddha has arrived": it is not that one is born in a good realm; this is based on the fact that by failing to provide food during the *upavāsa* (fasting) observance, one causes others to fall into hell.
It is not that one is born in an evil realm; rather, by being able to observe the fast and provide food, one can be born among humans, devas, and so forth (*et cetera*).

"Leaving suffering and attaining happiness" explains the preceding terms "compassion" (*karuṇā*) and "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*). Loving-kindness is able to bestow happiness, which is the attainment of happiness; compassion is able to extract [one from suffering].
"Suffering" refers to being free from suffering. As for the phrase "if one reaches the middle," it means not knowing the distinction between the Path and the secular.
The Path consists of preaching the Dharma; receiving offerings constitutes one's portion. The laity seek merit; practicing giving constitutes their portion.

Now, if a monk instead gives to the laity, this is precisely not knowing one's portion. Regarding "destroying the Three Refuges": the laity are originally entitled to give goods to the Sangha; now they come to beg [for them].
Regarding monastic property: how can there be the meaning of taking refuge in the Saṃgha? If one honors the Dharma, one should instead practice giving;
yet now you beg for monastic property—how can there be the meaning of taking refuge in the Dharma? If one reveres the Buddha, one ought to make offerings; yet now you instead beg from him.
There is also no sense of taking refuge in the Buddha [in this context]. Regarding "according to the characteristics," this refers to the precept against stealing.

As for the various methods concerning kings, ministers, wicked thieves, public officials, laborers, and so forth, these have been explained in detail in that [other] section and need not be recounted here.

Regarding the second point, citing authoritative scripture (*āgama-pramāṇa*): Now, there are three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely: direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*).
As for direct perception, the *Nyāyapraveśa* states: "In this context, direct perception refers to that which is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).

If there is correct cognition regarding objects such as form (*rūpa*) that is free from all conceptualization—such as names and categories—and which functions by directly confronting each [object], it is therefore called direct perception."

The meaning of this is as follows: Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) must take the five objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) as its conditions. It truly recollects their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) without forming conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
It functions spontaneously, taking its object simply by being free from discrimination. Because it illuminates the object through cultivation, it does not deliberate or measure;

it directly apprehends the specific characteristics of the five objects. For this reason, it is called direct perception. For example, when visual consciousness takes the specific characteristic of form (*rūpa*) as its object, it takes only the specific characteristic of form as its object, and not...
One forms conceptions of long, short, square, round, and so forth; this is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form.

A detailed explanation is as stated therein (*etc.*). Second, inference (*anumāna*): the treatise says, "It is the observation of an object by means of various signs (*liṅga*). There are three kinds of signs, as previously explained.
Taking those as the cause, there arises a correct cognition regarding that object, whereby one understands the presence of fire and so forth. This is...

This is called inference (*anumāna*). Its meaning is comprehensive. Now, as for inference, it requires a proponent to establish [the thesis] by means of the three members [of a syllogism], without excessive words, so as to produce understanding in the two opposing disputants; therefore, it is called inference.

Third, the authority of sacred scripture (*āptāgama*) refers here to the authority of the holy word (*āptavacana*). These are all explained in relation to the expressive text. This authority of the holy word is...

The ancient masters Maitreya, Asaṅga, and Vasubandhu established [all three]. From Dignāga onwards, however, they abandoned the discussion of the means of expression (*śabda*) to discuss the intended meaning (*artha*), establishing only the first two [perception and inference].
This implies that the authority of sacred scripture (*āptāgama-pramāṇa*) serves as the basis for formulating a treatise and is also a means of expression;

whereas perception and inference, the two [other] measures, are the intended meanings to be expressed. If both the means and the object are explained together, all three measures are fully manifested. If, however, one speaks only of...

That which is expressed is established as being only twofold. Furthermore, there is "non-valid cognition" (*apramāṇa*), such as when an object does not correspond to the mind—for instance, when one takes empty flowers, rabbit horns, and the like as objects;

these are all called non-valid cognition because they are not elegant or real objects. Now, according to the text of this *Chao* (Excerpts), since all that is cited below consists entirely of the teaching that expresses [the truth], it is designated as "the authority of the sacred word" (*āptavacana-pramāṇa*).
This is not the same as the explanations found in various commentaries (*ji*), [as indicated by the phrase "etc."].

Regarding the phrase "saying 'sa' until death": *Saṃghī* is another name for that which is permanently established (*cang-chu*). Alternatively, the Sanskrit term *saṃghī* means "the great assembly" (*tshogs chen-po*) in this language;
here, the latter explanation is taken as definitive. It refers to the time when the great assembly eats. As for the four signs:
striking the *gandi*, blowing the conch, beating the drum, and subsequently chanting so as not to lose the signal. "Summoning" refers to the resulting confusion. Or, it may be as follows:
In the various temples of Tiantai, the drum is struck first; only when the sound of the drum ceases may the bell be struck. Since this rule is fixed, it is not called "confused.

Regarding the phrase "the *Saṃghāṭī* from beginning to end at two or three locations": "beginning" refers to the initial establishment of the monastery, and "end" refers to the time the site falls into ruin.
That within this interval the communal meals never cease is what is meant by "from beginning to end. Question: Great... [text ends]
Within a single boundary (*sīmā*), how can there be two or three distinct locations for the beginning and end of the *saṃgha*? There are two explanations.

The first, based on the *Souxuan*, states that these are identical in terms of the Dharma but have separate boundaries for food (*bhojana*). Another interpretation says that within a single separate residence (*prativastu*), there are two or three courtyards.
Each has its own place for communal meals, such as the Sūtra Hall in a monastery today, where fields and property are provided to support those who study the sūtras.

When thirty-five or fifty people gather there at the appointed time, this meal does not constitute an offense of eating separately from the community (*pṛthaggaṇa-bhojana*). It is sufficient that they establish the mutual perception [of being together];
this applies equally to other halls, such as those dedicated to the Heavenly Kings or Avalokiteśvara. It is not necessarily fixed that these constitute separate boundaries for meals (and so forth).
"Clapping the hands three times" signifies the three rounds [of the ritual]. The remaining text may be understood in detail (*yún yún*).
Regarding the phrase "saying 'Sàzhì' (the arrival of the *sādhivihārin*)," the commentary states: "It should be because it was a time of scarcity; therefore, the rule is fixed.

This explains the preceding point that one should limit oneself to a single companion. However, if it were a time of abundance, there would be a surplus of people, and the number would not be restricted.

The meaning of the Commentary (*Śāstra*) is as follows: If one receives a portion of rice cakes by mistake, it constitutes an offense according to their value. Furthermore, this does not depend on whether it is a time of plenty or scarcity.
Regarding the offense of *pāyattika* for eating monastic food with partiality: this refers to cases where one receives a small amount of food that is already designated for a specific person.

However, there are those for whom this is inconvenient who do not accept it; they merely incur the offense of *pratigraha* (taking by hand). If one who is not ill demands fine food, and obtains it, one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*).

This means that if one makes an agreement with another and the food enters one's hand, one commits a grave *pārājika* offense. Even if one merely demands it, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense. Such is the meaning of the treatise (*śāstra*).
Now, the Master [Saṃghabhadra] re-examines the meaning and establishes it definitively: this applies only to those who maintain the precepts; for those who have broken the precepts, it is not so.
Regarding wealth and the Dharma: even if one does not personally give them oneself, there is no offense (and so forth). One who constantly watches for a bhikṣu’s shortcomings will mock him, saying:
"A śramaṇa only knows how to receive things from others; he does not know how to give to others. This is why he does not give with his own hands.

The original cause was giving food with one's own hands; later, because of the words of an outsider to a layperson, [the monk said]: "You take the śramaṇas as a field of merit. As for the śramaṇas..."

However, because [people] regarded me as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) and so forth, I established the rule that one must not give with one's own hand. Regarding "one monastery, one village, or one grove":

"monastery" (*vihāra*) is a term used here in this region; "village" (*grāma*) refers to the name for a place characterized by the four boundaries, explained in terms of a monastic dwelling (*saṃghārāma*) within a settlement;
"grove" (*vana*) is the original designation for Jetavana. That sutra states: "If it be a single monastery or temple, a single village, or a single..."
The "tree grove" (śāla-vana) is verified as being without error. The "five Dharma masters" refers to the five Vinaya masters;
they are called Dharma masters because they understand the Dharma and are able to adjudicate matters such as the conferral of precepts. All other details are as stated in the text (*etc.*).
Regarding the phrase "the third [case] up to the drawing of lots": concerning the application of the Dharma, this refers to *karmavācanā* (formal procedures) or methods of disciplinary punishment.

"Performing a separate *karmavācanā*" refers to such acts as requesting an extension of time (*āpattidina*), performing confession (*pratideśanā*), or receiving the precepts (*upasaṃpadā*). "The Sangha cannot reach a consensus" means that although the assembly has gathered to seek harmony, it is somewhat difficult to achieve.
These should be performed prior to the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*; the purpose is that the entire community of monks gathers together and does not disperse again. Furthermore...
At this time, the various karmas are performed. The Venerable One said: "Furthermore, one must know the proper timing for performing the ritual acts.

For example, when the Preceptor for the Precepts ascends the seat, recites the five-word introductory verse, and completes it, he then asks whether the Saṃgha is assembled in harmony, and so forth, up to the announcement regarding those who have not arrived and their proxy consent (*chanda*)."
Some may say, "There are those who desire [to participate]," or "There are none," and so forth; all such matters are as usual.

Before answering a question regarding a matter that has not yet been resolved, the Elder (Sthavira) among the assembly shall announce: "Preceptor, please wait a moment before speaking. There is currently a certain ritual matter [or other business] at hand."
Furthermore, when the Elder merely addresses Chen, there is no need for him to rise from his seat; this is the model for the proper procedure of formal acts (*karmavācanā*).
Gradually, people have failed to understand this and, unable to endure it, perform various ritual matters without first having made the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Or, at times when the Elder addresses the Sangha, those who rise from their beds and stand upon the ground all fail to comprehend the application of the characteristics of the Vinaya. Wait for...
When all the *karmavācanā* (formal procedures) have been completed, the Preceptor may then inquire into the essential points of the matter.

He shall then perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by one announcement) and recite the *Prātimokṣa*, from the extensive introduction down to the five categories of offenses (*pañcāpatti*), and so forth. Regarding the "wise person," Xuán says this refers to a senior monk (*sthavira*) within the Saṃgha who is well-versed in the Vinaya.

According to the law, one should deal with the person based on the specific accusation; for instance, if one has raised a charge of a *pārājika* offense against another but the matter remains unresolved, [one should proceed accordingly].
"Discipline the remainder. Thus, [the penalty] descends by one degree [and so forth]. "Lacking a basis" means lacking the three bases of seeing, hearing, or suspecting.
To falsely claim, "I have seen, heard, or suspected it. "Lacking the remainder" means that the aforementioned bhikṣu has not actually committed an offense;

yet the person who raises the charge either sees another offense or, through a mistaken perception, believes it to be this specific offense. Even if they raise the charge, it is not established; however—

One does not punish for the offense of slander if it is groundless and without remainder; however, if both conditions are met, one punishes for the offense of slander. Regarding whether the intent is false or true:

this refers to the disposition of the person who brings the charge. To have a mind seeking benefit is true; to have a mind seeking to diminish [the other's reputation] is false. Furthermore, if one possesses virtue oneself, [the charge] is false.
Furthermore, one does not possess the requisite virtues. The Vinaya texts do not clarify the true or false nature of such a case. Regarding "weighing the matter":
one who knows others must exercise careful deliberation and measurement. If the intent is false and the basis for the accusation is not established, the person must certainly be disciplined.
However, if the intent is true but the basis for the accusation is not established, leniency may be granted.

Regarding the statement that "the lightest [offense] pertains to time": this refers to a discussion based on temporal limits. When the sun has not yet set, it is a time when [the ritual] is performed according to the Dharma;

when it is dark and without lamps, it is a time when it is not according to the Dharma. Here, we rely on these times to distinguish the characteristics of what is conformable and what is non-conformable.
As for where the gravity of the offense lies, it is as in the case of the *Poṣadha* (confession of precepts), which is the very root of the Buddha-dharma and the basis for receiving the precepts.
The body serves as a field of merit for the world; repenting of sins and removing transgressions are all matters of grave importance. The rest of the text may be understood accordingly (*etc.*).
Regarding the phrase "as for those who face the Vinaya," whether they come or do not come refers to those among the quorum who must always be mindful and always present from the beginning.

This refers to those who are lightly ill. A question was raised regarding the previous section, which states: "Constantly mindful, constantly coming. Here, it says "perhaps coming," which seems to be contradictory. How can these be reconciled?
According to the commentary from Shu-chuan, the two characters "perhaps coming" (或來) here refer to the person described in the previous section as "constantly mindful, constantly coming.
This person constantly remembers [the appointed day] for fifteen days, and upon reaching that day, they come; therefore, it is said they "perhaps come."
This refers specifically to the day of the formal recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). Regarding those mentioned here as "not coming," these are also the previously mentioned sick persons;
or there may be circumstances that cause the recitation to be advanced or postponed, such that they do not know whether they should come or not.

This therefore refers to other days. This text presents both the actual day and other days together; however, within the context of fulfilling the quorum (*pūraka*), it refers exclusively to the actual day.
This explanation is likewise not contradictory. Regarding those who "do not remember and do not come," this refers to the second type of person, which concerns the most extreme case;
that is, the person mentioned in the preceding section who neither remembers nor comes. Regarding those who "remember and come," these constitute a quorum.

The third category consists of those who mutually remember or forget, and who come or do not come, being persons whose mental state is unstable due to the onset of illness. Within this context, it says "those who remember... [and so forth].

"Come. This first clarifies that when another’s illness is mild, they come to attend the *poṣadha* (confession ceremony). To conceal one's own recollection [of an offense] by not coming is likewise an instance of concealing and revealing.
At first glance, the textual phrasing seems contradictory; however, when reconciled in this manner, the underlying meaning is no different.
This point is of the utmost urgency. Neither the *Xuánjì* nor other records discuss it in detail; among later commentators, I have yet to see it mentioned (consider this).

Regarding why the first person must be granted [the rite] while the latter two do not: the first person has a minor illness and a separate assembly, so the *karmavācanā* ritual must be granted to them.
