Indeed. [The sequence is: 1. Seven excellences; 2. Eight arisings; 3. Nine departures; 4. Ten grants of reliance. In the Vinaya text, each item is followed by the two characters "ruo yan" (若言).
Regarding the question concerning "arriving at [the preceptor]," the phrase "at the time of the śrāmaṇera precepts," etc., means:

"At the time I previously received the ten precepts, I already requested [someone] to serve as my preceptor for the ten precepts; now that I am receiving full ordination, this very person shall be my master.
Why must I request the Dharma again? The answer states: According to the Great Virtuous One of Jing-shui, the text is interpreted through three sections. The first section says:

Regarding the statement that one may change based on a "guest" [preceptor] and not necessarily rely on the original teacher: this is merely to present the initial interpretation. The Venerable One says:
"Based on the fact that the 'guest' is not fixed, it is said that if ten people possess both sets of precepts and are all the same person acting as upādhyāya, there is no need to request them again;

it is also permissible. However, in the present case, at the time of receiving the full ordination (*upasampadā*), one requests other individuals separately to serve as upādhyāyas and does not employ the previous ones.
Because he came [to receive ordination] from the Upādhyāya of the Ten Precepts, it is said that "he changed his appearance," and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the second interpretation—that the requests made during the stage of a *śrāmaṇera* up until the reception of the Dharma were different—the Venerable One says: "This refers to the distinction in the Dharma itself; it is not discussed in terms of the person."

Even if ten individuals who have both received the two sets of precepts are all the same bhikṣu, one must still invite them separately. The *Chao* (the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan*) explains this itself:

"When he was a śrāmaṇera, he invited [the preceptors] with the intention of receiving the ten precepts; that he invites again now is for the purpose of receiving the full ordination (*mahāśramaṇa-saṃvara*).

Since the intentions regarding the dharma are distinct, the methods of invitation differ accordingly. Alternatively, it may be that the upādhyāya lacks sufficient virtue and is thus unfit to provide formal sponsorship.
This may be an indeterminate statement. It refers to when one receives the ten precepts and requests another to serve as one's preceptor (*upādhyāya*).

Later, if one sees that the preceptor has violated the precepts, or hears others say that this preceptor has faults and lacks virtuous conduct, doubt arises in the mind and one does not wish to request another.
Consequently, each teacher separately selects a person who maintains the precepts to act as their [preceptor].

This is because it serves as the basis for the full precepts (*upasampadā*) and so forth. The subsequent text states: "Because one has violated the rules of decorum (*airyāpatha*), one does not correspond to the virtue of a teacher.

Second, regarding the two occasions of formal invitation: at the time of the *śrāmaṇera* precepts, there was one face-to-face invitation; now, at the time of the full precepts, there is again one face-to-face invitation.
Therefore, it is said that there are "two occasions of formal invitation" (the above constitutes the direct explanation). According to the *Xuánjì*, however, it is taken to mean "to accommodate."

To alter [the text] and refuse to accept the original master’s version, using the two subsequent sections of the text to collectively explain the meaning of what was previously not altered, is a profound failure to grasp the intent of the *Chao*. I pray that you will reflect upon this.
Regarding "the next [category] that arrives" (as in the text). Regarding "because it ought to arrive," this correctly clarifies the request for the Dharma.

The phrasing and its analysis are no different from the previous explanation in the section on the Upādhyāya; since it would be redundant to describe them here, the textual characteristics may be understood from the context.

Regarding "the next [category] that arrives differently" (as in the text). Regarding "the next [category] limited by time," the meaning must be inferred based on the request; according to the intended meaning of our current Master, it may be...

"One requests [the preceptors] based on the three masters" (and so forth). Regarding "requesting according to the rules and principles of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*," this refers to the preceding passage which cites the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, stating:
"The person receiving the ordination shall first enter the saṃgha; instruct them to perform prostrations at the feet of each [master] in successive order, and then request [them].
Since the procedure requires each one to be done in succession, why would it be restricted solely to the *upādhyāya*? The same applies to the other two masters; all must be requested in this manner.
Therefore, it is said that this refers to the principles and precedents. It does not necessarily apply as a universal rule;
for instance, when one receives the precepts within a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) where more than a hundred people have gathered, it is impossible to invite all of them.

Although these individuals have come for the purpose of receiving the precepts from me, at present we simply follow the method of ordination used in China: beyond the ten people consisting of the three masters and seven witnesses, there is no further requirement.
This was stated in response to a request. Furthermore, any false explanations have not been recorded.

To clarify further the characteristics of whether the ten preceptors have succeeded or failed: "upholding the precepts according to the Dharma" refers to success; "breaking the precepts and lacking virtue while conferring ordination" refers to failure.
"Characteristics" (*xiàng*) refers to the specific signs or appearances. Regarding the phrase "the *Sifen* [Vinaya] states...": [The text continues with] "the younger brother... and so forth.

Regarding your question on whether one may know that the preceptor has violated the precepts and so forth: according to the fourfold formulation of the Vinaya, the first three cases permit it, while the last case does not.
In this present text, the fourth case is cited, as it was already explained in the section on "sufficiency of the quorum.

As for the point that "the other nine teachers may be inferred by analogy," although there is no explicit text in the Vinaya, the Master’s intention is that one simply infers the permissibility or impermissibility based on the aforementioned four cases. Thus, it is concluded.

"It can be known" (and so forth). Regarding "mutually knowing a grave offense": it means that the precept-teacher knows that the upādhyāya has committed an offense, and the upādhyāya knows that the precept-teacher has committed an offense;

the instruction-teacher knows that the precept-teacher has committed an offense, and the precept-teacher knows that the instruction-teacher has committed an offense. It is the same for the seven witnesses; they know one another in turn.

As for "knowing what is not comprehensive": "comprehensive" (*gai*) means pervasive. That is to say, if one knows that a grave offense has been committed, one may not perform the *poṣadha* or the *karmavācanā*.

Within the Saṃgha, one dwells together and does not live alone. If the preceptor knows that the *upādhyāya* has committed an offense, they may no longer dwell together; thus, the reception [of the precepts] is invalid.

If among those ten persons, each knows [the other’s offense], all are likewise unable to dwell together, and because the reception of the precepts is invalid, why would the formal announcement (*jñapti*) not apply?
Since the *upādhyāya* cannot be one of the ten masters, it follows by analogy that the reception is invalid; how could it fail to include the ten masters?
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "if one follows the Vinaya texts," this means that within those texts it is simply stated that the preceptor has violated a precept;

yet, since all five categories [of offenses] are collectively termed "precepts," it is not known which specific precept was violated—whether it was a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *sthūlātyaya*, or a *pāyattika*. Thus, the gravity of the offense is not explicitly revealed therein.

Regarding the phrase "according to the underlying meaning" (*yì*) and below: the present master, relying on the underlying meaning, maintains that even down to a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) is subsumed under the category of "precepts. It is also...
One must not serve as an upādhyāya. Why? Because the first chapter on incantations lists grave offenses; both are prohibited. The remaining texts may be understood in detail.
As for the statement "the upādhyāya reaches the bed and seat," regarding the "one hundred and thirty-odd types," according to the five texts of the Vinaya for monks, there are two [categories].

The sixteen persons and the five [qualifications] extensively demonstrate the teacher’s virtue. Regarding the *upādhyāya* of nine summer retreats (*navavarṣa*), when he confers full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon another, if the person receiving it obtains the precepts while the master incurs an offense, and so forth, this is detailed at length in the Vinaya texts (*yathā vinaya-sūtre*).

As for the two kinds of *ācāryas*, they are the *karmācārya* and the *śikṣācārya*. Regarding those with five summer retreats or more: "five summer retreats or more" refers to reaching six summer retreats up to thirty-five.
"Ten years, etc. refers to the Vinaya statement, "Having more than five years [of seniority], etc."; this is the scriptural proof.

In the present time, for one who has completed fewer than four summer retreats (catur-varṣa) to act as a preceptor (upādhyāya) or an instructor (ācārya) for others is logically improper. Since there are already established restrictions in the texts, violating these rules constitutes an illegality (*adharma*) and renders the ordination invalid.
For example, while a preceptor must definitively have ten years of seniority, nine years is permitted, and eight years and so forth are likewise fixed.

This is not permitted. Regarding "other masters" (*anye ācāryāḥ*): excluding the three primary masters, the seven witnesses are called "others. One merely needs to clearly understand the right and wrong of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) to be qualified;
it does not matter how many years of seniority one has. As for the meaning of "comprehensive master" (*saṃgraha-ācārya*): "comprehensive" (*saṃ*) means "thoroughly pervasive" (*samanta*).
Fortunately, there are those who are elder monks of great virtue. "Elder" (*lǎosù*) refers to one of advanced age; "great" (*shuò*) means vast.

It refers to those of renowned great virtue whom the multitude honors and respects. Regarding the phrase "producing goodness for those who come after," the commentary states that "those who come after" specifically refers to the *Sishipian* (Chapter on Teachers and Disciples).
In that section, it describes a disciple departing from his teacher because he perceives that the *upādhyāya* is acting contrary to the Dharma.
This matter is truly due to the fact that his virtue was not fully perfected, which is why he departed. The Venerable One said, "I do not know what intention lies behind this interpretation;
it deviates from the intent of the text. As for the current statement that "one generates goodness for the future," this too is spoken in broad terms.

The meaning is that when a venerable elder of great virtue acts as a teacher for others, it is not merely for a single session at the ordination platform; from the very moment they first receive the precepts, [they begin...]
With a sincere and earnest heart, and even over a long period of time, one acts for the sake of causing others to cultivate goodness;

thus, why must one necessarily point to the minor principles found in later sections? Regarding "not sitting together": those with five *kṣapaṇas* (years of seniority) and those with ten *kṣapaṇas* must not sit together.
One with five *kṣapaṇas* may sit first, but one with ten *kṣapaṇas* who arrives later may not sit with them; nor may those with ten *kṣapaṇas* share the same bed.
"Seated, etc.
[This is] the heading for "The Circumstances of Receiving the Precepts in the Three Teachings. It means that there is no need for an elaborate explanation of the matter.

Regarding the phrase "from the time of Śākyamuni onwards," the word "all" (凡) refers to various instances; it does not restrict itself solely to the moment of receiving the full precepts (upasaṃpadā), but rather applies to all five [precepts].
Regarding the "eighty [precepts]" and so forth, one must in all cases expound the Dharma in this manner to guide, open, and explain them.

As for the two characters "beginning" (chu) and "middle" (zhong), within these two sections, we are now at the section concerning the objective conditions (*ālambana*). Regarding the phrase "from that which is produced up to the essence," there is a separate manual (*biechao*) of thirty-odd sheets;

since ancient times, there have been masters who have separately issued a single fascicle on the characteristics of the preparatory stages of the precepts (*śīla-upāya*), which is consulted every time the precepts are received.
Regarding the exposition that guides, transforms, and provides clarification:

to summarize it, although the ancients might have produced texts of thirty sheets that seemed extensive and prolix, if one were to now extract and state the general outline, it is therefore called "essential" (and so forth).

Regarding "sentient and non-sentient": those possessing the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) are sentient; these range from the Tathāgata above down to all classes of wriggling, moving creatures with consciousness.
Non-sentient things are those that do not possess life; these range from Mount Sumeru above down to blades of grass, leaves, and even minute particles of dust.
In all cases, one should refrain from giving rise to a mind of harm. Regarding the two truths of emptiness and existence: emptiness is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

The Truths: "Existence" refers to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). "Cessation," which is the principle of *nirvāṇa*, is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), being neither empty nor existent.
The "Buddha’s holy teachings in written form and scrolls" refers to the present Tripiṭaka; these characters are the "teachings through names" (*nāma-śāsana*) that can express meaning.
"Images, stupas, and temples" refers to clay niches, paintings on silk, halls, caityas, and so forth—all of which should be treated with reverence and not subjected to destruction.
Slander refers to a mind of disbelief and destruction. Regarding "earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness," these are the six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*).
All of these are defined by the absence of any intent to steal or cause harm. As for "taking the dharma-realm as the measure," the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states:
"The sublime dharma of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas—because this sublime dharma accords with the minds of those sentient beings. Such sublime dharmas are each...
The distinction lies in the different classifications of the realms (*dhātu*); thus it is called the "Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*).

As for the statement that these are all the "essence" (*tattva*) of the precept-realm, according to the principle, it should properly be called the "precept-object" (*kṣetra*). That it is now called the "essence" is because the precepts are obtained by arising from this object;

therefore, this object is designated as the "essence. This is also a case of discussing the effect within the context of the cause. The phrase "therefore, [it] reverses" serves as a general corroboration of the preceding text.

"To possess virtue equal to that of a Buddha" means to pervade the entire dharma-realm. Because the object possesses a mind of protection and maintenance, and the mind is thus equal to that of a Buddha, it is called "equal virtue.
Alternatively, it refers to a person who has first received the precepts; being solemn, pure, and untransgressing, they are majestic, radiant, and pristine, no different from a Buddha.
They are superior even to the various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), for the wrong views and wrong practices of non-Buddhists are the source of birth and death, and they lack liberation.
Regarding the hope for liberation: although breaking the precepts leads to falling into the evil realms for a time, there is still a period of emergence after a long duration.
As for the statement in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* regarding "accepting [the precepts] and then breaking them," the *Sūtra on the Previous Life of the Bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā* says:

When the Buddha was in the world, this bhikṣuṇī had realized the fruit of arhatship. She would always enter the houses of nobles and praise the life of renunciation, saying to the women, "Sisters, you should all go forth together."
"Householder, remove the 'woman' [from your title] and say instead: 'In my youth, I was always possessed of great beauty, yet it was extremely difficult for me to maintain the precepts.

The nun said: 'Even if one breaks the precepts and falls into the evil realms, there will eventually be a time of escape. I myself recall that when I was a courtesan, I wore the robes of a bhikṣuṇī merely for the sake of jest and amusement.
By this causal connection, I became a bhikṣuṇī during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha; though I maintained my physical comeliness, it was for that very reason.'"

Having broken the precepts, he fell into hell. When his retribution for those crimes was exhausted, he encountered Śākyamuni Buddha, left the household life, and attained the six supernormal powers and the four fruits of arhatship.
The remainder of the text is as recorded in the *Chao* (copious notes), etc.

Regarding the phrase "thus it is most weighty": "Thus" (*ru*) is a term that points to the Dharma; "is" (*shi*) means "to be capable of" or "to constitute. "According to" (*sui*) means "to follow after.

"Faculties" (*ji*) refers to the spiritual capacities of the roots. If the faculties are dull, one speaks extensively; if the faculties are sharp, one speaks concisely. Although there is this distinction between the extensive and the concise...
Each and every one is made to attain realization; thus, the divine function does not sink into stagnation. The underlying intent of the *Sarvāstivāda* [Vinaya] can be understood from what follows.
The phrase "next, causing them to give rise to the precepts" serves as the heading.

Regarding the statement "it should be included among those to be established": *Vibhāṣā* (毗跋) means this is a Mahāyāna vinaya; however, its inclusion among the "doubtful and spurious" texts is incorrect.
Fa Bao states that it is a Hīnayāna vinaya and is not among the doubtful or spurious. If it were indeed doubtful or spurious, the *Chao* (the *Xu gaoseng zhuan lüechao*) would never have cited it.
As the text below states: "All that has been explained above is from authentic scriptures; it does not mean they are lost translations, doubtful, or spurious. Thus, [the *Vibhāṣā*] is cited here.
He realizes that this foundation is not erroneous. Regarding the phrase "I now seek the Way," the two characters for "seeking the Way" (求道) are synonymous with "receiving the precepts" (受戒).
If one were to adapt the phrasing, it should be said: "I now resolve my mind to receive the precepts.

Regarding "one should save all sentient beings," this means that non-killing is precisely saving their lives. As for "all sentient beings cherish their own life spans," [it refers to the fact that they fear death].

Life is a floating and provisional phenomenon that arises from joy; "evil" (pronounced *wū*) refers to death, which immediately softens the mind. The phrase "even though one possesses virtue, the Buddha, the precepts, and so forth" serves as a counter-explanation to clarify the meaning of this aforementioned softening.
Regarding the clarification of the remaining two based on their meaning: "the remaining" refers to the external. Outside of the lower grade of mind, the middle and upper grades constitute the "two.

"Based on their meaning" means according to the explanatory text. While the preceding section on the lower grade relied upon that specific Vinaya text, there is no such textual basis for the middle and upper grades of mind within the Vinaya itself.
This is an analysis according to the meaning. What is meant by "intermediate grade"? This interrogates the definition of the name and its characteristics.

"Rectifying the mind and turning toward the Path" means that severing all other thoughts is called rectifying the mind, while single-mindedly seeking the categories of precepts is designated as turning toward the Path.

"Dispelling the doubts of sentient beings" means that hesitation and indecision are called doubt; to deliver the spirit through the Dharma so that the mind awakens and enters it is termed "dispelling. (From the *Vinaya*).
As for "the beam" (*bimba*): because one does not sink into doubt or regret, it is called the "beam of the Vinaya. Regarding "benefiting oneself and others":
to resolve the doubts of others so that they do not sink [into despair] is benefiting others; the merit thereby obtained is benefiting oneself.
One who upholds the precepts with such a mind is of the middle grade.

"What is meant by 'superior grade'? This is a question. "I now resolve my mind to receive the precepts" clearly indicates that the preceding passages on seeking the Way and tending toward the Way are all alternative names for receiving the precepts;
here, it is stated directly as "receiving the precepts," where "receiving" (shou) refers to the act of accepting and internalizing them.
"Restraint and prevention" refers to the *śīla* (precepts). Regarding "for the purpose of accomplishing the three clusters of precepts":

this means that these three clusters of *śīla* serve as the cause, which subsequently brings about the fruit of the three bodies (*trikāya*). As the Sūtra says: "Vowing to sever all evil is called the *saṃvara-śīla* (restraint-precept); one thereby attains the *dharmakāya*."
The Buddha’s vow to cultivate all wholesome dharmas is called the *śīla* of collecting wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), by which one attains the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

The Buddha’s vow to deliver all sentient beings is called the *śīla* of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*), by which one attains the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) Buddha. Regarding the phrase "entering the three gates of liberation":

"entering" (*tsū*) means to move toward; "three" (*san*) is a number; "liberation" (*datsu*) means to be freed from. They are called "gates" (*mon*) because they are the places through which one travels. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The nature of all phenomena is emptiness."
The emptiness of the characteristics of all phenomena is called the liberation door of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣa-mukha*).
The emptiness of both the nature and characteristics of all phenomena is the liberation door of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa-mukha*), because there is no further mind of seeking or wishing.

In various sūtras and śāstras, these are also called the three samādhis, the three *samādhis*, or the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), and so forth. For those who correctly seek the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, [these are] two...
Riding upon analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), one looks toward the Buddha’s perfect nirvana; through this specific aspiration, the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi are finally realized.
Therefore, it is said: "One correctly seeks the fruit of Nirvāṇa. Among the four types of nirvana, this is precisely *apratisthita-nirvāṇa* (non-abiding nirvana).

What has been explained above is generally discussed in terms of oneself, following the text of the *Lun-chao*. From the passage beginning with "Furthermore, by means of this Dharma" onwards, the benefit of others (*parārtha*) is clarified.
To cause sentient beings to clearly perceive the Buddha-nature is called "reaching Nirvana. In this way, it proceeds successively without end, and the Buddha-dharma naturally abides for a long time.
As for the phrase "such as these," it refers to the aforementioned minds of the lower, middle, and superior grades. [End of] Erroneous [view].
Regarding "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*): it refers to the state of having a mind that seeks out what is feared; this is termed "perverse" (*mithyā*).

As for the phrase "how much more so when not generating [the resolve]," if even generating a profound and earnest mind (*adhimukti-citta*) is still termed perverse, how much more so when one does not generate it at all—how could one know with certainty that nothing will be attained?

Those who are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and beginners in their training within a perverse mind are called "beginners in training"; those who possess the seven stages of preparatory application (*prayoga-mārga*) are termed "beginners. "Beginner" (*śi*) means "initial. This is complete.

The nature of affliction (*kleśa*): although one performs various wholesome deeds, if there is a mind that grasps at attainment, this is called speech from a mind of perversion. Regarding "speech from a mind of conceit" (*māna-citta*):

although such a person has severed the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) of the three realms and the nine grades of doubt (*vicikitsā*) of the desire realm, they have not yet severed the greed, delusion, and conceit of the higher two realms; this is called speech from a mind of conceit. [This refers to] the Arhat.

Regarding "the language of names": this refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms, both those abandoned through vision and those abandoned through cultivation, which have all been completely severed.

Since there is no longer internal grasping, one merely accords with worldly convention and employs provisional names for circulation; thus it is called "the language of names. Regarding "thus knowing for oneself the limits of the mind":
this means that the mind seeking the precepts has [levels of] superior, middling, and inferior. It is like a person drinking cold water who knows its temperature for themselves.
That one attains the pure precepts of a Buddha also has its limits (*pramāṇa*). Since the precepts accord with the person's mind, they likewise have three types, each distinct from the others;
this is termed "limits. Thus, the preceding text states: "The precepts consist in the function of conforming to the vessel;
the practitioner takes reception as their aim," and so forth. Therefore, the passage concerning the lower [grade] can be understood accordingly.
Regarding the phrase "the question arising upon reaching the limit": this refers to the emergence of this inquiry based on what was previously stated.
"This teaching" (*jiao*) refers to the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, which is the teaching that expresses [the meaning]. "Principle" (*zong*) refers to the fundamental tenet.
"Which vehicle" (*he sheng*) asks whether this is the principle of the Mahāyāna or the path of the Hīnayāna. If it is said to be Mahāyāna, then it is the Vinaya.
The Vinaya-piṭaka is subsumed under the Hīnayāna. If it is said to be Hīnayāna, then its ultimate fruit is merely that of an Arhat;
why, then, would it cause one to resolve upon the Mahāyāna mind and seek the Buddha-way? In this text, the character *chih* (志) is glossed as "mind" (*citta*).

If the doctrinal tenets of these four divisions belong to the Mahāyāna—meaning, if one relies on the doctrinal positions of the Vinaya-piṭaka regarding the expressive words and so forth—then [it follows that they are Mahāyāna].
It certainly belongs to the Hīnayāna; however, within the five divisions [of the Vinaya], this Vinaya is categorized as Mahāyāna based on its underlying meaning.

It relies on the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*’s doctrine of provisional names (*prajñapti*), asserting the existence of seeds (*bīja*) and so forth. The passage beginning with "The text states... cites the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* to provide scriptural evidence for this classification of the Vinaya.

This is a case of the Vinaya being applicable to the Mahāyāna. There are many such authentic examples; indeed, there are numerous instances throughout the Vinaya texts where it is applied to the Mahāyāna.

For example, regarding the Arhat Trapuṣa (沓婆), who was free from further learning (*aśaikṣa*), he knew that the monks were not steadfast and wished to seek someone more reliable to manage monastic affairs. Furthermore, the Vinaya states:

The Son of the Buddha is also like this. Since he is called a "Son of the Buddha," one knows there is no other vehicle (*yāna*). Furthermore, it is like casting off clothes so that they become empty and unobstructed;
there is no attachment, but only the severing of continuity. It is not necessarily the case that one must discard physical garments and such items—all these are consistent examples.

Regarding Master Guang’s judgment concerning the limits of the Mahāyāna Vinaya: this refers to Vinaya Master Huiguang of the Wei dynasty. His *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vṛtti) states: "As in the past, Guang..."
The Master says: "Relying on principle to clarify the essence" means that because this is the fundamental nature of the mind, it accords with the Mahāyāna.

"As for 'reaching the great matter'" refers to the general conclusion indicating the ultimate aim. The two characters "conditioned object" (*yuánjìng*) cite the previously mentioned objects of perception.
"And the mind having supremacy" cites the *cittamātra* (mind-only). This term "supremacy" (*zēngshàng*) refers to the highest of the high.

The mind of the stage is called "increasing" (*vṛddhi*). The *Karmavibhaṅga-vyākhyā* states: "Increasing within [the world] to save all sentient beings is precisely the root of kindness and compassion;

this refers to the Buddha-mind" (the aforementioned text from the Commentary). Regarding these two paths, the object-condition (*ālambana*) is one, while the scope of the mind (*citta-pramāṇa*) is two.

One must receive [the precepts] according to the prior selection; it is not permitted to do so at the last moment, for fear of being superficial or confused. Regarding "the wise one who bestows the title":
one who is clear and proficient in the characteristics of the Vinaya is called a wise one. They shall individually cite the names and titles and bestow them upon the recipient and others.
There is an interpretation which says that "to lead and assist" does not mean one has exhausted the study of characters. "The mind succeeding the mind" means that the wholesome mind is uninterrupted.

"Seeing the object as bright and pure" is like looking with the eyes and seeing clearly and purely. From "one cannot wait until the moment [of death]" onwards, the refutation of this [interpretation] can be understood (and so forth).
Regarding the phrase "The fourth, etc.": "The fourth" serves as the heading of the section. The Venerable Jing-shui said: "According to principle, it should be called 'the fourth.
'Establishing the recipient' refers to the formal act of establishing the location; by simply mentioning 'the fourth,' one knows this is the section on the location for installation.
The Vinaya states: "One should establish the recipient... until the place where [the sound] is no longer heard. This precisely clarifies the installation.
"Placing [the recipient]" refers to establishing their position. If one is removed from the place of seeing and hearing: being removed from the place of hearing is the fundamental requirement;
however, if one is removed from the place of seeing, it constitutes an illegality (*adharma*). The Vinaya prescribes that the recipient stands in a place where they are seen but not heard.
Since both [conditions] are now absent, it is not a suitable location for placement. Regarding "outside the boundary" (*sīmā*) and so forth, the *Xuánjì* states: "Outside the *śīmaṇḍala*..."
Furthermore, according to the *Changjie* (Great Boundary), when the formal motion (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) is being performed, the recipient must be within the boundary.
If they are outside, the ritual action is not established because it is separated by the natural boundary; this is not called "receiving full ordination.

This explanation is based on the time of the formal motion, as the wording of the Vinaya text is general. However, the *Nanji* does not permit this interpretation. Moreover, this section is fundamentally...
In order to clarify the placement of the recipient and the establishment of the site while precluding obstacles, this has not yet even been asked;

how could one anticipate clarifying the time of the fourfold announcement (*jñapti-caturtha*)? Based on this passage of the text, it is not appropriate to discuss the measurements of the inside or outside of the *śīma* (boundary) as if they were irrelevant matters;

these shall be distinguished later when the essence of the reception [of the precepts] is properly explained. That commentary explains itself, saying: "Outside the boundary" refers to the Great Boundary (*mahā-śīma*).

This refers to the exterior. If there is a *kṣetra* (training ground) within a *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary), then the location for establishing [the *sīmā*] must be outside the *kṣetra* yet inside the *mahā-sīmā*.
Even if there is no *kṣetra* but only a *mahā-sīmā*, it must likewise be established inside the *mahā-sīmā* at a place neither too close nor too far from the Saṃgha.

It must absolutely not be established outside the *mahā-sīmā*; if it were, it would not be a valid location. The above presents two interpretations side by side; one may choose according to one’s own judgment.

Reflect upon this. There is a certain logic here regarding the point of focus: while it is visible to the eye, it is not heard by the ear. This can be explained by citing the *Śāstra* (抄文), which says:
"Fearing that [the candidate] might hear the *karmavācanā*, etc. (and so forth). Below, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* is cited to prove that the aforementioned procedure was illegal.

That text states: "At that time, a certain bhikṣu borrowed another’s robes and bowl to receive the precepts. After the ordination, the other bhikṣus said to him: 'Put on these robes and take up this bowl; let us go together.'"
He went away to beg for alms. They said to him, "I have no robes or bowl. The others asked, "Where did you obtain your robes and bowl when you just now received the precepts?
He replied, "I borrowed them for a short time. The bhikṣus said, "One cannot receive the precepts without robes and a bowl."
"Why have you borrowed another's robe and bowl? He replied, "The Buddha has not prohibited me from borrowing robes and bowls.

The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "From this day forward, those who receive the precepts at the proper time shall be placed outside the boundary of the ordination platform (*sīmā*), standing in a place where they are visible but out of earshot.
A person shall be dispatched there to inquire about their robes, bowls, and so forth... The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* text says: "The boundary..."

Regarding "asking about impediments outside": this refers to the practice of asking about impediments outside the *sīmāmaṇḍala* (ordination platform) when receiving the precepts within the *mahāsīmā* (great boundary).

By extension, the area outside the platform is referred to as being "outside the boundary. Some say that because the matter of impediments is minor, the small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) is situated outside the [great] boundary, and thus the questioning occurs there;

others say that according to the case where there is no platform, the great boundary itself is the location, and the questioning of impediments should take place outside that great boundary. Both views are consistent.

This is not a matter of misunderstanding. There is no logical flaw here. This refers to the formal questioning and examination (*paripṛcchā*) described in the Vinaya texts, where the Buddha instructed that the questioner should remain outside the precincts (*sīmā*).
Now, it may be that such a physical precinct does not exist; however, as long as there is a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), the majority of people will be within that boundary.

Since the questioner is a teacher (*śāstṛ*) who has been formally appointed for this task, even if they are within the same boundary, there is no logical flaw in their being considered separate from the assembly (*gaṇa*). This accords with the aforementioned Vinaya texts.
This accords with the preceding passage stating that if one is outside the boundary (*sīmā*), it is not called "receiving full ordination" (*upasampadā*), and so forth.

To explain the text in this manner follows the *Yiyi* (If-Dependent). The *Soushengji* says: "The previous interpretation, which takes 'outside the boundary' to mean 'outside the site,' may indeed have broad application in the Vinaya texts;
however, when reaching this specific passage, such an explanation seems inconvenient. Please consider this further. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* refers to a place that is neither too near nor too far.
[This] cannot be established as previously stated. Because it is situated outside the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), it is too far away. Yuanling says:

"If there is a field-great-boundary (*kṣetra-mahāsīmā*), it is located within the area outside the field, at a place neither near nor far. If it is a single great boundary, one may not go outside the boundary;
rather, one must remain within the same boundary at a place neither near nor far from the Saṃgha. If it is a small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*), the instructor is permitted [to be present]."

Regarding the recipient: they must remain entirely outside the boundary (*sīmā*), and furthermore, they must be separated from the Saṃgha at a distance that is neither too near nor too far; it is within this space that the questioning takes place.

"At the appropriate time, measure and employ one or many people to stand [in attendance]" (the character *hú* is read as *fǎn*) means, for example, if there are thirty or twenty-seven people who have not yet been questioned, they are stationed in one place, and so forth.
Second, "taking those who are about to be questioned" means: intending to question them. One intends to question.

Regarding "difficulties for three persons or one person, etc., in a place apart from the *saṃgha* and the *śrāmaṇeras*": "apart from the *saṃgha*" means apart from the monks on the ritual platform (*maṇḍala*).

"Apart from the *śrāmaṇeras*" refers to those who have not yet been interrogated. In the interval between these, even if one were to question them in the presence of various *śrāmaṇeras*, it would be impossible to cite the text of the *Chao* (the Vinaya commentary) as an answer;
it says, "one must certainly be in the same location," and so forth. [The candidate] then puts on the seven-fold robe (*saptakaṣāya*).

Regarding "standing there," Xuánzàng’s commentary states: "Because one is about to leave the lower rank, one removes the lower garment; yet, as one has not yet entered the higher stream, one instead dons the honorable robes.
Question: For what reason is it prescribed that one must stand there? Answer: The *Jiemo shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states:

"Between the two postures of walking and standing, the mind is distracted and scattered; sitting is tranquil, yet it does not necessarily signify the utmost respect. Standing allows one to look toward the Sangha with uplifted attention."
Thus it is said. The Venerable Jing-shui stated: "In current practice, one must take this as the standard.
If there are those who, while wearing the seven-strip robe (saptakaṣāya), put on arm-covers (upavīta), they have entirely failed to comprehend the intent of the teachings."

Regarding the phrase "as for the five things that must be done upon arrival": concerning the requirement to remove one's robes outside the boundary and so forth—when first establishing the conditions, there were those wishing to receive the precepts who were ordered to go outside the enclosure to remove their robes. This was done during the inspection for potential dangers and the like.

However, when there were those who were weak or timid, they felt shame and refused to comply, thereby delaying the ritual proceedings or refusing to receive the precepts altogether. The Buddha therefore decreed: "From this day forward, such a practice shall not be required."
However, by means of a *karmavācanā*, one person is appointed; he rises from his seat, goes outside, and inquires about those difficult matters.

This is the procedure for the second case, which includes the formal motion (*jñapti*). Regarding these four responses, each being performed as a single action according to a single rule: first, the appointment of the master of decorum (*airyāpathika-ācārya*).

Second, the summoning and entry; third, the formal announcement and the request for harmony (*saṃgha-sāmagrī*); fourth, the actual performance of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. This is based on the individual response.

One session of harmonizing the Saṃgha constitutes a single ritual act; thus, four such sessions require four rounds of harmony. If it is said that one responds collectively by saying "and so forth," [the same applies].

This is the general response. For example, as with the initial case of leading three people to receive the precepts, once this general response is completed, if no other individuals enter the enclosure from outside, then regardless of how many are led in, it is not necessary to perform further formalities until before the appearance of the dawn light;
prior to that, the procedure is entirely valid. Next, regarding the text for the single announcement (*jñapti*), the essential outline is as described above.
The section has been explained. However, within it, the character "pi" (彼) must not be mistaken. If someone mispronounces it as the character "ci" (此), the ritual will certainly not be accomplished;
this is because the distinction between "this" and "that" is not being maintained. The recipient stands outside the enclosure and says, "If he were among the assembly, he would be 'this' one.
Now, while the Preceptor within the altar performs the *jñapti* (single announcement), he points toward the person outside; how could this not be "that"?
Indeed. I have often seen people explain that when both parties are fully qualified, their ignorance is profound. An external objection states:

For instance, when five persons receive the precepts at the border regions, and the time comes for the *śuddhaka-vidhi* (the formal motion) to appoint a teacher of instruction, the first intermediate section says:

"So-and-so shall receive the precepts from the preceptor So-and-so. Once the name of the preceptor has been recorded and the procedure for entering the Dharma is completed, [the candidate] does not count toward the required quorum.

Furthermore, in the second intermediate section, it says: "Let such-and-such person act as the *śāstṛ* (instructor). By recording the name of the instructor and entering it into the ritual procedure (*dharma*), they do not count toward the required number.

Thus, there are five people in total, yet two are insufficient. Since three are not [valid] *saṃgha*, how can the ritual action (*karmavācanā*) be performed so that the Jewel of the Dharma (*dharmaratna*) is successfully established?

According to the *Jie-mo-shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā), it is said: "Because the positions are separated, they mutually fulfill one another. This is like the procedure for appointing the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults).

In the case of "two people," if both are listed together, entry into the ritual (*dharma*) is not permitted. Now, this is not so. When the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) is being listed, the instructor (*śikṣācārya*) has not yet been listed;
thus, [the candidate] still counts as part of the Saṃgha. When the instructor’s name is actually being listed, the preceptor’s name has not yet been designated;
therefore, the preceptor also counts as part of the Saṃgha. This is because they are separated by the intermediate structural phrases (*gaṅ-gu*). For this reason, there is no [violation].
This is the intention of Nanshan. Alternatively, according to Master Nan, the term "Upādhyāya" (Preceptor) refers merely to the conditions for the Master of Deportment (*airyāpathika-ācārya*).
From the perspective of a *śrāmaṇera* toward the Upādhyāya, the latter is called the "original" [preceptor] because the precepts were received from him.

From the perspective of the Master of Deportment toward the Upādhyāya, the former is merely the condition for what was performed by one who has emerged from the assembly. If, in the second intermediate stage, the Master of Deportment is formally cited...
The Preceptor is measured by the Saṃgha; because he is the one correctly appointed, he must certainly not be excluded from the count.

If, during the first or middle [announcements], the name of the Upādhyāya is cited, it is not for the purpose of being the actual officiant, and thus there is fundamentally no deficiency. Take, for example, the case of the Ācārya:
when wishing to summon a śrāmaṇera into the assembly, he makes the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Does he not cite the name of the Upādhyāya? Furthermore, the Ācārya is originally...

[The previous] division was insufficient for inclusion. Now, having cited the preceptor (upādhyāya) once more, it is clear that the preceptor is not included within the [insufficient] count. These three present individuals do not constitute a *saṃgha*;
thus, how could the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) possibly be accomplished? Therefore, we know that regarding the preceptor, there is no principle of insufficiency from the outset.
Although this interpretation contradicts the *Shu* (Commentary), it represents the views of a particular school; reflect upon this.

Regarding the phrase "that which reaches the conditions" (*yuan*), this is the heading. Regarding the phrase "that which is reached," this establishes the thesis. As the text says, "only that which reaches the habituation (*xi*)"—there are those who attain it and those who do not.
The *Xuanji* (Mysterious Record) addresses this point at length to clarify the difficult matter of attainment and non-attainment.

This principle is not accepted by the Great Virtuous One. He says that this is merely a general outline; whether [the precepts] are obtained or not will be explained in detail within each section of the *Chao-wen* (Excerpts) below.
He notes that if one were to explain everything in advance here, the text at the bottom would become overly prolix—this should be understood.

Furthermore, he says that if one asks a question but does not provide the explanation, it ultimately fails to serve the purpose of the questioner. His intention is to say: although one recites the words according to the text, if it is not understood in one's own mind...

Regarding "understanding through realization": since one has not understood it oneself, how can one cause others to comprehend it? Therefore, it is said that although there is questioning, there is no understanding.
Even so, what difference is there between questioning and not questioning? Thus, it is said that in the end, it does not constitute a question; "non-" (fei) here means "not.

As for the statement that "speech is not established because the central and peripheral regions do not understand each other," this serves as proof of the aforementioned lack of understanding. In the Central Kingdom and the borderlands, neither party understands the other, as their dialects are mutually unintelligible.

This is sufficient regarding the formal requirements (*saṃpad*). By contrast, it is revealed that although questions were asked and answers were given, neither party clearly understood the existence or non-existence [of the precepts].
How, then, could one know the details? Therefore, this is not permissible. If one follows the *Vinaya-mūla*, if one does not undergo the interrogation (*paripṛcchā*), one cannot obtain the precepts.

Since the *Vinaya* states that one cannot obtain the precepts [if unasked], why now is it said that one cannot obtain them despite having been asked? Although the answer was given, it was not understood; thus, it remains as if there had been no questioning at all.

Question: There is no difference in the examples provided, as they are presented in the same manner. Just as it is not said that the requisites such as the precepts are not established, so too is this not a case of stating the same thing twice.

If one refers to the Vinaya-mūla, it only asks about the thirteen grounds for defeat (*ānantarya*). Therefore, in the *Upasampadā-khandhaka*, the origin story (*nidāna*) of the thirteen grounds is listed first;
following that, after the origin stories of the various expulsions (*pārājika*) have been concluded, it concludes by stating: "Those who bring disgrace upon the Saṃgha."

When it was not possible to confer full ordination (*upasampadā*), there were those who wished to receive it. They were led outside the boundary (*sīmā*) and made to remove their robes before being ordained;
this caused them shame and delayed the ritual proceedings. When this was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said: "One must not allow such nakedness.

From now on, I permit that one be questioned regarding the thirteen grounds of disqualification (*antarāyika-dharma*). Only after this may the full ordination be conferred through the formal procedure of a motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*)."
It should be performed in this manner. The subsequent text then concludes the enumeration of the thirteen impediments (*antarāyika-dharma*). The Buddha declared:

"From this day forward, one must first inquire regarding the matters of the thirteen impediments, and only thereafter confer full ordination (*upasampadā*). According to the text of the aforementioned Vinaya-mūla, it simply speaks of "inquiring about the impediments."
Because it is never stated that one should inquire about all the prohibitions (*pratikṣepa*), it says only to ask about the thirteen impediments (*antarāyika-dharma*) and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) as discussed in the Vinaya, when the preceptor (*śikṣācārya*) is dispatched from the assembly to the recipient, he asks only about the prohibitions and not about the impediments.
When the ordination master (*karmācārya*) performs the ritual before the assembly, he likewise asks only about the prohibitions and not about the impediments.

This is difficult. Now, following the meaning and applying it to the sequence of the questions and prohibitions prior to the [formal] ritual, since the *vinaya* texts do not list the "difficulties" (*nān*) before the questions and prohibitions within their ritual procedures, the present commentator, following the meaning of the three stages in the *vinaya*, should place these difficulties before the questions and prohibitions.
As for what is called the meaning of the three stages: in the first stage, the conditions are listed; first, the conditions of the difficulties are listed.

The subsequent section lists the prohibitions (*parāpatti*). Section Two: The Vinaya states, "From this day forward, it is permitted to inquire about the thirteen impediments (*antarāyika-dharma*) before conferring full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Thus, it is appropriate that the impediments precede the prohibitions. Section Three: The Vinaya states, "From this day forward, it is permitted to first inquire about the thirteen impediments.
Since it says "first inquire about the impediments," one knows that the prohibitions follow. Based on the meaning of these three sections:

Therefore, it is said: "Now, according to the meaning, it is based on [the principle of] equality," and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the nature (*tǐ*) of the interrogation (*wènnàn*): the character *tǐ* has many interpretations, none of which are adopted here. Rather, one follows the *Sòuxuán*, which states: "Nature means 'to attain' (*dé*). This refers to the words and phrases of the interrogation; it is only when the questioner and the respondent mutually understand each other that it is truly attained. As for those who merely recite and study in a muddled manner... The *Moshu* (Commentary on the Commentary) states: "In my travels throughout the capitals and provinces of Jin and Wei, there was rarely a monastic seat (*lüxí*) that I did not visit;

yet regarding difficult conditions, I have never deliberated upon them at all. I fear that I may not even master the recitation of the texts, so how could I find the leisure to further recognize their characteristics? (The above is from the commentary).
According to this, it describes the aforementioned state of being "mōnglóng" (obscure), which signifies a lack of clarity.
Regarding the first case, "The Sinner": Master Tang said, "When the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, there was a bhikṣu named Nandika who attained the four dhyānas while seated.
Upon arising from samādhi, a female demon appeared before him. The bhikṣu seized her, but she vanished and did not appear.
The bhikṣu pursued and tried to seize her again; his lustful mind did not cease even unto death. He committed unwholesome conduct on horseback. [End of entry].

One does not conceal [the offense]. The Buddha said that after being granted the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) for repentance, if one commits it again, it is called a "count of extinction" (*nirodha-saṃkhyā*).

Regarding the "obstacle of a border-line offense" (*antya-āpatti-vighna*), the *Karmavibhāga-ṭīkā* states: "Having previously received the internal precepts, to now abandon them and remain outside the community is termed a 'border obstacle.
Because the precepts do not arise [again], it is called an 'obstacle' (*vighna*). As for laypeople receiving the five or eight precepts, this is compared to the ordinary [lay follower].
The common people of the road differ [in their views], collectively labeling it a "border offense" (*pārājika*). The remaining text is easy to understand (and so forth).

Regarding the statement, "one who commits two offenses against a *bhikṣuṇī*," the *Táng* says: The Vinaya states that at one time there were many *bhikṣus* traveling from the kingdom of Kośala toward Kāśi.
What was it that they all had in common? One *bhikṣu* said: "In this place, there was once a layperson who provided us with clothing."
Regarding the *kāṣāya*: it is a collective offense. The bhikṣus asked, "How did you come to know this? He replied, "I saw a numerical enumeration of names. The *Karmasūtra* states:

"To destroy the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) is called committing a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; it is a grave sin and a heavy obstruction such that the precepts cannot arise, which is termed a 'difficulty' (*duskara*)."

Regarding the statement "the four [texts] reach [this point]," the phrase "the Vinayas such as the *Dharmaguptaka*" includes, by extension, the *Mahīśāsaka* and the *Sarvāstivāda*, excluding the *Mahāsāṃghika*.

As for the lack of clarity regarding "purity and impurity," if one relies on the scriptural texts, it simply states that one who has previously engaged in sexual misconduct while wearing the *kāṣāya* incurs an obstacle (*antarāya*).

Furthermore, regarding the three groups of nuns who all wear the *kāṣāya*, it is unclear whether this constitutes an obstacle collectively for all of them, or whether it is restricted specifically to fully ordained nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*). Moreover...
The text states: "If one commits an offense against a bhikṣuṇī. This appears to exclude the lower assemblies; however, regarding bhikṣuṇīs, there are both pure objects and impure objects.

Is the offense committed universally across these, or is it committed only in relation to a pure object? Neither of these two points is clarified. The same holds true for the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
If that were so, then at present, during the time of receiving the precepts and performing the ritual, everyone says: "You shall not commit an offense against a pure practice (*brahmacarya*)."

"Is it not so for bhikṣuṇīs? [The questioner] asks, "On what teaching is this based? The *Chao* (the Commentary) answers: "Therefore, those who practice according to the worldly rites say that this is based on the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
As for 'those who have attained the two fruits, as well as ordinary women who observe the precepts,' the *srotāpanna* is the first fruit, and the *sakṛdāgāmin* is the second fruit.
It is understandable that the 'ordinary women who observe the precepts' refers to the first type of person."

Regarding those who have committed the offense of destroying a *bhikṣuṇī*: those for whom it does not constitute a "difficulty" (*antarāya*) later on refer to *bhikṣuṇīs* who are *phalastha* (abiding in the fruits). For a *bhikṣuṇī* who has attained the second fruit, the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-bhāvanā-heya*) have not yet been eliminated for the lower three grades;

for one who has attained the first fruit, the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm have not been severed in their entirety; and for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), neither the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) nor those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) have been eliminated.

Because all of these still possess a mind that experiences pleasure, at the time when the first person [the one who destroyed the *bhikṣuṇī*] conceived [the embryo], it was a pure object (*viśuddha-viṣaya*) and thus constituted a "difficulty. This applies to the middle and subsequent cases as well.

When a person is pregnant, it is already a defiled state; thus, it does not constitute a formal obstacle (*antarāyika*). As for those who are called obstacles both at the beginning and at the end—the *anāgāmin* (Non-returner) and the *arhat* (Worthy One):

the *anāgāmin* is one who has attained the third fruit, and the *arhat* is one who has attained the fourth fruit. If one violates these states, it constitutes an obstacle both at the beginning and at the end.

The reason this is so is that for the *anāgāmin*, the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) have been entirely exhausted through cultivation, while for the *arhat*, the afflictions of the three realms have been abandoned through insight (*darśana*).

Cultivating both [the wholesome and the unwholesome] while simultaneously eliminating them, one ultimately possesses no mind that seeks defiled pleasure; this refers to those who have destroyed [the roots of goodness] at the beginning and end.

These are all pure objects. Therefore, it is known that "only" (唯) refers to these [objects]. Thus, the two characters "therefore, it is known" (故知) are words of certainty; "only" (唯) carries the meaning of being exclusive or singular.
This, conversely, clarifies that there is no offense regarding an impure object. Regarding the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-vinaya* (*Shisong lü*) and other texts:

that Vinaya asks, "Is there a case where a person who has defiled a bhikṣuṇī is granted ordination and receives the precepts by the bhikṣus? The answer is: "There is. If eight people defile a bhikṣuṇī by means of the eight matters, this is called 'defiling' and constitutes an obstacle.
Furthermore, if a single person defiles her by means of the eight matters, it is likewise. As for the "eight matters": [they are as follows:]...
1. Grasping the hand; 2. Grasping the robe; 3. Entering a secluded place; 4. Standing together; 5. Speaking together; 6. Walking together; 7. Leaning the body against one another;
8. Making an appointment. The *Chao* (Commentary) states: "Regarding 'the eight [acts] of touching a *bhikṣuṇī*,' Xuanyue says: According to the text, it simply mentions 'eight matters.
It is because the *Chao* adds the word 'touching' (*mochu*) that this single phrase serves as a heading for the two initial sections on the precept regarding touching a *bhikṣuṇī*."

The gravity of these offenses is easy to understand: as soon as they touch upon the object, they constitute a transgression. Regarding the "Eight Matters of a Bhikṣuṇī Defiling a Bhikṣuṇī," this is the heading for the precepts.

By using the single character *ni* (Bhikṣuṇī), two precepts are governed. As for the phrase "eight persons together defile one person—one Bhikṣuṇī, using eight matters to defile one Bhikṣuṇī"—this seems difficult to understand;
the following section explains the "Eight Matters of Defiling a Bhikṣuṇī. Therefore, the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: "The eight [matters] of a Maṇi..."

Regarding the "equal offenses" (事等): there are eight laypeople; if a person uses a single act, there are eight acts by which they collectively defile one nun, or perhaps one person alone defiles the eight nuns.

(The above is the commentary text. The preceding citations of such extensive textual meanings serve to prove that within the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya), it simply states "offending a bhikṣuṇī" without weighing whether [the act] is pure or impure. This is what was just explained.

In general, it is by relying on the fundamental tenets that one achieves certainty, so that ritual actions may proceed without obstruction. Regarding the citation of the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* and other texts below:
although the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* mentions those who are "lustfully attached to the kāṣāya," it does not state that they are excluded. This applies to the two lower assemblies as well.
I now cite this passage: "If those in the two lower assemblies commit no offense, it does not obstruct their renunciation and so forth. The *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states:

"A minor offense in an incomplete stage does not constitute an obstacle; however, because it subsumes the full precepts which are venerable, it does indeed constitute an obstruction" (the above is from the commentary).

Regarding the phrase "if it reaches the *Chao*": "If one forcibly gives [clothing] to a nun and it constitutes a difficulty" means that although the nun does not wish to wear it, one forcibly provides her with lay clothing and compels her to wear it, thereby creating a difficulty. If the nun herself wishes to wear it, it does not obstruct her renunciation;

therefore, we know that the previous text’s mention of "forcibly giving and making her wear" must refer to cases where one insults her by forcing her to wear something she does not wish to wear—this is precisely what constitutes a pure object (*viśuddha-viṣaya*).
These two passages are, without exception, spoken in reference to the purity or impurity of the environment (this interpretation has its merit).

Alternatively, according to the *Xuanyi* (Profound Record), since one personally delights in and clings to the white robes [of a layperson], it signifies being like those with false views who have abandoned the precepts; therefore, it does not obstruct one's going forth into the monastic life.

The preceding passage forcefully links [the practitioner] with those [laypeople], thereby manifesting that wrong views do not arise because the precepts have not been lost; thus, it constitutes a difficulty [for the opponent].
Now, I fear this is not so. Even if one were to take pleasure in lightly donning the white robes of a layperson, one would merely be bound by the *kṣudrānuśaya* (minor offenses) of what is improper.

However, wrong views must arise in accordance with the scriptural texts through a mind that is fully perfected in its nine grades. Merely taking pleasure for a time in wearing secular clothing does not necessarily [constitute such a state].
"To abandon the essence of the precepts"—this interpretation is profoundly unreasonable. It is as follows:
if one knows that [the person] has received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) and so forth, the Master now seeks the meaning of this point.

If, with a clear mind, one knows for certain that the person before one is one who has received the full ordination, yet currently wears the white robes of a layperson due to the obstructive conditions of a difficult situation, this too constitutes a "difficult case" (*kaṣṭa*).
Regarding the destruction of the pure object (*pariśuddha-vastu*), it does not matter whether one knows it to be impure. The ancient masters said:

"If one knows that the object before one is pure and yet destroys it, this constitutes a difficulty [a violation]. If one destroys a pure object while my own mind does not recognize it as such, even though it is destroyed, it does not constitute a difficulty.
Now it is said: Provided that the object before one is pure, if one destroys it, it is an offense regardless; it is not contingent upon the mind, nor is it a matter of knowing or not knowing.

Regarding the *Yìchão* (Explanatory Commentary), the *Jīmēng Sūshù* (Commentary on the *Karmavācanā*) states: "According to the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, for a layperson (*upāsaka*), killing does not obstruct the precepts once they have attained the third fruit [of the path].

Now, if merely defiling a nun constitutes an obstacle, how can it be established as such? Answer: Killing obstructs the precepts because it involves taking the ultimate field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), which must be a person who has attained the fourth fruit [Arhatship].

This is because, in the previous three fruits, afflictions (*kleśa*) have not yet been exhausted. Defiling, however, is based on the act of insulting and being arrogant toward a superior object; therefore, it is an obstacle."
Each [point] has its own underlying principle.

Regarding the question, "Why does it not mention 'one who destroys a bhikṣu' when it comes to the section on inclusion? Fabao says: This refers to the questions asked at the time of receiving the precepts within the Saṃgha.
That is to say, just now it was only stated that one does not violate a bhikṣuṇī; why is it not seen to state that one violates a bhikṣu?
"Is it so? The response, "It also constitutes an obstacle," means that if one commits an offense against a *bhikṣu*, it likewise constitutes an obstacle.

Regarding the phrase "when receiving [ordination] from a *bhikṣuṇī*, one asks in return based on the matter in the text": this refers to bringing up the case of the *bhikṣuṇī* in reverse to provide an explanation. The intent is as follows:

when receiving [ordination] from a *saṃgha* (monks), one asks, "Have you not committed an offense against a *bhikṣuṇī*? When receiving [ordination] from a *bhikṣuṇī*, one asks, "Have you not committed an offense against a *bhikṣu*? [The interlocutor] asks: "Since previously..."
Master Yun said: "The passage concerning the time when one receives the precepts from the *saṃgha* is now being explained by way of a counter-example using a *bhikṣuṇī*.

The flow of the text seems inconsistent. Master Bao says: 'The author of the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanbu suiji jiemo*) had a hidden intention; he was not discussing it in relation to the *saṃgha* of monks.

However, because the matter is somewhat obscure and cannot be made clear [otherwise], he brought in the case of a *bhikṣuṇī* to explain it by way of contrast. The subsequent sentence states: 'Because such an incident is rare; were it otherwise, if a *bhikṣuṇī* were to defile the *saṃgha* of monks...'"
This occurs frequently; how can you say it is rare? Therefore, we know that this refers exclusively to the meaning of "easy" (*yi*).

As for the citation below regarding the Elder Śāṇakavāsin receiving the five precepts and so forth, it means that during the interrogation when the Elder Śāṇakavāsin received the five precepts, he was also asked:

"Have you not violated [the precept against] monks or nuns? The intent is clear from this. Thus, we know that these are likewise included within the category of "difficult" (*nan*) cases. This is the Master’s [view].
This is a definitive seal. Regarding the phrase "all for the sake of laypeople, etc.": Laypeople, based on the general rule, have never received [the full precepts];

those who receive the five or eight precepts are already difficult to manage as *śikṣamāṇās* (probationary nuns) because they have been defiled. If one who has received the five or eight precepts later commits an offense, it is merely designated as a "borderline transgression" (*sīmā-vyatikrama*).
The Venerable Master said: "The text of this *Chao* (Excerpts) is subtle and difficult for ordinary people to understand; the *Souxuan* (Investigating the Profound) does not cover it at all."
As he spoke: "Nowadays, when lecturers reach this point, they do not understand its original intent at all; how can they provide an explanation? Please consider this.

Regarding the phrase 'the three thieves of the mind,' the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: 'The dharma of śramaṇas and laypeople is not their original station; their outward forms are indistinct and presumptuous.'"
Furthermore, because they steal the wealth of the Noble Ones (*ārya-dhana*), they are called "thieves. Because they obstruct the arising of the precepts, this is termed a "difficulty.
As for the phrase "the Vinaya reached the household," the *Chao* (the *Vinayavibhāṣā*) briefly cites the origin story (*nidāna*).

According to the *Upasampadā-khandhaka*, when the Buddha was in the city of Vārāṇasī, the price of grain was high and the people were devouring one another; yet only the śramaṇas lived in peace, their food and drink never lacking. There was one...
A young non-Buddhist ascetic (tīrthika) shaved his own hair and entered the community to seek alms. When the monks asked him, "How many years of seniority (*kṣānti*) do you have?
and "Who is your preceptor?", he replied to both questions that he did not know. They further interrogated him, asking, "Who are you?
He replied, "I am a non-Buddhist. Because of this, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "He has a thieving mind; though he has entered the Way within my Dharma, he possesses no merit."

Yi et al. (as stated above) say: regarding those who have not yet reached the precepts, or those who should not receive them because they have not yet received them, this is understood in relation to the Saṃgha and cannot be taken as a fixed rule.

As for those who have already received the precepts, based on the fact that at the initial moment they did not know that he had left the household life for the sake of profit—that is, being a non-Buddhist and so forth—they nonetheless obtain the precepts.
Regarding those said to have previously been subject to expulsion, it simply means they have previously committed the offense of stealing the Dharma. That is all.

This refers to the formal act of expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*). Regarding the phrase "from four up to expulsion," Xuán states: according to the Vinaya text, there are six cases in total; the first two are grave offenses, while the latter four are minor.
The first case states: "If [an individual] goes to the place of one, two, three, or many monks, and they perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) and recite the *Prātimokṣa* together."

2. It is said that if one goes to the place of one, two, or three persons, or to the assembly of monks (*saṃgha*), and performs the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) together with them but does not recite the precepts;

(these two phrases constitute a difficulty). 3. It is said that if one goes to the place of one, two, or three persons, or to the assembly of monks, and neither performs the formal ritual together with them nor recites the precepts.
4. It is said that if one goes to the place of one, two, or three persons, but does not go to the assembly of monks, and does not perform the formal ritual together with them.

Regarding the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*): the fifth [clause] states, "If there are only one or two persons, and not three or more members of the Saṃgha present, they do not perform the *karmavācanā* together for the recitation of the precepts.

The sixth clause states, "If there is only one person, and not two or three members of the Saṃgha present, they do not perform the *karmavācanā* together for the recitation of the precepts" (these four clauses do not constitute a valid objection). These six clauses are as follows; the citation in the present commentary refers to the first clause.

This refers to the enshrinement following the prior verification of death. Regarding the phrase "the meaning is detailed and extremely difficult": it means that the Master’s intended meaning is now discussed in detail; hence, it is said that "the meaning is detailed.
As for the phrase "the *pratideśanīya* (confession) for the assembly and so forth," this *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) is a rule for the Saṃgha.

Now, since there is no Saṃgha within the boundary and only two persons are present, they have performed this rite. Furthermore, if one with a thieving mind goes there to steal [the requisites], this also constitutes a difficulty.

Regarding the claim that "the *cittavijñapti* (mental recitation) must necessarily become a *sāṃghika-dharma* (a formal act involving the assembly)," this refutes the views of the ancients. The ancients said:

"If one person performs the *cittavijñapti* for the *poṣadha* (confession of precepts), including oneself, there are effectively two people; therefore, it must be changed to a *sāṃghika-pratimukha* (formal act addressed to the assembly).

How can this be called a *cittavijñapti*? The Master [of the present school] says: This completely fails to grasp the meaning of the text. Since it states that one goes to another person's location to eavesdrop, it refers to the *sāṃghika* [procedure].

If one merely thinks it in the mind, it becomes difficult to restrain [the transgression]. What are the two persons? This refers to the principle of changing [the procedure] to the *pratyekamukha* (confession before another).
Regarding "three persons or fewer," this refers to the confession of the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses; this is the *pratyekamukha* method.

Since one must seek out and question those nearby within a concealed place, there are three persons. "Fewer" means two persons. Regarding "other harmonious methods (*saṃgha-karma*) and so forth," Xuán says: "Not yet performed..."
The *jñapti* (single-announcement) begins with the inquiry regarding the assembly of monks in harmony and so forth; this is termed "remaining harmony. Hearing this is not considered an obstacle.
When there are four persons, one immediately performs the *jñapti*. Prior to the *jñapti*, there is already the inquiry for harmony.

All instances numbering from one hundred thousand onwards first require harmony among the monks, and even when answering that a particular matter has been subject to *karmavācanā*, it does not constitute an obstacle.

Regarding the phrase "it is said that seeing [this] is difficult": the meaning of this passage is that although the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* mentions "stealing the form" (*touxing*), it does not set forth the specific characteristics of stealing the form;
therefore, the treatise is cited here to provide a detailed analysis. As for "leaving home by oneself without a teacher," etc., this refers to the actual manifestation of stealing the form.
It is like the present day, when one leaves home and shaves the hair without relying on a preceptor monk, but merely shaves it off by oneself.

[The phrase] "and so forth" refers to this. Regarding the statement "not relying on seniority by number of years (lǎ) up to not accepting offerings," it can be understood as an explanation that this does not constitute stealing the Dharma [as in the previous case], and so on.

Second, "stealing from a harmonious community" indicates the act of stealing the Dharma. The phrase "there is a teacher who has left the household life" explains that this is not stealing the form [of ordination].
The phrase "going to another region, etc. distinguishes the characteristics of the act of stealing the Dharma. It can be understood that both are cases of stealing; there is no [other category].

When a teacher leaves the household life, this constitutes "stealing the form" (stealing the appearance) by going to another region, receiving prostrations, entering the place for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), and so forth; this is "stealing the dharma.

Regarding those who steal the form, the following excerpt from the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*) provides a detailed analysis: according to the first phrase, such a person does not constitute a valid obstacle and may receive ordination.
Regarding the two cases where it is not appropriate: stealing the Dharma and stealing both [the Dharma and the precepts] are not appropriate for conferring the precepts.
As for the *Pañcaśataprśnasaṃgraha* and other such texts, they may be understood as providing general corroboration.

Regarding the statement that "the four cases constitute an obstacle": although it simply says "staying as a thief" (*caura-vāsa*) without specifying the circumstances of hearing or not hearing [the precepts], the *Caturvargika-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya), in its section on the offense of stealing the Dharma, merely states that "stealthily listening" while others recite the precepts constitutes an obstacle.

However, at the time of listening, there are various conditions—such as whether one hears or does not hear, or whether one is intelligent or dull-witted, and whether one can memorize them or not—which cannot be treated as a single uniform case; all such instances are included within the category of obstacles. Since...

Unexpectedly, "Jian" (簡) means "not to master" (不了). The following citation from the *Zhiwen* (祇文) establishes this as definitive. Regarding the "words of the beginning, middle, and end": the initial formal announcement (*jñapti*) constitutes the beginning;
the detailed introduction and the texts of the five categories of offenses constitute the middle; and the abbreviated teachings of the Seven Buddhas constitute the end.

To be able to memorize the chapters and phrases according to these three sections is considered difficult. As for those who are dull-witted and so forth, although they hear [the teachings], they do not memorize them.

It cannot be considered a difficult task to hold [the text]. As for those whose minds are distracted by other thoughts—though they may be intelligent, their minds are not single-minded—this is called being distracted by other thoughts and the like;
it is likewise not a difficult task (and so forth). Furthermore, there are those who read from the original text themselves; this can be understood by analogy.

Since their rank is not yet full and they have not attained [the requisite status], they do not yet deserve to see or hear [it]. Those who now privately and surreptitiously steal [it] are likewise stealing the Dharma.
