This is difficult; please do not doubt it. Regarding the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* and other texts, the intent of citing this passage is that although the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) states that if one has not completed six years [of residence], the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) is not established, it does not mention "staying like a thief" (*caura-vāsa*). This is incomplete.
Now, by citing the treatise which says, "If one undergoes the *poṣadha* and *karmavācanā* of the Saṃgha, this is called staying like a thief," it finally becomes comprehensive.
Regarding the "fourth part of the years": as for those whose age is not yet full and so forth, there are cases where one knows another’s age is not yet full and says, "Your age is still incomplete;

do not undergo the ritual of receiving the precepts, for the formal act will not be accomplished. Once you have reached [the required] age later on, you may receive them again. This is as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) and other texts.
It is said that when the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, there was a woman who, being harassed by her husband, mother-in-law, and maternal uncle, left the household life to become a nun.
Later, while living with her preceptress (upādhyāyī), she again experienced suffering and distress, and returned to lay life. A layperson rebuked her, saying:
"This is an inauspicious and wretched woman. We were her husbands before, yet in the interim, she has received our respect; she possesses no constancy."
He reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "If a bhikṣuṇī violates the precepts even once, she may not go forth again.

Regarding the phrase "those who break both internal and external paths," the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: "Their disposition is not constant; they bear the name of 'internal' or 'external' without attaining realization."
To break both internal and external obstacles, for the precepts not to arise—this is called "difficult. As for the phrase "those who have attained full ordination":
those who come to take refuge in the Buddha-Dharma break the external [obstacles]. Those who, after receiving full ordination, revert to their original path, break the internal [obstacles].

The *Chao* (Commentary) explains this by interpreting it as breaking both simultaneously, encompassing both the internal and external realms. According to the Vinaya, the *Jiefa juyuanqi* (The Origin Story of the Precept-Method Collection) states: "In the city of Rājagṛha..."
There was a naked ascetic named Posāla who was exceedingly intelligent. Fearing that his wisdom might overflow, he bound his abdomen with iron chains;
to illuminate those in darkness, he wore a large basin upon his head. He came to the monastery and declared, "Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, who dares to debate with me?
At that time, Śāriputra thought to himself, "This non-Buddhist Nirgrantha is a master of the land..."
The people honored him deeply. When he was asked about the meaning of a single phrase and could not answer, his fame inevitably spread widely, and he was certain to be drawn toward the Great Dharma.
He then engaged in debate with that opponent. From the first day until the sixth, they discussed various other matters, during which time the outsiders were all rendered speechless.
On the seventh day, Śāriputra established his thesis, stating: "Desire arises from reflection, not from opposition."
The outsider says: Desire arises from the object; it does not depend on the mind. This is because the *Abhidharmakośa* establishes its thesis by citing a verse which states:
"The various exquisite mirrors of the world are not true desire; true desire is the greed of human conceptualization.
Exquisite objects remain as they are in the world, yet the wise have already eliminated desire for them. Śāriputra said: "Exquisite objects are not themselves desire," and so forth. Why is this?
It is not true desire, for desire arises from the mind’s conceptualization; therefore, it is called "discriminative greed.

Because all exquisite objects have no end, it is called "abiding. Since the minds of worldly sages have already ceased after they have practiced and severed their afflictions, it is said that "desire has been eliminated.
Then the heterodox practitioner of wrong livelihood addressed the Venerable One, saying: "If you say..."
The wondrous object is not itself true desire; it is said that desire is the greed of human conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
A bhikṣu would then be called a person who experiences desire, because he gives rise to evil conceptualizations, discursive thoughts, and investigations (*vitarka-vicāra*). The non-Buddhists say:

"If you do not allow that desire arises from the object, but rather claim it arises from the mind, then the bhikṣu is instead the one who experiences desire. The following line states: "Because he gives rise to evil conceptualizations, discursive thoughts, and so forth."
"Because they constantly give rise to evil thoughts and seek out [objects] through investigation. At that time, Śāriputra further countered him, saying:

"If the sublime objects of the world are true desire, and you say that desire is not the greed of human conceptualization, then your teacher should be called one who experiences desire, for he is constantly surrounded by agreeable and sublime forms.
Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "At that time, having heard this verse, those non-Buddhists were unable to respond further."
He replied, and immediately gave rise to a virtuous mind; he returned to the Buddha and left the household life.

At that time, Baddhananda was among that assembly, his appearance being quite extraordinary, while Śāriputra was short and small in stature. He thought to himself, "If this small bhikṣu possesses such wisdom, how much more so must those who are dignified and imposing?
He then sought out Baddhananda to serve as his preceptor for the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), and having received it, he questioned him.
The Sūtras and Vinaya could not provide an answer at all. He then disparaged the Buddha-dharma, resented the bhikṣus for their lack of wisdom, and returned to his original path.
He reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "From now on, one must have ten years of seniority and possess wisdom before being permitted to confer the full precepts upon another.
Later, that non-Buddhist practitioner came again; this then became an obstacle. [He was then] ordained as a śrāmaṇera before the Saṃgha.

Regarding the *mi-jiè* (Mī-gati): first, one confers upon them the ten precepts. Regarding the four-month probation (*cāturmāsa-parivāsa*): one has the candidate come before the assembly of monks, join their palms, and request the four-month probation.
The community then performs the formal procedure (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) and grants him a four-month period of co-residence.

In the presence of the candidate, one recounts the evil deeds of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and reviles them. One observes his mind; if he does not give rise to anger, it is known that he is disciplined and compliant.
If one still defends that school of thought, it is known that they have not yet been subdued; therefore, it is untenable.

Regarding the question "What is meant by 'reaching clarity'?"—it means that those who believe in this and take refuge in this say, "I uphold the ten precepts," which constitutes being disciplined and gentle.

If one does not uphold the precepts, the contradiction with the characteristics becomes manifest. If one does not employ the ten precepts to test whether others are compliant or contrary, how can one discern them?
Regarding "attaining the heterodox or the orthodox," the meaning of the brief reference from this point downward can be understood.

As for the phrase "from 'five' to 'receiving,'" Master Tang says: According to the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*, at the time of the origin story, there was a eunuch who came seeking to leave the household life and receive ordination.
When the boundary for conferring the precepts was established, he summoned the bhikṣus and caused them to perform such acts. The bhikṣus rebuked him, telling him to depart and to vanish. Etc.
He went again to the place where the śrāmaṇeras were and called them to perform improper acts. He then went outside the boundary to the place where the cowherds were and summoned them to work.
A layperson criticized him, saying, "Among the bhikṣus, many are eunuchs. This was reported to the Buddha.

The Buddha established a rule prohibiting him from receiving [the precepts]. Next, regarding the explanation of the name, there are several interpretations. An ancient [commentary] states: "Yellow" refers to the color of the robe;

"gate" (*mēn*) refers to the sense-gates (*indriya-mukha*). [This is incorrect. Others say: In antiquity, there was a man who committed misconduct within the inner palace and was subsequently castrated.
Furthermore, at their dwelling place, yellow earth was smeared upon the door panels to signify that these were persons whose sexual organs had been severed.
Because they emerged from this yellow gate, they were successively referred to as "yellow-gated" (pandaka); thus, the name was established based on their dwelling place.
Now the Master says: "The gate is the imperial gate of the Son of Heaven. Yellow is the primary color among the colors of the five directions; it is the correct color of the central direction.
Thus, this inner restricted gate is designated as the 'Yellow Gate' (Huangmen). Since this person is now ordered to guard that gate, [he is called a eunuch]."
From the place of protection, the name is manifested. This is because it takes the name of another entirely and establishes it as one's own designation.

The *Jiewen su* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states: "Yellow is the color of the central direction; it is used because the central direction is the gate of prohibition" (this interpretation is correct).
First, in Sanskrit it is called *śaṇḍha*; here it is translated as "birth. This means that due to past karma, one is naturally so from birth. Second, in Sanskrit it is called *rūpa*.
1. *Na*: This is translated as "to remove by force. 2. Three words say *ilisa*; this is translated as "jealousy.
As explained in the *Chao* (Excerpts), it is self-explanatory. 3. In Sanskrit, *pannaga*; this is translated as "transformation. The *Chao* explains it as "suddenly transforming.
4. In Sanskrit, *pakṣanaka*; this is translated as "half-month. The text of the *Chao* provides its own explanation (*et cetera*).
Within this section, there are six parts, including the addition of the "nala-pō" (the castrated). Regarding the phrase "there are many such as these in the world":

although five types of *paṇḍaka* were previously listed, four of them are easily understood and thus not explained here; the present commentary explains only the *śaṇḍha-paṇḍaka*. Within this, there are roughly two sections:

first, a formal explanation based on the various Vinayas, speaking from the perspective of those who have already received the precepts; second, the following section concludes by identifying the essential nature of the difficulty.
It is explained whether those who have not yet received [the precepts] may obtain them. This section is further divided into two parts: first, a distinction based on self-mutilation;

second, from "dividing into four" onwards, a distinction based on retribution for enmity. The first part is further divided into two: first, regarding total mutilation, it concerns what is to be collected at the place of burial according to the current Vinaya.

Second, regarding the present time: a small portion of the *Yitabu* (依他部) is excerpted to clarify that [the precepts] may be received. (Based on the *Xuanyi* [玄記], this passage of the commentary seems easy to understand.
As for "that which should be excised but is not": this refers to the desire arising from the mind rather than originating from the body.

One must excise the afflictions within the mind; why would one need to excise the body? Thus it was rebuked by the Buddha (and so forth). Regarding repentance according to the chapters: if one were to excise one's head...

Regarding the case where one has half-reached the state of being "auspiciously departed" by having one egg removed: since there are two offenses of *sthūlātyaya*, one must perform the confession according to the respective category (*varga*).

Following this principle, even up to the point of "for the sake of receiving," all the aforementioned texts refer to cases occurring after the reception [of the precepts]. If, however, the cutting occurs before the reception [of the precepts], [the rules differ].

This is indeed difficult to manage. Since there is no authoritative scripture (āgama) that explicitly prohibits it, one must follow the text of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*. According to this, if one cuts off the head or half [of the egg], it is permissible;

if one removes a single ovum or the like, it is likewise acceptable. As for cutting [the whole] or not extinguishing [the fire] before enshrouding, based on the force of this textual passage, these are not considered difficulties.

Regarding the reception of the precepts: if one has completely severed [the parental relationship], various Vinayas state that such a person will certainly receive the precepts [of the deceased] and cannot obtain the precepts [of the living].

As for the sixth point, "mutual [relationship]," regarding those who kill their parents, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "The causal origin (*nidāna*) is as follows: there was a young non-Buddhist ascetic (*tīrthika*) who had previously killed his parents.
He constantly harbored grief and anxiety, and thought to himself: 'I shall rescue the Śramaṇas, the sons of Śākya,' and so forth."

If one receives the precepts at home and attains meditative concentration, their offenses may be removed. Yet, the bhikṣus did not first conduct an inquiry before hastily ordaining them for renunciation.
After they had left the household life, they spoke of this matter themselves, and they reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "They should be expelled. The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states:

Human beings are not born by transformation; their karma relies upon a womb for its retribution, using the residual aggregates of another to form their own bodies. Since the debt of upbringing is profound, it is only logical that one should repay it.

To now violate this by killing is termed a "perverse obstacle" (*ānantarya-āvaraṇa*). Because the precept against taking life is so difficult to observe, it is called "difficult to fulfill. (The above is from the Commentary.)
This is stated with reference to the biological mother. As for the foster mother, [killing her] does not constitute a *ānantarya* (immediate) offense.

The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Suppose there is a woman who has conceived a *kalala*; another woman takes it and places it in her own birth canal. If she gives birth to the child and kills that child, it does not constitute a *ānantarya* offense;

she incurs only a *pārājika* (defeat) offense. The verse of the treatise says: "'Mother' refers to the one whose blood [is the cause], or the one in whose womb [the child] develops. (The term "blood" refers to the biological mother.)
If one kills a living being who is not an Arhat, the act does not constitute a pācittiya offense; one merely incurs the sin of killing an animal, because the retribution is inferior.

Or, if one kills another enemy by mistake and kills one's own parents, it likewise does not constitute a pācittiya offense, because there was no intentional mind [to harm them]. As for killing an Arhat... [and so forth].
The Master of the Hall said: "According to the circumstances described in the Vinaya, there were bhikṣus who traveled through the country of Vatsa.
Among them, two bhikṣus saw a secluded place and pointed it out, saying, 'In this place, someone once killed an arhat.
The other bhikṣus asked, 'How do you know this? They replied, 'I am one of those people,' and reported this."

"Buddha. Regarding "Buddha," it is said that he has entered extinction and is enshrined. The *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vṛtti) states: "This person’s delusions were exhausted and his virtues were perfected;

as a field of merit, he was worthy of offerings. Yet, instead of showing respect, one inflicts harm upon him. Because the karma is as heavy as the aforementioned cases, it is termed a 'pārājika' (a grave offense).

It obstructs the arising of the precepts and is thus called a 'difficulty' (*duskarā*). 'Arhat' is a Sanskrit term; 'A' means 'no,' and 'Rahat' means 'birth. This refers to one whose delusions are exhausted and who no longer turns toward the three [realms]."

Because it involves taking birth within the realms, it is a term for non-arising. An external objection states: "In the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*, killing a pratyekabuddha is not considered difficult;
in the *Sudarśana-śāstra*, killing those who have attained the first three fruits of the path is not an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*);

yet here, why does killing an arhat constitute an immediate transgression that obstructs the precepts? The answer is: because the afflictions of those in the first three fruits are not yet exhausted, and they are not yet the ultimate field of merit.
It is not a transgression. Although the Pratyekabuddha has exhausted all afflictions, because his purpose in wandering and transforming others is inferior, it is not a transgression.
As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The Pratyekabuddha does not preach the Dharma among the houses of people. After receiving offerings, he throws a branch and soars into the sky.
He merely manifests the twelve links of dependent origination beneath his feet, causing them to observe this and practice to realize the Way," and so forth. These three...
The following [passage] refers to the summarized meaning, which can be understood accordingly.
Regarding the phrase "from nine up to the ear": the schism of the Wheel of Dharma (cakrabheda) has Devadatta as its causal condition, as will be explained in detail below (*et cetera*).
The *Karmasūtra* states: "When false dharma deviates from the truth, it is called 'schism of the Saṃgha' (saṃghabheda); it obstructs the attainment of the title [of Arhat]."

This is called a "difficulty" (*duskarā*). Regarding the breaking of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act), it is not considered a difficulty provided one obtains four persons of middle-grade *pārājika* offenses who repent;

thus, it does not constitute a difficulty (*na duṣkaraḥ*). (And so forth. As for shedding the blood of a Buddha, the causal conditions are the same as above. (And so forth. The *Karmasūtra-vyākhyā* states:

"The Tathāgata’s principle of transforming sentient beings through the path of the four immeasurable minds—when this is met with a reverent heart, yet one instead gives rise to rebellious harm and sheds his bodily blood, it is named 'rebellion' (*ānantarya*)."
[Obstruction]. Regarding the difficulty that "precepts do not arise" (the above is from the commentary): this refers to cases of malicious intent.

If the intention is wholesome—as when Jīvaka bled the Buddha to treat his illness, whereby [the Buddha] subsequently experienced celestial bliss—it does not fall under this category. The remaining text may be understood in detail (*yǔnyún*).

Regarding the statement "from the eleventh [chapter] to what is presented": As for the non-human, it was because of the son of an asura who, having contemplated the causes and conditions of birth, old age, and death, transformed himself into human form and came to seek ordination. At first, the bhikṣus did not recognize him and consequently ordained him.

He then consumed seven portions of food within the monastery and five hundred portions of food at the residences of laypeople outside. The householders discussed this with resentment. The various bhikṣus...
The Master asked in distress, "Who are you? He replied, "I am not a human being. [The monk] reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "A non-human being has no benefit within my Dharma;

therefore, [one must not ordain them]," and so forth. The *Karmavācanā-viniścaya* (羯磨疏) states: "Those with the retribution of non-humans or animals are of lowly status; their physical form and mind are not fit vessels [for the Dharma].
Because they thus obstruct the precepts, they are difficult to receive [ordination]. Regarding the eight classes of beings (*aṣṭau devanikāyāḥ*): first, the gods (*deva*).
Nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth—the rest may be understood accordingly.
As for animals (*tiryagyoni*), they arise from those various causes and conditions; among them is the dragon (nāga) Subhūti.
Disgusted with his dragon body, he transformed himself into a young man and went to the monks' quarters to seek ordination.

The bhikṣus, unaware of who he was, hastily conferred full ordination upon him. After his ordination, while he was staying in the same room as another bhikṣu, that co-resident bhikṣu went away on a journey.
It is the constant nature of dragons to assume their original forms at five specific times; these are referred to as the "five [times of] submission."
Regarding the "time," a verse states: "Birth and death are not the sleep of anger" (and so forth). Since he was asleep, his body filled the room.

When the bhikṣu returned and pushed the door open, his hand touched the nāga’s body. Realizing it was something extraordinary, he cried out in a loud voice, "A snake! A snake! At that moment, the nāga woke up;
he then rose and sat in the full lotus posture, fixing his mind with right attention upon the object before him. The bhikṣu asked:
"Who are you? He replied, "I am the dragon Suvīra. He reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "How can an animal bring benefit within my Dharma?

If it has not yet received [the precepts], do not confer them; if it has already received them, extinguish them through the rite of burial. However, if there should be one who is exceptionally gifted..."
This is due to negligence. For instance, there are those wearing robes and caps who come daily to receive the precepts (and so forth).

Regarding the "skillful means of inquiry," one should say: "Are you not an animal? You have been able to transform yourself into human form to come and receive [the precepts]," for this is a skillful means.
One must not speak directly, saying, "Are you not an animal? This is because it would appear as though one is treating the person before them with slighting contempt, as will be explained below.
"Cen" (陳) refers to the detailed explanation provided by the instructor during the formal questioning.
Regarding the phrase "from thirteen until the enshrinement": in the context of the Vinaya narrative, there was once a bhikṣu who transformed into both male and female sexual organs.
The bhikṣus did not know [what to do]. They reported this to the Buddha, who said, "Perform the funeral rites. Later, there was a bhikṣuṇī whose transformation was likewise.
According to the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Samantapāsādikā*), there are three types: first, those who can conceive a fetus themselves and can cause another to conceive;
second, those who can conceive themselves but cannot cause another to conceive; third, those who cannot conceive themselves but can cause another to conceive. All of these are...
It is difficult to restrain. The *Karmavācanā* states: "If one's physical form is narrow and both objective spheres are weak in resolve, then neither good nor evil can be accomplished.
Being able to obstruct the cultivation of the Path and preventing the arising of precepts is termed 'difficult. The rest is as stated in the text."
*Jiǎnzhèngjì* on the *Sifenlü chāo*, Scroll Seven, Part One.
Next, the various prohibitions (*śikṣāpada*) are distinguished.
The phrase "From 'Up' to 'One'" serves to conclude the preceding section and introduce the intent of the following one. The phrase "From 'The Vinaya' to 'Obtained'"... [text continues]
Regarding the "Brief Inquiry into the Sixteen": within the *Upasampadā-khandhaka*, there are ten combined inquiries in total.

By dividing the prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) and the separations (*vibhāga*), they become sixteen. These consist of two for parents, two for robes and bowl, and six from the five types of illness (excluding the original *niśraya*);
thus, including the original, they constitute sixteen. As for the other methods of receiving ordination explained in detail, beyond these sixteen, there are further [categories].
It is not uniform, as explained in the *Khandaka*. All state that one should not accept [the robe].

Regarding the various instances of obtaining or not obtaining, among these sixteen cases, one must distinguish between what is obtained and what is not. If it is redundant, it violates the fundamental principle; therefore, it is not obtained.

If [the commentary] were brief, it would merely repeat what has already been stated. Regarding this, the *Xuánjì* (Record of Profound Explanations) extensively cites the subsequent text. [The interlocutor asks: "Can you not analyze and distinguish [the meaning]?

The Venerable One does not permit this. This [section] serves as the introduction to the subsequent text; the subsequent text provides a detailed overview of each point, explaining their characteristics and clarifying their merits and faults.
If this were to provide an exhaustive analysis in advance, it would be redundant—amounting to a double repetition—and would result in excessive prolixity. Thus it is said:
Regarding those who have reached the stage of full ordination (*upasampadā*): one must not state one's own name, nor the name of the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or the instructor (*karmavācanācārya*).

If one has not yet reached twenty years of age, one certainly cannot receive it. Even if the period of gestation or intercalary months were to be calculated, this would merely address doubts arising after the ceremony;
if one knows before the reception that one is under age, or if the assembly knows it, the reception is strictly forbidden.
Regarding the phrase "five parts reaching the offense" (*pañcabhāga-āpatti*): "small and small, resembling a fragmentary matter. Xuánzàng says: "These matters are small and resemble evil;

one then relies upon these matters, which are not merely fragments [of fault], but obstruct another from receiving the precepts. 'Below, resembling blindness,' etc., refers to manifesting small and slight evil appearances.

There are those who change the character *xíng* (to practice) into *xiéng* (to act/shape), but this is an error. If the character *piàn* (fragment) is glossed as "few," it is according to the *Chāo* (Excerpts).
There is already the small character [“似”] within the main text. If it were glossed as “resembling,” there would also be the character “似” at the very end of the passage;

therefore, this interpretation is irrational. *Bì* (pinyin: bìng biàn; meaning: lame) and *yè* (pinyin: yú zhì fǎn): according to the *Guǎngyá*, it means to drag. *Kāo* (pinyin: kǔ dāo fǎn): Cāngjié says it refers to the hip bone (*kuān gǔ*).

"Whip-marks" refers to the scars left by a staff. *Tū* (with the *tu* and *jie* initials) means "to rise," according to the *Zi yuan*. *Āo* (with the *wu* and *jiao* initials) means "to sink. Regarding "seal-marks," the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states:

after the flesh has been broken open, one uses copper-green pigment (*tóngqīng*) and other substances to create characters or animal shapes. Regarding "animal-head shapes," the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
there were wives of various generals at home who had illicit relations with non-human beings and gave birth to children with heads like elephants or horses.
"Physical form. Regarding the "dwarf," Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that they were performers of ancient music.
As for the phrase "those who correspond to the recipients," "corresponding to this" refers to the various prohibitions listed under these five *gīti* and two *lǜ*.

All say "should not" because the *Gīti* states: "One should not grant ordination to those with the hundred [types of] impediments. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "All those who have committed [offenses]..."
"Those who have insulted the Saṃgha shall not be ordained. Regarding the two aforementioned Vinaya rules, neither permits the reception [of ordination];

therefore, it says "all. "Incurring an offense" means that the Saṃgha would incur what is not auspicious. "The following text" refers to the concluding passage after the *Vinayamātṛkā* lists the obstructing conditions (*antarāyika-dharma*).

"It says again" is a re-explanation of the hundred types of obstructed persons mentioned above; these are called those who do not truly receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). These are the hundred obstructed persons.

Since there are already prohibitions regarding the person's body, it is not called "receiving full ordination" (*upasampadā*). Regarding the phrase "in each and every case, one should not be expelled":
this refers to a person who has already become a *śrāmaṇera*, yet beneath each of the prohibitions, the words "should not be expelled" are attached.

"Among these" refers to the hundred types of prohibited persons within the context of leaving the household life to become a *śrāmaṇera*. "Pure and according to the Dharma" is like the example of a deaf person.

If one hears the name being called out in a loud voice and it is pure and in accordance with the Dharma, this person is said to have received full ordination (*upasampadā*). One who does not hear the name is likewise among those previously mentioned;

if they do not hear the loud voice, they are not said to have received ordination. Regarding the summary of the teacher’s offense: it is improper for the teacher to ordain such a person into the homeless life.
This constitutes an offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (requiring a formal meeting of the community). Why would there be any harm in there being those who do not attain it? [This is] because one desires...
The "Brief Examination" (Liaojian) begins with the arising of a difficulty. This refers to the difficulty that arose when the preceding hundred prohibitions were composed as a continuous text.

Since it was stated that [the person] is pure, yet further says they are not so called, one might ask: how does this not contradict the case of those who are impure? Regarding the phrase "cannot be like those who are mute, etc.," this means that the prohibition cannot be applied to such specific cases.
"Light prohibitions" (qingshe) refers to minor or small-scale prohibitions. "Pure" (qingjing) means not obstructing the precepts. "Living together" (gongzhu) is as follows:...
Regarding the Dharma: among the two types, such as the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), it refers to dwelling together in accordance with the Dharma.
As for "the mute who does not speak," this refers to using hand gestures to substitute for speech; the text below clarifies the intention behind making such gestures.

Furthermore, sending a letter saying, "Receive the precepts for me," or "I raise my hand in gesture, so grant me the precepts," as well as cases where the person from whom one receives them is not present—none of these result in the attainment of the precepts.
This is the limit [of the rule]. As for the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Vinayakṣudraka*, the intended meaning of the evidence can be understood (as explained at length).
It says that when one has reached the stage of the formal robe (*dharma-vastra*), if one does not possess both robe and bowl, one is not called a "fully ordained" (*upasampanna*) person.

In the narrative context (*nidāna*) of the Vinaya, regarding those receiving ordination who themselves possessed neither robe nor bowl and thus borrowed them from others, after the ordination, the various bhikṣus told them to put on and carry their robes and bowls. Thereupon...

"It is said that 'I have no equal'—this refers to the establishment of the rule (and so forth). Regarding the *Pañcavargika* and other schools: they permit borrowing another's robe and bowl, yet one must pay the value back as a tax.
Furthermore, the original owner must form the intention of relinquishment (*tyāga-citta*) for [the item] to be validly obtained.

If the value is not paid, or if the owner does not form the intention of relinquishment, it is contrary to the Dharma. In the *Sarvāstivāda*, the two characters 'If so' (*cet*) serve to acknowledge the preceding meaning. Since...
It is permitted to receive the precepts by borrowing robes and alms bowl; why must they necessarily be used? The answer is as stated in the *Shu* (Commentary) [et cetera].
Regarding the hunter wearing the *kāṣāya*: this refers to a deer-hunter. If he does not wear the *kāṣāya*, the deer will be terrified; however, if he wears the *kāṣāya*, [they are not afraid].

They say, "He is a śramaṇa," and thus they draw near to him without giving rise to fear or dread; that he realizes the meaning of rebirth in higher realms and so forth can be fully relied upon (as stated at length).

To cite those [other texts] as proof for this present text where they cannot be harmonized—such as citing the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (*Bahudhātuka-śāstra*) to prove this *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, which cannot be reconciled—is improper.
That the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* does not call it "receiving the precepts" refers to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* itself. One must possess the robes and bowl; if one asks...

"One certainly cannot obtain the precepts [in such cases]. Wanling says: "The Buddha established that one must possess the three robes and the alms bowl before one can receive the precepts. This is for three reasons:

first, because the Dharma is profound and difficult to clarify, one uses these external conditions to verify whether the attainment of the precepts was successful; second, to distinguish between those who enter the Path through heterodoxy and those who do so through orthodoxy, thereby verifying the truth or falsity of their realization;

and third, to use the three robes and the bowl as superior and favorable conditions to discern what has been realized. Furthermore, the alms bowl manifests that [realization] is not produced by oneself."

One may be liberated from hunger. Furthermore, this differs from the non-Buddhists who claim that the ten thousand dharmas are spontaneous (*svabhāva*). Now, by means of the bowl and robes, it is shown that the precepts are obtained through conditions (*pratyaya*).

To lack these at present would be to contravene the teaching; such a state is inherently contrary to the Dharma. If this is so, why do many schools permit the attainment of the precepts even without requiring robes and bowls?
The *Chao* (the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan*) answers: "This refers to the differences between the various sects (*nikāya-bheda*). One must recite the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
Regarding the term "etcetera" (*ādi*): if one has gone forth in that [other] school and performed its *karmavācanā*, it would be permissible for one to obtain the precepts even without robes or bowl.

However, since we now rely on our own *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is not permissible to arbitrarily judge the attainment of the precepts according to another school’s rules. As for the principle that "there is no harm in following what is urgent":

this means that even if one were to receive the precepts through the *karmavācanā* of another school, provided one possesses the robes and bowl according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, this is acceptable. This is the standard.

In times of urgency, one does not abandon the Great Principle (Mahā-vinaya). To secretly follow an urgent regulation while outwardly manifesting reliance on the *Caturvargika-vinaya*—which, according to other schools, lacks [the requirement for] robes and bowls—is precisely the latter case; thus, one certainly cannot obtain the precepts.

Regarding the phrase "ancient masters judging by analogy": the ancients said that, following the precedent of Master Zhun, one should apply a fourfold analysis based on whether one knows or does not know.
In the first three cases, where one does not know, it is permissible; however, in the fourth case, where one possesses full knowledge, it is not permissible.

Regarding this judgment of the ancients, the present Master says: This was merely a judgment based on the personal opinions of those ancients; I fear it ultimately violates the texts of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Moreover...

The Upādhyāya is a sentient being, and the śrāmaṇera is also a sentient being. When these two are compared with respect to their knowledge or lack thereof, it is permissible [to speak of them as such].

However, if one discusses the robes and bowl, they belong exclusively to that which is insentient; one must not take a sentient being and compare it to that which is insentient in order to argue about the principle of knowing or not knowing.
Such an error is grave. Regarding the re-ordination according to the Dharma, this too is a sincere exhortation. At the beginning...
If one lacks [the requisites] or borrows them and so forth, it is verified that the necessary conditions (*sāmagrī*) are incomplete and that there is no precept within one's person.

Since it is now stated that one must "know thoroughly," one should seek out robes and an alms bowl in accordance with the Dharma and receive them again according to the Vinaya. The wording in the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*) appears inverted; the text should now be rearranged to indicate receiving them again in accordance with the Dharma.

Regarding the statement that "Yuloka’s parents arrived at the place of ordination," according to the *nidāna* (circumstantial account) in the Vinaya: Śāriputra had unilaterally ordained Yuloka. When his father, the King, came and informed the Buddha, the Buddha commanded the bhikṣus:

"If one's parents do not permit it, one must not unilaterally ordain them. Because the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha, he established this rule; the text is simply as such. The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states:
"Since they are those upon whom one relies in this physical life, in principle they must be fully supported. For a bhikṣu to unilaterally ordain them [is a violation]."
It was established because it contradicts the [monastic] sentiment. The following citations from the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* make this easy to understand (etc.).
Regarding "one who is in debt until they attain [the goal]": according to the context of the Vinaya, various bhikṣus ordained a person who was in debt.
The owner of the wealth rebuked them, saying, "Bhikṣus are all people burdened by debt. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and consequently, he prohibited it. This is the meaning.

Regarding what is "justified by principle": although the texts do not permit it, our Master [Daoxuan] determines it based on the underlying meaning; according to this context, it is indeed appropriate.

That is to say, according to the laws of the Western Heavens (India), once one has left the household life, one may no longer demand the repayment of debts incurred prior to ordination. In this land (China), however, even after one has left the household life, one must still repay debts for wealth borrowed;
doing so does not incur public reproach, and it is justified by principle without causing harm.
Regarding the phrase "one who has reached the status of a slave": in the *Vinaya-nidāna*, it concerns the case of stealing and ordaining another person’s slave.

The owner criticized [the monks], saying, "Monks are nothing but a gathering of slaves. Because of this report to the Buddha, the rule was established. Those born in the household may be understood accordingly. "Bought" means acquired by paying wealth as a price.
"Seized" means captured by plunder. Regarding "that and this": "that" refers to a foreign country, and "this" refers to one's own country; these refer to male slaves (*dāsa*).
Because the master’s protective concern for his heart [servants] is deep, when someone brings a slave to offer him, he does not accept them by purchasing them with wealth;
they come of their own accord, willingly offering their service to their lord.

As for those obtained from other places, if this land does not permit it, then those from distant regions are permitted, because the master’s protective concern for his heart is somewhat thinner there. They come of their own accord.
Regarding those who have entered the Dharma and discipline: one does not speak of the master’s releasing them as being right or wrong, nor of their status as slaves or children.

When both parties agree upon the matter, even if they are the biological children of the head of the household, or slaves purchased or captured by him—regardless of these two causes, neither are permitted to receive the precepts;
it invariably constitutes a transgression. This applies to biological children, adopted children, slaves given by others, slaves brought from elsewhere, and those acquired through such causes.
To receive [the precepts] is what is right; this country does not permit what is wrong. Therefore, it is said that "right and wrong are based on slaves and children.
The literary structures of both passages correspond to one another, and their principles are appropriate; thus, it is said that "both sides are mutually consistent and correct.

The above interpretation follows the phrasing of the *Fayao Kechao*. Alternatively, according to the *Xuanji*, it says: "The 'right' and 'wrong' of the *Du* [scripture] are erroneous; they destroy..."
Furthermore, deleting these phrases makes the explanation of the meaning also inconvenient; reflect upon this. Regarding a "slave of the Buddha" (*buddhadāsa*) who commits a grave offense:

since a slave has no master, if one knowingly ordains such a person after having released them, it constitutes the same offense as theft; therefore, it is grave. Later, if one realizes they were not sent away, the principle remains the same as before.
As for the question regarding whether the person is a "Great Way practitioner" (*mahāmārgika*) and so forth: generally, a Great Way practitioner knows that the three realms are empty and afflicted.
Seeking the unsurpassed [enlightenment], one should now merely weary oneself of the toil of servitude and delight in the seclusion of the Saṃgha;

therefore, this is not the Great Way, and it offers no benefit to the Buddha-dharma. Regarding those such as "monastic slaves" (*saṃghanava*), their bodies belong to the ten directions and they have no formal master who can release them;
if they were to be ordained, it would likewise be a grave matter—hence it is said, "it is according to this. Hereafter, once this is understood, one must certainly resolve to...
He was sent back and returned to the monastic community; thus it is called the "stage of the thigh" (*ūru-bhūmi*).
Regarding the phrase "the official reached the status of a recipient," according to the context of the Vinaya: King Prasenajit had a brave and powerful general whom a bhikṣu had arbitrarily ordained.
Later, when the kingdom rebelled, the king could not find him. Upon learning that he had been ordained as a monk, the king then censured him.

He reported this to the Buddha, who declared that the national regulations did not permit it. The *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: "Those of the nine ranks and above, whether civil or military, fear they might fail their celestial mandate;

as for other miscellaneous officials, they are not mentioned. Regarding the criticism of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and other texts, there are four categories: first, those who have both titles and stipends, such as current incumbent officials;
second, those who have titles but no stipends, such as district or county magistrates who have resigned from office but have not yet accepted a new post.
Please consider these points. Third, there are those who have no official title but do receive a salary;

this refers to those currently holding office who, although stripped of their official titles, are granted half of their former salary because they previously rendered service to the state. Fourth, there are those with neither title nor salary;

this refers to those currently under indictment who have been dismissed from office. Among these four cases, the first two are not permitted by either of the two countries. As for the third case, this—
It is not permitted in the local area, but it is permitted in that other place. This is the fourth case, where both parties agree.
Following this principle—that is, according to this fourth case—if even for an official who currently lacks rank or emolument both sides permit it, how much more so for ordinary laypeople?
Therefore, one must indeed receive [the precepts]. However, by violating the royal regulations, one incurs a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).

As for the phrase "from the stage of a *śrāmaṇera* up to the stage of a *bhikṣu*": those who establish their resolve and aspire to the distant goal are those whose attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood is equal [to that of others]. Those whose pure conduct is peerless...
The Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*) is itself purity. Sparse eating is the regulation of one’s frugality. To stand far removed from the mundane world is why it is said he does not "form a crowd.
"Stands out prominently" (*zhuórán*) describes the manner of lofty establishment; since his conduct is already lofty, he is said to be "prominently standing out.

"Wind and frost" refers to the eight worldly dharmas—four favorable and four adverse—which are likened to wind and frost. That this person is not deluded or disturbed by them means he does not alter his will or integrity. *Kēng* (resonant).
[The character] *kǒng* (pronounced with the initial *k* and the final *-eng*) means "firm. His mind is extremely firm; this is called being "resonant" (*kāng*).

It is also an appearance of steel-like ferocity. Regarding "sorrow and joy": sorrow refers to suffering, and joy refers to pleasure. Hearing disparagement, he does not become angry; hearing praise, he does not rejoice.

Since neither affects his emotions nor causes them to be disturbed, it is said that "he has not yet moved his mind. The following line concludes by stating: "This constitutes the appearance of a true man (*puruṣa*)."

It is because it is due to this. The preceding discussion of suffering, pleasure, grief, and joy is likewise not separate from the favorable and the adverse; they are naturally subsumed within the eight winds (*aṣṭau loka-dharmāḥ*).
For now, the textual analysis has been conducted in this manner. Regarding the passage beginning with "The Vinaya says," [it refers to those] who have not yet reached twenty years of age.
If he is too young, it invites derision; if he is less than seventy years old, he is too old to be capable of fulfilling his duties, which again invites derision and reproach.
It is auspicious, however, for a bhikṣu to ordain such an elderly man, regarding him as one would his own father.
Regarding the phrase "the five [types of illness] up to insanity": the five types are: first, leprosy; second, carbuncles; third, white leprosy; fourth, consumption; and fifth, insanity.
According to the narrative context of the Vinaya, there were laypeople who suffered from illnesses and, when Jīvaka refused to treat them, they sought ordination in various monasteries.
Once Jīvaka had cured them, they abandoned the religious life. Jīvaka reported this to the Buddha, and thus the rule was established. [The following concerns] those other than the insane...

Regarding the two types of acquisition: if one acts with total disregard for the gravity of the offense, it is considered light; if one acts with neither disregard nor full gravity, it is considered middling—this is permitted.
However, if one is entirely unaware of what is good or evil, it is considered grave. As for those who do not contract leprosy or scabies: leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) has three varieties—black, white, and red.

Scabies (*pāmā*) includes all types of scabs and sores, which are classified under leprosy. These must not be present even if as small as a fingernail; they are prohibited whether in exposed areas or private places, regardless of their size.
Both increase and non-increase are attained, because it does not incur reproach. Regarding the *srotāpanna* afflicted with scabies and so forth:
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was a bhikṣu named Upagupta who entered a village for alms with his disciples.
They came to the house of a *caṇḍāla*, where there was a son who had attained the first fruit [of the path] but suffered from a foul disease. Upagupta said to his disciple: "This..."
A young boy attained the first fruit of the path and underwent such suffering. A disciple asked, "What sin led to this?
The Master said, "In a previous life, this child was an ordained monk serving as the *karmadāna*. Among the monks was an arhat who suffered from a foul disease;
as he scratched himself, it made a noise. The *karmadāna* remarked, 'Is a worm eating his body? He should go to the house of a *caṇḍāla*. He immediately repented."
Now, having received this retribution, one attains the realization of the first fruit through diligent practice.
Citing this passage as proof, since there is the benefit of attaining the fruit, it must necessarily take place in a secluded location, where one receives the precepts.

"All communal monastic affairs" refers to the formal procedures of the Sangha, such as the *pravāraṇā* ceremony. "Do not remain among the assembly during mealtime" is said because one might disturb the monks and cause them displeasure.
"Next, regarding those who perform prostrations": this refers to the sequence of subsequent matters. "Next" (*ci*) means order; "clearly manifest" (*mingxian*) means to elucidate.

It serves to exclude external obstacles and is termed the "four remaining [matters]". "Furthermore elucidating the reason why" (*geng ming suo yi*) means to reiterate; it is a further detailed examination of the time of receiving the precepts.
The phrase "the period of one lifetime" refers to the established rule. The statement "it should not be during times of clouds, mist, or darkness," etc., distinguishes this by way of time.
Since they have not previously known one another, there is a fear that obstacles or other impediments might prevent them from seeing each other; therefore, it must not be indistinct.

The phrase "if they have previously received full ordination," etc., distinguishes this by way of those who have already received full ordination. This means that having been pure until now, they receive it again; it is permitted because of this.

Regarding the "seven returns" and so forth, as for the absence of textual evidence in the *Caturvarga-vinaya*, it means that this specific passage questioned in the *Daśabhāṇaka-vinaya* does not exist there. There must be something analogous;

that is to say, if one was previously a bhikṣu and did not relinquish the essence of the dharma (the precepts), yet committed a transgression while still bearing those precepts, and now returns once more, this constitutes receiving the offense of a "limiting sin" (*antya-avadya*).
Furthermore, such a person would not be eligible for the thirteen grounds of defeat (*parājika*). A questioner asks: Xuanzang says this does not refer to the ten [grounds].
Prior to the recitation of the thirteen *antarāyika* obstacles (*dharmas*) in the Vinaya, there is this one question.

That Vinaya (the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*) asks only about the various prohibitions (*pratikṣepa-dharma*), but does not ask about the obstacles (*antarāyika-dharma*). This question is included within those prohibitions.

Now, the Master’s intention is that one should take this single question from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* and arrange it before the thirteen obstacles of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* to ask it. If the answers necessarily differ, then it constitutes the first obstacle.
This is a summary. Regarding the phrase "if there are obstacles and so forth" in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is distinguished according to the number of persons subject to those obstacles.
As for the reference to "the section on the recitation of the precepts," this points to the brief exposition within that text concerning the eight obstacles and other circumstances;

since these are no different from those mentioned here, it refers back to the subsequent passage, namely: "kings, thieves, water, fire, and so forth... [and so on]. Two or three people [form a group]... one.
Regarding "at that time, etc.": If there are no obstacles, a single motion (*jñapti*) constitutes one *dharma* and applies to only one person.

If there are circumstances involving obstacles, a single motion followed by a fourth proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha*) applies to two or three people; this is permitted in both cases. It must not extend to four, for fear that they might act as a formal assembly (*saṃgha*) themselves.
This is as described in the preceding section (etc.). Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika*, the *Ekottara*, and so forth: in those contexts, it was for the sake of separating them from existence.
There were two śrāmaṇeras. Fearing that if they received the precepts sequentially, one might harbor resentment, [the monks] wondered:
"May two people from a single assembly receive them at the same time under one upādhyāya and one preceptor? They reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "They may receive them.
If there are two upādhyāyas with one preceptor, because the formal recitation (*karmavācanā*) of the original texts differs, two or three people from a single assembly may not do so together.

As for "the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* and so forth," this is distinguished according to the person and the time. Regarding "not performing prostrations to one another," the treatise bases this on the point that those who have attained the Dharma are equal;
because there is no distinction of superior or inferior, great or small, it is prescribed that they do not prostrate to one another. The Venerable Jingshui said:
I fear this matter remains unresolved. Even if two or three people are grouped together as one unit, they must still be ranked;
those who first received the ten precepts are placed first. If none have yet received the ten precepts, they shall follow secular age, with the older being ranked above.
This is according to the Vinaya texts. Since there is a hierarchy of seniority, there is no need for mutual salutation. [If it is stipulated that they do not salute one another...]

Regarding ritual propriety (*li*): if one has not seen another for three years or five years, yet they have now become close associates, it is not permissible to conclude the meeting merely by joining the palms and exchanging greetings.
Nowadays, masters of the treatises (*lun-jia*) have established the custom of not performing formal salutations; this is based on the principle that they attained the Dharma at the same time.
However, if one speaks according to the ultimate principle, one must ultimately rely upon the Vinaya as the correct standard. Reflect on this.

"Regarding 'the aforementioned reaching up to the Dharma': this refers to the transition from the conclusion of the preceding section to the generation of the subsequent one (and so forth). Regarding 'the preceptor reaching down to instruct and transform':
this means that the preceptor, having received the Dharma within the ritual enclosure (*maṇḍala*), maintains the proper deportment (*īryāpatha*) and performs three prostrations within the Saṃgha.
Having finished, he exits the enclosure and proceeds to the place where the *śrāmaṇera* is stationed within the boundary. Once the sitting mat has been spread, he then instructs the *śrāmaṇera*..."
Spread out the sitting mat and perform three prostrations; this is to ensure that the four corners are straightened and arranged according to the Dharma. The *Chao* (Commentary) states:

"Regarding 'extending the hands within,' this refers for the time being to explaining it for use in the open air. If under a roof, it is sufficient provided that the distance between [the person and the object] is neither too close nor too far.

First, have them remove their *antarvāsaka* (inner robe), gather their *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe), and fold it over the left shoulder (*īrṣa-pi*). Then, have them put on their five-strip robe (*pañcaka*) and turn away from the other person.
Fold it and place it inside the inner cloth (*puṭa*). This constitutes one period. The *Xingshichao* states: "It cannot be described in detail;
the *Zhangji* should not be overly prolix, and if it is not clarified during the lecture, then at the time of actual practice, it will result in failure and omissions.
A Venerable One said: "There are those who act as instructors who themselves retreat to the upper part of the bed and sit in a grand manner, further ordering another bhikṣu [to perform the duties]."

If you give others spare robes or sitting mats, or if the Sangha takes a seven-strip robe (*saptaka*) for them to wear as their formal outer garment along with an arm-covering (*kaṭhina*), the priority lies in being concise and simple.
These instances are all due to those who do not understand the teachings, leading them to become objects of ridicule by others.

Thus, the detailed record concerning each article of clothing and deportment is concluded. Now, kneeling with the right knee touching the ground, one should follow the consolation provided in the *Vinayavibhāṣā*.
(As stated above). "Exalted and superior" means that one who has not long since received full ordination enters into the Sangha Jewel;
is this not indeed an exalted and superior station? "Displaying" means to unfold, to spread out, and to indicate. "Entrusting oneself to this for cultivation and guidance" means to rely upon it.
It means to rely upon these robes and alms bowl to unfold, display, and point the way, thereby serving as a means for training and leading others. The author of the *Chao* says: "Just as..."

A compassionate mother’s concern for her infant is no different [from her concern for others]. As for the statement that one does not receive the precepts even when approaching [the preceptor], this refers to opening the infant’s abdomen.
First, taking up the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṭika*), one says: "This five-strip robe is called *antarvāsaka* in Sanskrit.

Then, pointing to the seven-strip robe (*saptakaṭika*) worn on the body, one says: "This seven-strip robe is called *uttarāsaṅga* in Sanskrit. Finally, taking up the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*), one says: [as before].
The Sanskrit name for this robe is *saṃghāṭī*. The rest of the text is as described in the *Śāstra* (e.g., *Chao*). Thereafter, take the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*) and fold it downward;
next, place the great robe (*mahāsaṃghāṭī*) upon the five-strip robe. Regarding the reception of the robe and bowl at this point according to various schools, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"The instruction constitutes the reception," and so forth. As for "or in the midst of the assembly," etc., this refers to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

[The Master] said: "The *karmavācanā* master performs the conferral [of the precepts], and so forth" (etcetera). Regarding the absence of textual authority in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, that Vinaya merely states that one should receive and uphold [the precepts] without distinguishing between the prior and subsequent [stages].

As for the phrase "both are preserved according to the two [traditions]," this refers to the present Master’s definitive judgment. Whether received before or after [the formal ritual], both originate from the True Dharma;
they may be adopted according to one's preference and must not be rejected. Regarding the phrase "having taken up the alms-bowl," etc., the text says: "This..."
The alms bowl (pātra). Its Sanskrit name is *pātra* and so forth. Having shown it, one immediately covers the bowl and places it upon the two robes (*tricīvara*).

Furthermore, when asked, "Are these three robes and the bowl already yours? and so on, one then wraps them up; that is to say, one takes the inner cloth (*antarvāsaka*) and ties it to the bottom of the bowl.
In current practice, it is often seen that the bowl is placed face-up, and then [the robes are wrapped].

Regarding the two robes, upper and lower: if one folds the four corners directly into the bowl and ties the knots, yet leaves them on the surface of the bowl, this is a complete ignorance of the proper sequence.
The rest is as described in the *Shu* (Commentary) [and so forth]. As for the phrase "you have reached the point where you may receive it":

this means that while the precepts can be received because the matters of formal interrogation (*paripṛcchā*) are absent, there are still various prohibitions (*antarāyika-dharma*) that have not yet been inquired about; therefore, it says "precepts."
"One may receive [the precepts]. If one reaches the section below where the questions regarding the prohibitions (*parivāsa*) are concluded, it says:
"At the time of receiving the practice of the precepts and concentration (*śīla-samādhi*), one must rely on this text; it must not be altered. Some, upon reaching this point, also say:

"One may receive the precepts and concentration," or when the questions regarding the prohibitions are concluded, they instead say: "The precepts may be received," or they say: "In total, he does not understand," or they say: "He has failed. It says:
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, it arrives": "Who is your name now? What is the name of your preceptor?"—this asks for the *ming* (name) and the *zi* (style-name) as distinct entities.
Now, in the present text, it says: "As for the *zi*, one may simply state the *zi* without stating the *ming*. The previous commentary answers that the *ming* and the *zi* are essentially the same.

It is no different from [the distinction between] eyes and their function. The Venerable Jingshui said: "This is not so. A name is used to summon the bowl (the person), while a courtesy name (*zi*) is used to manifest one's virtue.

As it is said in secular custom: 'When a man reaches twenty, he receives the cincture and is given a courtesy name; when a woman reaches fifteen, she is counted [as an adult] and is given a courtesy name.
Now, when addressing the Preceptor or referring to oneself, it is permissible to use the name without the courtesy name, or to use the courtesy name without the name."
It is also permissible. According to the current method of practice, when asked "Whose name [or title] is it?", one may answer by providing the name;

there is no fault in this. Furthermore, it was asked: "In this context, using a title (字) does not apply to a personal name (名). Is it acceptable to use the personal name rather than the title during the *karmavācanā*?

The Venerable One replied: "It is entirely acceptable to state the personal name within the *karmavācanā*. To further append the title would be excessively prolix. [The instruction] "do not say... is definitive; it is certainly permissible.

Regarding the recipient of the precepts: if there were no obstacles (*antarāya*) previously and no prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) subsequently—meaning that both obstacles and prohibitions are absent—one will certainly obtain the precepts without further doubt;
thus it is called "certain" (*niyata*). As for the phrase "as if arriving," this refers to when one is properly wearing the seven-fold robe (*saptaka-kaṭhina*):

the teacher instructs him to stand up, temporarily remove the seven-fold robe, and put on the shoulder-cloth (*utsaṅga-kaṭhina*), after which he should properly don the seven-fold robe and adjust its folds and seams.
The sitting mat was [carried] on the shoulder; this was the ancient rule. Nowadays, it is placed upon the left arm and covered with the *kāṣāya*;
this follows the new method (as explained at length in the lower fascicle). Regarding "holding the robe and bowl level and flat":

one extends both hands together to support these two, holding the robe and bowl such that the surface of the bowl faces downward and the bottom faces upward. Nowadays, it is frequently seen that people hold the bowl by its two sides. The bowl...
"As for those whose faces are turned upward, they do not understand. The rest is as stated in the *Chao* (etc.).
Regarding the passage from "the seven *sambahula-śuddha-vācanas*" to "joining the palms," one must distinguish two points to explain this section of the *Chao*:

first, according to the standard procedure; second, harmonizing it with the text of the *Chao*. First, regarding the standard procedure: the instructor (*śikṣamāṇācārya*) comes into the midst of the assembly.

One must immediately unfold the sitting mat (*kaṭhina*) and, having performed three prostrations facing the Preceptor (*śīlācārya*), kneel with the right knee on the ground or sit cross-legged in the correct posture.
It is also permissible to first harmonize with the Saṃgha; the Preceptor will then provide the responses to the questions. Thereafter, one rises and stands to perform the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Whether the questioning is completed or not, the reason for sitting to harmonize with the Saṃgha and standing to uphold the ritual is that all the monks within the *maṇḍala*...

One must sit. If one were to perform the formal motion (*jñapti*) while standing now, other monks sitting would not be permitted [to hear it]; therefore, one must sit for the motion. Furthermore, the instructor acts as a servant to the Saṃgha and may not sit abruptly;
thus, he maintains the standing position when making the formal announcement. This can be illustrated by the case of the standing recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*.

Now, some say that since the single formal announcement (*ekajñapti*) is permitted to be maintained while standing, it is also permissible to perform the motion for the agreement of the Saṃgha while standing. This is the sort of practice belonging to those who follow the "expedited instructions" (*kṣipraśikṣā*). Hereafter...
When there is a time for performing the ritual, [the candidate] enters from outside and makes a verbal request. Other people engage in question and answer, yet they do not respond to the Preceptor;

thus, there is no sequential order at all (this is according to current common practice). If one follows the text of the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-śāstra*, once the Instructor has reached the midst of the Saṃgha, he stands at a distance where his hands can reach, and immediately makes the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Nowhere in that text is it mentioned that he should harmonize with the monks and so forth. How, then, are these two accounts to be reconciled?
Yes. The *Xuánjì* states: "This refers to one who has received the dharma through appointment by the Saṃgha; therefore, it does not depend on the harmony [of the assembly].

The Venerable [Dao]pò refuted this, saying: "If that were so, we would never see harmony at all nowadays. Since everyone originally obtains [the dharma] in this way, for what reason does the Vinaya command that one sit in harmony with the Saṃgha?"

To establish the *bingfa* (the formal pronouncement of the Dharma) at this point is a lack of principle. Although various masters of the past and present have revised the text here, they have all failed to explain it correctly.
Now, according to the *Fǎbǎo* (Treasury of the Dharma), this text is intended as a general response;

therefore, once the instruction has been introduced, one establishes the *bingfa* and does not repeat the *he* (the formal agreement). However, according to ordinary practice, when providing a specific response, one must perform the *he* again before it is valid.

The *baibai* (the formal announcement) follows; thus, there is a separate section below that poses the question: "If a newly ordained person comes from outside the boundary (*sīmā*), why is he not re-consecrated?
The answer states: "He is not one who has come from outside; he has newly arisen in this very place. This is intended to provide both a general and a specific proof.
This is a subtle point in the *Chao* (Commentary), difficult for people to understand; reflect upon it. After the announcement is made—

Regarding "having departed from among the monks," Wanling says: this refers to those who have come out to the boundary to pose questions and challenges; they do so because they are carrying out a mission.
Now that the questioning is finished and they have re-entered the assembly, it is improper for them to depart on their own before they have been instructed to request the precepts;

therefore, the rule restricts them to remaining within the limit, seeking their place inside while in the open air. Regarding "for the purpose of taking up their robes and bowls," the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "When they first enter the assembly..."

Since his deportment has not yet been fully integrated, for the time being, [the preceptor] shall act as a substitute to carry [the items] and demonstrate the expedient means (as stated in the commentary).
Regarding the instruction on grasping the three [monks'] robes and bowls: each person takes hold of them with both hands and brings them near to the Preceptor of the Precepts (*śīlācārya*).

Once the Preceptor of the Precepts has received them, he places them before the one observing the rains retreat (*varṣopavicāraka*), arranging them in order according to the first, second, and third [monks], ensuring they are not misaligned or out of sequence. The rest is as described in the text.
Regarding the phrase "from 'I say' to 'sits'": in the formula for requesting [permission], one says, "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. It is incorrect to say "one-pointed mindfulness" (ekāgracitta).
The rest is as in the text.
The phrase "the nine precept masters harmonize themselves" is the heading. The phrase "from that point until 'is'" refers to the *śuddhaka-vidhi* (simple announcement), which is easily understood.

Regarding the phrase "from the question until 'explains,'" the *Yìchāo* (Explanatory Commentary) cites the *Jīmēnsū* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā): "The precept master asks within the assembly; there is no need to appoint another.

If this is so, why was someone appointed when the *saṃgīti* (council) took place within the assembly? The answer is: that [instance] was for the sake of the *saṃgha*, and the sentiments of the *saṃgha* were difficult to manage.

First: Therefore, it is necessary to designate the person. Who asks and who answers? This is distinguished within the *śikṣamāṇā* [ordination]. Since the preceptor has already been designated, there is no further appointment.

The phrase "The tenth clearly explains the one who faces the questioning" is the heading; this is because the Preceptor of the Precepts (*śīla-ācārya*) directly faces the Sangha to ask the questions. Thus says the Vinaya.
Regarding "As for arriving at me": when performing the ritual, one should rely directly on this text without making any additions or alterations, as stated in the *Chao* (in extenso).
Regarding "You have arrived" and so forth: the differentiation of characteristics is already contained in the preceding text; here, it is sufficient simply to continue the text (in extenso).

Regarding the second major section, which correctly elucidates the essence of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*): while the preceding minor sections were numerous in their analytical distinctions, this second [section] marks the enumeration.

As for the "essence of the precepts," Xuánzàng states: "What has been explained previously—the capacity to receive [the precepts], the objects of reception, and the ten types of dharmas—are all preparatory stages prior to receiving;
they are not yet the actual essence of the arising of the precepts. This section correctly elucidates the dharma that is upheld, thereby giving rise to it."
This refers to the essential substance of the karma of the *prātimokṣa*. As for the phrase "if one is sincere," "profound precepts" (*gambhīra-śīla*) refers to those who seek *nirvāṇa*;

this is called "profound. "Supreme goodness" (*uttama-kuśala*) refers to that which is the most extreme among all virtues; this is called "supreme. Regarding the phrase "as in the preceding conditions":

the former cites the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*, while the latter clarifies the textual passages by way of their underlying meaning. The "three liberations" (*trivimokṣa*) refer to the establishment of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

Furthermore, the three clusters of precepts (*tri-saṃvara-śīla*) consist of the restraint of discipline (*saṃvara-śīla*), the cultivation of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the benefiting of sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*).

"The True Dharma abiding for a long time" and so forth refers to *nirvāṇa*. The term "supreme mind" (*uttama-citta*) summarizes its defining characteristics. As for the phrase "next, one arrives at," it indicates the subsequent stage.
The text consists of three sections: first, establishing the principle based on the teaching; second, citing treatises to provide proof; and third, "You should now...

which exhorts one to generate a sense of earnest reverence. Each point follows the text as written. Regarding the phrase "one should incur sin," the text here also provides a general response, meaning that one need not further reconcile with the Sangha.
Be aware of this; if it were a specific response, one would indeed have to reconcile with the Sangha, and so forth (as detailed elsewhere). — Great Virtue Jingshui.
It is said: When the robes and bowls of the three persons arrive at this point, they shall simply be placed before the Preceptor of the Precepts (Śīlācārya) and must not be moved or altered.
One must ensure that the śrāmaṇeras keep their eyes fixed solely on the robes and bowls and their ears fixed solely on the sound of the *karmavācanā*.

They must join their palms at the heart and must not look left or right. This is the authentic text of the Vinaya. As for those who perform the rites nowadays, when they reach this point... [they] uphold... (Note: The source text appears to be truncated at the end.)

At the time of the *dharma* (the formal ritual), the Preceptor for Precepts (*śīla-ācārya*) withdraws one by one and hands the robe and bowl to the *śrāmaṇera*, instructing him to hold them in his hands while listening to the *karmavācanā*.

I am uncertain as to which scriptural authority this derives from; the preceding commentary merely states that after the Preceptor for Instruction has summoned [the candidate] inside, he holds the robe and bowl and hands them over to the Preceptor for Precepts, who places them at the designated seat and then proceeds directly forward.
This text does not state that one should further hold up [the bowl] for a person who has received and maintains the precepts. How could one act so arbitrarily? Reflect on this.

Within the *śuddhaka-vidhi* (the single announcement), in the second intermediate section, it simply says: "I confer the full ordination upon [Name]. This is according to the original text of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure) in the Vinaya;
all such cases are determined in this manner. As for those who add the two characters "sengjin" (僧今—monks now), this is by no means permissible.
[The procedure] is accomplished. The Venerable One said: "This is the announcement to the Saṃgha. I do not yet know whether it is permitted or not.

How could there be the words 'the present Saṃgha' [in the announcement], when these words only appear within the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act)? They must necessarily be included there; if they are omitted, the act is not accomplished."
One asks the Saṃgha, "Is it accomplished? and they reply, "It is accomplished. This must be done for each instance from the first *karmavācanā* through the third;
one must ask and answer individually for each. That Vinaya states: "If one does not ask four times and answer four times, one incurs a *vyatikrama* (transgression) for each instance.

As for the statement that "one incurs an offense," this refers to failing to explain them distinctly by saying, "This is the first round," and so forth; such failure also constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Regarding the phrase "not yet having arrived": within the *karmavācanā*, in the first interval it says, "Venerable Sir, there is now a monk named [Name]";
in the second interval, one simply says, "The Saṃgha grants to [Name]," and the word "now" (*idānīm*) is absent;

when reaching the concluding formula, one simply says, "grant to [Name]," and the word "Saṃgha" is absent. In these three places, the formal model and procedure are fixed and must not be increased or decreased.
Many people are deluded by this, leading to the fault of falling into error at the critical moment. If one understands these three sections of the text, it is like a clear mirror;

the rest is as explained in the *Karmavācanā* section. Furthermore, the wording for the formal announcement (*niddesa*) regarding the *jñapti* at the three points must also follow the prescribed format.
If the single announcement (*jñapti*) is completed, one informs the recipient, saying: "The assembly of monks rejoices. When the first *karmavācanā* is completed...
He then announces, "Silence," or "Silence is acceptable. When the second *karmavācanā* is concluded, he announces, "The assembly is in harmony.

Although this does not violate the fundamental principle, the procedural logic of those who perform the rite must not be inverted; otherwise, it will deviate from the text of the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*. (And so forth.
One must rely directly on these words and must not add anything to them. This differs from the extensive version mentioned above. [End of] preceding section.
In the text that follows, when the Dharma is being enacted for a specific occasion, one may adjust it according to the circumstances. However, in this instance, additions are not permitted;

one must recite strictly according to the text. As for those assisting by joining their palms, from the third repetition of the *karmavācanā* (the formal ritual declaration), they should immediately focus their minds with single-minded concentration and, maintaining a sense of profound reverence, provide their assistance. They must not wait until the conclusion of the rite.
At that time, he merely raised his hand slightly; there was no ritual protocol whatsoever. Upon reaching the third *karmavācanā*, as soon as the final syllable was uttered, he would announce:

"The essence of the precepts has been received. Thereafter, he would perform the formal conclusion and so forth (as detailed elsewhere). The above concerns matters of vital urgency for this one occasion;
the account is somewhat prolix for the purpose of clarifying their practical application. Reflect upon this.
It is said that if many people approach the teacher, "many" refers to a hundred, fifty, or similar numbers. Regarding the recording of the time according to completion:
