The remaining text is as in the *Shuchao* (see *Yuezang zhenben chao*, etc.).
Regarding the phrase "as previously stated in the extensive explanation": one who is fully endowed with both practice and virtue. "Practice" refers to the skillful means from beginning to end;
"virtue" refers to the fulfillment achieved at the conclusion. It is necessary to possess both simultaneously before one may be free from dependence. An external objection asks:

Why were the previous seven [cases] not addressed in terms of the five-year summer retreat, such that only the loss of the subsequent three causes was discussed? [The answer is: It is required that virtue be established and practice be complete.

Regarding the phrase "only then can one leave behind dependence," the *Chao* (Commentary) provides the following response: "However, the loss [of status] after five summers is spoken in terms of the provisional period of the Vinaya teachings' formal characteristics.
As for the latter three [periods], they are explained in terms of the establishment of one's own practice (*svādhyāya*).

If we discuss one's own practice, it is only when the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*) is perfected that one may truly leave behind dependence on others. Furthermore, according to Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Nirvāṇa*, the Buddha himself also..."
The Master [said]: "That which is called the Dharma. For this reason, the Tathāgata always reveres the Dharma. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he surveyed all things and saw that none surpassed him. He then thought: "It is because of the Dharma I have obtained that I have become a Buddha;
I must therefore return to rely upon the Dharma. At that time, all Buddhas take the Dharma as their teacher. As for the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharma-kāya*), it serves as a defense...

Restraint from evil is called *śīla* (precept). Tranquil contemplation is called *samādhi* (concentration). Insightful observation is called *prajñā* (wisdom). The exhaustion of karmic burdens and the removal of delusions is called *vimukti* (liberation).

The clear and thorough knowledge of this is called *vimukti-jñāna-darśana* (knowledge and vision of liberation). One who explains it in this manner should say: "Those with five years of seniority rely upon those with ten years of seniority."
This extends even to those practicing for the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path], based on the fourth fruit and so forth (as detailed).

Regarding the second point, "clarifying the methods": there are seven types of dharmas practiced in common; because teacher and disciple practice them together, they are called "common practices" (*sādhāraṇa-caryā*).
As for "distinctive practices," the latter three apply exclusively to the disciple’s conduct; therefore, they are called "distinctive practices" (*asādhāraṇa-caryā*). Thus it is said.
Regarding the "seven dharmas at the beginning and middle": this indicates the seven kinds of common dharmas. As for the phrase "from one to discernment," in the first section, Xuán states:
"The latter two encompass and accord with the Saṃgha. First, one causes the Saṃgha not to act; second, even if they do act, the disciple [is affected].

He causes the Saṃgha not to perform what is contrary to the Dharma. He acts so as to cause the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) not to be in opposition [to the Saṃgha]. He seeks the removal of his offense from the Saṃgha. It is the same for the disciple;
it is likewise for the preceptor acting on behalf of the disciple. The following six cases are all explained by mutual reference. Understand this.
In the second section, the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the *mūlāpakarṣa* (punishment of returning to the beginning). In the third section, when the teacher is ill, the disciple personally...

[One] should act on their behalf. It is the same when a disciple is ill and the preceptor must attend to them personally. Regarding the fourth section, concerning "not being pleased with the dwelling place," Baoyun says:
this refers to a case where the Upādhyāya does not wish to remain at this monastery and intends to go to another boundary; the disciple must then move [elsewhere], and so forth.
Regarding the fifth section, if the Upādhyāya remains hesitant and indecisive concerning the causes and effects of upholding or violating the precepts, the disciple...
The disciple, relying on the Dharma and Vinaya, resolves his doubts and enables him to attain thorough understanding, and so forth (as detailed).
In the sixth section, regarding the arising of wrong views in the preceptor: this refers to the claim that desire does not obstruct the Path. The disciple says:

"The World-Honored One, through countless skillful means, has taught that committing [these acts] is an obstruction to the Path," which is called having right view. In the seventh section, the text contains three meanings.
First, the heading. There are two matters by which one provides protection: next, the explanation of protection through the Dharma; next, protection through food and clothing.
Protection through the Dharma nourishes the spirit, while food and clothing nourish the body. Xuán says: "According to the Vinaya, if a bhikṣu is fully endowed with and maintains the Prātimokṣa..."
To achieve proper deportment and to observe even minor precepts with such fear and caution as if they were as heavy as a vajra is called the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*).
If a bhikṣu is able to abandon all evils and even attain entry into the fourth dhyāna, it is called the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*).

If a bhikṣu is able to know, according to reality, the objects of the four noble truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—it is called the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*), and so forth.

The phrase "from 'it is said' to 'the same'" constitutes the conclusion. It is not only the *Caturvarga-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) that is thus; the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) and others are likewise the same;

hence it says "the same. Regarding the phrase "from 'the Saṃgha' to 'person': returning after one night outside the boundary," this means that if the dawn light appears while one is outside the boundary, one loses [the status] immediately upon spending one night there.

As for the two methods mentioned below, if one returns, one regains it. This refers to requesting another person to act as one's *niśraya* (reliance). Regarding "clarified butter" (*sarpis*): [text fragment].

The Master is able to skillfully expound the Dharma for his disciples, thereby eliminating the three poisons. This constitutes the most supreme excellence, comparable to *sarpirmaṇḍa* (the finest essence of ghee).
It is like the production of curd from milk, clarified butter (*sarpis*) from curd, and *sarpirmaṇḍa* from clarified butter; *sarpirmaṇḍa* is the highest and most excellent.
Now, the elimination of the three poisons to attain the fruit of sainthood is likewise so. For further details, as in the subsequent sections: as...
This is explained within the section on the method of expressing thanks. The remainder is as stated in the text.
Regarding the phrase "from the second to the planting," this is the restatement of the heading. Regarding the phrase "the first: announcing the matter to avoid transgression," there are two aspects:

first, in terms of the teaching (*śāsana*); second, according to the practice of the teaching. This means that the very moment one announces it to the teacher, one is free from transgression; if one does not announce it, one violates the teaching.

It is auspicious. Regarding the two types of practitioners: if one does not perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*), they will not know the instructions and may thus act in contradiction to them, committing an offense.
If the announcement is made, the teacher acts according to the instructions; it is said that "the measure is the same," whereby one becomes free from fault.
Regarding the statement in the Vinaya concerning "incurring an offense," the eight matters consist of three single cases, three pairs, and two combined cases.

As for "a companion," according to the *Vinaya* in the section on receiving the precepts, it says: "If a disciple travels far away, the Upādhyāya should ask: 'What business do you have to travel abroad?
Who is your companion? To what place are you going? and so forth. Regarding the three types of interconnected phrases concerning right and wrong actions, there are three... [text ends]

From among these, take one "good" [factor] as the head. For the first three permutations, they are: (1) the companion is appropriate, but the destination and the business are inappropriate; (2) the destination is appropriate, but the business and the companion are inappropriate;
(3) the business is appropriate, but the companion and the destination are inappropriate. Next, for the second set of three permutations with two "good" factors as the head, they are:

(1) the companion and the destination are appropriate, but the business is inappropriate; (2) the destination and the business are appropriate, but the companion is inappropriate; (3) the companion and the business are appropriate, but the destination is inappropriate.

The companion is not [in accordance with the rule]. The three—attending to affairs, the companion, and the destination—are likewise not [in accordance with the rule] (the above constitutes the first three pairs).
Next, one phrase is entirely non-conforming: the companion, the destination, and attending to affairs—all three are non-conforming. Next, the eighth phrase is entirely conforming:

the companion, the destination, and attending to affairs are all in accordance with the Dharma. Among the eight phrases above, only the eighth phrase is taken; these three aspects are collectively [conforming].

"If it is in accordance with the Dharma, then you may depart. Baoyun said: "Those who are 'in accordance with' refer to those who uphold the precepts, recognize the requirements for the *poṣadha* assembly, and so forth.
As for the 'place,' it refers to going to that residence where there are the Buddha’s teachings, enlightened teachers, and the like.

As for 'attending to affairs,' it refers to listening to and studying the Way, learning the Buddha-dharma, and so forth. When these three conditions are not fulfilled, one commits an offense; this may be understood by applying this principle to other cases."

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*. Regarding the desire to travel and inform the teacher so that he may know [of one's departure]: Xuán says, "If one knows there is doubt or fear on the road, and the teacher permits the departure, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if the teacher does not permit it and one departs by force, one incurs a light *sthūlātyaya* offense against the teacher.

As for "the rest is the same as the *Pañcavargika*," this refers to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, where, apart from the ritual of paying homage to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha, there is further the practice of requesting and informing, which is the same as in the *Pañcavargika*. Some have categorized this as contradicting the wording of the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*; however, this is understood [as being consistent].

"Regarding 'the same applies to the *jñapti* at an improper time': this means that when one performs the formal motion (*jñapti*) after having taken leave of one's teacher, it is the same as when one takes leave of the *upādhyāya* for an improper-time *jñapti*, even when entering a village.
Regarding 'one must weigh the suitability of one's companions': the reason one requires good companions is because there is the benefit of mutual correction and encouragement.
In the *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, it was because Nanda’s disciple acted as a companion to Upananda that [this rule was established]."
They reproached him. Nanda said: "Why do you disciples follow this foolish man? He does not know how to recite the precepts, perform the *poṣadha*, or carry out the *karmavācanā*.
One who knows the *poṣadha* should contemplate the remedies for transgressions; one who knows the *karmavācanā* should request from the Saṃgha that [the offense] be extinguished."

Regarding the *huìzuò* (assembly sitting): on the six monthly days of fasting—namely the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth—a monk who is free from illness should gather in one place to preach the Dharma; this is called the method of the assembly sitting.
As for "the offense is incurred when the dawn light appears," this refers to losing one's formal reliance (*niśraya*). If it is not auspicious, at that time...

One should tie it immediately, without waiting for the appearance of light. Regarding the term *xi* (細): the commentary on the *Zilin* says it means "rope" (*suo*, pronounced with the second tone like *zhēn*).
The *Qieyun* says that a single strand is called *xi*. This refers to a minor matter; how much more so for a major undertaking?
Therefore, one must announce it. To incur an offense would not be auspicious. As for the phrase "there is one who goes to the teacher," this refers to the tonsure master and others.
This means: if a bhikṣu comes to shave [the head], it is appropriate to inform the teacher.

If the teacher is temporarily away, one should inform another person to avoid the fault of failing to inform. When the teacher returns, one should immediately recount the previous matter in detail (and so forth).
Other matters are to be handled according to this principle; taking shaving as an example, the method and procedure for all other individual circumstances should be followed accordingly.
This is by way of illustration. "Great giving" refers to the act of *dāna* (generosity). "If there is a remainder" means that which remains outside of the three robes;
this refers to surplus robes (*atireka-cīvara*) that have been formally purified through the ritual of *viśuddhi*. Regarding "informing the community when dyeing robes":

according to the Vinaya texts, when one wishes to dye a robe, one must inform [the community]; whether it be washing, sewing, boiling, or dyeing, each step requires notification. If one is unable to do so, one should simply say:
"I wish to perform the task of dyeing robes. Having made this single announcement (*jñapti*), one proceeds to kindle the fire, seek firewood, and so forth;

all these belong to the task of dyeing robes. Regarding this, the *Xuán* (Xuánzàng) says that one should utter the following words of announcement. One should join the palms and bow the body, saying: "Venerable Sir, please take note:
from now until the boundary of tomorrow's dawn, I, [Name], shall perform all activities in accordance with the Dharma. I announce this to the Venerable One for his knowledge."

According to this, it is a general announcement. One must not go more than seven feet from the teacher for fear that, being too far away, one might not hear the voice should questions be asked in the interim;
thus, seven feet is prescribed as the limit. Furthermore, secular etiquette also states: "A disciple follows his teacher."
Looking forward, one’s gaze does not extend beyond seven feet; looking sideways, it does not extend beyond five feet. One expresses reverence by treading upon the shadow [of the teacher].

According to the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Observation), when approaching an upādhyāya, one must avoid six situations: first, being too close so as to tread upon the teacher’s shadow; second, being too far so that one's words cannot be heard;
third, not remaining upwind, lest one’s foul breath should perfume the other; fourth, not remaining in a high place, as this would fail to eliminate arrogance; fifth, not remaining directly in front.
It obstructs one’s gaze. Sixth, it is difficult to turn the face away if one is not behind; one should stand in attendance to the left or right.

Regarding the phrase "departing from this to inform," it means that one must inform [the preceptor] when departing at a distance of seven feet. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and other texts all concern matters requiring such notification;
this can be understood (as explained).

Regarding the passage from "The second" to "In the midst": this refers to the fifth [section], where, within the summary of the two masters, it cites the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* concerning the text on the three daily periods of instruction and so forth.
Regarding the passage from "The third" to "Praise": "The time has arrived" means that the time for the morning and evening meals has arrived.
Regarding the performance of two tasks during the *poṣadha* and other occasions: one performs them with one's own hands. First is the repair and maintenance of the dwelling;

second is the mending and washing of robes. One must not decline these labors. The rest is as stated in the text. As for the phrase "various [qualities] up to 'sincerity'": being straightforward is called "non-deceit.
Being forever free from falsehood is called "non-illusion. Being genuine is called "non-duplicity. This is one's nature...
To remain unyielding is called non-deception; to speak the truth to others is called non-delusion; to have no doubt regarding the Dharma is called faith;
to reform evil and follow what is good is called shame and remorse; to seek the Dharma without slackening is called diligence;
to reflect according to reality is called right mindfulness; and to sever the two obstacles of afflictions and the cognizable is called the mind abiding in seclusion.

To rather die than transgress [the precepts] is called "profoundly revering the Vinaya. To contemplate the Four Noble Truths and so forth while advancing in practice is called "observing the conduct of a śramaṇa.
Because one proceeds directly toward nirvāṇa, it is said that "one's resolve is exalted toward nirvāṇa" and that "one seeks only the supreme path"; this is termed "Dharma-leaving-home.
The upādhyāya should respect and love such a person and transmit the scriptures and Dharma to them, for their understanding of the principles is sufficient. This is what is meant.
The superior disciple is one who is able to cultivate the pure Brahma-faring and is able to establish the Buddha-dharma.

Regarding the phrase "the second section of the Great Gate: the two masters' reception," the "Great Gate" refers to distinguishing this from the preceding minor sections. The "two masters" are the Upādhyāya and the Ācārya.
"Reception" (saṃgraha) means gathering, transforming, and receiving [disciples]. "Dharma" (dharma) refers to the rules and principles. It says: its...
Regarding the passage "The Upādhyāya arrives at the gate," the Great Virtue Jing-shui stated: "The *Xuánjì* and later commentators alike do not understand the meaning of this text;
most have provided erroneous interpretations. Now, in the *Fǎbǎo kē*, this section is titled "The General Introduction through Synthesis and Analysis."

Only then can one accord with the profound principle. That is to say, the various commentaries (*cāo*) cited previously all primarily rely upon the *upādhyāya* at the ordination platform to explain the matter;

this does not preclude their partial application to the *ācārya*. However, this present section specifically discusses the *niśraya-ācārya*, while incidentally mentioning the methods for the *upādhyāya*’s reception of disciples.
If one were not to categorize it in this manner, then [the discussion] would necessarily pertain to the seven [categories] of the *upādhyāya*.

Regarding the three types of shared practice (*sādhāraṇa-caryā*) and the three types of distinct practice (*asādhāraṇa-caryā*), following these, the method for the preceptor’s (*upādhyāya*) reception of disciples is further clarified.
To avoid redundancy in the textual flow while ensuring that both sections are mutually illuminated, the text is concise yet comprehensive; this is a point of subtle and intricate detail.

It is difficult for people to understand; if one attains this realization, it constitutes thorough comprehension (the above briefly summarizes the general meaning). Next, regarding the commentary on the text:

as for the Venerable Master’s conduct of guidance, since it is identical to that of the *niśraya* (preceptor), meaning that the practice of receiving disciples is the same as that of the *niśrayācārya*, it will not be explained separately.
To clarify them together: they are explained in conjunction with the *niśrayācārya*, based on the underlying principle.

Separation must be distinct; now, because they are the same, they are collectively explained as "conjunction. Regarding the seven gates concerning the phenomena of dependence, this is the general heading, which will be described individually below.
Regarding "first, from 'relying upon' to 'benefit'": it is as stated in the text. Regarding "second, from 'to relying upon'":

according to the circumstances in the Vinaya, one was not permitted to wash one's feet or drink water without first having relied [upon a teacher]. Later, because he became confused and fainted and fell to the ground, he fell ill; therefore, he informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "From this day forward, I permit you to wash your feet and drink water, and then request a teacher for dependence (*niśraya*).

This rule is also like that. Regarding the Vinaya, it says: "The Buddha ordered that one should select and take a teacher for dependence. Because the terminology regarding "selection" is the same, it is said to be "also like that.

As for the daily offense of theft: if one has a teacher for dependence, one avoids transgression by reporting matters; now, not depending on another person, one constantly acts according to one's own will.

Regarding the matter: it constitutes the offense of theft because one has excessively and unrighteously damaged monastic property. As for "not reciting the precepts after ten years of ordination," Xuán states:
this refers to the gravity of the theft being equivalent to that of the previous day; it means that by not following the rules of the teaching, one has unrighteously damaged [the property].

Regarding the phrase "as for the three being the same": this distinguishes those who possess spiritual virtue; it refers to the *niśraya-ācārya* (reliance teacher). Regarding the phrase "explaining that various teachers differ":

this follows from the context to clarify that there are many types of *ācāryas*, all of whom occupy the rank of a teacher. Regarding the phrase "as for the four-part [Vinaya]... within the rules for the *upādhyāya*":
there are five types: first, the renunciant (*pravrajyā*); second, the instructor (*śikṣā-ācārya*); third, the ordination (*upasampadā*) teacher; fourth... [text fragment ends].
This is the receiving of the precepts; the fifth is the reliance [upon a teacher]. The Venerable One said:

"In this context, there should be a *śrāmaṇera-ācārya* (tonsure master), who is subsumed within the *pravrajyā-ācārya* (ordination master). If one follows the *Xuánjì*, 'leaving home' (*pravrajyā*) does not mean shaving the hair;
these two are distinct. Therefore, in the *Jīemó sū* (Karmavācanā-vibhāṣā), six types are distinguished, including the *śrāmaṇera-ācārya*. (Each has...)
[This refers to] its principle. Even regarding "relying on [a teacher] for one night," this is a case of citing a small instance to illustrate the many.

The Venerable One says: "In the present day, there are many who claim to rely on [teachers from] five or seven districts; this is surely because they have not mastered the teachings. Now, one who relies [on a teacher] must possess three factors:
first, the method of requesting [instruction]; second, the method of receiving instruction; and third, the method of dwelling in mutual dependence. How could there be otherwise?
In the various counties outside the prefecture, each nun resided with a *niśraya* (preceptor) and received instruction in the Dharma.

Furthermore, there were those of great virtue who served as *niśraya* for three hundred or two hundred nuns; at one time, they would all kneel in prostration and have a single person present their petition to request the Dharma and so forth.
These rules and others like them also contradict the Vinaya. Now, as for "relying" (*niśraya*), it was originally established in response to and for the sake of specific individuals;
how could it apply to many people at once? Furthermore, since a *bhikṣuṇī* may rely upon the Saṃgha in general and is not restricted to a single *bhikṣu*, how can one speak of a verse for "relying"?
This is utterly unreasonable. Regarding the exception for "relying," the original position of relying is to replace the *upādhyāya*. It is required that...
One must possess ten years of seniority; therefore, this [lower grade] must be excluded. Regarding those who have not yet attained the superior title:

according to the Vinaya, if one has not yet completed five years of seniority, although they may have mastered the recitation of the texts, they have not yet attained the distinguished title of *ācārya*. As for whether there is any harm in attaining such a title:
the current master follows the precedent of the nine-year *upādhyāya*, and even though his years of seniority were not yet complete, he conferred ordination and was called an *upādhyāya*.

Although this person has not yet completed five years of seniority (*pañca-varṣa*), since they have relied upon another for recitation and study, they may be designated as an *ācārya*. Furthermore, what harm could there be in this?

One who does not understand from beginning to end—the *upādhyāya* is the very root of receiving the precepts; starting from the beginning until the final abandonment of the four [grave offenses], it is otherwise for the rest.
Only the beginning is not understood through to the end. If one were to act as a teacher and further invite the Buddha, it would be just as in the original case.
This person is my *karmācārya* and *śikṣācārya*. Now, as I wish to take him as my *niśraya*, it is necessary to request him by reciting a verse;
one must not fail to request him. Just as in the rules for the *upādhyāya*, the sevenfold and threefold practices—both common and specific—are not possessed by the *upādhyāya* alone.
Since the *niśraya-ācārya* takes the place of the *upādhyāya*, these seven and three practices are likewise the same. According to principle, this...
It should further be clarified. However, because it was already explained previously, this serves to point out that they are the same.
Regarding the phrase "from *mā* to *yī*": "retinue" refers to those such as disciples. "Completely none" means there are no evil places whatsoever.
Regarding the "five [categories] of the *Mahāsāṃghika*," these all belong to the *upādhyāya*. To feel compassion for those below is called "loving concern."
To value those with virtue is called respect (*gaurava*). To feel shame upon seeing evil is called *hrī*. To cultivate goodness upon seeing it is called *apatrāpya*.

To always desire to remain in one place without frequent shifting or changing is called delighting in dwelling (*sthiti-ruci*). Only when these five qualities are possessed is one fit to be relied upon as a teacher.
Regarding a *bhikṣu* of two years’ standing and a disciple of one year’s standing: according to the Vinaya, this refers to a *bhikṣu* who has completed two rainy-season retreats (*varṣa*).
At that time, a disciple of one year’s standing went to the Buddha’s presence; knowing [who he was], the Buddha intentionally asked, “Who is this *bhikṣu? He replied, “He is my disciple.”
The Buddha asked you, "How many years of summer retreat (*varṣa*) have you completed? He replied, "Two. The World-Honored One rebuked him, saying, "Your body has not yet weaned itself from milk;
you ought to receive instruction from others. How can you instruct others? Thereupon, he established the rule that one must have completed ten years of summer retreat, and so forth.

Regarding "enticing a disciple away and committing a grave offense," the *Five Hundred Questions* states: "In the past, there was an elderly bhikṣu who had only one śrāmaṇera. He was enticed away by another person..."

He departed. With no one to look after him, he passed away before long. Based on this, he committed a grave offense of killing. Regarding the "Four Dharmas" of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:
"If one understands these four, one will resolve all doubts without exception; this is called 'superior mastery of the Vinaya. What is meant by 'having an offense'?

It is when the mental state and the external object correspond. What is meant by 'being without offense'? It is when one gives rise to an antidote. What is meant by 'light'? It is when the cause and effect are subtle."

Furthermore, what is meant by "heavy"? It refers to the coarseness of cause and effect. Regarding the "three thousand modes of deportment" and so forth, the Master here points to those many sentient beings, the two masters, and the teachings received from those two masters, as extensively detailed elsewhere. This indicates that this *Chao* (Digest) exists in a somewhat abbreviated form.
Regarding the statement that "the four [requirements] up to [the preceptor] are not fulfilled":

according to the Vinaya, when a preceptor (*upādhyāya*) passes away, there may be a newly ordained *bhikṣu* who, having no one to instruct him, fails to maintain proper deportment (*īryāpatha*), wears his robes unevenly, begs for food improperly, and speaks boisterously at mealtime like a gathering of Brahmins.
Having reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said: "From this day forward..."
[The character] "yǐ" (已) is a departing tone (qùshēng). It is taught that there is the term *ācārya*. Regarding the *ācārya*, one should regard him as a younger brother or like a son;
regarding the disciple (*śiṣya*), one should regard him as a parent, and so forth. In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sēngqǐ), the teacher is named "Zūn" (尊) with a departing tone.
There are those who pronounce it with a level tone (píngshēng), and those in the *Tiānyǒu chāo* (天有鈔) who write it as "Zhào" (召)—both are errors.
Regarding the statement "As for the five [categories] reaching the Dharma": this is largely the same as the preceding method.

It refers to the second "General Encompassing Gate" within the names and characteristics of the aforementioned master and disciple, which cites the *Ṣaḍdigvidhi-sūtra* (Sutra on Bowing to the Six Directions) and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* to demonstrate the mutual inclusion of the two sets of five and four masters and disciples.
Regarding the statement "From the *Mahāsāṃghika* to the analysis": it concerns the teaching of the Tripiṭaka three times each day. Xuán says:
The ritual for requesting instruction should be as follows: Ten or twenty people simultaneously prostrate to the teacher and then kneel facing one another.
One person speaks these words: "Venerable sir, please take heed. We, the disciples [Name] and others, request the venerable one’s instruction this morning.

May the venerable one grant us guidance out of compassion. Having said this once, the teacher then extensively demonstrates the characteristics of the teaching—the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma.
Having attained [realization], he then spoke, saying: "Do not be negligent. The disciple replied: "I shall carry this upon my head and uphold it," and so forth.

Regarding the gravity of the precepts in the *Śīla-sūtra*, there are five categories of ascending and descending severity; the preceding ones are grave and the subsequent ones are light. As for the meanings of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*), these are the three categories of phenomena.

The aggregates refer to the five aggregates; the elements refer to the eighteen elements; and the sense bases refer to the twelve sense bases (this has been briefly explained above). Next, the detailed explanation follows.

Regarding this, the *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: "Aggregation, gateway for arising, and lineage—these are the meanings of *skandha*, *āyatana*, and *dhātu*. That is to say, the five *skandhas* have the meaning of accumulation;
the twelve *āyatanas* have the meaning of gateways for arising; and the eighteen *dhātus* have the meaning of lineage. First, it says "the five *skandhas*."
The fifth [point] enumerates the number. The old Sanskrit term is *pātra* (or *pātrā*), which is translated as "shelter" (*yìn*). "Shelter" means to cover and protect.
Another interpretation holds that "shelter" refers to "darkness" (*yīn*), specifically the "yin" of yin and yang. Spring and summer belong to yang; autumn and winter belong to yin.
Winter is the season when all things accumulate. This is an explanation of the body according to its meaning. Alternatively, in Sanskrit it is called *skandha*. [This was the method of] Kumārajīva.
The Master translated [the term *skandha*] as "group" (*zhòng*). "Group" means "many. Thus, a sutra says: "The arising and ceasing of the five groups.

In the Tang dynasty, it was newly translated as "aggregate" (*yùn*). "Aggregate" carries the meaning of accumulation; that is to say, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are accumulations.

Now, this commentary states: "Shade" (*yīn*) still retains the old terminology. Regarding what is called the "aggregate of form," the treatise says: "Because it is subject to change and decay, it is named 'form' (*rūpa*)."

"Transformation of the aggregates" (*skandha-vipariṇāma*) reveals momentary impermanence (*kṣaṇika-anityatā*); "destruction" (*bhaṅga*) reveals the impermanence of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).

Furthermore, this transformation and destruction carries the sense of affliction and ruin (*upaghāta*). Second is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*): feeling is that which experiences (*anubhavati*).

It is called "feeling" because it conforms to its cause, which is contact (*sparśa*). This phrase "conforming to contact" is used to clarify the sense of causality; the cause is precisely contact, for contact is able to produce feeling. Contact... [text continues]

Because it conforms to feeling (*vedanā*), it is called "conforming to feeling" (*anu-vedanā*). Because it is able to experience the causes that conform to contact (*sparśa*), it is called "experiencing what conforms to contact.

Third, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has the grasping of images as its essence; because it is able to grasp the images of suffering and pleasure, enemies and friends, male and female, and so forth.
Regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*): the treatise states, "The four remaining [aggregates] are called the aggregate of formations.

This means that all mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) other than form, feeling, perception, and consciousness are collectively termed the aggregate of formations. They are called "formations" based on two meanings: volitional activity (*abhisamskāra*) and flux (*prasyanda*).

From this perspective, the five aggregates—including form—could all be designated as "formations," because the aggregate of formations subsumes a vast number of phenomena; thus, it is specifically highlighted as being "concordant with formations. As for the five consciousnesses...

Regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), the *Śāstra* states: "Consciousness (*vijñāna*) refers to individual discernment. This means there are six kinds of discernment; hence the term "individual" (*prati*). That is to say:

eye-consciousness discerns forms, and so on, up to mind-consciousness discerning phenomena (*dharma*), and so forth. Of the seventy-five dharmas of the Hīnayāna, these five aggregates subsume seventy-two.
Within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), eleven are subsumed: the five faculties, the five objects, and unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*). (2)

The aggregate of consciousness comprises the single dharma of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), which is the sovereign mind (citta-rāja). The aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) comprises the single dharma of perception among the mental factors (caitasika).

The aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) comprises the single dharma of feeling among the mental factors. The aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) comprises forty-four mental factors and fourteen dissociated phenomena (viprayukta-dharma).
There are fifty-eight factors in total; only the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are not included, because their meaning is incompatible [with the definition of an aggregate].

That is to say, since the three unconditioned phenomena are not accumulations, they cannot be established separately as aggregates (the preceding brief explanation concludes the inclusion of factors; this is what is termed "name"). Next, the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are explained.
This is the meaning of "gate of arising. "Twelve" indicates the number. The old Sanskrit term is *āyatana*, which here means "entry";
"entry" carries the sense of "extinction. The new [translation] is *praveśa*, which means "place," referring specifically to the six internal faculties and the six external objects.
This is the place where consciousness arises. That is to say, the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) can induce the six consciousnesses to produce their respective seeds.

If the external six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) act as conditions, they draw forth and give rise to the six consciousnesses. The mind does not arise in isolation; it arises only by relying upon objects. Thus, the sense organs and their objects are the locus where consciousness grows and develops.
If one distinguishes between matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), the five internal organs and the five external [objects]—these ten are matter. As for the mental organ (*manas*):

The *āyatana* (sphere) is a mental factor (*caitta*). The *āyatana* encompasses all mental concomitants (*cetasika*). These twelve *āyatanas* collectively subsume seventy-five dharmas: the five sense-faculties (*indriya*) are subsumed within the spheres of the five faculties;
the five objects (*viṣaya*) are subsumed within the spheres of the five objects; the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) is subsumed within the sphere of the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*);

and the sphere of the mental object (*dharma-āyatana*), which includes the sovereign mind (*citta-rāja*), subsumes forty-six mental concomitants, fourteen dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and one non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).

[There are] sixty-four dharmas in total (and so forth). Next, the eighteen *dhātus* are explained. "Eighteen" indicates the number. In Sanskrit, it is called *dhātu*; here it is translated as "realm" (*jie*).

These are the six sense-faculty realms, the six consciousness realms, and the six object realms. Because the six consciousnesses rely upon the six sense-faculties and gather the six objects, they are called "realms.
"Realm" (*dhātu*) has the meanings of cause, support, and lineage. Regarding the meaning of cause, it is like [the term] "distinctly maintaining" (*bié chí*), which means to take charge of...

It sustains the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). It also sustains the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) and the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). Furthermore, it is understood to sustain the six consciousnesses;

that is to say, at the time of the support (*āśraya*), there is that which is capable of sustaining. Regarding "lineage" (*gotra*): it refers to the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses being of the same kind as the flow of the faculties (*indriya-nisyanda*).

This should be understood by similar analogy. This includes all seventy-five dharmas, exhausting the five faculties and the five elements (*dhātu*). Within the classification of stages, it includes the matter of the five faculties and the five objects.

The *dhātu* (elements) comprise the five objects of the senses (*viṣaya*), the five material forms (*rūpa*), the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and the mind-element (*manodhātu*)—these together comprise one dharma, the mental monarch (*citta-rāja*).

The sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) comprises forty-six mental factors (*caitta*), fourteen dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and one non-informative matter (*avijñapti*);

these together comprise sixty-four dharmas. Question: The first five aggregates (*skandha*) do not include the unconditioned; why, then, do the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*) include the unconditioned? Answer: The aggregates... [text ends]
Because it is an accumulation, it is not included [in the aggregates]. The meaning of "realm" (*dhātu*) and "base" (*āyatana*) is that of growth;

since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is an object of mental engagement and a locus for growth, it is therefore included. Within the six objects of perception, first, regarding the object of form (*rūpa*), there are twelve types of manifest color (*varṇa*).
Blue, yellow, red, white, smoke, clouds, dust, mist, light, shadow, brightness, and darkness are exclusively of the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).

There are eight types of shape (*saṃsthāna*): long, short, high, low, square, round, regular, and irregular; these pertain to all three natures. Regarding the objective sphere of sound (*śabda*), there are eight kinds:
first, that which has appropriated primary elements (*upātta-mahābhūta*) as its cause, known as the sounds of sentient beings, namely the vocal sounds produced [by them].
These cause people to feel affection and delight. Second, there are those caused by appropriated primary elements (*mahābhūta*), which are sounds designated as "unpleasant" for sentient beings;
that is, the vocal sounds produced that do not please people. Even if these occur at the proper time, because they are not welcome, or they may be sounds produced at an improper time.
These two types of vocal sounds produced within the bodies of sentient beings are called "appropriated. Among these:
Vocal action results in sentient beings because it is capable of expressing meaning. It has as its cause the great elements (mahābhūta) that are appropriated by sentient beings.
Non-sentient things are called "agreeable sounds," such as laughter, clapping hands, and so forth; these have as their cause the four great elements that are not appropriated by sentient beings.
Non-sentient names refer to unpleasant sounds, such as those produced when striking with clubs or staves during a fit of anger;
these two types are called "appropriated" (*upātta*) because they are emitted from within the bodies of sentient beings. Since they cannot express meaning, they are designated as non-sentient.
Pleasant sounds that are sentient names have the five unappropriated great elements (*mahābhūta*) as their cause, such as those produced by a magically created person (*nirmāṇa-puruṣa*).

Regarding speech, the teaching of the Dharma, and so forth—these six have non-appropriated great elements (*mahābhūta*) as their cause. That which is called a "sentient being" refers to unpleasant sounds;
this refers to the case where a conjured person (*nirmāṇapuruṣa*) utters abusive words when reviling another. These two cases involve conjured persons, and are therefore termed "non-appropriated.

Although they are non-appropriated, they are nonetheless able to express the meaning of good or bad words; thus, they are designated by the term "sentient being. Seventh, non-appropriated... [text fragment].
Sound caused by appropriated great elements (*mahābhūta*) that is designated as non-sentient and agreeable refers to such things as bells and gongs.
Sound caused by eight types of unappropriated great elements that is designated as non-sentient and disagreeable refers to sounds produced by such things as winds stirring forests or river tides;
these are called "unappropriated. Because they cannot express meaning, they are called "non-sentient" (and so forth). This is the objective sphere of odor (*gandha-viṣaya*).
There are four types [of odors]: first, pleasant fragrances such as aloeswood (*agaru*) and sandalwood (*candana*); second, unpleasant odors such as onions and leeks;

third, those among pleasant and unpleasant fragrances that benefit the body, called "equal fragrances" (*sama-gandha*); and fourth, those that cause harm to the body, called "unequal fragrances" (*asama-gandha*).

Regarding the objective sphere of taste (*rasa-viṣaya*), there are six: bitter, sour, salty, pungent, sweet, and bland. Regarding the objective sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavya-viṣaya*), there are eleven: earth, water, fire, and wind (these four are capable of reaching afar).

Lightness, heaviness, smoothness, roughness, hunger, thirst, and cold (these seven are what are deluded by). Solidity is called earth. Moisture is called water. Warmth is called fire. Motion is called wind.
That which can be weighed is called heavy; the opposite of this is light. Softness is called smooth. Coarseness is called rough.

The desire for food is called hunger. The desire for warmth is called cold. The desire for drink is called thirst. Of the three—cold, hunger, and thirst mentioned above—these are what the mind desires; they are not [intrinsic properties of the elements].

Correct. Regarding the causes, there are three types of contact (*sparśa*). These are so called because they trigger these three desires: cold, hunger, and thirst. These are the fruits of contact rather than contact itself;
the term "contact" used here is established based on its fruit. Thus, the treatise states: "These three all apply the name of the fruit to the cause.

As for the objective realm of phenomena (*dharmaviṣaya*), it comprises forty-six mental factors (*caitta*) and fourteen non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*), as well as [certain] aspects of form (*rūpa*).
Non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) and the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are both subsumed within the objective sphere of dharmas (*dharmāyatana*).

Furthermore, what has been stated above—that the aggregates (*skandha*) have the sense of "accumulation," the twelve bases (*āyatana*) have the sense of "gateways for arising," and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) have the sense of "lineage"—is said according to their predominant characteristics.
If discussed in detail, however, these definitions overlap with one another, as explained extensively in the *Abhidharmakośa* (and so forth). Question: World-Honored One, [The text continues here.]

For what reason are these three categories of phenomena taught? The answer is given in a verse of the treatise: "Because of the three types of delusion, faculties, and inclinations, the three—aggregates, bases, and elements—are taught.
This means that because the sentient beings to be converted fall into three classes, the Buddha taught the three categories of aggregates and so forth.
There are three types of delusion regarding the mind. First, there is delusion concerning the mind but not concerning form; one grasps them collectively as a self.
To counter this, the Buddha taught the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), because four of the five aggregates are mental in nature—by teaching the five aggregates, he can shatter that grasping.

Second, there is delusion concerning form but not concerning the mind; one grasps them collectively as a self. To counter this, the Buddha taught the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), because among the twelve bases, eleven...
This is form (*rūpa*). Because only mental objects (*dharmas*) are non-form, the teaching on the bases (*āyatana*) is able to eliminate that attachment.

Third, there are two types of delusion: being deluded about form and being deluded about mind, whereby one grasps them collectively as a self. For this reason, the Buddha taught that among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), ten are form and the remaining eight are mind;
thus, the teaching on the elements is able to eliminate that attachment. Regarding the faculties (*indriya*), there are three levels: superior, middling, and inferior. The superior...

For those of sharp faculties, a brief explanation of the aggregates (*skandha*) is sufficient for them to understand. For those of middling faculties, who are somewhat slower, they understand only when the bases (*āyatana*) are explained.

For those of dull faculties, who are the most sluggish, a detailed explanation is required; therefore, the elements (*dhātu*) are discussed for them (this is explained according to the speed of their comprehension).

Alternatively, it may be explained according to the ease or difficulty of recitation: those of sharp faculties are taught the elements, those of middling faculties the bases, and those of dull faculties the aggregates. Thus, there are three types of preference.

First, for those who prefer the extensive but not the concise, one briefly explains the eighteen *dhātus*. Second, for those who prefer the concise but not the extensive, one extensively explains the five *skandhas*.
Third, for those who prefer the intermediate, one explains the twelve *āyatanas*. Regarding these three categories: according to the Sarvāstivāda school, all are real;
according to the Sautrāntika school, only the *dhātus* are real. If one follows Vasubandhu’s treatises, both the *āyatanas* and the *dhātus* are real; the rest is as previously stated.

The specific explanation (and so forth) is as follows. The *Yin-chao* text states: "The meanings of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) were analyzed and explained for the disciples," where "listening" refers to the listener’s reception and "explaining" refers to the teacher’s discourse.
Regarding "meditation and fasting" (*chan-ji*): "meditation" (*chan*) refers to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and "fasting" (*ji*) refers to the observance of precepts.

As for the intent of the repeated discussion: the method of requesting a teacher has already been clarified in the preceding section; however, the criteria for determining whether the person making the request is qualified or not has not yet been stated.
This is because this treatise establishes its arguments through inference (*anumāna*).
Regarding the phrase "reaching the flames," it is briefly similar to the "wild horse" (*yema*); as recorded in the *Xuanji*, it quotes the *Zhuangzi*: "The dust in a crack is called 'wild';

the dust of the wild horse is in the void, each flying separately and impossible to gather. This serves as a metaphor for those disciples who, although they have requested [instruction], [are like that dust].
It has never been the case that such a teacher existed before. With a single thought-moment, they encompass one another. "Briefly" means "to a small degree. That is, even a small portion is similar;
for instance, dust and grit eventually accumulate in one place. Here, we take the moment when it is blown by the wind as a metaphor, hence the phrase "briefly similar.
According to the *Huainanzi*, within the borders of the barbarians, there are many wild horses (*yema*) in remote and desolate places.
Regarding "a hundred horses, two hundred," and so forth: when one sees from afar that much is being given as alms, if people approach, they all flee and not a single one remains.
This case is also like that (this interpretation is also applicable). To speak in the ultimate sense, those who experience [the world] like a mirage—*Ratnamegha* states:
in the third month of spring, when the yang energy ascends, when viewed from a distance, it resembles ripples on water; because of this, coarse beings suffer from thirst.
He hurried forward until he reached that place, yet there was no water (this is the metaphor). To apply this to the Dharma:

on the day a candidate for ordination ascends the platform, they request a Venerable One to serve as their Preceptor (*upādhyāya*). The Preceptor then says, "Instruct you not to be negligent," and so forth;

thus, there appears to be a sense of mutual inclusion. However, after descending from the platform, there is fundamentally no longer any mutual inclusion between the two, just like [the aforementioned example].

Upon arriving there, not even a trace of water was to be found. In this text, the character "ji" (極) is glossed as "end. This is because while at the beginning it seems as though there is something present, in the end it must necessarily be absent;
hence it is called "extreme" (ji). Regarding the phrase "miscellaneous offenses": the "Great Master" refers to the Upādhyāya and the Ācārya.
"Managing affairs" means to travel between the superior and inferior [ranks], to expound upon principles, and to devise strategies for achieving liberation.
"Regarding 'avoiding calamity' and 'attaining auspiciousness,' these refer to the gravity of the offense of theft committed through expedient means.

As for what is now called 'the Dharma,' this refers to the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), elements (dhātus), and the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda). These three categories have already been described above."

Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), they shall be briefly analyzed by means of four sections: first, the enumeration of the names; second, the individual nature of each member;

third, the subsumption of the detailed under the concise; and fourth, the clarification of the purpose for their exposition. As for the first section: first, ignorance (*avidyā*); second, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); third, consciousness (*vijñāna*); fourth, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);

fifth, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); sixth, contact (*sparśa*); seventh, sensation (*vedanā*); eighth, craving (*tṛṣṇā*); ninth, grasping (*upādāna*); tenth, becoming (*bhava*); eleventh, birth (*jāti*).
Twelfth is old age and death. Therefore, the verse says: "Thus these dependent originations consist of twelve factors across three time periods;
two each for the prior and posterior limits, and eight for the middle, based on completeness. Regarding "two each for the prior and posterior limits," this means there are two factors in the past:

ignorance and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); and two in the future: birth and old age and death. The "eight in the middle" refers to the eight factors from consciousness (*vijñāna*) up to existence (*bhava*).
[This refers to] the middle limit (*madhyānta*) as spoken of in terms of those who reach full term. If one dies prematurely within the womb, then it is not fixed as eight [limbs].
Second, to specifically reveal the essential nature (*svabhāva*): regarding "ignorance" (*avidyā*), the treatise says: "Ignorance is the stage of afflictions in a previous existence.

Because the afflictions of a prior life possess the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), they are collectively termed "ignorance"; it is a single mass of past mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) that is defiled.

Regarding this principle: if the two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are designated by the name "feeling" (*vedanā*) by way of association, one may ask: why is it that only past afflictions are called ignorance (*avidyā*), while those manifest in the present are not? The answer is:

present afflictions such as craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth are merely causes that have not yet obtained their fruit; their functioning is grasped [as such], and they lack the characteristic of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

It is said to be "clear and sharp. Once the fruit has been attained, taking, giving, using, and playing are no longer clear and sharp; therefore, it is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*). Regarding the second, "formations" (*saṃskāra*):

the treatise states that they are the formations of names from previous lives; that is, the various karmas produced during past births, which have the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as their nature, are collectively termed "formations.
This is because "formation" carries the meaning of migrating, flowing, and performing actions. Regarding the third, "consciousness" (*vijñāna*): the treatise states that consciousness is precisely...

The aggregates of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi-skandha*): at the precise moment of rebirth-linking, the five aggregates for a single moment are termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), because consciousness is most predominant at the time of taking birth.

Regarding the four [aggregates] called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), the treatise states: that which precedes the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) is name-and-form; from the moment after rebirth-linking until the six sense bases arise.

The five stages prior to birth while in the womb are called *nāmarūpa*. "Form" (*rūpa*) refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); "name" (*nāma*) refers to the other four aggregates, which are collectively termed "name.
Regarding the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the treatise states: from the time the eye and other faculties arise until the three [aggregates] prior to that, there are the six bases.
This refers to the period from after the *bhalasakha* stage until just before emerging from the womb, during which the various faculties such as the eyes have not yet [functioned].

That which serves as the basis for contact is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Regarding the six contacts, the treatise states: "Contact is the name given to that which has not yet fully understood the distinctions among the three causes of sensation;
it refers to the period from after birth up until two or three years of age, during which the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness is capable of contact."
Regarding these five aggregates at this stage, they are collectively termed "contact" (*sparśa*). As for the seven types of feeling (*vedanā*), the treatise states: "Feeling prior to sexual desire;

that is, from the age of five or six onwards, one is able to discern the specific characteristics of the three feelings, which is termed 'feeling. The causes of the three feelings are the three: suffering, pleasure, and equanimity.
Regarding the eight types of feeling, the treatise states: "Possessing sexual desire through indulgence in craving; that is, at fifteen or sixteen."

Having already departed [from the previous stage], that which can give rise to craving toward the objects of the five desires is called *tṛṣṇā* (craving). Regarding the nine types of grasping (*upādāna*), the treatise says: "The term 'grasping' refers to the pervasive pursuit of various objects.
This means that once one has grown up, one is able to pursue the objects of the five desires everywhere. Regarding the ten types of existence (*bhava*), the treatise says:
"Existence is that which truly brings about an action; it is the karma that is destined to have a result. Since one has already pursued and grasped the aforementioned [objects]...

The object (*viṣaya*) is called a "limb of existence" (*bhavāṅga*) because it can bring about a future fruit. Regarding the eleventh, birth (*jāti*): the treatise states, "The connection to a future existence is called birth.
This refers to the connection to a future existence immediately following the single moment of death;

it is designated as "birth" because it manifests the future life, just as the present consciousness does. Regarding the twelfth, aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*): the treatise states, "Reaching the point of receiving [the fruit]..."

Old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*): This refers to the four stages—name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*)—which exist within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) following birth in a future body.
Collectively, these are termed "old age and death. This is just as in the present life, where name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are not distinct [from one another].

(The explanation of their essential nature is complete. According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, there are four types of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): first, the momentary (*kṣaṇika*); second, the continuous (*sāmbandhika*); [third, the progressive; fourth, the retrospective].
Bondage. [The following] three stages (which are those employed here). Fourth is distant succession; fearing prolixity, it is not described.

Third, regarding the summary of the extensive by means of the concise, this is called the "Twelvefold Intermingled" (*miśra-dvādaśāṅga*). It has only three or two as its intrinsic nature. The three refer to karma, afflictions, and entities;

the two refer to result and cause. Thus, a verse in the *Abhidharmakośa* says: "Three are afflictions, two are karma, and seven are entities, which are also called results. Regarding the three afflictions:

"Those" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*). What are called "the two karmas"? They refer to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and becoming (*bhava*). What are called "the seven things"?
This means that, excluding the five [factors], the remaining seven are termed "things" (*vastu*), because they are the bases upon which afflictions and karma depend.

These very seven things are themselves the fruit. Since these seven are known to be the fruit, it is by contrast revealed that the remaining five hundred [factors] are the causes—namely, ignorance and volitional formations.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like are the causes; consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the like are the effects. Craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) are the causes; birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are the effects. An external objection states:

What is the purpose of clarifying the meaning of the three time periods? Why is the past period abbreviated [as causes] and the future period abbreviated [as effects], while both cause and effect are presented for the middle period?
"Are all of them extensive? Answer: Therefore, the verse of the treatise says: "The fruit and the cause are both extensive; the intermediate [stages] allow for the inference of the two.
That is to say, by means of the intermediate [stages], the extensive fruit and the extensive cause, one may infer and know the three time-periods of the past and future.

Because they are abbreviated causes and abbreviated fruits, they are not mentioned separately. To mention them further would be redundant. As for the fourth section: Question: For what reason does the world...
"Venerable One, you have spoken of the twelve links of dependent origination and further analyzed them according to the three time periods. The answer is:
because sentient beings give rise to delusion regarding these three time periods. Delusion regarding the past refers to such thoughts as, 'Did I exist in the past, or did I not exist?
Delusion regarding the future refers to such thoughts as, 'Will I exist in the future, or will I not exist? Delusion regarding the present refers to [the present life]..."

Regarding the question, "In this world, what is my own self-nature? What are its distinctions?"—in order to remedy such ignorance, two layers of cause and effect are established to bring about clear understanding.
As stated in the treatise: "Because the twelve links continue in succession without interruption. The commentary says:
From afflictions arise afflictions and karma; from karma arises the actual entity; from the actual entity, the actual entity or [affliction] may arise. As for "from afflictions arise afflictions":

this refers to craving arising from feeling, and grasping arising from craving. As for "from afflictions arise karma": this refers to volitional formations arising from ignorance, and existence arising from grasping. As for "from karma arises the actual entity":

this refers to consciousness arising from volitional formations, and birth arising from existence. As for "arising from the actual entity": this refers to name-and-form arising from consciousness, and name-and-form...

The six sense bases arise. From the six sense bases, contact arises. From contact, feeling arises; from feeling, birth, aging, and death arise. Regarding that which arises from karma and afflictions: from feeling, craving arises;
this is precisely the arising of ignorance within aging and death. That is to say, the craving for this aging and death is itself ignorance.

This statement clearly demonstrates the uninterrupted continuity [of the cycle]. Apart from cultivating the path of antidotes, there is no end to birth and death. The rest is explained extensively in the treatise.

The text. This commentary was written for the sake of elder disciples. Now, by explaining these twelve links of dependent origination, it is intended to cause people to attain awakening, sever the continuity [of rebirth], and no longer undergo saṃsāra. The rest is as stated in the text.

Regarding the passage from "What are the six" to "emancipation," it is as stated in the text. Regarding the passage from "What is the first" to "that," these fifteen phrases are listed side-by-side in the *Chao* (Commentary), as can be seen.
Among them, "difficult to speak with" (*durvacas*) and "not accepting instruction" (*avavādāgrāhin*) appear somewhat similar; however, "difficult to speak with" refers to...
This is explained according to the Master’s teaching as a definitive refutation. If one does not accept this instruction, it refers to the time of the initial admonition;

that is, based on what follows, one would be unable to guide others in practice. Regarding "observing the turtle," this is not permitted because one fears the mind will become distracted, thereby neglecting the work of cultivating the Path.
Xuan says: If one follows the text of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it states that one must not go to the homes of those who catch fish or turtles; this is considered an evil [act].
Regarding the *vinaya* rules: because they invite censure, the text of the *vinaya* is as follows. Although there are fifteen items listed individually, there are actually eight phrases.

The first five are as stated in the *Chao-wen*: (1) lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), (2) lack of remorse (*anapatrāpya*), (3) not receiving instruction, (4) acting with improper decorum, and (5) lack of reverence.
The second group of five consists of those who, due to their lack of shame and lack of remorse, are difficult to speak with—namely, wicked persons.
He becomes a friend [to such people] and frequents the houses of courtesans. This continues up to the eighth phrase. The first four phrases follow the old version as separate sections;

the subsequent phrase, which includes "even watching turtles and tortoises," together with the preceding single items, constitutes eight phrases. In the *Chao* (the *Commentary*), fifteen items are listed individually.

The *Shoulüwen* (Excerpts from the Vinaya Texts) exhaustively covers fifty-eight and forty items. Baoyun states: "This is based on the Vinaya, which contains eight sets of five phrases. The first set of five is as in the *Chao* (Commentary).

The second set of five consists of those who lack shame (*ahrī*) and dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*), who are difficult to speak with, and who take evil people as friends; these four types serve as the heads [of the category]."

The *Lì* (歷) [section] states: "Passing through seven locations below the house of a courtesan constitutes seven phrases" (this does not differ in meaning from the preceding section on "capability"). Regarding those who do not inevitably fall into the three evil realms:
this refers to butchers who do not destroy the True Dharma and do not sever the lineage of the Buddhas, such as Qi Xū Gòutuó (氣噓搆陀羅).
And they attain rebirth in heaven. Aṅgulimāla, having killed a thousand people, later encountered the Buddha and still attained the fruits of the Path.
One who keeps wicked disciples and fails to instruct them destroys the True Wheel of Dharma, causes the Jewel of the Saṃgha to be severed, and further enters the evil realms.
Regarding the *Pañcaśata-praśna* and other such texts, they state: "In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who took on disciples and committed many [misdeeds]."
This was contrary to the Dharma. At the end of his life, he was reborn among the nāgas. According to the nature of nāgas, one undergoes retribution for seven days.
During this period of retribution, fire burns his body until the flesh is consumed and only the bones remain; yet, immediately thereafter, it is restored to its former state, only to be burned again.
Unable to endure this, he reflected: "For what offense have I incurred such suffering? He then examined his past lives and saw his own origin: that he had once been a śramaṇa.
While observing the precepts, he received no instruction from his teacher and consequently conceived a poisonous thought, feeling anger toward his own master and intending to harm him.
Later, he thought of his teacher who was with five hundred merchants; as they were crossing the sea by ship, a dragon emerged from the water and seized the prow of their vessel.
The crowd immediately asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am a nāga. If you release this bhikṣu into the water, I shall let you go.
The merchants asked, "In what way does the bhikṣu concern you? He replied, "He was originally my teacher."
He did not instruct me, causing me to suffer. When all my efforts were in vain, I intended to throw the bhikṣu into the water.
The bhikṣu said, "I shall enter the water myself," and he immediately cast himself into the water. The nāga killed him; [his blood flowed] into an ocean of blood... (and so forth).

Regarding the question of what constitutes "reaching the laws and regulations": An ancient said, "One must wait until fifteen [instances] have occurred before reprimanding. The Master now says, "One should reprimand immediately upon the commission of an offense;
only then does it constitute a proper correction. As for the *Saṃyukta Āgama* and other texts, that sutra states:
When the Buddha was in the city of Vaiśālī, there were many bhikṣus who went into the city to beg for food. Among them was a young bhikṣu who begged for food in an improper manner.
The bhikṣus returned and informed the Buddha. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Suppose there is a great lake in a desolate wilderness.
A large elephant pulls up lotus roots and departs; he eats them with the mud and his body is refreshed.

At that time, the young elephants also imitate him by taking lotus roots, but they eat them without washing. Having eaten them, they cannot digest them; they become emaciated and may even die. This is [the case]."
As for the analogy and its application to the Dharma: A bhikṣu of long-standing virtue, having studied the Path for many years, does not delight in wealth or profit.

Whatever robes and food he receives, he is neither stained by nor greedy for them; having eaten, his body is at ease. A young bhikṣu, however, being unacquainted with the Vinaya and relying upon a village, fails to guard his body and speech.
Whatever robes and food he receives, he becomes stained by and attached to them; greedily obsessed with food, his body is not at ease after eating.

On account of this food, one turns toward death. That which is called "death" refers to the loss of the precepts and the return to secular life; it means losing the True Law and Discipline (*saddharma-vinaya*).

To say that one is like those who suffer the pain of death, or that one shares the suffering of death, means that one has violated the Law and Discipline, not knowing the characteristics of offenses nor how to eliminate them—this is what is meant by sharing the suffering of death.
Xuan says: In the original text of that sutra, the subject is presented in two places; the present *Chao* (Excerpts) has omitted one of them.
This refers to those who share in the suffering of death; this is an addition by the author of the *Chao* (Excerpts).

Regarding the phrase "all those who reach the point of offering [the body]," it means that when fire erupts from within, it refers to the arising of anger within, which is called "erupting from within. Furthermore, regarding "advancing or retreating according to words of reproach," this refers to cases where the offense is grave or light.
To say "go far away" indicates a light offense; the light reprimand consists of saying things such as "I will not speak with you. "To set aside vulgar worldly sentiments" means to cease...
Setting aside the illegal staff, the punishment for base and evil corruption is to cause one who has transgressed the pure path to leave it.

This means that by giving rise to a mind of compassion, one relies on the path of renunciation to purify their prior transgression. Next, as for those who reprimand them for their offenses, they should be admonished according to the sequence of the five methods, in accordance with the gravity of the offense.
From the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) onwards, this is the formal procedure for expulsion. Regarding the phrase "you go," Xuán explains that it means "to leave."

The Sangha proceeds with the ritual of the Dharma-realm. The commentary states: "This is because it exceeds what is extremely grave. Xuánzàng says: "It is not that a transgression is designated as grave simply because it is heavy;
rather, even if one has committed only a light offense, it is considered grave because the locus of affliction for others is profound. The remaining text is easy to understand.
Regarding the statement "those who come of their own accord," this refers to the parable of the three sons from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
In the second chapter of that sutra, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa asks the Buddha about the cause of his long life. The Buddha replies:

"Kāśyapa, if you desire long life, you should protect and care for all sentient beings, regarding them as being identical to your own children. Kāśyapa then says: "The Tathāgata should not say that all sentient beings are..."

Regarding them as one’s own children. Why is this? Within the Buddha-dharma, there are those who break the precepts, those who commit crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), and those who destroy the true Dharma.

How can one regard such people as being the same as one’s own children? Immediately following this, he set forth the seven *karmavācanā* procedures for disciplining those who violate the prohibitions.
Kāśyapa then followed up with a challenge to the Tathāgata: "Suppose there were two men, and one of them..."
One person harmed the Buddha with a sword, while another person smeared the Buddha with sandalwood paste. How did the Buddha regard these two people? The Buddha said, "My mind is equal toward both.
Kāśyapa spoke again, saying, "If your mind is equal, why do you further speak of disciplining those who violate the precepts and not disciplining those who do not?
If you discipline one and not the other, it is not impartiality. The Buddha then gave a parable: It was like a high minister of state who fathered many sons.

They are handsome in appearance, intelligent, and wise. If you entrust two, three, or four of them to the Buddha Śrīghana, you may instruct them for me in the rules of deportment and etiquette, ensuring they all achieve perfection. Even if three of the sons should die from the staff, [it would be for their benefit].
"The remaining one son will surely suffer. Although I have lost three sons through this treatment, I shall never harbor resentment.
That the ancients administered the rod was based on this scriptural passage. Those who have not yet attained the teaching have not yet understood the intended meaning of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Regarding the statement that "the World-Honored Buddha dwells in the stage of regarding [all beings] as an only son with equal compassion," it means that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, regards those who destroy the Dharma, such as Rāhula and others, as no different [from his own son].

This is the compassion of the Stage of the Only Child. Therefore, out of pity for those who violate the precepts, he manifests the seven forms of disciplinary punishment to cause them to cease their future great suffering.
Furthermore, with respect to the Bodhisattva’s realization of the Pure Mind-ground, his mind is free from fluctuation;

only when he can exercise this punishment is it revealed that his mind possesses love and hatred, and thus he may not exercise it. What does this statement refer to? It means that if one is able to wield the staff [of discipline].
[The passage regarding] punishment is from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which admonishes: "Be careful not to wield the staff," and so forth. Why is it indicated in this way?
Even if one cites Master Yan, this is merely an allegorical explanation; it does not open up the literal text, and thus ultimately fails to reach the meaning of the teaching.
The allegory is as stated above. The *Yuanshu* commentary explains: "The king and others are metaphors for the Buddha; future learners are called 'the sons. Following the Buddha..."

Because they are born by transformation, they are called "procreated. Because the foundation of their path is not crooked, they are called "upright consciousness. Because they comprehend cause and effect, they are called "wise.
Whether there are two, three, four, or an indefinite number, there are six types of evil persons: first, the icchantika; second, those who slander [the Dharma] and so forth;

third, those who commit the five heinous crimes; fourth, those who violate the heavy precepts; fifth, those who commit the ten unwholesome actions; and sixth, those who violate all rules of decorum. Among these, the icchantika—
Those who lack faith and cannot be converted or disciplined are set aside and not discussed. Among those whose karmic conditions are slightly lighter, their offenses are likewise not mentioned.

Within the four categories [of offenses], committing the ten unwholesome actions and violating the four grave prohibitions are explained as two; adding to these the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), they are collectively explained as three.

Furthermore, there are four additional points regarding the slander of the Dharma. To entrust [the teaching] extensively for its transmission and conversion of beings in the future is called "entrusting it to the Master.

This may serve as a lower manifestation of the signs of entrustment, intended to bring about the accomplishment of the Three Studies. These are: the accomplishment of dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*) and ritual propriety;

the commission of the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*), the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), and the slander of the Dharma; and the abandonment and discarding of these three robes according to the Dharma, such that they are no longer fit for monastic use—these are called the "three children."

He dies from the staff of illness. Those who commit the ten evil deeds must likewise be punished; this is called "the remaining one son," and they shall certainly be subjected to severe treatment, and so forth.

As for the "ten evils" mentioned previously, they consist of the seven *karmavācanā* (formal procedures), with the addition of concealment and the six-night purification of transgressions, making ten.
