Regarding "the stage of the pure mind" (*śuddhabhūmi*) and so forth: attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye refers to a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*). That is to say, this Bodhisattva...
That which is associated with untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is called the "pure mind. When entering this mind, one does not perceive the grasper (*grāhaka*) or the grasped (*grāhya*);

therefore, it is termed non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). When this wisdom arises, because it is not associated with the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) such as greed and so forth, it is said that these ten matters are free from the fault of defilement and turbidity.
The passage beginning with "Now, at this time" [and following] serves to refute [the opposing view]. "Tong" (fear) describes the state of the mind and its objects.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "with utmost sincerity," the ancients cited that sutra concerning the three hundred strokes of punishment: for grave offenses, one receives three hundred strokes;
for middling offenses, two hundred; and for minor offenses, one hundred. Punishing in this manner yields immeasurable merit; hence it is so stated.

"Fu" (福) means punishment. "Shang guo" (上過) refers to the punishment for silence; it means to be excluded. When a bhikṣu commits one of the four pārājika offenses, this constitutes a "superior transgression";

he is excluded from the community and may not dwell with them. "Zhong fan zhe fu" (中犯折伏) refers to committing a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, such as undergoing the *mūlāpakarṣa* (treatment of the root) or the six-night penance.
"Xia fan ke ze" (下犯呵責) refers to repeatedly committing offenses of the three lower categories, which is punished by censure (*tarjanīya*). [End of excerpt]
Regarding "the blood of ten trillion Buddha-bodies," this refers to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, the *Sūryagarbha-parivarta*, where the Buddha addresses Kauṇḍinya (and so forth).
As for "those who fall back from the Path and go to Avīci," this speaks of those who strike a bhikṣu. Regarding "returning after staying overnight outside the boundary," [it refers to the following:]
There are three factors by which the reliance [on the higher stages] is lost; these are the two lower dharmas. Regarding these two lower ones:

if the mind still apprehends their characteristics, one returns to the two lower dharmas and they arise once more. If the mind feels revulsion and abandons them, then even if the matter of the two lower dharmas persists for a night, they will never arise again;
therefore, one must remain outside for at least one night. The rest is as stated in the text.
Regarding the statement "from the three knowledges down to a single robe": "for life" means from the first occurrence of an offense until the end of one's life.
"Having completed the retreat" refers to a single summer. Because both of these durations are too long, they would result in an improper censure.

As for the "sick person," because they are entangled by the pain and affliction of illness, it is not appropriate to censure them. "Not calling [them] to appear before [the assembly]" refers to those who have turned their backs [on the community].
"Subsequently, he censures from afar. Regarding "not coming forward to state one's transgression": although summoned, one does not first come forward to state the offense committed by another.
The *Xiangshu* (Commentary on the Mutual) states: "There are approximately three types of 'losing' the censure: first, the disciple being present; second, the transgression being present;
and third, the censure itself being present—such as saying, 'Go away! I will not speak with you! These three are called 'in accordance with the Dharma.'"
To act contrary to this constitutes a transgression and incurs guilt. Both the teacher and the disciple incur the *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing).

The teacher incurs it on account of violating his proper conduct (*śīla*), while the disciple incurs it on account of harboring resentment toward the teacher. Regarding the "co-resident disciple" (*sahacārin*) in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:

this refers to one who, having received the precepts at the ordination platform, shares in the seven types of conduct from the very moment of their spiritual birth; thus they are called "co-residents. As for "dependence" (*niśraya*): [text continues].
The name is given according to the time of the subsequent request. Regarding the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and other texts:

because there was a śrāmaṇera among the group of six who acted in defiance and was consequently shorn of his robes, people who saw him naked were displeased; therefore, the rule was established for the subjugation of śrāmaṇeras. As for "leaving one garment," this refers to the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*.
There are those who misread the text by breaking the phrasing, yet few recognize this.

Regarding the "four methods for declining and expressing gratitude": "declining" refers to taking leave of the teacher; "gratitude" (xie) refers to repentance and thanksgiving; and "methods" (fa) refers to the rules of conduct.

Regarding the phrase "from ten [days] until departing far away," and the distinction between dwelling in suffering or pleasure, there are likewise four phrases within the *Zhi* (the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*), hence it is said they are largely the same.
This [text] says "should dwell," while that [text] speaks of "dwelling in suffering" and "dwelling in happiness"; thus, they differ. Regarding "dwelling in suffering":
this refers to the third case, where there is no food but there is the Dharma; although it is painful, one cannot depart, and is therefore called dwelling in suffering.

The fourth case involves both Dharma and food, which together sustain the spirit and the body, constituting a state of joyful ease. If the teacher commands one to perform what is improper and calls for you, this refers to summoning the disciple.
"Come, take wine for me"—this is called *adharma* (unrighteous). It is not the same as the character [婬] (yin) as modified in the *Huainanzi*;
it contradicts the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. The rest is as in the text. Regarding the passage from "The Four-Part [Vinaya]" to "does not know," it is as in the text.
Regarding the passage from "Question" to "goes," it is as in the text.

Regarding the phrase "The seventh clarifies the method for losing one's preceptor," this is a formal citation of the title. Regarding the phrase "From harmony to the Dharma," this refers to obtaining the precepts based on [the preceptor];

it carries the meaning of not losing them through lack of formality. Alternatively, "there may be no attainment" means, as in the previous section on formal apologies, knowing that the *upādhyāya* is incapable [of fulfilling his duties].
To teach and cause wholesome dharmas to increase is called "having no virtue. Regarding the three different types of reliance (*niśraya*): Question:

Are these three types found in the Vinaya text itself, or are they added by way of interpretation? Answer: There are two explanations. First, according to Cihé (慈和), the Vinaya text contains only the formal request;
the latter two [types of reliance] arise based on the meaning. Now, I raise an objection: as for the formal request for reliance, it is fundamentally intended for mutual...

Regarding "reliance": since reliance and abiding are already admitted, there is consequently instruction. If the two lower functions of requesting were absent, for what purpose would the subsequent reliance exist?

*Souxuan* states: "Although the Vinaya text permits the two lower [functions], since the method of requesting exists, it inherently contains the other two. This is the perspective regarding this principle."
Gen-Tsuji Sōyu states:

"Next, clarifying the loss of the [three] dharmas of right and wrong" is the heading. He says, "If it reaches the 'flying' [stage]," which, according to the *Shō* (Commentary), means that one loses one dharma of instruction but does not lose the two higher dharmas.
Genki states: "In this context, further discrimination must be made; if [it reaches] the second..."
Regarding the teacher being subjected to the three types of formal charges (*tri-udghāta*) and so forth: as for the disciplinary measures, the latter two methods are both lost.

If he is subjected to the four [measures] such as censure (*tarjanīya*) and so forth, as well as the *parivāsa* (probation) and other such methods, then the second [method], the instruction (*anuśāsana*), is lost; this refers to the single method of the formal motion (*jñapti*). Regarding the three types that are not lost:

these refer to the necessity of the preceptor’s (*upādhyāya*) instruction. Thus, all three are not lost. The opening of the exemption from the offense of non-compliance (*anuvartana*) refers to the disciple.

If one is being disciplined by the Saṃgha, and another person [intercedes], they commit an offense of *anuvartana-sthūlātyaya*. Now, when the two teachers provide instruction and speak to their disciples, they cause them to quickly repent of the seven rules;
in the midst of such joint practice, there is no offense of *anuvartana*.
Regarding the statement "The Vinaya reaches the Great Commentary": first, "In the Vinaya, reaching the point of losing the *niśraya* (dependence)" cites the Vinaya text.

"Losing the two subsequent methods of dependence, yet not losing the method of requesting a teacher" is the explanation from the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*). As for the phrase "merely giving rise to the method of requesting," the wording seems difficult to understand;

it should be read as "merely giving rise to the request. When the method of requesting instruction arises, the method of depending upon and dwelling with [a teacher] immediately follows. It is as follows:

Regarding the *Great Commentary on the Vinaya* (*Vinaya-mahā-ṭīkā*), the initial commentary raises an objection: "If teacher and disciple have resolved [to leave], and their minds are separated by crossing the boundary, such that they return within a month, they would then lose their status as a dependent (*niśraya*).
If this were so, why is it that for the 'separation from robes' (*cīvara-vippavāsa*) and the 'breaking of the rains retreat' (*varṣā-bheda*), one must necessarily spend a night away?

The answer is: "In the case of dependence, there are two distinct mentalities regarding relinquishment; this is because the internal state of the mind is compared with the internal state of the mind. However, regarding the rains retreat and the robes, there is only the internal mentality of relinquishment directed toward the external object."

Furthermore, because it is not a sentient being and lacks a mind of relinquishment, there is no loss. Moreover, regarding robes during the summer retreat, the determination of loss or non-loss based on the appearance of dawn (āloka-nimitta) serves as the criterion for the night’s passage.
However, the criteria for the dependence [of the robe] on the mind and the realm (*dhātu*) are not analogous to this. Based on these four propositions, one may analyze:
first, when the mind is separated by a night, the dependence is lost, yet the robe is not lost during the summer; second, when the night is separated but the mind is not.

There is no separation; there is no loss. Regarding the basis of dependence (*niśraya*): it is like the case of a disciple following his teacher who, while holding the teacher’s robe for him, encounters someone preaching the Dharma.
Because the disciple is so intent on hearing the Dharma, he does not leave the basis of dependence, yet the teacher loses the robe. It should be understood that all three factors are included here.

Regarding what is called "the four causes for reaching the point of cessation": first, death. When the preceptor dies, all three dharmas are simultaneously lost. Second, departing far away. When the two persons depart from one another, [the relationship] is lost;
the latter two dharmas are lost when both cease their practice of the Way. Third, ceasing the path. When the two persons mutually cease, the latter two dharmas are lost.
Fourth, committing a grave offense. When the two persons mutually commit such an offense, the latter two dharmas are lost. Fifth, the teacher incurs censure. One dharma is lost.
Regarding those who enter the boundary of the *ṣaḍāyatana-śīla* (the six-fold precept field): two persons enter each other's space, which is called "different boundaries" (*bhinnadeśa*).

One loses the lower two rules; at seven years of seniority, one attains full purification (*pariśuddhi*). At five years of seniority, only the disciple [is affected]. One loses the lower two rules; at eight years of seniority, one sees [the fault]. Regarding the original *upādhyāya*:

this refers to when the disciple is within the boundary and has previously relied upon another person as their teacher, while the *upādhyāya* comes from outside and returns to reside in his own monastery. Once the disciple sees him...

Regarding the loss of the two lower dharmas: "The nine who return and dwell under the eye of the upādhyāya" refers to cases where the upādhyāya relinquishes the practice of maintaining disciples (*śiṣya*), yet the disciple subsequently requests another person as a teacher for reliance (*niśraya*). Now, the upādhyāya returns to his former practice of maintaining disciples, and because [the disciple] comes to dwell under his eye, the two lower [dharmas] are lost.
If one speaks in terms of the teaching regarding the loss of reliance (*niśraya*), the above cases all refer to the expressive medium (*vācaka*).

The clarification of errors in the teachings: If one considers the path of personal cultivation, it is necessary for the fivefold Dharma-body (pañca-dharmakāya) to be fully established before one may truly lose the basis of reliance.
This concludes the ninth chapter. The three preceding chapters have all been devoted to clarifying matters in relation to persons; this section is now complete.
*Jianzheng ji* (A Record of Simplification and Rectification) of the *Sifenlü chao* (Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya), Scroll Seven, Part Two;
*Jianzheng ji* of the *Sifenlü chao*, Scroll Eight (from the end of the "Section on the Uposatha" to the "Section on the Pravāraṇā").
Compiled by the Great Master Jingxiao, Qingliang, who was granted the purple robe for his long-term lecturing on the Vinaya and presiding over ordination platforms during the Wuyue Kingdom.

Next, regarding the section on the Precepts for Confession (*Poṣadha*) which distinguishes matters according to the Dharma, there are two major divisions: first, the citation of the title; second, the explanation according to the section. Regarding the initial statement from "Confession" to "ten," one first clarifies the intent of its inclusion.

Since the conduct between teacher and disciple has already been established as previously described, it is now logically appropriate to exhort them to cultivate their spiritual practice (*mārga-karma*). This spiritual practice must be maintained...

The foundation of upholding [the precepts] is that one must not prioritize excessive preaching; therefore, this chapter is established. Next, regarding the clarification of the rules and the explanation of the names:

proclaiming the sacred intent is termed "preaching" (shuo); admonishing and restraining body and speech is termed "precept" (jie); and being extensive according to the prescribed measures is termed "Vinaya" (lü).

Therefore, it is called the "Correct Ritual" (*zhèngyí*). Its rules and standards are designated as "Dharma" (*fǎ*). The rest is as explained in the usual commentaries (*yú rú chángjiě*). The commentary divides this into two sections (*zhùwén fēn liǎngkē).
Regarding the first point, "from the distribution [of the *poṣadha*] to the *saṃgha-sāmagrī*": *Poṣadha* is translated here as "Pure Abiding" (*jìngzhù*). An ancient outsider raises an objection:

"The title of the chapter says 'Reciting the Precepts' (*shuōjiè*), yet the sub-commentary below says 'Poṣadha. What is the meaning of this? The answer is as follows: ... [The text continues with the explanation of the term *poṣadha*, its etymology, and the resolution of the objection regarding the discrepancy between the title and the commentary. ... [End of excerpt]
The general purport is to refute the ancient view. The ancients claimed that *poṣadha* and the recitation of the precepts (*śīla-vyākhyāna*) are distinct:

they held that the recitation of the precepts prevents unarisen transgressions, while *poṣadha* eliminates transgressions already committed. Furthermore, they maintained that the term *poṣadha* refers to "pure dwelling" (*viśuddhi-vāsa*), which signifies the meaning of repenting for offenses.
Now, it is said that this is not so; *poṣadha* is a Sanskrit term, whereas the recitation of the precepts is a local (Chinese) practice.
These words [from the Chinese and Sanskrit] differ in expression but not in meaning or flavor. If one discusses the meaning of *poṣadha*, it does not refer solely to "pure dwelling" (*viśuddhivāsa*);
there are many other senses, and while it encompasses "pure dwelling," it should not be restricted to that alone. Therefore, the commentary states: "Poṣadha."
This implicitly reveals that the substance of the *Poṣadha* (confession of precepts) is fundamentally one and the same. Here, "Pure Abiding" (*jìngzhù*) refers to dwelling together in purity;
it thus indicates that those who have committed offenses and have not yet performed repentance are unfit to dwell together.

"Essential Vinaya Rules" (*chūyào lǜyí*) refers to the essential matters of the Vinaya compiled by Emperor Liang based on the Vinaya texts, intended as a ritual manual for the conduct of masters today. This is [the work of] Kauśāmbī... [text fragment].
Regarding the language of the Kingdom of Rāḥ: in the Shu dialect it is said that there are two Kośalas, one southern and one northern; this refers here to the southern Kośala.
That which is pointed out in the *Chuyao yi* (Ritual for the Essentials of Departure)—namely, the aforementioned *Poṣadha*—is the language of that country, as it originates from the western region.
As for the six-fascicle *Nirvāṇa*, according to the Southern [tradition], the reason it is designated as "six fascicles" is for this purpose.

Regarding the sūtras, there are those consisting of two fascicles and those consisting of six fascicles as complete sections. Now, fearing there may be oversight, I shall use the number of fascicles to distinguish them.
As for the two meanings of "nurturing" (*poṣadha*): the former refers to the *poṣadha* ceremony, which carries the meaning of nurturing.

The latter explains it itself, stating: "First, abiding in pure precepts. This is an exegesis of the aforementioned meaning of nurturing; that is to say, it refers to the wholesome qualities already produced.
Being unstained and undiminished is called abiding in pure precepts; it can nourish the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom. Second, regarding "increase":
the increase of merit explains the meaning of "growth" mentioned above. This means that because the essence is pure, unconditioned merit arises continuously from wholesome states not yet produced;
this is precisely what is meant by nurturing and growth. As for "various foods" and so forth, *Poṣadha* is also [included therein].
This is in the Sanskrit language. The original transliteration is *Upapudava*. This refers to the correct Sanskrit of Central India; hence it is called the "original transliterated sound.
Below, the text explains its own meaning: *Upa* means "to sever," signifying that all evils are ceased and severed so as not to defile the essence.
*Pudava* means "to increase," signifying that once one has distanced oneself from evil deeds, one must cultivate goodness.
Because it gives rise to the merit of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*). An external objection states: "The previous text mentions *poṣadha*, or *poṣadhasatva*, and also *upavāsa*.
Why is this inconsistent? One may cite the following commentary to answer: "This is due to differences in regional dialects. That which is above is the Sanskrit sound;
its expansion and abbreviation vary according to the phonetic emphasis. This is likely the language of the five regions of India (*pañca-videha*), used for calling out [to others]."
It is the same. Furthermore, there are two kinds of "assembling" (*saṃgha*): first, the community of monks assembling in one place;

second, the assembly of various merits for the sake of those who know. There are also two meanings to "knowing": first, to recognize the lightness and heaviness of the characteristics of the five categories of precepts;
second, to recognize whether or not one's own person possesses offenses. There are also two kinds of "appropriateness": first, this *poṣadha* ritual... [half].
To recite once a month is appropriate for a bhikṣu. If there are no conditions of the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), it is appropriate to recite in detail;

if there are causes and conditions of difficulty, it is appropriate to recite briefly. Regarding "being the same" (*sabhāga*), there are also two aspects: first, being common to all ordinary and noble beings throughout the ten directions;

second, being identical in the substance of the precepts received (*samādatta-śīla*). Regarding "the characteristics of communal residence" (*sārdha-vihāra-lakṣaṇa*), there are also two: first, that if one commits an offense, it is not [the case that they are still in communion].

Co-residing. Because of the purity of the two types of precepts, one may co-reside with others. There are also two ways of transformation: first, the transformation of evil, which is the turning back of defilement;
second, the transformation toward excellence, by means of pure dharmas. Even regarding that which takes nirvana as its constant characteristic, there are likewise two.
First, the Buddhas of the three periods of time do not alter this Dharma, making it eternal. Second, when I preach every half-month, there is no room for alteration or change.

Third, regarding the "three dignified demeanors" (*sān wēiyí*) and so forth: in the language of Qin, these are called *Jìngzhù* (Pure Abiding); that is, the Qin dynasty referred to them as Pure Abiding.
Regarding the term "nurturing" (*āhāra*), the explanation is the same as before. "Harmony" (*sāmagrī*) refers to the Sangha possessing the six kinds of harmony.

Next, the assembly for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) is no different [from what has been explained]. According to Xuánjì, this is further divided into two parts: the first concerns the Dharma that is received.
The names are not different. Regarding the statement "the two Vinayas say," this refers to the fact that when examining the expressive texts, the names are no different;
it means they both arrive at the same point. As for the phrase "both arrive," the *Abhidharmakośa* (referring to the old *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*) states:

"The eightfold precepts are called the *poṣadha-vrata*. "Eightfold precepts" refers to the eight types of precepts. It says: "There are eight kinds of *prātimokṣa*-vows: first, the bhikṣu precepts..."
1. The precepts for *bhikṣuṇīs*; 2. The *śikṣamāṇā* precepts; 3. The *śrāmaṇera* precepts; 4. The *śrāmaṇerī* precepts; 5. The *upāsaka* precepts; 6. The *upāsikā* precepts; 7.
The *upavāsa* precepts—namely, the eightfold precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*). These aforementioned eight types are all designated as *poṣadha-saṃvara*.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the term "many" (*bahu*) serves as a counter-explanation to the aforementioned *poṣadha-saṃvara*.
Furthermore, although it was previously stated that the two meanings of "upholding through the poṣadha" were not yet detailed, why is the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Yi-liao lun) cited here for explanation?

Regarding "that which resides in the mind is called 'upholding' (*saṃvara*)," this explains the meaning of "upholding. That is to say, when the stage [of restraint] has not yet arisen, merely guarding [the mind] is called "upholding," and it is also termed a "root.
Regarding "that which resides in body and speech, such as the *vinaya*-restraints, is called 'precept' (*śīla*)," this explains the meaning of "poṣadha. That is to say:
When this [restraint] extends to the seven branches of body and speech and is regulated so as not to reach the state of transgression, it is called *śīla* (precept).
Since *śīla* is used here to explain the aforementioned *poṣadha*, we know that *poṣadha* is itself *śīla*; it is merely a difference in terminology between the eastern and western lands.
Furthermore, *ārakṣā* (protection) and *poṣadha* are collectively termed *śīla*. Thus, in that very text, these eight are referred to by the name *poṣadha-ārakṣā*.
These are the eight kinds of precepts. Regarding the phrase "the Vinaya says, etc.," this refers to the text of the Five Hundred Bhikṣus' Council of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. It states:
"The matters concerning bhikṣus collected in one place are called the Bhikṣu-vinaya; even up to the matters concerning all the *poṣadha* rules collected in one place are called the *Poṣadha-khaṇḍa*.
This intends to clarify that the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*) is itself the *poṣadha*, just as *vinaya* and *dharma* (or *sūtra*) are two [terms for the same thing].

The names are not used interchangeably. As stated in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* regarding the *jñapti* for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), it simply says "poṣadha" and does not say "recitation of the precepts" (*śīla-deśanā*);
this preserves the original Sanskrit term. Furthermore, the Vinaya states: "When body, speech, and mind are pure, one then corresponds to the poṣadha. It also says: [and so forth].
The mind of purity, renunciation, and communal *poṣadha*. How could it be that while body, speech, and mind are pure, one still speaks of "confessing sins," my son?

What are its characteristics? The Vinaya states that *poṣadha* means "reciting the precepts. Answer: Originally, *poṣadha* was the name for the assemblies of non-Buddhists where they sat together to preach the Dharma.
According to the Vinaya, when kings invited the *bhikṣus* to assemble and preach the Dharma, the Buddha permitted it. Thus...
Reciting the precepts every day was exhausting. The Buddha therefore established the *poṣadha* (observance day) for the recitation of the precepts;
specifically, the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days were originally the half-monthly *poṣadha* days observed by non-Buddhists.

He directed that the first two be used for preaching the Dharma and receiving the refuges for laypeople, while the last one be used for the monks’ recitation of the precepts. Thus, it is known that *poṣadha* remains its original name. Therefore, the *karmavācanā*...

The *Moshu* (Commentary on the *Vibhāṣā*) states: "The non-Buddhists merely grasp the outward phenomenon (*vastu*), yet they do not act in accordance with the characteristics of the Dharma (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). The Buddha subsequently established the precepts to exhaustively investigate the root of principle.
Thus, we know that *poṣadha* is the recitation of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*), which does not preclude the inclusion of the confession of transgressions (*pāpadeśanā*).
This is simply to refute the fixed adherence of Master Ji. (etc.)

Next, regarding the explanation according to the chapters: first, as for the general intent, the phrase "the recitation of the precepts has arrived" refers to the ritual procedure for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).

The Tathāgata’s pure prohibitions are proclaimed every half-month; this is termed the "recitation of the precepts. The assembly of the Saṃgha, the incense, the water, the *śalākā* (voting sticks), the verses, the chanting, and the formal announcement—all these constitute the ritual procedure.
As for the "great outline of the Buddha-dharma," it means that this recitation of the precepts is the life-force of the Buddha-dharma.

It is the root of life; therefore, it is called the "Great Outline. Regarding the phrase "to encompass and uphold the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma," "encompass" means to protect, and "uphold" means to sustain.
"True" refers to the True Dharma (*saddharma*); "semblance" refers to the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*). "Kuang" (匡) means to rectify, and "wei" (維) means to sustain.

This clarifies that during the periods of the True and Semblance Dharmas, those who wish to rectify monastic affairs and maintain them so they do not cease must do so by means of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). Furthermore, this is because it is through the recitation of the precepts [that these ends are achieved].
Regarding the phrase "However, ordinary sentiments are easily satisfied," the character *rán* (然) is frequently glossed as "is" (*shì*). Here, however, it carries the sense of contradiction.

Since the preceding section clarified that the merit of the precepts is supreme, thereby urging one to revere and honor them, the current [attitude of] weariness and aversion is contradictory; hence, it is called *rán*.
"Ordinary" (*fán*) refers to the state of the lower [sentiments], which are easily gratified; thus, it is said they are "easily satisfied. This principle is the lifeblood of the Buddha-dharma.
This is not something ordinary people would do; therefore, it is called "seeing. There are none who, out of deep-seated aspiration, treat that which is revered and noble as base and insignificant.

This refers to the fact that if the monks and nuns today were to perform the *śīla-vyākhyāna* (recitation of the precepts) once or twice within a single year, it would be regarded as something precious.
If one were to perform [the *poṣadha*] every half-month, it would be considered base, lowly, and insipid.

Although those who practice this dharma are indeed bhikṣus, in recent times, even though the formalities cannot be fully accomplished, many have become arrogant and negligent regarding the performance of this *poṣadha* ritual.
To be "arrogant" (*māna*) means to be conceited; to be "negligent" (*pramāda*) means not to recite [the precepts]. This is truly due to being defiled by habitual listening and so forth.
"Zhě" (者) means "truly" or "in reality. "You" (由) refers to causes; "quān rǎnzhě" (曲染者) refers to defiled habituation, meaning that day by day one becomes defiled by the six sense objects.
Consequently, following this mind of defiled habituation, one treats the dharma of the precepts with negligence and superficiality.

"Yǐ cǐ lùn qíng qíng kě zhī" (以此論情情可知) means that by measuring one's feelings of delighting in evil and loathing the good through this, one ought to know for oneself that one's conduct violates the precepts.
Hearing that the Sangha was suffering from distress, one should simply remain thus; having no desire to hear of it, it is said that "the sentiment can be known.
Regarding the phrase "formerly arriving at Yi," this refers to Emperor Wenxuan of the Qi dynasty. "Qi" refers to the Southern Qi, also called Jingling. This "Wang" (King) was Xiao Ziliang.
That King once saw the Tathāgata Devendra in a dream at night, who commanded him to perform the *poṣadha* rites. Therefore...
The *Jingzhuzi* (Disciple of Pure Abiding), twenty fascicles, clarifies the ritual for the lay *poṣadha*.
Regarding the person known as Puzhao: "Śramaṇa" is a general title for those who have left the household life; "Da'an" is his personal name;

and "Kāśyapa" (開士) is his honorific title, meaning "one who is superior to the Path," that is, one who is supreme in the cultivation of the Path. Later, during the Yellow Turban Rebellion, he was falsely given this title.

[The people] called him "Renunciant. Those who were renunciant loathed him and thus abandoned him, refusing to acknowledge him. At that time, Fu Jian, the ruler of Former Qin, bestowed upon him the honorary title "Kaisi" (Opening the Gate).
This refers to one who is a scholar capable of opening [the gates of the Dharma]. These two Great Virtuous Ones (Mahāsattvas) composed the *Poṣadha* rules for renunciants.
Both sets of ritual procedures—those for the laity and those for the renunciants—are practiced together in the world.
Therefore, as for the statement that "the interpretations of the mind differ and the characteristics of the mind are distinct":

when laypeople recite the Bodhisattva precepts during the *poṣadha*, and monastics recite the Śrāvaka precepts, this is called "difference. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva precepts are Mahāyāna precepts that guard the mind;
the Śrāvaka precepts are Hīnayāna precepts that focus on the characteristics of body and speech. Thus, it is said they are "distinct. The above is based on...
This is the commentary by Yuanling. Among the various records, none of them explain this matter, which has led to many erroneous interpretations.

Those who have directly inherited and employed [the tradition] are said to be the two masters mentioned above, Puan and An; it was simply by following their example that the ritual for the *poṣadha* of those leaving the household life came to be practiced.
If so, why does your current *Chao* (Excerpts) further include this chapter to clarify the *poṣadha* method for leaving the household life? Below...

The *Jují* (Collection of Passages) states: "There is no basis upon which to rely when it is said that at the time of composition by the ancients, the sūtras and śāstras had not yet arrived in this land, and thus there was no foundation for their ritual practices.
As seen in the text of the present *Xíngshì* (Ritual Practices), every single practice cites the sūtras and śāstras;
only matters such as the reception of scented water and pure water have a basis. Now, in seeking the intent of the sūtras, I mark this distinction from the present [tradition]."

"Seeking" (qiú) refers to searching for the meaning of the scriptural texts. "With what I have heard" (yǐ suǒ wén zhě): "with" (yǐ) means to combine or intermingle. "Intermingled" (cān zá) means universally.

"The hearing of the Path and Delusion at the Poṣadha" (zhào dào wàng pǔ sà zhī suǒ wén): "hearing" (wén) refers to that which is roughly compiled; "roughly" (cōu lüè) means approximately, and "repeated" (chóng zài) means again. "To look back from the present" (yǐ jīn wàng zhě):
this means to recompile and seek the proper sequence. "As fully listed below" (bèi rú hòu liè zhě): "fully" (bèi) means complete and exhaustive; "as" (rú) refers to what follows.
The ten categories are arranged one by one in rows.

However, there are those who live during the period of the Semblance Dharma (xiangfa) and the end of the Dharma (mofa). "Semblance" refers to the Semblance Dharma; "the end" means that the Final Dharma (mofa) is about to increase.

The *Hōbōshō* states: "As for the composition of this text, calculating by means of the sexagenary cycle from the ninth year of the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, it is found to be fifteen hundred and seventy-four years ago.
The *Genki* says: "To say it is over one thousand seven hundred years ago is incorrect."

Furthermore, some say that the "image" (liangxiang) refers to the Semblance Dharma (xiangfa) and not yet the Final Dharma (mofa). This causes those who do not grasp the intended meaning to fall into such erroneous interpretations.
[The world is] decadent, corrupt, and degenerate; their dispositions are not sincere or reverent. When they encounter this Dharma, it brings them no benefit.
The phrase "Therefore, first citing [the passage] to provide proof" serves to conclude the preceding section and introduce the intent of the following one.

It may be said that "the meaning of 'well-attained' refers to the non-destruction of the precepts. Xuán explains: This is because when a bhikṣu’s practice is perfected, the precepts are thus not destroyed.
"Abandoning all evil and unwholesome dharmas": "abandoning" (*prahāṇa*) means to cast off and turn away from. "All evils" refers precisely to the ten unwholesome paths of action (*daśākuśala*).

Regarding "and all afflictions accompanied by craving" (*saratṛṣṇā-kleśa*): the *Zhongji* (Record of the Mean) states that the sixteenth fascicle of that treatise clarifies "with craving" (*sarata*) and "without craving" (*vītarata*).

"Craving" (*rāga*) refers to the fetters (*saṃyojana*). Having abandoned all afflictions accompanied by craving and thereby exhausted the source of outflows (*āsrava*), one immediately achieves [the state of an Arhat].
"Without craving. If one follows the *Xuánjì* (Record of Profundity), it is explained as the character "to receive" (*shòu*).

This means that by eliminating afflictions and karmic obstructions, one does not go on to receive birth within the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātu*). Furthermore, this is how the *Kēchāo* (Excerpts of the Commentary) breaks down the phrasing.

Nowadays, lecturers traditionally recite "and all afflictions" as a single phrase, placing the two characters "existence-reception" (*yǒushòu*) in the following phrase; this is entirely illogical—consider it well. [This is] the realization.
Regarding the statement "declared as ultimately equal": that which is called "white phenomena" (śukla-dharma) receives its name in contrast to "black phenomena" (kṛṣṇa-dharma).

However, black phenomena encompass both the wholesome and the unwholesome; it is not necessarily the case that they are exclusively unwholesome to warrant the designation "black phenomena. Now, according to the Jewel of the Dharma:
To elaborate further: if we discuss them in terms of their characteristics, what ordinary people call "black karma" is termed "white dharmas" by those who have left the household life;
this is a comparison between the secular and the monastic. If we look within the secular realm itself, the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds are called black karma.

The classes of scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants are termed "mixed occupations. Only within the Buddha-dharma do meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) states receive the name "white karma" (as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa*).

Furthermore, within the Buddha-dharma, according to the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), those who distinguish for themselves [the following]: first, black dharmas, which are the persons of the seven stages of preparation (*saptaprayoga*);
second, white dharmas, ranging from the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) up to the Arhat. Or, within the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*).

Regarding the differentiation between black and white: from the stage prior to the *bhūmis* (the stage of practice before the first ground), up to the first through tenth *bhūmis*, these constitute the white dharmas.

The above discussion is generally based on the distinction between the monastic and lay, as well as the Great and Small Vehicles. Now, the *Abhidharma-kośa-śāstra* states that the realization of the white dharma necessarily involves the attainment of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
From the immediate proximity of attaining the four fruits of the śramaṇa, to the distant goal of Nirvāṇa, one then achieves the ultimate holy life (*brahmacarya*). If one abandons evil...

The unwholesome is called "black phenomena" (*kṛṣṇadharma*). This refers specifically to the ten non-virtuous actions and the roots of perversity within the conventional world, which are described as black phenomena among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and must be abandoned.

Although, from the perspective of their own essential nature, these are analyzed and categorized as black phenomena during the seven stages of preparation in the Hīnayāna and prior to the [first] bhūmi in the Mahāyāna, one should reflect that they are now subsumed under "white phenomena" (*avadāta-dharma*) when considered in relation to the conventional world and the side of evil karma. Contemplate this.

(To explain it in such detail is what is truly elegant and appropriate). According to the *Huayan ji* (Record of the Avataṃsaka), taking up single-minded devotion without transformation is the first pure dharma (*śukladharma*);
being able to repent after having committed an offense is the second pure dharma. While this reasoning is not without merit, I fear it may contradict the literal text.

Furthermore, there are other ancient interpretations that are incorrect and thus not recorded here. It is also said regarding "every half-month": the *Fupian ji* (Record of the Auxiliary Treatise) states that within one month, it contains...
Because there are both the dark and the light fortnights, they are mentioned twice. Question: Why is the *poṣadha* (confession of precepts) observed during both the dark and light fortnights?
Answer: Because the fifteenth day of the light fortnight is already complete, it symbolizes that the wholesome dharmas are fully perfected and the observance is accomplished.
The "dark fortnight" (kṛṣṇapakṣa) refers to the day the moon has ended; it symbolizes the total extinction of all unwholesome dharmas.
It signifies the accomplishment of the practice of restraint and observance (saṃvara). Therefore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, ordained that this be performed every half-month.

This clearly demonstrates the accomplishment of the two aforementioned practices based on the two types of conduct (as stated in the Vinaya texts, which contains a specific intention). The remainder is as explained in the text (*etc.*).
"Regarding 'as for the distinctions'": this opens the two chapter-headings. "Regarding 'the first' to 'the dharma'": as in the text. "The different times and periods":

within the four categories, this refers to the first, the section on time; thus it says "beginning and middle. Furthermore, it is divided into four sections, all of which are occasions for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*.
"Regarding 'the former' to 'therefore'": the preceding three [sections] are from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations).
This refers to the three days of the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth, as well as the three periods of before and after meals during the day and night.
Regarding the "four divisions" listed above, according to the method for the *poṣadha* (confession of precepts), there are three days: namely, the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth.
These three were originally the three days for the *poṣadha* of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). King Bimbisāra and the various Buddhas followed the *poṣadha* of the non-Buddhists.
Therefore, it is established that they remain together for three days along the road: the first two days are for preaching the Dharma to the laity and administering the refuges;
the final day is for the monastic community to purify their minds by reciting the precepts (*śīla*). This differs slightly from the present text, which states: "As listed above. How is this so?

It means that within the *Caturvargika-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya), among the three added days, there are the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth; since these coincide with the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten-Recitation Vinaya), it refers back to what was stated above.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "on the day of the *poṣadha*, one should recite," etc., the term "etc. also refers to the text within the *Prātimokṣa* (the Code of Precepts).
The Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to recite the precepts, but they did not know on which day to do so. The Buddha said: "I permit it to be recited on the *poṣadha* day.
This *poṣadha* is the original name for the assemblies of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). After the king had invited [the Buddha], the Buddha employed...

This is distinct. The following citation from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* is precisely this point. Regarding the eighth and fourteenth days for preaching the Dharma and the fifteenth day for the *poṣadha*:
these refer to the recitation of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*), which was established by the Buddha and differs from that of the non-Buddhists.

As for the prohibition against performing the *poṣadha* at dawn and so forth, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* restricts it as being too early, but does not prohibit it before the morning meal. That text states: "In a village, there were bhikṣus who rose at dawn..."
Regarding the *poṣadha*: A visiting monk came and spoke to a resident monk, saying, "Venerable sir, let us perform the *poṣadha* together. He replied, "I have already performed it.

[The visitor] reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "One should prepare scented water and other necessities at the courtyard of the stūpa for nuns and wait for the visiting bhikṣus to arrive."

If one performs the *poṣadha* early in the morning, one incurs a *vyatikrama* (transgression of the discipline), and so forth. Regarding "day and night," since there is no conflict with the tenets of any of the various schools concerning these two periods of time, it is not explained here.

Regarding the statement "the four parts reach [the point] where it is not spoken," as for "increasing" and "decreasing": moving toward the future is called increasing; moving toward the past is called decreasing.

Regarding the phrase "coming on the fourteenth day and speaking on the thirteenth day, etc.," the *Vinaya* states in the section on prohibitions: "At that time, there were quarrelsome bhikṣus who came and took up the fourteenth-day recitation;
upon hearing that others were coming, they then held the recitation on the thirteenth day. Originally, it was to be held on the fifteenth day. Upon hearing [of the arrival], [they changed the date]."
[The Buddha] came. On the fourteenth day, he spoke: "This transformation of Śākyamuni was previously called 'extinction. As for those who enter the secular world:
once the wicked bhikṣus have arrived and entered the boundary, they shall announce, 'Virtuous ones have come; your bodies are defiled with filth; you should bathe.'"

One does not employ the language of ordinary people. If one enters among the lay-monks, it causes distress; therefore, one should quickly exit the boundary and establish a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) to perform the *pravāraṇā*.
If this is not possible—meaning the aforementioned bhikṣu does not use the [proper] language and refuses to enter the bath—one has no other expedient but to inform the Saṃgha:

"On the latter half of the fifteenth day, the *pravāraṇā* shall be performed. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "if he still does not go, [the time] is further increased," etc., this merely explains the subsequent procedure.

This is for the purpose of increasing [the assembly]. Regarding "forcibly bringing about harmony," the Venerable Daide of Jing-shui said: This means that one should exhort others to join in and not create obstacles;
even if the person in question is unwilling, one must still exert effort to urge them toward harmony. The ancient commentators explained:

Since it is called "forcibly bringing about harmony," if the assembly is already seated and that person stands up, there is no longer harmony; therefore, one must now employ those who possess power...
If one suppresses another person and forces them to sit, harmony is immediately achieved; thus it is called "forceful.

This interpretation is not particularly sound, as it mentions only two occasions and does not mention three occasions and so forth. An ancient master said: "If the Buddha-dharma is not preached after three attempts, it will perish.

For this reason, one must forcibly achieve harmony and is not permitted to approach [the assembly] again later. Now, it is said that the recitation of the precepts may be further increased by subsequent additions.
As for the fourth or fifth [day], in principle it is indeed permissible. That we do not allow it now is because we fear that those who practice *pravāraṇā* might take this as a precedent and say:
"Since the *poṣadha* was permitted to be held based on proximity, I may now likewise hold *pravāraṇā*. If it reaches the sixteenth day of the eighth month, one has already entered the winter season;
if the *poṣadha* were not permitted to be further increased, then one would not dare to apply the same precedent to *pravāraṇā*. This is because...
It merely says "two times"; the mention of "three" refers to the strong reconciliation of the minds. Furthermore, there is no statement that the Dharma would perish after three attempts;

thus, [your position] is entirely contrary to what the ancients established. Regarding the passage in the Vinaya concerning the Kausāmbī gate and so forth, it states: "The bhikṣus were quarreling, their mouths like swords and blades.
Since they were not in harmony, the six methods for settling disputes and so forth were applied; thus, [your claim] is a perverse refutation of the ancients.
What people have established is entirely incorrect. The Vinaya states that when the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī were quarreling, their words being like swords and spears, they failed to reach harmony;
thus for six years the [Prātimokṣa] was not recited. At that time, because the Buddha was still in the world, he prevented the strife and discord of the entire kingdom.

Regarding this, Xuán says: "This refers to the statement concerning the rescue [of the Dharma] when the Dharma is about to perish. It means that when the aforementioned [recitation of] the precepts is not performed, the Dharma perishes."
"It must be that because of such strife, the fruit of the Path cannot be attained; this is what is meant by the 'extinction of the Dharma.
Regarding Ānanda’s doubt concerning Ghoṣila and others, the Vinaya states: At that time, the bhikṣu Ghoṣila was the teacher of a householder.

The householder possessed a treasure storehouse, and on his deathbed, he entrusted it to Ghoṣila, saying: 'I have two sons; wait until they have grown up and become capable, then entrust this to them.'"

Ghoṣila later entrusted his estate to his second son. The eldest son, feeling aggrieved and resentful, went to the monastery and wept before Ānanda, saying, "Ghoṣila has taken my great possessions and given them all to one person. Having heard this, Ānanda...
He then whispered to Ghoṣila. After the great *poṣadha* ceremony, they did not recite the precepts together. At that time, Ghoṣila had a friend who was Rāhula’s maternal uncle.
Rāhula sent his maternal aunt with a young child to stand before Ānanda, saying: "If the child cries, you must take him away, for Ānanda cannot tolerate it.
You then said to her: "Venerable Sir, if he speaks with Ghoṣila, I will immediately [take him]."
As for the one who took the child, Ānanda, out of a compassionate heart, immediately asked, "Ghoṣila, why have you died?
Ghoṣila replied, "I was instructed by the fire regarding what was to be given; because my eldest son did not understand me, he would not give it.

Ānanda said, "Go now," [adding that] even if one does not commit a *duṣkṛta* offense, I believe that you have committed the offense of theft. Since the six [monks] did not assemble for the *poṣadha*, bring them here so that we may move together.
The Dharma perishes; it does not become a mixed transformation, remaining as if the ritual had not been performed, because it is not extinguished, and so forth.

Regarding the mutual disparagement for twenty years during which the *Poṣadha* was not recited, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* simply states: "In the village of Vakkala, the monks gathered together for a single *poṣadha*.
At that time, there was a forest-dwelling (*araṇya*) monk of great renown, and the village-dwelling monks conceived a mind of jealousy toward him."
At that time, an araṇyaka bhikṣu arrived on the fourteenth day and said to a village bhikṣu, "Venerable sir, let us perform the poṣadha together.
The village bhikṣu replied, "It should be performed five days from now. The araṇyaka bhikṣu then departed. After he had left, the village bhikṣu immediately recited the precepts.
When the other returned the following day wishing to perform the poṣadha together, [the village bhikṣu] answered, "It has already been completed. The village...
The bhikṣu spoke back to the araṇyaka bhikṣu, saying, "You have abandoned the *poṣadha*. I shall no longer share the Dharma-food with you.
From that time forward, the araṇyaka bhikṣu came every fourteenth and fifteenth day; yet for twenty years, he was unable to perform the *poṣadha*.
At that time, there was a benevolent deity who held the araṇyaka bhikṣu in high esteem and went [to him].
In Mount Pāṭi, the bhikṣu Jotidāsa fully recounted the aforementioned matters.
Having heard this, the Venerable Joti immediately summoned the protective deities of the village and returned to inform the forest-dwelling bhikṣu: "Joti is now in the village;
you may go there and ask him. Once permission was granted, the Venerable one asked, "Did you abandon the *poṣadha*? He replied, "For twenty years, fourteen times..."
"The Uposatha is on the fourteenth day; [you] come on the fourteenth. The Uposatha is on the fifteenth day; [you] come on the fifteenth.
Is this not a rebellion? Jyotiṣka said: "You follow the Buddha-dharma; it is merely that the *karmavācanā* performed by the village monks for twenty years has not been validly accomplished.
The preceding citations were also intended to refute ancient attachments.

Regarding the phrase "because the four parts have arrived" and "the strife has persisted for a long time," the Vinaya states: At that time, the Saṃgha in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī had split into two factions.
The bhikṣus wished to move to Śrāvastī in order to achieve reconciliation. The Buddha said: "From this day forward..."
Listen to the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Then, the *karmavācanā* (proclamation) is made as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Regarding the matter of dispute that caused the Saṃgha to quarrel and led to mutual discord—since that person committed an offense, he has been formally accused (*codita*), and his offense has now been resolved. The dust of the Saṃgha has been laid to rest."

If the time for the proclamation has arrived, may the Sangha listen with patience: the Sangha is now in harmony and makes this formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made the announcement, they act in harmony.

Regarding "on whichever day the dispute is extinguished, on that very day it is settled": this means that within either the dark or light fortnight of the month, on whatever specific day the dispute is extinguished, [it is settled] on that very day.
On this very day, the *jñapti* (formal motion) was completed; it was stated that there was no need to wait until the fifteenth day.
The Venerable Jing-shui said: "However, regarding the ritual procedures of the three schools, the additions and subtractions within the *ekajñapti* are not fixed.

For instance, from the third or fourth day of the waxing moon onwards, or from the first, second, or third day of the waning moon onwards, the performance of the *jñapti* follows the Nanshan tradition."

Regarding the addition of the terms "white" (*śukla*) or "black" (*kṛṣṇa*): if, for instance, on the third day of the month there is a dispute over the extinction [of the *poṣadha*] and one proceeds to recite the precepts, one must state, "Today is the third or fourth day of the white fortnight," and so forth;

the case of the black fortnight should be understood by analogy. According to both the new and old commentaries (*vṛtti*), however, they do not permit the addition of the terms "white" or "black," but simply say "the third or fourth day," etc.
The Great Virtuous One (Bhadanta) refutes this, saying: "Consider, for example, from the sixteenth or seventeenth day onwards..."
One should not omit the "black" (waxing) month. It is sufficient to simply state the first, second, or third day; how could such an omission be considered reasonable?
Now, following the Southern tradition, one must append the two characters "black" or "white" to each entry. Take note of this. The rest is as stated in the text.

Regarding the second point, the clarification of the various requisites for the *miśra-dharma* (miscellaneous teachings): Xuánzàng stated, "In the preceding introduction, it was said that 'the textual evidence lacks a firm basis,' which indicates that the scriptural texts of the explicit teaching (*nītārtha*) were insufficient.
Furthermore, it was said, 'Now, seeking the intent of the sūtras and supplementing this with what has been heard,' which means relying on the teachings as the basis;
every citation herein is based upon these. The Great Virtuous One further remarked, "This entire section is maintained by our current Master."
Furthermore, some say: "In this section, although it is stated that the assembly has fully understood the Dharma, it is then said once more;
is this not redundant? This is a request for clarification. It means that what was previously called "seeking the meaning of the sūtra" and so forth correctly introduces this second section.
This [second section] then extensively and specifically describes the events of a single period according to various sūtras and śāstras, each having its own [account].
This is based upon the following. In the third section, the "Gate of the Ritual for the Formal Exposition," one simply proceeds by standing upright throughout;
there is no further citation of individual scriptural titles. To provide an illustration, it is like the "Chapter on Repentance" (*Chānpiān*):

first, the established texts are cited as the basis for the practice according to the teachings, and subsequently, the formal procedures are clarified. Therein, the manner of performing the repentance ritual consists solely of standing upright; this case is likewise so.
Although the *Chao* (Commentary) is clear, its underlying intent is somewhat lacking;
consider this. Regarding the phrase "five up to five hundred," it is as the text states. Regarding the phrase "the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says... therefore," that Vinaya states:
When laypeople asked how many people were present at the time of the *Poṣadha*, the bhikṣus did not know the number and felt ashamed. The Buddha said, "I allow you to count [the number]. Furthermore—

[The text] was again forgotten. The Buddha said: "One should have voting sticks (*śalākā*) distributed; it is the same for *śrāmaṇeras*. As for the phrase 'from the fourth to others,' this refers to those who receive offerings on behalf of *śrāmaṇeras*.
Xuán says: 'This refers to *śrāmaṇeras* who have already received the ten precepts. Furthermore, this serves as evidence for the aforementioned fivefold division."

The five śrāmaṇeras may also be referred to by their names. If they have not yet received the ten precepts and so forth—referring to those who have never received the śrāmaṇera precepts—they may still receive offerings when addressed by name.
The following citation from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* explains the meaning of the scriptural passage cited above.
Regarding the "five-part measurement" (*pañcabhāga*) and the "measurement to the fingertips": these refer to the five fingers of the Buddha. Since each finger is two *cun* wide, it is one *chi* long.

This does not refer to the five fingers of a human being. One *zhǒu* (cubit) is eighteen *chi*. Based on this, [the measurement] refers to the Buddha’s [fingers], and not the other four [types of measurements].

As for "one who has left home" (*pravrajita*), they have departed from the house of the three realms (*tridhātu*) with the intent to seek *nirvāṇa*, thereby distinguishing them from householders. *Andha*... (Note: The term *jì* appears to be a transcription error or archaic variant; based on the context of measuring the Buddha's body, it likely refers to the specific measurement of his fingers.)

*He* (合) signifies "back-to-back" or "separate. *Śalākā* is a single term from India. In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the "śalākā for censuring misconduct" (*pāpadeśanā-śalākā*) takes this chapter as its tally-stick (*cū*), preserving the Sanskrit term.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* and *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* both use the term "tally-stick" (*cū*), which is the local vernacular equivalent.
Regarding the passage in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* where the Buddha permits laypeople to scatter flowers, at first the bhikṣus did not dare to accept them.
The laypeople (avadātavasana) derided him, saying, "He does not understand how to accept the offerings of others. Because of this, he reported the matter to the Buddha, who then gave permission.
When it was said that a bhikṣu may not [do so], the Vinaya context states that a bhikṣu scattered flowers upon a high seat;
the laypeople derided him, saying, "He is no different from a king or a great minister. The Buddha said, "A bhikṣu may not [do so]," and so forth. "There is no suffering" means there is no offense.

Regarding the statement, "When approaching the *vinaya*, the miscellaneous and minute textual passages are difficult to maintain," this accords with the twenty-seventh chapter of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* concerning the *poṣadha* ritual.
Therein, the Buddha asked Upāli, "Do you recite the *vinaya*? He replied, "The miscellaneous and minute textual passages are difficult to maintain.
The Buddha said, "You should count them using tally-sticks (*śalākā*). Later, he asked again, "Now that you have counted them using tally-sticks, do you recite the *vinaya*? He replied—
It is said: "The miscellaneous textual passages are so numerous that even counting them with tally-sticks would be difficult. The Buddha said: "From this day forward, there shall be two types:

first, five hundred; second, seven hundred" (the above is from the Vinaya text). Regarding the annotation stating "that which applies to both the monastic and lay precept texts," this is the interpretation of the present Master.
In this section, interpretations have differed between ancient and modern scholars. For now, following the orthodox teaching of our own school, it means: as appropriate...

Turning to the Vinaya text, it states that two kinds of tally-sticks were made—one set of five hundred and another of seven hundred. It is not clear for what reason these two numbers were established.
Therefore, the Master of the present day explains: this was done because the *Śrāmaṇeraka-śīla-sūtra* applies to both monks and nuns;

that is to say, the Buddha’s original intention was to have Upāli memorize the great treasury of the Vinaya and record its numerical counts so that he would always know the essential categories and ensure there was no omission or loss.
This is merely a time for leisurely examination; it is not a time for formal preaching from the high seat during the fortnightly assembly. Regarding the establishment of two types of enumerations:
the first records the number of rules established by the double regulations (*dvi-guṇa-vidhi*) for the two divisions of the monastic community, monks and nuns, which are not few in number.

The second records the number of rules established at the Council of Five Hundred for the nuns' discipline (*bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*), and the number recorded at the Council of Seven Hundred for the great assembly of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*). These two enumerations are thus established and each is set apart.

In one place, if the Saṃgha has committed an offense and the formulation of the precepts is concluded, one should subsequently check the number of voting sticks (*śalākā*) for the offenses within the Saṃgha and increase that count accordingly.

Later, when reciting from memory, if one checks those already confessed, and the number of voting sticks exceeds [the original count], then by the time the recitation is finished, one will know the number that was forgotten.
The same applies to the Bhikṣuṇīs. If one does not perform this counting of voting sticks, one must make a prediction based on memory.

Although this is so, because it relies entirely upon the inked script on the palm leaves at the end, some omissions have occurred. [The questioner asks: "The number of rules for nuns is many; the counting sticks (*śalākā*) should likewise be many.

Why, then, are they fewer? The number of precepts established for monks is few; why, then, are the counting sticks many? [The answer is: "In principle, the number of nuns' counting sticks should indeed be many.
That there are now only five hundred is merely to record the points where they differ from the monks. As for those that are the same,"
It is included within the numerical categories of the Vinaya for the Saṃgha. Therefore, we know that the character "tong" (comprehensive) in the commentary encompasses both positions:

the five hundred [rules] are comprehensive with respect to the nuns' precepts, while the seven hundred are comprehensive with respect to the monks' Prātimokṣa. (The first interpretation has now been concluded. Alternatively, according to the explanation in the *Xuánjì*, it is said:

"The five hundred are based on the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*, while the seven hundred are stated comprehensively according to both the *Bhikṣu-vinaya* and the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*. Furthermore, it says: "If one speaks of 'comprehensive'..."
As for this: there are five hundred precepts for nuns and two hundred and fifty for monks, totaling seven hundred and fifty.

That it is now stated as merely "seven hundred," lacking fifty, is a general approximation and does not necessarily conform to the exact number of individual precept articles (in the present day, many rely on this convention, interpreting it according to their own judgment).
An external objection states: According to the original context of the Vinaya, it was based on the fact that [the monks] had not yet committed [the rules] to writing;

fearing that it would be somewhat difficult for Upāli to maintain them in memory, these two kinds of counting sticks were created. Furthermore, this concerns ordinary recitation and practice, and is not related to the time of reciting from the high seat during the fortnightly assembly.
Now, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, once the collection [of the teachings] had been finalized, there were no omissions or deficiencies in the script upon the stone slabs (*śilā-paṭṭa*).
Even if something were forgotten during the session, it would have been pointed out [by others]; why then would there be a need to clarify it now? Now, Nanshan further cites that text;

among these four repetitions, is there not one that results in excessive prolixity? In response, some explain: "It is likely for the sake of those who have newly received the precepts, lest they [be confused] in a secluded place..."

When reciting [the precepts], one must keep track of the number of times they are completed. If the texts for the four *pārājika* offenses and the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules are difficult to memorize, there are seven hundred tally sticks (*śalākā*);
for those from the third category downward, which are easier, there are only five hundred. (This does not constitute a full explanation. The present commentary states:

although the preceding text has already clarified the length and size of the tally sticks, it has not yet discussed their quantity; therefore, this passage is cited here to determine the number of tally sticks.
Although there are now three thousand five hundred people gathered among the monks, they do not exceed seven hundred voting tallies (*śalākā*).

Even among the nuns, the number does not exceed five hundred. If we were to go further upward [in number], I fear there would be the fault of being endless. This, then, is the Master’s hidden intention.

It resides solely in this. Since those who have lost sight of the essential meaning are numerous, there arise thoughts of false interpretation. As for the question, "Who should perform the *jū* (blessing)?"—it is the *vinaya-dhara* (the *weina*) who now recites the proclamation.
Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "In the *poṣadha* ceremony for laypeople (*avadātavasana*), it is appropriate for the *vinaya-dhara* to perform the *jū* and other rites."

Regarding the "assignment of the senior seat": this is the first case among the four [sections of the *Caturvargika-vinaya*], wherein the assignment was originally performed by the senior monk himself.
Later, because he became exhausted, he ordered that a junior monk be assigned to perform it, and so forth.

Regarding the statement from the *Mahāsāṃghika* up to "error": it refers to the case where one who has not yet received the precepts speaks of the names of the five categories of offenses and incurs a fault.
This means that when making distinctions, one says, "This is a *pārājika*," or "The six friends [commit] a *duṣkṛta*," which means they commit a *duṣkṛta*.

Because he was originally speaking of the names of the five categories of offenses to laypeople, they then spoke lightly, saying, "This is a *pārājika* for a bhikṣu," and so forth. Based on the four [categories of offenses]...
Regarding the statement that "all offenses are *duṣkṛta* (吉羅)," this refers to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (祇文).

Because of this, it was not fully understood that below the *Caturvargika-vinaya* (四分戒), all [offenses] are concluded as *duṣkṛta*, yet the names of the four higher categories (*pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *sthūlātyaya*, and *pāyattika*) are not mentioned there.

However, one must further distinguish between cases: if addressing laypeople (*avadātavasana*), the names of all five categories are stated collectively; whereas, regarding those within the monastic community...

The three lower groups [of practitioners] may not, however, recite the names of the four higher categories of offenses. As for "the various *nidānas* (origins)," these refer to the day of receiving the precepts and so forth.

All these *karmans* (formal acts) are performed prior to the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts). According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the *bhikṣus* first perform the *poṣadha* and subsequently perform the *karman*.
It was because the group of six (*ṣaḍvargika*) departed as soon as the *poṣadha* was concluded that the Saṃgha failed to achieve harmony. Therefore...
"This refers to the preceding regulation" (and so forth). Regarding the rule that one should recite the precepts directly and not with a melodic chant, the Venerable Master said:
"This is a passage cited for its contextual connection; it does not mean that one should adopt the more convenient practice. The Preceptor Zhongping of Xishui said:

"The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* is the sublater, while the *Caturvargika-vinaya* is the sublated. One should take the latter as definitive. If this were the case, it would be identical to the fourth master’s position, which contradicts our own school's fundamental tenets.
They are eternally distinct. Is it not the case that they are identical? If there are difficulties regarding conditions, one may consult other sources without hindrance;
however, this must be during a time of leisure and should not rely entirely on a single school. To know the *poṣadha* offering is to understand the exposition of the precepts (*śīla-vyākhyāna*).
As for "at a time when there is no Buddha," etc., this explains the reason [for the practice] (and so forth).
Regarding the statement "from three to ten types," this clearly explains the ritual procedure, which refers specifically to the protocol for a single session of practice.
As for the point that it is not fully contained within the Vinaya, Xuánzàng states: "The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* lacks the verse for hearing the bell, the verse on purity, and other such verses.
We now universally adopt [verses] from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the *Āgamas*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and so forth, as will be explained below (etc.). Regarding the deletions and additions:

The *Shandangbu Shoujie Fa* (The Method for Reciting the Precepts in the Śāndhāna Section) eliminates non-essential texts and supplements the practice by citing various sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras to establish the ritual procedures.
"Ten kinds" indicates the enumeration of the categories.

Regarding the phrase "one *liàng* (measure) of the Dharma," the principle requires that it be based on the traditions of others. It must be understood as referring exclusively to the *Poṣadha-hall* (confession hall) in the Western lands [India].
There, they spread grass everywhere; here, one must instead sit upon mats on the ground. As for those in the Middle Kingdom who use rope beds and the like, Xuán says:
"The term 'like' (*lèi*) refers to raised platforms, small stools, and so forth. Regarding the frequent practice of spreading grass on the ground, it is because they mostly use grass.
This refers to sitting on the floor. Regarding the fact that in ancient times here [in China] people used beds, this is stated based on the customs of the Western Regions (India).

However, according to the local tradition of this land, for the most part since antiquity, people have sat on mats on the ground. Although beds were used, only those of the rank of Great Officer (*daifu*) or higher who held official positions were permitted to ascend them;
everyone below that rank sat entirely upon the floor. The phrase "after the Eastern Jin" and so forth refers to the period of the Jin dynasty when the Secretariat (Shangshu Sheng) was established.

Within the Hall of Fixed Examinations, there were eight *hang* (pronounced *hu* with the level tone) couches; those of the fifth rank and above, as well as provincial governors (*zhoumu*), were permitted to sit upon them.
It is also said that the hall had eight couches, which were called the "Eight Seats" (*bazuo*), referring to the six Ministers of State (*shangshu*) and the two Vice Presidents (*puyeshi*).
From the Eastern Jin dynasty onwards, continuing until the Tang dynasty, it was the custom for all to sit facing north on these seats, with no distinction made between their relative ranks or status.
Furthermore, regarding the many items commonly provided in monasteries today, "providing" means to establish them; this generally follows established precedent.

A typical example is the provision of beds and seats, as is the case throughout the lecture halls and dining halls nowadays. It is also permissible to use both together, meaning to spread mats on the floor in front of the beds.
In this practice, the officiant moves back and forth while the monks remain seated on their mats; this is a dual usage. However, regarding the original practice, there are many inconveniences.
Xuán says: "Rán" means "should. It should accord with the original practice of the Western Regions (India), which was to spread grass upon the ground.
When performing the rites here in this land, there are often many instances of instability. In this land, the two halls for lectures and meals are typically long corridors.
Regarding the bedding: in the Western lands, there is always grass available, which must be moved out every half-month; this is inconvenient.
Furthermore, the grass of the West consists entirely of pure, fragrant *māṇa* grass and the like, which are free from insects;

whereas here, the grass is impure and fodder-like, often infested with insects, thereby harming living beings—this too is inconvenient. Moreover, when a pure sitting mat is spread upon it, the assembly cannot perform their prostrations.
It is acceptable. However, if one touches the mats while wearing shoes during ritual activities, it also violates the Buddha’s regulations.
For these various reasons, it is not convenient. Regarding measuring according to the location: one should construct it as is appropriate for that specific place.
If there are no beds inside the hall, they may be used as substitutes; if they are long beds, there is no need to move or alter them, but they may simply be used together.

Regarding "from two to the discernment," it is as stated in the text. Regarding "from three to the midst," within the assembly’s network, the northern leader of the assembly inspects those who are healthy or ill, and so forth, including inducements and metaphors (and so on).
Regarding "from four to the matter," there are many instances where a novice (śrāmaṇera) from the north has a connection [to the assembly] and grants consent (*chanda*) according to the Dharma.
Initially, based on the *Xuánjì* (Record of Xuán), the formula for a novice’s declaration of consent is the same as that for the great monks (*bhikṣu*).
There is a slight difference. One should say, "Venerable sirs," while the rest of the wording remains the same. Now, the objection is raised:

even if there were a formal expression of consent (*chanda*), at what time would it be spoken? For instance, when the preceptor has sent those who have not yet received full ordination out, he then asks about those who did not come.
Since the novice who conveyed the consent has already followed the others out, it is illogical for him to re-enter the hall to transmit the words; this makes no sense whatsoever.

Regarding the second point concerning the reliance on the Dharma Jewel: it refers specifically to the procedure where a *śrāmaṇera* entrusts his consent to a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*) for the sake of receiving [the precepts] and so forth.

This is because, in the Western Land (India), whenever the *poṣadha* was observed, there were laypeople who would offer material goods. Therefore, the "consent" (*chanda*) mentioned here does not relate to the verbal expression of desire.

Based on this, the text merely explains the purpose of obtaining and receiving the tally (*śalākā*), but it does not clarify the underlying principle of how that consent is obtained. Now, following the interpretation of the Venerable Śīla from Dongyang...
Li explains: Mili requested that the assembly attend the hall to hear the five-character *Saṃghasūtra* and the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
However, because he had other karmic connections and could not fulfill his desire [to receive the precepts], he entrusted the matter to the Great Saṃgha to grant him one tally (*śalākā*).
Although the original purpose was to receive the offering by means of the tally, he now requests it to express his earnest aspiration. What prevents him from receiving a share?

Therefore, in the passage following the distribution of the *śrāmaṇera* counting-sticks (*śalākā*), it instructs that one should call out the names of those who are to be informed, making a general announcement throughout the Saṃgha.
This is because there may be occasions when a *śrāmaṇera* intends to come, and so forth; this is very clear in the *Śarīra-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. Furthermore, regarding those who have heard or seen signs:
if one sees clothing or armor, or if a door is open, or if there is the sound of human speech, one must immediately summon them. Thus, the Vinaya says: "Upon seeing such signs..."
Regarding the search for [the proper timing] (and so forth), one should explain the verse for hearing the bell. This verse is logically intended to be recited when the bell is struck three times.
Some say that to recite it upon first hearing the bell is too early; others say that to recite it when the sound of the bell has subsided is too late.
Below, the *Āgama* Sūtra is cited to clarify the phrasing, as in the text. Within this, it says: "Striking the *gandi* in an open space."
The Venerable One said: "In the Western lands (India), bell towers are mostly situated in the open air. According to the *Jetavana-vastu*, they were originally covered by multi-storied buildings;
