my current statement is based on the majority of cases. Some say that when Kāśyapa convened the council, he took the copper gong and went to the summit of Mount Sumeru to strike it, as that was an open space.
My present explanation follows this intent. As for those who gather here like clouds..."

The commentary explains: "This refers to within the fire-hall," or alternatively, "this refers to within the main hall. Both of these are partial and restricted interpretations. What is meant here by "this" is stated in a general sense;
it is not restricted to being either inside the hall or outside the hall. Take note of this. Regarding the subsequent entry into the hall to recite verses and so forth, Fabao says:
one may recite the verses either before the Sangha or behind the Buddha, and only afterwards proceed to one's own [seat].
As for sitting: it is also permissible to recite [the precepts] at one’s own seat before the bed in the present day. Regarding the phrase "what remains of the ultimate teaching" and so forth:

the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, and Ānanda asked the Buddha, "While the Tathāgata was in the world, we took the Buddha as our teacher," and so on, up to, "Until my parinirvāṇa, come once every half-month," and so forth.
As for the "root of gathering the Saṃgha": the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) is the root. Some say...
Regarding the dharma of the precepts (*śīla*), there are further ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) and codes; these others are the branches, while the former serves as the root.
All other ritual matters include such things as receiving the precepts and performing repentance (*pratideśanā*).
Regarding "From 'Five' to 'Contemplation'": *pán* (pronounced *qí jìng qíng*) refers to flower bowls and vessels for storing fragrant water or pure water;

there are three vessels, five vessels, and so forth—the remaining text may be understood in detail. Regarding "From 'Six' to 'Matters'": this correctly clarifies the ritual procedures for a single session.
Regarding "From 'Should' to 'Elder'": nowadays, many ritual practices do not conform to the Dharma; therefore, these are briefly clarified. As for the sound of the bell, just as it—
The *vina* (disciplinarian) performs the formal announcement (*bai*) while remaining in his original seat, or he may kneel with one knee on the ground before the Buddha or the Sangha.
He then proclaims: "The assembly has already gathered. Upon hearing this, everyone simultaneously kneels with one knee on the ground before their respective seats.
Once they have done so, he proclaims again: "Each of you requests the joy [of the Sangha]. The Elder then recites a verse, the first line of which says: "May the Great Assembly bear this in mind."
"I, [Name], do not need to say: 'Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind. There are many such instances; know this.
When these three persons have finished speaking, one immediately proclaims: "The Great Assembly, all at once, each requests your joyful approval. Or it is also acceptable to say:

"All at once, each requests your pleasure. The rest is as usual (etc.). When making this formal announcement (*jñapti*), the *karmadāna* (ritual master) should stand before the seats of those present.
"Kneeling with the right knee on the ground. When there are three or five young men, each observing the proper decorum, they may follow the practice of the Jiangxi region.
Three or five assistants shall, in order of seniority, come before the Buddha’s seat at the appointed time; having performed three prostrations, they then proceed to distribute the water and towels.

Alternatively, if there are two *xī* (assistants), they do not follow specific instructions, but rather coordinate with the *weina* (chant master); they then proceed from their own respective positions.

Observe the proper ritual decorum. Having performed three prostrations before the Buddha, withdraw to the place where the pure water is kept. After washing your hands, proceed before the Buddha to take the counting sticks (*śalākā*).
As for the assistant, they simply follow from their original position to bring the water jar and distribute the water. These two types of procedures each constitute a distinct method;
employ them as appropriate according to the occasion, provided you do not deviate from the fundamental principles. [This applies to] the Arhats and the Holy Sangha.

Regarding the phrase "the assembly, etc.," Xuán explains: This means that when the *karmadāna* (Venerable of the Assembly) chants, the members of the monastic community must also follow the vocal intonation of the *karmadāna* in reciting these verses.
If this were not the case, how could it be said that "each [member] recites the verses"? As for the term "Arhats," this refers to the gathering of those who have attained the ultimate fruit.
It is said that this *Poṣadha* (Recitation of the Precepts) is observed equally by both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and sages (*ārya*); how could it apply to ordinary beings alone?
It must be assembled. Question: For what reason is it that at this time only ordinary people have gathered, and no noble ones (*ārya*) are seen coming? Answer:
When the assembly of noble ones arrives, their appearance and disappearance are difficult to fathom. How is this known? The Venerable cites the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*:
"At Fǎróngjué Temple in Luoyang during the Sui dynasty, Dharma Master Tánwùchòu went to Chóngzūn Temple in Hándǎo to lecture on the *Lèizǐ* for the monks."
Every half-month, when the Dharma Master personally ascended the seat to recite the precepts, he would count the tally-sticks at the appointed time and find them to be suspiciously numerous;

upon counting them, he discovered there were sixty extra people. Furthermore, when he inquired about those from distant regions with four ears, he saw strange monks approaching from afar in the distance.
Someone asked him about the circumstances of this, and he replied: "I went to Handan to observe the Vinaya master Tanwulei reciting the precepts and so forth;
therefore, you may know that it is not an error."

Regarding the "eight meritorious qualities of water" mentioned in the *Jingshui-ge* (Verses on Pure Water): according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Lake Anavatapta possesses water with eight meritorious qualities.

As for the "eight," they are: first, lightness; second, softness; third, purity; fourth, coolness; fifth, fragrance; sixth, deliciousness; seventh, lack of foul odor; and eighth, freedom from harm when drunk.
As for the term "meritorious quality" (*guṇa*), "merit" (*gong*) refers to the causal effort, while "quality" (*de*) refers to the capacity of virtue. It is...
The fruit and cause are explained together. Furthermore, there is another interpretation: this water possesses only the capacity for eight functions;
it is not itself a "merit" (*guṇa*), though later people added the character *guǎn* (功). The rest is as usual (*yú rú cháng*). Regarding the method for distributing the ritual cloth (*xíng jīn fǎ*):

the person distributing the cloth holds the upper part with the left hand and the lower part with the right hand after having gathered the clean cloth in the middle (with a departing tone), grasping both ends with the hands. Each...
When it has emerged more than five or six inches, grasp it firmly so that it does not loosen. Hold the upper part with the left hand and hold the lower part with the right hand as you move it along.
When the assembly of monks uses the cloth to wipe their hands, they must distinguish between what is defiled and what is pure; they may only wipe the palms of the hands.

Nowadays, people wipe both the palms and the backs of the hands at once, completely failing to distinguish between the defiled and the pure. This method of using the cloth practiced in the region north of the River originated from twisting [the cloth].
"Binding the practice of conduct, etc. (and so forth). Regarding the phrase "the five parts are fulfilled" within the verse on fragrant water, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

this refers to the five aggregates of death (*maraṇaskandha*), namely, precept, concentration, and wisdom; these constitute fulfillment. Regarding "the perfect illumination of prajñā, etc.," it means that the two wisdoms of Mahāprajñā are perfectly luminous;
the liberation and dharma-body—the three virtues—are complete, pervading and encompassing the entire dharma-realm. All...
This is the One Suchness (*tathatā*).
As for the "Foolish Old Man" (*yusō*): in the regions of Qi and Lu, the elderly were called *sō*; because he was old and lacked wisdom, he was designated as the "Foolish Old Man.
Regarding the statement that those who reach [the state of] *sa* must also purify the mallet handle with scented water: this is because one fears [pollution] when grasping it with the hands.
Because of contact, pure water should not be used for the handle of a cleaning mallet. Regarding "in the section," this refers to the various miscellaneous chapters in the lower fascicle.
As for "Who among the assembly is the youngest? 'Gather and protect,' said three times," all three iterations must be recited in full.
In current tradition, these three full recitations are treated as two full and one abbreviated; by the third iteration, one simply says, "The youngest shall gather."
Fahao said: "This is entirely incorrect. Including the collection of voting tallies (shouchou) among the offerings has been the practice in both the two capitals throughout ancient and modern times.
The meaning of the *Chao* (the *Zunsheng jiaojie benmo chao*) is that since it was stated above that "the small [voting sticks] are collected and guarded," the statement is already exhaustive.
There is no need to further chant the words "and offering" or "collecting the voting sticks. Therefore, the commentary states: "As already fully detailed in the preceding text," and so forth.

As for those pure great śramaṇas from outside who enter during the third recitation, they likewise perform the extensive recitation three times. Now, as the time for the [fourth] recitation arrives...
The three repetitions are correct; however, to say only that "the Great Śramaṇa has entered" is incorrect. There is an interpretation that the "Great Śramaṇa" refers to Piṇḍola.

This was the interpretation of the ancients, as they were specifically summoning a saintly being. The passage beginning with "according to the Vinaya" and following is the explanation of the present master.

It is merely feared that there may be members of other assemblies who have not arrived; thus, they are made to inspect one another, rather than this being restricted solely to the noble personage Piṇḍola.

Therefore, it is said that it is not restricted to the worthy and the holy. As for the statement that "one *bai* [announcement] is added at the beginning," etc., this refers to ancient ritual practice:
adding one *bai* by saying, "Let those who have not received full ordination depart," and further saying, "as well as those who are impure. It is for this reason that...
The *karmadāna* (lay attendant) is not permitted to hear the precepts; they may only go out together with those who have not yet received full ordination.

This is because the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* itself prescribes that it is the reciter who must go out—this is the intention of the Master [of this school]. Since the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* differs from other schools, the reciter of the precepts himself proclaims: [the text continues with the specific verses].

Those who have not yet received full ordination must leave. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is the *karmadāna* (Venerable of Affairs) who calls out those to leave;

there is no need to mention "impurity" and so forth. Now, the Master says: if one is to exclude those who are defiled, whether according to our own school or other schools, there is no need to mention it at all.
Regarding those who are placed [in this position]: when the Preceptor recites the precepts, he states in the introduction, "Those who have committed an offense should confess.

Furthermore, there are three inquiries as to whether these individuals are pure or otherwise. When this point is reached, by openly disclosing their thoughts with an open mind, they immediately become entitled to hear the precepts;
what need is there to separately proclaim them?

Furthermore, it is said that this assembly of the junior members has already been gathered and protected. A pure Great Śramaṇa has already entered from outside; it is improper to add the word "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).

This constitutes the formal conclusion of the text. Regarding the three recitations: from the aspiration [of the precepts], the seats of the superior, middle, and junior members must be extensively explained three times over.
It is incorrect to now perform two extensive recitations and one abbreviated one. Thereupon, one should approach the senior monk (*sthavira*) and prostrate.
Regarding those who kneel: this applies only when there are three or more people. As for the person who collects the voting sticks (*śalākā*), it is likewise only this [person].

Some say that if there are ten or twenty people on a single bed, everyone must individually kneel upon their heels; however, I fear this is not correct. Furthermore, in some places where the voting sticks are distributed, they are placed into the hands of the *sthavira* Kauṇḍinya;
even the fragrant water and pure water are likewise washed into the hands of the *sthavira* Nīla.
This is ignorance; it is not to be called strange. Regarding the "Vajra, Fearlessness, Liberation," etc., in the verse for receiving the tally (*śalākā*):

this tally is firm and solid, and is thus metaphorically likened to a vajra. The Buddha possesses the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*); because he does not give rise to timidity or dread, they are called "fearlessnesses.
This is based on the interpretation in the *Fazheng ji*. If one follows the *Souxuan*, it interprets it with the character "obstruction" (*ài*), meaning that [the tally] is like a vajra.
It explains that all things are shattered and destroyed, leaving no further obstruction. The Venerable One said: "However, the characters *ài* (obstruction) and *wèi* (fear) are easily confused;
this was a scribal error that led to a false interpretation. Now, the previous explanation is taken as correct. As for the present fruit, it means that the *poṣadha* is the ritual of pure dwelling;
one is then fit for liberation and may participate in the monastic tally (*saṃgha-śalākā*), which is difficult to encounter.

Since it is now attained, it is called the "present fruit. Because this tally, which is so difficult to encounter, ought to be revered, it is said that one should "bear it upon the crown of one's head," and so forth.

Regarding "also identical in deportment": this refers to the manner of collecting the tallies—such as kneeling with the [left] foot placed forward—which is no different from the deportment of the person distributing the tallies;
hence it is called "identical. As for "firmness, joy, and equanimity" in the verse, it refers to seeing the purity of the precepts.
It is purified. His mind is joyful; because his mind is always far removed from the defilements of breaking the precepts, it is called "renunciation" (捨), and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the white procedure for distributing the *śrāmaṇera* voting sticks (*śalākā*):

when proceeding northward with the *śrāmaṇera* voting sticks, if there are no venerable monks present to listen, and one greatly distributes the voting sticks for lay inquiries on giving, and then counts them following the previous announcement, it is not in accordance with the rules. Nowadays, many possess jewels, yet they are still deluded.

The Elder recites three times; the Northern tradition recites three times with expanded wording. Now that we have reached the third repetition, it is also incorrect to omit the two characters "next line" (次行).

Regarding the phrase "each being pure and harmonious for the *poṣadha*," this follows the direct recitation of the *Chaozong* (Commentary School) and must not be augmented. If [the text] were otherwise...
The Commentary states: "Each emerges purely within the Buddha-dharma. This is said to distinguish [the Buddhist practitioner] from those who might be confused with him;

for non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are also called "renunciants" (*pravrajita*) and likewise observe the *poṣadha*. By now adding the phrase "within the Buddha-dharma," one knows that he is not a non-Buddhist. Now, [I] refute this:

Since the latter phrase is already understood, the former—conforming to the Buddha’s teachings—is also clearly evident. There is no need to add anything further; indeed, it is improper to do so. Regarding "conforming to the Buddha’s teachings":
this refers to the Buddha’s regulation that the *poṣadha* (confessional ceremony) be held every half-month. Regarding "repaying the four debts of gratitude" in the interim:
as the Sūtra states, these are first, the king; second, one's parents; third, teachers and the Saṃgha; and fourth, donors. Regarding "pure and wondrous verses," etc.: according to...
[The Buddha said: "It is exactly twenty-seven. Devadatta has split the Saṃgha and is heading toward Gayā City to perform separate *poṣadha*, *pravāraṇā*, and *karmas*.
We have already completed our *poṣadha*. Ānanda said, "I know; it is truly extraordinary that the Saṃgha has been split. He reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Those who act contrary to the Dharma have performed their *poṣadha*. Those who act according to the Dharma should recite the precepts. Recite the precepts!"
At that time, he recited these verses, etc. (as detailed). As for the statement "if a śrāmaṇera reaches the separate rules," this refers to the *Śrāmaṇera-viśeṣa-caryā* chapter.

Regarding the statement "from seven [steps] up to ascending the seat," as for "fully performing the dignified demeanor, joining the palms, and making a formal announcement," it means first bowing the body and then speaking the announcement with the mouth.

One does not perform the ritual of prostration. According to the *Pañcaśata-praśna-śāstra*, if one prostrates before a person in the presence of the Buddha, one commits a *thullaccaya* offense and so forth.

Furthermore, there is an interpretation which states: "The *thullaccaya* offense mentioned in the treatise refers to ordinary circumstances. Now, when one requests someone to recite the precepts on behalf of the Tathāgata, that person becomes equivalent to a new Buddha.
Because they are identical [to the Buddha], it is not permitted. Now, Master Dongyang provides an analogy: it is like a new king entering the temple of an old king.
Within this context, it is not appropriate to receive prostrations because the objects of veneration are distinct; thus, by citing that [case], the principle here is made manifest.

Now, one may simply squat on the heels (*prāṅmukha*) without performing a formal salutation, as the underlying reason is universally applicable. However, strictly following the text, it is more refined and appropriate to join the palms (*añjali*) while making the request.
Regarding the phrase "Venerable One, out of compassion, please preach the precepts for the Saṃgha," one may also say "Elder, out of compassion," and so forth—all of these are acceptable. However—
According to the text, it is established that one must not employ the words used when announcing to the assembly at dawn, such as: "Today is the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight;

the community of monks is harmonious. To add the phrase "sufficient speech" (*paryāptavāda*) here would constitute an unrighteous act (*adharmakarma*). Such instances are common today, likely because the underlying meaning has not been thoroughly investigated.

Regarding the statement, "The duty for this *poṣadha* ceremony shall rest upon [the responsibility of] so-and-so," various families explain that "resting upon" (*niyukta*) means "to be appropriate" (*yukta*).
"Yi" (依) and "cong" (從) are both incorrect. The Venerable Master said that within the character for "hǎo" (蒿) there is the character for "wei" (位).

His intention was that it should read "wei dang moujia" (位當某甲), meaning "the position belongs to so-and-so. Later scribes erroneously changed it to the character "ren" (任), which is entirely unreasonable.

Furthermore, one need not say that the presiding monk himself usurped the merit [of the candidate]. Nor should one say that the wording of the precept text is harsh or contravenes the intent of the Sage.
Furthermore, according to the text, one should not add or subtract anything; reflect upon this. Regarding the instruction to have the next seat in order recite:

if following the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, one should simply have the *sthavira* (elder) do so, or if he is unable, proceed directly to whoever is capable of reciting. The present instruction to have the next seat in order do so is according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

Within that text, it says: "The Saṃgha appoints a *vinayadhara*; such-and-such person who recites the Vinaya shall be cited," which refers to appointing someone capable of relinquishing [the responsibility]. If it says...
"Preceptor [Name], recite the precepts. This refers to the act of proclaiming what has been relinquished. In the present time, this has been changed to "Recite the Precepts" (*shuojie*).

The Venerable One says that the character *shuo* (recite) was used to avoid the imperial taboo, while the character *jie* (precepts) refers to the object being proclaimed. Below this, the preceptor recites all the verses.

Accordingly, this should be revised. When performing the ritual now, one should say: "The assembly, this is a careless oversight," or "This is entirely a failure to understand the meaning of appointing a *bhikṣu*.
Regarding the term "high seat" (*gāozuò*): it refers here to the teacher’s seat as distinguished from lower seats. Generally speaking, whatever is sat upon may be termed a "seat.
However, when the *Poṣadha* (confession of offenses) is being recited, one ascends the high seat; the new manual merely says "ascends the seat" (*shèngzuò*) without [specifying "high"].
The character "gāo" (high) is used; the same applies to the "xiàngsū" (commentary on characteristics). This seems to involve confusion, as has already been stated previously.
Furthermore, when first reading for the precept master (*śīlācārya*) and the *brahmacārin*, one should first invite the precept master, go before his seat, join the palms, bow the body, and say:

"The Sangha has appointed me to recite the precepts. Only then should one return and read for the *brahmacārin*. Nowadays, however, people first invite the *brahmacārin* teacher and only afterwards invite the precept master. Moreover—

When requesting [the precepts], one must not fail to present the formal petition; to instead act with negligence, indifference, or the like is contrary to the Dharma. One should be cautioned against this.
Only then should the written petition be submitted, as described above.

"Regarding the phrase 'as for the eight reaching the Dharma,' this is the heading. Regarding the phrase 'if one reaches [it],' this refers to the manner of performing *fanbai* (Brahmanic chanting). Fabao says:
'The term *fan* (Brahman) is designated according to its location, because the Five Regions are all the land of Brahmā; it refers to those people born there.'"
Because it originates from the Brahma Heaven, the method of adding phonetic characteristics to the sound is such that whatever is chanted or praised is called "Brahma-conch" (*brahmāṇī*).
This term *urvi* (鬱鞞) is the Sanskrit word for the country of Ujjayinī; in the Western lands, it refers to the country of Ujjayinī.

Translated here into this region’s language, it means "cessation" (*zhi*) and "severance" (*duan*). "Bai" (*bei*, chanting) is translated as "cessation," and "ni" (*ni*, *nir*) is translated as "severance. It means to sever all evils.

Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, it is said that [external] conditions naturally cease through stilling," etc.: whenever one wishes to listen to the precepts, the Buddha commanded that one should collect the ears and focus the single mind upon the sound of a single *gāthā*.
Thus, external conditions naturally cease. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The Brahma-sound is profound and wondrous, causing people to delight in hearing it.

The Venerable Master [Daoxuan] stated: "The origin of the Brahma-sound in this land dates back to the fourteenth year of Yongping, when the two Honored Ones, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna, [arrived]."

He competed with the Daoist masters of the Five Peaks and emerged victorious. Thereupon, he leaped into the air and performed great supernatural transformations, reciting a verse in *brahmaghoṣa* (Sanskrit-like) speech that begins:
"I am not of the lion lineage... (and so forth). He was also called "The *Brahma*-Sound of Mount Song. Nowadays, few obtain his original text.
Those who explain it based on the "Fish Mountain *Brahma*-Sound" found in the *Xuanyi* (Mysterious Record) are in error; [it refers to] the Fish [Mountain].
Regarding the *Shanfan* (Mount Baṇa) Sūtra: during the Wei dynasty, Cao Zhi, Prince of Chen-si and styled Zi-yuan, composed verses while walking.

One night, while lodging at Mount Yu-shan, he heard the sound of divine immortals chanting the *baṇa* (Sanskrit: *brahman*) in the air. He subsequently memorized it and understood its rhythmic patterns (*vidhi*).
Later, he transmitted it to various virtuous monks, who then established formal rules based upon the Sūtras and Vinaya; this is what is now called the *hebo* (chanting).

This refers to the *Brahmavihāra-gāthā* and similar verses. Regarding the phrase "he returns to his original position": the fragrant water and incense flowers are treated according to the same ritual procedure as the water.

This means that one sprinkles [the water] on the left and right sides before the Saṃgha, leaving the middle path open; this is called the "empty space. Because there is a middle section, it is designated as a separate reserved area.
As for the attendants and the initial sprinkling on both the left and right sides, it is not mentioned in the verses for the procession of incense.

"Wisdom-fragrance" refers to the self-restraint of precepts and meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Although "liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation" are not explicitly mentioned, they constitute the cloud-pavilion of radiance.
Furthermore, this fivefold dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*) is able to free one from all fetters and defilements; therefore, it is called "fragrance. The remaining text is easy to understand.
There is no need for further elaboration.

The phrase "The Nine Questions and Answers" serves as the heading. The phrase "As for 'that which reaches the ear,' one should recite it according to the method above" means that one should follow the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
The text of the recitation above states: "The Saṃgha is assembled in harmony; those who have not received the full ordination should depart. (From the *Śīla-vyākhyā*).

It says: "First, regarding 'harmony' (*saṃgha-sāmagrī*): when one intends to explain at length matters where the internal conditions are in conflict, the ritual procedure requires that there first be harmony before the assembly may subsequently convene.

Therefore, it is said, 'The harmonious Saṃgha assembles,' and 'the formal announcement (*jñapti*) for the detailed exposition. This is not carried out without the Saṃgha. Although harmony was previously sent forth,"

The dharma of becoming a *saṃgha* is not yet complete; it must necessarily possess the three qualities of precepts (*śīla*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and learning (*śruta*). These three names signify the aspect of perfect completion; therefore, it is said that the *saṃgha* assembles.

The *saṃgha* first distributes voting sticks (*śalākā*) to signify that the assembly has been harmonized. Now, when we simply say "the harmonious *saṃgha* assembles," the intent is specifically to distinguish this from the *śrāmaṇeras*.
Just as in the present-day recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), "the *saṃgha* assembles" comes first and "harmony" follows later; to do otherwise would violate the *Vinaya* commentary.
As for the phrase "the ritual is as in other methods," this refers to the procedures for the five qualities and the ten numbers, which are clearly explained in the *Śrāmaṇera-vibhaṅga*.
When answering, one says, "There is no one who has communicated their *kṣānti* (consent). This is a concise abbreviation preserved in the *Chao*. When asking, one must say:

"The bhikṣus who have not come have communicated their *kṣānti* and *viśuddhi* (purity). When answering, one should likewise follow this dual response; however, to say only "communicated their *kṣānti*" is a transgression that violates the Dharma.
This is because there is no distinct quality that can clarify it. Xuán says: "The instructions for instructing bhikṣuṇīs require the complete possession of ten qualities.
Even if this person possesses the aforementioned nine qualities, she is still not permitted [to instruct] if she has not yet completed twenty years of summer retreat (*varṣa*).

This tenth quality is a distinct quality among the ten; since the junior seat-holder has not yet fulfilled it, she lacks this specific quality that can be clarified. Therefore, [she is not qualified]."
"Having passed the time after sitting down. "By more than what? means that one is able to provide instruction in general. This is truly because of cherishing one's own karma and so forth;

this is also a term for the excellence of the *pānaka* (beverage). The commentary states: "The indication of signs and their application" refers to two texts: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* indicates that there was no [specific] person [to act as instructor], while the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* sets forth its abbreviated instructions. These two texts correspond with one another.
When [the monks and nuns] assemble in one place, they join together to perform the ritual proceedings. As for the other matters where there are clear evidentiary sources:

the above merely clarifies that the nuns come into the midst of the monks to request instruction; the monks receive their intent as the formal request, and the remaining nuns return to their own monastery to transmit the brief instructions of the monks.
This extends to such matters as those nuns ringing the bell to assemble the monks, and so forth; the words of the Elder are transmitted in this manner, and the rest is as before.
Although the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Wén-dāng-lù) does not explicitly state this, it is based on the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sēngqǐ-wén), which says, "all serve as clear evidence.

This has not been discussed at all; it only becomes manifest when one reaches the specific rules for nuns (*bhikṣuṇī-vidhi*). Therefore, one must practice reading through this entire section from beginning to end.

Other matters are as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "it is said... up to... etc.," the commentary notes: "Because the words are used interchangeably, the mutual relationship between the two parties is not clearly understood. The *Jièshū* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "There may be..."

The response states: Regarding "poṣadha" and "recitation of the precepts," *poṣadha* is the Western term and "recitation of the precepts" (*jie*) is the Eastern expression; these two names refer to one and the same essence and should not be spoken of redundantly.
The term *karmavācanā* (ritual procedure) is general, whereas the matter of reciting the precepts is specific; therefore, by presenting these two, the entirety of the communal rites is indicated.
This refers to the simultaneous application of the terms *poṣadha* (布薩) and *śīla-deśanā* (說戒).

If one uses [only] these, it is not understood that *poṣadha* is a term from the West (India) and *śīla-deśanā* is a term from this Eastern land (China); hence the expression "understood or not understood by both sides.

Regarding the phrase "the *karmadāna* returns to his original seat," etc., this is explained according to the ritual procedure where the *karmadāna* spreads his sitting mat near the wooden mallet (*ghaṇṭā*). At present...
The example regarding "taking one's place" is not so; the rest of the text may be understood accordingly.

As for the phrase "reaching ten [steps] to pay respects": if reaching [the teacher] involves a brief verbal salutation, it means that after reciting the *Saptabuddha-śīla-sūtra*, one should ring the bell, etc.
In this case, first strike the chime (*kṣaṇḍa*) within the hall, and then the bell on the upper pavilion is rung. Upon hearing the sound of the bell, the śrāmaṇeras...
[The assembly] gathers in the hall to hear the *Śramaṇera-śikṣāpada-sūtra*. [Question: Nowadays, if there are no śrāmaṇeras present, is it not necessary to strike the chime and ring the bell?

[Answer: There is an interpretation that says it is unnecessary; however, I fear this is not the case. Even though there may be no śrāmaṇeras to attend the hall, the established rules must still be strictly observed;
they must not be omitted. Furthermore, some say that on the night of the *Poṣadha* (confession ceremony), one must strike the bell.
This refers to the beginning of the night; if it is finished early, this [practice] is not required. This is a general statement that cannot be relied upon.

Regarding those who perform the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) of the immortals (*ṛṣi*), there is a modification of the characters within the verses; to say "those who compose various incantations" is an error.
How could the original intent of performing these two types of *brahmaghoṣa* (Buddhist chanting) be the same? The *Chao* (Commentary) answers: "It is for the purpose of causing them to speak."
"Those who, though possessing the full ritual decorum and expressions of courtesy... (and so forth). This is the Sanskrit text for the arrival of the merchant and the celestial being (*śramaṇa*);
it is likewise part of the liturgical text for the Vinaya assembly. Regarding the monks each reciting their own verses of congratulation: these are complete verses.

The old version of the treatise says "refreshment" (*kuài*), while the new version says "joy" (*lè*). The Venerable Jingshui said: "The wording of these verses should originally have been spoken by the Preceptor of Precepts."

Having finished the recitation, each person speaks while on their bed. Nowadays, there is no established standard for those who chant the Three Refuges and then recite [the precepts] before the ground;
therefore, the note below states: "Then they perform a prostration and disperse. Observe the flow of the text and reflect upon this.
Regarding the phrase "among these, the various characteristics": this refers to the detailed examination of various matters that were left unfinished within the preceding precepts (and so forth).
Regarding the phrase "if one arrives, etc.": this refers to those coming from outside the boundary, meaning they bring [the items] to attend the *poṣadha* ceremony.
"Upon reaching the place of recitation," one should proceed directly to the *śīla-hall*; one must not go toward private quarters or the like, even if the head of the hall is present.
When the bhikṣu Kang Bingfa entered the boundary, he did not commit the offense of a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*), because he was single-mindedly intent on hearing the precepts.

He came to recite the introduction, the inquiry into purity (*pariśuddhi-prcchā*), and so forth; however, the Preceptor had not yet recited the Extensive Introduction to the Teaching, nor had he yet performed the first of the three inquiries.

One should simply sit according to the order of seniority by summer, without further announcing purity (*śuddhi*). If a pure person arrives later, they should recite the extensive introduction to the teachings (*sūtra-pūrva-varga*) and complete the three inquiries;
only then may they come from outside. When the Preceptor sees them arrive, he must immediately stop [his recitation];

he must not continue chanting, but rather wait for a short while until that person announces their purity. If the newcomer is unwilling to stay and wait, the Preceptor should reprimand him and command him to remain, saying:

If the preceptor for the precepts does not understand [the procedure], the Elder shall immediately reprimand and stop him, instructing the preceptor to wait until the assembly has finished sitting. [The assembly] shall kneel on their right knees and announce their purity, etc.

(as detailed). Regarding monks from outside the boundary, even those who have been dealt with according to the Dharma, it is in accordance with the rules for the *poṣadha* ceremony that one must consider the relationship between the host and the guest;
this applies whether they are on the same day or different days. If they are on different days and the host and guest look toward one another, then there is [a formal connection].

Regarding strength and weakness: if the host and guest face each other on the same day, there is no distinction of strength and weakness. For now, I shall clarify the case of different days by dividing it into two positions:

first, viewing the host from the perspective of the guest; second, viewing the guest from the perspective of the host. In the first of these, for the guest, the period beyond the fourteenth day is the time of restraint (*śīla*).

It has been taught that once the *poṣadha* has been recited and one has departed from this boundary, the presiding host of this boundary does not recite it again until the fifteenth day; there are three cases regarding this:

first, if the guests who have arrived are few, they follow the host and recite again on the fifteenth day; second, if the guests who have arrived are equal in number to the residents, they likewise follow the host and recite again on the fifteenth day;
third, if the guests who have arrived are numerous, the host should request the guests to recite; if [the host] complies, they shall recite again on the fifteenth day.

It is said that it would be beneficial to recite [the precepts] again. The guest was unwilling to recite them again, so the host went outside himself to recite them. Regarding the second case, when the host looks toward the guest:

the host had already recited on the fourteenth day, while the guest was only just beginning to arrange the guest-recitation on the fifteenth day. This is also an instance of an incomplete *poṣadha*, and there are three points to it:
first, the number of guests arriving was small; they requested the host to recite again on the fifteenth day, but the host refused; consequently, the guests went outside themselves.
Regarding the external recitation: when two guests arrive and so forth, they also request that the host perform the recitation again on the fifteenth day.

If the host is unwilling, the guests may also go outside and recite it themselves. Thirdly, if many guests arrive, the host should follow the guests and perform the recitation again on the fifteenth day.
The above is based on dividing the fourteenth and fifteenth days into two positions; the same applies to the fifteenth and sixteenth days, which can be understood by analogy.
Second, regarding those who share the same day—whether it be the fourteenth, fifteenth, or sixteenth—it is likewise divided into two positions.

The first, "the host has already spoken," has been explained. The second is "the guest may speak. Now, to clarify the three phrases for when the host has already spoken: (1) the guest may come and briefly announce their purity;

(2) if the guests are equal in number to the host, the guests speak further; (3) if the guests are more numerous than the host, the guests speak further. The second position concerns when the guest has already spoken.
There are three cases: first, when the host is fewer than the guests, one announces purity; second, when the host is equal in number to the guests, one repeats the recitation;

third, when the host is more numerous than the guests, one repeats the recitation. The Vinaya text contains these two positions regarding similarity and difference. The present *Chao* (Commentary) omits the phrases concerning the differences in the number of days and so forth, and provides only the ritual procedures for the same-day case.
Therefore, the *Chao* states: "If [the host] is more numerous or equal [to the guests], even after the recitation is finished, all must repeat it. It does not [state otherwise].

This is to be dealt with according to the Dharma. This refers to the mutual relationship between host and guest; there is no question of strength or weakness. However, when many people are involved in general, it must be stated again.
If it is not so stated, it is not discussed; both host and guest are guilty of an offense. The *Shuochao* (Commentary) specifically explains this point.

Regarding the *Vinayamātṛkā* and other texts, they provide a detailed analysis based on the distinction between purity and impurity, as the text states. It says: "If the intention lies with the host, each [monastery] shall be listed."
Regarding the phrase "the bhikṣuṇīs by name," this refers to the monks of such-and-such monasteries and so forth, who dispatch bhikṣuṇīs to visit the bhikṣus and others.
The subsequent summary of the purpose of the invitation is expressed as: "Every half-month, we pay homage," and so on.
As for the phrase "if it reaches the *Zi* [commentary]," the note states: "As in the *Āgama*. This refers to the *Madhyama Āgama*. It is there that Ānanda replies to Kāśyapa, saying: [text follows].
Within a single verse, there are thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. What are they? "Commit no evil" is the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*);
"Practice all that is good" is the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*); "Purify one's own mind" is the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).
This is the summary of all the Buddha’s teachings, intended for people; none of the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths possess such a teaching. All of these belong to the Buddha.

Regarding "repeated exhortations" (*lei-zhu*): when matters are arranged in successive layers of importance, it is called a repeated exhortation. This is as in the preceding text: first, one orders them to recite a sutra;

if there is no one to recite, one orders them to recite a single verse; if they cannot do that either, one simply says, "Do not be negligent. Such successive layers of instruction constitute a repeated exhortation.
Regarding the statement "negligence in residing at a monastery is a light violation of the disciplinary net," according to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Sengzhuan*), there was...

At that time, the Dharma Master Sengyun was presiding over the assembly as the senior monk (*upādhyāya*). At the beginning of the summer retreat, when it was time to recite the precepts, he addressed the community, saying:

"The essence of the precepts is to prevent wrongdoing; if one is free from unwholesome thoughts, what need is there for such formalities? For the duration of this summer, let us temporarily suspend the recitation of the precepts and instead engage in discussions on the meaning of the teachings.
When the fifteenth day of the seventh month arrived and they were about to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, Master Yun suddenly disappeared. [Four characters missing.]
He then went to search for him. At a distance of several *li*, he found him among ancient tombs, his entire body covered in blood.

When people asked him the reason, he said: "A man wielding a three-foot-long great sword appeared; with a fierce and wrathful countenance, he changed the *poṣadha* ceremony and hacked at my body with his blade.
The pain was unbearable. Because I lightly spoke of the net of the precepts and teachings, I have received this retribution in this very life. Therefore, I did not comply."

As for "explaining," it refers to not transmitting [the precepts] every half-month. Regarding "defiling pure consciousness": at the time of first receiving [the precepts], there is no offense, hence it is called "pure";
subsequently, if an offense occurs, this is "defiled. "Great Dharma" refers to the dharma of the precepts;
because this is the foundation of the unsurpassed Bodhisattva, it is called "great. The rest is as in the text. As for the phrase "if one reaches the open air," it may be understood accordingly.
"Regarding the 'Brief Explanation of Miscellaneous Methods' by Siming: this is the heading. Regarding the section from 'The Four Parts' to 'The Precepts':

'The difficulty of kings' refers to military forces [yīng-yún; yún is pronounced *hú-láng*] entering the monastery. 'The difficulty of bandits' refers to violent robbers suddenly breaking in while the precepts are being recited;

the bhikṣus stop their recitation, and the bandits then inflict harm. 'The difficulty of water' refers to its power to sweep away and toss about. 'Fire' refers to its inherent nature to burn and consume. 'Sickness'..."
"Human" refers to the preceptor suddenly falling ill. "Non-human" refers to malevolent spirits and ghosts. "Insects" refers to snakes, scorpions, and the like.

Regarding the difficulties posed by humans, the text of the *Naishao* (Excerpts) clarifies this [and so forth]. "Other circumstances" refers to those collectively termed "other circumstances," which exist outside of the eight difficulties.
"Many illnesses" means that among the many people listening to the precepts, many are afflicted by illness and cannot remain seated for long; thus, the *poṣadha* has already lasted many nights.

Regarding the term "long ago" (jiǔ), the commentary explains it for itself. Question: Since this now permits the *poṣadha* as a ritual for the confession of offenses (*pāpadeśanā*), why was it previously refuted in the preceding text?
Answer: It does not preclude its inclusion within the ritual for confessing offenses; the Master of the present day does not hold to a fixed position, whereas the ancients adhered to it unilaterally.
The refutation in the preceding passage is intended solely to refute the fixed attachments of others; reflect upon this.
Regarding the statement "from ten [precepts] up to not being interrupted," this cites the texts of various schools. As for "practicing together with companions," Wanling says:

"This refers to acting as a companion by following the merchant’s journey. "Detailed exposition" means that when the merchant stops, one recollects the detailed precepts; "abbreviated exposition" refers to the brief summary.

"Approximately for a short time" refers to the abbreviated precepts; this is the formal cause (*nidāna*). Both of these refer to the performance of the *jñapti* motion in a small assembly within a defined boundary (*sīmā*).

Regarding "speaking in three statements": this refers to cases where traveling merchants do not stay even briefly, or when a bhikṣu conducts himself improperly and does not perform the *jñapti* motion, but instead speaks in three or five statements.
Although there may be many people present, they merely exchange words with one another because they are performing a separate ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*). Thus it is said of that [case].
This is discussed in terms of the *dharmadhātu* that is not subject to formal binding; understand this. Regarding the "five parts" and so forth, that Vinaya states:

When the *poṣadha* was being recited in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*), bandits arrived. Upon seeing them coming, the bhikṣus went up [to hide]. The bandits asked, "Why are you remaining silent like this?
They replied, "What we recite must not be heard by laypeople (*avadātavasana*). Because the bandits were angry with the bhikṣus, they seized their robes and helmets.
He reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "From now on, when bandits arrive, you should recite sūtras and so forth in a continuous voice" (and so forth).
As for what is meant by "if one arrives at the time of preaching": regarding minor matters, one should entrust the instruction; this is equivalent to transmitting the *chanda* (consent).

These are merely small affairs and do not constitute a formal occasion [for the full procedure]. "In a public place" excludes a private location, because a guest arriving there would not see [the proceedings].

Regarding the phrase "as for reaching the categories": first, the brief extraction of the titles from eight chapters, which marks the transition from the urgent toward the gradual, is the "Fifteen-Day Brief.
Second, the brief extraction that follows the categories of the chapters, which marks the transition from the gradual toward the urgent, is the "Seven Briefs" and the "Direct.
The Venerable Jing-shui said: "If one follows the new chapters and old commentaries, the 'brief extraction' is restricted to the former [the Fifteen-Day Brief], which consists of ten [chapters]."

The five types of omissions are for other circumstances (*pratyaya*) and do not apply during the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*). The latter type of omission, namely the "omission of the site" (*bhūmi-laghu*), applies only to the eight difficulties and does not apply to other circumstances.
Now, the Nanshan [Vinaya school] is not like this; these two types both apply to both circumstances and difficulties. Therefore, the *Jie-mo han-zhu shu* (Commentary on the *Karmavācanā*) states:

"The eight difficulties and other circumstances—according to the *Pañcavargika* and the *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinayas]—are all explained as being subject to omission, provided they follow the specific circumstances and difficulties."

There is both shifting and slowness; this is explained in detail and in brief (the above is from the commentary). If one were to say that the former brevity refers to conditions and the latter brevity refers to difficulties, one fears that the accommodation to capacities would not be fixed; consider this.

Regarding the statement "explaining the ultimate dharma," this refers to weighing matters such as urgency and so forth; that is, measuring the eight difficulties and the relative speed or slowness of other circumstances.
Regarding "observing whether the disposition is advancing or not," one observes the human condition, where slowness constitutes both advancement and non-advancement.
As for "explaining the preliminary expedients as in the extensive teaching," one should maintain the formal procedures exactly as usual; they must not be abbreviated. If...

If the *jñapti* (motion) has not been made and the *śikṣāpada* (precepts) have not been recited, it merely falls within the category of "increase or decrease" (*vṛddhi-hāni*) and is not called an "abbreviated" (*saṃkṣipta*) procedure.
Regarding the phrase "the introduction is reached," this means that the recitation of the extensive introduction to the teaching has been completed.

Regarding the question "Have you attained purity?"—this refers to the three inquiries following the first part of the introduction. The passage beginning with "Venerable sirs, [you should say]... and ending with "...the Saṃgha constantly hears" constitutes the formal core of the rite.

This clarifies the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*). With other conditions being somewhat leisurely, the latter [section] briefly extracts from the middle. At the beginning of the titles of the various chapters, two categories must be expanded;
these constitute the *Pañcāśad-uddāna-śīla* (The Fifty Brief Precepts). Fabao states: "Now, this is merely the text of the commentary.
It cites only from the beginning of the first among the five briefs up to the fifth among the third five, omitting the thirteen briefs in between."
This refers to the "abbreviations" (lue), up to and including the word "even" (zai). Bao further states: "These fifteen abbreviations are based on what may be said;
they must be applied when reciting the precepts fifteen times in succession, not suggesting that these fifteen exist within a single recitation.

Since the Vinaya text discusses them in terms of three or five [recitations], I shall now set forth their method (as follows). Regarding the first five abbreviations, they are as follows: [The text continues with the specific details of the five abbreviations.]

On the day of the *poṣadha*, it was known in advance that there would be obstacles due to external circumstances. The community of monks deliberated together and said, "Tonight we shall recite the precepts, but we shall proceed only as far as the 'Extensive Preface' (*keng-chiao hsü*).
Later, when they ascended the seat to recite, they had just finished the Preface. At that moment, someone reported that the obstacles were about to arrive.
Thus, one briefly takes up the titles of the four categories up to the eight sections of the *Śaikṣa* rules; this is the first of the five types of abbreviations.

As for the second abbreviation: the original intention was that tonight’s recitation of the precepts would proceed until the end of the introduction (*nidāna*), but as the Preceptor recited through it, the time for the *Pratideśanīya* offenses drew near.

Upon finishing the *Pratideśanīya*, the time for the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses drew near, so he then abbreviated the titles of the seven sections beginning with the thirteen *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules.

"Beginning with the head [of the precepts], etc. (as detailed above). Regarding the three types of abbreviated recitation: the original intention was that tonight’s recitation of the precepts would end at the *nidāna* (introduction).

When the *nidāna* was finished, the circumstances were difficult and time was pressing, so one further recited the four *pārājika* rules. When the four *pārājikas* were finished, the circumstances remained difficult and time was still pressing, so one further recited the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules.

When the thirteen were finished, the difficulty of the situation was about to arrive; thus, one simply took up the titles of the six sections beginning with the two *aniyata* rules (as detailed above). This is the original intention of the fourth type of abbreviated recitation.

Tonight, when reciting the precepts, one stops at the *Nidāna* (Introduction). When the *Nidāna* is finished, the *Pratideśanīya* (Confessions) has not yet been reached. One then recites the four *Pārājika* (Defeats) and the thirteen *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Formal Meetings).

When these are finished, the *Pratideśanīya* has still not been reached. One then recites the two *Aniyata* (Undetermined) rules. When the two *Aniyata* rules are completed, the *Pratideśanīya* is near.

Thereupon, one briefly takes up the titles of the five sections from the thirty [rules] downward (*etc.*). In the five abbreviated versions, one first recites the *Nidāna*. When the *Nidāna* is finished, the *Pratideśanīya* has not yet arrived. One then recites...
Regarding the four *pārājika*, the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and the two *aniyata* rules, the obstacles have not yet arrived; one should further recite the thirty [rules].

When the obstacles approach at the end of the thirty, one should briefly take up the titles and so forth of the four sections from the ninety rules downward (the "abbreviated precepts" used nowadays are this very abbreviation). Second, regarding the five abbreviations:

when the night for the *poṣadha* arrives, the community of monks should collectively deliberate, fearing that there may be difficult circumstances preventing a full recitation; thus, they may simply...

Regarding the four *pārājika* rules: when one reaches the point of ascending the seat and recites up to the four *pārājikas*, if the difficulties approach the monastery, one then briefly takes up the titles of the seven sections from the thirteenth rule downward;
this is called the "first abridgment. As for the "second abridgment," the original intent was: "Tonight’s recitation of the precepts shall end with the four *pārājikas.
Once the four *pārājikas* are finished and before the difficulties arrive, one further recites the thirteen [rules]; once the thirteen are finished..."
When approaching the temple, he briefly took up the titles of the six sections beginning with the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules (*etc.*). Regarding the three briefings:
his original intention was to reach the four *pārājika* (defeats), but before reaching them, he recalled the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meetings);
before finishing those, he further recited the two *aniyata* rules. Having mastered the two *aniyata* rules, he approached the temple and then briefly took up the thirty [rules].

The headings of the five sections below (etc.). Regarding the "Four Abbreviations": the original intention was to recite up to the four *pārājika* offenses. When the four *pārājikas* were finished, the recitation had not yet reached its end;
he then recited the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and two *aniyata* rules. As the recitation still did not reach the end, he then recited the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules.

Upon reaching the thirtieth rule, the recitation drew near to the temple, so he abbreviated it by taking only the headings of the four sections from the ninety *pāyattika* rules downward (this is the "abbreviated precepts" used at present).

Regarding the five abridgments: the original intention was to recite up to the four *pārājika* rules. When the four *pārājikas* were finished but the difficult questions had not yet arrived, one would further recite the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣas*, the two *aniyata*s, and the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*s. Because these too had not yet arrived, one would recite the ninety *pāyattika*s.

When the ninety *pāyattika*s were finished and the difficult questions drew near to the temple, one would then briefly take up the titles of the three sections from the four *pratideśanīya*s downward. The third abridgment occurs when reaching the *poṣadha* (confession of precepts).

That night, the assembly of monks deliberated, fearing that adverse circumstances might arise and thus prevent them from reciting the precepts in full. They decided they could only recite up to the thirteenth precept.

When the Preceptor ascended the seat and reached the thirteenth precept, and the difficulties were about to arrive, he briefly took up only the titles of the five sections beginning with the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules;
this constitutes the first abbreviated version. As for the second abbreviated version, the original intention was to recite up to the tenth precept tonight.
3. The thirteen [rules] concluded; the *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* had not yet arrived. He thought briefly of the two *Aniyata* rules. The two *Aniyata* rules were also not yet reached.
He then proceeded toward the monastery and briefly took up the titles of the four sections from the thirty [rules] downward. Regarding these three "brief" [recollections]:

originally he intended to recite from the *Śaikṣa* rules up to the thirteen [rules], but the thirteen [rules] concluded and the *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* had not yet arrived. He again thought of the two *Aniyata* rules, but they too had not yet arrived. He then thought of the conclusion of the thirty [rules].
It was difficult to approach. He then briefly took up the titles of the three sections from the ninety [pācittiyas] downward (the "Brief Precepts" used today is this very abridgment).

Regarding the four abridgments: he intended to recite up to the thirteenth [section], but before reaching the end of the thirteenth, it became difficult to approach. He then further recited the two *aniyata* rules and the thirty [nissaggiya pācittiyas].

Because he had not yet reached them, he further recited the ninety [pācittiyas]. Having finished the ninety, it was difficult to approach the monastery; he then briefly took up the four *thullaccaya* rules.
Regarding the titles at the beginning of the final two sections: the five abbreviated [recitations] are as follows. Originally, the intention was to recite up to the thirty rules.

When the thirty were completed but the difficult portion had not yet arrived, one further recited the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules and the thirty-ninth and fortieth rules. Because these had not yet arrived, one further recited the four *prātideśanīya* (offenses requiring confession).

As the difficult portion was about to arrive, one then briefly took up the title of the single section on the *śaikṣa* (rules of training). These aforementioned items are called the fifteen abbreviations.
All these are termed "abbreviated selections. They all proceed from the urgent toward the relaxed. Among the various commentaries (*ji*), none employ this method of sequential abbreviation.

As for those who are confused in their understanding, although I shall now explain it extensively, it will not be overly prolix; only thus can the principle of proceeding from the urgent to the relaxed be revealed.
Consider this. An external objection asks: "Why do these three or five abbreviated [rules] not extend to the *Śaikṣa-dharmas*? Regarding the Dharma:
Baoyun said: "The precepts consist of five sections. If one recites the *Śaikṣa* rules, it cannot be called 'abbreviated.

Regarding the fact that each section has its own title followed by a general concluding formula, the *Xuánjì* presents two interpretations. The first states: 'Listing the titles of the various sections constitutes the individual headings;

at the end, appending the single phrase "as constantly heard by the Saṃgha" constitutes the general conclusion. The second interpretation states: 'Following the beginning of each section, [the titles] are applied individually...'"
Zhu Sengchang heard this. As for what is now called "comprehensive" (tong), it simply refers to the fact that the words heard by the Sangha are comprehensive.
Faba said: "One should take the subsequent interpretation. The initial explanation does not fail to establish the brief precepts and meditative concentration;

however, this term "comprehensive" here refers to the seven points collectively functioning as a whole, which is why it is named "comprehensive. Why labor over such groundless assertions? Nowadays there are even those who label everything with a single "all" (zhu).
To place the heading "The Venerable Ones" at the beginning of each section would likewise constitute an improper practice.

Now, one should instead designate each of the Venerable Ones individually and record what the Saṃgha regularly hears; only then will it be appropriate. Since this matter concerns a point of urgent procedure, I have described it in detail.

Regarding the "Seven Methods for Settling Disputes," they are explained extensively below; an abbreviated treatment is certainly not permitted. An external objection asks: Why must the Seven Methods for Settling Disputes be explained in full detail?
"Why is it that you do not permit abbreviation? In response, it is said that practices differ between ancient and modern times. The Great Virtuous One (Dade) stated:

"The *Shoushu* and the Xiangbu school both say that abbreviation is permissible; it is simply that they did not follow the established tradition. Now, however, both the Nanshan and Dongta schools do not permit abbreviation.
Although the two schools are identical in this regard, their judgment cannot be considered cursory; yet when it comes to the interpretation of the ritual procedures (*vidhi*), they differ once more.

The Dongta school states: "The seven *vinayas* can eradicate the four types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*); thus, monks are exempt from the seven *duṣkṛtas*, and nuns are exempt from the seven *sthūlātyayas*. For this reason, [the ritual] is not permitted."
The Great Virtuous One (Bhadanta) raised this objection: "If that were so, why not recite the one hundred rules of the *Śaikṣa* and the one hundred *Duṣkṛta* offenses in full?
Therefore, [your position] is unreasonable. Our Master now replies: "It is simply because the Vinaya text contains only fifteen summaries (*saṃkṣepa*), beginning from the four *Pārājika* offenses."
It concludes with the *śaikṣa* rules. To abbreviate [the recitation], one stops only at the *śaikṣa* rules and does not include the seven points of contention (*adhikaraṇa*).

If such abbreviation were permitted, it would result in sixteen types of abridgment, which would contradict the texts of other Vinayas and naturally constitute what is not the Dharma (*adharma*). Therefore, the extensive recitation was established. Among the various commentaries:

This most urgent ritual is not described [in detail] elsewhere; let students know this. Regarding those points in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* that are incomplete, the Vinaya texts themselves contain three or five abbreviated explanations;
depending on the circumstances—whether distant or near—the wording is not explicit. What was just explained follows the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, which is as clear as this.

Regarding the phrase "if one reaches the point of departing," this section clarifies that "abridgment" (*lue*) means to proceed directly from the slow toward the rapid, which is termed "abridging and omitting" (*lueque*).

Whereas the preceding discussion on "abridgment" (*luequ*) involved taking from the front toward the back, the present "abridging and omitting" (*lueque*) refers to proceeding from the back toward the front.

This means that although one originally intended to recite extensively, unexpected circumstances suddenly arise; since these were not known beforehand, as soon as [calamities such as] water, fire, or bandits occur...
When urgent and difficult circumstances arise, one must not remain long at the Dharma seat.

According to whatever section comes to mind, one should immediately disperse according to the four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*) and the various precepts pertaining to the three poisons (*tri-viṣa*).

One cannot further retrieve the specific titles of the sections once they have been passed. If urgent circumstances numbering ninety arise, this refers to unexpected and pressing matters. This concludes the introduction.
Regarding the phrase "the rest has already been heard by the Saṃgha," this refers to the seventh abridgment among the seven.

If one is unable to recite the introduction and what follows, one may simply recite the words of the exhortation at once and disperse; this illustrates one direct method. Thus, the explanation according to one school is concluded for now.

Furthermore, according to various commentaries, it is said that if there are difficult circumstances, [one may recite] up to the ninety [verses] (this is the phrase regarding the "earth"). Upon reaching...

Regarding the phrase "having already stated the locations, as for the remainder": the collective intention is that within the five categories [of offenses], one should reflect upon which location [the offense] falls;

according to that location, difficult distinctions are omitted and the text proceeds downward. The *Chao* (Commentary) frequently uses the character "chù" (location), [which should be understood as "to contemplate"]. The above is a brief explanation of the text. Now, I shall further clarify the practical application (*xingxiang*).
That is to say, this is currently the fortnightly [observance], and it is not known whether there are circumstances involving difficulties; this is based on the regular practice.

Regarding the intention to recite the *Bhikṣu-Prātimokṣa* in full: the preceptor ascends the seat and recites up to the *Pratideśanīya* offenses. Suddenly, an abbreviated method arises. First, one says:
"The rest has been regularly heard by the Saṃgha"; this is the first abbreviation. Second, the recitation proceeds until the *Naiḥsargika-Pāyattika* (the ninety offenses) are reached.

Third, the recitation proceeds until the *Pāyattika* offenses are reached. Fourth, the recitation proceeds until the two *Aniyata* offenses arise. Fifth, the recitation reaches the thirteen *Śaikṣa* rules. Sixth, [the recitation] proceeds...

Upon reaching the fourth section, there are difficulties. When the sevenfold recitation of the extensive introduction (*prastāvanā*) is finished, the difficulties arise. The *Chao* (Commentary) cites this single phrase: "One simply does not yet recite the introduction;

rather, having finished the admonitions, one then departs. Regarding the above seven summaries, since it is said that they proceed from the gradual to the urgent, crossing over to the single point of setting the mind, all are intended for the extensive recitation.
This is the reason. However, because there are difficulties in the interim, they cannot be called "as extensive" as the full version.

This is called "urgent. It must be understood as referring to the seven types of *saṃkṣepa* (abbreviations) occurring across both preceding and subsequent [procedures], not that these seven abbreviations, such as the *sāvaśeṣa*, occur all at once in a single instance.

The Venerable Master says: "In general, there are twenty-two *saṃkṣepas* in total from what has preceded; if one includes the single direct [procedure], there are twenty-three instances in total. This is explained with reference to the Great Monks (*bhikṣu*).
For the community of Nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), there are no two *aniyata* (undetermined offenses). Among the aforementioned abbreviations, there are only two sets of five *saṃkṣepas*."
First is the Introduction; second, the Eight Grave Offenses; third, the Seventeen Saṃghāvaśeṣa; fourth, the Thirty Naiḥsargika-pāyattika; and fifth, the Prātideśanīya.
Regarding the two sets of five that are abbreviated: first, the Introduction and the Eight Grave Offenses; second, the Saṃghāvaśeṣa; and third, the Thirty Naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
The fourth is the *pācittiya*; the fifth is the *pātidesanīya*. If one were to discuss them in brief, there are only six brief categories, which are straightforward and easy to understand.
Nowadays, many people claim that the *bhikṣuṇī* community also has fifteen brief categories; such people have never examined the Vinaya texts and are merely speaking from their own conjectures.

Regarding what was stated above concerning "those who have reached the summit": if there is a violation regarding even a single matter, or if it is a difficult circumstance that makes compliance impossible, and others merely say "the rest," this is something the Saṃgha hears constantly;

thus, it is not a matter of urgent haste. This would contradict the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*. In all such cases, one incurs a formal offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa* or *pārājika*), and it should not be considered a minor fault (*duṣkṛta*).
All such instances should be judged according to the precedents set forth in the aforementioned *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*; one must not deviate from what has already been explained.

Furthermore, regarding those who collectively commit an offense: since there are already abbreviated conditions for providing a brief explanation to others, if one now fails to explain at all, the entire assembly incurs the offense of violating the teachings; hence it is said, "it applies to all" (and so forth).

Regarding the phrase "as for the method for two [or three] people": this refers to groups of two or three individuals. "Distinct method" means it is distinguished from the formal *saṃgha* procedure. Regarding the phrase "as for 'if one reaches three recitations'":
it is as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "if one reaches the third recitation": the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyāna* (Jie-mo-su) states:

"When the *saṃgha* performs the *poṣadha*, one person presides over the recitation while the rest remain silent. When it comes to the subsequent *pratyekamukha* (individual) procedure, each person must individually manifest their purity. Why is this not [done here]?"

The same. Answer: Regarding the *Saṃgha-dharma* (the legal procedure for the Saṃgha), it is accomplished when there are few people and they are weak, provided that internal purity is manifested (this is the text of the commentary).
As for the phrase "if one reaches the dharma," the meaning of the text is easy to understand.

Regarding the phrase "if one reaches the point of severance" or "if one confesses," the Vinaya states: There was a bhikṣu who had doubts and awareness regarding his offenses, yet he was unable to hear the *poṣadha* (precepts).

The Buddha said: "He should confess and then he may hear the precepts. Regarding the phrase "waiting for another person," the Vinaya states that he should face a pure bhikṣu and listen as he confesses.
As for the statement that the Vinaya does not clearly specify "severance," the intended meaning is as follows:
Now, there are those who dwell alone. Should they merely recite the precepts in their own minds as a full confession, or must they wait for another person to perform a face-to-face confession?
Since there is no explicit textual authority providing a definitive resolution on this matter, it is said that "the Vinaya lacks a clear determination."
Regarding the present school: it is said that the current Master, following the *Pañcavargika-vinaya-śāstra* and harmonizing it with the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, provides a joint commentary on them.
The Vinaya states: "One must confess before a pure bhikṣu. The Śāstra states: "First, one should repent before the Saṃgha of the four directions.
Based on these two texts, it is said that the universal explanation requires that one must first mentally confess. The Commentary (*Śū*) says: "If there is no one available..."
Form the thought: "If I have committed an offense against a pure bhikṣu, having removed it according to the Dharma, I shall now mentally reflect and verbally declare it.
Recite the *poṣadha* three times; this constitutes a confession before the Saṃgha of the four directions.
Next, citing the *Pañcaśataprakaraṇa-śāstra*, this indicates the recitation of the precepts for internal purity (the above concludes the section on the recitation of precepts).
Next, the commentary on the section "Distinguishing the Matters of Summer Retreat (An-ju) by Way of Realm and Person" is divided into two major parts.
First, the explanation of the title. Regarding the initial phrase "From 'Peace' (An) to 'Attachment' (Fu)," the intent of its inclusion is first clarified. Master Xuan states:

"Since the *Śīla-mātṛkā* (Precept Manual) has already been proclaimed above, and one has recognized transgressions and understood how to maintain the precepts, it is logically appropriate to rely upon a dwelling place for refined cultivation and to exert the three karmas [of body, speech, and mind]. This is the primary...

Regarding the suppression of sorrow: it serves to quell worldly censure and envy, as these were not previously discussed. To explain the meaning of the name according to this tradition, the *Karmasūtra-vyākhyā* states:
"The stillness and restraint of body and mind is called 'peace' (*an*); the commitment to abide therein is called 'dwelling' (*ju*); and the alerting of the three karmas is called 'exertion' (*ce*)."

The four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*) constitute the cultivation of power (*vīrya*). The details are as explained in the regular commentary. Regarding the term "receiving" (*shou*), it refers to the Dharma; the intent behind its inclusion and the explanation of its name follow the subsequent examples.

Within the general meaning of the explanation according to the chapters, it says: "Now, as for those who have attained the ultimate goal and those who contemplate the subtle in a quiet place"—here, "quiet" (*jing*) means stillness (*śānti*).

"Quietude" (*jing*). "Abiding" (*chu*)—the character is pronounced *chōng lǚ*—refers to resting from all conditions; thus, it is called the "abode of quietude. "Contemplation" (*si*) means reflection. "Subtle" (*wei*) means profound and subtle.
Since external conditions are already stilled, one internally reflects upon the subtle and profound Truth.

Regarding "the correct track of the Way": this refers to a standard or rule. Tranquil contemplation is the correct principle for practicing the Way. This principle necessarily requires the passage of days.

Regarding the term "etcetera" (ādi): the principles [of practice] are not accomplished in a single morning or evening; therefore, one must rely upon the accumulation of days to pursue and perfect one's efforts.

To "urge forward the mind and conduct" means that diligent perseverance without falling into decline is called "urging" (cakra), while cultivating meditative concentration and practicing wisdom is termed "urging the mind" (cittotsāha).

When the training in ethical discipline becomes increasingly firm, it serves as one's own "urging conduct. Regarding the phrase "relying on conditions and abiding in a place, with a resolve that accords with the aforementioned benefits": this refers to following [the teachings].

"Conditions" (*pratyaya*) refers to the conditions that provide provisional support and nourishment. "Secluded place" (*viveka-sthāna*) refers to a quiet location at night. "Volition" (*citta*) means the mind. "Concentration" (*samādhi*) means single-mindedness.
"Supreme benefit" (*viśeṣa-adhigama*) refers to the superior fruit of sainthood; because it is a benefit beyond which nothing surpasses it, it is called the "supreme benefit.
Regarding the prohibition against "wandering and scattering," to follow after [external objects] is called "wandering of the body"; external matters [disturb] the emotions entirely.
If the mind is distracted, one cannot cultivate the Path; it obstructs superior practice.

Regarding the statement, "Therefore, the Vinaya prescribes that one must sit [in meditation]," this universally regulates the three seasons. In the text of the *An-gu-jiàn-du* (Kṣudraka-vastu/Anuparīkṣā-vastu), it is prescribed that during the three seasons of spring, summer, and winter, when there are no affairs, one is not permitted to travel about;
to do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. The intent in relying upon the Path is to cause the practitioner to...

Based on the foundation of the path and its practice, an external objection is raised: "Since the Vinaya universally mandates the *an-gu* (rainy-season retreat) for all three seasons, why does the text mention only the summer *an-gu*, and not speak of spring or winter? One may cite the *Shō* (Commentary), which answers:

"Generally speaking, the focus is on the summer months because the [monastic] intention lies in avoiding the three faults" (*etc.*). Regarding the phrase "first, those without affairs," this refers to the ordained monks and nuns.

The honored guests of the three realms intend to take up the seven requisites; yet, if one does not cultivate the practice of renunciation but instead hastens to travel about, it is therefore said that this hinders the cultivation of the path of renunciation.
Regarding the second point, "harming and injuring," it refers to the time when first receiving [the precepts] toward all sentient beings.
They made a solemn vow and commitment to abstain from killing. If one were now to harm or injure living beings, it would not be a slight violation of their original compassionate heart;
