therefore, it is said that [the offense] is "profoundly deep. Regarding the phrase "since what was done is not equal," according to the narrative context of the Vinaya, the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) traveled about during the summer retreat, trampling and killing living beings.
Laypeople and others all reproached them, saying: "How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, lack a sense of shame?"

[Feeling] shame, [he thought: "I have trodden upon living plants and trees, severing the life-faculties of others. Even among the various non-Buddhist (tīrthika) traditions, they still observe a three-month summer retreat (varṣā).
As for insects and birds, they all possess nests and burrows. He reported this to the Buddha, who then established the rule for the summer retreat (anujñāta varṣā).

Furthermore, during the summer, non-Buddhists and laypeople claimed that plants and trees possess life-faculties; seeing bhikṣus trampling and injuring them, they all said, "This is no different from taking the life of a sentient being."

As for the statement that "the various meanings are not non-existent," this is indeed correct. Regarding the summer and winter retreats (*varṣā* and *hemanta*), it is not that there are no direct prohibitions or offenses concerning the loss of life;
rather, among the three seasons, the prohibition specifically applies to the summer because it concerns the loss of life that occurs particularly during the summer months.
Thus, the mention of even a square-foot of ground during the summer precisely clarifies that there are many insects within the summer period, and it establishes the prohibition.

Regarding the partial protection [of the rules] found in texts such as the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, Xuánzàng states: "According to the practice of eminent practitioners in the Western Regions during the summer retreat (*varṣā*), they beg for food only once;

when seated, they remain in one position throughout. Thus, we know that [the rule against lying down] applies only to the exclusion of defecating and urinating. As for the phrase "from '云故' to '云者': [this indicates the range of the cited passage].

"To necessarily contradict the words of the Sage" means to fail to comply with the scriptural texts; to enter the summer retreat (*varṣā*) [at an improper time] is to contradict the words of the Sage.

"The fault lies in not requesting" refers to the offense of violating the regulations, which may be expiated according to the relevant section of the code. However, the fundamental offense of taking life (*prāṇātipāta*) cannot be removed through confession;

therefore, it is said that "the fault lies in not requesting. Thus, the Sūtra states: "Only the calamities of past karma cannot be requested [to be averted]. "Karmic bonds entangle themselves" refers to the formation of...

Regarding "the karma of killing and harming," to be "perpetually flowing in the sea of suffering" means for a very long time. To "trample and injure the lives of sentient beings" incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
furthermore, there is the path of karma wherein failing to observe the summer retreat (*vassa*) gives rise to the *thullaccaya* offense and leads to rebirth in hell (*niraya*).
When will one see deliverance from this? Therefore, the phrase "perpetual sea of suffering" and so forth constitutes the Master’s concluding exhortation.
Regarding the statement "the beginning arrives at the non-": as for the division of the beginning into five parts, an external critic asks:

"In the opening chapters of all preceding sections, it is always said 'within this,' so why does this section alone say 'the beginning is divided into five'? Fabao says: "There is indeed a profound meaning in this."
That is to say, within other chapters there is generally only one major section; even if there are supplementary rules (*dharma*), they consist of at most two major sections.

This present chapter, however, contains three major sections: first, the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat); second, the receiving of days (*ādeśa*); and third, miscellaneous detailed analysis (*viniścaya*).

The reason a section on detailed analysis is added here is that while the *varṣā* encompasses both natural and formal procedures (*karmavācanā*), the receiving of days is not fixed; if it is received through the formal procedure of the Saṃgha...
The "day" (jī) refers exclusively to the formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*). If one receives the day’s permission through face-to-face confession (*pratimukha*), it applies to both realms.

For this reason, a third category is established to distinguish it from the aforementioned two categories. This clarifies the meaning of the commonality and exclusivity regarding the reception of the day for the rains retreat (*varṣā*). Now, within this section:

The latter two [sections] and the *Anāgamya* (preliminary concentration) are provisionally placed within the main body of the *Varsa* (Rainy Season Retreat). Therefore, it is said that they constitute the beginning and middle.
Since there are five distinct textual segments, it is stated that they are "divided into five. These are listed in full according to the text.

Furthermore, wherever there are rules that must be harmonized with other sections, they are all extracted as separate chapters beneath the titles of those sections. Having first clarified the general intent, the procedure for receiving the days [of retreat] is then appended.

It is categorized within the section on chapters (piān). Therefore, one should know that among the various records, this intention has not been fully elucidated. *Sòuxuán* and the *Huáinán* [commentaries] are both confused;
they take the third major section and force it into the category of "Treatises" (zǐ), as will be self-evident when the texts are compared below.
Regarding the phrase "the initial arrival is restricted," it is as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "the initial arrival for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat)," concerning those on trees:
according to the circumstances in the Vinaya, a bhikṣu was practicing the *varṣā* atop a tree; he discharged excrement and urine, thereby defiling the tree deity and nearly causing its death.
He reported this to the Buddha, who said, "One must not practice the *varṣā* atop a tree," and further, "One must not discharge excrement or urine to the left or right of the tree."
If it is a withered, dry tree, it is permitted to stay upon it without fault. At that time, the bhikṣus wished to observe the rains retreat under trees and informed the Buddha.

The Buddha permitted them to stay where they would not be obstructed by their heads, provided the branches and leaves were sufficient to shade a single seat. This applied even to those who wished to go toward small huts.
It is permitted for one to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*) in a small cave, provided that the head does not [expose]. However, if the head is superior [to other parts], it is permissible.
Regarding "the feet obstructing water and rain," Xuánzàng says: this means the feet are able to avoid water at both locations; it does not refer to a fixed rule regarding the hands and feet.

Regarding those who rely on cowherds and so forth: according to the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, the Buddha permitted monks observing the *varṣā* retreat to dwell in reliance upon cowherds, woodcutters, oil-pressers, and boatmen. If they must move or depart during the interval, they should go wherever they must.

Furthermore, monks, when relying on a village for the rains retreat (*vassa*), if that village is divided into two parts and provisions are supplied according to each location, one should remain in retreat where all necessities are fully provided.
If one moves from that place, it constitutes a violation of the monastic code (*vinaya*). Regarding the ambiguity of the code:
this refers to the fact that, in view of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there are two meanings, thus rendering it unclear. First, the *Caturvargika-vinaya* merely states: [text missing].
One may rely on cowherds and the like for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat). For now, let us not discuss the prior period of free choice.

Second, regarding relocation: it simply says to go wherever one goes. It does not say that by going elsewhere one loses the summer retreat, nor does it mention "faithful devotion," "abundance," and so forth.
Only when one examines the text of the five-part division below will one understand clearly. The commentary states: "It does not say 'the prior summer.'"

This is also a passage concerning the rules for the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat). At that time, some merchants were staying there. The bhikṣus wished to rely on them for the *varṣā*, so they informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to rely on the merchants for the *varṣā*. While staying there, an urgent matter suddenly arose, and the bhikṣus had to depart.
Not knowing what to do, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I allow you to go as you please. Furthermore, the merchants divided themselves into two groups. [The bhikṣus] compared...
The Master [Kāśyapa] did not know what to do. The Buddha said, "Go wherever you have faith and confidence; there, your needs shall be abundantly provided.

This applies equally to those who rely on cowherds or those who make bamboo-pole rafts. The *Śāstra* commentary notes that it does not say one loses the summer retreat (*varṣa*), and by principle, one should indeed be permitted to do so.
Regarding the phrase "if in a place without protection," it says: at one time, there was a bhikṣu who was in a place without protection...

Regarding the dwelling: "dwelling in seclusion" refers to being robbed by bandits; "having no place to flee to" refers to being exposed in the open air; and "being stripped of one's robes while dwelling in seclusion" refers to such instances as these.
Regarding the statement that "Yunming arrived at Datong": "Having a covering" means having a dwelling; if there is no shelter, one cannot reside there.
Regarding the dates for the preceding and subsequent *varṣā* retreats on the sixteenth day of the first month of summer:

the first month of summer refers to the sixteenth day of the fourth month, while the latter month of summer refers to the sixteenth day of the fifth month. As for "the eastern direction," etc., it is according to that Vinaya.
The commentary states: It is not as [some] hastily claim. When the ancients composed their commentaries, they held this divergent view:

one must necessarily spend the night of the fifteenth day at the place of retreat (*varṣā*), so that by adding the ritual formula on the following day, the formal establishment (*bandhana*) is successfully accomplished. If one does not reach the boundary within that night, it is not so.
If one arrives only after the appearance of dawn on the sixteenth day, the formal boundary-establishment (*sīmā-bandha*) is not valid. Now, the Master says:

"The fifteenth day is still the spring equinox and does not yet belong to the summer season; since spring and summer are distinct, why must one arrive prematurely? This is entirely a baseless fabrication.
Now, the *Chao* states that "the east is red," which refers to the conclusion of the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*. That is to say, it refers to the night of the fifteenth day.
"Exhaustion" refers to the eastern direction turning red; this is the limit of the sixteenth day.

This is clarified in the *Yinliao shu* (Commentary on the *Vinayamātṛkā*), which explains that when the commentary composed by Paramārtha states "the eastern direction turns red," it clearly indicates that the sixteenth day has arrived and the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is successfully established.

Thus, it refutes the interpretation found in the *Shisong lü shu* (Commentary on the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*). Consequently, none of the various commentaries have thoroughly elucidated this meaning. (*Souxuan*)

The *Huainan* [commentary] combines this with the third major section on miscellaneous rules and codifies it as a "Sub-section on Sons" (*zike*). This will be self-evident when compared with the following text. 4.
Regarding the phrase "if one previously resided there and gave rise to the intention for the summer retreat," the commentary (*shu*) explains this itself (as indicated by "etcetera").

5. Regarding the phrase "the place being free from the five faults and so forth," Xuán states: "In the *Karmavācanā*, these five are explained in full. As the textual structure is similar [to what follows], I cannot provide them here in their entirety."
Record: Regarding the fifth case, "having no donor": since this body is not like a gourd that does not depend on nourishment, how could it do without food?
Therefore, one must take medicinal food to sustain oneself through hunger and emptiness for a day or a night; if there is none, one cannot remain. Etc.
Regarding the phrase "as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*": according to that Vinaya, there was a bhikṣu in the kingdom of Kośala who dwelt alone in a deep forest.
At that time, a non-human female came and summoned the bhikṣu to engage in unchaste conduct. The bhikṣu did not comply with her.
The woman said, "If you do not submit to me, I shall bring ruin and distress upon you. The bhikṣu replied:
"Do as you wish. Later, while the bhikṣu was sleeping, the female ghost took the patched robe and embraced the bhikṣu, placing him beside a lady in the king’s inner palace.
The king suddenly woke up and asked, "Who are you? She replied, "I am a bhikṣu. The king asked again, "How did you come to be here?
The bhikṣu related the matter in detail. The king said, "Why did you go to this deep mountain? For what purpose?
He caused me distress. Out of reverence for the Buddha’s Dharma, I did not take this as a matter of concern; you must depart quickly.
He reported this to the Buddha, and because of it, the Buddha established a regulation, as described in the *Vinayavibhāṣā*.

Regarding the method for the great clarification of the *vinaya-mātṛkā* on the practical application of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat): the treatise states that the senior monk (*sthavira*) presiding over the retreat should inquire about the boundary markers of the great precinct (*mahā-sīmā*).

He should further inquire about the boundaries for robes and food, the location for the *poṣadha*, the appointment of the reciter of the precepts (*śīla-vācaka*), the appointer of blessings (*svastyayana-kartṛ*), the appointer of administrative affairs (*vaiyāvṛtya-kara*), and the mediator of monastic disputes (*saṃgha-raṇa-vinodaka*). Furthermore, he should inspect the cells and examine the bedding and furnishings to see who is using them in accordance with the Dharma.

Whoever acts contrary to the Dharma should not be instructed in the methods of encouragement, joy, and so forth; the full text is not recorded here for brevity. Regarding the phrase "the senior monk (*sthavira*) and others":
the senior monk should console them by saying, "The Great Assembly, observe impermanence! The days and months pass swiftly, and impermanence approaches in secret.
You should diligently cultivate the Path. Birth and death are to be feared; you must not be negligent. Such a senior monk is thus designated.
"Seng-fu-mu" (Parents of the Sangha) is also termed "Seng-shi" (Teacher of the Sangha), and so forth; the phrase "and so on" (*yun-yun*) indicates that the list is not exhaustive.

Regarding the statement "the two fetters reach the *luo* (robes)": this asks when the summer retreat (*an-ju*) for practicing the Way is no longer required, and why, among the seasons, the summer is specifically cited from the *Jiao* (Commentary).
The answer, beginning with "Because during the summer... and so on, is as follows. As for the statement "spring and winter pass with little [time]": [this refers to the brevity of those seasons].
The fault of inciting ridicule through improper conduct is relatively minor. Regarding the rule that one must not travel without informing others of one's absence:
if one travels during the three periods when there is no business, a *duṣkṛta* offense is incurred for a monk; for a nun, failing to observe the later retreat constitutes a *pāyattika*.

As for the question regarding the completion [of the period]: why is it that only a three-month period is established? It is because of the following reason. The intention is this: since the summer retreat consists of four months, why [is it only three]?

Does the Vinaya text permit a three-month *varṣā* (rainy season retreat)? Regarding "birth and death awaiting the form," "form" refers to the physical body, and "awaiting" refers to the form of karma.
"Opening the final month for robes to sustain the body" refers to the month of Kārttika;
thus, one may complete [the retreat] on the sixteenth day of the fourth month. This explains the previous passage: if the fourth month is summarized as the summer [retreat].
This refers exclusively to the sixteenth day of the fourth month, at which point the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is established.

If there is an omission or error such that this cannot be achieved, or if due to some circumstance the formal ritual for entering the retreat (*praveśana*) is suddenly not performed, then from the following day onward, it is not established.

Regarding the statement that "the teaching is too strict," Baoyun says: "If one summarizes [the period] as the fourth month, both the commencement of the retreat (*varṣā*) and the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) are fixed by this standard."
Now, although the four-month period is prescribed, one should conclude it after only three months, leaving the final month unconcluded.

Within those preceding three months, if one does not reach the prior *anvārambhaṇa* (pre-summer retreat), there is still the middle and later periods during which one may hope for a continuous conclusion. Therefore, it is said:
"To comply indirectly with the sentiments of sentient beings... even continuing the conclusion until now is accomplished," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "as for what was said above concerning the times": this refers to the general classification of the three seasons mentioned previously.

In the preceding text, it was established that there are three seasons—spring, summer, and winter—and that one must observe the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) during all of them; wandering without cause during these periods results in inauspiciousness.

Among these, however, excessive faults are most prevalent specifically during the summer, which is why the practice is strictly regulated for that season alone. Having already explained this, the present passage concludes the previous section; thus, for now, we shall proceed solely with respect to the summer.
Regarding the phrase "there are three times," this indicates that the present is different from the past.

It means that the current master, within the summer retreat (*varṣā*) alone, distinguishes three types of periods—the former, middle, and latter—which gives rise to the meaning explained below. As for the phrase "from the first to the last among the dharmas":
The sixteenth day of the fourth month is for those undertaking the *pūrvavārṣika* (early rains retreat). It is restricted to this single day;
from the seventeenth day until the fifteenth day of the fifth month, the twenty-nine days in between are called the *madhyamavārṣika* (middle rains retreat).

On the sixteenth day of the fifth month, it is likewise restricted to this single day and is called the *paścimavārṣika* (late rains retreat). This is the threefold system established by our present teacher. Therefore, the Vinaya states: "Equal increase in three texts."

This also serves to verify that the three aforementioned types are not erroneous. Regarding the passage "previously, during the first three months of the retreat," etc., this is the text from the *Aniyata-khandhaka* (The Chapter on the Retreat).
According to this text, there are only two types; therefore, while ancient masters sometimes established two or sometimes three, the latter was based on the expanded version of the text.
Furthermore, ancient masters stated that there are definitely only two, and they did not allow for a third.

Third. The reason for this is that ancient masters cited a passage from the *Khandhaka*: "At one time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana wished to observe the rains retreat together with the World-Honored One.
On the fifteenth day of the fourth month, they departed from their respective residences and arrived there on the seventeenth day.

Not knowing what to do, they asked the Buddha, who said: 'I allow you to enter the later rains retreat (*paścimikā varṣā*). If it is said that arriving after the seventeenth day constitutes the middle rains retreat (*antarvarṣā*')."

This would contradict the texts of other Vinayas. Now, the objection is raised: "If that were so, why are there three types—the beginning, middle, and end—within the *Upāli-vinaya* (the *Zengsan-wen*)?
If you say there are only two, do not contradict the *Upāli-vinaya* which mentions three. The ancient masters explain this by saying:
"Those are three methods for disciplining the mind; that is, the Buddha instructed the bhikṣus to contemplate [the body] during the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*)."
Singing is like weeping; watching a dance is like madness; frolicking and laughing is like a small child.

These are not what are called the three types of *vassa* (rainy-season retreat). Now, another objection is raised: "Why are these not listed within the text concerning the increase of the two [retreats]? In response, he counters:

"If there were three established, why did the Buddha, when the seventeen days had already passed during the *jetta* [first] month, command that the later *vassa* (*pacchima-vassa*) be observed? Furthermore, [he asks]: "But..."
It is said that one may enter the *an-gu* (rainy season retreat) in the first three months or in the last three months, yet there is no mention of entering the *an-gu* during the middle three months.
One might ask: "Is it permissible to enter the *an-gu* for the middle three months? This can be answered by citing the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü Shanding Chao*). The general response states:

"Although it does not explicitly mention the 'middle three months,' the text fully clarifies the number of days for both the preceding and succeeding periods. This is the Master’s response, establishing three principles.
The meaning is as follows: Although the Vinaya does not explicitly state "the middle three months," since the periods before and after are mentioned, the middle period is naturally included.

"The principle is self-evident" means that the reasoning for establishing [the retreat] during this time is inherently clear. Even if one arrives at a residence on the seventeenth day, the Buddha’s instruction is that one should observe the latter [retreat].
As for the distinct phrasing of the concluding texts, it refers to the textual formulations for the three types of *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat).

"Each has its own distinction. As for 'as in the subsequent section on the Dharma,' the following text sets forth the measurements for the *pātra* (alms bowl) by establishing fixed upper and lower limits;

although the intermediate measure is not explicitly stated, it is understood [by implication]. Having understood this, the subsequent passages are all explained according to the *Dharmaratna* (Treasury of the Dharma), differing from the various commentaries which are confused and disordered... and so forth.

Regarding the statement, "Because [the calculation] reaches the thirtieth day, one observes the *pravāraṇā* (end-of-retreat ceremony)": this is intended to generally clarify the sequence of before and after.

"Generally" (*fan*) means broadly; it does not refer to a specific interpretation. This refers to the broad clarification of the three types of *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) based on the differentiation of those three types.

As for the textual flow of the preceding and following sections, they follow one another without explicit explanation, so there is no need to elaborate further. First, regarding the date of the sixteenth day of the fourth month within the system of rewards and punishments, that is the "former."
Obtaining the five benefits is called a "reward. From the seventeenth day onward—namely, the eighteenth, nineteenth, and so forth—is the latter period;
since one does not obtain the benefits during these times, it is called a "penalty. Second, regarding obtaining the intermediate [period]:

the fifteen days prior to the fifteenth day of the fifth month are called the "former," meaning from the sixteenth day of the fourth month up until the fifteenth day of the fifth month; this entire month is collectively termed the "former. This applies when there are extenuating circumstances.

Regarding "no offense for not performing the formal act (*karmavācanā*"): this refers to circumstances involving difficulties; it does not mean following out of negligence. This is termed "in accordance with the Dharma.

If one has not yet received the additional ordination (*adhikāra*), the formal act is not established and thus no offense is committed. As for the statement in the text that "if there are no [special] conditions, the *jīva* [confession] is performed on the sixteenth day," this refers specifically to the sixteenth day of the fifth month;

this single day is designated as the "latter" period. Regarding "whether there are conditions or no conditions, it is a single offense": whether there are conditions or no conditions, [the offense remains the same].

And one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is because there is only this single day remaining for urgency. Regarding the rule that "if it accords with the removal of difficulties, it is opened as being without offense," and regarding the rule that "there is a separate *pāyattika* offense," the ancient masters explained:
"For a *bhikṣuṇī*, if she does not enter the *anvāraka-vassa* (the later retreat), she incurs a *duṣkṛta* because there is a subsequent [retreat] to look forward to;

if she does not enter the *paścima-vassa* (the final retreat), she incurs a *pāyattika* because there is no subsequent [retreat] to look forward to. (Master Xuán agrees with this explanation). Now, an objection is raised: "The *saṃgha* [monks] do not..."

Regarding the later retreat (*paścimikā varṣā*): there is likewise no expectation of a later one. Why is it that [the offense] is incurred only [at this time]? I suspect it is because the strength of one's karmic retribution (*indriya-vipāka*) varies;

thus, the gravity of the offense differs accordingly. Reflect on this. Among the three types of difficulties (*antarāya*), if a difficulty arises at the beginning of the summer such that the retreat cannot be formally established:
The sixteenth day of the fourth month is the first day of summer. From this day forward, there will be a succession of difficult circumstances;
one must not perform the formal ritual (*adhiṣṭhāna*) in the presence of others. If one does not depart from the original boundary, even if difficulties arise, the ritual cannot be completed.

Furthermore, if one has never stayed overnight outside [the boundary], when the subsequent summer arrives, those who were previously seated [in the assembly] will return on the sixteenth day of the fifth month. This is the latter period.
In the summer, on this day, it is difficult to remain in stillness; one should prepare to perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for others.

Although it is the sixteenth day of the fifth month, one only recites the verse for the *pūrvavarṣā* (the earlier rains retreat). Therefore, it is said that these are collectively called the "previously seated" and are termed the "thirty-day rains retreat.

From the sixteenth day of the fourth month until [the fifteenth of the seventh month], are these not indeed thirty days? Together, they culminate in the *pravāraṇā* ceremony on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
As for this: if the community attains the summer retreat on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, there is no fault in crossing the boundary again on the sixteenth.

Since the aforementioned circumstances constitute difficult situations, they are permitted as exceptions to the preceding rule. Regarding the statement that "only one day may be spent in formal confinement":

this explains the sixteenth day of the fifth month; is it not indeed one day? From the seventeenth onwards, the summer retreat is not established. "There is a difficulty on the fifteenth of the seventh month" refers to...

On this day, one should perform the *pravāraṇā* (the ceremony of self-indulgence) for the sake of receiving offerings. However, if there are sudden obstacles that prevent it, one may follow the schedule of those who do not encounter such difficulties.

From the sixteenth, seventeenth, eighteenth, or nineteenth after the mid-month of the seventh month, up until the fifteenth day of the eighth month, one may perform the *pravāraṇā* on whichever day within that interval is free from disturbances. This is called the "one-day *varṣā*"; it refers to the fifth month.

The sixteenth day is considered one day. Regarding the "thirty-day observance of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat)," this refers to the period from the middle of the seventh month to the middle of the eighth month, totaling thirty days.
This is because the sixteenth day of the eighth month does not yet constitute the entry into the winter period (*hemanta*).

Within this passage, the underlying intention is difficult to discern. To understand the purport of the text: the preceding section concerns encountering difficulties at the time of the initial commencement of the *varṣā*. The subsequent [section]...

Duan bases this on the case of encountering difficulties during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony. If one encounters difficulties during the *varṣā* retreat, one may wait until the difficulties subside to perform the formal addition [of days], allowing the ceremony to proceed until the sixteenth day of the fifth month.
If one encounters difficulties during the *pravāraṇā*, one may wait until the difficulties subside to perform the *pravāraṇā*, allowing it to proceed until the fifteenth day of the eighth month.
Reflect upon it in this manner.

Regarding the statement that the three summer months may be extended or shortened by an intercalary month: if one follows an intercalary month, it is called "extended" when it reaches one hundred and twenty days;
if one does not follow it, it is called "shortened" when the count reaches ninety days. As for the phrase "following means reaching," there is no formal textual authority for it.
In the Tripiṭaka teachings, there is no passage that mentions this. Fabao says: "It is not permissible to assume something when there is no textual basis;
furthermore, its meaning is absent. This means both the text and the meaning are lacking. As for the comparison with the Sarvāstivāda and other schools, it refers to this category.

That is to say, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, the acceptance of the rain-cloth includes the intercalary month; thus, the text states: "If there is an intercalary month, one accepts [the cloth] from the sixteenth day of the fourth month."
"Up until the fifteenth day of the seventh month; during that interval of one hundred and twenty days, one should store [the robe]" (as stated in the Treatise).

Regarding the fact that the method for opening the allowance for those robes still relies on the summer intercalary month, the Master here provides an explicit explanation to clarify it. His intention is as follows:

even though the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (the *Bahuśrutiya-śāstra*) permits the storage of rain-season robes for a period of one hundred and twenty days, this is an "allowance" (*anujñāta*), whereas the summer retreat is a "prohibitive teaching" (*pratiṣedha-śāsana*); therefore, it is logically appropriate [to calculate the limit] based on the summer retreat.

Regarding "universal protection": this refers to the rules for the summer retreat (*varṣā*), which are teachings personally ordained by the Buddha. According to principle, they ought to be universally observed to prevent difficulties;

if there is an intercalary month, one must rely upon it. This is cited as an example for other cases: even though the teaching regarding the relaxation of the rules for rain-cloths (*vassikasāṭikā*) is lenient, one still relies on the intercalary month to receive and store them.
By analogy, the present rules for the summer retreat are strict injunctions (*prajñapti-śāsana*); therefore, how could one fail to rely on the intercalary month to maintain them?

[The rule of] "maintaining" [the boundary]. Regarding those who go outside the boundary during an intercalary month when the summer retreat has not yet been completed: this clarifies the position established by the ancient masters. An ancient said:
"In the case of an intercalary fifth month, if it falls within the first five days, it is part of the original month and one must maintain [the boundary];

if it falls within the latter five days, it is an intercalary addition and does not count toward the full number of days for the retreat, so one should shorten the time spent outside the boundary and stay there without maintaining [the boundary]. This also applies to an intercalary sixth month.

Therefore, it is said that the intercalary month does not constitute "leaving the boundary" during the summer retreat. That is to say, it is not a continuous [period], and thus it breaks [the retreat]. Now, the Master refutes the errors of the ancients, stating:
if one leaves the boundary during an intercalary month, since the intercalary month belongs to the summer, even if one passes beyond it, the protection of the summer retreat is no longer beneficial;
because it is not a continuous fulfillment, the summer retreat is thereby broken.

Regarding the phrase "if it reaches two texts": if one does not perform the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) once the full count of days, including intercalary months, has been reached, there are two interpretations of this text.

The first, according to various schools, states that although a monk knows an intercalary month exists, he makes a mental resolve not to shorten the count; thus, when ninety days are complete, he may leave the boundary.
Alternatively, at the time of the formal assembly, even if he does not yet know an intercalary month will occur, he pre-emptively establishes a deadline, fearing what might happen later.

"If there is an intercalary month, I shall not rely on it either"—this interpretation is untenable. If one clearly knows in one's mind in advance that there will be one, then, according to the two-clothing precedent in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, one should observe the rains retreat based on the intercalary month.

One must not, following one's own arbitrary intention, falsely count the days as complete and leave the boundary; this would certainly constitute a violation of the summer retreat. Furthermore, it says: "Although some do not know [in advance], they generate [the intention] beforehand..."

Regarding the mind [of the practitioner], it is said: "I do not rely [on this]. Yet, there is no such principle; one does not establish the summer retreat (*varṣā*) merely by making a preliminary commitment.

Next, according to the *Fǎbǎo zhèngjiě* (Correct Explanation of the Dharma-Jewel), it is said that at the time of first entering the summer retreat, one was unaware that there would be an intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*) during this summer.

Having already fixed the ninety-day period until the conclusion of the retreat, one only realizes there is an intercalary month once the retreat is finished. Then, according to the text, one shortens the [remaining] nine [days].

When the ten days are complete, one may then perform the *pravāraṇā* and depart the boundary. This applies only if one knows [the date] in advance; it does not apply to cases where one must follow the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*. An external objection states:

"If there is a summer intercalary month, one would know it at the beginning of spring. How can you say, as previously stated, that it is 'at the time of the initial *anugata* (rainy season retreat)'?"

It was not known whether the summer retreat had concluded; only then did one realize that there was indeed an intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*). One may cite the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* (Chao) as proof, which states: "The *Mātṛkā* says:

'Once the summer retreat has been completed, [one proceeds] according to the intercalary month,' and so forth. The commentary by Shu states: "The calendrical systems established in the Western Regions differ from those of this land."

In this region, the calendar is produced at the beginning of the year, whereby one immediately knows whether there will be an intercalary month or not. In the Western lands (India), the calendar is regulated according to the three seasons;
consequently, discrepancies arise. For example, [the period] from the sixteenth day of the twelfth month to the fifteenth day of the fourth month [is calculated differently].
Consequently, the spring equinox marks the completion of one cycle, and the calendrical calculations are thus exhausted.

On the sixteenth day of the fourth month—the first day of summer—the new calendar has not yet been issued, and the bhikṣus enter the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat). This discrepancy in counting ninety days arises because they were unaware of the intercalary month;

thus, they are permitted to perform the *pravāraṇā* (ceremony of invitation). The above constitutes the correct interpretation according to the text. If, however, one follows the seating arrangement established by Xiachuan:
The Master said: "This is based on a location in deep mountains where one was initially unaware of the intercalary month and only later became certain of it;

since the ninety-day period had already been fixed, the count of days reached completion without regard for the intercalary month. Consider how this explanation contradicts the *Chao*. Reflect upon this.
Regarding those who receive the *kaṭhina* robe: it is received at the conclusion of the summer retreat (*varṣā*) through five advantages, honors, and labors.

As for whether this robe constitutes a valid reception or an invalid reception, there are many explanations of this text; however, following the interpretation of the *Huainan* [commentary], one’s understanding will be most elegant and appropriate.
Within that treatise, this section arises because of a discussion concerning whether the *bhikṣu*’s precept of receiving robes is established. The present *Chao* states: "This very robe..."
"Is the acceptance established or not established? This is the interrogative phrase within the treatise (*śāstra*). Its meaning is:

"When ninety days have been completed, is the monk’s acceptance of the robe established or not established? The subsequent line states, "That is, depending on whether an intercalary month is observed or not.

This is the explanation within the treatise. It means that if, at the beginning of the summer retreat, everyone was unaware that an intercalary month existed and had already fixed the ninety-day period, [the acceptance is established].

Even if one only realizes there is an intercalary month after the calendar has been issued later on, once the ninety days have been completed and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony has concluded, the robes are accepted;

thus, these robes are considered properly received. However, if it were certain at the beginning of the summer retreat that an intercalary month would occur, one should instead follow the urgent rule and observe the *varṣā* for one hundred and twenty days including the intercalary period.
If one now definitively counts only ninety days and accepts the robes after the *pravāraṇā*, then these robes are not [properly received].

This concerns the formal acceptance [of robes]. If one wishes to know whether the acceptance of robes is valid or invalid, it must be explained by relying on whether or not an intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*) is observed.
As for the explanations found in various commentaries, they do not fully exhaust the intent of the treatise; reflect upon this.

Alternatively, there may be a case where, within a single boundary (*sīmā*), half of the people accept the robes as invalid if they rely on an intercalary month, while the other half accept them as valid if they do not rely on an intercalary month. This...

This interpretation is also incorrect; understand this. An external objection states: "Since the preceding text already stated that the rainy season retreat (varṣā) is based on the intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*), there is no formal scriptural authority for it.

How then can what is now stated in the *Vinaya-ghaṭīkā* not be considered formal scriptural authority? The Venerable One replied: "The *Ghaṭīkā* is primarily clarifying whether the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* robe is valid or invalid.
It explains this by taking as its basis whether or not the retreat relies upon the intercalary month. If an intercalary month occurs within the summer [retreat]..."

"Residing" refers to not making it one's primary reliance; since this is not explicitly stated, there is likewise no textual authority for it. Nowadays, many people are confused regarding this meaning.
"Since both texts are present together" means that the textual passages from the *Mahāgama* and the two *Śāstras* are mutually complete and sufficient.

"When the time arrives, follow conditions" means that when the time for the intercalary retreat (*adhika-varṣa*) arrives, everything follows the preceding conditions. This concludes the section beginning with "at the start of summer. Below this, [the text] provides an analysis.

Regarding the principle of following conditions (*pratyaya*): if at the beginning of summer one knows there will be an intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*), one must certainly include it [in the retreat];
this follows the precedent of the two robes according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, and one must not rely on the text of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

If the opposite of the former occurs—that is, if at the beginning of summer one was unaware and made the resolve for the ninety-day summer retreat—then one follows the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*; this is the opposite of the former case. This [latter] is a contraction resulting from prior knowledge.
Furthermore, "not knowing" does not mean that one reverses another's intention regarding what is essential or non-essential. Regarding the reconciliation of the two texts from the two treatises:

this reconciles the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Daolun) based on the intercalary month text and the *Karmavācanā* (Jialun), rather than relying on the two types of textual passages in those treatises that do not concern the intercalary month.

The above follows the interpretation of Master Baohui. Master Xuán states: Within the *Karmavācanā*, there are two types of formal deliberation (*vinaya-viniścaya*). If the intercalary month is established after the summer retreat has already begun...

Thus, the ninety-day period is completed; this is one way of calculating. If one knows at the beginning of the summer retreat that there will be an intercalary month, one must remain for one hundred and twenty days;
this is the second way of calculating. [The commentator] fears that these are not the accepted positions.

Regarding the inquiry concerning the ultimate Dharma: first, the general meaning is distinguished; second, the text is analyzed. An external objection states: "This is the text concerning the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat).
Why is the receiving of the [additional] days explained in advance? The answer is: "The receiving of the days is contingent upon the *varṣā*.

Since it is already permitted that the *varṣā* may include an intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*), when I now receive the method for one month, it likewise conforms to the *varṣā* in being able to include an intercalary month. This is simply because they follow one another by way of convenience."
This question arises. The *Xiaowen chao* (Explanatory Notes on the Text) states: "Regarding one who receives [the precepts] for a period of one month:

if it is the intercalary fifth month, and one requests the Dharma-inclusion on the first day of the preceding five months, will one obtain the subsequent five months so as to complete a total of sixty days? The answer is: "No, and so forth."

It is said that the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is a restrictive teaching (*niyama-śāsana*). Remaining within the boundary (*sīmā*), one exerts oneself in practice and dwells in tranquil stillness; the benefits are not few. Answer:

Allowing the inclusion of an intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*) in the calculation of the days is a permissive teaching (*anujñā-śāsana*). Furthermore, if one goes outside the boundary, the body is driven about and the mind is scattered, thereby disturbing the work of the Path.
Now, calculating the days received [for the retreat] is a partial permission (*ku-pratimokṣa*). One must not further include a subsequent intercalary month; the limit must be shortened by one.
[The period] must not exceed [the month]. In the second round of questions and answers, I shall first clarify the general meaning and subsequently explain the text.
As for the objection: "Granting five months as a reward for labor is a matter for the subsequent section; how can this be explained here in advance? The answer is:

because the granting of labor rewards is based on the merit earned during the *anvaya* (rainy season retreat), it permits [extensions of] five months or one month and so forth. Since your calculation of the *anvaya* already includes the intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*), I now...
If there is an intercalary month within the period for rewarding labor, should that [period] also be subsumed? This is likely a clarification made in accordance with the circumstances.
Next, regarding the text stating "two sixes including the intercalary month," Fabao says: "If there is no *kaṭhina* robe, the original portion is the benefit of one month;
if there is now an intercalary month, should it not be two months? If there is a *kaṭhina* robe, this is originally the benefit of five months."
Since there is currently an intercalary month, one cannot simply have six months; therefore, it is said that "two sets of six" are required.

*Souxuan* (Investigating the Profundities) takes the two months without clothing and completes sixty days as one "six," while the six months with clothing constitute the second "six. This interpretation seems somewhat redundant.
Now, let us briefly summarize the previous explanation: taking approximately two months as six months constitutes the "two-six" [period] of the subtle dharma.

Regarding the statement in the answer that "the law of relaxation is opened by this," it refers to the benefit of the five-month period; since relaxation is opened by this, how could one further open it to include an intercalary month?

Therefore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Once the *guṇa-cīvara* (merit robe) has been accepted, if an intercalary month is established by the authorities, one must follow the full number of days until the end of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat);
the intercalary month itself cannot be included [in the calculation]. Therefore, it is not counted as an intercalary month."

Regarding the statement, "Now, as for reaching the *Shu* and *Chao* [commentaries], 'advancing' refers to the three examples": advancing means staying for four months, while not advancing means staying for three months.
These "three examples" refer to the three positions. Depending on whether the summer intercalary month (*rūna*) causes an extension or contraction of time, there are these three positions.
Even if the intercalary month falls in the fifth month, such that one stays for four months in all cases, this constitutes one example. From the second day of the intercalary month...

From "afterwards" up to "because of completing the formal act of ordination" constitutes the second example. From "if on the first day of the fifth month" onwards, including the concluding text, constitutes the third example.
The first example fixes [the period] at four months; the second example is indefinite as to length; the third example fixes the residence at three months.
This concludes the examination of the three types of examples. Based upon these three examples, the text is now interpreted.
Regarding the first example, it is easy to understand from the text; it refers to the fact that [the practitioner] stays for one hundred and twenty days in every case.
Regarding the second example, "after the second day of the intercalary month" refers to the second day of the intercalary fourth month;
"afterward" means the third and fourth days, and so on. "Gradually becoming fewer" refers to the second day of the intercalary month, because...
One may remain for one hundred and nineteen days. Regarding "binding [the rains retreat] on the third day," one remains for one hundred and eighteen days;
such are the gradual increments of the number of days. As for "passing beyond the intercalary month," this refers to passing beyond the fourth intercalary month.

Regarding "the fifth month being the actual summer and so forth," once the intercalary month has been passed, it constitutes the actual summer, and the formal binding of the retreat is accomplished. If, after the first day of the fifth month...

Regarding "the observance of the retreat" (*varṣā*) and so forth: these all refer to a three-month stay. This can be understood from the fact that the *Chao* (Commentary) calculates the duration by counting the days until they are complete.

As for the case of an intercalary seventh month and so forth, there are two interpretations: first, it is fixed as a three-month stay; second, it is fixed as a four-month stay, where the observance begins on the second day of the fifth month.
Because the second day of the fifth month falls short by one day, the period is not yet full, and one thus enters the intercalary seventh month.
Stepping on the *ling* [altar] does not count toward the full number. It was only on the second day of the eighth month that the count was finally complete.

"The rest is as in the *Shu* and *Chao*" refers to the *Shoushu* (Initial Commentary) and the *Yichao* (Commentary on the Meaning). Now, according to the *Jiemoshu* (Commentary on the *Karmavācanā*), there are three phrases:

the first two phrases refer to an intercalary fourth month (*rùn sìyuè*), and the last phrase refers to an intercalary seventh month (*rùn qīyuè*). The *Shu* states: "In some cases, the summer retreat (*anqu*) is separated by one month. From [this point], it is self-evident.
"Granting one day at will" refers to those who enter the summer retreat on the thirtieth day of the fourth month.

For those who enter the retreat on the first day of the fifth month, there is an intervening period of one intercalary month—the fourth month—between them; hence it is said that "the retreat is separated by one month.
Those who enter the summer retreat on the thirtieth day of the fourth month exit the boundary on the thirtieth day of the seventh month; thus it is called "five [months]."
Those who enter the summer retreat on the first day of the month depart on the first day of the eighth month; thus it is said they "descend one day.
The second line states: "There may be those who observe the *anvaya* (summer retreat) with a one-month interval, departing for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony simultaneously.

This means that while the former group enters the retreat on the first day of the intercalary fourth month, the latter group enters on the first day of the fifth month; hence it is called "separated by one month. This...
On the first day of the eighth month, both individuals simultaneously depart from the boundary.

This means that for the former person, the one hundred and twentieth day is completed, while for the latter person, the ninetieth day is completed; therefore, it is said they depart at the same time. Regarding the third case:

there may be an interval of one day between the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) and an interval of one month between the *pravāraṇā* (ceremony of invitation). This refers to the former person who performed the formal commencement (*pravarṣaṇā*) on the first day of the fifth month.
The latter person ties [the boundary] on the second day of the fifth month; hence it is said that there is "one day's interval.

The former person reaches the boundary on the first day of the intercalary seventh month, while the latter person does not reach the boundary until the second day of the eighth month; hence it is said that there is "one month's interval."
The reason for this is that because the intercalary month has been entered, treading upon the void is not accomplished.

Counting from the second day of the fifth month until the thirtieth day of the preceding seventh month, one only reaches eighty-nine days. Because of this deficiency of one day, the sentient beings must remain contained within the intercalary month until the end;
only in the eighth month may they depart.

Regarding the "Dharma of the Two Limits": whenever one intends to enter the summer retreat (*varṣā*), three conditions must be fulfilled. Among these, the repair and maintenance of the dwelling constitutes one requirement.

If it is not maintained for even a single lifetime, it will not continue through the three periods of existence. Since the practice of maintenance has been established, one must first divide [the responsibilities] (and so forth).
Regarding the phrase "possessing the four months": according to the time-periods of the Vinaya, there was a bhikṣu who, at his place of residence...
Upon inspecting the dwellings and bedding, he received an inferior room and became resentful toward the resident monks.

His mind was not impartial; he favored those he liked by giving them good rooms and gave bad ones to those he disliked. When this was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said: "From now on, the person who is staying there himself shall inspect the rooms and then assign others to distribute them.
The *karmavācanā* text is as in the *Śarīra-vibhāṣā* (or *Vinaya-śarīra*)... It says that those who arrive [at that time] shall not [be assigned rooms].
"Regarding 'having surplus items in the dwelling place': this refers to items belonging privately to one's own person; there must be no surplus.
As for items that originally accompanied the room, these may not be moved or altered. Regarding 'first asking the manager, the owner of the room, and others,' the *Śarīputravinaya* states:

if one has built a room using the funds from one's own robes and bowl, one may reside there for twelve years, because of the merit of having managed the construction; therefore, it is first assigned [to them]."

If the rooms are to be permanently assigned according to the principle of distribution, one may stay for six years. If they are merely being temporarily repaired, a stay of four months is permitted. Regarding the permission for visiting monks (*āgantuka-bhikṣu*) to stay:
one might fear that once the rooms have been fully distributed, it would be improper for them to obtain rooms; however, since there are now surplus rooms, what harm is there in allowing them to stay?

If it were at the time of the formal distribution of rooms, why distinguish between residents and visitors? They should be distributed according to a single uniform rule. The rest is as stated in the text.

Regarding the question of "selection": it is said that since preferences for beauty differ, the time limit should not be too short. Xuán explains: this refers to the fact that people’s inclinations are each distinct.
There may be an elder who values affairs and delights in tranquility, desiring a small room on the periphery;

there may be another elder who wishes to be near the dining hall or the Buddha hall. One must not restrict the quality of the rooms based on preference, as some may simply delight in cultivating merit.

As for "one who desires to stay," this refers to one who intends to stay in a poor-quality room and is preparing to repair it; or one who fears that the work will be interrupted and thus unable to complete the repairs, and therefore seeks to exchange the poor room for a good one regardless of distance.
Hence, it is said that "the fine and the poor are not the same. Because the summer retreat (*varṣā*) lasts for one season, the limit of days is not short;

this is why one must select a residence. Regarding the question as to what "taking" means: this refers to the current [distribution] where the portions are equal (pronounced levelly). It applies universally.
"One part" (qùhū): this object is divided equally according to the number of people, as it possesses two meanings: first, that it belongs to them permanently;

second, that it is a direct condition for sustaining the Path. It is not comparable to dwellings or rooms. "Throwing down a *ce* (cè)" refers to a tally-stick (*śalākā*), such as casting sticks or using a hook to take [a share] and so forth.

Regarding the statement "from the *saṃgha* to the one who departs": this fully encompasses both types of giving. First, giving for the purpose of enjoyment; second, giving for the purpose of maintaining the object.

This is not the same as the ancient records which state there are two types: first, a *bhikṣu*, and second, a *śrāmaṇera*. Regarding the phrase "one may not divide it at the place where the Song edition is located": [this refers to the specific regulations concerning distribution].
This refers to places such as dining halls and tea halls. If there are separate rooms, excellent caves, or the like, one should follow the circumstances described in the Vinaya:

"When the bhikṣus saw a fine cave in a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka), they said, 'I shall dwell in this place,' and later spoke further to the bhikṣus, saying, 'I shall observe the rains retreat (varṣā) here. On the sixteenth day at the beginning of summer, many bhikṣus together..."
They gathered together in their dwellings within the cave. Because many were afflicted by illness, they informed the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:

"If you wish to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*) in this place, you must first record your names according to the prescribed form, saying: 'So-and-so comes here to observe the rains retreat,' and so forth. Afterwards, the bhikṣus shall write down their names and occupy the space.
When the summer retreat is concluded, they shall depart, but they must not erase the names. Only then will those who come later dare to reside there. The Buddha spoke thus.

It should not be left unextinguished [uncancelled]. This is called "departing while leaving behind a name," which generally refers to cases where a donor constructs a separate dwelling upon monastic grounds, or builds a private room in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*), such that it does not belong to the Saṃgha. For this reason, it is permitted to preemptively reserve and register one's name.
If it is a monastic dwelling, one must divide [the day] into three periods; why then is there a need for prior calculation?

As for the statement "three times reaching the limit," this refers to the establishment of teachings according to conditions: there are conditions involving face-to-face interaction with another person, and conditions involving mental recitation when no other person is present.

Even up to the point where one becomes angry, opens one’s feet, or forgets the conditions for accomplishment—these are the [faults]. Second, regarding the delimitation of the application (*dharmaparyanta*):
this refers to the fact that each has its own specific limits in terms of time, person, and place. As for the four types of disciplinary judgments (*vinaya-viniścaya*) established at the beginning:

Regarding the establishment of the teachings in response to conditions, there are four types, namely *pratimukha* (face-to-face) and so forth (*etc.*). As for the phrase "from 'initially' to 'realms'":
this applies to all realms, meaning the spontaneous performance of ritual acts (*karmavācanā*). Since these ritual acts each have many different variations, it is said to apply to "all.
As for the phrase "from 'now' to 'question'": the *Karmasūtra-vyākhyā* states that within the initial *pratimukha* [category], the person upon whom one relies is...

The former refers to being in the presence of witnesses. The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "Even the Buddha observes the rains retreat (*varṣā*) without being in the presence of others, because he has attained all-encompassing wisdom and the four fearlessnesses;
thus, he does not rely on others to validate his speech. This is based on the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. (The above is from the commentary.)

The Venerable Jing-shui said: "Nowadays, many people claim that 'Mahāyāna *varṣā* (the rains retreat)' applies universally throughout the entire sphere of Śākyamuni’s transformation, and thus one need not observe the summer retreat.

This is a foolish teaching and a false assertion. Now, according to the two-fascicle *Niyata-artha Mahāyāna Sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatāra-jñānālokalaṃkāra-sūtra* (*Dacheng yuanjue liao yi jing*), specifically at the end of the second fascicle, the Mahāyāna *varṣā* is extensively explained as having three grades. First..."
For eighty days, ninety days, or one hundred days, one should establish a *maṇḍala* and practice. Except for the necessity of relieving oneself, one is not permitted to go outside even for a moment.
This is even more urgent than the recitation of mantras or the breath-holding (*ānāpāna*) of the Bodhisattvas of the Hīnayāna.

As for the worldly criticism that "memory and nature are no different," what text permits wandering during the summer retreat and so forth? (etc. Next is the section on performing the ritual procedures.
There are eight phrases. First, "Venerable One, please attend to me with one mind," which addresses the person present to ensure there are no other distracting thoughts.

Second, "I, [Name]," which distinguishes the speaker from others. Third, "relying on such-and-such monastery," which specifies the location where one is situated. Fourth, "the former," which distinguishes the beginning from the middle or end.
"Five or three months" means that the final month is excluded, as it is opened for the purpose of providing sustenance. "Six summer retreats" excludes those not occurring in spring or winter.
"Seven years of *an-gu* (rainy-season retreat)" excludes periods of wandering. "Repairing the dwellings" refers to the maintenance of one's requisites.
"Reciting three times" distinguishes this from reciting once. When that person says, "I inform you," it means the preceding witness must respond. "Do not be negligent" is a word of admonition.

"Responding that one accepts and upholds" signifies the understanding of the meaning. Regarding the addition of the term "equal" (*saha*), it is because during the summer retreat one must necessarily have a place of reliance;
thus, the following text prescribes relying upon a fifth *vinaya*-master. If there is doubt, go and ask.

This refers to being well-versed in the principles of penetration and obstruction. As for the phrase "if one arrives," it means that whether one is in a forest, a wilderness, a village, or a secular household, there is no mention of "cultivation" or "preparation.
The phrase "not the same as the former fools" and so forth refers to the lineage of the former fools, stating:

"In Jambudvīpa, in the Great Tang Kingdom, under the Emperor of the Li family, in such-and-such a prefecture and county, under such-and-such a high official, in such-and-such a village and hamlet, at such-and-such a monastery..."
[The previous cases of] indigo and so forth are not the same as this case.
Regarding the statement that "it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing)": this refers to the non-continuity of the three periods of time, because the past, future, and present do not connect [in this instance].

This concerns the three periods of a single lifetime (*ekakalpa*). Regarding "the offense is completed according to the day": this means it is completed during the middle or later part of the day. The regulation is based on the fifth [section].

Regarding the word "etcetera" (*ādi*): Xuánzàng states that the Vinaya adds five texts. During the summer retreat, if one does not rely on a fifth *vinayadhara*, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense; during spring and winter, if one exceeds [the limit] slightly, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.

As for the character "zhì" (至) in the phrase "from the middle," there are cases where the name exists but the rule does not; this refers to the three types of *varṣā* (rain-retreat) mentioned within the three added texts.
Regarding the name [of the retreat], it does not specify the rules for the middle *varṣā* (summer retreat).
As for the common practice in the world of using the later *varṣā*, this refers to the current era, from the seventeenth day of the fourth month until the sixteenth day of the fifth month;

the practical application of this one-month period constitutes the method for the later *varṣā*. However, concerning the three periods enumerated in the Vinaya, our Master says that these are [the results of] the increase...

Within the three texts, there are three distinct periods clearly delineated; here, we now clarify their specific differences. Regarding the phrase "according to the meaning, the three dharmas are not non-existent":

based on these three meanings, it is clear that the method for the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) among them is indeed present. As for the statement "having already clarified the preceding and succeeding [periods]," the intended meaning is as follows:
Since the Vinaya texts have omissions both before and after [the middle section], the middle portion is easy to understand; therefore, it is not set forth here.

Regarding the phrase "annotations and so forth," this cites examples to clarify the establishment of the middle placement. Regarding "certain strictures and so forth," this presents the method by way of illustration using the strictures of a cave;

there are no words concerning "cultivation and repair. Forests and wilds are to be inferred accordingly. As for the statement that one must employ the ancient methods to achieve completion, this is because the ancients did not establish a middle [section].
"Regarding the *paścimikā* (later) *varṣā*: from the seventeenth day of the fourth month onwards, it is entirely the later *varṣā*, which should be without hindrance.

As for the 'later *varṣā*' and so forth, they are the same as the methods previously addressed; that is, the formula for the face-to-face (*pratyakṣa*) procedure is no different from the one above, with the sole exception of changing the word 'earlier' (*pūrvikā*) to 'later' (*paścimikā*).
If one is in a monastery, there are words regarding its repair and maintenance; this must also apply if one is in a forest, a cave, or a mountain crag."
"There is no such statement" (and so forth).

Regarding the phrase "from the second clarification to the second amendment": in the Vinaya, there are those who serve as a basis of reliance; specifically, a *pratideśanīya* (*pratimukha*) bhikṣu is called a "person of reliance.
Since such a person is currently absent, the mind-attention method (*manasikāra*) is now permitted. Regarding the various types of dwellings: this refers to places where one resides.
Regarding the location: it may be in a village, a small wilderness, or an indefinite place; hence it is said to be of "many kinds.
As for "according to the preceding *pratideśanīya* (confession)," this refers to adding and modifying the words for "repairing" as appropriate at the time. The rest of the text is clear (*etc.*).

Regarding the phrase "the third is arrival": this refers to one who has previously made a formal commitment to come to this realm. For example, prior to the summer retreat, one resolves in the mind to arrive at this realm at a specific time to enter the rains retreat (*varṣā*).
As for "the mind and the object corresponding": "mind" refers to the mental state capable of making the commitment;

"object" refers to the location, which is the very place to which one is committed. Regarding the phrase "even if forgotten, it is established": this refers to cases where, after arriving, one’s mind becomes confused.

[The text] is omitted. This refers to the general rule of non-addition [of the formal act]. Once the seventeenth day of the fourth month has passed, one only then remembers that the summer retreat (*varṣā*) had not yet been formally entered;

therefore, the opening [of the retreat] is permitted, and it constitutes the "prior" summer retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*). The passage from "The Vinaya says... onwards serves as proof for the preceding text. Thus, we know that regarding those who reside [in the monastery], etc.
If one speaks in terms of not having made a prior agreement regarding the intention, then it is not opened. However, if there was indeed an agreement, one must then examine the case:

if there was previously an intentional commitment and permission, then even though those who arrive later are guest bhikṣus, because their original intent was not to make an agreement for this specific boundary due to other business, the Buddha [stipulated] that they should arrive on the sixteenth day of the fourth month. Since the formal ritual (*adhiṣṭhāna*) was forgotten, from the seventeenth day onwards...
Regarding "recollection": this does not include the fulfillment of the preceding summer retreat.
As for the phrase "from four [steps] up to the commentary," Xuánzàng says: According to the Vinaya, there were bhikṣus who went to other places to establish their lodgings;
when one leg had entered the garden and the boundary, and then the dawn light appeared; likewise, when both feet had entered the garden and the boundary, and then the dawn light appeared.

The Buddha said, "Both constitute the formal observance of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat). The commentary (*chao*) is obscure and abbreviated. Regarding "one foot enters within," it is evident that there are four types of cases involving both feet entering the garden or the boundary.

For the rest, as stated in the sub-commentary (*shu*): now, according to the *Jie-mo shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā), what is called the "boundary" (*jie*) refers to the boundary for gathering the Saṃgha;
"garden" (*yuan*) refers to the monastery garden, namely the Anāthapiṇḍika Garden. This is because of the current taking [of the boundary].

This is his title. The Commentary further asks: "Previously, when one had entered the boundary and the dawn light appeared, because of haste, there was no opportunity to perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*);

thus, the opening [of the retreat] did not constitute the commencement of the prior *varṣā*. Now, having entered the boundary both singly and in pairs while remaining within the monastery grounds, and having been inside the boundary for some time, there is leisure to perform the formal act before the dawn light has passed; this should therefore not be considered the prior summer retreat. The Buddha judged it as ten [days].
If one enters the boundary on the sixth night before the watch has ended, even if one does not recite the verse, it still constitutes the former [case]. Question:

If one foot has entered the boundary, or because of a certain reason an opening is permitted, it is established. However, if one foot has stepped outside the boundary, I do not yet know whether this breaks the summer retreat (varṣā).
Answer: It must be with both feet that the summer retreat is broken. With only one foot, it is not broken; this benefits the bhikṣu. All of the above is based upon...
The commentary (*shu*) explains this, stating:

"Regarding 'second, clarifying the limits' (*fen-chi*): the term 'limits' (*fen-chi*) refers to the fact that each of the four dharmas is distinct from the others; thus they are called 'limits. As for 'the aforementioned four dharmas establishing the dharma':

this refers to face-to-face confession (*dai-shou*), mental recollection (*hsin-nien*), confession through forgetfulness (*wang-ch'eng*), and the boundary (*chieh*). In terms of time, these apply to all three stages."

This refers to the early rains retreat (*pūrvavārṣika*) as well as the middle and late periods. Regarding the location, it applies to both realms (*dhātu*) by virtue of the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) and its natural occurrence.

Regarding the persons, it applies to the five assemblies (*pañca-saṃgha*), from *bhikṣu* down to *śrāmaṇerī*. According to the system established in the *Chao*, our Master has one hundred and twenty types of rain retreats;
how are these to be categorized? It is said that there are four types of the early rains retreat, including the face-to-face (*saṃmukha*) and the mental (*citta*) [retreats].
Recollection (smṛti). When the [stages of] accomplishment and the realms are combined, there are four for each of the preceding, middle, and subsequent [stages]. Thus, three times four makes twelve.
Applying these twelve to the two realms, there are naturally twelve of the ritual procedures (*dharmaparyāya*) and twelve of the ritual acts (*kriyā*), totaling twenty-four.

Applying this again to the five groups (*pañcagaṇa*), one group has twenty, and five groups have one hundred. Furthermore, there are another four times five, which is twenty; is this not one hundred and twenty?
(Ten [points], based on the *Chao wen*, further accord with the *Jie mo shu*. Now, our Master [Daoxuan] posits two hundred and ten types of *an-ju* (rainy-season retreat).
How are these to be categorized? Namely: first, face-to-face (*pratimukha*); second, mental recollection (*manasikāra*); third, completion through forgetfulness;

fourth, one foot within the boundary; fifth, both feet within the boundary; sixth, one foot having entered the monastery grounds; seventh, both feet having entered the monastery grounds. These seven are assigned to the three periods.)
The preceding and the middle [sections] each consist of three times seven, totaling twenty-one. When these are further assigned to the realms (*dhātu*), they naturally become twenty-one.
When the ritual procedures (*vidhi*) are added to these, they become forty-two. When these are further assigned to the five assemblies (*pañca-parṣad*), each assembly consists of forty-two.

"Are the five groups of practitioners not two hundred and ten [in number]? (and so forth). Regarding the Buddha’s regulation that the five groups must observe the *an-gu* (rainy season retreat) and so on, the *Xiangshu* (Commentary on Characteristics) poses the question:

"Among the five, the two groups of those with precepts and the *śrāmaṇera*s are permitted to observe the retreat at will. As for those who lack the precepts, should they also observe the retreat? The answer is:

"Their status as renunciants is identical, and because their spiritual capacities (*mūla*) are not distinct, the Vinaya prescribes three periods during which wandering is not permitted. All [must remain].

Regarding the matter of the five groups (*pañca-saṃgha*). An external objection states: "Previously, you distinguished the five groups based on all [of them] relying on the four methods [of confession].

Yet, for instance, when the *bhikṣuṇī* community has companions, why is it that they are required to perform *pratyākhyaṇa* (confession before another) rather than using mental recollection (*manasikāra*)?

The tradition received from Tiantai says: "This is explained in terms of what is permitted; it does not necessarily mean that within the *bhikṣuṇī* community, mental recollection is universally opened up. If there are companions, one is urged to perform *pratyākhyaṇa*, or..."

Regarding circumstances such as difficult conditions or dying together with a companion, it is permitted to be alone without offense. Since there is no one else present to face, what prevents one from engaging in mental recitation?

If one does not prepare for such contingencies, one’s capacity is insufficient; reflect on this. Furthermore, regarding external difficulties: within the Master’s *Jiaochan* (Excerpts), there is "one foot [of the robe] reaching the garden" and "one foot reaching the boundary.
In the *Shu* (Commentary), there is "both feet reaching the garden and the boundary," concerning the two locations of formal ritual action (*zuofa*) and the natural state (*ziran*).

Both [the natural and the formal] possess these [distinctions]. For instance, regarding the natural boundary (*prakṛtistha-sīmā*), the distinctions between the double and the single, as well as the precincts (*ārāma*), are not subject to doubt.

How, then, could there be such distinctions of double and single, or boundaries? Since it is said "and the boundary," this refers to the inclusion of the Saṃgha; is this not, therefore, subsumed under formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*)?

Furthermore, within a formal ritual boundary (*kṛtrimasīmā*), there exist the double, the single, and the precincts; these are likewise not subject to doubt. How, then, could there be such distinctions of double and single?

And there are gardens. A garden is a *saṃghārāma*. Is it not, therefore, subsumed under the "natural" (*prakṛta*) boundary? Since these two [the formal and natural boundaries] intersect with one another, how much confusion arises!
Having such a doubt, how is this objection to be resolved? Now it is said: this is explained according to the limits of the monastery grounds (*ārāmamaryādā*).

That is to say, when a guest arrives from outside and has not yet ascertained the demarcation between the two types of boundaries—the formal (*kṛtaka*) and the natural (*prakṛta*)—as soon as one foot crosses the threshold of the monastery gate...
Since these two characteristics are equal and indistinguishable, despite their relative strength, they both pertain to the *ārāma* (monastery) and both pertain to the *sīmā* (boundary).

If these were not explained reciprocally, the characteristics of the teaching would be incomplete. Among those who have recorded this in their commentaries and notes, few have observed it; apart from this interpretation, there is no other principle. Reflect upon this.

Regarding "in terms of the Dharma," this refers to the four types of methods for the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat). It begins with the face-to-face (*pratyakṣa*) and the mental (*manasikāra*) [procedures].
"Completing thirty-one days" refers to the period from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the sixteenth day of the fifth month; these constitute the thirty-one days.
"Sixty-one days" is calculated based on the intercalary fourth month; this has been consistent throughout both ancient and modern times.

Regarding the phrase "those who forgot the completion and the boundary markers," this refers to people prior to the time of Xiang Su. The interpretations of the ancients do not differ from those of today.
