The same applies here; therefore, it is mentioned first. Regarding the fact that only the two days at the beginning and end [of the period] are permitted: the former refers to the early retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*), and the latter refers to the late retreat (*paścimavarṣā*).
These two days—beginning and end—are those for which the allowance for "forgetting" (*vismṛti*) and the establishment of boundaries (*sīmā*) are opened.
As for the twenty-nine intermediate days, namely from the seventeenth day of the fourth month until the fifteenth day of the fifth month, one may not employ this allowance for forgetting.

And regarding the boundary (*sīmā*). The phrase "the latter two provisions relax [the rules] for those fearing the loss of the preceding and following [periods]" refers to the "forgetting" and "accomplishment within the boundary" mentioned above.

"Relaxing" means that the Buddha, out of compassion and for the benefit of the bhikṣus, granted further exceptions beyond the standard rule. Regarding "fearing the loss of the preceding and following":

ancient sources state that if one does not relax the rules for others' forgetting and accomplishment during the *pūrvavārṣika* (early rains retreat), one will fail to obtain the five privileges (*pañcānuśaṃsa*).

The "latter" retreat (*paścimā vārṣikī*) is not permitted [to be opened]. One would thus lose an entire summer; the loss incurred is no small matter. Therefore, it is permitted [for the former to be opened].
As for the phrase "among the middle [periods], one has already failed to reach the former, so why fear losing the latter": this refers to the twenty-ninth day of the middle retreat.

If, in comparison with the former, one has not reached it, then one has already lost the five benefits. Why then fear losing the latter? Thus, the summer season remains valid. This is a deliberation on the advantages and disadvantages.
[This is] the measure; therefore, it is not further divided (the above is from the *Qiucuo Chao*). Next, the limits [of the retreat] are explained.

Regarding this, there were one hundred types of *an-gu* (rainy-season retreat) among the ancients: four for the early retreat, four for the late retreat, and two for the intermediate retreat, totaling ten.

In terms of location, there are ten natural [locations] and ten formal [locations], making twenty. When these are applied to persons, there are twenty for a single assembly and one hundred for five assemblies.

"Et cetera" (and so forth). Furthermore, the phrase "it is also said" introduces the explanation of the second ancient master. "Only on the last day of the summer retreat" means that during the initial and middle periods of the retreat, no [formal] opening is permitted;
it is only at the final period of the retreat that the opening for forgetting the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and the boundaries is allowed.

Regarding the statement, "If one does not perform the formal binding (*bandhana*) for the single summer, one loses [the benefit]," this is because of urgency; fearing the loss of the entire summer retreat, this case allows for recitation as an opening, while other matters are performed according to memory and the time.

"Ample time" (*yōnyo*) means that there is sufficient time remaining outside [the current day]. Excluding the period of *an* (the day of the offense), this refers to the aforementioned "intermediate" period. Regarding "recalling as it occurs":

at the very moment the bhikṣu recalls [the offense], he must immediately seek someone to perform the ritual; it must be completed through face-to-face confession (*pratimukha-saṃvara*). One may not allow for forgetfulness.
Because there is ample time, even if the number of days is long and distant, one may recall it spontaneously whenever the opportunity arises.

One performs the face-to-face recitation (*pratimukha*); if there is no one present, one performs the mental recitation (*manasikāra*). Next, the boundaries (*sīmā*) are distinguished. Regarding this, the ancient masters enumerate eighty types:

two for the early rains retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*), two for the middle rains retreat (*madhyamavarṣā*), and four for the late rains retreat (*paścimavarṣā*), totaling eight. When categorized by location, these apply to both realms (*dhātu*), resulting in sixteen types (eight natural and eight established).
When these are applied to persons, there are sixteen types for a single assembly (*saṃgha*) and eighty types for an assembly of five (*pañcavarga*).
Furthermore, it is not that the sacred words were used according to one's own intent. Now, the Master generally permits the ancient interpretation.

Regarding the two types mentioned above, the ancients established them as principles without opening up scriptural evidence; they were not based on the sacred words. Rather, they were all employed through the arbitrary views of their own minds.
Therefore, it is said they "used them according to their own intent. Now, following the Venerable Jing-shui, we first refute the first [position].

Regarding the Master: if one says that during the twenty-nine days in between, it is not permitted for another to perform the formal act on one's behalf due to forgetfulness—for example, if one arrives on the seventeenth day of the fourth month and forgets to perform the rite of adding the [monastic] status, continuing until the sixteenth day of the fifth month—if one then remembers, one should immediately summon someone to perform the rite face-to-face.
If no person is available, one may perform it through mental recitation (*manasikāra*). However, this is only permissible if one remembers after the seventeenth day of the fifth month has passed.

Regarding the method of *pratideśanā* (confession before another) and mental recollection (*manasikāra*), how can these be successfully accomplished? Since one’s mind is deluded, it is impossible not to formally open the boundary for the summer retreat (*varṣā*).

Thus, we know that [the opposing view] lacks logical justification. Furthermore, regarding the different methods of entering the retreat and the boundaries among the ancient masters, the Venerable One said:
"In the case of an intercalary seventh month, if the boundary is not opened on the first day of the fifth month before the appearance of dawn, then an entire month will be lost."
If one remains for the entire day, will there not be some diminution [of merit]? Why then is it not opened? Next, regarding the refutation of the second master:

if one enters the *pūrvavārṣika* (early) retreat and does not open [the boundary], one loses five benefits; thus, the affliction of the location is not slight. If one enters the *madhyamavārṣika* (middle) retreat and does not open it, this is identical to what has just been refuted.
According to various records, the refutation of the ancient interpretation is not yet exhaustive; reflect upon this.

Regarding the passage from "It is said" to "not": "loss" refers to "non-loss. Regarding the passage from "It is said" to "difficulties": this opens two chapters. Regarding the passage from "In the beginning":
it first clarifies the shifting of the summer retreat; hence it says "in the beginning. An external objection states:

"Does the rule for the summer retreat follow the location or the person? (This is Master Fan posing a question. Huainan answers: "Neither does it rely on the location, nor does it rely on the person; it is simply as it is now."

On the day of entering the rains retreat (*varṣā*), this dharma is acquired simultaneously [with the retreat]. This is because it is a dharma associated with a mind that is currently distracted; therefore, there is no prior acquisition of the dharma.

If the rains retreat has concluded, or if a difficulty arises before the final day, this dharma is acquired subsequently. If one is currently engaged in the retreat and it is after the final day, non-possession (*aprāpti*) comes to take its place.
The Venerable One does not permit this interpretation, fearing it might contradict the text of the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Chao-wen*). As it says:

Regarding difficult circumstances: the Buddha permitted one to move away. Having diligently sought a place for oneself and arrived at that location, one generates the intention to enter the rains retreat (*varṣā*).

Thereupon, the Dharma of the summer retreat arises accordingly. If it is said that one has been replaced by someone who was not previously ordained (*aprāpti*), then there is no Dharma at all; how could it continue to arise?

There is no need for a face-to-face confession (*pratideśanā*); it is unnecessary to perform the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) again, nor is it termed "shifting the summer retreat" (*varṣā-saṃkrānti*).
Furthermore, since the subsequent text states, "If one obtains a dwelling place, the rules of the summer retreat follow one's person," how can such an interpretation be maintained?

Together with the previous question, both are unreasonable. The Venerable One further stated: "Now I shall separately present questions and answers to eliminate doubts and obstacles; one should ask as follows: its..."
Regarding the rules for the summer retreat (*varṣā*): do they correspond to the person, or do they correspond to the location?
Answer: Suppose it were so; what fault would there be? Objection: There are faults in both cases. If it corresponds to the location, then one would never be permitted to leave that place;

how then could one receive [permission] to go out of the boundary or move to another boundary? Logically, this would result in breaking the retreat (*varṣā-ccheda*). If, on the other hand, it corresponds to the person...
If there is a reason [to leave], one may simply depart; it is not necessary to request a formal day (*anujñā*). This still constitutes the completion of the summer retreat (*varṣa*). Answer:

If there is no legal reason (*dharmic cause*), one must remain according to the designated location. For this reason, staying overnight outside the boundary is not permitted; to do so would break the summer retreat.

However, if there is a reason such as being summoned by an invitation, or if there is danger from kings or non-Brahmins (*brahmadanda*), the rule then follows the person’s situation. Because there is a reason, one receives the formal permission for the day; because there is danger, one shifts the location of the summer retreat.

Therefore, it is not refuted. The subsequent text states: "The rules of summer follow the person," etc. (This question and answer exhaustively elucidate the root of the matter). Regarding the phrase "as for those who have departed": there are two difficulties;
life constitutes one, and Brahma constitutes the second. As for the term *brahmacarya* (the holy life): first, let us explain the difficulty regarding Brahma. The *Fǎbǎo* says:
Within the Western lands, if one follows the ascetic discipline and integrity of non-Buddhist practitioners, they are called a *brahmacārin* (Brahmin). "Brahma" (*brahman*) arises from purity.
Furthermore, within the Buddha-dharma, when a bhikṣu practices with refined sincerity and maintains his fundamental purity, this is also called *brahmacarya*, which is to say, pure conduct.
Because of defiled attachment, one may commit grave offenses, fail to achieve the fruits of the Path, and create obstacles that are not easily removed; these are described as "difficulties.

This refers to obstacles within the causal stage that hinder the fruit. As for the phrase "turning away from what comes through the person," this is a general explanation of the above meaning, intended to guide and harmonize the bhikṣus.
"Kiu" (丘) refers to the act of inducing and harmonizing; thus, each section of the Vinaya contains its own *nidāna* (origin story), as described in detail therein.
Second, regarding "ghosts and spirits," etc., this explains the danger to life. The "provisional being" of the five aggregates is sustained by the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

Ghosts, evil beasts, and venomous insects are capable of severing that life-force. As for "not obtaining food and drink at will": there is a life maintained which depends upon food and drink for its existence.
If one’s food is unsatisfactory, or if one’s life will not last long, these are called "difficulties" (*nāṇa*). For these two aforementioned reasons, the Buddha permitted departure.
The phrase "according to the arrival" (*jun-ti*) means that, based on these two difficulties, one may shift the summer retreat (*varṣā*), and the original commitment remains valid.

Someone has offered a false interpretation, stating: "When moving [the summer retreat], one must further perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*)," because the text says, "In accordance with this, it is established," and so forth.

This is refuted as follows: Since it says "further perform the ritual," what kind of *varṣa* (summer retreat) is this called? If it is the former *varṣa*, since that was already established, why labor to perform it again?
If it is the middle *varṣa*, then it cannot be called "moving the *varṣa*" (*saṃkrānti-varṣa*). This is utterly irrational. If...

Regarding those who have attained the status of "dwelling in the summer retreat" such that the rules of the retreat follow them: as soon as the intention for the *anvārambhaṇa* (summer retreat) arises, the rules of the retreat continue to apply;
it is nowhere stated that further formal procedures (*dharmas*) must be added. As for the rule that one may not return if there is no difficulty in one's original boundary:

this refers to cases where one has moved to another boundary because there was a difficulty in this one; now that the difficulty has subsided, one may not return. Since one is already established there in reliance upon the original boundary, [the retreat remains valid].

It is accomplished. Regarding the necessity of having both the conditions (*pratyaya*) and the Dharma: there must be the conditions for invoking [the deity] to give rise to goodness and extinguish evil;
only by performing the ritual for receiving the day (*āyur-dina*) can one return here once again.

Regarding the statement "five parts until summer": as for those whose food is insufficient, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: At one time, there was a bhikṣu who received a portion of coarse food that was insufficient.
He thought to himself, "I am observing the rains retreat here, yet my food is insufficient. He informed the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said, "I permit you to depart; there is no offense.
Regarding "suffering and pleasure, etc.": pleasure refers to the gathering of kinsmen and receiving palaces and such at the destination; suffering refers to...

[The monks] reported to the Buddha matters such as being robbed by bandits, encountering officials, or dying [therein], and the Buddha permitted them all to depart. Regarding the "eight difficulties" (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*):
if a king seizes one's dwelling or dispatches a renunciant on official business, it is called a "difficulty. "Bandits" refers to the loss of robes, bowls, and so forth (and so on).
Regarding the phrase "receiving a robe from either of two places," the *Caturvargika-vinaya* states: there was a disciple of a non-Buddhist who, within the Buddha-dharma...
He went forth into homelessness. His kinsmen among the various non-Buddhist sects said, "Why has he abandoned the path of an Arhat to go forth among the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas?
We shall take him back. They further thought, "If he hears of this, he will surely be able to escape. I have heard that the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, do not break the rains retreat;
we shall wait until the middle of the summer to go and take him back. We will certainly succeed, without a doubt. He, having learned of this, [acted accordingly].
Not knowing how to proceed, he then addressed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I permit you to break the *varṣā* (rain-retreat).

He then departed from that residence and went to the other location where the distribution of robes was to take place. Not knowing what to do, the Buddha said, "If you have spent more days at one place, you should receive a share from that place."

If the number of days spent residing in two locations is equal, one may receive robes according to the half-share. Regarding those who have broken their *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat), the Master here establishes a principle to prove that they have shifted their summer retreat;
it is permitted for them to receive robes in both locations, even taking robes at the place where the *pravāraṇā* (ceremony of invitation) is held.

Since, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, those who have broken their summer retreat do not receive a share of the robes, the fact that receiving a share is now permitted proves that they have successfully completed the summer retreat.

Next, within the three successive rounds of question and answer, the first—extending from the question to the response—concerns the "three repentances. This means that within a single summer retreat (*varṣā*), one may not exceed three [transgressions].
According to this statement, a single summer constitutes one "session" (*āsana*). The second—extending from the question to the mention of "summer"—differs from the preceding one.
The former refers to cases where one originally intended to receive [the formal authorization] for the days, but subsequently became confused and forgot.

He did not accept it. He cited the case of one who had gone outside the boundary for a specific reason, intending to return on that very day, but encountered a severance of the water and land routes and consequently stayed overnight.
He wondered whether this constituted a violation of the summer retreat (*varṣā*) or not. Regarding the "Ten Heads of the Gao Qi" (the character *tǒng* is pronounced *huǒ*):
Xuán says, "Gao" refers to Gao Yang; Yang’s surname was Di. "Qi" refers to the Northern Qi state. Because there were many instances of the name Qi, he specified the surname.

To distinguish this from others: because the Qi ruler revered and honored the Buddha-dharma, he established ten *mahāsattva* (Great Virtues) titled *Sengtong* (Patriarchs of the Sangha) to oversee the monks and nuns throughout the empire and to standardize the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the ten Great Virtues collectively deliberated on the matter of "ruining" (*huai*) through compassionate assistance; they judged that the summer retreat (*varṣa*) was not lost.
The intention of the various Virtuous Ones was also based on the principle of receiving [the precepts] while encountering difficulties, and thus it was judged that [the retreat] was valid. However...
Regarding the third point concerning "asking until one is unable to return": this refers to when one originally intends to go out for a short time and returns on the same day.

Upon returning, if the dawn light (*āloka*) is about to appear at the gate, does one count as having entered the summer retreat? In the response, it is determined according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* regarding the boundary for protecting robes, by way of analogy.
However, if separated by a great wall, one must logically enter so that hands and feet are visible before it is permitted; this is to indicate that one possesses a physical presence within the space.

Next, we shall analyze this in relation to the boundaries (*sīmā*). Regarding the statement, "If the robe reaches the one who has left [the boundary]," this passage contains four general points. First, it says:

"If one relies on the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) for the rains retreat (*varṣā*), even if one enters the intermediate space and breaks the summer retreat. This means that one must intentionally rely on the great boundary for the rains retreat.

As for "entering the *śīma-kaṇḍaka* (precept field)," it is for the purpose of separating oneself from the natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*) as well as other minor boundaries (*kṣudra-sīmā*). Xuánzàng says:

By this means, the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) for the gathering of the Saṃgha is established. Because it exists within the circular enclosure boundary (*parimaṇḍala-sīmā*), it is called "small" in relation to that enclosure;
thus, from the outside toward the inside, the [outer] status is lost, as it is naturally separated by the intermediate space. Regarding the second section:

if one relies on the monastery (*ārāma*) outside the great boundary, even if it is situated further back, this refers to a small area within the large boundary of the monastery, established based on the monastery situated outside.

"Abiding" refers to the fact that the mind must always be present there. The phrase "the note" (chùzhù) serves to harmonize the meaning of the subsequent text. Therefore, in the section on "Discrimination" (Liàojiǎn mén) below, it says:

"If the originally established great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) is smaller than the monastery (*ārāma*), and one sits according to the monastery, then because the Buddha prescribed that one must rely upon the boundary, if [the monastery] exists [within it], the 'receiving of the day' (*divasa-grahaṇa*) is not accomplished;
one may not remain, but may instead contract the boundaries to their defining marks (*sīmā-lakṣaṇa*)."

(This is the original text of the *Chao*). According to this, within a *sīmā* (*kṣetra*), there is a boundary where reliance on a *vihāra* (*ārāma*) is not permitted; one should rely solely on the *sīmā*.
Now, for what reason does this text allow it to apply to both types of boundaries without loss of validity, yet permit reliance on the *vihāra*? Does this not contradict the subsequent passage?
Therefore, the commentary states: "This means that the commencement of the summer retreat (*varṣā*) precedes the establishment of the boundary (*sīmā*). The intention is this:
if the boundary were already established first, one would have to rely solely upon the boundary and would not be permitted to rely upon the monastery grounds (*ārāma*).

Now, since at the beginning of the summer there is no yet-established boundary but only the monastery, it is therefore permitted to rely upon the monastery grounds to observe the summer retreat. Fabao says: "This is merely following ancient discourse; according to the masters of the present day, however—"

It is not restricted to the *sīmā* (boundary). Rather, whenever one finds a spacious location suitable for the occasion, one may rely upon it. Therefore, in the *Karmavibhāṣā-śāstra*, the "boundary of the monastery" (*vihāra-sīmā*) is permitted;

this is because it depends solely on the essential intention and lacks the three sections of the "definitive attachment. If one relies on the monastery within the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), the same principle applies:
that is, when the ritual boundary (*karmabhūmi-sīmā*) is large and the monastery is small, one may enter the monastery to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*) and depart from it.

Regarding the statement, "If the gate is broken, the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is ended; the same applies to a small boundary (*sīmā*)," there are two interpretations. According to Xuánzàng, this is the converse of the preceding sentence.

That is to say, in the previous case, the boundary was large and the monastery (*ārāma*) was small; one entered the monastery for the retreat and broke the retreat upon exiting the monastery gate. Now, however, the boundary is small and the monastery is large;
one enters the boundary to establish the retreat and breaks the retreat upon exiting the boundary. Thus, the meaning is derived by reversing the phrasing. It should be... [text ends].

The same applies to the minor boundary (kṣudra-sīmā) within the cloud-element (megha-dhātu). Alternatively, it may refer to the Dharma-jewel (dharma-ratna), meaning that within a great boundary (mahā-sīmā), there is a minor boundary for the gathering of the Saṃgha;

one may observe the rains retreat (varṣā) based on this minor boundary. If one leaves the minor boundary, the summer retreat is broken; therefore, it is said "the same applies. (This interpretation is superior.

Regarding the fourth section, "if the fundamental [boundary] generally depends on [others]," etc., it means that at the time of the initial formal establishment (jñapti), one was unaware that within this great boundary there were those who had not yet received the precepts (śīla).

Regarding the phrase "the site" (*kṣetra*): although there are distinctions such as the small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*) and others, as long as one remains within the original designated location, the [summer retreat] is not lost.

If this is so, why was it stated previously that entering the *sīmā-kṣetra* (the ritual enclosure) and so forth breaks the summer retreat? The *Chao* (Commentary) answers: "All these refer to cases where one acts in contradiction to the original intention," and so on.

This means that while the original intention was based upon the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), now entering the *śīla-kṣetra* (the ritual enclosure) or other small boundaries constitutes a departure from that original initial mind.

Regarding the contradiction where both sides incur faults: among the four preceding propositions, the first proposition—in which one enters the *sīmā* (ordination platform), etc.—constitutes one fault.

The third proposition—in which one relies on a monastery (*ārāma*) within the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) and now leaves the gate, thereby breaking the summer retreat (*varṣa*)—constitutes two faults.

"Both [cases] are lax regarding the reliance on the *dharmasīmā*" refers to the four propositions mentioned above: first, the great boundary; second, the great boundary within the monastery; third, the monastery...

Regarding the outer great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*): the four fundamental [boundaries] all depend upon the great boundary, and in each case, the violation occurs by proceeding from the lax to the strict.

As for "following the strictness according to the location of the room": suppose there is a three-room dwelling; if one initially resolves in mind, "I shall rely on the middle room," and subsequently exits through either of the two side rooms, one's summer retreat (*varṣa*) is broken because one followed the strict path.
This name is established in contrast to the lax. Regarding the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and other texts: within the causal narratives (*nidāna*) of the Vinaya, there is...
If a donor invites [a monk] to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*), and later a danger arises that he wishes to leave, he must seek permission from the donor himself to move.
If the donor grants permission, it is well; if not, he should [act] himself... (and so forth).
Regarding the phrase "breaking the summer retreat" (*varṣā-bheda*) upon reaching [a certain point], or "staying intentionally":

if there are circumstances such as the illness of one's parents, or the arising of wholesome states and the cessation of unwholesome ones, and if one is detained with insistence, the Noble Ones permit one to stay for the time being; this is not called breaking the summer retreat. However, if one is detained merely out of ordinary human sentiment, it constitutes a breach.

This is not permissible. It is likewise for those who have committed one of the eight difficulties or who have exceeded the time limit and do not return. According to these principles, the *Cīvara-vastu* states:

"If one receives a formal authorization (*jñapti*) based on a person resolving a dispute, if one receives it at dawn for the afternoon session, or receives it in the afternoon for the dawn session [it is invalid]."

One must not take a circuitous route; one should follow the direct path. If there are obstacles on the way, there is no offense. Upon reaching the point where the boundary is severed, the period of residence is terminated.

If one wishes to return and takes a detour, this constitutes a violation of the time limit, which results in the breaking of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat). Due to taking a circuitous route and violating the time limit, the *varṣā* is likewise broken.
If one takes a detour without violating the time limit, it is auspicious.

Regarding the phrase "the five [rules] up to the formal act" (*dharmakarma*), it is as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "from the beginning up to the subsequent formal act," two chapters were previously opened;

this is now the first, hence it says "the beginning. As for "the subsequent formal act following the *pravāraṇā*," this refers to the section where the *guṇadharmas* (meritorious rules) are appended and described in detail.
Some claim that robes kept for one month are called *kārttika*, while those kept for five months are called *kaṭhina*; such a view is profoundly erroneous.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "next, reaching the second condition," this refers to entering into understanding. As for the mention of "breaking the summer retreat" (*pakhā*), this is an explanation provided by ancient masters.

They state that because the Buddha commanded that the formal act of binding and releasing [the boundary] should be performed at the conclusion of the summer retreat, the ancients said: "Once the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) is completed according to the Vinaya, four matters ought to be carried out. First, oneself..."
1. Liberating the boundary (*sīmā-utsarga*); 2. Dissolving the boundary; 3. Establishing the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*); 4. Receiving the *kaṭhina* robe.

Since this summer retreat has not yet concluded, and because one originally relied upon a specific boundary for the retreat, dissolving that original boundary would cause one to lose the basis [of the retreat], thereby resulting in the loss of the summer [vassa].

This [argument] which falsely cites the words of the Noble Ones refutes the ancients. The Vinaya text’s instruction to dissolve and establish the boundaries at the conclusion of the summer refers to cases where various boundaries collectively receive the *kaṭhina*.

"Robe": this refers to causing [the monks] to dissolve the boundary (*sīmā*), not to opening it, breaking it, or relinquishing it individually—that is, each person dissolves their own original boundary.

"General binding": this means binding collectively to form one great boundary (*mahāsīmā*). "Shared reception": this means receiving the five benefits together. "Joint dissolution": this means that after having received them, they dissolve them together. "Separate binding":

this means that while remaining at a higher level, each person separately binds and takes up a great boundary. Regarding the extensive text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), it says: "That..."

Question: At the end of the summer retreat, many monasteries collectively establish a single boundary (*sīmā*). Once they have received the *kaṭhina* robe, they relinquish this great boundary (*mahāsīmā*).
Are all the bhikṣus therein said to have received the *kaṭhina* robe? Answer: All of them may indeed receive it. Furthermore, regarding the commentary:

This is the primary commentary. It also states: "If one dissolves the boundary (*sīmā*) during the summer retreat, the retreat is not broken. The *Xin zhang* (New Chapter) agrees with the Nanshan school. It refutes the ancients who say:
"If it is claimed that by relying on a boundary for the retreat, dissolving the boundary during the summer constitutes losing the basis [of the retreat], then consider this:

if one relies on a monastery (*ārāma*) for the retreat, and the monastery or its stupa collapses, should the retreat be broken? Regarding the phrase "the ancients and others," they refer to those who perform the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination).
This is difficult to understand and contemplate. If there are difficult circumstances, it is permitted to shorten the days for the *pravāraṇā*.

Since the *pravāraṇā* is already allowed even though the rainy-season retreat (*varṣāvāsa*) has not yet concluded, why should it not be permitted to dissolve the boundary (*sīmā*) during the summer? Therefore, it is said that the text encompasses both [cases] and requires mutual compatibility between the two.
In the commentaries, it is recorded that dissolving and re-establishing the boundary during the summer is a formal rule (*dharmatā*), as it certainly does not constitute a violation of the retreat.
Thesis: The reason is that this is a monastic (*saṃgha*) rule. The analogy is like the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) before the summer retreat has ended;

the *pravāraṇā* is a monastic rule, yet performing the *pravāraṇā* does not break the summer retreat. Dissolving the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*) is also a monastic rule, and likewise, performing the *pravāraṇā* together does not break the summer retreat.

Regarding the statement that there is no hindrance, the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) says: "However, the method of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is not restricted to a specific *dharmadhātu*; it may be undertaken anywhere."

If one is removed from the place of the original essential [boundary], and the boundary is dissolved, how could there be any obstruction? Because emotional limitations differ, those who distinguish [the cases] say:

if the emotional limitation lies within the *dharmadhātu*, then during the summer retreat (*varṣā*), the boundaries may be dissolved; since the great and small [monastic orders] differ, they are thus distinguished.

If the boundaries of one’s intention lie within the natural limits, whether they are established through formal ritual (*dharmakarma*) during the summer retreat or are otherwise wide or narrow, they must be distinguished according to the location of those intentional limits.

In cases where there are no difficulties, one should rely on the original location—that is, the place defined by one’s original intention. In cases where there are difficulties, one may follow the provisions opened up in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
The eighth fascicle of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "After the prior retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*) has already commenced, if a sudden difficulty arises and one wishes to go elsewhere..."
Within a distance of three *yojanas*. If there are monks in that monastery or temple, they should be summoned.

If one has already crossed the boundary and intends to go to another location after having performed the second binding (*bandhana*), one must relinquish the previous [boundary] and perform the binding anew.

This is because, after relinquishing the former, one establishes the subsequent [boundary] at a place that is equally suitable. Thus, even in times of difficulty, the three *yojanas* may be obtained. If the subsequent ritual procedure is narrower than the original.

Regarding "natural" (prakṛti): this refers simply to relying on the original natural [measurement] for its width or narrowness when subsequently tying the knot. If there is no difficulty with the original natural [measurement], one relies on it;
this is the first rule. If there is a difficulty, one opens [the space] toward the newly tied location; this is the second condition. (The above concludes the explanation of the *Zhengpian*.)

Next, the explanation of the procedure for receiving the *dharmas* (precepts) is presented in two major sections: first, the citation of the title; second, the explanation. Regarding the first, concerning the "two procedures for receiving the days," the initial intent is as follows:
Now, during the three-day period of seclusion and the long duration of the nine-month summer retreat, there may arise conditions for the perpetual increase of good and the extinction of evil;

logically, these must be urgently remedied. Since the Buddha has already granted permission, it is appropriate to include them here in this explanation. Next, regarding the explanation of the title, one cites that request.
The intention is to inform the Saṃgha individually; when the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is internalized within oneself, it is termed "receiving" (*pratigraha*).

Regarding the formal procedures for the assembly (*saṃghakarma*), if one grants permission to depart with a fixed time, and this is determined by the appearance of dawn (*aruṇodaya*), it is termed a "day. Each of these follows its own specific rule, which is called a "dharma. An external objection states:

I have not yet ascertained whether, on the sixteenth day of the fourth month, immediately after the summer retreat has commenced, one may receive the *ruìrì* (permission to leave) upon being summoned for some business.
Some say it is not permitted; one must wait until the night has passed before the *ruìrì* can be received.
Fǎbǎo says: "The Vinaya text permits receiving [the *ruìrì*] during the summer. Since the retreat is now entered on the sixteenth day, is this not indeed the summer? There is no need for doubt."
Regarding the phrase "claiming to have completed the summer retreat": to deceive one's own mind means to call what is not correct what is correct;
this is called self-deception. Regarding "wasting the offerings of the faithful": suppose there is a donor who provides requisites for several bhikṣus during the summer retreat.

If the days [of the retreat] are not fulfilled, yet the summer has been broken, they falsely count it as a full year and presumptuously accept the benefits; therefore, it is called wasting [the offerings]. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "To falsely extend one's own summer retreat."
"Receiving offerings and committing grave offenses, etc. (and so forth). "Thus, to show in detail" means to provide a thorough exposition that gives rise to the meaning of the subsequent text.
"Regarding 'down to the explanation'" is as the text states. "Regarding 'the first' down to 'identical'"—the three types refer to the seven-day, half-month, and one-month periods.
As for the statement "there is a saying," it refers to the days calculated according to the sequential inclusion within the boundaries. "Regarding 'from the first' down to 'receiving'"... [as above].

Regarding receiving [the precepts] from the five groups (*pañca-varga*): The Buddha established the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) for the five groups, each receiving the date in relation to one another.
This does not mean that a *bhikṣu* receives it in relation to a lower group; since they do not fulfill the requirements for mutual dependence, how could one receive it from them?

The current text of the *Chao* (Excerpts) provisionally sets forth the method based on a single period. Regarding the passage "from two to knowing," it is as the text states. Regarding the passage "from three to grinding," the ancients said:
Regarding the method for receiving the *poṣadha* (observance) days: first one receives the seven-day period, next the half-month, and finally the month;

this is the sequence that accords with the Vinaya texts. If one has already received the half-month period, one may not subsequently receive the seven-day period, as the longer period subsumes the shorter;
thus, one does not undertake the seven-day rite again. Other examples follow the same principle as the *kaṭhina* robe, which is obtained during the five months of the *kārttika* season.

Regarding the "Moon and Others" (the former section cites ancient views): the present Master says it is not so. The *kaṭhina* robe is determined by its specific time of application; furthermore, both possess five benefits. Therefore, the long [period] subsumes the short.

However, this present practice of receiving the *māsa* (month) is distinct in its conditions and circumstances. Conditions may be short or long, and their sequence is not fixed; one cannot determine another’s case.
It is impossible to apply the same rule when the period is first short and later long. Thus, it is now said that there are three grades for receiving the *māsa*.

Thus, it depends on the length of the conditions. If the longer condition arrives first, one receives the precepts through the formal *karmavācanā* ceremony first. If the shorter condition arrives first, one receives them first through the face-to-face (*pratyakṣa*) method.
Even though the sequence in the Vinaya text is arranged in such a way, this is merely the conventional method;

how can one stubbornly cling to the literal text? As for the phrase "the intent of the question," the meaning of the question is as follows: since it was just stated that one should request the day according to the priority of the long or short conditions, why...

In the formal motion (*karmavācanā*) for obtaining [the permission], it says: "one receives the seven-day rule. If one has previously received the seven-day rule and has already completed its use, one may say "it has passed.
However, if a long-term reason arose first, one would have previously requested a half-month [period] and so forth;

since one has never before requested the seven-day rule from the outset, it is not appropriate to say "it has passed. This citation is because the present master himself composed it to resolve doubts.

This question and answer arose because the meaning of the text concerns the Path (*mārga*). Since the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is superior as it is performed by the Saṃgha, whereas the seven-day [period] is inferior as it is a rite for individuals performed face-to-face (*pratyekam*).
If this were not based on the distinction between superior and inferior, the fault would not pertain to oneself.
When the seven days have concluded, one says, "It has passed. Reflect on this. Furthermore, the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* asks:
"In the formal motion for receiving the [one-month] method, why does it not say 'to receive [the period] until fifteen days have passed' or 'to go beyond the boundary for one month'? The answer is:

although the half-month and the month differ in length, they are both entirely the monastic law (*saṃghadharma*). Since there is no distinction of superiority or inferiority in the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, one cannot speak of "passing" [the limit].
The seven-day method is inferior. The Commentary further asks: "If one now receives the fortnightly or monthly method and encounters a small month, how should it be counted?
According to the Vinaya text, the fortnightly [method] is performed according to the law based on fifteen days;

thus, one does not inquire whether it is a large or small month, but simply counts until the days are complete and returns. This is also like the thirty-nine nights mentioned in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations).
If one receives [the precepts] for one month, one must not count the days based on the "large" or "small" months, as the Vinaya says regarding "residing for three months" and so forth;

the small month is included within that period (this first follows the *Śāstra*). Furthermore, Fabao explains: for example, if the fifteenth day of a small month coincides with the day of the invitation (*pravāraṇā*).
In subsequent months, one should simply count thirty days to complete the period; this is based on the varying lengths of days and months when receiving the precepts.
As for the phrase "reaching the fourth clarification," this section follows entirely the ancient interpretation of the *Shoushu* (Commentary on the Preface).

It is somewhat difficult to comprehend. For now, I have explained the text according to the ancient interpretation; subsequently, I shall briefly point out how the present master’s view differs slightly from that of the ancients. If...

Having completed the formal reception for the seven-day period. Regarding those who receive the *karmavācanā* and subsequently obtain it: the *Baoyun* commentary intends to clarify what is mutually inclusive by first clarifying what is not mutually inclusive.

"If the seven days have not yet been used" means that although there was an offering and an invitation to perform ritual recitations for seven days, one has now finished the procedure for requesting the seven-day period through face-to-face confession (*pratimukha*), but has not yet gone to the donor’s house; therefore, it is said they have "not yet used" it. Or...
Regarding "the period not yet exhausted": this refers to having already spent four days after arriving at the donor's house on the day of the invitation;

because three days still remain, it is said to be "not yet exhausted. Regarding "having other circumstances": these refer to separate matters concerning the Triple Gem, or perhaps circumstances such as being invited to preach the Dharma or to receive the precepts of refuge and discipline.
Regarding "or exceeding seven days": the current text should be revised to read, "or exceeding seven [days]."
The "daily basis" refers to the rules for the half-month and the month. In the present text, we provisionally cite the daily rules for the half-month;

this concerns the acceptance through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*). "The preceding rule has expired" means referring to the aforementioned seven-day rule, which is either entirely unused or has not been fully utilized;
thus, it has already fallen into disuse. The phrase "because the force of the ritual procedure [is superior]" explains the meaning of mutual inclusion.
This is because the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) can encompass the inferior rules for the seven-day period. Regarding "one cannot have two dharmas in succession":
within a single body, it is not possible for the two conditions of the seven-day and the half-month periods to arise in succession. The passage beginning with "The Vinaya says...
and below is an ancient master’s own citation of scriptural evidence. The phrase "it must necessarily" refers to the fixed rule of the seven-day period; it is indeed determined.
It is nullified.

As for "if one has previously received the *karman* for the duration of the days," this refers to having first received the rule for a half-month or a month in one's possession for the sake of the Triple Gem and other such matters;
yet now, perhaps due to a donor’s request for seven days of ritual recitation, it is necessary to wait for the conditions of the prior half-month.

Only after [the full period] has concluded may one be permitted to receive the seven-day [period]. If the half-month rule is already in effect for oneself, then requesting the seven-day period through face-to-face acknowledgment (*pratimukha*) will naturally not be valid.
Regarding the statement that "even until it becomes truly unacceptable," this is a personal commentary that refutes the ancient [position].
If there is a matter for which one month is insufficient, one may perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) to receive the "one-month rule.

Furthermore, by receiving the "seven-day rule" in conjunction with it, they together constitute thirty-seven days. This is because the former is indeed real, yet that [real duration] cannot be maintained; therefore, the one-month rule remains in effect.
One may not request an additional seven days; from this point on, it is contrary to the Dharma (the above constitutes the interpretation of the text according to the views of the ancient masters).

According to the present master, half of this is permitted while the other half is not. This is simply because the previously mentioned seven-day rule has not yet been employed, or has not been fully exhausted, and there are further conditions such as the fortnightly (*pakṣa*) rules and so forth. If these are concurrent conditions, they then constitute a mutual [requirement].
[The former] is subsumed [by the latter]. Both are objects of the donor’s veneration and mindfulness; alternatively, they may share the same conditions as the Three Jewels and so forth.

It is not permitted for one body to have two successive dharmas; logically, this is indeed impossible. This is what is meant by "half-acceptance. If they were distinct conditions, the two would not be mutually subsumed:

the former would be the donor’s invitation, while the latter would be the conditions of the Three Jewels and so forth. If the ancients had not permitted [the former], there would be no logical basis [for the latter].
This partially refutes our contemporary master. In the *Jie-mo-shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā), an example is cited:

"For instance, if one is ill and must take ghee, while two conditions have not yet been resolved, the oral ritual (*khou-fa*) follows the specific matter at hand. The three grades of 'receiving the day' (*shou-ri*) differ, all being based on various circumstances;

it is not permissible to follow [the rule] regarding the reception [of time], etc. (and so forth). According to this, our contemporary master permits [the practice] only when the conditions are identical, but does not permit it when the conditions differ. The ancients...
People do not distinguish between identical and different conditions; they all reject [the former]. The Vinaya states: "If one does not return on that very day...
If our current master were to cite this as scriptural proof, it would only prove that one may not [remain] under identical conditions for up to thirty-seven days.

Our current master also applies this to cases of different conditions, which is no contradiction to the text. Why is it that there is a one-month invitation for the Triple Gem, yet a seven-day invitation for a donor?

This cannot be established. If it were to share the same object of perception (*ālambana*), it would truly be untenable. One must rely on the ancient commentaries; this [current position] is entirely lacking in refinement.
It is merely because of a failure to comprehend the Vinaya texts that such a confused exposition has resulted.

Regarding the passage from "It is said, two to eight" to "the ordinary": Xuán says: "One receives the name 'progress' (*jin*) based on conditions. If it is not a day of receiving conditions, it is not accomplished; is this not so?
It is divided into eight parts, as described below in the *Chao* (copious notes) [etc.]. Regarding what is called 'determining whether conditions are correct or incorrect':

conditions that give rise to good and extinguish evil regarding the Three Jewels are called 'correct. Conditions such as breaking the precepts or seeking profit are called 'incorrect. Regarding the passage from "The ordinary" to... [end of excerpt].

Regarding those who later committed the same offense: as for one who commits a grave offense by giving property to the Sangha, suppose there is a person who intends to give goods to the Sangha but does not see anyone with ten years of seniority.
This bhikṣu is actually nine years senior, yet he claims to have ten years of seniority; because he causes another to fail to obtain what they ought to receive, it is a grave offense.
"Extensive as in the subsequent text" means that Xuánzàng says it refers to the precept against selling items according to their appearance, which states:
"If one sells items to make stūpas or images, one must not prostrate toward them; this applies even to making bedding, for every such transformation leads to a downfall," and so forth.
Regarding the statement, "dividing into five categories according to conditions": first, the Three Jewels, up to the fifth, the protection of the Sangha and the Dharma (and so forth).

Regarding the statement, "first, as for offenses": concerning matters pertaining to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, King Prasenajit provided testimony against a minister who was faithless and held a jealous, evil mind, wishing to dig a channel through the Jetavana Monastery. Compared with this...
The Buddha wished to go and inform [the King], but he thought that the road was too far for him to return on the same day.
Since the Buddha permitted the acceptance of the seven-day period, this constitutes a connection with the Triple Gem (*triratna*). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* is also like this;

the explanations in that Vinaya are largely the same, though it mentions only laypeople intending to pass water, rather than the unfaithful ministers. Regarding "Great Monasteries" (*mahāvihāra*), one interpretation says they refer to many monasteries.

The second interpretation states: "Even within a single monastery, for many various matters, one is permitted to request the *jīrì* (day of receiving the precepts) on all such occasions" (the former explanation is correct).

Xuán says: "In the present day, there are those who ask: 'Is it permissible for a monastery to grant permission to receive the *jīrì*? The answer is: it is exactly as prescribed in the *Sifenlü* (Four-Part Vinaya)."
King Prasenajit was leading his army to suppress a rebellion among the people of a bordering state.
The robes, food, drink, and other necessities previously offered by him to the Buddha and the Saṃgha were seized by an unfaithful minister.

The bhikṣus went to inform the king, but they reflected that the road was too long for them to return on the same day. The Buddha said, "In such a circumstance, I permit you to accept [the requisites]."

Seven days [after] departure. Examining the meaning of this passage, it concerns matters permitted by the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; one obtains the full duration of the *jīvitadivasa* (day of life).
The rest may be understood accordingly (*yathāyogam*). (And so forth.)

Regarding the statement that one should not go for two reasons, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* asks, "Is it for the sake of protecting the observance (*poṣadha*) and so forth? This is a question posed by Upāli to the Buddha. The answer states:

"It is for the sake of the seven classes of followers receiving the *karmavācanā* (formal authorization). That is, the seven classes of followers act as the hosts. The text enumerates two hundred and forty-two conditions, all of which are conditions related to the seven-day period (*saptāha*).
As for "sending a messenger" versus "not sending a messenger," when the person in front comes to invite [the monk], this is called [the former].

He sent a messenger to go [to the nun]. Even if she had previously not come for the invitation, it is called "not sending a messenger. Since this is a condition for generating wholesome states (*kuśala-dharma*) and so forth, going there in person is also permitted.
This is the position of other schools (*para-nikāya*). According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya), one must not go if no messenger was sent;

however, if one hears of her death or similar circumstances while on the way, according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ten-Recitation Vinaya), it says: "The Bhikṣu-saṃgha has come to grant the *smṛtivinaya* and *amūḍhavinaya* to the Bhikṣuṇī."

The Buddha said: "You should go. If, while on the way, you hear that the bhikṣuṇī has passed away, returned the precepts to enter the assembly of non-Buddhists, or fallen into one of the eight difficult conditions (aṣṭāvakṣaṇa), then if you proceed, you commit a *duṣkṛta* offense."

Regarding the third point, "visiting those who have come": the kindness of one's great parents in raising and nurturing one is profound; likewise, ministers possess the power to cause benefit or harm. Even if one lacks faith or devotion toward them, one must still visit;
if one already possesses faith and devotion, it is all the more appropriate to go. As for other laypeople, if they have faith and devotion, one may visit;

however, if they lack faith, going is not permitted. This is necessarily explained in terms of whether there is power; that is to say, it refers to a bhikṣu who possesses the power of the Path and is able to transform and guide others.
"Even though he does not believe now, once he arrives there, you should persuade him and cause him to have deep faith. If it is like this, one may go.

Regarding the statement that "the fourth [case] does not constitute [a valid reason for departure]," this is explained in the *An-ming nan* (Difficulties regarding the entrustment of life). It refers to moving during the *an-guo* (rainy season retreat). The fifth [case] states:
"If my life will certainly face obstacles," and the Buddha said, "I permit it. The *Jie-mo su* (Karmavācanā Commentary) says: "If one's own illness is severe and one cannot endure..."
"Receiving [the robes] on the day [of the full moon]" refers to a situation where life is at risk; in such a case, one may receive them directly. Regarding "losing the three and receiving the three":

this refers to the loss of the precept regarding the three robes within the context of following the formal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Our Master says: if one first receives two and has not yet exceeded the limit of sufficiency, yet commits an offense by receiving a third, this is cited as an extreme case to illustrate what follows.
"Discarding that which is prohibited and taking that which is permitted": the three robes are what is prohibited [to exceed], while extra items are what is permitted. Now, the three...

The robes were missing; this constitutes a violation of the prohibition (*śikṣāpada*). Possessing an excessive number of extra robes (*atirekacīvara*) constitutes a transgression of what is permitted.

Because one does not rely on the texts of the Noble Teaching, it is said that one has not yet followed the Buddha’s transformation. According to the *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* on the forfeiture of robes, this refers to loss according to the specific circumstances.
Regarding the *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* on the confiscation of the three robes, this refers to the absence of any one of them as it happens to be lacking. The rest is as stated in the text (etc.).
Regarding the phrase "because the five [factors] arrive": harmonizing the Saṃgha is the protection of the Dharma. This means that harmonizing the Saṃgha is itself the protection of the Dharma;

if one does not protect the Dharma, there will be internal disruption and external unwholesomeness, resulting in the destruction and extinction of the Buddha-Dharma. As for the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and other texts:

regarding those in the same boundary (*sīmā*) observing the rains retreat (*varṣā*), the Vinaya presents four cases. The first is when one sees a bhikṣu making preparations with the intent to split the Saṃgha; the second is when one hears of a bhikṣu...

Regarding the skillful means (*upāya*) for seeking to cause a schism in the Saṃgha, the case for a *bhikṣuṇī* is also twofold, as explained above. In both instances, it is because [the Buddha] is present here;

if he were to depart, they would immediately reconcile. The Buddha permitted those who are straightforward. According to the *Dongta Shu* (Commentary on the East Pagoda), these four cases are resolved simply by shifting the conditions for the summer retreat (*varṣā*).

Now, we rely on the conditions for receiving a formal authorization (*jñapti*). If one follows the intent of shifting the summer retreat, one may subsequently obtain [permission] from various locations, and the Saṃgha shall perform the act of settling [the matter].
Regarding "dwelling": even if these difficulties persist and one cannot remain, one must not return [to the original place]. This refers to the meaning of the preceding text.

If one intends to go away temporarily, then wherever one subsequently arrives, the intention of *varṣā* (the rains retreat) does not arise. To wait specifically for the difficulties to subside before returning is precisely the meaning of this passage (and so forth).
Regarding the "external boundary" (*bāhyasīman*), the Vinaya has four cases: first, hearing that there are bhikṣus there and employing skillful means with the intent to...
Regarding the schism of the Saṃgha: there are two cases where one hears that the Saṃgha has already been split; for the Bhikṣuṇīs, there are likewise two cases, identical to those above.

As for the Buddha’s permission in both instances, it is granted because such [schisms] exist within that boundary, and he requires that they be reconciled. The Dongta commentary states: "These four cases merely await the cessation of the difficulty;

one must then return to the boundary, even if it does not reach the end of the summer retreat. However, the characteristics of reconciliation and extinction are difficult to discern. According to the ancient masters:

All say that for a *saṃgha-karman*, the Vinaya permits one to go directly without mentioning the formal reception of days (*ādeśanā*). This is truly because, once the *saṃgha* has dissolved, its boundaries are difficult to discern;
it is unclear by what method one should receive the days to be valid. Now, the Master says: "Indeed, the characteristics of a dissolved *saṃgha* are difficult to discern."

The word "ran" (然) carries the sense of both concession and restriction. To concede is to state it directly; to restrict is to require that one receive [the precepts] on the appointed day. Thus, it is said "ran.

Regarding the phrase "it does not hinder the textual principle when considering the conditions": this means that with respect to the condition of harmonizing the Saṃgha—where the journey is long and the matter of dispute is great—one may rely on the procedure for receiving [the precepts] as described in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
This is, for example, like how before the Vinaya Piṭaka was divided, it was practiced and applied universally; even now, although...
It is divided. To apply it according to this principle does not contradict the general course of the Dharma; therefore, the *Jie-mo shu* (Karmavācanā Commentary) states:

"There must be limits for the harmony [of the assembly]; one relies on those who have received permission. As for matters that are unlimited, one may follow the text concerning the conclusion of affairs in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*" (the above is the text of the commentary).

Regarding the absence of a formal act of definitive resolution (*samyak-prahāṇa*) in the Vinaya: according to several sections of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* concerning the schism of the Saṃgha, it is stated that "one shall proceed with this very matter," and thus there is no need for the formal reception of the day (*divasa-grahaṇa*), and so forth.
Therefore, the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: "The Vinaya merely clarifies the conditions [for the schism] and does not explicitly clarify the reception [of the day]."

Regarding the phrase "the above refers to the ultimate": as for "one who begs for wheat," Xuán (玄) states: "This rule in the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya concerns the case where the group of six bhikṣuṇīs begged for raw grain."
To cultivate hemp, beans, rice, or wheat is censured by the world; therefore, for a *bhikṣuṇī* it is a *nihsargika-pāyattika*, and for a monk (*bhikṣu*) it is a *duṣkṛta*. Both are primary offenses.

As for "bending one's command to suit particular circumstances," this refers to entrusting a layperson to come with a written invitation when the silkworms are ripe, saying, "I, the poor monk, require silk and other such materials.
This is contrary to the Dharma. Since silk is inherently an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), such a request through an intermediary will certainly not be fulfilled.

To deceive one's own pure mind is to waste the offerings of donors in vain. Regarding those who make various requests in the Vinaya—whether they be bhikṣus, śramaṇas, or even lay patrons (dānapati)—each sends a messenger to invite them individually, saying, "Venerable Sir, please come to receive precepts, perform repentance for transgressions, or accept alms for me.
By requiring a messenger to be sent, this conversely reveals that such solicitation and entreaty constitute an unrighteous act. This applies to parents and others as well.

Regarding those who follow the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), the Vinaya states: "If one's parents are either faithful and joyful or not faithful and joyful, one may go [to them] provided they permit it;
as for others, it is the same. This refers to the preceding passage which says that if ordinary laypeople are generally joyful and have faith, they may listen;

if they lack faith, they are not permitted. The *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao* (The Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya) maintains this principle: if one's parents or other individuals [permit it], it is the same as in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, constituting the seventh [condition].

The multitude shall generate merit. Regarding those who inquire out of doubt, even if one is sent as a messenger or not sent, provided it is not for the sake of personal gain, all parties shall obtain [the merit].
This clearly shows that a biased command or a separate debt constitutes an easy means of profit; this is indeed not without reason.
Regarding the statement, "The second pair refers to arrival": as for the combination and separation of matters, "matter" refers to the object being confronted.

To receive [the precepts] separately according to individual conditions is called "separation"; to cite and enter [them] all at once through many conditions is called "combination. In the present text, only the combined reception is explained.

"Appropriate legal conditions" excludes those that are not legal. "According to how many there may be" refers to the number of conditions, whether more or less, such as three families or two families.
Regarding "being permitted to receive [the *poṣadha*] by combining [days]," the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states:

"If there are two conditions, such as those of the months of Zhang and Wang, each being a seven-day period, they cannot be combined into a half-month reception; this is because they are two separate seven-day conditions."

As for the matters: each is performed by a different person, and thus one may only recite [the precepts] for seven days in total, whether before or after. One should apply this principle accordingly (the above is the commentary).
If one [matter] lasts three days and another [matter] lasts four days, once both conditions have been met, the full seven days are used; at that point, it is appropriate to receive [the precepts].

Regarding cases such as the confession of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, this is cited as an example to explain the point: namely, that the confession of offenses also involves the principles of separation and combination.

This is explained according to the offenses of the same category. To confess a single offense is called "separation" (li). Alternatively, when three or five offenses are simultaneously concealed, one undergoes the six-night penance (ṣaḍrātra) and the purification of the offense (āpattivyutthāna) together.
The inclusion of titles [in the list] follows this precedent; they are fully enumerated and set forth in the Vinaya texts.

It should be said that this explains the established rules for requesting the assembly once they have already emerged from their retreat. As stated above, this is based on the *Shan-chao* (The Ritual Manual), specifically according to the rules for the seven-day separate observance (*pṛthag-dharma*).
The intent behind the separation and combination [of these rites] has been concluded; now, the separation and combination of the monastic laws (*saṃgha-dharma*) shall be set forth for your knowledge.

Although the *Shan-chao* does not explicitly clarify this, I shall briefly describe it here. For instance, when a donor (*dānapati*) requests a fortnightly ritual of veneration and recitation, or for the sake of the Three Jewels as objects of worship...

Regarding the *dhātu* (boundary): it is not permissible to undergo the half-month [observance] twice; rather, since both are now the same *karmavācanā*, one simply requests the method for the full month.
This can be accomplished by including the wording for both occasions within the formal document (*viniścaya*). This is the intended meaning.
As for the method of the month, the Venerable One divides the days and nights into two types, establishing them as three sets of ten-day periods for the Triple Gem. Thus, there are thirty days.

On this day, one performs the ritual for the donor; together with the preceding month, within these nights, one fully receives the one-month dharma. Thus, two conditions are obtained. The Venerable One said:
"This principle exists within the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* (羯磨疏). (Based on this, although there are two conditions according to the circumstances, it does not hinder their being combined in intent;
regarding the dharma itself, they have always been one, because both utilize the same period of one month.)"

Regarding the phrase "because it reaches three": that which is for the sake of a specific condition (*pratyaya*) is what is cited as the recipient. This refers either to an invitation from a donor (*dānapati*) or to conditions such as the Three Jewels;
these are the "for the sake of" (*sādhyārtha*). "Manifest" (*pratyakṣa*) means appearing in accordance with those conditions. For example, in the case of an invitation from a donor:

The "now" refers to having already sent the *śāstra* (explanatory notes) and so forth. Regarding "recording the matter for the sake of receiving": recording the previous location constitutes the "matter.
Granting seven days or half a month—the Venerable said there are two types of "suspended reception. To cite the method of the Sangha regarding half a month as an example:
suppose a donor takes [the precepts] on the twentieth day of this month and begins the recitation; this bhikṣu, on the fifteenth day of the [following] month, at the *poṣadha*...

At that time, because the Saṃgha has assembled, one next undergoes the *ardhamāsa* (fortnightly) rite. Although one has not yet gone to inform [the donor], the conditions for doing so have already manifested;
thus, one is already participating in the reception of the rite. Only when the time arrives is it termed "receiving in advance.

Furthermore, another explanation is that once the rite for the day has been completed, one intends to go and inform [the donor]; however, due to other matters at the donor’s household, one has not yet been able to perform the salutations and mindfulness rites.
"Returning from Yanyan, it will take another ten days or so. Once a bhikṣu has received the dharma into his person, he need not receive it again at that time;
the rules for the one-month and seven-day periods are explained accordingly. This principle is urgent; please record it clearly now.
Therefore, I have briefly discussed its application. To "fabricate conditions in vain" means that the matter has not yet... [text ends].
These are indeed empty fabrications; some claim seven days, half a month, or a month, while others rely on ancient sayings.
For instance, there was once a person with desires who spoke loosely during the springtime, saying: "In my village, there is a certain family home which, every summer..."

He constantly gave alms to the Sangha. [The disciple asked: "Would it be possible for the Upādhyāya to come at this time? When the Bhikṣu reached the summer retreat, he recalled what had been said during the spring.

He then wished to go there; thus it is said, "vaguely resembling but not yet real," meaning that while the matter was vaguely present before him, he had not yet attained its reality, and so he immediately accepted the day [of departure].
Regarding "the matter being false and the limit being obscured": since the previous matter was already false, he now again acts with concealment and ambiguity.

Limitation. To adopt fixed rules leads to error. Regarding the arbitrary setting of the number of days: it arises from taking the previous matter as a mere pretext and using it as a basis for such limitations.
It is not yet appropriate to debate matters of length or brevity. Now, some may receive [the precepts] for seven days, half a month, or one month;
such durations of days are all falsely established as distinct rules for the Saṃgha, and they do not grant them to one another.
Regarding the statement, "As for 'four days' up to what should be obtained,' it refers to using them for other purposes," this recalls the ancient interpretation. Master Shou said:
"The original intent was for the Buddhist community to receive [the seven-day period]. Having already used three days and completed those affairs, there remain four remaining days.
If there are further matters concerning the Dharma or the Sangha, one may take these residual days to use them without fault; therefore, it is permissible."
Regarding this: according to the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there is a formal announcement (*jñapti*) for using the remaining portion of the night; thus we know that it is permissible.

As for the statement "it is not permissible," this is the refutation by our Master [Hui-ying]. He means that at the time the initial resolve was made, it was originally for the Buddha to receive the seven-day period and was not for other circumstances.
Now, since the matters concerning the Buddha's affairs have been completed and the ritual has concluded, even if there are remaining days, they cannot be used because there is no [valid] basis.
Since this is the Dharma, why would one need it? Therefore, it cannot be obtained; there must necessarily be an underlying cause (*nidāna*).

How could there be any discrepancy regarding its universal application? Now, the Master explains it himself: at the time of the original recitation, it was universally applied to the Three Jewels, illnesses, and so forth, based on the reception of the seven-day period.

Now, for Buddhist rites (*buddhakārya*), the use is completed in three days. There remain four days, which may then be universally applied to other uses without any discrepancy. A discrepancy arises from failure.
Furthermore, an ancient master posed a counter-question: "If that is so, why does the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* mention 'informing the rest of the night' (*avaśeṣa-rātri-śeṣa*)?
The *Shoujue chao* provides a resolution, stating: "In the *Daśabhāṇavāra*, 'informing the rest of the night' refers to cases where it is the same single matter, etc.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: "The bhikṣus received a [seven-day] period; having arrived in a village, seven nights had not yet elapsed, and they performed..."
The task was not yet finished. Upon returning, he informed the Buddha. Consequently, the Buddha permitted the acceptance of "remaining nights" (*śeṣarātra*).
He said: "I have accepted seven nights, and two nights have already passed; there remain so many nights. I shall go beyond the boundary. Such is the text of the Vinaya.

Since it states that "what was to be done is not yet finished," it is clear that the original conditions for the formal act (*dharmakarma*) remain in force and have not been relinquished. Therefore, what loss is there in informing [the Sangha] of the remaining nights? This does not mean anything other than this.
Regarding the matter: the *Chao* (Commentary) again refutes the ancients for failing to understand the Vinaya text. It says: "The *Yi-jie-mo-su* (Commentary on the Intentional Karma) states:

'If there was originally no intention to receive [the precepts], how could one perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*)? If it were originally due to the Three Jewels and so forth, the *Jie-mo-su* states:
'If it concerns the Three Jewels, one need only manage the affairs; at the time of performing the ritual, these must be included within the text, as they are all mental phenomena. Subsequently...
This is a general rule. Regarding matters such as those concerning the Three Jewels for future generations and so forth, this section further provides a detailed analysis. Huainan said:

"Originally, for the purpose of producing the *Śākyamuni-buddha-saddharma-puṣpa-sūtra* and for the sake of the permanent endowment [of the Sangha] (and so forth), after receiving seven days [of leave], four days were already used.
The preceding matters were all explained. Now, perhaps for the purpose of producing the *Maitreya-buddha-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*, [for the sake of] the ten directions and the permanent..."
Regarding the matter of abiding: since it is also improper to employ the remaining days from a previous period, it is said that these are not the "three jewels of prior conditions.

As for "mixed conditions," these refer to receiving precepts, performing prostrations and recitations, and so forth. When one’s own family’s general conditions are deemed sufficient according to the mind, this refers to the interpretation of advancing or retreating.
That is to say, if the Zhang family invites [the master] for seven days but does not permit the acceptance of offerings, yet also invites [him] to receive precepts and perform repentance.
...and so forth. This means that at the very moment one accepts the day [of the observance], one attains it because the mind is present.

Regarding the phrase "because it has reached": this is even more effective for generating wholesome qualities. As for the word *mi* (彌), it means "extensive" or "vast"; it should not be interpreted by using the small character *wei* (微) [meaning minute].

The Vinaya prescribes two types of invitations (*pavāraṇā*): first, the sequential invitation (*saṅgha-krama*); second, the individual invitation (*viśeṣa-pavāraṇā*). Since one has specifically invited [the preceptor] to accept the day, [the procedure is fulfilled].
There is also a difference in the *Mahāyāna Brahmajāla Sūtra*. This is because it concerns one who was not originally intended by the donor.
That is to say, the donor (dānapati) originally invited a certain person, but now seeing another person arrive, they are ultimately displeased and thus do not permit it.

However, the text of the *Chao* (the sub-commentary) discusses this only in broad terms. Or, even if the donor originally invited a specific bhikṣu, if that person does not come now, a substitute may also [be accepted].
It is possible. As for "one who does not give rise to affliction," this is logically acceptable.

Regarding the statement "receiving in five layers," this refers to receiving [the precepts] in successive layers within the Three Jewels; this is the standard established according to the doctrine of the present Master.

Regarding the statement "those who formerly went to the administrative office," and the phrase "formerly it was said that during one summer retreat three methods were opened," the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) recounts the ancient tradition as follows:

"The establishment of the practice of *an-gu* (rainy-season retreat) takes the cultivation of the Path as its primary purpose. When circumstances are urgent, three [methods] are permitted to be opened in order to meet the essential needs of the time. Why would one permit the re-acceptance [of the precepts]?"

This is illogical. Therefore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "In order to prevent a schism in the Saṃgha, one is permitted to receive [an invitation] for seven nights, but not for fourteen nights;
even up to receiving it for thirty-nine nights, one must completely break the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat). Thus, we know that successive invitations are not permitted.
As for the current claim that successive invitations are allowed, this interpretation by the present masters—which permits them repeatedly—is entirely different from the ancient tradition.
As stated in the Commentary (*shu*), this refers to the initial commentary. Now, according to the *Karmavācanā-śu*, it says:

"If, as in the previous case of a donor, one is summoned to receive the seven-day [passage], yet afterwards there are matters for the Three Jewels that must be managed, how could it not be permitted?
