Furthermore, in the case of official business, if two or three days are required, how could one be able [to remain]?

The original intent of the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is to refrain from wandering without purpose; now, when circumstances arise, one may go forth after receiving [the authorization] according to the Dharma."
It is not that those who are solely donors cannot go; how could they not be permitted? However, if it is in accordance with the Dharma, one may go for all such occasions.

The remaining text is no different from the *Śarīra-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (the *Chao*). Regarding the enumeration of more than twenty conditions in the Vinaya, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* lists twenty-three conditions at length;
these are all seven-day conditions. Because the matter had not yet manifested and the Buddha had not yet granted permission, it simply does not say that one may not go. For now...

Regarding the four matters concerning parents who have faith and devotion: First, at that time there were parents with faith and devotion who invited a bhikṣu, saying, "Venerable Sir, I wish to see you, yet the Buddha has not yet permitted it. I have such-and-such a matter. He then informed the Buddha, and the Buddha granted permission.
Second, there were likewise parents with faith and devotion who sent a messenger to summon him; this was also the same. Third, at that time there was a mother...
"Requesting a bhikṣu" is also as described above. At that time, there were parents who requested [the Buddha], and it was likewise as above;

thus, these constitute the fourfold repetition of the Buddha. Since each instance states "if [the Buddha] permits," how much more so for others? This refers to the preceding and succeeding instances involving the parents.
If one may still incur [the offense] regarding the four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*), how much more so for a *dānapati* or the Triple Gem (*triratna*), which cannot be restricted or limited;
thus, the grave offense is not waived. As for the phrase "reaching five," the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* mentions "invited" and "uninvited" and so forth, citing another school. The *Pañcavargika* says:
Udāyin had faith and took delight in the Buddha’s Dharma. During the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), he built a dwelling for the Saṃgha and prepared a meal to be served inside it.
However, because the bhikṣus would not accept the dwelling, the elder became resentful and said, "I have spent my wealth for the sake of food, yet the bhikṣus will not accept it."

He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha permitted him to accept the invitation. As for those who do not receive an invitation: if a bhikṣu has a doubt and must go outside the boundary, the Buddha permits him to go for up to seven days.
Now, the Master says: "How could there be such a thing as opening the way for one to go and inquire immediately upon having a prior doubt?"
Later, such doubts may not be raised.
Regarding the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*’s listing of "many seven-night [periods]," it says: Upāli addressed the Buddha, "For whom is the seven-night [period] received? The Buddha said:

For the sake of the seven assemblies, he established the merit-receiving [practice] and extensively listed twenty-three conditions. For the *upāsaka*, twenty-three were listed, and so on down to the *śrāmaṇerī*;
each and every one of these was for a period of seven nights, all of which were permitted. An ancient master raised an objection, saying:
If this is so, why does the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* permit only one seven-night period and not two seven-night periods? One may cite the *Śāstra* (commentary) to resolve this, stating:

"The permission for one seven-night period and the prohibition against two seven-night periods mean that one cannot simultaneously claim two seven-night periods, as they would be used redundantly before and after.

Now, our Master says that the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* does not allow it; perhaps this refers to the fact that within a single matter, one cannot have two seven-night periods. How could it be otherwise?

Regarding the regulation of distinct matters: is it not permitted to receive [the *poṣadha*]? Furthermore, concerning the statement that "two periods of seven nights are not permitted," the method for receiving the days consists of only two categories:
first, seven nights; second, twenty-nine nights. Therefore, regarding the seven-night period received before the assembly (*pratimukha*), how could one add another layer?

Thus, it is said that two periods of seven nights are not permitted. What prevents those who depart before or after [the assembly] from all being granted [this privilege] by the ancients? It is not so.
He grasped the meaning of the text, but seeing only the statement "the two-week period is not permitted," he falsely interpreted it to mean that receiving [the robe] again is not allowed.

An ancient master further raised an objection, saying: "If that were so, since you have already granted permission for multiple receipts within a single instance, why then did the harmonious Saṃgha establish the *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rule?"

That Vinaya permits one who has broken the *anvāya* (rainy-season retreat) to do so; this may be cited as textual evidence. Generally speaking, if one follows the rule for reconciling the Saṃgha, it appears that on a single matter, receiving [the retreat] again is not permitted.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there was once a dispute among monks from different boundaries (*sīmā*).

When they requested monks to adjudicate the matter, if the preceding *anvāya* had already concluded, one should receive seven nights; if those seven nights were exhausted, one should receive thirty-nine nights, and so on until completion.
"Listen: breaking the *anvaya* (rainy-season retreat) is permitted. The ancients took this as their authority, not allowing for a second reception [of ordination] regarding a single matter.
Now the Master says: 'It seems that regarding a single matter, a second reception is not permitted. Since he uses the term 'seems,' it is not necessarily a definitive judgment.

As for the inability to grasp the intent of that Vinaya—stating that one may break the *anvaya* because the conditions for reconciliation (*samghāvaśeṣa*) are difficult to anticipate—if such a timeframe can be established, there is no opening [for the exception]."

[This section is] important. [The author] extensively cites the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* (羯磨疏) in his search for the profound mysteries; it is recorded here despite its prolixity. However, that text contains passages regarding "not being requested" (*apraṇihita*) that are more lenient than those in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (四分).

That Vinaya is intended for the seven classes of followers to cultivate merit, and when making offerings, receiving precepts, or inquiring about doubts, it permits the formalization of the day (*divasa-karma*) provided that the person before whom one acts gives rise to wholesome states of mind—even if no messenger is dispatched. In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, such authorization is only permitted if a messenger is sent. Since that [latter rule]...

Regarding the section on "broadness" (*kuan*) and "repeated reception" (*chong shou*): the text is not clear because the translators did not understand the stylistic force of the *huíwén* (reverted) style and its various implications.
It is not that the principle itself is unclear; rather, it requires thorough comprehension.

Since those are texts not explicitly requested, and there is further the text concerning "broadness" and "repeated reception," it is inappropriate to hastily interpret these two meanings. If one exercises thorough mastery, the principle will manifest of itself. However...
One must not dogmatically cling to a single passage, thereby failing to grasp the significance of the repeated requests made across various contexts.
Regarding the *Five Hundred Questions* and other texts: since those works state that one may receive [the precepts] again after seven days have passed, it is clear that such repetition is permitted.

Although this is not a case of "receiving again" (*chóngshòu*) in the strict sense, the text nonetheless conveys the meaning of repetition. Regarding the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (or *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*), Xuánzàng says: "Now..."

The *Shu* (Commentary) on the *Yinlun* states: "When the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha had finished his private affairs for which he had requested seven days' leave, he returned to the boundary on the eighth day.

This indicates that one may receive [the precepts] again due to external circumstances. Once the previous matter has been concluded, if there are further distinct circumstances, it is likewise necessary to receive them once more."

Since the text states that one "receives [the precepts] again," how could this not constitute a double reception? Based on this, although it is not a formal re-initiation (*punar-upasampadā*), the wording nonetheless carries the sense of repetition;

reflect upon this. Consequently, this has become the current practice. Since this treatise states that after the initial seven-day invitation is concluded, one returns to within the boundary and on the eighth day invites another seven days to go forth from the boundary, the current practice is to reach the seventh day [and then proceed].
Having completed the boundary, one requests seven days to go outside the boundary without staying overnight. It is uncertain whether this is valid. Someone, interpreting the principle broadly, says:
"The method of receiving the days involves remaining within the boundary; as long as the formal act remains in effect, it is not lost.

Thus, if one uses five or three days out of the seven, for the remaining days, before returning to the original boundary, one performs the previous formal act again. This is because [the formal act] remains [in force]."

There is no need to receive the precepts again, for they remain without being lost. Even if the seven-day period has now reached its full term and one returns to one's original boundary, when the dawn breaks, although the residual dharma from the previous night remains, it is permitted to be included within the renewed request; thus, one may still carry forward the previous dharma. Therefore, it is known.
When the seven days have just concluded, it is logically sound to return to the boundary and request [ordination] again; there is no fault in this.

Even if one were to go outside the boundary for another seven days as mentioned in the eighth chapter of the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*, that too is due to differences among the schools (*nikāya*). Our Master merely takes that [text] as evidence to support the prior re-initiation.
One should not act in dependence upon others. Although one possesses this [understanding], it cannot yet be relied upon; fortunately, do not rely on the commentaries or sub-commentaries.
For instance, the Vinaya also contains explicit regulations; thus the text says: "And returning within seven days.

Furthermore, regarding the principles established previously—just as when receiving the *saptāha* (seven-day) leave, one uses three or five days while the remaining days have not yet been used—if one returns to one's original boundary, one should then perform [the formal act].
Regarding the previous matter: this concerns a case where [the period] is not yet complete; it cannot be used as a precedent for a case where the period is already fulfilled.

To designate one's intention as "fulfilled" and then return to the monastery—once the formal procedure (*vidhi*) has been clearly completed, the [status] is lost. This is not the same as the case of being incomplete, where one merely turns back due to temporary circumstances;

how could the legal status be gained or lost [merely by such a change]? Now, following the profound tradition, if one returns to the boundary within seven days, one must necessarily spend the night there. Since the Vinaya follows what is urgent, is this not so?

Yes. Why rely on such redundant elaborations to establish the meaning? Please reflect upon this; the rest may be understood from the text [note: regarding this, the *Xuánjì* cites the treatise to explain the dimensions of the three thousandfold world-system, which I shall clarify here within the section on "following characteristics"].

Regarding the phrase "as for the rest, it reaches the *Śāstra*": within the *Karmavācanā-śāstra*, the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Liao lun) is cited as an explanation consisting of nine phrases, all of which concern receiving [the precepts] repeatedly;
this is done to refute the views of ancient masters. The *Śāstra* cites the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, stating:

"In the case of a seven-day period with obstacles, one may freely practice wholesome deeds," thereby explaining the three kinds and nine categories. The commentary states: "The 'three kinds' refers to the seven-day period and so forth; the 'nine categories' refers to the three periods..."
By combining these variations as the primary cases, nine are formed. It should be stated that there are three types: first, those where seven-day limits are established;

second, those where seven-day limits are established later; and third, those where difficult circumstances (an-antara) are established later. First, those where seven-day limits are established; second, those where seven-day limits are established later;

and third, those where *yathāsammuti* (consent-based) limits are established later. Second, taking the case of impending difficulties as the primary case, it is said: first, difficulties are established; later, difficulties are established; first, difficulties are established; later, seven-day limits are established.
Day. First completion with difficulty; later completion at will (sixth). Third, taking "completion at will" as the head: first completion at will, later completion at will;
first completion at will, later completion with difficulty; first completion at will, later completion within seven days (ninth).
Although these names are briefly cited in various records, confusion regarding their meaning is frequent. Now, I rely upon the *Jingshui* [Mirror Water].

The Venerable Master, citing the *Śāstra*, provides a brief explanation as follows: Regarding the "first seven-day period" and the "subsequent seven-day period," this clarifies that although one may initially request a seven-day leave of absence, if the matter is not resolved, one commits a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) by breaking the *varṣā* retreat. If the matter remains unresolved, one may at most remain for six nights.
On the seventh night, one must return to the boundary. On the eighth day, one should again request permission to go out of the boundary for seven days.

Having previously received permission to go out of the boundary for seven days due to the illness of one's preceptor, if the illness is cured after three nights, one must immediately return to the original location, as there is another donor present.
Furthermore, one may request to remain outside the boundary for three days after the initial period. If it is still not completed by then, one may request an additional seven days;

thus, both the preceding and succeeding periods together constitute seven days (the Venerable Master explains that the mutual application of these periods is permitted because when the teacher is ill, the donor’s purity is maintained, which is why they are mentioned together).

Second, regarding the case where the initial seven days are completed but there is a difficulty during the subsequent period: the commentary states this refers to having requested seven days from a donor and then using only three of them.
Having finished [the retreat], he returns to his original location. Hearing that a great calamity has arisen, he nevertheless travels to various places.

Regarding the statement, "First completing the seven days, afterwards completing the *svairakārya* (the period for personal choice)," the commentary explains: Previously, when the donor had invited him for the seven-day period, he was required to return immediately upon its conclusion.
However, now because his residence lacks good provisions and companions, there is much clamor and noise which hinders the practice of the Way, and furthermore, he is destitute...
Regarding food and medicine: one should not now further divert oneself by selecting a separate quiet place, nor should one long for fine companions or places where food and medicine are available;
rather, one should act according to one's inclination. If these three points are understood, the remaining phrases may be interpreted by analogy, so they will not be described here at length.
Regarding the statement "on the sixth day," it means that on both the first and second days, one must [perform the rite] for seven days.

The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "This is because the Dharma encompasses the conditions. The passage from the *Vinaya* cited below makes this clear. An external objection is raised: "This may be acceptable during the summer retreat (*varṣā*), but..."

Question: If there is a seven-day period for those with business on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, and by the sixteenth day it has already passed—since this is no longer within the summer retreat period—how can this be?
The *Chao* (Commentary) answers: "If one day remains at the end of the summer retreat, the seven-day rite may still be performed; others say it may be done for six days.

Although it is not within the limit of the summer retreat, because there is no rite for receiving [the *śikṣādattaka*] for a single day, [it is permissible]. Question: Regarding the protection of the bright boundary (*sīmā*) during the retreat.
If one has not yet gone outside, one does not incur an offense by being outside after the dawn light (*āloka*) has appeared.

Since it is now the sixteenth day, which was originally the time for going out of the boundary, why is it necessary to further receive the *anujñā* (authorization)? Answer: At the very moment the dawn light appears, one’s body must be within the boundary.

If one has not obtained the legal authorization (*dharma*) and one’s body is outside the boundary when the dawn light appears, one then incurs a breach of the rains retreat (*varṣa*). This is also like the case on the ninth day of the seventh month.
One must request seven days' leave from the boundary. Upon reaching the fifteenth day, one must likewise return within the boundary;
for at the moment the dawn of the sixteenth day appears, one's body must be within the boundary (and so forth).
Regarding the statement "up to seven days": the Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya permits seven days without specifying a greater number. This refers to the precept concerning wandering during the three seasons;

it is based on oral tradition that no more than [seven] days are permitted. In the *Mahāsāṃghika-bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*, the thirty rules state that these are received through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*).

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika*, during the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), there is no ritual for requesting permission to leave; however, for the sake of the Saṃgha or the stūpa, one is merely granted leave.
They were permitted to depart for seven days. Regarding those who have confused this with the monastic rules, I shall now describe the ancient protocol. The ancients said:

"Since the monks were granted the three methods for receiving [the *poṣadha*] on designated days, the nuns followed suit. This was not further detailed [in later texts]. (The *Xinzhang* supports this interpretation. This is according to the *Sifen lü* and subsequent codes.
Now, the Master refutes this. The following section explains the principle that [the period] is not fixed at seven days.
Regarding the statement that even opening [the retreat] for seven days can still provide the conditions for other circumstances: there are occasions lasting thirty days or half-months;
yet, once those seven days are completed, if one requests [the ritual] again according to the situation, it will likewise serve as a condition for generating goodness and extinguishing evil.

Regarding the phrase "those who have come for the eight [days]," the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: Some say that if one does not return after the matter has been concluded, it does not constitute a violation of the summer retreat (*varṣā*), because the formal authority (*dharma*) remains.
Thus we know that the seven-day medicine, the granting of consent (*chanda*), insanity, illness, recovery from illness, and failure to return are treated according to these precedents.

However, the current interpretation differs: when the matter is concluded, the formal authority ceases; this is because the procedure for receiving the day’s extension (*ādeśa-dharma*) is contingent upon the specific circumstance, and once that circumstance has passed, the authority lapses.
Regarding the Dharma: if one has not previously granted consent (*chanda*), it is like medicinal medicine that has ceased to be effective once the illness has ended;
it will not cure madness, and thus one must formally request the Dharma. (The above is the commentary. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Daśabhāṇavāra) clearly states that going is not permitted.

Within a single recitation, if a nun falls ill and is purified, and one goes to preach the Dharma to her only halfway when she dies and returns to the laity, one should not go in either case. To "go" here means to travel there (some versions erroneously read the character for "sutra" instead).
Regarding those who follow the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: within the boundaries of the *śīma*, monks may not wander about; they must reach their destination before midday and return after midday.

If they stay longer, they lose their summer retreat (*varṣa*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* does not permit going there, and the *Mahāsāṃghika* text does not permit staying; the wording differs slightly.
All feared that it would break the summer retreat; thus, their intentions were the same.

Regarding the phrase "adding three methods," this refers to adding the rules for the Saṃgha and the individual (pudgala). Regarding the phrase "the preceding leads to the individual rules," there are five types of persons:

first, those living alone; second, those in an araṇya (forest hermitage); third, those on a long journey; fourth, those with chronic illness; and fifth, those during times of famine. These rely upon kinship.
Because one dwells in the village, one performs the mental recitation (*cittānuvartana*). Regarding "being capable of coming but not waiting":

this refers to pure persons who are capable of coming and sufficient to fulfill the required number for my face-to-face ceremony; if one does not summon them now, this constitutes a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*), and the mental recitation is not accomplished.
Nowadays, there are many ignorant groups who, upon reaching the commencement of the summer retreat (*varṣā*), recite verses before the Buddha themselves. This is extreme folly. If...
"Cannot wait," etc., refers to opening up the practice of mental recitation (*manasikāra*). The remaining text may be understood in detail (*yathāyogam*). The Venerable One said:

"Since the *pratimokṣa* (confession) rites performed before another person in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* are already applicable to mental recitation, then by analogy, the communal rites (*saṃghakarma*) performed every half-month or month should likewise be applicable to mental recitation.
However, at present, no one dares to perform them; yet from the standpoint of principle (*nyāya*), there is no fault. Know this."

Regarding the phrase "the two [methods] for addressing an individual, up to 'until it is exhausted'": these words and phrases originate from the formal rules (*dharma*). As explained in the text, the practice of the present day differs.
Some say that a monk who is to be addressed must belong to the same boundary (*sīmā*) and be a fellow resident in retreat (*samvāsaka*);

furthermore, he must remain within the boundary to uphold this rite for one's sake. If they all depart at once, one may not receive [the rite] from another's side. One must receive it [from such a person].
That would not be valid. First, one must inquire in detail, and only then perform the ritual act. The Venerable One said:

"If that were so, then for instance, when requesting the *poṣadha* for a half-month or a month, if there is no one within the boundary to preside over the ritual, one may invite someone from outside the boundary to come, and once the ritual has been performed, they depart."
He did not instruct others, saying, "The external community of monks should come to this boundary of the monastic assembly to uphold the Dharma for me.

Now, regarding this *pratimokṣa* (confession before another), it refers only to the procedure performed in the presence of another. Once the days of mutual invitation have concluded, it is permissible for all to depart at once.
Who would discuss the distinction between other boundaries and one's own, or whether those departing together or separately? There is no such principle; this is merely a figurative expression.
As for the statement, "The ritual procedures are correct and without error": when performing a *karmavācanā* (formal motion), one relies on the assembly and requests a specific day.

Now, in the case of the *pratimukha* (face-to-face) and *manasikāra* (mental recitation) methods, one follows the wording of the previous formal motion to request the day; since this principle is universally applicable, what error could there be?

Regarding the statement, "If one receives [the medicine] on a day but uses it after seven days have passed, it is likewise permissible," this has the same intent as the previous passage concerning receiving [medicine] in advance.
The former distinguishes what is improper based on circumstances, whereas here the distinction is made based on whether the medicine has been used; thus, there is no redundancy.

As for "not being the same as the seven-day [rule]," even if a potent medicinal drug remains for a full seven days, the legal status of the medicine is forfeited if the illness has not yet been cured. Regarding "the essence of the illness":

This means that once the illness has been cured, the [seven-day] period is lost even if the days have not yet expired; therefore, both conditions are cited together. [The opponent] raises an objection:

"If the illness has been cured, it is reasonable to allow that the legal status (*dharma*) is lost. If that were so, then as long as the illness persists, the legal status should remain" (this is the self-reflection found in the *Chao*).

The phrase "due to the Buddha’s regulation," etc., is the explanation. This is because the seven-day limit was established by regulation. As the *Śāstra* says: "When the persistent illness is eliminated. Master Xuán says: "The *Śāstra* establishes this."

There are two passages [in the texts] that contain this statement. Regarding the question, "As for 'reaching the Dharma'": this refers to the request for seven days according to the *Caturvargika-vinaya*;
does it permit including the seventh night as well? In the answer, it is not permitted because the Vinaya text restricts it to the seventh night and the boundary (*sīmā*).

Therefore, we know that it does not include the night. As for its difference from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Shisong), at first glance the textual flow seems to imply that the seven nights are exhausted, and on the eighth day, after dawn has broken, one must return to the boundary;

however, according to the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā), this is no different from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen), as it also requires protection until the appearance of the dawn light on the eighth day. Furthermore, the commentary states: "The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* [states] seven..."
"Night and seven days are treated the same as in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), excluding the night [from the calculation]. (The above is from the *Śāstra*).

This is perfectly clear, yet even to this day there are those who do not understand it and offer a false interpretation, saying: "According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong lü), if one obtains the legal authorization (*dharmakarma*) at night, even if one is outside the boundary when the dawn appears, the summer retreat (*varṣa*) is not broken.
This is because the invitation (*pravāraṇā*) is said to be for 'seven nights' on a clear day. However, since the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* does not... [text continues]

Regarding the term "night," it can only provide protection until the seventh day; at the dawn of the eighth day, because [the protection] no longer exists, if one interprets it in this way, then even if one follows that Vinaya (the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*), it would still constitute a breach of the summer retreat (*varṣā*), which contradicts the *Śāstra* (the *Vinayavibhāṣā*). An external objection:

"If that is so, although the terminology regarding 'day and night' differs between the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, their protective function is no different. Now, the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya masters [claim] seven..."
Regarding the phrase "the time of the Dharma-sun," it should be amended to read "obtained after seven nights. One must not cite the *Chao* (Excerpts). The answer states:

"Furthermore, from 'having obtained' onwards, these are differences in the specific schools (*bhedaka-nikāya*); one must invoke them according to their respective traditions" (and so forth). Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika* rule concerning "the completion of the matter":

that [text] states that as soon as the duration of the preceding matter has concluded, it is immediately termed the "completion of the matter. This "completion of the matter" is a legal principle (*dharma*) of an external school; it is fully contained therein.
The Section on the Various Schools clarifies this.

Regarding the statement "from three up to the explanation": as for the conditions (*pratyaya*) for which it is intended, these are the first, the condition of the Three Jewels, through to the fifth, the condition of protecting the Dharma by harmonizing the Saṃgha.

As for what is commonly applicable as before: both the mental recitation (*manasikāra*) and the face-to-face method (*saṃmukhībhāva*) employ these same conditions; therefore, they are said to be "common."

As for its application: since the current circumstances involve slightly longer durations, one employs the methods of the half-month or the month. This differs from the "preservation of the single [period]" (cun dan) and so forth;
this phrase serves as a refutation. Within a single summer retreat, only three periods are preserved: first, the single seven-day period; next, the single half-month period;
and finally, the single month period. Therefore, it is called "preserving the single. Consequently, he cites the seven-day period to allow for longer durations. Xuán says: "This is not [the case]."

This means that it draws forth the conditions to cause them to grow; it simply employs the method of growth. Since the formal reception (*upasaṃpadā*) is not established, there is no violation of the summer retreat (*varṣā*), yet the offense incurred is a punishment.
Regarding the phrase "the rest is as explained previously," this refers to the explanation within the fifth section on the "repeated reception.
As for the statement "there are four differences in what has arrived now," the first is the *karmavācanā* (ritual manual) produced by Tandi during the Cao Wei period.
The second refers to the time of the Yao Qin dynasty. Regarding the *Karmavācanā* produced by Jueming, the author of the *Chao* states that he once saw it, but did not encounter it again later;
hence, he says it was "rarely seen."
Regarding the third method: Master Guang of the Northern Qi dynasty produced a version that added the formal request for the *jī* (confession).
Although he added this request, it was modeled after the procedure for requesting *pārivāsika* (probation for concealment). When reciting the matter twice, he listed the previously added request;

thereafter, once the assembly had granted their consent (*kṣānti*), he abbreviated the rest of the proceedings. This method of Master Guang was widely practiced in his time. Thus, he stated: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Bhikṣu..."

I, [Name], am observing the rains retreat at this location. Having received the *saptarātra-atireka* (seven-day extension) rule, I shall go outside the boundary on the fifteenth day for a certain purpose, and then return here to observe the rains retreat.
I now request from the Sangha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the fifteen-day period to receive the seven-day extension rule.
If the Saṃgha is ready, may the Saṃgha listen with patience. Now, for the sake of the bhikṣu [Name], we grant him the *karmavācanā* of exceeding seven days up to fifteen days;
the motion (*jñapti*) is as follows. This is merely an example of the formal text for the motion; as for the *karmavācanā*, it should follow its general framework.
Specifically, one should follow the four-line formula for the "granting of days" found in the Vinaya text, which constitutes the essential framework of the teaching for the basis of the motion.

Regarding the question concerning "reaching the point of loss": the intent of the question is clear. In the response, although the phrasing of the request is expanded, there is no fundamental error in the main substance.

This refers to the formal citation of the conditions and the citation of the request, which are merely the second and fourth phrases; in relation to the core essence of the *karmavācanā*, there is no error. Thus, the *Karmasūtra* states:
"Some definitively judge that one must rely on the formal acceptance [of the precepts] to break the summer retreat. Our current interpretation is not so; both [positions] are compliant."

Because of the teachings, the *saṃgha* requests the lifting of the formal act (*jñapti-karman*). Each has its own basis. The general outline of the presentation remains as it was, so that nothing is lost (the above is the text of the commentary).
Regarding the phrase "from the fourth [day] to the fifteenth day": the "fourth person" refers to the Vinaya Master Fayan; his textual output contains no further additions.
The present *Chao* follows this precedent in its usage. The *karman* text is as found in the *Chao* (etcetera); follow the preceding [text] in its application.
As for this, it means that one should apply the rules according to whether it is for fifteen days or for one month; all related conditions are to be applied accordingly.

One must not recite both "fifteen days" and so forth. Now, following this intent, fearing that people might fail to understand the Vinaya text, I shall carefully recite the original Vinaya scripture as it says:
"The method for receiving [the *pārivāsika* status] for more than seven days: whether for fifteen days or for one month, it is issued..."

Outside the boundaries (*sīmā*). If one now receives [the *poṣadha*] for fifteen days, one must not additionally observe the month-long period; or if one receives the month-long method, one must exclude the fifteen days.
One may not recite both together in a single document. (The above concludes the explanation of the second section: the method for receiving the day-period).
The third major section, the "Discrimination of the Three," states: Regarding the discrimination of the various characteristics of the three [categories], there are altogether three schools.

This first section follows the *Xuánjì* (Commentary on the Profound); within the second part, the "Method for Receiving the Day" (*shòurìfǎfù*), it is divided into three sections concerning the "Receiving the Day" according to the rules for the Sangha (*sēngfǎ*).

First, the "General Clarification of the Long-term Conditions" refutes the errors of past masters. Second, from "Now, adding the ritual for receiving [the precepts]" onwards, the actual method of reception is presented.

Third, this section provides a miscellaneous analysis (*viniścaya*) of it; because the *karmavācanā* for receiving the days is performed at a time and place that are inappropriate, it is termed "miscellaneous characteristics.

Alternatively, according to the *Huainan Shunzheng Ji*, this section on receiving the days is also divided into three parts: first, the formal recitation (*uddāna*); second, the explanation; and third, the miscellaneous analysis.
[Commentary: If that were so, then the three characters "da" (大), "ke" (科), and "zi" (字) in this current [text] would not correspond to the topical divisions (*yike*).

Thus, both of the two preceding schools have incorrectly divided the text; the *Pochao Wenshu* is not an elegant or accurate interpretation. Now, following Fabao’s view, according to the meaning of the preceding text:
from the beginning, it is divided into five parts, which constitute the first major section, the main body on the *an-guo* (rainy-season retreat). Second...
The first major section is titled "First: Clarifying the Receipt of the Day. Now, this third major section is titled "Third: Miscellaneous Analysis.

Should it not have included the first two characters from the preceding section? This is likely the commentator’s own topical outline; later readers, being superficial, failed to grasp the intent of the text.
Furthermore, as for why this is called "Miscellaneous Analysis," it refers to the analysis of the receipt of the day and—
Regarding the place of *varṣā* (the rainy season retreat): because they are surrounded by [other] boundaries (*sīmā*), it is necessary to establish this distinction.

If you say that this merely analyzes the monastic rules concerning the formal authorization for the duration of the retreat (*jñapti-cāra*), then consider why the subsequent text further explains the distinctions regarding the dependence on a monastery (*ārāma*) or a boundary (*sīmā*) for the *varṣā*. Reflect upon this.
In the commentary it says: "As for those who reach the limit of opening [the rule], 'those whose heat is extreme'—this refers to other circumstances.
'Common circumstances' means they share the same period, such as half a month or one month. Regarding 'two or three people,' it may not exceed four. This is like the conferral of precepts:
when there are no [other] circumstances, one person constitutes a single *karmavācanā*; because there are circumstances involving two or three people, an exception is made. This...

This is also consistent with the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which permits it. As for the statement, "If one reaches the robe [boundary]," and other small boundaries (*kṣudraka-sīmā*), these are still subsumed within the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) of the Saṃgha.

Now, in relation to the great boundary of the enclosure, they receive the name "small. This means that originally, based on the external great boundary, one must have the intention (*citta*) to dwell in retreat (*vāsa*).
The small boundary of the *śīlākṣetra* (precept-field) is not the original place intended for such a commitment; therefore, one may not receive [the precepts] therein.

Furthermore, regarding the subsequent establishment of the two boundaries: the first is the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary), and the second is the *śīla-maṇḍala* (precept platform). This permits the acceptance of the [rainy season] retreat days. The passage beginning with "Truly not... is explained by the text of the *Śāstra* itself.

Even if one enters the platform and does not break the summer retreat, yet becomes separated from one's robes, this is because the precept platform is originally a place where one maintains the intention that it is "my own" territory;
thus, by entering therein, the summer retreat is not broken. This is due to the fact that it is separated from the natural ground. It is... [end of fragment].

This [rule] regarding being separated from one's robes is also stated with reference to the formal demarcation of a robe-holding boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*). If one has not formally demarcated a robe-holding boundary, then even if one relies on a monastery (*ārāma*) to protect one's robes, one is not considered separated from them.
Regarding the phrase "if it was originally within reach": this refers to the time when the summer retreat (*varṣa*) was first established;

at that time, there was already a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), and reliance on a monastery was not permitted because the Buddha had prescribed reliance on the boundary itself. As for the statement "those who have [the boundary] do not achieve [it]": this refers to those who rely on a monastery.

Regarding the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat): if the *varṣā* is not established and one is unable to receive the formal authorization (*jñapti*) for the days, it means that since the monastery grounds are naturally open space, one merely employs the specific procedure for seven days.

As for the method of performing the *karmavācanā* to receive the authorization for half a month or a full month, because [the original boundary] cannot be maintained, one may only contract the limits of the boundary.
One interpretation states: from the interior contracting toward the exterior, the original boundary becomes smaller; since now...
Furthermore, there is another interpretation that clarifies and expands upon the connection. A second explanation states: from the outside, one contracts [the boundary] toward the inside;

thus, one must enter the *sīmā* (boundary) to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*), and may not reside based on the monastery grounds alone. This means that within the boundary, the three methods of receiving [the invitation] and so forth are all universally applicable.

For further details, refer to the commentary. Regarding the "Great Commentary" mentioned at the beginning: it recounts the principles established by two masters. One [master] maintains that the rains retreat must necessarily rely upon...

A monastery (*ārāma*) cannot serve as the basis for a boundary (*sīmā*), because it has been so established by the Buddha’s regulations. Thus, the text states: "The double and single boundaries are reversed. The two masters say:
"The monastery is large and the great boundary is small; however, one may rely on the monastery but not on the boundary for the sake of the precepts.

The text says: "Relying on such-and-such a monastery," and so forth. According to these two interpretations, each addresses one aspect. The current text of the *Chao* follows the procedure of the first master out of necessity. From this, the matter is understood.
According to the *Jie-mo-shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā), there is likewise no fixed adherence; one simply relies upon whichever is more spacious.

If the monastery (*ārāma*) is spacious and the boundary (*sīmā*) is small, one relies upon the monastery, which is identical to the position of the second master. If the boundary is large and the monastery is small, one is made to rely upon the boundary.

These two texts provide for both cases, so that when the time comes, one may deliberate accordingly. An external objection states: "If the boundary is small and the monastery is large, one should reside within the monastery; now, one is instead directed toward the interior of the boundary."

"May I receive the *jñapti* (formal authorization)? He replied, "You may. This is within the monastery (*ārāma*). Since the interior boundary (*antar-sīmā*) is originally the very ground required [for the rains retreat], entering it does not constitute a breach of the summer retreat.

Why fear that receiving the *jñapti* would fail to be accomplished? Therefore, according to the previous text, based on the monastery, regarding the two boundaries—the inner and outer—receiving the *jñapti* according to the boundary is still judged to be valid.
Now, within the monastery, how could the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) not be valid? Furthermore, it is difficult to object: if that were so, then within the monastery..."

The boundary of the *śīmaṇḍala* (戒場) should likewise be established at the lower level. Answer: Although the *śīmaṇḍala* is within the monastery grounds (*vihāra*), it is not fundamentally required that one enter into it;
thus, there is no loss of the summer retreat or the violation regarding robes. This follows the superior method and is not analogous to the subsequent establishment [of the boundary].

The above is from the *Yi-jue* (儀決); it is not something found in the original texts. Some people do not understand the intent of the *Chao* (抄), and thus claim that the statement "the above is from the Nanshan *Yi-jue*" is an error.
This refers to what our original teacher pointed out in the preceding text: "Because the Buddha established the reliance on boundaries (*sīmā*) and the contraction of boundary marks.

This is the definitive judgment of the ancient masters based on ritual protocol. The following sentence rebuts this, stating: "It is not found in the text," meaning that such a statement does not exist within the Vinaya text itself.
That is to say, the boundary was originally intended to encompass the Saṃgha and was not for the purpose of the *vassa* (rainy-season retreat); the *vassa* is determined by persons.
Regarding the focus of the mind: why restrict it to a specific boundary? It is sufficient that one protects it wherever one dwells. Furthermore, there is another interpretation which says:

the Master [Sengyou] feared that people might doubt him, thinking, "I am now observing the rains retreat (*varṣā*) based on a monastery (*ārāma*), not based on a formal boundary (*sīmā*)," or that they might receive the fortnightly or monthly disciplinary procedures (*poṣadha*) without such a basis.

If one attempts to perform the *jñapti-karman* and receive the *anujñā* (permission) for the day outside of the boundary (*sīmā*)—that is, within a natural grove (*ārāma*)—this reception of the day is not valid.

As the commentary explains: because the Buddha ordained that [the ritual] must rely upon a boundary, if one performs the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) within a natural grove while facing toward it, the reception of the day is tacitly invalid.
It is certainly impossible to obtain it; one can only obtain it by contracting the direction [of the ritual] back into the boundary and receiving it therein.

This merely establishes that the period of receiving [the precepts] depends upon the *sīmā* (boundary), but it does not mean that the establishment of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) depends upon the *sīmā*.

If one follows this interpretation, it contradicts the text of the *Shu* (Commentary) and confuses the intent of the *Chao* (Excerpts). Reflect on this. The explanation of the twelfth section is hereby concluded.
○ Fourth, regarding the classification of matters by correlating the Dharma with persons, specifically the *Pravāraṇā-vastu*, is divided into two main sections:
first, the citation of the title; second, the explanation. Regarding the first section, from "Now, concerning *pravāraṇā*" up to "attached," the intent of the passage is first established.
The preceding chapter concerned the summer retreat (*varṣā*), during which one dwells together for ninety days.

Fearing that there may be transgressions that one does not perceive or recognize oneself, it is necessary to personally confess the three types of action (*trikarma*) and allow the Saṃgha to freely investigate and censure them; thus, following the conclusion of the retreat, this chapter follows (the *Xuánjì* notes that listing the origins here would be too prolix, so they are omitted).

Regarding the explanation of the title: it consists of words for personally confessing the three dharmas and freely allowing the seven groups of offenses (*saptāpatti-skandha*) to be raised, thereby crushing black karma.

The principal master [of this treatise]. It constitutes the pivotal key to the pure Dharma (*śukla-dharma*). It is intended to cause those who know [their faults] to surely reform themselves, to reflect upon their own conduct, and to increase their cultivation.

That the *śīla* (precepts) be as bright and pure as a clear ocean—this is the further explanation of the "Dharma Jewel. Furthermore, regarding the term "master" (*zong*), it refers to the principal authority. As for "essential matters," these refer to the primary duties;

specifically, the dispatching of attendants and so forth are the essential duties of the householder. The sections and so on are as usual (*etc.*). This concludes the commentary explaining the underlying intent of the text.
[This is] the name. As will be fully illustrated later.
Next, regarding the general intent of the explanation according to the chapters, as for the phrase "Thus it is... until... [in the section on] the ninety-day cultivation of the path:
the particle *ran* (thus) is frequently glossed as "this" (*shi*) in various commentaries. However, the Venerable Jing-shui provides an interpretation based on the sense of contradiction (*xi-wang*).

It is said that during the summer retreat one should cultivate diligent exertion so that body and speech are free from flaw; when the summer is complete and the practice perfected, it is logically fitting to ascend into the air to manifest the attainment of the fruit-stage.
Yet now, while being told to continue practicing, one is not permitted to go wherever one wishes, but instead says, "I fear the monks will punish me.
Is this not a contradiction? Thus it is said. *Jiuxun* (九旬) refers to the number [of days]; *souxuan* (搜玄) means the period of ten days (*jun*); *zhili* (支歷) refers to the progression [of time].
There are twelve *śīrṣaka* (deities): zi, chou, yin, mao, chen, si, wu, wei, shen, you, xu, and hai. There are ten *gān* (trunk) deities: jia, yi, bing, ding, wu, ji, geng, xin, ren, and gui.
When the twelve *zhī* (branch) deities cycle through the ten *gān* deities during the day, it is called one "decade" (*xiún*).
One summer consists of nine such cycles; hence the term "nine decades" (*jiǔxún*). The Venerable Master did not approve of this interpretation. If...
"Yún" (旬) is a variant of "xún" (巡). It should be written as this character "xún. In current texts, it is used interchangeably with characters such as "yóu" (由), "xún" (旬), and "jiǎ" (假).
According to the interpretation of Fǎbǎo, ten days constitute a "xún. This is like the state establishing one hundred and twenty offices.
Each office is allotted ten days as a "decade" (*xún*). During these nine days, one attends to official duties; after midday, one returns to their quarters to attend to private affairs.
If one re-enters the office on the tenth day, that constitutes a single day of "decade-holiday" (*xúnjiǎ*), during which all administrative matters are suspended for rest.
Now, according to the Buddhist precepts, a *bhikṣu* enters the summer retreat for ninety days; hence the term "nine decades" (*jiǔxún*).

Because one exerts effort through preparatory application (*prayoga*), it is called the "Path of Cultivation" (*bhāvanāmārga*). Regarding "refining the body and mind": alerting and restraining the body and speech constitutes refining the body, which is the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*).
Cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and practicing wisdom (*prajñā*) constitute refining the mind, which refers to the other two trainings.

As for the statement that "many people are deluded about themselves," the *Lüfa Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Three Samādhis of the Dharma and Vinaya) says: "Worldly people see only the faults of others and are largely deluded regarding their own transgressions."
Therefore, by relying upon collective governance, one can finally attain purity; thus it is said, "It is appropriate to rely upon [the Sangha] with reverence," and so forth.

Regarding the passage, "Even if one confesses one's own offenses and allows the monks to freely enumerate one's transgressions," this means that one personally declares the three roots [of sin] and permits others to freely present their accusations.

To say "internally manifesting the absence of private concealment" means that since I have already confessed, it demonstrates that I do not hide my offenses. To say "externally manifesting the presence of flaws" refers to the fact that there are indeed...

"Damage constitutes a flaw; even a jade with a protruding point has a blemish. The text states: "The Great Virtuous Elder, out of compassion, spoke to me," which clearly indicates that there are transgressions externally.
"The body and speech deceive others" refers to the faults of the seven branches [of karma].
These are entirely entrusted to the five virtues for correction and admonition. The reason why only body and speech are mentioned and not the mind is that the Hīnayāna...
Because one has violated the mind through transgression, one is not "not solitary. This means that if a transgression is not eliminated, it is contrary to the Dharma of the Saṃgha;

such a person is cast outside the assembly and excluded from the count of the Saṃgha, which is called being "solitary. Now, having completed the repentance, one returns to the former state and is thus called "not solitary.

Furthermore, another interpretation is that if one commits a transgression and does not repent, one will enter the evil realms in the future, which is called being "solitary. Now, having finished the remorseful elimination [of the offense], one is spared from summoning [rebirth in] evil.

The Way is thus not solitary. If one speaks of "subduing" (*vinaya*), it is so called because one is punished according to the law; if one speaks of "subduing" because one does not transgress the teachings, it is so called because one follows them.

As for "rejoicing in liberation," once the cleansing of the limbs is complete and the seven branches are pure and bright, one personally experiences joy and gladness, knowing that there is no longer any offense.

Regarding the reason for reaching the *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence ceremony): it is intended to establish a formal agreement (*sāṃketika*). The *Shuowen* states that "agreement" (*sāṃketika*) refers to emotional desire.

"Agreement" (*qi*) means to fix a specific time; "meeting" (*zhì*) means to assemble. At the beginning of summer, when emotional desires are fixed and the assembly of sages dwells together, they establish a solemn covenant for the ninety-day period.
Within these ninety days, they practice and advance toward [liberation].

The "superior fruit" transcends the three realms (*tridhātu*). If one were to raise [accusations] based on contrary characteristics—for instance, if immediately after the initial summer retreat (*varṣā*) one were to mutually accuse and expose [others]—then there would be no intention to cultivate the Path;
instead, it would result in enmity, which is the root of disputes. "Each according to their direction" refers to place (*deśa*); "to go to" (*yāti*) means to arrive at.

"Those whose obstacles to the Path are profound" refers to those whose *śīla* (precepts) are impure and whose *samādhi* (concentration) does not manifest, having committed offenses of transgression (*duṣkṛta*).

[They fall] into the *āpatti* [of defeat]. For ninety thousand years, they shall fall into the *niraya* hells. This can be understood from the textual evidence in the lower section of the *Vinayamātṛkā*.

As for the statement "this applies to the practitioner," it does not mean that one may act wickedly during the period of self-indulgence (*pravāraṇā*). It refutes the former ignorance. Former people said:
"During the summer retreat, one must focus one's resolve on self-examination and must not engage in committing evil deeds. Now, at the conclusion of the summer retreat, one is permitted to relax.
"To act according to one's whims and create evil" means this. Now the Master says: "This does not mean that one should indulge oneself in doing evil.

Although this [explanation] clearly reveals the characteristics of what is being discussed—namely, the state of self-indulgence—there are still those of this class of foolish people who, lacking knowledge, fail to grasp it.

Regarding the phrase "as for the middle, the practice is as stated in the text": this is divided into two parts at the beginning. Within the first section, it is further divided into two sub-sections, as listed below.

Regarding the phrase "from the preceding up to the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination)": if one follows the regional custom, the country observes the *pūrvavārṣika* (early summer) retreat from the fourth, fifth, or sixth month;
the practitioners remain for a fixed period of one hundred and twenty days and perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.

If one enters the rains retreat during the middle or latter periods, it is not fixed. Regarding those who do not wait for the intercalary month but perform the *pravāraṇā* on the ninety days themselves, they simply count until the full number is reached.
If one encounters an intercalary month before the *pravāraṇā*, such a person belongs to neither the preceding summer retreat nor the middle or latter ones.

If one has entered the retreat on or before the first day of the fifth month, they may depart on the first day of the seventh month when an intercalary month occurs. If [one enters] on the second day of the fifth month...

After this, when the subsequent summer retreat (varṣā) is concluded, all [dates] shall skip the intercalary month. Once the period has passed until the second day of the eighth month and beyond, the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) is performed once the ninety days are complete.
Regarding the phrase "from the second to the middle": this refers to what was previously stated in the section on the *Poṣadha* (confession ceremony).

It cites the case from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* where a monk who had been fighting in a foreign region arrived; the Buddha then permitted the increase or decrease of the *poṣadha* date. If one knows that the fourteenth day will arrive, [one may adjust accordingly]. If the tenth... [text ends].

It is recited three times. If one knows that the fifteenth day is approaching, one should perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fourteenth day. If [the monks] have already entered the boundary, they should be made to bathe;
the bhikṣus shall then go outside the boundary to perform the *pravāraṇā*. If they are unwilling, one should inform the Saṃgha, saying: "We may not perform the *pravāraṇā* now;

we shall wait until the next fifteenth day to perform it. This must not exceed three occasions; one should forcibly bring about the assembly to perform it. The current practice of the *pravāraṇā* is also like this; only...

The *saṃghāṭī* (confession) is changed to the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish); the rest of the text is identical. Therefore, it is referred to as being "like that. What was previously called "reducing" refers to the preceding day, while "increasing" refers to waiting for the subsequent month.
Regarding the phrase "on the third day," according to the *Pravāraṇā-karman* (the ritual of invitation) in the Vinaya, it says:
"At that time, there was a residence where many bhikṣus had entered the rains retreat (*varṣā*). They practiced the Path with diligence and attained superior fruits. The bhikṣus..."
They made this thought: "We who are performing the *pravāraṇā* today must move to another location; we fear we shall not obtain such peace and happiness here.
They informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "If there is a dwelling place where such circumstances as these exist, one should perform a *pravāraṇā* for the sake of increasing one's own merit.
One should announce: 'Venerable Saṃgha, listen! If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, we shall not perform the *pravāraṇā* now, but [postpone it] until the fourth month.'"

"The full [term] shall be for the *pravāraṇā*. The announcement is as follows. This refers to those who have entered the first *varṣā* (rainy season retreat). When the eighth month reaches the fifteenth day, this constitutes the completion of the four months.
As for the statement "thus until the *pravāraṇā*," according to the *Pravāraṇā-khandhaka*, it simply mentions the two days: the fourteenth and the fifteenth.

Regarding the *pravāraṇā* (the invitation for criticism), within the section on "clothing offered as an urgent gift" (*ātyayika-cīvara*), there are sixteen days; in the sequence of increasing [the number of days], it likewise clarifies these sixteen days.

As for what is called "clothing offered as an urgent gift," the Vinaya states: "There are kings and high ministers who provide monks with clothing as a reward for their labor during the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat)."
When the summer retreat was nearly concluded, [a donor] intended to make a gift. However, having urgent business requiring a distant journey, he pre-emptively offered it to the Saṃgha.

The bhikṣus thought, "The summer retreat is not yet finished; we dare not accept this," and they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha asked, "How many days remain of the summer retreat? They replied, "Ten days.

The Buddha said, "In such circumstances, from this day forward, I authorize you to accept [the gift] up to ten days before the end of the retreat. Therefore, it is called "urgent gift-cloth" (ātyayika-cīvara).

According to this principle, it is on the sixth day of the seventh month that the opening of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony may take place. If it has not yet reached the sixth day of the seventh month, then receiving [the precepts] beforehand is termed "receiving prior to the proper time," which constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense.
The intent of the *Chao* (Commentary) states: since it is said that ten days remain until the *pravāraṇā*, one knows that [the proper time begins on] the sixteenth day.
This is the day of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony. Regarding the "successive increases," the Venerable [Master] says that according to the Vinaya, there are nine levels of increase.

*Souxuan* states that there are ten levels, as in the case of obtaining robes on the sixth day of the seventh month until the sixteenth day; once the ten days are full, one ought to perform the *śuddhika-pravāraṇā*.
Due to the *kārttika* month, this falls within the period of relaxation where no offense is committed. This continues until the fifteenth day of the eighth month, when...

To explain: if one obtains [the robe] on the seventh day of the seventh month, and the *Kārttika* month is exceeded, one gains an additional day, such that it is only on the sixteenth day of the eighth month that the recitation [of the *Kaṭhina*] takes place.
If one obtains the robe from the eighth day up to the fifteenth day, and the *Kārttika* month is exceeded, nine days are added;

this is called "sequential addition. This means that by taking the subsequent time—though not the specific day—and adding it to the previous period of obtaining the robe, the ten-day limit is fulfilled.

Furthermore, if there is a *kaṭhina* robe, after the five months have passed, the increase is likewise the same. The *Chao* (the *Shishi Yaolan*) cites this because the text on the ten successive increases all reaches the sixteenth day;
it says that if one has exceeded the *kārttika* month, one should perform the *śuddhi* (purification) when the ten days are complete.
This makes it clear that the sixteenth day is the time for the *pravāraṇā*. Within the three texts concerning the increase, there are also three days. Thus...
[This concerns] the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth days. The preceding [section] extensively cites various passages from the Vinaya, which differ in three respects;

it remains uncertain which day is definitively established as the time for the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination). The *Chao* states: "According to the Vinaya, during the three days following the conclusion of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), the sixteenth day is taken as the day the retreat concludes.
An external objection is raised: "Since it is stated that the sixteenth day is the day the retreat concludes..."
Regarding the *Pravāraṇā* (Self-Examination): For what reason does the Vinaya text state that the Saṃgha performs *pravāraṇā* on the fourteenth day, while the Bhikṣuṇīs do so on the fifteenth?

The *Shuochao* (Commentary) first records the aforementioned objection and subsequently provides the following explanation to resolve it: This refers to the practice of mutual inquiry regarding offenses; therefore, different days are prescribed.

It means that the Bhikṣuṇīs must first come among the monks to perform *pravāraṇā*, and only afterwards return to their own community to perform *pravāraṇā*. If they were to perform *pravāraṇā* first [among themselves] and then enter [the monks' assembly], [it would violate the rule].

Within the Saṃgha, this would then constitute an illegal act. Conversely, regarding the method of questioning on offenses by relying upon a *ni* (nun) for debate, it may be performed generally over three days;
it does not necessarily require the fifteenth day. Xuán further explains: "Conversely, one performs the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) rite."
These three days are all acceptable; according to general discussion, the fourteenth day may be taken. Therefore, it is said they are "universally applicable.

Now, the sixteenth day is specifically fixed as the date for the *pravāraṇā*. Thus, the Vinaya states: "At the conclusion of the summer retreat, one should perform the *pravāraṇā* and receive the *kāṭhina* robe."
If one receives the robe on the fifteenth day, it is not permitted; it is merely called "out-of-season robe" (akālacīvara). Therefore, one takes it on the sixteenth day.
When a nun arrives, she may stay for a short while; why must it necessarily be the fifteenth day? This is because there may be obstacles.
This can be understood according to the text. Regarding the phrase "from two up to those who have attained fulfillment," it is as stated in the text.
Regarding the phrase "the second clarification of 'up to,'" this refers to three types of people. Fazhao says: "This refers to three categories of persons;
it does not mean merely three individuals. That is to say, the first category consists of groups of five or more, extending all the way up to hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, and so forth."

Furthermore, groups of four or fewer persons constitute one category; groups of three persons, where each individual’s mental intention is distinct, constitute another category—hence the mention of "three persons.
Regarding the phrase "proceeding to the actual matter": among those consisting of five or more persons, they are divided into four [categories].

The *Baokē* (Precious Section) serves as the general heading for the two types of monastic laws; this is Chapter One. Five persons constitute one [category], and "five or more" refers to six persons, and so forth.

"Dividing those numbering one hundred thousand into four groups" refers to the enumeration in the *Chao* (the *Vinayamātṛkā*), and so forth. An external objection states: "The rubric of the *Chao* says that 'dividing into four' applies to groups of five or more.

While it is acceptable for those numbering six up to one hundred thousand to be divided into four, since the *pravāraṇā* (self-exhortation) is performed by five people, the method of appointing the five virtuous ones (*pañcavarga*) would apply to groups of six or even one hundred thousand; however, how can this ritual procedure be carried out [in such cases]?"
The application of the Dharma is categorically different; it is not necessary to exclude the five persons. Rather, one should simply distinguish the four categories based on six persons or more.

Answering Fabao, [the Master] said: "There is indeed profound significance in this. It means that when the five persons perform the *pravāraṇā*, these same four gates are no different from those used for six persons or even hundreds of thousands.
However, during the procedure for the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* within the second section on 'not entering' (*anupraveśa*), there is a difference."
The procedure for admitting two people simultaneously differs slightly from that for six people; here, we proceed with only five people and divide them into four sections.
The first and third sections are identical, while only the second section—concerning the five qualifications (*pañcavarga*)—differs.
Below, one may briefly identify the points of divergence as they arise. If these sections were not established, [the procedure for] six people would be [confused].

The section on the "Thousand [Monks]" has already been divided into four gates. Regarding the legal procedures for a community of five monks (*pañcavargika-saṃgha*), it is essential that they be fully detailed.

Although the second gate differs slightly, this will be clarified below. For now, we shall simply divide the categories starting from groups of five or more; this will encompass both types of monastic procedures.
This is a skillful use of literary structure, intended to avoid prolixity and to provide a concise indication of their mutual relationship—is this not the very purpose of a digest (*saṃgraha*)?
Reflect upon this.
Regarding the statement "from the beginning until dawn," it means that five or more persons must obtain a formal appointment (*śuklavihāra*).

This is intended to contrast with the case where, although four persons constitute a *saṃgha*, they may only perform the *paryāya-pratimukha-dharma* (the method of mutual face-to-face confession). As for the phrase "the posture of sitting on a bed is not yet severed," it refers to the present situation.
Sitting on the ground signifies that one’s status is low and that one’s person is situated within transgression. The Venerable Master said:

"It is like when those with offenses wear white private caps while sitting on the ground; or even if there is a bed, it is a bed placed beneath the feet, which likewise signifies that one's own body possesses transgression.
This case is also like this. "Not being permitted to be on a bed" refers to sitting upon a bed. This serves as proof for what was stated above.
Regarding the phrase "one must not sit on the ground": this means that it is improper to sit directly upon the bare earth.

The subsequent citation of sitting on grass spread in five layers serves as proof for the preceding point that one must not sit on the ground. Spreading the *kuśa* grass signifies respect; following ancient custom, it ensures auspiciousness.
Kneeling on the ground signifies humility; joining the palms signifies single-minded devotion. As for the requirement that even *śrāmaṇeras* must attend the hall, the *Chao* (Commentary) states:

"The phrase 'even including' refers to those such as *bhikṣuṇīs* who might otherwise bypass [the assembly] and perform the *pravāraṇā* in a separate location. The *Chao* speaks of a "separate location" based on the existence of such a place.
If no such separate location exists, one should wait for the opportunity and then return to the midst of the *saṃgha* to perform the *pravāraṇā* before the assembly.
Furthermore, regarding the "Explanation of Separate Dharmas," this refers to the *Śrāmaṇera-varga*.
As for the statement, "The two sets of five virtues reach the dharmas": the first six persons and above constitute the "dharmas";

from six persons upward, even up to hundreds or thousands, whether the five virtues advance or not, there is no difference whatsoever. The latter five persons constitute the "dharmas," which refers to the five virtues themselves.
The method of appointment differs from the above; therefore, this section is set forth. The remaining protocols will be described further below (etc.).

Regarding the phrase "from the beginning to the ritual": it is as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "from the beginning to the arrival": first, "not being partial" means having no special affection or favoritism toward any particular members of the Saṃgha.
Second, "not being resentful" means not becoming angry or seeking out faults like a blade drawn from its sheath.

Regarding the three types of fearlessness: first, even if a monk possesses the power and influence of kings or ministers and has committed an offense, one should not be afraid of others and must still censure him.
Fourth is non-delusion, which means understanding the formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) as being either valid or invalid.

Regarding the "five knowledges for the *pravāraṇā* (self-exhortation)" and so forth: one knows that when there are no obstacles, the full *pravāraṇā* is performed; one knows that when there are obstacles, the abbreviated method is used;

furthermore, one knows that if two people are virtuous, they may perform the *pravāraṇā* together; and one knows that those who have committed the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) or whose integrity is impaired are ineligible for the *pravāraṇā*.

The Vinaya text further specifies the knowledge of the proper time, such as not performing it at an improper time. These five points are explained by the text of the *Śāstra* itself; their intent is to bring about harmony.
"Those who do not contend" explains the aforementioned "knowing the proper time," meaning one does not act at an improper time. This refers to raising faults;

if one does not know the proper time, it conversely becomes the root of contention. "Having committed an offense that is not erroneous" explains the aforementioned "according to reality," meaning without falsehood.

This means that although there are three bases for the names of offenses, one does not take pleasure in them according to those three bases; therefore, it is said to be "not erroneous. This is intended to cause [the offender] to repent beforehand.
"From repentance up to external difficulties" clarifies that the aforementioned "benefiting others" does not involve causing harm or diminution.

"Therefore, one is able to exhort and persuade" explains that the aforementioned "gentleness" does not involve harshness; "exhorting and persuading" refers to soft speech, whereas "the blade" refers to harshness.
"Compassionately bestowing happiness upon beings and not desiring what is unrighteous" explains that the aforementioned "loving mind" does not involve anger.
It is *dveṣa* (hatred). The opposite of this is precisely *pratigha* (anger). The five types mentioned above have already been explained by the *Chao* itself;
there is no need for further separate commentary. This differs from the ancient records (*yǔnyún*). Regarding the unclear passages in the text of the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka Vinaya):

within the *pravāraṇā* (self-invitation) ritual, it merely states that one should authorize someone to receive the *pravāraṇā*, but does not mention two people. This is the first point of obscurity. Furthermore, within the *karmavācanā* (formal motion), it merely...
Regarding the appointment of a monk named "So-and-so" by the Saṃgha: in cases where two persons are not appointed, the second name "So-and-so" is not included;

this refers to the case where these two are not finalized. As for the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and others, both the *Daśabhāṇavāra* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* state that two persons are appointed for the sake of the Buddha, while the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that two persons are appointed and further many more are appointed for the sake of the Dharma. Although these three Vinayas mention two or many persons, [the context remains as follows].

The ritual procedures are not yet fully understood. For now, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, two persons are appointed to perform the rite for one another in turn; the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* follows the same principle.

In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, many persons are appointed, though the specific number is not stated; alternatively, ten persons may be appointed as five pairs, with each pair entering into the rite together.

If they become exhausted, they should rest in turns; two people should then be dispatched to alternate [the duties], as clarified in the commentary to the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanbu suiji jiemo chao*).

Since this matter was not yet fully resolved, the *Chao* cites the passage from the *Sanqian weiyi* (Three Thousand Dignified Deportments) to provide a definitive conclusion. Regarding the phrase "each person being individually distinct":

the masters of ritual practice in ancient times observed that within the *Sifenlü* (Dharmaguptaka Vinaya), when a single person was appointed, they would perform the *karmavācanā* (formal motion and proclamation) twice.

"Appointing. Having first appointed one person, another is then appointed; thus it is said that "each person is appointed separately. Regarding "one who has not mastered the various schools": "mastered" means to have attained proficiency.
This refers to the case where two people are appointed at once without having yet mastered the *Daśabhāṇavāra*, the *Pañcavargika*, or the *Mahāsāṃghika*.
If five people perform the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination), they must be appointed separately. If there are six or more people, why would it be necessary for each to be appointed individually?
[The answer is] "It is permitted. It says that within a single session, the names of two persons are recorded and entered into the ritual; the rest of the text may be understood in detail.

Regarding the phrase "from the second [person] to the holder," the wording for the request is as in the text. Within this, one must invariably say "self-exhortation" (*pravāraṇā*). Nowadays, however, it is often stated [otherwise].

To say that "pure" (*qingjing*) refers to something other than this is incorrect. The *Chao* (the Sub-commentary) further cites the text, fearing that the meaning might be misunderstood; take note of this. Regarding why this Vinaya permits [the *pravāraṇā*] in a manner different from other schools:
it is to distinguish it from the *Mahāsāṃghika*, which does not permit the *chanda* (consent). That school states: first, one must have someone assist the sick person in coming;

second, fearing that the illness might worsen, the monks go to where he is to perform the ceremony. If the illness is severe, the monks themselves go outside the boundary to perform the *pravāraṇā*. *Souxuan* says:

I appreciate the meaning of your text. For this reason, when raising a formal accusation (*āpatti-udbhāvana*), it must be done in the presence of the accused. If one were to suppress the mind [of the accused], I fear they might rebel against their offense;
therefore, I have not permitted it. There are also cases of both general and specific responses as mentioned above. If one says, "The *pravāraṇā* *karma*," this is the general response.

If one says, "Appointing a person to receive the *pravāraṇā*," or "The *karma* for appointing those with five virtues (*pañcavarga-guṇa*)," this is the specific response. This continues until later...

Regarding the performance of the five virtuous acts (*pañca-kuśala-karma*): when holding the *jñapti-caturtha* (the motion with one proclamation), it must be further harmonized. The text for the *karmavācanā* is as found in the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* (the *Chao*, etc.).
