As for "going out three times and following [the assembly]," this refers to going before the elder (*sthavira*). In current practice, however, it is customary to face toward the Buddha. Some say:

One must not deviate from the text of the *Śāstra* (鈔文). It may now be interpreted flexibly; this does not harm the fundamental principle. Regarding the addition of the word "Saṃgha" (僧) within the *karmavācanā* (羯磨文) of the *śuddha-ekajñapti* (單白):
the text of the *Śāstra* lacks the word "Saṃgha. It is unclear whether this is valid or not. Answer: If it is present, it is an addition (*adhika*);

if it is absent, it is a subtraction (*ūna*). Both presence and absence are permissible. Nowadays, there are those lacking in knowledge who, seeing the omission of the word "Saṃgha," rebuke [the practitioner], saying: "This is not..."
It is accomplished. This is a matter of harmony, which is equivalent to the category of formal procedures (*dharma*).

The statement that "one may not universally apply subsequent procedures" means that one may not universally apply this act of reconciliation when performing the subsequent single-announcement procedure (*ekoddeśa-vācanā*).

As for the phrase "directly applying both methods of harmony," this refers to the aforementioned universal response; both are matters of *pravāraṇā* (self-examination), after which there is no need for further reconciliation. This is a single instance.
This refers to the procedure for the two types of *karmavācanā* (formal acts). Regarding the instruction that the junior monks should perform [the ritual] in sequence, Xuánzàng says:

"The five virtuous ones (*pañcavarga*) must not perform it; it should be performed by the juniors. The Great Virtue says: "Nowadays, most cases have the five virtuous ones performing it themselves, which greatly contradicts the text.
Once the five virtuous ones have reached a consensus, they remain before the Saṃgha and wait until the juniors have completed the performance of the ritual. Then, the five virtuous ones...

This is the initial request made to the Saṃgha. When performing the *cāruka* (the ritual of walking), one proceeds before the three elders; one must also kneel with the feet together (*zhīguì*), and so forth. The commentary states:

"That all the monks follow according to the announcement means that once the *pañcavārṣika* (the official of five virtues) has announced [the procedure] and [the candidate] has gone to the *cāruka* seat, each monk shall follow him accordingly.
The *Dàdé* says: "When first performing the *cāruka*, having received [the instructions], one should simply sit down for now."
[The text] continues as above. Upon reaching this point, one places the grass *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) beneath [the seat], joins the palms, and each recites the verse:

"The Auspicious Youth offered soft grass; The Tathāgata, having accepted it, attained Perfect Enlightenment. We bhikṣus, emulating the Buddha, Sit upon the grass to purify our three karmas through the *pravāraṇā*.
(From the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, Upper Scroll. Xuán’s Record states: "At the time of spreading the grass, as soon as it has been accepted..."

He was ordered to recite this verse. At present, such is the general practice; it is merely acting without having reached the original intent of the scriptural texts, and thus lacks any distinguishing merit.
Regarding the phrase "from the fourth to the middle":
as for the *Xiánsuì jīng* (Sūtra on the New Year), Xuán says that there is a separate translation in five sheets; for now, I shall cite the *Zēngyī Āhán Jīng* (Ekottarika Āgama).
The Sūtra says: When the Tathāgata had taken his seat upon a grass mat within the lecture hall, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying, "Each of you take your seats upon grass mats.

I wish to receive the *varṣā* (rain-retreat) precepts. Have I committed any offense against the assembly? Furthermore, have I committed any transgression of body, speech, or mind? He asked this three times.
At that time, Śāriputra rose from his seat and said to those who were without a counterpart for confession: ... [text continues] ... [Note: The provided source text ends abruptly here.]
The Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus rejoiced that the Tathāgata was free from faults of body, speech, and mind. Why was this so?

Because today the World-Honored One causes those who have not yet crossed over to cross over, and those who have not yet attained liberation to attain liberation; he causes those who have not yet entered nirvāṇa to enter nirvāṇa.
He acts as eyes for the blind and as a path for the lost. For these reasons, the assembly is without reproach.
Regarding human beings, there was likewise no transgression of body, speech, or mind. Next, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have just reported my three karmas to the Tathāgata myself. Am I without fault before the Tathāgata and the Saṃgha? The Buddha said: "You now have no transgressions whatsoever of body, speech, or mind.
The reason for this is that your wisdom is immeasurable, and you possess the dhāraṇī-samādhi, as well as morality, concentration, and wisdom."
They have attained liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation; their actions accord with the Dharma and never deviate from principle.
In this manner, each of these five hundred bhikṣus likewise observed the annual retreat (varṣā). Now, according to the intent of this sūtra, it includes both the Buddha and his śrāvakas.
"If even the Sages were thus, how much more so should we, mere ordinary beings? Following this model, each person should sit on grass.
Regarding the phrase "next comes," the commentary states: "As for the *Mahāsāṃghika* text, that text says:

'If two people perform the *pravāraṇā*, one receives the *pravāraṇā* from the elder (*sthavira*), while the other stands before him at the lower seat. Once the elder has finished speaking, the [junior]..."

Regarding the discussion on seating order: although it was explained in this manner through successive transmission, because the text of the *Catuṣpariṣat-sūtra* (Fourfold Assembly) was not fully clear, the text from the *Jñānaprasthāna* (or *Caturvarga-vinaya*)—specifically the passage concerning "one sitting and one standing"—was adopted.
Question: Does this not constitute the offense of a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*)? Answer: This separate assembly is formed in contrast to a single person possessing the five virtues.

Even if one confesses one's own offenses there, since that person is also appointed by the Dharma, although the sitting and standing differ, there is no offense of a separate assembly. (The above is the correct interpretation. Now, some people say [regarding the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*]: [End of excerpt]

This citation from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* establishes the rule that two persons are to be appointed as Dharma-officers, thereby clarifying the ambiguous passage in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. When performing the ritual, both must kneel with their calves on the ground;

they may not remain standing in a single posture. If one were to follow the manner of sitting and standing [prescribed elsewhere], one would be employing the textual conventions and procedural matters of another school.

For this reason, the Master of the present commentary has clarified the ambiguity by specifying that "this is the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*," lest it be entirely taken as such [without qualification].
One sits and makes the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Then, joining the palms, one says: "The *saṃgha* [declares]... and so forth, as in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

Since this commentary extracts the hidden intent (*sandhyā-bhāṣita*) and does not adopt it, I fear it may not be correct. The regulations for the formal announcement (*jñapti*) do not allow for such adaptations.
Why restrict yourself to this commentary? Reflect upon it carefully; your interpretation is far too forced. You should add words to complete the sense. The *Jie-mo-shu* (Karmavācanā-vṛtti) states:
"According to the ten Vinayas, two persons are both dispatched to attend to the *upādhyāya*; they perform the five duties (*pañca-guṇa*).
When the junior monk comes before the senior monk, he takes hold of his feet and speaks to request permission. If he is a junior monk, it would be improper for him not to follow this ritual."
Regarding the addition of the phrase "with single-minded mindfulness" (*ekacittena smṛtim upasthāpya*) in the *Chao* (Commentary) during the ritual procedures:

since this is absent from both the Vinaya texts and the *Karmavācanā* manuals, the reason for its insertion is that the *Chao* follows only the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, which contains the expression "with single-minded mindfulness. This refers to the act of addressing an individual who possesses the fivefold virtue (*pañcaguṇa*).
If one applies oneself with single-minded attention, what harm could there be? This passage consists of five textual divisions:

first, "Venerable Sir," which is a direct address to the person before one, requesting that they listen; second, "The Sangha today performs the *pravāraṇā*," which records the time for the Sangha's *pravāraṇā*.

"Third, 'I, [Name], also invite [the Sangha] to admonish me freely': this follows the method described above; it means that even if one confesses one's faults, one allows the Sangha to point them out freely.

Fourth, 'If there be anything seen, heard, or suspected, even down to speaking to me': this indicates that the three roots [of seeing, hearing, and suspecting] exist, and that one extends compassion by requesting instruction."
If I see my own transgressions, up to the point of reciting them, this constitutes my own practice of mindfulness regarding purity.
As for the threefold recitation, it expresses the teacher’s earnest exhortation; it is not a matter of idle or superficial reliance.

Regarding the fourth phrase, "Venerable Elder" (Bhadanta Āyuṣmat), the ancients said that these are terms of the Dharma and should not be used together. If one uses "Great" (Mahā), one says "Venerable" (Bhadanta), and the other is omitted.
Regarding the words "Elder" (sthavira) and "Virtuous One" (bhadanta): if [the person addressed] is junior, one says "Elder," and in that case, one must not use "Virtuous One.
If both titles are listed together, it constitutes redundancy. However, our Master does not hold this view; rather, both must be listed together. Thus, the *Chao-yi* states:

"In the past, it was said that among the Sangha, those who were senior were called 'Virtuous Ones' and those who were junior were called 'Elders. Now, this is challenged: if that were so, then above..."
When seated, whom does one call "Mahānāma" (Great Virtue)? When descending from the seat, whom does one call "Sthavira" (Elder)? Now it is said that both are called "Pañcavarga" (the Five Virtues).

One whose conduct and realization are complete is named Mahānāma; one whose years and virtue are lofty and remote is an Sthavira. Thus, while their names differ, the virtues they manifest are likewise distinct;
therefore, they are not called repeatedly. If this is so, why not first call him "Sthavira"? Answer: If there were no such precedence... Furthermore, [if there were no such precedence...]
Why is doubt not placed at the end? At present, it may be positioned wherever it is convenient according to the wording; this is acceptable.
Regarding the division into Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna within the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), that is merely a provisional statement for a single occasion and does not fully exhaust the principle.

As the Sūtra says, "The Elder Śāriputra and others," which serves as excellent evidence (*Shangyi chao*, main text). Furthermore, in current practice, there are also those who recite this verse and then inquire whether the procedure is complete.
No. Furthermore, there are those who say that when the formal words of the motion have been completed, it is incorrect for the five virtuous ones (pañcavarga) to respond, "So be it.
Regarding "remaining as one finds comfort in one's body," the Vinaya states: At one time, a sick bhikṣu knelt with palms joined for a long duration, and his illness intensified.
He informed the Buddha, who said: "I permit a sick person to remain as they find comfort in their own body; they need not necessarily pre-emptively kneel according to the manner of the elders."

When it is time to speak before taking one's seat, only then should one kneel. The commentary states: "Those who follow this rule" refers solely to the aforementioned cases where an exception was made due to illness.
Now, if there is a bhikṣu who is not ill, he must immediately kneel before the elder (upādhyāya). He waits until he reaches his seat, and once the verse has been recited, he sits down again;
therefore, it says "finished. There is another interpretation: one may wait until everything is concluded before finally sitting down again.
To say that "sitting" refers to the speaker is not a correct interpretation; it contradicts the rules of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitation School). That text states:

"From the senior monk (*sthavira*) down to the junior monk (*navaka*), they finish their invitation to confession (*pravāraṇā*). Then two monks of virtuous conduct face one another and perform the invitation to confession.

Now, this [practice] is not so; each returns to his own seat and performs the invitation to confession facing one another. This is identical to the sequence of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya), proceeding from the senior monk one by one in order.

Regarding the *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence), the meanings and contexts are mutually illuminating; however, one must rely on the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. Since [other versions] are too lax, they are not adopted.
If the community of monks has finished their discourse, the matter is concluded according to the text. This may be understood by following the sequence of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

Regarding the statement "if one reaches the point of being accused": the intent of the *Chao* (the *Shishi Yaolan Chao*) is that those who have been accused of offenses belonging to the six categories (*ṣaḍ-varga*) should first undergo disciplinary treatment, and only thereafter participate in the *pravāraṇā*.

If one is accused of the four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*), those with concealment (*sa-praticchāda*) are to be treated with expulsion (*parivāsa*), while those without concealment are to be treated with penance (*śikṣādattaka*).

For the second category of offenses, whether concealed or unconcealed, one must first confess them and then proceed with the *pravāraṇā*. For the third category and below, all must be fully repented before the *pravāraṇā*. This is done for fear of causing undue delay.

Regarding the formal ritual (*dharmakarma*): once everyone has confessed their transgressions, they perform the *pravāraṇā*. If a specific individual has been accused, they must first grant permission for them to undergo disciplinary treatment before the *pravāraṇā* may proceed.

If the basis of the accusation is not clarified—such as when one has actually committed a *pārājika* offense but says it was a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or when one hears of it and suspects it but cannot distinguish the truth—the procedure cannot be finalized.

Once [the truth] is realized, one immediately treats the offense of slander. The commentary states: "As in the case of those within a net. That text says: "If it is not established as clear. The Vinaya states:

"If one does not raise the issue, does not perform the formal recollection (*smṛti*), and does not confess the offense, or if there is no offense, then even if an offense were committed, it should not be subject to confession."

Once the offense has been confessed and concluded, it does not constitute an *adharma-vivāda* (unlawful division) in the presence of others; these twenty-seven [cases] are likewise *adharma* and invalid.

Regarding the "five virtues for raising a charge" and so forth, the textual characteristics are easy to understand (*yìjiě*). As for the progression being unlike what is explained among the four types of persons, that text states:
"If one commits an offense from *thullaccaya* downward, regardless of whether it is raised through self-accusation or by another, it shall all be confessed beforehand."

To perform the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) is called "proceeding. If one has committed offenses such as *sthūlātyaya* or even *saṃghāvaśeṣa* involving four or more people, and the number of monks is too small to carry out the formal punishment for the offense, one should follow the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:
after the announcement (*jñapti*), wait until the assembly is complete and then deal with it according to the Dharma.

One must not proceed with the *pravāraṇā*; this is called "not [proceeding]. This refers to cases identical to those mentioned above; therefore, it is said: "within the rules concerning the four persons."
[This section] concludes.

Regarding the statement, "The three nuns request the procedure for going forth," this is the heading. An external objection states: In the second section on the "Gate of Advancing" in the *Chao* (Commentary), the initial topical outline (*ke*) opens with:
"First, explaining the procedure for six or more persons; next, [the procedure for] five persons"; subsequently, it distinguishes the procedure for five persons. Just now...

Since it has already been clarified that the procedure for the advancement and non-advancement of those with the five virtues (pañcavarga) consisting of six or more persons is complete, one would logically proceed next to explain the procedure for groups of five persons according to the established sequence (*koṭi*).
Why then does this text instead introduce the third section—the request for confession by nuns—here? Answer:

If the gate of advancement and non-advancement for the six-person group with the five virtues were explained first, and the procedure for the five-person group were explained immediately thereafter, then how much more so [should this be the case] for a new...
This leads to confusion in the study [of the text]. The preceding section’s outline stated: "Regarding those with five or more persons, they are divided into four [sections].

Now, if one were to further extract a group of five persons from within that [first category], there might be such a redundancy. If that were the case, why did the previous division of the sections not divide them into two within the *saṃgha-dharma* (monastic rules):
first, explaining the rules for six or more persons, and second, distinguishing the rules for five persons? Would this not have been more convenient? How can you [allow this]?
The general heading is divided into four sections based on groups of five or more persons; it is categorized in this manner. [Objection:

If one were to combine the subsequent sections to form these divisions, there would be the fault of being either redundant or too concise, making it impossible to proceed or retreat [from this structure].

For instance, within the rules for groups of five persons, if one were to mention only the rules for appointing a *vaiyāvṛtyakara* (steward) and the procedures for those possessing the five virtues (*pañcaguṇa*), and omit further discussion, then both the first section and the third section would likewise [be left incomplete].
This is too brief. New students might think that the five-person *pravāraṇā* lacks the first and the last two of the three gates.
If one were to further elaborate on the three gates—preceding and following—within the five-person procedure, this would have already been explained in the section on the six-person assembly;
to recount it again now would be excessively prolix. Therefore, for the time being, we shall simply address the procedure for assemblies of six or more people in general.
Having completed the departure through the four gates, one then briefly distinguishes the dharma of five persons from that of six persons; they differ slightly in their respective positions.
If the first [set] and the latter two were identical, it would be as explained in the preceding text. For this reason, the timing for the five persons is not recounted here.
Regarding the profound intent that they need not recite the precepts together with the nuns—whether such a case exists or not—Xuán says: "This means..."

Regarding the question of toward whom one should direct the confession of precepts (*śīla-āpatti*): the rule of dispatching bhikṣuṇīs and others was established so that designated individuals would go to instruct the community of nuns, thereby ensuring their purity and bringing benefit to both sides.
As for the present *pravāraṇā*, it is simply a matter of the nuns coming themselves to request the monks to point out their transgressions.
Since the Noble One did not establish a rule regarding whether they should come or not, there is no need for such a procedure here.

Regarding the phrase "if a bhikṣuṇī comes," etc., this is stated for the sake of convenience based on those who share the same name. As for the matter of timing—whether it is early or late in the day—instructing the bhikṣuṇī to return:

if it is early in the day, one should simply wait until the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) of the monks is concluded. If it is late in the day, fearing that the bhikṣuṇī might not be able to return to her monastery, the *sthavira* (senior monk) shall command two *pañcavarga* (groups of five virtuous ones):
"Stay here for a moment and wait for the bhikṣuṇīs' *pravāraṇā*. Those two groups of five virtuous ones shall each return to their respective places for the time being.

[Regarding] the position: it is incorrect that one frequently sees [a nun] currently standing before the Saṃgha. As for "one who is to be summoned," this means requesting someone to call the Bhikṣuṇī into the midst of the Saṃgha.
Regarding the question of whether, after she has been summoned but before the *pravāraṇā* (self-criticism) has been recited, it is necessary to harmonize with the Saṃgha once more:
those who say today that this is unnecessary do not understand the meaning. The Venerable One said: "It must be harmonized again," meaning that the previous harmonization [was insufficient].
From that time on, he was a monk; now she is a nun—is this not discordant? A monk possesses the authority to raise charges against all; yet if even one person is in discord, it cannot be done.

Furthermore, when a nun who has been away for several days comes and reports matters seen, heard, or suspected, the assembly must likewise seek her *chanda* (consent) and inquire whether she has been asked [about the matter];
this is not treated as an exception [to the rule]... [etc. An external objection: "Even if there is a transmission of *chanda*, within the words of that *chanda*..."
Should one say "self-indulgence" (*pravāraṇā*) or "purity"? The Venerable One said: "One should simply say 'purity.
This is for the sake of harmony among the nuns; they need only bring purity. Those who are to be informed beforehand by the Saṃgha should say 'self-indulgence. This applies even on subsequent days."
The Saṃgha has already performed the *pravāraṇā*; it is not permissible to speak of it again (reflect on this). This is what is called the "daytime rite," which is identical to the "same-day rite.
Regarding the phrase "now, as for the demonstration": the remainder is the same as previously demonstrated. As stated before: "The great assembly remained for a long while," and so forth.

Regarding the question concerning "arriving": the intent of the question is as follows. Based on the preceding text, which states that those who do not come must transmit their *chanda* (consent), this is the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) performed by the *bhikṣuṇīs*.

Since it is not a formal procedure (*saṃghakarma*) of the *bhikṣu* Saṃgha and there is no separate assembly, for what reason would one transmit *chanda* and so forth? The answer can be understood from the text [as indicated by "云云"].

Therefore, the phrase "the Vinaya says" and so forth is cited as scriptural evidence. One should not follow the procedure for the extensive *pravāraṇā*, but rather perform only the prostrations and other such acts.
One must not speak of the three matters—what has been seen, heard, or suspected—this is called the "extensive dharma.

It is a mistaken interpretation to claim, as some masters explain, that if the *saṃgha* is incomplete or discordant, the *bhikṣuṇī* community may not return to the monastery to perform the *bhikṣuṇī* *pravāraṇā* ceremony, but may only perform prostrations and inquiries.
Reflect on this. Regarding the passage "as in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* instructions," the *Mahāsāṃghika* states:

On the following day, when the nuns come among the monks, they shall request an instructor. The instruction and exhortation shall be transmitted by the senior monk (*sthavira*) among the great assembly of monks, who shall then have the nuns return to their own monastery to explain it.
If there are nuns who do not come, they must also send their formal consent (*chanda*). Both of these are the monastic rules for the Saṃgha.
The principle is one of equality; it must not be partial or applied separately. It is simply that this specific practice is requested; there is no doubt that it is being requested.

Regarding those who have committed grave offenses: among the seventeen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (residual) offenses, acting alone is not permitted. This is considered grave in comparison to the lower category of offenses, but it does not mean that it is as grave as a *pārājika* (defeat).
"Regarding 'The Four Ming [Masters] Briefly Explain Miscellaneous Practices,' this is the citation of the title. Regarding 'From the words "until...

and so forth,' the phrase 'the eight difficulties and other conditions as explained in the *Vinaya*' refers back to what has already been analyzed; these are the abbreviated conditions (*saṃkṣipta-pratyaya*). (And so forth. Regarding 'If one reaches the point of chanting...
and so forth, the phrase 'when the Saṃgha is large, hot, or cramped' indicates that these remaining conditions permit abbreviation. 'Whispering' is [defined] in the *Vinaya*..."
Regarding the six groups [of monks] speaking in whispers and performing the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) with hurried speech, the Buddha declared it to be contrary to the Dharma.

As for "double-headed," this refers to when two sets of five virtuous qualities (*pañcavarga*) each perform the *pravāraṇā* in the presence of a single person; this is contrary to the Dharma. Regarding the statement in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* that one should follow the senior monk for the *pravāraṇā*, Xuánzhì states:

"This is the text from the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*; the *Chao* (the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan*) points to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* as the source. This is a scribal error.
This is an error. Regarding the "inverse order" (*niṣyanda-krama*): the *Ji jie* (Record of Explanations) states that proceeding from bottom to top in reverse is the inverse order.

The Venerable Master says that turning to the left to establish the order is the inverse order. This is like the practice in modern-day dining halls, where the eastern end is considered the seat of honor;

however, this is not the case during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony. This is because the *pravāraṇā* is for the purpose of purifying offenses (*āpatti-vinodana*), and thus differs from ordinary custom, just as when facing [a person].
At the Southern Monastery, the entrance is laid out on a platform in front of the main hall. One proceeds from the eastern narrow side of the door within the hall to serve as the seat of honor.
When the five virtuous officials perform their duties, they circumambulate to the right, just as when performing the ritual circuit for the Buddha;
if one follows the ordinary seating arrangement, this would be a counter-clockwise turn, hence it is called "contrary. As for the placement of people in each row, it is like adding more food.

Regarding the *dharma* (the ritual procedure), various records state: "If there are ten practitioners sitting in a row, one person shall perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) while observing the five virtues, according to the method for adding food.
The Great Virtuous One said: "This interpretation contains two points that are not fully understood.

Since it says 'if there are ten practitioners,' and because the *pravāraṇā* for the expiation of offenses requires a formal *karmavācanā*, the monks must spread their mats longways facing each other."
Regarding the seating: there is one row of seats in the middle that is reserved for those not sitting [in the assembly] to be provided with the duties of the five virtuous ones (*pañcavarga*).

If, at present, one arranges the seating in ten or five rows, this is contrary to the Dharma; this is the first point of misunderstanding. Furthermore, it is said that "one person sits in each row with one of the five virtuous ones.
Now, since there are only two such persons among the five virtuous ones, where could there be ten? This is the second point of misunderstanding. Now...
According to the *Fǎbǎo* (Treasury of the Dharma), regarding the arrangement of rows for the people: it is like the seating within a dining hall where ten rows are established;
five rows are placed in front and five behind, such that they sit facing each other across from one another. Regarding the method for serving food:

when the two virtuous ones (*pañca-varga*) go through the various rows during the *pravāraṇā*, it is no different from the current practice of serving food within the hall. This is called "leaping over" (*chāoyuè*).
"Without following the sequence" means that one does not proceed from the first person to the third person and so on in order. Regarding "reciting collectively," the *Huainan* [Commentary] says:
"For example, if there are thirty people in a single row, the first person at the head of the row says:
'I, bhikṣu [Name], and the others, such-and-such persons, also perform the *pravāraṇā*. The remaining twenty-nine people do not recite the verse. (This does not constitute a valid resolution). Now...

According to the *Xuánjì* (Commentary by Xuánzàng): "All virtuous monks [should grant] the invitation for confession (*pravāraṇā*) regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected. This is excerpted from that Vinaya text.
The term "etc. further includes other matters that are contrary to the Dharma.

Regarding the statement "when four parts have reached the point of going directly," it means that one must not be lax or slow. Although there may have been circumstances for delay previously, such delay would be difficult to justify;

thus, it might be permissible to perform the recitation briefly before the five virtuous ones (*pañcavarga*). However, since the current difficulty involves the door being barred and the situation is urgent, it is not permissible [to be slow].

As for "each person facing another and reciting three times," if there are one hundred people, they form fifty pairs; each individual within these pairs recites three times separately. This is the textual explanation.

The procedure is the same as before. The wording and phrasing do not differ from what was previously stated regarding the five qualities. If the matter of the obstacle becomes more imminent, one should perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*) twice;
if it is even more urgent, one should perform the formal announcement once. Thus, there are these three types: the single announcement, the threefold announcement, and the [single] announcement.
The second [announcement] is stated twice; the third is stated once; thus, three are established. These do not correspond to the five virtues (*pañca-guṇa*). Dharmabhadra says:

"One must understand that these three are discussed in terms of the three universal [applications], and do not refer to a single instance. Because the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) occurs at one time, these three announcements are made.

Many are confused by this thought, thinking it is similar to the previous abbreviated version that corresponds to the five virtues. This means it cannot be compared to the previous abbreviated version corresponding to the five virtues."

Regarding the brief explanation of the four divisions and six types: first, there are two [procedures] for those facing the five virtuous qualities (*pañca-guṇa*), namely: (1) the second recitation (*dvir-vācana*) and (2) the single recitation (*sakṛd-vācana*).

In the second [category], the single recitation according to the abridged text lacks the second recitation mentioned above. Second, there are briefly four [procedures] for those not facing the five virtuous qualities:

(1) announcing to the Saṃgha with a face-to-face procedure and three recitations; (2) announcing to the Saṃgha with a face-to-face procedure and two recitations; (3) announcing to the Saṃgha with a face-to-face procedure and one recitation; and (4) ...
"One must not say [this]; one should simply go directly. This completes the six summaries (*ṣaḍ-saṃkṣepa*). Regarding the sixth, 'going directly in a state of alarm,' Baoyun says:
this refers to the formal declaration of the *pravāraṇā* alone. However, since the *pravāraṇā* has not yet been recited, it is difficult [to proceed]; one should instead enter immediately."

This is the sixth abbreviated procedure (*saṃkṣipta-kalpa*). If, while the five virtues have not yet performed the *jñapti* motion to harmonize the Saṃgha, an obstacle arises before the *pravāraṇā* has been completed, it is subsumed under the category of "abbreviated procedures" involving increase or decrease.
In various commentaries, it is merely stated that if an emergency arises and one departs immediately, this constitutes the sixth abbreviated procedure;
however, they do not specify whether it occurs before or after the *jñapti* motion. Such a treatment is extremely superficial and confused.
Reflect on this.

Regarding the statement "the two [cases] are as above," the Vinaya says: when a wicked bhikṣu creates obstacles and yet enters to compel others to bathe, or when one quickly leaves the boundary with fellow teachers and virtuous friends, etc., because such actions are rarely performed when establishing a small boundary (kṣudrasīmā), they are treated as such.

The *Chao* (Excerpts) indicates a summary. Regarding the phrase "the dharma for a group of six monks is as above," this means that from a group of six up to a hundred thousand, all possess these four gates without exception;
it is also a concluding statement. As for the phrase "next, reaching the dharma," it is because one fears confusion with the practice [of other groups];
that is to say, among the four gates of the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) for a group of five monks, there are one gate before and two gates after.

It is the same as before; however, regarding the second set of five virtues (*pañca-guṇa*), there is a difference in the method of proceeding with the *pratideśanīya* (offenses requiring confession) compared to the six persons.
Fearing that others might not understand and might assume these two groups are identical, this is further clarified. As stated at the beginning of the second section above:
"Second, pointing to the subsequent explanation of the dharma for the five persons"—this refers precisely to these individuals. The remainder is the same as previously explained.

Regarding the Dharma: the first [section] concerns the origin of the assembly of monks; the third concerns the arrival of nuns to request absolution for their offenses; and the fourth concerns the miscellaneous rules regarding the emergence of various characteristics, all of which are the same as those in the section on the six persons.

Regarding the statement "it is said that two or four persons have arrived": when four or fewer persons perform the *pratideśanīya* (confession before another) rite, they do not yet constitute a *saṃgha*.
For this reason, those below the *pratideśanīya* rite refer to three or two persons.

If one commits a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) involving four or more persons—meaning one person commits the offense while there are only three others present—one cannot perform the confession. This rule applies exclusively to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya).
Four persons constitute a "small group. This refers to offenses of medium-grade *sthūlātyaya* and above, for which there is no provision for formal disciplinary punishment (*daṇḍa*).

If one follows the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, a "small group" that extinguishes disputes consists of two or three persons; thus, even for the confession of medium-grade *sthūlātyaya* or minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*), this applies.

The statement here that "four persons or more" constitutes a small group refers to offenses of superior-grade *sthūlātyaya* (this follows the interpretation of Master Xuánzàng). However, as for those included within the explanation of *sthūlātyaya*: this...

This refers to having committed a *sthūlātyaya* offense and brought it before the Saṃgha; before the punishment could be administered, one was startled by a sudden calamity and fled—this is what is meant by "entering into the category of the *sthūlātyaya* confession.
It means that the offense has already become manifest, as stated in the teachings. Regarding the phrase "up to the confession of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*" and so forth:
this means that one has bypassed the *pārājika* offenses; hence the word "up to" (*yāvat*). Because the assembly was insufficient and there was no further way to administer the punishment...
This is because of the underlying principle (*artha*). Regarding the statement that one should not be obstructed from the *pravāraṇā*:

this refers to cases where one has been accused of grave offenses such as the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or other serious *pārājika*-like transgressions, and because the quorum of the Saṃgha is incomplete, one is unable to perform the formal confession (*pratideśanā*). For the time being, the matter of suspending the confession is set aside;

once the offense has been formally raised and everyone is fully aware of it, it is equivalent to a public disclosure (*vibhūta*), and thus one may proceed with the *pravāraṇā*. The phrase "as stated in the *Caturvarga-vinaya* regarding the recitation of the precepts" provides an illustrative example.

This refers to the commonality of the number [of participants]. Once the recitation of the *Poṣadha* and the disclosure of offenses have been completed, even if the offenses have not yet been expiated, one is nonetheless permitted to hear the precepts.
Likewise, during the *Pravāraṇā*, even if an offense has been raised and not yet expiated, one is still permitted to perform the *Pravāraṇā*.

Since both are equally practitioners of pure conduct, the recitation of the *Poṣadha* prevents non-virtuous acts that have not yet arisen, while the *Pravāraṇā* prevents offenses that have already arisen; because their function in preventing transgressions is identical, both constitute pure conduct. Furthermore, the *Poṣadha* and *Pravāraṇā* are both...
These various dharmas serve to unify the Sangha’s merit; they require that all members within the boundary assemble, and they unify the merit of the disciplinary proceedings.

Those who have committed an offense are not permitted to hear the *śīla*, nor are those with offenses permitted to perform the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination), and so forth. Since the *pravāraṇā* follows the same procedure as the recitation of the *śīla*, what obstacle could there be?
The phrase "the principle requires that one must state the origin [of the offense] and so forth" is likewise a statement of the formal wording.

When two or three persons perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish), or when one is accused of having committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal ecclesiastical offense), one should say: "May the two virtuous ones attend to me with one mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed such-and-such a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Because the assembly was incomplete, I have not yet received its formal treatment; the rest [of the assembly] is pure. This follows the same format as the procedure for the *poṣadha* (confession ceremony).

Furthermore, regarding the different cases of silent falsehood during the recitation of the *Poṣadha*: when one is actually impure yet claims purity in the presence of others, this constitutes a deliberate lie (*mṛṣāvāda*).

Since there are three types of objects [of the offense], three *pārājika* offenses are incurred. This differs from the case of silent falsehood during the *Poṣadha*, where one merely expresses purity; in that instance, one incurs only a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Regarding the phrase "if one arrives before [others]," it states that one should not perform the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination/invitation to admonish). Xuán explains: "When one has reached the level of 'repeated auspiciousness' (*chóngjí*) and above, there is no one else with whom to face;

thus, the principle of repentance (*huǐ*) does not apply. Furthermore, since one cannot disclose [one's faults] alone, one should not perform the *pravāraṇā*. This is the meaning according to the principles.

As for the phrase "the rest follows what precedes," the intent of the *Chāo* (Commentary) conforms to the section on the "mindful recitation of the precepts" (*xīnniàn shuōjiè*). That text says: "Or it is said..."
"Exposed. Some say it means "waiting for others. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If no guest arrives, one should form this thought:

'If I obtain a pure bhikṣu, this offense shall be removed according to the Dharma. Having formed this thought, one should recite it three times mentally and verbally. This is from the *Poṣadha-khandhaka*.
Furthermore, it cites the *Pañcaśata-praśna-śāstra*: "One should join the palms and confess before the Saṃgha of the four directions; thereafter, one should recite the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra at length.
Since both parties are members of the community of pure conduct, their efficacy in governance is equal. One should then enumerate the offenses committed, while the remainder are declared pure.
Only then should one perform the *pravāraṇā* by means of mental reflection and verbal declaration, reciting it three times. Thus it is said.

Regarding what is called "the miscellaneous characteristics of the three great vidyās," there are multiple layers of question and answer; these are set aside for detailed analysis because they serve to resolve the doubts concerning meanings left unfinished in the preceding text (and so forth).
Within the questions and answers, the initial statement "the question reaches the Saṃgha" makes the intent of the inquiry clear.

As for the response which "generally includes the sense of formal censure and suspension," this refers to the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) according to the Saṃgha’s legal procedures, wherein one may be charged with a *pārājika* offense.
He shall immediately expel him. If he has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that is concealed, he shall undergo the six-night *parivāsa* and the *āvarhaṇa* (formal rehabilitation), and so forth;

even for offenses of *duṣkṛta* or *durbhāṣita*, he shall all be subject to disciplinary treatment. When adding the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*), the number may be made complete with twenty persons.

They may all be treated accordingly; this is the case where [the quorum] is fully met. If only six or seven people emerge to deal with the residual offenses, one cannot discard the heavy *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting) offense.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, eight people must be present; thus, this [smaller number] is insufficient, which is why it is said that "it may occur. Consequently, it is not fixed.
Therefore, even if individual members have the authority to treat and manage [offenses], as long as the management and governance are not yet complete, if it is... [as stated above].

"Te-ji. Immediately, the punishment is administered. If it is a *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or heavy *sthūlātyaya*, and there are too few people to perform the formal confession and purification, one cannot yet achieve complete eradication [of the offense];
therefore, they simply say "pure. Second, regarding the phrase "the inquiry has arrived": the intent of the question is clear.

As for why the *prātimokṣa* (precepts) are recited first and the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) follows in the response, it says: "If five persons perform the *pravāraṇā*, they must first recite the *mūla-vinaya* (Prātimokṣa) in its entirety, and only then..."

One person rises, kneels with palms joined, and requests to be the presiding master for the confession of offenses. He announces the offenses regarding what was seen, heard, or suspected. He requests others [to announce their own offenses] regarding what was not seen, heard, or suspected.

This "invitation" (*pravāraṇā*) is another name for the fivefold virtue (referring to the procedure for the *poṣadha*, as this treatise explains at length). Regarding the statement in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* that the *pravāraṇā* is the same as the *poṣadha*:

in the introductory narrative of the Vinaya, after the *pravāraṇā* they performed the *poṣadha*, and because they were utterly exhausted, the Buddha said that one should not perform the *pravāraṇā* [immediately followed by the *poṣadha*].

"Perform the *pravāraṇā* and then recite the *prātimokṣa*; the *pravāraṇā* is itself the recitation of the precepts. **Objection:** The recitation of the precepts (*prātimokṣa*) is for the purpose of knowing the characteristics of the precepts and preventing unarisen transgressions.

The *pravāraṇā* is for the purpose of purifying body and speech and removing transgressions that have already arisen. Since their respective remedies (*pratipakṣa*) are different, how can it be said that the *pravāraṇā* is itself the recitation of the precepts?
**Response:** Although there is a distinction between what has already occurred and what has not yet occurred, there is no difference in the intention to bring about purity. (Third, the question.)
Regarding "that which has been explained": it is as previously explained. As stated in the *Dharmas of the Four Groups of Venerable Ones*:

"May the Venerable Ones attend with one mind," and so forth, up to the threefold recitation for purity. Fourth, regarding "the inquiry leading back to the returner" and "one who is separated from his robe":

this refers to a person who entered the previous *anvārohaṇa* (summer retreat) and, based on the five advantages of the *kārttika* month, has not yet completed the summer retreat; he places his robe outside the boundary and departs, but has not yet entered the [next] *kārttika*.
"Ti" means to be separated from one's robes. The remainder of the text is easy to understand. Regarding the fifth point, "inquiring about offenses":

Xuán says that according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), if one has received a formal extension of time (*ādeśa*) for the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) at this location, it is permissible to go to another location for the *pravāraṇā*. However, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Zhiji lü) does not allow this. It states:

"To perform the *varṣā* ceremony at this location and the *pravāraṇā* at another location constitutes a violation of the *vinaya*. This applies whether one has received an extension of time, or for a period of one month, or even until later."

If one proceeds with the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) at will, one also incurs an offense of transgression (*vyañjana-āpatti*). However, if there are difficulties on the road such that one fears for one's life, there is no offense in performing the *pravāraṇā* there.
Regarding the sixth point, "asking about arrival": Xuán explains that this refers to the property obtained by the Saṃgha during the intermediate period;

it does not distinguish between before or after the rainy season retreat, nor between the boundaries of "this" or "that," as the gift is universally bestowed upon the monks of the entire transformation-field. This applies to items present before the Saṃgha.

It is entirely inappropriate [to divide the property] because the objects present at that time possess four defining characteristics: first, the certainty of time, as it is the same day, the sixteenth of the seventh month;

second, the certainty of place, being restricted to those observing the rains retreat within this specific boundary; third, the certainty of persons, being restricted to those currently residing together who entered the retreat early;

and fourth, the certainty of dharma, as there is no need for a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), but rather the property is divided directly according to the number of individuals. Thus, one should know that [the division applies only to] the latter...
Those who have completed the *varṣā* retreat are not entitled to receive these items [for the sake of those yet to come].

For the sake of future recipients, the Vinaya text states that when the former *varṣā* residents and those traveling after the summer retreat divide the dwellings at the time of the *pravāraṇā*, may those who entered the latter *varṣā* before it was complete also receive a share?

The Buddha, knowing this, permitted them to accept [the share] for the sake of the future; they may look forward to spending the summer retreat through this means, but they must not take [the property] arbitrarily.

Regarding the phrase "receiving [the dwelling]": at the present time, one receives a winter room; even if it is later occupied by another person, it still counts as a winter [allotment]. When the rooms are being divided, receiving [a room] with the expectation of winter is called "future.
Regarding the seventh point, "asking until [the lips move]": this refers to speech that does not leave the lips; it is a private, clandestine whisper. This is contrary to the Dharma and improper.
Even if the speech is rapid and the lips close together, if others do not understand what was placed [therein], it is called "improper. Ānanda gathered the assembly without...

Regarding the phrase "the Dharma and so forth": this refers to the consensus reached within the monastic community (*saṃgha*). Now, to cite only the previous case of the left side is to fail to understand that this constitutes a partial illustration.

How can it be said that [the rule] does not apply? (and so forth). Regarding the question in the eighth [section] concerning "equality" and so forth: this means that among those observing the rains retreat (*varṣā*), there may be those who entered early and those who entered late.
If one does not know the status of the earlier entrant, one should follow the principle of the later entrant; the determination is made based on the majority.
As it is stated in the Vinaya: when the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) of the Saṃgha has concluded, if many guests arrive, they must perform their own *pravāraṇā* as well;
the few shall follow the majority. This case is also like that. Regarding the question "What is the Ultimate Virtue? in the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* and other texts, it says:

"When a donor invites [the community] for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), even if the *bhikṣuṇīs* [arrive] at the conclusion of the retreat for the sake of food and drink, one does not say that the donor has become weary or disgusted."

He reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "If one has completed the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) and stays for even one night beyond that, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. Furthermore, among the *niḥsargika-pācattika* rules for nuns, it states:

"If a nun has accepted an invitation to complete the *varṣā* and does not depart, she also commits a *pācattika* offense. However, if the invitation was not restricted to the summer period and was made with a deceptive mind, there is no offense.
Moreover, in places such as monasteries, mountain caves, and the like, there is no offense at all; if [the rule] increases by one grade, there is evidence for this above.

The *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) has concluded. To remain for a long time without departing from this place involves faults and disadvantages. [As explained above, the main section on the *pravāraṇā* ceremony is finished.
Next, the method for the *kaṭhina-cīvara* (the robe of merit) is clarified as an appendix. Regarding the *kaṭhina-cīvara* method: first, the purpose of its introduction is distinguished.

Because those who previously entered the *varṣā* to advance in their practice have fulfilled their summer retreat with merit, performed the *pravāraṇā* without transgression, and possess a reputation for excellence that extends afar, they are pure both internally and externally.

It moves the hearts of sentient beings. Regarding this period, it separately invites blessings; the Sage opens five benefits to reward virtue, and the Confucian tradition exhausts its efforts to support merit.
It is also called "recompense for service," and thus it is explained next. Next, the commentary lists the names in their Sanskrit order and explains their meanings.
Below the term *kaṭhina*, the *Vinayavibhaṅga* (Liao lun) is cited and translated as "solidity. Next, the meaning of "solidity" is explained: it is that which can evoke...
"Many robes. This refers to a path where robes do not become spoiled. If one receives these robes, one immediately gains five benefits from their abundance:

even if one keeps extra robes (*dīrgha-cīvara*) without performing the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification), no offense is incurred; this is called "not being spoiled. If one does not receive these robes but keeps them, and they exceed the time limit for extra robes, [an offense occurs].

Because it constitutes an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), it is termed "ruined. Regarding "difficult to sustain," the *Śāstra-vivaraṇa* states: "For a poor person, resources for livelihood are deficient;
since sustaining life is difficult, even a small amount that can be extracted and placed into this robe yields exceedingly superior merit.
This serves as the response to the aforementioned objection. As for "one who gives a great mass of robes like Mount Sumeru," this refers to those who are wealthy.

What difficulty is there in giving even a small amount? It is only for the sake of the poor that even a very small amount of wealth is extremely difficult to give, as evidenced by the great gift of Mount Sumeru.
When the Buddha ordered this robe to be made, he specifically sought the materials from the poor;

thus, it is named after the source from which the recommended material was obtained. As for "firm" (*khakkhaṭa*), it means "indestructible. If so, how does this differ from the previous term "solid" (*sāra*)?

The previous response stated that being "solid and substantial" refers only to the ability to procure many robes such that the robes do not fall into ruin; thus, with respect to the robes, there is no offense.

The present statement regarding being "firm and stable" refers to the absence of offense with respect to the precepts; for by receiving benefits on account of the robes, one does not violate the five kinds of prohibitions.
Therefore, Zhi says: "Because one accepts the robe, yet does not violate the five precepts, it is called 'firm and solid' (*kaṭhina*).

As for 'sheltering' (*kaṭa*), because by accepting this robe one is able to provide shelter and protection against the five [sensual] pleasures, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* designates this as the 'sheltering robe.

Regarding 'rewarding the good and punishing the evil,' this is the author's own interpretation. As for the 'robe of merit' (*kaṭhina-cīvara*), it is also explained as in the preceding text (*et cetera*)."

Regarding the "arrival at the characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*), as the text states: first, regarding the inclusion of the intercalary month, it says that after the *cāturmāsika* (four-month) *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) is completed, there is the *kāṭhina* robe of summer merit.

According to the narrative context of the Vinaya, on the sixteenth day after the completion of the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism), one who carries a *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) or a new robe goes to see the Buddha.
On the way, he encounters rain and becomes utterly exhausted; he reports this to the Buddha, and the Buddha consequently assembles the Saṃgha and addresses them.

It is said: "Once the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) is concluded, four matters should be performed: namely, the *pravāraṇā*, the dissolution of the boundary (*sīmā*), the re-establishment of the boundary, and the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* robe.
Regarding those who entered the retreat early and received the robe on the sixteenth day of the seventh month, this is intended to exclude those who might otherwise be confused with them.

The text states: "One receives the robe once the *varṣā* is concluded," which refers to both before and after the retreat; thus, it serves as a distinction. As for discarding [the robe] at the end of the four winter months, the Buddha said: "No."

Regarding the "receiving of robes": this refers to receiving robes for one month. Since it is stated that this period extends through the four months of winter, this corresponds to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month.
To claim that one may likewise receive robes up until the fifteenth day of the eighth month is cited as a refutation of the ancient [view].
The ancients maintained that it was restricted solely to the sixteenth day of the seventh month, with anything beyond that being prohibited. How is this known? Therefore—
The Vinaya states: "To come on the same day and not spend the night" refers to the sixteenth day of the seventh month. If one obtains a robe on that very day, it must be accepted immediately;
even staying overnight is not permitted, so how could one be allowed to depart for seven days? Now, the Master says this is not so:
from the sixteenth day of the seventh month until the fifteenth day of the eighth month, within this period...
Within one month, it may be opened for acceptance day by day. Fabao says: "The statement that it 'may be accepted day by day' is said in terms of what is permissible;
although a month-long period is opened, this is the time for receiving robes, and those robes may only be accepted once."
This does not mean thirty days; rather, it means that one may receive [the robe] within thirty days. An ancient critic raised an objection, saying:
"If you say that receiving the robe is permitted within a single month, how do you reconcile this with the Vinaya which states: 'It must come on the very same day and not remain overnight'?
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) text then cites the passage held by the opponent, stating: "'It comes on the very same day and does not remain overnight'—this latter phrase serves as..."
The ancient commentator said: "This means that on the very day one obtains the robe, one must accept it immediately; it is not permitted to let it remain overnight. The present Master says:
"This means that according to the Vinaya, within the course of a month, whenever one obtains a robe, one must accept it upon receipt; it is not permitted to let it remain overnight.

This does not restrict 'that very day' to the sixteenth day of the seventh month alone. It is because those of old did not grasp the intent of the text that they fell into such erroneous descriptions. Question: Why?

Therefore, the Vinaya regulations do not permit [an object] to remain overnight. The answer, as stated in the *Xuánjì*, says: "Furthermore, if it becomes subject to defiled contact, the ritual procedure (*dharmakarma*) will not be valid.

This is just like [an object] remaining overnight on pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*), where one may not perform acts such as the formal assignment of ownership (*parikarma*). This also refers to the case when [the object] has already been offered to the Sangha.
"If it has not been given away for even one night, there is no offense, as it is purified by being treated like another's property. This interpretation is entirely incorrect;
clothing cannot be used as an analogy for food. Food may become defiled through contact, but clothing does not. Contemporary practitioners have largely followed this explanation.
Now, according to the tradition of Shu, it possesses three meanings: first, to avoid the fault of wearing garments with pride; second, to prevent the loss of the five benefits for bhikṣus;
and third, to prevent the loss of the five merits for the donor. Therefore, as each day arrives, one should immediately cause [the robes] to be accepted. Reflect upon this.
Therefore, regarding the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*’s mention of "the first day of the month," the commentary itself explains that this refers to the sixteenth day of the seventh month.
Since this is the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), one may accept the robe immediately; this is stated in reference to that specific day.
As for "the second or third day," this refers to the seventeenth or eighteenth. The same applies up to the fifteenth day of the eighth month. To exceed [this limit]...
Because the intervening days are excluded, it says "up to" (*yāvat*). Because one may accept the robe on the very day it is obtained, it says "likewise.

This cited passage serves as further proof for the previously mentioned allowance of thirty days for the robe. Regarding the statement in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* that there are thirty days for acceptance and thirty days for relinquishment:
from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month—is this not indeed so?

The period of receiving is thirty days. Those who enter the *pūrvavārṣika* (early rains retreat) receive it on the sixteenth day of the seventh month and relinquish it on the fifteenth day of the eleventh month;
if they receive it on the seventeenth day of the seventh month, they relinquish it on the sixteenth day of the eleventh month.

This continues until those who receive it on the fifteenth day of the eighth month relinquish it on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month. Question: Receiving on the sixteenth day of the seventh month is what is fundamentally prescribed.
It is abandoned on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month; how can it be said that it is abandoned on the fifteenth day of the eleventh month? The *Chao* text answers:
"He only receives the benefits of four months, which differs from the five-month benefits of the *Sifen* [Vinaya].

If one follows the five-month benefits of the *Sifen*, then the determination is made by the middle of the twelfth month. However, since the *Wufen* [Vinaya] provides four months of benefits, the abandonment extends into the latter period."

Because of the one-month period. Furthermore, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, those who later take up residence also obtain the five benefits, whereas according to the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, they do not.

Here, we simply adopt the "thirty days of receiving" from others to refute the views of the ancients; we do not adopt the "thirty days of relinquishing" from others, but merely cite it for the sake of convenience.
The *Vinayamātṛkā* and other texts likewise corroborate the preceding passage. Regarding the phrase "if one exceeds this, one does not obtain [the benefits]":
This means that one must depart on the fifteenth day of the eighth month; it is not permissible to remain after that, as the winter period has already begun.
Regarding the relinquishment of the intermediate [period], it likewise concludes on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month. From the sixteenth day onward, it is relinquished automatically.
As for the intermediate duration, which can be inferred by comparison, it is at its maximum one hundred and forty-nine days, and at its minimum one hundred [days].
Twenty days. The intervals between descents are not fixed; they may be one hundred, forty-eight, forty-seven, forty-six, or forty-five [days], and these can all be understood by analogy.
"The intercalary month cannot be included" means that once an opening has been made, it is not opened again.
Regarding the statement "the two lead to the completion of receiving [the robe]": the substance of the robe is the very substance of this merit.

Within the *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) category, there are two types. According to the Vinaya texts: if it is a new robe, or if it is an old robe—for an old robe, one performs the purification (*parikarma*) by folding it with a new material;

for a robe made from rags, one performs the purification by sewing it together. As for "wrong livelihood," this refers to the four or five types of wrong livelihood and so forth; these are the ways of flattery and crookedness.

Coveting wealth and profit, being sycophantic and deceitful while feigning few desires, and acting with crooked compliance to suit human sentiments—these are instances of not obtaining [an object] through its proper characteristics.
Wearing summer clothing in winter or winter clothing in summer, hoping that others obtain an object, and instigating others together;

speaking before a person named Zhang about five people obtaining an object with the intention that Zhang himself might also obtain it from another—these do not constitute an offense of expiation (naiḥsargika-pāyattika), as they involve one's own excess.

It is a material object. "Pure" means that which accords with the Dharma. Having excluded the aforementioned categories, the name "in accordance with the Dharma" refers to the purity of this robe's substance.
Regarding the phrase "if it exceeds these strips": Xuán says, "This clarifies the characteristics of the robes.

What was previously stated regarding 'five strips and ten partitions' was spoken in reference to the lower-grade [robes]. By extension, the medium-grade two robes and the seven-strip *kaṣāya* (great robe) may all be received."

Regarding the term *zhàn* (pronounced with the *ní* and *zhǎn* finals): it also has the pronunciation *zhǎn*. As for the "five great colors" (*wǔ dàsè*), the Vinaya text records that because the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) made robes of five great colors, the Buddha said they were permitted to use the color of the *kāṣāya*, namely blue, yellow, white, and black; these are called the "great colors."

Blue-black and madder-red are called the color of the *kāṣāya*; this is translated here as "improper color. If it is not cut into patches (*saṃghāṭī*), it is categorized as "leaf-like" and is not permitted.
Therefore, regarding "that which is decayed," the Venerable [Master] merely relies on common usage; he frequently cites "decayed" as referring to tattered clothing.
As for "clothing that covered a dead person," the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanbu suiji jiemo*) explains its own text: "That which was taken from a cemetery. The Venerable [Master] relies on this.
The tradition of the Western Lands (India) states that when a person dies, there is no coffin or shroud;

rather, they simply move the body along with its bed to the Śītavana forest, where it is either given to crows or buried in the earth. At the time of departure, the clothing worn by the deceased is used to cover the corpse.

As soon as they arrive at the cemetery, they do not remove these garments but return immediately, bestowing them upon the bhikṣus. Because it is considered a taboo among laypeople, the clothes are not collected again.

The above concludes the correct interpretation. According to the *Souxuan* (Investigating the Profundities), the "previously worn and decayed" and the "cloth used to shroud a dead person" are combined into a single interpretation.

This means that because this cloth had covered a dead person for a long time and had become decayed, those who go to the cemetery to retrieve it obtain the upper garment from the corpse during a reburial and bring it to offer to a bhikṣu.
To cite this as a non-interpretation [of the original meaning] is incorrect; if it were indeed decayed, it would refer to a replacement garment.
Clothes obtained by divination are likewise unfit for bestowal upon a bhikṣu. Furthermore, this *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is based solely on the traditions of India;
even in that region, there is no custom of reburial. Consider this. An external objection states:

"If it is said that clothes used to shroud a corpse may not be made [into robes], why was it permitted in the preceding text for 'rag-robe' (*pāṃśukūla*) to serve as the substance of a robe in accordance with the Dharma? This should be cited as a commentary."

The commentary states: "The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* [mentions] rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*) and so forth (etc.). Regarding the rag-robes of the aforementioned *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, these refer to items discarded by people along the road that are no longer used;
after a bhikṣu has collected them, he may use them. However, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, this is not permissible in the case of the corpse of a brave warrior (*vīra*).

Therefore, the sub-commentary provides this clarification to distinguish it from such confusion. Furthermore, regarding a brave warrior who accepts [the robes] to perform the *kaṭhina* ceremony, it is said: [text continues].
What was previously raised has already been addressed; it cannot be done again now. This [section] is brought forward to resolve a doubt regarding the folding of leaf-like robes (*patracīvara*).
The preceding text stated that "it must not be cut," which might lead someone to suspect that even the folding of leaf-like robes is not permitted.
Therefore, this is set forth as a clarification. This robe is continuous with its strips; one merely folds the leaves to create the divisions. This also applies to old robes.
Regarding "become old": even if it has been worn on the body only once, it is called "old clothing. As stated in the *Śayanāsana-śikṣāpada* (the precept concerning sitting mats):
"Even if it has been sat upon by the body only once, it is immediately termed 'old'; it does not require being folded [or used extensively]. Regarding "clothing given in haste":

if at the time of its original acceptance it was intended for later use as a *kaṭhina* robe, then it is not permitted; however, that which is permitted in the present text refers to when it was accepted by another.
Because there was originally no intention [to receive it], when one later sees that there is none, one may immediately make it into a *kaṭhina* robe and complete the formal acceptance (*parigraha*).

Regarding the "timely robe" (*kālacīvara*), this refers to a robe offered by someone at the end of the summer retreat for the monks who have observed the rains retreat. This also applies to the case where there was originally no intention at the time of first receiving it;

it would be improper to acquire it if one had such an intention. As for those who have never used the three robes (*tricīvara*), according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, although they have finished making them, they have not yet performed the ritual of formal dedication (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
[He] maintains [the robes]. Or, on this day, if he sees that there are no other robes available, he may make [them]. This serves as a counter-illustration to the preceding text:

the three robes of a deceased bhikṣu, having already been used by oneself, are in every respect improper [to keep]. If one discards them out of greed for gain and offerings, this refers to the perspective of a bhikṣu who thinks:
"This year, there is no offering of the *kaṭhina* robe from laypeople; thus I shall not obtain the five privileges. I shall now discard them myself."

"One's own robe" refers to one that has been offered to the Saṃgha for the purpose of making [a robe]. According to principle, when a bhikṣu offers a robe, it constitutes a valid acceptance by the donor.

That it is said here not to be valid is based on the fact that it is improper from the perspective of seeking personal gain. Regarding "all five matters being invalid": the five matters refer to the five types of gain;
"all" means that they are all invalid in the same manner. Conversely, those that are valid are cases where there is no intention to covet gain.

This constitutes the formal acceptance of the robe. According to the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, regarding the evidence for the completion of the seven classes of robes, the passage on a bhikṣu receiving a gift of robes states that it is not for the sake of personal gain from the donor;
thus, the acquisition is not restricted solely to the lay donor. One may accept either one or two [robes] as appropriate.
The intention applies to all three robes, and one may receive them to make a *guṇa-kaṭhina* (merit robe).
It is not necessarily as prescribed in the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (Shisong); it must be a *saṃghāṭī*. The lower three robes must not be those with four-fold stitching (*bun*).

"Stitching" (*bun*) refers to the successive weaving of threads around the edges. "Fine hooking" (*gō*) refers to the fine strips of leather on the front and back. Without these, [the robe] is not completed.
Regarding "the three who are not persons [qualified]": this refers to the selection of those who receive the robe, and the selection of those who hold the robe.

Regarding "the four who do not constitute [a valid assembly]": the commentary states that as for the person who has given their consent (*yadṛcchā*), since this person is already in a private room and thus not before the *saṃgha*, they are not entitled to the five benefits.
As for those with obstacles: a person subject to the thirteen obstacles is not qualified to receive [the robe]. Below are the ten...
If even those who recite the *Śikṣamāṇā* and *Śrāmaṇera* precepts do not yet obtain it, one can know [the situation] by analogy with this. Regarding the absence of the *saṃghāṭī*:
according to the context of the Vinaya, because the *saṃghāṭī* (great robe) is heavy, the *kaṭhina* (merit-cloth) was established so that one might receive its five benefits.

Now that the *saṃghāṭī* is absent, it is not appropriate to use the two lower robes [in its place]. There is no obstacle to asking about this deficiency. Since the formal *saṃghāṭī* has been permitted, one may now take the two lower robes [as substitutes].
Regarding the *saṃghāṭī*, it can be received [as a substitute] when its proper location is occupied. An unexplained note states: "The Vinaya lacks a definitive ruling;

however, since the robe is applicable to both the primary and secondary [categories], according to the principles of the text, it is appropriate to receive it. Furthermore, another interpretation says: "Since the *antarvāsaka* (inner robe) is the primary robe, even the receiving of the precepts allows for such substitution;

the present case should follow this precedent. Now, it is said: "The Vinaya does not permit substituting the two lower robes (*uttarāsaṅga* and *antarvāsaka*). This temporary measure merely avoids the deficiency of being without robes for a single period."
The fault of violating the rules of decorum has already been granted as one exception; it must not be granted again.

For example, if there is an intercalary month for receiving the day [of the Uposatha], one may receive it for that single month, but one cannot include the intercalary month in a subsequent reception. This is also a case of granting an exception that is not to be granted repeatedly;

this should be understood by analogy (reflect on this). As for those who reside outside the boundary, since they were previously inside the boundary, their offering of consent (*chanda*) was not valid; how much more so now, when they are physically outside?
It is certainly improper to be outside the boundary (*sīmā*). If there are four *bhikṣus* or more at the residence, an external objection might be raised:
"A *śrāmaṇera* has only just received the precepts and becomes a newly ordained *bhikṣu*. He does not yet understand the right and wrong of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedures).

How can he count toward the quorum for receiving robes and obtaining the five benefits? [The response is: "Dharma-ratna, you should rely on an established *bhikṣu* who understands the Dharma to instruct him; it simply requires a long period of training."
And thus, one immediately attains it. Regarding "one bhikṣu and four śrāmaṇeras," an external objection states:

"At the beginning of the summer retreat they were śrāmaṇeras, and only within the summer retreat did they receive full ordination; for what reason do they obtain the five benefits? One may cite the commentary to answer, saying:

"Because the śrāmaṇeras, etc. [as explained at length]. As for "if the residence, etc.," this refers to these five persons: since none of them understand the Dharma, they are permitted to request [the ritual].
When outsiders come to receive [the robe], they are not entitled to receive the benefit.
Regarding the passage in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* concerning "monks from different territories," one must understand its general meaning as follows:

it means that although monks from outside this territory were previously permitted to serve as the quorum for a monk of this territory to perform the legal act (*dharmakarma*) and receive the robe, they themselves are not entitled to the five benefits, because those who belong to a different territory do not obtain them.

Now, it is not yet clear whether it is permitted for the Sangha to collectively receive this benefit at different locations. This is why the *Chao* (the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan*) cites this passage;
there is indeed a principle that permits it. Only the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: Venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, "When the bhikṣus have completed their summer retreat..."
When many monasteries within a single boundary collectively receive robes, have they all relinquished their robes? Answer: It depends on whether they relinquish them.
Regarding those who do and do not relinquish them, this is determined by the subsequent dissolution of the boundary.

If one originally intended to relinquish them, then at the time of dissolving the boundary, one loses the five privileges. If one did not intend to relinquish them, then even though the boundary is dissolved, one does not lose them.
The five benefits depend upon these benefits. If one relies on the Dharma-jewel, it is calculated according to the number of persons who hold the robe.

If the person holding the robe remains within the boundary and does not sleep apart from the community of monks, one does not lose the five benefits; hence they are called "benefits based [on the Dharma].
If one sleeps apart from the robe outside the boundary of the community of monks, one commits an offense such as the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Saṃghādisesa) and so forth, as stated in the text.

Regarding the statement that "in two cases it is not necessary to grant permission": the "holder of the robe" refers to one who possesses the five virtues; the same applies to the "guardian of the robe. One must call upon someone who is specifically knowledgeable.

Those who may receive [the robe] are those who clearly and distinctly understand whether it has been received or not received: namely, one who has broken [the precepts], one who is not settled, one who was settled later, and one who lacks the *saṃghāṭī*.
