These are those who may not receive it. Conversely, those who do not fall into these categories constitute those who may receive it. This is what should be done.

"Receiving one robe" refers to a robe offered by a single donor. Regarding the formula, whether it concerns one donor or three robes being offered for the sake of merit, this is intended to distinguish the *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe);

however, it is also permissible to do so with the two lower robes. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, this applies exclusively to the *saṃghāṭī*, and the two lower robes are not permitted to be accepted in this manner.
Following the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, however, there is no restriction to the *saṃghāṭī* alone. The rest is the same.
Regarding "light items": Xuán says that this refers to merit, as they are acquired during that specific time; therefore, they belong to both categories [the Sangha and the individual].

Regarding "heavy items" entering the permanent property (*sthavira-sāṃghika*): the *Huainan ji* states that when citing cases where a donor provides many garments or clothing of high value, one accepts the money for the purpose of maintaining the precepts.
If there are no garments, the items all become money, which is then used to purchase silk and cloth to make [robes].
One should accept the robes. Any remaining money beyond that must be entered into the common property (*sādhāraṇa*), because this is a gift given during the proper season.
If it is the fifteenth day of the seventh month, it is merely called a "gift received out of season" (*akāla-labdha-dāna*); it is not appropriate to divide it according to its weight or value.

Even if there are gold, silver, or coins, one must exchange them for light goods and then perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) to divide them. If one performs the *karmavācanā* to divide heavy goods, that constitutes the offense of *vada-ja-mṛṣā* (false speech regarding the ritual).
This is the Dharma. As recorded in the *Xuánjì*: furthermore, regarding the calculation of advancing or retreating [the retreat], it depends on the robe offered by the donor.

If one says, "I offer this to the boundary," then for those who have entered the *pūrvavarsa* (early retreat), it is termed "present before" (*pratyakṣa*) during that period; no formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is required because the four principles are fixed.
These four are: first, time; second, place; third, persons; and fourth, the Dharma, as previously described (*et cetera*). If, however, one says, "I offer this to all those in retreat," then...

Regarding those who are "identical in prior and subsequent" (i.e., belonging to the same time period), they are called "monks who have obtained [the robes] during that time"; therefore, it is necessary to establish limits through *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedures) regarding the two portions, light and heavy, and so forth.
The determination of the sections is explained in the same manner here. It is incorrect for the *Xiangxu* (Commentary on the Characteristics) to state that *karmavācanā* is not performed.
If a donor says, "Make [a robe] using these three robes," Baoyun explains this as meaning the donor has brought the three robes with the intention of having them all made together.

Regarding the *guṇa-cīvara* (merit robe), it must necessarily be sewn together to form the appearance of a single garment. Furthermore, the explanations by the monks of Huainan and Dongyang are not orthodox and shall not be recorded.
As for "giving the robes in their entirety to the one who maintains them," this refers to giving the three robes (*tricīvara*) to the five virtuous ones (*pañcavarga*).
This reflects the original intention of the donor to create merit through the three robes; one must follow the donor’s intent and may not transgress it. Now that...

The five benefits are said to be "sufficient. These robes are to be given to the robe-holder (*cīvaradhara*). According to the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vṛtti), the robe-holder is not permitted to receive the [other] five benefits;

therefore, these are bestowed upon him as a reward. The statement in the *Huainanzi* that "one may simply not be separated from the robe, while the other four are all permitted" is a mistaken interpretation.
In the *Jie-mo-ji-na-yi* (Karmavācanā on the Kaṭhina), the phrase "given to one whose robes are ruined" refers specifically to the robe-holder.

It is not accepted. This applies to one whose *saṃghāṭī* has been torn among the assembly of monks; if many people in the assembly have their robes torn, then it is distinguished according to the text of the *Chao* (as stated at length).
Such clear explanations regarding the place where the robe is [to be kept] exist, yet some who do not understand them provide false interpretations, saying:
"The text of the *Chao* does not clarify that after the robe of merit (*guṇavastuka*) has gone to its destination, one merely performs the 'non-seasonal' (*akāla*) [procedure]."

When the Sangha obtains property and divides it equally, those who wish to receive the *kāṭhina* robe at the time of the initial retreat should be considered in relation to the person holding the robe.

At the time of the first formal commencement of the summer retreat, if the individual monk personally desires to guard the robe and does not accept the five privileges, the Sangha must examine whether this is in accordance with the Dharma;
they should then grant permission. To act contrary to this would be improper, and the robe should not be held.
Regarding the phrase "the four matters up to the Dharma," this opens two chapters; it is as the text explains.

Regarding the phrase "the four matters up to departure," "one must not speak of one's own moral virtue to cause a delay" means that one must not say, "That Great Virtuous One is a master craftsman of the Tripitaka," and thus attempt to prevent him from leaving by calling for him to stay.
Because it involves requesting that he not depart, it is called a "difficulty. If one were to describe one's own moral virtue, then...
This is self-authorization. Regarding the phrase "not together with the ten thousand six thousand, etc.," that treatise states:
The Dharma Master asks, "Why such earnestness regarding the *kaṭhina* robe? It is for the sake of praising the Buddha's dwelling. In the past, there was a Buddha named Padma Tathāgata.
He had a śrāvaka disciple named Sujāta who, while preparing the *kaṭhina*, had not yet finished it. Padma...
The Tathāgata was surrounded by sixteen thousand bhikṣus; because they collectively made this robe, it is that which is intended and held in high esteem.
Regarding the phrase "two up to five": there are five patches in this manner. Fearing that [the robe] might come apart, four [patches] are joined together to form five patches.
Xuán yún: "If one receives both the five robes and the six robes together, they must be joined crosswise so that they connect and form five seams.

If one leaves these robes aside and does not receive them, then the five benefits will not arise; it shall not be called a 'meritorious deed,' but merely 'monastic property acquired during the proper time.
If they cannot be divided immediately and thus enter the category of 'improper time,' they must likewise be treated as 'monastic property acquired at an improper time. If one simply [acts]..."
Regarding the "present portion" (*pratyutpanna-bhāga*), it ultimately does not reach the scriptural teaching. As for the phrase "from two up to the top," it is as stated in the text.
As for the phrase "from two up to the *mala*," the Venerable One says: at the time of receiving the robes, the arrangement of seats is different from that during the *pravāraṇā*.

If it is the *pravāraṇā*, the five virtuous ones perform a circumambulation to the right, like a tiered structure before a hall; specifically, in the east of the middle gate, they establish the seat for the presiding elder (*sthavira*).

Now, regarding the receiving of the robe: the five virtuous practices for receiving the robe involve circumambulating to the left and taking it from the narrow passage west of the central gate of the hall.

This is where the seat upon the mat is located. The reason for this is that if one were to circumambulate to the right, it would be inconvenient for the movement of the robe, nor would there be any other logical basis for doing so.

This matter is of the utmost importance; therefore, it must be treated with meticulous care. Regarding the phrase "the superior ones arrive," the statement by the *upādhyāya* (senior monk) and others constitutes a *jñapti* (formal motion).
The *Wenchaos* states [as follows]. The commentary notes: "That 'so-and-so' is able to uphold [the precepts]" refers to one possessing the five virtues (*pañcaguṇa*).

"One should perform the *karmavācanā*" and so forth means that one should appoint a person by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, as per the text [as follows]. Question: As in the *pravāraṇā*, one first appoints those with the five virtues via a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, and then performs a *jñapti-prathama-karman* to harmonize the Saṃgha.
Why is it that in this present case of receiving robes, one first harmonizes the Saṃgha via a *jñapti-prathama-karman* and only afterwards performs the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*?

Regarding the appointment: the answer is that because the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) is a formal enactment, the prior appointment followed by the subsequent announcement for receiving robes is permitted.

If someone does not receive the robe, there is no fault. Now, it is not yet determined whether one will receive the robe later; therefore, first the five virtuous ones (*pañcavarga*) are harmonized, and subsequently they are appointed.
As for "the great [robe] reaching the holder," this refers to the method of entrusting the robe. "Holding it at this residence" means...

The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "To demonstrate that for such a person, the benefit of receiving robes is not considered paramount; this robe is thus conferred upon them through the ritual of *karmavācanā*.
The rest is as stated in the text (*etc.*)."
Regarding the phrase "that which reaches its ultimate limit," concerning the threefold recitation of "shall receive," "now receiving," and "have already received":

according to the *Kaṭhina-vastra-dharma* (the rules for the robe of merit), Upāli asked the Buddha whether one should receive the *kaṭhina* robe by means of the three past phrases, the three future phrases, or the three present phrases.
The Buddha said to Upāli: "These nine phrases are spoken for the sake of completeness; they are not [to be understood] by means of the past."
The *kaṭhina* robe is received by means of the three phrases of the present; it is not received by means of the three phrases of the future, but only by means of the three phrases of the present.
The reason for this is that the past has already ceased and the future has not yet arrived; therefore, one receives it as the present.

Regarding the *guṇa-cīvara* (merit robe): it is said that "one shall receive this" for the future; next, "one now receives this" for the present; and subsequently, "it has already been received" for the past.
As for the recipient who has "already properly received" it, the *Xiangshu* (Commentary on the Characteristics) states: "This refers to the receiving and accepting by the Saṃgha;
in order to manifest the holding of the robe, it says 'already properly received. In this context, the merit belonging to me refers to the five benefits (*pañca-lābha*)."
It constitutes a meritorious deed; as its beautiful reputation is manifested outwardly, it is called "renown. Since the benefit does not reside in another, it is said to "belong to me.

To answer "so be it" means that the person holding the robe speaks to grant his consent. "Having completed the reception of the merit-cloth" means that the matter is finished and one stands with upright and respectful demeanor.
Having finished the announcement, he withdraws; this refers to the dispersal after the ritual prostrations (and so forth).

As for the "five kinds of characteristics," this is a restatement of the chapter headings. "Abandoning" means emerging. Because there are many different varieties, they are called "various characteristics."
Regarding the phrase "the four months have arrived": this refers to the completion of the fourth month of winter, which is the fifteenth day of the twelfth month.

Furthermore, to explain in detail the loss and relinquishment of the essential mind, Xuán states: according to the *Kṣudraka-vastu*, there are eight causes and conditions by which one relinquishes the *guṇa-cīvara* (robe of merit).
1. Departure; 2. Completion; 3. Non-completion; 4. Loss; 5. Severance of expectation; 6. Hearing [of the robe being given away]; 7. Crossing the boundary; 8. Departing together.

Of these, the first six involve the essential mental resolve (*citta*), while the latter two constitute formal acts of relinquishment (*karmavācanā*). Regarding what is called "essential mental resolve," it refers to the state at the initial moment of receiving the robe.

Because it involves a mental commitment based on the duration of one's stay, it is called a "vow of intent" (*yācitaka-citta*). Because one loses the benefit of this robe, it is termed "renunciation" (*utsarga*). Regarding the first case, "departing":
this refers to when, at the time of originally receiving the robe, one makes a vow of intent saying, "If I remain here, I shall accept the benefit; if I depart, I shall relinquish the *kaṭhina* robe.
Now, having departed according to that original intention, one relinquishes it immediately. Regarding the second case, "completion": this refers to the thought made at the time of receiving the robe.
"I have finished making the two lower robes; I shall now relinquish the *kaṭhina* robe. Since he has now completed the two lower robes and fulfilled his original intention, he relinquishes it.

Regarding the "three cases where it is not finished": this refers to a person who leaves the materials for the two lower robes within the boundary, and later, when going outside the boundary, makes a formal resolve, saying:
"Even if I do not make the robes, I will not return to the place where I left the materials. Once [this resolve is made]...
Having gone outside the boundary, he reflects within his mind: "I am also unable to make the robe; it will hinder my cultivation of the path.
Once he has resolved not to make it, he does not return to his original location; therefore, this is called "abandoning before completion. Regarding the four losses:
when he receives the robe, he makes a mental vow, saying: "I receive this *kaṭhina* robe for the purpose of making a robe. If I lose either of the two lower robes..."

One immediately relinquishes the *guṇa-cīvara* (robe of merit). Because it now fulfills its original condition, it is called "lost through relinquishment. Fifth, regarding the severance of expectations:

when receiving the robe, one makes a mental resolve, thinking, "If I do not obtain a robe at the first house, I shall go to the next house to seek one. Now, having gone to the first house and not obtaining one, there is no subsequent house to which one can proceed;
thus, the continuity is broken and the robe is lost. Sixth, regarding "hearing": this refers to the mental resolve made after having received the robe.

One goes outside the boundary to make a robe. If one hears that the Saṃgha is performing the formal act of relinquishing robes (*cīvara-utsarga*), thinking, "I too shall relinquish my robe," yet later hears that the Saṃgha has already relinquished them, one then adheres to one's original intention;
this is called "losing [the robe] by hearing. Seventh, "going outside the boundary": having received the robe, one goes outside the boundary to make it.
Hearing that the Saṃgha within the boundary is in harmony and is relinquishing the robe, one remains outside the boundary, unaware of it; this also [constitutes a loss].

This refers to the loss of robes. Some commentators explain that if one is aware [of the loss], it constitutes a forfeiture; if unaware, there is no forfeiture. However, such a principle does not exist.

Regarding "the eight formal acts performed together," this means they are collectively and harmoniously relinquished. If the designated time passes without relinquishment, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Regarding the "many kinds in the *Mahāsāṃghika*": that Vinaya includes relinquishment through a formal resolve (*cittotpāda*), up to relinquishment through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), and so forth.

Regarding "until the end of the winter month" (*kārttika-pūrṇimā*) and so on: this clarifies that when the time has passed, [the robe] is relinquished spontaneously. Regarding the "eight kinds and ten kinds": the *Pañcavargika* has eight; the *Daśabhāṇavāra* also has eight matters of relinquishment;
the *Vinayavibhāṣā* has eight, which are largely the same as those in the *Dharmaguptaka*. The *Mahāsāṃghika* has ten, which are largely the same with minor differences.
It is not that they lack clarity regarding what is urgent.
As for the statement "next comes the explanation," regarding the five benefits and their obstructions: there are many such obstructions and openings.

If distinguished according to the precepts, the opening of the five minor rules constitutes an "opening," while the non-opening of the remaining precepts constitutes an "obstruction. If one explains it based on this, it is still merely addressing each case individually.

This is also what was said regarding the boundaries. If we consider it in terms of time, one interpretation states that five months with robes is "open" (tong), while one month without robes is "closed" (se).
The Venerable One did not approve of this interpretation. Alternatively, it might be said that five months with robes is considered "open" because one is permitted to receive benefits.

Beyond the fifth month, it may not be considered "blocked" (*sai*). For one month without robes, it is considered "open" (*tong*). Beyond that period, it cannot be [considered] blocked. If one distinguishes this according to the person:

the Great Virtue (Bhadanta) says that for the recipient of the robe, obtaining the five benefits constitutes being "open," whereas for the holder of the robe, not obtaining them constitutes being "blocked.
Others say that those who later cause the robe to be settled, unsettled, or who destroy its settlement, do not obtain the benefit; this constitutes being "blocked. It is not otherwise.

Furthermore, Fabao stated: "The Sangha obtains five benefits; not receiving robes is 'penetration' (tong). Holding robes and receiving robes but not obtaining the [other] benefits is 'obstruction' (se).
In the *Xuanji*, the meaning of penetration and obstruction was not understood, thus remaining incomplete. Reflect upon this: according to this principle, it constitutes an obstruction.
This is also stated from one particular perspective; we do not rely upon it here. Next, the sub-commentary explains the five advantages. Regarding "carefully managing wealth":
if, during ordinary times, one fails to perform the *śuddhi* (declaration of purity) within ten days, one incurs an offense at the end of the ground on the eleventh day;

however, once the robe has been received, it is permitted not to perform the declaration for up to one hundred and fifty days. Second, regarding "being separated from the robe": this refers only to being separated from the Saṃgha.

Regarding the *kāṭhina* robe: the two lower robes are not permitted [to be used as such]. Such are the conditions. Third, regarding "turning away from invitations": whether one turns away from the front toward the back, or from the back toward the front, both are permitted.
Fourth, regarding "separate groups": if four persons who are the leaders eat together in one place, while others are separate and do not join them, there is likewise no offense.
Fifth, regarding "going to another's house before or after a meal": it is also permitted to go without having announced one's intention.

Regarding the statement "each is obtained as previously according to their respective characteristics": the rules for keeping extra robes (*ātyaya-cīvara*) and being separated from one's robes are explained in the section on the thirty [offenses], while the remaining three precepts are distinguished in the section on the ninety [offenses].
As for those who perform the *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (purification by declaration) at once on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month regarding extra robes kept for more than twelve months:
this refers to robes obtained from the sixteenth day of the seventh month onwards, which must all be declared [as pure] by the fifteenth day of the twelfth month.
It is said: "One must not wait for the following day. This is unlike the case of the *ātyayika-cīvara* (emergency robe), which is increased sequentially until the twentieth day;

such confusion might arise, therefore this is clearly explained. (The *Xiangshu* further notes that taking the example of the *ātyayika-cīvara* by adding ten more days fails to grasp the teaching. Even if one followed that example, it would only allow nine days, let alone [the proposed] impossibility).
Regarding other cases where the "timely" (*kāla*) and "untimely" (*akāla*) periods mutually encompass one another: this refers to when there is a *kaṭhina* robe, starting from the seventh month...
The period from the latter half [of the summer retreat] until the end of winter is all designated as "proper time" (*kāla*).

From the sixteenth day of the seventh month onwards, for the twelve and a half days preceding it, all are termed "improper time" (*akāla*). Regarding what is called "continuity": the *kāṭhina* robe is received during the proper time and continues into the month of Kārttika for three reasons:
first, they share the same temporal status; second, both permit the five privileges; and third, there is a causal relationship between the original and the subsequent.

The *kārttika* month is the root; the *kaṭhina* robe is the branch. Regarding their mutual dependence: because the opening of the one-month period was insufficient, another four months were added, making five months in total.
The "out-of-season" [period] naturally encompasses the out-of-season [robe]. It also possesses five meanings: first, it is identical to the position of the out-of-season period;
second, it is identical in preventing the offense of keeping [the robe] too long; third, the root and the branch are mutually dependent—the ten months are the root and the one month is the branch.
Furthermore, regarding "mutual inclusion": because ten days were opened up, if they were insufficient, twenty more days could be added to complete one month.

Since the long period subsumes the short, they are mutually inclusive. By extension, this further clarifies what is not mutually inclusive: the one-month *kārttika* period does not include the ten-day cloth.

This is for three reasons: first, the distinction between the timely and the untimely; second, the distinction between the broad and the narrow; and third, the distinction between the root and the branch.

They are mutually dependent. Thus, the ten-day period also possesses these three meanings. Regarding the aforementioned breadth and narrowness: the *kārttika* month is broad; the ten-day period is narrow because it permits only one long robe.
As for "both according to the *Anuvyañjana*," this refers to what is explained below in the section on the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules concerning the "urgent gift of robes.
In some manuscript copies of the *Chao*, there is a later citation of the *Sāgaramati-paripṛcchā-sūtra* and other texts; the Venerable Master says that this is the latter [part].
These are later interpolations added erroneously; they cannot be explained. If they exist, please remove them. (The preceding section on the Dharma is concluded.
Above, there were two discrepancies. This concludes the entire fourth chapter, "The Chapter on the *Pravāraṇā* Ceremony Regarding Persons and Affairs Based on the Dharma.

Second Main Gate: Regarding Self-Cultivation. This scroll contains four sections, with the text divided into three distinct parts (*etc.*).

Regarding the phrase "from the fourth [fascicle] to the middle fascicle": the general title is as explained previously. As for "middle fascicle" (*juan zhong*): "fascicle" (*juan*) is as explained previously;

"middle" (*zhong*) refers to the fact that while the structural framework of the various practices above has already been established, anyone who wishes to uphold the communal laws must first ensure their own conduct is pure.

Therefore, it is placed after the section on individual practices and before the section on communal practices, and is thus termed the "middle. The commentary provides two interpretations regarding the person capable of performing these acts.
The titles and so forth are all as at the beginning of the preceding fascicle (and so on). Regarding the listing of the names of the four chapters:

since the preceding [fascicle] first indicated the middle fascicle and subsequently listed the four chapters, this demonstrates that within the text of the middle fascicle’s own practice, these four chapters of matters and dharmas are subsumed.
One may examine whatever matters are required and act accordingly. Next, the explanation of the sections (p’ien) is divided into two parts;
we shall now address the first. Regarding the statement "from the section up to the sixteenth," the intention for its inclusion is as follows:

although the twelve preceding sections have already clearly established the communal laws (saṃghadharma), it is nevertheless necessary to thoroughly understand the relative gravity of the precepts (śīla). This is the essential point of such thorough understanding.
Do not prioritize the titles of the various chapters and sections. To understand the gravity of an offense, one must know the distance of its karmic retribution.
Therefore, this chapter follows the twelve chapters on the various practices. Question: Why do the four chapters on personal conduct (*xingxing*) occupy the very beginning? Answer:

Because they follow the essence of the precepts (*jie-ti*), which is precisely the subject of this chapter; it is intended to ensure that monks and nuns uphold the prohibitions without transgression, and thus these matters are shown first.
The names and their retributive fruits are therefore placed at the beginning. Next, regarding the explanation of the names, there is first a brief account, followed by a detailed one.

As for the brief account: "pian" (sections) refers to the five sections; "ju" (clusters) contains six or seven; these are none other than titles of chapters and articles, which are divided into segments and established individually within a single position across three functions to determine their gravity.
Next, as for the detailed account: according to the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), the character "pian" is first explained through four gates, the first of which concerns the five positions.

This section comprises both the analysis of the chapters and the clarification of their meanings. Second, it establishes the titles and provides translations. Third, it explains why only five categories are established rather than four or six.
Fourth, it discusses the sequential order. Regarding the establishment of the five categories in the first position: first, there are eight *pārājika* offenses—four for monks and four for nuns.

The second section, consisting of thirteen rules for monks and seventeen for nuns, is the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Saṅghādisesa) chapter. The third section, consisting of one hundred and twenty rules for monks and two hundred and eight for nuns, is the *Pāyattika* (Pācittiya) chapter.
The fourth section, consisting of four rules for monks and eight for nuns, is the *Pratideśanīya* (Pāṭidesanīya) chapter.

The fifth section, consisting of one hundred rules each for both monks and nuns, is the *Duṣkṛta* (Dukkaṭa) chapter. Next, regarding the explanation of the meaning of these chapters, there are four masters in total. The first master says:

Regarding the titles of the chapters, which differ in their relative gravity and hierarchical order: the first chapter is titled "Expiation through Banishment" (*pārājika*), and the second is "Confession before the Saṃgha" (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), continuing thus until the fifth chapter, where the degrees of gravity vary.
Now, you ask: since the twenty categories of dharma (*dharmaskandha*) are arranged sequentially, what difference in gravity exists between them?

Furthermore, there are two meanings for the character *piān* (chapter): first, derived from the radical for "person," it carries the sense of partiality or bias; second, derived from the radical for "bamboo," it refers to a scroll or section.
"Chapter" (pǐn). This is now the "Chapter" of the chapters. The second master says: "What is called a 'chapter' here takes similar categories as its basis for forming a chapter.
In establishing the term 'chapter,' three types of equality must be present. For example, the first four precepts are all designated by the same name, *pārājika*;

this is called equality of function (*gōngqí*). They must be dealt with through expulsion and disciplinary treatment; this is equality of substance (*tǐqí*). The offense is not a preliminary act but the final consummation; this is equality of completion (*jiùjìngqí*)."
The three *jūn* (harmonies) are all complete up to the fifth *pǐn* (section). Now it is asked: "If that is so, secular books also have names; should they also possess the three *jūn*?
Regarding the third [harmony], the Fire, the Master of the Sub-commentary (*shūsǔ*) says: "What is now called a *pǐn* begins from the Four Exclusions (*sìqì*)."

Finally, with the seven *nirodhas*, there are eight chapters (*pāda*). Because they consist of a multitude of characters and sections, they are given the name "chapters. Regarding the fourth [point], the present Master says:

"The establishment of the meaning of 'chapters' is nothing other than the auspicious names of sections and the distinct titles of divisions. Even if they are gathered according to the five [categories] and established, their meanings are fully present in the three [groups] and equalized.

The names of the chapters reside in the seven; fundamentally, they are identical in being subsumed within the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Thus, we know that 'chapters' and 'aggregates' (*skandha*) are mutually pervasive."

Regarding the primary and secondary branches, the offenses are determined as being either uniform or mixed across five or seven stages. The second section is titled "On the Translation. The details of the translation are self-evident from the *Shuchao* (Commentary).
Herein, we shall examine the significance of establishing these five names. The answer in the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) states:

"The Great Sage Tathāgata deeply discerned the dispositions of sentient beings; since those in the turbid age have dull faculties, he had to establish coarse regulations to accommodate their capacities. Upon hearing [these teachings],..."

This is called "the cessation of transgressions. Just as in secular tradition, the willow whip was used to indicate shame; yet in later ages, punishments became so severe and cruel that banishment and exile could serve as a general deterrent.
Regarding the statement "three but five wrongs, four and six," the commentary says: According to the ancient interpretation, there are five methods of medicine (*bhaiṣajya*).

In contrast to these five medicines, the five categories (*pañca-vastu*) were established. If that were the case, since seven groups (*sapta-nikāya*) are explained later, there would have to be seven medicines, clarifying the seven *vinaya* [categories].
There are seven types of disputes among *bhikṣuṇīs*; thus, we know it is not as [you] claim. Furthermore, the administration of medicine according to the illness is not fixed;

sometimes the illnesses are many while the medicines are few, such as the four wheels subduing the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*). Sometimes the illnesses are few while the medicines are many, such as the seven methods for extinguishing disputes (*saptadharmā vivādaśamathāḥ*) resolving the four types of contention.
Sometimes the medicines are equal in number, namely these five categories of offenses (*pañcāpatti*). To establish a further principle: this is indeed the Buddha’s singular method of transformation.

Regarding the ritual procedures (*vidhi*) for teaching according to the faculties of the disciples, it is appropriate to hear that there are five [categories]. As for the sequence and order of these four: first, they are established in relation to what is to be prevented (*pratiṣedhya*).

If one relies on what is to be prevented, there is originally no fixed order; rather, whatever offense was committed first is the one for which the rule is enacted first. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:

The first four precepts possess a sequential order, whereas the remainder have no such sequence. Regarding the establishment of the sequential order for the five sections (*pañca-vastu*), the Commentary states:

"It was because the Great Sage, at the time of his parinirvāṇa, desired that the teachings transmitted to future generations should possess a formal protocol, that he commanded those who uphold the Vinaya to extensively expound these essentials.
Therefore, the text of the *Saṃgīti* says: "All monks and nuns, as well as all the *khandakas*..."
All the teachings are gathered in one place; the text is indeed verified. Among the five categories of offenses (*pañcāpatti*), the offense of immediate death (*sadyomaraṇa*) should be placed first;
the remaining offenses follow as the second, and so on, gradually descending down to the fifth.

To cause the monks and nuns to observe their transgressions and give rise to world-weariness, one begins with the coarse and proceeds to the subtle, thereby severing unwholesome karma and attaining the benefit of the Path;

this is the natural order of things. Next, as for that which can prevent [transgression], it is the substance of the first category [of precepts]. It is the root of being able to maintain practice and the primary source for entering the Path.

If the initial root is destroyed, there is no way for the branches of the latter four categories to grow. Thus we know that when the practice of the first category is established, all other practices follow accordingly.
Birth must be most earnestly cultivated and practiced; therefore, it must be established first. Second, the framework of the communal laws (*saṃgha-dharma*) must be perfected;

if matters are contrary to these, how can one rectify and transform others? Therefore, it must be established next. Regarding the rules for body and speech, if one’s conduct transgresses dignified decorum (*īryāpatha*), one’s own practice will not be accomplished;
how then can one purify one’s karma? Therefore, the third is established. Although the three karmas may be without flaw, which constitutes profound purity of practice, if one is defiled by...

The worldly dust has afflicted his True Dharma such that it has not yet attained glory and distinction; therefore, the fourth [stage] is required. Having first practiced self-cultivation and transformed others, one subsequently cultivates clarity.

If one does not reverently accord with the Three Jewels and restrain the four modes of deportment, then the bestowal of teachings will deviate from skillful means, and the net of the Dharma will be cast in error.

Therefore, one must practice the correct conduct that leads to the fifth destination (the preceding is from the commentary). Next, the character *zu* (aggregate) is explained; it also possesses four sections.

First, the seven aggregates in their initial stage and the meaning of "aggregate. Second, the intent behind the classification of stages. Third, the explanation of the different names by which the seven aggregates are designated.

Fourth, clarifying the characteristics of the concealment and manifestation of various offenses. Regarding the establishment of the seven aggregates in the first stage: *pārājika* constitutes one [aggregate], and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* constitutes...

Second is the *pāyattika* (Pāli: *pācittiya*); third is the *lai* (Pāli: *thullaccaya*); fourth is the *ti* (Pāli: *dubbhāsita*); fifth is the *shani* (Pāli: *sikkhāpada*); sixth is the *ji* (Pāli: *dukkaṭa*); and seventh is the *e-shuo* (Pāli: *dukkata*).

These are all as explained in the "Increase of Seven" section of the Vinaya texts. Collectively, they comprise the preparatory stages (*upakrama*) of the various categories of offenses, which, when brought to completion, constitute the full offense.
Taking this as a chapter, it also constitutes one school of thought; it cannot be suppressed. What is meant by "accumulation" (*caya*)? The ancients said:

when various offenses are not merely one, they are designated as an "accumulation. If explained in this way, the five offenses may be so described. However, regarding the *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), where does its "accumulation" reside?

My current interpretation is that, when subsumed under the meaning of the term, there is simply the nature of the offense—whether light or heavy—which remains constant, whether numbering seven or five.

"Unified by means of gathering them. Assigned to their respective categories according to their names, they are employed to comprehensively encompass the *piñjū* (sections on precepts). (The above is from the sub-commentary [Sū-wén]). Second, regarding the meaning of distinguishing the levels of the stages (*pin-wei*):
the sub-commentary states, "The Great Sage established the teachings to manifest the mentalities of the times; or he categorized them based on the karma of the compilers."
The Martial [Code] establishes names and characteristics based on the offenses of the East. One attains understanding according to what is accessible and stops there.

This can be understood by analogy with the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*), which are differentiated according to delusion. Although the offenses are grouped into one category with three stages, their lightness or gravity is determined;

yet when taking the ultimate perspective, none fail to align with the five. Thus, there are the five accumulations, the five transgressions, the five regulations, the five grades, the five articles, and the five...
Regarding the determination of the retribution for these classes [of offenses] and the duration of their maturation over years or kalpas, none fail to be uniform in being sixfold;

thus there are six categories of transgressions, which are precisely these six types of offenses. It is said that results are produced by causes, yet there are cases where a cause exists without bringing about its result.

There are none that do not align with the seven; thus there are the seven categories of offenses (*saptāpatti-skandha*) and the seven types of transgressions, such as those in the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* and its seven sections.

Third, regarding the derivation of these names, it is as described in the *Shuochao* (see *Yichao* for details). Fourth, concerning the relationship between the hidden and the manifest: the *Shu* (Commentary) asks, "I have originally established the characteristics as clarified in the respective sections;
why then are the *sthūlātyaya* and *duṣkṛta* not mentioned? The answer is: "These arise from the Sage’s mind; they are not matters to be determined by ordinary beings."
In the Vinaya, it is frequently stated that the two hundred and fifty precepts constitute the primary substance of practice; therefore, this *Śīla-sūtra* (Prātimokṣa) has reached such a great number.
As for the remaining offenses that do not enter the *Śīla-sūtra*, they are beyond my understanding and cannot be sought through mere sentiment.
Some have explained it as follows: "The two hundred and fifty" is merely a numerical convention; the measure of the precepts realized by a bhikṣu is equal to the Dharma-realm. It may be...

This is not so. As for the offense of *sthūlātyaya* (偷蘭) which is not included in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, is it not because its essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are dissimilar [to the other offenses] and its cause and effect are difficult to determine?

Therefore, it was extracted separately and subsumed within the category of "aggregates" (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*). Consequently, whether it appears earlier or later, or whether it is open or restricted, is not fixed.

Now, speaking in general terms, both are called "precepts. Thus, the Vinaya says: "The very first violation of a precept. If explained according to their specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are uniform...

It is called "dignified deportment" (*īryāpatha*). Therefore, the Vinaya is not itself dignified deportment. Generally speaking, it is divided according to gravity: the first three categories (*skandha*) consist of coarse transgressions;

that which can remedy them is called "precept" (*śīla*). The *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) falls within the third category. The final four categories involve lighter transgressions; the conduct that can remedy them is termed "dignified deportment.
If one divides them based on their uniformity or mixture, the first four are uniform, while the last three are mixed. The *sthūlātyaya*...

This is the most important point among the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (Lánzá), and therefore it is placed fifth. (The above is from the commentary. The preceding section, based on the *Jièshù* (Commentary on the Precepts), concludes the explanation of the two characters "piānjù" (sections and clusters).

As for the term "míngbào" (name and retribution): "míng" refers to the *pārājika* offenses and so forth; "bào" refers to the karmic fruit. This is as extensively demonstrated by the scriptural citations below.
The remainder is as explained in the usual commentaries (*yú rú chángjiě*). (etc.)
In the introductory general meaning of the first chapter, it says: "As for 'emerging into the ultimate characteristics,' 'emerging from the mundane' refers to the five assemblies.
These consist of two types of monks and three types of nuns, totaling five assemblies; this is said in reference to those who possess the precepts.

If one merely shaves their hair, they are identical in outward form but lack the superior Dharma, and thus have not emerged from the mundane world. Therefore, they are [merely] good people of the world."

Regarding the "field," there are two aspects: that which is one's own and that which belongs to others. First, it is explained in terms of oneself: because there was no emergence [of purity], one has long endured saṃsāra;
now that there is a pure emergence, one is able to transcend birth and death and attain nirvāṇa. This is precisely what can produce the seeds of goodness.
It is called "excellent field" (*kṣetra*). Next, there is an explanation based on others:

because there are those who produce offerings that are pure and bright for the sake of the world, and who practice giving with faith and reverence toward this [field], they increase immeasurable merit; thus, these five assemblies are designated as the "excellent and virtuous field of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*) of the world.

Therefore, regarding the passage from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and so forth, it cites this to prove that the essence of the precepts (*śīlaskandha*) is inherently designated as an "excellent field."

The two characters "shì yǐ" (is therefore) serve as a recapitulation of the preceding meaning and an introduction to the following discourse. Regarding that meaning, the *Jiě xìng xiāng yì* (Explanation of the Nature and Characteristics) states:
"What is the distinction between nature (*xìng*) and characteristics (*xiàng*)? There are two masters' explanations. The first says: "In terms of its own essence, it is nature;

in terms of its dependence on other conditions, it is a characteristic. According to this interpretation, nature and characteristics are not different. The second says: "Nature and characteristics are not the same," just as...
For example, a śramaṇa has the observance of prohibitive precepts as his nature and the shaving of hair and dyeing of robes as his characteristic.

Furthermore, fire has combustion as its nature and smoke and flames as its characteristic; proximity is its nature and distance is its characteristic. Now, this master’s doctrine is cited to corroborate the preceding text.

Master Xuánjì provides a fourfold analysis: 1. Having the nature [of a monk] but lacking the form: as in the case of Vimalakīrti and others, who manifest having wives and children while constantly practicing pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
2. Having the form but lacking the nature: as in the case of *śrāmaṇeras* who have committed one of the thirteen grave offenses and thus lack the precepts. 3. Possessing both:
namely, the virtuous and exemplary *bhikṣu*, who internally contains the virtue of the precepts and externally possesses proper deportment. 4. Lacking both: namely, the worldly laity.
It is so. Regarding the phrase "now arriving at loss": "water cleanses the mind" means that the precepts are solemn and firm, causing the mind to be pure;

thus it is likened to water cleansing—this refers to the mind that upholds the precepts. Regarding the phrase "inquire into its virtue": this refers to the five virtues found in the world. First, dryness... [text ends]
First, it is not treated with contempt; second, it is moist yet not heavy; third, it does not conceal flaws; fourth, it does not tolerate filth; fifth, it is always luminous.
The bhikṣu’s mind that upholds the precepts accomplishes the virtues of the fivefold Dharma-body in the same way. Therefore, this leads to the next metaphor:

that which produces the seeds of goodness is called a "field of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*). Above, regarding the three vehicles, one sows the seeds of the cause in the field and brings forth the purity of the precepts.
It is the same for those who serve as fields of merit for the six realms of existence. "Otherwise" means that they are not individuals like those mentioned above, who are pure and untainted like ice.
"Even if they reject" means to indulge in negligence and transgress the scriptural prohibitions established by the Buddha.
"To bring grief upon oneself" means to cause one's own loss and ruin. "Yi" (伊) refers to "who."
"Sorrow" (*qi*) means grief. It refers to those who give rein to the three poisons and defy the Buddha’s precepts, thereby losing their own seeds of goodness and fields of merit for themselves.
Who else would receive this sorrow? A Confucian text says: "These are the words of Zhao Xuānzǐ lamenting for himself.
Zhao Dun, styled Xuānzǐ, was the Chancellor of Jìn Línggōng. He was a man of loyalty and integrity, yet his Lord Línggōng was unrighteous and lacked virtue.

Tao Dun was able to admonish and transform him, yet he repeatedly offered remonstrances that were not accepted. Furthermore, the Duke had a fondness for meat and a habit of eating it. He dispatched his kitchen steward to prepare it;
when it was past the proper time and still not cooked, the Duke’s anger flared up, and he struck the man to death with a copper staff, carrying him out on a cart and covering him with vegetables.

On the road, he encountered Tao Dun, who thought to himself, "These are coarse vegetables; they should only be brought in from the outside. How could they have come out from within? [He realized the truth of the matter.]
He then looked back and questioned him. Upon examining beneath the vegetables, he saw a corpse. He sent someone to recount the previous events in detail.
Jizhi Dun subsequently entered the court and reprimanded him, saying, "Eating is a minor matter; how could you go so far as to kill a person?

The official was ashamed and enraged, and that night he ordered the assassin Chumi (the *Zuǒzhuan* states that *Chú* is his nature and *Mí* is his name; the modern readings *Ní* or *Ní* are incorrect) to enter Dun’s residence.
Having arrived at the residence, he saw Xun, who was dressed in full ceremonial robes and cap, gazing at the stars and the moon; he had been awake since dawn and had not slept day or night.
This was a loyal minister. He thought to himself: "If I do not obey the king's command, I shall be disloyal.

Yet, if I were to execute an innocent man unjustly, that would be unkind. To be neither a loyal subject nor a benevolent person would result in a twofold failure. Thereupon, he struck a catalpa tree and died.

Regarding this, some based on the *Jiashi* (家史) claim he touched a locust tree; others say he ended his life by cutting his own throat. I fear these are not correct. His younger brother Zhao Chuan said to him:
"Now, apart from what is recorded here, it is said that bhikṣus have become licentious and negligent, defying and opposing the Buddha’s precepts, thereby losing their seeds of goodness.
This is something they have done themselves and must suffer for themselves; it does not involve others, yet it brings upon them the guilt of the six classes of offenses."
The *pārājika* offenses down to the *duṣkṛta* are the causes. Entering the hells of the two spheres of existence (*āyatana*) is the experiencing of the fruit.
What is called "hell" refers to the hell realms (*naraka*). This is the general abode for those who have committed offenses.

In the Xia dynasty it was called Xiatai; in the Yin (Pan) period it was named Youli; during the Zhou era it was called Lingyu, also known as Huangsha. In the older Buddhist scriptures it is called *niraya*. This—
It is called "placeless" (an-avasthāna) because sentient beings born there have no place to go and no place of refuge.
In the new [translation], it is called *naraka*; here it means "vessel of suffering. If one says *nāraka*, it means "one who undergoes suffering," which refers generally to sentient beings.
Next, the specific enumeration: this refers to the sixteen hells formed by the eight hot and eight cold hells.

Speaking according to their primary roots, within each of the eight hot hells there are sixteen minor hells that serve as their retinues. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Twenty thousand [yojanas] below this is the Avīci hell, equal in depth and breadth;
above it are the seven other *naraka*s, and all eight [sets of] secondary hells (*utsada*) consist of sixteen each. These are known as the Pit of Hot Ashes (*Kukūla*), and so forth.
Excrement and filth; blades of weapons arranged in rows at the *āpaya* (hells of swords); each situated at those four gates (these are the eight hot hells).

As for the other eight cold hells, regarding the phrase "beneath this," two thousand *yojanas* below the ground of this Southern Continent (*Jambudvīpa*), there is a hell called *Avīci* in Sanskrit, which means "Without Interval.
It is twenty thousand *yojana*s in both depth and breadth. Above it, [at a distance of] twenty thousand...
Within this *yojana*, there are seven other hells: from Saṃjīva (Reviving) up to Pratāpana (Extreme Heat).
While the treatises describe these from bottom to top, here they are described from top to bottom. First, five hundred *yojanas* below this ground is the surface of the earth;
next, five hundred *yojanas* down is the palace of King Yama. Ten thousand nine hundred *yojanas* further down are situated the remaining seven hells. One source states:
They exist in layers, or, as another says, they dwell side by side (and so forth). First is the Reviving Hell (*saṃjīva*):

it is said that because of the power of the evil karma of those sentient beings, various instruments of suffering arise there; once these have appeared, they harm one another until they faint, which is figuratively called "death.
Then, when a cool breeze briefly blows upon them, they immediately revive and return to life just as before; thus it is called "reviving."
It is named Saṃjīva (Reviving). Another explanation is that there is a voice crying out from the air, "Saṃjīva!
Because of this sound, sentient beings desire to revive; thus, after dying, they are born again. Only when their karma is exhausted do they emerge.

For these reasons, it is named Saṃjīva (some say it is so called because the mountain-demons trample the ground and cry out "Live!"). Second is Kālasūtra (Black Rope), which refers to those sentient beings whom the hell-wardens lead away.
Black cords are stretched across them; they are divided into four, five, or eight parts, or variously marked with drawings.

According to where these lines are drawn, the ground is either dug, scrubbed, or cut. For this reason, it is called the Black Cord Hell (some say that when sentient beings were previously oppressed by suffering, veins emerged from their bodies like cords).
Third is the Hell of Crushing: it refers to those sentient beings being driven by the hell-wardens into between two iron mountains.
In that place, two mountains press together from both sides. Furthermore, the multitude collectively joins forces to crush them with iron troughs.

For these reasons, it is named Saṃghāta (Crushing). Fourth is Raurava (Howling): oppressed by manifold sufferings, various beings wail piteously; as they give vent to cries of resentment, it is named Raurava.
The Great Crying (Mahāraurava) hell: Tormented by extreme suffering, the beings there utter loud, piteous cries of lamentation and resentment; hence it is called "Great Crying.

The Sixth is the Heat (Tapana) hell: This refers to sentient beings whom the hell-wardens place upon a floor of hot iron and roast over a blazing fire on their right side, while also skewering them with iron rods so that flames erupt from every pore; for these reasons, it is called "Heat."
Seventh is the Extremely Hot (Pratāpana) Hell. Whether internally or externally, within one’s own body or that of others, fierce fires break forth and they burn and harm one another;

because this is far more intense than the preceding [hells], it is called "Extremely Hot. Eighth is the Uninterrupted (Avīci) Hell. This refers to the uninterrupted succession of the fruit, the matter, and the time within the body, or the absence of any interval of pleasure amidst the suffering, and so forth.
Next are the Peripheral Hells (*utsada*). The first is the Pit of Hot Ashes (*Kukūla-utsada*); that is, within this peripheral region, there is hot ash.
It reaches up to the knees. When sentient beings wander there, as soon as they set foot down, their skin, flesh, and bones are all scorched and fall away;
when they lift their feet, these regenerate. Second is the Increase of Excrement and Filth (*Gūthodaka*). This means that within this increase, the ground is filled with mud of excrement and filth.
Within it dwell many *narkakṣa* worms, over a foot long, with needle-sharp beaks, white bodies, and black heads. When sentient beings wander there, they are all...
These insects bore into their skin and break their bones, devouring their marrow on all sides. Regarding the "Increase of the Three Blades," there are three parts within it:

First, the Great Road of Blade-Edges (*kṣuradhāramārga*). Sentient beings wander upon it; as soon as they set foot down, their skin, flesh, and blood are all sliced into fragments and fall away, yet as soon as they lift their feet, these grow back again.
Second, the Forest of Sword-Leaves (*asipattravana*). Its upper surface is composed entirely of sharp, keen sword-blades.
Leaves. When sentient beings wander there, the wind blows and the leaves fall, severing their limbs and bodies until their flesh and bones are scattered.
There are variegated crows and dogs that tear them apart and devour them. Third is the Forest of Iron Thorns; this forest has sharp iron thorns sixteen finger-widths long.
When sentient beings climb up or down the trees, these thorns pierce them as sharply as needles. There are also iron-beaked birds that peck at them.

They peck out the eyes, hearts, and livers of the sinners and devour them in competition (*The Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Although the three types, such as the Path of Sword-Blades, differ, they are all made of iron;

therefore, they are subsumed under a single *ūṣmaghāta*. One should know this). Fourth is the River *Ūṣmaghāta* (the River of Heat), which refers to this *ūṣmaghāta* being filled with hot, salty water into which sentient beings enter.
Sometimes floating and sometimes sinking; sometimes moving against the current and sometimes with it; being steamed and boiled until their flesh and bones are disintegrated.
Even if they wish to escape, there are wardens upon the southern bank holding swords and spears, who block them and force them back, leaving no way to get out.

(The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "This [Avīci] is the first of the three [hot hells], like four [layers of] iron walls; its four faces are likewise. It asks: What is meant by "increasing" (*utsada*)? It answers, as the *Abhidharmakośa* says: These are the increasing [sufferings].)

Because their bodies are further afflicted by harm, they are called "increased" (*utsada*). Another interpretation is that because sentient beings emerge from the fundamental hells and encounter this suffering again, they are called "increased.
There are four gates for each, with sixteen sub-hells at each gate; thus, the eight [peripheral] hells together comprise one hundred twenty-eight.
Together with the eight primary hot hells, they total one hundred thirty-six, all of which are termed the Hot Hells. Next...
The eight cold hells are: first, Arbuda, which means "blister"; because the body is afflicted by the freezing wind, blisters arise.
Second, Nirarbuda, which means "blistered rows. Third, Aṭaṭa. Fourth, Hahava. Fifth, Huhuva.
Sixth, Utpala, which means "blue lotus. Seventh, Padma, which means "red lotus. Eighth, Mahāpadma.
*Ma*. This translates as "Great Red Lotus. Of these, the first two are named according to their location; the middle three are designated based on sound;
and the final three are distinguished by color. All of them are cold hells. These eight hells are situated at the four corners of the royal palace of the preceding eight [hot hells].
According to the Mahāyāna *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, each of the seven hells above the eight hot hells is ten thousand [yojanas] deep.
[This makes seventy thousand. The eighth, the Avīci Hell, is forty-two thousand [yojanas] deep [adding this to the previous total makes one hundred twelve thousand].

The distance between each of the eight hells is two thousand [yojanas] (thus making sixteen thousand). Calculating from the bottom of the Avīci Hell, it is one hundred twenty-eight thousand yojanas away, as extensively described in the treatises.
Outside of these, there are further solitary hells (*pratyeka-naraka*), which are caused by individual karma; they may be many, or two, or...
1. The distinctions of their locations are manifold and indeterminate. They may be near rivers, mountains, or wildernesses; or they may be beneath the earth, in the air, or in other places.

Such is the arrangement of the receptacles of the various hells: their primary location is below, though their distribution is not fixed. As for the dwelling places of animals (*tiryag-yoni*), these are water, land, and air;
their primary location is the great ocean, though they later gradually spread to other places. Regarding the various hungry ghosts (*preta*)... [their primary location is...]
[They dwell] in the realm of King Yama. From there, they wander on and reside scattered in other places. Some possess upright features yet emit a foul odor;

others possess great majesty and enjoy various riches and pleasures like the god Īśvara. Others are famished and their countenances are hideous. Such categories as these are explained at length in the sūtras.
Question: Are the various hell-wardens sentient beings? Answer: There are two interpretations. One school says they are not.

If that is so, how can it produce movement? The answer is: because it is brought about by the karmic power of sentient beings (*sattva*). It is like the winds at the beginning of the eon (*vivartakalpa*);
although the winds are not sentient, they are nonetheless capable of forming the eon. According to another interpretation, they are sentient. Thus, the verse says:
With a mind constantly filled with the poison of anger, delighting in the accumulation of all evil karma, he rejoices at the suffering of others;
upon death, he becomes a henchman of Yama.
(According to this verse, is he not a non-sentient being? If so, for what reason is he not burned by fire? Answer: This is certainly due to the intervention and obstruction of the power of karma.
Therefore, it may be that they can evoke distinct primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and thus they are not burned (and so forth). Question: What is the lifespan in the eight fundamental hells?
Answer: The *Abhidharmakośa* states: For the sixteen hells, beginning with Saṃjīva, one day and night corresponds respectively to the lifespans of the six heavens of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Their lifespans are likewise equal to those [heavens]. Now, first we shall calculate the celestial realms based on the human realm, and subsequently, based on the celestial realms...
Calculating the lifespan in the hells, the verse says:
Fifty years among humans Is one day and night in the lowest heaven; Based on this, their lifespan is five hundred [years], And for each of the five higher heavens, it doubles successively.
Fifty years among human beings constitute one day and night in the palace of the Four Great Kings. Thirty such days make a month, and twelve months make a year.
Their full lifespan is five hundred such years, which constitutes one day and night in the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell.
In this hell as well, thirty days make a month and twelve months make a year; their full lifespan is likewise five hundred years.
One hundred years in the human realm constitutes one day and night in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. There too, thirty such days make a month, and twelve such months make a year;
their full lifespan is one thousand such years. This constitutes one day and night in the Kālasūtra Hell.
There too, thirty such days make a month, and twelve such months make a year; their full lifespan is likewise one thousand such years. Two hundred [human years]...
One year [of the human realm] constitutes one day and night in the Yāma Heaven palace. There too, thirty such days make a month, and twelve months make a year.
A full lifespan there is two thousand years, which constitutes one day and night in the Saṃghāta Hell. There too, thirty such days make a month, and twelve months make a year.
A full lifespan there is two thousand years. Four hundred years of the human realm [constitute one day and night in the Yāma Heaven].
One day and night of the Śuddhāvāsa devas is equal to that [period]. They also have thirty such days in a month and twelve months in a year.
Their full lifespan is four thousand years. This constitutes one day and night in the Raurava hell. They also have thirty such days in a month and twelve months in a year.
Their full lifespan is four thousand years. Eight hundred human years constitute one day and night in the Nirmāṇarati heaven.
One day and night of the Nirmāṇarati devas is equal to thirty such days making a month, and twelve such months making a year;
their full lifespan is eight thousand years. This constitutes one day and night in the Mahāraurava hell, where thirty such days make a month and twelve such months make a year;
their full lifespan is likewise eight thousand years. By human reckoning, this is equivalent to sixteen hundred years.
One day and night of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods is equal to thirty such days making a month, and twelve such months making a year;
their full lifespan is sixteen thousand years. This constitutes one day and night in the Tapana (Great Heat) Hell.
There too, thirty such days make a month, and twelve such months make a year; their full lifespan is likewise sixteen thousand years. Seven... [kalpas].

The lifespan in the hot hells is half an *kalpa*. Regarding the eight uninterrupted (*avīci*) hells, it is said that their lifespan is one intermediate *kalpa* (*antarakalpa*); both the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* agree on this.

Next, the eight cold hells are distinguished. The verse states: "Suppose there were a *vaha* of sesame seeds; if one seed were removed every hundred years until they were all exhausted, each subsequent [cold hell] would be twenty times longer.
Here, *vaha* is a Sanskrit term; one explanation says it refers to a vessel capable of holding twenty *shi* (石). Suppose it were filled with sesame seeds.
Suppose there were someone who, once every hundred years, removed a single sesame seed from a vessel until all the seeds were exhausted;
this duration constitutes the life span in the first Cold Hell (*Arbuda*). Thereafter, the seven [subsequent] hells increase by multiples of twenty vessels:

the second Cold Hell is twenty vessels, the third is forty vessels, the fourth is sixty vessels, the fifth is eighty vessels, the sixth is one hundred vessels, and the seventh is one hundred [vessels].
Twenty ships; the eighth [set] consists of four hundred and forty ships. In each case, one grain is removed every hundred years (and so forth).
Furthermore, there is the Mahāyāna interpretation, as he himself has described it. Regarding the five categories clarifying transgressions (*āpatti*), this refers to those laws concerning offenses.

As for "transgressing while maintaining the practice naturally accomplishes [the precepts]," transgressing here means not committing evil; therefore, the two types of observance (*saṃvara*) are spontaneously accomplished. This is based on the *Upāli-śāstra*.

The "five characters" refers to this. Regarding "the seven aggregates manifesting observance": "manifesting" means making clear. This refers to clarifying the observance of conduct and its compliance;
as for "all transgressions being darkly excluded," compliance with observance means strictly guarding the precepts, whereby all offenses are darkly and utterly not permitted.
This is based on the increased version of the seven characters.

"Coming from afar" refers to those who have newly arrived as respondents; that is, those who have just begun to enter the Dharma. "For the most part foolish and coarse": "for the most part" (率) means collectively (it does not mean to follow or encourage).

"Foolish" (愚) means being deluded and failing to understand the teachings. "Coarse" (魯) means dull-witted. "Not yet knowing the regulations and precedents" refers to not yet understanding the regulations and precedents of the five categories (pañca-nikāya) and seven groups (sapta-saṃghāvaśeṣa);
how then could they distinguish between the two types of upholding and the two types of transgressing? Thus it is called "the constitution" (憲).

"Chapter. The *Erya* states: "Constitution" (*xianfa*) means law; "chapter" (*zhang*) means a section. "Wandering like one confused by mist while following the precepts" refers to being dim-sighted and lacking clarity regarding each individual precept—whether it be a *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *sthūlātyaya*, or *pāyattika*—just as a person wandering through mist cannot distinguish anything.

Their transgressions and retributions are analogous to this. As for "one who gazes at the ocean," because they do not recognize its characteristics, they do not know the gravity of the offenses they have committed; this is likewise [analogous].
It is like a person observing the ocean who cannot fathom its boundaries. This causes those who follow the current far away to do so;
it is truly because they have lacked knowledge and failed to comprehend the teachings up until now that they commit various unrighteous acts and follow the stream of birth and death.

Because they do not sink into the wheel [of saṃsāra], it is said they "go far away. "Going" (*śì*) means to depart. Regarding "greedily craving drops of honey while forgetting the way back," Master [Dao]xuan cites: [The Master] says: The Great Master (the Buddha) cited...
The Parable of the Pit: Suppose a person has committed an offense against another, who then orders his guards to hand that offender over to a fierce, intoxicated elephant.
The elephant pursues the offender, who flees in terror. He encounters a dry well and leaps into it with several bounds. The man follows suit and leaps into the well.
At the bottom of the well are three dragons, and on its four sides are four snakes; they all look up toward the top of the well in a frenzy.

The elephant has already approached. Furthermore, there are two mice, one black and one white, gnawing at the vine. Next, he sees a wandering bee dripping residual honey, which he catches with his mouth;
for a brief moment, all his fears subside. (The above is the parable; the following is the application. His body is like a dried-up well, pressed by old age until it reaches death.

The elephant symbolizes impermanence (*anitya*); the vine symbolizes the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); the three dragons represent the three poisons (*triviṣa*); and the four snakes [represent the four great elements].
These are the four signs [of decay]. The two mice represent the sun and moon; the drops of honey are a metaphor for the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).

One who merely craves the five desires and fears not the three poisons (*triviṣa*) will find the four signs gradually advancing and the sun and moon pressing on from behind, until the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is severed—this is to forget one's return home.

Having committed grave karma, one fails to repent for the transgressions; following that karma, one undergoes rebirth and falls downward into the three miserable realms (*tricātya*). How could such a person ever transcend the five desires?
Regarding the "object" (*viṣaya*): it refers to awakening to the principle of *nirvāṇa* and returning to the original source; hence, it is said that one "knows the reversal.
As for the *Vinayamātṛkā* and other texts, they mean that those who are foolish and indulge their passions will create offenses and undergo suffering in the future, not in the present.

This does not mean that the retribution appears immediately before one's eyes. The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "If a bhikṣu receives the faithful offerings of others but does not act in accordance with the Dharma, he will be [reprimanded] by the donor..."
"Fallen" means practicing the Way contrary to the Dharma and allowing the mind to become negligent; because of this, one shall fall into the three miserable realms to undergo retribution.
If one does not undergo it in the future, then in the present life, food will tear open one's belly and clothing will detach from one's body.

The phrase "it is thus, it is thus" precisely clarifies the intent of this chapter. Regarding "karma follows the mind in its formation," the *Śīlavarga* explains that there are eight kinds of minds through which karma—whether light or heavy—is formed. All such light and heavy karmas follow the mind;

that is to say, the mind is able to create karma, and whether one performs good or evil, neither departs from the mind. Therefore, the Vinaya states: "When an offense is committed, one immediately questions the mind. There is no...
"The mind does not transgress" refers specifically to the mind as the cause of karma. "Retribution follows the mind in its formation" means that the fruit is presented in recompense for the cause.
Based on the eight aforementioned types of light and heavy mental states, the gravity of the retribution received in the future is achieved in accordance with one's present mind.

The reason for first setting forth cause and effect is to establish the causal relationship between the two observances and the two transgressions; this is first introduced by citing the *Liao* [Sūtra].

The treatise explains the eight kinds of guarding the precepts, which are the causes and effects of upholding them. Below, it cites the *Maudgalyāyana-paripṛcchā-sūtra* and other texts to clarify the causes and effects of violating them.

Regarding the "extensive clarification of characteristics and names," this refers to the detailed explanation in the following text of the characteristics and designations of the five categories and seven groups (*pañca-āpatti-prakaraṇa-sapta-samghāvaśeṣa*).
As for "knowing the cause by observing the fruit," this means that one desires to lead practitioners to observe that by upholding the precepts, one attains fruits such as *nirvāṇa*.

Breaking the precepts results in the fruit of dwelling in hell for a duration determined by the length of the kalpas; this is because one knows there exist the two causes of good and evil, namely upholding and breaking [the precepts].

Regarding what is called "reaching the ultimate characteristics," it is as the text states. Regarding what is called "from the beginning to the retribution," the reason why the retribution for violating the precepts is so immense is that, as Xuan says, this section comes to resolve doubts.
He fears that people might doubt, asking: "For what reason is the offense of violating the precepts so extremely heavy?"

"And why not hold it lightly? This is explained by the phrase "protecting through the precepts" (*śīla-rakṣā*). This means that the precepts are the foundational basis for all wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*). As the text says:

"Relying upon and depending on these precepts, one can give rise to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), as well as the wisdom regarding suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-prajñā*), and so forth. Among all that gives birth to the wholesome, they are the foremost;
they are the dwelling place of all wholesome dharmas. Regarding the maintenance of merit, as stated in the Preface: "Abiding in and maintaining..."

Regarding the phrase "The Buddha-dharma: the various scriptures cease their discourse here," and so forth—it is for this reason that violating [the precepts] brings about retribution that is not slight.

As for the statement "From 'clearly understanding' up to the eight kinds" and "The many types of guarding the precepts": in the older sūtras and śāstras, these are called *rakṣā* (guarding); in the newer sūtras and śāstras, they are called *saṃvara* (restraint).
If one uses the term *rakṣā*, the *Mingdi shu* (Commentary on the Ultimate Truth) states there are four meanings: first, it can separate one from evil matters; second, ... [text continues].

It is able to guard the gates of the six sense faculties, preventing mental karma from arising. Thirdly, it is "guarding" because it causes one to leave the stage of ordinary beings and enter the stage of the noble ones.
For these many reasons, it is called "guarding" (*ārakṣā*). If one speaks of "restraint of the faculties" (*indriya-saṃvara*), [it refers to this].

The "faculties" (*indriya*) refer to the six faculties, beginning with the eye; "restraint" (*saṃvara*) refers to that which is able to guard these six faculties, and is thus called "faculty-restraint.

Regarding its designation as "guarding" (*ārakṣā*) when it pertains to the mind, the treatise states: "Abandoning evil of the mental level is called guarding. Regarding its designation as "precept" (*śīla*) when it pertains to body and speech, the treatise states:
"Abandoning evil of body and speech is called precept. The statement that "there may be guarding without necessarily being precept" is a citation of the fourfold formulation from the treatise.
First is protection that is not precept (*śīla*). This protection protects the mind so that various thoughts do not arise;

even when confronted with the five sensory objects, because the mind does not stir, there is as yet no need to guard body and speech. Therefore, it cannot be called a precept. Hence it is said: "There may be protection, but it is not necessarily a precept.
If body and speech do not commit various evils, this must be due to mindfulness, wisdom, and the mind of renunciation. Hence it is said: "Where there is a precept, there is necessarily protection."

Second, that which is morality but not protection: although one possesses the essence of having received the precepts, because one gives rise to improper reflection (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), there is no protective mind;

thus, even if body and speech do not move, one does not necessarily transgress the precepts. Third, that which is both morality and protection: this is because one must rely on mindfulness (*smṛti*) and other factors to enable [the precepts] to flow forth into body and speech to prevent what is non-virtuous.
Fourth, that which is neither morality nor protection: if one moves body and speech, one will necessarily give rise to improper reflection.
Therefore, among these four statements, the *Chao* (the Sub-commentary) cites the first and third. Regarding the phrase "in the sutras" and so forth:

in the commentary on the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*, it is indicated generally that various sutras contain these eight similes, all of which serve as metaphors for the person who attains the protection of the precepts.
Regarding the phrase "from one up to all evils": this means that these eight [examples] are all general illustrations using the metaphor of the eight dharmas.

The *Lun shu* (Commentary on the Treatise) states: "A king is able to exercise sovereign control over all his subjects; because he is born into the royal lineage and will certainly become a king in the future, he is revered by the people.
As for the application of the dharma (*dharmasaṃprayoga*): the king is a metaphor for the Great Sage, and the sons are a metaphor for the bhikṣus. From the Dharma...
Thus, he gave birth; hence the expression "giving birth to a son. The "people" metaphorically represent all sentient beings.
"Succeeding to the royal throne" metaphorically represents how the bhikṣus, by virtue of upholding the precepts, attain Buddhahood.

In the second analogy, through the five factors of the Dharma-body—precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—they are made complete. Regarding the third analogy, the treatise states: "As one wishes..."
The "Precious Jewel" (maṇi). It is also called the "Priceless Precious Jewel. This means that by possessing this jewel, all things required are obtained according to one's wishes.
As for the term "priceless," it means there is no person who sets a price for the jewel; rather, the jewel itself sets its own value.

If one wishes to purchase this jewel and places money or goods upon it, and the jewel passes through them, the price is still not equal to its worth. If the jewel does not... [pass through]... [the price is likewise insufficient].
He went out and departed with the jewel. Someone asked, "What is the substance of this jewel? He replied and explained: First, it is said that this jewel comes from camphor (*karpūra*).
If one possesses this jewel, poison cannot harm them, and fire or water cannot burn or sweep them away (this explanation is not seen in the scriptural texts).
