Next, regarding the sequence from beginning to end: in the case of sexual misconduct, the gravity is determined by the initial invasion of the boundary; for killing, it is based on the severance of life; for theft and false speech, it is based on the intermediate stage.

Although the property has been separated from another in theft, it has not yet been put to use; although the words of falsehood have been uttered, the benefit has not yet been obtained. This can be inferred accordingly. [The six teachings.]
Regarding their origin: the Buddha’s establishment of the precepts was fundamentally intended to cease unwholesome karma. This was because it was essential to remain free from the three poisons.
As the text states concerning the peacock-crowned brāhmaṇa, the Venerable Ānanda, and others (etc.). Seventh, the sequence of priority:
Some say that the precepts are established in opposition to the poisons. Since greed is primary, sexual misconduct is ranked first. As stated in the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya:
after attaining the Way of the Buddha, in the fifth year, during the winter season, in the fifth fortnight of the twelfth month, at midday when one and a half shadows remained.
The first precept was established because of Yaśas’s transgression (which corresponds to the seventh day of the tenth month in this land).

The second precept was established during the winter season of the sixth year, on the tenth day of the second fortnight after the midday meal, when one and a half shadow-lengths remained (which corresponds to the tenth day of the ninth month in this land).

The third precept was established at the same time, during the winter season of the sixth year, on the ninth day of the second fortnight before the midday meal, when one and a half shadow-lengths remained.
(That is, it corresponds to the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month in this land). The fourth precept:

On the thirteenth day of the fourth half-month of the winter season in the sixth year, after the meal, when three and a half shadow-lengths remain, the rule was established (that is, it corresponds to the thirteenth day of the tenth month in this land).
If one follows the sequence of offenses as prescribed above, the textual characteristics are very clear. (The analysis of these doctrinal points is hereby concluded).

The first is the precept against sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*). Regarding what is called the "precept against sexual misconduct," it means that each single precept is divided into four sections.

However, the ancient arrangements differ. According to Xuánzàng’s record (*Xuánjì*), the first section concerns the origin (*nidāna*); the second explains the name of the precept; and the third describes the intent behind its establishment.

As for clarifying the root text of the precept (*śīla-mūla*), one must wait for the commentary (*chāo-wén*) before the meaning can be categorized; otherwise, it would seem to contradict the text. Furthermore, the purpose of the commentary itself is for the sake of explanation.
Regarding the commentary on the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*: if it were placed at the end, it would be entirely inverted and fail to establish the ritual procedures.

Now, following the intention of the original compilation by the attendants in the capital, there are four sections: first, the explanation of the name; second, the origin (*nidāna*); third, the *Prātimokṣa* itself; and finally, the commentary on the sub-commentary (*śāstra*).

As for the intention behind the compilation, if the sub-commentary does not provide its own analysis by citing treatises, then the *Karmavācanā* and the *Śīlacitta* are cited; this is clarified in both commentaries.

I shall not elaborate further here for fear of being too prolix, as it can also be understood through four sections. First, regarding the principle of establishing the intention [to abstain], the *Chao* (Commentary) text itself clarifies this.
Second, concerning the explanation of the name: "Yin" (lust) means to be dissolute and unrestrained, or to be addicted and attached.

This refers to the sensory objects of form which cause the emotions to become dissolute and ruined, leading to defiled attachment from which one cannot separate; thus, it is called "yin. This is the object to be guarded against, while the "precept" (*śīla*) is the practice that serves as the remedy.
Both the agent and the object are mentioned together; thus it is said that the three conditions for the precept against sexual misconduct arise in four ways.

This, along with the root text of the precepts and the ten points of meaning, is explained in detail as set forth in the *Commentary on the Precepts* (*Jie zhujie*). Regarding the phrase "up to the middle," Xuán says: "The intent of the abridgment is to avoid prolixity;

however, the headings state that the sections extend below. For all the precepts, one should divide them according to the text; where the meaning is sufficient, they may be accepted and followed," and so forth. This provides a brief understanding of the observance and violation of the extensive [precepts].

As for the phrase "as in the latter section": this refers only to cases where one commits an offense regarding the *mātṛkā* (the disciplinary matrix) by violating both [precepts] simultaneously; thus it is said, "briefly known. To correctly present the meaning of the text:
if one explains the mental states of perception and doubt regarding the object, it is as explained in the "Holding and Violating" (*dhāraṇa-aticāra*) section below.

Regarding the phrase "other meanings are as in the *Śīla-vinaya-śāstra*": this indicates that the detailed text is to be found there. As for the phrase "from 'initially' to 'therefore'": this refers to the most extreme form of dread, namely, that which can plunder a person's merit.

"Good man, it is for this reason that it is called 'terrible. The *Zhi* [text] says: At the beginning of the kalpa there were no humans. Beings from the upper realms descended to eat *gao* (fat/essence).
Once the *gao* was exhausted, they next ate naturally grown non-glutinous rice. Their bodies gradually became coarse and heavy, and they could no longer fly. Then women were born.
The multitude cried out, 'An evil thing has been born here!'—referring to the woman. The nuns, however, say the opposite."

Thus it is said: "A man... [and so forth]. To "corrupt what is right and destroy virtue" means to sell off one's right mindfulness and right conduct, and to destroy one's own and shared virtues by making them like those of the laity.
That one's family is ruined and the state is destroyed from of old is just like this.

As for the statement that "lustful desire does not afflict sentient beings," while killing, stealing, and lying afflict the objects before one, lust involves acting in common with others; yet, it is claimed that doing so does not constitute affliction.
Furthermore, regarding "the mind being bound by mind": it is simply that this binds the human heart, causing such deep attachment that it is difficult to relinquish;

it further binds one to the commission of preceptual transgressions, and is therefore called a "great sin. Moreover, it is called "great" for three reasons: first, it can initiate karma; second, it can moisten rebirth; and third, it is black karma.
Regarding those who attain *nirvāṇa* in this very life, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Sexual desire is an obstacle to the Path."

Regarding the source [of this]: if one commits [an offense], the fruit of Nirvāṇa cannot be attained. The precepts for Śrāvakas are established primarily at the beginning. As for the statement "from four up to the *jāti* (birth/period)," the "three realms" (*tridhātu*) are mentioned.

Question: Since the objects of transgression (*āpatti-viṣaya*) are six, why are only three mentioned here? Answer: The two realms of humans and animals do not encompass their own respective categories [in this context].

Regarding the realm of non-humans (*amanuṣya-gati*), it includes celestial beings (*devaputra*). Although asuras, ghosts, spirits, and hell-beings (*nāraka*) are not explicitly mentioned, they are nonetheless included within the non-human realm.

This is also subsumed within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Because the spiritual functions of these four realms are identical, they are combined into one;

they do not constitute a separate realm of non-humans (*amanuṣya*). While the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* combines them with the gates [of the Vinaya] to form three realms, and the *Śāstra* opens them up into six destinies (*gati*), the latter is divided based on the presence of good and evil, whereas this Vinaya combines them based on their manifest activity. Both are explained by taking the three realms as the basis. Regarding the male retribution..."
Regarding women with two sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjanā*): they are divided into five types—women, female householders, young girls, those with two sexual organs, and eunuchs among humans.
It is the same for non-humans. Based on three types of females and two types of males, these constitute the objects of sexual misconduct that constitute an offense.
Among the fifteen aforementioned types of objects, there are also four states such as being asleep and so forth. As for "a hair’s breadth" (*vālāgra*), this refers to the measure of an offense.

Regarding the boundaries and characteristics [of offenses], even minor infractions constitute violations, let alone others. *Pārājika* refers to the name of the offense committed, as analyzed previously (*et cetera*).
In the Vinaya text itself, there are six hundred and twenty-four permutations concerning one’s own sphere and the sphere of another.

There are three thousand seven hundred and forty-four phrases regarding the pressure of resentment; in total, there are four thousand three hundred and sixty-eight phrases, all of which constitute offenses.
However, I have merely provided a rough estimate of the total number and have not engaged in a detailed enumeration. Do not ask those who harbor doubts or suspicions in their hearts.

In this Vinaya, regarding the precept against sexual misconduct, neither mistaken perception nor doubt is exempted. Provided it is the "right path," even if one forms the perception or doubt that it is not the right path, one commits a *pārājika* offense.
As for the boundaries of the offense, it is said: Upāli questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha replied: "If it passes through the path of excrement..."
It passes through the urinary tract; the joints, the mouth, and the teeth are all leveled, serving as the boundary.

As for the phrase "thus reaching the point of emission," this refers to the definitive conclusion of the offense, meaning it is the ultimate fruit of the transgression rather than a preliminary stage (*upāya*). Regarding those who feel "strange" or suspicious, this refers to those of the same path;

they harbor doubts because this was spoken by the Buddha. They say it is a mind of passionate attachment, which increases their resentment and gives rise to suspicion. The Buddha is the World-Honored One... [text ends].
"How can the Honored King speak such coarse and wicked words? (and so forth). "The Dharma Master" refers to the author of the treatise.
If the Buddha had not taught the precepts and so on, how could one know today that there is such a thing as a *pārājika* offense? Regarding "laughing and being driven away":

if one who expounds the Dharma uses a fan to shield their face, they must take care not to expose their teeth while laughing. If there is someone who laughs, [they should do so with their face covered].
"Drive them out! Why? Because the Buddha, out of compassion for sentient beings, has spoken with his golden mouth.
You all should give rise to a sense of shame and remorse and listen attentively. Why do you laugh? It is for this reason that they are being driven out."

Regarding the phrase "next, the characteristics of the offense": "next" refers to the sequence; "accomplishment" refers to the completion [of the act]. "Offense" (*āpatti*) refers to that which is transgressed; "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the specific features [of the act].

It is because one does not yet know how many conditions each—such as acting on one's own initiative toward another, or being coerced by an enemy—must possess for the offense to be established as a formal characteristic, that this is explained next.

Regarding the phrase "there are two conditions": first is acting on one's own initiative toward another; second is the condition of being coerced by an enemy. Regarding the phrase "first, to the offense": [this indicates the first condition].

"Those who have lustful minds of their own" means to exclude those who have been coerced by an enemy; it refers to one's own body. "With an internal barrier" means to prevent others from defiling [the body].

Therefore, fearing that others might [violate the precept], one says, "I am currently protected by a barrier; there should be no offense. This is why it is said. The full conditions are as stated in the *Śāstra* (etc.). Regarding the deficiency of conditions:
for the first condition, if one perceives it as a non-path or has doubt, one incurs two *sthūlātyaya* offenses. If the second or third [conditions] are deficient...

There is no offense when two conditions are absent. When the fourth condition is lacking, there are two types of *sthūlātyaya* (grave offenses): one for the distant preparatory stage and one for the proximate preparatory stage; these are the two *sthūlātyaya*s of the preliminary effort (*prayoga*). Regarding the phrase "reaching the boundary":

this refers either to bringing [the object] to another's territory, which constitutes creating an offense against another's domain, or to approaching one's own body, which constitutes creating an offense against one's own domain.

The note states, "without distinguishing between self and other," which refers to the pervasiveness of the aforementioned two cases. As for "bringing it oneself": [The text continues: ...or taking it oneself. The note says, "whether by oneself or by another" refers to the two preceding cases being universal. As for "taking it oneself":... [text ends]

One brings the correct object (*samyag-viṣaya*) into another’s right path; another brings the correct object into one’s own right path. Regarding the deficiency of conditions, it is to be understood through analogy as previously explained.
The passage from "In the *Sudarsana*" onwards clarifies the characteristic of non-attachment. As for the phrase "from 'Question' to 'no opening,'" this means not engaging in idle chatter.
Regarding "a child playing with his genitals in his mouth," the Vinaya text states: there was a bhikṣu begging for alms who saw a child...

[Regarding] the male organ (*mūla*): [If one] raises it and inserts it into one's own mouth, [one commits a *pārājika* offense]. [If one] inserts it into another’s mouth, the *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "At that time, there was a bhikṣu who inserted his male organ into the mouth of another bhikṣu. Later, both gave rise to doubt. The Buddha said: 'If it was done in jest, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.'"* *Iyer: *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). it does not depend on the object itself. This should be understood. (The above discussion regarding the theft of Dharma objects is hereby concluded.)

Next, regarding the theft of property belonging to the Saṃgha, the following section concerns the most serious cases of theft. This passage is intended to refute the interpretation of the ancient masters (*pūrvācāryas*). According to the judgment of the ancient masters:

with respect to the monks of the ten directions, there is no principle of a "full five" [karṣāpaṇas] for which one would incur a light offense; however, if there is a guardian, then with respect to that guardian, the offense is grave. The present master does not hold this view.

If there is a guardian, the offense is determined as grave with respect to that guardian, just as it would be if the guardian themselves committed the theft. This is to be understood according to the *Śīlaparivarta* (or *Kuśalamūla-samparigraha*).
Regarding the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Views): When an administrator takes monastic property for the dual purposes of the Buddha and the Dharma, the Buddha declared this a *pārājika* offense.
This is because the Sangha of the ten directions is collectively regarded as one; thus, it constitutes the full five-fold grave offense (*pañca-guru-dharma*).

As for the statement that there are four kinds of Sangha, the Master [Zhiyi] now explains the five kinds of permanent property (*zhangchang*). The four names are listed in detail below (*et cetera*). Dongta Zhi did not permit the Southern [tradition].
Shanli established four categories. He refuted [the previous view] by saying: "One should forcibly combine the stages into two:

first, the 'permanently abiding for the ten directions' (śāśvata-sarvadik), and second, the 'presently abiding for the ten directions' (pratyutpanna-sarvadik). One does not need the pair of 'permanently abiding permanently abiding' and 'presently abiding presently abiding.
Fabao countered his refutation, saying: "If one must divide them into only two, then what about the various implements, fields, and gardens [of the Sangha]?"

[Items such as these] should be shared equally with the Sangha of the ten directions according to what they deserve to receive. Now, it is said that this property belongs exclusively to this specific realm.

Second, even if the Sangha from all the great lands of the ten directions were to assemble together, they still could not divide it; it is termed "permanently established permanent" (*sthāvara-sthāvara*). If this category were not established, under what classification would it be subsumed?

Furthermore, regarding the division of "present" (*pratyutpanna*) and "present permanently established" (*pratyutpanna-sthāvara*) property back into the "ten directions present" category: [this is incorrect].
Furthermore, suppose there is someone who gives an object directly to the *saṃgha* present in this realm. May it now be divided among the *saṃghas* of the ten directions?
We say that since this object has arrived in person, the object is present; however, the number of people is limited, and thus these people are present.
If one were to distribute this object to the Sangha of the ten directions, considering those currently present, whether it should be obtained or not, what offense would one incur?
To pass judgment in such a manner is a profound case of dark reliance [on ignorance]. The commentaries on the *Xitā* (Western Pagoda) all reach this point and do not permit further measurement;

they merely state that "this is a teaching according to capacity" and so forth. Now, the Master specifically establishes four names to encompass [these cases], which alone constitute [the correct standard].

This concludes the principle. Regarding the initial statement "up to 'permanently fixed' (*sthāvara*)," that which is "permanently fixed" refers to an entity restricted to its own location and not extending to other realms;
therefore, it is called "permanently fixed. Furthermore, because it is permitted only for communal enjoyment and not for sale or division, it is also termed "permanently fixed.
Thus, it is said. As for the mention of "flowers and fruits," they must be distinguished. The Venerable Master said: "If it is a fully ripened fruit..."

Regarding "picking and plucking": ten *shí* or fifteen *shí*. This belongs to the perpetual property of the ten directions; because the substance of the object pervades the ten directions, it cannot be divided.
As for the flowers and fruits mentioned here that are not to be divided, this refers to the period before they have been taken from the tree;
one may not take ten or five trees and divide them into one's own possession. In the commentary, the discussion concerns the measurement of rice and flour.

...and so forth. These are added within the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts). For example, if there are one hundred *shí* of rice and fifty *shí* of flour in the storehouse, these belong to the "perpetual property of the Sangha" (*changzhu changchu*).
If they are made into cooked rice, cakes, and the like, they then enter the category of "perpetual property for the ten directions" (*shifang changzhu*).

Salt, sauce, vinegar, and so forth, which remain in the storehouse, are collected under this specific heading. Regarding those items placed on the offering table on a given day, these belong to the "perpetual property for the ten directions."

This is categorized according to the commentary; it is certainly not a mere speculative claim. This is because it is stated that the "permanently abiding [property] of the ten directions" is distinguished from within the "permanently abiding permanently abiding [property].

Alternatively, there are those who do not permit this, asserting that fruits on trees, grains, rice, flour, salt, vinegar, and so forth, are subsumed under the "permanently abiding permanently abiding [property]" and are collectively judged to be included within the "permanently abiding [property] of the ten directions. Such people then provide a false interpretation, saying: "Fruits..."
Rice, grain, flour, and other edible items must necessarily be shared, for these substances pervade the ten directions and thus belong to the permanent endowment (*sādhāraṇa*) of the ten directions.
Now, an objection is raised: for instance, when rice in a field has not yet been harvested, the Vinaya states that it is the "permanent endowment of the permanent endowment" (*sādhāraṇa-sādhāraṇa*).
This rice and grain should likewise be used as food to provide for the Sangha; since its substance pervades the ten directions, [it should be shared].

What difference is there between this and giving tree fruits, grains, rice, or flour? Furthermore, this same intent is present in the current master’s *Qingzhong yi* (Ritual of Light and Heavy Matters).

It states: "If one intends to offer raw rice and the like as permanent offerings for the ten directions, as soon as the bell sounds, one may bring basins and bowls to request the rice and flour; these may then be distributed," and so forth, as detailed therein. In sum:

Regarding the reference to the Saṃgha: as for the determination of gravity according to the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*, if one habitually steals from oneself, then with respect to the Saṃgha of the ten directions, one incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) as a single master.
If another person steals, the offense is incurred with respect to the protector of that property. This is as stated in the passage on determining gravity in the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

Furthermore, the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is cited as evidence; previously, it was explained generally that with respect to the entire Saṃgha, it constitutes a single unified sense—even if they were all assembled together.

"It shall not be divided. Regarding the statement "the two [cases] constitute a *sthūlātyaya*": that which belongs to the permanent endowment (*sādhāraṇa*) of the ten directions has its substance pervading the Dharma-realm and is for the use of the Saṃgha;
therefore, it is designated by the name "ten directions. Furthermore, within the delimited boundaries (*sīmā*), it is again called "permanent endowment" (*nitya*).

Since it is permitted to divide and consume this, it is mentioned alone. Regarding the food constantly provided by the monastic community for the monks, the *Śīla-śāstra* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Such as cakes, rice, and so forth, currently..."

"Thoroughly cooked food" refers to the substance. "Its essence pervades the ten directions" explains the two characters for "upper" and "lower" directions. "It is restricted solely to its original location" interprets the two characters for "permanently abiding" (śāśvata).
Regarding the gravity of the offense, it is said that if one steals this cooked food belonging to another person, it constitutes a grave transgression.

Regarding the expectation of protection by others: if five conditions are fulfilled, it constitutes a grave offense (duṣkṛta) for theft committed in common. As for those who should incur a light offense, Xuan states:

"This follows the interpretation of the ancient masters. The ancients said that regardless of whether the food was raw or cooked, one who steals any utensil for eating incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

Regarding the Sangha of the ten directions, there are five reasons why it does not constitute a "fulfillment" (pūrṇa). Therefore, it is now stated that for items such as raw food, the Buddha did not permit their distribution;

rather, they universally take the Sangha of the ten directions as their primary recipients, which is why this is established as a grave offense. However, if one distributes cooked food after striking the bell, it is permissible.
In that case, there is no offense of theft. If a community of monks does not ring the bell before eating, it is termed "collective theft and damage.

Since it is permitted to share the food, one does not expect it for oneself alone; rather, everyone has a share of the food. Regarding the criteria for theft, because the value does not reach five *māṣakas*, the offense is minor when considered in relation to the Sangha, as the property of the Sangha does not reach the full value of five.
Below, the text from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is cited regarding "the surplus food of the Sangha," etc.; Xuanzang says: "The Sangha..."
If food is in excess, it is beyond one's personal share and ought to be returned to the Saṃgha. Since it is not now returned, how can this not be considered theft?
It is said that if food is in excess, it belongs to the ten directions; this corroborates the previous point regarding common theft and damage, for which one should incur a light offense.

This is because, in relation to the Saṃgha, the amount does not reach five [units]. The above is the correct interpretation. Alternatively, according to the *Huainan ji*, it is considered *cangzhu* (permanent property).
Regarding the practice of stretching out food [to others]: if one obtains food on the following day, the administrator (karmadāna) commits a *thullaccaya* offense by stealing it for himself.

However, if he takes it back [after realizing his error], there is no offense; this is an incorrect interpretation. As for the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* and other texts, these refer specifically to the administrator.

Taking monastic property for personal use, as if it were one's own property and giving it away to others: according to the commentary, this is equivalent to stealing monastic food together with others;

that is to say, one incurs the offense of *thullaccaya* (grave offense) based on the first half of the verse. Based on the intent of the treatise (*śāstra*), it is proven that since the damage is shared equally in the act of theft, the penalty should be light.
Regarding the statement, "If one takes [something] with a thieving mind, this is called the fifth great thief," the eleventh fascicle of the *Śāstra* says:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "There are five kinds of great thieves in the world. What are the five? First, if a bhikṣu commits an offense of the five categories of transgressions..."
First, receiving offerings and sustenance while failing to cultivate the practice of the Path;
second, hearing the Dharma from another wise person, yet when asked by others from whom one heard it, replying that one understood it oneself, thereby obtaining offerings and the like;

third, being an ārya who has attained one of the four fruits, or being an ordinary person who observes the precepts, yet harboring malice toward others and proclaiming one’s own name [to claim superiority], which constitutes slandering the noble ones; fourth, taking the Saṃgha...
Regarding garden bamboo and trees, or any other heavy items, if one offers them to a layperson with a mind of fear or expectation, this constitutes an offense.

Fifth, taking monastic property as if it were one’s own; if one uses it or gives it away, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (light offense). The commentary states that this is analogous to property belonging to others;

that is, if one steals cooked food, both acts together constitute a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). The treatise states that the offense is determined according to the value of the object; in most cases, this reaches the threshold of five *māsaka* coins.

The gravity of the offense depends on the value; if it is small, the offense is light. This statement should serve as evidence that there is a guardian or owner, and the transgression is incurred in relation to that owner.
"The *Vinayamātṛkā* is also like this" means it is identical to the passage from the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* cited above.

Regarding "the *Sarvāstivāda* and other schools," if such a text exists in those two treatises, the interlinear note should be understood accordingly. "As with the *sthūlātyaya* mentioned above" refers to the preceding text, which states that one mistakenly considers the Saṃgha to be oneself.

Regarding the citation of the *Vinayavibhaṅga*: since it states that theft constitutes an offense according to the value of the object, one would have committed a grave offense (*pārājika*) based on the aforementioned *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.
However, because [the objects] such as empty space are seen to be without anyone to guard them, the commentary notes that it is only a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
Regarding the statement "the third [offense] arises from the completion of the act": this refers to three conditions. First, the object is present before one, such as an offering or the like.

Second, the person is present before one, meaning that when an object is offered to the *saṃgha* present before one, it belongs to that very *saṃgha*; therefore, it is stated twice. If one steals this object, the offense is grave;

this is because even though the donor has relinquished ownership, the object has not yet been formally transferred to the *saṃgha*, and thus the thief is still held accountable with respect to the original owner.

This refers to gravity. If many people share an object equally, this is determined based on the act of taking after it has been entrusted; furthermore, the offense is judged in relation to the original recipient-monk.
If it has not yet been distributed, and is merely entrusted to one person for custody and record-keeping, the thief is also judged in relation to this custodian.

Regarding the phrase "the fourth [offense] constitutes a sin," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Since these items belong collectively to the Sangha and all may obtain them, it is called 'ten'."

It is now employed as the function of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Regarding those who gather according to their manifestation, all possess their respective portions; hence it is said, "manifesting before one, manifesting before one.

As for the light belongings of a deceased person, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "For example, when the Sangha receives offerings, as well as the belongings of the five groups [of practitioners] upon their death..."

Its substance belongs to the ten directions. Regarding texts such as the *Sūtra on the Good Birth* (*Śraddhājanana-sūtra*), these refer to the period before the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has been performed.

As for the note stating that if one calculates five people but they do not actually total five, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense: this is based on the Buddha’s words. It means that all items for which the *karmavācanā* has not yet been performed belong to the ten directions;

thus, regarding theft, one must look to the ten directions to reach the full amount. Since there is no sense of "totaling five" when looking toward the ten directions, one incurs the *sthūlātyaya* offense immediately. Furthermore...
Regarding the phrase "there is that which is unjust and not properly arranged," if it has already been *karmavācanā* (formal ritual action) and so forth, the commentary explains this [at length].
As for "the offense is incurred in relation to the person to whom it was given": this refers to a case where one says, "Entrust this object to such-and-such a person.

Here, the deceased person is the giver (*dātṛ*), and that person is the recipient (*pratigrahītṛ*). The thief incurs the offense in relation to that recipient. Regarding the phrase "from four up to Chen," this refers to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
The *Śayanāsana-vastu* (Chapter on Lodgings) states: At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the human realm with five hundred disciples and arrived at the kingdom of Kollāga.
There was a monastery there where several bhikṣus were residing: first, Aśvajit; second, Kālodāyin;
third, Aśvaśīrṣa; and fourth, Pūrṇaśīrṣa. When they heard it said that the Buddha, along with Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, had come to this place, they consequently gave rise to [a thought].
The monks said, "The Buddha is the dragon among dragons, and his disciples are likewise men of virtuous reputation.
If he remains here for long, we shall surely lose our fame and profit. They then selected one of the finest upper rooms and left it for the Buddha, while dividing the remainder into four parts.
Thus, they made the monastery grounds into one portion and gave them to the first bhikṣu, along with the jars, basins, and other articles.
[He] divided [the items] into two parts. He gave the two wooden beds and so forth to his two disciple-monks as three parts.
He gave the grass, flowers, and so forth to the third monk as four parts.
Because the noble guest monks had come with nothing to enjoy and could not remain for long, the Buddha later, together with the monks, arrived at a monastery in this country. The Buddha...
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana: "You may tell the long-term residents to prepare bedding and mats. They replied, "The Buddha is the Dharma King;
we have already set aside the best room for his veneration, and the remainder has been divided into four portions. Śāriputra reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "This is the property of the Saṃgha from the four directions. Whether it belongs to the Saṃgha, to a large group of people, or to a single individual—"
"It should be sold and distributed; it must not be kept for oneself. [If one does so,] one commits a sthūlātyaya. (Having established this scriptural passage as the thesis, some people then say:
"The ancient masters state that since the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) had already divided the property of the Saṃgha at that time, the Buddha ordered Śāriputra to go and seize it back.
Therefore, we know that although they previously divided it into four parts and took it for themselves, it did not constitute theft. For if it were necessarily theft, then Śāriputra..."

One who knows the Dharma likewise ought not to further seize [the property]. By this analogy, it is known that if there is one today who steals the property of the Sangha, it does not constitute theft;

seizing it carries no guilt. (The above briefly recounts the ancient view. As for the phrase "this has not yet been seen in the various Vinaya sections," this refers to the Master’s refutation of the ancient interpretation.

He means that the ancients did not clearly understand that the various Vinaya teachings contain explicit texts stating that if one seizes or steals the property of another, it likewise [constitutes an offense].
This constitutes the offense of theft, because the property was seized by thieves. If that is so, why is the passage from the preceding *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* cited? It states:
"The group of six monks divided [the goods] into four parts and took them for themselves; Śāriputra seized them. One may answer this by citing the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*, which says:

"In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it refers to temporarily obstructing the use of the Sangha, and so forth. This means that the preceding text concerns the initial intention to divide [the goods] temporarily, as the guest monks were not expected to remain for long.
If there is no intention to appropriate [the property] for oneself, it merely obstructs the Sangha’s use; therefore, one commits a light offense of *duṣkṛta*.

However, if one has the intention to divide it and take it for one's own possession, it constitutes the grave offense of theft (*steya*), and even in such a case, taking it by force is not permitted. This is as stated in the *Sāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (Shanjian wen) regarding the theft of property by a steward.

It is expected that the Saṃgha as a whole shall be considered the single perpetrator of a grave offense; hence it is said that, according to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, this constitutes a grave transgression.

Regarding the statement that "the offenses of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* are equal to the five heinous crimes," Xuán explains: this refers to the heinous crime of schism (*saṃghabheda*). Now, the Saṃgha of the ten directions relies upon food for its existence;

taking food as a condition, they are able to cultivate the Path. Since it has now been stolen and damaged, the Saṃgha has nothing on which to rely, and the cultivation of the Path is cut off; therefore, it is equated [with the five heinous crimes].

"An offense of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma). 'I am among the number of the Saṃgha' means that the preceding text clarifies how each individual incurs an offense in relation to the holy ones and ordinary beings of the ten directions.

"The *Divyāvadāna* section (*Dīrghāgama*, *Rìzàng fēn*) refers to the Buddha’s discourse addressed to the Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha concerning the suffering endured by various nāgas. A portion of that scripture states:

'Recall in the past, when we had left the household life, we committed all manner of evils; we devoured the flowers and fruits belonging to the Saṃgha, and consumed the offerings of faith given by people.'"
It will not end; they shall undergo various sufferings. As for the account of Saṃgharakṣita, he was named after the person [who told it].
The bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita followed merchants into the sea to gather treasures and saw fifty-two hells: fifty for monks and nuns, one for a śrāmaṇera, and one for a layperson.
Because he had committed illegal acts on behalf of a monastery for others, he entered these hells, and so forth, as described.
Regarding the passage beginning with "He" and continuing through "five hundred," concerning the Tripiṭaka Master’s repayment of a debt:
the *Upāliparipṛcchā* (Five Hundred Questions), in its first fascicle, states that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was a bhikṣu who was diligent and intelligent.

A certain brāhmaṇa, seeing that the bhikṣu was intelligent, offered his daughter to him to become a nun and study the Path. The bhikṣu accepted her. That woman was beautiful, and the bhikṣu lost [his composure].
[The Buddha] said: "He reflected: 'We have together committed an unrighteous act by using the property of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—each worth one thousand coins.

This bhikṣu was intelligent and skilled in expounding the Dharma; he contemplated repenting his offense and wished to repay the debt. He went to another country to beg for alms and obtained a great amount of wealth.
On the way back, he was bitten by a seven-step snake (the pronunciation of *shí* is provided). The bhikṣu knew that once he had taken seven steps, he would certainly die."
Within six paces, he then instructed his disciple to take the goods and repay the debt, saying, "I shall remain standing here and wait for you.
The disciple, obeying his teacher's command, went to repay the debt and returned to report to him.

As soon as the teacher took a single step forward, his life ended and he fell into hell, which was the Warm Bath (Jentāka) Hell; thereupon, he raised a great voice and recited sūtras and incantations. There was...
Several thousand people heard the sound of the sutra and dharanis and were all liberated.

The hell-warden grew angry with the bhikṣu and struck him with an iron fork until he died, whereupon he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and other realms. (The above passages clarify the successful application [of the rite].)
Regarding "mutual exchange between the two [limits]," it is as stated in the text. Regarding "concerning the limit of the controller," the *Zhi* (祇) states:

If a bhikṣu acts as a *māmādī* (steward), and the Buddha’s stūpa has no property while the Saṃgha possesses property, he then thinks: "The Saṃgha receives the grace of the Buddha; therefore, to make offerings solely to the Buddha is equivalent to making offerings to the Saṃgha.
He then takes the property of the Saṃgha to repair the Buddha’s stūpa. This constitutes a grave offense of *pārājika*. If the stūpa [has property...]
Regarding property: if the Sangha has no property, one should think, "The Buddha is within the Sangha," and thus offer the temple property to the Sangha.
(The term *māmāte* is a Sanskrit word; here it is translated as "manager" and so forth. Question: At present, there are images of Maitreya in various monasteries.
If someone receives offerings or profits [from them], how should this be adjudicated? Master Jiahuai ruled that they should be offered to the Sangha.
Regarding the use by the Saṃgha: since the stage of Maitreya is that of a Bodhisattva, and Bodhisattvas are subsumed within the Saṃgha, this serves as an illustration.
For example, the Venerable Sengqie (Saṅgha) of Sizhou was an emanation of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; all offerings and benefits he received were entirely entered into the Saṃgha.

Now this case is also like that: at Xianggao Temple on Yangzhou, there was an iron statue of Maitreya to which people offered an immense amount of goods; the Southern Ācārya issued a general order that these be used for the support of the monks. The Venerable One said: [this is the same].

Maitreya is currently at the stage of the causal ground; he is a bodhisattva who dwells in the midst of striving. Yet, how can one blame him for bestowing gifts while manifesting the appearance of a Buddha?
This is not the same as Master Sizhou, who manifests the deportment of a monk. The examples are not uniform; [to insist otherwise] would be nothing but ignorant attachment.
(This is spoken of here because it is a matter of urgency; students must understand this.)

Regarding the phrase "because the Jewel [Sūtras] have arrived," the *Ratnarāśi* and other sūtras are mentioned; the term "others" includes the *Mahāsannipāta*. The first fascicle of the *Ratnarāśi* states:

"If there is something required for a Tathāgata’s stūpa, or if it has fallen into ruin, and if the property belonging to the permanent endowment (*saṃghika*) or the property belonging to the universal community (*caityika*) is abundant, the bhikṣu in charge of affairs should assemble the Saṃgha, distribute voting tallies (*śalākā*), and seek their consent (*chanda*), speaking as follows: 'The Buddha’s stūpa is in ruins.'"
Now there is a need. The property of this permanent monastery (*sthavira-saṃgha*) is abundant, as is that of the *cāturmahāyānika-saṃgha* (the universal saṃgha).

These may now be used for the repair and maintenance of the Buddha-stūpa. If the Saṃgha is in harmony, they may be used; if they are not in accord, then one should exhort laypeople to perform the repairs.

Seeking funds and goods from the homes of householders thus implicitly demonstrates that the two types of property belonging to the Buddha and the Dharma have no fixed owner and cannot be settled through internal arbitration.
"Mao" (皃) means "not appropriate. The rest is as stated in the *Chao* (鈔文) [and so forth]. Regarding the phrase "if it reaches":
if one follows this principle, it refers to the aforementioned point that they must not be used interchangeably. As for setting up a monk’s bedding within a Buddha hall: [it is not permitted].
This would obstruct the affairs of the Buddha’s family. To install scriptures and images within the monastic quarters (saṃghārāma) is to obstruct the affairs of the Saṃgha’s family.

Is this not a case of mutual interference? This is explained in terms of long-term usage; if it is for a temporary period, as permitted in the *Śarīra-piṭaka* (or *Vinaya-śarīra-vibhāṣā*), it is allowed (and so forth).
Regarding the prohibition against installing [images] in lower rooms and the like: if there is a multi-storied pavilion, then [the image should be placed] on the upper floor.

The upper stories constitute the "superior," while the ground floors constitute the "inferior. If it is merely an ordinary residential courtyard, one takes a fine room as superior and a coarse or dilapidated one as inferior.
This passage is cited to demonstrate that what was previously mentioned regarding taking [a room] temporarily applies to taking [one] in general.

By contrast, this shows that if one takes a monastic cell for long-term use to enshrine a Buddha or scriptures, leaving it without a lock and not providing it for the monks' residence, this constitutes "mutual misappropriation" (interchangeable use). Reflect upon this.

Regarding the question concerning "dedicated property" (*sthitikā-vastu*): The meaning of this passage is as follows. In the preceding text, it was stated that "permanent property and property for the visiting community (*āgantuka*) are mutually required for the Saṃgha to use.
However, it was not yet understood how to distinguish between these two types of monastic communities—those of permanent residents and those of visitors.
Therefore, this question was raised. Regarding Ānanda receiving a separate room: this refers to lay devotees (*gṛhapati*) erecting rooms and halls within the monastery grounds.
The four requisites were provided to Ānanda, who in turn distributed them as offerings for the *caityas* (shrines).
Regarding the statement that the courtesan Āmrapālī offered her grove to the Buddha first, this refers to King Bimbisāra, who, using a golden pitcher to pour water, said to the Buddha:
"Of all the gardens and groves in the city of Vaiśālī, my garden is the most excellent; I now offer it to the World-Honored One. I pray only that you will accept it. The Buddha said:

It may be offered to the Buddha as the foremost and to the *cāturdisa* (universal) Saṃgha. Regarding the ambiguity in the scriptural text, the intention of the author of the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*) is that the wording of the sutra is unclear;
according to the underlying principle, dwellings and the like are property belonging to the *cāturdisa* Saṃgha. Thus, the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vibhāṣā) states:

[The text] continues: "There is a separate provision for offerings; thus the Vinaya says: 'How many rooms possess abundant merit? (referring to those built by *dānapati* which are permanently occupied).

This cites an ancient interpretation, referring to flowers and fruits as the permanent property of the *saṃgha*. If one follows the *Jieshu* [the *Sifenlü Shu*], the author of the *Chao* personally questioned the Great Tang [monks]."

*Saṃghāṭa*. The *Sanzang* (Tripitaka) states that the Sanskrit term *saṃghāṭa* means "giving face-to-face" (*duimian shi*). Among the four types of Saṃghas, this refers to the property of the *pratyakṣa-saṃgha* (the present Saṃgha).
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "One who does not misappropriate the property of the *saṃghāṭa* shall be reborn in the Immovable Land (*Acalā*).

The *Chao* (Excerpts) states that according to ancient usage it was called "permanent property" (*changzhu wu*), because [its meaning] had not yet been fully understood; it was only within the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) that its definitive meaning was established.

However, as the *Chao* (Excerpts) has already been widely circulated, it cannot be further revised or altered; for now, we shall take the *Shu* (Commentary) as our primary source. The Tripitaka Master further stated:
"According to the Sanskrit language, it should be called *cātus-tarika*, which means 'the property of the Sangha of the four directions.
The translators abbreviated it by omitting the two characters *duo-xie*. It should now properly be written as *zhāoti* (招提). Later scribes have erroneously transmitted it [in other forms]."
The character "zhao" (招) was erroneously written [for "ti" (提)]; it has not been corrected to this day, and thus remains as "Zhao-ti" (招提).

Furthermore, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the mother of Viśākhā offered precious treasures to the Saṃgha of the four directions and said to Śāriputra, "They may be used for the saṃgha hall. The Buddha permitted her to accept them.

Based on this, it refers to the monastic quarters for the Saṃgha of the four directions. However, while the name "permanent property" (chángzhù) is general and applies to everything, the term "invited residence" (zhāotí) is specific, referring only to the rooms and halls.

Regarding the statement that "if there is a mutual need, it is permitted to use the property of the harmonious Saṃgha," and so forth—up to the point where it says "the five [types of] grave matters"—if one is obstructed by the boundaries of the Saṃgha, one does not commit an offense. Xuán states: "Thus, although the respectful etiquette is the same, even within the same room..."

Next, he cites a passage from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which states that since monasteries and Buddhist shrines each have their own designated attendants—even down to the livestock—it is improper to employ those of one establishment as proxies for another. Furthermore...

One may then use it as they wish for making offerings to the Buddha and the Dharma. As for "flowers being beyond measure," this means that because they have no fixed value, they are taken according to need.

Regarding those who have no one to consult or inform: this refers to later bhikṣus who are not familiar with the previous demarcations of the Three Jewels.
If they distribute things according to their own convenience—allocating some to the Buddha and some to the Dharma and Saṃgha, etc.—it belongs to the water of the stūpa.
This refers to the original state: within the grounds of a Buddhist stūpa, water belongs to the stūpa and may not be used for other purposes.
Alternatively, even if it is stūpa ground, if the Saṃgha has previously expended labor to cultivate and maintain it, one must account for that labor when taking water.
If the value exceeds five *māṣaka*, a grave offense (*pārājika*) is committed; this is stated in reference to times when there is no other water available.
Regarding the statement in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* concerning "offenses": as for "flowers and so forth from the monastery grove," that Vinaya states:

since the monastic community does not use them, one may take them according to one's own preference. This also applies to items such as cauldrons, pots, jars, and basins.
Furthermore, it is based on new [materials], nor are they for common use; if they have already been used, there would be an unpleasant tactile sensation.

Regarding the *Vinayamātṛkā*, it states that when one has already demarcated a site for building and plants trees there, it is not necessary to inform the Saṃgha. Xuán explains: "Since the ground has already been demarcated, the trees follow the ground;

This is truly unacceptable. Baoyun said: "This was planted intentionally; that is to say, it was originally intended for constructing a dwelling of a specific size, but now [it is used] because of the timber."
It has not yet been prepared. For now, construct a small hut or a shelter sufficient to contain one's body. Plant trees on the vacant land surrounding it that are fit for timber use;

Regarding trees, firewood, and the like within the *saṃghika* (monastic) compound, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If there is a visiting bhikṣu who cuts dry grass or wood..."

Fuel was piled up in front of the rooms. A bhikṣu who had gone out for alms returned, saw it, and rebuked them. He reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "Regarding the method for burning wood:
so much should be provided for the heated bathhouse, so much for the kitchen, so much for the bath hall, and so much for the separate rooms.

He dies immediately. The fields and houses are transferred; this refers to "monastic fields" and the like.

Regarding "treasures hidden underground" and so forth, the ninth [chapter] of the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: if one finds buried treasure, one should form the thought of acquisition and dedicate it to the Triple Gem.

If one uses [items] equally for the sake of the Saṃgha, there is no offense. This refers merely to the initial intention; as long as it is generally for the purpose of performing the ritual action, there is no offense of mutual misappropriation.

One need not consider whether they were hidden treasures; rather, one should reflect upon the principles regarding the establishment of offenses based on the specific ownership and the relationship to the owner.

Regarding the phrase "those who have reached the ultimate": "identical in both wealth and Dharma" means that sharing the same material offerings constitutes identity in wealth, while the communal recitation of the precepts constitutes identity in Dharma.
"As explained extensively in the aforementioned sūtras" refers to such texts as the *Mahāsannipāta Saṃgharakṣita Sūtra*, which state:

Inside the casket were documents recording the registers of the offenses of the monks; these were all slips of tree bark taken from the monastery, which had been dyed for various uses.
Their bodies were all entering hell to undergo suffering. This monk revived and recounted this matter in full. This was because his precepts were not pure.

It is not permissible to take [the leaves] oneself. Regarding "taking them by secretly consulting": the previous statement that an individual may use them or a monastic may use the leaves from a family tree applies only if one is upholding the precepts.
One should first privately and discreetly deliberate whether it constitutes upholding or breaking [the precepts], and only after such careful consideration should one use them.

It is said that there is mutual application within each respective category (*dangphen*). "Mutual application within each respective category" means mutual application within the Buddha, mutual application within the Dharma, and mutual application within the Sangha;
therefore, it is called "respective category. This differs from the mutual relationship among the three jewels mentioned previously. Regarding the phrase "it is said... reaching [the point]":
when the original creation of Śākyamuni was changed to Amitābha, this constitutes mutual application within the respective category of the Buddha. (From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*)

"Nirvana" refers to mutual interchangeability among the various categories of phenomena (*dharma*). "Monastic dwellings and vehicles" refers to mutual interchangeability among the various categories within the Sangha.
In all these cases, when viewed in relation to their respective objects, the principles and meanings are logically consistent. This collectively explains the aforementioned thirteen items;
although they differ slightly from one another, they are fully consistent in both principle and meaning. This is because both Śākyamuni and Amitābha are Buddhas. Six.

Because the ten titles of virtue are fully perfected in both, and because the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* are likewise both Mahāyāna teachings that equally generate merit, as well as because monastic dwellings and vehicles are used in common by the Saṃgha—such principles may be harmonized through their underlying meaning.

It is not appropriate for their names to be interchanged. Now, on what basis is the offense of mutual use committed by others determined? The commentary on the subsequent line explains: "It merely violates..."

If one uses what was intended for another, one incurs an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*). This is merely a formal determination that it is improper; it does not mean that one incurs a *pārājika* offense as in the previous case. Be aware of this.
Regarding "the value of the assembly hall and so forth," this citation from the Vinaya text serves to prove that violating the intent of a gift constitutes an offense of wrongdoing.
The Twenty-fourth [Khandhaka] of the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya states: There were a group of bhikṣuṇīs reciting the precepts in the open air. A layperson saw them and asked:
[The layperson] asked, "Auntie, for what reason are you reciting the precepts in the open air? The nun replied, "I have no hall for recitation.
The layperson then offered the funds for a hall and ordered it to be built. Once the nun had received the money, she thought to herself:

"The recitation of the precepts occurs only once every half-month; one may simply go wherever a place is available. However, clothing is difficult to obtain and is needed at all times. I should divert this [money]..."

Regarding money and goods: [if one] makes them into five robes for personal use and maintains them, it later incurs the censure and suspicion of the laity; it was on this account that the rule was established. For a nun, the offense is a *pāyattika*; for a monk, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

This is because [the funds] were originally intended as a gift for the currently present Saṃgha hall, yet they were diverted to make [personal] requisites; thus, the offense is a *pāyattika* for the nun and a *dukkaṭa* for the monk.

If the gift had been intended for the Saṃgha of the four directions and was diverted to make a precept hall for nuns, or if it was diverted to make a fixed [monastery], it constitutes a grave offense of theft (*steya*). As for the phrase "if it reaches its destination": [it refers to when the object has been delivered].

This means that one first transcribes the sūtras and subsequently transcribes the śāstras; hence it is said, "The sūtras are primary, and the śāstras are secondary" (the above is the correct interpretation).

(This latter explanation contradicts the *Chao*). Regarding "contrary to both human sentiment and rational principle": this is because it contradicts both human feeling and logical reasoning. [Regarding] cause and effect...

according to the authentic scriptures and the primary records, these constitute supramundane cause and effect; whereas the spurious scriptures and miscellaneous records do not constitute supramundane cause and effect.
Such cause and effect are therefore completely discordant (this interpretation is also valid). Regarding the distinction between merit and non-merit: if...
