this explains that the miscellaneous records are not merely internal variations within their own respective categories. Fearing that people might become confused in their understanding, these [authentic works] have been extracted and set apart.

Regarding "that which has a patron is not permitted to be used in common with that which has no patron": this refers to the case where [the images] belong to the same Buddha, yet the two niches are located in the east and west respectively.
If a patron exists and restricts their intention to one specific [niche], then it is not permissible.

If there is no patron and both are managed by the bhikṣus themselves, then although the two niches differ, they may be used interchangeably without restriction. Regarding "originally shared between teacher and disciples," the teacher...
The Buddha refers to these [figures]; the disciples refer to the assembly of Bodhisattvas, noble *saṃgha*, and so forth;

and the various requisites refer to the groves, ponds, flowers, fruits, platforms, thrones, auspicious birds, exotic fowl, and even the Vajra-gods, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings.
This means that when one intends to paint a transformation tableau (*pariṇāmika-bimba*) of Amitābha, it is logically appropriate and permissible to include all such requisites. It is not otherwise.

Regarding "the form of unrighteousness between men and women" and so forth, this refers to the illicit physical forms of male and female. The rest of the text is self-evident. As for the statement "it is a grave offense up to the *sūci-vardhana* [needle-point] transgression":

if a donor originally intended to give a garden or fruit orchard, but the recipient diverts it for personal consumption, resulting in a grave offense, there are two interpretations in the *Xuánjì* (Records of Profound Meaning).
The first [view] says: These four types of offerings are for the enjoyment of the *saṃgha* present before one. Since he stole and consumed them as food, he violated the donor’s original intention;

calculating the value, it constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). The second [view] says: Regarding the robes and medicine given to poor monks from the four directions, since he now consumed them entirely with a thieving mind, he caused others to be deprived of what they ought to have received at a later time;
therefore, it is grave. Baozhi says: These two interpretations are difficult to justify logically. If, regarding...

The Saṃgha of the four directions states that this does not constitute a grave offense (*pārājika*). However, we now base our judgment solely on the fact that the donor gave these items specifically for the thirty or fifty people currently present within this monastery.
If one diverts these goods to summon monks from the ten directions and consumes them all, then compared to those currently present, one fails to obtain what they rightfully deserve;
it is for this reason that the offense is established. This refers to the object of the act (*viṣaya*), and not to the intention (*citta*) itself. Reflect on this. If one diverts [the goods] to...

Regarding the offense of *thullaccaya* (grave offense) concerning monastic quarters and the like: this refers to the use of dwellings that have no specific owner and belong collectively to the Sangha of the four directions;

therefore, the offense is classified as light. If one takes even a small amount of food or provisions from a residence—referring to the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, which states that if a garden is donated for the purpose of providing robes and requisites, diverting it for food constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*)—in cases where such items are currently scarce and one wishes to distribute them, the rule is relaxed to permit the Sangha to use them collectively. The Sangha...

Regarding items such as bedding and clothing that have accompanied one during times of banditry and chaos: these are light articles that may be kept as personal requisites for the sake of maintaining stability amidst turmoil.
However, if one later wishes to offer them to this very image at its original location, both [the image and the object] are equally images; their essential nature is no different.

According to principle, there is no fault; however, it constitutes a transgression (*vyañjana*) and should not be performed. Regarding the phrase "the robe is offered to a bhikṣu," that treatise asks:

"If a layperson (*avadātavasana*) renounces the world for the sake of the Path but has not yet received the precepts, may they receive food from the Saṃgha? The answer is: "They must inform the Saṃgha."

Only when the Sangha has granted permission may one eat; to eat without having made such a request constitutes an offense of *pāyattika*. If it is an ordinary layperson, one may not request permission from the Sangha to give them food.

However, in this case, although the person wishes to leave the household life and their body remains that of a layman, their mind is already set upon the Path; therefore, the rule is relaxed to permit requesting permission to give them food.
In the lower fascicle of the Treatise, it further asks: "If one is on the road begging for the sake of the Sangha, may one receive food intended for the Sangha?"

"No. He replied: "If, when departing, one first informs the Sangha and the Sangha grants permission, it is well. If one does not inform them when departing, it is also well to inform them upon returning.

If one informed them when departing but was not granted permission, one must repay [the debt] upon returning; otherwise, one commits a grave offense" (Xuán says: "This refers to the mutual relationship between the monastic and the lay").

Furthermore, in the first volume of the *Lùn* (Treatise), it asks: "Regarding rice for a monastic feast, if the Sangha has departed, may the host of the feast use it to provide for subsequent [feasts]?"

"Is it permissible for the Saṃgha [to eat]? "Will those who come later be able to obtain food? He replied: "If the *ghanṭā* is struck, they may obtain food; if it is not struck, even eating a single meal constitutes a grave offense. (This is first cited from the Śāstra.
This refers to a case where a donor brings rice to provide for the monks of the ten directions; once the monks have departed, he intends to bring it to provide for subsequent monks.

Once the offerings for the ten directions have been determined, if the monks later have no intention to steal, but merely strike the bell to assemble everyone from the ten directions to eat together, there is no offense.
However, if one acts with the intent to steal and eats without sounding the bell—even if eating only until full—one commits a grave offense (Xuán says:
these three grave offenses are *sthūlātyaya*). Furthermore, according to the two preceding texts, if one does not manifest the signs of stealing, the *Chao* likewise classifies this as *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding the phrase "as prescribed above": "Arriving" (zhì) means that as prescribed above, one must be on the road; only after informing the Saṃgha does one obtain [permission], for without informing them, one does not.

As for the statement that "even though the bell is struck, one is not exempt from the offense of theft," this refers to the fact that one commits the offense the moment one carries the item across the boundary; it is not because the bell is struck outside the boundary.

Thus, one is exempted from [the offense]. Regarding those who have been appointed by the Saṃgha and so forth: as explained above in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, one who guards the monastery and harmonizes with the Saṃgha may use the property of the Saṃgha from the four quarters;
now, for one acting on behalf of the Saṃgha, it is likewise permissible to harmonize with the Saṃgha to take food out of the boundary.

Furthermore, there is no need to perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), as this would indicate that there was no prior consultation with the Saṃgha. Regarding "monastery estates" and the like: this refers to the locations where the monastery’s estates are managed; in such cases, it is simply...

He made a formal agreement but did not repay it, claiming that the estate and the monastery were one family. If he were led outside [the monastery], even for the property of a monastic family, one would still commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Therefore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "When the bell is struck to summon the assembly, all the monks shall eat."

It is not yet known whether it is permissible to keep slaves or livestock at another temple. Answer: If it is permissible, the Sangha possesses the six harmonies (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*), and thus [the property] belongs to all locations.

Since humans and livestock belong to distinct categories, the principle does not permit their being sent as messengers; a messenger is likewise restricted to food. Question: What constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*)? Answer: [As follows:]...

Because both are permanent property, as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: "If one gives monastic property to another monastery, since it is likewise permanent property, it is not permissible to give rise to a mind of theft;
therefore, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. This case is the same.
Regarding "the three arrive": this refers to the maintenance of these images, namely the physical statues, stupas, and temples; the paper, silk, bamboo, and cloth [of scriptures];

and the shaving of hair and donning of dyed robes—these are the three. Regarding "the principle is the Three Jewels": this refers to the Three Jewels as a single essence within True Suchness (*tathatā*). Regarding "from 'sa' to 'great portion'":

this means that during the Buddha's lifetime, when receiving offerings, one received the same share as the *saṃgha*, but obtained only a single person’s portion. After his parinirvāṇa, [one obtained] one...
"Taking a large portion" means receiving a fixed share for oneself alone, as when the property of the Three Jewels is currently distributed equally:
the Sangha receives ten *zi*, the Dharma receives ten *qian*, and the Buddha likewise takes ten *qian*.

As for the phrase "because it is answered," this refers to the fact that during the Buddha's lifetime, offerings were made to his physical body (*rūpakāya*), whereas after his passing, offerings are made to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which is superior to the Jewel of the Sangha.
Therefore, among these three parts, one part is taken. Regarding the placing [of these items] within a stūpa for nails and hair:

this means that all hair shorn and nails clipped after the Buddha attained enlightenment were used to erect stūpas for the purpose of making offerings. As for the giving of Dharma and so forth, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun) states:
"If it is said that one gives to the Three Jewels, one should divide it into three portions: one portion is given to the Buddha Jewel, and one portion should be suspended for the Dharma Jewel."
It should be placed within a Buddha stūpa; it must not be used for Buddhist scriptures. One portion is given to those who recite the Dharma;

one portion is given to the Saṃgha-ratna. The Saṃgha must not take this object; it should be returned to the donor and placed within the stūpa as an offering to the Saṃgha of the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-saṃgha).
Question: This treatise does not state that the gift to the Dharma is divided into two portions. Why, then, has the text been arbitrarily altered here?
Answering by way of analysis: The *Śāstra* states that when the Dharma-treasure is offered, it should be placed within a stūpa and not given to those who preach the Dharma or recite the sūtras.
However, if it is simply stated that "the Dharma is being given," one should divide it into two portions: one portion for the scriptural Dharma and one portion for the person who preaches it.

Therefore, the *Jie shu* (Commentary on the Precepts) says: "According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, if there is a gift of the Dharma, the Dharma Master who preaches and recites the sūtras may also take [a portion]."
Regarding the distribution: it is said that the Dharma must be propagated by people. In the present time, when one receives money for reciting sutras, this rule must be applied accordingly;

thus, one should receive a half-share. Looking toward the benefit of the monks, when seven people recite the sutra, the proceeds are divided into eight portions, and one of these portions is allocated to the Dharma.

This is still to manifest respect; if nothing at all is given, it is not appropriate to divide [the offering]. If one gives to the Sangha Jewel and so forth, this refers to the First Noble Truth (paramārtha-satya), meaning that in principle there is no contradiction with the pure essence, and one should give rise to harmony; this is also called the ultimate truth (paramārtha).

Regarding the statement that "words do not correspond," it means that one should not speak of giving to either the noble ones or ordinary people at inappropriate times, but should simply give to the Sangha, because the Sangha encompasses both the ordinary and the noble. Thus it is said.

Regarding "it is deemed a loss": this refers to the distinction between the ultimate and conventional jewels, and the divergence between the paths of the ordinary and the sage. At the time of receiving a gift, one must discern whether it is open or obstructed.
If an object is given to the Three Jewels, the act of giving is "open"; however, if it is restricted solely to the Buddha Jewel, it is "obstructed.

Furthermore, if the gift is for an image that sustains the Dharma, it is "open"; if it is for the Buddha Jewel alone, it is "obstructed. As for the Dharma: if one says the gift to the Dharma is "open," it is divided into two parts, both of which are "open."

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the Dharma-jewel," it serves as a restriction. As for "the Sangha": if one says "giving to the assembly of monks," it applies universally to both ordinary and noble ones.
If, however, one says "for the sake of the Sangha-jewel," one must distinguish and inquire thoroughly to ensure clarity, so that there is no confusion between the two.
This is to avoid the fault of mutual confusion.
Regarding the statement "fourfold mutual [usage]": what has been explained above clarifies the mutual description of images and jewels;

what follows below clarifies that among the various objects belonging to the images themselves, there is likewise mutual [usage]. The statement "first, regarding the objects of the Buddha, there are four kinds" serves as a heading.

This refers to the numerical category. The commentary states that "from one up to the middle" means that if it is an object for the Buddha’s personal use, it is absolutely improper to move or transfer it, and so forth.
As for the reference to what was said previously in the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra*, it says: "Whatever objects there may be in a Buddhist stūpa, even down to a single coin..."
Because they renounce with a mind of profound devotion, it should be understood that gods and humans constantly perceive the marks of a Buddha within these objects.
One must not sell the silk used for the Buddha’s body to make robes for him. The Venerable [Master] said:

"This refers to secular households in India who, after the silkworms have finished spinning, produce silk to offer to the Buddha; this substance is made purely of cotton, resembling a six-fold (ṣaḍvidha) bedstead."
Great! There are those who are discerning. Nowadays, everyone paints the Buddha wearing a *saṃkakṣikā* (undergarment) draped over both shoulders;

this follows the style of the Venerable Xuanzang, which will become the standard for the future. This is precisely what defines a *bhikṣu*. Furthermore, the Tripitaka Master from India has manifested this very point.
All were designated as the "Stainless Sangha" (*vimala-saṃgha*). Their appearance was like that of those wearing cotton; they mostly dyed their robes in purple, crimson, and other such colors.
Nowadays, when lecturers are questioned about this, none recognize it. Knowing this, some people nowadays bring [such materials] to offer to the Buddha.
When the bhikṣus see that there is a surplus, they immediately sell them off and purchase silk and cloth to make *kāṣāya* robes and the like for the Buddha. This is truly not permissible.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the garden, the seating implements, and so forth are all [part of] the stūpa," a question is raised:
For instance, if a garden, a well, a field, or a hall belong to the Buddha, are they included within the category of "seating implements" for use? The answer is as stated in the Vinaya:

King Bimbisāra offered the Bamboo Grove (Veṇuvana) to the Buddha and established a vihāra there. The Buddha said to the king: "You have now offered this Bamboo Grove of the Buddha to the Buddha and..."
The Saṃgha of the four quarters. Why is this? If the Tathāgata exists, then objects such as those belonging to the gardens, the dwellings, the robes, and the bowls constitute his stūpa;
these are things that neither devas nor worldly people dare to use (the above is from the Vinaya text). Xuan says:

This mention of "gardens" refers to the gardens of the monasteries (*saṃghārāma*) that are actually used for their maintenance, not referring to other wells or gardens outside the temple grounds. As for the statement "it constitutes a grave offense," it means:

Regarding items donated to the Buddha: these items are given to the Buddha and thus belong to the Buddha. Concerning the acquisition of Buddha-property to purchase articles for worship, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:
"The reason this property may be acquired is that the original donor intended it generally for the Buddha’s use; therefore, it may be traded.
This differs from the previous category [of items dedicated to specific individuals], where because a superior mental image was formed, the object must remain fixed. This refers to Buddha-property.

One must not move or discard [the items] belonging to another; this means that if the donor’s intention is restricted to a specific location, to act contrary to their intent constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*).
Regarding whether a bhikṣu may fashion Buddha images or transcribe scriptures, the Venerable One said: "There is no fault in a bhikṣu making Buddha images or writing scriptures."

However, taking money is not permitted. This is because such money was originally intended for the sake of the scriptures; for a bhikṣu to take it for the purpose of copying [the texts] is entirely improper.
If a layperson offers it as a gift for their own sake and not for this specific task, taking it does not constitute an offense.
Some say that it is entirely improper for a bhikṣu to copy scriptures. If that were so, then when transcribing onto palm leaves during the assemblies of the Councils, would one not have to...?
Regarding the question of whether white cloth may be written upon: it is said that "three times" refers to not altering its original substance.

Whether one joins many banners and canopies together to form a curtain, or patches small banners to make a large banner, or constructs them for use as a Buddha-bed and so forth—all such uses are permissible, as they do not sever the donor’s merit.
However, if one tears or breaks them, the original substance is destroyed and the field of merit is severed. As it is said:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dàlùn) states that "equal" refers to the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Zhìlùn). That text says: "Suppose one were to paint a Buddha image.
One person destroys it because the likeness is not good; another destroys it out of an evil mind. The one with a good heart gains merit, while the one with an evil mind incurs sin.

Citing this passage from the treatise, [the author] explains that destroying [an image] because it is not beautiful is what prompts one to make it magnificent and beautiful, so that it does not change.
The nature of the image is analogous to this; by applying this principle to adjust the practice, it does not contradict the intention of the donor, and thus there is no fault and merit is gained.

Regarding the passage from the *Sūtra* cited as "From the fourth [section] to the *Sūtra*," the *Shoushu* (Commentary on the Preface) asks: "How are objects offered to the Buddha distinguished from objects used for the worship of the Buddha? It answers:

"Objects for the worship of the Buddha belong to the Buddha permanently, whereas those offered [to the Buddha] are returned to their original owner temporarily; therefore, there is a distinction. This is quoted in the *Chao*.
The Vinaya text states that those who repair stupas may receive food; furthermore, it cites a śāstra passage stating that bhikṣus who attend upon the Buddha may receive food.

Both of these cases pertain to those who have rendered service. If [the offering] does not belong to the Buddha, it should not be given to others. Therefore, we know that in this context, it refers to what is temporarily offered.
By analogy, regarding "Buddha-dishes" and so forth in lay households, this means that according to the preceding text, the offering of rice does not belong to the Buddha permanently.
It belongs solely to its original owner. Thus, when a layperson has finished providing a meal at their own home, the host may collect it themselves without offense.

As for the statement that "it is not to be assigned money," the claim that it "belongs" [to someone else] is from a spurious sutra. Since this is the case for the *pātra*, the other two [requisites] are likewise the same.
All are returned to their owners.
Regarding the phrase "next, those who know," the *Fǎshòuyòng shūsū* (Commentary on the Use of Dharma Objects) states:

"Whether it be scriptures or images inscribed upon paper, silk, bamboo, or wood, or objects such as chests, boxes, vessels, or miscellaneous items that have previously been used for storage—if they have been formally designated for perpetual offering, they may not be altered or transferred. This refers to...

It is certain that this accords with the sacred teachings, for all are based upon the principle of cessation (*nirodha*). Should there be any loss or gain, both result in the production of demerit or merit in relation to *nirvāṇa*.

As for the other three types of acquisitions that were not deliberated upon—namely, items belonging to the Dharma, offerings made to the Dharma, and gifts presented to the Dharma—these three are treated the same as items belonging to the Buddha.
Depending on the circumstances, they may be advanced or not; therefore, it is said that "they may be understood by analogy with what precedes."
Regarding the phrase "the three knowledges (trividyā) up to the offenses": the two types that are permanent and restricted to specific locations are called "two" because they are permanent.

Since it is not permitted to take them out of the boundary at will, they are said to be "restricted to specific locations. Regarding the phrase "the two types may be used interchangeably, as they are known to be obtained, etc.":
Xuán says, "According to the aforementioned passage from the *Jiàn lùn* concerning the guarding of monasteries, it states: 'Those who lack sufficient food and provisions...'"
This means that when the property of the perpetual endowment for the ten directions is scarce, one may be permitted to use the gardens, fields, and buildings belonging to the perpetual endowment;
by selling such items to provide food, they are thereby returned to the perpetual endowment for the ten directions. Regarding the gravity of the offense according to the scriptures:

based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, the buying and selling of male and female slaves, oxen, horses, and other livestock constitutes the offense of a minor defilement (*āpatti-laghu-mala*), which can be understood through reflection.

Zhi said: "If one says, 'I give these slaves,' they should not be accepted. If one says, 'I give these garden-slaves,' or if one gives a slave belonging to the Saṃgha, or a servant of the Saṃgha, in all such cases they should not be accepted.
If one says, 'I give this male attendant to provide for the Saṃgha,' then it may be accepted.
Thus, while the sūtra text concludes with the offense, the Vinaya states that it is not permitted; the meaning of the term "not permitted" is as intended here.
Observe this; do not fear the fault of buying or selling. As for the discussion regarding the two types of "present before" (pratyakṣa) and so forth, ancient records exist elsewhere.

Here, we simply take the case of stealing property belonging to the Saṃgha—specifically that which is "present before" and "present before throughout the ten directions"—to clarify their mutual application.

For example, the property of one's own fivefold assembly is originally "present before throughout the ten directions"; if one now does not perform the formal ritual but enters directly into [the category of] "present before," [it constitutes an offense].
The previous case was a division of what was already shared, resulting in countless gains; this is the case of mutual exchange.

If, however, the items were originally present before [the community]—such as robes offered to those who have completed the preceding *anvāraka* (summer retreat)—and they are now returned to the presence of the ten directions, one universally summons the ten directions to divide them together.
This is also a case of mutual [classification]. Next is specific damage. If it reaches five *kaṭhina* offenses, it is heavy; if it does not reach five, it is light.
These two offenses can be mutually interchangeable, as explained in the preceding section on "mutual establishment. Regarding the light and heavy [distinctions]:

for example, if property belonging to the deceased is adjudged heavy but falls into the category of light, then damaging the permanent property (*saṃghika*) results in a *pārājika* offense. If what is adjudged light falls into the category of heavy, one incurs numerous *sthūlātyaya* offenses. This is...

"Mutual severance" refers to the interaction [of offenses]. Regarding the "double binding of two offenses," the *Xuánjì* (Record of Profundity) states that one simply takes the preceding light and heavy offenses as the two offenses.

Now, an objection is raised: when severing a light offense and entering into a heavy one, there is only a *duṣkṛta* (light offense); furthermore, when severing a heavy offense and entering into a light one, one commits only the heavy offense.
In these cases, there is a single offense mutually established for each; they cannot be called the "double binding of two offenses. Now, it says: "severing the heavy..."
When one enters a light offense while the original bond was a grave *pārājika*, and on top of this offense there is further ignorance, would this not constitute the simultaneous bond of two offenses?
The severing of the light to enter the grave may be understood by reversing this logic. Among the various commentaries, this has been handed down as a point of distinction.

Regarding the theft of property belonging to a *piṇḍola*, there are two explanations. One interpretation states that a *piṇḍola* is a monk of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) who has received the Buddha’s command.
In the present world, if one now steals this object with the intent that another shall be its master, one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*).

Even if the donor intends to offer the object to a senior elder (*sthavira*), although it has not yet been formally accepted, it already belongs to him by right, because the donor’s mind is firmly resolved upon it.

If one steals the property of other monks who have entered *parinirvāṇa*, there is only the fault of karma (*karmāpatti*), because they are not the intended masters. This is further explained as follows:
This is the interpretation of our school; those that are incorrect have not been recorded (the preceding passages have all concluded the explanation of mutual application).
Regarding the statement "from 'three' to 'precepts,'" the character *dài* (貸) has two uses: if it refers to giving goods to another, it is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*);
if it refers to borrowing goods from another, it is pronounced with the entering tone (*rùshēng*). As for "a written contract," this is like the division slips used today. Read the commentary.
This refers to the accounts of income and expenditure. To violate these constitutes an offense. Regarding the calculation of value and the restitution to the stūpa or the Saṃgha:
if there is an equivalent amount, it should be returned; if not, one should provide compensation such as a network of silk cords, and so forth.
As for the "tenfold restitution," *Śrāddhakarman* states: "If an ordained Bodhisattva takes on a disciple, he must first instruct and admonish them not to..."
Regarding negligence: if one is impoverished and has needs, or is ill, one should seek what is required on their behalf. If one lacks it oneself, one may borrow items belonging to the Triple Gem;

once recovered from illness, one must repay them according to worldly custom with a tenfold increase. As for that which differs from the Vinaya, this refers to the text of this sutra differing from the aforementioned *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
The Vinaya states that borrowing is permitted for individuals, but requires that the value be calculated and returned; it does not mention a tenfold increase.

Regarding the "number" and so forth: the doubt is that these refer to the two assemblies among the laity. As for the passage that appears similar to [the rules for] the five assemblies of the ordained, it means that if one were required to repay tenfold, the meaning would be excessively strict.
It is suspected that this refers to a layperson lending property belonging to the Triple Gem; the text states: "Once assigned, they shall repay tenfold according to secular custom.
Furthermore, based on the scriptural text, it also says: "One may keep ordained disciples," which again seems to pertain to the five assemblies of the ordained.

Assembly: Now, I shall extract and cite the meaning of the text. If [the value] is not full, be careful not to lend it. If one lends it due to illness, one must repay the principal according to the Vinaya.
Regarding the precept on possessing precious objects, the text says: if there are weapons, order them to be broken; they are not permitted to be sold, for fear they might be used for evil purposes.
The dharma of a bhikṣu is that he should encourage the abandonment of evil. As for musical instruments, they may be sold but must not be used.
(The above passages have completed the explanation of lending.

Regarding the phrase "the fourth is reaching the Dharma," it is as the text states. Regarding the phrase "the fourth is reaching the provision," the Vinaya clarifies that when Upāli arrived at a certain residence and was not provided with hospitality, he departed on that very day.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha: "If one knows [the situation] to be equal to the Dharma, one should [share] half."

[The distance] such as a *yojana* for welcoming [the guest], and so forth; if one does not act accordingly, one shall be dealt with according to the law. As for those said to "know the Dharma," they are those well-versed in the Sūtras;
those who "know the Vinaya" are those well-versed in the Vinaya; and those who "know the Mātṛkā" are those well-versed in the Abhidharma.

Regarding the "person of comprehensive knowledge" mentioned therein, this refers to the *karmavācanā* in the Vinaya concerning the *kaṭhina* robe, which is the property of the *saṃgha* present in the ten directions.

At present, those who provide for those who know the Dharma should also follow this principle. One who takes my place is one who propagates the teaching; such a person is no different from the Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "from five [reasons] up to the explanation": during the first period of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, whenever there was food, it was never given to laypeople.
They consequently criticized them, saying: "The śramaṇas only know how to receive things from others; they do not know how to practice giving to others. Because of this...
He reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "One should give him food for a guest. The bhikṣus then placed it in his hands and did not provide him with a vessel.
He again complained, saying, "The bhikṣus look upon me as if I were a small child. The Buddha said, "One should give him food using a vessel.
The bhikṣus then gave him a coarse, broken vessel, and he again felt resentment. The Buddha said, "Give him a fine vessel. This is [the rule].

Those who wander about seek only the faults of the monks. As for the two groups of householders—those who observe the five or eight precepts, those who are learned laypeople, and even those who, though not having received the precepts, possess faith and knowledge of the Buddha-dharma and have the capacity for discernment—one should preach the Dharma to them and show them cause and effect, and so forth.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one should provide offerings to kings, ministers, and others.
Regarding this, the text states: At that time, there was a royal minister who frequently went to the Bamboo Grove Monastery for recreation.

Whenever he arrived, he would request food, firewood, and lit candles and lamps. The bhikṣus wished to provide these things but feared committing an offense; yet if they did not provide them, they feared causing him distress.

Not knowing what to do, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "From now on, I authorize you to establish a formal arrangement. You may use [the monastery's resources] without having to announce it to the entire Saṃgha. (19)
Regarding the provision of money: if more is required, one should inform the Saṃgha and give it to them. As for the "nineteen coins," these were the large ancient copper coins;
they were equivalent to sixteen small coins, totaling three hundred and four [small] coins. Regarding the phrase "when wicked robbers arrive," the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
there was a thief who asked the monk in charge of food for [some of] it, but he did not give it to him. The thief said, "I am preparing this food for the Saṃgha, not for myself."
"You all," [he said], "should strike the bhikṣu; his hands and feet shall be broken and his waist severed. The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there is such a place of fear, one may beg little and give little, beg half and give half, beg much and give much, or beg everything and give everything.

One must not, on account of this, bring about the loss of life or similar harm. As for those things that can cause harm or benefit, the *Ji* (Śīla-skandha) says: 'Both causing harm and providing benefit are permitted.'"

Regarding giving food: "Detrimental" refers to when thieves come to the monastery and demand various kinds of food and drink; if one does not give them, they may burn down the monastery and so forth (as detailed).
"Beneficial" refers to those who repair the monastic dwellings, such as craftsmen and painters, as well as those who manage the property of the Sangha;
to these, one should provide morning and evening meals, as well as non-timely drinks (*vikāla-pāna*) and the like. If it is a king or someone of great power, one should likewise [provide for them].

Giving food and drink [to those who are not ordained] is not called stealing. Regarding the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun), which states that it is improper to give to those who are not beneficial, this differs from the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (Zhi).
This refers to one who defiles the household, as in the precept on defiling households (*kuladūṣaka*). The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* cites:

"Because one gives objects offered in faith to laypeople, one violates the prior mind of equanimity; furthermore, it is a perversion and confusion of the Buddha-dharma," and so forth. If [this applies] to both parties...
Regarding "knowing the Dharma and also obtaining [the item]": this refers to the distinction between the monastic and the lay.

When the monastics and the laity know that a woman is pregnant, or when a faithful donor (*dānapati*) knows [of her condition], they may equally permit [the gift] even while she is in prison. As for the layperson who knows the Dharma, it means they recognize:

"It is not appropriate for me to take the property of another’s preceptor or monk; how could I do so? Yet this destitute nun has brought it here. Thus, constrained by the circumstances, they [accept it] for the time being.
"Receiving" (or "accepting") may later be compensated for by doubling the amount, and so forth;

as for the phrase "as explained extensively in the second section," this refers to the passage in the *Anuvyañjana-śikṣāpada* on defiling families that provides an exception, which is precisely what was cited just now. Regarding the phrase "from ten up to the middle," the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"At that time, there was a householder who prepared various medicines—namely, ghee, oil, honey, ginger, pepper, *pi-pa-lie*, and so forth—and sent them [to the monks]."

They went to the Bamboo Grove Monastery (Veṇuvana-vihāra). At that time, the group of six monks rose early and stood by the gate. Seeing those who were bringing medicine for the monastery, they asked, "What is this?
They were told, "It is such-and-such medicine. The group of six said, "We wish to travel far away; first give us our share of the medicine.
They then selected the fine medicines, such as ghee and rock honey, and left behind only the dregs, which they carried into the monastery.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "From now on, you should appoint a person to distribute the medicines, dividing them equally.
If expensive medicine arrives, it should be set aside for sale. If a sick bhikṣu requests it, one should give him two and a half coins' worth.
If he requests more than that, one should seek the full value from him. Regarding what was called "two and a half coins," this is based on the ancient large coin.
"Copper coins" refers to the forty small coins currently in circulation. "Those of lower rank do not receive them" means they have no meritorious service.
"High officials do [receive them]" because they have performed meritorious deeds; thus it is so ordained. The remaining text is easy to understand and need not be elaborated upon further.
(The above passages constitute the first major section, concluding the discussion on stealing property belonging to the Triple Gem.)

Regarding the phrase "from the 'gate of arrival' (*yūshishu*) to the 'middle'": "the gate" refers to being designated by way of excluding various minor categories. "Arrival at the master" (*yūshishu*) means that because of this person, there is a master;
it is not the case that [the object] is protected [by the person] as if it were their own. Now, regarding the theft of these objects, they are categorized under two types of offenses.

Therefore, the names are listed below: first, the "primary" (*sei*), and second, the "protective" (*go*). Regarding the phrase "concerning the offense of arrival": first, there is guarding with the thought of "mine-ness" (*mamakāra*).
To reckon that an object is "mine" and to personally guard and maintain it constitutes "guarding.

This refers to the objective sphere of objects one has taken possession of and raised for oneself, such as cotton stored within a chest, and so forth. Second, there is the state of having the thought "it is mine" without personal guarding;
this is like the fields belonging to the Zhang family, where each person reckons "this field is mine," yet none of them actually guards it. The *Chao* (Excerpts) also explains this for itself.

(As stated above). Regarding hidden treasures (*pātāla-nidhi*), the *Xuánjì* (Records of the Mysterious) cites secular law and the two Vinayas and the Tripiṭaka to adjudicate them. First, according to the ten views:
if they are found within the grounds of the Triple Gem, the adjudication is based on the grounds as the primary owner.

Second, if they are on the grounds of commoners, following the Vinaya-piṭaka’s principle that "a blade and its sheath are distinct implements," [the former] should belong to the state, whereas gold, silver, and the like belong to the commoners, even if they are ancient.

The name of a person does not, furthermore, qualify them as the owner for the purpose of an inscription. Third, if [an object] is in a deserted mountain, wild field, or marsh, and there is no mind of "mine" to guard it, it is precisely an ownerless thing;
taking it involves no offense. Now, in this case, there is no mind and no one to guard it.
This is not a third category of ownerless property. It refers to the first two types of owned land;

regarding the case where a previous person buried something there and that person has since died, it is because they lack the sense of "mine," and subsequent people do not know of it, thus there is no guardian or owner.

Regarding the two phrases beginning with "as for the guardians": this refers to items that can be physically divided and are present before one, such as robes distributed at the end of the summer retreat as rewards for labor, where each person has calculated their own share;
thus it is said there is "the mind of 'mine'. Because these are entrusted to a single individual to manage, it is called "separate guardianship.
If a bhikṣu steals such an item, he incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) in relation to the guardian, just as if he had seized it at a checkpoint.

Regarding "forbidden items" and so forth: this refers to items that are illegal because they violate official decrees. Since the original owner has already severed their attachment to these objects, they possess a mind of "non-mineness" (*amama-citta*).
When such items are seized by customs officials and recorded, they are termed "separately guarded. Furthermore, it is like when a bhikṣu loses an object;

because he has severed his attachment to it, it is also called a state of "non-mineness. If the authorities recover it from a thief and take possession of it for recording, it is likewise termed "separately guarded."

Now, regarding the theft of these objects, all [the rules] are based on the expectation that the person who guards them will incur a grave offense; this is explained as the limit of severing the mind through the application of the precepts.
This is called the "mind of non-possession" (amama-citta). Ancient records failed to understand this and falsely claimed it was not the text of the *Shō*.

Regarding the phrase "now, as for the various [cases]": this refers to the seven types of offenses categorized from the two cases of "guarding" (*shouhu*) down to "mixed" (*zahui*), which extensively distinguish the characteristics of theft.

Regarding the phrase "first, as for the commission of the offense": the character "shang" (賞) in "recompensing the owner for loss" is stated by the Venerable Master (*Dade*) to be a scribal error made during translation;
it should now be read as the character "zhang" (掌), meaning to take charge of and record the guarding. If one follows the *Xuanji* (玄記), it says: [text continues].

The term *shǎng* (pronounced with the initial *cháng* and the final *shì-zhǎng*) has two meanings. First, it refers to looking upon (*zhān*) and is thus called "reward" (*shǎng*); this means protecting objects by looking after them.

Second, it refers to recompensing merit (*chóu gōng*) and is thus called "reward"; this means that when one has performed a task with merit, one bestows things as a reward. Of these two meanings, the former is intended here.

In the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* and other texts, there are two passages of text. The first passage concerns the person who guards; it describes how they diligently act as a guardian, yet unexpectedly encounter a thief.

If a bhikṣu breaks through a wall, pierces a hole, or steals by way of clandestine means, or perhaps seizes it face-to-face or robs it with a staff, this certainly does not fall within the scope of [the owner's] protection.
Thus, the aforementioned thief incurs a heavier penalty in relation to the actual owner than in relation to the person providing protection.

Furthermore, the actual owner is not entitled to demand from others that they provide restitution for the property under their protection, because this is not a fault of the person themselves. If one were to demand such property from others...

Acquisition. This constitutes a grave offense for the primary owner. Regarding the second section: this refers to a case where, due to the custodian’s failure to diligently guard the property, it is stolen.

The thief incurs an offense with respect to the custodian, not with respect to the actual owner. The custodian must repay the loss according to the teachings; if they do not repay it, the custodian incurs a grave offense.
In the text, the character for "repay" (償) is pronounced with the rising tone (*shāng*). Furthermore, the *Xiangxu* (Commentary on the Mutual Relations) states:

It is said: Regarding the two types of owners mentioned above, if one considers them from the perspective of formal ownership (*svāmya*), one does not consider them from the perspective of protection (*ārakṣā*); if one considers them from the perspective of protection, one does not consider them from the perspective of formal ownership.
One cannot incur an offense by combining both types of owners, for wealth cannot belong to two parties simultaneously; thus, the offense is not doubly incurred. Know this.

Regarding the phrase "the two most serious [offenses]," as for the character *fu* (to entrust) appearing in the *Chao* (the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan*) instead of *ji* (to entrust), the Great Virtuous One says:

"This is also an error in transcription that occurred during the time of translation. As for the *Shisong* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) and so forth, the *Chao* fully quotes the four lines from the *Shisong*.
1. A bhikṣu entrusts an object belonging to a bhikṣu to another bhikṣu. 2. Two bhikṣus entrust an object belonging to a householder to a bhikṣu. 3.
Three bhikṣus entrust an object belonging to a householder to a householder. 4. A householder entrusts an object belonging to a bhikṣu to a bhikṣu.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), chapter twenty-seven, in the context of the six groups of bhikṣus (*ṣaḍvargika-bhikṣu*), these bhikṣus were friends with another bhikṣu; that bhikṣu entrusted [an object]...
A certain man had a single alms-bowl which he gave to the group of six monks (ṣaḍvargika). On the road, he diligently guarded and protected it, but by chance he accidentally broke it.
Later, seeing the group of six monks, he explained the circumstances of what had happened. The group of six asked, "Is your bowl broken? He replied, "My bowl is not broken.

The group of six then persistently pressed him for compensation. He sought redress from them and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "If it was broken by accident, there is no need for compensation. However, if..."
"Destroying what was taken with an evil mind" (this explains the first phrase). The second [point] should be sought out and understood. Regarding "entrusting goods to a layperson":
this refers to a bhikṣu taking an object and entrusting it to one layperson to give to another layperson.

As for the two aforementioned explanations: the first is that if it was done with a good heart, there is no need to repay; the second is that if it was done with an evil mind, one must repay. If one borrows another's property, it is logically appropriate...
To repay him; regardless of whether [the recipient] is good or evil, one should have no dualistic mind. The rest is as in the text.
Regarding the phrase "reaching the third stage," the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and other sources state: "The group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) enticed away the disciples of others.
The Buddha declared this an offense of *duṣkṛta*. Because the group of six each made a vow, saying: 'If I entice away your disciples, I shall perform the Buddha-mantra.'"
Regarding the spells of the Dharma and the spells of the Saṃgha: from this day forward, bhikṣus shall not cast spells upon themselves, nor shall they cast spells upon others;
to do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. Later in the text it says: At that time, the group of six lost their robes and bowls and were about to flee together.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "From this day forward, you shall not flee yourselves, nor shall you instruct others to flee."
"Concealment. If one performs it oneself, it is auspicious. Why? Because incantation and concealment are of one kind. (The above is the Vinaya text.
As for what is called "concealment," it means causing a thief to deposit an object in one place while concealing their own form, so that people do not know [where they are].
Now, when the leader of the assembly performs the ritual for the purpose of recovering stolen goods, he should go to the place where the items were lost.

Several people shall each enter an empty room with a single robe. If the thief has already taken the goods and departed, and on the following morning the items are found therein, yet it remains unknown who took them—provided that the intent is solely upon the objects and there is no desire to identify the person—the Buddha said this is not permitted.
As for the recitation of mantras: these are evil incantations and contentious words; they are not the dharma of a śramaṇa and should not be practiced.

A newly added method for "probing with oil" is explained elsewhere. Regarding the establishment of a separate position [for the *kaji-shi*], Gen states: "This is the tradition of the masters of the past."
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) cites this; the following text will cite it itself.

Regarding the phrase "from one up to taking": as for the meaning that the owner’s mind of protection is weak and so forth, it refers to a case where the object is in another location and is stolen without being in the presence of the bhikṣu.
This concerns the thief’s mind being resolute and thorough, while the owner does not know and there is no pursuit whatsoever.

Regarding the mind toward objects: this refers to the principle of the protective mind (*ārakṣaka-citta*). If one has not yet lost the intention [to protect], it means that one maintains a mind of ownership toward the object;
that is, while the object is in storage, the mind has fundamentally not relinquished it. Later, when one sees this object in another location, one must not seize it.

Once the object has left its original place, the formal act is completed, and the status of belonging to the thief is established. In this regard, there was a case where a bhikṣu’s robes were stolen by a thief.
Not knowing that the object had been lost, he did not steal it face-to-face. Furthermore, the Vinayavibhaṅga states:

"At one time there was a bhikṣu who, when another person stole an object, took back that stolen object from the thief. He felt doubt [regarding his own action]. The Buddha said: 'This is a pārājika offense. This is the second citation of scriptural evidence.

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* contains four propositions. The first clarifies that the owner has not relinquished [the object] and the thief has not yet formed the perception of possession. The second is the reverse of the first two cases: the owner has relinquished it and the thief has formed the perception of possession.
The third is when, following one's own inclination, the owner has not relinquished it and the thief has formed the perception of possession.

The fourth is when there is no relinquishment: the owner has relinquished it and the thief has not yet formed the perception of possession. Regarding the first proposition, it says: "The original owner has not relinquished it; the one who seizes it has not yet..."

One forms the perception [that the object belongs to oneself]. In the two cases mentioned above, since the relinquishment and the acquisition have not yet been finalized, taking it away does not constitute an offense. Regarding the reversal of the two aforementioned conditions:
if the owner has already relinquished it and the thief has already formed the perception [of ownership], one must never take it back. This refers to the third case of stealing.
Once the act has been completed and the intention to take possession is formed, it cannot be taken back.

Therefore, in the third phrase of the fourfold classification regarding theft in that Vinaya, any bhikṣu who commits the theft is charged with a grave offense (pārājika). The text states: "There was a visiting bhikṣu who, departing at dawn, forgot his robes and bowl.
At that time, a resident of the monastery, while inspecting the rooms, saw these robes and bowl and immediately gave rise to the intent to steal."

The mind shifts toward one place and conceals it. Since there is already the intent to steal (*steya-citta*) and the object has been lifted from its original location, the offense of *pārājika* is established.
Furthermore, another bhikṣu arrives later, sees this robe and bowl, and again gives rise to the intent to steal;

he moves them and places them in another location, and likewise the offense of *pārājika* is established with equal gravity (as stated in the Vinaya). Now, according to this principle, if [the items] do not yet belong to the thief, how can the offense of *pārājika* be established?

Since the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Wen) has already concluded the case of the "barbarian," we know that the previous person [the owner] had made a definitive claim. Why, then, would one need to wait for the owner to develop the intention to relinquish it?

Therefore, it says: "Even if one's own mind does not relinquish it... and so forth. The later text of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "At that time, the owner of those clothes and goods traveled to a place ahead.
Suddenly remembering them, he returned to take them back; having taken them, there was no offense" (the above is the Vinaya text). — Ancient Record.

This phrase is frequently cited, yet it does not refer to the *Chao-wen* (Excerpts). Since it states that the previous person has definitely taken [the robe] and the offense of *pārājika* is established, one must not take it back even if one later sees the object, provided the owner did not form an intention to relinquish it.

Now, according to this Vinaya text, even if the owner of the robe does not form an intention to relinquish it but returns to take it away, there is no offense in either case. How, then, could there be a discrepancy? This is what [the present commentator] reconciles.

However, according to the Vinaya, if one takes back an object previously forgotten, provided there was not even a single thought that someone had stolen it and one simply took it away as one's own property,
what offense could there be? According to the *Śarīptra-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Chao), if one hides an object and another person steals it, and later when the object returns,

one recognizes it as having been stolen by a thief and forms the conviction that one has acquired it, one is definitely charged with the offense of *pārājika*, even if it was one's own intention [to hide it].
It is not abandoned, nor is it appropriate to seize it. This passage from the *Yao* (Excerpts) is cited as the textual basis for judging theft in ritual practice.
One must consider that citing the text is difficult because its circumstances differ from the meaning of the *Chao* (Copies). As for the fourth case:

it refers to when a thief-monk takes an object away, but the monk’s mental connection to it is severed; subsequently, the thief is either mocked on the road or pursued and caught by others, and he abandons the object.
The object was then left behind and given to two thieves; regarding this object, both parties were without any intention [of ownership]. This object remained in a state of indeterminate ownership.
Later, when a virtuous person recovered this object and lifted it from the ground, it immediately belonged to that subsequent taker.
If the original owner-monk were to seize it back from the latter, he would properly incur a grave offense (pārājika); therefore, such an act is not permitted.
Regarding "the second is seizing face-to-face": this refers to when a thief robs someone directly in their presence; hence, it is called "seizing face-to-face before one's eyes.

Regarding "because the sense of guarding and protecting is strong," etc.: this means that the owner has a conscious intention to guard and protect the object, and thus it is said that "the sense [of ownership] is strong.

As for the one who seizes the object, since they have taken it directly from the owner, even though the object has entered their hands, they remain hesitant in their mind, fearing what might happen later.

However, in cases such as being robbed, because one has not yet attained a state of decisive realization regarding the characteristics [of the object], the original owner’s property has been taken away;

yet, since one has partially developed the intention [to claim it] while not having completely relinquished it, it is said that "the mind is weak and has not yet abandoned [it]. If the mind is in such a state, it can also be considered stolen.

In the second section, the citation of scriptural evidence, the meaning is divided into two parts. First, the text consisting of three phrases from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and other sources is cited as proof.
Second, the conclusion as stated above summarizes the characteristics of the perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*) regarding whether one obtains or does not obtain [the offense].

Regarding the first part, concerning the *Mahāsāṃghika*, it says: "At that time, there was a bhikṣu traveling on a road who was plundered by bandits. The bhikṣus said to one another: 'These bandits are few.'"
"We are many; let us join forces with our companions and recover our belongings. They then seized bricks and stones and pursued the thieves.
From afar, the bhikṣu reviled them, saying, "You wretched thieves! Although we have shaved off our hair and beards, do you now think we have shaved off both our hands as well?
At that, the thieves were terrified; they immediately dropped their robes and bowls and scattered in all directions. Since that bhikṣu had not yet...
If one forms the thought that [the items] have been lost, there is no offense in taking back the original objects.

If one has already formed the thought that they were lost and then takes them back, it constitutes a case of a thief seizing the property of another thief. Now, having briefly taken this up and formed the thought that they were lost, the following summarizes the three points.
Furthermore, "darkly pursuing thieves" and so forth refers to the second point: there was a bhikṣu traveling on a road who was plundered by thieves and lost his robes and bowl.
Having done so, he entered the forest and hid it. At that time, the thief thought to himself, "My companions are many, yet this object is small;

it would be better to seek more to add to our share. He then hid his robes and bowl, covering them in one place. When the bhikṣu saw this, he waited until the thief had departed and then took the robes and bowl.
If that bhikṣu originally had no intention of relinquishing them, he incurs no offense in taking them.
[This constitutes] an offense. If one has formed the intent to abandon [the object], it is improper to take it; if one does take it, it constitutes the theft of stolen property from a thief.

If the value reaches five [units], it constitutes a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*). Regarding the term "in secret" mentioned in the text, this refers to hiding the object on one's person so that the thief cannot see it;

it does not mean that darkness of night is called "secret. Furthermore, "the thief arriving and informing others" refers to the third case. There was a bhikṣu traveling on a road who was [attacked] by thieves.
They plundered his robes and bowl. The thieves then proceeded along the road. The bhikṣu followed behind, watching them from afar and pursuing them without ceasing.
As they gradually drew near a village, the thieves began to divide the goods. The bhikṣu said to them, "We are renunciants who rely entirely upon others for our livelihood;
you should give me back my robes and bowl. The thieves replied, "You wretched śramaṇa! We have already spared your life; how could we possibly give it back?"
He immediately went to seek his robes. The bhikṣu said, "The village is nearby now; you would endanger my life, and [the robes] could not be obtained.
The ministers and elders in the village are all your kinsmen or disciples; if I were to speak of you to them, you would surely suffer harm.
Through such intimidation, the thief released the items and departed. The bhikṣu took possession of them; he does not commit an offense. This applies even if the thief becomes angry.
"Blame! Entrust you with telling others; I am ultimately not afraid. I will not return your property.

If a bhikṣu uses skillful means to speak thus to a village headman and thereby obtains the object through consolation and persuasion, there is no offense. However, if one tells others to kill or harm [the owner], that is impermissible.
(The above three sentences all refer to cases where the owner has not yet formed the intention to relinquish the object; in such cases, taking it is not an offense.)

Regarding the phrase "the various clauses above" and so forth: this refers to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, where each clause concludes [with a specific judgment]. The intent of the *Chao* (the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-ṭīkā*) is that it fears prolixity;

therefore, it merely summarizes the preceding three clauses at this point. That is to say: if one simply forms the thought that [the object] has been lost—regardless of whether the thief’s intent is certain or uncertain—one must not seize it.

This constitutes the mental state of relinquishment (*tyāga-citta*). If the thief’s intent is certain—that is, if they have definitely resolved to take it and possess no fear of being caught—the *Chao* states that [it is not relinquished].

The Master, based on the previous case of a bhikṣu stealing property, clarified that it constitutes a grave offense. Now, this decision regarding taking [property] out of fear is also established according to the principle of belonging to a thief;

even if one does not have the thought that it has been lost, it is still improper to take it. As for what is called "extremely grave" (*pārājika*), it refers to the Vinaya, which states that if the authorities confiscate property and one takes it back, there is no offense.
Thus, we know that the principle of official confiscation is stronger than the mind of a thief’s seizure.
Weakness. To seize the weak by means of strength: if a bhikṣu anticipates that an official will act as the master and take it for himself, there is no offense.

Regarding theft where the face is not present before one: according to the Vinaya, based on the principle of seizing the weak by means of strength, it is known that the intent of theft is decisive and thorough.

In this sense of "theft," the strength [of the force] prevails; the bhikṣu’s mind of protection is weak, and thus he cannot prevail over the strength of the seizure. Even if he knows the place of concealment, he likewise...
Regarding the statement, "It is not permissible to take [them]; as for a bhikṣu being captured by bandits," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

"The disciple already belongs to the bandits; because this is a case of violent seizure, it is grave. The disciple’s physical body is the primary retribution (*vipāka*), whereas the bandits’ power and utility are weak.
When fleeing, the strong retribution pursues, while the weak utility follows along; therefore, there is no offense."

Regarding the phrase "from the four [types of objects] to their application," the *Śīla-śāstra* (Commentary on the Precepts) concerning the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and other texts states: "In principle, the formal acceptance (*upasaṃpadā*) is established because the object is not fixedly assigned;
rather, one becomes the owner [of it] subsequently. This is unlike worldly currency, which can be fixedly assigned according to the person, the place, the use, and the determination."
This refers to causing damage and forming a bond [of debt] accordingly. "Do not follow a thief who possesses nothing" means fearing that the person ahead might commit theft because of the request;
thus, it is the bhikṣu who is capable of providing instruction. "If one obtains [clothing] from a thief" and so forth means that after purchasing clothing from him, the clothing is subsequently seen.

Although one knows that these are one's own belongings, one must not seize them without compensation; rather, one should return their value. To seize them without returning the value constitutes an offense, calculated according to the monetary amount.

As for the present case where one might steal property belonging to the Triple Gem and so forth: this means that if one originally knew it was property of the Buddha, one may subsequently use it for the Buddha’s purposes;

the same applies to the Sangha, though they may not be used interchangeably. If, however, one is utterly unaware of this, then it is not discussed [as an offense]. Regarding the phrase "the five arrivals":
The text says: At that time, there was a high official who had violated the king’s law; his wealth and property were rightfully to be confiscated by the state.
The authorities dispatched men to guard the door of his house. Then, the nun Nanda went on her alms-round and arrived at that residence.

The woman said to the nun, "Āryā, my husband has committed a crime for which he deserves the death penalty, and his property has been seized by the state. I wish to entrust you with some precious ornaments. If I am..."
“...be released. I shall pay you the wage due; if I die, I shall give it to you as a gift. The bhikṣuṇī filled the bowl with earth, covered it, and departed.
When the gatekeeper saw this, he asked, “What is in the bowl? But the bhikṣuṇī would not show him.
He called out to her again and again, and she showed him out of fear. The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, “From now on, [it shall not be done].”
If one finds concealed valuables, and if they belong to a person who has committed an offense against the king’s law but has not yet been apprehended, the one who finds them may take them.

If the owner has already been apprehended, the finder should say: “The World-Honored One has established a precept that does not permit me to accept this. If the owner says, “Give it to the stūpa,” then one may take it;

however, one must not conceal it. Instead, one should openly carry it along the road. If anyone asks about it, one should say, “It is property for the stūpa,” and so forth. If permission is granted, one may carry it away.

If one departs from the wholesome, they shall immediately return if they do not comply. According to the *Yuanzhong* (The Source), this refers to a *bhikṣuṇī*. The *Chao* (The Abstract) states that "a *bhikṣu*" implies that monks and nuns share the same precepts.

If the authorities have not yet confiscated [the property], it is expected to be returned to its original owner; if it has already been confiscated, it is expected to be protected for the owner. Regarding the phrase "sixth, taking": it refers to the act of seizing.
The *Vinaya-śāstra* asks: "May one accept clothing from a madman? Answer: "Sometimes it may be accepted, and sometimes it may not. How may it be accepted?
If a bhikṣu does not know the whereabouts of his parents, brothers, sisters, or others, and [the madman] offers an object to the bhikṣu, it may be accepted;
this refers to the case where the primary owner is unknown. How may it not be accepted? If the parents and others can be identified, yet [the madman] does not offer it with his own hand...
"Given; it cannot be taken. This refers to the expectation of the guardian.
Regarding the phrase "the seventh case arrives," the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing) states: The Dharma Master said, "I wish to manifest that the thief is without offense.
Why is there no offense? The answer is: "Because there is no owner, there is no offense. If a person's child falls away from the path [of discipline], and the parents... [text ends].
If a person is sent away by their parents through the ritual of water-consecration (*abhiṣeka*), or if their parents have died, a bhikṣu who takes such a person incurs no offense.

If the person owes a debt to another, the bhikṣu may take them away without committing a transgression. (The above is from the *Śāstra*). Xuan says: According to the intent of the aforementioned treatise, a child does not belong to the king, but belongs only to their parents.
Since they have been sent away by their parents, or because the parents have died, the matter lacks an owner; therefore, the present case is compared [to that].

The Master [Kāśyapa] said: "I shall depart without incurring offense. Furthermore, this child previously owed a debt; now I am merely taking the person away, not taking the debt. The commentary states:
"By analogy with this, those who cross boundaries privately are like thieves. They do not pay royal taxes, yet they possess merit and commit no crime.
Thus, Saccaka Nigaṇṭha said: "Not paying the king’s tribute does not constitute theft. An external objection states: "The text of the *Chao* clearly explains that it is [the duty of] guarding..."
Regarding the meaning of "viewing" (*dṛṣṭi*). Why is it said that there is no offense for one who steals from such a person? Answer:

"Viewing" clarifies that [the person] is not the actual owner, but merely a guardian who watches over the property. Now, as for the thief, he regards the person as having already been dispatched by his parents;
thus, he is also not the actual owner. This is like a guardian who comes to watch because of the thief; if it were a debtor, he would merely owe the person wealth, but [in this case], the body...
It is not bound to that [place]. To keep watch over a person and know their whereabouts is also called "keeping watch.

Regarding a slave who commits a grave offense, this occurs because he came for the purpose of stealing a person; it does not carry the meaning of "keeping watch. This is also seen in the treatises (*śāstra*).
It says: "If another's slave, a bhikṣu says to him: 'You are suffering here; why do you not run away? If you go to that place, you will certainly...'"
"One shall obtain peace and happiness. Upon hearing these words, the slave first resolves to go; this is auspicious. If he lifts one foot, it is light; if he lifts both feet, it is heavy.

If the slave has already fled and [the master] urges him to depart quickly, he incurs the heavy offense according to the words [spoken]. Or, if it is said, "It is a time of scarcity here, but abundance there," and the slave immediately flees, there is no offense as he was not instructed [to stay].
Or, having heard of abundance and joy, he pursues a bhikṣu; if he encounters difficulties on the way and calls out for him to be pursued, in all such cases, there is no offense.
Regarding the offense: this alone constitutes an offense when there is no intention to employ a stratagem to cause the person to turn their back on their master and so forth;

in all other cases, there is no offense. As for "the watchman giving robes and such," this refers to the act of guarding and watching; it is merely a different term for "summoning. That Vinaya states:

"When a watchman gave a robe to a bhikṣu, he did not accept it because he suspected that [the watchman] was not the rightful owner. He reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said: 'Let it be according to the donor's disposition.'"
In the following passage, it concerns the person guarding the food and the thief who gave *khajjaka* (solid food) to a bhikṣu. The bhikṣu thought to himself, "This is not his [the owner's] food;

I will not accept it. The Buddha said, "This is indeed the donor’s food. It is permitted to receive it after washing one's hands. However, it is not appropriate to beg for it from the one who stole it."
This means that knowing an object does not belong to another and then begging for it from them constitutes teaching another to steal; therefore, it is improper.

Regarding the statement in the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* concerning the determination [of the offense]: "The meaning of 'stealing' is extremely manifold," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "It encompasses both animate and inanimate objects."

The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "If a bhikṣu, based on the conditions of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, gives rise to unwholesome conduct toward their respective objects—whether committing grave or light offenses, and so forth—if such a person consumes poison or is bitten by a snake..."

The Venerable One said: "The character 'shè' (螫) has two meanings. The minor sense is pronounced 'shì' (釋) or 'zhé' (哲), referring to the venomous water contained within the folds at the edges of a snake's wide-open mouth; one can perceive this when it penetrates the flesh.

The major sense is pronounced 'shè' (螫), as seen with the large snakes common in Lingnan, which spit poisonous gas from their open mouths, killing a person upon contact. (The *Huozi* [豁子] says: "Liu [劉] refers to the spitting...")
Poisonous gas harms people. One who commits such an offense refers to the crime of theft. This is judged according to twelve factors:
the "able to steal" refers to the six sense organs, such as the eye; the "object stolen" refers to the six sensory objects, such as form.
Because the conduct violates the Vinaya, it is called "unlawful practice. One commits such an offense because of that person's consumption of poison or being bitten by a snake.
To secretly look at forms and so forth constitutes a grave or light offense; therefore, it is said that one commits such offenses.
If a person steals earth, water, fire, wind, and so on, these are all judged according to the six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*) and subsumed under the precept against stealing.

As for the phrase "the explanation reaches," this cites the commentary by Paramārtha. Regarding the stealing of the six objects (*ṣad-viṣaya*), just as with the internal six sense organs (*ṣad-āyatana*), so too regarding the external six...

Regarding the "dust" (kleśa), it is categorized into four types: first, stealing of form; second, stealing of sound by reciting [the scriptures] below; third, stealing of fragrance, taste, and touch by smelling [the objects] below;
and fourth, stealing of the Dharma by means of secret formulas and the like. As for the "various seers" (ṛṣi), they are the Āraṇas.
As for the "chest-crawling snakes," this refers to all footless snakes that move along the ground using their chests. Poisonous drugs may be understood accordingly.
If someone is bitten by this snake or at some time afflicted by poison, one should simply draw a rishi or write a single character upon his heart;
this character is a mantra. If the person who has been poisoned should see it, the poison will immediately be withdrawn and all illnesses will be cured.
One should only pay the price set by the rishi; now, having stolen [this method] and recovered, you have not paid the price.

[If the value is] "straight" (i.e., full), it constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*); if not full, it is light. Thus the text says: "Whether one commits a grave offense or a light offense, etc. (and so forth).
The commentaries, such as the *Mishu Shu*, do not permit others to transmit [these teachings]; the same applies to stealing a look [at them] (this clarifies the theft of color/form).

As for "reciting," etc., it means that there may be someone who understands [them] and recites incantations or arts to cure illness; these are secret methods, and if one wishes to learn them, one must pay directly. Now, a bhikṣu [steals them] secretly...
"Listen. To calculate the value [of the object] constitutes an offense (this clarifies the theft of sound). The same should be understood for smelling, tasting, and touching. The Commentary states:

There are teachers who can prepare medicines such that a patient is cured simply by smelling them. If a bhikṣu steals to smell them, he commits an offense according to their calculated value (this clarifies the theft of [insects]).

Or there may be a marvelous medicine such that the disease is cured by tasting it. If a bhikṣu steals to taste it, he commits an offense according to its calculated value (this clarifies the theft of flavor). Or there may be a person..."
"Excellent medicinal arts: touching [the patient] can cure the illness. A bhikṣu steals the touch; calculating its value constitutes an offense" (this clarifies "stealing by touch").

Regarding "secret formulas, essential arts, and so forth," this clarifies "stealing the Dharma through the mind. When a bhikṣu receives the Dharma from a teacher, he observes it with his mind and perceives that it will cure [his ailment].
Having received the Dharma from another teacher, he does not pay the fee; this constitutes theft. As for the phrase "next, up to 'knowing,'" the previous three [cases]...
"Those who know" refers to earth, water, and fire. "Earth" means encroaching upon another's boundary. "Water" also concerns times of drought; for one bucket of water, the price is five *qián*.
If one does not pay for it, or even if it is not a time of drought, if there is good water in a well fit for use such as boiling tea and so forth, and one requires it—one bucket costs five *wén*.
If one comes here and steals this water, it constitutes an offense. As for "fire," it is as follows:

In the winter months, there were charcoal fires within rooms. If one waits until another is absent and steals the fire away, the offense is determined according to the value of what was taken and the location where it was left behind.
A Venerable One said: "Furthermore, in Taiyuan during the winter months, when the market is held and the cold is extreme, there are those who set up rice-fermentation rooms;

anyone who enters them briefly must pay a fee. Also, at the marketplaces in the Eastern Capital, there are people selling fire to warm their hands; if one does not pay for it now," [the same principle applies].
"Directly. This refers to the total completion of the offense. Regarding the phrase "there being [a value] up to the direct," Xuán says:

In the commentaries on the *Śāstra*, it is merely stated that by chanting incantations over a fan to produce wind that touches the body, the illness is cured. If a bhikṣu shakes it stealthily, he commits an offense based on the calculated value; this is the theft of wind.
