When returning silk on the balance, one relies upon its weight (*jin-liang*); as for the horizontal beam atop the balance, it is used for measurement, yet here it is erroneous.
The *dou*, *chi*, and *cun*. These three types were used in government markets; there was nothing that did not accord with these small measures.
This small *shi* (one *nanfu* unit) was universally used in the Southern Regions. It was not a contraction, but was unique to the Ji-Zhou dynasty in the land of Han.

Since it is cited as proof for the measurement of the *bō* (alms bowl), we know that it was also used in Western countries. As for "six feet being one *bu*," this refers to approximately the six feet of the Ji-Zhou dynasty.
One *bu* (step). Regarding "the *hu* (suddenly) being the precursor to the *si* (fibre)": the *Suanjing* (Arithmetic Classic) states that this measurement originates from the *hu-hu* (the sudden).

When the silk emerges from the mouth of the silkworm for the first time, it is called the *hu-si* (sudden-fibre); this refers to how it suddenly exists and suddenly vanishes, or suddenly appears and suddenly disappears.
Ten *hu* make one *si*; ten *si* make one *hao*; ten *hao* make one *li*; ten *li* make one *fen*; ten *fen* make one *cun*; ten *cun* [make one *chi*].
Ten *chi* make one *zhang*; ten *zhang* make one *yin*; ten *yin* make one *pi*.

These measurements take the *hu* as their primary unit, all of which accumulate to form the *Ji-Zhou* (Western Zhou) foot-measure. Regarding "the Guanzhong region": "Guan" refers to the capital within the passes;

in the eastern province there was early on the Tongguan Pass, and in the northeast, Puzhou has the Pujin Pass and Longmen Pass. "Fu" refers to the Three Fu (the three commanderies surrounding the capital).
[The regions include] Dongfufeng, Dongxi, Zhunyi, Zhong, and Jingzhao (and so forth). Regarding the statement "now reaching one chi":
as for the fivefold inch-measure (*cun*), this is one *jianchi* (span-measure), which is two feet. Furthermore, among the five types of measures, this is the Zhou measure of the Ji dynasty.

"Rate" (shuì) means the standard rule (*dharma*). Using this as the basis, the dimensions of two *zhàng* and four *chǐ* in width and one *zhàng* and two *chǐ* in length precisely define the measurements of the longitudinal and transverse spans.
A question arises: the original text of the *Prātimokṣa* states that the length is twelve *vitasti* of the Buddha and the width is seven *vitasti*.
This would logically correspond to a length of two *zhàng* and four *chǐ* and a width of one *zhàng* and four *chǐ*. Why, then, does the commentary instead state [the following]?
[The measurement] is two *zhang* and four *chi* wide, which contradicts the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*. Answer: There are several interpretations. First, Xuán says:

"What is the length in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) is the width in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Wufen lü); what is the width in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* is the length in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. (This is entirely unreasonable. Next, Zuónán says:

"In India, they refer to this by taking 'length' as 'width'. (This is also only partially explanatory. Now, following Bǎo, it is said that in Western countries, the east is considered the superior direction; [this applies to] the monastery (*saṃghārāma*).
The gates are mostly oriented toward the east, and the rooms are likewise;

is it not the case that they are long from east to west, measuring twelve *vitasti* (two zhang four chi), from the front pillar to the rear pillar? They are wide from south to north, measuring seven *vitasti*.

It measures one *zhang* and four *chi*. From the pillar of the southern ridge-beam to this [current] ridge-beam pillar—that is, within the text of the *Prātimokṣa*—it is twelve units long and seven wide;

this is specifically calculated according to the Western Land (India). As for the current text of the *Chao* stating it is two *zhang* and four *chi* wide, this is stated according to this land (China);
that is to say, south of the Divine Continent (China), monasteries and dwellings are mostly oriented toward the south. From the front steps...
From the central pillar to the rear pillar, it is logically appropriate to state that they are twenty-four *zhang* long and fourteen *zhang* wide.
Following the convention of the Western Regions (India), where north and south are termed "width" (*guǎng*) and east and west are termed "length" (*cháng*), there is no further need for elaboration.

If one adheres to this explanation, one merely converts the measurements from *chi* [Chinese feet] while leaving the width and length unchanged; this constitutes the definitive rule. If calculated using the Tang *chi*, the length would be twenty *zhang*.

It is slightly less than one zhang, one chi, six cun, and eight li in width. Regarding the statement that "the interior is taken as the limit," the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), fascicle 13, states:
"This refers to the central line drawn from the pillars beneath the front and rear eaves. Three chi outside this line constitute the exterior;
two chi beneath the eave are considered the exterior and are not included within the limit. Thus, the interior is taken as the limit, specifically the threshold of the inner door."

"Outside is for the purpose of illuminating the exterior. This refers to the "light" within the context of light and darkness. Regarding the phrase "the walls are one *zhang* and two *chi* high," Master Xuán says:
"The *Chao* follows the measurement of two *chi* as a *jieshou* (cubit). However, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, two *zhang*, four *chi*, and four *cun* constitute a *jieshou*.
Thus, if the height is only one *zhang*, it means that one *chi* used here corresponds to two [standard] *chi*. As for the phrase "if it reaches the master":

As stated in the text. Regarding "a place difficult to reach" and "a place protected by the King’s decree": Xuánzàng says these refer to places such as the imperial gardens, parks, and mausoleums of the present dynasty.
Regarding "not allowing passage for a ladder with twelve rungs": this means the ladder has twelve rungs, with a distance of one *quan* (fist-width) between each rung.
One *zhǒu* (cubit) consists of eight *chí* (feet). Calculating the total length of the twelve rungs, it measures two *zhàng*, one *chí*, and six *cùn*.
If the four sides are not open, such that this ladder cannot move back and forth across the vermilion [floor] or a grass cart cannot turn around, it is a "constricted space" (vighāta-sthāna).

The citation below from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* regarding "one *vyāma*" intends to clarify that if there is no wide space, one is permitted to take [the measurement] from another school; the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* contains no such text.
Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "A constricted space refers to within one *vyāma* on all four sides of a house where there is ground for a stūpa, or even a deep pit."

In such cases, the formal procedures for making an assignment (*pradeśana*) are entirely invalid. Since they are already invalid when only one of the two conditions is present as described in the Vinaya, how much more so when both are present?
If the condition was absent at the time of the initial assignment but suddenly appears later, it constitutes a hindrance; yet the prior legal act remains intact.

Regarding the statement "even reaching [the tree] constitutes an offense," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) explains that a "hollow tree" refers to a large tree with a hollow interior that is suitable for use as a dwelling place.
"Shady side of a mountain cliff" refers to a cave beneath a cliff that is also suitable for use as a dwelling. "Downward-facing mountain forest" means being situated below a mountain;
these two are called "shady sides of a cliff. They are suitable for use as dwellings. Regarding the necessity of establishing boundaries:

if one dwells in such places as caves on these mountain cliffs, and if the space within is spacious, it requires great effort to partition it; therefore, one must establish limits by partitioning it off.

Furthermore, one must obtain the formal authorization (*jñapti*) and consent of the Saṃgha. If the construction exceeds the prescribed dimensions or if the ground has not been prepared beforehand, one incurs a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

Because failing to adhere to the measurements results in excessive labor and the neglect of one's spiritual practice (*mārgakarma*), it is clear that both monastic and private grounds must be formally requested for permission to build;
this refutes the views of the ancient masters. The ancients said: "In the case of monastic grounds, fearing they might obstruct the Saṃgha’s enjoyment [of the site], one must [seek permission]."

The question is raised: "If it is necessarily one's own private ground, what is the use of performing the formal act of begging (*yācanā*)? Now it is said that since there are both monastic grounds and private grounds, one must beg for them both.

Below, the *Cīvara-vastu* of the *Mahāsāṃghika* is cited to explain the characteristics in detail. The *Śrīlāta-śikṣā-saṃgraha* (or *Shan-chao*) presents three points: first, when there is no person capable of performing the *karmavācana*, the method of oral assignment is used;
second, although one is capable of performing the *karmavācana*, if the residence is somewhat distant, then given these circumstances, one may simply appoint a person to go [in one's stead].

Disposal. Third, regarding the four types of "inferior" cases, this clarifies that [the rite] is not accomplished according to the Dharma. Following the previous two sections, these are analyzed according to the text.
Within the third section, "one who has passed a year" refers to someone who requested the ritual last year but only begins the construction this year;

such a person is difficult to determine [as qualified] and is negligent, and thus one should not provide them with instructions. Second, "one from another boundary" refers to those who are members of a monastic community belonging to a different boundary.
One does not know of such matters as obstructions or difficulties within this boundary. Third, regarding those who construct many private rooms:
if among the community of monks one person does not build a room, or even two or three do not, while the rest all build rooms, this is also not called "directing" (authorization).

This means that since the construction of so many rooms causes distress and disorder for both [the builders and the residents], it is not permitted. If it is a place of obstruction or difficulty, it refers to the inhabitants of that difficult location.
This is not called "instructing. It means that one remains personally obstructive and parsimonious toward others, and is unable to cause others to be free from parsimony;
therefore, it is not permitted. This very Vinaya states: "A trustworthy person shall oversee. Since those mentioned above are clearly not trustworthy persons, they are in no way fit to assign duties.
Regarding the *Sarvāstivāda* and other schools, the question asks: "In this assignment of duties..."

"One may construct [a dwelling] upon a portion of land that has been formally assigned; it may not be done in other places. If this is so, since it already corresponds with the location, why is it not permitted for another person to build a room upon it?

This is because the two phrases from the *Śāstra* are cited together as constituting a total violation; hence it is said that "all are *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. The *Jie shu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "However, regarding this mutual..."
Exceeding these two rooms in both width and length constitutes one room; this is a single offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* resulting from a single act.
Xuan says: The Vinaya contains nine distinct cases. Now, in contrast to the precept regarding robes, these are divided into three groups of three. As for the first three cases:

1. Exceeding the limit in length and exceeding the limit in width (an offense of *niḥsargika-pāyattika* regarding leftover robe-cloth). 2. Exceeding the limit in length and equal to the limit in width (an offense of *niḥsargika-pāyattika* regarding leftover robe-cloth).

3. Exceeding the limit in length and less than the limit in width (no offense regarding leftover robe-cloth). Regarding the next three phrases: 1. Equal to the limit in length and exceeding the limit in width (an offense of *pāyattika* regarding leftover robe-cloth).

2. Equal to the limit in length and equal to the limit in width (no offense regarding the robe; an offense of *pāyattika*). 3. Equal to the limit in length and less than the limit in width (no offense for either the robe or the dwelling).
Regarding the latter three cases: first, when the length is less than the prescribed measure but the width exceeds it (the residual cloth of the robe does not constitute an offense);

second, when the length is less than the prescribed measure but the width is exactly as prescribed (both are without offense); third, when both the length and the width are less than the prescribed measure (both are without offense). Furthermore, to clarify that the robe is not an offense:

the Vinaya text provisionally refers only to the non-offense regarding the *pāyattika* (offense of expiation), but according to the Śāstra, there is no lack of a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense). Know this. If the robe is being made but not yet finished...

Regarding "one who acts for the sake of inclusion": this refers to a single person acting alone to construct a dwelling of excessive size. Now, "one who acts for the sake of inclusion" refers to two people acting together;
since each individual has no share of a full dwelling, but only a half-share, because it is small, there is no offense.

If one were to calculate the share per person and find that it reaches the full measure, then even though many people have constructed it together, since the dwelling is large, [the offense is incurred].

When calculating the number of people, beyond each person's allotted share, there are still those who possess more; thus, everyone commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. As for the question regarding the gravity of the offense, the intent of the question is as follows:

"Regarding extra robes, one commits the offense only when they exceed the limit collectively; however, regarding dwellings, one commits the offense even if they exceed the limit individually. Why are these cases not the same?

If, according to the rules on robes, one commits the offense when they exceed the limit collectively, why is it now cited that one commits the offense when they exceed the limit individually? [The answer follows: *Note: This passage addresses a technical point in the Vinaya concerning the distinction between collective and individual transgressions regarding the possession of extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*) and the construction of monastic dwellings.*

The meaning is this: a dwelling is something one constructs oneself; because the potential for causing disturbance and confusion is profound, even mutual transgressions constitute an offense. The substance of the robe, however, is not something one constructs oneself; it is merely due to greed and accumulation that an offense occurs, and thus the nature of the transgression is somewhat lighter. It requires both factors to coincide for an offense to be committed. If that is so, since a dwelling constitutes an offense even through mutual transgression, why would a robe require both factors to coincide for an offense? Answer: A dwelling is regulated within the category of "transgressions" (*āpatti*); a mutual transgression is immediately established as an offense. A robe, however, is regulated within the category of "prohibitions" (*pratiṣedha*); it is only when both conditions coincide that an offense is established. Furthermore, regarding a dwelling, the act of construction itself is the primary factor; therefore, even if the materials are provided by another, the act of building it oneself constitutes an offense. Regarding a robe, the act of acquisition is the primary factor; therefore, even if one has no intention to wear it, the mere act of obtaining it constitutes an offense. Thus, although the two cases appear similar, their underlying principles differ. Regarding robes, this is a full offense (*sāpattika*). Thus, both [the one who makes it] and [the one who wears it] likewise commit an offense. As for the offense of exceeding the prescribed measurements when receiving instructions, Xuán says:
"This refers to the second instruction among the final four clauses of the Vinaya. These four clauses were not recorded because they were not urgent."
Question: Why is it said only "offense" (*āpatti*)? What are the names of these indeterminate offenses (*aniyata-āpatti*)? The *Xiāngsū* (Commentary on Characteristics) states:

"Because one wishes for a single term to comprehensively conclude two offenses, it is stated simply as 'offense. Therefore, the subsequent sentence says: 'If the owner of the dwelling incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the teacher who was defiled incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If it were definitively stated that he commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, it would not include the *sthūlātyaya* of the defiling teacher; if it were definitively stated that he commits a *sthūlātyaya*..."

Furthermore, the *thullaccaya* (grave offense) of the householder is not included here. Now, it is simply stated as "offense" (*āpatti*). This means that one must act according to the circumstances at the time.
Since the *thullaccaya* is not fixed, if the householder is the primary owner of the construction and commits an offense of excess himself, both the householder and the builder are at fault.

If the householder measures and calculates according to the rules, but the person receiving the instruction does not follow suit and exceeds the limit, then the person receiving the instruction commits a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense).

Furthermore, it must be understood that if a skilled craftsman who has received instructions builds a house in conjunction with another and exceeds the prescribed measurements, he too commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense;

this is because he possesses a share in the dwelling and is also the owner. If the craftsman has no share in the dwelling himself and merely constructs an excessive building for another, he commits only a *sthūlātyaya* offense, as he is not the owner and thus lacks a personal claim to the property. As it is said:

A "master craftsman" refers to someone within the Sangha who is skilled in construction and capable of building dwellings; such a person is designated as a master craftsman, and for him, this offense applies.
If it concerns worldly artisans and the like, they are not included in this deliberation. It is not the same as what the *Huainanzi* says—that it refers to a layperson.
If one who has previously received the five or eight precepts commits this, they incur a *thullaccaya* (grave offense); this would then completely result in a foolish teaching.
Regarding "obstructing [the path] or causing separation from two locations," etc.: according to the Vinaya text, there are three sets of four and one set of twelve phrases.
This is the first complete phrase; the remaining eleven phrases are all abbreviated versions. The Vinaya states:

"If one has not been assigned a location by the Saṃgha, and it exceeds the prescribed measure, or there is difficulty or obstruction, there are two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and two *duṣkṛta* offenses. This refers to the second phrase above.
This follows the previous pattern; however, within the obstructing and difficult conditions, they are mutually reduced. In the third case, there are obstructions but no difficulties;

in these two instances, both result in two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and one *dukkaṭa*. In the final three cases, the obstructions and difficulties are mutually extinguished, or both are present, as previously described.
Only the Saṃgha does not assign [the site]; it is neither excessive nor mutually deficient. This is the second triad. The Saṃgha does not assign [the site] and it is not excessive;
this serves as the heading. Obstacles and difficulties may both exist or be absent. This is the first triad of the Saṃgha. The third triad:

the Saṃgha assigns [the site], it is excessive, and it follows the heading; this yields three phrases. The fourth triad: the Saṃgha assigns [the site], it is not excessive, and it serves as the heading. It is also...
It is so. Now, this *Chao* (Excerpts) cites only the first three phrases; the first, the "complete phrase" (*juzu ju*), encompasses all the subsequent "mutually inclusive phrases" (*huju*).
As for the expression "the Vinaya states," it specifically clarifies non-offenses, as in the text.
Regarding the statement "up to seven": first, the explanation of the name. It is constructed for one who has a patron (*sāmi*) and is intended for exclusive, independent use.
The two locations where begging is prohibited constitute what is to be guarded against; the precept (*śīla*) is that which serves as the remedy (and so forth). The *Śīla-ṭīkā* asks:

Since it is built for one who has a patron, why is it necessary to cut down trees? Answer: To clear the ground below in order to provide a foundation for the site. The rest is as previously stated. Regarding the "intention behind the regulation" (*vinaya-saṃvaraṇa-abhiprāya*).

It is the same as the previous case; it is no different from a room that has no owner. Regarding the phrase "it constitutes an offense": this refers to a room that is six *zhang* long and four *zhang* wide or larger;
conversely, it indicates that there is no offense for rooms smaller than these dimensions. Regarding the phrase "this... [is] so": Xuán says, "These are all from the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya*.
As for "the Sangha incurs an offense if it does not permit the sale of a room," this means that although the room belongs to oneself, one informs the community of monks [of the transaction].

Selling is not permitted; rather, it is the entire Saṃgha that incurs the *jīva* (minor) offense. Some say that the individual monk who sells incurs the offense, claiming that this refers to the sin of selling [the property].

This does not constitute a correct interpretation and furthermore suffers from the fault of breaking the syntax. When it says "the Vinaya reaches the offense," it specifically refers to the gravity of the offense incurred. The Vinaya states:

"If the Saṃgha has not assigned [the property] and there is an obstacle or hindrance, there are two types of offenses: one is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting), and the other is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation). There is... [text fragment ends].

Where there is difficulty, there is no obstruction; where there is no difficulty, there is obstruction. In both cases, it is uniformly auspicious. If the Saṃgha has not made a formal assignment and there is neither difficulty nor obstruction, it is simply a single *śeṣa* offense.

As for the statement "opening until one obtains [the fruit]," this specifically clarifies that there is no transgression. The commentary states "provided it is not excessive" in order to resolve a doubt. The preceding precept prohibited excessiveness;
since a house small enough to accommodate the body does not constitute such excess, there is no offense. This present precept, however, was not originally intended to prohibit such a case.

Question: What is the use of discussing its dimensions? Answer: Although there is no offense for exceeding the measurements, if it is six units long and four units wide, one must still perform the formal procedure of requesting [permission].
This clarifies that because it is small, the formal procedure of requesting is not required, as there is no offense.

Regarding the statement "up to eight [cases of] speaking falsely": first, the explanation of the name. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Because there are no three realities within, it is called 'rootless' (*amūlaka*).

When a grave matter is subject to false accusation, it is termed 'slander' (*paiśunya*). This is that which is to be prevented; the precept is that which can remedy it (and so forth). The rest is as described elsewhere.

Regarding the statement "because many [cases] reach [this point]," it is for the sake of protecting one's own practice and ensuring the long endurance of the Dharma. *Xuán* says: "Slandering others..."
If one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, one immediately ruins one's own practice. Because one’s practice is ruined, one cannot preside over the performance of the Dharma.

If, in this case, one does not slander [the preceptor], it is the opposite of the two points mentioned above. As for the phrase "The question reaches the commentary," the meaning of the question is as follows:
Generally speaking, what is called "slander" must be false and groundless. If it is not false, then it is not termed "slander. Now, when one slanders another, is there merely the offense of slander?

Regarding the question of whether there is a further offense of lying (*mṛṣāvāda*), the answer cites the *Abhidharma-darśana-śāstra*, which states: "There is no separate offense of *pāyattika* (offense of expiation);

it means there is only the offense of slander (*abhyākhyāna-pāyattika*). There is no other separate *pāyattika* for lying. As for how a falsehood is established as being true, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"The Brahmin woman Ciñcā tied a wooden basin to her belly and slandered the Buddha, saying, 'The Buddha has had intercourse with me, which is why I am pregnant.'"
The Buddha said, "I possess the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses; how could such a thing as this exist?

Śāriputra then used his supernatural power to transform himself into a mouse, whereby the cord was gnawed through and the basin fell to the ground. This serves to clarify the matter; thus we know that slander is established based on mere falsehoods.
Regarding "now explaining by way of principle": this means that the Master now explains and clarifies through the underlying meaning.
If one slanders without such intent—that is, if one falsely constructs [the charge] merely for the sake of vilification—the object of the slander remains distinct and there is no other mental state;

thus, there is only a single offense. If the Sangha is also involved, it means the intention is marked by these two factors; therefore, two offenses are established. In relation to the previous object of slander, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense is incurred.

It is expected that one incurs a *pāyattika* offense regarding the Sangha for [lying about] killing one’s father or an Arhat, or for engaging in false speech and slander by speaking to one person what was said by another;

this citation serves as an example to establish the formation of two offenses. The *Fǎbǎo* (Dharma Jewel) states: "This refers to forming the perception of an Arhat regarding one's father and then killing him, thereby incurring two *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses.
The *Śāstra* says: "In the past, there was a king who, being advanced in years, entrusted his position to the crown prince and entered the mountains to practice, whereupon he attained realization..."

He attained the fruit of Arhatship. After the Crown Prince ascended the throne, he did not practice righteous governance. A foolish minister entered the mountains and invited the Father King to return, admonishing the Crown Prince.
Once the Prince learned of this, he sent men to intercept and kill the King on the road. As the King was being killed, he cried out: "Tell the Crown Prince:
if one kills, two offenses are incurred—namely, the severing of the sustenance of life and the destruction of a field of merit. If...

To discuss this in detail: there are three offenses in total. If one perceives the person as a human being, one commits a *pārājika* offense; for violating one who has provided sustenance, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*;

and for destroying a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), one also incurs a *sthūlātyaya*. If one merely perceives the person as a human being and does not know they are an Arhat, one incurs only a *pārājika*.

If one knows they are one's father but does not know he has attained the fruit [of Arhatship], one incurs only one *sthūlātyaya*. The above is based on the original text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. For now, we shall set aside the case of the human being.
One contemplates the gravity of these offenses; hence they are called "the two offenses. Regarding this, the Venerable Master cites four propositions from the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts):

First, one who provides sustenance and support is a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). This refers to a father who has left the household life and attained the fruits [of the path]. Killing him constitutes two *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses and one *pārājika* (defeat).

Second, one who provides sustenance and support but is not a field of merit. This refers to killing a father who has not realized the fruits [of the path]. This incurs one *ānantarya* offense and one grave offense. Third, one who is a field of merit... [text continues]

It is not one who has provided sustenance; however, killing an Arhat who is not one's father incurs two offenses: one is a *ānantarya* (immediate) offense and the other is a *pārājika* (defeat) offense.

Regarding those who are neither benefactors nor fields of merit—that is, ordinary people—one incurs only a *pārājika* offense. As for lying and divisive speech (*paiśunya*), this refers to the intention to cause separation;
therefore, by the mere utterance of the words, one incurs two offenses. If there is only the intention to deceive another, but no [actual] division...
Apart from the mind, there is only one offense, as explained in detail in the section on the minor precept against false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*).

Here, the two preceding matters are cited to collectively corroborate the previous text, establishing that both the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and *pāyattika* offenses are incurred. As for the remaining points, they are as stated in the commentary;

since those contain detailed questions and answers that do not differ significantly from the general outline of this summary, they are omitted here. Regarding the phrase "one who possesses [the conditions] up to the point of committing [the offense]," the first refers to a *mahābhikṣu* and...
Regarding the term "nun" (*bhikṣuṇī*): Question—Why is it that slandering a nun constitutes the same offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* as with a monk, yet striking a nun results only in a *duṣkṛta*?

Answer—the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: Striking is based on the inferiority of status, whereas slandering concerns the cultivation of practice; therefore, the resulting offenses are not fixed [in the same manner]. Regarding the exclusion of the three lower groups [of disciples]: The *Shu* (Commentary) states:

Because the intent behind slandering and causing distress is slight, it does not hinder their spiritual cultivation. Furthermore, the name of the offense committed is light, and since the act of slandering is not grave, there is only a *duṣkṛta*.

"Regarding the second point, 'the perception and mind [of the accused] being pure,' this refutes the ancient interpretation. The ancients held that one commits an offense only if they slander someone after perceiving them as pure;

however, the present view maintains that when discussing the communal legal procedures (*saṃghakarma*), one must rely on what has been seen or heard. Thus, even if one slanders another based merely on the perception of purity, it constitutes an offense.

Therefore, the *Chao* (Commentary) states: 'It does not matter whether the person is actually impure. Accordingly, the Vinaya says: 'If that person is not pure, yet one slanders them without having seen them commit an offense, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting) offense. — *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts).

One raises an objection: "If one conceives a pure perception toward an impure object and thereby incurs the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (defamation), then if one kills a non-human being while mistakenly perceiving it as a human, should one not incur the offense of *pārājika*?
The answer is: "Defamation is defined by the falsity of the intention; killing is defined by both the object and the intention being real."

Therefore, it does not constitute a *pārājika*. For instance, if one breaks a precept and commits a *pāyattika*, how could this be cited as proof? Thus, the text says "and so forth," which refers to the text of the *Śaikṣa-dharmas* (the Chapter on Prohibitions).

"Prohibition" (*śikṣā*) here carries the sense of "to raise up" or "to cite. "Lack of basis" (*amūlaka*) means the absence of the three bases [of perception]. "Lack of remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*) refers to the four *pārājikas*.
Regarding the phrase "having acted thus": although the offense was indeed committed, if the three requisites (*trīṇi mūlāni*) are absent, then the formal accusation (*codanā*) is not established.

Since the accusation is false, one is punished for slander. Second, regarding "the perception of him as a great bhikṣu": the Great Virtuous One (Dade) says that this is the current master’s second restatement of the conditions. As for why it is restated:
it is because the conditions established by former masters were not fully understood, and thus they are clarified further. However...
If one perceives [the person] as a great bhikṣu, one immediately incurs the offense of slander, regardless of whether the person is pure or impure.

If one perceives them as belonging to the three lower assemblies, one commits a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). Third, "possessing a mind of anger" refers to a heart of resentment. Fourth, "lacking the three roots" consists of:
first, the root of seeing—meaning seeing by oneself or seeing through another; second, the root of hearing—meaning hearing by oneself or hearing through another; and third, doubt.
There are cases of doubt after having seen, and doubt after having heard. According to the Vinaya, there are seven chapters regarding the six mental states (*ṣaḍ-citta-pada*).

First, the actual state of being impure without the three roots (*trīṇi mūlāni*). Second, the three roots proceeding to slander. Regarding the six phrases: first, that person is impure and lacks the three roots.

1. One goes about slandering with the three faculties [of seeing, hearing, and knowing], yet there is no thought of non-perception (asaṃjñin) nor any thought of not forgetting. 2. That person’s mind is impure and lacks the three faculties;

having previously conceived the notion of the three faculties, they later look back upon that conceptualizing mind and say, "I have seen, heard, and [known]"—this refers to a mind characterized by perception and forgetfulness. 3. That person is impure.

There are no three roots [of knowledge]. [In the first case,] one who previously gave rise to doubt later says, "I truly saw, heard, or suspected" (meaning that although there was doubt, the mind did not forget it).

Fourth, such a person is impure and lacks the three roots; having previously given rise to doubt, they later say, "I truly saw, heard, or suspected" (meaning that although there was doubt, the mind forgot it).
Fifth, that person is impure and lacks the three roots; nor do they possess the three roots, yet they lack a mind of doubt.

Later, forgetting this absence of doubt, they say, "I truly saw, heard, or doubted" (thus falsely claiming doubt when there was no doubt). Second, lacking the root of seeing, they proceed to slander based on hearing and doubt.
Third, lacking the root of hearing, they proceed to slander based on the two roots of seeing and doubt. Fourth, lacking the root of doubt...
The first two cases involve slander based on the two faculties of seeing and hearing. The fifth case lacks the faculties of seeing and hearing, yet one slanders solely based on the faculty of doubt.

The sixth case lacks the faculties of hearing and doubt, yet one slanders solely based on the faculty of seeing. The seventh case lacks the faculty of seeing, yet one slanders solely based on the faculty of hearing.
Each of these contains six permutations. As clarified above, these constitute forty-two permutations. This applies even if one is actually pure.
There are no three roots (*trīṇi mūlāni*). Regarding slander by means of the three roots, there are likewise forty-two phrases; these are explained by reversing the above [analysis] (and so forth).

From the fifth [category], down to speaking in the presence of a single *bhikṣu*: this is based on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (*Caturvargika*), which maintains that when slandering another, one must face the object [of the accusation], whether it be many people or even just a single person.
Below, the text cites the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (*Śāriputra-abhidharma*); that is, according to that *vinaya*, it concerns the slanderer facing the one being slandered.
The offense is established according to the words spoken; that is, one must slander another face-to-face. The conditions for offenses six, seven, and eight may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the term "one who is good and arrives," "懦" (nuǎo) means weak (also read as nuò or nù luàn; both are glossed as "weak"). The rest is as stated in the text. As for the phrase "the Vinaya states they are the same," this clarifies the circumstances under which there is no offense.
First, "truthfulness" refers to when the person before one has actually committed an offense; it means seeing another person commit such acts as killing or stealing.
Regarding the second case, "the fact is real": although the person before one has not actually committed an offense, my own mind considers that they have indeed committed it;
this is not a false accusation. This refers to the state of perception at the time of speaking. One must truly form the perception that the person before one has committed an offense;

if one deviates from this characteristic, it constitutes slander. Regarding the third case, "the fact is the killing of a king, and one says, 'He killed the king,'" this means seeing that person kill the king.

Regarding the person: it is currently also called "killing Wangren" (王人), which is factually correct; if one says "killing Zhang," it constitutes slander. Furthermore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If one kills one's father but calls him 'mother,' it is still a *sthūlātyaya* offense. Regarding the four cases where the three faculties do not correspond to reality: such as seeing or hearing something but claiming to have seen it, and so forth.
They are not mutually name and reality. If one sees yet speaks of hearing and so forth, they become mutually contradictory and are thus false. The rest is as in the text.
Regarding the statement "provisionally reaching nine," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) says: This precept differs from the preceding ones in its name, cause, and category.

This precept involves falsely attributing the characteristics of the faculty of sight (*cakṣur-indriya*) upon a different object; that is, taking this faculty of sight to be used for slander, it thus constitutes a "false root. This is...
Regarding "that which is guarded" and "this up to the second": these explain the different characteristics of this analysis of the precepts. Question:

For what causes and conditions was the Arhat Trapusa slandered in this way? Answer: According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Duōlùn), in the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a Bhikṣu named Dabba (Tápiāo).
At that time, he served as the distributor of food (*bhattuddesaka*). There was also a forest-dwelling (*araññavāsin*) Bhikṣu who...
An Arhat, whose physical appearance was upright and handsome, was walking along a road. At that time, a woman saw him and gave rise to lustful attachment;
she followed him with her gaze and would not leave. When a man who was watching for food saw this, he assumed that this bhikṣu had previously had an illicit affair with that woman.

He consequently slandered the noble ones, and for this act of calumny, he fell into hell. Once his retribution was exhausted and he emerged from there, by virtue of his original wholesome karma, he encountered the Buddha.

He attained the Path. Due to the power of residual karma, he received this slanderous statement (measuring it according to this, it constitutes a major prohibition). As for the phrase "the conditions for the offense are the same," they are the same as the precept on groundless slander; the eight conditions are modified according to the occasion and are not listed again here. As for the phrase "the Vinaya reaches the 'seemingly'": (Note: This passage concerns the gravity of false accusations against those who have realized the Path, illustrating how karmic retribution follows.

It further clarifies that while the formal requirements for the offense remain consistent with the rules regarding baseless slander, specific contextual factors may vary. Finally, it refers to the application of the Vinaya principles to cases where the transgression appears similar to, though perhaps distinct from, the formal categories.)
"Different destinies" refers to the two categories of humans and animals. "Different offenses" refers to the six classes of offenses being distinct.
"Different persons" refers to those who share the same name, surname, and so forth; when one person commits an offense, that person is slandered by claiming it was committed by another.

"Different times" refers to committing an offense while a layperson and then claiming it was committed after the other had left the household life; or committing an offense with the hand and then claiming it was committed with the current hand, and so on.
"Simulating an echo" refers to speaking aloud to oneself within a mountain valley or a cave, shouting out as if saying, "There is someone there," and so forth.

Regarding the "different category," the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* cites the scriptural commentary for its own explanation (which may be understood). As for the phrase "the remaining characteristics may be known," this opens up the conditions for non-offense;
the similarities and differences are the same as in the preceding precept.

Regarding the explanation of the name "breaking the Saṃgha" (saṃghabheda) as the tenth [topic]: when false dharmas subvert the truth and cause the community to split into divergent paths, it is termed "breaking the Saṃgha.

Thus, because one stubbornly clings to [false views] and refuses to relinquish them, thereby breaking [the harmony], it is called "defying admonition" (and so forth). The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* asks:

"Since the breaking of the Saṃgha is a false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*), why is it specifically named 'breaking the Saṃgha'? The answer provides two masters' interpretations. The first states: it is named after its cause; that is, it is a false speech.
This is the cause; the schism of the Saṃgha is the result. It is because of deceptive speech that the Saṃgha is subsequently split. Second, it is said:

"Because this deceptive speech is able to split the Saṃgha, the name is designated according to its function. Regarding the phrase "this reaches [the ear]," the word "this" refers to the precept on the formal schism of the Saṃgha.
The word "etcetera" includes the three [precepts] concerning assisting in a schism, defiling families, and being of an evil nature. This extends to the subsequent sections.
"Zhe" (者) means "to reach" or "to attain. "Yu" (于) is a particle used for "at" or "in. Regarding the subsequent section concerning the *Pāyattika* (Single-Expiation) rules:
first, not accepting a private admonition; second, persisting in a *liṭṭha* offense despite a private admonition; third, the precept against treating those who provide instruction with contempt.

Alternatively, these refer to rare matters or hidden cases, such as those mentioned in the commentary regarding slandering the Saṃgha or rejecting the Saṃgha—such matters being infrequent. The reason for this is that even in the present day, there are wicked *bhikṣus*.

The Master said: "To claim that 'desiring to leave does not obstruct the Path'—since there was no Sangha present to offer admonition and exhortation according to the Vinaya, and since there was no occasion for the act of rejecting and slandering through such admonition, how could there have arisen an act of rejection and slander?
Furthermore, since the formal procedure for settling a charge of slander was not manifested, it is said to be 'rarely concealed' (or 'hidden')."
"Those who rarely employ [the means]" refers to the bhikṣus of the final age; although they commit many evils, there is no punishment at all for them, hence they are said to be "rare.
Or, "those who ultimately do not discern the fruit" refers to this matter of schism:

since there is currently no Buddha in the world, they compete in proselytizing to cause disharmony among the monastic community, which constitutes the cause. Since the act of causing a schism in the Saṃgha does not exist, it is therefore lacking.

The cruelty of one who defies admonition; therefore, the fruit [of such an act] is not distinguished. To restrict it to the time when the Buddha was in the world and to claim it does not exist after his parinirvāṇa is precisely what the sub-commentary points out.
Because it is said that there is no "schism of the wheel-turning Saṃgha" (*cakrabheda*) at the present time, it is analyzed through five sections: first, the essence of the schism;

second, the precepts, time, and place of the schismatic; third, the requisite conditions; fourth, the distinction between the two types of schisms; and fifth, the absence of [the former] at the present time.

Regarding the schism of the Wheel-turning Saṃgha (*cakrabheda-saṃgha*): first, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that the essence of a schism is non-concordance (*asaṃvāsa*). Its essence consists in the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) [of concord] within what was previously concordant.

When the Saṃgha has not yet been split, the community is in harmony, and it is accepted that the noble path can be entered. Once the Saṃgha has been split, it is termed "non-concordant," and its essence is non-acquisition.
Among the four types of minds, it is subsumed under the mind-in-action (*citta-vartamāna*), and it does not include the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*). It is non-existent.
It is subsumed under the nature of obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta). An objection is raised: "If it is unspecified, how can it constitute an immediate transgression (ānantarya)?

The answer is: The treatise states that such schisming of the Saṃgha arises from deceptive speech; since deception is an immediate transgression, the schisming of the Saṃgha is the fruit of an immediate transgression rather than the essence of one.
Because the cause receives the name of the fruit, it is called an "immediate transgression" when referring to the schisming of the Saṃgha. Furthermore, this schisming of the Saṃgha is unspecified.
It is not established by the one who breaks [the Saṃgha], but is established solely by the monastic community that is being broken (the eight entities above are concluded).

Second, regarding the time and place of the establishment of the one who breaks [the Saṃgha]: this refers to Devadatta, the one who breaks the Saṃgha. He incurs the offense of breaking the Saṃgha, which has deceptive speech as its nature;
he will certainly fall into the Avīci Great Hell and suffer there for one kalpa. The rest is as described in detail in the treatise. Third, the possession of conditions.

Regarding the schism of the Saṃgha, the verse says: "A bhikṣu who perceives [others] as pure acts to split them; at a different location, a fool, when he endures a different teacher and a different path, it is called a schism that does not last overnight.
As for the term "bhikṣu," it must be a *mahā-bhikṣu* who is capable of splitting the Saṃgha; it certainly cannot be a layperson, a bhikṣuṇī, or others.
"Perceives [others] as pure" means perceiving that the person is not one who has transgressed the precepts. "Pure conduct" refers to...

This means that one who upholds the precepts and does not violate them, yet lacks dignified deportment and breaks [the rules] in a different location—specifically, in a place other than in the presence of the Buddha—is intended.

Because the Tathāgata’s speech is so majestic and awe-inspiring, one would certainly be unable [to transgress] in his presence; therefore, "a different location" refers specifically to Mount Gajaśīrṣa.
Devadatta split the Saṃgha there, at a distance of about three or four *li* to the north of Vulture Peak. Regarding the "foolish ones" (*bāla*), there are two interpretations among the Śākya masters:

first, that they are so called because they have initially realized the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); second, that they are so called because even those who have attained *kṣānti* (receptivity) cannot be split from the Saṃgha. According to the former explanation, one is designated a "foolish one" based on having attained the status of an Ārya;

according to the latter, one is designated a "foolish one" because they have not yet attained the *kṣānti* of the West (the irreversible stage). The verse says: "The 'foolish one' encompasses these two."

Regarding "one who holds a different view and follows a different teacher": "patience" here refers to faith. It means having faith in a teacher other than the Buddha and faith in teachings other than those spoken by the Buddha.
At such a time, this is called "breaking the Wheel of Dharma. Devadatta spoke thus: "I am the Great Teacher, not the śramaṇa Gautama.
The five dharmas I have taught are the Path; it is not the eightfold path taught by Gautama."
The Way. The foolish bhikṣus, such as Traipusa and others, faithfully believed Devadatta, thinking: "He is our Great Teacher; these five dharmas are the path to liberation.
As they gave rise to this faith, they immediately broke the Wheel of Dharma (the five dharmas are explained in the cited section on the conditions).

Fourth, regarding the distinction between breaking the two types of Saṃgha: the verse says: "In Jambudvīpa, when nine [or more] [bhikṣus] exist, one can break the Wheel of Dharma Saṃgha; only the breaking of the *karma*..."

Regarding "Ma-seng" (the grinding of the Saṃgha): it applies generally to three regions and eight [conditions]. As for the term "Jambudvīpa," this distinguishes it from other locations, as only here does a Buddha exist.

Regarding "nine persons": the number nine refers to nine individuals; that is to say, the eight *bhikṣus* who constitute the two factions of the schismatic group—four representing the side of the correct doctrine and four representing the side of the heterodox faction—and the ninth being the one capable of causing the schism. Therefore, even at the very minimum, nine people are required. If there are more, then...

It is incalculable. Regarding the phrase "penetrating three continents and eight [people]": this refers to the *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act) of schism, which occurs across the three continents because the noble Dharma exists there.

At its minimum, it requires eight people; at its maximum, there is no limit. This refers to a case where the Saṃgha within a single boundary (*sīmā*) divides into two factions and performs the *karmavācanā*.

The fifth section clarifies that in the present age, there is no schism of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-bheda*). The verse says: "At the beginning and the end, the two tumors; before the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and before the formal establishment [of the rules]."

Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): among these six stages, there is no schism of the Wheel-turning Sangha (*cakrabheda*). As for "the first," this refers to when the Buddha has not long since turned the Wheel of Dharma;
as for "the last," this refers to the time near his *parinirvāṇa*. During these two periods, the Sangha is of one flavor (*ekarasa*), and thus a schism cannot be spoken of.

Regarding "the pair of blisters" (*phalgu-yugala*): "blister" (*phalgu*) refers to a boil or sore. When wrong precepts arise upon right precepts, and wrong views arise upon right views, it is called [a blister].
This refers to the "blister. Before the blister has arisen, it is called the "pre-stage. It requires the arising of two blisters before they burst;
these five factors constitute wrong precepts. To slander the Noble Eightfold Path is wrong view. The "pair of leaders" refers to Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra, the pair of noble disciples.
Maudgalyāyana was foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), and Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom (*prajñā*). There were none [among the disciples] who surpassed them in spiritual knowledge.

"Before the [Buddha's] passing" (referring to both periods before his passing). Regarding those who have not yet established the boundary (*sīmā*) after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa: because after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa there is no true Great Teacher with whom one might contend;
and regarding those who have not yet established the boundary: because within a single boundary, the Saṃgha has not been divided into two. Thus, the five preceding sections differ.
The general analysis of the categories of meaning is now complete.

The phrase "those who defile the household and are expelled and slander" refers to those monks who, having defiled a household, were consequently expelled from the village; once they had been driven out and expelled, they in turn slandered the Sangha.

The Saṃgha consequently offered a formal admonition. Because he did not accept the admonition, the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* was established. Since this practice is no longer carried out today, it is equivalent in meaning to being obsolete.

Regarding the phrase "it does not hinder evil conduct; such conduct truly ensnares living beings": this means that although the formal admonition has been abolished, there are still instances of defiling families and committing evil acts through slander;
however, as there are many such cases nowadays that are improper, they are omitted from discussion here. Thus it is said, "it does not hinder. Now, since such evil [conduct] is absent...
An admonition is set forth: because the net of one's conduct ensnares them within the web of the Teaching and gives rise to offenses, it must now be clarified.

Alternatively, "discerning the characteristics" refers to manifesting the characteristics of the transgressions of defiling families and evil conduct found among the lower precepts. "The matter is practiced universally" means that this matter of defiling families and evil conduct is currently practiced by people in common;
thus, it is described here as the practice of the lower precepts. One should be commanded to recognize these characteristics and conduct oneself accordingly.

Because it is for protection, or because it is an opening of the conditions (*kai-en*) that is essential at that time. In the texts of the Vinaya’s *kaidō* (opening and permitting), it is permitted to offer flowers as seeds for the Three Jewels, or to offer them on behalf of a donor (*dānapati*).
Carrying a letter to those in prison, the pregnant, the sick, one's parents, and so forth, and giving them food, does not constitute an offense.
Is this not indeed essential for the present age? Regarding the phrase "using the divine to supplement the divine," it refers to providing great assistance.

This is for the benefit of those who are newly learning; it is the application of the Buddha’s divine grace. As for the statement "as for those who would commit [an offense]," in principle, such an offense is not possible.
This means that since the Great Master [Bodhidharma] concealed his traces and competed in the transformation of others to open the conditions for enlightenment, such a thing simply does not exist.

Therefore, according to the underlying principle, there can be no commission of an offense. Question: Since this is currently non-existent, it is equivalent to being abolished and should be deleted and not used. For what reason is it [included] below?
The text further enumerates the requisite conditions and clarifies the characteristics of transgressions. One may cite the *Chao-da* (Excerpts and Answers), which states:

"It is essential to list them fully so that those newly studying [the path] may understand the characteristics of the teachings; thus they may look toward [realization]. The meaning of this is clear. First, regarding the intention of being heterodox toward the Triple Gem:

The Commentary on the Precepts concludes: Admonition is never established in vain; it must have a specific purpose. Therefore, first, the false Three Jewels are established to perform the act of schism within the Sangha. Regarding the "false Three Jewels":

Devadatta claimed for himself the title of Buddha, thereby usurping the place of the True Buddha as the Jewel. He preached the five heterodox dharmas, thereby usurping the place of the four reliances and the eightfold noble path.
As for the five heterodox dharmas: first, begging for food for the duration of one's life; second, [begging for food] for the duration of one's life...

1. Wearing rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*). 2. Sitting on the open ground for as long as one lives. 3. Not consuming ghee or salt for as long as one lives. 4. Not eating fish or meat for as long as one lives.
The first three are similar dharmas, resembling the Buddha’s four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*); the latter two are false claims.

They say that ghee and salt have heavy flavors, and that fish and meat harm living beings and the Buddha-treasure; thus, while not actually discontinuing them, they falsely claim to have discontinued them. [This refers to] Śrīlāta and others.
Fourth, regarding the substitution of Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others for the Saṃgha-ratna (the Jewel of the Sangha), and the period during which they traveled to transform beings:

the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states that although the three heterodox teachers were established, if [the disciples] had not traveled to transform beings, there would have been no occasion to offer admonitions.

This is because the Tathāgata’s Wheel of Dharma pervades the trichiliocosm and is taught to reach both monastics and laity. Therefore, when Devadatta proclaimed the five practices, he was merely explaining the four reliances (*catvāri pratiśaraṇāni*) and was not competing with the Buddha in his transformative work.
The announcement reaches even the Earth Deity, such that throughout the trichiliocosm, the Wheel of Dharma cannot turn, meditation and recitation are suspended, and heaven and earth are overturned;
during this interval, there is no one who attains the Way. Regarding the third formal admonition by the Sangha acting in accordance with the Dharma, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:
"If one transforms [the offender] but does not admonish, it is neither accomplished nor is there fault; therefore, a third formal admonition must be performed in accordance with the Dharma."
Regarding the fourth [offense], "insistence and refusal to relinquish": although one hears the admonition offered by the Saṃgha and complies with it, there is still no fault [in the act itself].

For this reason, the fourth [category of] "refusal to relinquish" must be established. Regarding the fifth, "committing an offense after the completion of the three *karmavācanās*": although one persists in holding to the view and refuses to relinquish it, no offense has been committed as long as the procedure is not yet finished;

it is only when the three formal acts are completed that the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*) is incurred. As for the phrase "contravening until the end," it refers to the resulting offense incurred in contravening the Saṃgha’s admonition.
Furthermore, "Lan" (蘭) refers to the *saṃghabheda* (schism of the Wheel-Dharma), which is the "fruit-Lan.

The reason why the schism of the Saṃgha is the "fruit-Lan" is that Tīrthika (Devadatta) originally intended in his heart to usurp the Buddha’s position, destroy the Saṃgha, and sever the Dharma. Now that he has succeeded in breaking the Saṃgha and won over its followers, his original design is complete;
his thoughts are fulfilled, and this constitutes the ultimate [result]. Regarding "disobeying the admonitions of others," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: If...

Regarding private admonition (*paṭicchanāpatti*), it does not matter whether the monk or nun is of full or incomplete status, nor the number of monastics or laypeople present; the established rule is that it is conducted as a collective admonition. For monks, four [monks] are required;
for private admonition, other various skillful means may be employed until the offense is ceased, at which point the procedure ends.

The *Chao* (Commentary) states that "residual" (*sāvaśeṣa*) and "grave" (*guru*) offenses refer to the results [of the transgression]. If one considers the causes as well, there are many offenses (as explained in detail elsewhere). This is extensive as found in the *Jieben shu* (Commentary on the Prātimokṣa).
Regarding this, he says: there are ten sections concerning the two admonitions given in private by the Saṃgha, which clarify the differences between cause and effect.
There are another ten sections, but they are omitted here as they are too numerous. As for the statement "the Vinaya says it is not an offense," this refers to a specific exemption from the offense.
"To act as one who has no dwelling place" means to drive [the offender] out of the monastery and not allow them to reside there. The remaining text is easy to understand.
Regarding "saying 'assisting in the schism' up to the eleventh": this is an explanation of the terminology. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

"When the Saṃgha performs the formal act of admonition, four companions act as shadows and echoes, assisting in the accomplishment of the schism. The Saṃgha then offers an admonition, but [the offender] refuses and does not accept it;
this is what is to be prevented, and so forth. Regarding "saying 'possessing' up to 'immediately forming the offense'": first, it clarifies that there is a person, namely Devadatta. Third...
Regarding the four companions who assisted in the schism: the first was named Svāgata;
the second, Khaṇḍadravya; the third, Guptaka; and the fourth, Kokālika. The rest may be understood as before.
Regarding the phrase "from 'defiling' to 'twelve,'" as for the explanation of the names: to soil pure faith is called "defiling the household" (*kuṭikāra*).

To raise faults and expose the assembly is termed "burying" (*śava*). To slander by falsely attributing guilt where none exists, and to reject it through reasoning, is called "contravening the admonition of the Saṃgha.

These are the things to be prevented, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "from 'possessing' to 'offense,'" concerning one who slanders the Saṃgha unreasonably, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:
The Saṃgha proceeded to perform the funeral rites. However, because their conduct was tainted by increasing attachment and there was a sense of partiality, this led to verbal slander against them.
This is just as stated in the Vinaya text: "Now, the Saṃgha possesses attachment, aversion, and delusion," and so forth. This refers to the six individuals who committed the offense together;
among them, Upāli, Māṣila, and Daḍhapaṭṭa fled to the royal palace and the villages, and since they did not appear in person, the rites could not be performed for them (as they shared the same fear).
The two individuals, Kālodāyin and Channa, opposed the path but reformed their ways; they were without fault and could not be punished (this is the same as having affection).
The two individuals, Aśvajit and Punabbasu, did not depart from the present state nor did they repent; the Saṃgha then interred them (this is the same as having hatred).
Now, [you] have reversed your former intent and are treating them according to the Dharma—what ignorance can there be? The rest of the text is easy to understand. It says: "defiled."

Regarding "arriving": "defiling the household through non-precepts" refers to committing an offense that defiles a household; however, this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) and not a formal offense (*āpatti*).

As for the phrase "the original cause of this precept is slandering the Saṃgha," this precept arises fundamentally from the act of slandering the Saṃgha; although the Saṃgha offered admonitions and exhortations, he did not accept their counsel.

The offense is committed when the three factors are complete. Regarding the phrase "reaching the fourth": if one hears of a place where one has received [offerings] and feels displeasure, one destroys the profound field of merit belonging to the former person.
If one thinks of repaying the kindness toward a place where one has given [offerings], one breaks the impartial mind of that former person.
Both conditions thus defile [the practitioner]. The rest of the text is understandable. Regarding the phrase "walking up to laughing": irrigation...

(“Gu” is pronounced as “gù” [in the ancient reading]; today it is simply read with the phonetic “jì,” meaning to encircle halfway). “Guan-chang-ji-zhe” (灌倡伎者): The *Shuowen* says this means to perform music. “Pai-shuo-zhe” (排說者): One who acts as a master of ceremonies, advancing forward to tell stories for the sake of provoking laughter.

It says, “From ‘Sengqi’ (Saṃghāṭī) to ‘reaching the house,’ one looks back at what was previously. The rest is as in the text. It says, “If one reaches the point of ‘seeing. This refers to what is in the text. It says, “From ‘many’ to ‘body.
That which is “unconditioned” (*wuwei*) and “desireless” (*wuyu*) arises from action (*zuo*). “Desire” (*yu*) means longing or expectation. Now...

This is because there is neither intentional action nor expectation. The remainder is as in the text. As for the phrase "if one reaches the point of cessation," this refers to those who are exclusively capable of causing harm and incapable of providing benefit;
that is, the class of those lacking faith. Therefore, it is permitted to give them what they leave behind, so as to avoid misfortune.

Regarding the statement in the Vinaya that "there is no offense," this separately opens up the conditions under which one does not commit an offense regarding the misconduct of defiling families, as explained in the text.
Regarding the phrase "one of an evil nature" up to the thirteenth [offense]: as for the explanation of the name, harboring resentment, anger, and perversity is called an "evil nature.

To incite a group of like-minded people to strike at the life of a monk is called "resisting the Saṃgha and defying admonition" (this is what is to be prevented). Regarding the phrase "possessing [these qualities] up to the offense":
"not accepting admonition while relying on oneself to insult others"—the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states: "Chanda did not accept the instructions of the various bhikṣus, and said to them..."
The bhikṣu said: "You should not instruct me; I should instruct you. Why is this? Because the Buddha is my family's Buddha.
I entered the mountains with the Buddha to practice the Way, yet I did not see the elder monks. Only one person attended upon the Buddha. Having attained the Way, he turned the Wheel of Dharma;
therefore, the Dharma is also our family dharma. Question: You do not say that the Saṃgha is your family. Answer: Fundamentally...
Because he had quarreled with the Saṃgha, he did not say, "The monks of my household. As for the aforementioned Chanda, he is Chandaka;
he was originally a servant of the Buddha's household. The statement "this person has arrived" precisely explains the intent of the admonition: do not cling to abbreviated teachings.

Regarding the phrase "many [cases] up to contradictions," this refers to the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya* (the *Duḷvā*), which itself cites the scriptural passages from the *Saptabuddha-saṃkṣipta-śāsana-sūtra*.

It specifically points to the passage in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* concerning the precept on those of "evil nature who reject the Saṃgha. Therefore, it contains both. Regarding the phrase "the answer up to 'identical'," this means that the precepts were established according to the faculties and the timing of the occasion.
As for the enumeration of the brief precepts, it says: "One should simply observe one's own bodily conduct; the Vinaya commands that one instruct others in turn."
Although these two texts differ in wording and expression, their intent is identical in seeking to cause one to leave the evil realms and proceed toward the fivefold Dharma-body;
thus it is said that "their destination is the same. Regarding the six different types, the enumeration is as follows and will be explained below.

As for the phrase "from one to [ten]," although the first half of each of these six sections need not be accepted, the second half must be accepted. Regarding the character *bǔ* (supplement) in the phrase "uttering words without supplement": this character...

"Instruction is for the sake of benefit. Regarding "for the sake of happiness in the present life," speaking in terms of general characteristics, attaining the Noble Path is called happiness in the present life.

Speaking in terms of specific characteristics, the four fundamental dhyānas are called happiness in the present life. It is for the sake of this happiness in the present life that the one who offers admonition acts.

It is simply intended for self-restraint, as stated in the sūtra. The other preceding and following contexts are easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "the Vinaya says one does not incur an offense":
if you say, "Your preceptor and ācārya were also like this," this refers to those who lack wisdom. One should rebuke them, saying: "Do not sit in meditation or recite the sūtras;

you should perform manual labor for the Saṃgha. This indicates various types of miscellaneous work. One may then respond with a counter-argument, saying: "Tell your preceptor [that he too should do so]."
[He] likewise sat in meditation and recited the sūtras. Why did [the others] not speak to him to have him perform various duties for the Saṃgha?

If the matter were indeed as described, the Venerable One said: "In this context, the word 'er' (爾) means 'is. As for the task one has undertaken oneself, it is truly not in violation of the scriptural texts.
If another person offers erroneous admonition, I do not accept it; there is no offense. Or perhaps they mistakenly spoke words of contrary admonition."
"None are transgressed.
Regarding "the two indeterminate [rules]": this is the general heading for the two indeterminate rules.

As for the phrase "placed in the commentary on the *Prātimokṣa* by ancient textual exegesis," this refers to the fact that in the commentaries of antiquity, these were not originally listed within the *Prātimokṣa* itself, but were instead placed in the explanatory sections of the Vinaya commentaries (*śāstra*). Now...

This has been omitted for brevity. To briefly outline the general meaning: it serves to introduce the subsequent text and clarify the sense of committing an offense through the fulfillment of specific conditions (*paccaya*).

Although this is not explicitly stated in the *Chao* (the abridgment), I shall now analyze it according to three sections: first, the intent of its placement; second, the explanation of the name and the determination of its essential substance (*svabhāva*);

third, whether it applies to both monks and nuns. Regarding the first, the intent of its placement: as for why it is situated below the two preceding categories (*varga*) and above the three subsequent ones, if we discuss it in general terms:

The disciplinary practices for the five categories of offenses possess the merit of preventing wrongdoing; all are termed *śīla* (precepts). Therefore, the text says, "the first offense against the precepts," and also says, "he established the precepts for the bhikṣus," and so forth.
If one refers to the various rules governing the movements and postures of body and speech, these are called *airyāpatha* (dignified deportment).
Therefore, the text says, "the first offense," and also says, "it is not dignified deportment," and so forth. If judged according to these specific distinctions, the former...

The transgressions prevented by the first two [categories] are coarse, and their remedies are termed "precepts" (*śīla*). The latter three involve subtle offenses whose remedies eliminate lapses in dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).

Now, because the characteristics of these offenses are difficult to discern, they give rise to doubts and suspicions. If one commits an offense of the first category (*pārājika*), it is logically appropriate that they be permanently discarded.

For offenses of the second category (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), which are next to death, the Saṃgha must administer the remedy. If one violates dignified conduct and defiles the Saṃgha, this constitutes a confusion; therefore, an investigation is required. Question: Is it necessary to purify one's conduct and practice? Answer: Yes.

Answer: Matters that are inconsistent must be subject to disciplinary punishment. If they were placed at the beginning, the legal principles would not yet be manifest; by what law could one distinguish between the apparent and the real?

If they were listed later on, it would be utterly discordant with their logical sequence. Thus, these two *aniyata-dharmas* (undetermined rules) appear below the second category (*pārājika*) and above the third category (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*).

Second, regarding the explanation of the names and the determination of their essence: first, the explanation of the names. According to ancient tradition, three were established for secluded places and two for open places.
The nature [of these offenses] is indeterminate. Now it is said that this is not so; for the natures, names, and categories of the three or two offenses are each distinct.
How can they be bundled together to constitute a single precept? Our Master now says: Sexual intimacy is a practice commonly performed by the laity.

When a bhikṣu, being without a companion, speaks coarse words in the presence of a single woman, it causes others to suspect and find it strange among the three types of offenses. Because the characteristics of the transgression are difficult to clarify, it gives rise to [confusion].

Doubt. To reprimand the fault of their intention, the *duṣkṛta* (吉羅) constitutes the essence [of the offense]. Regarding why the three [offenses] exist for monks but not for nuns—specifically why there are no two *aniyata* (不定) offenses for nuns—the Master now says:
because when a monk sits with a woman in a place that invites scandal, the head of the household may lose faith and perhaps drive him out;

since the harm caused by such a situation is profound, the rule was established that these [two *aniyata* offenses] apply to monks but not to nuns. This is because even if a nun sits alone with a man...

This incurs censure. Furthermore, regarding the principle of a wife without [a husband], a minor transgression does not result in formal binding. As for the phrase "the many discourses, etc.," this clarifies the intention behind the regulation.
Regarding this question, Xuán (Xuanzang) stated: "In most precepts, the conditions (*pratyaya*) are listed first, and only afterwards is the intention of the regulation established.

Why is it that here the intention is established first and the conditions are listed afterwards? The Venerable One replied: "This is an error in the intention of the compilers of the records. [The text continues: "The preceding [cases]..."

In all precepts, the underlying intention (*saṃdhāya*) is established first, followed by the enumeration of the conditions (*pratyaya*). There has never been a case where the conditions were fully enumerated first and the intention established later.
Now one should ask: "In all the preceding precepts, the name of the precept is listed first, and only afterwards is the intention established.

Why is it that here, without first indicating the name of the initial *aniyata* (undetermined) offense, the intention is instead set forth? Answer: If the intention had been explained immediately following the initial precept, it would have merely...
Now, within this general heading, it is clarified that both sets of precepts are fully subsumed; this is why they differ from other categories of precepts.

Furthermore, the fact that even a single category of precept is included reflects the intention that the formulation is slightly different (reflect on this). Regarding the phrase "among the first *aniyata* [undetermined offenses]," the explanation of the name is as before.

Regarding the phrase "from four... to the offense," the enumeration of conditions is as in the text. Regarding the phrase "from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*... to the section," it is as in the text. Regarding the phrase "it is said":
Regarding the differences in the subsequent [sections],
the second precept may be understood therefrom. *Sifenlü Chao Jianzheng Ji*,
Scroll 14 (Scroll 11 of the *Sifenlü Chao Jianzheng Ji*, from the explanation of the thirtieth precept through the ninety precepts).
Compiled by the Great Master Jingxiao (Cīngliáng), who lectured on the Vinaya for many years in the Wuyue Kingdom and was granted the purple robe while presiding over ordination platforms.

Section Four: The Major Headings of the Thirty *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* Dharmas, Part Two. First, a general indication of the brief reliance [on the source]; now, the direct explanation. Second, the explanation according to the precepts.
The initial statement, "The thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses," is the general heading. This is briefly divided into two parts:
first, the definition and establishment of the names; second, the reasons for their sequence. Regarding the phrase "The method of confession is as follows," this refers to the abbreviated version.
The Venerable Master says that this also serves as a secondary refutation of ancient errors, specifically those of the ancient masters who, under each individual precept...
The *Chàn-fǎ* (Methods for Confession) produced [in the past] were extremely voluminous; now, however, it is not so. There is but a single chapter, as described below.
As for "directly clarifying the categories" (*zhí míng xiàng zhǒng*), this refers to the direct clarification according to the present [text].

Since we do not rely on the ancient *Chàn-fǎ*, we merely clarify the characteristics of committing an offense when all conditions are met, and the characteristics of not committing an offense when conditions are lacking. "Categories" (*zhǒng*) means types; these arise from wealth and consist of thirty [offenses], all of which...
Because it is a category of greed, the term *niḥsargika* is a Western Indic (Sanskrit) expression; in the Eastern lands (China), it is translated as "to be relinquished" (*she*).
