As the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* states, there are three kinds of relinquishment: first, relinquishing material wealth; second, relinquishing the continuous stream of mind; and third, relinquishing the offense.

Regarding the *pāyattika*, as explained in the preceding section, they are termed "falling" (*pan-duo*). Therefore, these are called the "thirty relinquishments and falls. If one discusses the ninety [offenses], [the same principle applies].

Second, regarding the principle of eradication (*utkṣepa*), it is also appropriately termed "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*). However, it is called "abandonment" because one does not merely abandon the material object but must repent for the fundamental downfall (*pārājika*) itself.
Second, concerning the sequence of priority: according to the essential nature of the offense, it is consistent with the various categories of transgressions (*skandhaka*).

This is because the acceptance of material wealth through improper means harms sentient beings and destroys the Path; thus, to wash the heart and repent, one must rely upon a superior object (*viṣaya*) before the continuity [of the offense] can be severed and extinguished.

Once matters concerning a covetous mind have been relinquished, obstructive karma must be dispelled; therefore, the offenses are explained next. Since the formal procedures for these are difficult, they are listed first.

As for the ninety *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses, which are dealt with in the *Prakīrṇaka*, one merely needs to sever future transgressions to achieve purification through repentance; thus, their formal procedures are easy.
Therefore, I shall explain them next. I wish to enable students to first recognize what is difficult and subsequently proceed to what is easy.

If categorized according to the distinction between prohibitive (*pratikṣepa*) and inherent (*prakṛti*) offenses, only the transgression regarding monastic property is an inherent offense; the remaining twenty-nine are all subsumed under the category of prohibitive offenses.

Regarding the explanation based on the *Śīla-vibhaṅga*, there are thirty distinct sections, corresponding to thirty chapters. Now we shall address the first. As for the "Precept on Exceeding the Limit on Extra Robes" (*Ādhika-cīvara-sīmātikrānta-śīla*):

regarding its definition, the *Śīla-ṭīkā* states: "That which remains after the allotted portion is called 'extra' (*dīrgha*); to exceed that fixed limit is called 'exceeding the limit' (*sīmātikrānta*).
This is what is to be guarded against... [and so forth]. Regarding the phrase "because it reaches a great amount": it destroys the merit of the Path.
"Wealth" refers to the three [roots] beginning with non-attachment; these are able to give rise to the myriad virtues and merits.

These merits can nourish the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom, and are thus metaphorically termed "wealth. Now, if one covets worldly profit, the myriad virtues will have no means by which to arise—is this not destruction?
The rest is as stated in the text.

"Regarding the phrase 'possessing six conditions,' this is a general heading indicating the conditions for an offense. Regarding the passage from 'one' to 'purification by declaration' (śuddhi-viśuddhi), it is asked:

why is this precept merely marked with a general heading of conditions, rather than listing them individually as is done for other precepts? The Venerable One says: the other precepts are explained according to specific difficulties;
here, the first [condition] is explained separately, while the latter five are analyzed collectively. This is also the method of the author."

This transformation and mastery [of the rules] possesses no further underlying principle. Regarding the phrase "one's own extra robes" (*dīrgha-cīvara*), the *Śarīra-vibhāṣā* (or *Chao*) itself explains below:

it refers to wealth other than the three robes (*tricīvara*). Since the three robes are not items classified as "extra robes," they are distinguished from them. As for those who write the character "self" (*ji*) instead, this is a mistaken reading;
it implies that one commits an offense by treating what is one's own extra robe as such. The passage concerning the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and other texts serves to distinguish the "extra" [robe].
This refers to the measurement of the robe. The *Chao* (Commentary) discusses this according to the Zhou cubit;

however, in terms of the current Tang cubit, it is slightly less than one chi and three cun in length, and slightly more than six cun and six fen in width. If either the length or the width exceeds or falls short of these measurements, no offense is incurred.

It is only when both exceed [the prescribed limits] that an offense occurs. Regarding the nine permutations mentioned in the Vinaya text: four permutations constitute an offense, while five permutations do not. As for these nine permutations:

These are established by grouping them in threes. First, three statements are formulated using "excessive" (*atireka*) to demonstrate the cases; next, three statements are formulated using "as it is" (*yathā*) to demonstrate the cases;
and finally, three statements are formulated using "deficient" (*ūna*) to demonstrate the cases. Regarding the first set of three: (1) an offense involving excess in length and excess in width;
(2) an offense involving excess in length and conformity in width; (3) no offense involving excess in length and deficiency in width. Next...

Regarding the three phrases: first, [a case] where there is an offense as described in detail within the long [period]; second, [a case] where there is an offense as described in detail within the long [period];

third, [a case] where there is no offense because it is less than what is described in detail within the long [period]. Regarding the latter three phrases: first, [a case] where there is no offense because it is less than the offense described in detail within the long [period];

second, [a case] where there is no offense because it is as described in the reduction within the long [period]; third, [a case] where there is no offense because it is reduced within the reduction within the long [period]. Thus it is said.

Regarding the nine phrases above, there are differences between ancient and modern interpretations. Ancient masters, seeing nine phrases in the Vinaya—four phrases as offenses and five phrases as non-offenses—arbitrarily maintained that an offense occurs only when both conditions are fulfilled (i.e., both being "as it is" and both being "excessive");
they claimed that if either were excessive, there would be no offense. The Master of the present [tradition] says this is not so.
When the Vinaya states "no offense," this refers merely to the absence of a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation), not the absence of a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). Based on this, the aforementioned...

There are nine phrases [regarding the offense]. Four phrases constitute a *pāyattika* (提), while the fifth phrase constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (吉). Below, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (多論) is cited to discuss the aforementioned five phrases.

Although the Vinaya text does not mention two *pāyattikas* for the cases where there is no offense, according to the *Śāstra*, there is a *duṣkṛta*. Consequently, the conclusion is drawn: "Therefore, both must be mentioned. An ancient record states:

"According to the Vinaya regulations, both are like the two offenses; why then does the *Shan-chao* (Commentary) require both to be transgressions? If that were so, then 'both' would be as if non-existent."
[The offense] is not committed. If it is not committed, does this not contradict the scriptural text? The Venerable One said: "Not so. This merely cites both faults for the sake of self-restraint;
both are as explained in the *Śāstra* (Chao). For fear of prolixity, I cannot repeat them here, yet it is not that I am not thorough."

Regarding the statement that "the three robes have no surplus to prevent": this means that when one possesses the three robes, they are subject to the *śuddhaka-dharma* (the rule of purification) in relation to other garments, which prevents them from becoming surplus.
Now, if one lacks the three robes, then in their very substance there is nothing further to prevent as a surplus; thus, the *śuddhaka-dharma* is lost.

Therefore, if one discards [the robes], one must perform the *śuddhi-vyākaraṇa* (declaration of purification), because each individual item constitutes a surplus. As for those who, due to specific circumstances, obtain cloth and designate it as the three robes and so forth:
This refers to the presence of circumstances such as loss or theft. Suppose a person obtains a piece of fine cloth but has not yet manufactured it into a robe to receive and maintain;
fearing that the day will pass and they would commit the offense of "excess" (*atireka*), they may temporarily designate the three robes [as their current possession] to avoid the offense of excess.

Regarding the *Souxuan* (Investigating the Profound), it restricts this to cloth that is "proper in color"; however, the present text says otherwise, simply clarifying "fine cloth. Upon what treatise does this rely? There are three cases: dyed, undyed, and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "beyond five cubits [in length] there is the 'excess' (*atireka*) for which one must perform the ritual of *śuddhika* (purification by declaration)," the Venerable says: "If there is more remaining, one should cut off the excess and perform the *śuddhika*. Xuan says:

"One performs the *śuddhika* on the portion outside the body of the robe, including the finger-widths. Both interpretations are correct. As for the question, "What is meant by 'reaching the ears'? This refers to the *māsa-pakṣa-cīvara* (the robe obtained during the fortnight).

It raises an objection to the previous point regarding obtaining a *khaṇḍa-cīvara* (patchwork robe) and making it into the three robes (*tricīvara*): if one does so, one avoids the fault of having an excess. Why then [is there mention of] the *māsa-pakṣa*?
"Cutting the hairpin to sew over transgressions" refers to those with long hairpins. This means breaking thin bamboo into pieces to insert as hairpins and stitch the monk's *kāṣāya* (robe).
Sewing refers to joining [the fabric] with thread. (As stated in the *Dawen Chao*, etc.)

Regarding the phrase "because it has reached [the limit]," this indicates the correct topical division (*vibhāga*). Fearing that it might contradict the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), I shall first interpret the text according to this [division], and subsequently provide a separate detailed analysis and judgment.
As for the phrase "the aforementioned texts," Baoyun says: "This clearly sets forth the eight parts;

it makes it known that if one possesses an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) and does not declare it by the end of the day, one commits an offense. The *Pinaiye* (Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya) states that "it is accomplished in one day"; this refers to the first [part].
This refers to the causal conditions. That text states: "A long robe (atireka-cīvara) becomes a five-strip robe in one day; a seven-strip robe in two days;
a great robe (saṃghāṭī) in four days; and a long robe in five days. It is 'easily obtained' because it is made in a single day.

Second, although one knows it is a long robe—meaning although one knows it is a garment belonging to oneself beyond the three robes, such as wealth or silk—if there is no fault due to causes such as forgetfulness, [it is permissible].

Baoyun said: "This is explained in terms of confusion and forgetfulness. Because the mind is deluded, even if one transgresses the limit and does not speak [of the excess], it is a non-preventable offense (akaraṇīya-āpatti) that cannot be learned from.
Above, I have finished explaining the *Śāstra* according to its topical outline. The Venerable One said: 'Fearing that it might contradict the *Jieshu*, he stated:
'Even if one knows it is an excess, if there is confusion or forgetfulness, or if one does not yet know it belongs to oneself, it shows there is no offense for having an excess.'"
One must know that this belongs to the section on "Certainty" (*niyata*). The two characters "彼無" (pi wú) are not present in the original text; they have been added by the *Chao* (Commentary).

If one follows this principle, although it is known from the second [section] that this is a long [passage], this is the second sub-section (*ke*) for clarification; it should not be compressed [into the first]. Question:

Within the first analytical section (*liao*), it was stated that even if one acts based on delusion, there is no offense. Below, there is a fear that a separate door titled "Delusion and Forgetting" (*mi-wang*) might be opened to establish non-offense. How can this be?

To clarify this point in advance would not be elegant or appropriate. The Venerable Master further stated: "Now one may form the intention of concluding the preceding section and leading over to the subsequent one;
from the preceding petition up until what is accomplished in a single day. This, for now, concludes the first causal condition of the preceding text."
Although one may know it is long from these two [criteria], if there are conditions such as forgetfulness, then no offense occurs. Second, this clarifies the determination of what belongs to oneself.
Up to this point, this constitutes the second condition for giving rise to fear. If one relies on this interpretation, the structural outline (*ko-wen*) should be revised accordingly.

The detailed explanation of the lower section is divided into two parts: first, the individual explanation of the first [category]; second, the combined discussion of the latter five, beginning with "Although...

This follows the *Shu* (Commentary) rather than the *Chao* (Notes). Regarding the note stating that items such as cotton wool are not included within the category of clothing, the *Jie Shu* (Precepts Commentary) says:
Now, regarding the general form of the letter: only those items made of cloth, silk, wool, or cotton that can be measured and limited in quantity constitute the category of "robes.

All others are not yet formed; their dimensions are indefinite, such as bundles of wool or lengths of cotton, which by nature are not robes. How could they possibly correspond [to the prescribed measurements]?
Therefore, it is inappropriate to speak of them in this context. The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.

Regarding "many lead to offenses": this refers to robes that are either of proper measure or improper measure. "Proper measure" means six feet and eight inches; "improper measure" means less than six feet and eight inches.
"It is better to perform the *śuddhika* (purification) immediately" means that as soon as the robe enters one's hands, it is good to perform the *parivāsa* (formal declaration);

it is not necessary to wait until ten days have passed. "There is no fault upon reaching ten days" means that [if one has not yet performed the purification], there is no offense up until the tenth day. Unfinished... [text ends].

This violates the time limit. Regarding the phrase "if one does not perform the ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*) until the eleventh day, at the time the ground is finished," the text states: "One may remain for up to ten days;
if one exceeds this, one commits an offense. *Souxuan* asks: "For what reason is it that one only commits the offense on the eleventh day, at the time the ground is finished?"
That commentary explains: "The tenth day is defined by the appearance of light; if one says it has passed, that too is based on the appearance of light as the limit of passing.
Now, from dawn until night on the eleventh day, before the light has appeared, it is not yet the state of having passed;
therefore, there is no offense. This is just like those who share a room: they may not stay for more than two nights and reach a third night, for fear of [the rule] regarding the sequence."
"The third [view] holds that the appearance of dawn constitutes the transgression. The Venerable One says:

'If one follows this interpretation, since it is stated that from the eleventh day until before the appearance of dawn one has not yet committed the offense, then the morning of the twelfth day would be the point at which the offense occurs.

This [interpretation] fails to grasp the intent of the teaching, leading to such a groundless fallacy. Furthermore, citing the rule on 'staying overnight' as an analogy is incorrect, for the cases are not equivalent."
Now, on the tenth day, from dawn until the light has not yet appeared, there is no offense.
As soon as it reaches the appearance of light, the boundary of the eleventh day is reached, and an offense is incurred. How can you allow yourself to be confused about this?

If items are bound together in one place, they constitute a single offense—just as many garments gathered in one place result in only one offense. If they are scattered in various places, [the offenses] correspond to the objects.
Each of these locations constitutes a separate offense. Regarding what is called "the appearance of light" (*ālokanimitta*), the Vinaya states it is the time when flowers bloom and birds sing.

However, our Master [Daoxuan] now says that in winter months there may be no flowers, or in certain places there may be no birdsong; thus, it is difficult to rely upon this as a standard. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, it is said that there are signs of light:
when the sun shines upon the trunk of a Jambu tree, it appears black; when it shines upon the leaves, they appear green; and if it shines upon...

When empty, it is white. These three colors together constitute the characteristics of the luminous family. The previous mention of "earth" being clear means that the color of earth is distinct and vivid;
among the three characteristics, this is the characteristic of white. Now, one must definitively maintain the observance of precepts and take this as the focal point.

Regarding the question concerning "one [garment] that is subject to defilement": if the defiling agent (*rañjaka*) is of the proper measure, how can that which is defiled be so? This question likely does not arise;

for if the defiling agent is of the proper measure, there is no fear of committing a *thullaccaya* offense on the eleventh day regarding an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*). Among those things being defiled, some may be of the proper measure and some may not.

If it is of the proper measure, one undoubtedly commits an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). Even if it measures less than sixteen or eighteen inches [in width], [the same applies].

As for this, does it constitute a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), or does it constitute only a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing)? [This question applies specifically to the case of dyeing cloth that is not of the proper measure. Answer:
Regarding the aforementioned "proper" and "improper," this means that among the cloths to be dyed, whether they are of the proper measure or improper, one commits a *thullaccaya* in both cases.

Question: If that which causes defilement is of a permissible measure, one should incur a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) by consent; if it is not of a permissible measure, one should originally incur a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).

Why, then, is it said that one incurs a *thullaccaya*? Answer: It is because the offense is determined according to the nature of the defiling agent; [the gravity] is such that one fears incurring the forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) offense.

Thus, when the meal is finished, whether the food is "proper" or "improper," both constitute an offense. This is now explained by the Master through analogy. For example, suppose one has finished eating the proper meal since morning.

Although one has not yet passed the midday meal limit, if one eats further staple foods such as rice or *kaṅkuka*, it constitutes a fundamental offense (*maulāpatti*). Even if one eats non-staple foods that have been finely ground, the same offense applies.

Now, having finished eating to satiety, if the food that causes the transgression is of the proper measure (*pramāṇika*), and one subsequently eats more staple or non-staple food, both the food of proper measure and improper measure (*apramāṇika*) that is consumed will constitute an offense. The agent [of the transgression] is thus improper.

Regarding "equal in measure": this is a counter-question concerning whether that which defiles is an improper measure (*amātrā*) or, among those things that are defiled, whether it is a proper measure (*mātrā*).

The intended meaning of the answer is as follows: although they differ in size, that which is of proper measure is considered "large" and that which is of improper measure is considered "small"; both must be relinquished through confession.

Therefore, it is said that the meaning is one. According to the Vinaya, if one constructs something large that exceeds the prescribed measurement, one incurs a *pāyattika*; according to the Śāstra, if one constructs something small that does not meet the measurement, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
Thus, both cases involve the same defilement (the difference is not mentioned in the *Jiyi*).

Regarding the phrase "from *asaṃkhyeya* down to numbers": when one who is skilled in the *vinaya* acts as a representative for the assembly to perform the *śuddhi* (purification), there is no offense.

This refers to the case where many people share a common object; one person provisionally acts on their behalf to recite the declaration, so that the others are spared from committing an offense. An external objection is raised:

"In the previous case, if two people share an object and do not divide it, yet fail to recite the declaration after the day has passed, they still do not commit an offense. Now, in this case of many people sharing a common object, why [is it different]?"

"Is it necessary for one person to speak on behalf [of others]? One may answer by citing the commentary, which states: "This refers to those who live together. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* itself raises the objection:
"If clothing and wealth are held in common, and many people commit an offense together, yet only one person speaks on their behalf, do the others not become guilty?

Furthermore, if many people commit an offense together, can the offenses of the many be extinguished if only one person performs repentance on their behalf? The answer is: "It is treated as being hypothetically assigned to another."

One person acts on behalf of the group; thus the assembly is exempt from the fault of exceeding the limit, and they repent to eliminate their own offenses. One person performs the ritual of confession (*sāṃghāṭī-sāmagrī*), while the others do not cease [their transgressions].
Regarding the five allowances for remote regions mentioned in the Vinaya, Fabao says that there are three stages to the allowance for extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*).
Dade says there are four stages. First, Aniruddha was unable to complete a robe in one day; consequently, the allowance for one day was opened.
Regarding the offense: When two summer retreats had concluded, the Buddha permitted a bhikṣu who maintained *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) practices to accept five privileges.

If he possessed robes, he was permitted to keep them for five months without performing the *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (declaration of purity); if he lacked robes, he was permitted to do so for one month. Thirdly, regarding the disciple of Kātyāyana, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa:

while staying in the district of Ārṭīya, he received the full ordination (*upasampadā*). Because there were few monks in that border region, it took three years before he could find ten persons to observe the requirements for receiving the full ordination.
Later, he went to pay his respects to the Tathāgata. Kātyāyana instructed Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa to report five matters to the Buddha, requesting that they be permitted:

first, that monks from remote regions who have fewer than ten members be allowed to receive full ordination with a group of five who uphold the Vinaya; second, that the *saṭha* (monks) be permitted to wear double-layered straw sandals;
third, that in cold weather, skins may be used as bedding; fourth, that those with much dust and grime may bathe frequently; and fifth, that monks with few companions may travel alone.

The *kṣudrakavastu* (minor matters) state that when a long robe (*dīrgha-cīvara*) enters one's possession, it may be kept for ten days before being formally declared. The Tathāgata granted this as a flexible dispensation;
thus, although the ten-day period is permitted in the border regions, it is not permitted at this time in the central lands. Section Four: Because Ānanda had a robe he wished to offer to Kāśyapa.

Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, asking after how much time [the robe] would be completed. The Buddha replied that it should be returned within ten days. Because of this, the Buddha permitted a ten-day period;

this single opening applies universally to all places. Regarding "other regions" (*anyadeśa*) based on this: it refers to applying the allowance for border regions, or viewing the central lands as "other regions.
As for "not necessarily having been carried by hand to constitute an offense," the *Chao* (Commentary) states that because there are few monks in border regions, [one may keep] extra robes...
One must carry it by hand; the offense is incurred only when ten days have been completed. According to this principle, monks in China are numerous; it is not only necessary to carry it by hand.
Whether on one's knees, on one's shoulder, before one's eyes, out of one's sight, or upon one's body—whenever one forms the thought that it belongs to oneself [the offense applies].

When the [period] is full, one commits the offense. Regarding the citation of the *Vinayavibhaṅga* and other texts below, it serves as proof that in other cases, the robe need not necessarily be held in hand.
The *Vinayavibhaṅga* sets forth four modes of acquiring robes, as stated in the text. The *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* presents four propositions.

Regarding "attainment through the eye," the *Śīla-śāstra* states: "It is like when someone offers a robe; even if the butter (or the robe) reaches before the bhikṣu’s eyes without touching them, it becomes his own."

[Note: It is not said that the purification (*viśuddhi*) is calculated according to the days for the medicinal substances or the seven robes (*sapta-cīvara*). As for "entering the calculation," it refers to the number of days on which the robe was obtained;

this designation of the number of days constitutes "entering the calculation. Regarding the second phrase, "there is the object and there is the person, yet it is obtained by reaching [the object] rather than by the eye reaching it," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:
"For example, if one gives in the dark, that person says aloud, 'I give this to the bhikṣu named So-and-so. In the darkness..."

Therefore, it is not seen. When one touches an object with the body and forms the intention that it belongs to oneself, if it has not been declared pure (*asuddhika*) and enters into the calculation [of the full offense], the full offense is committed.

Regarding "the three cases where the eye and body reach the object": this refers to seeing with the eye and touching with the body; these three instances of reaching the object do not constitute the calculation [of the full offense].
Although one receives the robe, it does not belong to the bhikṣu and is not included within the count [of his possessions]. Why is this?

It is said that although the donor previously entered [the act of giving], he did not permit the bhikṣu to personally accept or use it; rather, he placed it by the side of the bhikṣu intending to offer it to the Triple Gem.

Regarding the four cases where there is neither [the donor nor the recipient] present at the time of acquisition, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "It is like giving in the dark, where the eyes do not see and the body does not touch, yet one merely forms the thought that it is one's own."
The day on which the item is obtained is immediately included in the calculation.

Regarding the statement "up to ten days according to the *Dharmaguptaka*," this clarifies non-offense from the perspective of whether the item was obtained or not. It simply means that if one takes into account the day the robe was not obtained, there is no possibility of transgression;
thus it is called "non-offense. For example, in the *Dharmaguptaka* tradition, if one obtains the robe on the first day and does not obtain it on the second day [and so forth].
Regarding the statement, "up to the eleventh day, those who do not obtain [the robe] at all do not commit an offense," there are two interpretations of this text.
First, *Yisou xuán* (The Profound Search of Robes) states: "Obtaining the robe on the first day" refers to the first day of the second chapter;
"not obtaining it on the second day" refers to the second day of the second chapter. This means that the second day of the second chapter is the very first day on which one does not obtain the robe.
Up to the citation of the eleventh day in the tenth chapter at the end, it says that up to the eleventh day, one is entirely free from offense.
As for the first chapter, starting from the first day, the second day, and so on up to the tenth day, since this chapter constitutes a general offense, it is set aside and not discussed.
The *Chao* (Commentary) skips this chapter and takes the second chapter [as the basis]... (end of excerpt).
[This is] the explanatory text. Next, following the interpretations of former masters, it is composed based solely on the tenth chapter.

"Obtaining the robe on the first day" refers to the first day of the tenth chapter; if one obtains the robe on this day for the purpose of dyeing and it emerges on the eleventh day, it is certainly an offense.
"Not obtaining it on the second day" refers to the second day of the tenth chapter, and so on through the eleventh day.

Regarding "none of these constitute an offense": according to the underlying principle, it should be stated that one may not [keep] it for three days; likewise, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten days are all impermissible.
The intent of the *Chao* (the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā*) is to be concise; therefore, it employs the term "up to and including" (*zhì yǐ zhì*).

As for "the eleventh day," this means that from the second day following the previous [period] through the ninth day of the middle month, one may obtain the robe; when the dawn light appears on the eleventh day, [the period ends].
At that time, within the context of what is being dyed, there is no offense; therefore, it is said that "in all cases there is no offense. "In all cases" (tōng) means "generally" (zǒng).

This is because on the ninth day, when one has no garment, there is generally no offense. It does not mean that the one who dyes the cloth incurs no offense. If it were the case that the dyer incurs no offense, it would contradict the scriptural text.

Furthermore, it says: "On the first day, if one obtains a robe, there is *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* [offense]. The above represents the two interpretations presented by Feishen. As for various lecturers...

All [the preceding views] rely on the first interpretation and refute the second. It is incorrect to restrict [the analysis] solely to the tenth chapter, for that would fail to encompass the entirety of the preceding chapters.
Now, Fabao instead supports the second interpretation. Although at first glance it may seem narrow, upon examining the underlying principle, it proves to be comprehensive.
Since, according to this view, one incurs no offense whatsoever regarding the nine days of dyeing without robes during the tenth chapter, it consequently extends to...

This clarifies that in the first chapter, obtaining robes over ten days—with one day acting as the "dyeing agent" and the subsequent nine days as the "dyed object"—constitutes an offense in all instances.

The text uses this to reveal by contrast that there are both offenses and non-offenses regarding the intermediate eight chapters; by citing the latter to constrain the former, it fully captures the underlying principle.
The present *Chao* (Commentary) is precisely composed based on this tenth chapter. If one were to follow the *Souxuan*, it would instead result in a mere collection [of fragments].
The meaning is not yet exhausted. Since Chapter One has been bypassed and Chapter Two is being composed as unfinished, reflect upon this:
herein there are further instances of descending, reversing, hooking, leaping, and intervening phrases; these will not be set forth unless they are urgent.
"Categories such as these" refers to the ten chapters on attainment and non-attainment and their like. "Possessing eight gates that universally do not defile one another" refers to the second day.
If one does not obtain the robe, there is nothing to be dyed. On the second day, there is the *śuddhi-dharma* (the rite of purification); therefore, they do not become defiled by one another.

Regarding the other six cases, such as when it is given to another person or due to causes such as forgetfulness, they likewise do not become defiled. As for the remaining cases where there is no cause for non-offense, this refers to the aforementioned obtaining of the robe without the conditions for non-obtainment;
furthermore, if on the first day one obtains a robe but does not perform the *pariṣkāra-dāna* (the formal act of relinquishment), that constitutes a lack of purity.
Regarding the conditions for giving: in the latter six gates, there is no condition of "giving to another," and therefore one commits an offense in all of them.

Second, regarding "pure giving in the interim": this refers to the second gate through the eighth gate. If on the first day one obtains cloth but does not perform pure giving, and on the second day one obtains cloth and performs pure giving, there may be ten chapters of offenses to fear.
Third, regarding "sending to another": if on the first day one obtains cloth but does not send it [to another], [one commits an offense].
Regarding the section on "Giving to Others," it is modeled after the preceding [section] and also consists of ten chapters; even the eighth chapter, which was omitted, is likewise [treated].

I have not listed them all here, as they are abbreviated in the actual text. In the commentary, the character [火*句] (pronounced *jù*, meaning "to enlighten") appears; the rest of the text is intelligible.
Regarding the statement, "The Vinaya says it reaches this point": this refers to the textual passage concerning the *atireka-cīvara* (extra robe). As for "if one gives wealth and departs," etc.:

in ancient times, when one was about to commit the offense of possessing an extra robe, one would greedily seek a new robe; although the physical substance of the robe had been relinquished, the mental intention to possess it was not severed, and thus the defilement of attachment remained.

When the subsequent robe entered one's possession, one immediately committed the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture). "Light" (*ji*) refers to the light offense of wearing [the robe]. Now, the Master [Daoxuan] marks this as a refutation, stating that according to the *Śāstra*:
The *Madhyama-āgama* is not like this; that is, it does not state such things as in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*. Regarding the phrase "from 'many' up to 'ra':

" based on this, since it says that for the subsequent robe there is no defilement, and that one does not confess this robe but confesses the previous *thullaccaya* offense, we should know that the mind of possession did not defile the subsequent robe.

Regarding the phrase "the two robes, not having been relinquished, enter into purification": this refers to the two robes obtained through support (*upakaraṇa*). Since they were not defiled [by the mind of possession], they may be purified.
What need is there to abandon it? Therefore, it is said that one does not abandon it. Since there is no fault, its essence is pure; thus, it is said that "the person is already pure.

Regarding the phrase "up to [the point where]... this passage has two parts: first, the presentation of the correct principle; second, the citation of the Vinaya to prove that it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense).

This means that although the previous robe has been removed, the offense remains because it has not yet been confessed; therefore, there is a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture), as one has committed the offense of failing to relinquish the robe.
One should sell [the item] without discarding it; by contravening the Buddha’s words, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. This does not mean that wearing it is auspicious, as some ancients have claimed.

Regarding the statement "it does not constitute an offense": within the ten-day period, this is precisely the permitted state, and thus there is no offense. If one performs the ritual of *pariśuddha-pariśuddha-dāna* (pure-to-pure giving), there is no offense because the formal procedure has been performed.
If one gives it away to another person, there is no offense because it is no longer one's own property. If it is seized by a thief...

Regarding the term "etcetera," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "When wealth is kept with the intention of discarding it, there is no offense because it is not [intended as] one's own.

For example, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one sees the original property later, an additional ten days are permitted; this is because, in principle, it is considered newly acquired. The note states:

"To say that one may again obtain ten days for *śuddhi* (purification) and re-undertake the vow refers to the aforementioned Vinaya passage concerning the separation from robes (*cīvara-vipravāsa*), which lists four conditions under which the undertaking is lost and there is no offense. Now, in this case..."
Not so. If one encounters the four conditions and subsequently obtains [the robes] again, it is as if newly acquired; one may perform the *śuddhika* (purification) rite for ten days.

If all three robes are obtained together, one should once more formally accept and maintain them; this does not refer to the formal acceptance of extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*). Consider this carefully. As for those who take and wear [them]:

The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Because one previously received and maintained the three robes, but they were subsequently lost due to circumstances, and since the three robes are no longer present while a surplus robe (*dīrgha-cīvara*) remains, one takes that [surplus] to receive and maintain [as the three robes].
Therefore, it is said 'taking and wearing the robe. This means there is no fault, provided one directly confesses the previously committed offense.
The following citation of the *Gāthā-śāstra* intends to prove that although one commits the offense of possessing a surplus robe, it is not an offense to make it into the three robes. Why?

Therefore, what was stated previously—that one who commits an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*) is not permitted to make the three robes—was intended precisely to resolve a point of doubt and difficulty.

That is to say, the preceding citation of the Vinaya text states that a forfeitable robe (*naiḥsargika-cīvara*) "should not be given to others," and so forth, up to "it should not be made into the three robes.

Now, why is it that here one is permitted to make the three robes without incurring the offense of forfeiture? The answer is: "This is based on [the following]... This means that such a statement is based on the existence of... [text truncated].
This refers to one's own robes; thus it is said that this is based on that. Regarding the permission to wear the five primary colors:
this means that while such improper colors are not permitted according to the Buddha’s regulations, they are now temporarily allowed for wearing due to the loss of one's robes.

When people see a bhikṣu wearing these robes, they immediately know he has encountered bandits. As for borrowing laypeople's robes from the *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya] and maintaining them as one's own, the robes likely refer to those worn temporarily as coverings.
One may borrow from An-rèn to receive [the robe], because it is identical to the three robes (*tricīvara*).

The *Vinaya* states that if another gives one a cloak (*saṃkakṣikā*), there is no offense. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) says: "Since this property is a heavy object, it is not appropriate to apply the ritual of purification (*pariśuddhi*).
Although it exceeds the time limit, it does not fall under the category of 'excess' (*atireka*). Regarding the commentary, as no explicit authorization has been seen, I have cited many explanations.

*Sou Xuan* says: "If another person makes it into a robe for one, and this object has not yet attained the characteristics of a robe—remaining merely as a bolt of cloth—it ought to be subject to *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (the declaration of purity).

However, because it is being made into a robe for the sake of warmth, it does not require such a declaration. Now, it is said that no explicit permission has been seen for a bhikṣu to possess a robe [other than the three].

This refers to when winter arrives in the Western Regions, where one covers the body with the three robes. Below, he cites the *Shi tan shang seng ji* (Record of the Upper Monks of the Ten Discourses).

A single person may also receive [the robe]. Furthermore, another explanation states: while the characteristics [of the robe] have not yet been finalized, it remains merely a bolt of cloth and must likewise be declared as pure (*śuddha*).

Below, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is cited, which discusses that both the Saṃgha and a single person may receive [it], but does not mention its storage. The above presents three interpretations in full;
one may choose among them according to one’s own judgment (etc.). Regarding "entrusting the robe to one traveling afar," this refers to a bhikṣu who has received [the robe].
Having finished, he entrusted it to another person to keep. The one who received it hid it in a chest and traveled far away, being absent for more than ten days;
yet there was no offense, because this was still a case of physical obstruction rather than a fault of the mind. The same applies when the northern route is cut off.

Regarding the precept on being separated from the three robes overnight (*trīṇi cīvarāṇi*): Second, as for the explanation of the name: when a person and their robe are in different locations, it is called "separation" (*viyoga*).

Because it violates the prescribed limits and is defined by the appearance of dawn (*āloka-lakṣaṇa*), it is termed "overnight" (*rātri*). This is what is prohibited, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "when the conditions are met, one commits an offense":

as for the obstacle of the robe and the person being in different locations, the reason why "different realms" (*sīmā-bheda*) is not mentioned is that within a single realm there may be obstacles; even if...
This refers to the boundary. Since one cannot avoid losing the robe, it is not called a "boundary. Furthermore, it obstructs the broad inclusion of the boundary.

Regarding "not relinquishing the assembly": since one has not attained the assembly, one also lacks the leisure to relinquish it. "Lacking causes and conditions" refers to the obstruction of heavy robes and the month of Kārttika, and so forth.

Regarding the statement "the third [case] refers to the original commentary": concerning the fact that obtaining the three robes or five robes constitutes a *pāyattika* offense—[one might ask], why is there no *naiḥsargika* (offense involving forfeiture)?
The answer is: from the perspective of the robe itself, there is already forfeiture; here, however, the offense is established based on the person, and therefore it is not mentioned.

As for "other robes constitute a *dukkaṭa*," this refers to external items. Outside of the three robes are the "extra robes" (*atirekacīvara*); fearing that one might not separate from them, [the rule states] "if separated... [the offense follows].

This constitutes an offense of *dukkaṭa*. Consequently, the established precedent states: "One hundred [rules] were permitted by the Buddha; because staying overnight [with extra robes] constitutes an offense, it is *dukkaṭa*.

Extra robes (*atirekacīvara*) were also permitted by the Buddha; why then is there no offense of *dukkaṭa*? The *Śāstra* (Commentary) says: "It does not mean that one may store extra robes and so forth. Our Master now says:

Regarding the aforementioned mention of "other robes," these refer precisely to the one hundred and one garments for personal use. Although their use was permitted, the Buddha commanded that they be received and maintained; to now violate this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Although the *atireka-cīvara* (extra robe) is similar in nature, it is subject to the rules of purification and donation (*pariśuddhi-dāna*). It must be entered separately into the inventory and its private possession is not permitted; furthermore, it is not to be maintained [as a constant possession].

What offense would there be in being separated from it? This does not accord with the interpretations of past masters. Furthermore, the three robes (*tricīvara*) are [subject to] the formal prohibitions (*pratikṣepa-sāvadya*), and so forth.
"Those" refers to the Buddha who personally established the regulations for persons of the three grades. Now, by violating the formal precepts, one incurs a grave offense.

The "one hundred and one" are permissions rather than prohibitions; because they merely violate what has been undertaken and maintained, they are minor. "The long [period] for those of lower class" refers to persons of the lowest grade.
The Buddha opened the way of skillful means by separately bestowing [the surplus] upon others; because he himself had no mind to store or accumulate it, he was entirely without fault.

As for the rest, as stated in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts): A question is raised: "Among the three robes and the one hundred and one items, these are what are to be maintained through formal acceptance (*parigraha*).

Why is it that if the three robes are separated from the person overnight, the acceptance is lost and one incurs a *pāyattika* offense, whereas if the one hundred and one items are separated overnight, the acceptance is not lost and there is only a *duṣkṛta* offense? The answer is: "The three robes are primarily regulated regarding their formal acceptance."
There are three grades. Now, if one stays apart from [the robe] overnight, the offense of violating the regulation is grave, and one loses the validity of the formal acceptance (*upasaṃpadā*).

Regarding the "one hundred and one" robes, for those of middle and lower quality, although there is a violation, it is merely an *ājñapti* offense; one does not lose the formal acceptance. If that is so, since the bowl is also subject to the regulation against staying apart overnight, why is it merely an *ājñapti* offense and one does not lose the formal acceptance?
The answer is: because the use of the robe is broad, its temporary separation is permitted; therefore, [in the case of the robe], one incurs a *pāyattika* offense and loses the formal acceptance.
The *pātra* (alms bowl) is used for only one purpose and is subject to temporal limits;

therefore, its lightness does not cause one to lose the method of receiving it. Regarding the phrase "from two up to the middle," it is as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "up to three," this refers to the aforementioned three obstacles that exist throughout the boundaries:

namely, the three obstacles of defilement, separation, and mental state (*citta*). This applies regardless of whether they are produced by formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) or arise naturally; if these three are present, they all constitute [obstacles].

[The boundary] is lost; therefore, it is said that they "interpenetrate" (and so forth). If one discusses the obstruction of spatial limits such that this and that do not interpenetrate, it refers to the fact that natural boundaries (*jātideśa*) create mutual obstructions for one another, and thus do not interpenetrate.
Within these natural boundaries, there are fifteen types, namely the monastery boundary (*sīmā*) and so forth; each of these is mutually non-interpenetrating.
As for those established by formal ritual (*kṛtadeśa*), such as the *śīlākṣetra* (precept field) and the small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*), these likewise [do not interpenetrate].
[Answer: They are distinct. Regarding the various boundaries within a *saṃghārāma*: these correspond exactly to the physical characteristics of the monastery’s perimeter.

If no laypeople enter, and the area throughout the monastery is occupied solely by renunciants, there is no separate boundary; this is called "one boundary. However, if women or others enter the monastery, multiple boundaries arise;
hence it is said to have "various boundaries. The commentary states: "There are no more than three obstructions. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* says: "One boundary..."
[The practitioner] attains mastery in coming and going therein, because they are free from the three obstructions. Regarding the phrase "from the beginning up to 'following the body'":
this refers to a passage in the Vinaya commentary (*vinaya-śāstra*) concerning a bhikṣu who leaves his robe in a village. When he goes to retrieve it, he fails to untie the fastening;
consequently, his body is exposed, leading to shame and embarrassment. Because of this, he informed the Buddha, and the Buddha declared: "From this day forward, [it shall not be so]."
"One may leave one's robes within a village. If one wishes to establish a robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*), one must first exclude the village" (as stated in the Vinaya text).

The Venerable Master says: "A village has no fixed substance; it is merely designated based on the indeterminate coming and going of men and women. Therefore, it is not permitted to place [the robes] there. Later, if the village departs, it is permitted to remain as before.
Furthermore, according to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, a village has five meanings: first, the village boundary is not fixed, whereas the robe-boundary is.

This is meditative concentration (*samādhi*). [It serves to] first, stop slander; second, eliminate strife and contention; third, protect the holy life (*brahmacarya*); and fourth, remove lustful doubts.
The *Chao* (Excerpts) sets forth three meanings; the remaining two are subsumed within the character "etc. (*diǎng*) [in the original text]. As for "the nature and characteristics being in conflict":

The *Shuowen* states: "To contradict (*wu*) means to leave a trace. This refers to the fact that the nature of a bhikṣu consists in upholding the prohibitive precepts, whereas the nature of a woman consists in carnal desire.
Because these two natures are mutually opposed, it is said they are "discordant in nature. Furthermore, the characteristic of a bhikṣu is to restrain body and speech through prohibitions.

Women take the unrestrained use of body and speech as their characteristic; hence it is said they "contradict" [the precepts]. Regarding "staying in the same room" and so forth, these are all explained as in the ninety [rules] mentioned above.

As for the phrase "the second through the eighth being coarse and difficult," Baoshou says: this refers to the occurrence of the eight difficulties (aṣṭāvaraṇa), which are obstructions caused by external circumstances rather than a fault of the person.

Therefore, the rule is relaxed such that there is no offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; however, one merely loses the ritual propriety (*mukhadharma*) of the robe. Later, upon seeing the robe, one should retrieve it again.

This refers to receiving [the benefit of] protection. Regarding "not taking the door key": if the gate is closed and lacks a door-bolt such that one can enter, yet the robe is separated from oneself, then one loses possession of the robe.
If one takes the door-bolt and goes to meet [the gate], there is no separation; therefore, one does not lose it. Regarding "no ladder of twelve rungs":
they say that a bhikṣu places his robe on an upper shelf while he stays overnight below; provided there is a ladder or a path for ascending and descending, [it is not lost].

[The robe] is not lost because the *Saṃghāṭī* lacks the "sphere of influence" (*śeṣabhāga*). Regarding the statement "losing the robe after three [days]": "obstruction of sentiment" (*cittavighna*) means that there is a hindrance in one's feelings; thus it is called an "obstruction.

In the Vinaya of this particular school, all cases are based on an obstruction of one's own feelings—such as the fear that the robe might be seized or that one’s life might be endangered by wild beasts—and so forth.
As for the *Mahāsāṃghika* and others, they define the boundary based on the limits of brotherly relations; this is what is termed a "household" (*kula*).

Regarding the *sīmā* (boundary): the text states that concerning the "domestic boundary" (*gṛha-sīmā*), if two brothers live together in a household and have established separate internal divisions such that the elder brother does not permit the younger to enter, and the younger does not allow the elder to enter;

if a bhikṣu stays overnight with the elder brother while his robe remains with the younger, this is called "losing the robe. If those brothers say to the bhikṣu, "Although laypeople [act] according to their own inclinations..."

"Obstructed" means there is no impediment regarding the Saṃgha; one may act as one pleases with respect to either side. At that time, if one places robes according to one's convenience, they are not lost.

Regarding the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun) and other texts: those refer to cases such as kings or illusions; it is based on the fact that one’s mind is obstructed by them. The treatise says:

"If a king enters the boundary and sets up a tent to stay, the areas for food and drink near the king’s left and right, as well as the places for large and small excretions, are all not [suitable] for robes."
Regarding the phrase "the realms (*dhātu*), as well as the making of agreements and so forth, are also like the royal law":

when musicians enter a monastery, they may place their robes near him on his left or right, just as the king does not distinguish [between them]. Therefore, it is said, "also like the royal law. Question:

Since people such as illusionists do not hinder a bhikṣu’s coming and going or the gathering of robes, why is it called an "obstruction of the mind" (*sāmantaka-pratibandha*)? Answer: It does not hinder the coming and going; however, because these people, such as illusionists, are numerous...

It causes a bhikṣu’s mind to become dissolute; this may also be termed an "obstruction of the mind. As for the phrase "reaching the same boundary," it means that while the robe is in its natural state and the person is within the ritual enclosure (*karmabhūmi*), the robe and the body are in different locations—this is termed an "obstruction of the boundary. This refers only to the case of the natural boundary.

In the case of various types of enclosures such as houses or groves, if the body and the robe are in two separate locations, both are termed obstructions of the boundary. Regarding the loss of the robe through the common boundary, it refers to the aforementioned...

If there are three obstructions, one enters the *dharmadhātu* (the formal boundary), and the loss of the robe is determined by the *dharmadhātu*. If it is a natural boundary (*prakṛtistha-sīmā*), the loss of the robe follows the natural boundary.
Regarding "obtaining protection for the robe through commonality": this means that when there are no three obstructions, one enters within two boundaries;

each of the two boundaries separately provides protection for the robe through their own commonality. This term "commonality" is stated with reference to the respective boundary itself; it does not mean that they are made to merge. Reflect on this.
The following citation from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* serves as proof: "This is called a separate boundary (*pṛthag-sīma*), not a shared robe-boundary (*sādhāraṇa-cīvara-sīma*).

As with the three aforementioned obstructions, when one enters these two types of boundaries and loses one's robe, this is indeed an obstruction caused by defilement and mental attachment that impedes the boundary.

Why, then, is it specifically termed a "boundary-obstruction"? Answer: Because these three matters come to obstruct the boundary, preventing the boundary from exercising autonomous protection over the robe. Thus...

Because many *dhātu*s (elements/realms) arise, it is called "obstruction of the *dhātu*. If there were no superior three obstructions, entering the *dhātu* would be universal across one realm and thus not be called an obstruction of the *dhātu*.

As for the phrase "if one reaches [it]": "Dharma" refers to the performance of the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to demarcate the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*), specifically referring to the two lower types of robes.

The commentary states: "Now, regarding the fifteen realms (*dhātu*). As extensively explained in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the *Ekottara-śikṣāpada*, and other schools: [The text continues with the detailed exposition.]
The following (and so forth). Regarding the phrase "the four boundaries": first, the boundary of a *saṃghārāma*; the Sanskrit term is *saṃghārāma*, which is here abbreviated.
Second, the boundary of a village; this refers to the boundary of a village settlement. Each has four types, as listed in full in the text. It says: "This..."
"Reaching such [a state]" refers to the fact that these various characteristics differ, even extending to as many as several *dhātu*s (spheres/regions); this describes the views of the ancients.

It means that according to the Vinaya text, for one who does not lose their robe, there is a single *sīmā* (boundary) within the monastery (*saṃghārāma*); for one who loses their robe, there are several *sīmā*s within the monastery.
The ancient masters erroneously explained this by saying that these various characteristics are incomplete, meaning that there are no walls on all four sides.

Furthermore, regarding "leaving the fences and so forth," this refers to the destruction of the boundary markers (*sīmā-lakṣaṇa*). As for "trees, vehicles, and the like within the boundaries, or thickets of vegetation," once the boundary markers have been destroyed, if there are trees therein, they are called the "tree boundary" (*vṛkṣa-sīmā*);
or if there are vehicles and the like, they are also called the "vehicle boundary" (*śakaṭa-sīmā*). Therefore, it is said that there are "various [boundaries].

This constitutes a distinct boundary (*pṛthag-sīmā*) and is not termed either a "monastic community" (*saṃgha*) or a "village" (*grāma*). This is the refutation by the present Master. His intention is as follows: if...

If the boundaries of a monastery (*saṃghārāma*) are surrounded by trees or carts, they are renamed as "Non-Manifest" (*apratyakṣa*). If the characteristics of the monastery boundary are destroyed, there is no longer a monastery boundary;
within that space, where there are cart-boundaries and so forth, these are merely designated as "tree-boundary," "cart-boundary," and so on, each with its own distinct name for its location.

Furthermore, it is said that within a monastery there may be several boundaries; if they are continuous, the individual distinctions are lost, but if they are not continuous, [the distinctions remain].

Since it is impossible for both [conditions] to be absent simultaneously, one knows that this is incorrect. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) indicates: "If it is deficient, is it not a *sīmā*? It says, "It should be in the wilderness.
The present statement of "etcetera" (*ādi*) is the author of the *Chao* (Sub-commentary) choosing his own examples; that is to say, these three obstacles exist within the *sīmā*.
A bhikṣu cannot travel freely back and forth; therefore, it is said that within the monastery grounds (ārāma) there are various boundaries.

This applies even to the boundaries of houses, paths, and so forth. This means that, as indicated above, if there are three types of obstructions within the monastery, one loses possession of one's robes;
if there are none, one does not lose them—the same principle applies here.
Regarding the statement "from three trees to the offense": "equal to a person" means that when one stands up, there is no obstruction to the head.
"Sufficient shade" means it is sufficient to provide shade for the body. This merely clarifies the minor characteristics; this defines the smallest boundary for lifting the *kaṭhina*.
If this [boundary] is destroyed, it is not permissible. "Trees whose branches do not touch" means that the branches and leaves on the four sides are not connected. To take [this as the measure]:
Regarding the phrase "at midday," this distinguishes the protective nature of the *kāṣāya* (robe) precept; the textual characteristics are clear. Some interpret it as follows:
"If a tree stands directly in the path, and one relies on that tree for protection of the robe, the robe must be hung upon a branch and not placed on the ground below.

This is because the boundary of the tree (*vṛkṣa-sīmā*) is inferior to the boundary of the path (*mārga-sīmā*), and thus [the robe] is lost. This interpretation has entirely failed to perceive the underlying principle and is a base fabrication.
It says: "Simply rely on the text. According to the interpretation in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one obtains the protection of the robe as long as it is covered by the shadow of the tree.
Regarding trees that are joined together, Xuán says: 'Trees that are not joined constitute a tree-boundary (*vṛkṣa-sīmā*); if they are joined, this also constitutes a single boundary of one *krośa*.
This correctly defines the substance of the boundary. As for the phrase 'from the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* to the point of loss,' and 'excessive length' and so forth, these are merely..."

A single tree: within it, there may be one branch that is somewhat longer than the others. Although this branch is long, since the other branches are only one or two *zhàng* [in length], this constitutes the boundary of the tree.
For those who come and go, women and the like do not constitute a "garment-boundary" (*cīvara-sīmā*).
Regarding the phrase "upwards to": "upwards" refers to a great forest; furthermore, it is free from obstacles for a distance of one *krośa*, though its influence does not extend further.
As for the phrase "the nature of trees," it means that because the area covered by them is not extensive, it can be explained without difficulty. Regarding the phrase "because the monks arrived":
*manjia* (pronounced *man* with the second tone) refers to the grapevine, which grows as a creeping plant; *guo'na* is similar, meaning [a structure] in the center of a trellis.
Taking twenty-five cubits on each of the four sides constitutes the natural garment-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*).
This refers to the fact that these grapevines and the like are like a small grove; because their extent is not vast, the measurement is calculated in cubits within this space.
Regarding the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* and other such works, the *Liaoshu* (Commentary on the Clarification) states: "Prajāpati-loka is translated here as 'Victorious Virtue' (*Jiǎngdé*).

This palace of Śakra is one thousand *yojanas* high, while the Jambu tree is one hundred *yojanas* high. The boundary of this [rain] realm is defined by the reach of the raindrops from these palaces and trees;
if one wears the robe upon the upper body while remaining within the lower boundary, one does not lose the overnight [retention of the precepts]."
Regarding the robe: the reason for this is twofold. First, because it falls from above; second, because it would not be stolen by others.

If the body were positioned above, it would contradict these two principles and is therefore improper. The intent of citing this passage is to explain and establish the aforementioned tree-shelves and so forth, as well as the positioning of the body and the robe, one above and the other below.
Regarding "the four points of arrival": "a place empty and quiet outside the village" means that if one is inside the village, the name [of such a place] does not apply;
as for protecting the robes, it refers to the actual size of the area. Regarding "the five points of arrival leading to an offense":
"both being on land" refers to when the vehicle is stationary. If the vehicle or boat is turning around, this correctly defines the boundary for protecting the robes.

It is as follows: when the robe is within a carriage or boat and one’s body is outside, provided that one remains stationary and turns so as not to lose [the connection between] the interior and exterior, it is permissible.

Regarding "carriages and the like" in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, this refers to a person who rides in a carriage and drives oxen without ever mounting them; he merely sits in the carriage and strikes the oxen with a staff.
Now, regarding this staff: suppose there are many carriages traveling together in a line, and either the person is in the front carriage while the robe is in [a rear one], or...
Regarding the preceding and following carts: if the carts face one another and the ox-whips reach across them, this is called a single boundary (*ekasīman*), regardless of their number.

Even if people or robes are separated by a thousand carts, as long as there is no obstacle between them, it is all termed a "robe-boundary" (*cīvarasīman*). Furthermore, one must know that these carts belong to a single household;
if they have different owners, such as Zhang or Wang, they may not be maintained as a common unit. This applies even when they are loaded onto a boat upon the water.

Regarding the term "and so forth": according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Chapter Eight, it is said: "If a bhikṣu travels on the same boat as an outsider (tīrthika), but they have separate dwellings, and the outsider’s dwelling is secure and firm—may he entrust his robes there and stay overnight? If there is an outsider who permits him to come and go at will, and they do not meet, there is no offense.

This means that if there is no obstruction of intent, there is no violation. However, in the present day, many cabins are situated upon riverboats; if one leaves his robes there, this does not conform to the rule for an offense.
This is the measure.

Regarding the statement "seven [rods] for attainment," the *Caturvargika-vinaya* mentions "signlessness" (*animitta*). In the Vinaya, there is only the name of the entire boundary (*sīmā*), along with the rule regarding not leaving one's robes unsecured.
As for the phrase "signs," this refers to separate designations outside the village. Now, our Master explains this dwelling (*śālā*) based on the textual evidence.

It is currently outside the village. If it were inside, then the village would be strong and the dwelling weak; how could its name be established and its presence made manifest? Therefore, it is said to be "outside the village.

Since it is distinguished as being outside the village, it is called a "dwelling" (*śālā*). Based on this, the similarities and differences between a village and a settlement (*sanniveśa*) are distinguished;

these will be explained extensively later, hence the statement: "it shall be explained in detail later. Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya] mention of twenty-five cubits outside the stairs and pathways of a multi-storied pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), that...

It is said: "A 'double-roofed building' (chùng-sa) refers to a multi-storied pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*). Measuring twenty-five *hasta* from the base of the stairs outward on each side constitutes the boundary substance (*sīmā-vastu*).

This applies regardless of the size of the pavilion or whether the stairs are located inside or outside. Regarding the boundary of storehouses and granaries, the *Ming-nei* (Within the Light) is specified;

according to the *Jiaochao* based on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the boundary of storehouses and granaries is established according to the *Ming-nei*, which serves as the substance of the robe-precept (*cīvara-śikṣāpada*). (*Ming-nei* means within the walls)."
Regarding the two cases where neither [boundary] can be obtained: this refers to the *caturvargika* (four-part) *śīman* (boundary), which exists only in name and has no other reality;
and the *Mahāsāṃghika* boundary of twenty-five cubits (*hasta*) for the purpose of protecting robes, as well as the boundary of storehouses.

Because these two measurements are absent from what is called the "inner" [boundary], they are termed "neither of the two. Now, between these two, one adopts one kind to serve as the substance of this *śīman* for protecting robes; therefore—
It is said that it may be accepted as is; furthermore, there are those who do not understand it and thus do not record it.
Regarding the phrase "facing until falling": the preceding text mentioned "villages and settlements," and the subsequent detailed explanation specifically refers to this passage.

This means that while the previous section clarified the four parts of the *śālā*-boundary (*sīmā*), it only provided their names without determining the actual location of the *śālā*. Now, the Master [explains] it according to its meaning...

The judgment states: "A separate dwelling outside the village is similar to, yet distinct from, a 'zhūzhī' (a cluster of villages). How can one clarify the distinctions between a village and a cluster based on this alone?"
Regarding the phrase "it reaches four parts": "the village boundary of the *Caturvargika*" is the heading.

Within the Vinaya, there are only names for villages, but it does not distinguish how they are designated as "villages," nor what is not designated as a "village" and so forth. Below, external sources are cited to clarify these characteristics.
"A market is called a 'village,' and a market is called a 'cluster' (*kheṭa*)" is the explanation from the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*. It states: "The four characteristics are the courtyard walls."
That which is fully provided with [facilities] is called a *cun* (village). Because people dwell together there, it is further called a *ju* (settlement).

As for *luo* (market town), it derives its name from the fact that it is a place where [goods] are carved and displayed. Thus one knows that there is no difference in outward appearance between a village and a settlement.

Regarding what is called a *shi* (market), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A place where people of various natures gather to trade. Having understood what a settlement is, one further notes that within such a settlement, there are two distinct types of households.
Next, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* is cited regarding how names are established through mutual relation. If they were not mutually related, the name would vanish and remain unmanifest.

Regarding the statement that "one is a cluster (*grāma*) but not a household (*kula*"), it means that while it receives the name of a "cluster," it does not receive the name of a "household. The internal commentary explains:

for example, if there are two clusters each containing one household, and these two clusters, east and west, stand in relation to one another, they then receive the name of "clusters. Within a single cluster, however, each [household]...
Regarding "family" (*kula*): there is no other family that stands in contrast to a family by which it could be made manifest.
That is to say, within the eastern cluster (*grāma*), there is only one *Kula* family, and no other families such as Wang or Li;

within the two clusters, assuming there is one *Wang* family, there are no other families such as Ya or Zheng, and thus the name "family" disappears and is manifested only in relation to the cluster (*grāma*). (This explains the characteristics of the family and the cluster, but does not yet discuss the meaning of protecting the robe. Second.

A "house" (*kula*) is not a "collection" (*saṃghāta*). This refers to those such as the Ayāras, Vajjis, Licchavis, and Nattaputtas; they receive the designation "house" because they exist in contrast to what is not a collection.

Furthermore, regarding the third [point], that it also possesses both [characteristics] such as the two realms: because there are two collections in contrast to one another, they receive the name "collection.
Within these two collections, there are multiple houses; through the mutual relation of these multiple houses, they further receive [the designation].
The fourth phrase may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the statement "from a village to a boundary," this is said in general terms; however, it receives the designation "village" specifically by virtue of people living together there.
This serves to reveal that the previous citation from the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, which discusses the matter based on the existence or absence of a marketplace, is entirely narrow and limited.

If one bases it on a "household" (*kula*), it is restricted solely to a single clan; father, son, and grandson share the same surname and dwell together, as clarified previously. As for the statement "extending to the boundary" (*sīmā*):

this refers to the fact that while the aforementioned elegant names clarify the distinction between a household and a village settlement, the characteristics of protecting one's robes remain unknown; therefore, [this must be explained].

The two paths of "common" and "distinct" shall be discussed next. "Distinct boundary" (*bhedasīman*) refers to the designation. Regarding "the distance a cock cannot fly," etc., this indicates the actual substance of this boundary.
Beyond the limit, there exists another boundary, which is all termed a "distinct boundary. A "cock" refers to the domestic fowl belonging to a person;
the place where its flight does not reach belongs to the boundary of another person. If one is guarding robes, [the robes] do not belong to that person.
One attains mutual separation. Outside the range where a rooster can fly, one loses the robe. Regarding the phrase "because they arrive together": "same boundary" (*sīmā*) is the heading.
As for "each village on the four sides having a single household," this refers to four villages extending to one another; within the range of a rooster’s flight, they constitute a single boundary.
That treatise further mentions two types of boundary villages, which the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*) omits and does not clarify. Alternatively, it may simply be...
Citing the four categories to illustrate the two internal categories of one's own dwelling:

regarding "a vehicle, a ladder, or a revolving [mechanism]," one interpretation states that the characteristic of a vehicle’s rotation and a ladder are called "reaching toward" because one can ascend to the top of a wall, enter or exit, and move with ease;

furthermore, when descending from the ladder onto a vehicle, one does not lose the robe because there is no obstruction. A second interpretation states that there is an axle beneath the ladder, by means of which it can be rotated.

It is turned around; this is called "the carriage and the ladder. There are two types: first, the *kaṭhina* robe, which is established by the Saṃgha acting in harmony; second, [the permission] for those traveling afar or for the sick, which is also established by the Saṃgha acting in harmony.

Regarding what is done in an open space: for example, when a bhikṣu is traveling on a road, if he stays within forty-nine paces of the place where he crossed [the boundary], covers the ground, keeps his body straight with arms extended, and holds the corners of his robe so that they reach one another, it is permitted for him to be separated from his robes. This applies even if two people are pursuing one another.

A person was carrying his robes. Sometimes [the companion] was ahead and sometimes behind; suddenly, realizing it was dawn, he looked ahead and behind and saw that the distance between the two people carrying the robes was great.
Suspecting that he might have lost them, he did not know whether they were gone or not. He immediately spoke to the person holding the robes, telling him to stop.

He himself also stopped and told the person holding the robes to lean against a spot one *xing* (尋) and one *zhi* (枳) away. He also measured the ground with a bow; at a distance of forty-nine bows, the ground was level.
This is the limit. Furthermore, one takes up the three robes [as prescribed by the *Song* edition], folds them, and pulls both corners diagonally.

At that time, they cover the ground. With the body straight, one extends the feet toward the point where the bow-tip reaches, facing this person. This person likewise covers [the ground] as the previous person did. If they touch each other, the robes are not lost.
Regarding the dwelling place, the season, and the dimensions of the area: this refers to the time of being in an *āraṇya* (forest hermitage) and the summer retreat (*varṣa*).

Regarding dwelling in the center: furthermore, fearing one might lose the robe, the Buddha permitted one to entrust the robe to another place; thus, one may also stay overnight apart from the robe without it being lost.
Regarding "turning the cart": this refers to the wall of the enclosure, out of compassion. The *Liaoshu* states:
