Question: Why is it that one speaks only of misappropriating the property of the Saṃgha, and not of misappropriating the property of the Buddha or the Dharma? Answer:

Some say that regarding the property of the Saṃgha, since it is permitted for the Saṃgha, there is a risk of confusion with what belongs to oneself; thus, if one were to divert it according to one's own desires, the offense would be grave. Regarding the property of the Buddha and the Dharma, such confusion is rare;

therefore, even if one diverts it, the offense is light. As for the phrase "the Vinaya has reached [this point]": that which was initially permitted to the Saṃgha is definitively not [to be considered as] belonging [to the individual].

1. If one has designated [the property] for the Saṃgha, yet it is for a large group, a specific individual, or a small number, because the mind has not yet reached a definitive decision, diverting it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. 2.

If it is for the sake of the Saṃgha but has not yet been formally granted to the Saṃgha, although it does not belong to oneself, since the distinction between the assembly and the individual has not yet been made, diverting it constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.

3. If it has already been granted to the Saṃgha, it definitively belongs to the owner; diverting it constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), as it is equivalent to stealing communal property (*saṃghika-vastu*). This concludes the section on "The Saṃgha."
Regarding the phrase "As for those who use it": "I have already given to the Saṃgha; now I give to the Venerable" refers to the donor.

This is itself contrary to the Dharma, though there is no fault in the recipient—just as in the case of receiving a gift from a thief. However, one must not ask for it; to ask would constitute diverting property belonging to the Saṃgha.

As for the statement in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* that "it is extremely grave," this is all intended for cases where [the status of the object] is not yet determined; even though the object has been distributed among the monks, because it is not yet...
If it has already been definitively assigned, one incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) by diverting it into one's own possession, and a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) by diverting it to another.

If the gift has been definitively determined as belonging to the donor, and one diverts this object with the intent to cause loss to that other person, one commits a grave offense according to the preceding case. Regarding the diversion of property held in reserve, this is treated according to the rules for "keeping" (*parikkhāra*).

If one diverts this property intended for the *pavāraṇā* ceremony of the Saṅgha and gives it to someone else, one should perform a *dukkaṭa* confession; this is because the ownership has already been definitively established. Diverting...

This constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). Why, then, is it said that one may be "fortunate" (*śubha*) through repentance? It means that if one encourages [the donor] to redirect the gift to another, one attains fortune; however, the object has not yet actually been given to that other person.

If the object were given to that other person, it would mean it is no longer returned to this Sangha, and thus a grave offense would be incurred, because the object would have become the definitive property of either the former or the latter individual.
Therefore, by redirecting it, one commits a grave offense. Based on this, the ownership of a single individual is fixed; there is no other relative factor to distinguish it.
It has not yet been divided. When a monk arrives according to the turn of the assembly, that person who is currently on duty is also definitively assigned [to receive the offering].
If one diverts it to another with the intent to harm this person—thereby depriving them of what they ought to receive—it constitutes a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*).

Regarding the statement in the Vinaya that "there is no offense": this permits the recommendation of the "bad" for the sake of the "good"; here, observing the precepts is considered "good," while violating the precepts is considered "bad. (The above two sections, though distinct, complete the explanation of the fourth chapter.)
Next, the ninety *pāyattika* (offenses requiring expiation) are explained.
This section is divided into two parts: first, a general heading; second, a detailed exposition. Regarding the initial mention of the "ninety precepts," from "minor false speech" down to "the first":
as for the definition of the names, that which does not accord with reality is called "false"; that which is manifested through the mouth is called "speech. This distinguishes it from...

Because [the former] is great, the name of the minor [offense] is designated. This refers to that which is to be prevented (and so forth). Regarding the phrase "from this up to 'all fall into [transgression]'" (*sarvavasthā-patita*):

it means that all those established as prohibitions and contained within the chapters [of the Vinaya] reside in transgressions arising from anger. Therefore, it is questioned here: "Is anger the primary factor in transgression?"

For what reason is this stated? The passage beginning with "Those who uphold the precepts often commit offenses out of anger" serves as the introduction; the section following "This is truly due to... correctly explains the underlying cause.
This means that since time immemorial, one has practiced the karma of false speech, which has perfumed and formed seeds that accumulate within the *ālayavijñāna*.
Therefore, it is said that "false karma has been perfumed and accumulated. These false seeds reside in the *ālayavijñāna* in no small measure.

Therefore, it is said that "the left is often excessive. Thus, "following the objects of the senses" means that these [defilements] arise from seeds as active manifestations; hence they are called "following the objects.
When the objects of defilement and so forth move, one falsely constructs mental frameworks and thereby creates evil karma.

Regarding "not contemplating the beginning of the reversal of the flow," the ancients said this means not contemplating the beginning of reversing the flow of birth and death to return to the source of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Now...
This means that on the very day one first receives the precepts, one vows to sever all evil. Now is the time for sincere resolve;

now is the time for truthful speech. These are the beginnings of reversing the flow [of saṃsāra]. Yet, if one does not reflect at this moment, but merely follows the seeds of one's karma and constantly engages in false speech, one will surely fall into the form of a beast.
To settle one’s life upon such things—upon such hollow fabrications and deluded karma—is to ensure that one’s entire life must end in this way.
It persists until death; therefore, it is said that one must certainly die. If this is the case, one cannot eradicate the seeds of deluded karma within the *ālayavijñāna*.

To leave the household life while following the karmic activities of birth and death—believing in such a thing is truly pitiable; hence, it is said, "Truly it is to be lamented. This expresses a sense of sighing and regret.
(The preceding section, based on the *Sōgen*, concludes the explanation by analyzing the phrases. Alternatively, according to the *Hōbō-kashō* (Commentary on the Dharma-treasure), the phrase states:

"Taking this [life] as the priority for securing one's existence" (this is the first phrase). "When death arrives, it is certainly not possible to cast off karma" (this is the second phrase). The meaning is this:

using the karma of such false speech to secure the body of this life is considered its essential excellence; yet when the time of death arrives, it is certainly impossible to shake off or dispel this karma (this interpretation is also one approach).
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, etc.," the preceding false karma has been cultivated through habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*); as soon as it is activated, it becomes manifest.
"Falsehood": this is done intentionally. Now, based again on whether the object is real or unreal, one incurs the offense simply by contradicting one's own perception;
hence it is said, "furthermore. Regarding "the offense has no fixed object": this means the object is indeterminate, as it may be either existent or non-existent.
It suffices that one contradicts their internal perception; for example, when one does not actually see person Zhang, yet perceives and thinks they have seen him, and later someone asks [about it].
If one answers that they do not see it, this is precisely the distant internal conceptual mind. Why discuss whether external conditions are real or false?
To say "not seeing" is real and the conceptual mind is false; if one sees, the opposite is true. Other cases may be understood by analogy.

Regarding the statement "six conditions leading to liberation," it is as in the text. Regarding the statement "the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* [on] karmic paths," there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). The first is as in the *Chao* (commentary) [and so forth].

The second is double-tongued speech (*paiśunya*) that is not false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) or harsh speech (*pāruṣya*). One transmits these words from one person to another with the intention of causing division;
therefore, it is double-tongued speech. Because one speaks according to the facts, it is not false speech; because one speaks with gentleness, it is not harsh speech.
It is not harsh speech (*pāruṣya*). This is the third phrase. It is evil speech (*durukta*) but not false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) or divisive speech (*paiśunya*).
Because one conveys these words from one person to another and speaks perversely, it is harsh speech; because it is according to the facts, it is not false speech;

and because one does not speak to cause separation, it is not divisive speech. In the fourth phrase, all three offenses are incurred. "Rescuing speech" refers to speaking at an improper time and speaking that is meaningless (*asaṃbaddha-pralāpa*).
All are the playful mind; they are called "saving speech" (*jìyǔ*). As for the other three types of action—whether combined or separate—the one type of saving speech cannot be separated from them.
The commentary explains: "The other three types of action" refers to false speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech.

Since these three mental states all involve saving speech, it is said that they are not separate. For instance, even in the case of false speech, if it is spoken at an inappropriate time, it is [a form of] saving speech.
If one speaks falsely, it is necessarily meaningless. Sometimes false speech is uttered with a mind of mere playfulness;
however, all such false speech is of the same category as divisive speech and harsh speech. When two, three, or four [of these] are committed at once:
when two are committed simultaneously, there is false speech together with divisive speech; when three, there is divisive speech; and when four, there is further the addition of harsh abuse.
Among the ten courses of action (*karmapatha*), two are excluded from the mental [realm]. Therefore, it is said that there are "up to eight matters. Why does it not reach ten?

This is because the three mental states—greed and so forth—do not arise simultaneously within the mental ground (*manobhūmi*). Greed and hatred are contradictory states of mind and do not coexist at the same time.
If one considers both performing the two acts oneself and instructing another to perform six, there are eight precepts for a single occasion. If one only causes another to act, there are only six:
namely, the four verbal transgressions together with the two physical acts of killing and stealing. Sexual misconduct requires one's own body as a medium;
when added to the lack of karma-path [involving] delusion, these constitute eight. Within a single moment, these eight karmas are accomplished.

As for the statement that [the offenses] range from the *pāyattika* to the *duskṛta*: regarding the "Dharmācāryas of the *Caturvarga*" and "Bhikṣus," the *Caturvarga-vinaya* refers to the Śākya son named Hastibala, while the *Pañcavarga-vinaya* refers to the Bhikṣu Śāraṇa; both were exceptionally intelligent and eloquent among all four assemblies of followers.
No śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas were able to equal him in the Way. Consequently, he took what was wrong to be right and what was right to be wrong;

he claimed to know what he did not know and claimed not to know what he did know. He constantly used his skillful eloquence to defeat others, so that none among the bhikṣus failed to sigh in admiration and submission.
They asked him, "When you debate on the meaning of the Dharma, do you consider yourself to be right or wrong? He replied, "In truth, I know I am wrong."
One speaks falsely because of the shame of falling into a state of defeat. A bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha, and it was consequently proscribed.
Regarding "speaking falsely within the Saṃgha" and so forth: Xuán states that this is from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*. It was because Cīrā slandered Trapusa that the Buddha spoke to Cīrā.
If one speaks falsehood before a bhikṣu of firm faith, the offense is more grave than killing countless sentient beings.
If one speaks falsehood before a single bhikṣu of firm Dharma, the offense incurred exceeds that of a hundred bhikṣus of firm faith.

Thus, proceeding by degrees, if one speaks falsehood before the Saṃgha, the offense is more grave than that of speaking falsely before a hundred Arhats. This refers to the gravity of the offense of deception committed before four [bhikṣus]. Why is this so?
Therefore, when ordinary monks receive deception and yet give rise to faith, it is grave; for the noble ones, because they recognize what is not [true] and do not believe [in it], it is light.

As for the previous mention of "firm faith," this refers to those from the stage of the Inner Worldlings (āryapudgala) onward, who have attained the four unshakeable faiths (*avetyaprasāda*). Regarding "firm in the Dharma" (*dharmadṛḍha*):

this refers to having attained the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) among the untainted dharmas (*anāsravadharma*). From the first moment of that mind onward, this dharma is firm and difficult to destroy; therefore, it is called "firm in the Dharma."

One should always cause those who have a basis [for their claims] to provide a referral. That is to say, if one has something to assert, it is appropriate to refer it back to one's teacher or to the sacred teachings;

in doing so, there will be no fault. Even if a fault does occur, it belongs to the person from whom the reference was originally derived. Otherwise, the axe remains in one’s own mouth. Thus, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"When a person is born into this world, an axe resides within their mouth. This means that the speech one utters can wound others, much like a blade.
The *Fǔ* (The Axe). The Master of the Confucian School said: "A single word that injures another is like a sword or a halberd.
The Vinaya says: "That which is seen, heard, touched, and known. The *Sarvāstivāda* school says: "If an object is cognized by visual consciousness, it is called 'seen';
this refers to form (*rūpa*). It requires five conditions: first, a pure eye; second, the object of form; third, space; fourth, light..."
[The fifth is] the intention that initiates consciousness. If an object is cognized by the auditory consciousness, it is called "that which is heard," namely sound.

It is heard through the presence of four conditions; among the five previously mentioned, only the condition of light is excluded. If the object is [cognized] by the olfactory, gustatory, or tactile [consciousnesses],...

That which is realized by the three consciousnesses is called "the perceived" (*vijñāta*), namely the apprehension of odors, tastes, and tangibles. This requires three conditions: first, the three faculties must be unimpaired; second, there must be contact between the object and the faculty;
and third, there must be the mental activity that initiates the consciousness. If an object is realized by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it is called "the cognized" (*vijñāta*).

This refers to the mental consciousness knowing all phenomena (*dharma*); that is, the objective sphere of phenomena. However, this requires only two conditions: first, the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*); and second, [the presence of the object].
The *vijñapti-mati* (consciousness-intent) asks: Why are the three—nose, tongue, and body—combined and designated as "contact" (*saṃsparśa*)? Answer:

Because they apprehend objects internally, it is necessary for the three types of objects to impinge upon their respective faculties before cognition can be attained. However, there must be a slight interval between them:

the nose-faculty is separated from its object by three subtle particles (*paramāṇu*), the tongue-faculty by two, and the body-faculty by one. Nevertheless, they are collectively termed "cognition through contact," meaning:

Because these four constitute the basis for both contrariety and compliance, all eight permutations involve an offense. That is to say, regarding what was not heard, touched, or known, one claims to have seen, heard, touched, or known (forming four permutations);
or, having seen, heard, touched, or known, one instead says one did not see, hear, touch, or know (forming eight permutations).

The first category—concerning cases where one does not externally hear, touch, or know, yet deceives another—consists of twenty-four permutations. First, regarding the six permutations based on not having seen: [the first] is when the fact is fundamentally not so...

1. One sees a mind without conceptualization (*asaṃjñika-citta*), yet deceives others by saying "I see it" (this is a case where both the object and the mind are contrary to the statement). 2. In reality one has not seen;

although one had previously seen a mind with conceptualization (*saṃjñika-citta*), one now deceives others by saying "I have not seen it" (this is a case where the object accords with the mind, but the statement is contrary). 3. In reality one has not seen;

doubt arises within the mind, yet one deceives others by saying "I have truly seen it without doubt" (this is a case where both the object and the mind are contrary to the statement). 4. In reality one has not seen; doubt arose within the mind previously, yet one deceives others by saying [“I have not seen it”]... (text fragmentary).

1. Having seen, one has no doubt (this is a case where the object accords with the mind, but the statement contradicts it). 2. Not having actually seen, one has no groundless doubt; yet one deceives others by saying, "I saw with doubt" (this is a case where both the mind and the object contradict the statement). 3. Not having actually seen, one has no groundless doubt; yet one deceives others by saying, "I saw with doubt" (this is a case where the object accords with the mind, but the statement contradicts it).

4. Not having actually seen, one has no groundless doubt; yet one deceives others by saying, "I saw with doubt" (this is a case where both the mind and the object contradict the statement). 5. Not having actually seen, one has no groundless doubt; yet one deceives others by saying, "I saw with doubt" (this is a case where the object accords with the mind, but the statement contradicts it).

6. Not having actually seen, one has no groundless doubt; yet one deceives others by saying, "I saw with doubt" (this is a case where both the mind and the object contradict the statement). The remaining cases—of not hearing, not touching, and not knowing—are each to be treated according to this pattern, resulting in twenty-four permutations. Next, regarding actual seeing, hearing, touching, and knowing, the same applies.

The twenty-four phrases (can be understood by referring back to the preceding section). Regarding the phrase "differences in what is seen" (*dṛṣṭi-bheda*) and so forth: the Vinaya text further contains six phrases.

As for "differences in what is seen," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "While in a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one sees an evil image and speaks of it as a good one; furthermore, when questioned by others..."

The answer is that they differ from what was seen in their original texts; thus it is said that "what was seen differs. Regarding "what is endured differs": to subtly oppose [the rule] while accepting suffering is called "endurance" (*kṣānti*).

To speak of pleasure to others and further perform the *karmavācanā* together while not actually enduring [the suffering], yet claiming to endure it—this is what is meant by "what is thought differs."
To speak of an enemy as a friend is [an offense]. Furthermore, regarding the "three times" and so forth: these are the three stages of the preliminary, the fundamental, and the subsequent.
There are only eight permutations; four result in a *pāyattika*, three in a *dukkaṭa*, and one is without offense. The Vinaya states:

if one knows it is such at the time of acting, knows it is such at the time of speaking the lie, and knows it is such after the lie has been completed—possessing knowledge across all three times—one incurs a *pāyattika*. Two cases involve knowing at the beginning and middle but not at the end; three... [The text ends here.]

One knows it after the middle part, but does not know it at the beginning; one knows it at the time of the fourfold false speech, but does not know it at the beginning or the end—these four cases all constitute a *pārājika* offense.

Regarding the next three cases which are *duṣkṛta*: first, one knows it at the beginning and the end, but does not know it in the middle; second, one knows it at the beginning, but does not know it in the middle or the end;

third, one does not know it at the beginning or the middle, but knows it immediately at the end—these three are *duṣkṛta*. The eighth case, the single phrase, involves being without intention (*acittaka*) during all three periods.

There is no offense. If, during the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) or similar occasions, one remains silent while harboring a false intention, a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) is incurred at the edge of that transgression.

Regarding the statement "according to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, it constitutes a *pārājika* (defeat)": this refers to one who has a doubtful mind. For example, seeing a person walking past before oneself, one truly suspects whether it is Zhang or Wang. When asked, "Who is it?
and having already reached a conclusion, one answers, "It is Wang," and so forth—if one does not answer when asked... [text ends].
Regarding "the questioner": it does not matter whether the person before one has come to ask or not; if one merely deceives them, one commits the offense.

Regarding "a sound different from the original": this refers to vocal sound. A sound that differs from what was originally spoken—such as a Chinese person using a barbarian (Hū) dialect, or employing the language of Silla and so forth—with the intent of making the person before one fail to understand, all constitute false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*). This is not widely seen [in other texts].
Regarding "those who hear": nowadays it is said that such people are neither seen nor heard much. Regarding "one who explains by destroying characteristics":

this is like a person who clings to the existence of a self or a person, and now [the teacher] refutes it by saying that neither exists. Regarding "uncovered ground" (*anāvṛta-bhūmi*): this refers to speaking in accordance with reality. Regarding "different sounds":

the former person does not understand them. Regarding "inverted": in this land, one first states the agent (*kartṛ*) and then the object (*karman*), whereas here one first states the object and then the agent; this constitutes an error.

For example, if one asks, "Did you hear the sound? and the other replies, "I did not wish to hear the sound," or if one makes a loud noise in response, or speaks indistinctly—these constitute cases where the preceding text applies to those with inferior faculties. Regarding the instruction that one should be made to look at their fingernails, the Venerable One said:
this refers to the hooves of animals, not to making another look at their own fingernails. He questioned the bhikṣu.
"Did you see where the animal went? If one has actually seen it and answers "I did not see it," this constitutes a lie. If one answers "I saw it," this reveals the location.

Now, by simply having the other person look at their own fingernails, both faults are avoided. (The correct explanation above is concluded. Some cite a commentary on the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* which states:
"Fingernail" is a foreign (Hū) pronunciation; here it means 'not seen. Although this appears in the *Mahāsāṃghika* text, it avoids [the fault]."

Regarding the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary): The current *Vyākhyā* itself provides a self-commentary, stating: "This method is for the purpose of guiding and leading [the person] away by having them carry [the object] for a distance.
One must know for certain that they have already gone far; even if one pursues them, one cannot catch them. Only then may one tell them, 'Go from this path.

If one were to simply tell them the husband's location immediately, that would constitute 'indicating the place,' which contradicts the text of the *Vyākhyā*. As for the phrase 'reaching the middle' in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*:"
The specific clarification regarding non-offenses is as stated in the text.

Regarding the second precept on "Abusive Speech": the explanation of the name and the citation from the *Chao* (Commentary) [is as follows] (*etc.*). Regarding the passage from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Zhilun) stating "reaching the world":
according to the *Śāstra*, the Bodhisattva purifies the three karmas of body, speech, and mind as the cause for purifying a future Buddha-field; thus, one's own person is made perfectly pure.
They also purify others. Why is this? Because even if only one person is born in the land, all together create the causes and conditions;
internal phenomena act as causes and conditions for external phenomena. Whether it be good or not-good, because of much unwholesome verbal karma, thorns grow upon the earth.

The remainder is as stated in the *Chao* (Commentary). According to the intent of the treatise (*śāstra*), because there is the cause of a corrupt mind within, internal dharmas induce the external world to have lands that are either pure or defiled.

As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* explains, the external receptacle world is differentiated according to collective karma (*sādhāraṇa-karman*). This is analyzed through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):
first, "common among the common," meaning that all beings together, by means of their ālayavijñāna, collectively transform and project the receptacle world.
Because it is commonly enjoyed by the world, it is "common. Within the category of the common, there is that which is not common [to all], namely humans and animals and so forth;

because they transform it together, it is called "common enjoyment. Yet, due to their respective causes, it is also not common. For example, fish take water as their dwelling place; the various devas see the water as lapis lazuli;
hell-beings and hungry ghosts see the water as transforming into fierce fire; and humans see it as clear, cool water. This is...
It is not shared (*asādhāraṇa*). Third, it is shared within the unshared: the male and female sexual organs (*indriya*). Their seeds transform individually; this is called "unshared.
However, their engagement with tactile contact and the experience of smoothness is "shared. Fourth, it is unshared within the unshared:

for example, each person’s five sense organs (*pañcendriya*) are distinct, and thus they are called "unshared. Furthermore, among these five organs, their sharpness or dullness, clarity or dimness, differs from one to another. Moreover...
This is not common [to all]. As for the statement in the present text that they "act as common causes and conditions," this refers to the first of the four propositions.
Furthermore, regarding the passage about animals hearing insults and feeling shame, the Vinaya states: At that time, a Brahmin had a cow located far to the north.
He then broke off one horn. He and the elder’s ox engaged in a contest of strength to pull a cart, wagering a thousand pieces of gold.
While they were contending, the brahmin cried out before the assembly, “The broken-horned one pulls well; pull by the horn! The ox felt shame and was unable to exert its strength to pull it out.
This caused the elder to win the thousand pieces of gold, while the owner of the ox forfeited it. He then said to the ox: “I...”
"I have always fed you and cherished you, stroking you with affection. Why have you caused me to lose the golden ox?
He replied, "It is not right for you to revile me in the midst of the assembly, causing my strength to fail. You may change your previous words and wager another two thousand *liǎng* of gold.
Later, during the next contest of strength, the Brahmin praised him before the assembly, saying, "The excellent golden [ox] is as majestic and dignified as..."
The Dharma pulls the chariot; hearing it within, the mind rejoices and exerts itself with vigor to emerge. One obtains two thousand pieces of gold.
If even animals are thus, why do you now revile and disparage human beings who possess mantras?

Regarding the statement "six conditions lead to knowledge," it is as stated in the text. Regarding the statement "the *Daśabhāṇavāra* [Vinaya] leads to auspiciousness," the six roots of dispute are listed therein.
Alternatively, one may, due to anger or resentment, disparage others, even up to holding wrong views, thereby defaming the object before them.

Regarding the "four types of people who disparage those of evil dharmas": "evil dharmas" distinguishes them from wholesome dharmas. "Various kinds" refers to the differences in their lineages (*gotra*).
"Types" means that within each of these lineages, there are further specific categories. "Disparaging" refers to actual verbal abuse.

As for the "six classes," the first three pertain to external factors, speaking in terms of lineage, occupation, and craft; the latter three pertain to internal retribution, speaking in terms of body and mind.
They confess their transgressions. First, those of low birth include the Caṇḍāla caste, the scavenger caste, the leather-worker caste, and the like.
As for "clan," this refers to the Kauśika, Vatsa, Bhāradvāja, and so forth. Those of low occupation include pig and sheep sellers, thieves, prison guards, and the like.
As for craftsmen, these include smiths, carpenters, potters, winnowing-basket makers, and the like.

If one says that another has committed such an offense—ranging from a *pārājika* down to a mere *durbhāṣita*—and the person has indeed actually committed it, then by censuring them on this account, one also commits an offense;
therefore, [the rule] remains in force. Fifth, those with many fetters (*saṃyojana*) refers to afflictions (*kleśa*) such as anger and resentment.
Sixth, the blind, the sightless, the bald, the lame, the crippled, the deaf, the mute, and so forth. There are three methods of verbal abuse.
These six aspects are divided into three categories of abuse. First, "face-to-face abuse" refers to speaking directly to one's face.

Second, "abuse by analogy" refers to speaking through comparison. Third, "abusive comparison" refers to saying things such as "I am not that person. Regarding the second category, "good abuse," this is the heading;
it also has three parts, which are the division into three based on shared evil dharmas. "You are a [product of] karma... and so forth.

Regarding the practitioner of *zazen*: the Vinaya text initially cites the forest-dweller (*āraṇyaka*), the alms-seeker (*piṇḍapātika*), the wearer of rag-robes (*pāṃsukūlika*), and the practitioner of meditation (*dhyāyin*).

The present passage states that this extends even to those who transgress the intermediate [precepts]. However, among these, only the abuse of "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*) constitutes an offense; the other two types of abuse are merely metaphors for the other two [categories]. This can be understood by analogy. Question:
If "wholesome dharmas" are considered good abuse and [the others] are considered evil abuse, how is the offense established? The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:
With the intent of the one who reviles, desiring to slaughter and dismember [the other], even a slight fault is magnified into something vast.

You are a person living in seclusion; how can you still wear these robes? Even those beyond training (aśaikṣa) still take up their water-jars and robes. Thus, on account of minor circumstances, they secretly incite one another;
since the emotional transgression is not grave, it is classified as light. (The above is from the Commentary.)
Regarding the statement "as it says in the *Saṃghāṭa*": according to that Vinaya, there are seven types of disparagement: first, lineage; second, occupation; third, physical appearance;
fourth, illness; fifth, offenses; sixth, verbal abuse; and seventh, latent afflictions (*anuśaya*). For the first three categories, each has three grades: superior, middling, and inferior.
The four lower [categories] consist exclusively of the inferior grade and lack the middling and superior grades.
What is now called "superior unwholesome dharmas" refers to taking the most severe of the third category—the inferior grade—and transforming it into a superior unwholesome dharma.

Regarding "inferior lineage," it means saying, "You are of the Caṇḍāla caste," or "You are of the Kośika, Śvapāka, or Vena castes. Regarding "inferior karma," it refers to those such as butchers and hunters. Regarding "inferior marks..."

Regarding "appearance": this refers to those such as the "blind worm" on the head. One who holds these three lower dharmas and reviles other bhikṣus or their parents incurs a *thullaccaya* offense for the parents.
This is because, since the parents gave birth to one's physical body (*rūpakāya*), reviling a bhikṣu is equivalent to reviling them; thus, the *thullaccaya* is established.
Preceptors (*upādhyāya*) and instructors (*ācārya*) are able to give rise to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), just like parents; however, they serve merely as the lineage and the karma.

Their mutual relationship with oneself is not the same; they are ranked one degree lower. However, because their karma and offenses are similar, and since their lineage (*gotra*) regarding the branches of the Path is even more remote, it is merely auspicious.

As for the "other middling and inferior evil dharmas," "middling" refers to those who are neutral, such as the *śūdras* and others; these constitute the middling lineage. Selling flowers, operating a general store, and so forth constitute the middling karma.

[Regarding] "too white, too black, too... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on Buddhist ritual or Vinaya texts concerning the classification of individuals based on caste, karma, and spiritual lineage.)
Blue and so forth are the characteristics therein. If one uses these to revile one’s parents, the preceptor (upādhyāya), or the instructor (ācārya), it is a grave offense;
if toward a fellow practitioner, it is a minor offense. As for the inferior and evil [cases]: "You are of the Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa caste; you are of a superior lineage.
You are engaged in superior crafts such as those of a goldsmith; you possess the thirty-two marks and so forth; you have superior physical characteristics. By means of these...
Abusing one’s parents is the heaviest offense; abusing one’s preceptors and the like is next in gravity; abusing one’s companions is the lightest.

This means that for the middle grade there is no *pārājika* (defeat), and for the lower grade there is no *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting); thus it is said that the gravity decreases by one degree. As for the passage "The earth contains a hidden treasure, which is good at inciting people to fight," this is based on the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. It clarifies the prohibition against those of evil character.

In the past, he was once a servant to an elder named Āmāyu. He beat a subordinate of a certain Brahmin, and although the other Brahmins told him not to beat him, he would not stop because of his beating. Then Āmāyu attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Observing the site of the conflict from above, he saw a treasury of gold beneath the ground. He had a man dig it up, and indeed they obtained the gold. Furthermore—
That Vinaya text states: Before the king’s palace was a hidden treasure of gold. When a man stood upon it, he immediately said, "I wish to solicit the king’s daughter.

The king, finding this strange, had him moved to another place; thereupon, the man did not dare speak. Later, when he returned to his former spot, he repeated his previous words and was consequently compelled to submit.

...it also results in the acquisition of gold. Although this passage is cited in succession within various records, none have yet understood the intent of the *Chao* (the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā*).

A Venerable One said: "The previous citation from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* regarding the six types of disputes (*ṣaḍadhikaraṇa*) was entirely concerned with the internal mind and had no bearing on external objects.

Now, citing the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, [it is shown that] even if internal states could resolve them, disputes would not arise; rather, it is truly because they are pulled by external objects that they cause others [to fall into conflict]."

"Causing disputes" refers to cases where there is a treasure of gold beneath the ground; those with little merit cannot digest it while standing upon it, which leads them to act with cruelty, and thus disputes arise from this.
Reflect on this. Regarding Kāśyapa’s mention of the faults of monks who build dwellings and so forth, this accords with the thirteen precepts in the Vinaya.
There was a certain bhikṣu who built a large dwelling; as he went about begging for alms in the village, everyone grew weary of him.
When Kāśyapa entered the village to beg for food, the householder fled to avoid him. Upon being questioned as to the reason, the elder gave a full account. Kāśyapa reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "If you wish to stay overnight outside the boundary tonight, do so. That night, there were again non-human beings (amanuṣya) who reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha—
When you were ordered to spend the night outside the boundary this evening, that very night another non-human being came to inform the Buddha:
"A bhikṣu was cutting trees and injured my child’s limbs. Out of faith, I did not inflict further harm upon him; may the Buddha take note of this.
The following morning, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha and rebuked the bhikṣu who had built the hut, saying directly: "Last night, a non-human being came to inform me [of these events]."
It is said that Kāśyapa, out of a desire to protect the mind of the bhikṣu who had built the dwelling, feared that [the offender] would harbor resentment and bring up Kāśyapa’s own faults;
for this reason, he censured Kāśyapa. If one were to expose the transgressions of such a person, they would certainly not dare to disparage him.

Even a sage protects the minds of others; how much more so should ordinary bhikṣus refrain from mutual disparagement. Regarding "other similar cases," Xuán explains: it is like the dragon and the bird requesting the scales and feathers [of the Nāga-king].
This is an example of such usage. The following [particle] "kyo" (況且) means "moreover. Now, it is said: "I do not know what intention there is in citing this interpretation.

Please consider this. Regarding the statement "it does not reach the world," it says: "Do not harbor anger or engage in contentious speech. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "At the time of the *pravāraṇā*, there was a bhikṣu..."

When one speaks of another bhikṣu’s offenses, citing what was seen, heard, or suspected, the other bhikṣus should recognize that the person accusing them is themselves impure—capable of committing acts such as sexual misconduct, theft, up to and including destroying living beings or drinking alcohol—and they should not place trust in this person’s words. They should immediately say:
"Venerable sir, do not engage in strife; do not speak to one another; do not obstruct the *pravāraṇā* ceremony of others. According to the intent of the *Chao*, the community...
Although the Saṃgha may know that the person who brings forth the charge is impure in their physical conduct, they must not utter words such as, "You have broken the precepts and are impure;

why do you point out another's faults? If one speaks such words, it constitutes slander. One should simply say, "Do not engage in strife or mutual accusation," and this does not violate the principles of the Dharma.

Regarding the third precept, the prohibition against divisive speech (*paiśunya*): The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states, "To transmit words between two parties in order to cause a breach is called 'divisive speech' (*liangshe*).

This is what is being guarded against. (If one follows the translation of the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang, it is rendered as the "precept against slanderous speech" [*pāruṣya-virati*]; the current term "divisive speech" is somewhat crude. Regarding the phrase "one who possesses [knowledge] up to the point of knowing":

those who speak base and evil matters include such individuals as the "refuse-remover" (*saṃkaradhamika*) and those placed in cages, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "according to the Vinaya, all are *duṣkṛta*": [this refers to the classification of offenses].
"Those who incite strife between oneself and another to cause their division" means to transmit these words in order to separate them.
"Such-and-such says you are [this]" refers to being one of the outcaste *caṇḍālas*, sweepers, jailers, leather-workers, or flour-sellers.

Regarding the statement that there are no superior, middling, or inferior dharmas: this refers only to the seven kinds of abusive speech; among those, the first three possess the distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior. Only.
Regarding the commission of offenses, there are also gradations of severity. In the present case of divisive speech (*paiśunya*), one transmits the insults of another;

regardless of whether the subject matter concerns superior, middling, or inferior dharmas, if one harbors a mind toward oneself that seeks to cause division, it constitutes a single grade of *thullaccaya* (grave offense), with no further reduction to *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).

This is understood by those who have read the *Pōchǎo* (Commentary on the Vinaya). To speak further of what constitutes a *pācittiya* (offense requiring expiation): it is when one transmits the words of another [to create discord].

"Repeatedly speaking to others [of one's offenses] constitutes repeated violations of the *thullaccaya* (grave offense). The passage beginning 'The Vinaya states there is no offense' is as written in the text.

Regarding the passage 'Engaging with a woman up to four times,' this explains the name and cites the *Chao* (the *Vinayavibhāṣā*). Regarding the passage 'Five conditions leading to a *pārājika* (defeat),' it is as written in the text."
Regarding the statement in the Vinaya concerning "reaching the point of an offense": "A human female who possesses discernment" excludes non-human females and female animals.

"One who is without offense" means that if she possesses discernment, it excludes young girls who have not yet attained understanding; furthermore, "as long as the life-faculty is not severed" excludes deceased females.
In the commentary, regarding "that which does not accord with the treatise," this is frequently seen in the two treatises and will be clarified below. First, "open at the front and without walls":
according to the analogy, even under a modern bright-hall (*mingting*) roof, this constitutes an offense. Third, "though covered, it is not complete":
this refers to being enclosed on all sides with both ends covered, but the center remaining uncovered. Fourth, "though the covering is complete, there are openings": above...
"Opening the ceiling to take in light" refers to this. While the preceding chamber has many openings, this chamber differs in that it has only a light-hole.
"If one lies in a slanting position" means leaning askew; it simply means not lying with the body straight, but perhaps leaning against the eastern or western wall, a rope-bed, or similar objects.
All are termed *āśraya* (lying down). Thus, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "If one lies on one's side leaning against something, it is termed 'staying' (*śayana*).
Other incorrect interpretations will not be recorded. Regarding the passage from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* up to the Arhats, it says: The Buddha told Panlu (Bhāradvāja): [text continues].
Although you are an Arhat, you should not sleep in the same room as a woman. Just as cooked food and drink are what people crave, so too is a woman’s desire for a man.
This Vinaya master was also Nanda. A bhikṣu is not satisfied by empty space.
The woman repented her transgression. If even those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) may still be subject to such insults and defilement, how much more so for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*)?

One must not insist on claiming that they do not fear or resist; this is what the Buddha has prescribed. Regarding the statement "many cases constitute a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing)": the preceding commentary in the *Chao-wen* (Excerpts) notes:

This conforms to the treatise and is precisely what this text describes. The commentary states, "as well as the various regions," meaning that in many parts of Da Yuan (Dali), such houses are commonly built;
they have no ridgepole above and are made flat, entirely covered with earth, with an opening in the center to drain water.
It is extremely long, measuring ten bays by five bays. The interior is not partitioned or blocked off; they share a single door. The rest is as stated in the text.
Regarding the statement in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* that "one does not commit an offense": if there is bright light, even if many people are present, one must not sit in darkness.

If there is a lamp and one neither sleeps nor lies down, there is no offense. However, if one lies down while not sleeping, it is still an offense. Note: This does not apply only to chests and beds; this is recorded in various commentaries.
This is not explained in the *Madhyama-āgama*. The Venerable One said: "This was stated to prevent people from harboring defiled thoughts.
Fearing that some might surround their beds with baskets, curtains, and the like, claiming they would thus not commit an offense, this commentary was written to exclude such cases.

Regarding the phrase "men of various schools accompanying [the nun]," this refers to the citation below from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, which states that when a man of understanding accompanies her, he does not sleep. The passage beginning with "there is no offense" follows.

There are nine cases where there is a covering but no obstruction; in these, the characteristics of a "room" (śālā) are not established, and the situation is equivalent to being in the open air. Therefore, it is opened up as non-offensive.
One may find the meaning by examining the text itself.
Regarding the phrase "stating that they go together up to five," this is a citation from the *Shiming* (Explanation of Names). Regarding the phrase "stating that the five lead to an offense;
the remaining meanings are as in other [texts]," the ancients listed the conditions [for the offense] simply as "a male who has not yet received full ordination," excluding women.
The reason for this is that the ancients said: "The Buddha prohibited co-sleeping with women; even a single night was not permitted, let alone three."

Regarding the offense of spending the night [with a woman]: the *Gā-sūtra* states that if one continues to stay with a woman for up to three nights, there is only the offense of cohabitation (*tong-xiu-zui*), but no offense of exceeding three nights.
This text is not the school followed by our present *Shao* (the *Biqiujie-jing-shao*); it is not recorded here in full, so I refer you to other sources for details.

Our present Master says, however, that this applies to both men and women; thus, the *Jieshu* states: "In the past, it was said that men commit the offense while women do not, because the precept was established according to [the specific circumstances]."

Regarding "staying overnight": according to the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*, there is no allowance for three nights; the current interpretation holds that one commits an offense in both cases. Thus, the *Gāthā-śāstra* states:

"If one has previously stayed two nights with a man and stays a third night, then for every time one lies down or turns over, one incurs two *pāyattika* offenses. Based on this, our Master [Saṃghabhadra] treats this as a continuous offense (*saṃtati-patti*).
Therefore, among the enumerated conditions, it says "man and woman. Both ancient and modern scholars have cited various passages from the treatises to provide their respective explanations.
The meaning is distinct. There are other points that are not urgent, as described in the *Mahā-vinaya*. Regarding the "two, three, and four conditions being the same as the preceding precept":
(1) the two rooms are interconnected; (2) staying together overnight; (3) knowing one is staying together overnight; (5) committing an offense after exceeding three nights.
The third night is when the dawn has not yet appeared; this is "having passed two nights. As soon as the dawn appears, it is the third night, which constitutes the actual offense.

Regarding the statement in the Vinaya that it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing): according to the commentary, where it does not specifically say *duṣkṛta*, this refers to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
If one does not avoid [the act] before the dawn appears, one incurs the preparatory *duṣkṛta*; thus it should be understood.
When the light of dawn appears, one incurs the offense of *pācittiya* for exceeding [the time limit] by two or three [units]. If one departs before the light of dawn has appeared, there is no fault;

however, once the light of dawn has appeared, one commits a *pācittiya*. Even if one circumambulates [the boundary] three times and departs before the light of dawn has appeared, by the fourth watch of the night, it will certainly not be permitted;
therefore, one must have oneself leave or cause the other to leave. The *Vibhaṅga-śāstra* (Jian lun) further states: "Before the light of dawn has appeared..."

One who avoids [the offense] also does not commit it; this means that "not committing" is not the same as "non-existence. Regarding the note: "If one sits during the first watch of the night, the exception is not established. *Souxuan* says:
This means that even if one sits during the first watch of the fourth night, it is likewise not permitted; therefore, it is said that the exception is not established.

This implies that from the third night onward, sitting is permitted and does not constitute an offense. Since an exception is not to be applied repeatedly, it is not established [as an exception]. One must...

Regarding "sending [the guest] away" or "leaving on one's own," the following citation from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* regarding the long sitting (*dīrghāsana*) not constituting an offense makes it clear: "One lies down for the first two nights;

reaching the fourth night does not constitute a violation [of the rule]. (This is already recorded in the commentary. According to this statement, not lying down on the fourth night constitutes the "first watch" (*pūrvayāma*).

The Venerable One did not approve of this interpretation. Since one has been sitting from the beginning of the fourth watch of the night until dawn without resting one's side upon the mat, it is uncertain at what point the time for incurring the offense occurs; therefore, that [previous] view is incorrect.

Now, according to the *Fǎbǎo* (Treasury of the Dharma), from the first watch of the night until the fourth watch, if one sits and reaches dawn without [resting], there is no offense. Thus it says: "If one sits at the very beginning of the night..."

[The opponent] argues that this does not constitute an exception (*anujñā*). That is to say, it does not establish the principle of an exception regarding staying overnight with one who has not received full ordination (*upasampadā*), because [the practitioner] does not lie down.
Below, he cites the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Wufen lü), which states that sitting upright or sitting and lying alternately constitutes no offense in its original context;
this serves as proof for the aforementioned point. Furthermore, the commentary notes that in all cases, if one remains awake throughout the four watches of the night, it is permissible.
This indicates that even if one does not lie down throughout the entire night, it is still not considered "one night. Regarding the increase of the offense:

if one has not yet performed confession, then even after many days have passed, if one sleeps together again, each time the side touches the bed, there is a *pāyattika* (offense); with every turning over, there is a *pāyattika*. Thus, one incurs the offense repeatedly.
Therefore, it is said that the offense increases over time. The phrase "no allowance for two nights" explains the meaning of the preceding point.

That is to say, if this bhikṣu has stayed overnight with a śrāmaṇera and committed an offense that he has not yet confessed, then even if many days have passed, because the offense has not been eliminated, there is no interval of innocence.

Consequently, each night he lies on his side together [with the offender], the offense becomes increasingly grave. How could there be any further allowance for two nights of staying together with one who has not received full ordination?

"Staying in a separate room for two additional nights" means that one must repent for one's transgression; one may not stay in the same room on the same day. Only after staying in a separate room for one night may one then obtain the further two nights.
Regarding the "four propositions" (*catuskoṭi*) and so forth mentioned in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*:

this precept refers exclusively to those who have not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*); it does not distinguish between whether the person staying with one is the same or different. Although the four propositions differ, [the principle remains the same].

If all three conditions are met, one commits the offense. Regarding the phrase "the same conditions as above": if, as in the cases above, one is unaware [of the presence of a person], or if it lacks the characteristics of a private room (*agāra*), or if there are other conditions such as being commanded by a *brahman* or a *śramaṇa*, in all such cases there is no offense.
Regarding "associating with one who has not received full ordination for up to six nights," this is the title from the *Shichao* (Excerpts from the Commentary).

Regarding "the five conditions leading to an offense," this refers to the three categories of *zì* (characters), *jù* (phrases), and *wèi* (flavor). These constitute the essence of the teaching (*jiàotǐ*). "Characters" (*zì*) refers to names; "phrases" (*jù*) refers to chapters and sentences; "flavor" (*wèi*) refers to the literary expression.

The new terminology uses "name, phrase, and character" (*míng-jù-wén*), while the old terminology uses "character, phrase, and flavor. In Sanskrit, this is called *nāma-kāya*. In Chinese, it is translated as...

"Name" (*nāman*). "Name" refers to conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). Conceptualization has two meanings: first, conceptualization as the grasping of images, which is among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*);

second, conceptualization as conventional designation, meaning that the noble ones (*ārya*) have collectively established designations such as "form" (*rūpa*) through mutual agreement, as when one says, "that which is deep, vast, and boundless is called the ocean," and so forth.
Here, the term "name" is explained by means of the function of conventional designation. It was formerly called [the *nāmakāya*].
"Letter" (*akṣara*). "Phrase" (*pada*) refers to a chapter or section; in Sanskrit it is called *varga*, which here means "chapter. The Sanskrit term *pada* is translated as "phrase.

In secular texts, chapters are numerous while phrases are few; however, within the Buddhist teachings, a chapter is itself a phrase. This is because the term "phrase" is applied specifically to that which exhaustively expresses a meaning.
For example, "all conditioned phenomena" (*sarvasaṃskāra*) is the name, and "are impermanent" (*anityāḥ*) is the phrase. "Text" (*vyañjana*): in Sanskrit it is called *vyañjana*.
Now, it is said that "syllables" (*vyañjana*) are that which can manifest meaning; they manifest "phrases" (*pada*) and "names" (*nāman*) proximately, and manifest "meaning" (*artha*) distantly.

Regarding their proximate manifestation of phrases and names, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Names signify intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); phrases signify distinctions (*viśeṣa*); syllables are the characters (*akṣara*), serving as the basis for these two.
That is to say, the two factors of name and phrase depend upon characters, and characters are established based on sound. Thus, the *Abhidharma*...
The treatise cites the analogy of weaving brocade: first, according to the text, threads are interlaced to form dragons and phoenixes, which subsequently constitute the pattern of the brocade.
However, these forms arise based upon the texture of the silk (the application of the Dharma may be understood in detail). As for that which reveals the meaning from afar:

it is like the custom in India, where fans, salt, and vinegar are all called *piṇḍana*. This is also a case of being able to reveal a meaning: a fan can reveal wind, while salt and vinegar can reveal food.
The middle flavor. Therefore, the translations of the past that rendered this as "flavor" (rasa) were erroneous. This refers to cases where one recites these names and phrases together with others;
it constitutes an offense because it fails to fully represent the essence of the teaching and usurps the preceding words.

Regarding the phrase "in the Vinaya, up to 'more or less,'" "oral transmission" (mukhāgama) means that there is no written manuscript, and the teacher imparts it orally, reciting it in unison with the student; thus, [to do otherwise] constitutes an offense.

Regarding the phrase "one who receives by writing," one commentator explains this as "holding the original text while receiving [the teaching]. Master Xuán does not accept this interpretation. Although one may hold the original text, it must also be recited orally;
thus, it still constitutes "receiving by oral transmission. Now, according to the section below on "non-offenses," where one person finishes reciting and another writes it down, there is no offense.

However, if one writes it down before the recitation is finished, fearing that the phrasing and meaning will be incomplete, it constitutes an offense. Thus, the Venerable One refutes [the first interpretation].
It says: Previously it was called "oral reception" (*kǒu shòu*), which was based on the fact that one did not hold a physical copy of the sūtra in the dark;

now it is called "oral instruction" (*kǒu shòu*), based on the fact that there is a textual basis for what is being held. The principle is self-evident; why trouble oneself with doubt? Now, it is decided that the initial interpretation is superior. The commentary states:
"Decisively returning to the indeterminate passages" refers to the four lines which merely say, "spoken by śrāvakas, celestial seers (*deva-rṣi*), and so forth," and do not...
Regarding the statement that what has been approved by the Buddha as a sūtra entails guilt for those who recite it together: this now cites the text of the *Cīvara-vastu* to resolve the matter.

That one does not distinguish between the number of words and phrases is likewise an incomplete understanding. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* cited above [demonstrates] that according to its specific sections, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
This is what constitutes a definitive resolution. Regarding the statement in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (or *Vinayamātṛkā*) concerning "proper decorum":

if two individuals who are both proficient in the scriptures recite side by side, and the names, phrases, and syllables are complete such that the substance of the teaching is not deficient, then this does not constitute an offense. Furthermore, if they maintain their composure and do not lose their dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*), [there is no fault].

This means that if you simply attend to yourself and do not lose the decorum of the Saṃgha, you will succeed. The passage beginning with "The Vinaya states that there is no offense" is as it appears in the text.

The passage beginning with "Regarding the seventh [category]" is an explanation of the title and a citation from the *Shuochao* (Commentary on the Essentials), and so forth. The passage beginning with "The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* states... down to 'falling'" means:
To destroy stupas and damage images can only harm oneself; it cannot harm others. Others may still gain merit by showing reverence toward the stupas.
Yet, by speaking of another’s grave offenses, one ruins oneself and ruins others, causing all people to lose faith in the teachings of this branch of the Dharma.

When a bhikṣu upholds the True Dharma, they will not believe or accept [such slander]. Since they do not believe or accept the Dharma, does this not equally constitute the destruction of the Dharmakāya? Thus it is said:
Regarding "the seventh, reaching those who know": the four cases where there is no *saṃgha* [to be addressed] refer to when Devadatta split the *saṃgha*.

The Buddha ordered the community of monks to perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) to appoint Śāriputra to go and inform the lay followers that Devadatta’s actions were contrary to the Dharma, and so forth. Regarding "the fifth, reaching those who exist":
if it concerns one who has already performed the formal act (*karman*), this refers to having already performed the *karman* to appoint a person to speak. Question: Is the formal act correct?

The Dharma should be expounded. Why, then, was the question asked in reverse? The answer is: one who is permitted to expound must be a person appointed for that purpose; only when the requisite qualities reside within them may they do so.

Since he was not appointed, it would have been improper for him to expound it arbitrarily; therefore, the question had to be asked in reverse. Thus it is said, "I also heard it at such-and-such a place.
Regarding "because of a laywoman," etc., this means that the woman was an acquaintance of the bhikṣu who had committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, and [the rule] arose because of her questioning him.

Therefore, Nanda said, "Your preceptor has not yet outgrown his childhood games. The woman replied, "My preceptor is still like this," and she then entered her room, closed the door, and spoke this verse (as recorded in the *Dengchao*).
Regarding the statement in the Vinaya that [an offense] reaches the level of a *pārājika* or a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*:

the two upper categories refer to grave offenses for which one commits a *thullaccaya*; the lower category refers to minor offenses for which one cannot cause [the community] to be split, and thus it is a *dukkaṭa*.

Regarding the confession of one's own offenses as being light: this is because they are rare. "Stating the name" refers to declaring within the assembly that a certain bhikṣu has committed a certain offense.
"Lineage" refers to [the case of] the bhikṣu Li and others. "Robes" refers to the offense committed by a bhikṣu wearing robes of the *kāṇḍa* color.
"Dwelling" refers to [specifying] the first room from the east and so forth. "Physical appearance" refers to having white eyes and a black face.
This refers to a bhikṣu’s transgression. Regarding the statement "not guilty because of ignorance," this was originally explained in reference to those who have not studied the precepts.

Now, I suspect these may be followers of the *liǎojiào* (those who have mastered the teachings), who, at the time of speaking, were mentally confused and thus did not realize they had committed an offense.

As for "coarse [action] without the perception of it being a coarse offense," this also refers to mental confusion; although one recounts the matter of another person's transgression, one’s own mind does not yet perceive it as coarse.
Because of the perception of evil, one does not commit [the offense].

Regarding the phrase "in truth, up to eight," the explanation of the terminology is as usual (*et cetera*). The *Chao* (Excerpts) omits the enumeration of the conditions; here, following the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), there are five conditions:

first, internally having truly attained the Path while being free from overweening pride; second, personally declaring that one has realized it; third, [declaring this] toward one who is not yet fully ordained...

People say: "The fourth [category] is 'understanding through explanation' (liao), and the fifth is 'understanding through hearing' (jie). Because these are rare, the *Chao* does not explain them in detail. Regarding the phrase "it reaches the question":

this refers to the regulation for the noble ones (ārya) which excludes the ordinary person (pṛthagjana). Since the noble one has truly attained the Path, if they speak of it to a layperson, they commit a *thullaccaya* offense; this is what is meant by "regulating the noble ones."
The Noble Ones uphold the precepts; thus, although they do not commit transgressions, the existence of these precepts now serves to distinguish them from ordinary people.

Should others later see them speak [falsely], they will know that such persons are not Noble Ones, for the Noble Ones, in upholding the precepts, never commit a transgression. Therefore, the precept against great falsehood was established for the sake of protection.

If an ordinary person claims to have attained the state of a sage, they commit a grave falsehood. Now, the sages are established to distinguish themselves from the ordinary; since the sages do not speak [of such attainment], to speak of it is to remain an ordinary person.
Thus, this prevents ordinary people from committing such an offense. Therefore, this must not be dismissed as irrelevant; what is required for the present time must certainly be recounted.

Regarding the phrase "from 'yun' (cloud) up to nine": this is the citation of the title [of the commentary]. In the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (Jieben), within the section on its origin (*nidāna*), it says: "The father-in-law previously gave his son’s wife to me.

Regarding the term "shuofa" (speaker of the Dharma), the Venerable Master cites the *Erya*, in the section explaining kinship, which states: "The mother of one's husband is called *gū* (father-in-law)."

While she is alive, one refers to her as "the lady mother-in-law" (jūngu); after she has passed away, one says "the former mother-in-law" (xiāngū). The father of one's husband is called "uncle" (jiù). While he is alive, one refers to him as "the lord uncle" (jūnjiù).
There is someone who has misinterpreted this; I shall now refute and clarify it. Regarding the statement "if six conditions are met, it constitutes an offense," it is as the text says.
Regarding the statement "if [five or six] words are spoken, one incurs a *pāyattika* (falling offense)," the explanation is as follows: there was a woman whose menses had begun. A bhikṣu...
He did not preach the Dharma for him. Day after day, a wind arose; because of this, he informed the Buddha. The Buddha asked the bhikṣu, "How many words are required to bring understanding?
The bhikṣu replied, "Five or six words are sufficient to bring understanding. The Buddha sighed deeply in admiration and immediately established this rule.
Furthermore, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when the mother of Viśākhā was ill, she heard Ānanda speak five or six words and was immediately cured. May you quickly bring an end to suffering.

Having finished explaining the five aggregates (*skandha*) and six sense bases (*āyatana*), he further says: "You must sever all outflows (*āsrava*), exhaust all suffering, and attain *arhatship* (*arhattva*), for you have exceeded the limit.
Regarding the phrase "the Vinaya reaches the *ra*": this means that those who have left the household life may not serve as witnesses for one another when their offenses are identical;
that is, if monastics commit the same offense more than five or six times, they cannot testify for each other. One must instead obtain a layperson to serve as a witness.

Regarding the discernment of what is good and what is bad, as for those who speak of the meaning [of these matters], the rest is as explained in the *Great Commentary* (*Dàshù*). The opening section of that commentary states:
"For example, after having spoken five or six words, one escorts [the guest] out the door and performs the rites of parting. If one says, 'May you dwell in peace and happiness,' there is no offense.

If one says, 'May you swiftly exhaust the source of suffering and realize the fruit of Bodhi,' and if there is no pure attendant (*paricāraka*) to provide guidance along the path or at the gate, or if the guidance is interrupted... [The text continues in this vein.]

At the gate: if one sees or hears from afar, there is no offense; the opposite of this constitutes an offense. Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the *Madhyama Āgama*, the *Souxuan* states:

"Whenever someone comes to inquire, it includes both men and women. Regarding the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka Vinaya): if it is a woman who requests instruction, one may speak more than five or six words provided one reflects on the matter within the context of the Vinaya;
if she does not request instruction, yet one speaks more than five or six words of one's own accord, it is an offense.
"Speech constitutes an offense. 'Not yet finished' means a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense): if one stops after five or six words before finishing, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.

This is the preparatory offense; once finished, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation). (The above is the correct explanation. Furthermore, there is another interpretation which states that the text of the *Śāstra* (Commentary) contains the phrase 'up to and including "one should reflect,"' which is the wording of the Sūtra.
The portion from 'In the Vinaya' onwards is the text of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. (This is a false explanation; the commentary itself is clear on this point.)"

Regarding the phrase "not an offense," etc.: excluding [the presence of] men and excluding [the request for initiation], these are all grounds for exemption. This is briefly clarified in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.

One exemption does not mention "excluding the request," but simply states "excluding a knowledgeable man" when bestowing the five precepts. The essence of the three refuges is this. As for the method of the five precepts, it refers to the explanation of their characteristics.
The eightfold fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*) refers to the eight precepts. It means to close and conceal the gates of the sense faculties. And as for the explanation...

The method of the fast (*upavāsa*) is also explained by its characteristics. The Eightfold Noble Path consists of right speech, right action, right livelihood, right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
The ten unwholesome paths of action consist of three of the body, four of speech, and three of the mind.
If a woman does not understand what has just been said, and asks for further explanation, one may explain it more extensively; in all such cases, there is no offense.

Regarding the ten rules on digging the earth: the explanation of the names and the citations from the *Śāstra* (as indicated by "云云"). Regarding the passage from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* up to "great protection" (*mahārakṣā*):

the intent of the regulation is as stated in the text. Regarding the passage from "five conditions" up to "offense of falling" (*pātayantika*): as stated in the text. Regarding the passage from "conditions for the precept" up to "how much more so" (*cai*): [as stated in the text].
The conditions are as previously stated. Regarding "those who seek luck": this refers to those who incur sin by digging the earth while falsely imagining they are performing meritorious deeds;

thus, the text censures them. As for the statement in the Vinaya that it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (an offense of wrong-doing): this distinguishes cases where the earth has already been dug from those where it has not yet been dug, because [the latter] is merely natural ground.
Now, within the category of already-dug earth, there are further two types: if one touches it after four months have passed...

This constitutes an offense; it does not matter whether it was during the rainy season. Second, regarding "being soaked by rain": this refers to when a pit is freshly dug and encounters rain, such that it becomes identical to its original state.

Thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If the earth from wells, ponds, ditches, water jars, or vessels placed on the ground is dead soil, and it is soaked by rain, one must have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a 'pure person') know of it and take it up for oneself;

otherwise, one commits a *pācittiya* offense. "Returning to its original state" means that due to the time factor of four months and the causal condition of being rained upon, the earth [returns to its natural condition].
"Because it is a living thing. Regarding the phrase "as in the original, if one uses [it]," the *jue* (pronounced *jué*) and *lu* (pronounced *lù*) are hand-tools for plowing.

Regarding the phrase "if one pinches or pries," or if one does not instruct [another] by saying "look at these," one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one digs according to those words, one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense.
This excludes cases where one makes a model for the sake of a monastery or a stūpa; this also applies to making a model of a *saṃghārāma*.

It is so. Previously, when the mold was made from clay, it was opened and found to be inauspicious. Regarding the many commentators on the Shu edition, according to the Da Zhou edition of the sutra, there were originally eight fascicles among them;
however, from the "Explanation of the Ninety" down to the sixty-eighth precept, they were subsequently missing.
Master Shou, suspecting that the text was incomplete, constantly sought it out extensively. Later, he encountered a monk from Shu named Bao Yun who arrived in the capital.
The Master Shou (Shou-lüshi) inquired, "I do not know how many fascicles of the *Duolun* (Treatise on Many Topics) there are in Shu. The other replied, "There are nine fascicles.

The ninth fascicle begins with the explanation of 'precepts arising from destruction' and continues right through to the end of the text. Master Shou earnestly requested that it be sent back so he might copy it and send it along.
After one year had passed, it finally arrived; because of this, it was titled the *Shuguo Duolun* (The Shu Edition of the Treatise on Many Topics).
The Master Vinayadhara [Vasubandhu], at the beginning of the treatise, composed a preface in which he fully set forth the causes and conditions (as detailed above).

Within the treatise, he distinguishes between "arisen ground" (*jātā bhūmi*) and "non-arisen ground" (*ajātā bhūmi*) based on the natural state of the soil. Regarding the fourth and eighth months: these two months are the rainy season;

even if it does not rain, the moisture from beneath the earth rises to the surface, making the ground wet, and this is collectively termed "arisen ground. Apart from these two periods, it is "non-arisen ground."

When it rains, the ground becomes parched by the sun; when the wind blows, the soil rises up—this is called "non-arising. The rest of the text may be understood in detail. Regarding the phrase "from the *Mahāsāṃghika* to 'taking'":
as for "turning over stones" and so forth, this refers to having the intention to disturb the earth; therefore, one commits an offense regarding clods of earth.
"One person cannot carry it" means that one person is unable to lift it; it then drops down and naturally connects with the moisture of the earth because the portion to be produced is large.

"To break it" constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense. "If one tears it apart" (*che*)—meaning to pull it out—and "to pick out two or three rows" (*zhe*)—meaning to take them by hand—refers to piling up earth against the ground to form a wall, thereby creating three rows of moats for the rain. "To scoop it out" (*shu*)...

(“Xu” [pronounced with the *lǚ* rhyme] according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to discharge water). Regarding the fact that rain can cause the earth to sprout, the *Ji* states: "If it has recently rained, a bhikṣu must not draw water himself from a well;
he should instead employ a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person). If the *kappiya-kāraka* is small [in stature], he should first have him stir the water, and afterwards the bhikṣu may draw it himself."

Regarding the statement "The *Four-Part Vinaya* (Dharmaguptaka) extends to the point of non-comprehension": according to our own school, it is permissible to protect one's dwelling place [by striking the bell].

As for the phrase "the rest is as in the various schools," this refers to the *Three Thousand Dignified Manners*, which states: "If fire, water, wind, kings, or thieves approach, summon the śrāmaṇeras; there is a method for striking the bell. The previous [passage] concerns cases where people are present.
If it is a forest hermitage (*araṇya*) where no people are present, it is as stated in the commentary on the *Five-Part Vinaya* (Mahīśāsaka), which says: "The *Four-Part Vinaya*..."
Regarding the point that is not clear in the text: because the text lists "bent earth" (*ku-nei-tu*) within the interior soil, it explains itself by saying, "This is dead floating soil.

If one were to remove the bent earth within, one would then obtain the excavated interior soil. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, this refers to dead soil found in exposed areas or within the bends [of the terrain].
