one must invite the monks in their proper order. If even one person does not do so, they must send a portion of food [to them]. If this is not done, the members of that *saṃgha* commit the offense of a separate assembly (*pṛthag-varga-doṣa*).
If a donor separately invites four or more monks in their order, the aforementioned rules shall first be applied according to a single boundary (*sīmā*) and two locations.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there may be occasions when a donor invites four monks from outside to enter the boundary for the *poṣadha* ceremony (this refers to the people coming from outside while the food is within the boundary);
or when one brings food into the boundary to invite specific bhikṣus separately (this refers to the food coming from outside while the Sangha is within the boundary).
Regarding these two cases, if there are monks within the boundary at the time of the formal meal who do not assemble together, they all incur the offense of eating in a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇa*).
Regarding the person mentioned earlier in the text who is called "a bhikṣu invited in the sequence of a separate invitation":

this refers to four bhikṣus invited in the sequence of a separate invitation, not to a single individual specifically named for the invitation. Therefore, the text says: "This is according to the precedent of four persons invited in a separate invitation.
If that is so, since a group is constituted by these four persons, why does the text refer to them as "a bhikṣu invited in a separate invitation"? Answer: According to the sūtras and śāstras...

In the text, the term "the assembly" (saṃgha) is mostly used in reference to bhikṣus. This may be intended to distinguish them from the other four groups of followers; thus, "bhikṣu" is specifically designated.

If it were referring to a single individual, why would there be a need for a formal act of the community (karmavācanā)? Many are confused by this—reflect upon it. Regarding the place where the poṣadha should be performed:
Regarding the phrase "requesting one person from the sequence of monks" and so forth, this refers to establishing the Dharma while remaining free from transgressions.

As for the statement "if the boundary of the path is distant," this is based on a single *karmabhūmi* (area of ritual action); three *yojanas* is the distance at which the road becomes remote. Thus, one first selects those who follow the sequential order.
This indicates that one has already partaken of the monastic meal; after taking a single mouthful, one proceeds. The meaning of this food is simply that it serves as a supplement.

As for the phrase "if one arrives at [a place where] there is not": "within the boundary of a village" refers to what can be distinguished and what cannot be distinguished, which is explained as the limit for assembling the Sangha.
"There is no *saṃgha*-boundary" means there is no boundary established by formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*); it is entirely natural. One eats in these two locations.
[The area] of the two donors' houses is within sixty-three paces [of each other], and the *gandī* should be struck; the following establishes the method, which may be understood accordingly.
One must ensure it is well-concealed yet thoroughly known. Regarding whether a village exists or not: one must perform this concealment.
If the natural boundary of the village is enclosed by the four marks, it is equivalent to a village. If the four marks of the natural boundary are not complete, [it is not].
The length and breadth are sixty-three paces. Regarding these two locations above, there may be a bhikṣu who is separate within [the boundary] but not separate outside;
he does not join [the assembly], yet there is no fault. One should know that if someone falsely interprets this, it will lead to confusion. As for the phrase "or reaching [the limit]" and so forth:

if the turn of the monastic order (*saṃgha-krama*) is obstructed, it changes into a separate invitation (*pṛthak-nimantraṇa*); conversely, a separate invitation does not hinder the change into the turn of the monastic order. Thus it is said: "Or reaching... and so on.

Regarding the phrase "up to chanting for one person," this refers to the aforementioned ritual procedure for inviting monks one by one. This explains the mutual transformation of the two types of invitations.
As for the passage from "according to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*" to "one who commits an offense," the phrase "separately begging in four lines" serves as a general heading.
"Or four people begging at once" means that four bhikṣus go on alms-round simultaneously and together see a single donor, and speak to him... [text continues].
[The Buddha said: "Suppose [a donor] says, 'Please give four portions of food to us.

If the *dānapati* (donor) immediately grants this, or if they beg separately without knowing one another—meaning four bhikṣus walk one after another and all approach a single *dānapati*, each begging separately, saying, 'Please give one portion of food to me'—and thus the four do not know of one another, yet they are from the same *dānapati* and share the same host, and they go at the same time to receive the food: [in such a case,] there is an offense."
This explains the meaning of the preceding two lines. Either four people may request [the gift] from the donor simultaneously;

since the donor has already consented for four people to go together to receive the food, or they may request individually. Although they do not know of one another at the time of requesting, the donor has nonetheless granted permission.

Although there are differences regarding the sequence of arrival and departure, the timing of receiving the food is the same (the first phrase is concluded). Second, regarding those who go at different times and receive food at separate locations:

this refers to four bhikṣus who together request permission from a donor; having obtained permission for four people, they each depart for the donor’s house and, receiving the food simultaneously, return and eat individually.
According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, this does not constitute an offense of falling (*pāyattika*). This means:
Regarding the fourfold division based on the place of eating: if it constitutes a *saṃgha*, one commits an offense. Now, since they are eating separately and not as a group, there is no offense.
The treatise refers only to the simultaneous reception of food as constituting an offense; it does not concern whether the meal time constitutes a *saṃgha* or not.

As for the third case—going separately and eating separately without offense—this refers to four people begging together, such as when four people each go to the house of a donor and eat individually.

If each person receives food separately, neither the Vinaya nor the Śāstra considers it an offense. This is because the conditions for constituting a *saṃgha* (an assembly) are not met at the place of eating. According to the Vinaya, there is no offense. Furthermore, they do not receive [the food] simultaneously.
This is based on the rule that there is no fault in begging separately more than four times. Regarding the offense of receiving [food] simultaneously while going separately:

this refers to four people walking one after another, all approaching a single donor to beg separately, saying, "Give it to me alone," and each being permitted by the donor; each having been permitted previously.

Regarding "having given permission": if one goes first to the donor's house and later gives permission, or if one goes later to the donor's house after having already given permission—although there is a difference in the timing of arrival, because the food is received at one and the same time—one commits an offense.
The above four cases are determined as offenses according to the three cases set forth in the *Śāstra*.

According to the third case, there is no offense. If one follows the scriptural text (*vinaya*), there is an offense for the first and last cases, while for the middle two cases, there is no offense regarding external difficulties.

In the first case, it is a separate act; if one begs separately at one time and goes to receive food, there is an offense. The fourth case is likewise a separate act; if one begs separately at one time and receives food, there is an offense.
If one acts for the sake of obtaining something different, then in the first case, [the food] is already in the house of the donor.

Regarding the fourth phrase of the verse: "Taking food back to another place," this refers to four people eating together. This passage in the *Chao* (Commentary) is extremely difficult to understand;

the interpretations and judgments provided above are all based on the *Fǎbǎo* (Jewel of the Dharma). If one follows Xuanzang’s interpretation, taking [food] separately and begging separately would constitute all four phrases, which becomes quite prolix.

Moreover, the force of this current text merely cites "begging separately" (*biéqǐ*) and does not discuss "inviting" (*qǐng*); since it is not followed or utilized [in that way], [the former interpretation is preferred].
I shall not record further details here; rather, I will rely on the *Zhengyi* (Correct Meaning). As stated previously, the *Yi* (Meaning) commentary says:

"As for 'reaching a separate assembly' (*biezhong*), this refers to when one is originally in the sequence of the *saṃgha*, yet having been invited, their status becomes distinct. Because the assembly blocks the entrance, the bhikṣu is not permitted to enter; thus, he enters this separate sequence of the *saṃgha*."
This then becomes a "separate invitation" (*pṛthag-āmantraṇa*). The essence of this separate invitation is a "separate assembly" (*pṛthak-saṃgha*).

Whether there are people outside the gate or not at the time of the subsequent meal, one commits the offense in either case. Baoyun says: "If one were to fix the name [of the offense], it would be called 'separate from the Saṃgha,' followed by 'separate assembly.'"

If [the monks] are outside the gate, once the Sangha has already descended from their seats, according to this order of precedence, it already constitutes the meaning of a separate invitation (*pṛthag-āmantraṇa*).
Even if the monks outside the gate are more than sixty-three paces away, as long as they have the intention to obstruct [the meal] at the time of eating—if one were to definitively name it [as such]:

This is what is called "inviting separately and forming a separate assembly. The *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya-śāstra* (Duo lun) merely states that within the boundary (*sīmā*), when following the order of the *saṃgha*, one does not form a separate assembly;
it does not mention the area outside the boundary, which is sixty-three paces away, where other monks may be present.

Therefore, the author of the *Shanbu suiji jiemo chao* clarifies this point based on its underlying meaning, establishing it as "inviting separately and forming a separate assembly. Alternatively, some interpret this term "outside" as being relative to the monks within the household.
"Obtaining a name outside" does not mean beyond sixty-three paces; if one is in a natural state, what offense would there be outside?
(This explanation is entirely incomplete. Regarding "four places of eating constitute a *saṃgha*": this cites the conditions for the offense. Regarding "from the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* to 'a bhikṣu'":
as for "the other three being finished," it means that after three people have finished eating, one person eating alone indicates that a *saṃgha* is not constituted.
Regarding the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*: the *Sijù-chāo* (Excerpts on the Four Categories) cites three cases; furthermore, there are three bhikṣus—one on the ground and one in the air.

The commentary below explains that this establishes the principle of "not being separate. As for the passage from the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* stating that "there is no offense if they eat in the same place":
this refers to each holding their own food and eating together in one location. If four people each beg for alms separately and then eat together in one place, there is likewise no offense.
[Regarding] the offense: If this is so, according to which section of the Vinaya is the offense established? The *Shan-chao* (Commentary) quotes the Vinaya as saying:
"According to one school, if one requests food from four people simultaneously, it constitutes an offense. However, if it is as stated in the *Śāstra*, there is no fault. It says:

"There are cases where one incurs a *pārājika* [or *pāyattika*] downfall; if one eats two flavors at the same location, there is no offense. If there is someone within the boundary who obstructs the giving of food, both locations constitute an offense. This...
"Regarding 'in the open air' (*abbhokāsa*)," this explains the preceding passage. For one who is in the open air, [the food] must be within reach of the hand.
If it is outside [that reach], it constitutes a separate meal (*bhojanavikappana*), as it is identical to the fourth case; therefore, it must be distinguished and restricted to form the third case.

It is necessary that these four persons occupy the same location and are simultaneously in the open air, such that [the food] must be within reach of the hand. In a covered place, this requirement does not apply, provided they are adjacent to one another.
It is natural that it constitutes a single location. Regarding the statement, "it is not gathered within the five boundaries," this refers to the conditions for the offense.
Regarding the statement, "because the five divisions have arrived," those who go forth among the five assemblies do so none other than for the sake of liberation.

As for the "monastic boundary" (*saṃgha-sīmā*), this refers to the boundary established through formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*). As for the "village boundary" (*grāma-sīmā*), it is naturally divisible and cannot [be otherwise].
[This refers to] the division [of the community]. Regarding the "household boundary" (*grāmakṣetra*): this is also explained as being sixty-three paces for a residential area.

Regarding the "wilderness" (*araṇya*): it is five *li*. One *krośa* is six hundred paces when traveling on a road. Regarding the note above concerning the *śrāmaṇera*s and so forth, "not a separate assembly":

according to the *Śāstra*, three *śrāmaṇera*s who are insane or deceased do not constitute a separate assembly. There have been those in antiquity who produced erroneous commentaries, saying that [this is not the case].
Giving food to a śrāmaṇera or to those attending a funeral constitutes stealing from the *saṃghika* (monastic) property; it is not an offense against the deceased themselves.

Because both wealth and the Dharma have already been relinquished [to the Saṃgha], it is said that "evil precepts and the like are excluded. Xuánzhì says: "The *Chāo* speaks in general terms, whereas this text specifically refers to cases where a śrāmaṇera has been invited.

This exempts groups of four bhikṣus or more from being considered a 'separate assembly' (*biezòng*). As for the aforementioned case of a madman’s funeral, it is merely cited as a supplementary example."

It is not something different. Regarding the statement "the four parts reach the point of obtaining food": this refers to separate invitations and separate begging, as the treatises treat them identically.

As for the phrase "according to the Vinaya, with the addition of 'not assembling'": when invited according to the sequence of the *saṃgha*, those within the same boundary do not assemble, as listed previously. Therefore, the commentary states:

As listed above, there are five types of *sujñapti* (proper announcements). Regarding the four cases where one does not incur an offense, the commentary notes that these refer to inviting those who are insane or deluded, in order to exclude improper applications.

In the subsequent section on permitted conditions (*pratyaya*), although it is permitted for one who is suffering from a physical ailment such as a lame foot, the other three cases still constitute an offense;
however, this is not the case here. Question: In the preceding text, the conditions were listed as seven for the commission of an offense against the precepts. Now, regarding this...

Within the commentary, why is it that only five conditions are explained, while the five types of formal food (*bhojana*), the state of insanity, and the seventh swallow—the conditions for an offense regarding swallowing—are omitted?
The Venerable One says: "As for offenses committed with every swallow, these all depend on the substance being consumed; if it is one of the five types of formal food, then there is an offense.
If it is not one of the five types of formal food, then even if there is no swallowing, there is still no offense regarding swallowing. Therefore, these two [categories]..."

The "conditioning through penetration" (*pratyaya-saṃprayoga*) has already been explained within the preceding five [categories]; it is clear upon examining the text itself and need not be listed and explained again. (Reflect on this;
it is not due to a lack of notes. The *Jia* school says that the text of the *Chao* is abbreviated.)
It is said that according to the Vinaya, there is no offense; this refers to the opening of seven conditions, as found in the section on the precepts.

Regarding the phrase "from one [place] to another," this concerns the time for giving robes, which extends throughout the twelve months. Wherever robes are given, one may generally proceed on the journey.

This constitutes the fourth type of boat-journey and is the fifth [category]. On a journey where many difficulties arise, the formal practice is relaxed; even a temporary pause is regulated. How is this so?
[One] knows [this]. Thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one arrives yesterday and eats today, it is a *pācittiya*. If one travels on that very day and eats separately, there is no offense.

It is the same for traveling by boat" (many people are confused regarding this meaning; know it). As for the phrase "the six groups of people arrive," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) follows the *Liubei* (Accompanying Retention).
In the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*, it is not mentioned that [the matter] was announced. The *Vistara-vyākhyā* (Extensive Commentary) states: "The 'great assembly' refers to four persons or more.
Regarding the phrase "four persons suffice for food; one additional person becomes a source of trouble," this refers to two households in a village:
the eastern household limited its offering to four persons, while the western household limited its offering to one person. Thus, the intention to give from these two households was restricted.
No one was able to accommodate one another. Since it was a time of scarcity, alms were difficult to obtain everywhere;

if this [rule] were not relaxed, then one person from the western house would become a source of trouble for four people in the eastern house. Because of such trouble—where the word "trouble" (*huàn*) is glossed as "offense" (*fàn*)—it was permitted so that there would be no trouble.
This applied even up to the case of hundreds or thousands of people, where only one person being a source of trouble would suffice, provided that food remained difficult to obtain.
It is obtained. All [cases] where one opens [the door] are non-offenses; this is called "when the great assembly has gathered. The annotation may be relied upon for detail.

The above concerns the precept on robes for the time being; the commentary provides an explanation here. As for other interpretations, fearing they would be too voluminous, they are left in the *Daji* (Great Record).

"Jing" (Capital) refers to the place where the Son of Heaven resides; it is glossed as "great. "Lüan" (Palanquin) refers to the precious carriage ridden by the Emperor; it means that one cannot lift it.
To "honor as supreme" means merely to point toward the object one is riding upon, just as one says "Your Majesty" (陛下) to point toward the steps (*biè*) beneath which one sits;
this present case is also like that. As for "vulgar and base people," these are those who are contemptible, ignorant, and worldly—the kind of people found in the wine shops of the Qin wards.
When they eat and drink, they treat their guests with such indifference that they divide the food and withdraw their presence; [the text] exhorts one not to practice such behavior.
This is the procedure. As detailed in the section on the invitation (*pṛcchā*), it refers to the method for taking one’s seat and welcoming the guests in the lower fascicle:
announcing to the donor to enter, and so forth, up to indicating that there are monks for a meal in a certain monastery (*saṃghārāma*), etc. (and so on).

Regarding the "food offerings to the seven types of śramaṇas," this refers to the fact that in the Western lands, all ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist practitioners are called *śramaṇas*; here, it follows that same convention.
The Vinaya text states: The sister of King Bimbisāra went to the place of the Nirgranthas and left the household life to study the Way.

Desiring to go to a monastery to provide a meal, the bhikṣus did not dare to accept it, so they reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha permitted śramaṇas to receive and accept food offerings (this is a provisional allowance regarding the circumstances of receiving).
Furthermore, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, the second [sister] of King Bimbisāra was an outsider śramaṇa who invited the assembly for a meal and exerted herself [to provide it].

It could not be provided in full detail. Thereupon, the multitude, filled with anxiety, informed the Buddha. The Buddha granted permission for *śramaṇas* to receive food offerings; at that time, separate groups were permitted to eat together.

Regarding the phrase "furthermore, according to the *Jìdǐng*" (or similar): as for those who do not commit an offense during the turn of the *saṃgha*, their nature is not that of a separate group, and furthermore, it is because they are not prohibited [from doing so].
Regarding the "time for the five-part clothing" (*pañcavastuka-cīvara*): the text states that this applies throughout the twelve months for making the two lower robes; it does not mean...
The fifth month is one month [of the rainy season retreat]. Regarding the total of nine conditions: these consist of the four divisions, the seven, and the two from external schools.

These are all "exceptional conditions" (*āpatti-kāraṇa*). As for "increasing by one, etc.": when the Buddha was in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a householder named Siṃha who went to Śāriputra’s place, prostrated, and said:
"I pray that you will accept my invitation. He then went to Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, and Rāhula.
At that place, he invited five hundred eminent leaders and prepared a grand offering. Later, the Buddha asked Rāhula, "How many people were there today?
Who was the senior elder? Rāhula replied, "My preceptor Śāriputra was the leader, along with five hundred others of divine virtue.
The Buddha asked Rāhula, "Did that householder obtain much merit? Rāhula answered, "He obtained immeasurable merit."
[Limitation. If a person were to provide for even a single arhat, the merit obtained would still be immeasurable; how much more so for five hundred? The Buddha said:
"It is not equal to inviting a single śramaṇa bhikṣu according to the monastic order. A hundred thousand billion worldly people cannot serve as a comparison.

The remainder of the text is as in the *Chao* [commentary] (etc.). Regarding the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* and other texts: it says that at that time, the maternal aunt personally spun thread with her own hands and produced one end of cloth.

There was a golden-colored woolen cloth. He waited for the Buddha to return to the palace in order to offer it to him. The Buddha said, "You may give this as an offering to the Saṃgha; you shall obtain immeasurable merit.
Thereupon, he passed it through the ranks of the monks in succession, but none dared to accept it. When it came before Maitreya, he then accepted it.
Having put it on, he entered the city. As the multitude begged for alms, they all gazed upon his golden-colored *kāṣāya* without ever tiring of it.

Regarding the statement that "according to the Vinaya, this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing)": "benefiting oneself" means that one has personal benefit. The commentary states that "benefiting others" or "separately" refers to this context;

here, the character *yi* (益) is glossed as "to transmit" (*chuan*). The *Chao* text mentions entering after announcing [one's purpose] when there is a reason, and entering and exiting after announcing it when there is no reason.

The reason why one must announce [one's movements] when entering or leaving is as follows: "entering" refers to protecting the bhikṣus within the household; "leaving" refers to protecting the *dānapati* (donors).

This is done entirely for the sake of people's minds, so how much more so when suspicion or strangeness might arise? If one fails to announce it and violates the regulation, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is another interpretation which states that there is no offense; however, regarding the exemptions mentioned above, it should be understood that all nine conditions constitute exemptions.
Regarding the statement, "Taking [food] from a woman returning home up to thirty-four [mouthfuls]," this is an enumeration of the names [of the rules], etc.
As for the transgressor, there are two conditions: first, a woman returning home; second, a merchant. Regarding the absence of conditions, it is permitted during times of illness.

Now, if one takes more than three bowls when not ill, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, there are three grades of bowls: taking one of the superior bowl does not constitute an offense; taking two constitutes an offense regarding the medium bowl.
Taking two does not constitute an offense. Taking three constitutes an offense; taking three from a smaller bowl does not constitute an offense.

Regarding the fourth point, which states that "taking more than three bowls" constitutes an offense: this refers to taking from a smaller bowl. If one person takes [alms], taking more than three bowls constitutes an offense.
If four people take [alms] together, those before the third do not commit an offense because they have not exceeded the limit; the last person commits an offense because he has exceeded it.

Regarding the thirty-fifth precept on "having finished eating" (*kṛtabhaktika*): [the explanation of] its definition and so forth is as stated [in the text]. Regarding the five conditions that lead to an offense: this is as in the text.
Regarding the Vinaya rule stating that it is an offense for each swallow (*ghrāsa-ghrāsa*): these five [conditions] are not inherently complete causes; they are simply the wording of the Vinaya text.
In the *Guangshi* (Extensive Commentary), Upāli asks the Buddha: "How many instances constitute 'having had enough to eat' (*paryāpta-bhakta*)? The Buddha replies: "There are five instances;

based on knowing that one has had enough, to eat further constitutes an offense. Both the *Chao* (Commentary) and the *Jieshu* (Explanation of the Precepts) refer to these as "conditions" (*pratyaya*). "Knowing" refers to the condition of knowing that [the meal] has been brought forth.
"Up to the fifth [act], one knows to abandon the causal conditions such as deportment. Regarding the phrase "from the *Saṃghāṭī* until it becomes an invalid obstruction":
this means that once the food in the bowl has sufficiently satisfied one's hunger, one no longer intends to receive further benefit from it.

Regarding the phrase "having already [eaten] one mouthful less" in the commentary: this refers to the point when one intends to finish eating and is short by only one mouthful; thus it is said "already.

As for the statement that this does not constitute a "severing of the mind," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) says: Some interpret this as follows: "The object being 'sufficient' means 'I have eaten my fill.
If I have not yet eaten my fill, even if I rise from my seat abruptly, there is no fault in eating again. This is not the correct authority (*pramāṇa*). According to...

Regarding the *Nyāyamukha-śāstra*, there are three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and authoritative testimony (*āptāgama*). Each of these has fallacious counterparts.

Since the present [position] contradicts the text, it is not a valid cognition according to the correct words of the Holy Teaching. As for "having no time of satiety when eating": if one follows the ordinary mind and waits for satiety, when will one ever be satisfied?
One must sever these fourfold conceptual distinctions. First, the state of being satisfied by eating is not [truly] sufficient; that is to say, not...

First, although one is full, no offense has been committed. Second, when the object of the meal is sufficient while the food itself is insufficient, this refers to a case where the formal meal is small.

Third, when both the object of the meal and the food are sufficient, this refers to eating a large amount of the formal meal; even a single mouthful constitutes an offense. Fourth, when both are insufficient, it is not a formal meal. Furthermore, there is a minor concession:

regarding those who drink parched flour (maṇḍa) or gruel, it means that because parched flour and gruel are not pure [solid] food, drinking them is permitted even if they satisfy one's hunger. "Millet" (bèi) refers to dry rice; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is "dried grain."
The *Fǔpiān* (Supplementary Treatise) states: "Take dry rice and fry it; then grind it and sift it to make flour. When ten measures are full, one may prepare *bèi* (dried provisions).

The rest is the same as in the *Sifenlü* (Four-Part Vinaya)," which refers to rice, parched grain (*māṣa*), fish, and meat. Regarding *māṣa*, the Venerable One said: "Take wheat and steam it; once steamed, parch it.
Soak it in water, and after soaking, fry it until it resembles wheat porridge. Some do not [agree with this].
[The interlocutor] said: "It is false to claim that barley is parched, pounded, and ground to be called *māṣa* (flour).

This is an error. *Mí* (pronounced *pí*) refers to what is called *mí* in the regions of Guānxī and Jīngzhōu; however, people from the north, such as those of Jìzhōu, call it *jì*. Here [in this region], it is also called *jì*.
Furthermore, regarding *sù* (millet) and *guǎngmài* (broad-barley), the latter is great barley (*yava*). As for *yǒuzǐ*, it is *biè* (weed-grain)."

“*Saktu-maṣa*”: *saktu* means “groats” (*mài*) and *maṣa* means “flour” (*jiā*). These are the words of this land (China); they correspond to *yava-maṣa*, which is the language of Western India (Sanskrit).
This is likely a case of citing both terms together. “A single root” refers to all types of grass roots. “Five fruits”: the fifth is fruit from trees.

Regarding the five [foods] in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, those that exactly match this [text] are called the “five regular foods” (*pañca-bhojanīya*); their names and essential natures are largely the same as in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

As for *jī*, there is no such thing as dry rice. Regarding the "five types of mixed [food] that are not proper" (*pañca-vyañjanāni avyavahārāṇi*): among these, what is called "mixed" refers to that which is improper; "proper" refers to the fourfold [meal], such as cooked grain and so forth.

As for "branches and leaves," these are not places where proper food is found; eating at such locations constitutes no offense. Furthermore, there is no mention of "eating separately from the community" (*pṛthag-bhaktatva*).

Regarding "correcting the name" (*zhèng míng*) and "not correcting the name": if one says "rice gruel," it is correct and thus prohibited; if one simply says "leaf-gruel," it is incorrect and thus not prohibited. Regarding "the meaning being reached implies prohibition":
this refers to establishing a name based on the object [of the food], regardless of whether it provides satiety or is seasonal. As for "there are those who... and so forth:
this means that if there are young people who do not rise when seeing an elder approach, they commit an offense; therefore, one must express one's intention [to apologize]. *Nikāya* (Monastic Code).

Regarding "not showing respect" within the monastic precepts (*saṃgha-śīla*): this refers to seeing a nun observe the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*). Even if one has newly received the precepts, one must rise [in her presence].

Now, for the sake of eating while seated together (*ekāsana-bhojana*), although one does not rise upon seeing her, one should express one's intention by saying, "I shall not perform the *kṛtānna-vidhi* (the ritual of finished food).

Once this has been declared, it does not violate the rules of respect. Regarding the eight prohibitions in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: first, the invitation for self-examination (*pravāraṇā*); second, [the prohibition against] accepting gifts from a donor once one is full... [and so forth].

*Pārivāsika*. When given *pañcabhojanīya* (the five kinds of staple foods) or various other staple foods, and invited to eat at will, if a bhikṣu says, "I am already full," and thus rises and leaves his seat without performing the *atiriktabhojana-vidhi* (the ritual for leftover food), it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense. Second, regarding being content with few desires: when a donor gives staple food...

A bhikṣu makes a gesture with his hand to manifest an appearance of few desires; thus he leaves his seat. Regarding the offense of *pāyattika* for not performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of leaving food remaining):
when the food is being served, the attendant has sores or scabies on his hands, or his hands, body, or robes are impure.
The bhikṣu speaks ill of it, saying, "I will not take it," and thus leaves his seat. As before, he does not perform the ritual himself. Fourth, regarding "mixed" [impurity]:

A *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) was carrying vessels of milk and curd while walking along with cooked rice and parched grain flour (*maṇḍa*). When a bhikṣu saw this, he disapproved of it and said, "I do not need these;
five [items] are sufficient. As the *kappiya-kāraka* was serving the food, the bhikṣu asked, "What is this food? He replied, "It is parched grain flour (*maṇḍa*). The bhikṣu said:

"I have a wind ailment, so I cannot go. This is the sixth [case]: being crooked and deceitful. A person of pure conduct partakes of the five kinds of formal meals, whether mixed with or equal to the formal meals.
A bhikṣu shakes his head over his alms-bowl and makes a gesture of not eating. This is the seventh [case]: standing still. A person of pure conduct partakes of the five kinds of formal meals.
The bhikṣu said, "Do not serve the rice first; for now, distribute the cakes and fruits. We ourselves shall suffice with eight [mouthfuls].
The bhikṣu had previously received some parched flour (maṇḍa) which he had left with a donor's family. He went to the donor to request water to mix with the flour.
The layperson asked, "Do you need flour? The bhikṣu thought, "He is giving me both water and flour. The layperson then took the bhikṣu’s bag of flour and handed it back to him.
Regarding the giving to a bhikṣu: one who perceives [the recipient] as oneself cherishes them in their heart; thus, they say, "Place it on the ground," thinking, "I have no need for this.

By thus relinquishing the deportment, one does not commit the offense of *pācittiya* regarding leftover food (*atiritta*). This applies even more so to a case where the intention is lax rather than urgent.

According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, once the food has been accepted and entered the hand, even a single mouthful is designated as being within the "boundary" (*viṣaya*). However, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, it is not yet considered "entered the hand."
Regarding the phrase "and when eating, one merely speaks [of it] in the mouth" and so forth, this is for the purpose of precluding [the need for further formalities] hereafter.

As for the statement in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* concerning the addition of the ritual formula (*adhikāra-dharma*): both monastic and lay food may have the formula added. The Vinaya states: "At one time, there was a bhikṣu who rose early and received monastic food.

He placed it in his bowl and entered a village. There, he accepted an invitation and returned; he then performed the 'remaining-food' rite (*kṛtāvadāna*) before the other bhikṣus, and they divided it."
[They] eat, or perhaps eat it all up (this refers to the occasion of communal monastic food). At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went to a donor’s house and obtained food;

he did not know whether he had obtained it in accordance with the prescribed ritual. The Buddha said, “It is permissible. Now, this *Chao* follows this precedent, and therefore says that both are permissible.

Regarding the phrase "if one acts according to the Vinaya text": as for "concealing food," if the coarse covering is given by the donor, [the intention] above is that one fears the person performing the face-to-face confession (*pratideśanā*) might eat it.

Regarding the statement that [the rule] does not apply to the *Pañcavargika* (Five-Part Vinaya) because it is incomplete: the old commentary states that nuns possess the *śeṣabhaktavidhi* (rule concerning leftover food), for nuns are of the female class and their food is not easily digested;
thus, they do not incur an offense for eating until full. Now, this is said to be incorrect, for the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* provides an exception, as the text itself makes clear.
Furthermore, after the *Pañcavargika* has extensively explained the rules for monks regarding leftover food (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), it then states: "It is the same for bhikṣus as well."

This is based on the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts). Regarding the statement, "As for the meaning of 'reaching the precepts' (*zhijie*)," this refers to the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) undertaken with a specific intention.

It is performed for the sake of eating even a single mouthful, as prescribed in other schools. If one does not eat at all, yet says, "This is my leftover; you may take it," according to this principle, since the meal has not yet been finished, the ritual procedure is not required.
Zhen says, "If I give you my leftovers, it will be valid. This is based on the fact that the person before him wishes to receive the food.

If one knows that the other person does not wish to do so, yet strongly urges them until they commit the offense, they acquire the precept [of the offense]. Regarding the phrase "as for the Vinaya rule on committing [the offense]":

"not receiving the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (remaining-food) ritual" refers to a case of absolute non-reception; that is, from dawn until the rice has never been received as food. The rest is as stated in the text.
Regarding the passage "explaining the exhortation up to thirty-six," this refers to the *Shiming* (Explanation of Names) [and so forth].

Regarding the passage "explaining the five conditions up to the offense," after the textual analysis is complete, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "How does this differ from the previous precept concerning 'sufficient food' (*pūrva-bhakta*)?

Why are they divided into two? The answer is: the former precept is an offense committed by oneself alone; this precept is an offense committed by both oneself and others. Furthermore, for four reasons, they are opened into two. First, the former precept...

The former offense is committed by the body; this precept is committed by the mouth. Second, regarding the causal condition of illness, the former precept permits [the violation], whereas this precept does not permit it.

Third, the former precept is committed through a mind of greed, while this precept applies to all three types of mind. Fourth, the former precept is committed by eating for oneself, whereas this precept concerns the swallowing of food by another;
this is because it is committed through the act of emptying [the mouth].
Regarding the statement "it is said that 'non-time' reaches thirty-seven," this explains the name of what is to be known.

Regarding the phrase "it is said that the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* [reaches it]," that is the first cause for understanding the meaning of "Thus have I heard at one time. This dismantles the characteristic of time (*kāla-lakṣaṇa*), because it cannot be apprehended.

Consequently, a question is raised: "If dharmas have no time and so forth. This question is posed from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Its intent refers to the principle of *tathatā*.

The nature [of reality] is fundamentally without temporal divisions. Why, then, is it established as a precept by restricting time, specifically prohibiting food at improper times? (End of question. In the response, it says:
"I have already explained that one should not raise objections regarding the world. The intent of the treatise is this:

I have previously stated that within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) of the world, there are phenomena provisionally designated with names such as "time. Although they exist, they are not real. You should not now apply the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) to them.

"Regarding the objection: 'My [position] is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). It is also within the Vinaya,' this means that when the Vinaya establishes precepts, it does so in accordance with worldly conventions.

For the sake of sentient beings, a time is permitted; however, if it were treated as the absolute truth, it would not be permissible at other times. To criticize something as being at the wrong time is like the case of Kālodāyin.
This is precisely why [the Buddha] prohibited [certain acts] at improper times and established the precepts to protect the minds of people."
"Furthermore, desiring to protect the Buddha-dharma and so forth" means that the Buddha established the precepts so that the True Dharma would abide for a long time.
As the *Śāstra* also states: "The Vinaya-piṭaka alone ensures that the Buddha-dharma abides. Regarding "the ritual laws for the disciples of the Buddha":

while the regulations of external texts constitute the ritual laws of the secular world, the rules for eating and the protocols established by the Buddha at the present time are the ritual laws for the disciples of the Buddha.
[The character] "ze" (則) [is explained according to Xuánzàng’s commentary]. Bǎoyún states: "When formally receiving the precepts, one must divide the summer retreat (*varṣā*) into three periods;

one enters the teacher’s quarters to seek instruction and admonition. [This interpretation is restrictive. Therefore, regarding the phrase "the World-Honored One," etc., it means that the Buddha established the precepts to prevent censure;

one should not seek worldly fame or titles, nor should one attempt to distinguish between what is consistent or inconsistent with the nature of *tathatā* (suchness). Regarding the phrase "if this were so," etc.:

This explains the preceding point. "The actual time is not [the time for] preaching" is the explanation. It means that within the Vinaya teachings, which are the fundamental principle, one must not allow confusion.
If laypeople or non-Buddhists were to hear that the Truth (Paramārtha-satya) has no fixed time, they would immediately give rise to false views.
Furthermore, as for the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*), even the Lesser Sages (*śrāvaka*) are unable to comprehend it;

however, because many people can collectively understand the temporal divisions of the world, it is said that "it is common to the majority" and "it has now been reached. This is from the *Vīra-samādhi-sūtra*, where King Bimbisāra questioned the Buddha.

For what reason is one to eat at midday? The Buddha said: "The various devas eat at dawn and so forth; now, eating at midday is prescribed in order to sever the causes for rebirth in the six realms of existence.
Furthermore, it symbolizes the Middle Way, which was practiced by the seven Buddhas. All details are as stated in the text.

Regarding the phrase "as stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*," and the term "etcetera" (*ādi*): this means that while the previous discussion was based on coarse characteristics, the present one provides a more detailed analysis.
Furthermore, in India there are three seasons, which are also divided according to the twelve months:

from the sixteenth day of the twelfth month to the fifteenth day of the fourth month constitutes spring; from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month constitutes summer.
From the sixteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month constitutes winter.
In this land as well, the four seasons are likewise distinguished according to these twelve months, with the addition of autumn. During these four seasons, the length of days and nights is not fixed.
On the day of the summer solstice, the days are at their longest and the nights at their shortest. On the day of the winter solstice, the days are at their shortest and the nights are long.

On the two days of the spring and autumn equinoxes, day and night are equal. Beyond these points, the duration of the days and nights is not fixed. Now, if one were to distinguish between the proper time (*kāla*) and the improper time (*akāla*):
The Commentary states: "Day and night are each divided into nine periods, yet they are identical to a *muhūrta*.

This is intended to mean that according to the *Mahīśāsaka-śāstra*, day and night each have nine periods, which is the same as the thirty *muhūrtas* in the *Saṃghika* and *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. Now, first we shall clarify the *muhūrta*."
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: one hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* constitute one *tatkṣaṇa*;
ten *tatkṣaṇas* constitute one *lava*; thirty *lavas* constitute one *muhūrta*; and thirty *muhūrtas* constitute one day and night.
On the two days of the spring and autumn equinoxes, day and night are equal, each having fifteen *muhūrtas*. From dawn until midday, there are seven...

Half a *muhūrta* at this time, plus seven and a half *muhūrtas* after midday, together with fifteen *muhūrtas* of the night, totaling twenty-one and a half *muhūrtas*, are all designated as "non-time" (*akāla*).
According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, there are nine periods: from dawn until midday.

Three and a half *muhūrtas* constitute the period of *kāla* (proper time). After midday has passed, there remain another three and a half *muhūrtas*, together with nine *muhūrtas* of the night, totaling thirteen and a half *muhūrtas*, all of which are designated as *vikāla* (improper time).
On the summer solstice, the day is at its longest; according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, it consists of eighteen *muhūrtas*.

Among these, nine *muhūrta* after midday are called "past midday. These nine *muhūrta*, together with the twelve *muhūrta* of the night, constitute a total of twenty-one *muhūrta*, which are termed "improper time" (*akāla*).
On the winter solstice day, the reverse is stated (and so forth). For the intervening days, the duration is not fixed;
it may be inferred accordingly. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, there are eighteen periods in a day and night, which are likewise analogous to this.
To what extent? When asking about the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Manyūron), it states that there are eighteen periods (*kāla*) in a day and night.
In the *Saṃghabhedavastu* (Sengqi) and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Kusharon), there are thirty *muhūrta* in a day and night.

Since these numbers do not agree, why does the *Chao-wen* (Commentary) equate the eighteen periods of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* with the thirty *muhūrta* of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*? Please provide a reconciliation. The Venerable One explains: "In the *Abhidharmakośa*, there are thirty..."
Thirty *lava*s constitute one *muhūrta*. One day and night consists of thirty *muhūrtas*.
Now, since one *muhūrta* already contains thirty *lava*s, ten *muhūrtas* would contain three hundred *lava*s, and thirty *muhūrtas* would contain nine hundred *lava*s in total.

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*), one period (*yāma*) contains fifty *lava*s; thus, ten periods contain five hundred, and there are eight such periods. Five...
Eight times forty is four hundred; added to the previous total, this amounts to nine hundred *lava*s.
Although eighteen *muhūrta*s and thirty *kṣaṇa*s appear to differ slightly, they are both equally nine hundred *lava*s without distinction;
thus it is said that "the matter is the same as a *kṣaṇa*. None of the various commentaries have yet clarified this meaning, merely reciting the words to explain the text.

Some say this refers to the times of the winter and summer solstices, when the days are at their longest and shortest, as in the *Saṃghabhedavastu* and the *Abhidharmakośa*, where the *muhūrta* is not distinguished [from the solar day].
(I fear this interpretation may not yet be fully understood. My own intention differs; I shall not explain it further here. Regarding "the sun being near the earth" and so forth:

this refers to the sun’s passage along the southern course, passing close over the ice mountains, which is equivalent to being near the earth. Consequently, heat gradually recedes and cold gradually increases; it is not [otherwise].
This means that, as stated below, because the sun revolves level with the midpoint of Mount Sumeru, there are one hundred and eighty paths in the heavens.
On the summer solstice, the sun travels along this first path; on the following day, it moves one path toward the south.
Passing forty-five *dao* (measures) from here is the commencement of autumn (*liqiu*). Passing another forty-five *dao* is the autumnal equinox (*qiufen*).
Passing another forty-five *dao* is the commencement of winter (*lidong*). Passing another forty-five *dao* is the winter solstice (*dongzhi*), located at the first *dao* to the south.
On the preceding day, there were twelve hours of daylight and eighteen hours of night. From this point, moving back toward the north for forty-five *daos*, it is the beginning of spring (*li-chun*).
Another forty-five *daos* is the spring equinox (*chun-fen*). Another forty-five is the beginning of summer (*li-xia*). Another forty-five is the summer solstice (*xia-zhi*).
On this day, there are eighteen hours of daylight and twelve hours of night. As for the heat during the summer months, it is because...
Because the sun travels on its northern course, it approaches Mount Sumeru and the seven golden mountains; the nature of gold is hot.

Furthermore, it is closer to human beings, and because the northern side of Jambudvīpa is broad, it captures much of the sun’s light; therefore, winter is cold. The opposite occurs [during the southern course].
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* further states: "In winter, there are ice mountains in the southern ocean. This is because the sun is close to the land of those ice mountains. (24.5)
Regarding the phases of the moon: this refers to the twelve months of a year, each divided into a half-month, thus making twenty-four.

If measured according to the twenty-four seasonal nodes (*caturviṃśati-ṛtu*) of the secular calendar—wherein there are twenty-four nodes in common usage, and each node likewise consists of a half-month—the twenty-four half-months constitute the twenty-four seasonal nodes. If one were to calculate it by means of footprints or shadows, the principle would be the same.

The aforementioned scripture takes the length of one’s own body as the measure for the steps based on the shadow of the feet. For example, from the first day of the first month to the fifteenth is one half;
these fifteen days are used according to the corresponding seasonal breaths (*qi*). When the shadow of the body is nine and a half feet long, it constitutes a period of time.
When the shadow is seven feet long minus three finger-breadths, it is considered the improper time (*akāla*). From the sixteenth day to the thirtieth day, this is the second period of the breath.
During these fifteen days, nine feet is the proper time (*kāla*), and six feet minus three finger-breadths is the improper time.

Examples such as these could not be recorded in full detail. Regarding the *ke* (unit of time), the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "In the land of Tang, the divisions of time (*gui-lou*) are divided into one hundred *ke*.
For the timing of leaving the household life, the day and night are divided into one hundred *ke*. At the summer solstice, when the days are at their longest, the daytime consists of sixty [ke]."
Regarding the fourth [section] on nights: "The longest day is eighteen [muhūrtas] and the night twelve" refers approximately to the summer solstice.
Regarding the "longest night in summer," the Venerable [Xuanzang] notes that the phrasing has been reversed;
thus, it means the night is eighteen and the day is twelve, which is spoken of in reference to the winter solstice.
Regarding the statement "the four conditions reach [the point of] falling" (as in the text), and regarding the statement "the Vinaya reaches [the point of] falling":

that the four continents (*caturdvīpa*) are likewise means that all four continents are aligned at the same time before noon. At present, the sun and moon complete one day and night across the four continents;
for example, when the sun rises in the southern continent (*Jambudvīpa*), it sets in the east, and it is midnight in the north. Thus they shift.

This can be understood through comparison. If one possesses supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), having finished eating here in this direction, one may go to the western direction to eat again without committing an offense.
In this manner, one may eat four times within a single day without offense, because it is all before midday.
That which is called "non-time" (*akāla*) at the time of solar noon refers to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, which states that there is a specific brief interval known as "the time that is non-time."

Regarding eating at this [forbidden] time, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. Some people, breaking the phrasing of the *Śīlaskandhaka-śāstra*, state: "The time when the sun is at its zenith is called 'time' (kāla);
it is a single phrase. Eating at a non-time (*vikāla*) results in a *duṣkṛta*. This differs from the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, where eating at a non-time constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

[This interpretation] completely fails to grasp the intended meaning. Regarding "non-time beverages" (*vikāla-pāna*) and so forth, the *Śīlaskandhaka-śāstra* states: "The two methods of receiving—by mouth and by hand—are performed before the appearance of the dawn light (*aruṇodgama*)."
"Not lost" means it is called "timely" (*kāla*). If the ritual for consuming [medicinal ghee] has been lost, one incurs an offense; it should not be consumed, as this is called "untimely" (*akāla*).

Regarding medicinal ghee and oil, if the ritual for oral consumption has not been lost, it is called "timely. If the eight periods of the day have passed and the ritual is lost, it is called "untimely.

As for medicines taken for life, if one consumes them additionally when ill, it is called "timely"; if one consumes them abruptly when not ill, it is called "untimely. Note: Because the ritual for oral consumption was previously added, there is no [offense].

Regarding those illnesses for which [the medicine] is not permitted to be taken: this generally explains the three types of medicine. That is to say, when these aforementioned three medicines are available and one is not ill, they must not be consumed;

the violations carry degrees of gravity. This means that these three medicines are collectively termed "non-timely" (*akāla*). If one further consumes two of these medicines, one incurs the offense of a *pāyattika* (falling sin) for taking them at the wrong time;
only for the single medicine that may be taken for life does one incur a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) for taking it at the wrong time. Therefore, it is said that there are violations...

This concerns the gravity [of the offense]. If the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is not added, down to the point of falling into an offense, then all three medicines—those for non-timely use, those for seven days, and those for life—are permitted for the sake of illness.

If the formal ritual is added, it is known that they are for the purpose of illness; since the text specifies the causal condition of the illness, once the time has passed and the illness has ended, it is improper to take them.
If one were to merely receive them by hand, there would be the fear of taking them indiscriminately when not ill. If one takes the four medicines while ill, [it is permissible].
Because it constitutes a simultaneous offense of falling (pāyattika). Regarding the exclusion of water and tooth-sticks in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, this cites the rule on not eating;

that [rule] clarifies that although tooth-sticks and water may enter the mouth without being formally received, because they have not been received, they are not fit to be swallowed. This [passage] is cited here for that reason.
The meaning of these two cases is distinct. If it concerns water or tooth-sticks used at an improper time (*akāla*) for the purpose of rinsing the mouth, they may enter the mouth;
yet, although entry is permitted, because it is an improper time and one is not ill, one must not swallow them.

Some people do not grasp this and mistakenly interpret the *Vinayavibhaṅga* (or *Śīlaskandhaka*), concluding that one may taste food. However, in the specific context of that Vinaya rule, it describes how various bhikṣus hired laborers to cook for them.
Regarding food that is bland or sour, the bhikṣus were dissatisfied with its quality. He said, "I am unable to cook it for the bhikṣus. They reported this matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha permitted [the cooking] provided one tastes it while it is being cooked. Following the logic of this passage, the aforementioned items such as tooth-sticks and water are explained as being permissible to place in the mouth, though they must not be swallowed.
This is because they are treated the same as the four medicines taken at improper times or by those who are not ill. Next, he cites the *Daśottara-sūtra*...
Regarding the passage "reciting until both commit a *pāyattika* offense": if one follows other schools (*tāntrika*), the aforementioned subjects and objects of the action both incur a *pāyattika*.

However, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, for eating at an improper time or keeping food overnight, the instructor incurs only a *dukkaṭa*. The intent of the present *Chao* (Commentary) is to adopt the view that they are equally guilty;

thus it says, "The precepts strictly prohibit this, which serves as both a warning and an exhortation. As for "if not [done], one falls [into an offense]," the *Wubai wen* (Five Hundred Questions) states that once the meal is finished, one must [dispose of the leftovers].
Regarding ash and other such substances: if one does not use them, fearing that there may be residual flavors of food in the mouth, swallowing [the saliva] would constitute an offense.

As for the statement in the *Zhonglü* (Central Code) that this constitutes a *pārājika* (falling) offense: "emetic and purgative medicines" refers to those for inducing vomiting and those for inducing diarrhea; "diarrhea" here refers to the downward flow. Regarding "boiled barley heads that have not broken":

barley is a "timely medicine" (*kālika-bhaiṣajya*); because it was boiled without breaking, its use is permitted. If it is swallowed back down the throat, there is no offense. If it passes out of the throat, as if...
This is the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Views).

Regarding the statement "from 'eating leftovers' up to thirty-eight," the *Shiming* (Explanation of Names) cites the *Chao* [text] (etc.). Regarding the statement "three offenses," it is as the text says.
Regarding the statement "in the Vinaya, up to 'overnight,'" Xuán [Zàng] says: "There are three points here; the first is the formal explanation of 'leftover overnight' (*śeṣabhakta-śayita*)."

[This is] the name. Second, regarding "all [food]" and below, it explains and establishes impurity (*aśubha*). Third and fourth, regarding "the four medicines" and below, it comprehensively distinguishes the four types of medicine;

each point follows the text. As for the phrase "The question asks... and so forth: the *Chao* (Excerpts) first presents four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) concerning "leftover overnight food" (*śeṣa-rātri*), and subsequently presents four permutations concerning "internally stored overnight food" (*antaḥ-rātri*).
This is done to avoid confusion; the text is easy to understand upon examination. However, as for the third permutation within the preceding four permutations:
How does this differ from the third of the four subsequent phrases? Therefore, it must be distinguished. The former refers to food placed outside the boundary;
eating it the following day incurs a *pāyattika*. The latter refers to food placed within the boundary; eating it the following day incurs both a *pāyattika* and a *dukkaṭa*.
Some say that in a pure area (*pariśuddha-bhūmi*) there is no "overnight storage" (*antara-saya*). An ancient master said: "Once the purification has been established, there may be a bhikṣu who..."

Within the purified ground (*śuddhasthāna*), eating together and staying overnight does not constitute an offense. If one cannot avoid committing an offense, what is the use of performing the formal demarcation (*sīmābandha*)?
Now it is said: "If one does not demarcate, there is an offense throughout the entire area; now that the boundary has been demarcated, there is no offense within it—is this not a benefit?
Regarding the exclusion of *bhikṣus* in the text: I now cite the Vinaya text; since it is not permitted for anyone to be present within the purified ground, it says "excluding" [them].

"Depart! Thus, one knows that the phrase "there is" is a term of definitive certainty. Since there is a bhikṣu within, it is certain that there has been an overnight stay indoors, thereby constituting an offense.
As for the statement in the Vinaya, "How profound!"—the bhikṣu practicing dhyāna serves as the *nidāna* (the causal occasion).
Objection: Those who violate the precepts do so out of an evil mind. Now, a bhikṣu practicing seated meditation does so merely for the sake of conditions;
this is for the purpose of frugality. Why, then, were the precepts established? Response: To prevent [transgressions] in the future, and so forth—this explains and resolves the objection.
"Dreading and leaning upon the practitioner of the Way" means that the dreading mind relies upon True Suchness (*tathatā*). The ultimate principle is primordial.

Those who lack the perception of signlessness (animitta) tend to treat with contempt the noble precepts and the Three Vehicles. Regarding those who do not disparage the precepts, it is said that for a Bodhisattva who maintains the precepts for the sake of calming the world, these are no different from the naturally grave offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
As for the statement in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* regarding the offense of *duṣkṛta* for eating impure, leftover, or overnight salt:

this refers to its salty and bitter nature; since its substance is something to be maintained throughout one's life, although it is merely leftover or overnight, the rule prescribes only *duṣkṛta*. The *Shunzhengji* states:
The substance of salt is pure and does not retain grease; originally, it was not permissible for it to remain overnight.

However, because it can manifest the flavors within food and humans constantly require it, the rule against keeping it overnight was established. If one eats it [after it has become stale], it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense (this interpretation perfectly captures the intent of the text). As for the commentary:

in the section on medicinal substances (*bhaiṣajya*) in the Vinaya, the group of six bhikṣus used salt that had been kept overnight and deemed it unfit to eat. Since it states "it is unfit," this is likewise a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"Nor shall one kindle fire," because it prevents self-cooking. "Nor shall one blow upon or stir [the food]," because it prevents improper contact (*duṣṭa-sparśa*).

Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the commentary is to be inferred accordingly": this means it is to be inferred according to the principle established above regarding purifying the mind through renunciation.

"One should receive [food] from a *śrāmaṇera*": Xuán says this is out of fear that there might be oily residue; however, if there is certainly no oil, although one has touched it, it is permissible to accept it. This is stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

"Regarding 'the eater' and 'the one who plucks away' (the latter being pronounced *suo zhong fan*; the *Shuowen* says it means to take from above): 'like those of Uttarakuru' refers to the principle of having no sense of 'mine.

As for the statement that there is no offense according to the *Mahāsāṃghika*, this is because two periods are distinguished: the period after midday and the period after a *muhūrta*. Thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika* states:

'If one receives [food] during the proper time, but eats it after a hair's breadth or a blink of an eye has passed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; if it is set aside and a *muhūrta* has passed, it is a [full] offense.'"

One commits two *pāyattika* offenses: namely, eating at an improper time and storing food. This refers to setting food aside. If it is for medicinal purposes and remains for more than a *muhūrta*, there is no offense;
the supplementary note is clear on this point. Regarding "a pure cloth without fault": this means it has never been used to hold fruit, and it is called "pure" because it is washed daily.
Regarding "if one who begs for alms makes a mental resolve for a *śrāmaṇera*": this refers to the case where an unreceived object falls into [the bowl] while [the resolve is being made].
"Confused. If a bhikṣu holds it in his hand, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; this is because he intentionally employed such a means.
As for the statement in the Vinaya that "there is no offense," it refers to a *hǎo* (pronounced huà; the *Shuowén* glosses it as a fissure or crack).
Regarding "not receiving food" up to the thirty-ninth [item]: this is the *Shiming* (Explanation of Names) and the *Dieliao* (Citation of Texts), etc.

Regarding "the ten gates" up to "explanation": these are the general enumeration of names and numbers; there is no need for laborious explanation or judgment at this stage. Regarding "the first" up to "end":

the intent of the regulation and its origin are as stated in the text. Regarding "the second" up to "therefore": this passage consists of three sections: first, clarifying the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); second, seeking and obtaining; third...

"Eat here" refers to the phrase "crossing over," etc.; this location applies to all places, as will be made clear below. Regarding those who have broken the precepts and so forth, they are not persons from whom one may receive food;
these points are easy to understand according to the text. As for the statement that "the three objects of offering do not constitute [a valid recipient]," this excludes oneself;
that is to say, one must not pass food with one's own right hand, as it does not constitute [a valid act] when held in the left hand.
"Receiving" and "those of a similar class": those of a similar class are great bhikṣus; one may not personally confer [ordination] upon other bhikṣus.
"The other three classes of sentient beings" refers to humans, non-humans, and animals. "Being initiated" means teaching another so that they first understand.
This is originally for the purpose of providing testimony; if one is among humans, the other two realms are inferior and cannot serve as witnesses. *Niu shang* (Cattle on High).
Regarding the recipient of the food: Zhi says that there was a bhikṣu who wished to travel far. He borrowed a lay attendant (kappiya-kāraka) from another. At the time of departure, he said:
"I have no lay attendant; I do have an ox. If you need one, you may take it. He then had the lay attendant carry provisions such as grain in a long sack.

The method is as stated in the text (*et cetera*). Regarding the fact that humans, devas, animals, and flying birds can all achieve [this], the Venerable [Śīlabhadra] cites the *Lokaprajñapti-śāstra*, which states:
"Animals are exemplified by oxen and macaques; flying birds are exemplified by orioles and mynas.

Regarding Kāśyapa receiving food from Śakra, the Venerable [Śīlabhadra] cites the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, which states: "Śakra saw the appearance of the five minor signs of decline and became terrified; he descended..."
He came at an interval to question the Buddha. The Buddha instructed him to seek merit by offering a meal to monks who had recently emerged from meditative absorption.
Śakra, wishing to offer food to Kāśyapa, observed that Kāśyapa was abandoning the wealthy for the poor; having just arisen from meditation, he was wandering everywhere to beg for alms.
Śakra then transformed himself into a weaver in a poor neighborhood and gave him rice. Later, when Kāśyapa returned to the monastery and ate it, he perceived that it possessed [a divine quality].

Regarding the "divine flavor": Kāśyapa subsequently entered meditative concentration and observed that this was a meal offered by Śakra. Fearing that the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) would not be valid, he addressed the Buddha.
The Buddha said it was a valid acceptance. This is cited as proof for the principle of receiving food from a deity. Regarding the honey received from the side of a monkey:
the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states that when the Buddha was by the side of the Rṛjupāta River, a monkey was walking along. Suddenly, it saw a tree in the air [or a tree] free of bees.
It was ripe honey. The monkey then came to take the Buddha’s bowl. The bhikṣus tried to stop him, but the Buddha said, "Do not stop him; he has no ill intent.
The monkey then took the bowl, scooped out the honey, and offered it to the Buddha. The Buddha did not accept it, saying that it was not yet pure.

The monkey, not understanding the Buddha's meaning and thinking there were insects [in the honey], turned the bowl over on all four sides to scrape it clean. Seeing that there was still dripping honey inside the bowl, he then took hold of it.

He went to the water’s edge to wash it, but water splashed into the bowl. He brought it back and offered it to the Buddha, who accepted it immediately. It is said that the Buddha accepted it because he considered his own water to be pure, yet its flavor had been spoiled.
This citation is used to prove the principle that what has been stored overnight may still be accepted as food. Regarding those bound lightly in hell, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"Maudgalyāyana was receiving food by the side of the Mahā-Sudarśana Lake," and furthermore, Śroṇakoṭikarṇa saw the human world during the day.

"Painful nights and pleasant [days]" refers to the shores of the great ocean and the slopes of various mountains, where there are minor hells (*kṣudranaraka*) in which the suffering experienced is not severe;

these are called "light fetters" (*laghupratisaṃyukta*). This does not apply to the eight cold and eight hot great hells (*mahānaraka*), and so forth. The remainder of the text, concerning the summary and explanation, is clear.

Regarding the phrase "from four up to transformation," this cites the name of the fourth [section] and opens it up to provide a general explanation of both "contact" (*sparśa*) and "transformation of perception" (*saṃjñāpariṇāma*).
This is the chapter.

Regarding the statement, "The initial, middle, and final [stages] are mutually received," the five types of sensory objects (*viṣaya*) are fully enumerated in the *Chen-yao* (Excerpts). Now, the Master’s commentary states:

"It is likely because those that are subtle cannot be seen; therefore, they do not undergo reception (*vedanā*). If they were coarse and visible, it would clearly follow that they must undergo reception."

As for those that do not constitute an offense: this refers to coarse dust that can be removed; although other food may be covered by dust, because it does not lose its status through contact, it is said that there is no offense.
Regarding "fine [dust] must be received again": this means that if there is fine dust which cannot be removed and remains adhered to the food, one must receive it once more. An objection is raised:

in the previous section on the Ten Recitations (*daśajñapti*), it was stated that five types of dust do not require re-receiving. The Master of the *Chao* (the Sub-commentary) explains that this should be...
Regarding "this subtle [particle]": why must even a subtle particle be considered "received" (*pratigṛhīta*) in this treatise?
This can be answered by citing the commentary on the following passage (as follows). As for "splashing into the bowl constitutes receiving": this refers to when monks are sitting together;
once that monk has received food, if other food splashes into one's own bowl, it thereby becomes "received. If [the food] splashes from the hands of the original pure person...
Regarding "placing [food] into the bowl": this does not constitute a valid reception (*pratigraha*). Regarding "monks and nuns mutually purifying and mutually receiving":
Xuan says that if a monk has food that is "touched by remnants" (*śeṣa-sparśita*), it becomes pure for a nun; the same applies in reverse for a nun.

When they receive from one another by hand, both constitute a valid reception of food, because their physical forms and roles are distinct (the *Shunzhengji* notes that according to the current commentary, washing hands again and receiving once more from a *kappiya-kāraka* is called "mutual reception," but this is incorrect). Regarding "as stated in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, 'up until it has not yet been taken'": this refers to a single pinch.

"Taking" (pronounced *chê* [as in *chê-hsüeh*], meaning to receive). "Great marsh" refers to the place where the empty vessel for the dead is located. Regarding "not yet taken," the text should be rearranged to read: "first, purify and take the rice.
As for the phrase "from the *Saṃghāṭī* down to 'excellent,'" it means that when arm-sweat flows into the hand, one should immediately receive it.
The *You-shi* (Commentary on the Profound) states: "Because the forehead has already separated from the body, it must be received; as for the arm-sweat flowing into the hand, because..."
It does not leave the body; as soon as it enters the hand, one should receive it. The commentary states:
"In accordance with this" means that just as arm-sweat flowing into the hand constitutes receiving, so too does the mental intention regarding forehead-sweat constitute receiving.

"In accordance with the *Mahāsāṃghika*" means that if one receives by swallowing the liquid, only then is it properly received. Regarding the phrase "from two onwards," "arising mutually without losing the reception" refers to the reception of ginger.

Once purified, a sprout subsequently grows. The area where the sprout has emerged is cut away and further purified, but the area where the sprout grew does not lose its status as a "receiving" (paribhoga) object, even though it remains connected to the sign of growth;
this is because the prior act of purification was originally performed to prevent growth. If that is so, what is the purpose of purifying the area where the sprout grew? The answer is:

because the newly arisen sign of growth is distinct from the original substance, the original area of prevention does not lose its status. Regarding the new [growth]: it is distinct from the original substance. Thus, the original area of prevention is not lost. Regarding the new...

"The place where [the seed] grows must necessarily undergo [the formal act of] receiving [the precept]. (This is one interpretation. Furthermore, another explanation states: "The place where the sprout grows is touched once by a pure person;
because it is pressed by the hand, the method of receiving [the precept] is not lost. This may be illustrated by the case of a person touching food:
if they press down on the vessel with their hand, the food is not lost. This interpretation is also correct. Regarding the note that the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya) is also like this: Ānanda...
The Buddha was warming his rice outside the gate of Jetavana; this refers to that. Regarding "recording what was recognized before the midday meal":

it means that when curd-food (*dadhi*) has not been finished, one records and recognizes it, saying, "A pure substance has arisen within this; I shall prepare it as a seven-day medicine for an improper time (*akāla-bhaiṣajya*).

It is like butter being extracted from curd, or rock honey (*phāṇita*) produced from sugarcane; although they have transformed, their essence is not lost. As for "the five kinds of received food until the recitation," it refers to the ground.
And as for those who receive food while in water: one receives food in no more than these two locations.
If the body is in the air and receives food—since there is no support in space—receiving food in such a place is not valid.

As for the previous discussion regarding receiving food [while in water], this is further cited from the *Śāstra-vivaraṇa* (Commentary on the Treatise), which is largely identical to what was already explained in the second section on the "recipient."
Regarding the phrase "from six to all": the titles [of the sections] are self-evident. Regarding the phrase "from one to 'attainment'":
"reaching the edge of the object" means causing the bhikṣu to extend his hand so that he himself reaches the edge of the object. The remaining text is easy to understand.
Regarding the statement, "In two cases, the act of receiving is accomplished," there are four phrases in the text. As for "the body is not the mind," the commentary states:

when a bhikṣu extends his alms-bowl while his mind is focused on another matter, he places food into it without being mindful of what he is receiving; nevertheless, because he was previously possessed of the intention [to receive], the act of receiving is nonetheless accomplished.
In the second sentence, there are three points. First, the meaning of the phrase is explained. Second, from "the Vinaya" onwards, scriptural citations are introduced as proof.

Third, "if one follows the instruction" indicates the addition of further details. The commentary states: "If a person sends food for a bhikṣu, it is included within [the donor's] intention; it is included within [the donor's] own intention."
The donor placed the food down and departed; except for cases where it was not received directly by hand, this food also constitutes a valid acceptance.
