The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: In the kingdom of Vaiśālī, grain was expensive and alms were difficult to obtain. A bhikṣu with supernormal powers went to the country of the non-Buddhists to beg for food.
The outsiders, finding him impure, placed the food on the ground and left. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "Bring it here and place it [on the ground]."

"Previously" means that the act of giving is completed and the reception is established. Regarding "the equality of body and mind," the *Liaoshu* (Explanatory Commentary) states: "Because the hand is extended and received, and the mind does not dwell upon anything else, it is called 'equality.
That which has already been offered at the feet is not what is prohibited; once it has been offered, it constitutes a prohibition, and thus the reception is not established.

Regarding "not [of] body and mind," the text of the *Shu* (Commentary) is as in the *Chao* (Extracts). Regarding "body and mind being unrelated," it refers to the time when one is currently eating. Body...
The mind and food do not interact; for even that which is not the mind constitutes "receiving. Regarding the phrase "a single-minded person approaching a pure individual":
"single-minded" means without a counterpart; it refers to having the intention to receive alone, without using hands or body to receive that food from another.
Regarding the statement that a person with wrong views does not give food to a bhikṣu, the *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya* says: "There was a country called Dengqu, which was a frontier region."
This is a wrong view. Because he is an evil bhikṣu, one should not give him food. One should perform the *maṇḍala* ritual—here translated as "altar.

This involves marking out the ground with a compass. The *Shuowen* says that a compass is used for making circles. Using the compass to mark the ground, one completes the form and places the food within it.
If leaves are used to cover the bowl, one may use tree leaves to cover the ground where the mark has been made, thereby completing the bowl.
If one establishes the characteristic of a single household, the formal reception [of food] is accomplished for all. Regarding those who do not understand one another:
people from different countries who cannot communicate and are unwilling to offer food to a bhikṣu—this is also the same as what was previously stated regarding "reception upon reception.

The characteristic of the horse stable being burned by fire is found in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*. At that time, there was a horse merchant who invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha; after they had received water, the people...
The report arrived that the horse stable had been burned by fire. He said to the bhikṣu, "You may take food for yourself," and having said this, he departed. The Buddha said:

"If there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible), it is permitted to accept [the food] on the basis of the donor’s words. Regarding "meditating or sleeping": this refers to the *saṃghāṭī*.
If a bhikṣu sits in meditation or sleeps upon his bed, and a *kappiya-kāraka* brings food and places it within the *kuṭi* (cell), if he awakens... [he may then partake].
This refers to receiving [the food]. If one is unaware [of the rules], when wishing to eat, one should have another person receive it on one's behalf.

If one does not wish to eat, one should hold it oneself and give it to a *pariśuddha* (pure person) or the like. Regarding what is called "fourfold continuous entanglement and obstruction": this means that because objects are interconnected, one cannot act with autonomy.
It is called "linked-counting" (*liánjì*). When an object is thrown from afar, it is intercepted midway before finally falling; therefore, it is said that there is contact and obstruction.
Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika* definition of "receiving at the place of arrival": this refers to the *Mahāsāṃghika* school.

For instance, when a bhikṣu is begging for food, a shopkeeper fills a measure with roasted flour (*mañca*) and gives it to the bhikṣu. The measures are linked by a chain, whether five *sheng* or four *sheng* are connected together. Thus...

At that time, the Bhikṣu should say to the donor: "Once you have untied the subsequent measures and handed them over to me—if the lock cannot be opened, then place the roasted flour inside and hand it to the Bhikṣu.
As for the remaining measures and the connected lock, they shall remain in the hands of the layperson.
This is called "the continuity of the utensils being unbroken. Or, receiving [the gift] in a manner that is not decorous... [and so forth], as found in that Vinaya.

There are ten cases. Because these exceed [the standard] by involving taking, touching, or obstructing, the text says "up to and including. The *Ji* states: A lay attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*) climbs a tree to gather fruit.

The bhikṣu says, "Give me the fruit. The attendant shakes the tree, and the fruit falls into the bhikṣu’s vessel; this is called "receiving [fruit] that is not in accordance with the rules of decorum" (*na-vinaya*).

If, when the fruit is being lowered, it touches the branches or leaves, or if while falling it lands on branches or leaves between [the tree and the bhikṣu], [and the bhikṣu receives it], the lay attendant and the bhikṣu... [both incur an offense].
"Kiu! Both minds were startled, and thus the previous ritual was lost. It should be that the mind arises and the reception is accomplished through that reception.

Regarding "because there is no oral addition," the *Jianlun* (見論) states that the reception is accomplished without an oral addition; however, it is merely non-ritualistic (*a-vinaya*). In the *Sifenlü* (四分律), if one does not touch or encounter an obstruction in the interim, the reception is accomplished;
in the *Shisonglü* (十誦律), an oral formula is further added. Regarding "the *Sengqilü* (僧祇律) [mentions] food suspended over a well, etc.," this refers to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

It is said that a monk in an araṇya (forest hermitage) has no attendant (kappiya-kāraka). When drawing water from the well himself at mealtime, he has no leisure to come out for fear that the water will refill.

He therefore attaches the rope to his food and lowers it down. While lowering it, he must avoid any grass or wood that may be inside his stomach. [This is] the rule for a monk at the bottom of the well.
With one hand he holds the cord, and with the other he receives the food, saying "I receive, I receive. However, it is said that one should avoid grass and wood;
it does not say whether contact constitutes a valid reception or not (this refers to the obstruction by contact within the *Lianjie*). Therefore, the *Chao* states:

"Do not collide with living fruit-bearing trees," for fear of further obstructing contact, as both the attendant (*jìngrén*) and the bhikṣu would each be startled in their minds. Thus, one should distance oneself from the base when receiving or being granted food.

Regarding the mind: furthermore, one must follow the previous analogy of the fruit on the upper and lower parts of a tree. Through contact, obstruction, and permeation, it enters [the consciousness], giving rise to the mental and verbal expression "I receive, I receive.
Were it not so, it would not be established; therefore, it says "do not snatch" (*mōt*). As for that which is on top of a house, it is *kan* (pronounced *han-dàn*).
The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To take with the hand by warding off. This means the intention of receiving by grasping the rope with the hand. That Vinaya states: "An *āraṇyaka* bhikṣu..."

Holding the upper end of the rope with one hand, when the attendant (kappiya-kāraka) places the food and hangs it [on the line], the bhikkhu holds the rope with one hand, forming the intention of receiving, and says aloud: "I receive, I receive."

Regarding the statement in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* that "receiving [food] from two [hands] is permitted": it says there that a layperson was holding a jar of ghee or oil and poured it into a bhikṣu’s bowl in an unbroken stream.
The bhikṣu became doubtful and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "This is pouring downward, not upward;

it does not violate the rule for receiving [food]. This constitutes a continuous flow. As for the phrase "those who travel on the path in the central lands," these are those who practice the Way. [The bhikṣu] sat upon a clean cloth.

"Sitting" refers to the people of the Western lands (India), who customarily remain in a kneeling posture with their feet on the ground. Because their feet are often covered in mud, they fear it might soil their three robes (*trīṇi cīvarāṇi*);
for the sake of keeping the robes clean, they are made to sit in a squatting position with both feet planted firmly on the earth, which is called "squatting" (*utkuṭuka*).

As for the food table placed before them, this refers to a raised earthen mound upon which grass is spread and a bowl is set; in this manner they eat. If the food is served on leaves or grass, [it is considered] small...

If it does not stop and fall away, it accords with the mind that intends to receive, and thus constitutes "reception" (this is termed *sparśāvaraṇa-vedanā*). If it were to immediately fall away, it would contradict the mind that intends to receive, and therefore it would not constitute reception.
"Gradually receiving for oneself" means bestowing upon oneself step by step. It is like a basket of rice:
first one lifts one side and bestows it upon a bhikṣu, then one lifts another side and bestows it upon a bhikṣu; this is what is meant by "gradual. This...

This refers to the ground that is mutually separated from one side. Because it is received as being connected to the earth, even when treading upon water with the feet, if one descends into the cauldron, one must verbally add:

"I receive, I receive, I receive. This is the reception of tactile obstruction (*spraṣṭavya-pratighāta*). That is to say, when touching the water being stepped upon, there is an obstruction such that one does not reach the ground;

because this accords with the original mind of the vow, it is successfully accomplished. As for the phrase, "The five mental objects reach the center": (Note: The character 㝵 is a variant of 礙, meaning "obstruction" or "impediment.")

Regarding this, there are three factors for the *kappiya-kāraka* (the one who makes things permissible): first, knowing what is food and what is not; second, having a donor; third, bestowing it according to the Dharma. There are three factors for the bhikṣu:

first, the bhikṣu’s giving corresponds to what the *kappiya-kāraka* has bestowed; second, it is for the purpose of food and nothing else; third, the food is bestowed with the hand according to the Dharma.

There are seven faults to be avoided: first, storing overnight inside; second, cooking inside; third, cooking oneself; fourth, improper contact; [fifth, touching with a non-permissible hand]; sixth, [receiving from a non-permissible person]; seventh, [receiving from one who is not a *kappiya-kāraka*].

(The first four are auspicious). Five: not from leftover overnight food. Six: not from what was purchased or sold. Seven: not from the body of one who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and is consuming medicine for the purpose of fattening or nourishing.

(The detailed explanation of these five observations is as found in the section on "Giving to Others"). Regarding the statement that "all phrases and sentences are the broad path (*prthu-mārga*) which one should know," the *Liaoshu* identifies the Vinaya as the "broad path.
One travels this path to reach all meanings; therefore, it is called the "broad path. Within the Vinaya—
This meaning is explained extensively; therefore, it says, "One should know. The section beginning with "The commentary states" and following is the *Liaoshu* (Explanatory Commentary).
Regarding "all other phrases and sentences," this refers to all remaining phrases concerning the protection of right precepts, excluding the formal regulations of the five categories of the Vinaya.

To expand upon these formal regulations is called the "Extensive Path" (*zòngguǎng dào*), which refers precisely to the aforementioned five points on the method of contemplating food. Therefore, they were established as prohibitions.

It should be understood that the *Śāstra* explains that for a renunciant, receiving food and so forth is the formal regulation of the Vinaya; to receive it otherwise constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
One must first observe the gate [of the mouth] before eating or drinking. In light of the original text of the formal precept, this observation constitutes the thorough and expansive path.
Regarding the phrase "the eightfold attainment of right reception": it is as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "all who reach the Dharma":

this is the citation of the title. Regarding the phrase "first, [concerning] defilement": the text of the *Chao* consists of six sections. The passage "the formal act (*karmavācanā*) is completed when the time has passed, and there is no further reception, etc.

is as explained in the tenth section of the subsequent commentary according to the text. The passage "the seven-day period for [staying outside the monastery] at an improper time exceeds its limit, and likewise... is also as stated in the text. This refers to the time.
The time has already passed, and the period for the Dharma has again expired. Within this, there are further two types of reception: by mouth and by hand.

This refers to "recording and recognizing" during the proper time; it accords with the preceding *Ji* (Sīla) text. If one does not record and recognize [the transgression], and it changes, then the reception is lost.
The note does not mean that there is defilement; the ancient masters said that pure water might have impurities or oily contact upon the hands. Now it is said: but...
This expresses a pure mind. It is like the daughter of King Bimbisāra who offered a garden; when she poured water from a golden pitcher, where could there be any impurity on her hands?

Regarding the explanation based on the text of the *Daśādhyāya-vinaya*, this refers to citing the title, as it is specifically an explanation based on the text of the precepts. The *Shan-chao* (Commentary) omits the full causal conditions.

Now, according to the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), the offense is complete when all conditions are met: first, it concerns the four types of medicine; second, one takes them oneself without having received them;

third, the offense is incurred upon swallowing. As for the statement that "the fourth [condition] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (*jīlúo*)": this refers to cases where the aforementioned condition of illness is absent. If one eats without having received the medicine, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.

Why does one not incur a *pāyattika* (*tí*)? Because the formal rite of receiving (*pratigraha*) still exists; therefore, one does not incur a *pāyattika*. This is because, while there is no illness, the condition of not having received the medicine is present.
Because they are not equivalent, it is improper. Regarding "not committing an offense" and below, it is as stated in the text.
As for the fortieth [precept], "Seeking Fine Food," the *Shichiao* (Explanatory Notes) comments [as follows].

Regarding the statement "four conditions lead to an offense," "fine food" (*praṇītabhojana*) is defined in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun) as being expensive, difficult to obtain, and capable of curing illness. There are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). First: that which is fine and is food.
1. Neither a fine medicine nor a fine food: milk and curd. 2. A fine medicine but not a fine food: fresh ghee and oil. 3. Both a fine food and a fine medicine:
meat and *pūtimukta* (putrefied fruit). 4. Neither a fine food nor a fine medicine: *harītakī*.
Regarding what is considered most important: it refers to meat broth that can be boiled down to make fat, which is capable of treating wind-related illnesses;

thus, one may go to beg for it. As for the eight kinds of milk and curds, the *Śīla* states: unless one is ill, one must not go [to beg]. One may, however, go to a butter-maker’s house to beg for butter;
to an oil-presser’s house, to a honey-gatherer’s house, to a sugarcane-presser’s house to beg for rock sugar (*śarkarā*), or to a cowherd’s house to beg for milk and to make curds.

One may beg for fish from a fisherman’s house and meat from a butcher’s house. Regarding those who commit a grave offense (*guru-āpatti*), the *Pañcaśata-praśna* states that calling out [the name] constitutes a grave offense.
As for the statement in the Vinaya, "one does not commit an offense up until one obtains everything," it is as the text says.
Regarding the statement "from the Cloud [Sūtra] to the forty-first [offense]" and "five conditions leading to an offense": 1. "The first is a non-Buddhist (tīrthika)":
The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states that this refers to a renunciant non-Buddhist. This is because for a layperson, it constitutes only a minor offense;

however, since the names are identical for renunciants, it is difficult to distinguish the true from the false, thereby giving rise to delusion and confusion among people, and thus it is treated as a grave offense. 3. "One gives food oneself": The Vinaya permits this in the case of a relative.

The kindness of one's parents is profound. According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, this matter is not even mentioned; nevertheless, if one must provide [food], one should employ a pure attendant (*śuci-puruṣa*).

If they express dissatisfaction or reproach, simply reply: "Those who have left the household life may not [do so]; the Buddha has already established this precept. If they still refuse to eat, then let them do as they please.
It is not that one places food on the ground and sends someone else to eat it; rather, because the flavor of food is common to all, it is logical that one should eat it alone.

It is permitted to place food on the ground and send someone else to eat it only so as not to give rise to delusion or perversion. As for the statement in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* regarding "giving to another," this refers to one who lacks right view—that is, a person with nihilistic views.
This person does not discriminate between victory and defeat, good and evil, self and other, nor do they seize upon the faults of the Saṃgha.
Regarding the statement "not to inform until the forty-second [day]," this is explained in the *Shiming lidiao* (云云).

Regarding the statement "five conditions leading to an offense," as for "before or after a meal," it refers to the period after the great meal (*mahābhojana*) or the small meal (*laghubhojana*). If one enters a village after the great meal, it is as prescribed in the following precept.

These are not offenses under this [rule]. Regarding the "four cases of no cause": these refer to the month of Kārttika, the distribution of robes, the making of robes, and having made the formal announcement (*jñapti*), one departs;
these are all due to specific causes and conditions. As for the phrase "the *saṃgha-kaṭhina* robe reaches the point of announcing it to the donor," there are two *pāyattika* offenses:

first, as in the precept on "turning away from an invitation," failing to announce to the household that has invited one; second, turning away from where there is no invitation. One incurs two *thullaccaya* offenses. According to the underlying principle, our Master now bases [his explanation] upon...
Regarding the precept on a single person’s invitation: there is no rule against multiple invitations. This is consistent with the precept concerning "turning away from an invitation.
If one is begging for food among various households, one should inform the donor who gives the beans. If one is inside the monastery, one should inform a lay attendant (*karmadāna*).

When the donor arrives later and asks the attendant, the attendant will know where [the monks] have gone. It is simply stated: "There were two bhikṣus, each separately accepting an invitation from the head of a household. If...
If one bhikṣu says to a second bhikṣu, "Venerable sir, let us go together today to my donor’s house for a meal," this constitutes an invitation.
The second bhikṣu should inform his own original donor; if he does so, there is no offense. Otherwise, it is a *thullaccaya*.

The second bhikṣu should also act in this manner; the same principle applies by analogy. Regarding the statement in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* that "one falls [into an offense] upon entering the gate," if this is compared to the *Sūtra on the Measurement of Time*, they are identical.
That sūtra distinguishes between "proper time" (*kāla*) and "improper time" (*akāla*) based on twenty-four half-months.

For instance, from the first day of the first month to the fifteenth day, measured by the shadow cast by one's footsteps, nine and a half steps constitute "proper time," which is precisely the time for eating.

At that time, this sutra discusses the period generally as being before midday, totaling nine feet and a half shadows, plus four *caturthas*. Regarding the division of before and after midday, there are two periods:

the time before eating and the time after eating. As for the time before eating, two feet and a half shadows, plus three fingers, constitute the "time for eating" (*bhojana-kāla*), starting from the appearance of the dawn light until the time of the morning meal (*prahāṇa-bhakta*).
As for the time after eating, seven feet minus three fingers constitutes the "improper time" (*akāla*). From...

"Ten [units] after eating" refers to the period before midday. The *Chao* (Commentary) broadly adopts the two periods—before and after eating—from the *Four-Part Vinaya*, totaling nine and a half *jiao*.
Since this is discussed in conjunction with the sutras, it is said that "the time is the same as the mealtime in the *Sūtra on Time*.

As for what is not the same as "non-time" (*vikāla*), it means entering a village during non-time; wherever there is a bhikṣu, or if one sees a white-clad person on the road, [the rule] applies. This requires...

Instruct those who have received the invitation together to complete it; seek out the location and ensure it does not cause distress to others. The wording of the formal announcement (*jñapti*) is as follows: "Venerable sir, please bear this in mind:
I, [Name], while traveling among various households for the purpose of eating together with others... The response is: "So be it.

Regarding the statement in the lower fascicle of the *Vinaya* that one does not commit an offense, the *Śīla-śāstra* (Commentary on the Precepts) explains: "When many people are gathered at various houses, one waits at each location."
Regarding the Sangha: wherever they go, it is all a place of invitation; there is no offense if one does not give prior notice.

If one goes to a donor's house first on the day before the meal is served, it causes distress to the patron, as described in the section on "Invitations. The Venerable Master said: "In this precept, 'sharing the same benefit' refers to..."
This refers to receiving offerings from lay donors in common with the Sangha. Nowadays, in monasteries across various regions, they collect alms money and take ten percent of every hundred coins;
this is called "sharing profits. This is contrary to the Dharma. If one asks where this is documented, it is found within the Tripitaka.
There is no place where this is explicitly stated.
Regarding the passage from "In a house where food is being eaten" up to "forty-three," the *Shiming* (Explanation of Names) cites the *Chao* (Extracts) [and so forth].

Regarding the passage from "The four kinds of food" up to "also," as for the four kinds of food, they are divided into two parts: first, a general clarification; second, an explanation of the *Chao*. First, regarding the general clarification, therefore, it is said in the *Jù*...
Śāriputra said: As it is stated in the sūtras, the World-Honored One, amidst the assembly of devas and humans, spoke these words:
"Beneath the Bodhi tree, I attained perfect enlightenment and truly realized a single dharma: that all sentient beings subsist by depending upon food and drink.
When the non-Buddhists heard this, they clapped their hands and laughed loudly, saying, "All sentient beings rely upon and look up to food and drink; who would not [agree]?"
"I know it. Why rely on the Bodhi tree? Only a Buddha attains awakening. The World-Honored One then questioned him in return:

"Since you already know that all sentient beings subsist by means of food, why do you starve yourself? Furthermore, how many kinds of food are there? Do they exist within the three realms or not? How are they distinguished?
And what is the meaning of 'with outflows' (sāsrava) and 'without outflows' (anāsrava)? Thereupon, the outsider was unable [to respond].

It is capable of providing a response. Therefore, the Buddha explained the nature of nutriment to each of them individually. Now, according to the commentaries on the treatise (*śāstra*), this will be briefly divided into five sections:

first, the explanation of the name; second, the determination of its essence (*svabhāva*); third, its connection to the realms of existence (*dhātu-bandhana*); fourth, whether it is with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*); and fifth, the clarification of its establishment and abrogation. Within the first section, there is both a general and a specific explanation.
Question: What is the meaning of "nutriment" (*āhāra*)? Answer: It has the meaning of "sustaining and benefiting. That is to say, it is that which is capable of sustaining and benefiting.

Because they are the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the sense faculties (*indriya*). Next, regarding the specific names: first, morsel food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*); second, contact (*sparśa*); third, volition (*manasikāra*); and fourth, consciousness (*vijñāna*).

As for "morsel food," it refers to the physical substance formed by the four sensory objects (*viṣaya*). The ancient term was *tuánshí* (lump-food), so called because it can be grasped and rolled together;

however, this definition does not fully encompass its meaning. The new term is *duànshí* (segmented food), so called because it consists of distinct portions. Within this category, there are two types. The first is subtle segmented food, which refers to that of the various devas.
Furthermore, at the beginning of the kalpa, as well as during infancy, there was no excrement or urine at all; [the food] dispersed into the limbs like oil poured onto sand.
Second, coarse material food refers to what is eaten today. Moreover, light, shade, heat, and cold are also called "food" when they are beneficial to humans;
what people see today are merely the implements of food, which have not yet provided sustenance, just as music [is an instrument of pleasure].
[It is] complete. Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "As for 'eating,' it does not constitute the act of eating merely by being in the hand or in a vessel;
it must necessarily pass through the throat, be chewed by the teeth, and fall into the stomach (*āmāśaya*), benefiting the internal organs, only then does it constitute the act of eating."

Second, the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*): the conjunction of the three—sense faculty, object, and consciousness—is called contact. Third, the nutriment of volition (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*): the mental application that seeks and anticipates an object of experience is called volition.

Fourth, the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*): that which performs the discernment of all aggregates of consciousness is called consciousness. Regarding the second [point], the determination of their essential nature:
Although edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) is established as consisting of eight factors, its essence consists only of the three—odor, taste, and tangibility—and does not include visible form.

Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "That which is not visible cannot provide benefit, because it is liberated from its own sense organ. For example, when one sees a form while asleep, it cannot provide nourishment;
indeed, it cannot even sustain the great elements (mahābhūta) of its own sense organ, let alone nourish the great elements of the various sense organs. Furthermore...
It cannot benefit the liberation of those who have attained liberation—namely, those who have realized the third fruit and the arhats—even though they have severed sensual desire.
When they perceive forms, it provides no benefit; they must still obtain food and the second type of nutriment, contact (*sparśa*). This contact has as its essence the mental factor of contact.

It is not the case that the physical substance of food constitutes the essence of the bowl. Regarding the three types of nutriment consisting of volition (*manahsaṃcetanāhāra*), the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The nutriment of volition corresponds to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

The four nutriments consisting of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) are the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). Regarding their association with the three realms: the nutriment of physical morsels (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) is restricted to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while the remaining three pertain to all three realms.
Question: Why does the nutriment of physical morsels not extend to the two higher realms? Answer: One must first become free from craving for physical morsels before [attaining those realms].
Because they can produce the higher [realms]. Regarding the four types—contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*): edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is exclusively contaminated;

although the other three may be both contaminated and uncontaminated, here, as "food," we take only the contaminated category. Why not include the uncontaminated? Answer: "Food" has the meaning of providing nourishment and benefit.

Uncontaminated contact, volition, and consciousness destroy the three realms of existence (*tridhātu-bhava*); because they cannot provide nourishment and benefit, they are not included. As the treatise quotes from a sutra:
Food enables *bhūta* sentient beings to abide securely and provides nourishment for those seeking birth. "Bhūta" refers to those already born within the five destinies;
"those seeking birth" refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) body, which constantly and eagerly seeks its future place of birth and thus takes fragrance as food.
Because the untainted (*anāsrava*) contact, volition, and consciousness lack this characteristic, they do not take it as food. Regarding the presiding lord of the five sciences, he asks:

All contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) possess the quality of providing sustenance and benefit to the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*). Why, then, does the World-Honored One speak of only four nutriments (*āhāra*)? Answer: There is no fault in speaking of four based on their predominance. Question: What is it that makes them predominant?

Answer: The verse says: "The first two benefit this life; they are the support and the supported. This clarifies that the first two nutriments are predominant (the first two being *kavaḍīkāra-āhāra* and *sparśa-āhāra*). As for "the support": [The commentary continues: It refers to the physical body (*rūpa-kāya*), which is the basis for the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). Since these two [nutriments] provide the primary sustenance for the maintenance of this body, they are called predominant.

Furthermore, because the first two nourish both the present life and the future life, they are superior. The third [nutriment, *manahsaṃcetanā-āhāra*], while it can produce future existence, does not sustain the present body. The fourth [nutriment, *vijñāna-āhāra*], though it sustains the present body, does not produce future existence. Therefore, by virtue of their mutual efficacy in sustaining both the present and the future, the first two are established as predominant. Thus, there is no contradiction in the teaching of the four nutriments.

This refers to the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) of sentient beings; because edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) can provide nourishment and benefit to it. As for the "supported" (*āśrita*), this refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*);
because contact as nutriment (*sparśāhāra*) can provide nourishment and benefit to them. Thus, these two types of nutriment possess the functional capacity to sustain those already born.
It is the most excellent. Therefore, it is said that these are the support and the supported in this world. Regarding the latter two nutriments, the verse says:
"The latter two [nutriments] act upon future existence as its projection and its arising. This means they serve as the sense of sustenance for the body in future existence;

that is, volitional karma (*cetanā-karman*) is able to project future existence, and once projected by the power of volition, the power of the seed of consciousness (*vijñāna-bīja*) is able to proceed toward that future existence. By means of karma...
The power of the seeds perfumed in consciousness shall arise through the application of power (*bala-upāya*). Therefore, these two nutriments are the most excellent for benefiting the future.
The first two are like a foster mother, because they sustain the body already born; the latter two are like a biological mother, because they give birth to that which is yet unborn.

According to the treatise, there is a fourfold classification (*catuṣkoṭi*): first, that which is edible matter (*kavaḍīkāra*) but not nutriment—namely, that which is consumed as a condition [for the body] but does not itself provide sustenance.

The first [category] consists of those things that damage the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the sense faculties; the second consists of nutriment that is not "morsel-like," namely the three nutriments such as contact (*sparśa*) and so forth;

the third consists of both morsels and nutriment, namely those things consumed and swallowed that serve as conditions to nourish and benefit the primary elements; the fourth category is for the purpose of excluding the aforementioned characteristics.

The three nutriments beginning with contact all fall within these four categories. Among them, that which is contact but not nutriment refers to untainted (anāsrava) contact acting as a condition to impair the sense faculties and the primary elements;
the remaining four cases can be understood accordingly. Question: Regarding the five destinies and the four modes of birth...

"Do all possess these four types of nutriment? "They all possess them. "If that is so, how can there be edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) in the hells? "Answer: They swallow hot iron balls and drink molten copper.
Although these cause injury, they are nonetheless able to temporarily alleviate hunger and thirst;

because they possess the characteristics of food, they are also considered food. Furthermore, in the *pratyekanaraka* (solitary hells), food and drink are like those of humans. Therefore, among the five destinies (*gati*), all possess [the four nutriments]."

There are four kinds of nutriment (the above five sections, totaling many general explanations of the meaning of the four nutriments, are now concluded). Next, regarding the conclusion that returns to the intent of the *Śāstra*, the text states:

"Among the four nutriments, this belongs to the category of contact-nutriment (*sparśāhāra*). Because the eye-faculty encounters visible forms, it is called contact-nutriment. Thus the Vinaya says: 'Women take men as their nutriment; men take women as their nutriment.
This contact is a real dharma among the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*); it is what women desire, and because it resembles food, it is called nutriment."
Therefore, regarding the phrase "the four reach [the treasure]," it means that by wearing garments adorned with jewels and the like, this constitutes the sense of "much exhortation.
As for the second meaning, taking men and women as the treasure: when a lady has not yet covered her body with other clothes, it is called "not having hidden the treasure."

The characteristics of non-offenses are omitted here for brevity. The Vinaya states: "If one sits within arm's reach of the door, or if two bhikṣus are companions, or if there are other such difficult circumstances, there is no offense."
Regarding "sitting with a woman until the forty-fourth [day]," see the *Shiming diechao* (云云). Regarding "the four conditions leading to an offense," it is as stated in the text.
Regarding "the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* on non-offenses," it is as stated in the text. Regarding "the *Vinaya* on non-offenses and the exceptions," it is as stated in the text.

Regarding the passage from "It is said that [one] alone" up to "the forty-fifth": this is the *Shiming diacao* (Explanatory Notes on the Names), etc. Regarding the passage from "It is said that four" up to "offenses":

the commentary states, "A *śuddhaka-puruṣa* (pure person) sees or hears in a secluded place. This is based on the two *aniyata-dharmas* (undetermined rules), which clarify that seeing or hearing [the act] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for the tooth-separation [act].

Regarding "Kuladūṣaka" (one who corrupts families): as for the statement that "ten [offenses] up to a *duṣkṛta*," and "not committing an offense while eating at a family home," these refer to the preceding precept on sitting forcefully.
Regarding "mutually receiving the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*) without committing an offense," this means that one does not commit a *pācittiya* offense, as has already been clarified above.
Regarding the two precepts hereafter: even if one has received them alternately, violating either constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), because it invites public censure.
Since the husband was absent, the former precept remained concealed; this [offense] only becomes manifest now. Although the phrasing appears difficult, upon investigation it is easily understood.
"From 'It is said that *tadyathā* up to forty-six' is the explanation of the name and the citation of the text.

From 'From "four" up to "offense"' refers to those who lack various obstructing conditions, such as being ill or lacking proper decorum (*īryāpatha*); these are those for whom the offense is waived. According to the Vinaya, the offense is incurred immediately upon being out of sight or hearing.
From 'According to the Vinaya up to "dissatisfaction"' is as stated in the text."
Regarding the statement "exceeding the acceptance for four months up to forty-seven," this is a citation from the *Shiming* (Explanation of Names).

Regarding the statement "six conditions leading to an offense," the first is "various medicines. The *Shijing* (Mirror of Affairs) states: "Among the four types of medicine, exceeding the acceptance of three types constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

According to the *Gālun* (Sutra Commentary), eating [these] at the time of receiving them also constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. This applies to the seven-day and lifetime medicines; as stated in the lower section of this Vinaya, these are those prescribed by a physician for consumption.

Medicine. Therefore, it is known that this constitutes an offense. If it is a non-time medicine (*akālabhaiṣajya*), its value is low, its therapeutic purpose is inferior, and the sense of "receiving beyond [the limit]" is rare;

thus, one merely commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. Hence, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "After four months have passed, if one further requests ghee and so forth for seven days or for life, [requesting] pepper, ginger, and the like constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense;
if one requests *āmalaka*, *vibhītaka*, or fermented gruel, it is merely a *duṣkṛta*. This concludes the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

Regarding "exceeding [the limit]": if one exceeds the limits of either spring or summer, one commits an offense. This refers to the origin story (*nidāna*) of this Vinaya rule: it concerns the invitation for the four months of the summer retreat.

Now, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (the *Cīvara-vastu*), exceeding the limit in spring also constitutes an offense; however, it is simply a matter of exceeding the time limit, regardless of whether it is three seasons, half a month, or a full month.

As for the statement in the Vinaya that it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing): excluding the four conditions as stated in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, the first is "one who constantly invites," which refers to a donor.

The Master said: "Regarding 'constant invitation' (*nitya-nimantraṇā*): it means that after one has already finished eating, one continues to offer food. Regarding 'invitation by division' (*vibhāga-nimantraṇā*):

one personally carries [the food] to the monastery (*ārāma*) and, having divided it into portions, gives the good portions to the bhikṣus; this fivefold type is called 'self-delivered invitation. Regarding 'invitation for as long as life lasts' (*yāvaj-jīva-nimantraṇā*):"

"I shall provide medicine for as long as my life lasts. *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts). Question: What is the distinction between "regularly providing" (*changqing*) and "for as long as one's life lasts" (*jinxing*)?

Answer: It is simply distinguished according to the capacity and the object [of the act]. Alternatively, it is said that because it involves the two individuals for the duration of their lives, it is called "for as long as one's life lasts" (*jinxing*).

Regarding the offenses of exceeding the limit for medicine and exceeding the limit for the night: the Vinaya text provides a fourfold analysis (*liaojian*) of medicine and night, and of the time and day.

Regarding the limits of time (*kāla-pariccheda*): as for the medicines, they are *śuṇṭhī* (ginger) and *piṇḍaluka* (chebulic myrobalan). The flavors are divided into two fruits. The first phrase states:

"The night has a limit" (fixed at four months for the seasonal invitation), while "the medicine has no limit" (meaning various kinds of medicine may be given). The second phrase: "The night has no limit" (one should always invite [the monks]), while "the medicine has a limit" (giving *śuṇṭhī* but not *piṇḍaluka*).
The third case has both; the fourth has neither, which can be understood accordingly. This is based on the fourfold classification (*catuṣkoṭi*) in the Vinaya. Not... [text ends].

Distinguishing between light and heavy offenses: The present commentary distinguishes between light and heavy offenses based on the meaning of the established precepts (*śikṣāpada*). Originally, a *pāyattika* offense was incurred for requesting medicine beyond the permitted limit.
However, if one stops [requesting] after four months and the night has ended, it is not a case of requesting medicine; because it is a matter of exceeding the time limit, a *pāyattika* is incurred.

If one stops during the fourth month and while the night is still ongoing, this does not constitute the characteristic of "requesting medicine"; since one should not be requesting at that point, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*. Reflect upon this.
Regarding the phrase "from 'cloud' (yun) to 'forty-eight'": the explanation is as can be understood from the text. Regarding the phrase "from 'many' (duo) to 'therefore' (gu)":

the intent of the regulation is as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "from 'four' (si) to 'offense' (fan)": first, "one is a military array" (jun chen). In the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), it says:

"A long gathering is called an army (*jun*); when ranks face one another, it is called an array (*chen*). The Great Virtuous One said: "An elephant army uses four men; a cavalry army uses eight men; [a chariot army uses]..."
There were sixteen men; the infantry numbered thirty-two. This differs from the present time, when twenty-five men constitute one banner (*dhvaja*) and one hundred men constitute one unit (*gaṇa*).
Regarding the statement that it does not constitute an offense if [the army] consists of four divisions: "Heavenly King" (*devendra*) refers to the Son of Heaven (*cakravartin*).
If one goes out, it constitutes a military formation obstructing [one's] departure.

Regarding the statement "having a reason to go among the troops up to forty-nine [days]," the *Shiming* (Explanation of Names) explains [this at length]. Regarding the statement "from four days up to the point of transgression," [it means as follows].

Regarding the unsurpassed fruits of the śramaṇa—namely, the three fruits beginning with that of the arhat—if one wishes to cause another person to attain these fruits, one may go [to them] for up to two nights.
This means that once the person has earnestly requested and the matter is accomplished, one should depart immediately;

as soon as the task is finished, one should return. If it is not yet complete, one should stay for one night; if it is still not completed, for a second night; and if it is still not finished, until...
The third watch: one must depart before the dawn has appeared. If one does not depart and the dawn appears, an offense is committed.
Regarding the phrase "observing until fifty," this is an explanation of the name [of the rule]. Regarding the phrase "committing four offenses at forty," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If one is staying within a city and bandits come to surround it, they may compel the bhikṣus to all leave the city. Even if many people are seen, one does not intentionally put on [the robes]."
Regarding "offense": the preparatory act (*prayoga*) of consuming it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
As for "drinking alcohol, fifty-one": the *Shiming lidiao* (Explanation of Names and Citation of Extracts) explains [as follows]... Regarding "the third leading to an offense":
first, as for "alcohol," the Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty states there are three names. First, in Sanskrit it is called *surā*, which here means "rice wine."
The second is *miliye*, which here means "alcohol made from roots, stalks, flowers, and fruits. The third is *madhu*, cited as "grape wine. The Venerable Master, citing a commentary, says:

"This is a poisonous water that can cause people to become dazed and intoxicated; it is further associated with all forms of negligence. It is written with the radical for 'water' (*shui*) and the character for 'wine' (*you*).

When the sun enters the hour of *you* (the fifth double-hour), it gradually becomes dark and one can no longer rise up. Regarding the second [category], "without cause," this refers to the allowance in cases of illness.

Regarding the statement that the Vinaya has arrived: alcohol constitutes ten faults. First, it impairs one’s complexion. Second, it diminishes one’s strength. Third, it causes the vision to become unclear. Fourth, it manifests signs of anger and resentment.
Fifth, it destroys the karma of a field of merit and leads to the loss of the means of livelihood. Sixth, it increases various illnesses. Seventh, it promotes strife and litigation.
Eighth, it results in a lack of good reputation. Ninth, it causes wisdom to diminish. Tenth, at the end of life, one falls into the evil realms.
Regarding the passage on "Subduing the Poisonous Dragon with the Fivefold Path and Obtaining Wine": it is said that the Buddha traveled from Śrāvastī to the village of Bhadrayāṇī.

There dwelt a poisonous dragon that constantly sent down great thunder and rain, destroying the crops of the people's fields. A householder was constantly wondering, "Who possesses the power to subdue this poisonous dragon?
Suddenly, he heard that the Buddha, accompanied by twelve hundred disciples, was arriving. He rejoiced with great joy.
He came out to meet him and paid his respects, saying to the Buddha, "I pray that you will subdue this dragon. At that time, Sāgata was behind the Buddha fanning him.
The Buddha turned his head and commanded him, "Go and subdue it. He obeyed the Buddha’s command, paid his respects and took his leave, heading toward the dragon’s palace.
He sat down to one side; the dragon first emitted smoke, and the bhikṣu also emitted smoke. The dragon then raised a firebrand, and the bhikṣu also [raised one].
He raised a torch, and the dragon emitted fire of five colors; the bhikṣu likewise emitted fire of five colors.

Thereupon, he transformed his dragon body to be as small as a chopstick, placed it inside his alms bowl, and brought it to the Buddha. The Buddha commanded that it be sent toward the intermediate spaces between the worlds.
In the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he had finished delivering the thief and soon returned. The householder was greatly delighted and made a vow.
He accepted my invitation, remaining silent and accepting it. This bhikṣu, while still a layman, was fond of drinking alcohol.

He went to the house of an elder and drank a great deal of *kālaja* liquor (black wine). Upon returning, he lay down intoxicated outside the monastery at Śrāvastī, spitting everywhere in disarray, with his robes and bowl strewn about.
[The text continues as follows: ...and so forth, until the gradual prohibition of alcohol; the text should be amended to read "gradually."
The prohibition against drinking alcohol was established. After the Buddha had instituted this rule, [the bhikṣu] did not dare to drink again.

However, due to the force of his past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), if he did not obtain alcohol, all his ailments would flare up and his food and drink would not be digested. Not knowing what to do, he reported this to the Buddha.

The Buddha ordered him to smell the aroma of alcohol; yet even after smelling it, he was not cured. The Buddha then ordered him to boil alcohol into a soup or gruel (*maṇḍa*); still, he was not cured. Finally, the Buddha permitted [the use of alcohol].
He gave him a small amount of wine, and having received it, he was cured. The Buddha said: "Once he has recovered, gradually cease drinking it.

With the exception of those who cause a schism in the Saṃgha, if one calls them 'Teacher of Gods and Humans' while they are intoxicated, no one will believe it. Regarding the statement in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* that [the prohibition] is relaxed:
this applies even to wine made from grasses and trees. Within the Vinaya, there is mention of wine made from pear juice and wine made from jambu fruit.

This includes grape wine and the like. Regarding that which lacks the color, fragrance, and taste of alcohol, the Vinaya establishes four categories: first, that which is alcohol possessing the color, fragrance, and taste of alcohol;
second, that which is alcohol lacking the color and fragrance of alcohol but possessing its taste; third, that which is alcohol lacking the color and fragrance of alcohol but possessing its taste;

and fourth, that which is alcohol lacking the color, fragrance, and taste of alcohol (all four categories constitute a *pārājika* offense, as the rule is established based on the objective conditions). The *Śāstra* states: "That which lacks alcohol..."

Regarding "color, fragrance, and taste," this refers to the fourth phrase, which is contrasted with the preceding three phrases. As for "if it is not liquor, etc.," the Vinaya also contains four phrases:
first, that which is not liquor but possesses the color, fragrance, and taste of liquor; second, that which is not liquor and lacks the color of liquor but possesses its fragrance and taste.

Third, that which is not wine, lacking color and fragrance but possessing flavor. Fourth, that which is not wine, lacking the color, fragrance, and flavor of wine. The *Chao* states: "That which is not wine possesses color, fragrance, and flavor.

Among these four propositions, the first proposition is cited, which subsumes the latter three. According to the text of these four propositions, regarding the four cases of non-wine, it merely says one should not drink;
it does not state that one incurs an offense. Now, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) in both instances. Both are [prohibited].
It is an offense. Therefore, the *Dharmapada* (or *Vinaya* text) states: "In no case is it permissible to drink. Regarding "sweet wine" (*madhu*), the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says:

"Once the fermentation is complete, it begins to turn from raw [grain] into sweetness. Regarding "sour [wine]" (*śukta*), it means the flavor has deteriorated and become sour. Regarding "dregs for medicine" (*kāñjika*; pronounced *jiàn* in the commentary), this refers to the sediment at the bottom of clarified wine.
The note stating that "the offense is not incurred by taking the object" is the interpretation of the ancients; it means that there must first have been an intentional disposition (*abhiprāya*).

This is the Master’s current explanation. When the ancients saw the precept regarding drinking alcohol, they interpreted the three phrases concerning the "perception of the object" (*sañjñā*) within the fivefold classification as all referring to actual alcohol.
Thus, even if a bhikṣu suspects it is not alcohol, or if his mind is deluded by the appearance of it being something other than alcohol, he still commits a *pāyattika* offense.
It is said that there is no offense that does not involve a specific object (*viṣaya*), rather than being discussed solely in terms of the mind. Now, the Master says:

How could there be a wise person who, throughout their entire life, has never even smelled the scent of wine? If one desires to drink wine but mistakenly swallows water, can this be classified as a *thullaccaya* (grave offense)?

Regarding the current Vinaya texts, where a formal grave offense is established based on a state of doubt, misconception, or confusion of mind, this is determined by the prior existence of an intentional disposition (*abhiprāya*) to drink that wine. Or...
When raising the cup, if one instead gives rise to the thought or suspicion that it is not wine, from the perspective of the mind, one should only incur a *duṣkṛta* offense;

however, because there was a prior preparatory intention that secretly coincides [with the act], a *pāyattika* offense is established. If there were no prior intention, and one merely entertains such a thought or suspicion, [the case is different].

"One shall never commit a grave offense" (the above is interpreted according to the *Jieshu*). Those who study the *Xiangzong* school refute the Nanshan tradition, claiming that the precept against alcohol is already clearly defined by its objective basis (*viṣaya*), and that it is now merely a matter of arbitrary speculation to claim there is no manifest action (*vijñapti*) arising from the mind.
One may rely on the *Fobao* (Fa Bao), which states that our own school does not understand this;

one must not follow the view that the alcohol precept arises from the mind rather than being a precept based on an objective basis. Therefore, the author of the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*) cites the following ten [points]...

The proof regarding alcohol establishes the aforementioned principle. As for those cases opened above: if one knows it is not [alcohol] yet drinks it by mistake—such as in the second clause above where there is no perception of it being alcohol—then it is opened and there is no offense.
Furthermore, it must indeed be alcohol; however, if it lacks color, fragrance, or taste, there may be the possibility of error.

Alternatively, it may pertain to the tongue not distinguishing flavors, or the olfactory faculty being impaired, and so forth. This is a clear textual authority that provides such an opening; it is certainly so.

This is not a mere conjecture. As for the statement that it is not a violation according to the Vinaya: "Āka" (pronounced *yízhé*; the *Shuowén* says it is the sprout of rice) is that which can cause rice to ferment.
By using this fermenting agent to make wine, consuming it excessively causes people to become intoxicated; therefore [it is prohibited].
Regarding "playing in the water," the fifty-second [offense]: this is the citation of the title. Regarding "frequently reaching to thoughts":

the regulation of the mind is as stated in the text. Regarding "three... to violations": the enumeration of the conditions can be understood. Regarding "in the Vinaya... to *lā*": [the explanation follows].
As in the text. Regarding the passage beginning with "How one does not commit an offense," it is as in the text.

Regarding the passage from "Tying up at the stable" up to the fifty-third [item], this explains the names and cites the *Chao* (the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā*), etc. Regarding the passage from "The four" up to "offenses," [it is as follows].
The sequence of conditions can be understood. Regarding the statement "from *saṃghāvaśeṣa* down to *duṣkṛta*," this refers to the act of pointing with the finger.
In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, among the ninety rules, there is the precept concerning "pointing with the finger" (*aṅgulipratoda*), which is similar to this.

In its origin story (*nidāna*), because the sixteen groups of monks saw a nun sitting improperly and laughed while pointing at her from a distance with their hands, the rule was established. As for "pointing with the finger" in the context of assigning duties, that refers to the month... [text ends].

The *karmadāna* (officer in charge of affairs) assigns the meals in sequence, pointing with his finger and saying: "So-and-so commits an offense. Regarding the statement "not committing," up to the point where it says "opening [the rule]," it is as in the text.

Regarding the statement "not receiving," up to the fifty-fourth [item], the formal citation (*uddiśya*) is clear. Regarding the statement "five conditions," up to the *pāyattika* (offense), it follows accordingly.
Regarding "that which constitutes the root": among the five categories [of offenses], whichever offense one commits, it is a *pāyattika* (forfeiture) for each instance of transgression;

thus, this applies to every single one of the five categories. As for the phrase "it means 'to reach'": it means that when the root offense violates the admonition, the two offenses are simultaneously established.

Regarding the subsequent establishment of the six groups as general *pāyattikas*: since one does not accept the admonition, the preceding offenses—such as *pārājika* (defeat) or *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting)—are established accordingly.

The six cases, such as that of Laṇḍika and others, all constitute the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for violating a formal admonition (*pratisaṃharaṇa*) only after the preliminary act has been performed. Thus, one should know that for this offense, it is necessary for the preliminary act to be carried out before the offense of violating the admonition is incurred.

If one does not accept the formal admonition during the actual admonition itself, one incurs only a *duṣkṛta*. Question: In the previous case of violating the Saṃgha, the offense was committed immediately upon the conclusion of the admonition, without waiting for the preliminary act to be performed.
Why is this different from the present case, where the offense is incurred only after the preliminary act has been performed? Answer: In the previous case, there was already a Saṃgha [present].

The Dharma may be transgressed; one commits an offense immediately upon the conclusion of the admonition. This refers to the private admonition (*raho-’nuśāsana*). Regarding "transgressing the Dharma without faith":

this means that because one intentionally persists in the aforementioned conduct, one subsequently commits an offense. As for the phrase "not committing an offense until [the other] arrives," this refers to those of a bad character who do not accept admonitions.
They say: "If an ignorant person comes to admonish me, I shall reply: 'You should ask your teacher; once you have learned the method of admonition, then come back and admonish me.'"
"If I [act] contrary to the Dharma, such as when one does not accept admonition, there is no offense whatsoever.

Regarding "from 'fear' up to fifty-five," this refers to the *Cāo* (Excerpts) [and so forth]. Regarding "from 'five conditions' up to *duṣkṛta*," it means that each of the six objects of the senses (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) is explained individually;
that is to say, taking the six objects such as form (*rūpa*), one shows them to others to let them see, and then says, "I..."

Regarding the seeing of evil insects, beasts, and the like, although the text extensively lists the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), the characteristics of fear are not clearly revealed. Now, this commentary cites the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* to explain it. That text states:
"As for 'fear of form' (*rūpa-bhaya*), it refers to such things as cowering in a dark place, flapping the ears, knitting the brows, rolling back the eyes, and protruding the tongue;
even down to making fearful gestures with a single finger and so forth. As for "sound" (*śabda*), it refers to either long-drawn-out sounds or short sounds, and so forth. Even down to making...
Regarding sounds such as those of bells and drums, they cause fear. Regarding odors: some say it is the scent of snakes, armies, or ghosts.
Regarding tastes: one may ask, "What flavor are you eating today? or say, "If you eat this flavor, you will surely die of leprosy or other diseases. Regarding tactile sensations:

one may press down with an extremely heavy object and say, "The wall is collapsing," or cover [the person] with light clothing and say, "Your mouth is falling out," or bring flowers... [and so forth].

Regarding "contact" (*sparśa*): it refers to [the perception of] things such as centipedes and the like. Regarding "phenomena" (*dharma*): it refers to speaking words intended to terrify others, such as saying, "You have urinated and defecated upon living grass;

you shall fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. Regarding "each individual sign appearing": this means that among the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), each respective sign appears.
There is an interpretation which says: two signs appear, namely the bodily sign and the verbal sign. This also refers to the bodily sign of pleasure and the verbal sign. This too...

Regarding the ancients, they merely indicated fear but did not speak of it; now, this [text] possesses both (this interpretation indicates attainment). As for "not questioning the one who fears," the *Jieshu* states:

"To clarify that even the most holy encounter light fear, how much more so those of lower classes; the meaning requires the elimination of the *shu* (commentary). The text clearly shows that the Buddha has no fearful mind;
it merely belongs to the defilements (*saṃyojana*) that cause fear and constitute an offense. Regarding the phrase "not an offense" and so forth:
As in the text.

Regarding the statement "from the half-month to the fifty-sixth," this refers to the *Shiming* (Explanation of Names) and the *Dieliao* (Excerpts). Regarding the statement "the fifth to the offense," it is as in the text.
Regarding the statement "from the *Sifen* (Four-Part Vinaya) to 'no offense,'" it means that the forty-five days following the end of the retreat period begin from the third month.

One day, from the middle of the fourth month until the beginning of the summer, and from the sixteenth day of the fourth month until the middle of the fifth month, constitutes the combined two periods of seventy-five days;
this is according to the explanation of the Western Heaven (India). Now, in the Eastern Land (China), it is extremely late;
thus, the timing may be adjusted. Therefore, the *Mahā-saṃghika-vinaya-śāstra* states: "It should be used according to the early or late seasons of the country. This limit refers to bathing.
Regarding the requirement to wear the *saṃkakṣikā*, various records handed down by tradition identify it as the *saṃghāṭī*. The Venerable Master did not approve of this interpretation.
One must not use a *saṃkakṣikā* for bathing; this is the *nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī*, also called the *śalaka*, which is the same as the skirt currently worn today.
It is not of the same category as thigh-length trousers. Regarding those who are prone to lust, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, there was once a *ra...* [text fragment].
While the bhikṣus of Han were bathing, one bhikṣu entered later and saw that the body of an arhat was fresh, pure, delicate, and soft.
He immediately conceived a lustful mind; before long, his male organ fell away and a female organ appeared. He subsequently abandoned the path and became a layman, fathering a son.
Later, he encountered him again by chance and recognized him at once. Knowing the cause of what had happened, he invited him back to his home and begged for mercy.
Through repentance and with single-minded devotion, he regained his male organ. Thus we know that one must not bathe naked at present.

Regarding the statement "in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, from the lower fascicle": it says that when all the monks enter in succession, Xuán states that based on the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika*, one may use the property of the permanent monastery (sangha) to provide what is required for bathing; this is clearly indicated by the striking of the wooden gong before entering in succession.

Thus, it is known that this is property belonging to the Saṃgha. "The remainder is as in the lower fascicle" refers to the various miscellaneous sections, which extensively clarify the benefits of bathing as well as the methods and so forth.

Regarding the passage from "clouds and dew" to "fifty-seven": this is the explanation of the names as recorded in the *Jiejiao* (云云). Regarding the passage from "four" to "offense": it is as stated in the text.
Regarding the passage from "Wufen" (The Five-Part Vinaya) to "place of birth": "a flame four finger-widths high" refers to the aforementioned conditions.

According to the *Sifen* (The Four-Part Vinaya), it merely states that there is a flame, without specifying its height or brevity; therefore, one adopts the "four fingers" standard from the *Wufen*, at which point an offense occurs (these are also human fingers).

[The measure is] one chi and four cun. "Acting according to the task" means following up by adding fuel or more wood, or roasting the body, boiling things, arranging the previous fire-pile, gathering [embers], and so forth;
all such acts constitute a *thullaccaya* offense. "Spinning the fire into a wheel" means holding such fires in one's hands and spinning them into a circle;

this also constitutes an offense. Regarding "ruined" or "growing" and so forth, these exist according to the application of the principle. If it is on ground that has not been cleared (*ajātakhette*), [the same applies].
This constitutes an offense; therefore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is cited as proof. As the text says, "the Vinaya states there is no offense.

Regarding the phrase "fifty-eight types of concealment," the definition of the name can be understood from the text. Regarding the phrase "three conditions leading to permission," this refers to the commentary.

As for the statement that "the five primary colors are not permitted by the Buddha," this means they are contrary to the Dharma (*adharma*); since their storage and possession are not permitted, one incurs a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*). This applies when [the material] has not yet been dyed.

Although the alms bowl is not a primary requisite, the Buddha permitted its possession and did not prohibit it; therefore, one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense [for failing to maintain it properly]. (Based on the trend of this passage, the reconciliation of the textual points is hereby concluded.)
Regarding the statement "when the Vinaya reaches the *lao*": the commentary states that this refers to one who does not commit the offense of failing to maintain [the robes].

That is to say, it means not committing the offense of being deficient in the maintenance of the robes. Xuan says: if the judicial authorities are urgent and do not permit [the practice], one may wear secular clothing and store away the three robes for a time. One family.
One should not incur the offense of failing to maintain one's robes (this may be explained by citing the *Fǎbǎo* [Dharma Jewel] regarding the purging of monks and nuns; this is also acceptable).

Regarding the statement "From 'True' up to fifty-nine," this is the explanation of the title from the *Nièchāo* [Excerpts], etc. Regarding the statement "From 'Four' up to 'all obtain'," the *Jièběn* [Precept Text] lists five groups of practitioners.
The *Jièshū* [Commentary on the Precepts] states: "The two divisions of the True Dharma and the Two Vehicles do not harmonize; they do not perform [ceremonies] for one another."
Why are the names listed collectively in the precept text? The answer is: it is intended to clarify that the five classes of practitioners all possess the characteristics of transgression;

although there are differences in the gravity of these offenses, the principle of "pure giving" (*śuddha-dāna*) is the same for all. Therefore, their names are listed collectively. As for the ritual of pure giving itself, it pertains specifically to the particular assembly concerned.

Thus, the text explaining the characteristics states: "Now, for the sake of purity, I give this to the Elder as a true act of pure giving. By examining this, one knows that [the term] is restricted solely to the cause.
This is of the same category. There is no offense if one acts while harboring doubt. According to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, this applies mutatis mutandis to all five groups of monastics.

Regarding the statement that "whether one asks or does not ask successively, it is permissible in both cases": this refers to the fact that when performing the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), one is facing an individual; therefore, the object is not handed over to them.
Consequently, when using the object later, it is not necessary to ask the original donor again.

Regarding "up to sixty years": this refers to the *Shiming* (Explanation of Terms), the *Dieliao* (Excerpts from the Text), and so forth. Regarding "the four conditions leading to an offense": as stated in the text. Regarding "good [cloth] up to clothing":

this refers to circumstances such as encountering bandits; the term "etc. includes being burned or swept away by water. That which is first obtained is also called "new": this means it was first obtained from another;
even if its color is not according to the Dharma, it is designated as "new clothing" because it has not been dyed in a discolored hue (*raṅga-vikṛta*). Both [cases] apply.

This constitutes an offense of *thullaccaya*. Regarding the phrase "from four up to 'not seen,'" this refers to bedding, quilts, and so forth, as well as secular clothing; if these are not marked with the *pāṭidesanīya* (or *pariśuddhi*) seal, it is an offense of *dukkaṭa*.
"Light clothing" refers to garments other than the three robes (*tricīvara*); if one keeps such items without having them marked with the seal, it is likewise an offense of *dukkaṭa*.

The note stating "the commentary follows this pattern" means that the present master, based on these two principles of defilement and purity, has followed the explanations of the various schools (*nikāyas*). [End of] Ancient [Commentary].
It was previously stated that the three robes need not be dyed; however, it is now stated that the three robes and the extra robe must both be dyed and further purified by marking (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

If they are not dyed, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense; if they are not purified, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. Regarding the "three types of marking," according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, a bhikṣu and a non-Buddhist practitioner were both robbed of their robes by bandits.
When they were captured by the guards, the guards ordered them to each identify and reclaim their own belongings. Consequently, the non-Buddhist practitioner [was first...]
He came to select [a robe], taking fine garments with him. He reported this matter to the Buddha, who consequently prescribed three types of color: blue, black, and madder-brown.

If one uses any of these individually without authorization, one commits an offense for every instance of wearing it. Furthermore, some say that regarding the "three types," the first refers to the dyeing process itself.
Two dots and three slashes distinguish [the robe] from that of laypeople as well as non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Regarding the statement in the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya-mātṛkā* (Duo lun):
"Luo sha" is here translated as "blood-nature. Furthermore, Sengliang’s commentary on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states:

"Luo sha emerges from the *palaśa* flower; when it emerges, it kills insects, yet it may be used for dyeing. If one applies it [to the robe], it is auspicious; otherwise, this constitutes an offense."
Regarding "falling" (into a fault): these five major colors, according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, are applied without dots.
*Kauśeya* refers to that which is the finest among silks. *Kambala* is translated here as "fine woolen cloth," or alternatively as "fragmented cloth.
There are two kinds of purity for fine garments: first, purity by cutting the threads; second, purity by dotting. What is meant by "cutting" refers to cutting three or five threads.
Because the dye-liquid is coarse, let two types [of robes] be purified for now; however, when they are worn, they must ultimately be dyed. For other robes, add one further method:

that is to say, apart from the two aforementioned fine and soft garments, they must be dyed. Regarding "blue" being covered by a copper vessel with fermented vinegar (*ka-sui*), the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"Blue is of three kinds: first, copper-blue, as in the text; second, 'nurtured blue' (*jōyō-ao*), which is indigo-dye blue."
The third is *śilāpīta* (stone-yellow), which is the same as *kaṅgīpīta* (stone-blue). One does not perform the ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*) by means of the latter two types of yellow.

Regarding "black" (*kṛṣṇa*): the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states it refers to "named mud" (*nāmamṛttikā*) and "unnamed mud. Now, regarding "named mud," this refers to *harītakī*, *bibhītaka*, and *āmalaka*;
when these are placed within an iron vessel, they constitute "named mud. "Unnamed mud" refers to actual soil. Mud is... [text ends]... that is, it is indeed [so].
"Pond mud" and "well mud"—these and all such varieties constitute "mud. As for *mūlāṇa* (wood-lac):

it refers to the juice of the three fruits, such as the *harītakī*, which is placed upon raw iron and ground; this is used for the purpose of purification (*pratyavekṣaṇa*). Bronze and the like are considered "blue-colored";
fruit juices, mud, and so forth are "black-colored"; and *mūlāṇa* is "red-colored. These are the three colors that accord with the Dharma, just as in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Regarding "fruit skin" (*phala-tvac*): the commentary states that it refers to a piece of wood with a vertical grain. Xuan says it resembles the color of the *mùlán* tree found in the Shu region;

since this was translated and revised in the northern lands where four parts [of the Vinaya] were used, it takes the *mùlán* of the Shu region as the standard. It is the color of the fruit of the *mùgǎo* tree.

As for the statement that "in the Five-Part Vinaya (*Pañcavargika*), when performing the purification (*parikarman*), one folds it finely," it is the same here. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "One performs the purification by directing it toward a single corner; if it is a single strip..."
Patches are also made pure (*parikarman*). This applies to all garments, even those with fine pleats (*sūkṣma-puṭa*), which are also made pure.

That is to say, when a new object is fashioned into a garment by means of fine pleats—and since such pleated objects are generally numerous—one need only perform the rite of purification at one corner to remove the "stitches" (*kaṇṭaka*);
it is not necessary to perform it separately for each individual section. Therefore, it is said that "it is likewise."

Regarding the passage from "It is said, 'seizing' up to sixty-one": this refers to the *Shiming* (Explanation of Terms) and the *Diyao* (Excerpts), and so forth. Regarding the passage from "It is said, 'many' up to 'precepts'":
as for the five conditions: first, it is an animal; second, the perception that it is an animal; third, the intention to kill; fourth, the application of means; and fifth, the severing of life.
Regarding the statement "drinking up to sixty-two [insects]," the *Shiming diacao* (Excerpts on Explaining the Names) states [as follows].

Regarding the statement "from the previous [rule] up to 'killing,'" it means that the former precept is a regulation within the category of "limited divisions" (*xiànfēn zhōng zhì*), which requires the actual severing of life. This [present rule], however, is a regulation within the category of "deep prevention" (*shēnfáng zhōng zhì*), established for the sake of protecting the lives of sentient beings.

It is sufficient to know that there are insects; the offense is incurred upon drinking and using [the water], without waiting for their lives to be severed. If death does occur, it is then subsumed under the jurisdiction of the former precept.
Regarding the five conditions for committing an offense: the fourth is drinking and consuming; the fifth is swallowing with each gulp, without waiting for death in the interim.
Regarding the passage from the *Vinaya* concerning the body: it says that there were two bhikṣus living in deep mountains who had never seen the Buddha and desired to go pay their respects to him.
After spring, the heat was intense; they traveled through a vast wilderness where water was scarce and insects were numerous. One of the two...
The Buddha spoke to a certain bhikṣu, saying, "Drink this water; by crossing this vast marsh, you shall behold the Buddha.
A companion replied, "I have received the Buddha’s precepts; how could I violate them? He then did not drink. Because of this, he passed away and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Wearing a crown of a hundred jewels, he came before the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and stood to one side. The Buddha—

He preached the Dharma to them, and they immediately attained the vision of the Truth (*satyadarśana*). Those who had drunk the water containing insects arrived later. The Buddha saw them coming from afar;
he took off his *uttarāsaṅga* robe and revealed his golden body, saying: "You are foolish people! You have drunk as if it were a mere draught.

Regarding the statement that those who arrive after [the meal] may use [leaves], those who wipe with tree leaves should use dried ones; it is not permitted to use fresh ones. [This refers to] the *śarīra*.

Regarding the phrase "not by means of the pure divine eye (*divyacakṣus*)," it means that the Venerable One, using his pure divine eye, saw insects in the air as numerous as the sands along a riverbank, existing everywhere.
He consequently abstained from food for three days. The Buddha, knowing this, spoke to him and ordered him to eat.
