Generally, the prohibition regarding water containing insects applies to what is visible to the physical eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) and what is caught by a water-strainer; it does not apply to the divine eye. Furthermore, there are even more minute insects.
The divine eye does not see it; only the Buddha’s eye sees it, as small as one-tenth of a mote of dust—it is exceedingly subtle.

Regarding the phrase "from a *saṃkhyeya* until its application," this means that one must not grow weary of reciting or cease from observing; this is the colloquial expression used by people of that time.
The phrase "now here it is said: shadow and echo, look at them both together" describes a state of lack of refinement.

Having no other recourse, one feels deep aversion in the heart while the body merely forces itself to endure; hence the expression "aversion to the recitation. It is like a great elephant pulling a bamboo or wooden cart:
if it tips over even once, the instruction is simply this: "Do not go too fast, do not linger too long; you must proceed just as a great elephant turns once."
Recently, [this practice] has been used only when there are no insects; if there are insects, one should strain the water before using it.
One must not say, "Do not harm or kill the insects. The *Śīla-sūtra* states: "If you cannot trust the other person, you should sprinkle the insects yourself.

You must not tell them to sprinkle it or not to kill or harm the insects, for you fear that the other person may hold wrong views, or perhaps they are by nature fond of killing living beings; if they hear the advice 'do not kill,' they might intentionally kill them all the more."

Regarding "not digesting for seven days": since insects undergo a transformation every seven days, one is permitted to leave [the medicine] in water for seven days without it being digested, as there is no offense of taking life.
Regarding "one must not lend vessels or ropes to others": this is because one fears that such acts would be equivalent to instructing another to take life.
One must not announce, "This water contains insects. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

When pouring water into a reservoir, if one sees insects therein, one must not announce to others, "Venerable sir, this water contains insects," thereby causing others to harbor doubts or feel displeasure.

If one is unaware or perceives the water as being free of insects, one may still avoid the offense. However, if one has informed others and they have reached the certain perception that there are insects, [the offense is incurred].

For this reason, I have encouraged him to compose it himself. As for the statement "this reaches the middle," that text, following its discussion of the water-strainer (*parisrāvaṇa*), extensively elucidates the proper methods for using water and so forth.

Regarding the passage from "It is said that the doubt extends to sixty-three" to "The explanation of the names in the *Diyao* (云云)": Regarding the passage from "It is said there are five conditions" to "One is known to be a bhikṣu":
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (*Duolun*) states: "For a bhikṣu who has committed one of the thirteen *antarāyika*-offenses or is insane, [the offense] is merely a *duṣkṛta*.

However, for those undergoing the *parivāsa* of six nights or the four *karmas* of *mānāpya*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. Regarding the phrase "if the person hears and knows": if they have not yet heard or known...
[Regarding] the transgression. An external objection states: "The text of the precepts says that one commits an offense only when another person has been made unhappy for even a brief moment;

why is it that now, upon merely hearing or knowing [of the act], one immediately commits an offense? Is this not contradictory? Answer: It is not the case that one commits an offense based on another person’s unhappiness.

Rather, it is because one possesses the intent to disturb others, desiring to cause the object before them to be unhappy for even a short time. (This is explained according to the *Jieshu*). Thus, the Vinaya says...
"Opening" refers to the six matters of stinginess; this is the general enumeration of the headings. In the first instance, "receiving" is raised as stinginess regarding doubt;

in the second, "following" is raised as stinginess regarding doubt. If it concerns the time of birth, such as saying, "You were not born at such a time," one causes distress by referring to the common secular age.

If it concerns the years, such as saying, "You have not reached such an age," one expresses stinginess regarding the number of years since ordination (the *varṣa*). If it concerns receiving the precepts...
Regarding the statement, "Your age is not yet full": this refers to the affliction caused by a separate assembly within the boundary. Regarding the *karmavācanā*:

if you perform the formal motion (*jñapti*) when receiving [the precepts], the *karmavācanā* is not accomplished; this refers to the seven types of parsimony regarding non-transgression. Regarding the commission of the six classes of offenses (*ṣaḍvarga*):

the statement, "You have committed a *pārājika* offense" up to "a *prāyaścittika* offense," refers generally to parsimony regarding the six classes of offenses. Regarding the commission of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*): the statement, "You... [refers to the same].

Regarding the "gate of what is [permissible]," one commits a *pārājika* offense and is no longer a *bhikṣu*. This distinction concerns specifically the great falsehood (*mahāmṛṣāvāda*) and stinginess (*mātsarya*).

Therefore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a *bhikṣu* is on the verge of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), but the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is not completed, he should snap his fingers and say:
'Venerable sir, your *karmavācanā* has not been accomplished. If he does not speak thus when about to receive and maintain [the precepts], he shall not be permitted [to remain] hereafter."
Regarding doubt and regret: if one uses the words exactly as noted, and the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* permits it, then according to both these two Vinayas, there is no offense of causing distress or doubt.
As for why the Vinaya states there is no transgression: "the fact is indeed so" means that the person actually had such circumstances, yet it was not with a sincere [malicious] intent;
rather, it was with the aim of benefiting them, without any desire to be stingy, and speaking so as to make them understand and return their property.

Regarding "receiving [the precepts] at the original location": this refers to the third and fourth matters in the Vinaya text, both of which require returning to the original location to receive them.

Therefore, the commentary states: "The Buddha ordered them to return to their original locations so that it might be determined whether they obtained the precepts or not, for the reception of the precepts depends upon specific conditions."
The characteristics [of the recipient] are not easily discerned. If there is any doubt regarding the person, one must return to the original place where the precepts were conferred;

only after a detailed examination confirms the encounter may one receive them, so that there will be no confusion hereafter. Question: Since you have already heard the *karmavācanā*, this is merely a case of stealing the Dharma.
"It would then be difficult to recover; how could it be received again? Answer: "Because it was permitted for him to hear [the teaching], it is not theft.

It does not constitute a case of being difficult to recover, and thus it may be received again. As for one whose nature is coarse and who does not understand speech: this refers to a person whose disposition is negligent and arrogant."

If one does not recognize that what was said was improper and attempts to rectify the gravity of the offense, fearing that the words spoken might violate the rules for interacting with others, and then says,
"What you have said violates the Noble Dharma," with the intention of reforming the other person rather than out of a deliberate intent to cause distress and so forth— in all such cases,
there is no offense.
"Clouds covering up to sixty-four" refers to the *Shiming Dier Chao*. "Five conditions up to the appearance of light" is as stated in the text.
Regarding "good up to all *duṣkṛta* offenses": "a hundred thousand together covering" means that a hundred thousand people are collectively aware [of the offense] and simultaneously conceal it;
therefore, each incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. This is not a case of successive concealment. The commentary on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* cited below states: "toward one person."

It is said that there is no offense; therefore, one should know that concealment does not constitute a transgression through successive stages. As for "if the offender is fierce and evil," this refers to those who are violent, coarse, and cruel.
It means that if, by relying on the power of the king, the power of a great minister, or the power of fierce and evil men, it might lead to the cause and condition of losing one's life.

Regarding "corrupting the holy life" (brahmacarya): one who is endowed with the guarding of the sense-faculties (indriya) maintains their own faculties and does not concern themselves with the affairs of others.

Even if another person has committed an offense, if my mind remains hesitant [to report it], this is not called concealing a fault (paticchādana). "Excluding the gross": the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses are the "gross"; to conceal these constitutes a *thullaccaya*.

To conceal other offenses refers to those belonging to the three lower categories; concealing these incurs a *dukkaṭa*. Question: If one conceals a *sthūlātyaya* (saṅghādisesa), what offense is incurred?

The Venerable One said: According to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, concealing two of the *pārājika* offenses incurs a *pratyekadeśanīya-sthūlātyaya*; this is no different from the *sthūlātyaya* for a *pācittiya* offense (this is the explanation according to the Dharma, whereas the *Bhāṣya* [the *Vinayavibhāṣā*] does not include the term "bowl").
Regarding one who conceals their own offenses, the *Śīla-śāstra* states: "If one commits seven [offenses] and conceals seven, one incurs one *sthūlātyaya* for each;

there is one *duṣkṛta* for each, but no *pācittiya*. As for the exclusion of the *bhikṣuṇīs*: this means that if a *bhikṣu* conceals an offense of a *bhikṣuṇī*, he also incurs a *pācittiya*; therefore, it is said that they are excluded.
If a nun conceals a monastic offense, she incurs a *duṣkṛta* (sthūlātyaya). [Question: Since concealing it constitutes an offense, she must certainly confess it.

If she confesses her offense, would this not constitute an act of formal accusation (*codanā*) against a *bhikṣu*, thereby violating the Eight Rules of Respect (*gurudharma*)? [Answer: The Venerable One said: Not so.

She should merely confess within her own assembly and not go before the assembly of *bhikṣus*. This is not called an act of accusation. Consider this. As for "other persons," [it refers to] those below...

The three groups [of practitioners] obtain auspiciousness. Regarding the statement "not committing an offense" up to "opening [the path]," it means that if no one speaks to them about it, the *Vinayavibhaṅga* alone states:
Suppose there is a bhikṣu who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; he stays among the bhikṣus by day and stays where there are no bhikṣus by night.
If he remains where there are no bhikṣus by night and never confesses for the rest of his life, he does not commit the offense of revealing another's sin. If...
Regarding the case of having resolved to speak to someone: it refers to the situation where one has already gone to a secluded place with the intention of speaking.
Alternatively, it may refer to a case where one has just begun to realize the intent and is about to speak when the dawn light appears; therefore, this is opened as being without offense.

Regarding the passage "From 'it is said' to 'sixty-five years old': this is an excerpt from the *Shiming* (Explanation of Terms) [and so forth]. Regarding the passage "From 'it is said' to 'four conditions leading to an offense':
the preceptor commits a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), while the others commit minor offenses. Regarding the passage "From 'it is said' to 'no harm':

the upper scroll concerns the section on receiving the precepts, while the lower scroll concerns the section on *śrāmaṇeras*; both clarify the age of those being ordained, whether they are older or younger. As for 'the spear and the shield':"

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Manyūi-ron) states that those aged sixty and above may not [be ordained], whereas the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi-lü) permits it for those aged seventy and above who are incapable of performing monastic duties;
this constitutes a point of contradiction between the two. Regarding the statement that both positions are compatible and cause no harm:

the intent of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* in prohibiting those aged sixty and above is that they are unable to uphold the precepts due to their weak resolve, whereas the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* permits those aged seventy and above.

Regarding "the receiver": this refers to one whose disposition is resilient and capable of upholding the precepts. If we discuss "capability," both texts agree that it is permitted; if the disposition is inferior, both texts prohibit it.
As for the statement in the Vinaya regarding the *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing): the Vinaya poses five criteria. First, not knowing [the offense] beforehand;
second, accepting the words of another who believes [it]; third, testimony from a bystander; fourth, the word of one's parents; and fifth, frequency.
The womb is the cause. Furthermore, there are three positions: first, calculating the year of conception; second, counting the months of gestation; third, reckoning by the *poṣadha* days.
As for the matter of the parents' testimony, it is simply said: "If the parents do not know, and there is no record of the year of birth, one observes the facial features."
The son of a wealthy and prosperous family may have a large physique despite being young in years; in such cases, one should examine the development of his hands and feet.

If he still does not know [the date], one should ask what king was reigning and what year it was, as well as whether the country was experiencing abundance or scarcity, drought or flooding, and the seasonal conditions of birth and so forth. Regarding the opening of the preceptor’s status and the auspiciousness for others:

once the moisture of the womb has been calculated, there is no doubt that the precepts are obtained; the preceptor is exempt from the formal lifting [of the prohibition], though the assembly of monks lacks the auspicious sign. If one relies on...

Regarding the characteristics of the offense, there are sixteen permutations based on four factors concerning the preceptor (*upādhyāya*)—namely, whether the Sangha knows or does not know [the age], and so forth—which result in different degrees of transgression.
These are: first, knowing; second, asserting; third, doubting; and fourth, not knowing. "Knowing" refers to when the preceptor clearly knows that the candidate has not yet reached the required age.

"Asserting" refers to when one perceives the signs of the candidate as being complete and forms the conviction that they have reached the age, even though they have not yet reached it. "Doubting" refers to remaining in hesitation...
The decision is: "doubtful. To have no understanding at all is called "not knowing. The four mental states of the other monks regarding that preceding object are likewise.
One establishes four propositions by comparing the four mental states of the assembly of monks with the knowledge of the preceptor: first, the preceptor knows and the assembly of monks knows;
second, the preceptor knows and the assembly of monks is certain; third, the preceptor knows and the assembly of monks is doubtful; fourth, the preceptor knows... [and so forth].

If the assembly of monks is unaware [of the offense], the preceptor incurs four *thullaccaya* offenses and the assembly incurs two *dukkaṭa* offenses; in the first and third phrases, the assembly incurs *dukkaṭa*. Next, regarding the four mental states of the assembly toward the preceptor, there are likewise four phrases:

first, the preceptor says the assembly knows [the offense], and so forth. This is explained by analogy [as follows]: it is said that the preceptor is without offense, while the assembly is the same as previously described.

Next, regarding the four mental states of the Saṃgha in relation to the Upādhyāya, there are likewise four permutations. First: the Upādhyāya is doubtful while the Saṃgha knows [the offense], and so forth (for the Upādhyāya, this constitutes four *pārājika* offenses;
for the Saṃgha, it is as before). Next, regarding the four mental states of the Saṃgha in relation to the Upādhyāya, where the Upādhyāya does not know [the offense]:

there are likewise four permutations. First: the Upādhyāya does not know while the Saṃgha knows, and so forth (the Upādhyāya incurs no offense; for the Saṃgha, it is as before). Question: Since the Upādhyāya’s state of doubt is light, why...
Regarding the offense of *thullaccaya* (grave offense): When receiving the precepts with another person, one ought to inquire with care, composure, and thorough discernment before accepting them.

If there is already doubt regarding their integrity, it is improper to accept them; one must not lead others astray. Even if the matter is not certain, yet one harbors a suspicious mind, this also constitutes an offense of *thullaccaya*.
As for the phrase "until resolution": this refers to the consensus of the various schools, namely the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (Wufen lü) and the *Mātṛkā* (Mo jian er lun) distinguish three types of cases regarding the attainment of precepts through sequential ordination;

these are reconciled with the two passages from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Shi ji). Furthermore, the *Caturvargika-vinaya* (Sifen lü) and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Wubian lü) likewise state that if the years and months are not yet complete, one still attains the precepts in all such instances.

Regarding those who examine other calendrical systems (*li*) and mathematical techniques (*shu*): these rely on secular conventions and involve comparative analysis of written texts to verify the *yin-yang*, *lü-lü* (pitch-pipes), and the full range of *zhi-gan* (trigrams and stems).
Therefore, they are called "calendars" (*li*). Because their methods calculate temporal durations with precision, they are termed "techniques" (*shu*).

This refers, for example, to the calendrical systems of six or seven schools in the Tang dynasty. These are now all compared and examined (this concludes according to the interpretations of various masters). Fabao says: "It is capable."
"Kan" (堪) refers to a clan name (*xing*), while "Yu" (餘) is a personal name. In antiquity there was a calculation method known as "Kan-yu" (堪餘);

the present *Chao* (鈔) follows this. Later copyists erroneously transcribed it as "Kanzu" (勘字). As for "comprehensively encompassing and clearly mastering" (*zongkuo minglian*): because one has sought out and exhausted all [details], it is called "comprehensively encompassing";
because nothing subtle is left unexamined, it is called "clearly mastering. Such a passage is pointed to in the *Shoushu* (首疏), hence it is so stated.

This is as stated in the *Great Commentary* (*Dàshù*). Regarding the brief citation of a single phrase from the *Cùtōng*: "To look at the present from the perspective of the past is called 'penetrating' (*tōng*).

This refers to the ancients citing the case of an extremely young novice (*śrāmaṇera*) who was nearly, but not quite, a full year old; they permitted him to receive the precepts by relying on the three types [of ordination] according to the Vinaya, thereby attaining the number of precepts through this dispensation.
Now, the Master cites the case of the most junior śrāmaṇera. According to the three types of exemptions found in the Vinaya, one may obtain the precepts by counting [the days].

Now, citing this single phrase regarding the most junior śrāmaṇera: although the principle is the same in both ancient and modern times, if one allows for the counting according to the three types of exemptions in the Vinaya text, then [the precepts are obtained].

As for the point that the years and months were not yet complete, this is raised below to refute the erroneous interpretation held by some of the ancients, who claimed that one obtains the precepts only when the years and months are not yet full.

Thus, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Regarding the interpretations of the ancients concerning those who receive [the precepts]: in their secular reckoning, both the years and the days and months were deficient."

The *garbha-māsa* (conception month) is not counted as an intercalary month. When the conventional year is complete, but the days and months are not yet full, only then is it opened [for calculation]. The current interpretation merely counts the months of gestation;
once these reach twenty, even if the conventional year is not yet full, it is opened [for ordination], and there is no offense committed. (The above is from the commentary.)
Regarding the phrase "it is said that 'to arrive' means... the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "For now, let us take the case of the smallest possible śrāmaṇera.
On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, his birth year completes twenty; he receives full ordination (*upasampadā*) at dawn. Calculating by actual age, he is only eighteen years and two days old.
He lacks twenty-three months and twenty-eight days before reaching twenty. Therefore, following the ancients, we shall generally cite this as the smallest possible [age]."

"Position. Regarding the opening of the calculation for the year above and the addition of the intercalary year below: "one thus adds the fetal intercalary [days]" and so forth refers to the subsequent calculation after receiving [the precepts].
The Vinaya text contains only three positions; based on this, the ancient masters further added the "frequent large [intercalary month]," thereby forming four positions.

As for the "four positions," they are: first, the five stages within the womb; second, the remainder of the intercalary [days]; third, the frequent [intercalary month]; and fourth, the *bimāsa* (double-month).
Great. Fourth, regarding the *poṣadha* (confession) on all fourteen days: "within the womb" excludes those outside the womb.

According to the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, there are five stages even for those outside the womb (infant, child, middle age, prime, and fifth, senility). As for "within the womb," this means that even being in the womb is not fixed; as the Indian monk Rāhuṇa said:
"A bhikṣu [who has experienced] the suffering of birth and death remained in the womb for six years. Another bhikṣu remained in the womb for sixty years.
Regarding the womb: here in this land, Laozi remained in the womb for eighty years; some say he remained for twelve months, followed by another eight or nine months.
Now, speaking according to the majority of cases, the standard is to remain in the womb for nine months. As the *Sūtra of the Five Kings* says:
In the first week, it is like thin curd; in the second week, like thick curd; in the third week, like congealed butter (*navanīta*);
in the fourth week, like a soft mass of flesh; in the fifth week, like a firm mass of flesh; in the sixth week, the five swellings expand and the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) become complete;
in the seventh week, it becomes a human being. Regarding these five stages, the first four stages each last for seven days.
Only in the fifth stage are there thirty-four [days] remaining of the current seven-day period;

together with the previous thirty-eight seven-day periods—wherein three sevens make twenty-one, totaling two hundred and ten days—and the five six-weeks (seven times eight) which amount to fifty-six days added to the previous two hundred and ten days, it totals two hundred and sixty-six days.
Throughout all these days, the fetus shares the same vital energy as the mother and desires to proceed toward birth.
The Gate. Sharing breath with the mother, he further receives four days (the mother inhales while the child exhales). Together with the preceding period, this totals two hundred and seventy days.
Now, calculating these days into months, one obtains nine months. Within these nine months, four are large months.

Furthermore, subtracting another four months, and adding the two days of birth, along with the previous six days, this constitutes the age of eighteen years, nine months, and six days for a śrāmaṇera.

Regarding the calculation of intercalary months (*māsa-śeṣa*), the methods of calculation used by various schools differ at this stage. For now, we shall calculate according to one school, which is quite elegant and refined.
The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "There are three kinds of days and months: namely, the days and months of the heavens above, the days and months of the human world," and so forth.

Regarding the Yin and Yang and the sun and moon: the former two are indeterminate, while the latter one is determinate. Now, by employing the Yin and Yang and the sun and moon, one determines the days and months of the human realm so as to correspond with the four seasons of Heaven;

therefore, the others are set aside. Furthermore, the *Wenchang Guanguo Shi* (Poem on Observing the State from Wenchang) and the *Nanshan Guijing Yi* (Ceremonial for Returning Reverence at the Southern Mountain) state:
"The celestial body moves to the right, while the sun and moon revolve to the left. They rise at Fusan in the morning and enter [the west] at dusk."
Mong’s Record: Day and night, one travels through the twelve divine stations (*devatā*), each separated by thirty degrees, plus sixteen-sevenths of a degree.
Completing the circuit of the twelve stations totals three hundred and sixty-five degrees and one-quarter of a degree, which constitutes one full revolution of the celestial sphere.
At this point, the sun and moon each return to their original positions. Thus, there are twelve months in a year, and each month consists of thirty days.
There are two divisions: the first day of the month and the last day of the month. On these two days, the daily motion equals the full zodiacal circle, totaling thirty-two *kalās*.
During the twenty-eight intermediate days, because the sun moves more rapidly, it travels only thirty-one and a half *kalās* each day.
Since the first and last days of the month are excluded from the calculation, for each of the twenty-eight intermediate days, there is a surplus of half a *kalā*.
Thus, one month yields fourteen parts; ten months yield one hundred and forty parts. Furthermore, two months yield twenty-eight parts.
Calculated for one year, this totals one hundred and sixty-eight parts. Using thirty-two parts as the measure for one day:
Divide one hundred and sixty [days] by five; there remain eight additional parts. These eight are minor parts (*kṣudrabhāga*), being one of the four such parts.
Thus it is said: "one-fourth of a *caturtha-bhāga*. This means that in one year, five days and eight minor parts are obtained.
Furthermore, in one year there are twelve days; for now, let us approximate this as six major and six minor [parts].
Small. Within six great months, six days are extracted; together with the preceding period, this totals eleven days and eight small fractions.

Now, calculating the total for the previous eighteen years, including the *śrāmaṇera* [period] of the sixth day of the ninth month, there are six intercalary months and an additional twenty-seven days.
Furthermore, one year yields eleven days and eight small fractions. As for these eight small fractions, they are set aside for now.
Treatise: Now, calculating the number of days: in one year, eleven days are produced; in ten years, one hundred and ten days are produced.
Furthermore, in eight years, eighty-eight days are produced; added to the previous total, this makes one hundred and ninety-eight days.
Taking these as days—where thirty days constitute a month—and taking one hundred and eighty days as six months, it is thus established.
Externally, eighteen days remain. Furthermore, as previously mentioned, there are eight small fractions for each year that were not yet discussed;
we shall now calculate based on these future years. Since eight fractions are left over each year, we will now take the four years’ worth of remaining fractions, which amounts to four times eight.
Thus, thirty-two *kalās* constitute one day; eight years constitute two days; twelve years constitute three days; sixteen years constitute four days.
Beyond this, the remaining two years are divided into twenty-eight *kalās*, which form half a day. Adding this to the previous four and a half days makes four and a half days.
Adding these four and a half days to the preceding eighteen days results in twenty-two and a half days.
Furthermore, there were previously nine months and six days within the womb that had not yet been discussed. Now, within those nine months, ninety parts are obtained.
Additionally, four times nine is thirty-six; combined with the previous total, this makes one hundred and twenty-six parts.
Furthermore, from the six days, three parts are obtained, making a total of one hundred and twenty-nine parts. Dividing these by four days results in thirty-four [days].

Two [units] consist of one hundred and twenty *kalās*. Furthermore, two sets of four [units] are equal to eight; together with the previous one hundred and twenty-eight *kalās*, these are consolidated into four days, leaving one *kalā* remaining.
Now, taking these four days and adding them to the previous twenty-two and a half days results in twenty-six and a half days.
Then, by adding the one remaining *kalā* to the preceding half-day to make a full day—this being done so as to strengthen the weak—the total is thus established.
In this calculation, six leap months are determined, with a remainder of twenty-seven days.

Now, taking three of these leap months and adding them to the eighteen years previously calculated, plus the nine remaining months, constitutes one year. There remain three months and twenty-seven days beyond that.
Taking three days from the previous six days and adding them to the twenty-seven days makes one month; together with the preceding months, this completes four months. Still...
Three days remain; this is the year of the śrāmaṇera’s nineteenth year, the third day of the fourth month (transcribed with meticulous detail). Regarding the "three frequent [small months]":

this refers to three months occurring consecutively as large months (for it is certain that [if] three months were consecutive small months, they would not constitute "frequent small" months; if such a case occurs nowadays, it is due to the irregularity of the lunar days).
This means that counting back from the opening of the fourth month of the nineteenth year, there are ten years of one hundred and twenty months, plus nine months and another two sets of nine.

Eighteen [months] make one hundred and eight months; together with the previous two hundred and twenty-eight days, and the additional four odd months, there are a total of two hundred and thirty-two months.
Grouping these into forty-nine months constitutes one chapter. This yields four chapters, with thirty-six months remaining;
fifteen months are still lacking to complete another chapter. Thus, the first chapter begins from the first month.
Upon reaching the sixteenth month, one obtains one *pinda*. Furthermore, from the seventeenth month onward, following the same calculation, one obtains one *pinda* after the sixteenth month.
Again, from the beginning until the seventeenth month, one subsequently obtains one *pinda*.
Thus, one chapter yields three days; four chapters yield twelve days. After thirty-six months, one chapter is not yet complete; [the days] are subtracted.
Taking two days [from each cycle], the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The method of frequent *mahāpavāraṇā* consists of forty-nine months to complete one chapter.
A chapter contains three frequent *mahāpavāraṇās*: the first two are sixteen months each, and the last is seventeen months; each has one frequent *mahāpavāraṇā*.
Thus, from the end of one cycle to the beginning of the next, the preceding period uses one hundred and ninety-six months to form four chapters, with each chapter consisting of three months."
In total, this amounts to twelve days. Adding the thirty-six days outside of that, it approximates two full months, totaling fourteen days.

When added to the previous nineteen days of the śrāmaṇera’s [training], it becomes seventeen days on the third day of the fourth month (this is based on the commentary as the standard; all other records calculate this incorrectly).
Regarding the fourth point, concerning the *poṣadha* on every fourteenth day: this is explained by taking the non-leap year as the basis for one cycle.

In the twelfth month of the year, there are six large months and six small months. From the large months, two days are deducted from each of the bright and dark fortnights, totaling twelve days deducted.
From the small months, one day is deducted from only the bright fortnight, totaling six days deducted. Calculating this for one year, eighteen days are deducted;
for ten years, one hundred and eighty days; for nine years, ninety days; and likewise for eight, seven, and six years.
Two. A total of three hundred and forty-two days. Within the previous four months, another six days were deducted, making a grand total of three hundred and forty-eight days.
Now, twenty-eight days are set aside as one month; three hundred and thirty-six days constitute one year.
With twelve remaining days, together with the previous seventeen, they form twenty-nine days, which are likewise set aside.
Twenty-eight days constitute one month; with one day remaining, would this not be the first day of the fifth month? All of these are "empty years" (*kūn-nen*).

According to the calculation of all [schools] regarding the fourteen-day *poṣadha*, even after completing the four stages of the full-year and the *śrāmaṇera* [stages], there still remains the first day of the fifth month.
The present masters do not hold this view; since this is already an empty year, it is complete.

The former [view] permits [ordination] prior [to the full age]. This is because the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "There is permission to calculate prior to receiving [the precepts], and permission to calculate after receiving [the precepts].

Regarding the calculation after receiving [the precepts], the answer is that the attainment of the precepts arises at the time of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of motion and three proclamations); it is not obtained only by means of the subsequent calculation.

Based on this clarification, since the nominal age (*vṛddha-varṣa*) has already been reached, there is no doubt that one may receive [the precepts]. What harm is there in the prior permission? If that is so, what constitutes the doubt regarding the arising [of the precepts] after receiving them?
Answer: This refers to years and months. For one who has not yet completed both [the required periods], they simply retreat to the rank of a junior *śrāmaṇera* among the former elders;
once the surplus days are subtracted, it is then considered nineteen years. (The above concludes the calculation according to the four ranks of the ancients.)
Regarding the statement, "This refers to the long winter solstice observance (*dīrgha-dīkṣā*)," this establishes the present single phrase.

It definitively refutes the erroneous interpretation of former times, which took the "long" (pronounced *qùshēng*) to refer to the remaining first day of the fifth month following the preceding [period], claiming it was drawn from the position of the *poṣadha* and constituted a month by including the twenty-eight days of the "empty" [lunar cycle].
Now, one must rely on reality, strictly following the common practice: two months are large and three are small, according to the standard rule.
In the *Śīla-ṭīkā*, during the fifth month, five days are returned from the first half-month, and two days are returned from the second half (making seven).

On the first day of the fifth month, these seven days are deducted; one day is used to offset the first day of the fifth month, and the final six days are deducted from the fourth month, resulting in a total of twenty-three days for the fourth month (this is according to the actual calculation). Next, it is reduced and extinguished.
On the first day of the first month of the year [X], he was demoted from his position.
On the twenty-third day of the fourth month, he first deducted one day for the previous occasion and one day for the reception of the precepts. Next, he deducted nineteen years from the fourth month.
Furthermore, from the latter part of the fourth month, he deducted twenty-two days. In the eighth month, after deducting the final twenty-two days, it reached the eighth day of the eighth month.
The day was the eighth of the eighth month of the nineteenth year of the Xū era. Because he harbored doubts regarding the conferral of the precepts, this calculation was opened up.
Neither the Upādhyāya nor the assembly of monks committed the *tīkṣṇa* (transgression); the śrāmaṇera obtained the precepts. This is what is stated in the accounts.

Regarding the calendrical systems of the six or seven schools, from the Emperor’s time down to the Kāiyuán calendar, there were a total of twenty-four schools that elucidated these calendrical methods.
There are also variations involving addition and subtraction. Thus, Li Chunfeng, the Dhyāna Master Yi-xing, the *Dayan*, Liu Xin, the *Zhoubi*, and others have now been excerpted.
As for those who speak of "one school," all records state that they rely on the calculation methods of the Linde era, as briefly described above;

yet [the calculation] still exceeds [the actual date] by five months and one day. Furthermore, there is the *Yiwei* calculation method composed by Wang Bi, which cannot be recounted here again; therefore, it is said "moreover."

Regarding the point that [the Vinaya] does not reiterate [the requirement for full age] (as the *Fǎbǎo* commentary explains: "The *Chāo* follows our own school’s view that this applies to others as well, such as the calculation of years, as has already been analyzed above"), it is stated in the *Jièshū* (Commentary on the Precepts) that various schools do not require one to be of full age to obtain the precepts.

As the *Shūsòng* says: "The *Śāriputra-abhidharma-vinaya* states: 'If one is less than twenty years old, or forgets and is unaware [of one's age], and the Saṃgha asks whether one is of full age, if one answers that one is of full age, one obtains the precepts.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: 'If one is less than [twenty], yet claims to be already twenty and thus obtains the precepts,' and so forth."
The *Dṛṣṭigata-vastu* consists of five parts, each having its introductory text (which is omitted here as it is verbose).

Regarding the passage from "speaking" (*yuan*) up to "sixty-six": this is the explanation of the title and the formal citation (*yúnyù*). Regarding the passage from "five" (*wǔ*) up to "conclusion" (*jié*):

if there are other matters of private purity, these distinguish them from other disputes (*raṇa*), which cannot cause the Saṃgha to fall into ruin. If one's own four types of disputes have already been extinguished, yet one initiates [them] again...

An offense is light because it is rare; however, it is heavy if it incites further disputes due to their frequency. Regarding this precept, if either a monk or a nun incites a dispute against the other, it constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

When the two communities extinguish the dispute according to the Dharma, this refers to extinguishing it through the Dharma and the Vinaya, as taught by the Buddha; recognizing both the "sickness" and the "medicine" is called extinguishing according to the Dharma.

"Knowing" means knowing that the dispute has been extinguished according to the Dharma; if one incites it again after such knowledge, it is a *pāyattika*. If one does not know [it has been extinguished], there is no offense.
It is not an offense. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Observing the action but not observing the thought, it is likewise not an offense to observe.

This means that one who has deeply penetrated the arising and ceasing of the medicine and the illness, yet now gives rise to a pure [thought], does not know how to extinguish it according to the Dharma; thus, they extinguish it in a manner contrary to the Dharma. For this reason, even if they impulsively give rise to [a thought], there is no offense.

Regarding the fourth point, "impulsively giving rise to," according to the three clauses of the Vinaya, all such instances of giving rise to [an offense] constitute a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation). First, if one observes improperly...
Regarding "forming a contemplation" (*chengguan*), the commentary explains: "The monastics do not recognize the essential nature, characteristics, causes, and origins of the four types of disputes.

They hastily use their obscured minds to adjudicate principles; therefore, it is said that they do not contemplate well (contemplation refers to observation; if one contemplates in such a manner, it does not constitute contemplation). Second, they do not understand well."

Regarding "not forming a correct understanding," the Commentary states: "The Daoist and the Monk do not comprehend the meaning of the distinctions between the essential natures and characteristics of the seven medicines;

this is called 'not understanding well' (where 'understanding' means decisive realization; if one forms such an interpretation, it will ultimately be of no benefit because it does not constitute a correct understanding). Regarding "the three types of improper extinction and non-extinction" and "forming [an improper] extinction," the Commentary states:
"The Daoist and the Monk do not recognize the method for eliminating [defilements] through the correspondence of medicine and illness; they judge purity in violation of principle."

Therefore, as for the cessation of unwholesome [states], because it cannot be ultimately extinguished, it is said that "cessation is not accomplished. These all constitute *thullaccaya* (grave offenses).
Regarding the phrase "from 'giving' up to sixty-seven," this is an enumeration of names [and so forth]. Regarding the phrase "from 'six' up to *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing)," [it is explained as follows].
Regarding the "debtor": one who owes a debt but fails to repay it possesses the "atmospheric influence" (*vāyu-gati*) of a thief; this refers to the auspiciousness of a scheduled journey.

As for the statement "evil reaches sixty-eight," the *Shiming Dier Chao* (Explanations of Names and Notes on the Ordination Certificate) explains [this at length]. Regarding the statement "five reaches *thullaccaya*," it refers to declaring that sensual desire does not obstruct the Path.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun) states: "This is an outsider (*tīrthika*). Because his disciples were exceptionally intelligent and sharp, [the Buddha] intended..."

Within the Buddha-dharma, such a person acts with perversion and confusion. Because that person will not long remain in thorough mastery of the Tripiṭaka, they will perversely explain it, seeking to exhaust its wisdom;
their sophistry shall not be able to bring it to completion.
Regarding the phrase "from 'it is said' up to sixty-nine," this refers to the *Shiming* (Explanation of Names) and the *Nieliao* (Citation of Texts), and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "from 'it is said four' up to 'conclusion,'" it concerns those who act in accordance with the same purpose (*samānārthatā*). According to the Vinaya texts, among the requisites provided, there are those pertaining to the Dharma;

that is to say, teaching and training in concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), as well as study, questioning, and reciting the scriptures. These include providing robes, food and drink, bedding, seats, and medicinal supplies—all of these being supplied one by one.

Regarding the *pāyattika* (offense of expiation): The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that even if one has abandoned an evil view, if the *saṃgha* has not yet performed the *karman* of release, it is still a *pāyattika*.

Regarding the phrase "following the enshrinement up to seventy," the commentary explains the name [of the rule] as follows (*et cetera*). Regarding the phrase "the offense occurs upon reaching [the limit]," there are four conditions for the offense:
first, the person being enshrined is a *śrāmaṇera*; second, knowing this; third, staying overnight together with them; and fourth, the offense is incurred by following along with them.

Regarding the phrase "from 'cloud' (yún) to 'seventy-one'": this refers to the *Chao* (Excerpts). Regarding the phrase "from 'five' (wǔ) to 'conclusion' (jié)": it addresses the objection that the previous [rule] regarding not accepting [admonition] during private counsel (*bìngjiàn*) was not yet established.
At the very moment one refuses to accept [admonition], one commits a *duṣkṛta* (light offense); one must necessarily wait for the subsequent formal act.

Only when the preliminary action has been completed does one incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension) according to the six categories of offenses, specifically the *pratideśanīya* (offense of confession) for violating private counsel. Now, since one likewise violates private counsel here, how can you say that the offense is concluded only when the words have finished?

"Thullaccaya. This refers to the offense incurred when one has already committed the act; it is only upon the actual performance that the offense is formally established. Since this admonition serves to prevent the commission of the offense, it is said that "the offense is complete" (this interpretation follows the *Jieshu*).
Regarding the phrase "from ten down to five": the "four matters" refer to the four pārājikas. As for the statement "I do not train," this is why the offense of thullaccaya is established.
Regarding the "five persons who do not explain the Vinaya," although there are various sections below, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (*Shisong lü*) is cited, stating: "First, testing..."
Question: The second is the question of no doubt; the third is the question of not being moved by remorse for an offense; the fourth is the question of not accepting the words;
and the fifth is the concluding question. These do not require an answer; one answers only when the opposite conditions apply.

Regarding the passage from "it is said, 'destruction' up to 'seventy-two'" (*yún huǐ zhì qīshí'èr zhě*): this refers to the *Shìmíng diéchão* (Excerpts on the Explanation of Terms), and so forth. Regarding the passage from "it is said, 'many' up to 'fragmentary'" (*yún duō zhì suì zhě*):

a single verse is a brief teaching for examination. That is, "skillfully guarding" one's body, speech, and words. These "five categories of miscellaneous fragmentary rules" (*wǔpiān zásuì*) refer to the extensive [code].

Because the transgressions are not few in their varieties, they are truly called "miscellaneous fragmentary" due to their great number. Regarding the passage from "it is said, 'five' up to 'abiding'" (*yún wǔ zhì zhù zhě*).
The *Chao* (Commentary) provides a general outline of five points, yet lists the sequence of three conditions: fourth, verbal disparagement; fifth, the completion of the offense.
This is added based on the *Shu* (Sub-commentary). Regarding the phrase "from the *Pañcavargika* to the *Loka-varga*," it means causing others to distance themselves [from the Dharma].

This explains the third point: the intention to cause the extinction of the Dharma. "In accordance with the Sūtras and Vinaya" refers to wherever within the Sūtra texts there are explanations concerning the precepts and discipline, such as in the *Nirvāṇa*.

In texts such as the *Pāṇḍulohitaka-vastu*, even a general reproach (*pātayantika*) is mentioned. If [the *Pratimokṣa*] were merely for general reproaches, what would be the use of this precept? [If one argues:

"A single *pātayantika* occurs when reciting the introductory text (*nidāna*), which is not itself a specific rule; why then is it said that one commits an offense? The answer is: "It is because one explains the meaning of the two hundred and fifty precepts, and so forth.
Furthermore, if one reproaches the introduction, since the introduction already explains the meaning of the two hundred and fifty precepts in their entirety, this constitutes a general reproach.

"Only one offense is committed" refers to the case where violating the *Abhidharma* (*Vibhāṣā*) or the *Sūtra* incurs a light transgression; this is discussed in terms of relative superiority and inferiority.
"Regarding 'not committing' up to 'opening'" is as stated in the text.
"Fearing being raised [as a charge] up to seventy-three" explains the name: the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states that some masters call it "sudden alarm."
Zhang Jie: If one were not paying close attention, why would one say, "I have only now come to know"?

Furthermore, if one is not paying close attention while within another's mind, how could one realize that they have previously heard it? If one were not paying close attention, one should be permitted to hear again. (The above summarizes the ancient interpretation.)
Now the Master raises an objection: "If that were so, it would be a lie and a deception of the Saṃgha; I have only now heard this. [The author] now establishes two names:

at the time of the cause, it is called "not listening attentively" (*na-śrotra-grahaṇa*); at the time of the result, it is called "fearing being accused" (*utkṣepa-śaṅkā*). This is because he previously stated that, in reality, he was not listening attentively.

For this reason, they were unaware. Now that they have begun to know, fearing they might be prosecuted and punished, they first confess their transgressions; this is what was being prevented (and so forth).

Regarding the passage from "The four" to "the conclusion of the offense," it is as the text states. Regarding the passage from "Only" to "those who listen," for the four, three, or two assemblies, it is as in the first sentence.
As the first sentence says: "If one cannot recite one *āgama*, one should recite the five groups of precepts. Now...

If following the sequential order, one should say: "If unable to recite the five groups [of precepts], one should recite four groups, three groups, two groups, or one group, as well as the verses" (the term *zhòng* refers to the *pǐn*;
the five *pǐn* are called the "five groups"). One must not sit in meditation, for fear that the student will not listen with single-minded attention.
Regarding the phrase "as stated in the *Karmavācanā*, up to number seventy-four," this refers to the explanation of the names and the citations from the *Śarīraka* (Commentary) [and so forth].

Regarding the phrase "from four up to the offense," the first point—concerning that which is the property of the Saṃgha—is addressed in both the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, which state that it is "an object given to the present assembly that should be divided," and not an object belonging to the permanent endowment (*sthavira*).
Therefore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "At that time, Dharmapāla’s robe was worn out, and a lay devotee gave many [robes] to the present Saṃgha."

Regarding the distribution of property: when the Saṃgha takes items to reward others, the *Catuṣpariṣat-sūtra* states that if someone gives clothing of high value to the Saṃgha and does not specify it as "for the permanent endowment" (*sthavira*) or "for those currently present" (*pratyutpanna*), this is also not clearly defined. Second, regarding rewarding others collectively:
many say that whenever the Saṃgha is in harmony, whether a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has been performed or not, anyone who rebukes them commits an offense.

Regarding "not giving consent" (na-dattānujñā), the seventy-fifth [rule], the *Jiaochao* (Excerpts) states [as follows]. Regarding "the five [factors] up to the formal conclusion," as for "a monastic matter conducted according to the Dharma," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) says:

"This refers exclusively to cases concerning the settlement of the four types of disputes (*catur-vivāda-mūla*); failing to give consent constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. For other monastic matters, it is merely a *dukkaṭa*.

This is because if the four disputes are not extinguished, there is the possibility of a schism in the Saṃgha. Regarding "both feet having crossed the threshold": if one intends to [perform an action] through such means...

To depart—whether with one foot already outside the door—is in all cases auspicious. As for the statement in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* that [departing] constitutes a *duṣkṛta*, it refers to those cases where three *karmans* (formal procedures)—namely, the *jñapti*, the *jñapti-dvitīya*, or the *jñapti-caturtha*—are to be performed, yet one departs from under the roof before the procedure is completed; in such instances, each departure constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"For however many times one departs, there is a *sthūlātyaya* for each; and for every time one departs and then returns and departs again, the offense is established according to the number of departures. Now, our Master [interprets] this based on...

Regarding this matter: when one intends to enter the Saṃgha but departs before having spoken, or when one wishes to leave the assembly for reasons such as [avoiding] the loss of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, there are two conditions.

First, it concerns the teaching of the Dharma and the Vinaya; second, it concerns the performance of the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation), up to and including the *parivāsa-karman* (act of probation).

If one has a reason to depart, one must announce one's intention and grant one's consent (*chanda*). Regarding the teaching of the Dharma and the Vinaya, if one is to announce it, one must do so; if one does not announce it, [there is a fault].

"Regarding 'one who bypasses the intermediate [seat] and stops to engage in other speech': this refers to when one has listened to another person receive and recite the scriptures, and then departs to engage in other conversation;
if one does not inform [the teacher], there is no offense. Regarding 'if a śrāmaṇera is in the midst [of the group], if he also rises, it is auspicious': the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:"

If the Saṃgha has not performed a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to settle a matter, a *śrāmaṇera* may participate in a private adjudication; if a *bhikṣu* rises [to leave], he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This does not mean that a *śrāmaṇera* who leaves arbitrarily incurs a *duṣkṛta*; it refers to the *bhikṣu*. As for the phrase "the Vinaya allows it," it is as stated in the text.
Regarding "the phrase 'up to seventy-six' (etc.)": it refers to the four conditions leading to the formal act of binding (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*).
Regarding "the phrase 'mostly [resulting in] a *duṣkṛta* offense'": it is as stated in the text.

From "The Cloud Screen" up to the seventy-seventh [item] (as detailed above). Regarding the passage from "The Five Conditions" up to "the speaker": concerning "one who commits an offense upon merely hearing," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:
"If one hears these words but has not yet spoken them to the other person, it is a *thullaccaya* (offense of wrong-doing); however, the offense is committed immediately upon hearing.

If one waits until they have actually spoken them to the other, it would fall under the category of the precept against divisive speech (*paisunya*). If this is so, why does the text of the *Jieshu* state: 'If one hears these words and speaks them to that person'?"
[Upāli] asked: "This refers to the listener’s mind hearing this matter of purification; it is intentional in that one addresses it to them.

It does not mean that an offense is committed at the moment one goes there to speak. Question: "For what reason, regarding double-tongued speech (*paiśunya*), must one first address it to the other party for the offense to be incurred?

Why is the offense established as soon as it is heard? Answer: "In the former case, there was no dispute yet; the dispute arose only upon the speaking. Therefore, the offense was established at the time of speaking. In the present case,"

There was already a prior dispute; how could one wait for what was said later? Therefore, one commits an offense as soon as one hears it. Regarding the passage in the Vinaya concerning "reaching the *lao*":
the *Śāriputra-vinaya* states that if two bhikṣus are present—one inside the hall and one outside—and the bhikṣu outside wishes to enter, he should snap his fingers or move his foot to make a sound.
If the bhikṣu inside the hall hears a human voice and remains silent without speaking, the incoming bhikṣu must retreat. If he nevertheless speaks...
"Regarding 'not ceasing': this refers to entering [the state of] non-offense. "Regarding 'not reaching the exemption': as stated in the text.

"Regarding 'striking out of anger up to seventy-eight [blows]': (as elaborated in the text). "Regarding 'four [cases] constituting an offense': as stated in the text. "Regarding 'according to the Vinaya, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing)':

because for one who has already received the precepts, even if they strike someone with a heavy blow, it constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation); however, if it concerns the thirteen difficulties (*trayodaśa-antarāyika-dharma*), [it is different]."
Regarding those who originally received [the precepts] but failed to obtain them: striking [them] constitutes only a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is similar to tying up a handful of sand;
each grain corresponds to a single bean in the calculation of the offense incurred. It is not determined by the number of people involved.

As for the phrase "in the Vinaya, etc.," it refers to passages in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other Vinaya texts. In that treatise, while discussing offerings, it is explained that making offerings to both the true Buddha and the transformation Buddha yields limitless merit.
If one destroys either a true Buddha or a manifested (nirmāṇa) Buddha with an evil mind, one incurs the same offense.

If that is so, why is it that killing a manifested person does not constitute an offense within the Vinaya? One may cite the *Shuochao* (Commentary), which explains: "The precepts established in the Vinaya are for the sake of worldly affairs, and so forth."
"Provisional designation" refers to the provisional establishment of names such as "human" or "beast" upon the basis of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

Regarding these humans and beasts, the gravity of the precepts established based on worldly censure or respect concerns the amount of offense incurred in this life, without regard for the amount of offense incurred in future lives; this is explained in terms of karmic offenses.
The phrase "such as whipping oxen or sheep" correctly explains the preceding text, clarifying the intent regarding the gravity of the karma of the transgression.
Regarding the passage beginning with "If one strikes... up to "seventy-nine" (and so forth): an offense is complete when four conditions are met:

first, a *bhikṣu*; second, a mind of anger; third, the intentional act; and fourth, the raising of the hand, at which point the offense is incurred. The full text is abbreviated here; it is now listed according to the commentary (*śāstra*).

Regarding the phrase "the previous [passage] up to the *pāyattika*": the former refers to the section on limitations, where the offense is incurred only when the blow actually lands; this [latter] refers to the section on deep prohibitions, where the offense is incurred upon the mere raising of the hand.

If one merely intends to strike, one must determine the specific characteristics of the offense. If the original intent was to strike but one does not actually lash out, one commits only a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing);
this is the preliminary preparation for striking. If the mind is set on lashing out, yet at the moment of the motion one does not strike, this constitutes the preparation for lashing out;

by merely intending it, one commits the root offense. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "The group of six monks used the side of their palms as an instrument of force; because they intended [to strike] others, it is so called."
Regarding "as for striking": if one raises a hand toward [another], one commits an offense according to the number of persons involved in the situation.
Regarding "from 'unfounded' to eighty": this refers to the *Shiming* (Explanation of Names) and the *Dieliao* (Excerpts from the Vinaya), etc. Regarding "from 'briefly' to 'distinct'":
this points to the second precept on unfounded slander (*anuvāda*), including the eight conditions for its commission, and so forth. Regarding "as in that [text]": [it refers to the aforementioned].
Regarding "entering by force up to eighty-one" (and so forth). Regarding "four cases up to an offense": first, a *kṣatriya* king;

according to the fourfold formula of the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, if one enters who is a king but not a *kṣatriya*, there is no offense. Second, one who is a king and a *kṣatriya*, but has not undergone the consecration (*abhiṣeka*);
entering here also does not constitute an offense. Third, one who is a king, a *kṣatriya*, and has been consecrated, yet possesses no kingdom...
Taking possession of a portion of land is not an offense (in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, these three phrases are all auspicious). Fourth:

if one is a king, a Kṣatriya, who has been consecrated (*abhiṣikta*) and possesses a portion of territory, [taking it] is a *thullaccaya* (the *Caturvargika* is likewise). As for what is called "consecration," the text of the *Caturvargika-prātimokṣa* states that it is the pouring of water upon the head;
this is the ritual for assuming office. The Vinaya says: take the right horn of a white ox and fill it with the waters of the four great oceans.

Together with all the seeds [of the royal lineage], these were placed upon a golden palanquin. The minor kings were made to lift it, while the king and his chief consort remained together upon the palanquin.
A Brahmin then performed the consecration by pouring water over their heads, thereby establishing him as king; thus he is called one of the Kṣatriya royal caste.
If those of the Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes are likewise established through such a consecration by pouring water over their heads, they too [become kings].
He is named a Kṣatriya of the consecrated lineage (*abhiṣeka*). "Washing the seed with water" takes the sense of moistening and causing it to sprout.
"The right channel for nourishing the myriad people" takes the sense of auspiciousness. As for the passage in the Vinaya concerning "reaching the *la*," it is as the text states.

Regarding the phrase "if one seizes [them], up to eighty-two," this refers to the *Shiming nieliao* (云云). Regarding the phrase "this... to the words," the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (多論) provides a clear explanation.
According to that treatise: "If one seizes gold, silver, and the other seven treasures, as well as vessels made of precious materials, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense."

If one receives or speaks of a pure jewel, it is all an offense (*pācittiya*). Now, this is cited in order to refute the former interpretation. Regarding the reason for not using the old terminology, the *Daoshu* states:
"This is called the precept against seizing lost property. If one seizes what is not lost, one commits an offense of equal gravity."
Now it is said that this is not so. Although one may have received precious objects as gifts, once the prohibitions have been established, merely taking hold of them constitutes an offense;

what need is there to discuss whether they were given as gifts or not? Regarding the statement "only when all conditions are met is there an offense," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) sets forth four conditions:

first, the object must be a precious item; second, it must not be an ornamental article belonging to a stūpa; third, it must not be for any other purpose; and fourth, taking hold of it constitutes an offense of possession. It is based on these four factors that the offense is established.
This may be accepted. The commentary states that it is not appropriate to permit [the handling of treasures], as this constitutes the initial condition for opening [the allowance] (reflect on this).

Regarding "heavy treasures" and so forth, this differs from the ancient *Shoushu* (Commentary by Shou), which says: "The first refers to lost treasures. As for "applying to both oneself and others," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) asks:

"The Buddha prohibited the grasping of precious objects; since it is improper to grasp them oneself, how can it be that causing another to do so also constitutes an offense? The answer is: "If one examines whether it is contrary to the Dharma, for both oneself and others..."
The same offense applies. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If one causes another to do it, one also commits the offense. There must be exceptions;

for instance, there is no offense when one holds [the items] oneself, or when they are decorative implements—meaning various ornaments made of copper, iron, lead, tin, white brass, and other precious materials. Regarding 'not staying or lodging':
if one is not in these two places, it constitutes an offense. As for the exception regarding staying in these two places, it refers to staying in a *saṃghārāma* (monastery) or a *vīhāra* (dwelling)."

Regarding Śakrā’s mother entering Jetavana and seeing the Buddha, she cast off her necklace; as for "opening" and "the place of lodging," "opening" refers to entrusting it to a craftsman, and "place" refers to holding gold.
Regarding the four types of theft without intention: if there is a thieving mind, one commits a *pārājika* offense when the object is grasped and moved away;

this is not what I am referring to here. As for the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* stating "until releasing": one must not release it later, nor may one leave it with a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle property).

Regarding "afterwards": when releasing [the weapon] while holding it, a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) should be in front; when first releasing it, the monk should be in front, which constitutes assistance.
If one first holds it and subsequently releases it, this is merely holding it oneself and does not constitute assistance.

Regarding the phrase "many cases leading to a *pācittiya* offense": excluding spears (*kunta*) and javelins (*śakti*). According to the treatises, both spears and javelins are *thullaccaya* offenses; therefore, they are excluded here. Regarding the passage from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:
"Fallen" refers to that which is not a monastery (*ārāma*) nor a lodging; all such places are called "other locations.

As for the phrase "from the *Saṃghika* up to those who have stayed for two or three years," this indicates that no one has been there for a long time. When someone comes to take these objects, they are considered ownerless property (*asvāmika-vastu*), even though they possess their own inherent names.

"Since it has been long abandoned and is without an owner; 'advancing or retreating as mentioned above' refers to what was clearly explained in the section on the precept against stealing regarding the discovery of hidden treasure (nidhi).
Alternatively, some point to the section on 'keeping precious objects' [in the *Abhidharmakośa*], saying that the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* refers to such things."
The "Giver of Solitude" (Anāthapiṇḍada) was the elder Sudatta; because he delighted in providing for those who were alone and destitute, he was thus given this title.

When he wished to purchase Prince Jeta’s grove, he spread gold over it, but when it was not yet complete, he reflected: "From which treasury shall I take enough gold to finish this? He then took from a hidden treasure (nidhi).
Since even Sudatta, who was one who had attained the second fruit [of the path], took such wealth, we know that it does not belong to the king. If...
"Belonging to the King": at that time, it would likewise not be permissible to take [the property]. The rest is as stated in the text.
Regarding the statement "Non-seasonal [food] up to eighty-three," this is the commentary on the title of the *Chao* (Excerpts) [and so forth].

Regarding the statement "Five conditions up to the conclusion," the note refers to the *śramaṇera* (pure attendant) within the monastery. There is much confusion regarding this; some say it is because it is not a village. Now, the note...

[This refers to] departing. Regarding the statement that according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* it is "not permitted," the *Caturvargika-vinaya* states that once the sun has passed its zenith, it is called "improper time" (*akāla*).
Regarding the phrase "there being no bhikṣus," the wording appears inverted; logically, it should read "if there are no bhikṣus. If one sees [them] on the road, one should inform them.

Furthermore, regarding "if there are none," it means if one sees nuns or the other three assemblies, one should inform them. Furthermore, regarding "if there are none," it means after having already formed the intention [to depart], now...

The commentary states that this refers to "emerging. Regarding the text on "restraining food": although one may eat according to the treatise, if one finishes early and leaves, it constitutes an act performed at an improper time (*akālacaryā*).
As for the phrase "informing the elders," this is the formal presentation of the speech. There are two reasons why such notification is required:

first, to avoid obstructing the monastic community's legal procedures (*saṃghadharma*), for there might be a fear that a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) will be performed without knowing where [the person] has gone, thereby causing distress to the monks; second, it is intended for the sake of the person in question.

"One does not have the freedom to enter the homes of laypeople. Regarding "turning to the left and right," this indicates a sign of not encountering [the person] directly, as both enter the village together.

As for "binding the five parts" and so forth, if one passes through a secular area from within a village or settlement and must go to a lodging place by sunset, such that it constitutes one of the eight difficulties (aṣṭāvaraṇa) and so on, and one does not inform [the preceptor] or make a formal selection—this refers to selecting the person who is being addressed.

"He is a bhikṣu. The commentary explains this itself, saying: "This refers to one who has undergone the formal announcement (*jñapti*), shares the same precepts, observes correct conduct, and maintains the monastic deportment with the *saṃghāṭī* robe and other requisites.
Such a person may be formally announced; others who do not know the Dharma may not be so announced, hence it is said they are 'inappropriate.
Regarding the phrase 'the Vinaya reaches the aforementioned,' it is as stated in the text."

Regarding the statement "exceeding the measure up to eighty-four [inches]," the *Shiming niéchāo* (Explanation of Names from the Nièchāo) provides the commentary (*yúnyún*). Regarding the statement "from five [inches] up to the offense," concerning "the beds of the two types of Saṃgha as well as one's own":

the *Nièchāo* follows the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, stating that the offense occurs at the limit of the Saṃgha’s use. The *Jièshū* (Commentary on the Precepts), however, refers only to one's own boundary bed;
thus, it establishes the offense according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Regarding the statement "originally... up to eight fingers," "not cutting [the excess] constitutes the offense": this...
This means that at the time of the original action, when intending to cut it into shape, there is no offense; however, if one does not cut it, an offense is incurred.
If the intention was originally not to cut it into shape, an offense is incurred as soon as it is cut and completed. Regarding "one chi and three cun plus a quarter":
Bao says that one *zhou* chi and two cun is equivalent to one *tang* chi, and three cun and six fen is equivalent to three *tang* cun. Furthermore, there is the *zhou*...
"Four parts" (sì fēn): here, the character is *qiáng* (strong), which encompasses the four parts. Reflect on this; if it appears as *ruò* (weak) in certain commentaries (*chāo*), it is an error.
Furthermore, the claim that there are "four parts and five parts" is incorrect. The "four parts" above (with the level tone) refers to a measurement of one chi or more;
the "five parts" below are to be understood as the name of the Vinaya itself. Regarding "falling for each sitting": if one completes a single sitting...

First, it is a downfall because one possesses a share [in the offense]. If it is another's bed or seat, it is a *dubbhāsita* (wrong speech) because it is not one's own share; however, one simply should not sit upon it, for this is an improper bed.
Regarding "the water-tube, the foot-stand, the burial, etc.," the intent is that the enemy will quickly rot and decay.

While our own school (*nikāya*) explains this from the perspective of the path of action (*karmapatha*), the *Mahīśāsaka* text explains it from the perspective of usage (*paribhoga*). Why is the measurement not specified? Answer: It is used in various countries.
The Dharma does not conform to worldly sentiments, nor is it merely fixed by the Buddha alone; by using this constant measure, one will never deviate from the truth.
Regarding the measurement taken from the human body: it is based on doubling the human unit, which results in a bed-leg height of eight *cun* above the ground.

As for the division into four equal parts, the *Shisong-lü shu* (Commentary on the Ten Recitations Vinaya) provides this interpretation: by calculating four times eight as thirty-two, it results in three *chi*.
Two *cun*. Now, taking two [units] of eight *cun* as the legs: the third eight *cun* enters the socket (*kaṭaka*), and the fourth eight *cun* is cut off; it is used again to support the leg.
According to this, one can verify that the upper part is moist while the lower part is dry; this allows for the use of a human finger [as a measure].

Regarding "reducing by four years for those who sit together": this means to reduce or decrease. When four people look at one another, if they are eligible to reduce their age by four years, they may sit together. If they are full [of years], [they must not].

Five. This refers to the rank of an ācārya; it is not permissible to sit together [with one of lower rank]. A bed or chair [for such a person] shall not exceed eight finger-widths [in height], as stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* regarding non-offenses. As the text says: "There is no offense."
Regarding the passage from "yun dou" (云兜) to "eighty-five": this is the explanation of the names as recorded in the *Niediao* (釋名牒鈔). Regarding the passage from "yun wu" (云五) to "hui" (悔):
"pu tai" (蒱臺) refers to the *puhua* (蒱華) plant of the winter months. As for "first distinguishing and then repenting," it means that one must first distinguish this matting before giving it away;
only then may one repent for the transgression.
Regarding the passage from "As for bones" to "eighty-six," the *Shìmíngdiéchāo* (釋名牒鈔) explains it as follows (*etc.*).

Regarding the passage from "As for the five conditions" to "discard," since it states "the same as above," one should simply modify the "offense of *dū*," etc., as follows: first, bone, ivory, or horn; second, a case for needles; third, for oneself;
fourth, doing it oneself or employing another; fifth, the completion of the act constitutes an offense. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because of desire," it must first...

One should break through the offense of regret. As for returning it to the owner who does not accept it: one should hold the intention to act as such because there is no use in returning it to an owner who does not accept it.

If the non-accepting owner becomes distressed, one should indicate, "This was made for someone else; I am now returning it to him. Since he is already an unrighteous monk (*adharma-bhikṣu*), [one should act accordingly].
Furthermore, because it is not used, it is set aside as a case of "determination through exclusion" (*thāpanīya*). An external objection states: "This offense arises from the acquisition of wealth;

why is it not included among the thirty [Nissaggiya Pācittiyas]? The answer is: "Because it is a minor matter, it is not included. If that is so, then wild silk (*vāla*) is also a minor object, and its destruction is likewise the same;
why is it included among the thirty? The answer is: although that [wild silk] is already destroyed, it can still be used for applications such as ointments; therefore, it is not [included].
The same. Regarding the statement that "according to the Vinaya, one commits no offense in all cases," concerning the *máo-zàn* (a type of prong) at the head of the *khakkhara* (monk’s staff):
various records state that this tiered structure is marked upon the head of the staff; its construction follows these specifications (based on this, it is entirely one *chi* in height).

The Venerable Master says: Tripiṭaka Master Yijing explains that the *khakkhara* consists of three parts in total: the upper part is metal (*śīla*), the middle part is wood, and the lower [part is...]

[The parts] are divided; sometimes the teeth, bones, horns, and so forth are not fixed. What is now called the *biao* (handle) is simply the very top end, just like the *zuan* (top-piece) of a staff here [in China], with no difference.
Regarding the "umbrella canopy" (*sang zizi*): *sang* refers to making this canopy to ward off wind and rain;

*zi* refers to the decorative ornaments beneath the canopy. The *biāo* at the head of the *dou* (the central ring) [pǐ shāo fǎn; the *Shuowén* says it is the ornament below a sword hilt]. This refers to the canopy.

Below is the *doubu* (the bowl). This is the decorative fitting for this bowl. "Wrapping around the *dou*" refers to the ornamental band that encircles the mouth of the *dou* (this follows the interpretations of various scholars).
