[If] the mouth [acts alone], there is no completion of either observance or transgression, because of the absence of volition (*citta*). Therefore, one should know that body and speech are the instruments for creating good and evil;

they require the assistance of the mind to bring them to completion. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Body and speech are the instruments for creating wholesome and unwholesome karma; they are not the essence of goodness itself."

Xuán says: This refers to the mind that is capable of upholding or violating conduct as being the act of upholding or violating. Since the four types of conduct constitute the substance of karma through their formation, they are not analogous to a solitary mind;
thus, one knows that it is still matter and mind together that constitute the substance. For now, we have singled out the basis for the completion of karma.

Therefore, it is concise. Next, the scriptural evidence is cited. Regarding the phrase "Therefore... to understanding," this refers to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, which states: "These three types of karma are all merely mind.
Apart from mind, there is no volition (*cetanā*) and no karma of body or speech. This means that the proof for the three karmas is that they all take mind as their essence. Now, regarding the body...

The mouth cannot initiate action on its own; it all depends upon the mind. First, one perceives an external object, and subsequently, the volitional mind (*cetanā*) arises, moving the body to perform a prior act;
only then can karma be established. The karma of speech is likewise so, for because it arises in dependence upon the mind, its essence is not separate from the mind.
Therefore, know that the three types of karma cannot be self-generated; they must arise through the mind. As the treatise says: "If there is no mind, there is no killing."

It establishes bodily karma (*kāyakarman*) and the absence of mental false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*), while not establishing verbal karma (*vākkarman*) and so forth. This statement refutes many schools who claim that apart from the mind there is no volition (*cetanā*).
They assert that when the mind-king (*cittarāja*) arises, there is a separate mental factor of volition that arises simultaneously with it.

Now, [the text] states that the mind-king and its mental factors (*caitta*) arise sequentially; apart from the mind, there is no separate volition whatsoever. This refutes those who maintain that there is no bodily or verbal karma.
This is the view of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). They reckon that the two karmas of body and speech do not depend upon the mind, but arise solely from external objects.

What the Buddha’s teachings state—that everything arises from the mind—is precisely this meaning; as the *Abhidharmakośa* says: "The various wonderful objects of the world are not true desire," and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the Vinaya and other texts," this cites the introductory text of the Vinaya, which states: "Now, in wishing to perform good or evil, one must fully possess the three [karmas]."
When planting karmic seeds, one should carefully examine the intention. Whatever action is performed, it is always first known by the mind;

only afterwards is it spoken by the mouth or executed by the body. This constitutes the fulfillment of the three types of karma. If one observes with thorough discernment, and if that intention within the mental ground is patient, then no [unwholesome] thought arises, and there is no karma of body or speech.
Therefore, know that all [karma] has the mind as its essence. The term "etc. implies inclusion of other texts, such as the Rāhula-sūtra.

When this was said, Śāriputra and Rāhula were on their alms-round. At that time, a frivolous brāhmaṇa, harboring malice, placed sand and gravel into Rāhula’s bowl and struck him on the head, breaking it and causing blood to flow down his face.
Śāriputra said to Rāhula, "You should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness. As Rāhula washed the blood by the water, he spoke this verse: "I myself..."
While I am out begging for alms, you have needlessly disturbed me. My pain lasts but a moment; how can it compare to your long-term suffering?
This refers to patience on the level of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), which further establishes that the essence [of patience] is the mind. As for the subsequent explanation, Xuán says:

"As in the 'Section on Superiority and Inferiority' below, one distinguishes lightness and heaviness based on the three periods of the mind; and in the section on 'Expedient Means Leading to the Fruit,' one distinguishes them based on the movement of body and speech."
This is explained in the section on the formation of karma through volition (*cetanā*).

Regarding the second point concerning that which is maintained: as for the phrase "reaching two," the former [case] was based on the capacity to maintain [the precept], taking the mind as its essence;

in the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), a single moment of mind alone does not constitute an offense. It is necessary to encounter an object (*viṣaya*) before the karma is formally established. I do not yet understand upon what basis this is determined with respect to the object.

Because there are [factors] that accord with and those that oppose [the precepts], it is necessary to rely on what is upheld in order to distinguish their essential nature and characteristics. In the commentary, the phrase "upholding until clarity" refers to the two types of upholding and violating, namely, abstention (*saṃvara*) and performance (*kriyā*).
Regarding the "two teachings," these refer to prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) and permission (*anujñā*). If one does not rely upon these teachings, the four modes of conduct are difficult to clarify.
One upholds [the precepts] by relying on the teachings; the mind acts as the agent, while the teachings serve as the object. Furthermore, it may be asked:

"Since all objects of transgression are included within what is upheld, why are there only two types of teachings? The answer is: although the objects encountered are numerous, they do not exceed these two teachings, which encompass them entirely.
When the mind accords with the two teachings, one achieves upholding; when it violates the two teachings, one incurs transgression. For now, I shall briefly explain the Great Teachings.
The details are provided in the subsequent text.
The statement that "the formulated teachings (zhìjiào) are of two kinds" cites their number. The phrase "namely, formulation and prohibition" is the explanation of the text.

The phrase "from one up to offenses" clarifies the formulation. Thus, the *Jieshu* states: "Restricting all those who have left the household life so that they may cultivate what is wholesome is called..."

"Fabrication" refers to the three robes, the alms bowl, and the textual teachings of the Tripiṭaka. It causes one to cultivate all wholesome matters and wholesome dharmas. Within these texts, there are also two aspects of observance and transgression:
first, regarding the fabrication of robes, bowls, and so forth, one must act in accordance with the teachings; to do so is "observance through action" (*kriyā-śīla*), which is free from fault.

To refrain from doing so is "transgression through non-action" (*akriyā-vyatikrama*). Regarding the second point up to "contrary to": it refers to prohibitions against evils such as sexual misconduct and theft.

To cause [an action] not to be performed is, when one follows the teaching by ceasing [the action], termed "maintaining through cessation" (*zhi-chi*). To act in violation of the teaching is termed "committing an offense through performance" (*zuo-fan*). This is no different from what was stated previously; thus, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) says:

"Prohibiting all those who have left the household life so that any evil is severed is called 'cessation and restraint' (*zhi-zhen*). Second, regarding the "teaching on permissions" (*ting-jiao*), there are two parts:

the heading and the explanation. As for the phrase "permitting until [reaching] an offense": this differs from the section on prohibitions (*zhi-men*). Whereas in the previous case of cessation and restraint, if one performs [the prohibited act], there is [an offense].

[This is] contrary. To engage in making [the image] would immediately constitute an offense. However, in this present context of the "gate of permission" (*kṣama-mukha*), there is no fault whether one makes it or does not make it.

If one makes it, it is for those of middling or inferior faculties (*madhyamādhama-indriya*) who accord with the gate of permission; if one does not make it, it is explained in reference to those of superior faculties (*uttama-indriya*).

Generally speaking, there is no fault in either case. Yet, if one restricts the scope specifically to those of middling and inferior faculties, even within the gate of permission, it is not without [a specific purpose].

Regarding these faults: for instance, one must properly receive and maintain the one hundred and one articles of clothing; furthermore, regarding extra robes and dwellings, one must comply with the teachings.

Only if the robes are in accordance with the Dharma can they be subject to the ritual of *śuddhika* (purity); only if the dwelling is in accordance with the Dharma can it be requested [and the permission to build it granted].

If there are transgressions concerning the material, or obstacles and difficulties such as exceeding the prescribed dimensions, the request will not be fulfilled (this refers to the prohibition). Therefore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "In this matter..."

The Dharma also permits its construction. Since there must be materials for the dwelling, it is necessary in principle to apply the ritual procedure (*adhikāra*); therefore, its construction is permitted.

If there are obstacles or difficulties, or if the materials for the garment exceed the prescribed measure, it is improper to apply the ritual procedure; therefore, its cessation is permitted. (The above is from the commentary. The above concerns materials for a dwelling that accord with the Dharma.

To apply the *anujñā* (authorization) rite is *kriyā-dhāraṇa* (active observance). To refrain from applying the *anujñā* rite constitutes *sthiti-āpatti* (passive violation). Regarding the property of a room that requires the *anujñā* rite, to refrain from applying it is *sthiti-dhāraṇa* (passive observance);

if one violates the instruction and proceeds with the construction, it constitutes *kriyā-āpatti* (active violation). In the *Xuánjì*, there is another distinct interpretation, which need not be detailed here (*et cetera*).

Next, the necessity of their mutual requirement is distinguished. The text has three parts: the inquiry, the explanation, and the conclusion. Regarding the phrase "Why [is it] necessary": this means that what was previously distinguished as the substance of that which is upheld is the teaching;
since the teaching possesses a restrictive substance, the present inquiry asks: why employ these two? Regarding the phrase "If [it is] so... until 'exertion'": [the text proceeds as follows].

The correct explanation requires the intent of two teachings. Regarding those of middling and inferior capacities who are excluded [from the aforementioned path], it is determined that they must hear the teaching.

While practitioners of the aforementioned type may sustain their bodies and cultivate the Path merely by begging for food, wearing rag-robes, and sitting under trees, this [teaching] now directs those of middling and inferior faculties.

Those who are equal to the superior person (uttamapudgala)—who do not eat the food of the Saṃgha, do not wear robes offered by donors, and do not dwell in monastic quarters—may find their strength insufficient and be unable to enter the Path.

This would cause them to lose heart and retreat, like the heavenly Subhūti, who, after long enjoying celestial pleasures, realized the fruit of the Path upon staying for but one night in a chamber of the seven treasures. If, however, one were to [restrain them] from dwelling under trees or in cemeteries...

There is no way for one to realize the fruit in a single night; it is necessary to listen to the teachings. For those who act with superior pride and seek [realization], it is necessary to establish and regulate the teachings.
If one were to establish only the practice of listening, it would cause those of superior capacity to become equal to those of middling and inferior capacity;

thus, the teaching would not accord with their faculties, and they would instead become indolent and fail to diligently seek penetration, like the cases of Garbha-kāśyapa and others. Therefore, it is necessary to establish regulated teachings to guide them. It is said:

Therefore, that which is ultimately sufficient must integrate the intent of both types of teaching. First, the prohibitive teaching (*prātimokṣa*) must be established to gather those of superior faculties;

next, the door of permission (*anujñā*) must be instituted to encompass those of middling and inferior faculties. In this way, all who come will be fully included. This differs from the five heterodox paths, which merely prohibit and thus fail to provide a comprehensive system for gathering living beings.
The second section, "Distinguishing the Scope of the Two Teachings through Their Mutual Inclusion," consists of two parts: first, the general heading; second, the explanation according to the stages.

Regarding the initial statement, "Now, distinguishing the scope of the inclusion of phenomena within the two teachings," the Master [Wonhyo] says: "The *Shoushu* (Initial Commentary) does not contain this heading;

this is my current general heading formulated in accordance with ancient traditions. The general meaning is that, regarding the phenomena of the two teachings as categorized by the four practices, they are directed toward—

Among the four modes of conduct (*caturvidha-caryā*), how many modes encompass the matters (*vastu*)? Furthermore, how many modes encompass both the matters and the dharmas? There are cases where only the matters are included and the dharmas are not;

this is termed "partial" (*pradeśa*) because it does not extend universally to the dharmas. If the matters were to pervade all four modes of conduct, one would not speak of the "partiality of encompassing matters. Next, following the ancient tradition to clarify the boundaries:

the statement that "abstaining from what is prohibited and performing what is required" (*śīla-vṛtti-karaṇa-āpatti*) refers exclusively to the matters within the two teachings—that is, the prohibitions and prescriptions—will now be explained.

The two practices of "abiding-in-observance" (*zhi-chí*) and "committing-transgression" (*zuò-fàn*) are distinguished by way of their objective basis (*shì*) within the context of the two types of teaching (*jiào*). "Only" (*wéi*) means exclusively;

it refers to cases where there is only an objective basis but no formal rule (*fǎ*). For now, let us distinguish "abiding-in-observance" in relation to the two teachings. First, regarding the distinction of "abiding-in-observance" in relation to the prohibition of evil deeds:

one should say that within abiding-in-observance, under the prohibitive teaching (*zhì-jìào*), one prohibits specific deeds, such as the third [offense] of sexual misconduct and the fourth [offense] of theft, which accord with the teaching.

Abstaining from faults constitutes the observance of restraint (*śīla-dhāraṇa*) (the first layer). Second is the performance of prescribed acts (*kṛtya-karaṇa*). For example, regarding the substance and dimensions of the robe and alms bowl, one performs them in accordance with the Dharma by following the teachings and remaining free from what is contrary to the Dharma;

thus, the observance of restraint is established. It should be understood that within the observance of restraint, the performance of prescribed acts under the rules of prohibition (*pratiṣedha-śikṣāpada*)—namely, the substance and dimensions of the robe and alms bowl being in accord with the teachings and the abstention from faults—constitutes the observance of restraint (the second layer). Next, one brings this observance of restraint into [the category of]...

Within the context of "abiding by the precepts through listening" (*śīla-śravaṇa*), this is distinguished from the case of robes for an unlawful dwelling. One should state: within "abiding by the precepts," and within "listening," one listens to the performance of the ritual act.
Regarding long robes and dwellings, following the teaching and remaining free from transgressions constitutes "abiding by the precepts" (the three layers).

Next, taking the commission of an offense and reversing it [to the position of non-transgression], one likewise obtains the three layers, as extensively described previously (thus forming six layers of matters). Therefore, it is said that "abiding by the precepts" and "committing an offense" correspond only to the two teachings.
The middle matter is clarified by this. Regarding the statement "acting as the ultimate seed": the previous two lines spoke only of attaining the matter (*vastu*);

these current two lines, however, state that it penetrates universally into the phenomena (*dharma*). First, taking "active maintenance" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*) and "prescriptive teaching" (*vidhi-śāsana*) as a pair for analysis:

one should say that within active maintenance and within prescriptive teaching, one performs the matter. When this is clearly manifest in the mind, it constitutes the fulfillment of training in accordance with the teaching; thus, it is established.

[The category of] *dhāraṇa-kāraṇa* (the act of maintaining). For example, regarding the substance and measure of a robe or alms bowl, which constitute the first layer (*ekāvacara*). Next, regarding the method of composition (*kriyā-vidhi*) in contrast to this: one should say, "Within *dhāraṇa-kāraṇa*, within the prescriptive teaching (*prajñapti-śāsana*), the method of composition.

One acts in accordance with the teaching, thereby accomplishing *dhāraṇa-kāraṇa*. For example, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedures) and the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, etc., constitute the second layer (*dvayāvacara*).

Next, regarding the person who listens to the teaching in contrast to this: one should say, "Within *dhāraṇa-kāraṇa*, within listening to the teaching (*śruta-śāsana*), [one performs] the act of listening to the composition. This is the study.

Conformity with the teaching constitutes both the act of performing (*kṛta-kriyā*) and the act of maintaining (*dhṛta-kriyā*). This refers specifically to the long robe and the dwelling (the threefold [requirements]). Next, regarding the procedure for listening according to the gate of the teaching, one should say:

"Within the acts of performing and maintaining, this is the procedure for listening within the teaching; it conforms to the side of the teaching and constitutes both the act of performing and the act of maintaining," which is the formal authorization (*anujñā*).

The pure dharmas (śukladharma) are fourfold. This is the gate of "active observance" (*kṛtadhāraṇa*) contrasted with "listening" (*śravaṇa*). Having already encompassed the four grave matters of the *vastu-dharma*, one next applies the cessation of transgressions (*virati-āpatti*);

when inverted, these likewise constitute four grave categories (and so forth). Taken together in detail, they total eight. Therefore, it is said that "active observance" and "cessation of transgression" universally correspond to the two types of teaching:

*dharma* and *vastu*. (In the case of "cessation of observance" and "active transgression," there are six grave matters and no *dharma*; in the case of "active observance" and "cessation of transgression," both *vastu* and *dharma* are universally subsumed, totaling eight grave categories. 4.

The practice of the *duìjì* (counter-measures) comprises fourteen categories of dharmas as their boundaries. The above concludes the explanation by the ancient masters regarding the boundaries of upholding and violating.

Next is the investigation and explanation of the reasons why [certain acts] are included or excluded. This section has two parts: first, the inquiry; second, the explanation. Regarding the statement that the preceding [categories] do not encompass the dharmas:

this refers to the two practices of "abstaining from what is maintained" (*zhǐchí*) and "acting in violation" (*zuòfàn*), which exist prior to "maintaining through action" (*zuòchí*) and "abstaining from violation" (*zhǐfàn*). These are now restated here to be analyzed.

Because they do not understand the reason for this, they raise this inquiry. Regarding the statement that "the Dharma is known only through progressive cultivation" and so forth, the intention of the ancient masters is as follows:

Generally speaking, what is called "Dharma" refers entirely to the dharmas of progressive cultivation, study, and practice; therefore, it exists within the stage of active observance (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*).
Since the observance of restraint (*vārya-dhāraṇa*) is not progressive cultivation, how could there be "Dharma" therein? If this is the case, one must distinguish these dharmas and exclude them.
This is subsumed within the practice of "active observance and passive transgression. Active engagement constitutes observance, while passive withdrawal constitutes transgression.

If this is so, since the phenomena (*dharma*) have already been excluded, why are the objective events (*vastu*) not also eliminated? The answer is: objective events merely avoid faults through self-restraint; therefore, they can be clearly elucidated. As the ancients said:
Deeds such as sexual misconduct, theft, and killing, as well as unlawful robes, alms bowls, and dwellings, are all unwholesome matters; therefore, one need not cultivate them.

By merely refraining from transgressions and not committing them, one achieves cessation and maintains restraint. Within these two modes of conduct—refraining and abstaining—one naturally encompasses [all training].

Thus it is said: "Matters are simply avoided, and one naturally gathers [the precepts] within oneself. "Therefore, clarity is attained" concludes the preceding section, meaning that it is by way of avoidance [that this is achieved].

Because it exceeds the limit, one may take the matter and apply it within the context of "abstaining from what is prohibited" (*zhi-chi*) to clarify "committing an offense" (*zuò-fàn*). If one studies the matters of sexual misconduct and theft, this causes them to be fully understood;

furthermore, as these belong to the dharma of active practice (*jiao-xing-fa*), they constitute "active observance" (*zuò-chí*). Conversely, if one abstains from studying and understanding them, this further constitutes "passive violation" (*zhǐ-fàn*). (Reflect on this.)

The above explanations from the *Shō* (Commentary) all serve to establish the interpretations of the ancients; they are not yet refined. They fail to encompass the entirety of the objects [of discipline] and do not fully establish the general meaning (*sōgi*).
Take, for instance, the chapter on "Following the Characteristics" (*Zuishō*), which is titled "Distinguishing Holding and Violating.

Since it includes evil dharmas such as matchmaking, coarse speech, and the two types of slander, how could it be that there are no evil dharmas within what is now called the "general meaning"? If one does not understand this, the five [categories of] heterodoxy...

Regarding the seven *fei* (non-prohibitions), in which category are they subsumed? Therefore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "As established above, regarding the 'cessation and maintenance' (*zhichi*), it pertains only to matters (*shi*) and does not extend to dharmas (*fa*).
For instance, the five *ye* (deviations) and seven *fei* are not the true Dharma; if one were to engage in them, there would necessarily be a violation, and thus they must be restricted by cessation.

Since these dharmas and matters are no different from [the prohibitions against] killing and stealing, for what reason are they not included under cessation? As the ancient interpretation of cessation held only..."
Regarding the matter of *śīla* (precepts), there is a discrepancy in meaning. We do not follow that [view] here; we do not distinguish between the specific acts (*vastu*).

When the Noble One prohibits an action, it applies universally to both observance and violation. Below, these are categorized by rank, yet there is no difference in their essential nature. (The above is from the Commentary.

If one follows this statement, then among the four types of conduct, regardless of the specific act, whatever the Noble One prohibits constitutes both observance and violation. Thus, we know that according to the two preceding types of conduct from ancient times...

To not include the unwholesome dharmas within the "Middle" [category] is utterly contrary to principle. Now that this error has been recognized, we shall follow the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) and add the five *yāna* and seven *abrahmacarya* dharmas.

First, regarding the *prativedha-dhāraṇī* (observance) in contrast to the *prajñapti-dvāra* (prescriptive gate), the method of prohibition should be termed: "The method of prohibition within the prescriptive teachings of the *prativedha-dhāraṇī*.

The five *yāna* dharmas constitute one grave offense (*guru-dharma*). Next, regarding the composition [of the text], it should be stated: "Within the *prativedha-dhāraṇī*, under the prescriptive teachings..."
The method for the middle [category] of performance (*kṛti*). Departing from the seven non-transgressions (the second *dvi-guṇa*). Next, regarding the gate of listening:

one should say, "In the middle of cessation-and-maintenance (*saṃvara-dhāraṇa*), within the middle of listening to the teaching, the method of listening is performed. Regarding the rules for rooms and robes, departing from the seven non-transgressions (the third *tri-guṇa*).

These three methods above are to be mastered clearly within the mind; by following the teaching and avoiding faults, one achieves cessation-and-maintenance. Since cessation-and-maintenance is thus established in three stages, the transgression of performance (*kṛti-āpatti*) follows.

These also consist of three [categories], thus forming six. By adding these six layers of dharmas to the two preceding rows of the ancients—which did not encompass the dharma—since they now do encompass the dharma, the matters and the dharmas are discussed in conjunction, resulting in twelve layers. These are coarser than the latter two rows.

The eightfold method of affairs becomes twentyfold. These twenty stages are clear and can be studied; however, if one knows that subsequent delusions and illusions arise in mutual succession, they become unstudyable.

Reversing this also results in twenty stages. Are these not forty stages in total? Is it not the case that these have been entirely transformed into the current master’s system of affairs and their respective limits?
Question: Regarding the four practices of the ancients, two of the practices possess the Dharma, while two lack the Dharma.

When viewed from the perspective of their mutual non-communication, they may be described as having "delimitations" (*pradeśa*). Now, since the Master’s Dharma encompasses all four practices and his activities pervade all four practices, why can he also be called one who possesses "delimitations"?

The Ācārya Jingshui explained: "The Master’s difficulty lies in the fact that while his Dharma and activities pervade the four practices, when viewed from the perspective of their mutual non-communication, they are likewise termed 'delimitations.
This is like the Dharma and activity of *zhi-chi* (maintaining through cessation), which is not [the same as] *bu-zuo-chi* (maintaining through non-action)."

Regarding the *shifa* (matters and dharmas): other cases should be understood by analogy with this. Question: Since ancient times, it has been held that the two practices of "abiding in restraint" (*zhichi*) and "committing an offense" (*zuofan*) do not apply to the *fa* (dharmas).

Now that the Master has added them [to the dharmas], why does the text of the *Chao* (the *Nanshan Shu*) not simply add them as well? Furthermore, why does it still follow the ancient restriction to only the *shi* (matters)?

Answer: There are two explanations. First, Xuán says: The *Chao* was written to guide beginners. If it were to apply the *fa* universally within the practice of abiding in restraint, there is a fear that...

Excessive [attachment to] other wholesome dharmas causes all diligent cultivation to be neglected; furthermore, this has followed ancient precedent and was not established [by us]. Within the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), regarding both observance and transgression, the four practices are universally applicable.

As for the two interpretations based on the school’s records (*zongji*), it is said: "This is intended to preserve the 'ailments' of the ancient masters and to reveal that the characteristics of observance and transgression are superficial."

Both interpretations have their own logic; one may choose between them according to one's inclination. Question: Why does this section only speak of "delimitations" (*pramāṇa*) and not yet name the "substantial essence" (*svabhāva*)?
Master Jing-shui replied: This text consists merely of three omissions. First, it has not yet distinguished the two teachings—this is the first omission.

Second, it has not yet distinguished the four types of practice—this is the second omission. Third, it has not yet distinguished what is to be learned from what is not to be learned—this is the third omission. It is for these reasons that it is merely named [as such].

Regarding the delimitation of the phenomena of affairs (*dharmas*), their essential substance (*tattva*) has not yet been extracted; it is only within the "Three Extensive [Sections]" below that their substance is finally established.

As for the claim in various commentaries that this section "discerns the substance," I fear it contradicts the intent of the text. Furthermore, to simply designate the objective realm of the forty phrases of affairs as the "substance" (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) is truly untenable.

Those of wisdom, I pray, will reflect deeply upon this. Moreover, [the text says] *xuan*... (Note: The final character *xuan* appears to be an incomplete or fragmentary reference to the title *Xuanzan* [Profound Praise] or a similar term.)
In the *Ji* (Commentary), this is explained in detail. The *Fazheng pojie shu* (Exposition on the Correct Breaking of Precepts) fears prolixity and thus is not recorded here;
it says as follows (*et cetera*). Second, regarding the detailed exposition of the essential characteristics (*tǐzhuàng*), it states:

"With respect to the preceding 'cessation and maintenance' (*zhǐchí*) in relation to the two teachings, 'with respect to the preceding' refers to taking up one line from the 'cessation and maintenance' section within the brief analysis of the boundaries (*fēnzhì*) mentioned previously. This is the exposition of the essential characteristics in relation to the two.

The dharma of the teachings serves as the object. When accomplished through a clear and enlightened mind, it constitutes the essence of the "restraint and maintenance" (*śīla*) that can be learned. When accomplished through a deluded and ignorant mind, it does not constitute the essence of the "restraint and maintenance" that can be learned.
Question: Why is the essence extensively presented in this section? Answer: Because it possesses three kinds of extensiveness, it is logically appropriate to present the essence.

The commentary already divides the two types of teaching; this is the first extensiveness. Furthermore, it divides the four modes of conduct; this is the second extensiveness. It has already been divided...

"Those that may be practiced and those that may not be practiced" constitutes the three broad categories; this immediately follows and clarifies the three concise categories mentioned in the preceding text, which is why they were not previously combined.

Regarding the statement that "within the section on prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*), there are two matters," this means that having already extracted the single practice of "abiding in restraint" (*śīla*) from the preceding section, one now establishes the essential nature (*svabhāva*) by correlating it with the objects (*vastu*), phenomena (*dharma*), and spheres (*viṣaya*) of the two types of teachings.
For now, we shall first clarify this in relation to the teaching of prohibitions; within the section on prohibitions itself, it is divided into two.

They are distinct. The first refers to matters that can be learned; the second refers to matters that cannot be learned. Regarding the phrase "first" and so forth, it precisely sets forth the essence of what can be learned within the gates of *zhi* (stopping) and *chi* (maintaining), as well as the prohibitions.
To explain this passage, one must first distinguish between the two perspectives of the ancient and the modern.

According to the various masters of antiquity, within the gate of *zhi-chi*, they first clarified what cannot be learned, and subsequently clarified what can be learned. Therefore, the opening commentary states: "The first is not..."
There are two types of matters that may be practiced as if they were permissible. First, regarding the perception of a human being as a non-human being.

Second, regarding the perception of an object such as a robe or alms bowl as having a certain substance or quantity [when it does not]. (The above is from the Commentary. This refers to the opinion of the ancient masters: "Acts such as stealing are evil deeds;

one must not train with a clear, conscious intent to kill a human being while perceiving them as a non-human being, or to steal property belonging to another while perceiving it as ownerless. This is a definitive [rule].
It is not "not to be learned. There is nothing that cannot be learned. If it concerns virtuous matters such as robes and alms bowls, one must certainly cultivate them through practice;
there is nothing among these that cannot be learned. Now, the Master does not distinguish between good and evil; first, one must learn to know them, which is termed "that which can be learned.

If, later, when encountering objects, deluded thoughts arise and one commits a transgression despite the Sage’s prohibitions, this is termed "that which cannot be learned. Therefore, the phrase "not to be learned" is placed [in contrast] to "that which can be learned."
The former cannot be learned by looking toward the latter; the distinction in meaning is also different. The general purport from ancient times to the present is as such. Question:

What is the difference between this "that which can be learned" and "that which cannot be learned" and the "that which can be learned" and "that which cannot be learned" within the context of the successive stages (*kalāpa*)? Answer: Although the names are the same, the meanings are entirely different.
This refers to the roots of the four practices, whereas that refers to the branches and twigs. This should be understood. Next, to explain the text of the *Chao*: it says "can be learned."

Regarding "training in the prohibitions": after having received the precepts, one must train; this is called "that which is to be learned. That which is not permitted to be committed is called a "prohibition.
As for "sexual misconduct involving three objects": these are (1) humans, (2) non-humans, and (3) animals. In principle, all six destinies (*ṣadgati*) are indeed objects of transgression.
The reason only three are mentioned here is stated in the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā): "In clarifying the conditions according to the Vinaya, only three are spoken of."

Because the forms of the two realms of humans and animals are manifest and easy to recognize, whereas those of devas, asuras, pretas, and hell-beings are hidden and difficult to discern, these four are combined into one;

thus, there is no one who does not receive a share. As for the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), they differ from those of the human race, and are therefore collectively termed "non-humans" (*amanuṣya*). Regarding the four types of property owners whose goods are stolen:
first, the property of the Triple Gem; second, humans; third, non-humans; and fourth, animals. Question: Why is sexual misconduct referred to as "pervasion" (*sambheda*), while theft is not?

This is called "dividing. The answer is that there are three types of objects regarding which it is not difficult [to commit an offense]. Because one commits a *pārājika* offense equally against all of them, they are termed "common" (*sādhāraṇa*).

Regarding theft, the offenses vary in their degree of gravity depending on the four types of owners; therefore, it is said to be "divided. The term "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes all matters of prohibition. Alternatively, it may also include the five types of wrong livelihood (*pañca-mithyājīva*).
If one discusses the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of these acts, they are defined in relation to the mind that maintains virtuous conduct when confronted with sexual misconduct, theft, and so forth.

Regarding the objective sphere (*vastu-viṣaya*): to refrain from performing [an act] is to depart from its extreme; to comply with the teaching of restraint constitutes the essence of *śīla-dhāraṇa* (maintaining through restraint).

Within the preceding objective sphere, that which is designated is called a "characteristic mark" (*nimitta*). (One should say: within the maintenance through restraint (*śīla-dhāraṇa*) and the prohibitive teaching (*pratiṣedha-śāsana*), the refraining from the three types of theft and the four types of sexual misconduct—this constitutes one grave offense.

In distinguishing between dual maintenance and dual violation based on the cause, regarding acts such as sexual misconduct and theft, if explained in terms of the application of the mind, there are instances of both dual maintenance and dual violation.

If one considers the observance of prohibitions in accordance with the teachings, it constitutes *śīla* (observance) through restraint; if one considers the application of antidotes, it constitutes *śīla* through active practice. If discussed in terms of the teachings themselves:

to refrain from and not commit acts such as sexual misconduct or theft is to be in accord with the teachings and thus constitutes *śīla* through restraint (*virati-śīla*); to engage in them and thereby violate the precepts constitutes an offense through action (*kriyā-āpatti*).

This refers to the case where only one aspect is present, forming a "single" or "isolated" observance. Now, this exposition of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) specifically concerns the essential nature of the single observance and the single offense. [End of] excerpted text.

At this point, it is logically appropriate to present the *dharmas* [of training]. One should say that these are the *dharmas* of restraint that ought to be studied, such as the five types of misconduct (*pañca-kuśīla*) and so forth.

They have not been mentioned here because, for the sake of guiding beginners, there is a fear that they might be confused with wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), thereby hindering their progress in cultivation.

Alternatively, it may be to show that the characteristics of observance and violation (*dhāraṇa-vilopa-lakṣaṇa*) have been superficial in the past. Although this is the case in the text of the *Śāstra*, we shall now clarify it in accordance with the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts). Thus, the *Śāstra* says: "Second..."
Such a person may study the Dharma of restraint (*saṃvara*). For instance, the five heterodoxies and seven non-practices are in essence contrary to the holy teachings;

their common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) are clearly understood, and thus one must not rely upon them for practice. Therefore, they are called "restraint" (*śamatha*). (The above is from the commentary. Now, to specifically identify their nature:

regarding these five heterodox practices, after having received the precepts, one ought by principle to understand the essentials and distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox. Just as the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*) were established by the Buddha, one may rely upon and practice them. As for the five heterodoxies...

It is not a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). It cannot be relied upon for application. One should give rise to a mind of wholesome conduct and restrain [the transgression], thereby following the teaching with the mind to perfect the essential substance of the method of "restraint-maintenance" (*saṃvara-ādhāra-dharma*). Within that dharma, there is that which marks it out, called its "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*). (One should say:

among the methods of restraint-maintenance, those that are prohibitive teachings—such as the five types of wrong livelihood—are included here, along with the two preceding categories. Therefore, next, the matters of "prescriptive acts" (*vidhi-karman*) are distinguished. As for the phrase "from the second to... and so forth, this is the principle.
In truth, one should say there are two types [of things]: those that can be manufactured through study, such as the three robes and the alms bowl.
These three robes and the alms bowl are the insignia of the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; they are not possessed by any non-Buddhists.

After receiving the precepts, one must necessarily possess and maintain them until the final relinquishment at death, and it is not permitted to be separated from them overnight. Because the Buddha personally established these, they are called "manufactured."

Regarding the substance and dimensions of the robe and bowl: the robe and bowl are made of fine, tightly woven silk or cotton cloth. If they are thin, coarse, or light and translucent, they do not constitute the proper substance.
As for the dimensions of the robe: three cubits in width and five cubits in length is the standard measure. Alternatively, it may be equal in size to the Buddha’s robe, though this is not permitted;
furthermore, the colors should be contracted [to the prescribed ones]. The *Chao* text is brief on this point. Blue, black, and madder-brown are the colors that accord with the Dharma.

The five primary colors of the cardinal directions are not [permissible]. As for the substance of the bowl, it consists of two types: clay and iron; copper, stone, hemp, and linen are not the proper substances.
Regarding the capacity of the bowl, the superior is three *dō* (pecks) and the inferior is one and a half *dō*; if it exceeds or falls short of these, it is not the proper measure.
Regarding the color of the bowl, the color of a peacock’s throat is [permissible]; anything other than that is not. The term "etc. includes other manufactured items.

For example, regarding items such as sitting mats or water filters, as soon as one has received full ordination (*upasampadā*), one must learn them from a teacher; these are called "things to be learned.

If one intends to construct or create something, one first ceases what is improper. By following the mind’s compliance with the prohibitive teachings, the essence of "cessation through observance" (*virati-dhāraṇa*) is established.

Within the preceding object, that which is manifested is called a "characteristic mark" (*nimitta*). (One should say: among the prohibitive teachings within cessation through observance, the matters of construction refer to the substance, dimensions, and so forth of robes and alms bowls.)

(These constitute the three layers). The *Xiaochao* (Explanatory Notes) concludes. Question: These three robes and the alms bowl are fashioned in accordance with the teachings; thus, they constitute "active observance" (*zuochi*). Why, then, are they called "restraint" (*zhi*)? Answer:
There are two kinds of restraint and observance (*zhichi*): first, that of identical substance (*tongti*); second, that of distinct substance (*bieti*).

For example, when one intends to fashion robes and bowls, first restraining oneself from transgressions and faults constitutes "restraint through distinct substance" (*bieti zhichi*). This is because, by turning away from unrighteous robes and bowls, the restraint is accomplished. With...

This constitutes the distinct substance of the "active observance" (*kṛta-śīla*). Subsequently, when one employs materials such as silk cloth to perform the act, and having completed it, maintains it without daring to violate or regret it, this further constitutes the "restraint observance" (*vārita-śīla*).

Thus, these two observances together apply to the three robes and so forth; since they are perfected upon the alms bowl, they are called the "restraint observance of identical substance" (*ekadravya-vārita-śīla*).

Question: Regarding this analysis of the essence (*tattva*), is it based on a single essence (*ekātman*) or on distinct essences? Answer: If one discusses a single essence, every precept is fully present;

this is likewise true when one contemplates [the transgressions of] sexual misconduct, stealing, and killing. However, the essence discussed here is based solely on distinct essences, specifically the side of avoiding faults (*doṣa-parihāra*).

If it pertains to the side of active performance (*abhisamskāra*), it is subsumed under "observance through action" (*kriyā-samvara*); it is not appropriate to include "observance through cessation" (*vāraṇa-samvara*) based on a single essence (reflect on this).
Next, the Dharma is explained. According to the *Chao* (Excerpts), the text at this point should logically state:

"Second, the methods for learning and performing ritual procedures (*dharmas*), namely the teachings and practices of the Vinaya-piṭaka, as well as the three types of formal acts (*karmas*) that avoid the seven kinds of non-validity (*saptān-āpatti*). One who wishes to perform a ritual act must avoid these seven non-validities.

The seven non-validities are as described in the *Karma-skandha* section; that is to say, after receiving the precepts, one must immediately study and understand them, and regarding these rituals, one must remain free from [the seven faults]."
The seven non-transgressions (saptā-vyatikrama) are the essence of the dharma of restraint and maintenance (śīla-dhāraṇa), which follows the teachings of the mind.

They serve to characterize the aforementioned dharmas and are termed "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa). [One should say: within the restraint and maintenance of the prohibitive teachings (pratiṣedha-śāsana), the performance of rituals (karmavācanā) is free from the seven non-transgressions, thereby accomplishing the four grave offenses.

The term "etc. includes all such ritual performances. Next, the matters that cannot be learned are distinguished. Regarding the statement "the two things that cannot be learned... up to this point," this clarifies the delusion.

"Delusion is not something that can be learned" refers to the essence of the *śīla* (precepts) regarding what is to be maintained and what is to be observed. This means that this "not being able to learn" is also a matter among those previously mentioned as things that can be learned.

Previously, these were explained clearly so that they were fully understood; however, now, when encountering objects within the sphere of understanding, one instead gives rise to confusion and delusion.

The Sage has declared that there is no offense in such cases, which is why it is called "not being able to learn. "Matters that cannot be learned" is the heading. "Because the mind is confused and inverted" explains the reason.
The "explanation of delusion" refers to fundamental delusion, which is the inversion known as the transformation of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*).

"Failing to understand according to the object" means failing to understand, in accordance with the prohibitions, the objects such as sexual misconduct, theft, and killing; furthermore, it means failing to understand the objects involved in the performance of tasks such as making robes and bowls.

Such a person has merely achieved "cessation" (*śīla*) and cannot be said to be "learning. If one distinguishes the matters of cessation and maintenance that cannot be learned, this is the nature and state of delusive confusion.
The Master Jingshui said: "If it is difficult, then transform the perception; or perhaps it is fundamental delusion.

One fails to clearly understand the objective realm as it presents itself, yet for the time being, one does not proceed to engage in actions such as the aforementioned sexual misconduct, theft, or killing, so as to avoid violating the teachings that prohibit them."
This is termed "stopping and maintaining" (*śīla*). However, from the perspective of delusion and lack of understanding, it constitutes the essence of that which cannot be learned.

Because it manifests certain characteristics regarding the aforementioned matters, it is called a "mark" (*nimitta*). Thus, the *Śīla-śāstra* states: "That which cannot be learned as a matter arises because the mind is confused and inverted;

following objects without understanding, one fails to distinguish between doubt and certainty regarding the objects of killing and stealing. In relation to the state of non-offense, this is therefore 'stopping' (*sthiti*)."
[One] maintains [the precept], yet the mind does not comprehend it; this is what cannot be learned (the above is from the *Shu*).

According to the *Zongji*, if one approaches an object with the intent to steal or kill, even though it is merely due to a deluded mind and there is no offense of violating the teaching, it conversely constitutes "maintaining through cessation.
The detailed explanation is as found therein; here I shall briefly state the general meaning. This interpretation also does not contradict the *Chao*; please reflect upon this. This is based on...
The analysis of delusion regarding phenomena has been concluded.
Next, to analyze the essence of delusion regarding the Dharma, the *Chao* (Excerpts) states in its prose and verse: "Second, the unlearnable dharmas;

due to the mind’s delusive confusion, one fails to comprehend objects as they are," and so forth. However, because it merely follows the ancient tradition, I shall not discuss it here. Since the preceding text has already set forth [the matter]...
In the *Jieshu*, it says: "Now one must also distinguish between delusion and falsehood. Master Jingshui said:
"The practices of the five heterodoxies and seven non-practices are originally objects to be ceased. Because the mind is deluded, one claims these to be the four reliances and other such dharmas;
thus, one fails to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox. Nevertheless, one does not perform the five dharmas of Devadatta for life, nor does one commit the seven non-practices."

The method of not performing [forbidden acts] in accordance with the Dharma is called "maintaining through cessation" (*zhi-chi*). Because the mind is deluded, this cannot be learned [by mere effort];

furthermore, regarding the deluded mind, its essence as delusion consists in not violating the teachings. When there is something manifested upon the preceding object, it is termed a "characteristic mark" (*xiang-zhuang*).

Therefore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The second [category] consists of things that should not be learned, such as the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*), the five wrongs (*pañca-kudharmāḥ*), and the seven non-dharmas (*sapta-adharmāḥ*).

Because these are confused with what is right and wrong, one lacks understanding even when reflecting upon them. Although one does not yet act upon them, this is called 'maintaining through cessation' (*zhi-chi*).

It is not something to be learned; it is that which should not be learned" (the above is from the commentary). Alternatively, according to the *Zongji* (Record of the School), this refers simply to the failure to understand the preceding objects, yet one nonetheless proceeds to act.

Regarding the aforementioned unwholesome dharmas, according to principle they would constitute an offense; however, because one is currently deluded, the Noble One has opened [the path] such that there is no fault.
Thus, what was previously an offense becomes the observance of restraint (*saṃvara*). This interpretation does not contradict reason; take this to heart.

The second section has two parts: first, the statement of the doctrine to be discarded; second, the commentary. One should distinguish between the ancient and the modern. Regarding the "discarding of the former doctrine":

this refers to the current masters who, based on the *vinaya*’s principles of objective conditions (*ālambana*) and mental perception (*saṃjñā*), maintain that because the mind is deluded and inverted, it cannot be learned;

thus, for the sake of those who cannot learn, they discard the views of former masters. They hold that since evil deeds are manifest, the mind cannot be learned [in their commission], and thus they establish the doctrine that such acts are "unlearnable" (*aśikṣamāṇa*).
Question: Since the former interpretation has been discarded and the present one established, I do not yet understand how they differ. The commentary on the *Zhuzhu* (Notes) explains this as follows:

"The former [view] held that certain matters could not be learned; this was to clarify the Great Master’s [position]. Later, in the *Great Commentary* (*Dashi*), within the section on the prohibitions of the *Zhichi* (Precepts for Abstaining from Transgressions), he states:
'Within the category of prohibitions, there are two types: first, matters that cannot be learned, such as perceiving a human as a non-human.'"
This refers to matters that may be practiced, such as the dimensions of robes and alms bowls (as stated in the commentary above). This concerns the third case regarding the perception of the object:

when one mistakes a human for a non-human, the Vinaya permits this and there is no offense. However, if one were now to teach others to practice this—such that a person is killed while being perceived as a non-human—this would constitute an offense, thereby resulting in a transgression. Therefore, one must not learn to perform this act, as it is something that should not be learned.

One must not learn from evil deeds. Within the category of "abstaining through observance" (*śīla*), one establishes the principle of "not learning" by analogy with the aforementioned mental perception of an object.
In those cases, a person who is confused kills another while perceiving them as a non-human; because the conditions were not fully understood, there is no fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*).

Now, regarding evil deeds performed with a clear mind, if the conditions are not fully understood—just as in the case of that confused person who perceives a non-human—the same logical principle applies.

They are similar. This is because, in relation to that which is neither to be learned nor known, one establishes "evil matters" within the category of *zhi-chi* (abstention and maintenance) as being "not to be learned.
One simply ensures that no transgression occurs; thus, there is no violation of the teaching, and this is termed *zhi-chi*. Now, examining this intent:

it takes the case of delusion regarding the object (*viṣaya*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) in the Vinaya texts—where there is no root [of offense]—and applies it by analogy to cases where one clearly understands [the rule] but does not practice or learn it, resulting in no branches [of offense]. Since ancient times...

All are thus. Fearing that it may not be possible, he says: "In the past, because the matter could not be learned"; this refers to the present state through mental conceptions (*citta-vikalpa*) and so forth.
This precisely establishes the meaning of the present. That the mind is deluded is the root; delusive falsehood is the transformation of conceptions (*vikalpa*).

Taking these conceptions and doubts as the basis for "that which cannot be learned," the phrase "all mental objects and states" (*sarva-citta-dharmādi*) serves to further elaborate upon the meaning of the Master of the present. Regarding "all minds": when they first arise...

First, there is the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*). Next, the fundamental mind (*maula-citta*) arises. Finally, the mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodana-citta*) arises. These consist of the three wholesome minds, such as non-attachment, and the three unwholesome minds, such as attachment.
Regarding "all objects": these include objects of prohibition and performance; objects of permission to cease and permission to act; objects that are sentient or insentient;
objects of the truth of emptiness and the truth of existence; the object of the principle of cessation and nirvāṇa; objects consisting of written texts and scrolls; and the object of empty space.
One must learn to recognize the objects of consciousness; such mental objects, whether wholesome or unwholesome, all require study and knowledge, which is why it is said that "all are learnable.

Now, if delusion should suddenly arise regarding the matters and dharmas previously explained—such as when a confused person mistakes a non-animal for a wooden post or similar object and performs an act—the Vinaya texts still permit [the act] based on the fundamental principle of the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*). Yet, in the present case, one does not face such circumstances...

When one has attained full understanding, there is no "ignorance through lack of study," and thus, as a general rule, no offense is incurred; hence it is said that "all are exempted. Therefore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

"One must not learn in delusion, for it is not through mere study that one can attain such realization—even those who have attained the four fruits of the path may still harbor confusion regarding specific phenomena, let alone ordinary worldlings who could possibly discern them all clearly.

Thus, regarding the phenomena of the phenomenal world, whether in matters of abstention or performance, there is a state of mind characterized by confusion that is not subsumed under the category of offenses."

He asked again: "What difference is there between such arising of delusion and the case of those who are ignorant of the teachings? He replied: "Those who are ignorant of the teachings have not studied from birth;

therefore, they fall into error according to their circumstances and are collectively bound by ignorance. This is not the case here. These individuals were originally well-versed and proficient, yet suddenly gave rise to delusion and falsehood.

Since this was not something they could have known through study, no fault can be imputed to them regarding the characteristics of the teachings. (The above is the text of the commentary. The above is the exegesis.
The explanation is complete.

Furthermore, regarding the question of why ancient sages stated that certain things should not be practiced: does this mean they were designated as "unfit for practice" because the actions themselves are unfit to be performed?

Or was it because of the delusion of perceiving a person as a non-person that they were designated as "unfit for practice"? If one says they were unfit for practice because the actions themselves were unfit to be performed...
One should immediately listen to the gate. Regarding exceeding the prescribed dimensions or improper placement, as well as the division of rooms, these are not permitted.

Furthermore, in the making of the three robes (*tricīvara*), one must not exceed the proper colors or dimensions. One should listen to the gate regarding the practice of holding [the robes] within [the proper limits].

There are also things that should not be learned; if one acts with a deluded mind, this constitutes a transgression of the gate of listening. Even in matters such as the placement [of items], there may be instances where one acts with a deluded mind.
"How can it be that there is nothing that cannot be learned? He further questioned the ancients: "How is it that wholesome matters can only be learned?

They replied: "First, one is capable of advancing in practice; second, one is capable of relying on the teachings to generate understanding. Regarding unwholesome matters, these likewise can only not be learned.
If that were so, then the manufacture of non-Dharmic robes and bowls, as well as the construction of non-Dharmic rooms, clothing, and so forth, would also be incapable of being practiced.

Cultivation should universally apply to what is not subject to formal training (*aśaikṣa*). Regarding sexual misconduct, theft, and other evil deeds, if one’s understanding does not arise from relying on the teachings, how could one know that violating the third [precept] regarding sex or the fourth [precept] regarding theft constitutes an offense?
In that case, these evil deeds would instead become matters subject to formal training. To argue in this manner, there are obstacles both in advancing and in retreating.

Therefore, the *Xin zhang* (New Chapter) refutes this, stating: "Merely by allowing these four meanings to detract from the orthodox teaching, it causes those who study it to become mired in stagnation."

This is a deluded thought. Those who seek it become confused by the text and cling to the words. Now, Nanshan follows the principle that regarding phenomena (dharmas), whether good or evil, one must study and know them all;
these all constitute what can be learned. When one does not perform an evil act, this constitutes "abstaining while maintaining" (zhi-chi).

When the mind of delusion arises and one fails to comprehend the preceding phenomena of good or evil, this is called "that which cannot be learned. This is termed "pervading the four modes of conduct" (si-xing).
It encompasses both teachings and includes both mundane matters (*dharma*) and the categories of good and evil; all of these possess aspects that may be learned and those that may not.

This constitutes the meaning of "proficiency" (*khyad par*). Thus far, we have applied the practice of restraint and observance (*śīla*) to the section on prohibitions, comprehensively collecting mundane matters and *dharmas* in four layers:

first, the prohibition against the acts of sexual misconduct and theft; second, the prohibition against the five types of wrong livelihood; third, the regulation of robes and alms bowls; and fourth...

The ritual procedure for formal enactment (*karmavācanā*) is translated as "delusion" and likewise consists of four types; together they constitute eight categories. This concludes the section on their essential characteristics.
Next is the explanation of the section on "allowance," which has two parts: first, a general enumeration, and second, the detailed explanation.

Regarding the statement that within the section on allowance, "the matters apply to both [the preceding categories]," Xuánzàng says: "It is just as in the preceding section on 'prohibition,' where there was no distinction between matters that may be practiced and matters that may not."

In the commentary, regarding the phrase "the dimensions of the dwelling that may be constructed": this refers to the construction of a dwelling for which no donor has been designated. It must conform to the scriptural texts:

it shall be twelve *vitasti* (spans) of the Buddha’s hand in length, and seven *vitasti* in internal width—specifically two *zhang* four *chi* and one *zhang* four *chi*, respectively, calculated according to the Zhou dynasty *chi*.
One must seek formal authorization (*jñapti*) for its construction. Regarding the "large and small extra robes": these refer to a robe that is one foot six inches in length and eight inches in width.
The aforementioned [garments] exceeding the proper measure are "large"; those measuring sixteen or eighteen inches or less are "small" and are not of the proper measure.
Both must be formally dedicated (*śuddhi-vyavahāra*). One must understand these rules regarding robes for the dwelling; this is called that which is to be learned.

If one wishes to manufacture them, one must avoid what is improper and, with a mind of virtuous conduct, comply with the instructions for making them. This is the essence of the practice of restraint (*saṃvara-dhāraṇa*). Regarding...

Regarding the preceding matter, that which is specifically designated is called a "characteristic mark" (*lakṣaṇa*). (One should say: among the *śīla* of restraint and maintenance, within the category of listening to the teachings, there are matters to be performed. Items such as extra robes and dwellings constitute one group.

Within this [category], there are the formal procedures of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* and the method for declaring purity (*śuddhi-vidhi*). Although these are logically consistent with the textual principles and should be recorded, they are not listed here because they merely follow ancient precedent and do not accord with the current system.
One should state: "Second, the methods for learning and listening to the performance of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* and the declaration of purity."

This means one must be thoroughly proficient; this is the sense of "that which can be learned. When performing this rite, one must avoid the seven non-prohibitions (*saptāparādha*) and unite the mind with the teaching;

this is the essence of the "observance through cessation" (*śamatha-dhāraṇa*). Within the aforementioned ritual, that which is manifested is termed the "characteristic mark" (*lakṣaṇa*). (It should be stated:

within the observance through cessation, regarding the permitted teachings, the performance of rites, the distribution of duties, and the declaration of purity—avoiding the seven non-prohibitions constitutes the second category. The *Jieshu* states: "Second, clarifying the matters and rituals within the section on the gate of permitted teachings concerning the observance through cessation."

This refers to the measurement of dwellings in cubits, the length and breadth of extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), the formal assignment (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), the application of ritual procedures (*adhikāra*), and the declaration of purity (*viśuddhi*).

Regarding such matters of dharma, there are instances where it is permitted to perform them and instances where they are prohibited. If one possesses a dwelling or material resources, it is necessary to apply the ritual procedure; therefore, its performance is permitted.

However, if there are obstacles or difficulties, or if the robe or material would constitute a transgression, it is improper to apply the procedure; therefore, its cessation is permitted. (The above is from the *Śāstra*. Second, those things which must not be learned.

Regarding the phrase "not mentioned previously" (*bushi shu*): Fabao states that this follows the same format as the preceding section on prohibitions (*zhimen*), clarifying the principle that certain matters are not to be learned [by imitation].

There is no separate instruction regarding the size of the dwelling, the property, or the status of the individuals involved; rather, these were already understood through prior study. Later, however, one’s mind may suddenly become deluded, failing to comprehend the circumstances—just as in cases of sexual misconduct or theft, where the arising of delusion is no different.
Therefore, it is pointed out here as being the same as what was discussed previously. Thus, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) says: "Matters that must not be learned."

Regarding the Dharma: this refers to matters such as dwellings, wealth, and the scale of one’s status, where delusions and false views arise alternately, and rules and prohibitions emerge from confusion and ignorance.

To look toward the future without transgressing the teachings is called "stopping and maintaining" (zhīchí). Because delusion is not something that can be learned [as a virtue], it is therefore prescribed that one must not commit [transgressions]. (The above is from the *Shu-wen*). In the *Xuánjì*:
This refers back to the section on "That Which Can Be Learned. It means that while previously [the mind] was clear and bright, learning served to cease errors and transgressions;

now, having suddenly fallen into delusion and falsehood, it is "that which cannot be learned. Regarding its essential substance (*tattva*), it is no different from before; therefore, it is referred back to what was stated previously (fearing it may not equal the former). In the second passage, there are two parts:

first, based on the fundamental delusion of the shifting perceptions, the state of "that which cannot be learned" is established; second, the "hidden penetration" objection, which says: "But as for reaching..."

Regarding "contradictions": there have been many interpretations of this section since ancient times; as they are not correct, none are recorded here. Only the correct meaning is preserved. Xuán says:
"Delusion" refers to fundamental delusion, while "falsehood" refers to derivative conceptualization. If a subsequent mind does not recall the state of the preceding mind, it is termed "falsehood.

For example, if one constructs an oversized room, there is no offense if both the preceding and succeeding states of mind were deluded. However, if one knows it is oversized both before and after, until the point of... [text ends]... arriving at the act itself.
At that time, the perception shifts. If one perceives it as not exceeding the limit, one incurs only the *pācittiya* offense of the preceding thought-moment (*pūrvacitta*).

If one initially acts with the perception that it does not exceed the limit, but upon reaching the point of completion, realizes it does exceed the limit, one incurs the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense of the subsequent thought-moment (*paścāccitta*). If the original delusion does not shift, then according to the teaching, there is no offense from beginning to end.

Even if the shifting of the perception is forgotten, no offense is incurred. Thus, we know that delusion and forgetfulness are not things that can be fully understood through mere study; they are precisely [the domain of the realized].
The meaning of "not being able to learn" is as follows: by establishing this meaning as "not being able to learn," there is no contradiction with the Buddha’s revealed teaching.

This section serves to overturn deluded thoughts and fundamental confusion, providing a simultaneous explanation of both [aspects]. (End of the upper excerpt). Question: I do not yet understand the original intent behind establishing this section. Answer:
It is because one fears that, based on the preceding [discussion], the mind remains deluded and the principle of "not being able to learn" has not yet been established.

Citing the *Vinaya* regarding the perception of the object (*ālambana-saṃjñā*), it is proven that being deluded [about the object] constitutes no offense; this is something that cannot be learned [by mere rule].
This same intent is also found in the "Gate of Observance" (*dhāraṇa-mukha*) section of the *Śīla-śāstra*. Thus, the commentary states:

"The preceding mind intended to construct an oversized, undivided dwelling, but the subsequent mind shifted its perception, thinking it was a dwelling of proper measure and with divisions" (the above is from the commentary). Since the perception has shifted between the preceding and succeeding moments, the formal act (*saṃvara*) is indeterminate (*aniyata*).
Such indeterminate offenses (*aniyata-āpatti*) are not deluded states of mind; they merely conclude the preceding section on preparatory means (*prayoga*).

Now, regarding the excerpted rules for cessation, maintenance, and permission (*śikṣāpada*), since the matter concerns dwellings and the permitted teachings are likewise the same, these are subsumed under this category from the perspective of avoiding transgressions.

Regarding this gate of listening (*śravaṇa-mukha*): once the dwelling has been established, there is that which cannot be learned. This reaches down to the gate of practice and maintenance (*dhāraṇā-mukha*), where there is likewise that which cannot be learned;

thus its meaning is well-established. [The author] secretly refutes the ancients regarding these gates of listening and practice and maintenance, asserting that there is no fault in not establishing "that which cannot be learned" therein.
Second, he secretly addresses and subdues the objection. First, the objection is raised: "If fundamental delusion does not turn back, from beginning to end..."
There is no offense; there is no violation of the principles of the Teaching. This refers to a case where the meaning was not intended to be learned.

Now, when one suddenly shifts one's perception between what precedes and what follows, the offense of *thullaccaya* (grave transgression) is incurred, and there is indeed a violation of the Teaching. How can it be said that in all such cases there is no violation? The abbreviated response states:

Because the perception shifts between what precedes and what follows, the formal act (*sīla*) is indeterminate. This means that while the preceding state of mind and the object were congruent, the subsequent shifting of the mind was not.
If the preceding mind was directed toward the object, but the subsequent mind was not, there is no offense for the latter mind.

If the preceding mind was not directed toward the object, but the subsequent mind shifted so that the mind and the object corresponded, one incurs only the fundamental *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, with no offense of preliminary effort (*prayoga*). This is based on the case where the preceding and succeeding minds were both directed toward the object.

Because the gravity of the offense incurred varies, there is thus no fixed rule; however, when the preceding or succeeding moments of mind do not encounter the object [of the transgression], no offense is incurred, and this likewise does not contradict the teaching.
Is this not the meaning of "that which cannot be learned"? (The formal response to the external objection is hereby concluded). Therefore, the *Jieshu* states:

If there is no formal offense of transgression, why does the Vinaya text establish this as a *sthūlātyaya*? Answer: This is with regard to what would otherwise be a *sthūlātyaya*, yet here only the conceptualization and the mental preparation (*citta-upāya*) are established.

For example, if one initially intends to construct an oversized dwelling that is not properly demarcated, but later changes one's mind and thinks it is a properly demarcated and measured dwelling, the subsequent state differs from the preceding cause; since the final result is not reached, it is established as a *sthūlātyaya*. This is acceptable.
"I do not understand" (the above is the commentary). Based on this, the principle that [certain matters] cannot be learned is clarified. This is entirely consistent with the past;

however, it refers only to cases where, due to a deluded mind, one fails to incur an offense—this constitutes "that which cannot be learned. Above, there are two layers regarding the procedures for listening: first, the matter of the dwelling;

second, the formal procedure (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for declaring purity (*śuddhi*). Conversely, regarding delusion and forgetfulness, there are likewise two. Altogether, there are four layers. If...
The section on the dual practice (*samyukta-pratipatti*) consists of eight gates; when calculated together with the preceding, they comprise twelve gates in total regarding their essential forms.
These all pertain to *śīla* as cessation-and-maintenance (*śamatha-dhāraṇa*). Next is the gate of active practice (*pravṛtti-dhāraṇa*). Regarding "active practice": "next" means sequential order.

Since evil has already been abandoned, one must cultivate goodness; this is termed "active. "Maintenance" (*dhāraṇa*) is explained as before. Question: In the preceding section on the "gates of demarcation," following cessation-and-maintenance...

[The text] clarifies the commission of offenses (*āpatti*). Now, having established the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of "abstention" (*virati*) following [the discussion on] "maintaining" (*dhāraṇa*), why does it then clarify "active maintaining" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*)?

The answer, as stated by Master Bao, is that the two types of offenses have no distinct essential natures; they are formed by reversing the state of "maintaining. However, after extensively setting forth the two types of "maintaining," the text briefly reverses them to form the offenses.

This was done for the convenience of the author; there is no other underlying principle. Now, perhaps following the sequence within its own section according to the names, it establishes the essential natures accordingly.

It is thus. That is to say, following the ancients below while relying on the present, both are explained together. "Function" and "sustenance" are designated as the essence (of the precepts). (The two sections below differ from the old classification; take note of this.)

Regarding the initial statement "within the section on the gates of counter-regulation," the term "Dharma-affairs" (hōji) refers to the simultaneous presentation of both "affairs" (ji) and "Dharma" (hō).

This means that the two teachings of "performance" (sā) and "observance" (jū), as well as "entry into prohibitions" (nyūsei) and "permission" (chōju), collectively encompass all affairs; therefore, they are first set forth. As for the phrase "Dharma and so forth" (hōtō), it is not yet clear what kind of Dharma is intended.

According to the commentaries of the past, "Dharma" refers to teaching (kyō) and practice (gyō); "teaching" refers to the Three Baskets (Tripitaka), and "practice" refers to the Three Studies (Trishikṣā). However, this present copy has been revised.

It says: "Teaching" refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka. As for "practice," what kind of practice is it? The *Chao* (the Sub-commentary) explains: "Practice" refers to the application of remedies (*pratipakṣa*).

The reason this differs from the *Da shou* (Great Summary) is that, as Xuan states, the *Chao* relies on the beginner—those who have not yet completed five summer retreats—and thus explains the matter gradually, focusing specifically on the Vinaya.
The *Da shou*, however, broadly elucidates both the new and old schools of learning; therefore, it encompasses all three piṭakas. Alternatively, one may simply refer to the Vinaya alone.

This includes the other two collections [of the Tripiṭaka] within itself. "Practice" refers to the remedy; that is, beneath the teaching that expresses it (*abhidhāna*), there are the three kinds of remedies for the pure precepts (*śīla*) that are expressed by it (*abhidheya*), namely:
