those of the assembly (*saṃgha*), the individual (*pudgala*), and both together. Examples include the formal ritual acts (*karmavācanā*) such as the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations) and the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults).

Avoiding what is improper and conforming to what is proper constitutes the remedy for communal practice. Cultivating various meditative contemplations and practices constitutes the remedy for personal practice. This includes matters such as the *pratimokṣa* (confession before another), the wearing of robes, and so forth.

Purifying the application of medicine is precisely practicing the remedies in tandem. Therefore, the introduction states: "These three are called practices; there is no practice that is not subsumed herein.
This means that regarding the aforementioned expressive terms and expressed meanings—the dharmas of teaching and practice—one is enjoined to learn and know them after receiving the precepts;

this is the sense of being "capable of learning. By means of the three mental states beginning with non-attachment, one advances toward and cultivates these dharmas, acting in accordance with their composition.

The Teaching (*śāsana*). To unite the mind with the Teaching is the essence of "active observance" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*). Within the aforementioned phenomena (*dharma*), that which provides a designation is called a "characteristic mark" (*nimitta*). [One should say:

within active observance, the prescriptive teachings (*vidhi-śāsana*) and the methods for performing actions (*kriyā-karaṇa-dharma*) are one and the same category. Regarding the statement "matters can only be learned," etc.: the question is, why was it not stated in the preceding section on phenomena that "phenomena can only be learned"?
The answer is: according to the ancients, phenomena are the methods for progressive cultivation; originally, they did not exist [as independent entities].

It need not be studied; there is no need for such distinction. Such matters pertain to both good and evil. Regarding evil matters, there are indeed things that must not be learned, which consist solely of "abstaining from what is prohibited" (*zhi-chi*).

However, the present case concerns "engaging in what is prescribed" (*zuo-chi*), which pertains exclusively to virtuous matters; therefore, it is solely something that ought to be learned. This is why it is distinguished [from the former].

If one were now to establish that this too is "not to be learned," I fear that beginners would become confused, not knowing which specific matters or dharmas constitute that which is "not to be learned."

Therefore, this has not yet been established. Furthermore, it was already established in the preceding commentary; it can be understood that it is not mentioned here. Thus, for now, the word "only" (*kevala*) is used. Question:

In the previous section on "maintaining through cessation" (*śīla-dhāraṇā*), one distinguished between "cessation" (*nirodha*) and "performance" (*kriyā*). Why, in the present section on "maintaining through performance," do you discuss only performance and not cessation? Answer:

The previous [section] was based on the aspect of avoiding transgressions, which is termed "maintaining through cessation. If one avoids transgressions regarding evil matters, [that is what is meant].

This is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*). Now, regarding the aspect of performing virtuous deeds by remaining free from transgressions and practicing according to the teachings, this is collectively termed "active observance" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*);
therefore, it is not distinguished as "restraint. Next, to explain the text: regarding the substance and dimensions of the robe and bowl, "robe" refers to processed silk, cotton cloth, or silk gauze.
The substance of the ten types of robes measures five cubits. The substance of the alms bowl refers to clay or iron; its capacity is three or three-and-a-half *dō*.
The term "and so forth" includes the sitting mat, needle case, water-strainer pouch, and all other manufactured items as well as articles for receiving the precepts.
After receiving the precepts, one clearly understands them within the mind and is enjoined to train in their practice; this is the meaning of "that which can be learned.

Because one is able to maintain the mind in accordance with the teachings received, one accomplishes the substance of "observance through action" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*). Regarding the aforementioned matters, that which serves to manifest them is called "characteristic marks" (*lakṣaṇa*).

(One should say: among the observances through action and the enjoined teachings, the performance of the matter regarding the substance, dimensions, and so forth of the robes and bowl constitutes the second category.)

Next, the section on the "Gate of Listening" (*śravaṇa-mukha*) is explained. Regarding the phrase "also facing a legal matter" (*dharmakārya*), this refers to the point when one is about to enter the Gate of Listening;
it involves two types of legal matters, which are no different from those previously discussed in the "Gate of Regulation. Regarding the phrase "the Dharma reaches... and so forth:

since it was stated above that one is "also facing a legal matter," it is not yet clear what kind of Dharma or what kind of matter is intended. The *Chao* (Excerpts) itself provides the commentary: "Dharma" refers to the formal act of assignment (*jñapti*).

Regarding purification (*viśuddhi*): this matter is solely a matter of training; the long robe (*atireka-cīvara*) and the dwelling (*layana*) are examples. As for "assignment" (*parikarman*), it refers to requesting the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) to designate the site and ground for these buildings.
Furthermore, regarding the possession of a lawful long robe, one must perform the *viśuddhi* declaration within ten days.

The term "etcetera" includes all other permitted actions, such as requesting the *nir-cīvara-śākhā-karman* (the formal act concerning the exemption from the rule against being separated from one's robes) and the *kāṭhina-karman* (the formal act concerning the *kāṭhina* robe).

Regarding these dharmas, it is logically appropriate to advance in their practice and study; this is termed "performing and maintaining" (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*). Its essence consists in the mind following the teachings.

Within these dharmas, there are those that serve as markers or indicators, which are termed "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*). (One should say: "Within performing and maintaining, within listening to the teachings, the procedure for listening, the *jñapti-dvitīya* [motion-and-second-vote] rite, and the rite of purification (*śuddhi*).
This is a single point. As for the statement that "matters can only be studied regarding extra robes and dwellings," this revision also accords with the ancient tradition. Ancient...
Regarding the "Dharma-robes for the Superior Good Deeds" as mentioned above: they should be clearly understood within the mind as solely the sphere of diligent cultivation;
one must certainly learn them. If one does not learn them, it constitutes a transgression of omission. Therefore, only that which is learnable is established; there is nothing that is not learnable.

Regarding the statement, "Now, in selecting the text, I follow the ancients," this means that these matters concerning extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*) and dwellings (*layana*) must be clearly understood within one's mind and thoroughly mastered.

Furthermore, the phrase "that which may be learned" (*śikṣamāṇa*) and so forth refers, by way of inclusion, to all virtuous practices within the category of what is permitted (*anujñāta*), such as the two robes for covering wounds and the like;

since one learns them all after receiving [the precepts], they are called "that which may be learned. Thus, by following the permission with the mind, one acts according to the teaching, thereby establishing the substance of the practice (*dhāraṇa*).

Regarding the aforementioned matters, that which serves to characterize them is called a "mark" (lakṣaṇa). (One should say: among the items to be maintained, among the teachings to be heard, and among the tasks to be performed—such as long [robes] and dwellings—these constitute two pairs.)

The second [section] refutes the ancient [view] and establishes the present text, consisting of two parts. First, the formal refutation of the ancient view: it does not accord with the reason why [the state of] "inability to learn" cannot be cultivated. Second, the establishment by the present master:

he separately establishes "inability to learn" and points toward its detailed exposition later [in the text]. (These two minor sections also differ from the old schema; if one follows the old version, it would deviate from the meaning—consider this carefully.

Regarding the statement that it does not accord with the reason why "inability to learn" cannot be cultivated: this refers to the present master’s intended establishment of the "mind of delusion and forgetfulness."

Because it is something that cannot be learned, [the author] first cites the ancients. Within the context of "making and maintaining" (*zuo-chí*), specifically regarding the internal practice of "making" (*zhìzuò*) and "listening to making" (*tīng zuò*), why is it stated exclusively that matters can only be learned and that there are none that cannot be learned? Therefore, it says: "The reason it does not extend to what cannot be learned.

Although the *Chao* (Commentary) contains the words of the citation from the ancients, it conceals the response of the ancient master; it is only in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) that [this is clarified].

[The commentary] says: "Now, I shall respond to that text by providing the answer of the ancients. Thus, it says: 'In the section on the gate of active observance (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*), there are matters and dharmas that can be studied and none that cannot be studied;
however, these are not what is being clarified here. Because they do not involve progressive cultivation (*abhyāsa*), the Sage did not enjoin their study.

This differs from the gate of passive observance (*sthita-dhāraṇa*), which universally includes that which cannot be studied, because it consists solely of abstaining from transgressions. Therefore, [this] can be clarified [here]. (The above is the text of the *Śāstra*). According to the intent of the ancients, only...

Regarding evil matters, they cannot be pursued for cultivation and thus are not to be studied. Now, this practice of *sahajagṛhīta-śīla* (inherent precepts) is indeed a matter of cultivation; therefore, it can be studied.
This is the intended meaning of the response in the *Xiangjie shu* (Commentary on the Resonance Precepts).

If one wishes to establish the doctrine of the present master, one may borrow the aforementioned words used to challenge the ancients, omitting the character "not" (*bu*), and simply state: "The reason the present master maintains that [certain things] are universally not to be studied is because... [the rest of the argument follows].
Since ancient times, within the gate of "practice and maintenance" (zuochi), there has been only that which is learnable; as for that which is unlearnable, its principle was not yet complete.

Now, our Master [Daoxuan], within the gate of practice and maintenance, comprehensively includes the unlearnable. On what basis does he do so? He cites the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*) to answer:

because the mind is deluded and forgetful, it cannot be understood through mere learning. This is explained in detail later. Since our Master established this anew, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The present interpretation..."
This is not so. It is impossible for one who is deluded regarding what is not [proper] to understand it through mere study, even up to the level of the four fruits of the path.

Since this applies to those with such confusion regarding material matters, how much more so for ordinary people who could possibly discern everything? Therefore, regarding material dharmas, whether in relation to what is prohibited or what is permitted, there is forgetfulness and confusion;

yet these are not subsumed under transgression. This can be clarified by the following: according to the Vinaya, regarding surplus wealth, forgetting is permitted and does not constitute defilement; likewise, regarding the assignment of a dwelling, the mental conception [of the space] is also permitted.

Doubt. Since it was not formally adjudicated as an offense, it is clear that no transgression occurred (the above is from the *Śāstra*). According to this passage, it is evident that the excerpted text represents the response of the Master [Daoshi].

One must establish here that [the rule] is to be observed, yet it is "not to be learned" (*aśikṣamāṇa*). That is to say, regarding the precept on the dwelling room (*vihāra-śikṣāpada*), the Vinaya permits the application of the notion of doubt (*saṃśaya*).
If one forgets to perform the *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (ritual purification) for an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*), no offense is incurred; this is an allowance for delusion.

Is it not the case that such matters are not to be learned? Why did the ancients not establish [this principle] here? As will be explained in detail later, within the "Analysis of the Successive Stages," regarding the nine phrases on "Non-learning in the Maintenance of Restraint" (*śamatha-dhāraṇa-aśikṣaṇīya*), when examining the three cases of "not recognizing the object," it is simply because the object itself is learnable through conceptualization.

Doubt and forgetfulness give rise [to offenses]. Although the object may not be fully discerned, the Sage does not establish it as an offense. By citing the perception of the object, our present Master establishes the principle that [certain] matters cannot be learned.
According to the ancients, among the nine cases, in the first half where confusion arises regarding the matter, the offense is immediately relinquished;

in the second half, where there is doubt and lack of recognition regarding the legal transgression, twelve offenses are incurred. Our present Master objects: "If that were so, then regarding the subsequent factors of the dharma..."
There is also the occurrence of perception (*saṃjñā*). Furthermore, he raises an objection based on the *śikṣāpada* regarding the perception of an object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*):

for instance, if one perceives something as not having been formally assigned when it has been assigned, or if there is doubt [regarding its assignment], no offense is committed. Why, then, are the twelve offenses of the latter half [of the *Prātimokṣa*] established here? He replies:

This is stated according to the "abstention and maintenance" (*virati-dhāraṇa*) section, speaking in terms of the specific matter (*vastu*). It must be as cited from the *Abhidharma*, which contains two sets of nine propositions (*navaka*). In the subsequent "performance and maintenance" (*anuvṛtti-dhāraṇa*) section, furthermore...

This is for the sake of clarification. When we reach the section on the "Gate of Active Maintenance" (*kṛtya-dhāraṇī*) below, our current Master, in contrast to Dharmottara, maintains that one may only study nine propositions regarding the first [category].
Later, it is said that there are also nine propositions regarding the "unstudiable dharma-delusion," as explained in the nine propositions at the end of the preceding section.

Within the "cessation of transgressions" (*pratiṣedha-āpatti*), two sets of nine are established in relation to specific matters; the intention is to reverse cessation into activity. Regarding active maintenance in relation to specific matters, there are likewise [nine].
29. Thus, within the gate of "practice and maintenance" (zuochi), there are nine items to be studied for each of the categories of phenomena (*vastu*) and principles (*dharma*).
These will be pointed out later; therefore, it is said: "Extensively as described below" (the detailed explanations are omitted here as they would be cumbersome).

The third major section. Regarding the phrase "this [refers to] the attainable," the opening commentary states: "Within these two [categories], [the distinction between] prohibition and permission constitutes the two.

Simply ensuring that one acts in accordance with the teachings without transgression is all termed 'observance through action' (*kṛta-dhāraṇā*). (The above is the text of the commentary. This [text] only concludes what is learnable.
Now, since our Master has established here that which is unlearnable, we shall borrow this passage to conclude the unlearnable as well. One should first raise the following objection:
If one’s deluded mind perceives an oversized, unassigned room as being of the prescribed size, and constructs an illegal dwelling, this constitutes an offense of construction.

How, then, can one now perform the ritual of formal authorization (*dhāraṇa-mukha*) therein? One may cite the *Chao-da* (Excerpts and Answers) for this; it states that such cases refer to those who are "equal" [to the ignorant].

That is to say, one cannot learn from the deluded; it is not through learning that one can truly understand. Since the Noble Ones do not establish an offense for such a person, this is termed "conforming to the teaching without transgression."
This may also be termed "active upholding" (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*). Furthermore, regarding this active upholding:

if one clearly and consciously gives rise to a wholesome mind and accords with the two teachings, taking the union of mind and teaching as its essence—as previously analyzed—then even if one is deluded, it is determined that the mind, though deluded, does not violate the teachings;

thus, one is bound to the side of non-offense, which constitutes the essence of delusion (reflect on this). The above clarifies how the four grave offenses are established through conscious intention; the opposite applies when one is deluded or forgetful.
There are also four [aspects], which together constitute eight layers of essential form.
The third section concerns the commission of offenses, consisting of three parts: first, stating what is being translated; second, discerning the essence; and third, the concluding statement.

Regarding the clarification of "commission of offense" (*kṛta-āpatti*) as the counterpart to "abstention through observance" (*virati-dhāraṇa*): this refers to the two types of teachings—the prohibitions and the permissions—which do they not constitute the three layers of matters? In contrast to the preceding objects and conditions...

[The term] "making" (作) refers to acting in accordance with the prohibitive teachings, thereby constituting "abstention through observance" (止持). Now, this [term] refers to acting in violation of the teachings, thereby constituting "active transgression" (作犯). This can be expressed by reversing the meaning:
simply not relying on the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*) and completing the act constitutes what is termed "active transgression.

Here, we shall now reverse it. That is to say, within the preceding section on prohibitions, there are two types of matters: the prohibition of the three [unwholesome acts] regarding sexual misconduct and the four [unwholesome acts] regarding theft; these prohibit that which is contrary to the Dharma.

Regarding the robe and bowl: now, when the three poisons arise and the conduct of the mind violates the teachings, such that the act is fully accomplished, this is termed the "substantial offense" (*karmabhāva-āpatti*).

When there is a specific manifestation within the objective matter, this is termed the "characteristic mark" (*lakṣaṇa*). It should be said: among the offenses of commission, within the prohibitive teachings, there are prohibited matters of the offense of commission.

Sexual misconduct and the fourth [offense] of stealing are the one grave [offense]. Among the offenses of commission, within the prohibitive teachings, there are enacted matters of the offense of commission.

The substance and dimensions of an unlawful robe and bowl are [defined as] "double-layered. In the previous section on "Abstaining from What Is Prohibited," there was an unwholesome practice that the *Chao* did not clarify;

since it was previously added by citing the *Jieshu*, it is now likewise reversed as a transgression. It should be stated: among the transgressions of commission, within the prescriptive teachings (*zhìjiào*), regarding the prohibitive rules (*zhǐzhìfǎ*), it constitutes a transgression of commission.

The five types of false practices constitute three [categories]: among the transgressions of commission, within the prescriptive teachings, regarding the prescriptive rules (*zhìzuòfǎ*), it constitutes a transgression of commission. The *karmavācanā*...
The seven acts of grinding are not included [in the four]. Next, regarding the reversal from the perspective of the "listening gate" (*śravaṇa-mukha*):

in the previous section on "abstaining and maintaining" (*zhi-chi*), it was stated that the first is a matter of training (*śikṣāpada*), such as the measurements of rooms and dwellings or the dimensions of extra robes. Now, however, one gives rise to an unwholesome mind and carries out actions in violation of the teachings.
Because an unwholesome mind violates the listening to the teachings, this constitutes the essence [of the offense]; it manifests its mark upon the preceding object.
This is called the "aspect" (lakṣaṇa). It should be stated as follows: within the category of transgression through performance, there is the permission to perform an act within the teaching;

this refers to the performance of an act. [The cases of] extra robes and the relinquishment of a dwelling constitute one layer. Within this section on permissions, there is also a formal rule (*dharma*). Since this was not previously discussed, it likely follows the ancient tradition. This is also a dark passage; it should be stated as:

within the category of transgression through performance, there is the permission to perform an act within the teaching, specifically the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) of assignment and the declaration of purity (*viśuddhi-vyākaraṇa*); these seven are not [transgressions].

(Second layer). Together with the four [layers] from the preceding section on the "Gate of Regulation," this forms six layers. To clarify the essential nature [of the offense], when reversed to form delusion and forgetfulness, there are likewise six layers.
This constitutes the essence that cannot be learned, totaling twelve layers. (The above concludes the textual analysis).

Although the above has distinguished offenses committed through clarity and awareness, we shall now distinguish offenses committed through delusion and forgetfulness. What constitutes their essence? One interpretation, based on the *Zongji* (Record of the School), states:
This refers to what was explained previously regarding the case of building a hut on top of another structure. That is to say, it was originally an oversized hut;

at the outset, one had the perception that it was oversized, but upon its completion, one reversed this and formed the perception that it was within the proper measure. Because of such mental confusion, the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (requiring suspension from the community) was not incurred.

However, there was a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) at the time when the initial perception of oversize arose. Now, this offense is taken as the actual substance of the transgression committed through delusion and forgetfulness. Now...
An objection is raised: "The *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) prior to the [actual] mind is a manifest offense (*vijñapti-pāpa*). How can it be taken as the essence of delusion and forgetfulness?
This seems untenable. One who seeks to defend this point says: "Although it is a manifest offense, it exists because of a deluded mind.

That is to say, when the subsequent mind transforms its perception (*saṃjñā*) and forms a perception of [the object] as it actually is (*yathābhūta-saṃjñā*), one does not commit the root offense; thus, the preceding *sthūlātyaya* occurs. If it were not due to delusion, [it would not arise]."

To establish the root offense and thereby constitute a clear transgression—could it not be otherwise? Now, to raise this objection in order to support one's own position is also logically untenable. [The opponent] objects again:

"If that is so, and there is an offense when the perception shifts, then let this interpretation be granted; however, there is no offense when there was original delusion. Furthermore, how can this be?
If the shifted perception has substance while the original delusion lacks substance, it would result in the fault of inconsistency. No.

This has been explained (reflect on this). Second, regarding the explanation: according to Master Jingshui, this "learned transgression" (*śikṣāpatti*) cannot be learned; it exists only in name without substance.
Nevertheless, one must actually perform the preceding act for it to be called a "committed transgression. Since this arises from a deluded mind, the Sage did not establish it as a formal offense;

therefore, it is not something that can be learned. Thus, the *Shouyong Chao* below states: "Furthermore, it necessarily arises through the performance of the preceding act; it is generally termed 'committed' (*kṛta*)."
This pertains to the inclusion of transgressions.

The fourth section, "Cessation of Transgressions," consists of two parts: first, citing what has been translated; second, correctly explaining the essence. Regarding the phrase "The four... up to this":

it refers to the aforementioned gate of precepts, wherein the two types of practice—affairs and dharmas—constitute "active observance" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*). Now, this also corresponds to the preceding category of affairs.

Regarding the Dharma: it is simply through indolence that one fails to study, which conversely constitutes a transgression of omission (*pratikṣepa-virati*). This is likewise the case within the category of "listening" (*śravaṇa*). As stated in the aforementioned *Chao* (Excerpts): "It also pertains to Dharma-matters.
'Dharma' refers to formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) and the declaration of purity (*śuddhi-uddeśana*); 'matter' (*vastu*) refers to what may be studied, such as extra robes and dwellings.

With clarity in one's mind, one performs the formal procedures before these matters and thereby accomplishes the act of possession (*parigraha*). Now, due to indolence, one does not study this; conversely, this constitutes a transgression of omission."

Regarding the transgression: I shall now take this cessation of transgression and, within the context of the two teachings, rely on the transcribed text to examine the matters of the rules for training.

These collectively encompass the four grave offenses (*catur-guru-dharma*). As for these four grave offenses, they should be stated as follows: first, the cessation of transgression regarding the rules for training in the composition of [monastic] objects;

that is, not training in the practice of the teachings constitutes one grave offense. Second, the cessation of transgression regarding the training in the composition of material objects; that is, the substance and dimensions of the robes and bowl constitute [the second grave offense]. Within the section on "Listening" (*śravaṇa*), there is that which may be learned...

The methods for the performance of acts that prevent transgressions and the rules for the formal declaration of purity (*śuddhi*) constitute three categories. One may study and listen to these matters concerning the performance of tasks that prevent transgressions.

The long robes and dwellings constitute four categories. Thus, there are four categories of clear and manifest matters; when inverted as confused or forgotten, they likewise become four, totaling eight categories.

It should be understood that the transgressions prevented by confusion or forgetfulness possess only names and meanings but no substantial form. The same applies to the transgressions resulting from completed acts.
Twelve [categories] multiplied by two become twenty-four. By establishing the eightfold observance (*dhāraṇa*) and its corresponding eightfold transgression (*āpatti*), they become sixteen.
Together with the previous twenty-four, they constitute forty modes of essential form. This is merely the formal method; for those who have attained realization, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
The second section concludes here.

The third section, the Gate of Accomplishment (*siddhi-mukha*), consists of two parts: first, the citation of the title; second, the preliminary opening of the chapters for explanation based on the following text.

The phrase "From 'three' to 'object'" (*tri-āyatanam*) is the citation. Since the names and essential natures (*svabhāva*) have already been understood, it remains to be examined in which nature and state of mind the four practices (*caryā*) are accomplished;

therefore, this is explained next. Regarding "accomplishment" (*siddhi*), the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "To obtain and acquire is called accomplishment," meaning that the substance of the dharma is acquired and resides within one's person.

This is collectively termed "attainment" (*samanvāgama*). If discussed specifically: when the essence of a dharma first reaches the phase of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), it is called "acquisition" (*pratilambha*) or "attainment" (*lābha*);
when it flows on into the present, it is called "possession" (*samanvāgama*). At the time of possession, it is not called acquisition, because it has already been attained.

At the time of acquisition, it is not called possession, because it has not yet been attained. Thus, there is a distinction between acquisition/attainment and possession. Now, we shall discuss only...
To have attained the Dharma within one’s person is called "accomplishment.

Regarding the explanation, the statement that it first distinguishes [the subject] by way of mind means, as Xuánzàng says: "The five aggregates constitute the body; four aggregates are mind, and one aggregate is matter.
Now, excluding matter, it is distinguished solely by way of the four aggregates of mind. As for the statement that "retention (dhāraṇī) has two types," it refers only to...

The analysis of the single practice of "stopping and maintaining" (*śīla*) itself has two aspects. First, regarding the three mental factors of sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*): when no evil comes to defile them, there is "stopping and maintaining.

Second, regarding the mind of application (*prayoga-citta*) and its counteractives (*pratipakṣa*): when these are present, there is "stopping and maintaining. As for the remaining three practices, they exist solely within the mind of application.
Because there is no distinction between them. Now, first we shall distinguish *śīla* as cessation-and-maintenance (*zhi-chí*). Regarding the statement "first, up to the second part":

"no evil comes to defile [one]" means that, according to the ancients, "cessation-and-maintenance" refers to sitting with hands folded (*duàn-gǒng*) after receiving the precepts; by remaining in this state of folded hands, one does not engage in either good or evil, thereby accomplishing cessation-and-maintenance.

Now, I refute this: if one merely sits with hands folded without cultivating various virtues, one accomplishes a state of "folded-hand cessation-of-transgression" (*duàn-gǒng zhǐ-fàn*), which is not permissible.
Regarding other practices: as for the statement that "no evil comes to defile [them]," this refers to the period from after receiving the precepts until the four points of abandonment;

during this interval, if one does not give rise to an evil mind, with respect to the non-defilement of the precepts, it is termed "observance through cessation" (*zhi-chí*). This is not restricted solely to the initial reception of the precepts.
Regarding "the three preceding minds during practice" and so forth: this means that once the essence of the precepts (*śīla-sarīra*) has been received, it resides within the mind.

As long as it is not defiled by unwholesome characteristics, even if one enters a state of moral neutrality (*avyākṛta*), one does not yet violate the essence of what was received and may thus be called a "holder. These three are not [karmic] actions; they are consciousness (*vijñāna*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and feeling (*vedanā*).

When the mind of consciousness first arises, it merely cognizes general characteristics. Subsequently, the mind of perception arises to apprehend objects, at which point there arise suffering, pleasure, equanimity, enmity, affection, and so forth.

Next, the perception-generating mind (*saṃjñā-citta*) arises. One perceives an enemy as producing painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*), a loved one as producing pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*), and a neutral person as producing neutral feeling (*upekṣāvedanā*).
At this stage, the mind is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and has not yet become karmically formative.

When it flows into the volitional mind (*saṃskāra-citta*), meaning upon reaching the fourth stage of the volitional mind, it is able to generate the three poisons and can then perform action. Facing an enemy object, it gives rise to the volition of hatred and commits killing.

When one gives rise to greed toward an attractive object, it constitutes sexual misconduct and stealing. Toward a neutral object, one gives rise to delusion, which constitutes the practice of false speech;

thus, two transgressions can be established. The two observances are explained in reverse: non-greed establishes the practice of abstaining from sexual misconduct, non-hatred establishes the practice of abstaining from killing, and non-delusion establishes the practice of abstaining from false speech.
Only when reaching this level of mental action can karma be fully established. Question: Regarding the enumeration of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), [what of] form (*rūpa*)...
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness follow the same sequence. Now, which consciousness occupies the first position? The answer is:

according to the sequence of meditative practice (*yogācāra*), one should first contemplate form—such as through the contemplation of impurity—and subsequently contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

However, this current enumeration is explained in terms of karma; therefore, consciousness is clarified first. Furthermore, according to the sequence of arising in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, consciousness also occupies the first place. Consciousness is...

The mind-king (citta-rāja) and the other three mental factors (caitta). The *Śata-śāstra* states: "The mind-king apprehends their general characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa), while the mental factors apprehend their specific characteristics (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa).

For example, when consciousness first arises, it merely takes as its object a general characteristic such as blue; this is the stage of the *vijñāna*-citta. Subsequently, the image of the object is reflected upon;

this is the *saṃjñā*-citta. Next, one experiences the preceding object; this is the *vedanā*-citta. Following that, afflictions such as craving engage in formative activity; this is the *saṃskāra*-citta. [Question: Regarding consciousness, perception, feeling, and...
Question: Since these are already the *saṃskāra-citta* (active mind), why is it said that one "enters" the *saṃskāra-citta*? Answer: There are two meanings of "activity" (*saṃskāra*).

First, in the sense of "flux" (*prabandha*), all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are *saṃskāras*; thus, the three [aggregates] beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) are also called *saṃskāras*. Second, in the sense of "volitional construction" (*abhisaṃskāra*).

It is capable of initiating bodily and vocal karma; because it serves as a distinct cause, it is termed "formative action" (*saṃskāra*). This refers specifically to the fourth mental state, which alone is designated as "formative action. Therefore, they are divided into two groups:

consciousness (*vijñāna*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and feeling (*vedanā*) are grouped as one, while the mind of formative action is grouped as another. Regarding the phrase "due to reaching and maintaining," this explains the reason for establishing the "maintaining" (*dhāraṇa*) precept.
According to the *Great Commentary* (*Dàshù*), one should first raise the following objection: "In the three mental states prior to formative action, there is 'stopping-maintenance' (*zhǐchí*)."

Is this [the state of] being determined (*vyākṛta*) or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) karma? If it were determined karma, then since the three minds are not [wholesome] conduct (*caryā*), how could they constitute karma?
If it were indeterminate, it should not be called "maintaining" (*dhāraṇa*). The current text answers by saying, "By virtue of the original undertaking (*samādāna*) and so forth.

Although one may be within an indeterminate state of mind, with respect to the side of non-transgression, the essence of the precept (*śīla-tattva*) remains pure; thus, it is designated as "maintaining. If that is so, prior to conduct...

Regarding the three minds: if one does not cultivate various virtues, one should incur a "cessation-offense" (*zhi-fan*). Answer: Since evil has fundamentally never been acquired, there is no virtue to come and reform it;
thus, it is not called a cessation-offense. As for the statement that "the reception [of the precepts] reaches [them]," one should first raise this objection:

practicing the three preceding minds is neutral (*avyākṛta*). Neutral minds possess "cessation-maintenance" (*zhi-chi*). Since cessation-maintenance exists within these three minds, cessation-maintenance ought to be...

[Question: Is the essence of the undertaking (*samādāna*) itself indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)? [Answer in the *Chao* (Commentary): The essence of the undertaking is determinate (*vyākṛta*), and so forth.

This means that when one first receives the precepts, it is established within a mind of wholesome conduct; thus, the essence of the undertaking is determinate. The three minds [of the subsequent stages] are neither wholesome nor unwholesome; they are indeterminate.
Now, the determinate "stopping and maintaining" (*śīla-saṃvara*) operates within these three indeterminate minds. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Although his mind..."
Regarding the unwholesome and the neutral (*avyākṛta*): the precepts originally received are not called "lost," yet they are still termed "maintaining the precepts.

Question: What is meant by "neutral"? Answer: It refers to that which cannot be defined (*avyākaraṇīya*) in terms of being wholesome or unwholesome; furthermore, it means there is no future fruit to be defined.
This differs from the wholesome and unwholesome, which can be defined as having future results that are either beneficial or detrimental. Question: How many kinds of the neutral are there?
The answer is that there are four types. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Vipāka (maturation), airyāpathika (postures), śailpasthānika (crafts), and nairmāṇika (transformation).

Regarding "vipāka": the distinction between cause and effect in terms of their nature is called "vi" (different); the arising of the fruit as a recompense for the cause is called "pāka" (maturation). This refers, for example, to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

The karmic causes that can summon it are by nature wholesome or unwholesome, yet the eighth consciousness itself is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). As for the "discrimination" of the six consciousnesses: "vi" belongs to the cause, and "pāka" refers to the fruit.

(This is a *tatpuruṣa* [dependent determinative] compound. If both "ripening" (*vipāka*) and "concomitant" (*sahaja*) belong to the fruit, it is a *karmadhāraya* [appositional determinative] compound. Regarding "dignified deportment" (*airyāpathika*): it refers to walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; picking up and putting down; bending and stretching.

That which possesses a standard of propriety is called dignified deportment. Regarding "craftsmanship" (*śailpasthānika*): it refers to things such as long and short, square and round, and so forth. Regarding "transformation" (*nairmāṇika*):

"transformation" (*pariṇāma*) means to alter or change the fundamental substance; "creation" (*nirmāṇa*) means that which suddenly comes into being where there was previously nothing. [This is the extensive explanation.]

As stated in the treatise: Question—Regarding the statement in this compendium that [the three minds] are designated as "indeterminate" (avyākṛta), among the four types of indeterminate states mentioned above, which one do they correspond to?
Answer—They are the first type, the retributive (vipāka) indeterminate. This is because these three are non-defiled (akliṣṭa).

In the second section, which comprehensively explains the four modes of practice as antidotes: first, regarding the statement from "stopping" (*śamatha*) up to "non-existence," this refers to the process from the preceding three moments of mind to the fourth moment of mind, wherein one is able to counteract and protect; this is termed "practice" (*caryā*). "Practice" carries the meaning of "constructive activity.
That is to say, when the three objects—suffering, pleasure, and so forth—manifest, first a consciousness arises that discerns them, and subsequently a perception (*saṃjñā*) arises that grasps them.

First, there arises the *ālaya-vijñāna* (image-consciousness); next, the *vedanā-citta* (feeling-consciousness) arises to experience [the three aforementioned neutral states]; finally, the *saṃskāra-citta* (volitional-formation consciousness) arises to perform action, which then brings about results such as suffering and pleasure.

Therefore, one knows that the *saṃskāra-citta* is karma, while the preceding three are not. This distinction is made according to the establishment of our own school’s tenet. Because they arise sequentially, there is this order.
However, according to many other schools, the primary mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) must necessarily arise simultaneously; thus, [this sequence] would not exist.

Regarding this sequence, the phrase "that which possesses a virtuous nature" refers to the differentiation of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). "Three" refers to the number. "Nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to essential nature; all possess these three.
It also carries the sense of "category," meaning that both mundane and supramundane phenomena comprise these three categories, which are called the "three natures.
What is now termed "virtuous nature" is a specific name. "Virtuous" (*kuśala*) has the meaning of being "conducive and beneficial"; it is to be in accord with the correct [path].

Principle (*nyāya*). Because it benefits both oneself and others, it is called "virtuous nature" (*kuśala-svabhāva*). Now, these two observances (*dhāraṇī*) accord with correct principle and their merit benefits both self and others;
therefore, they are exclusively virtuous. These three natures are not different from the four minds; one should understand that they are merely distinct categories.
Next, regarding the two types of transgressions, the phrase "ceasing the distracted mind" refers to the unwholesome mental activity that, through its completion, constitutes a transgression. (Note)
The elimination of redundancy can be understood. Regarding those restricted to the nature of the unwholesome (*akuśala*), they are also distinguished by way of the three natures.

"Unwholesome" has the meaning of contrariness and harm; because it contravenes correct principle and harms both oneself and others, it is termed "unwholesome. Now, only two types of transgressions are established.
Since this contradicts correct principle and harms both oneself and others, it is restricted solely to this case.

Regarding the phrase "if one reaches [the act]": previously, it was based on the premise that the preceding and succeeding moments of mind are one, and thus the observance (*dhāraṇa*) and violation (*āpatti*) are also one;

now, this is based on the premise that the preceding and succeeding moments of mind are distinct, and thus the observance and violation are also distinct. Alternatively, if one first gives rise to a mind of anger and intends to carry out an act of killing, this immediately constitutes the performance of a transgression (*karmapatha*).

If one subsequently gives rise to a wholesome mind and ceases from killing, it becomes "abstention through observance" (*virati-samvara*). Alternatively, if prior to encountering the object one gives rise to non-anger and other such states, and the mind remains free from killing and so forth, this constitutes "observant conduct.
However, if one subsequently gives rise to a mind of anger and commits the act of killing, it constitutes "offensive conduct.

Thus, depending on whether the preceding or succeeding moments arise, and depending on the differences between the preceding and succeeding mental states, the distinction between observance and offense likewise differs; hence it is said that there are distinct forms of observance and offense. The former case is generally categorized as wholesome.
The mind of unwholesome conduct has been distinguished. Now, it is explained separately by way of the sequential arising of the three wholesome roots and the three poisons.

Although there are differences between upholding and violating them individually, they are all instances of the mind of conduct; in principle, they are not difficult to discern. Therefore, it is said that they "can be known."

Regarding the second section, which distinguishes [the offenses] by way of the three types of action (*karma*), the introductory text may be understood accordingly. In the explanation, the first two—the bodily and the two forms of retention—are as stated in the text.
Regarding the combined analysis of the transgressions, the opposite of the above may be understood (and so forth). Next is the single mental action (*manas-karma*).

As for the statement "single [action] leading to a transgression," it is because the body and speech have not yet been moved. The text of the *Mahīśāsaka* school states: "At that time, there was a bhikṣu who thought of releasing another's piglet."
Furthermore, seeing a boat floating on the waters of the Ganges, he thought of stealing it; yet, without moving his body or hands, he raised all manner of questions to the Buddha.

The Buddha said, "There is no offense. It is only when one moves the body or speaks that a karmic act is fully established. This is because for Śrāvakas, offenses of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) are not proscribed.

The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Ordinary people are constantly conditioned by objects of desire; if a noble one were to establish a precept for the mind alone, there would be no one who could achieve liberation."

Regarding the "period": to say that one has reached [the point of completion] means that having moved the body and speech with the intention of performing such an act toward that object, one immediately incurs the offense of distant preparation (*dūre-prayoga*).
As for what is further explained later, it is as in the section on the subsequent attainment of the fruit;

concerning the first precept, when the internal mind harbors lustful intent while body and speech have not yet manifested, this is termed "distant preparation," and so forth—this should be understood. (The section on the door of accomplishment is concluded).
Now follows the fourth section, the Gate of Penetration and Obstruction. The text has two parts: the heading and the explanation.

Since it has already been clarified—by way of the mind and by way of the nature—that the four practices constitute the locus for the formation of karma, this is already known. However, regarding the two distinct aspects of penetration and obstruction, one has not yet thoroughly mastered them; therefore, they are explained next.

Regarding the explanation of the names: "four" indicates the number; "manifesting" (*ming*) means to reveal and clarify. When within a single practice one accomplishes it equally with other practices, it is called "universal" (*tong*);
if within a single practice one accomplishes only that single practice, it is termed "obstructed" (*se*). As for the statement that these are divided into four gates:
This refers to the characteristics of pervasion and obstruction, which are profound and difficult to clarify; they cannot be distinguished by means of only one or two gates.
Therefore, it is necessary to explain them through four gates: the first gate concerns the activity of karma as being exclusively obstructed and non-pervasive;

the second gate is both pervasive and obstructed; the third gate is exclusively pervasive and not obstructed; and the fourth gate is both obstructed and pervasive. If the upholding and violating [of precepts] are pervasive...

In these instances, non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is predominant. Regarding the points where transgression and observance intersect, non-informative action is present. This is intended to make people recognize the quantity of karma involved, so that by avoiding transgression, one achieves observance.
Regarding the statement "one [mind] to one [object]": this means that a single mind confronts a single object.

Now, the reason we speak only of the mind and not of the object is to avoid confusion with the two subsequent sections on objects. As for "only in relation to the action": this refers to the moment when one is actually abstaining from killing and the karma is completed;
at that instant, one only accomplishes the "abstention-and-maintenance" (*śīla-dhāraṇa*), and can no longer engage with the other three modes of conduct. This applies to all four types of conduct.

The mind has no simultaneous objects of concern because a single mind does not take two things as its conditions (*ālambana*). When the mind correctly arises taking as its condition an object of abstention from killing, it cannot simultaneously take other objects, such as those for the purification of transgressions (*śuddhi*), as its conditions.
This is because when the object of restraint (*saṃvara*) is present before one, the object of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) cannot appear simultaneously.

This is stated solely with reference to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) of performing an action. (If one were to engage in contemplative practice regarding sexual misconduct, theft, and so forth, these would belong to the subsequent category.)
[This is] excluded from this section). Section Two consists of two parts:
the heading and the explanation. Regarding the phrase "from 'two' to 'obstructing,'" this refers to a single mind in relation to two objects.
For example, when a single mind of wholesome action arises, it universally relates to both the objects of abstention and engagement;

likewise, when a single mind of unwholesome action arises, it universally relates to both the objects of abstention and engagement regarding transgressions. This section specifically concerns the meaning of simultaneous observance and violation within a single essence.

When the mind relates to its object, the transgressions of the respective categories are simultaneously established; because they are established through the universal presence of the two types of observance, there are no such designations as "two transgressions" and so forth.
Therefore, it is said that there is both penetration and obstruction.

To say that obstruction reaches existence means that upholding [the precepts] is without transgression, while transgressing is without upholding. Upholding is good; transgressing is evil; because they do not coexist.

To say that upholding and transgressing mutually penetrate one another means that within the upholding by cessation (*śīla-saṃvara*) there is upholding by action (*kriyā-saṃvara*), and upholding by action likewise...

The categories of "observance" (*śīla*) and "cessation" (*virati*) are mutually inclusive; their violations are explained as the reverse of this, meaning that both observance and violation are mutually pervasive.

In the subsequent detailed explanation, the phrase "as with observance" indicates that observance and violation are mutually inclusive of one another. For example, the cessation of the act of killing is "observance by cessation" (*virati-śīla*);

the performance of contemplative practice is "observance by action" (*kriyā-śīla*); and the making of robes and bowls according to the Dharma is "observance by action. Likewise, the cessation of improper conduct and measurements is "observance by cessation."

The same applies to the two types of offenses (*āpatti*). To state it conversely: for instance, constructing a dwelling without having requested permission is an offense of abstention (*virati-āpatti*);

violating the instruction constitutes an offense of action (*kriyā-āpatti*), which is to say, there is action within the context of abstention. Conversely, making an unlawful robe or bowl is an offense of action;

abstaining from exceeding the prescribed dimensions is an offense of abstention, which is to say, there is abstention within the context of action. Regarding the initial inquiry in the "Discrimination" (*vibhaṅga*) section, it may be understood as follows. It says:

Answer: Regarding the term "up to the pervasive" (*yāvat-spharaṇa*), this precisely clarifies the meaning of mutual inclusion. For example, the cessation of killing is "cessation-maintenance" (*pratiṣedha-śīla*); the performance of contemplation is "performance-maintenance" (*vidhi-śīla*).

In this case, performance-maintenance serves as a secondary cause (*pāratantrya-hetu*), while cessation-maintenance is the primary subject (*mukhya-artha*). By including the secondary cause of performance-maintenance, one establishes the definitive state of cessation-maintenance;
this is what is meant by "including performance as cessation. The same applies within the context of performance: for instance, performing according to the Dharma.

When performing the act of wearing robes, this constitutes "observance through action" (*kriyā-samvara*), which is not merely an observance of restraint (*vāraṇa-samvara*) based on the physical dimensions of the robe.

Restraint serves as a secondary cause, while action is the primary subject. By incorporating the secondary cause of restraint, it completes the primary subject of action; thus, by subsuming restraint within action, it is simply termed "observance through action.
The same applies to the two types of offenses; they can be understood by reversing this explanation.

"Manifestly distinct" (*jùzōng lìrán*) refers to the appearance of clarity. "Pervasive and diffuse" (*tōngmàn*) refers to the appearance of non-distinction. Furthermore, when water flows level and wide, it is called "diffuse.
Since the present case is not like this, it says, "How could this be pervasive and diffuse? The next four lines provide a response by distinguishing [the two].
Although the preceding section raised the fundamental tenet and reached a conclusion, it had not yet specified the differences between the mind and its objects; therefore, [this section] is composed.

Dividing this into four propositions: first, the distinction between the mind of restraint and the mind of performance. For example, in the construction of a house, the restraint of the mind from exceeding the prescribed dimensions is the mind of restraint-and-maintenance (*śīla-dhāraṇa-citta*);

subsequently proceeding with the construction is the mind of performance-and-maintenance (*kriyā-dhāraṇa-citta*). Second, the distinction between the objects of restraint and performance. For example, the restraint against constructing [a house] that exceeds the prescribed dimensions.

Third, the correspondence between the restrained mind and the object of performance. As in the aforementioned case of not exceeding the dimensions for a house, this is the object of restraint-and-maintenance.
A house of the proper measure is the object for the observance of performance (*kriyā-śīla*). Regarding the four types of mental application toward the object of restraint (*niṣedha-śīla*):

the intention to construct a house according to the Dharma is the mind of performance-observance; it is specifically directed toward the object of restraint, which is a house exceeding the proper measure.

Alternatively, it may also be explained as the restraint of an act that was about to be committed. In the former two cases, the mind and the object differ; in the latter two, the mind and its corresponding object are distinct—namely, the two categories of restraint and performance.

[The text] maintains that although characteristics exist, their distinctions are clearly evident. The two offenses are explained in reverse order as being identical. Next, the explanation by way of specific instances is given:

regarding the phrase "if one reaches [the state]," the two contemplations constitute the antidote for detachment; subsequently, with respect to the objective sphere, one does not commit killing or stealing.

This refers to the separation from the fruition and the practice. First, performing the antidote is "active treatment" (*pratipakṣa*); subsequently, abstaining from killing and stealing is "restraint through observance" (*samvara*). This is precisely the transformation of active engagement into restraint.

As for the phrase "if one reaches cessation," it means first ceasing external conditions; looking toward the abandonment of gross transgressions, this is called "cessation. This constitutes separation through the antidote.

When wholesome conduct is accomplished, it is called "action" (*kṛti*); this refers to the fruit of action being free from [faults]. First, one ceases external conditions. Xuán says: "The explanation of the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*) concerns freedom from gross transgressions;

the explanation of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts) concerns the fifty-odd *dharmas* of the *karma*. To distinguish the person, it suffices that one is free from gross transgressions to obtain [the result]."
Regarding the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*), even minor transgressions (*duṣkṛta*) must be confessed; however, one must not speak of them at all, whether they be grave or minor.
If one is free from such faults, one must eliminate external conditions. In this context, a wicked bhikṣu constitutes an external condition.

Knowing that the [Uposatha] falls on the fourteenth day, one should perform the recitation on the thirteenth day, and so forth (all schools follow this explanation). Alternatively, one may rely on Master Jing-shui, following the *Shou-sū* (Commentary on the *Śrāmaṇera-śīla*).
The self-commentary states: First, one must cease the coarse, agitated mind that dwells upon external objects; only when there is tranquility can [the precept] be accomplished.

Because it aims to distance oneself from gross transgressions, it is called "observance through cessation" (*śīla-virati*). Subsequently, when the karmic practice is perfected, it is called "observance through action" (*kriyā-śīla*). (This interpretation is precise.)

Regarding the statement "active transgressions reach the category [of offenses]": for example, when a person commits evil, this is an active offense (*kṛta-āpatti*); failing to first train in the wholesome is a passive offense (*vārita-āpatti*).
Thus, within the active, there is also the passive. As for the term "extremes" (*anta*) here, Xuánzàng says: "The characteristics of these two offenses involve 'following' and 'raising';

both the middle and the extremes are applicable, and there is no separate principle [for distinguishing them]. Alternatively, some explain that the extremes differ from the middle: the passive offense occurs first, while the active offense follows.
Subsequently, this *śamatha* (stopping) of the mind exists on the outer edge of the *kriyā* (active) mind; therefore, it is called "the edge" (*anta*). If that is so, one might ask:

previously, in the section on *kriyā-dhṛti*, it was stated that first stopping external objects is *śamatha-dhṛti*, and subsequently the successful accomplishment of good conduct is named *kriyā-dhṛti*.

Since this *śamatha-dhṛti* would likewise exist on the outer edge of the *kriyā-dhṛti* mind, why was it not mentioned there? It is not so. Later, another interpretation states: "This refers to the transgression of *kriyā*."

There may be cases of abstention-offense (*virati-āpatti*). If one does not personally train in committing an offense but instead instructs another to do so, then within this very act-offense (*kriyā-āpatti*), there is necessarily an abstention-offense.

One should say that within the mind of the act-offense, there is an abstention-offense. If, however, one personally trains in committing an offense and instructs another to do so, then within this very act-offense...

There is certainly no such thing as "stopping-off transgression" (*zhìfàn*). One should say "committed transgression" (*zuòfàn*). This is because there is no stopping-off transgression within the mind. Thus, the excerpted text states:

"As for 'similar categories,' this refers to those who have received the training precepts; when they commit an offense, there is no stopping-off transgression. The term "no" here merely means that there is no "stopping-off transgression" regarding the performance of the formal instruction (*jiàoxíng*); it does not mean that the objective act itself is absent.

Regarding "stopping-off transgression," as seen in the second section on the two types of transgressions in the *Shǒushù*, both the "objective act" (*shì*) and the "performance" (*xíng*) include the character "limit" (*biān*). Therefore, that text [states]: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the omission of the specific passage from the source text.*

It is said: Regarding the presence of *kṛta-āpatti* (active offense) within the sphere of *avijñapti-āpatti* (non-informative offense), if one considers it from the perspective of non-learning (*aśikṣita*), there is no *kṛta-āpatti* within *avijñapti-āpatti*.
However, when contrasted with spiritual practice (*bhāvanā*) in order to clarify *avijñapti-āpatti*, there is indeed *kṛta-āpatti* within *avijñapti-āpatti*.

For example, when a person builds a house, keeps extra robes without having requested formal permission (*jñapti*), or fails to perform the ritual of "purification" (*viśuddhi*) after the designated day has passed—these are instances where *kṛta-āpatti* exists within the sphere of the mind of *avijñapti-āpatti*.

[The above is the text of the *Shu* (Commentary). Regarding that [text], it classifies transgressions according to teaching (*jiao*), practice (*xing*), and understanding (*jie*). The fourth category, "cessation of transgression" (*zhifan*), refers to non-manifest transgression (*wuzuo fan*). Therefore, it says:

"The *Bianchao* (Borderline Excerpts) classifies 'cessation of transgression' based on the understanding of the matter; it definitely concerns manifest transgression (*youzuo fan*). Thus, it states that the middle section clarifies the third category, "manifest transgression.
When a transgression is completed, whether there is cessation of transgression with respect to the teaching and practice is indeterminate; hence, it is termed "borderline" (*bian*).

The section on the four types of *śikṣāpada*-violation (*śikṣā-vyatikrama*) has two parts. First, following the previous [discussion], it establishes the common characteristics of the two types of violations.

Second, if one considers the lower [stages], it permits non-learning as a form of *śikṣā-vyatikrama*; this does not mean there is no subsequent training. Regarding the statement "ceasing until this point," it refers to the case where one keeps extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*) but ceases to perform the ritual of *viśuddhi* (purification).
This constitutes a *śikṣā-vyatikrama*. After eleven days have passed, when the dawn appears (*aruṇa-udaya*), the misconduct becomes established as a formal offense (*kṛta-āpatti*). That is to say:

Within the state of *sthiti* (abiding) there is *kriyā* (action); the completion of action is subsumed within *sthiti*. It is like building a house: if one does not request formal authorization from the Saṃgha while abiding [in the process], this constitutes a transgression of *sthiti*;

subsequently, the construction of an illegal house constitutes an evil deed (*duṣkṛta*). When the work is completed, it constitutes a transgression of *kriyā*. This is precisely "action within abiding," wherein the completion of action is subsumed within abiding.
As for the statement, "If one looks toward non-learning, there is a transgression of *sthiti* and a transgression of non-action (*akriyā*)," this phrase is an excerpt.

This is the meaning of the opening commentary. The intention of the ancients was this: if one does not study the teachings and thereby incurs a *saṃvara-āpatti* (an offense of restraint), then within that very *saṃvara-āpatti*, there is certainly no *kriyā-āpatti* (an offense of action).
For example, today, as soon as the thought of not studying arises, at that moment one incurs a *saṃvara-āpatti*.
However, since one has not yet acted toward an object, there is no *kriyā-āpatti* among the five categories of offenses (*pañcāpatti*). Thus, [the *kriyā-āpatti*] has not yet been incurred.

"An offense. This refers specifically to the offense committed at that very moment; it does not extend to the commission of an offense through habitual practice. Since the general meaning cannot be established [in this way], it is necessary to distinguish them.

Regarding the statement, "It is not that they do not inherit one another, yet there is no subsequent habituation," this is the current master’s interpretation. It means that if one restrains the mind today but does not train, there is only the fault of non-training;
there is no offense of non-action (*avijñapti*). Nevertheless, this principle is not without merit. From the perspective of the long term, it occurs spontaneously.

This is established by practice; it also establishes the general principle. To illustrate this with an example: suppose one currently practices *śamatha* (calm abiding) but does not train in attaining it, thereby committing an offense of non-training.
Later, when confronted with objects such as sexual misconduct or theft, one commits transgressions according to what is done, resulting in the commission of root offenses (*mūlāpatti*).

These root offenses also arise because of the failure to train in *śamatha* in the past, which leads to a lack of recognition regarding the objects encountered. If the offense of non-training in *śamatha* were first established, then [the subsequent offenses would follow].
Let this be set aside for now and not further discussed. However, based on the presence or absence of ignorance regarding the offense at the moment of transgression against the object:

if one is entirely ignorant of the root offense, one commits a *thullaccaya*; if there is doubt, one incurs a *dukkaṭa*. This is also a case where both the abstention from the offense and the commission of the offense are simultaneously habituated;

is this not a universal principle? Therefore it is said: "It is not that subsequent habituation is absent" (if one wishes to provide a false interpretation, one may take whatever one likes from various schools).
The third section. Regarding the statement "the three lead to penetration" (*tṛtīya-mukha*):

the general meaning of this passage is that one first instructs others to perform four practices, and subsequently cultivates them oneself, entering into these four modes of conduct. When the four practices are performed within the mind simultaneously, their activity is accomplished;

this is explained as the meaning of "penetration. If there were necessarily a sequence of before and after, it would not constitute the meaning of penetration. As for the "four phrases" (*catuṣkoṭi*):

This refers to the distinction between preceding and succeeding actions. One personally cultivates four practices: first, the personal cultivation of *śīla-vāraṇa* (maintaining restraint), which may consist of maintaining restraint, committing an offense, or ceasing an offense.
These four personally cultivated practices constitute the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). Within these four propositions, each universally applies to teaching others;

since all four practices are accomplished simultaneously, it is said that one both acts oneself and teaches others. Thus, all four propositions are universally applicable, meaning that within each individual proposition, there is the act of teaching.

There are four modes of conduct for a person. These four multiplied by four make sixteen modes of conduct; when combined with the four modes of self-initiated conduct, there are twenty modes in total.
In the commentary, the phrase "as one who maintains [the precepts]" refers to the preceding preparatory mind (*pūrvopāya-citta*).

For example, at midday, if one intends to practice the conduct of maintaining through cessation (*śamatha-dhāraṇa*), one prepares the preliminary means before the conduct is fully accomplished. Suppose, for instance, that—
"Monks, each shall practice a single duty. First, have one monk bring me water filtered by midday to protect the lives of insects;
this is 'abstention-and-maintenance' (śīla-saṃvara). In principle, the practice of abstention-and-maintenance is perfected when the water is actually being filtered.

Although it is not yet being filtered at present, this is nevertheless a preparatory means for abstention-and-maintenance, just as the effect is spoken of within its cause. Next, he commanded another monk...

"Kauṇḍinya, to hold an intention and declare it within the Saṃgha constitutes an *āśraya-karman* (act of formal undertaking). Furthermore, to command another bhikṣu to take life, or to act against an enemy, and so forth, constitutes an *ārambha-karman* (act of commencement).
Moreover, to command another bhikṣu to construct a dwelling without having requested the formal procedure (*jñapti-dharma*), this constitutes a *samāpti-karman* (act of completion).
These four matters above, though not yet fully executed, are all considered the mind of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*). Once the four bhikṣus..."

Each has understood the meaning. Therefore it is said, "Having performed the four matters. This word "having" (已) refers to the completion of the monks' understanding of the meaning, not to the conclusion of performing the four matters;
it means "at that time, having [understood]. Thereafter, at the hour of noon, one personally cultivates the practice of one restraint (止持).
Thus it is said, "The subsequent mind applies its attention to depart from all transgressions and offenses. One correctly cultivates this practice.
At the moment of completion, the four types of conduct previously taught by the preceding mind each cultivate a single matter and are all set in motion:

the first bhikṣu, at the exact hour of noon, filters water, thereby accomplishing the practice of "maintaining through restraint" (*śīla-saṃvara*); the second bhikṣu is in the process of reciting the *poṣadha* invitation, thereby accomplishing the practice of "maintaining through performance" (*kriyā-saṃvara*);
the third bhikṣu kills a living being before him, whereby his livelihood is severed and he accomplishes the practice of "offense through performance"; the fourth bhikṣu constructs...

Regarding the practice of not begging for a dwelling, once it is established, one commits an offense through non-performance; however, by being able to instruct a bhikṣu, one subsequently forms the intention to abandon faults and maintains restraint through performance.

This universally includes that which is taught, such that when the four types of conduct are complete, it should be said that within the category of "maintaining through restraint" (śīla-saṃvara), there is both "restraint through non-performance" and "performance through action."

There is the offense of commission and the offense of omission. Because the *Chao* (the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan*) preserves only the essentials, it cites just one example of these four modes of conduct; this serves as a model for understanding the remaining three.

Next, regarding the explanation of the three modes of conduct being common [to all], the phrase "up to and including the Dharma" means that these transcend both the acts of commission and non-commission.

One directly takes up the single practice of "cessation-offense" (*zhi-fan*) as a general characteristic according to the treatise; even within the mind of cessation-offense, both "observance" (*chi*) and "offense" (*fan*) are fully present.
If the four preparatory practices (*upāya*) of what is taught are no different from those in the section on "observance-through-cessation" (*zhi-chi*), it is therefore said:

"As previously explained, after having dispatched another person to perform the four aspects, one subsequently cultivates for oneself the single practice of cessation-offense until its completion. Hence it is said: "Thereafter, one simply ceases [the action]."

This refers to training in wholesome dharmas. One is able to instruct a bhikṣu. When the training in wholesome dharmas ceases and an offense is committed, the four modes of conduct previously taught are simultaneously accomplished within the mind that commits the offense. Thus, even within the commission of an offense, all four modes of conduct are present;
that is, within the commission of an offense, there exists the commission of an offense and so forth.

The fourth section. The text has two parts: stating the number and the explanation. Regarding the phrase "from four to penetration": this means that one first employs four types of preparatory practices (*upāya*) out of fear of their subsequent results.

Later, one’s own mind again enters into a single practice. When the time comes for the subsequent result of the four prior preparations to be realized, it is simultaneously accomplished by the single practice performed by the later mind.
Therefore, it is said that the self-activity of the preceding and succeeding moments mutually completes one another.
Regarding the latter line, to connect it with all four lines is called "penetration" (tōng); to establish only the preceding line is "obstruction" (sè).
In the commentary, where it says obstruction is easy to understand, it is simply as follows: one first makes a water-strainer for oneself, intending to use it later to filter water.
This is the cause of the practice of restraint (*śīla-saṃvara*). Once the water-strainer has been prepared, the subsequent mind personally takes hold of it to filter the water;

this is the fruit of the practice of restraint. This subsequent mental fruit-action is established precisely by virtue of the preceding mental cause-action. Thus, the preceding and succeeding moments of one's own karma mutually establish one another.
There is only the single practice of restraint, with no other three [practices] present; this is the meaning of "blocking. It is also like the preceding mind.
The act of killing itself constitutes the cause of the transgression of commission; subsequently, the actual execution of the killing is the fruit of that commission.

This resultant karma is established through the prior mind and is founded upon causal conduct. Thus, it constitutes only a single course of action (*eka-karmapatha*) and does not extend to other courses of action.

This principle is not difficult to grasp; therefore, it is said to be "easy to understand. Furthermore, this section is unlike the first section, where the single mind remains undifferentiated with respect to its objects.

It is "obstructed" (*sita*). Furthermore, it is not the same [as the previous case]. In the second gate, maintaining [the practice] without transgression is called "obstructed. This refers only to one's own karma across preceding and succeeding moments;
since these are all part of a single course of action, they are described as being "obstructed. Reflect on this. Regarding the statement that what is general extends to the specific:

it means that within the preceding state of mind, one personally cultivates the causes of the four practices and makes preparatory arrangements; then, within the subsequent state of mind, one further engages in the four distinct practices that follow.
Into what state of mind does one enter? The first four practices are accomplished simultaneously and are termed "penetrations" (*abhijñā*).

Within each of the four practices of the subsequent mind, all are permeated by the four practices of the preceding mind; thus, within a single practice there are four sets of four practices, which should be understood accordingly.

Therefore, it is said that penetration requires skillful means (*upāya*) and so forth. "As before, without difference" means it is largely the same as the section on "performing it oneself" within the "instructing others" chapter.

Regarding the slight difference in the concluding characteristics: Xuán says this means that while in the previous section one causes others to perform the fourfold expedient means (*upāya*), in this section one personally cultivates the fourfold expedient means;
thus it differs slightly from the former. Alternatively, according to Fǎzhèng, in the previous section one maintains the desire within the Saṃgha.

This section explains the characteristics of the expedient means for active practice (*kriyā-vidhi*). This gate restricts the *śrāmaṇera* and clarifies the characteristics of the expedient means for active practice.
The preceding gate prevents people from requesting permission to build a dwelling, thereby clarifying the characteristics of the expedient means for abstaining from transgressions (*virati-vidhi*).

This gate closes the door, manifesting the signs that clarify the characteristics of abstaining from transgressions. Thus, between these two types of characteristics, there are two differences; therefore, it is said: "The characteristics differ slightly."

It is so. Next, the general meaning is explained. Regarding the phrase "as previously... up to 'placing it oneself'": "as previously" refers to the aforementioned. "Placing the strainer oneself" refers to the preparatory mind as described before;

that is, placing the strainer oneself upon returning from the morning alms-round. This is the preparatory practice for the *śīla* of cessation and maintenance (hence the mention of "placing the strainer oneself," etc.).
Furthermore, if one raises a śrāmaṇera but fails to instruct and admonish him, there is the fear that he will commit an offense of omission;
thus, one restrains him and commands him to recite scriptures and so forth—this is the preparatory stage for the performance of a positive act (hence the phrase "restraining the śrāmaṇera," etc.).
