Alternatively, if one sees a person or an animal constantly passing by and subsequently sets out an instrument of killing, this is the preparatory stage for the commission of an offense of commission (hence the phrase "setting out instruments of killing," etc.). Furthermore, when one definitively knows that today...

When the Abbot performs various *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts), if one cannot bear it in one's heart and, furthermore, does not grant consent (*chanda*), but instead closes the door and manifests the appearance of being absent—this constitutes the preparation for a transgression of the precept of non-action (hence the mention of "closing the door," etc.).

After these four types of actions have been performed, one who practices the observance of restraint (*śīla*) correctly distinguishes the general meaning: namely, that the preceding mind has performed the four kinds of preparations until the time of noon, when the object of resentment [is encountered].

Upon arrival, one directs the mind toward subsequent mental engagement and cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and so forth. By contemplating the departure from all faults and transgressions, one accomplishes the practice of restraint through cessation (*śamatha-dhāraṇa*).

When this practice of restraint through cessation—free from killing—is accomplished, the four preceding signs simultaneously shift and transform. This refers to the instance when a person at a well filters water;

it should be joined with the preliminary preparatory mind (*pūrvaprayoga-citta*). Once the practice of restraint through cessation is accomplished, the novice (*śrāmaṇera*) within the dwelling maintains right mindfulness.

When the *sūtras* and so forth are completed, the act of holding is established; when the place for the lethal instrument is settled and life is precisely severed, the act of committing the offense is established;

when the head of the hall is performing the *karmavācanā* and the door is closed to manifest the sign, the act of ceasing the commission is established. These four aforementioned acts correspond precisely to the mental attention of the subsequent mind.
Free from all faults and transgressions, the practice of *śīla* (stopping and maintaining) is accomplished all at once; this constitutes the general meaning.

Within the practice of stopping and maintaining, there are both the two types of maintenance (*dhāraṇa*)—stopping and acting—and the two types of transgression (*āpatti*)—stopping and acting. All four modes of conduct are universally applicable; the text of the *Chao* (the sub-commentary) preserves this by being concise.

Regarding the phrase "even including stopping transgressions," it refers to the preliminary mental preparation and expedient means; thus, while only the single mode of stopping and maintaining is explicitly mentioned, it is understood to encompass all four modes of conduct.

The remaining three lines are concluded. Within each line, following the previous section on "stopping and maintaining" (*zhǐchí*), the preliminary mental application (*qiánxīn fāngbiàn*) and the four characteristics (*sìxiàng*) are distinguished as being general rather than specific.
These are further combined with the three degrees [of transgression] to clarify the intent of the *Tongchāo*. This is abbreviated; only the headings are indicated.

Regarding the three lines for the subsequent mental state (*hòuxīn*), within these three lines, the "active maintenance" (*zuòchí*) and "active transgression" (*zuòfàn*) are further abbreviated, leaving only the heading for "stopping transgression" (*zhǐfàn*). This is an abbreviation within an abbreviation.
Therefore it is said: "up to and including the cessation of transgressions," leaving a small remainder to indicate that they are not entirely absent (the preceding four sections are thus concluded).

Following the second section of detailed analysis, there are two sections on the cessation of transgressions. Regarding the statement "this leads to transgression," these refer to the latter two gates.

This refers to the third [section], the gate of performing it oneself or instructing others; and the fourth, the gate of the mutual establishment of one's own karma through preceding and succeeding factors.
Regarding the phrase "all in relation to the actual performance of construction and so forth," this follows the *Shoushu* (Initial Commentary) as a refutation of ancient interpretations.

According to the *Shoushu*, previous masters had never clarified these matters in relation to specific actions; they spoke only in terms of the Dharma, explaining the offense of non-learning regarding cessation (*śamatha*) by positing only three types of conduct.

It does not pertain to the offense of non-restraint; therefore, it carries the meaning of "blocking. As the ancients said: "For instance, within the third category [of offenses], there is no offense of non-restraint.
Suppose in the morning one instructs a bhikṣu: 'When it is time for the recitation, do not study the teachings of the Tripiṭaka.

If the person uses these words and the other gives rise to the intention not to study, at that moment the offense of *śikṣāpratyākhyāna* (refusal to train) is incurred as a *duṣkṛta*. This offense of restraint also belongs to the preceding category."
Regarding the person being instructed: for this reason, within this gate, there is no instance where one does not incur an offense of non-training (*aśikṣamāṇa-sāvadya*).

Furthermore, regarding the fourth gate, the "Gate of Accomplishment through the Characteristics of One's Own Action": suppose that in the morning one gives rise to the thought of non-training and makes a formal commitment (*samādāna*) not to train until noon;

at the very moment that thought arises, one immediately incurs the offense of non-training. It is not permissible to wait until the time of midday; it occurs simultaneously with the other three modes of action.

[The practice] is accomplished. Therefore, within this gate, it is likewise not applicable. As for why the opening commentary (*shūsō*) states that it is applicable, this does not refer to cases where one fails to train or merely commits an offense;
rather, it refers to arranging the matter at hand and waiting until other practices are attained, whereby they are all accomplished simultaneously.

As for the case where one does not request the formal act (*dharmakarma*), but instead sends someone to build a dwelling, closes the door to manifest a sign, and does not grant consent (*chanda*)—this constitutes the preliminary mental preparation (*pūrvamanas-kauśalya*).

One does not incur the offense immediately; rather, it is only when the dwelling is completed and the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is performed by the Head of the Community (*sthavira*) that the offense of cessation (*niḥsargika-pāyattika*) is incurred.

Regarding this matter of the offense of cessation, the guest is already involved. Once the remaining three modes of action are obtained, they are simultaneously perfected within the subsequent mind. As for the first two...
Regarding the section on "Passage and Obstruction": there is also a rule concerning the offense incurred when a messenger stops at the gate. As the preceding text states:
"Thereafter, one does not train in the wholesome dharmas," and so forth. (The fourth section, "Passage and Obstruction," is hereby concluded.)

The fifth is the Gate of the Gradual and the Sudden. This section has two parts: citing the title and explaining it. Regarding the phrase "explaining the five types of gradual and sudden," this is the citation of the title.

Xuán says: "Above, the principles of penetration and obstruction were clarified; however, although these are known, the logic of the gradual and the sudden has not yet been refined, and therefore they are distinguished next.

As for the explanation of the names: when categorized according to practice, each being established individually is called "gradual"; when analyzed collectively from the perspective of the mind, it is called "sudden. Question: What is the relationship between the gradual, the sudden, and the universal (tōng)?

What is the distinction between "obstructing" (*sè*) and "blocking" (*bì*)? Answer: "Gradual" (*jiàn*) is somewhat similar to "obstructing," while "sudden" (*dùn*) is entirely different from "penetrating" (*tōng*).

For instance, within a single practice (*yī xíng*), if one conforms to and accomplishes that single practice without allowing other practices to intermingle, this is "gradual. This is necessarily somewhat similar to the "obstructing" of the preceding section.

If "sudden" were entirely distinct from "penetrating," then the presence of other practices within a single practice would constitute the meaning of "penetration" as defined in the preceding section; however, within a single practice, there is only...

To accomplish one’s own manifold single practice is the meaning of suddenness in this gate. That is, when the four practices are compared to one another, there are differences in horizontal and vertical alignment, as well as in what is permeable or obstructed.

When the four practices are compared to one another, one must carefully contemplate both the gradual and sudden aspects discussed horizontally, as well as the vertical explanations made by comparing each practice to itself.

In the commentary, the passage from "initial" to "sudden" is explained according to the clarity of the mind. Because the power of the mind is unimpeded, as it arises and encounters objects, there is a sense of suddenness.
Regarding the passage from "if" to "sudden," Xuán states: This means that at the time of first receiving the precepts, one intends to sever all evils;

if one now severs them all, this accords with the essence of the reception [of the precepts] and is called the "suddenness of the mind of cessation-and-maintenance. If, however, one forms the intention to simultaneously commit various evils...

This would contradict the nature of the undertaking (*samādāna*). It is called "the immediate transgressive mind. The rest may be inferred accordingly. As for the statement, "If one discusses the gradual [development] of the mind, it can be known by analogy," this means:
when the mind ceases and is simply separated from a single evil, this is the gradual development of the mind of cessation-and-maintenance (*niṣedha-samvara*).

If, according to that, one performs a single good deed, this is the gradual development of the mind of active maintenance (*vidhi-samvara*). If one intends to perform a single evil for the time being, this is the gradual development of the mind of active transgression (*vidhi-āpatti*). If one ceases [evil] and cultivates...

"First, the gradual [arising] of the mind that violates through improper cessation. The *Chao* (Commentary) states: "The categories can be understood by analogy; therefore, specific instances are not pointed out.

Regarding the phrase "there is nothing that does not reach the two divisions," this distinguishes between the two divisions of upholding and violating. One should first raise the following objection: "In general, for the completion of upholding or violating, it necessarily requires the mind to engage with an object before they are established.
Now, since the mind has not yet engaged with any object at all, how can there be the upholding or violating of the precepts? The *Chao* states: "There is nothing that does not..."
This is the answer to the following [question]. It means that while the substance of the precept (*śīla*) already exists, one now merely considers the arising of the mind:

if it accords with the substance of the precept, it constitutes observance (*dhāraṇa*); if it opposes the substance of the precept, it constitutes an offense (*āpatti*). Within this, there is a fourfold analysis: 1. Accordance within accordance:

for example, forming the intention to universally abandon evil and cultivate good; this is the second type of observance through the sudden application of the mind. 2. Opposition within accordance: for example, forming the intention to abandon [evil] partially.

1. Cultivating evil while practicing good: these two represent the gradual progression of the sustained mind (*citta-dhāraṇa*). 2. Contradiction within conformity: as when one initiates the mind to partially perform evil and partially cease good;

these two represent the gradual progression of the transgressing mind (*citta-āpatti*). 3. Contradiction within contradiction: as when one initiates the mind to entirely perform evil and entirely cease good;

these two represent the sudden occurrence of the transgressing mind. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Because at the time of initial reception, both were generated; now, one contradicts the essence of the vow."

"Sudden" (ton). One incurs many offenses. Regarding the second point, "in relation to practice" (dui xing zhong): from "two" up to "sudden," it means that "practice" (xing) refers to performing an action in relation to an object.
Since one cannot simultaneously cultivate two [opposing] practices, this follows the gradual approach. Regarding the phrase "from one to three":

for instance, when wearing the three robes, each of the three types of "wearing" (zhi) is established individually; one cannot say they are done "suddenly. This is true not only for these, but for others as well. Regarding "cessation" (zhi)...

Regarding "reaching" (*zhì*): for example, when one does not kill within the context of an enemy, this constitutes the observance of non-killing (*zhǐchí*), but it is not the observance of non-stealing (*zhǐchí*) and so forth.

The text on transgressions through action (*zuòfàn*) has two parts: first, an explanation following the general meaning; second, a detailed interpretation by citing specific instances. The first is as the text states. As for the phrase "now, reaching the explanation":

*qiě* (and/now) is a term indicating that the discussion is not yet exhaustive. Killing (*shā*) applies to all six realms of existence; here, we have not yet discussed the other five, but are addressing only human beings.
According to the treatise: furthermore, among human beings, there are the two distinctions of male and female; here, the discussion is restricted solely to males.
Moreover, for now, the explanation is based upon the body of a single male; therefore, it says "for the time being" (*qie*). As for the seven mental states:

they consist of the three singles—greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*)—the three pairs—greed-and-hatred, greed-and-delusion, and hatred-and-delusion—and the three [neutral] minds, which together constitute [the group].
First: This constitutes the sevenfold poisonous mind. For example, regarding the object of a single man, there are originally seven branches;
when the branch of sexual misconduct is added as two, they become eight. At the time one first receives the precepts, these seven poisons are applied across those objects to form fifty-six precepts.

Now, if one gives rise to a greedy mind and commits a single transgression against the precept against killing, there remain six other precepts against killing, as well as the remaining forty-nine [precepts].
Regarding the precepts: as for those who do not transgress any of the fifty-six precepts, the *Huainan Shunzheng* states that this is discussed in reference to other men.
The meaning is that since one man alone has not yet fully committed [transgressions], how much more so for the countless and boundless men who have not yet transgressed?
Since even one man possesses these fifty-six precepts, they are thus countless and boundless; all fifty-six precepts are likewise [infinite].

Regarding "not committing offenses" and so forth: the phrase "and so forth" includes the female object. Originally there were seven branches; by dividing sexual misconduct into three, they become nine.

When these are multiplied by the seven types of poisonous minds, they form sixty-three precepts. Now, even if one commits a single offense of greed and does not commit the other sixty-two precepts—such as killing—one is still considered to have fully refrained from them.
How much more so when it concerns many women, each of whom possesses all sixty-three precepts?
That is to say, one does not transgress any of the sixty-three immeasurable and boundless precepts; therefore, it is known that this is gradual.

As for the phrase "all as previously explained," this refers to what is stated in the *Piàn-zù* (Varga) and in the section on the arising of the precepts (*shòu-jì*). Reflect upon this interpretation as definitive.
If one follows the *Àn-jì* (Record of Cases), it states that the forty-nine precepts are taught with reference to a single man, while the fifty-six precepts are taught with reference to a single son.
If one man and one woman violate one [precept] regarding greed and kill the other six, they do not kill at all and thus do not violate [those precepts].
If one adds the six to the forty-nine for men, it becomes fifty-five precepts; if one adds the six to those for women, it becomes fifty-six.
Regarding the sixty-two precepts (this interpretation may perhaps contradict the *Chao-wen*): the *Xuan-ji* states that the fifty-sixth precept is also explained sequentially based on a single man;
however, various schools do not accept this—consider it well.

Regarding the phrase "three cases of reaching [the limit]": this refers to the transgression of ceasing [practice]. There are two aspects to the first practice; if it concerns the cessation of transgression regarding a specific matter, as well as the cessation of transgression regarding the Dharma-family (dharmakula) in relation to that matter, such cessation is exclusively gradual.

Its formation is no different from the previous three practices, so it will not be discussed again here. If, however, we consider the transgression of ceasing due to failing to study within the teachings, this applies to both the gradual and the sudden approaches, and thus it is explained separately.

Regarding the phrase "one case of not reaching [the limit]": (Note: The provided text appears to be a commentary on technical Buddhist scholastic terminology concerning the classification of transgressions (*āpatti*) related to the cessation of practice, specifically distinguishing between gradual (*anupūrva*) and sudden (*tadātva*) realizations.)

Regarding the term "hence" (*gù*): this section of the text intends to distinguish between the gradual and the sudden by contrasting "non-learning" (*bùxué*) with "ignorance" (*wúzhī*). Xuán says: "Non-learning is sudden;
ignorance corresponds to the gradual. If one clarifies only non-learning, then non-learning itself encompasses both the gradual and the sudden, as will be clarified below.

The reason for explaining these two offenses in relation to one another differs from the ancient tradition. The ancients said: "Both offenses are established based on the moment of sudden realization; they are both tied to the time of non-learning.

When the offense of non-learning is incurred, there is no room for the conditions of the object [of ignorance] to arise; since one has not yet understood, the offense of ignorance is incurred immediately.

Thus, both offenses are doubly established as being simultaneous. Now, the Master says: "At the time when the offense of non-learning is incurred, the offense of ignorance has not yet been incurred; it must wait..."

Wait. Only after five years of summer retreat (*varṣā*), when one’s understanding of the teachings remains incomplete, does one incur the offense of ignorance (*ajñāna*). This is explained in terms of the sequence in which the offenses are incurred to clarify the gradual and sudden [approaches].
Not studying first and then giving rise [to the offense] is the sudden; ignorance arising later is therefore gradual. Within this context, "not studying" refers to the sudden sense.

However, understand that defining "sudden" (dun) merely in terms of the arising of the mind does not contradict the meaning of "sudden" when referring to the immediate engagement with the objects of the teachings below.

Regarding those who, in their commentaries, do not accept this explanation, I request that you reconsider them. To cite the scriptural authority: the Buddha asked the bhikṣus, "Do you recite the *prātimokṣa* and the *karmavācanā*?
They replied, "We do not. Consequently, he established the rule that one must have spent five summer retreats (*pañca-varṣa*) before being permitted to recite the *prātimokṣa* and the *karmavācanā*.
"Not so. [This refers to] "governing according to the Dharma," and so forth (as detailed).

In the second section, the specific explanation means separating these two offenses and discussing them individually. Whether gradual or sudden, and whether indeterminate, the headings follow the text.
Regarding the explanation of the phrase "according to... the offense": "according to what is required by the mind" refers to that which is required by one's formal resolve (*samādāna*).
Regarding "the mind may learn regarding objects": this means that with respect to all ten thousand objects, they are all subjects of learning.

To form the intention not to learn is to apply this to the mind, wherein one does not practice or study at all. Regarding "instantly incurring many offenses for each and every dharma": this refers to the number of objects;

for as many such objects as there are, one instantly incurs a multitude of offenses. This citation from the fundamental school (zong) concerns both objects and the mind, whereby one instantly incurs [offenses].

There are many offenses. They do not share the same vows regarding light; they are determined by approximating the objective sphere (*viṣaya*) to establish the offense. Now, the objection is raised: "If there is no intention to commit an offense, how can an offense be established?

Furthermore, the offense of abstaining from transgression (*virati-pāpa*) is not the same as that of the East Pagoda school, which explains it solely in terms of the mind. Therefore, their commentary states:

One does not train [in the precepts] when the mind is withdrawn and lacks cognition of the object; if one generally ceases [transgression] by taking the Three Pitakas as the object, one incurs only a single offense.

If, however, it arises according to specific instances, it also constitutes a mental fetter (*citta-saṃyojana*). This differs from the ancients, who held that even when the object is not clearly understood at each individual stage of perception, one incurs the offense of non-learning (*aśikṣita*).
Yet, since the offense of non-learning does not arise solely from the objective conditions (*viṣaya-pratyaya*), how could it be incurred in every single instance of an object?

[The above is the text of the memorial. Now, an objection is raised: If it is held that one incurs only a single offense for failing to study all three Piṭakas while intending to master them, then if one gradually ceases the study of one Piṭaka, should one not incur a corresponding partial offense? Therefore, it is as when the offenses are formally defined.
One must consider how much offense is incurred by directing the mind toward an object; it is equal in number to the objects themselves.
Regarding the phrase "incurring the maximum offense," Xuán says this explains the reason why one suddenly incurs many offenses. One should first ask:

"How is it that by forming the intention not to train regarding an object that ought to be trained in, one suddenly incurs many offenses? This may be answered by citing the *Chāo* (Excerpts), which states that at the outset, regarding what was taught by the Buddha...
Regarding the Three Piṭakas: all wish to study them as the cause [of ordination]. It is only by giving rise to the mind of aspiration that one can obtain the precepts.

Now, if one ceases the mind and does not study, one violates the essence of that aspiration and thus incurs many offenses at once. This explains two points within the gradual [approach]. First, the question is clear. As for the statement "if one reaches the gradual [approach]," the answer is:
if one has the intention not to study the *karmavācanā* (ritual formulas) among the one hundred and eighty-four rules, then regarding these now...

Not learning the *śikṣāpada-uddāna* (recitation of the precepts) and the single motion (*jñapti*)—this does not mean it applies universally to all formal acts (*karmavācanā*). Rather, consider that there is only one offense [for failing to learn these].

As for "learning the rest," "the rest" refers to those outside [of the aforementioned]. Excluding the recitation of the precepts and the single motion, the remaining one hundred and eighty-three repetitions constitute "the rest";
this is because one must practice and learn them. From the perspective of the formal act (*karman*), one incurs an offense of cessation (*pratiṣedha-āpatti*) for failing to do so.
This means that, with respect to a single *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), it requires that one’s mind not yet have learned [the rule] and that one commits a single transgression;
this constitutes gradualism. Next, the separate explanation of the passage on "ignorance" has two parts: first, establishing the core tenet; second, the commentary.

Regarding the phrase "if it reaches," this means that while facing the conditions of a specific matter or dharma, one fails to understand them before the formal act is concluded; therefore, it is not instantaneous. Regarding the phrase "it refers to reaching gradualism": as for one who is ignorant—

In all cases, when one encounters objective conditions yet fails to comprehend them, this constitutes the formation of "ignorance" (*ajñāna*). This is explained with reference to the realm of form (*rūpa*).

As for the mental object (*dharmadhātu*), it is simply that which is being contemplated. The reason for this is that the minds of ordinary people never rest even for a moment; they fail to comprehend as they follow along with conditions.
Thus, at the time of encountering an object through ignorance, the mind does not have simultaneous deliberations, nor do objects appear all at once; therefore, it occurs only gradually.

[This is] also [the case]. Regarding the lightness or heaviness of the offense, first there are the two questions as in the text. As for the statement "the answer reaches the offense," the ancients said: according to the *Upasampadā-vidhi* (Method for Receiving Ordination), the formal conclusion (*niṣṭhāpana*) states, "You should study and inquire";
the concluding formula (*niṣṭhāpana-vākya*) states, "If you do not study in accordance with the Dharma... This passage is cited for the purpose of disciplinary treatment.

[The Vinaya] Master [Seng]zheng states: "Not learning this is auspicious. Regarding the second case of ignorance: as recited previously in the lower section of the *Vinaya*, one has now completely forgotten it;

the rule is established that one must be dealt with according to the law. Both instances mention being "dealt with according to the law," which definitively establishes it as a *duṣkṛta* (吉羅). Second, the current Master’s text has two parts.
At first, there was no formal study; the ancient masters were as described in the *Śāstra*. Next, ignorance is distinguished.

Regarding the statement "there is no arrival," if one is entirely ignorant of the fundamental source, one relies on the present analogy to cite what came before: it is said that one incurs a *pāyattika* offense regarding the precepts.

Thus, in the *Vinaya-nidāna*, there is a case where a bhikṣu had previously committed an offense and, fearing that a pure bhikṣu would cite his prior transgression, he went to a pure person and declared: "I have only now [realized this]."
[The monk] says, "I know. Regarding this section of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, the Buddha rebuked him, saying: "Why do you fear a pure bhikṣu? You say you only now realize it as soon as you are accused.
Since you say, 'I only now realize it,' it is clear that you were already possessed of ignorance (*ajānan*) prior to this. Furthermore, the Vinaya commentary on the characteristics states:

'Because of an unwholesome mental state, one listens to the Dharma with a single-minded focus while being ignorant; therefore, a *pāyattika* offense is again incurred. Moreover, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: 'Fundamentally...'"

Regarding the offenses: because one does not understand the underlying conditions (*pratyaya*), one further incurs the offense of ignorance (*ajñāna*); thus it is said that [the offense] is "increased.

In the lower section of the admonitions, it states that ignorance constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation). (The above is from the Commentary. If one suspects but has not yet fully understood, ignorance is treated as the same; this is because it is a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*). Therefore, the *Śīla-śāstra* says:

If one first recognizes the delusion and doubt, then the gravity [of the offense] depends on the conditions of one's training; there are thus distinctions between clarity and obscurity in the matter. Therefore, within the context of mental objects (*ālambana*) and perceptions (*saṃjñā*), doubt is judged according to its gravity;
whereas present-day delusion, characterized by a failure to recognize [the truth], is precisely what constitutes the downfall of grasping (*upādāna*). (The above is from the Commentary.)

In the third section, regarding the phrase "from three up to the individual," this refers to clarifying the boundaries of the preceding and succeeding offenses by means of the two transgressions of non-learning and ignorance, within the three types [of gravity] according to the teaching and practice from the perspective of the roots. Regarding the phrase "from each word up to the conclusion":

This is an explanation. Regarding the determination of the timing for the incurrence of offenses according to the Vinaya teachings, "from beginning to end" means that the initial reception [of the precepts] is the beginning, and the completion of one's entire life is the end.
The Vinaya mandates that one study for as long as one lives; therefore, at whatever time one fails to study, the offense of non-study is immediately incurred.

As for the statement regarding the "incurrence [of the offense] after five years of ignorance," this refers to citing the offense of ignorance, which applies only to the end and not the beginning, because one has studied prior to the five-year period.

If one has not yet mastered [the precepts], it is until the fifth summer retreat that the formal interrogation (*pravāraṇā*) is subsequently conducted. Why must this interrogation necessarily be deferred until after the fifth summer?

The answer, as stated by Xuán, is because three conditions are fulfilled: first, it is appropriate for the stage of "one who knows," since a person who studies with diligence attains understanding through their study.

Now, because he does not yet know [the teachings], the rule for dependence (*niśraya*) is established. This refers to those before five years of ordination who do not yet understand the characteristics of the doctrine;
thus, dependence is mandated. Now, because his own practice is not yet established, the rule is established. Third, this combines with the four stages of the teacher’s rank (*ācārya*).

Since he has not yet clarified the characteristics of the doctrine and has not attained the status of a teacher, the rule is established for those before five years of ordination, as well as these three types. Therefore, it is not [the case that the rule applies otherwise].

[The section on] Binding. Within the two [sections on] "practice in relation to" (*pratipakṣa*), the term "practice in relation to" refers to the previous explanation of the five years of summer retreats (*pañca-varṣa*) as taught according to the doctrine.

Now, it is explained in terms of practice, clarifying the progression from the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) to the noble one (*ārya*). It is because the precepts give rise to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), and only when one applies effort and practices the Dharma does the body finally become established. Now...

To distinguish the degrees of transgression regarding conduct, it is said that one must fear falling into degradation. This refers to the Noble Teachings of the Tripiṭaka, which must necessarily be studied and understood for the sake of severing delusions and attaining realization.
Now, having completed five summer retreats (*varṣa*), if one does not rely upon a teacher, there is a fear that the mind will become dissipated and laxity and pride will arise.
Merely understanding the contemplation of the five stopping-minds (*pañca-vipaśyanā*) and deeming oneself a peer to the Arhats—since the Arhats also understand this—is insufficient.
Because of this contemplation, the rule is established that the inferior shall follow the superior, and that the ordinary person shall dwell in reliance upon the noble one.

Regarding the phrase "the text stops here," it serves as evidence for the characteristics of descending from the superior to the inferior. In the text of the Vinaya’s method for receiving the precepts, it is stated that even a bhikṣu of five years’ standing whose conduct and understanding remain inferior must rely upon a bhikṣu of ten years’ standing, despite having completed five summer retreats. This is because the conduct and understanding of the ten-year bhikṣu are superior.

For the first five years, one thus restrains the inferior with the superior and relies upon the superior through the inferior, continuing until reaching many years of seniority and the state of an Arya.

Regarding the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*), the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 32, states: "The discipline of body and speech of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as right livelihood, are called the aggregate of morality (*śīla-skandha*).
The wishless samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*) is called the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*). Right view and right knowledge are called..."

The aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*) consists of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), as well as the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) associated with them; this is called the aggregate of liberation (*vimukti-skandha*).

[The name "liberation" is established here] because of mastery over the object, and does not refer to the unconditioned liberation that is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). The knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising are called the aggregate of the vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha*).
It is only when the fruit of Arhatship is attained that these five constituent bodies are fully established and one is finally freed from dependence.

Third, [the classification] is according to the faculties (*indriya*). Regarding the statement "in terms of the faculties": although previously it was discussed in terms of conduct (*caryā*), it is now further distinguished by way of those with sharp or dull faculties.

Regarding the phrase "if one reaches": this refers to those of sharp faculties. Baorui said: "As has been the case since antiquity, there were those who did not wait for the majority of the *qīngbiàn* (clear and complete) [period];
how could they require five years of summer retreat (*pañca-varṣa*)? Rather, following a single matter from beginning to end, one immediately incurs two offenses; from beginning to end..."

From the initial reception [of the precepts] until the end of life, during that interval, at whatever time one ceases to apply the mind, if one does not train, one incurs the offense of non-training (*aśikṣā*).

If, due to the conditions being unclear, one fails to understand, one incurs the offense of ignorance (*ajñāna*). Next, regarding those of dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*): it is said that "if they are established [in this category]," it means that because these faculties are dull, even if they train, they will ultimately not understand;
therefore, this person is regulated such that for as long as life lasts they must rely on others. If they do not rely [on others], [they incur an offense].
Other scholars merely incur the offense of not having studied; it is not due to a lack of intellectual power, for there is no such thing as ignorance [in this sense].

Regarding the phrase "as stated in the Vinaya" and so forth, the citation of the evidence can be understood accordingly. Xuán says: This refers to those who are extremely dull-witted, speaking of those who fail to master their studies throughout an entire lifetime.
If one is of middling capacity, the offense is determined according to their strength and understanding at the time of analysis—namely, whether they have studied for ten or twenty years.

If one has attained understanding through study, there is no offense for not having studied previously; however, if one has not studied for ten or twenty years and has completed that period, they incur the offense of ignorance (*ajñāna*).

Regarding the fourth category, "those that may be confessed": from the word "fourth" to "confessed," this refers to the offenses of non-learning and ignorance, which can be purified through confession.
It does not say that both types may be confessed; rather, the Master here directly answers that both are permitted to be confessed.
This immediately refutes the errors of the ancients. The ancients said: "If one does not commit the offense of non-learning, then it is permissible to repent for the offense of ignorance;

however, that [offense of non-learning] itself cannot be repented of. The reason for this is that the ancients said: "Suppose, for instance, that on a previous day one ceased learning with a settled mind, thereby incurring the offense of non-learning.

If today one resolves to learn again, this constitutes severing the continuous stream of the mind that previously refrained from learning. Since there is the sense of severance," [the offense can be removed].
Therefore, we permit repentance. If one speaks of ignorance, even if one were to study again today with renewed diligence, that study would still not be refined;

how could there be a sense of severance? Only if, in the future, one becomes thoroughly proficient and free from doubt—thereby attaining mastery of the teachings—would it no longer depend upon repentance.

Therefore, there is no sense of ignorance or severance; it cannot be expiated (the above is from the *Śāstra*). In the commentary, the phrase "from 'as if' to 'can be expiated'" means that the Master now wishes to clarify that while there is the principle of ignorance, there is also the principle of severance such that it can be expiated. First, he sets forth the reasons for the commission of the offense:

for instance, if one has not yet completed five years of summer retreat (*varṣa*), and previously ceased [one's practice] and did not study; or if, after completing five years of summer retreat, one encounters the same object or circumstance as before.

Yet they do not understand; this is entirely because they previously ceased their practice and did not learn through coming [to the teacher]. Thus, they incur the offense of ignorance (hence it is said: "if one ceases intention and does not learn," etc.).

Later, upon reaching six years of summer retreat (*varṣa*), they again resolve to learn. From the time of this resolution onward, when encountering phenomena or matters, they have doubts and fail to recognize them.

Because they are learning from a teacher, it is difficult for them to achieve clear understanding immediately; thus, while facing such objects, they do not incur the offense of ignorance (hence it is said: "if one makes the effort to learn, yet remains unaware," etc.).

If this is the case, one does not learn from the mind; rather, further learning leads to severance. Regarding ignorance, it is in relation to learning: since present learning has not yet been refined, ignorance is not yet bound.

Likewise, clear knowledge is not yet bound, yet there is severance. Since learning involves severance, and you have already granted that ignorance may be expiated through repentance, it should be understood by analogy that the same applies to non-learning (*aśikṣā*). (The fifth section, the Gate of Gradual and Sudden, is hereby concluded.)

The sixth section is the Gate of Superiority and Inferiority. The text has two parts: the heading and the explanation. Regarding the phrase "from the sixth to the inferior" (the underlying intent is as can be understood):

"superior" (*yū*) means strong; "inferior" (*re*) means weak. This gate differs from the preceding one in four respects: it specifically clarifies the gradual and the sudden, and it concerns present observance and violation.

This is to distinguish between the superior and the inferior. First, regarding the explanation of the two types of observance through ten gates: since these constitute the initial stage of generating the aspiration, they are placed first.

As it is difficult to discern superiority and inferiority in detail, one must divide them into ten gates so that students may abandon the inferior and follow the superior, thereby protecting the essence of their vows.
Regarding the phrase "from one to identical," this refers to discussing the four types of precepts and the methods for practicing and guarding them.
Second, because it maintains the superior and the inferior. To speak in terms of the Dharma, there are four distinct types. Regarding the first, "precepts" (*śīla*):

this refers to *iriyāpatha* (dignified deportment), which is the present *prātimokṣa*. It may exist solely in a state of non-concentration (*vīkṣepa*), merely guarding the seven branches of body and speech.

Because it manifests faults in contrast [to higher states], it is called "dignified deportment. It is also termed "turning away from following the mind," or said to be established upon the seeds of volition (*cetanā-bīja*). Above [this level]...

It is established as not following the three natures and four minds, for it functions [independently]. Regarding "guarding the faculties" (*indriya-saṃvara*): "guarding" means protection; "faculties" refers to the six sense-faculties.

A person possessing the four roots of goodness mostly dwells in a state of meditative stability, guarding the six faculties so that they do not give rise to defilement; this is called "guarding the faculties."

The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "The restraint of the faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*) of a śrāvaka becomes fully perfected only after beginning with the stage of training and continuing until the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Regarding what is called "precept co-existent with concentration" (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*), it refers to the sevenfold bodily and vocal restraints that prevent evil; these arise simultaneously when one dwells in a lower realm and attains the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), and so forth (and is thus named "co-existent with concentration").
Alternatively, it is called "non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) co-existent with concentration," which arises together with concentration.

Both [the dhyāna and the formless realms] possess this untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*), which cannot be manifested to others; therefore, it is called "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*). It is also termed "dhyāna-restraint" (*dhyāna-saṃvara*). "Dhyāna" means tranquility (*śamatha*);

"yāna" (here rendered as *lǜ*, meaning deliberation) refers to mental reflection, because it takes all objects of cognition as its focus. "Restraint" (*saṃvara*) signifies the cessation of evil and the prevention of wrongdoing.

Thus, one should know that meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) can prevent transgression and is therefore designated as "precept" (*śīla*). (If explained according to their general characteristics, the four fundamental dhyānas...)

The four *ārūpya-samāpattis* are termed "concentration-concomitant precepts" (*samādhi-sahabhū-śīla*). If discussed according to their specific distinctions, the term "precepts of concentration" (*samādhi-śīla*) applies exclusively to the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-dhyāna*), whereas the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) are termed only "dhyāna-precepts. (In this present excerpt, both are included).

Alternatively, they are called "precepts that follow the mind" (*cittānuvartin-śīla*), meaning that they possess the function of preventing wrongdoing precisely while one is in a state of meditative concentration. If one is in a distracted state of mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), these precepts lack that aforementioned quality;

for these precepts are established based on the actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) of volition (*cetanā*), unlike the prātimokṣa precepts, which are established based on the seeds (*bīja*) of volition.

Question: Since seeds lack cognitive engagement (*ālambana*), they may be called "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*). But since active manifestations (*samudācāra*) possess cognitive engagement, why are they called "unmanifest"?

Answer: This is a matter of the true nature of the jewels of principle. While it is said that [active manifestations] are "with manifestation" (*savijñapti*), the unmanifest possesses cognitive engagement because it is self-cognized; therefore, it is called "with manifestation."

It has no physical form or substance; it cannot be manifested to others, and is therefore also called "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*). Question: Both the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*) and the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) possess the precepts of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-śīla*).

How are they distinguished? Answer: In the Lesser Vehicle, these are exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*); in the Great Vehicle, they include both the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) and the with-outflows.

Furthermore, when the mind is in a state of meditative concentration in the Lesser Vehicle, it is termed "precept" because, by virtue of being able to restrain the seven branches of body and speech, one does not give rise to evil; moreover—
It is capable of giving rise to the sevenfold virtuous courses of action of body and speech;

when the mind is concentrated in the Mahāyāna, it can prevent the sevenfold unwholesome courses of action of body and speech while simultaneously giving rise to the sevenfold virtuous courses of action of body and speech. Thus, a sutra says:

"Furthermore, one sees a bodhisattva sitting in meditative concentration with palms joined, praising the Kings of Dharma with ten million verses," and so forth, as explained elsewhere. This is what is called the "precept concurrent with the path."
This refers to the period from the moment of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) up until the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).

Whenever one attains the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), there arises an unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) consisting of seven factors that coexist with the path; because it is associated with the untainted path, it is called "the offering of the path" (*mārga-pūjā*).

Alternatively, it is called the "unmanifest form coexisting with the path. This untainted wisdom cannot be manifested to others; it pertains exclusively to the untainted state and does not extend to the tainted (*sāsrava*).
Regarding the outflows (*āsrava*): Question—both the Great and Small Vehicles possess these precepts; how are they distinguished? Answer—there is indeed some slight distinction.
In the Small Vehicle, the eight [levels] consist of the four fundamental dhyānas, the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*) of the first dhyāna, and the lower three formless attainments (*ārūpya*).

When one reaches the various untainted (*anāsrava*) precepts (excluding the "non-place" [asaṃsthāna] because the Great Brahmā King dwells at the periphery), these are called the "unmanifest concomitant with the Path" (*mārga-sahabhū-avijñapti*). In the Mahāyāna teaching, there are four...

The four dhyānas, the four formless bases (*ārūpya*), and both the preparatory (*sāmantaka*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) concentrations are all collectively termed "concomitant with the path" (*mārga-samprayukta*), as they are all wisdom (*prajñā*).

Furthermore, according to the Mahāyāna, whenever there is an unmanifest [action] concomitant with the path, there must necessarily be an unmanifest [action] concomitant with concentration; however, it is not necessary that there be an unmanifest [action] concomitant with the path.

Moreover, "concomitant with concentration" is broad, encompassing both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted states, whereas "concomitant with the path" is narrow, applying only to the untainted. Furthermore, this precept is also...
This is established based on the manifestation of volition (*cetanā*). The rest will not be described in detail.

Next, regarding the assignment [of stages] throughout the sequence of levels, there are three positions in total. As for the phrase "from the beginning up to morality": the "beginning" refers to the first of the four dharmas, namely the morality of deportment (*īryāpatha-śīla*), which is assigned to the stage of the outer ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).
It is called "outer" because one has not yet contemplated the principle of the truths (*satya-dharma*) and has not yet attained non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*).

"Leakage" (*āsrava*) refers to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), namely the three preceding types of practitioners who apply the preparatory means (*prayoga*). Those at the stage of the five mental abidings (*pañca-vastu-sthiti-citta*) who contemplate the general and specific characteristics (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*) are said to be in this position.

They have not yet attained the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) harmony with the true principle; they merely attain harmony regarding phenomena (*vastu-sāmagrī*). Because they possess the functional utility of a Saṃgha in a provisional sense, they are called the "provisionally named Saṃgha.

Regarding the "two [types of] precepts" within the section on morality, these refer to the two precepts of guarding the sense faculties (*indriya-rakṣaṇa-śīla*) and that which is co-existent with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*). These are assigned to the maintenance of the stage of the internal ordinary person (*adhyātma-pṛthagjana*). This refers to oneself.
Contemplating the principles of the Truths (satya) constitutes the internal [aspect]. One who has not yet attained the untainted (anāsrava) state is an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).

This refers to the stages of the four roots of goodness (kuśalamūla)—namely, Heat (uṣmagata), Summits (mūrdhan), Patience (kṣānti), and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (laukikāgradharma)—which are associated with the principles of the Truths; these are called the Saṃgha of Union. If one lacks Heat and the others, even if one attains the four dhyānas, [one is not such a Saṃgha].
Nor are they ordinary practitioners (*pṛthagjana*), such as the non-Buddhists and others; this refers specifically to those who have attained [the fruit].
Regarding the "one type" mentioned later, this refers to the common precepts of the fourth path, which belong exclusively to the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*).

That is to say, the four fruits of the noble ones, being conjoined with the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) and remaining without further change, are called the "True Saṃgha. Alternatively, it refers to the first fruit, which abandons the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the three realms, and the second fruit.

Simultaneously abandoning the first six grades of the afflictions of cultivation results in the third fruit; simultaneously abandoning all nine grades of the afflictions of cultivation in the desire realm results in the fourth fruit.
When the afflictions of both seeing and cultivation in the three realms are exhausted, one is named a true *saṃgha*. Next, the section determining superiority and inferiority has two parts:

first, the heading as in the text; second, the formal analysis beginning with "Holding... The phrase "holding [the precepts] to the highest degree" means that through the protection of the *vinaya* of majestic deportment, one easily disciplines the body and speech.

Therefore, it is inferior. The restraint of the faculty-guarding precepts protects the mind slightly better. The restraint concomitant with meditative concentration (samādhi-samvara) is next best, as it arises from concentration.

The restraint concomitant with the Path (mārga-samvara), being untainted (anāsrava), is the most excellent. Since the text mentions the restraint concomitant with concentration, it says "up to" (yāvat).
Regarding the statement "the two most weak": the preceding section discussed this in terms of the *dharma* (teachings); thus, it cited persons to manifest the *dharma*.

In the present text, which discusses this in terms of stages (*avasthā*), the stages of those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and the inner ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) are presented to clarify the supremacy of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Because all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms have been exhausted, what was to be done has been accomplished, and the two kinds of liberation have been attained, it is called "liberation of mind. Because all outflows (*āsrava*) have been severed and eliminated, it is called [liberation by wisdom].

Regarding "liberation through wisdom" (*prajñā-vimukti*) and "one whose virtues are perfected": because both the virtue of abandonment and the virtue of knowledge are fully perfected, they are so designated.

Regarding "those who aspire for the three superior fruits through the practice of precepts": this refers to aspiring for the first fruit from the perspective of the second fruit, the second fruit from the perspective of the third, and the third fruit from the perspective of the fourth;

for as long as afflictions are not yet exhausted, there remains a subsequent fruit to be hoped for. This is the mutual comparison between those within the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those outside it.

Regarding those who are "gradually weaker": from the perspective of the internal ordinary person (*ābhyantarapṛthagjana*) looking toward the first fruit (*prathamaphala*), they are inferior; yet from the perspective of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), they are superior.

Furthermore, they are superior to the four stages of the internal ordinary person and the three stages of the external ordinary person. Consider how these are distinguished as superior or inferior when compared among themselves; this differs from various commentaries (and so forth).
Regarding the statement "the three are most excellent," this is explained in terms of human beings. This refers to ordinary persons among the sevenfold assembly of the laity and the ordained.
By means of this, we distinguish that among laywomen, five [faculties] are most inferior; men are next best. A *śrāmaṇerī* is not equal to a *śrāmaṇera*;
a *śrāmaṇera* is not equal to a *śikṣamāṇā*; a *śikṣamāṇā* is not equal to a *bhikṣuṇī*; and a *bhikṣuṇī* is not equal to a *bhikṣu*.

Regarding "because it is fulfilled, there is no aspiration": one originally sought the precepts with a mind of aspiration; now that they have been obtained in their entirety, the aspirational mind has ceased, and is thus called "no aspiration.
Furthermore, the two thousand training rules of the four directions flow constantly day and night; because there is nothing further to be sought or desired, it is superior.
Regarding the statement "fourfold according to practice," this is distinguished by way of the two occasions of cessation (*sthiti*) and performance (*kriyā*).

Regarding the statement "from cessation to expectation," this is distinguished based on the gravity of the offenses to be remedied: maintaining cessation (*sthiti-śīla*) by avoiding grave transgressions such as sexual misconduct and theft is superior;

maintaining performance (*kriyā-śīla*) by avoiding minor transgressions such as *thullaccaya* and *dukkaṭa* is inferior. Regarding the statement "if [it is] to the superior," this is distinguished by the ease or difficulty of the remedy.
They are distinguished as follows: they are superior because it is difficult to avoid the fault of being too light; they are inferior because it is easy to avoid the fault of being too heavy.
Regarding the statement "from five down to three," this distinguishes the three mental states in relation to what is wholesome and unwholesome. Regarding the statement "from one down to [one],"...
If one abandons evil and cultivates goodness, seeking the fruit of Buddhahood above, this is the wholesome mind that ceases and does not accept pleasure.
That is to say, one cultivates the wholesome root of non-attachment through detachment from defilement as a pure practice.

Since the three poisons, such as greed, can serve as the source of birth and death, one now does not give rise to these states of mind and refrains from all evils in order to seek liberation; this is the wholesome mind. In contrast to fundamental evil, [the following is] below...
This is an explanation by way of indicating the thing itself (*nirukti*), as in the text. Regarding the phrase "two do not reach [the path]," this clarifies the unwholesome mind.

Because one seeks fame and profit, or the retribution of birth in the human or celestial worlds, and because one's observance of the precepts has not yet transcended the boundaries [of worldly existence], one remains bound by this unwholesome mind.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "There are four matters that result in evil retribution: first, to surpass others; second, for fame and profit;
third, for the sake of one's retinue; and fourth, for worldly rewards. Regarding the phrase "the three are not ultimate," this refers to the indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*).

Even if one performs the aforementioned acts while in a state of delusion, madness, sleep, or the like—acts which are permitted by the Noble Ones—it still constitutes the observance of precepts, though it is the lowest grade of mind.

This is inferior. Regarding the phrase "if one uses it for equality" and so forth: the three minds previously listed were explained in terms of *śīla-vṛtti* (maintaining through restraint); now they are explained in terms of *kriyā-vṛtti* (maintaining through action).

When these three minds are compared, they likewise comprise three grades. For example, as in the case of becoming a Buddha: if one maintains the three robes and the alms bowl with a virtuous mind, this mind is the most excellent.
If it is for the sake of fame, profit, and so forth, it is a middling mind; if it is due to madness, sleep, and so forth, it is an inferior mind.
Regarding the statement, "If one looks toward the ultimate sincerity," this refers to the confusion arising from doubt. One should first raise the objection:

"While it may be acceptable for the middle grade [of practitioners] to act for the sake of fame and profit, how can those who perform the aforementioned evil deeds while in a state of non-defined (avyākṛta) madness or sleep, or who improperly maintain their three robes (tricīvara), be said to be 'maintaining the precepts'?
The *Chao* answers: "If one looks toward compliance with the teaching, as long as there is no violation of the teaching itself, it is generally [considered such]."

This is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*). That is, one does not differentiate among the three types of mind. The reason for differentiating them here is to determine their relative superiority and inferiority.
Regarding the sixth [point], within the context of "that which is sought," the phrase "from the six to the seeds" refers to having expectations regarding the mind that upholds the precepts;

this is termed "that which is sought" in order to distinguish their relative superiority and inferiority. In the commentary, the phrase "the boundaries of a single thief" and so forth means that it is solely the upholding of the precepts and solely the seeking [of results].

Fame and profit give rise to unwholesome states of mind; because they damage the wealth of merit, they are called "thieves. They are distinguished from other mental states and are termed "delimitations" (*pradeśa*).

The fundamental purpose of upholding the precepts is to seek the fruit of Buddhahood and *bodhi*; yet now, through flattery and wrong livelihood, one seeks to surpass others in order to pursue fame and profit.
This damages the very mind that correctly seeks *bodhi*—it is an unwholesome state of mind. Alternatively, it may be understood as maintaining a mind of flattery.

Regarding the precepts: to bewitch another person, to seek wealth with a depraved mind in the hope of sustaining one's own life, or to assume a solemn external appearance with the intent to deceive others, or to devote oneself exclusively to majestic deportment in order to attract fame and profit—all such acts are contrary to the Dharma. This concludes the second section on the limits of offenses.

This can be understood. Third, regarding the limits of the *puṇya-bhāga* (meritorious portion): various sūtras state that one who dies will be reborn in the heavens, or that those who wish to be reborn in the heavens should always protect the "feet of the precepts" (*śīla-pāda*).
Since the heavens represent the most excellent among all tainted pleasures (*sāsrava-sukha*), one now aspires for this fruit and consequently maintains the precepts;
this is thus superior to the former [category]. Fourth, regarding the limits of the *mārga-bhāga* (path portion) and so forth: when one possesses pure precepts and wisdom, then...

One attains the supreme path, eliminating fetters and becoming free from obstruction. Because of bondage and attachment, there is this liberation; "bondage" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*), while "attachment" refers to the notions of self and person (*ātman* and *pudgala*).
Now, seeking to sever these, one upholds the precepts and practices cultivation until the fruit of the path is achieved. This mind is the most excellent.
Regarding the statement that they are "extremely weak": this is explained in terms of their capacity for sustained practice (*dhāraṇa*) according to their respective locations.

Because the defilements of the people in the Southern Continent are heavy and their weariness with suffering is sharp and intense, they are able to practice for one day and one night in a manner superior to those of the Eastern and Western Continents over the course of fifty minor eons (*antarakalpa*).

This can be understood by comparing the Eastern and Western continents progressively; however, the Northern continent is not included because it lacks the Buddha-dharma and is thus subsumed under the eight unfavorable conditions (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*).

Regarding the eighth statement, "the eight [periods] reach [their respective stages]," this is in reference to the *vidyādhara* (knowledge-holders). During the time of the Buddha, sentient beings possessed sharp faculties;

they were able to receive and uphold [the teachings], thereby attaining the realization of the fruit, and thus [that period] was superior. In the final age (*paścimakāla*), faculties are dull; although one may uphold [the teachings], there are none who attain the Way, and thus it is inferior.

By comparing these three periods—the *saddharma*, *pratirūpaka*, and *antardharma*—in their sequence from beginning to end, their relative superiority and inferiority can be known. The *Kubjita-avadāna* is based on the principle of constancy.
Regarding the statement "based on hearing":

when it is expressed through discourse, the ninth [category] refers to the nine types of "weakness. This is explained in terms of restraint (*saṃvara*). From the perspective of the relative weight of the nature of the vow itself, the nature of the vow is strong while the prohibitory aspect is weak.
However, from the perspective of the difficulty or ease of guarding them, the prohibitory aspect is strong and the nature of the vow is weak; thus, they are said to be mutually strong and weak.
The tenth statement, "the ten [categories] from strongest to weakest," is distinguished according to the various aggregates (*skandhas*). The first section is the root of practice;
because the transgressions it prevents are grave, its observance is strong. The offenses in the subsequent sections prevent transgressions that are lighter, and are therefore weak.
If explained in terms of difficulty or ease, it can be understood that those which follow are stronger, while those which precede them are weaker.

The second section clarifies the two types of offenses, which is divided into two parts. First, the names are stated and their number enumerated (as in the text). Second, the explanation is divided into ten sections. Now, for the first part, there are two divisions.

First, regarding the statement "distinguishing by way of stages": this distinguishes between ordinary beings and sages, as well as those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Regarding the phrase "the gravity reaches its utmost": [this refers to the most severe degree].

This distinguishes those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) from the three fruits [of the path]. Since afflictions (*kleśa*) no longer exist for those beyond training, there are only transgressions committed through a mistaken mind (*viparyāsa-citta*).

Alternatively, among those transgressions, they may be solely prohibitory precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*), such as: when one is asleep, someone places one on a high bed; or staying overnight in a woman’s room by mistake;
or staying for more than two nights with one who has not received full ordination (*upasampadā*); or staying overnight with one who has stolen [an item]; or [staying] for a long time...

Regarding such matters as forgetting to perform the *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (declaration of purity) for robes: these three fruits [of the path] have not yet exhausted the afflictions (*kleśa*), so it is possible for them to intentionally violate the precepts;

furthermore, what they violate consists of prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepa-śīla*). Because they have exhausted the afflictions of desire (*kāma-kleśa*), if one were to consider the two lower fruits [of the stream-enterer and once-returner], there would be the sense of violating the nature of the precepts (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).

As the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "In the case of the two lower fruits, if a nun is coerced and loses mindfulness while experiencing pleasure, etc., this is because she has exhausted the afflictions of desire."

Because [the defilements] have not yet been exhausted. Furthermore, there is only the loss of mindfulness; ultimately, one never commits [new offenses] against others, because one does not create new karma.
This means that the afflictions are light. Regarding what is said to be "up to the most serious": this is distinguished by comparing the three fruits to the stage of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana).

As for the noble ones (ārya) of the three fruits, although they possess the support of the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga), even if they commit intentional transgressions, they certainly do not enter the three evil realms; therefore, they are light. This refers to the internal ordinary beings (antarapudgala).

"Although one has been moistened by the water of principle, because one has not yet attained the state of outflow-free (anāsrava), it is grave. Regarding the phrase "and so forth," this distinguishes the stage of the inner ordinary person (antarapudgala) from the stage of the outer ordinary person (bāhyapudgala).
Because the outer ordinary person has not yet seen the Truths at all, whatever they commit is equally grave. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:

The offenses committed by the foolish and the wise differ in their gravity. When a fool commits even a small sin, he falls into the evil realms; when a wise person commits a great sin, they are nonetheless liberated from suffering.
It is like a lump of iron that sinks in water despite being small, while a bowl made of iron floats despite being large.

Regarding the statement that "the two [types of offenses] are very light," this is distinguished based on the violation of conduct (*caryā-vipatti*). An active offense (*kṛta-āpatti*) is grave because it corresponds to the first category of the Pratimokṣa;

a passive offense (*vārita-āpatti*) is light because it corresponds to the second category and below. Examples include constructing a dwelling without requesting the formal authorization (*dharmatā*), and so forth.
As for the phrase "it may also be," this means that regardless of whether it is an active or passive offense, intentional commission is grave, whereas accidental commission is always light.

Regarding the statement "the three types of arrival," this is distinguished according to the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral—as explained previously in the section on the *skandhas* (aggregates).

Specifically, as clarified in the section on the *pārājika* offenses, if one acts with an unwholesome mind, one commits a grave offense; if the mind is wholesome or neutral, the offense is light. One might ask: "In the previous case of the neutral mind, it was stated that this opens the possibility of maintaining the precepts."
The present case is likewise indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). How, then, does it constitute an offense? The answer is: the previous indeterminate state was one of insanity, sleep, or lack of awareness;

therefore, it was permitted as two forms of restraint (*saṃvara*). This present indeterminate state, however, is neither wholesome nor unwholesome in intention, and because it does not encompass dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*), it cannot be treated as an analogy to that case.
Regarding the statement "from the four precepts up to knowledge," this is distinguished in terms of the *vinaya* of deportment (*īryāpatha-śīla*). Violating the first three precepts is grave;

violating the latter four [precepts of deportment] is distinguished as light. Within the five categories (*pañca-varga*) and six groups (*ṣat-saṃghādiṣeṣa*), each preceding category is more grave than the one following it.

Regarding the statement "from the five [precepts] up to the prohibitions": this distinguishes offenses based on the nature of the prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). While the prohibition itself is light, its nature is grave; thus, although one may repent for violating a disciplinary rule (*prajñapti*), the karmic path (*karmapatha*) remains.

As the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (or *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*) states: "If one violates the ten wholesome precepts, although one repents, the sin leading to the three evil realms is not removed. This is like the retribution for a bhikṣu who kills an animal:
because he was involved with Devadatta in causing a schism in the Saṃgha, even though he repented within the Saṃgha, he still fell into hell.
The nose: none can save one from this; this refers to the violation of the nature-precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*).

Regarding "the sixth, up to liberation": this is distinguished according to time. During the Buddha's lifetime, the two [offenses] were light; after his parinirvāṇa, the two became grave because the defilement was heavy.
This is as can be understood from what preceded.

The seventh statement, "taking the mind and directing it toward the object," means taking the mind capable of committing an offense and, in relation to the object of that offense, discerning its relative superiority or inferiority.

This is like [the term] *zhì* (to arrive). Now, for an offense to be established, one must necessarily confront the external object; only when it engages with the internal mind can the karmic action be completed.

When the mind arises in relation to a superior object, the force is intensified, as in the case of killing a human being. When the mind arises in relation to an inferior object, the force is diminished, as in the case of...

This refers to the killing of non-humans or animals. Regarding the statement "the precept applies to the perception [of the object]": the first phrase concerns the characteristics of the objective field (*ālambana*). Since it constitutes a *pārājika* offense, the gravity of the precept corresponds to the gravity of the object.

In the case of a lower object with an inferior mental state, one perceives it as the actual object; this third phrase constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (light offense) due to the inferiority of the mind, as it does not correspond to the actual object.

Alternatively, when the object is light or inferior, yet the mind is superior, one perceives it as the actual object; this fourth phrase constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* because the object is not commensurate [with the gravity of the offense].

This refers to the mind. Regarding the discussion that culminates in the precepts, let us take the single case of killing as an illustration; this may be used to clarify other precepts by analogy. Therefore, it is said to apply universally to all. Next, the first point is explained by citing specific instances.

Regarding "the gravity [of the offense] is the same while the retribution differs" within the category of sexual misconduct: the gravity is the same because both incur the *pārājika* (defeat) offense;

however, the retribution differs based on the superiority or inferiority of the object, which opens the way for the formation of karmic bonds with varying degrees of lightness or heaviness. Thus, the retribution is not fixed.

Furthermore, offenses against animals are light while those against humans are heavy; householders are inferior while monastics are superior—this can be understood by comparison. Second, regarding theft:
stealing property belonging to the Sangha as a collective is the gravest among the paths of karma. Thus, the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says: "Those who commit the four pārājika offenses..."
I am also able to save [others], but one who steals the property of the Saṃgha, I do not save.

Regarding the third [category] of killing, the citation of the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma* refers to the text from the "Chapter on False Views" (*mithyādṛṣṭi-varga*) of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*. As for the citations of the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma* provided here, according to the *Samayabhedoparacanacakra*, there are seven [versions].
The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* constitutes the body, while the other six treatises constitute the feet. First is the *Saṃgītiparyāya-pāda*, consisting of twelve thousand verses, composed by Śāriputra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang Dynasty. Second is the *Dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra*, consisting of six thousand verses, composed by Mahāmaudgalyāyana;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang Dynasty. Third is the *Prajñapti-pāda-śāstra*, consisting of eighteen thousand verses, composed by Mahākātyāyanīputra.
Untranslated (the three preceding works were all composed during the Buddha’s lifetime). 4. *Jñānaprasthāna* (The Foundation of Knowledge): seven thousand stanzas;
composed by Devaśarman within one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. 5. *Prakaraṇapāda* (The Section on Categories): six thousand stanzas;
composed by Vasumitra at the beginning of the third century after the Buddha’s extinction. 6. *Dhātukāya* (The Body of Elements): six thousand stanzas; also composed by Vasumitra.

The latter three versions were translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty. At the end of the third century, Kātyāyanīputra composed the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* in twenty-five thousand verses.
Although it appeared later, it extensively elucidates the tenets of the Sarvāstivāda school for the masters of subsequent generations.
The *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* takes [the first chapter] as its body and the remaining six chapters as its feet. That treatise states:
"To lack faith in the Three Jewels, one's parents, and Arhats, and to lack faith in cause and effect, the Four Noble Truths, and so forth, is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
To lack faith in sin and merit, and in the retribution of evil karma, is called the severing of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla-ccheda*). Such a person is certain to fall into the Avīci Hell. (4)

Regarding speaking of minor offenses to those who have left the household life, as stated in the Vinaya: "If one has truly attained the Path and speaks of it to a fellow bhikṣu of like mind, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* [offense].

This is because, knowing that the person who has left the household life will not believe it, there is no sense of causing harm or diminution. However, if one falsely speaks to such a person, it opens up the karmic knots of the mind and is therefore a minor offense.
Conversely, with householders, they are easily led to believe and easily understand; therefore, [falsely speaking to them] constitutes a grave offense."

Eighth. Regarding the statement that "the eight [offenses] are extremely grave": this refers to distinguishing the relative gravity of the offenses established by the Buddha’s precepts when compared to the offenses of karmic retribution in the future.
Regarding the statement that they are "as [heavy as]... appropriate": this means that although the offense is grave, the retribution is light.

This is because [acts such as] plotting the marriage of a woman with or without a husband, or the three offenses regarding a dwelling, were committed out of joy; thus, they are designated with the names of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Since these are prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-śikṣāpada*), one will receive [retribution] in the future.
The retribution is not heavy. The cited treatise states: "Regarding the difference in the method of establishing the precepts (*śikṣāpada*):

because the method of establishing the precepts is formulated according to what is rare, although the offense itself is light, it is considered heavy because it obstructs many instances. This method of establishing the precepts differs from that which addresses minor obstructions;

however, the resulting dharma of the offense is established differently than it is today. Because the cause for the minor obstruction of today results in retribution, it is said that cause and effect correspond."
Regarding the statement that "the precepts reach their due measure," this clarifies that although the offense is minor, the retribution is grave.

Acts such as striking or fighting, though they are natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), are prescribed as minor *pāyattika* offenses because they are rarely committed. Nevertheless, because they are natural transgressions and involve heavy karma that violates the principle of reality, the resulting retribution is likewise grave.

The preceding argument may be reconciled by citing evidence to the contrary: since these are *prakṛti-sāvadya* (inherent) precepts, the gravity of the offense is already significant; consequently, the retribution received at the time of fruition is also severe.
