Thus, it is said that "cause and effect correspond. Regarding the latter two phrases, the expression "or reaching [the limit]" refers to cases such as the emission of semen, the two types of slander, the three instances of violating admonitions, and physical contact, wherein both cause and effect are grave.
This is illustrated by the hundred *śaikṣa* (training) rules and others, which involve a mind of forgetfulness or error.

If one occasionally commits an offense, both the cause and the effect are light. Regarding the mind of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*): it is like feeling ashamed of one's own lack of virtue while feeling abashed before those who possess virtue;
with a heart full of reverence, one bows the body in humble adoration—this is what is meant by "the garment trailing on the ground. As for the term "and so forth" (*ādi*):

This includes other offenses committed with a deluded mind. Regarding the phrase "this... therefore," it refers to the two points concerning whether the offense and its retribution are both light or both heavy.
That the nature of the restraint and the gravity of the retribution do not differ is also a case of cause and effect being commensurate.

The ninth point, stating that "the nine are most serious," clarifies the previous section by viewing the mind in relation to its objects; now, however, it distinguishes them solely in terms of the mind itself.
Regarding the phrase "the three times of the single mind," this refers to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), the fundamental stage (*maula*), and the subsequent stage (*pṛṣṭha*).

As for the expression "as explained in detail," this cites the *Śrāmaṇyaphala-sūtra* (or *Upāsakaśīla-sūtra*) and restricts the analysis to the precept against killing, using it as the paradigmatic case; other cases are to be understood by analogy, which is why the word "merely" (*qie*) is used. (4)
As for "distinctive," this refers to the grouping of eight [factors] into four positions. Regarding the phrase "initial resolve": this is the first position.

As for "expedient means" (*upāya*), the new sūtras and śāstras state that once the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is completed, it is the subsequent stage. In the initial expedient means, one raises turbid and heavy thoughts; with a mind of envy and malice, one intends to commit killing.
At the moment of actual killing, one gives rise to a mind of reckless abandon; having finished the killing, one does not contemplate repentance, but instead generates further [afflictions].
This refers to a mind of joy. The following cases are all analogous. Regarding the phrase "the lightest of the second degree": this refers to the second category.

Specifically, among the eight propositions, the second, third, and fourth propositions are all heavy at two times. First, regarding the initial proposition, it says: "The preparatory and the fundamental are heavy.

This means that the preparatory stage involves giving rise to a harmful intent (a "boil" of malice), while the fundamental stage involves giving rise to a sense of satisfaction in having caused that harm; therefore, they constitute a grave offense.

Regarding "light offenses" (*kṣudra-āpatti*): Xuán says that because the subsequent mind involves repentance and reform, the offense is light. Zōng’s commentary does not permit this, and his refutation of that interpretation states:

"If the subsequent mind involved repentance and reform, it would instead constitute maintaining the precepts (*dhāraṇa*). Since it is now said to be 'light,' it is clear that there is still a transgression."
He explains it himself as follows: It refers merely to having completed the acts of killing or stealing without giving rise to a turbid or heavy mind, nor having yet produced a sense of remorse.

Since the cause—the state of mind—is light, the resulting offense is also somewhat light. Regarding the phrase "within the middle" (*zhōng yú*), it means within the three phrases of that particular stage.
As for "light in the preliminary stage" (*fāngbiàn qīng*), it refers to not giving rise to a turbid, heavy mind of resentment when others come to oppress one.

It is not obtained. Having already moved forward to kill, because that mind’s cause was light, the offense committed is also light. Once the root [offense] is established, the heavy [type] arises from turbidity;

once the heavy mind is established, it arises from a sense of exhilaration. Regarding the phrase "after the heavy" (*zhòng hòu yún*), this refers to the third line of its respective position and is the very last one.
Regarding the heavy [type] after the preparatory stage (*fāngbiàn*) is completed, this refers to the preparatory stage arising from turbidity.

Regarding the emphasis on the mental state (*citta*): because one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) after the act is completed, the emphasis is on the fundamental [intent] while the [external] factor is light.
This means that at the actual moment of killing, if there is no turbid or heavy mental state, although one incurs the offense of *pārājika*, the resulting karma is nonetheless light.
As for the phrase "the third is the lightest": the "third" refers to the third position among the four positions; the "three phrases" refer to the fifth, sixth, and seventh among the eight phrases.
Regarding these three phrases: "one is heavy and two are light" means that within each phrase, at one time it is heavy and at two times it is light.
"The first" refers to the head of the three phrases within its own position. "The root is heavy" means it is heavy because the root gives rise to a turbid and heavy mind.

"The beginning and end are light" means that the preparatory stages (*upāya*) do not give rise to a turbid and heavy mind; this is the lightness of the beginning. As for "accomplishing for oneself," it is not... [text ends].
To give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) is "light" in its aftermath. Regarding the statement that the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) is heavy while the aftermath is light:

this refers to cases where one gives rise to a turbid and heavy mind during the preparatory stage, yet does not give rise to a mind of malice (*ghātana-citta*) at the fundamental stage (*maula*), nor gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy upon completion.

Regarding the statement that the act of completion is heavy while the beginning and middle are light: this means that because one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy upon completion, it is heavy; whereas both the preparatory and fundamental stages are light.
"One does not give rise to a turbid or heavy mind. Regarding the phrase "the fourth and so forth," the "fourth" refers to the first phrase of the fourth position;
that is, the eighth phrase among the eight phrases. "Light in all three times" means that at the beginning, middle, and end, there is no turbid, heavy, or harmful mind.

Subsequently, because there was no mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), [the offense] was light. Next, he cites a scriptural case as proof: "Mahallaka" is a term from the Sanskrit language; here it means a foolish person.
One who does not know the characteristics of the precepts and speaks with the words of a worldly person—such a person may be provoked to anger;

it would be better for him to die quickly. If he follows their words, it constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*); if he does not follow their words, it is auspicious and immediate. Furthermore, by following their words, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (evidence that in all three instances the offense is light).
Next, the *Shansheng jing* (Sūtra on the Birth of Goodness) may be cited for corroboration (the same proof as above). Third, regarding the conclusion that summarizes the essential point:

concerning the statement in the *Vinaya*, "For one who has attained the state of a person," one should first ask: "Since the eight karmas are distinct, why is there no further gradation [of severity]?

This refers to the passage in the *Jieyichao* (Commentary on the Concluding Rules for Defeat) which answers: "The Vinaya, based on the perception of the person, treats all eight karmas as grave offenses. This means that although such thoughts may arise...

The gravity of the offenses differs according to the Vinaya texts; however, based on the clarity of one’s intention, if one kills another while perceiving them as such, it constitutes a violation of the regulations and thus results in a *pārājika* offense.
Question: Since the resulting offenses are identical, why was it previously stated that the former is superior and the latter inferior?

Answer: Because karma follows the mind, the retribution it draws forth differs. That is to say, although the formal offense (*prajñapti-āpatti*) is the same, there are differences in the lightness or gravity of the mental karma.
This is different. Next, the treatise is cited as proof; this can be understood through the tenth section.
Regarding the statement "ten [cases] up to 'in relation to,'" this means that within the three periods of time, one distinguishes by contrasting the presence and absence of mind.

Regarding the statement "eight [cases] up to 'prior to,'" this means there are eight propositions, which are condensed into four positions to be distinguished as previously described. This refers to the method of the single-mind propositions.
There is no distinction. To say that the first phrase refers to "the mind being present during the three periods" means that the mind is present throughout the three stages:

the preliminary application (*prayoga*), the fundamental act (*maula*), and the subsequent completion (*pṛṣṭha*). This refers specifically to the four precepts of the first category; because all result in the fundamental offense of *pārājika*, they are grave.
As for the statement that "the next [category] reaches the level of *duṣkṛta*," this means that among these three phrases, in the first two, all four precepts are grave.

This means that because there is a mind at the time of the fundamental act, the final phrase—referring to one who commits the first grave offense—indicates that this refers to the grave offense of the precept against sexual misconduct.

This means that although there is no mind experiencing pleasure during the interval between entry and exit, because there is a mind experiencing pleasure at the moments of entry and exit, it constitutes a grave offense.
The three offenses of *sthūlātyaya* and *duṣkṛta* refer to the three precepts against killing, stealing, and lying; this refers to the initial arising of the intention.
Auspicious. Next, regarding the two *laṅghana* [offenses] of the preliminary (*upāya*) and near-preliminary (*sāmantaka*) stages:

when performing the actual root act, if one steals while perceiving what belongs to another as belonging to no one, or kills a person while perceiving them as a wooden stump, or deceives with false speech while perceiving it as not false—these constitute *pārājika*.

If one is possessed by madness, delusion, mental derangement, or affliction by disease, there is no root offense. After the threefold renunciation of the precepts, if one subsequently realizes they have killed a person or stolen, [the offense is established].

Regarding objects belonging to an owner, if one recognizes them as stolen goods and so forth, yet has not yet repented, one incurs one *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) based on the factor of such recognition.

According to the *Śāstra* and in accordance with the Vinaya, for a single precept there should be two *duṣkṛtas*. Since the names are identical, the two *sthūlātyaya* (grave offenses) and four [instances of] *duṣkṛta* are collectively referred to as "grave offenses and minor offenses" (*sthūlātyaya-duṣkṛta*).

According to Xuánzàng’s interpretation, once one has passed through the three stages of the precept (*śīla*) and recognizes it as killing or the like, one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), thereby forming a "favorable" (*kalyāṇa*) bond.
Previously, I followed the *Zōngjì* (Record of the School), which merely posited the formation of a favorable bond based on the aspect of recognition, without discussing other meanings.

This favorable bond is somewhat light; if one further gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy, then according to principle, a more serious favorable bond is formed. I hope you will consider this carefully; let your own judgment decide.

Regarding the selection and rejection [of cases]: as for the statement that "arriving later is auspicious," this refers to the three phrases of the third position. In all [these cases], there is a state of mind at one time and an absence of mind at another time.

In the first phrase, four precepts are all violated at their root; therefore, it says "one commits the four grave offenses. In the second phrase, only the precept against sexual misconduct is violated; therefore...
This refers to committing the first grave offense (*pārājika*). Regarding the statement that the remaining three precepts may result in *sthūlātyaya* or *duṣkṛta*, Master Xuán says:

"The 'remaining three precepts' are considered in relation to the initial presence of intention. Depending on whether it is a preparatory act (*prayoga*), one may incur either *duṣkṛta* or *sthūlātyaya*.

For instance, in the case of the precept against killing: the initial movement of the body and the volition constitutes the commission of *duṣkṛta*; if it is a distant preparatory act, one incurs *sthūlātyaya*; and if it is a proximate preparatory act, one incurs a grave *sthūlātyaya*."

If one merely intends for body and speech and stops without acting, one incurs only a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). If one reaches the distant preparatory stage (*pūrvaprayoga*), by remaining [in that state], one incurs a *duṣkṛta* as well as a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).

If one reaches the proximate preparatory stage, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* along with either a light or heavy *sthūlātyaya*, or two *sthūlātyayas* and three *śikṣāpada*-violations; these vary according to the specific circumstances.

The offenses differ according to the location; therefore, it is said that "it may be in an araṇya. There is another interpretation, which shall be explained below. For now, we shall take the former interpretation as definitive.
Regarding the statement "the two preceding [cases] are without mind," this refers to being without mind during both the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and the fundamental stage (*maula*).

As for the precept against sexual misconduct, it constitutes a grave offense because of the pleasure experienced at the time of emission; this is discussed in relation to the specific exception regarding being coerced by an enemy. The preceding...

The subsequent rules regarding the precept against sexual misconduct are all like this. If one reaches the stage of transgression through these conditions, it constitutes an offense from the very first moment—like a hair-tip—regardless of whether one experiences pleasure or not.
As for the other three offenses that result in a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), namely theft, killing, and lying: the final mind constitutes the *duṣkṛta*.

For example, in the case of the precept against killing, if one mistakes a person for a tree stump, and at the very moment of killing, one still thinks it is a stump, but only realizes after the act has been completed that it was actually a person, [the offense is established].

Rejoicing [in another's offense] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense). False speech may be understood by analogy. The *Zongji* states: "Among these, regarding the precept against stealing, there is a distinction between it and [the offenses of] killing and false speech in terms of the object being present before one.
First, when seeing the object, one recognizes that the environment has an owner; yet one immediately becomes confused and perceives it as having no owner.

At the very moment of lifting it and moving it from its place, one likewise acts with the thought that it has no owner. During both of these preceding stages, there is no offense. Only after having obtained the object does one realize [the truth]."
This concerns property belonging to another. Regarding the aspect of knowing it belongs to another, one commits a *duṣkṛta* (light offense).

If one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and decides that the object belongs to oneself, intending not to return it to the other, one certainly commits a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). If one returns it immediately, there is no offense.

This present excerpt is based solely on the mental factor of knowing the object belongs to another; it does not discuss all the various meanings. Xuán states: "If one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy, one commits an offense."
It is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). Once an object has been acquired, if one knows it does not belong to oneself and returns it to the other, no offense is committed.

Now, because one forms the intention not to return it, one commits a *duṣkṛta*. I fear that this interpretation may create an obstacle; since it is said that one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) while forming the intention not to return it, logically a grave offense must be incurred.

One cannot say it is merely a *duṣkṛta*. My school’s position is based on the aspect of "knowing," whereby one incurs only a *duṣkṛta* for the time being, without yet discussing the distinct underlying principles. This is profoundly [significant].

This is my view; please reflect upon it. Regarding the statement that "even a single instance constitutes an offense," this refers to the precept against sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*), which—consistent with the preceding discussion—is explained in terms of being coerced by an adversary.
If one remains free from defilement throughout the three times [of preparation, execution, and completion], there is no offense. The same applies to the remaining precepts as well.

Regarding the phrase "citing the *Vinaya* to reach [the conclusion]": this refers to citing the *Vinaya* as evidence to establish the positions of "with mind" (*sacitta*) and "without mind" (*acitta*).

Specifically, within the *Vinaya* precept against minor lying (*mṛṣāvāda*), one establishes "with mind" and "without mind" across three stages—the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), the fundamental stage (*maula*), and the subsequent stage (*pṛṣṭha*)—thereby forming four positions and eight propositions.
If one is without mind during these three stages, the offense of lying is not established. The present commentary likewise relies upon these three stages.

Distinguishing cases where there is intention (*cetanā*), even when there is no [actual] speech, eight permutations (*aṣṭapada*) are established. In four positions and three times, there is no intention; following that analogy, there is no offense.

Thus the Vinaya says: "One originally forms this thought: 'I shall speak falsely' (intention at the stage of preparation); while actually speaking falsely, one knows it is false (intention at the root act);
having finished speaking falsely, one knows it was false (intention at the subsequent stage). This constitutes a *pāyattika*. The second [text] says: "One originally forms this..."
[The first case: One thinks, "I shall speak falsely" (the preparatory stage with volition). While speaking the falsehood, one knows it is a falsehood (the fundamental stage with volition).

After finishing the falsehood, one does not know it was such speech (the subsequent stage without volition). This is also a *pāyattika*. [The second case: One does not originally think, "I shall speak falsely" (the preparatory stage without volition).
While speaking the falsehood, one knows it is a falsehood (the fundamental stage with volition). After finishing the falsehood, one knows it was a falsehood.

(The subsequent action involves a state of mind). Regarding the fourth *pāyattika*, it says: "One does not initially form the thought, 'I shall speak falsely' (the preparatory stage lacks the intent);

while speaking falsely, one knows it is false (the fundamental stage possesses the intent); having finished speaking falsely, one does not realize it was false (the subsequent stage lacks the intent).

This concludes the *pāyattikas*. Among these four cases, are they not all instances where the fundamental stage possesses the intent? In all such cases, the offense of falsehood is established. Furthermore, there should be...
There are four phrases. In the first three phrases, at the very moment of speaking a false word, one does not know it is a lie;

because there is fundamentally no intentional mind, there is no grave offense, but only a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense), as there is intentional mind before and after. In the final phrase, throughout all three stages [of preparation, execution, and completion], there is entirely no intentional mind, and thus there is no offense at all.

Now, citing the intent of this text, it means that since the precepts for those [other classes] are thus, the present eight phrases should be understood accordingly. This third point serves as a general conclusion and reference.

Regarding the statement "later, with a sincere mind," the preceding section raised an objection, saying: "In the previous case of 'single mind,' where there were eight phrases and four positions, all were considered grave offenses based on the three periods of time.
In this present section, where there are likewise eight phrases and four positions, they are also divided into three periods; why, then, would there be an offense?"
"Is there also non-offense? In response, it is said: "The latter eight cases differ regarding offense and non-offense based on the presence or absence of intention (*citta*);

they are not like the former eight, where none are without intention. This means that although these eight cases also involve the three periods [of time], within those three periods—whether occurring at one period, two periods, or otherwise—there is a distinction between offense and non-offense due to the absence of intention; whereas if there is intention..."

[In these cases,] there is an offense. Where there is no intentional mind, there is no offense. Regarding the first eight phrases, although they are divided into four positions and further into three periods, within those three periods, despite the differences between a light and a heavy mind, they are all invariably characterized by clear and conscious intent; therefore, they are consistently classified as constituting the position of an offense.

Furthermore, it is difficult to ascertain: what are the characteristics of the unintentional state in the latter eight phrases? The answer is as in the *Chao* (Excerpts), which explains this according to the general principle.

There are two further distinctions. Regarding sexual misconduct, the specific conditions are defined by being unstained by passion during the three periods [of time]. Regarding theft, the specific conditions concern whether the object has an owner or not.

Homicide and falsehood are easily understood. If, however, these are committed under general conditions—such as when one is insane or otherwise lacks the conscious intent and awareness—then with respect to all precepts, there is no offense. Thus ends the sixth section.

Part Seven: Miscellaneous Explanations, Section Two.

First, the formal heading; second, the five-part sub-commentary. Regarding the phrase "from seven to middle," first, the intent of its inclusion is as follows: [The text continues with the specific commentary.]
The six gates distinguish these four types of conduct, each elucidating them according to a single principle; however, this treatise discusses only the fundamental [offenses].

Now, within this gate, one distinguishes variously upon the fundamental offenses of the four types of conduct: first, regarding the four types of conduct, one distinguishes the characteristics of the presence or absence of the two offenses of "not training" and "ignorance";
second, regarding the fundamental [offense], one clarifies the presence or absence of the preparatory and causal offenses.
The characteristics [of the offenses]. Third, regarding the fundamental [offenses], it clarifies the presence or absence of transgressions and their lightness or gravity.
Fourth, regarding the fundamental [offenses], it clarifies the presence or absence of the object, perception, phrasing, and method, as well as their lightness or gravity.

Fifth, regarding the fundamental [offenses], it clarifies the characteristics of transgression and non-transgression through six categories, such as specific versus general [intent]. Therefore, it is called "miscellaneous" (*saṃkīrṇa*). As for the phrase "dividing down to the particulars":
As stated in the text, within the commentary, this is the first of five [sections]. Regarding the phrase "first, not learning out of ignorance": "first" refers to the head of the five gates.

"Not learning" means that after receiving the precepts, one gives rise to a mind of indolence, violating the original vow by failing to apply oneself to the textual teachings of the Tripiṭaka, and thus ceasing to learn;
for this, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). "Ignorance" refers to [failing to understand] the objects and phenomena (*dharmas*) as conditions.

Yet they do not understand, thereby incurring the offense of ignorance (*ajñāna*). Now, taking these two offenses and traversing them through the four stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), we shall examine their presence or absence, their frequency, and their gravity within the framework of the nine propositions concerning those who are "trainable" (*śaikṣa*) and "untrainable" (*aśaikṣa*), thereby distinguishing the training of the two types of persons.

Question: Previously, you stated that you would "traverse the stages to make distinctions," yet now, when citing the matter, you speak only of the "ignorance of non-training" (*aśikṣita-ajñāna*) and do not mention [the other]. Why is this?
What are the two characters "passing through stages" (*liwei*)? The answer has two interpretations. First, Baoyun says:

Because they were extensively indicated above, they are briefly cited below. Second, Xuanyuan says: The previous heading fully stated "the non-learning and non-knowing that distinguishes the passing through stages.
In this current commentary, we first explain "non-learning and non-knowing," but have not yet discussed "distinguishing the passing through stages. How do we know this? Therefore...

The passage in the *Chao* beginning with "From the point where its characteristics are subtle and hidden... and so forth, all serves to clarify that the characteristics of the presence or absence of non-learning and non-knowing cannot be [discussed] here.

From the second section, where the *Chao* states, "Since the summary and conclusion have been briefly provided, one must now correlate them with the stages of the path," and so forth, it is only then that the characteristics of the detailed differentiation of the successive stages can be explained separately. Therefore, it is known that because the extensive explanation follows below, what precedes it is merely a brief restatement.

[The text] says that its characteristics are subtle and hidden; this is a general praise of the fact that the appearance of this gate is subtle, profound, and difficult to know. It is not something easily seen by those who have not accumulated learning.

Now, relying on the Dharma-treasure, I shall collect the meanings of both ancient and modern [traditions]. There are four kinds of difficulty in knowing: first, the difficulty of knowing whether there is bondage or lack of bondage with respect to persons;
second, the difficulty of knowing whether there is bondage or lack of bondage with respect to delusion regarding what can be learned versus delusion regarding what cannot be learned.
[The text] knows [the following]. Third, regarding the textual evidence of the teachings, it is difficult to know what is opened or not opened, as well as what is light or heavy.

Fourth, regarding the classification into two [categories], it is difficult to know how the nine fetters (saṃyojana) constitute offenses. Now, first, concerning whether or not an offense is incurred based on the person:

according to the Vinaya, when correlating the teachings with the faculties (indriya), there are three types of persons—superior, middling, and inferior. If one correlates the faculties with the teachings, there are six people who study the teachings and three people who do not study the teachings. Furthermore...

Regarding the three types of persons who study the teachings: first, those who study to master the teachings. As the *Chao* (Excerpts) states: "This refers to those who, since receiving the precepts, have diligently studied the Tripiṭaka and so forth.

Such persons understand the dharmas of human conduct; they incur no offense of duality. This applies to both the superior and middling faculties among the two types of learners—those who know half and those who do not know half.
In matters they understand, there is no offense of duality; in matters they do not understand, likewise there is no offense of duality."

Regarding the offense of not learning: because one is training, there is no offense of not learning; because there is nothing unknown, there is no ignorance. This also applies to those of superior and middling faculties. As for the third type, the beginner:

because they are training, there is no offense of not learning; because they have things yet to know, there is no ignorance. Furthermore, regarding those of dull faculties who do not fully comprehend despite training:
because they have not yet abandoned their reliance [on the teacher], there is no offense of not learning; yet, even at the conclusion of their training, they do not reach full comprehension.

The transgression of ignorance. This applies generally to those of the three grades of faculties (the above distinguishes those who do not incur the offense at all). Next, we consider those of the three types regarding the failure to study the teachings:

first, those who have never studied from the outset. Thus the *Chao* states: "If one has never studied the matters and dharmas and is ignorant of them, this applies generally to those of the superior and middling faculties.
If one of superior faculty does not study, they incur both offenses [of ignorance and non-inquiry] from beginning to end; if one of middling faculty does not study..."
1. Five years of *varṣa*. First, one binds [the offense] for not training during the five years; later, one binds [the offense] for ignorance.

Second, for those who stop training in the interim, there is no offense of the two types at the point where they previously understood. If there is doubt or lack of recognition, one binds the two offenses. This also applies to those of superior and middling faculties.
3. Those of dull faculties who do not train: from beginning to end they do not train; they incur only the offense of not training, as it is not within their capacity.
Therefore, ignorance is not established [as a separate category]. The above exposition of the six persons according to the correct principle is concluded.

Second, regarding the description of the "trainable" (*śaikṣa*) and the "untrainable" (*aśaikṣa*), and the reason why ignorance is not established as a distinct difficulty: if, within a clear mind, one encounters a phenomenon (*dharma*) and has doubt or fails to recognize it, this is called the "untrainable" description.
If, however, one previously understood and then later becomes confused, such that the mind encounters the object but does not comprehend it, this is...

One cannot learn delusion. If one who studies the teachings is clear regarding all matters and dharmas, yet fails to comprehend them due to external conditions, this constitutes "delusion regarding what can be learned" (*śikṣaṇīya-moha*) concerning those matters;
both offenses are incurred. If, however, it is one who does not study the teachings who gives rise to such delusion, then both offenses are fully established.
If one who studies the teachings experiences delusion or forgetfulness regarding a point of understanding, this is indeed "what can be learned."
Regarding serving one's superior: if one has never studied and is thus deluded, two offenses are incurred.

If it is a person who has not studied, or one who by nature has never studied, and whose mind is so clear that they do not even know [the rules], then there is no offense of delusion or forgetfulness.

However, if it is someone who has previously studied but has since ceased their practice, they will still harbor a deluded mind regarding what was previously understood; this likewise constitutes an offense of negligence. This is based on the precedent of how those of antiquity served their superiors when in doubt.
If one does not recognize [the offense], one simply releases it; if there is doubt regarding a violation of the law and one does not recognize it, one simply does not formalize the charge.

This has been the case throughout successive dynasties. Now, the Master opens [all cases] without exception, which may be called subtle and profound (the second section clarifies this). Third, regarding the discernment of whether a case is opened or not, as well as the difficulty of knowing lightness or gravity according to the scriptural teachings:
if a person studying the teachings possesses a clear mind regarding the phenomena of the matter and has previously recognized them, [they understand the rules].

Later, he suddenly became confused and forgot. According to the Vinaya’s categories of perception regarding the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), the second and third cases allow for the absence of a fundamental offense.
Now, our Master follows this precedent and further relaxes the minor details; thus the following text says: "It depends on the perception of the object and the perception of the perception.

If one who has not studied the teachings, regarding a specific matter or dharma, clearly perceives it in their mind but fails to fully comprehend its conditions, this constitutes confusion that can be learned from; according to the Vinaya, this constitutes an offense.

[The text] continues: One establishes the root offense according to what was committed, further increasing the transgression of ignorance (*ajñāna*). (For now, this is discussed primarily from the perspective of the teaching. Next, to distinguish between light and heavy offenses:
the ancients said that failing to learn out of ignorance constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). Now it is said that failing to learn constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. There are two types of ignorance:

if one suspects [the rule] but has not yet understood it, according to the Vinaya, if one recites [the precepts] first and later forgets them, this is a *duṣkṛta*. If one answers that one does not recognize the fundamental [rule] at all, then...

It is established that listening without covering one's ears constitutes a *pāyattika* offense of increased ignorance. Since ancient times, this has not been distinguished, which may be called subtle and obscure.

The third section is concluded. Regarding the fourth point, which divides [the offenses] into two groups of nine phrases where the determination of the offense is difficult to know: one should study these nine phrases.

Regarding the four categories of one-off offenses: in the superior grade, there is one sentence with no offense; in the middle grade, there are four sentences, where the first half contains no offense and the second half contains eight offenses;

in the inferior grade, there are four sentences containing sixteen offenses. If one who is learning the teachings commits an offense in this matter, and there is doubt regarding the point of non-recognition, it constitutes twenty-four instances of *thitibhūta* (cessation of offense) and thirty-six instances of *kamma-bhūta* (performance of holding). If one does not learn the teachings...
A person incurs twenty-four offenses through their fetters. Regarding the nine sets of three phrases for training: in the superior grade, there is no offense in the first phrase;
in the middle grade, there is no offense in the first half; in the inferior grade, both the upper and lower halves involve offenses, as detailed in the subsequent text.

According to our own master, when a trainee encounters these nine phrases regarding matters of offenses, being conscious of them constitutes a state of clarity of mind and is therefore without offense.
When there is doubt regarding what is not recognized, this is a deluded and forgetful mind; twenty-four offenses are released.

If one stops midway and does not study, then in relation to these nine cases, having doubts or failing to recognize what constitutes an offense in a given matter, all are deluded minds; likewise, the offenses are released.

If one follows the ancient masters, the first half of the matter pertains to the upper [category], while the latter half is set aside; there is doubt regarding the violation of the upper [category] due to the lack of clear identification of the point.

This has been so because successive generations have consistently followed this precedent. Our present master, however, finds it difficult to open up [the explanation] following the section on "abstaining and maintaining" (*zhi-chi*), which may be described as subtle and obscure.
(The Fourth Section concludes. What has been summarized above is merely the general outline; the detailed exposition is found in the subsequent text.

In the second section of the structural analysis (*ko-p'an*), the phrase "from the beginning to 'opening'" refers to two chapters. "Narration" (*xu*) means to introduce the subject; "conclusion" (*jie*) means to summarize and assign.
First, it narrates the person who diligently studies: from the time they receive the precepts, they diligently study the Tripitaka; later, if their mind becomes confused or forgetful...

Failing to understand the conditions, and based on the Vinaya’s principles regarding the object, perception, matter, and offense, it is opened up that there are no two offenses; the formal act of confession belongs to this person.

Next, he further describes those who do not train: because they have never trained from the outset, they commit violations in every encounter; according to the Vinaya, these constitute actual offenses.
The textual connection establishes the fundamental basis. Furthermore, the factors of ignorance are added, and these fetters belong to this person. This is merely a brief exposition;

if one were to discuss it exhaustively according to principle, there should be six types of persons. [These] are concealed beneath the two mentioned persons, which is why the word "merely" (qie) is used.

As for the subsequent classification by analogy: since the preceding section has already described the two types of persons—the learner and the non-learner—this now corresponds them to the four modes of practice.

Above, the examples are divided into two sets of nine phrases. For those who are not yet learners (*aśaikṣa*), these are applied to the nine phrases for those still in training (*śaikṣa*) to conclude twenty-four instances of non-offense.
If they are learners, these are applied to the nine phrases for those beyond training, resulting in no offense at all.

As with this one precept, so it is for all the remaining two hundred and forty-nine precepts. Therefore, the text below states: "For now, based on a single matter, this principle is extended to the other precepts."

Above all precepts, there are four modes of practice. Within each mode of practice, they are each expanded by analogy into two sets of nine phrases; hence it is said, "thereafter, they are expanded by analogy.

For now, I shall follow the commentary of the *Chaojie* (Excerpts and Explanations). Even if there were alternative interpretations, they would not be free from confusion, so I shall not record them here.
In the commentary, the phrase "speaking of the characteristics of their offenses" is a formal restatement (*niddesa*).

This means that since it has already been explained whether or not the two types of persons—the diligent student and the non-student—incurred an offense, the current mention of "the characteristics of their offenses" specifically restates that for the diligent student there is no characteristic of offense consisting of non-studying or ignorance, whereas for the non-student there is indeed a characteristic of offense consisting of non-studying and ignorance. This is the principle.
In reality, this refers to the characteristics of both observance (*dhāraṇa*) and violation (*āpatti*). Now, "observance" is not mentioned;

rather, it speaks only of the characteristics of violation because it concerns the moment one engages in a prior action. The phrase "one who reaches [the point]" refers to a person studying the teachings.

Such a person, after receiving the precepts, diligently studies the teachings of the Tripiṭaka until they are as clear as looking at the palm of their hand. Later, when encountering an object, confusion and forgetfulness suddenly arise. Regarding...

The object may be doubted or unrecognized; hence it is said that one is "deluded or forgetful regarding the object. "Object" refers here to the three categories of grave offenses within the teachings on prohibitions and permissions (*saṃvara* and *anujñā*).
These constitute the objects for "abstaining from what is prohibited" (*śīla-dhāraṇa*) and "committing what is forbidden" (*āpatti-karaṇa*).

The two categories of wholesome matters constitute the objects for "engaging in what is permitted" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*) and "abstaining from what is forbidden" (*śīla-dhāraṇa*). Now, having previously mastered these objects through thorough cultivation, one suddenly becomes forgetful, deluded, or experiences doubt regarding them.
This refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*). "To act upon conditions" means that "acting" refers to the performance of an action;

it is when a person, being deluded regarding a previous event or a present object, conceives the notion of it being a non-human being, a beast, a stump, or a log, and thus performs the act of killing. The phrase "possessing the characteristics, the object, and the perception" precisely clarifies the intention of dispelling delusion;

that is to say, within the Vinaya texts, after citing and explaining the precepts of the *Prātimokṣa*, the characteristics of each precept are subsequently explained in detail, including the object and the perception.

The text consisting of five propositions is established upon the matter of the precept prohibiting killing. Regarding these five propositions: (1) one person kills another person with the perception of a person (resulting in a *pārājika* offense);

(2) one acts toward a non-human being while suspecting it to be a human (resulting in a *sthūlātyaya* offense); (3) one acts toward a non-human being with the perception of a non-human being (the same as above); (4) one acts toward a non-human being with the perception of a human (also a *sthūlātyaya* offense);
(5) one acts toward a non-human being while suspecting it to be a human (the same as above). Of these five propositions, the first alone constitutes a clear and definitive offense.

Regarding the root [offense]: for the latter four cases, both delusion and forgetfulness result in a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). From the perspective of not having committed the root offense, this constitutes observance of the precept.

Now, when a person training in the teachings gives rise to a mind of delusion or forgetfulness, even if they act due to encountering certain conditions, it is strictly governed by the text concerning the latter four cases of perception regarding the object.
"Opening [the offense] because there is no fundamental basis" means that since the person is deluded regarding the mind but not deluded regarding the teaching, the offense is opened.

As for the statement "if it reaches an offense," this refers to the case where one who has not studied is deluded regarding the teaching but not deluded regarding the mind; thus, the offense is established.
This means that after receiving the precepts, such a person treats all matters of good and evil within the textual teachings of the Tripiṭaka as if they had not studied them.

It is intended to cause one not to recognize [the offense] and to harbor doubts; thus, when encountering objects before one's eyes, it constitutes a transgression. Therefore, it says: "If one has never studied [the precepts] from the beginning," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "concluding the root offense according to what was done," this follows the text on the commission of offenses, whereby the guilt is concluded according to the five categories (*pañcāpatti*).

Furthermore, regarding the addition of the offense of ignorance: the ancient interpretation followed the text on the commission of offenses, stating that if one speaks based on a doubtful mind, it is a *duṣkṛta* (misdeed); now, however, it is interpreted as follows:

If one does not lend an ear [to the precepts], the offense of ignorance increases further. Question: Since it is stated that the root offense is determined according to what is actually done, this would pertain only to active transgressions (*kṛta-āpatti*);

why then is there an allowance for omissive transgressions (*vārita-āpatti*)? Answer: This is because the phrasing of the cited text follows its general tendency; thus, while it contains the expression "offending against the root," we now take only the omissive transgression consisting of non-learning and ignorance.

Regarding the statement that "the words are concise," this refers to the necessity of correlating the summary with the ritual procedures (*vidhi*). This means taking the two types of persons—the learner and the non-learner—and correlating them with the four stages of practice;

this constitutes the phrasing for the rules of cessation (*śamatha*) and action (*pravṛtti*). Regarding the phrase "now, as for the precepts": "now established" means being different from those of former times.
As for the "two persons and nine phrases": first, the nine regarding the learner; second, the nine regarding that which is not to be learned. It is permissible...

Regarding the nine types of training: these correspond to those who do not train as previously described. Within the aforementioned nine phrases, there are three instances of transgression through consciousness (*vijñāna*) and three instances of transgression regarding each matter according to the Tripiṭaka;
thus, there are six instances of consciousness in total. Upon each instance of consciousness, two modes of "active maintenance" (*karmasamādāna*) are established.

Calculating across the six instances of consciousness, this results in twelve modes of active maintenance. Furthermore, there remain twelve and a half phrases; within a clear and lucid mind, there are transgressions regarding doubtful matters and...

Not recognizing the nature of an offense constitutes a doubt regarding what is not recognized; this arises because one has previously failed to train. Together, these form twenty-four branches that result in the cessation of offenses. Thus, the preceding text states:
"If there is a person who has never trained from the outset and is ignorant of matters and the Dharma, they commit a transgression upon contact [with the object].

The Buddha said: 'In accordance with what was done, the root offense is established, and furthermore, the offense of ignorance is added. Therefore, it is known that there are nine [categories] that can be learned."

This phrase applies only to those who have not yet studied the teachings. If one is a person currently studying the teachings and clearly perceives within their mind that there are doubts or things they do not recognize, this is "having studied but not yet understood," which opens up the possibility of being free from offense.
One must not study the nine [precepts]; this applies to those who previously applied themselves diligently to study.

After learning through study, one becomes deluded and forgetful when confronted with objects; having doubts and failing to recognize them, the twelve and a half phrases are transformed into twenty-four *karmavācanā* (formal acts).
Furthermore, the remaining six and a half phrases, which involve recognizing the facts of an offense, also become twelve *karmavācanā*.

Together with the previous ones, these constitute thirty-six instances of *zuochi* (active engagement). This differs from the harmful practices of antiquity, which serve as conditions that must not be learned;

when one does not understand them, there is no offense. However, regarding the transgressions of the Dharma, which are conditions that can be learned, if one does not understand them, twelve offenses are incurred.

Now, the Master, based on the deluded mind, does not distinguish between the act and the offense, and thus grants amnesty to both. As the preceding text states: "That is to say, the previously received..."

Since one has already received the precepts, one diligently studies the Tripiṭaka; yet, due to confusion or forgetfulness regarding the objects [of the precepts], one may commit an offense when encountering certain conditions.

This occurs when the characteristics, the object, and the perception are all present. Therefore, it is known that the "nine [cases] not to be studied" apply only to those who are studying the teachings. Question: Regarding the two sets of nine phrases established above...
"What is the intended meaning? The *Chao* (the Sub-commentary) answers: "It is for the sake of the rules governing observance and violation (*dhāraṇa-vilopa*).

That is to say, these two sets of nine propositions—concerning what may be learned and what may not be learned—are established as the superior methodological rules for the four practices of the two types of observance and the two types of violation.
Furthermore, 'taking one matter to apply it to the remaining precepts' refers to one matter [such as] addressing a person, two matters [such as] ancient precedents, and so forth."

The two sets of nine rules are established first within the *Pratikṣepaṇa-saṃvara* (the prohibitions); above these, the one set of nine rules on what "should not be learned" (*na śikṣitavya*) is established.

Furthermore, within the *Pravartana-saṃvara* (the prescriptions), regarding the virtuous matters of robes and alms bowls, the one set of nine rules on what "should be learned" (*śikṣitavya*) is established above. This has been the case since antiquity.

Now, in the text of the Master [Buddhayaśas], the two sets of nine are established directly above [the prohibitions]. For instance, regarding the prohibitions against evil deeds, they are placed directly above the "clarifying the mind within."

All must be learned and known. There are nine cases where it is permissible to train; after having learned and known them, if one becomes confused or forgetful such that the conditions for understanding are absent, even if one performs the aforementioned acts, they are all permitted and non-offensive. These constitute the nine cases where training is not required (hence it is said: "this is based on a single instance").

As for those that apply to other precepts, this holds true for all two hundred and fifty or three hundred and forty-eight rules; in each case, there are both instances where training is possible and instances where it is not.

This can be learned (one should not explain it by way of false speech or various essential dharmas). Therefore, the subsequent text says: "Following the indication of a single precept, one penetrates its universality throughout the Dharma-realm."

Regarding the phrase "first reaching the *jī*": this refers to the general heading of the two sets of nine phrases, clarifying the meanings of what may or may not be learned, ignorance, existence or non-existence, lightness or heaviness, and much or little.
First, as for the analysis of the nine phrases concerning what may be learned: one phrase of the superior grade concerns the offense regarding the recognition of the matter;

and four phrases of the middle grade concern the first two which involve recognizing the matter and the latter two which involve recognizing the offense—these constitute the category of being without fault.

The *Cīvara-vastu*: the second half of four middle-grade clauses and the four full clauses of the low-grade [clauses]. Regarding transgressions, there are six instances of doubt and six instances of non-recognition;

this constitutes the limit of what constitutes an offense (*sāvadya-vibhāga*). Within these offenses, regarding the clauses where one doubts both the matter and the transgression, there is only a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) and no *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

This is the limit of the offense. Regarding the clauses where one does not recognize either the matter or the transgression, there is both a *pāyattika* and a *duṣkṛta*; the *pāyattika* is the grave [offense].
The "delimitation of offenses" (*āpatti-paryanta*): "Auspicious" refers to the delimitation of light offenses. Regarding the nine phrases concerning what "should not be learned" hereafter:
in the first half of these nine phrases, there is no offense at all; as for the lower half, there is an offense. Among the fourth and seventh [phrases] above, likewise no offense arises.

This is the delimitation of non-offense. As for the remaining six phrases, there is an offense in the lower half. Regarding the upper half, there is doubt as to whether an offense has been committed or lack of recognition that an offense was committed; this constitutes the delimitation of offense.

Regarding offenses: if one is doubtful about having committed a transgression, it is categorized as a *duṣkṛta* (light offense); this is the limit for light offenses. If one commits an offense without recognizing it, it is categorized as a *pāyattika* (heavy offense);
this is the limit for heavy offenses. This follows the current master’s division of *pāyattika* and *duṣkṛta*, which thus establishes lightness and heaviness.

If, like the ancients, one were to judge all such cases as *duṣkṛta*, then there would be no distinction between light and heavy. Furthermore, regarding the determination of offenses based on these nine propositions, this still accords with the ancients. If, however, one relies on... [text ends]

Now, if one is confused regarding both the matter and the offense, then neither the matter nor the offense constitutes an established transgression. These nine phrases collectively constitute the boundary of being without fault.

Next, in the detailed explanation according to the stages, it says that "first, clarifying the matters that can be learned" means that within a clear and conscious mind, one must learn to know all objects;
these are the matters that can be learned. Now, in contrast to those who are learning and those who are not learning, [the text speaks of] clarity...
Discriminated within the mind. Now, the excerpted text first clarifies the matters that can be studied; this is identical to the text of the *Shoushu* (Initial Commentary).
Therein, it likewise first discriminates what can be studied and subsequently discriminates what cannot be studied.

This differs from the "Gate of Differentiating Characteristics," which first clarifies what cannot be studied and subsequently discriminates what can be studied (*Jizong ji* contains an error in its presentation of the sequence of past and present). Regarding the statement "forming nine phrases divided into three grades," this refers to [the classification] according to the phrases.

The Dharma distinguishes the degree of the offense. According to the *Jieben shu* (Commentary on the Precepts), one may study nine or ten [precepts], but these are applied exclusively to those who do not teach others.

There are nine phrases in total, with each phrase assigned to one person; that is, they are explained in reference to nine individuals who do not teach others (this does not mean the "Nine People of Searching the Profundity," as most have seen Bing explain).
That is to say, these nine people each cultivate one practice of "stopping and maintaining" (*zhi-chi*) regarding the aforementioned killing.
Regarding the objective field (*viṣaya*): when it remains inactive and does not serve as a basis, even if the observance of conduct is established, one merely clarifies the mind;

however, because the conditions for the preceding objects of training are not fully understood, nine phrases regarding the objects of training are thus formed. Excluding the actual transgressions, these consist of the cessation of the six consciousnesses, which naturally constitute twelve instances of active observance.

There are twelve remaining doubts and instances of not recognizing the phrases; in total, these comprise twenty-four branches. If one does not study and lacks knowledge, one merely commits an offense.

If one studies and instructs others, assigning [the offenses] accordingly, it results in thirty-six *karmas* (this is according to the *Jieshu* [Commentary on the Precepts], which assigns these nine persons).

According to the *Cihewaji* [Record of Compassion and Harmony], it is incorrect to say that for a single person, the preceding and succeeding [cases] naturally constitute nine phrases. This is the established doctrine.
Poyun said: "If one speaks of 'a single person,' then since they have already recognized both the matter and the offense during the first instance, they are clearly proficient.

If, however, when encountering the same conditions again, they harbor doubts and fail to recognize it, they would be as if deluded and confused; this would constitute a failure to learn for themselves. How, then, could there be an offense?

(Therefore, it is only by considering nine types of persons that the principle becomes subtle. In contrast to this, one must understand that the formulations of ancient and modern masters differ; they are distinct, yet both are worthy of study."

The "Untrainable Nine" (fùkěxué jiǔ) are all formulated based on the three propositions concerning the object and the perception (*ālambana-saṃjñā*). As stated in the *Shūsō* (Commentary on the Preface):
"The Untrainable Nine are formulated by taking the three propositions regarding the object and perception and arranging them into groups of three.

If it were the "Trainable Nine" (kěxué jiǔ), they would not be formulated according to the Vinaya text, but rather by forming groups of four. The text of this present *Chāo* follows the *Shūsō* in its formulation; however...
Regarding the four phrases of the lower grade, they differ slightly from the initial commentary.

Now, first we shall establish the nine phrases of the "unlearnable," followed by the nine phrases of the "learnable," lest one fall into error. Question: Why are the nine phrases of the unlearnable established first? Answer:

It is because the nine phrases of the learnable originally derive from within the unlearnable. Since one wishes to clarify the learnable, one first clarifies the unlearnable. Furthermore, one wishes to...

It cannot be learned [as a mere rule]. First, let us set forth the categories of objects (*viṣaya*), perceptions (*saṃjñā*), and formal phrases (*pada*). The reason for doing so is that these cannot be learned apart from the objects and perceptions within the Vinaya;
therefore, they must be explained first. Regarding the categories of objects, perceptions, and formal phrases, we shall first list five cases according to the precept against killing:
1. A person, with the perception of a person (this is a mind that recognizes the object). 2. A non-person, with doubt regarding a person (this is a mind that doubts the object). 3. A non-person...

1. Perception of what is not a person as a person (this is a mind that does not recognize the object). 2. Perception of what is not a person as not a person (also a non-recognition of the object). 3. Doubt regarding what is not a person (this is a mind that doubts the object).

Now, taking the first three of these, they are arranged horizontally to form the three categories of: perception of the object, doubt regarding the object, and non-perception of the object. These constitute the three mental states regarding the object.

If we discuss the commission of an offense, this refers specifically to the "perception" (*saṃjñā*) regarding the object of the precept against concealing a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). As for the five permutations (*pañca-vākya*), take for example the case of killing: [The text continues with the application of these five permutations to the act of killing.]

When a person commits a *pārājika*, it is termed a "gross offense" (*sthūlātyaya*). There are five mental states regarding this: (1) perceiving a gross offense as a gross offense while concealing it (this is a mind of conscious transgression);

(2) perceiving two gross offenses as not being gross offenses with doubt (this is a mind of doubtful transgression); (3) perceiving a gross offense as not being a gross offense (a mind of unconscious transgression);

(4) perceiving what is not a gross offense as a gross offense (also a mind of unconscious transgression); (5) doubting whether what is not a gross offense is a gross offense (this is a mind of doubtful transgression). Now, we take the first three.
The three phrases—“knowing the offense,” “suspecting the offense,” and “not knowing the offense”—are laid out horizontally beneath the three matters.

First, taking the phrase “knowing the matter” as the subject, one proceeds through the three phrases above regarding the offense, thereby forming the three phrases of the upper grade: (1) knowing the matter and knowing the offense;

(2) knowing the matter and suspecting the offense; (3) knowing the matter and not knowing the offense. Next, taking the phrase “suspecting the matter” as the head, one proceeds through the offenses...

The first three phrases constitute the middle grade of three phrases: (1) doubting the matter while recognizing the offense; (2) doubting both the matter and the offense; (3) doubting the matter while not recognizing the offense.
Next, taking "not recognizing the matter" as the primary term, one proceeds through the aforementioned three phrases to form the lower grade of three phrases:
(1) not recognizing the matter while recognizing the offense; (2) not recognizing the matter while doubting the offense; (3) not recognizing the matter while not recognizing the offense.
This concludes the nine propositions regarding that which cannot be learned.

Next, to clarify the nine propositions regarding that which can be learned: among those cases where one does not recognize the object within the perception of the object, yet recognizes the offense while engaging with the matter, this constitutes the first proposition of the superior grade—namely, recognizing both the matter and the offense. Subsequently, one again employs the mind that recognizes the matter.

When one sequentially commits an offense with doubt regarding the object and lack of recognition of the object, and subsequently applies the first form of recognition (the first *vijñapti*) to commit the offense with doubt regarding the object and lack of recognition of the object, the four phrases of the middle grade (*madhyama-pakṣa*) are established.

Nine phrases. First, the source of these phrase-methods is clarified. Since it has already been established that deluded mind cannot be learned [from external objects], the discussion here focuses exclusively on the mind’s engagement with phenomena.

Regarding the three types of mind: for example, in the case of the precept against killing, the first three phrases are: (1) taking a human as a human and killing them (this is the mind that recognizes the object);

(2) taking a human as a non-human with doubt (this is the mind that doubts the object); (3) taking a human as a non-human (this is the mind that fails to recognize the object). These are the three minds regarding the conditions for the offense.
For example, regarding the concealment of a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), with respect to the object of the precept and the perception thereof:

the first three phrases consist of perceiving a grave offense as a grave offense (this is the mind that recognizes the offense), perceiving a grave offense while doubting it (this is the mind that doubts the offense), and concealing a grave offense while perceiving it as not being a grave offense (this is the mind that does not recognize the offense).

Now, taking the recognition of the fact as the primary focus, one proceeds through the three minds associated with the underlying offense to constitute the three phrases of the highest grade (*adhimātra*): first, recognizing the fact and recognizing the transgression; second... [text continues].

[The first set] consists of those who recognize the offense but have doubt regarding the matter. [The second set] consists of those who recognize the matter but do not recognize the offense. Next, taking the state of doubt regarding the matter as the single mind, there are three states of mind for the offenses committed throughout the conditions;

these constitute the middle grade, consisting of three phrases: first, doubting the matter while recognizing the offense; second, doubting both the matter and the offense; third, doubting the matter while not recognizing the offense.

Next, taking the state of not recognizing the matter as the single mind, there are three states of mind for the offenses committed throughout the conditions; these constitute the lower grade, consisting of three phrases: first...
1. Doubt regarding the offense while not recognizing the matter; 2. Doubt regarding the offense while not recognizing the matter; 3. Not recognizing the matter and not recognizing the offense.

In all these cases, with respect to the mind that takes the object and the offense as its conditions, there is delusion regarding the objective matter and the objective offense; thus, they are considered "untrainable" (asikṣya).
Regarding the statement "the first arrival constitutes an offense," the initial three phrases serve as the heading.

Taking the consciousness of the object as the primary factor, one traverses the three mental states regarding the offenses to establish the three phrases of the superior grade. As for the "three consciousnesses of the object in the first half," this refers to cases such as the final consciousness:

when a person perceives another as a human being within their own mind and desists without killing, this constitutes the three instances of superior-grade *śīla* (abstention) within the category of *saṃvara* (restraint).

Regarding the matter: if one recognizes the matter and is not deluded, there is no offense whatsoever. Regarding "recognizing the offense" in the second half [of the verse]: it means recognizing the four types of transgressions and being undeluded;
since this refers to an enlightened person, there is likewise no fault. It can be understood that if one does not recognize the offense, there is no fault.

According to the intention of the present Master, if one has fully studied and known the rules regarding offenses, even if one subsequently forgets or becomes deluded, it is universally permitted as being without fault. In the present text...
"Still bound" refers to following ancient bonds. The ancients said: "Evil matters are not to be learned.
Now, within a clear and enlightened mind, if one contemplates evil matters and does not understand them, it is because one is neither bound by nor has learned them through ignorance.

If there are offenses that ought to be learned, yet one does not understand them within a clear and enlightened mind, this is entirely because one did not learn them previously. If one harbors doubts and simultaneously fails to recognize the bonds, these constitute two offenses.
Now, according to our Master’s assessment based on delusion, regarding matters that cannot be learned, both doubt and ignorance are equally granted as non-offenses.

Furthermore, if one relies on the explanation concerning the side of offenses opened up in relation to specific matters, our Master and the ancients are identical in granting such exemptions. However, if one examines this from the perspective of its underlying principle, it is entirely distinct, as previously explained.
If one commits an offense but harbors doubt or lacks clear recognition, both ancient and modern masters have generally resolved such cases by concluding the offense based on clarity. I ask:

do you fully understand the intent of the ancient masters in concluding an offense based on a "clear mind" (*mingbai xin*) when the causal conditions for the offense were not fully realized? I wonder, what is the distinction between this and the conclusion of an offense based on a "clear mind" when the causal conditions for the offense were not fully realized according to the views of contemporary masters?
The answer is found in the *Jie shu* (Commentary on the Precepts), which states: "The latter nine phrases consist of three grades, each with three [subdivisions]."

If one does not recognize the nature of the object or situation, it cannot be understood through study alone; however, this does not preclude the possibility of understanding it through training regarding transgressions, which is why their characteristics are enumerated here.
(The above is from the *Śāstra*). In response to this question, why does the *Chao* text not mention "confusion" and "forgetfulness" at this point?

Regarding the "concordant practice" (samānārthatā), the absolution of transgressions is achieved by following ancient precedents. The answer is that this "abstention and maintenance" (vāritasamvara) has as its essence the singular attainment of avoiding unwholesome matters;

therefore, within the interval of such matters, one establishes the practice of abstention and maintenance through non-delusion. If the nature of the offense falls within the category of progressive cultivation, [it is addressed accordingly].

This pertains to the section on the maintenance of observances (*śīla*) through performance and cessation, and the transgression thereof. Performance constitutes maintenance, while cessation constitutes transgression.

One must wait until reaching the section on the "gates of performance-maintenance and cessation-transgression" to distinguish the opening of delusions and the release from offenses. If so, why is this [other category] cited here? The answer is: this is a provisional borrowing from that [other section].

Next, in listing the middle grade, the statement from "the two" up to "violation" takes a doubtful matter as the premise and traverses the three mental states regarding violation to form the three phrases of the middle grade. This constitutes the first half [of the section].

Since there is also a transformation of perception and fundamental delusion therein, why are offenses such as the *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) incurred based on this transformation of perception and fundamental delusion?

He did not speak of it. The answer is that the present discussion concerns the third phrase regarding the perception of the object (*ālambana-saṃjñā*). If one is confused regarding the original object, there is no offense, and one achieves the lower grade of *śīla-dhāraṇa* (maintaining the precepts).
This, in turn, serves as a counter-illustration for the second phrase regarding the object: since there is no primary offense (*maula-āpatti*) with respect to the person who is the original object.

In the realm of objects, there may be clarity or obscurity. If one suspects that one does not recognize the object, then [the mental consciousness] opens up. this does not depend on the other five consciousnesses. If one suspects that one does not recognize it, this indicates that one has not yet mastered the principle.

It is not because of confusion or forgetfulness that the Dharma is not opened [to them]. The Upādhyāya refutes this, saying: "If that were so, the Vinaya texts allow for concealment regarding gross offenses (*sthūlātyaya*) and the perception of the boundaries of a dwelling;
how then can confusion be permitted? Are these gross offenses and the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion followed by one proclamation) not solely matters of mental engagement?
The text follows the previous passage: it is simply because they are confused and have not yet mastered the training that the Buddha permits everything. Since it says 'everything is permitted'..."
This very [matter] must still be released; that it is still being tied now is merely following the ancients.
The second section restricts itself to the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*) and establishes two sets of nine phrases by way of association. The reason for dividing them into two is as follows:

first, it clarifies [the matter] by associating the cessation and the commission of the offense; second, from "Furthermore, the explanation below," it distinguishes [the matter] by whether or not there is a fundamental offense. The former...

Three [sections]: First, the objection that there is no offense regarding the initial commission (some also say this includes the objection that there is no offense regarding the root act); second, the response by following the characteristics of the cessation of the offense (it is incorrect to call this the "response concerning offenses arising from a different object";

for example, a person is the primary object and a stump is the different object; since one is confused about the primary object, there is absolutely no minor offense regarding the different object—how then can it be called a response concerning offenses arising from a different object?);

third, the objection that there is an offense which is not the tenet, and the response by following the performance of the act; fourth, the objection that the recognition of the offense consists only of eight [cases], and the response by following the phrasing of the rules.

Regarding the phrase "because the inquiry has reached its conclusion": the reason this section is established is that, within the extensive explanation provided previously, it was not fundamentally understood that, according to the *Chao*, there might be no offense—namely, when one is entirely without intention from beginning to end.

Now, excluding these three phrases of the "lower grade," only six phrases remain as having an offense. As for why the three phrases of the lower grade are without offense, it is because they concern fundamental delusion (*mūla-moha*).

Furthermore, one should consider the third case regarding the object of perception. When a deluded person perceives a human being as a tree stump, there is no offense for the human object because it is not perceived as such, and no offense for the stump object because it is not perceived as auspicious.
Thus, in the three lower grades, there is a complete absence of offense. In the three middle grades, there is doubt; although there is no offense regarding the stump, one doubts its nature.

Furthermore, regarding those who harbor even a partial doubt, they incur three *duṣkṛta* offenses; for those of the superior grade who do not recognize [the offense], they incur three *pārājika* offenses.
Now, excluding the three lower grades, among the six superior cases there are offenses. How can it be said that one commits nine offenses? (The question concludes.)
The answer consists of two parts: first, a response that accords with the question, which provides only six answers; second, a response that restates the intent of the preceding question.

Regarding the first, it should be understood that based on the fundamental [classification], there are truly only six phrases. As for the words "However, etc.," these state the response that restates the intent of the preceding question. Here, "however" (ran) means "indeed" (ni).
This is also referred to as "allowing and excluding. If the above [categories] are allowed, there are only six phrases; if they are excluded, it again results in nine phrases.
Regarding the phrase "under the three [cases] mentioned above," this refers to the section following the three "not knowing" phrases previously questioned.
Under these three phrases, there are cases of "not knowing" an offense, "doubting" an offense, and also the fault of "not having studied or being ignorant," which likewise results in nine [phrases].
Regarding the phrases: the ninth phrase concerns "not recognizing" an offense; the eighth phrase concerns "doubting" an offense.

If the seventh phrase is included generally within the former, its presence or absence has not yet been specified. Now, by taking the two phrases—the eighth and ninth—which concern doubt and non-recognition, and adding them to the characteristics of the commission of an offense, they likewise constitute nine phrases.
The second [section], "The Response to the Objection that There Are Faults and That the Three Categories Do Not Follow from the Formation of the Act," is divided into two parts:
first, the inquiry; second, the response. Regarding the phrase "If it reaches the point": this means "If that were so," which is the inquiry.

It refers to the inquiry into whether, since the three categories were previously established below, ignorance and doubt also constitute offenses, such that they would be added together to form nine categories—fearing that this might not be the case. Furthermore, regarding this offense of ignorance and...

Regarding the doubt concerning the offense: the offense established is one of "not learning," which was originally known as a "cessation-offense" (*śikṣāpada-āpatti*). Now, by bringing this cessation-offense to augment it, it becomes an "active-offense.
If it thus forms nine propositions, is this not a violation of the fundamental principle of the active-offense? (The inquiry concluded. In the response, there are two parts.

First, following the ancients, an explanation that the derivative follows the root. Second, from "Furthermore, necessarily... onwards, the explanation of the present master’s assistance in the prior matter. [The word] "following" refers to...
Regarding "being designated by virtue of the root": this means that performing the act of killing constitutes the commission of the root offense.

If one kills while being under the influence of doubt or ignorance regarding the *pārājika* offense of killing, one is instead charged with the offenses of "not training" (*aśikṣita*) and "lack of knowledge" (*ajñāna*). This transgression is based upon the person who is the object of the root act of killing;

thus, it is designated by taking the secondary factors from the root, and is likewise considered a commission of the offense. Furthermore, it necessarily depends on the assistance provided by those below [the perpetrator]. (From the *Shoushu*).
