Fearing that the bhikṣus would report them to others, the bandits intended to kill them all. One among the bandits, however, knew the dharma of the bhikṣus and advised them to bind the bhikṣus with grass and leave them.
While the bhikṣus were being tormented by mosquitoes, gadflies, and the scorching sun, the senior monk (sthavira) addressed the assembly, saying: 'Human life is impermanent.'"
Like the swift current of a river, even if one dwells in the heavens, one will soon be worn away and destroyed; how much more so for human life—how can it be preserved?
Why, for the sake of life, would one destroy the precepts? All you people should know that a human body is difficult to obtain, and so forth.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus each rectified their own bodies and minds. Because the king had gone out on a hunt, they saw him and subsequently spoke a verse, asking: "Observe the time."
"You appear healthy, robust, and full of vigor; why then are you entangled by this thick grass? Day and night you cannot turn over.

The bhikṣu answered with a verse: "This grass is extremely fragile; it would not be difficult to destroy it. It is only because I am restrained by the Vajra-like precepts of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Having heard this, the king had the man released and spoke a verse: "Excellent! You are able to maintain the teachings of the Śākya Master with such firm resolve."
As you have said: "One would rather sacrifice one's own body and life than violate the Dharma;

I now likewise take refuge in the Muni, the Honored One of Liberation, who firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts. I now likewise take refuge in him. Regarding the term "board for the ocean," the eighth fascicle of the *Śāstra* states:
There were certain bhikṣus who accompanied merchants into the sea. Encountering a storm, their ship was wrecked and they fell into the water. A junior monk managed to catch hold of a board.
A wooden board. The senior monk (upādhyāya) submerged himself in the water and spoke a verse to request it, saying: "The Buddha ordained that one must respect the seniors;
why then do you withhold the board? The junior monk replied: "I did not consider the Buddha’s words; I withheld the board for the sake of my life. Now I offer this with sincere resolve."
Offering his body and life as a raft, he then handed the board to the Elder and submerged himself in the water.
At that time, the sea deity, moved by his sincerity, received the bhikṣus and the merchants onto the shore. Thereupon, the sea deity spoke a verse in praise, saying:
"Homage to the Great Faithful One! In risking his life, he was able to uphold the precepts. By the power of your single-minded resolve, You have inspired my courageous heart. [He] received them.
"You ascend; let us ascend together to a place of safety. By virtue of this faith and reverence, you shall surely attain the fruit of liberation. Regarding the word "etcetera" (*ādi*):

it includes the case of the monk who took the swan's pearl, which was entrusted to him. There is no contradiction in citing such instances to corroborate the preceding discussion on natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*).

Regarding the statement "others are permitted": this refers to cases where one's power of the Path has not yet been perfected, and upon encountering circumstances involving a threat to life, one is permitted to relax the prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepaṇīya-śikṣāpada*) found within the first three categories of offenses.
If that is so, are the prohibitive precepts in the second category also not relaxed? Answer: They likewise are not relaxed.

For example, acting as a matchmaker to give rise to sexual desire—sexual desire being the source of obstacles to the Path and the root of wandering in saṃsāra—and possessing two dwellings, which waste wealth and furthermore hinder [spiritual progress].
The path of cultivation is also not opened [for them].

Regarding what is called the "five most difficult [situations]": "Brahma" means purity; fearing that pure conduct might be ruined, they permit transgressions in these cases. As for "going to the extreme":

for a young maiden or a widow, it is difficult to maintain the precept against sexual misconduct; for buried treasure, it is difficult to maintain the precept against stealing; for water... [it is difficult to maintain the precept against taking what is not given].

Because there are many minute insects on land, it is for the sake of the precept against killing; because evil companions are difficult to avoid and verbal excesses are frequent, it is for the sake of avoiding false accusations.

The phrase "the text says" refers to the passage in the *An-gu-fa-jù* (The Collection of Rules for the Rain Retreat). It states that if any of the aforementioned conditions exist, one is permitted to break the retreat and depart without fault.

Regarding the statement "only up to the [third] category of offenses," this follows from the preceding text which says: "As for those who break the retreat and depart, it is only permitted within the three categories of offenses (*triprakāra*)."

Regarding prohibitions such as *pācittiya* and *dukkaṭa*: if they concern actions by nature that involve striking, beating, consuming [intoxicants], and so forth, they are never permitted. As for the statement "until one knows," this refers to the prohibition of evil acts;
because it prohibits cutting down trees, felling timber, digging the earth, and so on—acts that would incur the censure of the laity—it is permitted when there is an obstacle.

Regarding matters that are light: as in the case of the *śaikṣa* rules, there may be two difficulties where exceptions are made for running with one's head covered or entering a village without informing others.

Regarding cases where a light matter obstructs a heavy one: if due to the four obstacles such as gender and so forth, one is unable to assemble for the distribution of robes (*kaṭhina*), then the remote relinquishment (*dūrasamnyāsa*) is permitted;

by doing so, one incurs only a light offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*) and avoids committing a major offense of expiation (*sthūlātyaya*). The opposite cases can be understood accordingly; this refers to the various heavy obstructions not included in the three aforementioned categories.
In cases such as drinking alcohol and the like, it is not permitted. If there is a difficulty as mentioned above, it is permitted;

if there is no difficulty, it is not allowed (there are further non-permissible cases as recorded in the *Hongji*). Regarding the statement "the Vinaya reaches the teacher," this serves to verify the characteristics of what is permitted and what is prohibited through superior discernment.

First, regarding the origin of the transgression: second, the initial promulgation (*prathama-prajñapti*); third, the repeated promulgation (*punar-prajñapti*), such as [the case of] being with livestock in the forest.

Regarding those who have committed sexual misconduct and violate the precept against unchaste conduct: for one whose observance of the full precepts is lax, it is permitted to relinquish the precepts and return to lay life; having done so, they may later return to receive the precepts again.

For one who is strict, it is prescribed that they must maintain them alongside their peers. As for the three points of definitive resolution: first, the origin story (*nidāna*); second, the core of the precepts (*sūtravastu*).

Third, the extensive explanation: This proves that for the *dharmatā-śīla* (inherent precepts), no exemptions are permitted; whereas for the *prajñapti-śīla* (provisional prohibitions), exemptions are allowed when urgent.
Furthermore, when there is no difficulty, exemptions are not granted even if the matter is urgent. One who makes such decisive judgments is called a Vinaya master (*vinayadhara*) and so forth.

Regarding the sixth [section], which is titled "The Designation of the Original Object": as for the phrase "the sixfold designation of the original object," one may ask: what is the difference between this designation of the original object and the previously mentioned mental state directed toward its object?
The answer is: the former was distinguished by differences in perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*), whereas this is distinguished by differences in the preceding objects.

If one refers to the original object of the offense, one universally commits all transgressions; if one does not refer to the original object, then one universally does not commit the root offense, though there are still the *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) and *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) due to deficiencies in the conditions.
The phrase "to reach" means to arrive at. Regarding "conceiving what is not the path to be the path," this is an explanation based on the first precept.

Furthermore, there are four primary objects for the precept against sexual misconduct: first, a waking woman; second, a sleeping woman; third, a recently deceased woman; and fourth, a partially decomposed woman.
All of the above constitute the primary objects (*maula-vastu*); if one approaches them to commit the act, one incurs the offense of *pārājika*. As for a "half-object" woman...

Alternatively, it may be a woman who is mostly corrupted, which is subsumed under the category of "improper path. If one approaches her and commits an offense involving *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, consider first the original object:
she was a woman who was only slightly corrupted and was not the proper object [for intercourse]. With a clear mind, one proceeded with the thought that she was on the "proper path.

Upon reaching the midpoint of the act, the original object had already transformed into one who was half-corrupted or mostly corrupted; thus, she now belongs to the category of the "proper and proper object. Now...
Regarding an object that is not the proper path, one constantly perceives it as being the proper path. When union with the object occurs, one becomes attached to what is not the path;

this does not constitute a fundamental *pārājika* offense, but rather incurs two *sthūlātyaya* offenses. When the nature of the object changes midway, one incurs one *sthūlātyaya* for the discrepancy of the object.
Following the change of the object, if one again perceives the improper object as being the proper path and engages in union with it...

At that time, there was no "when," nor was there the non-path. The non-path deviated from the fundamental mind. Furthermore, one obtained one *laṇ* (in the *Shuōjì*, it is simply stated as "one *laṇ*"; this refers to a state of confusion and disorder).

Regarding the phrase "there is no perception of it as having an owner": although this statement is clear, it refers to a case where an object has been left behind within one's own territory, and the owner has not yet definitively abandoned their claim to it; thus, the object remains as if it still had an owner. Now, upon seeing this object...

One forms the perception that the object has an owner and proceeds to steal it. While traveling toward the destination, the original owner has already relinquished their claim; thus, the object’s status as a domain of ownership has vanished.

Now, regarding this object which is actually without an owner, one continues to maintain the perception that it has an owner. If one moves the object from its location under such conditions, the offense of *pārājika* (defeat) is not incurred. This is based on the principle of "intermediate change":

when the object has become something without an owner, there is a discrepancy in the objective condition (*ālambana*), resulting in a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). This is determined according to the nature of the object.

After the transformation, if one falsely gives rise to the perception that there is a master [of the object], and when lifting it away, one also gives rise to the mind that there is a master, it is a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense).

This is not analogous to the precept against sexual misconduct, which results in a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). Therefore, the text below states: "In the case of sexual misconduct (*abrahmacarya*), whether through a shift in perception or through delusion, one incurs both a *pārājika* (defeat) and a *sthūlātyaya*."

Only in the case of sexual misconduct is there an external emission that constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense; all subsequent mental states are associated with a *dukkaṭa*. Know this. Regarding the phrase "perceiving one who is not a human as a human":

this refers to a situation where the object before one is actually a human, and one perceives them as such while killing. However, during the interval, a non-human (*amanussa*) comes to take their place.
Throughout this time, one continues to perceive that non-human as a human. When the blow is struck and the killing occurs upon that non-human, it is [not a *pārājika*].

When a human life is severed, one does not incur the offense of *pārājika*. There is only the *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) arising from the discrepancy between the prior mental state and the actual object. Regarding the moment of changing objects during the interval:

from the point after the object has changed, because one harbors a false intent to kill a person, one incurs only the *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). This *duṣkṛta* also applies specifically when there is a discrepancy between the person and the object;
if it were a non-human being or a different object entirely, there would be no offense at all. Why? Because there was no intention [to kill] that specific object. Each case is distinct.

The following provides a general summary: In the precept against sexual misconduct, the "proper path" is the primary object (*maulaviṣaya*), while the "improper path" is the secondary object (*viṣayāntara*).

In the precept against stealing, that which has an owner is the primary object, while that which has no owner is the secondary object. In the precept against killing, a human being is the primary object, while a non-human being is the secondary object.

The three precepts above all involve the substitution of one object for another; however, they constitute the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) due to a discrepancy in the object, as only the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) is committed.

This principle regarding discrepancies in the object within this section is most profound and subtle. It is explained extensively according to a single school [of thought], which may serve as a mirror for reflection; consider it well.

The seventh gate. Regarding the phrase "the seven factors for reaching [the offense]": although one possesses the preceding six, if one has not yet progressed toward the fruit and has not yet committed the transgression, this condition is established.

Suppose the original object was a human being, and at the present time when one intends to kill that person, the thought and mind are resolute and penetrating.
Upon reaching the moment of accomplishment, both the perception of the person and the murderous intent remain uninterrupted, and one incurs the ultimate offense of *pārājika*.

However, if one encounters the original object and gives rise to doubt—where the mind wavers between two possibilities, fearing that it might not be a human being—and consequently desists, one incurs only the preparatory offense (*prayoga*). This has been the established principle since antiquity.

Commentary: Regarding the tradition handed down here, it defines the *pārājika* offenses based on differences in the sixth category of objects (*viṣaya*), while also incorporating the seventh category of mental intention (*citta*).

By means of the "cessation of doubt," "mental state," and "forceful cessation" and so forth, it establishes the meaning of the *pārājika* offenses through differences in the object. The *Shoushu* (Initial Commentary) lists eighteen *pārājikas*; the *Xiangshu* (Mutual Commentary) lists thirty-eight;

the Dongta school lists eight (as detailed in the *Yitu*, these are not included in this record); and the Nanshan school lists seven. These seven conditions are fully contained within the text of the *Chao* (Commentary), where they are used to apply [the rules] universally to all cases.

The third section concludes with the binding statement. Regarding the phrase "extending upward to the 'leaving'" (*chū*), it clarifies two types of offenses: those committed through general conditions (*sāmānya-pratyaya*) and those committed through specific conditions (*viśeṣa-pratyaya*).

(The above is the interpretation of Hong. Alternatively, it may be understood that both general and specific conditions together clarify the commission of an offense; or that general and specific conditions together clarify the superior offense (*uparimaka-āpatti*).

If the commission of an offense is clarified within both conditions, this is as discussed in the *Shō* (the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*). If both conditions together clarify the cessation of an offense (*nivṛtti-āpatti*), [the same applies].

Just as in the case of constructing a dwelling without begging for materials, one must likewise rely on both the general and specific conditions. Therefore, it is said that "both clarify two offenses" (this interpretation is also applicable).

When two conditions are deficient, this constitutes the cause but not the result; when the two conditions are complete, this constitutes the result but not the cause. Upon reaching the result, the offense is grave.
If [the offense] was committed due to causes, it is light. One must understand this in detail before entering into the rite of repentance.
If one does not clearly discern the gravity or lightness of causes and effects, the confession of faults will be vague and ineffective. (The third section above is concluded.)
Regarding the fourth section, the "Gate of Perceptions of Objects": first is the formal citation. As for the phrase "the four perceptions of objects," etc., the intent behind it is as follows:

Therefore, they are not explicitly indicated. Alternatively, they could have been included within the section on "doubt regarding the object" (*viṣaya-saṃśaya*), such as the doubt concerning whether the victim is a human or a non-human, or the doubt concerning whether it is a human or a non-human.

Regarding all precepts, whenever there is a perception of an object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), it is all determined by reference to this [perception]. There may be cases where [an act] exists, or cases where it does not;
cases where it ought not to exist according to principle, or cases where it is omitted within the Vinaya texts; cases where it is few or many, or light or heavy, and so forth.
As for the statement "the formulation reaches the ear," it asks: what is the reason for formulating [the rule] based on the perception of the object? If one were to answer...

If one were to establish the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*) and definitively determine the offense, there would be no means by which to know the distinctions between its presence or absence, or its gravity or lightness.

By establishing this method of the "perception of the object" (*viṣaya-saṃjñā-pada*), one immediately knows the gravity or lightness, and its presence or absence. That is to say, regarding the fivefold textual formulation of the Vinaya:

the first phrase constitutes a *pārājika* (defeat), while each of the subsequent four phrases constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting). Among these, the preceding offenses are more serious, and the succeeding offenses are lighter. Within these five phrases:

The four subsequent lines each have their own skillful means (*upāya*) but lack a fundamental basis. Alternatively, they may be categorized according to fundamental delusion, as in the case of the precept against killing. Regarding the third line:

if one is deludedly attached to a non-animal that possesses the characteristics of an object of transgression, there is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing); if one is deluded regarding a tree stump [mistaking it for a human], there is no offense.
One can only know this through the perception of the object (*ālambana-saṃjñā*). Therefore, in all the precepts, even before the Buddha, these were fully established.
[This] is a listing. Under each of the two hundred and fifty-one precepts, the text of five phrases regarding the objective conditions (*viṣaya*) is listed in parallel.

If this is so, why is it that within the current version of the Vinaya text, while twenty-six precepts contain these [phrases], other precepts lack them entirely? The *Śāstra* (the *Nanhai Jiguai Neifa Zhuan* or *Shanbu Suishu Yichao*) answers:

"Even if there are missing passages, they are mostly merely abbreviated. That is to say, wherever the current Vinaya text lacks the method of phrases concerning the perception of the objective condition (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), [it is due to abbreviation]."

These were originally absent; they have been added here by the present commentator. Fearing prolixity, I have deleted them, or perhaps the original author of the section omitted them as being too cumbersome.

Regarding the phrase "from the two [categories] up to the offenses": "fan" (汎) means broad or extensive. To clarify the characteristics of transgressions, one must first distinguish the objective spheres (*viṣaya*).

In total, there are five types, which will be comprehensively summarized for the sake of brevity. Subsequently, within these spheres, one shall determine their presence or absence according to the Vinaya.

Regarding "internal retribution" (*antaravipāka*): sentient beings are termed "internal," and that which recompenses past causes is termed "retribution. This does not include the categories of *piśāca*, hell-beings, or *asura*.
For the first precept, the four objects [of killing] are termed "offenses" because the rule is established in relation to those objects; for the others, it is not fixed.

It should be understood that for killing, stealing, and lying, if they are committed against human objects, they are grave and thus constitute an ascent; if committed against non-humans or animals, they are light and thus constitute a descent.
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, [the offenses] such as 'equal to' (*tulya*)": among the four previously mentioned, these pertain solely to the human realm (*manuṣya-gati*).

Within them, there are precepts concerning the laity and the clergy regarding buying and selling, which—like the offense of sitting by force (*balāt-saṃsthāpana*) found among the ninety [offenses]—have only laypeople as the objective field for the commission of the offense. This also includes the two offenses of slander, both major and minor.

The precept on concealing gross offenses; the precept on speaking of gross offenses; the precept on striking or beating a bhikṣu; the precept on causing doubt or vexation; the precept on hiding another’s robes or bowl—these apply exclusively to the monastic community.
Regarding the offense of staying for two nights: the first is staying overnight with a woman; the second is staying for more than three nights with one who has not received full ordination.
Sexual misconduct refers to the precept against sexual intercourse. Physical contact refers to the precept against touching. Regarding the two types of harsh speech: the first is harsh speech itself.

The second is praising one's own body. This applies equally to both monastics and laypeople; both commit the offense. The phrase "extending to both" excludes the lay community and refers specifically to the monastic order.

Within the monastic order, there are further distinctions between those within our own tradition (insiders) and outsiders. Regarding outsiders—those who are preoccupied with food and clothing—the offense occurs when a monk gives food with his own hands to an outsider;

nuns commit the same offense as the monks. As for "personally recording what is incorrect and failing to report it," the internal cases are like the two instances of disparagement [discussed previously].

"Defaming" refers to disparaging [others]. "The two" refers to divisive speech (*paiśunya*). These apply exclusively to those within the community. Regarding the phrase "having reached the age," this concerns the internal community and is discussed in terms of seniority and juniority.
"Slandering and seizing" refers to slandering the precepts and seizing the robes and bowl; this constitutes an offense only when committed against a *bhikṣu*.

Granting full ordination to one who has not yet reached the required age results in a *thullaccaya* offense for the preceptor; by analogy, this applies when the offense is committed against a *śrāmaṇera*.

Regarding the statement "furthermore, it is known": within the context of possessing the full precepts (*saṃvara*), this is distinguished according to the physical form and status of monks and nuns as being compliant with the act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*).
When a *bhikṣu* incurs this offense, it constitutes a transgression only in relation to another *bhikṣu* as the object of the offense; it does not extend to a *bhikṣuṇī*.

This is because monks and nuns do not share communal formal acts (*karmavācanā*), nor do they share such activities as staying overnight together or conversing. Traveling on the same road is equivalent to traveling on the same path, and traveling by boat is equivalent to traveling on the same boat.
Regarding the precept on making robes for a nun, and the precept on accepting food praised by a nun: although these take a nun as the object of the offense, they are offenses against both assemblies.
As for the meaning of "slander and concealment" applying to both assemblies, the *Hongshi* (Great Commentary) states: "This refers to the fact that monks and nuns serve as mutual objects of offense.

Since there is no separate introductory narrative (*nidāna*) in the *Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa* but the rules are listed directly, we know that both major and minor slanders constitute *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and *pāyattika* offenses respectively for both groups.

It is said that for concealing a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), both [monks and nuns] incur a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) through mutual concealment. If one conceals a *sthūlātyaya* committed by a nun, one incurs a *pārājika*; if a nun conceals one of the eight *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meetings) offenses, she incurs a *pāyattika*.

As for concealing offenses from the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* downward, both incur a *pāyattika* through mutual concealment (this is the interpretation transmitted in the tradition). However, the meaning of the current interpretation is different:

it states that when concealing these [offenses], both assemblies are the objects of my transgression; it does not mean "mutual" [concealment]. This is like the case of concealing a slanderous statement, where both great bhikṣus incur a *pāyattika*.
Regarding a *mahābhikṣu*: this is my object of transgression (*āpatti-viṣaya*). If one slanders or conceals [an offense] against him, a *mahābhikṣuṇī* also commits a *thullaccaya*.

Regarding a *mahābhikṣuṇī*: this is my object of transgression. The underlying meaning is that these three higher precepts apply to both assemblies; therefore, it is said that they are explained according to the two groups.

If one were to discuss them reciprocally, taking only one side as the object, I fear this would contradict the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* (the *Chao*). Reflect upon this, for there is significance therein.

Regarding "the others that can be understood": this refers to those [offenses] other than the three aforementioned precepts. Furthermore, there are cases that apply universally to both assemblies as the objects of transgression, yet they are not all explicitly listed;
therefore, it is said that "they can be known" (reflect upon this). The *Hongji* states: "For instance, offenses such as killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct apply to both assemblies.

This is because in the *Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa*, there are no separate introductory narratives (*nidāna*); the precepts are listed directly, and since the offenses are identical for both, they are easily recognized."
It is said: "It may be known" (this should not be considered incorrect).
As for the statement that "speech and form are distinct," the preceding passage was based on the retribution of form; thus, the forms of all sentient beings are entirely *vipāka* (maturation).

Now, within the context of the ripening retribution of form, we further discuss the objects of transgression in terms of both matter and mind. For example, when the scope of sexual misconduct is considered broad, it is defined in terms of matter;
that is, among the five aggregates (*skandha*), only the single aggregate of matter (*rūpa-skandha*) constitutes the object of the offense of sexual misconduct. A corpse is matter.

It is like committing a root offense; provided that the correct path is involved, whether one has doubt or certainty, it constitutes an offense. This applies universally to humans and devas, not to animals.

By this, it is proven that the four aggregates do not depend on the mind [to constitute the act]. The scriptural passage stating "the path and the perception of the path" is likewise proof that matter (*rūpa*) constitutes the offense.
As for the statement that "leakage is the same," this is indeed so; it means that the leakage of the precepts is equally an object of offense, and the object remains [the same].

This "broad" refers to the aforementioned precept against sexual misconduct. Although it was defined in terms of physical form (*rūpa*), it remains narrow; this [precept regarding] emission is even broader.

Internal forms, external forms, in space, in water, in wind, whether facing toward or away, and so forth—all these are objects of transgression. Regarding the phrase "coming oneself to eat," there is that which pertains to the mind: the intention of taking [the food].
This is because one’s own capacity for the transgressive mind is compared to the mind of another person; this is what is meant.

This refers to the object of the offense (*āpatti-viṣaya*). Regarding "such as observing the consent" (*anumati*) and so forth: "observing" (*anupaśyanā*) refers to the four types of offenses involving the giving of consent;

"consent" (*anumati*) refers to the precept against diverting property belonging to the Saṃgha. From this point upward, the object is defined by the mental state of another. For example, when the members of the Saṃgha possess a mind that seeks to settle a dispute in accordance with the Dharma, a bhikṣu forms a wholesome perception of them.

If he subsequently raises the issue again, hoping for the Saṃgha to maintain that wholesome perception of settling the dispute, he incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) in relation to that side of their mind seeking to settle the dispute. Therefore.

The text states: "If one contemplates [the object] and forms the perception [of it as such], even if [the object] is permitted to have ceased, if the Saṃgha still performs an unwholesome contemplation, then for a bhikṣu who has extinguished his mind, even if he subsequently forms the contemplation and perception, he incurs only the preparatory offense of *duṣkṛta*. This would result in the deficiency of the Saṃgha’s wholesome contemplation regarding the object of the extinguished mind.
If one permits the action and permits the perception, once the person has already determined that the property belongs to the Saṃgha, the bhikṣu..."

Furthermore, one may form the perception that [the donor] has granted permission. this is because the objective condition of the donor’s consenting mind is lacking. Regarding "food and clothing with a defiled mind":

this refers to a nun who knows that a man has a defiled mind toward her, yet she gives him food and clothing. When the mind and the object correspond, taking them constitutes an offense. If [it is] a man...

One acts for the sake of merit; therefore, one gives with an undefiled mind. Even if one were to act with a defiled mind, there would be no transgression, provided that the object of the defiled mind is absent.
One must generally understand that this does not encompass every specific division. The preceding text began with the four realms of existence and concluded with form and mind;
while this broad outline roughly encompasses everything, beyond this, there are further details that cannot be minutely categorized.
This is the judgment (the above concludes the explanation of internal retribution).
Next, regarding external matters: as for the phrase "up to two," this section exclusively concerns non-sentient things, which are termed "external matters.

The phrase "it may also be" means that while, according to principle, robes and bowls kept beyond ten days constitute an offense where time serves as the objective condition (*ālambana*) for the violation, here we take the robes and bowls themselves [as the object].
This concerns external matters; it is cited here for clarification, which is why the *Chao* text uses the phrase "it may also be.

If that is so, since the offense of keeping food overnight (*śeṣabhakta*) is also determined by time, why does it lack the phrase "it may also be"? Answer: This refers to the case where the object of the offense is food kept overnight, rather than the formation of the substance of the offense itself being kept overnight.

Regarding the substance that applies to both internal and external factors: in the precept against stealing, the owner is internal and the property is external. In the case of taking back a robe [after it has been relinquished], it is similar.

The robe is external; the bhikṣu is internal (the personal note states this is incorrect). The insect is internal; the water is external. This constitutes an internal retribution and an external object combined to form the sphere of the offense.
The third section, concerning the dharma-text, has two parts. First, the citation of the text as it appears. In the commentary:
regarding the phrase "first, etc.," (1) "that which one refers to oneself" means taking as the object the dharma spoken from one's own mouth, such as acts of matchmaking or coarse speech;
(2) "that which is performed by another" refers to the dharma upheld by the Saṃgha, such as the act of formal authorization (*jñapti-karman*); (3) "punishment" [is the third].

This refers to knowing that the *uddhata-vinaya* (the method of correction for arrogance) applies to oneself; now, in accordance with that, one regards the *uddhata-vinaya* within the other person's body as the object of the offense.

Regarding the four characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*): these are the phenomena of names and numbers, all of which constitute the characteristics of phenomena. Upon these phenomena, one discerns the principles of the heterodox and the orthodox.
The Buddha taught the nine orthodox [points], while Devadatta taught the nine heterodox. When the Sangha is split, one issues a formal admonition by observing these eighteen phenomena.
Thus one knows that the principles of the heterodox and the orthodox are contradictory, and one recognizes whether that bhikṣu speaks according to the Dharma or not according to the Dharma.

If one now studies this non-Dharma which destroys the True Dharma, then by reason of these characteristics of the phenomenon (dharmalakṣaṇa), the arising of an offense is ceased; thus it is taken as the object of the offense.
Fourth, regarding time: as for the mention of "the four [periods]" and so forth, the evening is designated as the improper time for teaching nuns; that is, it is an improper time.

Regarding the precept on eating and the summer retreat (*varṣā*): during the summer, if one does not observe the *anvārohaṇa* (the supplementary retreat), one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense; if one does not rely upon a fifth *vinayadhara*, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

Alternatively, one may "steal" the summer by proclaiming [one's seniority] and receiving great benefits; such a person also attains the year [of seniority]. If one has not yet completed five years and yet leaves the *niśraya* (dependence) or ordains others, [the penalty is as follows]:

some explain that for two years one studies the six rules (*ṣaddharma*) and then receives full ordination (*upasampadā*); for a nun, this is a *sthūlātyaya* offense, while for a monk it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one stays away for two or three nights...

These are: first, staying with one who has not received full ordination for more than three nights; second, staying in an army for more than three nights, or staying overnight within the camp during the remaining night.

In all these cases, the limit of the offense is defined by the appearance of dawn (*āloka*). The term "etc. includes such matters as being separated from one's robes, keeping extra robes, and the medicinal bowl.

Regarding the fifth point, "the fifth refers to the limit and so forth": this means that, for example, as with concealing gross offenses (*sthūlātyaya*) and similar cases, if one conceals a *bhikṣuṇī*’s eight grave offenses (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*), one also incurs a *pāyattika*.

If a *bhikṣuṇī* herself conceals her own eight gross offenses, or conceals four [grave offenses] of a *saṃgha*, these are likewise grave. All are classified as offenses based on the nature of the concealment.
Regarding the third section, the "Gate of Presence and Absence": the statement "three to none" refers to the aforementioned five categories of objects of offense (*viṣaya*).

Regarding perception (*saṃjñā*): according to the Vinaya texts and the Monastic Codes (*Prātimokṣa*) for monks and nuns, there are cases where the object is perceived and cases where it is not. Therefore, the following section clarifies this;
as for the remaining cases that are omitted, they are either logically absent or intentionally omitted. In the commentary, the phrase "referring to those who have reached the precepts" means:

These can be understood by reference to the four categories of precepts. Regarding the six offenses of the second category (the *dvādaśa-nissaggiya-pācittiya*): they are touching [a woman], the two types of coarse speech, the two types of matchmaking, and the two regarding dwellings.

Among the thirty offenses (*pācittiya*), the first is the offense of diverting the property of the Saṃgha. Among the ninety offenses (*pācittiya*), the fifteenth consists of seven items: first, speaking of a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) once; second, digging the earth; third, destroying living plants;
fourth, using water containing insects; fifth, instructing a nun to announce the time of sunset; sixth, eating food praised by a nun; and seventh, eating after having finished one's meal.
Eight: encouraging another to eat to fullness; nine: eating food kept overnight; ten: eating at the improper time; eleven: eating food not formally offered; twelve: drinking alcohol; thirteen:

drinking water containing insects; fourteen: concealing a grave offense (pārājika); fifteen: inciting the four types of disputes. These are the twenty-six precepts established in the present [Vinaya].

The Vinaya texts fully contain the distinctions of "object" and "perception. However, regarding the precept on sexual misconduct, it is said that the perception of the object does not apply. Why is this?

There is this method of phrasing [the rules]. The answer is that it is intended to prevent clever rationalizations; that is to say, one might claim that if one perceives an act as being "not the proper way," no offense is committed.
Therefore, it is necessary to distinguish [the cases]. Next, regarding the analysis by contrast, the phrase "contrasting with the 'arrival'" (*prāpti*) means:

based on the aforementioned twenty-six precepts, there are further perceptions regarding grave objects (*gurutara-vastu*) within those twenty-six, which together constitute thirty-five. Second, the two dwellings (*dvau vihārau*).
"Containing seven" refers to the sevenfold categories of objects, perceptions, and phrases. There are four types of ownerless dwellings: first, those not authorized by the Saṃgha;

second, those exceeding the prescribed dimensions; third, those in difficult locations; and fourth, those that obstruct others. Thus, the Vinaya text states: first, the Saṃgha has not authorized it and one perceives it as unauthorized;

second, the Saṃgha has not authorized it but one suspects it is authorized; third, the Saṃgha has not authorized it but one perceives it as authorized; and fourth, it is authorized and one acts accordingly.

[1] Not having obtained formal authorization (anujñāta), yet perceiving it as not authorized; [2] having doubt regarding whether authorization was obtained or not (the first phrase is incomplete, with the other four phrases constituting a *pācittiya* offense). The five cases concerning exceeding the prescribed dimensions are likewise [as detailed above].

Regarding difficult locations (*kṛcchra-sthāna*), there are five cases: [1] a difficult location, perceived as a difficult location; [2] a difficult location, with doubt as to whether it is a difficult location; [3] a difficult location, perceived as not a difficult location; [4] a non-difficult location, perceived as a difficult location;
[5] a non-difficult location, with doubt as to whether it is a difficult location. Regarding obstructed locations (*vighna-sthāna*)... [five cases follow].

The same applies to the case of the *pada* (phrase/section), and so forth. Regarding dwellings with an owner, excluding those that exceed the prescribed dimensions, the remaining three cases should be treated according to the above principle, and so forth.

For dwellings without an owner, there are four layers; for those with an owner, there are three layers. Together with the preceding cases, this constitutes seven fundamental instances. As for the two external remaining cases, they may reach five layers. Regarding the two layers in the precept on stealing:
first, when it is another person's property and one perceives it as such, and so forth; second, when it is another person's property and one perceives it as such, and so forth.
...and so forth. Regarding the two types of matchmaking: first, one person [perceives] a woman as a woman, and so forth; second, matchmaking while perceiving it as matchmaking, and so forth.
Regarding the two types of harsh speech: first, one person [perceives] a woman as a woman, and so forth;
second, harsh speech while perceiving it as harsh speech, and so forth. Regarding the two types of destroying life: first, a seed while perceiving it as a seed, and so forth; second, living beings...
"Regarding grasses and trees, one has the perception of grasses and trees," and so forth (as detailed). The four precepts above each have one additional category, thus forming four;

combined with the previous five, they become nine times nine. When paired with the twenty-six [categories], they correctly total thirty-five (the *Bun'i ki* states that thirty-five are paired, and further notes that "perception" and "doubt" are paired together).

Regarding the statement "from the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya down to the [Prātimokṣa]": this refers to the twenty-six rules for bhikṣuṇīs in relation to the saṃgha. Among these, ten rules lack the distinction of "perception regarding the object" (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*). These ten are:

sexual intercourse, physical contact, coarse speech, praising one's own body, the two types of building dwellings, soliciting food, praising food, eating at the improper time, eating after having finished a meal, and encouraging another to finish their meal.

Since these ten differ from those of the bhikṣus, they lack the distinction of perception regarding the object. As for the remaining ten rules, they may be understood as being the same as the six major rules for bhikṣus. [These concern] coarse touch and defiled intention.
Regarding food and clothing, there are distinct objects and perceptions; thus, eighteen precepts are established. Therefore, it is said that they are not non-existent.

In the *Chao*, because of the desire to avoid prolixity, these have been abbreviated and omitted. As stated previously, even where there are missing passages, they are mostly merely omissions. Hence it is said, "as described at the beginning."
Regarding the statement that "the fifth follows next," this refers to the aforementioned five categories, which clarify the objects of transgression.

According to the Vinaya, with the exception of twenty-six precepts, all others lack the *mūla-pada* (root-text) formulas. Here, we shall again examine them in light of the preceding principles to determine whether they are absent due to a logical reason, or whether they have been omitted by the masters of the schools or the translators.

In the commentary, the phrase "or reaching the [full] state" refers to cases such as the violation of the precept against emission. Since this offense is committed against all objects, whether sentient or non-sentient, why would it require the specific formulation of the words?

Therefore, the principle of the *pārājika* (defeat) is here omitted. Next, within the section on omissions, the phrase "or reaching the abbreviated [form]" refers to the aforementioned precept against emission. It involves the perception of the object;
that is, if one perceives it as a non-path and acts upon it with the thought or suspicion that it is a non-path, [the offense is established]. However, [if the perception is otherwise, it is not].

Regarding those who incur the offense of *thullaccaya* (grave offense): this can only be explained in detail by considering both the primary object (*maulaviṣaya*) and the secondary object (*anyaviṣaya*).

The non-path is the primary object (such as when more than half [of the female organ] is damaged); thus, it is the domain of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension). The path is the secondary object (such as when a female is slightly damaged); thus, it is the domain of the *pārājika* (offense involving expulsion).
Now, if the initial object is a non-path, and at the time of first approaching it, one clearly perceives it as a non-path, [the offense is determined accordingly].

When one has traveled halfway and then develops the perception that the right path is partially obstructed, or when one entertains doubt regarding the right path, one first incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense for the provisional means of forming the perception that it is not the right path.
Once the perception shifts back to perceiving it as the right path, and when that doubt coincides with the actual object, there is no longer a question of it being the wrong path;
yet, because one falsely gave rise to the perception of it being the right path, one further incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. This is clearly understood.

The emission [of semen] necessarily involves the perception of a sexual object; this is omitted in the text. According to the *Hongji* (Great Record), if one perceives it as a non-path or has doubt regarding it, this constitutes only a *duṣkṛta* offense for lacking the necessary conditions (*pratyaya*) under the first precept;

it does not constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. This is because [the offender] merely incurs a *duṣkṛta* for the subsequent thought arising falsely regarding the "correct path," while the primary offense upon the actual object has not yet been discussed.

It should be stated: (1) a non-path with the perception of a non-path is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; (2) a non-path with the doubt that it is a path. In the former case, there is a *duṣkṛta* for the initial thought regarding the primary object, and a *duṣkṛta* for the subsequent thought regarding the different object; thus, there are two *duṣkṛta* offenses, one for each object.

This refers to the "double offense" (dvi-saṃghāvaśeṣa) due to the presence of two mental states: 3. Perceiving what is not the path as the path (*amārga-mārga-saṃjñin*). [The first mental state constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* regarding its original object;

the subsequent mental state constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* regarding a different object. 4. Perceiving the path as not the path (*mārga-amārga-saṃjñin*). [The first mental state constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* regarding a different object; the subsequent mental state also constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* regarding the original object. Regarding the different object, one incurs a *pārājika* offense. 5. Doubting whether it is the path or not the path (*mārga-amārga-vicikitsā*). [The first mental state constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* regarding a different object;

the subsequent mental state also constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* regarding the original object—this is because by falsely giving rise to doubt, one incurs a *pārājika* offense regarding the different object. In these cases of emission, the non-path is the primary object (*mūla-viṣaya*), while the correct path is the secondary object (*anya-viṣaya*).

This is so. In principle, it should be explained solely in terms of the original object and the preceding mind: the former incurs one *thullaccaya* (residue) and the latter incurs four *dukkaṭa* (faults).

If both the original and the differing [minds] are mentioned together regarding the original object, there is one *thullaccaya* and seven *dukkaṭas*. It is impossible for two *dukkaṭas* and two *pārājikas* to occur regarding a differing object.

Consider this in terms of a single differing object alone; the sequence of reasoning and the supporting citations can be understood from this. As for the phrase "from two to brief," it refers specifically to this object.

Regarding the offenses: as with slandering a great bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Taking a bhikṣu’s robe, engaging in double-tongued speech, disparaging a bhikṣu, or reviling one who has been appointed by a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* incurs a *pāyattika*.
If one does so toward other assemblies, it incurs a *duṣkṛta*. As for cases where it ought to be combined with a *sthūlātyaya*, the absence of such a text is merely an abbreviation.

Regarding the second point on external matters: as for the phrase "the two, etc.," it refers to the two instances of destroying monastic property—whether in private or in public—which constitutes an offense.

One should say, "monastic bedding" or "monastic bedding," and so forth; if one perceives it as not being monastic property, there is no offense. However, lighting a fire on open ground constitutes an offense.

There is no offense if it is merely covered; however, there is an offense immediately upon concealing the robe of a *bhikṣu*. For the three lower assemblies of disciples, it is merely a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
The scriptural texts should include both cases, but this [passage] is merely an abbreviation.

The third section has two parts: the heading and the explanation. Regarding the phrase "the principle reaches its limit" (*li zhi deng*) in the explanation: for instance, in the two precepts against killing and stealing, an offense is incurred simply by the severing of life or the removal of an object from its place;
it is not determined by the formal ritual (*dharma*). Therefore, according to the *Abhidharma* principle, such [formal] action does not exist.

If this is so, then when one instructs another to kill or steal, is that not a formal act? Answer: At the very moment of the verbal instruction, the offense is not yet established; thus, it must await the physical action (*kāyakarman*) of the other.
"At the time of performing [the act], it is both an offense and contrary to the Dharma" (and so forth). Regarding the phrase "in the absence of [the full statement]" within the abbreviated [formula]:

since both the major and minor falsehoods constitute an offense upon the completion of the speech, there must accordingly be the perception of the object (*dharmālambana-saṃjñā*). That is to say, there should be the perception of the noble Dharma as the noble Dharma, and the perception of false speech as false speech, and so on;

thus, the "absence in the abbreviated [formula]" is appropriate. As for "those who admonish," this refers to the four types of admonition regarding transgressions and the formal procedure of suspension (*pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman*).

This applies accordingly to *bhikṣus* and *śrāmaṇeras*, and the basis for an offense is defined by the actions performed toward another; that is, to admonish while perceiving it as an occasion for admonition, to suspend while perceiving it as an occasion for suspension, and so forth.

These involve both the objective condition (*viṣaya*) and the perception thereof (*saṃjñā*), though the text omits them for brevity. Question: According to the Vinaya, a great falsehood (*mahāvadya*) is based on one's own perception regarding the object.
The preceding text also mentions the four rules of the first category (*āpatti-pada*). Why, then, is it said here that there is none? Answer: The preceding [passage] was based on...
This is a topical correspondence regarding the person being deceived by means of a formal argument (*vāda*). For example, it is like deceiving someone while perceiving them as a human being;

however, since this has never been explained at all in relation to the Dharma, it is clarified here once more. Next, the scriptural evidence is cited, beginning with the words "As for... and ending with "...the two types of followers.

Regarding the four cases concerning a monk who has been subject to formal suspension (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*): the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), volume eighteen, states: first, following [the action] while perceiving one who has been suspended as not suspended (no offense); second, following one who has not been suspended...

1. Having performed an act of suspension (*ukkhepana*), one perceives it as such and complies with it: an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). 2. Having performed an act of suspension, one perceives it as such and complies with it:

an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*pācittiya*). 3. Not having performed an act of suspension, one perceives it as not having been performed and complies with it: no offense. There are likewise four cases regarding compliance with a *śrāmaṇera* who has been suspended:

1. Having expelled him, one perceives it as not having been expelled and complies with it: no offense. 2. Not having expelled him, one perceives it as having been expelled: an offense of wrong-doing. 3. Having expelled him, one perceives it as having been expelled: an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. 4. Not having expelled him, one perceives it as not having been expelled: [no offense].

[The text says] "perception" (saññā) [is without fault]. However, there are only phrases concerning doubt; there are only phrases concerning perception. The *Chao* (Excerpts) cites this passage, yet that [work] has the evidence while this text lacks it; it is merely an abbreviation.
Regarding the statement "mediation up to perception," this refers to the coarse language regarding matchmaking found in the Vinaya.

Since there is currently the perception of a dharma, the fact that this text lacks it is certainly an abbreviation. Regarding the statement "it may also be," this refers to the four types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*) as set forth in the Vinaya.

Regarding the precepts: this refers to an act performed by another that possesses the perception of being in accordance with the Dharma; that is, the person who initiates it forms the perception that it is in accordance with the Dharma.

If one observes and views it as such, and then initiates a formal accusation (*ukkhepana*), one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense. This means that the Saṅgha has properly investigated and extinguished the dispute.

Furthermore, having personally formed the perception of a proper investigation and initiated the accusation, one incurs a *thullaccaya*. This serves as proof that all admonitions are also acts performed by others: "The Saṅgha has admonished me in accordance with the Dharma."
I further form the thought that my admonition is in accordance with the Dharma; only if one intentionally contravenes it does one incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*.

Therefore, it is said: "It may also be... and so forth. Regarding "unlawful [admonitions]" and so on: this means that if the Saṃgha has settled a dispute in accordance with the Dharma, yet a bhikṣu fails to properly contemplate the situation and so forth, he does not commit a root offense, but only a *duṣkṛta* for the preparatory act.
This proves that regarding all such contraventions of admonitions, even though the Saṃgha has performed [the formal act], [the offender is not guilty of a grave offense].

Regarding the formal act of admonition (*dharmakarma*) performed according to the Dharma, I maintain that even if one perceives it as an illegal admonition (*adharmasaṃjñā*) and so forth, one likewise incurs no offense regarding the root transgression;
there is only an offense of preliminary preparation (*prayoga*). This is because the rules for those admonitions where another person performs the formal act already contain the specific phrasing;
by analogy with these various admonitions, they all constitute formal acts performed by others, and it is logical that such textual passages exist, though they have been omitted here.

Regarding the fourth point, "at the wrong time" (*akāla*) and so forth: for example, if the fifteenth day is considered the proper time, and one has already bathed on the fifteenth day previously, bathing again now constitutes bathing at the wrong time.
One should state: "at the wrong time," with the perception that it is the wrong time, and so forth. Some say that bathing during the heat of the season and so on is also permissible.
Regarding the two instances of entering a village: first, entering a village at the wrong time; second, entering a village before or after a meal.

The same applies to the cases of "at the proper time" (*kāla*) and "clear perception of the object" (*saṃjñā*). One should state: "not at the proper time, with the perception of not being at the proper time," and so forth;
"before a meal, after a meal," and so forth. Where the text lacks such details, they have been omitted for brevity.

Regarding the statement that "the offenses are abbreviated and there is no middle [category]," Master Hong says: this refers to cases where one has a coarse offense with the perception of a coarse offense, or a coarse offense with doubt as to whether it is coarse or not;

these involve the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), though the text omits them and thus they are abbreviated. Regarding the statement that "for other precepts, logically there is no [perception of the object] because they do not face an offense," Master Hong says:
except for the two precepts concerning the concealment of a coarse offense and the speaking of a coarse offense—which possess the perception of the object—all others [do not].
In the principle of the precepts, there is truly no such thing [as a "counter-offense"]. That is to say, there is no offense that can serve as its counterpart;

it is not like those two [cases], where an offense serves as the objective field of transgression (hence the phrase "not by way of countering an offense"). The personal commentary states: "When a nun conceals another's grave offense, this one precept alone has a further principle for which there is no counterpart, because it does not counter an offense.

(If one follows this explanation, the intended meaning is: concealing an offense and the original offense itself are termed "counter-offenses" due to their gravity; other offenses shared by both monks and nuns constitute the essential requirements for transgression, yet they do not mutually counter one another.)

Therefore it is said that this is because [the offense] does not correspond to the *pārājika* offenses. (I fear the previous interpretation may not be correct; consider this further. Question: Why is only the *bhikṣuṇī* rule on concealment cited, rather than referring to the *bhikṣu* rules?

Answer: The original text refers specifically to a *bhikṣuṇī* concealing a fault because she lacked the perception that it was an offense; therefore, she is singled out for mention. As for the concealment of an offense by a *saṃgha*, since this is already established within the monastic disciplinary texts (*vinaya*), what need is there to state it again?

Regarding the "Section on Quantity" (Dì-sì duō-shǎo mén), the statement that "the fifth is the many" means that five phrases regarding the object and perception (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*) constitute the "many," while four phrases constitute the "few.
Question: Previously it was said that they are "fixed and reciprocal" (*dìng-hù*), yet here it only speaks of "quantity" (*duō-shǎo*). What does "fixed and reciprocal" mean? Answer:

If one follows Master Hóng’s interpretation, the previous mention of "reciprocity" refers to the ancient masters’ system of headings and explanations, which incorporates the views of the present master. For example, as the ancients did...

When light and heavy offenses are compared, the five transgressions are established as fixed, while the non-transgressions are established through mutual comparison. Alternatively, one might say that the five are mutually fixed.
However, within the two categories—the gate of light and heavy and the gate of transgression and non-transgression—there are both four and five [offenses] present;

therefore, there is no fixed mutual correspondence. (If one follows this interpretation, the following objection may be raised: "Furthermore, within the Master’s two categories of light/heavy and transgression/non-transgression, three positions are established: first, the fixed five; second, the four; and third, the five. Regarding the two precepts for killing and stealing, the five [offenses] are indeed uniform. )

The four [offenses] correspond to the four [categories]. If one intends to kill four, it is also permissible to steal five; if one intends to kill five, it is likewise applicable to steal four. This is not like the ancients, who fixed killing at five and stealing at four—claiming that these two pairs are logically equivalent and that the texts merely alternate between "killing five" and "stealing four.

Is this not precisely the Master’s [Sengyou’s] established principle of alternating between more and less? Why do you falsely attribute this fixed alternation to the ancients, while claiming the Master only spoke of "more or less"?

My intention is not so. It is simply that because the preceding section provides a broad indication, the subsequent section briefly restates it. Such brevity in composition serves no other purpose. (If you wish to offer a fallacious interpretation, please follow...)

In the commentaries of various masters, regarding the phrase "fearing that one might reach this [point]," it is explained as follows: while the precept against sexual misconduct does not involve the conceptualization of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), and the precept against stealing consists merely of four permutations according to the Vinaya text, only the precept against killing possesses all five permutations. Now, following the explanation:

furthermore, these five permutations of the object and conceptualization may be described in relation to a single person, referring simply to the five successive stages of approaching the act; or they may be described in relation to five different persons, occurring at each [stage].

The first case corresponds to one person. Furthermore, when one who is a person is perceived as a person, and the object and the mind correspond—meaning the object before one is actually a person and one perceives them as such—the perception of the object and the mind coincide.
Therefore, the Vinaya states: "If it is a person and one perceives them as a person, killing constitutes a *pārājika* offense.

This first case is the absence of the result [of the full offense], being merely the preliminary effort (*prayoga*). Regarding the second case, the commentary notes: "The object is certain while the mind is doubtful. According to the Vinaya...

It is said: Others suspect it is a *sthūlātyaya*, yet there is no mention of the character "non-" (*a-*) [in the definition]. This means that one originally intended to kill a human being, but upon reaching the person's side, suspects they might be a non-human (*amanusya*).
Because the original object was indeed a human, the objective basis (*ālambana*) is fixed; however, the primary intention has shifted as one now suspects they are a non-human.
This is called "doubtful mind. It refers to the preparatory effort directed toward the original person as the object.

Third, "error regarding the person" (*pudgala-viparyāsa*) means that although one initially intended to kill a specific human being as the fixed object, while on the way, one develops the perception that it is not a human being;

this is called an error of the mind (the three preceding points all involve the original object). Fourth, "error regarding the perception" (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) means that one initially suspected whether it was a human or a non-human coming toward them.

Regarding the substitution: the mind takes a non-human being as its object, yet it is actually a human being; thus, one forms the perception of a human being, and the murderous intent does not change.

This is called "the mind is fixed while the object is substituted by a non-human. Therefore, it is said that "the object has shifted. Furthermore, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for the deficiency of conditions regarding the original object.

Regarding the fifth case, from "non-human" down to the second condition: it should be stated in full as "non-human, human, doubt," meaning the original doubt. However, [in this case] a human being is [perceived as] a non-human being.

The place where one comes to take over is precisely the "deficient object" (*kua-jing*). This is called "lacking two conditions. Therefore, the text below states: "Non-humans lack the condition; the object is deficient; the mind lacks its original intent.

This also refers to the shifting of the mind when there is a discrepancy in the object. When the offense is incurred upon the original object (the first two lines take the difference in conditions as the basis for the original object;

within these five lines, one fruit and four causes all pertain to the offense of the original object), the five lines are presented in this manner to provide a definitive indication so that [the practitioner] may understand. This is it.
Based on the text concerning the precept against killing, the characteristics of the five phrases are enumerated as follows.

As for the statement that there are "five [phrases] at most," this refers to the fact that among the five phrases, the phrase regarding killing possesses all five, whereas the precept against stealing has only four. Why is it that some have more and others fewer, such that they are not fixed?
The answer is: it is solely due to the third phrase—the perception of a human or a non-human—which is indeterminate. Thus, there are five phrases.

In the first and last [of the four] cases, there is definitely an offense. Only in the third case is it indeterminate as to whether an offense exists (it is also acceptable not to restrict this to the three types of persons mentioned previously).

Take, for example, the precept against killing: if one’s perception shifts such that there is the *duṣkṛta* of the preliminary thought (*pūrvacitta*) and the fundamental delusion, yet one acts toward a non-animal object that is actually an animal, this is also a *duṣkṛta*.
Thus, it constitutes either five [offenses]. If one is fundamentally deluded regarding a stump and there is no animal object, then in this case there is no offense.
The substance of the offense does not stand; rather, it results in either four [offenses], thereby making it indeterminate.
This is according to our own Master, who explains the number [of offenses] based solely upon a single precept. Since this principle holds for one precept, it applies to all ten thousand objects.
This differs from the ancients, who distinguished the number [of offenses] based on two precepts and rigidly adhered to the scriptural texts that specify five for killing and four for stealing.
The statement "the reason for which it is so" is an inquiry. It asks: what is the underlying principle? Why is the third phrase indeterminate, such that there might be four or five [categories]?

In the response, the first part records the explanations of former scholars as being incorrect; the second part, beginning with "Furthermore," reveals the correctness of the present master’s explanation.
Regarding the "explanations of the ancients," this refers to the interpretations of Yunhui and Huiyuan. These ancient masters categorized [the offenses] based on their relative gravity.
Correct. Only one category is established; there is certainly a third alternative. For example, sexual misconduct with a legitimate path is grave, while that with a non-path is light;

likewise, killing a human being is grave, while killing an animal is light. When these two levels of gravity—grave and light—are contrasted with respect to the fundamental delusion and the transformation of perception, a third case exists for both, thereby forming five definite categories.
However, only one category is established when contrasting those who have committed an offense with those who have not.
Regarding fundamental delusion (*mūla-moha*), there are four permutations of perception based on non-offenses, and five based on offenses; thus, two positions are established.

Furthermore, one must understand the meaning of the gravity of offenses and non-offenses across the four objects: humans, non-humans, animals, and wooden stumps. Among these, the first three constitute offenses, while the last one does not.
Moreover, within the first three, the object of a human is grave, while the latter two are light. Within those first three, there is further gradation of gravity and lightness.

In contrast, there is definitely a third category that completes the five propositions. If one contrasts "having committed" with "not having committed," the third category becomes indeterminate, thereby resulting in either four or five [propositions] (as will be explained in detail below).
Regarding the statement that "lightness and heaviness reach five stages," take, for example, the precept against killing.

Regarding the distinction between the light and the heavy as they relate to one another: this is explained in terms of human and non-human [beings]. A human is a heavy object of delusion; a non-human is a light object.
It is because the offenses arising from these two objects differ that they are designated as light and heavy. Although they differ in degree, both are conditions for transgression.
There must necessarily be a third [category]; once this is established, there are thus five propositions. Therefore, it is said: "Whether light or heavy, etc."
(As stated above). Regarding the cases where one commits a *pārājika* offense through a shift in perception (*saṃjñā-viparyaya*) or through delusion (*moha*), both result in a *pārājika* offense.

This means that while the prohibition regarding sexual misconduct is established in relation to the specific object, both the initial shift in perception and the underlying delusion constitute the formal offense. Thirdly, five fixed propositions are established; for now, let us discuss them in terms of the shift in perception.

This refers to a case where one originally intends the "right path" (*mārga*), but upon reaching the object, gives rise to the perception of it being the "wrong path" (*amārga*). At the time of union with that object, however, it is actually the "right path."

If one summarizes the preliminary preparations, they constitute one *pārājika* offense; looking toward the intermediate stage, when the thought that it is not the proper way (*amārga-saṃjñā*) arises, one incurs one *thullaccaya* offense.

Therefore, two offenses are combined and established. If explained according to the primary delusion, when the primary delusion forms the thought that it is not the proper way, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense for the deficiency of conditions;

when it coincides with the actual path, one incurs a *pārājika* offense based on the object. Since this is of the same nature as the "change of perception" (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), it is said that both are established as *pārājika*.

*Āna*. The above constitutes the general transmission of the exegesis. (According to the *Jizong ji*, there appears to be a different view: it states that when one originally intends the right path but, while traveling halfway, conceives the thought that it is not the right path, and upon meeting with the object, this still constitutes a *pārājika* offense for the right path and two *thullaccaya* offenses.

This means that because it was the right path, one incurs a *pārājika*; as for the "two *thullaccayas*," the first is incurred during the initial formation of the thought of the right path which is subsequently transformed into the thought of it being not the right path; at the moment of transformation, one incurs one *thullaccaya* for the deviation of the thought regarding the right path.

The second is incurred when, from the subsequent mind, one falsely gives rise to the thought of it being not the right path, incurring one *thullaccaya* for the deviation of the thought regarding what is not the right path. This is explained in terms of the transformation of thoughts. If, however, one considers the original delusion of taking the right path to be not the right path...)

The Path-Master (Dàotái) further maintains that one must rely on the correct path; only through the correct path is one delivered. Fundamentally, delusion does not lie at the edge of the Path; rather, it arises falsely as the perception of the Path where there is no Path. This constitutes a *pārājika* offense (*lán*). It is the same as the category of "shifting perception" (*zhuǎnxiǎng*), both resulting in a *pārājika*. (This current explanation within the *Xiángzhōng* [Commentary] is also one approach.

As for the phrase "if one kills while forgetting," this is explained here by way of the precept against killing with a shifted perception. For example, if one originally intends to kill a person and also perceives the object as a person...

Upon arriving at the location of the object, one transforms it into the perception of a non-human being (*amanuṣya*) and binds the original object. Since the preceding mental state was based on the condition of perceiving a non-human being, there is a discrepancy in timing;

this is auspicious when explained in terms of the transformation of perception. As for "the original delusion is also auspicious," it means that even if one falsely gives rise to such a thought regarding a different object, it is auspicious.

The phrase "the rest, such as forgetfulness," etc., is explained by analogy. (According to the *Jizong ji*, it says: "If the subsequent mind arises in vain without the perception of a non-human being, and one obtains the object of a non-human being while there is a discrepancy, it is auspicious (*kṣema*). It is not permitted that a shift in perception results in a discrepancy [whereby it is not auspicious]. This refers to a shift in perception;

if one speaks in terms of original delusion, one maintains the perception of a non-human being from beginning to end without shifting the original object, and thus there is no formal act (*anabhisamskāra*). However, even when merely conditioned by the aspect of the perception of a non-human being, it is still auspicious due to the discrepancy regarding the object of a non-human being.

This interpretation should be reasonable; one should reflect upon it. The above are the annotations representing the interpretations of their respective schools. These are the explanations presented by Jizong; they are left to [the reader's] discretion.
Regarding the emotional grasping and rejection: the statement that "one must have a third [factor] to complete the five stages" refers to the intent of establishing the five propositions.

This means that based on the fundamental delusion of shifting perceptions (*vipariṇāma-saṃjñā*), when facing non-human beings, animals, and so forth, one distinguishes between *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) or *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) by way of the objective field of the offense as it relates to the shifting perception.
There is also a third [category], which completes the five propositions (*pañca-vākya*). (The above concludes the exposition on the ancient masters' views regarding the gravity of offenses.

As for the phrase "if it reaches," this refers to the application of the perception of the object (*ālambana-saṃjñā*) with respect to whether an offense has been committed or not. When this perception is applied to the object, it results in either four or five positions. Regarding the precept against building a hut without requesting permission and the precept against stealing, these clarify the four and five [positions].

As for the phrase "stealing... perception": *Note: This passage discusses the technical classification of offenses within the Vinaya, specifically concerning the mental state (*saṃjñā*) regarding the object of an action and how that state determines the gravity of the offense (e.g., *duṣkṛta*, *sthūlātyaya*, *pārājika*, etc.), resulting in a framework of four or five possible legal categories.*

This refers to the precept against stealing, which consists of four propositions. In the third proposition—where there is an owner, but one perceives it as ownerless—one does not commit an offense, because the original perception was mistaken;
thus, this case is entirely excluded from the formal classification, leaving only four propositions. 1. There is an owner, and one perceives it as having an owner: *pārājika* (defeat). 2.

There is an owner, but one is mistaken and suspects it is ownerless: *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). 3. There is no owner, but one is mistaken and perceives it as having an owner: *sthūlātyaya*. 4. There is no owner, and one is mistaken [perceiving it as having an owner]: *sthūlātyaya*.

"Doubt is auspicious. "Not having performed the formal act (anujñā) while perceiving it as such" refers to the third case. When one has not performed the formal act but perceives it as having been performed, there is an offense; this refers to a change of perception (*vikalpa*).

This establishes the prior state of mind as a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), while the subsequent state is an *āpatti* (offense). Since this phrase is established, it likewise constitutes five cases: 1. Not having performed the formal act and perceiving it as such: a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal offense requiring suspension). 2.

Not having performed the formal act but doubting whether it was performed: the prior state of mind is a *sthūlātyaya*, and the subsequent state is an *āpatti*. 3. Not having performed... [the third case continues].
1. Perceiving it as *avavāda* (formal authorization) when it is not: the preceding thought is a *sthūlātyaya*, while the subsequent thought is without offense.
