as will be seen in the following text, there are mentions of bedding made of black and white wool. In this land (China), they are mostly made of cloth or silk.

As for the note stating that the *kāṣāya* derives its name from its color, this refers to the robes originally worn [by the Buddha]; they were not called *kāṣāya*. In the Western Regions, there is a plant named *kāṣāya-grass*.
This is taken as "dye" because it serves to produce a discolored hue; thus, the name of this garment is established based on the place of its dyeing. Therefore, the *Karmasūtra* states:
"Now, as for the *kāṣāya*, it is originally a dyed color and is not actually the name of a garment. The Vinaya says: 'One should make it the color of a *kāṣāya*,' which refers to a discolored hue.

What does this have to do with the name or the substance? Regarding the phrase "dyeing it to make the color of a *kāṣāya*" mentioned in the text below, [it is explained in] the *Shuchao* (Commentary), Part Two.

In the section on "Civilized Colors," it quotes the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) regarding the method for preparing robes, stating: "Robes dyed with superior colors should be altered to produce the color of a *kāṣāya*.

This refers to that passage. Regarding the phrase "possessing the flavor of the *kāṣāya*": among the six flavors, there is the flavor of *kāṣāya*; could this "pale flavor" (*dàn wèi*) possibly refer to the robe?
As for the term "bedding and requisites" (*wòjù*) used in the translations of this land [China], it means that the three robes are translated generically as "bedding."

It is complete. The *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: "The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* translates it as 'reclining equipment' (*śayanāsana*), meaning that the appearance of the robe resembles a woolen mat or similar items.

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* translates it as 'bedding equipment' (*śayanāsana*) because those robes consist of multiple layers—perhaps three or four—and thus their appearance is not distinct from that of a blanket in this land.
The *Jie-shu* (Precepts Commentary) states: "The three robes are translated as 'bedding equipment'; this captures their general characteristics in brief. However...

They have lost the essential meaning. Regarding the "bedding and requisites" (*śayanāsana*) among the thirty [articles], such as silk-cotton, black and white [wool], and those reduced by six years, these are all *tricīvara* (the three robes).
They are all translated as "bedding and requisites" because this garment did not previously exist in this land and could not be translated through direct correspondence.
It merely takes the measurement as its primary characteristic; three or five cubits are the same, for this is the reverse of the characteristics of bedding and furniture.

Regarding the various translations of its meaning: the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* calls it the "stain-free robe" (*viraja-cīvara*); the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* names it the "transcendent robe";

the *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* calls it the "three dharma-robes," or alternatively the "robe for emaciation," because it diminishes afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, as for the passage from the *Lotus Sūtra*, it refers to the "Tathāgata’s robe."

The above citations are by no means few. Why is this so? Regarding terms such as "the great robe" (*saṃghāṭī*), these are explained according to their specific characteristics, whether in terms of their meaning or their numerical count, as listed in the *Shouluo chao*.
If we consider them in terms of the number of strips, the *Caturvargika-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) on the Dharma of Robes states:
"The bhikṣus did not know how many strips they should make. The Buddha said: 'One should make it with five strips; one should not make it with six.'"
There should be seven [sections] that are permissible and eight that are not; nine that are permissible and ten that are not; and so on up to nineteen sections, but not twenty sections and so forth.
The *Chao* (Excerpts) lists them from the greater number to the lesser. As for the absence of specific names such as "five," "seven," or "nine" in the *Vinaya*, this is to avoid ambiguity.
The *Vinaya* text simply states: "From now on, I permit the bhikṣus to make [robes] by cutting and patching."
Regarding the *uttarāsaṅga* and the *saṃghāṭī*, one does not yet speak of the five-strip robe; rather, the *antarvāsaka* up to the nine-strip robe is the *saṃghāṭī*.
Nowadays, people call the seven-strip robe the *uttarāsaṅga* and the nine-strip robe the *saṃghāṭī*;
this is merely a matter of common nomenclature. If one considers them according to their general characteristics, they can be applied universally in relation to the aforementioned number of strips.

Regarding the term "general" (sāmānya): it is like the term "general" used for the three robes (*tricīvara*) when they are made as a single whole. As for "according to what can be procured according to one's means":
if there are many pieces of cloth, one makes many strips; if there are few, one makes fewer strips. If even this is insufficient, one should fold the layers;

furthermore, if nothing is available, one should simply make them as a whole. Regarding "dividing into three according to use": since a robe made as a whole has no other distinguishing characteristics, one merely divides it into superior, middling, and [inferior] grades according to its utility.
Regarding the use of the lower robe (*antaravāsaka*), it is divided into three types. This is not because there is no fundamental distinction in their essential nature (*dharmatā*).

Although the *saṃkakṣikā* (side-covering cloth) is divided into three according to its function, when considering the status of the "great robes" (*mahākāṣāya*) as a category, the dimensions and essential natures of each are distinct.
That is to say, even the *saṃkakṣikā* must take its strips and leaves as its fundamental basis; furthermore, the dimensions of the *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe) cannot be discussed in isolation.
Regarding "mant-yi" (mant-robe): it should be called "mant-saṃghāṭī. The other two [robes] are to be understood accordingly.
Regarding the phrase "from three up to": "gong" (merit) refers to functional capacity; "yong" (utility) refers to superior application. Regarding the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* and so forth:
its third chapter states, "The Buddha told Ānanda: 'In a future age when the Dharma is about to perish, there will be bhikṣus and..."
“Bhikṣuṇī, you have gone forth within my Dharma, yet you walk about together with others, openly extending your arms from one tavern to another.
Although you have committed the pārājika offense of unchaste conduct, because of this very cause of your drinking, you shall all attain parinirvāṇa within this Bhadrakalpa.
In this Bhadrakalpa, one thousand Buddhas will appear in the world; I am the fourth, followed immediately by Maitreya.”
"You should succeed me," and so on, until finally reaching the Tathāgata; you should know this sequence (the above is the scriptural text).

The *Chao* [commentary] cites this in brief. Within the text, it says: "One whose nature is that of a śramaṇa" refers to one who upholds the precepts. "One who defiles the conduct of a śramaṇa" refers to one who violates the precepts.
"One whose form is that of a śramaṇa" refers to one who entirely lacks the essence of the precepts (*śīla-samvara*), such as those mentioned in the *Daśa-śīla-sūtra*.

Third, refuting the analogy of the layperson. Regarding the aforementioned term "Louti" (樓至), which here means "Weeping" (啼泣), many schools generally claim that this refers to the Vajrapāṇi deity at the entrance of the monastery;
this is an error. Baoshou says: The texts of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* all contain their respective introductory narratives (*nidāna*).
For now, let us follow what is explained in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*. Long ago, there was a king named King Kṣemavikrama (犀勇王).
There were two queens. The first queen gave birth to a thousand sons, all of whom practiced the path and were destined to attain Buddhahood together.
When the king’s city was about to witness these thousand sons achieve the Way, he eventually took them all and placed them inside a golden jar, which he set atop a tower of purple gold.
He then ordered the thousand sons to draw lots from it; Kūṭadanta drew the first lot, and Śākyamuni drew the fourth. Thus it was.
When Lohitī reached the one-thousandth [living being], he thought to himself, "All sentient beings have been delivered by my elder brothers;
who remains for me to deliver? He then wept. His father, the King, told him, "The realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible."
"Do not weep in sorrow. Furthermore, this Louti is also called Huluzhi; here it is translated as 'Beloved Son,' because he was the king's youngest son and was cherished with great affection.
The second queen had two sons: the first was named Zhengnian (Right Mindfulness), and the second was named Fayi (Dharma-Intent).
Having heard that their thousand elder brothers would successively attain Buddhahood, they then made a vow, saying: 'We shall not become Buddhas. This is our first vow.'"
He became the Brahma King and requested his thousand elder brothers to turn the Wheel of Dharma;
one made the vow to become the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada to protect the teachings of his thousand elder brothers (all that is listed above is from the sūtra).

According to this, the Vajra Spirit is the second son of the second queen, Prince Dharmamati, and is not an emanation of Ruci Tathāgata. Know this. According to the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and other texts, it says: Śākya...
In a past life, Kāśyapa was once a brahmin named Ratnasāgara. Within the Buddha-dharma of Ratnagarbha, he developed reverent faith in the Triple Gem and served them with the four requisites.
He then resolved his mind upon Bodhicitta, whereupon that Buddha bestowed upon him a prophecy: "After kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and beyond measure (asaṃkhyeya),..."
In the latter part of the second *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* eon, during the Bhadrakalpa, he shall attain Buddhahood.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s prophecy, the brahmin made a vow regarding the five merits of the *kāṣāya*, as set forth in the excerpt.
Then, that Buddha extended his golden arm, rubbed the crown of the brahmin’s head, and praised him, saying: "Excellent, O Great Being! It shall be just as you have said."

He is called the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion. Regarding the fourth section of the text, concerning how one gives rise to a heart of compassion when sentient beings act in opposition [to the Dharma]:

for example, if someone steals property belonging to the Sangha, even though the Sangha has apprehended the thief and his offense is such that he must die according to the laws of the Sangha, they should not disclose this to others.

Is this not indeed giving rise to a heart of compassion through mindfulness of the power of the *kāṣāya*? The fifth section of the sutra states: "Four inches [of the robe] shall remain attached to the body."

"Strife and contention shall both cease. This was asked regarding the power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). [Question: "If one holds even a small portion [of this power] while amidst the ranks of an army, one will achieve victory.
But what if both sides possess it? [Answer: "If both sides hold it and their soldiers are harmonious, neither side will invade the other."

Regarding the statement "the two [types] differ," it is as the text says. Regarding the statement "the one [type] is equal," this may be understood. Regarding the statement "because of the two [types]," this distinguishes the substance of the material.
Even if silk, damask, brocade, and fine gauze are subsequently thick and heavy, because they possess patterns and images, their use is not permitted.
The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "The colors of brocade are brilliant and dazzling, which agitates the mind; as for fine gauze, it is thin and coarse, and thus [its use] is not permitted."
Regarding *xiāo* (pronounced *yè*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is raw silk produced from *juàn* (silk). As for "escaping the calamity of the *garuḍa*," the *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya* says:
In a past age, there was a *śāmbalī* tree on the shore of the great ocean, upon which lived a *garuḍa*. This bird’s body was immense, with its two wings spanning fifty *yojanas*.
It took dragons as its food; whenever it wished to eat a dragon, it would first strike the ocean with its wings.
Water causes the dragon’s body to open; it then appears and immediately seizes and eats it. Because all dragons are constantly afraid, they seek to wear the *kāṣāya* upon the palace gate.
When the bird sees the *kāṣāya*, a mind of reverence arises, and it dares not eat.

These dragons and birds each have the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*), as described in the usual accounts (etc.). The phrase "the three colors are like" serves as the heading. The phrase "the four parts reach... [and so forth].
"Also" refers to the causal conditions within the dharma of robes. "The superior colors of the six groups" refers to the primary colors of the five directions.
Regarding the note stating that there is a direct translation for "dyeing," the subsequent text says: "In the language of Qin, it means 'to dye,' and so forth.

If one makes [robes] such as the five-patch robe (*pañcakaṇḍuka*), Śāriputra obtained materials consisting of fragments of superior-colored cloth and wished to make a five-patch robe. He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha permitted it, saying: "It is likewise..."

If one obtains a piece of cloth that is wide and long, it is permitted to cut and tailor it [into robes]. Regarding "棧" (*zàn*), it refers to blue or red; this refers to the color of *mùlán* (magnolia). "紺" (*gàn*) means a blending;
it is the mixture of blue and red, which is also another name for the color of *mùlán*. "With the exception of the three robes" refers to those of superior quality and so forth.

If one makes the three robes, they must necessarily be dyed to change their appearance. If one uses only these three colors [for other items], one may apply them as spots, but they cannot be made [into formal robes].
The three robes are excluded because they are already established. Regarding the fact that all [robes] dyed in black or madder may be accepted: these are colors that accord with the Dharma.

The reason they may be accepted while not being "pure" primary colors is that they do not consist entirely of the five great primary colors; rather, it is simply that the dyeing process was not fully perfected, hence they are called "impure.
Furthermore, one may apply spots of these colors to other garments; this intention is no different from that of the light blue mentioned above. [This applies to] the *kāṣāya*.
The term "one who dyes" (*rañjaka*) is the Qin (Chinese) translation. The preceding text states that "dyeing" has a direct equivalent; this refers to the present section.

That is to say, the three robes one wears are not called *kāṣāya* [in their original sense], but because they are dyed with this grass to produce a "defiled color" (*kāsāya*), we know the name is established based on the dyeing process.
The phrase "such as the fetters of craving," etc., provides an illustration. It means that the truly pure mind is falsely affected by form and the other [sense objects]. Five.

"Dust" refers to that which is defiled by craving; "fetters" (saṃyojana) arise from this—these two are termed "defilement. How much more so for primary colors such as blue and the like? If they were not covered by non-color, there would be no primary color at all. Why is this?

It is because the very manifestation of the primary color itself carries the meaning of "defilement. The passage on "true purple" and below clarifies that colors not in accordance with the Dharma are not permitted for use.
From the passage beginning "from what is permitted for use" and below, it clarifies that colors in accordance with the Dharma are permitted for use. The sub-commentary reconciles these points.
The color *múlán* (mulberry). This was translated during the Qin period; there is a *múlán* bark in that region which resembles dried *śīrṣa* (śirīṣa) bark.

By soaking it in fermented rice water (*sukta*) and pounding it to extract the juice, one dyes [the cloth] into a dark red-black color. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* was translated in the Wu region during the Zong dynasty;
since they lacked this bark there, they simulated this color. Now, our Master, having personally witnessed it, takes it as authoritative, as stated in the *Sudarsana-vinaya*.

The *kāṣāya* robe is a vivid crimson; this is precisely the dye derived from *mólán* (madder). Regarding the *Yìjiào fǎlǜ jīng* (Sūtra on the Bequeathed Teaching and the Vinaya), it is permitted according to the citations in the *Xínggǔ* (Practice of the Ancients) that wearing the five primary colors constitutes a transgression.
It is also titled the *Yìjiào fǎlǜ sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Bequeathed Teaching and the Vinaya).
This passage from the *Wen* (Exegesis) clarifies that the five Vinaya schools each designate a specific color for their robes: the Mahāsāṃghika wear yellow; the Pañcavargīya wear blue;
the Dharmaguptaka wear black; the Kāśyapīya wear mūlāna (wood-brown); and the Sarvāstivāda wear vermilion. This [tradition] is spurious; it was not included in the orthodox records (*zhènglù*).
Although ancient masters cited it, modern masters judge it to be the result of ignorance. The *Jiemo shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā), citing Paramārtha, states: "The middle..."

Although the monastic robes of the country consist of five types, they are all of the same color; therefore, this [text] rejects [other colors]. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* (Shanjian lü piposha) cites evidence below regarding the color red.
Baoyun says: "The alms bowl, when suspended over the shoulder, is blue-green; that is, the color of a peacock's throat, a lush green-blue."

The subsequent phrase states: "The *kāṣāya* is a vivid crimson. This is because the preceding context follows suit; the phrasing here lacks independent intent and serves merely as a corroboration that the *kāṣāya* is crimson.
As for Master Xuán’s commentary, which assigns the character "blue" (*qīng*) to the subsequent phrase, this misses the intended meaning of the text.
Reflect upon this.
Regarding the statement that "four *cun* equal one *zhǒu*": when the lower robe (*antaravāsaka*) is extremely tight and small, its length is seven feet and six inches;

therefore, this serves as the standard. Regarding the establishment of three grades for each of the ten *śīla* (or *daśādhyāya*): the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states, "The Buddha permitted bhikṣus to establish three types of robes, namely:
superior, middle, and inferior. The superior robe is five *zhǒu* in length; the lower robe is four *zhǒu* in length and two *zhǒu* in width."

Half [of that]. That which is between these two is called the middle robe (*antaravāsaka*). Alternatively, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, within a single robe there are three grades of measurement:
the superior *saṃghāṭī* is five cubits in length and three cubits in width; the middle is five cubits in length minus one span and three cubits in width minus one span;
the inferior is four and a half cubits in length and three cubits in width minus one span.
The *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe) has three grades. For the large country, the superior *antarvāsaka* (inner robe) is five and a half cubits in length and two cubits in width;
the middling is three cubits in length and two cubits in width minus one span of the hand; the inferior is four cubits in length and two cubits in width minus one span of the hand.

Regarding the two Vinaya texts mentioned above, receiving [the robe] that conforms to these measurements constitutes its formal acceptance; receiving one that exceeds these measurements does not constitute it.

The *Śariputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*) states that for the four types of robes, one may receive them in sizes both large and small provided they conform to the textual measurements; thus, the bowl is not included [in this category].
Now, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, the three robes are also generally permitted [to exceed these limits], each having its own specific number, length, and width as detailed in the texts.

Whether they exceed or fall short of these measures, they all constitute valid possession (*parigraha*), because they can be cut or joined. Therefore, they are accepted as being similar in principle to the "measuring the body" rule in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, which concerns the robes' looseness. Thus, they are taken [as permissible].
Regarding the statement that "the declaration [of purity] occurs after the acceptance": this means that beyond the dimensions of the three robes (*tricīvara*), no further cutting is permitted;

anything exceeding those dimensions is considered surplus and must undergo the rite of *śuddhaka* (purification). One must first perform the formal ritual (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of acceptance and only thereafter perform the *śuddhaka*.

If one were to perform the *śuddhaka* first and then accept [the robe], it would contradict the principle of the purification rite. Regarding the measurement of five *pañcahasta* (five cubits) and so forth: since the text states that it must necessarily conform to the size of the body...

Based on the *cubit* (*hasta*), it is clearly understood that this does not adopt the textual explanation for "purification outside the measurement. The intent in the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* is likewise the same. Therefore, it says:

"The meaning is identical to the *Pañcavargika*, where 'according to the body' is best. Now, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, the passage concerning "exceeding" corresponds in meaning to the "measuring the body" in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the "according to the body" in the *Pañcavargika*;
these meanings are equivalent. As for the phrase "five strips reaching [the body]," this distinguishes the strips.

"Number" refers to the quantity [of items]. Regarding the *Shuchao* (Commentary on the Essentials): this is the primary commentary (*shu*) and this is the explanatory sub-commentary (*chao*). For now, following the *Jiemoluoshi* (Commentary on the *Karmavācanā*), it says:

"The reason for using only an odd number is that the practice of a śramaṇa is rooted in compassion and benevolent nurturing; thus, it acts in accordance with the Yang (the masculine/active principle) of the world, and is therefore not even.
This is like the *Yijing*, where the single line (*zhi*) represents Yang and the paired lines (*ou*) represent Yin; Yang brings forth life, while Yin brings about death. Now, as for wearing...
This robe symbolizes the generation of the myriad virtues; therefore, its count corresponds to that of a single-layered garment. Regarding the absence of a formal scriptural injunction permitting it:

although there are now thirty-three strips [of cloth], we have never seen the *saṃghāṭī* (great robe) prescribed by the holy teachings as something permitted for a bhikṣu to receive, maintain, and wear.
As for the records of sacred sites (*ārya-vihāra*) and so forth, they state: "At midnight, the Bodhisattva leaped over the city wall to leave the household life and traveled twelve..."
Traveling for a *yojana*, he arrived at the forest retreat of the seer Bhārgava.

There, he shaved his hair with a blade, traded his exquisite robes for a coarse *saṃghāṭī*, and performed austerities for six years on the banks of the Nairañjanā River; such is the purport of this passage.
Since the Buddha wore only the thirteen-strip robe and displayed coarse cloth to demonstrate the dharma of few desires, this should be taken as the standard.
One should now prepare it according to one's means; why is there a need for a twenty-five-strip robe, especially since there are no such things as thirty-three-strip robes?
Regarding the phrase "from six to [ten]," this distinguishes the number of *vitasti* (spans). A dam that holds back water is called a *tīra*.

As for the unclear passage in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, it merely refers generally to "ten intervals" (*daśa-vidhāna*) and so forth. The citation in the present *Shō* (Commentary) simply establishes the length at five or seven *hasta*;

the *saṃghāṭī* is to be understood by the same standard. It does not state that the number of *vitasti* is indeterminate; rather, one must now clarify this according to other schools, as the text explains.
Question: Why is it that they only increase in length and do not become wider? Answer: The *Yeshu* (Outline of Karma) states:
"The reason for demonstrating [robes] of varying lengths is that, in the world, rice paddies differ in height depending on whether they are near water or elevated ground.

Likewise, when śramaṇas wear robes of different lengths, it is because the Dharma robe serves as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) for those seeking benefit; thus, while the holy increase, the ordinary diminish. This is metaphorically illustrated by the abundance of the long."*
"Short" means deficient. "Not being stripped by enemies or bandits" means one avoids being plundered. Alternatively, there is an interpretation based on the character *li* (profit/benefit):
since there are many kinds of inferior [materials], they are not fit for the use of thieves; therefore, they do not provide them with profit.

Regarding the definition of the "seventh": this distinguishes the number of repetitions. If one uses new cloth dyed with vermilion, it is auspicious when made; if it exceeds the limit, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

This refers to the prohibition against making [robes] with one new layer over two old layers; whereas now, with three layers all new, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense due to violating the rule at the time of manufacture.

Furthermore, regarding the fault of including [a robe] in the count of the three robes (*tricīvara*) without having performed the ritual of dedication (*pariṣkāra*), which constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense after ten days have passed:

even if one subsequently removes it through disrespect, there is still a *duṣkṛta* offense for the act of removal itself. As for "according to whatever amount," this refers to [the case of] excrement.

Because sweeping [the robe] is not restricted by a specific number of layers, it is not termed "separated from the robe. Even if one or two layers are left behind, since the substance of the robe remains with the body, there is no fault of being separated overnight.
The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "The great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) must necessarily have multiple layers; however, many nowadays make it single-layered. This is not a Dharma-compliant garment.
To wear it after receiving it constitutes an offense. If one performs the formal act of receiving it, it is successfully accomplished. [This applies to] the single-layered robe."

One receives the precepts and thereby attains them; however, one merely obtains what is inappropriate [to keep]. If, before death, one causes those within the original boundary to take it, the former master judges:
"Since it was removed from inside the robe yet left within the boundary, it belongs to the light items of the boundary and should be divided.
The latter master decides: "It should be awarded to the caregiver, because it was originally a single garment. The Vinaya Master says: "The latter is the definitive rule."

The *vinayadhara* is the author of the treatise (*śāstrakāra*). Since he was originally one who maintained [the rules regarding] robes, and because the patient has already obtained what is suitable for him, he is entitled to receive items from a different territory;

thus it is explained extensively in the following text. Regarding the phrase "if the robe is lost elsewhere and brought here for distribution," if this merit is not complete, then it shall be divided according to that [original location].
The statement "the eight methods of making robes" is the heading.

Regarding the phrase "four parts" and so forth: as for the five strips being permitted to include the leaf-edges, it is because the Vinaya fears that the edges of the leaves will quickly break and dust or grime will enter within;
therefore, it permits them not to be cut off, yet requires them to be gathered and made into the two upper robes, so as to prevent them from breaking even at a distance.
"Simply having the edges bound with bird-foot stitching and the like" refers to the first allowance.

The Buddha’s regulation was that it should be completed in a single day, using a running stitch for a rough assembly so as to be immediately usable; otherwise, there would be fear of incurring the offense of keeping an extra robe.

"The *Madhyama Āgama* and other texts" cite specific instances to corroborate the preceding passage. "The *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* and other texts" represent the second allowance: that a nun may have a companion.
Therefore, it is said: "The Saṃgha has no companion, hence it is auspicious. Regarding the Sarvāstivāda and other schools, this refers to the final allowance for an exception.

Because it is intended for many days, one does not incur the offense of keeping an extra robe (*dīrgha*). This is entirely without the characteristics of a robe, unlike the preceding and following cases where the formal acceptance (*parigraha*) is performed and only then explained.
The two aforementioned points both concern the initial condition: fearing the fault of keeping an extra robe, one should not make the three robes (*tricīvara*) from such items at the outset.

Because the ten-day limit had not yet been established, its prompt completion was mandated; later, one exception was opened, which refers to making [a robe] without surplus, and thus does not concern the number of days spent making the robe.
As for the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and others, they clarify the sewing of patches, which is not the standard marked by the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

The instructions for the sewing also state "sew it on. This refers to the *pañcavargika* (five-part) robe, which is made with attached patches (*pattra*). Regarding the lower part of the *caturvargika* (four-part) robe, one should fold the patches over onto the other section.
One should not [use] the *caturvargika* method; this is because the *pañcavargika* was a later innovation, whereas the former is the original regulation.

Furthermore, those patches should all be closed at the top and open at the bottom, forming a single strip with two internal partitions: one half is open at the top, and the other half is open at the bottom.
This is contrary to the Dharma. As for Ānanda following the instructions to make robes and so forth, this refers to a passage in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
The text is not particularly refined or elegant; thus, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "Ānanda instructed the bhikṣus: 'This is a long strip; this is a short strip.'"
"This is the first seam; this is the second seam; this is the central strip. The markings on both sides are exactly like this.
Now, let us take another school’s version. Furthermore, it says: "The Buddha was traveling through the south with one thousand two hundred and fifty followers.
From the foot of a mountain, he saw a fire-pit field with its ridges and furrows, and thought: 'The bhikṣus should fashion their robes in accordance with this. He asked Ānanda: 'You..."
"Do you see this field of fire? "I see it. He then instructed Ānanda and the bhikṣus: "The robes should be made in this manner.
Are you able to do so? They replied, "We are able. He then instructed the bhikṣus: "Some should have one long strip and one short; some two long and one short; some three long and one short.
The left strips should slant toward the left, the right strips should slant toward the right, and the middle strips should slant in both directions. Thus they made them.
He eventually brought him to see the Buddha. The Buddha said, "You possess great wisdom. Having heard my brief explanation, you have acted in accordance with the Dharma.
This is called the 'cut-and-sewn robe for exclusive use,' which differs from that of the non-Buddhists; it shall not be seized by enemies or thieves."
The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* asks: When the Tathāgata first addressed Cunda and the other four by saying "Come, Bhikṣu," their three robes were already complete.
Furthermore, when Ānanda performed the *karmavācanā*, the five bhikṣus already possessed their kāṣāyas.

For what reason is it now that Ānanda is first instructed to have the bhikṣus imitate the cultivation of worldly fields to produce their robes? Answer: It is because, through the words "Come, Bhikṣu," the place of instruction was transformed.
Because ready-made garments are difficult to emulate, we now take the fields of the world as our model to establish a standard; thus they are called "fields of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*) robes.

Just as a field uses water to grow fine seedlings and nourish the physical body, so too this field of the Dharma-robes employs the water of the four benefits to increase the seedlings of the three wholesome minds, thereby nourishing the life of wisdom of the Dharma-body (the above is from the commentary). If one obtains [them]...

Regarding the phrase "insufficient [material]," this clarifies that when the cloth and resources are scant, there is the allowance for making a lower robe (*antarvāsa*). According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* rules on robes:
if a monk receives one robe-measure of cloth, it is too long to make an upper or middle robe; therefore, the Buddha said: "If it is insufficient, it should be made with three lengths and one width;
if it is still insufficient, it should be made with two lengths and one width. If it remains insufficient, patching is permitted.
[The robe] is made of strips. Even if it is insufficient [to make a full one], it is permitted to make a *maṇḍala-antarvāsa*. This is another instance of a specific occasion (*paccaya-kāla*).
Furthermore, a bhikkhu obtains another robe. The Buddha says: "It is permitted to make a *saṃghāṭī* of cut pieces. If it is slightly insufficient, it is not permitted to make an *uttarāsaṅga*;
if it is still insufficient, it is not permitted to make a *maṇḍala-antarvāsa*. The commentator’s main point states: "In the Vinaya, this was originally..."
Because the *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe) was insufficient, it was permitted to be made into an *antaravāsaka* (inner robe). Regarding the example of its subsequent completion:

this means that because the upper [robe] was originally a *saṃghāṭī* but was insufficient, it was permitted to be made into a plain *antaravāsaka*; now, it is returned to being a *saṃghāṭī*, and its acceptance is performed according to the procedure for the two lower robes.
If it is still insufficient, it is completed as the upper *saṃghāṭī*. The rest is as stated in the text.
Regarding the statement "from the saṃgha to the laity" and "narrow as a barley grain": this refers to the fact that a barley leaf is as large as a reed leaf;

one must not sew the cloth with leaves aligned horizontally. This means that when bhikṣus sew a garment by joining the two ends face-to-face, the Buddha said that the leaves must not be aligned horizontally.
"Aligned" is simply another term for "joining the two ends face-to-face. That is to say, the lengths of the two ends must match; one must not [sew] the ends [in such a way that they do not align].
The heads [of the cloth] face each other; thus, the subsequent garment is easily removed. Regarding that which should be made with "horse-tooth" (aśvadaṃṣṭrā) seams:

fearing that the edges of the strips might fray, one gathers the edges inward and, using thread, turns them back onto the outer edge—either by horizontal or vertical stitching—so that they are as wide as a horse's tooth.
Hence, it is called a "horse-tooth seam. In times of urgency, it is as described above. "Discriminating" refers to many people assisting in its completion.

Having finished the coarse lines and the concealed [seams], one subsequently makes further cuts and so forth. According to the Vinaya, there are three types of "leaf-pressing" (patra-pīḍana) for the "t-shaped" (dīrghākāra) [sewing]:

the leaf-pressing, the nail-pressing, and the bird's-foot seam (*pakṣa-pada*). Nowadays, however, one simply makes straight cuts. Regarding those [cuts] of half an inch or less, these are the "previously purified" (*pūrva-kalpa*), which refers to the "purification by marking" (*parikarman*).

As for "installing the stitching" (*sīvana-pratisthāpana*), this must be installed because it was not previously present; if one does not install the stitching, the acceptance [of the robe] is not valid.
This is established. This is the mark of the smooth skin covering the joints. Depending on its size, it extends forward from the preceding part as before.

When four fingers are applied, it is the *xuan* (pronounced like "hu" and "quan") ear. Following this standard, it extends forward; thus, the appearance of the hook-like mark resembles the handle of a tripod.
"Stitching" (*ni*) refers to the long strips on the back; because a knot is made at the head of each strip, it is called "stitching.

Alternatively, it is said that one uses these strips to tie the leather straps of the hook so that they remain continuous and unbroken; thus it is called "stitching. The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "Within four finger-widths from the edge of the border."

The *an-guǒzhì* (the "hook-and-fastener" or "hook-and-loop") is positioned eight finger-widths behind [the shoulder], taking a measurement to cover the left shoulder; thus, there is a distinction between distant and near.
Furthermore, the four fingers and eight fingers refer to the measurement from the inner edge of the border. Moreover, regarding the prevention of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*):

initially, when a bhikṣu did not withdraw the border, his robe was pulled by a non-Buddhist so that the lining fell apart. Therefore, the regulation was established that the border should be withdrawn and cut away; as for what should be given to the Saṃgha, it refers to...

Once this item has been sewn on, it is no longer subsumed under the category of the *kāṣāya*. If the owner of the robe dies, this patched material should be removed and treated as light property to be shared with the Saṃgha;
thus, the main body of the robe remains with the patient. Therefore, in the text, there are two instances of "giving.

Regarding the folding of the four corners of the three robes, the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "To assist one another in providing strength," and further says: "One should attach hooks and fastenings."
This refers to the practice of securing the hem of a patched garment with a needle and thread; it is done for fear that the garment might easily tear when being pulled.
Regarding "obstructing soiled areas," this means that because the original garment would likely be quickly ruined by frequent washing, one merely tears out the damaged section and patches it.
As for the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* regarding rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*), that Vinaya states: there was once a bhikṣu who possessed a rag-robe and heard the Buddha establish [the rules concerning them].
The precepts do not permit wearing [such garments], nor do they restrict the cutting of robes. While entering a village, he reflected: "I have a rag-robe (*pāṃśukūla*) that is torn;

it should be patched. I shall attach hooks and borders. He immediately took up needle and thread and, near the gate of Jetavana, began patching and attaching borders, intending to cut them into strips.
The Buddha, while walking for exercise, saw him and asked what he was doing. He related the matter in detail. The Buddha said, "Well done."
When making a *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) with patches, one should use cloth cut into strips. Regarding the term "hook-and-lantern" (*gōuran*): this refers to folding the edges of the strips and leaves;

because they are bent and turned like a hook, it is called "hook-and-lantern. Placing these folds upon the upper part constitutes the formal acceptance and wearing of the robe; this distinguishes the characteristics of the robe.

If one accomplishes the possession [of a robe] with five strips, or seven, or even nine, or if it exceeds the standard measurements for robes, one should receive and maintain it according to the two categories based on the teachings of the *Sūtra*.
Regarding the explicit text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and so forth, the *Chao* (the Commentary) further cites them separately;
following the principle that "one may wear what is obtained by the poor," this is easy to understand.

Regarding the phrase "the third arrival," it is as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "the first arrival among the four [sections] of the *Śāstra*," the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) simply states, "The three robes should be accepted," and so forth.

Since there is both relinquishing and accepting, it is clearly known that there is a formal rule (*dharma*); if one possesses the robe but does not carry it, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. Regarding the passage beginning with "In the past, some people... and so on:
although ancient masters have cited this as an interpretation, the analogies are not equivalent. As for the marginal note: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* permits [carrying the robe] for one night.

"Assembly" (saṃgha) refers to any gathering at any time during the night; it does not require the four parts [of the day] to be reached by the appearance of light, nor does it depend on whether the assembly is slow or fast.
Now, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, those who maintain the practice of similar characteristics—namely, maintaining the appearance of light—are equivalent to the four-part system.
Since they are equivalent, one takes up the text and receives the robe; thus, they form a corresponding category. The *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe) properly consists of ten [parts].
Regarding the eight types: from nine strips to twenty-five strips, meaning that for those with nine folds, there are nine layers;
two nines make eighteen. Regarding those with six types: taking the seven-strip robe, there are exactly two types, namely the cut-and-sewn and the folded-layered.
The five-strip robe has exactly three types: the cut-and-sewn, the folded-layered, and the gathered-layered, along with the seamless robe (*sāṇa-vastra*). Thus, there are [eight].
Sixth: The primary [robes] together with the secondary ones total twenty-four. Regarding the seven-strip robe (*saptaka*), as mentioned above, there are two primary types;

the secondary ones number twenty-two, which, when combined with eighteen from the outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*), three from the five-strip robe (*pañcaka*), and one from the seamless robe (*sāṇḍasaṃghāṭī*), also total twenty-four.
Regarding the five-strip robe, as mentioned above, there are three primary types; the secondary ones number twenty-one, namely the outer robe...
The eighteen and seven types of robes, when combined with the *maṇḍala* (patched) robes, total twenty-four. Three sets of twenty-four make seventy-two types of *maṇḍala* robes.
Regarding those that apply to all three categories: as previously stated concerning the *maṇḍala* robe, it is not without its substantial core;
logically, it should apply to all three categories—primary, secondary, and derivative. This is likewise the case in the subsequent section on the method for making robes. Now, it says:

Regarding the combination into one: this is based on the explicit text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. There is currently a method for receiving and maintaining the *mañca-saṃghāṭī* (the patchwork outer robe);

I now cite the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and combine [these sections] into one. As for "as in the *Shuchao*" (Explanatory Notes), this refers to the *Yi-chao* (Notes on Meaning) of the primary commentary (*shu*).

Now, according to the *Jie-mo-shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā), it asks: "The methods for receiving the three robes differ in name and substance; may they be mutually applied? The answer states: "According to..."

Regarding the five parts [of the robe], if one obtains the cloth and material, one first performs the cutting and piecing. This continues until, if it is insufficient to make an *antarvāsa*, one cuts it down;
or if it is still insufficient, one folds the layers to make the others. The rest need not be described in detail. As for the phrase "now it has arrived," this differs from the ancients.

The ancient masters all first received the *saṃghāṭī*, followed by the seven-strip robe (*saptaka*), and finally the five-strip robe (*pañcaka*). The present master, however, proceeds from the subtle to the coarse.

Regarding the wearing [of robes] and the method for taking them up: one first receives the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṭika*), and finally the great outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*). As for what is called "adding the *uttarāsaṅga*":
if it is folded in pleats, when holding it, one follows the rule of one long and one short side; as stated below, "folding and pleating the robe to hold it," and so forth.

Regarding those points identical to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Xuánzàng states: "According to our own school (the *Mahīśāsaka*), among the five types of robes, there are only the three mentioned above.
However, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there is additionally the 'continuous robe' (*sāntarottara*). The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* merely says:

'If one obtains a continuous robe that is wide and long, if it is cut into pieces, one should fold the sections to make it smaller'; it does not say that one hears of making a continuous *antarvāsaka*."
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there is indeed a passage permitting [the practice], yet it lacks a specific location for its retention; therefore, we do not adopt it here.

We follow the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* as the basis for the *maṇḍala-saṃghāṭī*, for it contains explicit textual evidence regarding its formal acceptance and retention. Thus it is said: "The rest is the same as the *Daśabhāṇavāra*" (further unexplained points are not recorded).

As for the phrase "if one arrives at it," this means that one must first formally designate the *antarvāsaka* as the foundation, and subsequently take [the cloth] from among those of twenty-five strips or more.
"Substitute. This refers to cutting [the cloth] into pieces; it takes the highest-grade garment among the nine grades as the standard for the Dharma.

To cite the intent of this passage, it is from the twenty-first fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), concerning the text on the method of receiving the precepts. Regarding "folding the leaves according to the circle":

if there are folded leaves, the highest grade among the nine is also called "a robe held by folding four lengths and one short length," extending even to the seven-strip robe (*saptaka*). According to this...
Regarding the phrase "to alter it," it is also said: "up to [altering] two long and one short [patch], or cutting and piercing the robe for wearing, etc.

As for the statement "if it reaches the point of alteration," the text contains two meanings. The first restates the various subordinate items mentioned above to generally demonstrate that they apply to all three types of robes; the second refers specifically to the *saṃghāṭī* (great robe) from below.
Regarding the *saṃghāṭī* robe made of uncut cloth, the method for its formal acceptance is shown as follows: from the upper part down to the middle, this refers to the *antarvāsaka*.

If it is used as a subordinate [robe] for others, all instances should be modified accordingly. If the *uttarāsaṅga* takes the *saṃghāṭī* and other robes as its subordinates, one should modify the formula to say:
"I accept this twenty-five-fold *uttarāsaṅga* robe, consisting of four lengths and one short piece, as a robe of cut cloth. If...

The *saṃghāṭī* takes other robes as its attendants; one should receive this *saṃghāṭī* as a five-panel robe (*pañcaka*) and maintain it as a robe of cut and pieced strips (*khaṇḍa-cīvara*) of appropriate length.
Regarding the *sāṃkakṣikā*, it is renamed "the distinct one" because the *sāṃkakṣikā* lacks distinct characteristics; however, if one simply changes [the name] for each, it becomes an *antarvāsaka*.
One should say: "This is a *sāṃkakṣikā* *antarvāsaka*," and so on, up to: "This is a *sāṃkakṣikā* *uttarāsaṅga*."
The following citation from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* establishes the legal basis for the outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*), as stated in the text.

Regarding the phrase "if one is a principal master of the Dharma," the text clearly refers to the method for receiving the robe through cutting and patching (*khaṇḍa-sīvana*), with specific notes on the folding of the cloth; this may be understood by analogy with what precedes it.

Regarding the phrase "if one is superior, up to being enlightened," this refers to the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) cut into patches, which comprises nine grades in total. Since these cannot be definitively specified, it is said that "one receives it in several strips."
The same applies to the counting of the strips (*vīci*) for robes of various lengths. Because the two lower robes are fewer in number, their characteristics are easily understood;

therefore, they are explained separately according to their specific categories. Thus, the *Karmavācanā-vṛtti* states: "The number of strips for the preceding two robes is fixed by rule, with no further extension or reduction.

The phrase "How great it is! (*yue shang zhi cai*) precisely distinguishes the amount of the strips, while simultaneously intending to clarify that this also applies generally to the *maṇḍala-saṃghāṭī*.
This is merely the meaning of the original text. Since it is permitted that one will receive the precepts in the future, how could it be said that [the robes] exist prior to the reception?
One receives them and immediately knows they are robes fit for use in receiving the precepts. However, in the *Vinaya*’s method for receiving the precepts, it says:

"One should instruct them, saying: 'You shall follow my words; I, [Name], etc. If it were as you claim—that [the robes] exist prior to the reception—then there would be no mention of the title "bhikṣu. It has not yet...
"Cutting" refers to either a *maṇḍala* robe or a regular robe. An ancient master said: "That which has not been cut is a single bolt;
how could one take a full piece of white cotton cloth (*pata*) and, having received it as one of the three robes, come to receive the precepts?

To say that the aforementioned cases do not constitute [a valid robe] means that when citing various Vinayas and treatises regarding the characteristics of color, they all state that what is not in accordance with the Dharma does not constitute a valid reception [of the robe]. It says:

Next, regarding the *Vinaya*: there is no text concerning this in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü). Why, then, is it not taken from other schools, but specifically from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Shengqi lü)?

It is said that it is taken because the meaning of "renunciation" (*śikṣāpada-tyāga*) is the same. The *Karmasūtra* states: "In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there is doubt as to whether one should renounce [the robe].

In the *Mahāsāṃghika*, when traveling at night and unable to reach the assembly to perform the formal act, the Buddha then permitted 'remote renunciation' (*dūratyāga*), treating the light matter as heavy, just like the method for renouncing the precepts. (1)

It is said that the relinquishment is accomplished. Since even the fundamental substance of the acceptance becomes a robe through a single recitation, what need is there to labor over three recitations to manifest the "conformity" (*anuvartana*)?

Furthermore, the four doubts regarding relinquishment do not accord with the characteristics of the two types of urgency; thus, the meaning of taking [the robe] is the same as the intent of the single recitation.
As for the phrase "if a nun arrives," etc., Xuán says: "The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā* of the *Daśabhāṇaka-vinaya* also..."
These four sections of the *Cīvara-vastu* differ only in their Sanskrit phonetics. As for the "shoulder-covering robe" (*saṃkakṣikā*), it refers precisely to the nun’s cross-worn upper garment;

the Buddha prohibited baring the shoulders and mandated its wearing. Regarding its application within the Saṃgha, Ānanda established the rule that it must be worn, lest one’s upright appearance provoke lustful thoughts in others.
Nowadays, most members of the Saṃgha wear it; although there is no specific scriptural authority to cite, in principle this does not hinder the practice. (Note)

The text does not state that the measurement in *cubits* (*hasta*) must be specified for it to be valid. Now, when a nun makes the two superior robes (*uttarāsaṅga* and *saṃghāṭī*), since she does not rely on the standard measurements, she does not recite the number of cubits;

rather, she simply says, "I shall make them according to the Dharma, and they shall be valid. Therefore, the *Karmavibhaṅga-vṛtti* states: "Sister, attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], am making these *saṃghāṭī* robes according to the Dharma;

I accept and maintain this. This is recited three times. This is the text from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. "According to the Dharma, I... refers to the acceptance and maintenance. It is recited three times.

The procedure for receiving the *saṃkakṣikā* (shoulder-covering robe) follows the regulations set forth in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, with modifications as appropriate. Regarding the differences between the other two [robes], the fact that offenses are incurred for other garments is due to the nature of the convenience [of the rule].
As for the second point, the "mental reflection" (*cetanā*), the phrase "from two... up to following" refers to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, which requires three recitations.

According to the *Karmasūtra*, however, if there is no one present within the boundary (*sīmā*), it is permitted to accomplish it through mental reflection alone; this is established even if [the formal procedure] were later to be performed.

If there are people present, one need not trouble oneself to perform the ritual of "purifying through difference" (*visamāna-sādhāraṇa*) again. However, if one encounters more people, it must still be recited anew.

Within the fourfold analysis of the distinctions, the names [of the sections] can be understood from the headings. The commentary on the text has three parts. First, from the beginning up to the "elder," constitutes the major section.
Regarding "not speaking upon first arrival" and "non-completion": these clarify the characteristics of the formation of receiving and relinquishing, as is evident from the text itself.
Next, from "all those who receive and maintain" down to "having copied the commentary," this clarifies the method of receiving and the characteristics of non-loss.

Regarding the "broad side," this refers to the vertical length from top to bottom. Since the measurement is small, it is eight finger-widths; this constitutes the loss of the received [robe], referring to the long side, which means the two ends measured horizontally. Since the measurement is...

The *Mahīśāsaka* school states that one must extend the hands beyond [the robe] by at least one *muṣṭi* (a handful) for the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) to be lost; thus there are four such cases.

The following points regarding obstructions are all as explained in the *Naiḥsargika-vastra* (Rules on Separation from Robes), the *Yìshāo* (Commentary on the Meaning), and the initial commentary (*śū*), and so forth. The *Sarvāstivāda* school, below, distinguishes that there is no offense of "staying overnight separated from one's robes" when one does not possess them, because the necessary conditions (*pratyaya*) are lacking;
this differs from the *Dṛṣṭānta-vibhāga* (Treatise on Views), which holds that even if one has not formally accepted [the robe], there is still the offense of being separated from it.

If, after the initial *śuddhika* (purification) has been performed, one intends to use the purified material to make the three robes (*tricīvara*) and undergoes the formal rite of acceptance (*parigraha*), the previous purification is lost.
If another robe is separately accepted to replace this robe, this [new] robe must once again be purified. Second, regarding mending, washing, and dyeing.

Regarding the statement "from two up to *hā*": as for obtaining two offenses for each segment, this refers to the violation of the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) and the *pratideśanīya* (offense requiring confession), because the cloth has not been joined with its proper substance.

Regarding the phrase "applying both types of purification methods," the *Jiumoluoshi* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states: "There is purification through the joining of the cloth and purification through the joining of the color.
Thus, the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* says: "If the patches of a robe have not yet been declared pure (*adhiṣṭhita*), one should apply the purification by marking (*tilaka*) before sewing the robe."

Regarding "having already been purified": this refers to the purification through the combination of robes (*cīvara-saṃsarga-śuddhi*). If the color is not in accordance with the Dharma, but one wears what is in accordance with the Dharma, this is called purification through the combination of colors (*varṇa-saṃsarga-śuddhi*).
There is no need for further individual purification. The citation from the *Śāstra* (the *Shanbu erzhi jiaojie xuanyi*) does not differ from this;

it means that by combining previously purified colors, one causes the subsequent robe to be purified through its connection with those colors. The following section on "excellent preparation" clarifies the method of mending.

The characteristics can be known. As for "the double lines being separated," this is a textual error. Regarding "weaving the edges (bù mí fǎn), stretching the frame (zhòu yīn lǜ), and having the low parts patched":

the measurements of the holes in the frame are not fixed; thus, the loss of the formal reception (*upasampadā*) and so forth may be considered identical. The boundaries are as explained above in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
"Both usages cause no harm" means that although the conditions are not severed, if there is a breach in the middle, it constitutes a loss as clarified in the *Samantapāsādikā*.

If, while in the middle [of the process], one hears that it has not yet been pierced and the cord breaks, then according to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, this constitutes a failure. Regarding the term "vivid color" (*he-se*):
Xuán says it refers to red-colored earth; the Dàdé (Venerable) says that the original text read "all" (*zhū*) rather than "various" (*zǔ*), and that this was a scribal error by later generations.
"Dù" refers to a mound of earth. As for "not scolding," this is to protect the minds of non-human beings (*amanuṣya*) and to raise up those who are obscure, let alone those who are manifest.

Third is "receiving and holding," the title of which can be understood from its name. Regarding the section stating "the ten cases where there is no offense," it first cites the *Daśādhyāya-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) and the *Xiuzhanchanbing jing* (Sutra on Treating the Illnesses of Meditation) to clarify the method for respectfully using celestial robes (*deva-vastra*); the textual characteristics of these passages are self-evident. The Venerable Master said:

"The character 'háo' (蒿) was originally [intended for] 'bēn' (奔), as in 'running chariots, elephants, and horses'; later generations mistakenly wrote it as 'yì' (逸). Second, from the passage following the *Daśādhyāya-vinaya*...

This clarifies the method of following what is beneficial and accompanying the person. Regarding "not acting at improper times": knowing that one cannot produce wholesome states due to broken precepts, wrong views, and so forth, one immediately restrains oneself from such actions.
Regarding "feathers and quills accompanying one another," the Great Virtuous One cites the *Shangshu*:

"The fine hair beneath the belly is called *chui*; the longest hair on the head of the wing is the feather (*yu*); the tube that enters the flesh is the quill (*he*). Now, these two [categories] are taken."

According to the rule regarding the addition of thread, we now follow the principle of adding to the edge without cutting it, but taking the total dimensions as five units in length and four in width, making them into one.

in this case, too, there is no offense. This refers to adding an extra foot [of cloth], which is merely new supplementary thread added to the center of the fabric, rather than a further increase beyond the original prescribed measurement of the garment itself;
this is termed "not cutting. According to this principle, there is no offense; thus, even if the *bhañja* exceeds the measure, there is no transgression.
It is also improper to commit [these offenses] or to stake them as collateral. Regarding "Bāḷha": after the First Council, Bāḷha questioned [the monks].

"Only below" clarifies the ritual procedures for sitting and using [the robe]. "Long-folded" refers to folding it vertically from top to bottom.
"Folded in the middle" refers to folding it by bending it in half. "Folding it in the center" refers to the pleating within the hall; nowadays, this is located in the inner pure area.
The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* clarifies the place where it is to be placed. Xuán says: In the tenth fascicle of that [text], it states: "In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, [King] Prasenajit..."
Anāthapiṇḍika, a minister of King Prasenajit, went to the royal city to seek a wife for his son. There, upon seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, he realized the fruit [of the path].

He wished to invite the Buddha back to Śrāvastī, so the Buddha instructed Śāriputra to designate a place for him to reside. Anāthapiṇḍika then purchased Prince Jeta’s grove with gold to establish a monastery.
The six heretical teachers became envious and jealous; they went to the king and requested that a contest of dharma be held between them and Śāriputra. The hall...

He placed his sitting mat upon his shoulder and entered the assembly to take his seat. A disciple of the Six Heretics named Raudrākṣa manifested lotus ponds, mountains, dragons, oxen, yakṣas, ghosts, and so forth;
the Buddha’s disciples manifested fierce winds, elephants, garuḍas, lions, Vaiśravaṇa, and others to confront them.
Since he was no match for them, he wept and submitted his heart, subsequently renouncing the world and becoming a monk. Thus it is.
That which is currently on the left arm and is contrary to the Dharma is the original intention. This is clarified according to the teachings.

Next, following the *Gantong zhuan* (Records of Spiritual Resonance), one receives the indication of a celestial being who says: "This is not the fault of the Master; it was merely opened later. The teaching had not yet reached this land."

Now, let us simply rectify our former delusions and hasten toward later enlightenment. When the Buddha first delivered the five bhikṣus and ordained the brothers Kāśyapa, he prescribed that the *kāṣāya* be worn upon the upper arm.
In the Western Land (India), kings and ministers alike all wear golden brocade over their shoulders.
Therefore, the Buddha’s robe was worn over the left arm to distinguish it from the common people. At that time, the bhikṣu Aśvajit’s sitting mat was likewise kept on his left arm.
Later, as his followers gradually increased, young bhikṣus with handsome and dignified appearances went into the city for alms and were frequently pursued by the affections of women;
consequently, the rule was established that the corner of the robe should be placed on the left shoulder. Subsequently, because the robe was blown away by the wind, the Buddha ordered that—
He used heavy objects to weigh it down. The bhikṣus, failing to grasp the Buddha’s intention, fashioned elaborate shoulder-weights with many ornaments.
This drew the censure and reproach of the laity. The Buddha rebuked them, saying: "When I instructed that heavy objects be used to weigh it down, I was referring to the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat).
How could you separately create such unlawful items? Consequently, the sitting mat was used to weigh down the three robes while they were carried on the left arm. At that time, the Tathāgata...
He ascended to heaven to preach the Dharma to the Brahma King. Later, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Dharmatrāta who claimed to possess all-encompassing knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
He waited for the bhikṣus as they entered the city to beg for alms and sought to debate them; when the bhikṣu engaged him in debate, the non-Buddhist was defeated.
Pāpīyān asked, "What is the name of the garment you wear? The śramaṇa replied, "It is the robe of patience. He asked again, "What is its functional efficacy?
He answered, "Above, it subdues the celestial Māras; below, it overcomes external paths. He asked again, "What is that cloth upon your shoulder called?
He answered, "It is a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat). He asked, "What is its use? The śramaṇa said, "It is intended for..."
He sat down and used it. A non-Buddhist remarked, "To wear [the robe] while sitting is a mark of noble endurance; it possesses great majesty and spiritual power.
This is the garment for sitting beneath [the teacher]. How can you instead place it upon yourself? If this is your teacher’s instruction, your teacher is not worthy of such high honor.
If this is something you did yourself, why did your teacher not instruct you? Later, the Tathāgata descended from heaven.

The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, who then ordained that it be moved to the left arm beneath the robe. Later, because the wind blew the robe away from the body, he ordained that a hook and thread be attached to the upper part [of the robe].
According to this explanation, its current placement on the left arm perfectly accords with the proper ritual procedure;
if one refers to the Vinaya and Sūtras, it is because the original intention has been preserved.
The document concerning the method for the three water-bags is as written. The phrase "do not go" expresses the underlying intent.
"Jue" (厥) means "that which. The mind of compassion resides therein. "Bei" (背) means "resembling"; it refers to those who do not uphold the precepts, mostly mentioned below.

Regarding the clarification of the straining method as previously explained, this refers to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā* (Shang-duo-lun), specifically the section on constructing other wells and so forth. Its shape is like a hook.

The character [for "handle"] should be written with the "gold" (金) radical. Xuán said: "Do not write it as the character for 'hook' (鉤). It should be described as an object that has a handle by which it can be grasped;
the form currently used for 'to cut' (截) is this very shape. As for the "large outer coffin" (宏槨), it refers to a wooden outer coffin shaped like a well or other such forms.
The "filtering jar" (漉瓶) is the same as the "yin-yang jar"; one filters water using a silk cloth as the bottom, placing it inside a sand bag like when straining lime.

"Equality of dharmas," and so forth. The phrase "this reaches the middle" is an admonition and exhortation; it means that if one cannot even maintain these natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*), it goes without saying that one will fail in other matters such as livelihood and deportment.

The second section, the Gate of Listening (*śravaṇa-mukha*), consists of two subsections: the citation of names and so forth, and the first [subdivision] as it appears in the text. Regarding the phrase "From 'initially' to 'different'":

the initial passage cites the fundamental school’s general clarification that the hundred and one types of long robes differ in their methods of receiving purification (*pariśuddhi*). As for "the hundred and one" (*śata-eka*): "hundred" (*śata*) is used to indicate the maximum number;
this is spoken in reference to the formal rules (*dharma*). "One" (*eka*) means that within these hundreds, one [robe] is kept for each specific item; it does not mean exactly one hundred.
Regarding the "one-for-one" (bai-yi) rule: this generally permits the accumulation of various purified items.
If one does not maintain these as "one-for-one"—that is, beyond the three robes and the sitting mat—then they become surplus items and are no longer subject to the "one-for-one" designation.

As for "things resembling jewels," Xuán says that items such as crystal and amber used as prayer beads fall within the "one-for-one" count and do not require the ritual of *shuo-jing* (purification by declaration); other items resembling jewels are considered heavy [in terms of value].
All these are termed "remnants" (*śeṣa*). "Vessels" refers to jars, pots, and the like; "non-vessels" refers to copper and iron fragments and so forth. All of these are to be given to laypeople.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Fenbie sengqi lü), in its lower section, clarifies the opening of the one hundred and one items as found in the text. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (Wufen lü), in its lower section, clarifies the substance of the one hundred and one items. Regarding the "single-layered covering robe":
according to the circumstances [of the Vinaya], it was established for use as bedding for monks when they were defiled by filth. It was permitted for the purpose of protecting the monastic bedding.

Regarding the storage of bedding for the Saṃgha, it is explained as indicated in the commentary. "If it resembles clothing" refers to all other types of robes. *Pārikkāra* is a general term for "one hundred";
here it is translated as "clothing that assists the body. As for its color, Xuán says: "This refers to the designation of the colors of various robes;
it does not mean specific hues such as blue or yellow. Regarding the phrase "to be applied according to the dharma," it means—
"Facing the eyes of the assembly" refers to the *zuo-fa zá-yī* (作法雜衣). "According to how much [is available]" refers to what is called *bù-yī-bó* (補衣帛) here.

Regarding "there is no fault if one does not accept it": while robes and bowls must necessarily be formally accepted (*shòuchí*), as for other items such as the hundred [miscellaneous] articles, if one does not accept them, no offense is incurred.
As stated in the preceding text: whether they are made or not made, there is in all cases no offense. Regarding the two robes, upper and lower, for a *śrāmaṇera*, as follows...

The *Śrāmaṇera-vibhaṅga* states: Regarding one *uttarāsaṅga* and one *antarvāsaka*, with the exception of money, grain, or rice, these must be relinquished to a layperson; one must speak to the layperson while performing the act of relinquishment.

If one does not speak, it constitutes an offense. This is excluded because, unlike long robes (*atireka-cīvara*), which may be kept for ten days by obtaining the consent of the assembly, these items do not permit such an allowance.

Regarding the two types of *dīrghacīvara* (extra robes), the topical divisions may be understood as follows. First, the characteristics of the "extra" are clarified. As for the phrase "beginning with...

(*yún chū zhì yě*), this refers to the original classification and distinction. Regarding "completed in one day": according to that text, it states that a *saṃghāṭī* is completed in five days, a seven-strip robe in four days, a five-strip robe in two days, and an extra robe in one day.
This is because they are easy to make; that is to say, the material substance of the three robes can never constitute an offense regarding excess.

The meaning: what is called *dīrgha-dhana* (long wealth) in foreign lands [refers to this]. Regarding the rules for the *saṃkakṣikā* (undershirt), along with its commentary, these are the names in the Chinese translation.

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), in its lower section, distinguishes its characteristics; its form is like that which covers the knees, as explained by Master Houguang—it is a garment cut so that it is narrow at the top and wide at the bottom.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong lü), in its lower section, prescribes the purpose of wearing it when entering a village, as stated in the text. In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Monǐzhēn lü), in its section on the *saṃkakṣikā*, it clarifies the measurement of the elbow; the commentary notes that it is still intended to cover [the breasts].
Regarding the measurement of the shoulder: it is made according to the measurement of the elbow (*kūpara*), resembling the appearance of a garment that covers the shoulders.

Some masters who have modified the methods state that during the Later Wei dynasty there was a master of the Mahāsāṃghika school who produced a commentary clarifying the method for making robes. He stated that the *saṃkakṣikā* (shoulder-cloth) should be made with four parts, being narrow at the top and wide at the bottom;
however, he merely said to "make it according to the dharma" and did not specify the size of the elbow measurements. Below the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (inner robe), the following is first cited:

The *Mahāsāṃghika* and other vinayas clarify the rules for the dharma-robes. In the Western lands (India), the *mañca-tārā* (waist-cloth) is used to encircle the waist; the waist-string comes around from above.
The Buddha instructed the bhikṣus that it must not be too high, level with the knees, nor too low, level with the ankles.

The two front corners should hang down like the tail of a fish, one corner slanting like an elephant’s trunk, or rising up in folds like the leaves of a *tāla* tree. Among the three thousand [rules], there is not even one that does not [prohibit] this.
"To hold the lower part upward" means to wear it inverted. "To obtain the binding for the feet" means to unfasten and break the ties at the sides of both knees.
"To fold back" means not to bind it with a strap, but merely to fold it back and turn it over. "It should consist of two, three, or four strips."

In the *Caturvarga-vinaya*, the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) made waistbands that were wide and long. The Buddha said this was not permissible; they should be three finger-widths wide and wrap around the waist three times.

If one obtains [a belt] that has already been completed, it should consist of two strips and so forth. If it is disordered, one may listen to [the rules on] sewing them together and so forth, as in the text.

In the *Fǔpiān jì* (Record of the Auxiliary Chapters), making strips is not permitted; the character should be read as "dié" (a slip of paper or label). This means that if one obtains a finished product, it must be dismantled into two, three, or four [strips].

The colophon states that it is "one. If there were three or four colophons, they would be disordered; therefore, they are joined together by stitching. In the current Vinaya text, the character *tiáo* (條) is erroneously written [instead of *zhì* (至)].
Regarding the phrase "later passing through the gaps" (*qíjiān guòděng*), this is to avoid exposing the body. As for *kūśūra*, there is no standard Chinese equivalent;

therefore, the *Wǔfēn lǜ* (Five-Part Vinaya) is cited to clarify its appearance as a garment, which is the *guàn tóu yī* (貫頭衣, "head-piercing robe"). The phrase "now explaining... until... refers to distinguishing [the types] according to region.
It is a mark [of the Buddha]. As for "exposing one shoulder," this refers to the right side of the present-day *pianshan* (short-sleeved robe).

According to the *Zhudaozu lu*, when the palace ladies of the Wei dynasty saw monks exposing their shoulders during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, they did not conceive wholesome thoughts; they therefore fashioned a garment to cover the monks' shoulders by sewing it onto the left side.
Because the *saṃkakṣikā* was joined together, it followed that mark and was called the *pianshan*. The Venerable Master permits those who make new ones to have them regulated accordingly.

Regarding the example of raising the sitting mat (and so forth). As for the *dabban* (sleeve-cover): it resembles a *pianshan* (short tunic), but with a patch added to the left side of the back, covering the shoulder like a single piece of cloth.
It is short, and when worn, the fold hangs toward the right shoulder. The Venerable One said: "In the northern regions, the *śikṣamāṇā*s mostly wear this garment;
its purpose is to distinguish them from *bhikṣuṇīs* and *śrāmaṇerīs*. Later generations moved the placement [of the patch] to the left side of the *pianshan*."
On the upper sleeves, they are called *bōyī* (播衣). This is the *biǎnshān* (褊衫) that emerged from the *zhīzhī* (祇支), from which the *dàshuǒ* (襠膞) emerged, and from which the *bōzǐ* (播子) emerged.
However, the trailing banner (*yèfán*) is merely a sham of renunciation and expresses nothing; this is because the masters (*lùnshī*) of the Western Lands (India) hold only to the red banner.
As for the square skirt (*fāngqún*), it was bestowed upon the monks by the Princess of Jun during the Liang dynasty.
The large skirt worn by palace attendants when mounting their horses is folded at the waist and opened like a *fangxiang* (a ritual mask).

As for the various skirts, these are further types made according to the occasion. The "arm-clothing" (*biyi*) refers to arm-sleeved garments; the "leaping-clothing" (*tiaoyi*) refers to padded trousers with high boots and the like.

All of these were created according to the customs of this region; they did not originally exist in the Western lands (India). Next, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* clarifies that it is improper to wear garments with distinctive features.
A "tight-fitting shirt" (*biànshān*) refers to a garment with narrow sleeves. A "double-layered garment" (*fùyī*) refers to a garment padded with cotton or silk floss.

A "tunic-like garment" (*guàntóuyī*) is the skirt worn by women. A "two-sleeved garment" is the secular style of wearing the arms bare. Regarding the "pleated skirt" (*zhé*), various explanations differ, all of which...
The characteristics have not yet been identified. Now, according to the *Yifuzhiminglu* (Record of the Names and Meanings of Clothing), this is the lower garment (*chang*) of antiquity.

During the time of King Wu of Zhou, it was made of plain cloth and called a *xie*. During the time of King Jing, it was made of *chan* silk; however, its opening was not sewn shut, as it was worn by commoners.
During the reign of Emperor Luo, it was made of *ling* silk and a hem was added below, which was called the "mouth" (*kou*); consequently, it was renamed.

Regarding trousers (*hakama*): On the *Go-tsuba* (Dragon Boat) festival, the various officials were granted trousers made of *suisha-ryō* silk. This was intended to symbolize their upright integrity and their governance of the people, and so forth.

In the present day, such things no longer exist; even if they did, it would likely not be appropriate. Regarding the practice of *gyōtō*, [the author] cites the sutra, saying: "Because he strides with his ankles crossed and leaps forward, his body is light.
