As for those who avoid what I have prescribed: *Hakama*. On the *Go-tsuba* day, the various officials were bestowed trousers of *suisha-ryō* silk. The intention was to signify upright integrity and the governing of the people, and so forth.

In the present age, these do not exist; even if they were to exist, they would likely not be fitting. Regarding *gyōtō*, [the author] cites the sutra, saying: "He strides by crossing his ankles and leaping along, because his body is light. As for those who evade what I have established:

The *Zhì* (the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*) treats the three robes as a single entity; now [the present school] avoids this and does not follow it. Furthermore, the accumulation of various surplus items is termed "engaging in other matters" (*anyakārya*).
The *Madhyamāgama* (Middle Discourses), lower fascicle, clarifies that for those of middle and lower capacities, providing for the body while practicing the Way increases wholesome dharmas;

it permits such accumulation, whereas the opposite is not permitted, as stated in the text. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, lower fascicle, clarifies the items possessed and used by the Saṃgha and individuals. [King...]
Regarding the offering of expensive robes: as previously established, these are indeed *dharmakāya* robes (monastic garments). It is not permitted for one to lead [the Buddha] over them.
When Prince Bodhi invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha, he spread out expensive robes upon the ground and requested that the Buddha tread upon them. The Buddha ordered Ānanda to remove them.

For the sake of future bhikṣus: regarding the meditation belt (*dhyāna-bandhana*), it refers to that which is used to bind the body and provide support when one becomes weary from sitting in meditation for a long time.

As for the waistband—specifically those with three or four strips sewn together—if one is a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) or even further advanced, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there was a case where a layperson was stripped by bandits and came to the place of the bhikṣus to borrow a robe.
He informed the Buddha, who said: "Examine [the person] before lending; if they return it, it is appropriate. If they do not return it, it is not.
"Returning, it is finished. "Finished" means to cease. In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the section on leather goods distinguishes [the rules]. Regarding the "five matters of the border regions":
Kātyāyana was in the country of Aparāntaka when he conferred the precepts upon Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa; it took three years for him to obtain the full assembly (*saṃgha*).
Consequently, he requested five matters, as detailed in the text (etc.). Regarding the "white wooden strips" and so forth, the Vinaya states: "In the east there is a country named Śvetavaktra."
Section. Outside the white wooden beam, listen! To the south there is a stupa named Jingxian (Tranquil Goodness). Outside Jingxian, listen!
To the west there is a mountain named Shilifo (Śrī-buddha), outside which are the people of the Buddha-lineage; listen! To the north there is a country named Zhu (Pillar).

The Pillar then listened. Regarding the "Illustrations of Tribute" (*Gongzhi tu*): these were paintings depicting high-ranking officials and their duties, as well as the quantities of tribute items presented by various foreign states.
One such illustration stated: "The State of White Wood Strips (*Baimutiao*) in the West presents one steed of vermilion hue and white color, and one jade elephant," and so forth.

By verifying this, it was known that this place lay to the east of those [western regions] and belonged to the frontier lands. The remaining text may be understood in detail. It is said to be according to the *Vinaya* (*Lü*).

Regarding "possessing" (畜): this is further clarified by reference to hides. The group of six (ṣaḍvargika) monks possessed the skins of dogs, lions, tigers, leopards, otters, wild boars, wild cats, foxes, and so forth.
The Buddha declared that these should not be possessed. In the text, the term for "otter" (獺) is pronounced *tālù* (with the second syllable as *tā* and *lù*).

Its form is like that of a small dog; it dwells in water and eats fish. In the Vinaya, it is sometimes written as *zhuò* (丁曷反), which resembles [the character for] *zhèng* with the radical for "wild" (*kuáng*) substituted for "king" (*wáng*), but nowadays it is mostly written as *jū* (七餘反).
The *Shuowen* states that "small" means "subsequent. Regarding the prohibition against begging for raw hide: the group of six monks saw a fine, variegated calf and asked for it;

the ox-skinning man, being faithful and respectful, skinned the animal and gave it to them. The mother cow then went to the Jetavana Monastery and bellowed in distress, which led to the establishment of this rule.

As for the prohibition against making canopies or awnings, this follows the rules for robes (*cīvara*); it simply states that one must not do so, without further discussion of whether the material is hide or not.

It is a garment. The meditation belt (*dhyāna-bandha*) has five characteristics: first, it is one foot wide; second, it is eight feet long; third, it has a hook at the head; fourth, it should have three or four layers;
fifth, gold hooks must not be used. It is wound from behind and turned forward to hook [the waist];

thus, when both knees remain completely motionless, it is called "Aid to Goodness" (*kalyāṇamitra*). Regarding the protection of the garment: if defined by the sense of obstructing dust and defilement, the *śamī* (sleeve or hem) is also a garment. If...

Because they were worn on the ground with the sleeves tucked up, they would brush against the upper robes when sitting later; therefore, the use of straw sandals and the rules concerning them were permitted.
As for protecting the bedding, they were allowed to be worn so as not to soil the Dharma robes. Regarding the practice of baring one shoulder, there are exceptions:
in the Western Regions, removing one's shoes and baring one shoulder is considered a mark of respect; thus, while traveling on this path, one removes straw sandals to fetch water.
When giving [a sandal] to one's teacher, it may sometimes be lost or bitten by venomous insects. When this was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:

"One need not remove the sandals or the *biantan* (exposed shoulder garment). Therefore, it is said that there is no fault. Thus, one should simply give whatever object is at hand to the teacher; there is no requirement to remove grass sandals or the *biantan*.
Regarding the four kinds of precious shoes—those made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and various jewels—the rest of the text is easily understood.

Regarding the second section on the *dharmas for purifying* (śuddhi-dharma): first, the titles are listed, which can be understood individually. The commentary contains six parts. The phrase "From 'the first' to 'ear'" clarifies the underlying intent of the regulation.

As for "providing through skillful means," it means that the Great Compassionate One established this teaching and formulated these *śuddhi-dharmas* so that one may constantly maintain the intention that [possessions] belong to others;
thus, one avoids the fault of personal hoarding while still obtaining clothing and requisites to support the body, thereby benefiting the donor and escaping [retribution].

Because he was reviled by the world, he was not [a true] arhat. Regarding the passage "As at one time in the past," Xuan quotes the *Fenbie gongde lun* (Treatise on the Differentiation of Merit), which says:
"The heavenly Subhūti was originally of royal lineage. For five hundred lifetimes, he was constantly born in the heavens. Now, descending from heaven, he was born into a royal family;
his karmic rewards were exquisite. Later, he joined the Buddha and left the household life. Upon hearing the teaching of the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*), his mind did not..."

Enduring this, he wished to return home. Ānanda detained him for one night, and he immediately went to the royal palace to borrow various precious objects and requisites for adornment, where he stayed overnight.
[He thought: "I must attain the fruits of the Path. The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for clothing, it may be used with intimacy, yet it may also not be used with intimacy.
If wearing fine clothes benefits the Path, they may be used with intimacy; if they damage the mind for the Path, then they should not."
One should not rely on external things. For some attain the Way through fine clothing, while others attain the Way through the five precepts;

thus we know that awakening and understanding reside in the mind and are not constrained by physical form or dress. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* also contains instructions on the method of giving, which states:
"The Bodhisattva first, for the sake of purifying all the requisites he possesses, relinquishes them to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions by means of the four pure [offerings]."

Just as a bhikṣu, when about to present his robes and requisites, relinquishes them to his preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya) for the sake of performing the ritual of purification (viśuddhi), so too is it with nirvāṇa.
As the Sūtra says: "Although one is permitted to accept and keep impure objects, they must necessarily be purified through a formal gift (pariṣkāra-dāna) to a donor of sincere faith.
Second, regarding the distinction of the donors: their names may be recorded for identification. The three types of donors mentioned previously refer to those who provide robes and medicine.

The *pātra* (alms bowl) invites the monastic community to act as donors; the precious jewel and other items invite laypeople to act as donors. The commentary (*chao*) follows this section to divide the categories, stating:

"First, reaching the pure ones" refers to distinguishing them from the three aforementioned masters. "Obtaining anyone according to circumstances" means that one may proceed through five successive stages.

This applies to the entire assembly of pure monks. When it comes to the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), one may designate any single person according to one's intention to act as the guardian of that object.
It is not said that this must be done in the presence of a *śrāmaṇera*; this refers to "true purification" (*bhūta-pariśuddhi*), which necessarily requires the presence of the assembly.

Now, this method of protection is unlike the "successive transfer" (*paramparā*); among the five types [of purity], any one of them suffices. As for the category of "improper time," since it has already been obtained through prior preparation, [it does not require further formalities].

Regarding the fear that it would be difficult to obtain the robe: "one who cannot praise another" refers to someone who, having received the precepts of the Hīnayāna, sees that others do not commit the offense of *atireka* (excess) when receiving pure gifts (*śuddha-dāna*), and thus acquires a good reputation. Now, because one does not wish for the aforementioned person to have such a reputation, one may not invite them.
As for those who should receive pure gifts from the five assemblies: this means that [the gift] is transmitted through the five assemblies. That is to say:

It simply means that among the five [categories], one may give to any single individual. Xuán says: "If this person does not personally perform the ritual of *pariśuddha-dāna* (pure giving), it is improper to invite the five groups of monastics;
it would not constitute a valid formal act (*samyag-vidhi*) and should not be granted. There are versions that add the character "light" (*qīng*), but this is incorrect.

Regarding "laypeople" (*báiyī*): this refers to fathers, brothers, and other secular persons; it is improper for them to give to others [on behalf of the Sangha]. Next, as for the "five and four," since these pertain to the two types of giving, [the preceding rules apply].

This may be understood in detail according to the text. One must not designate two or three people as the *śuddhikara* (purifier), for fear that the person acting as the purifier might become confused regarding the six types of items and fail to record their specific characteristics (*varṇa-nāman*).
Regarding the failure to return another’s purified object: Vaddhananda took a robe from a disciple who had performed a *śuddhidāna* (pure gift) to him;

later, out of anger toward his preceptor, he refused to return the robe. Because he seized it, a dispute arose. This was reported to the Buddha, who consequently established the rule that one must carefully examine and select [the recipient].

"Person": This refers to the person before whom one receives the purification (*śuddhi*). That is, the person who performs the purification in their presence. "Śrāmaṇera who has received the precepts":

This refers to those undergoing penance for transgressions (*śikṣādattaka*). "Persons of five qualities": These include two who have completed the formal practice (*karmavācanā*), two who have finished the practice, and those undergoing the *mūlāpakarṣa* (penance for a fundamental offense).

Because these superior persons do not count toward the quorum, they do not give rise to strife. "Fearing that a wicked person might claim this object": This means that if such a person were to recognize the object as theirs, it would result in the loss of the purification.
The phrase "practicing the ultimate teaching" clarifies that money and treasures are for worldly purposes. "As explained below" refers to the terminology cited from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā*.

The second section, "Requesting the Dharma," indicates the title; this can be understood accordingly. Regarding the passage "From 'first' to 'must,'" it clarifies whether a request is necessary or unnecessary.

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā* contains only the intent of requesting, while other schools have no textual record of it. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* merely states that one should give according to who arrives.
This seems not to require a formal request. The three types of methods for requesting [permission] are all as stated in the text (etc.). Regarding the phrase "next, until the clear and pure":

this indicates that it is appropriate to state that [the items] are not subject to the rule of following [the ten-day limit]. This means that for money and precious objects, one must specify how many days they will be kept;

for grain and other such things, one must state whether they are essential or non-essential. Therefore, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* is cited, stating that all must be declared within ten days. Fourth, the method for performing the purification (*viśuddhi*). First...
This clarifies the mental reflection. Regarding the phrase "five [steps] up to 'transferring'": first, one relies on the fivefold procedure (*pañcavastuka*). The *Karmasūtra-vyākhyā* states:

"Since it is difficult to exhaust the intention to relinquish [the object] if one does not face another person, one should first cause it to be transferred so as to extend the time limit; ultimately, one must speak [of the relinquishment] in person before it is finalized. (The above is the text of the commentary.

Regarding the phrase "purely giving [it] to someone named X and taking it from them for use": this means forming the intention that it belongs to that person, and then taking it for use from their side.
After ten days have passed, he again directs his mind toward taking it from that person and stores it by his side.
After another ten days have passed, he again gives it to that person. Regarding "discarding the old and accepting the new":

this means that giving it to another is called "discarding the old," while taking it back from that person as if newly acquired is called "accepting the new" (according to the meaning of this passage, this refers specifically to a single garment). The section beginning with "inner mind" explains the above.
The *Saṃghāṭi* [Vinaya] states that this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is because the Vinaya clarifies below that one must relinquish the old [robe] before receiving the new.

Regarding the phrase "in the Vinaya," this refers to the text of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* cited above. It should refer to those who have not performed the *viśuddhi* (purification/declaration of purity).

The Venerable Master says: "In the *Karmasūtra*, it is explained generally with respect to persons of the three faculties. However, the 'not performing the *viśuddhi*' mentioned here refers specifically to those of the upper and middle faculties. Such individuals...
Such a person has traditionally never kept extra items (*dīrgha-vastu*) and has had nothing to formally purify through ritual declaration (*śuddhi*).

Now, if someone should offer the three robes (*tricīvara*) and so forth, once accepted, they immediately become "extra. Since one originally maintains only the three robes, one does not fear violating the rule against keeping extras;

yet, there is no avoiding the offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) when these extras remain for more than ten days. Therefore, within ten days, one should exchange them with others as a skillful means (*upāya*) to maintain them as new. (Note)

The text states: "Regarding those who say 'one may perform the *śuddhi* (purification) and so forth," this is spoken for persons of inferior faculties. Originally, when one acquires an extra robe through defilement, it is appropriate to perform the *śuddhi* in the presence of another person (*pratimukha*).

Now, since there is no one present to whom one may speak, and fearing that the day will pass and an offense be committed, one is first permitted to perform a mental recitation (*manasikāra*) and exchange [the robes] with others in turn.
One must still wait until someone is available to whom one can speak before finally ceasing; thus, one relinquishes the old and receives the new.

Although the *śuddhivāda* (declaration of purity) and this differ, there is no distinction in changing them once every ten days; therefore, they are made to circulate in succession. (This interpretation does not contradict the *Chao*;
it is said that the *Jie-mo-su* [Karmavācanā] contains further incorrect meanings which are not recorded here.)

Next, the method of face-to-face transmission in succession is explained. Regarding the phrase "reaching from here to there": "face-to-face" refers to the person with whom one is directly confronting; "succession" refers to the donor.

Xuán states that according to the *Jǐemó Shū* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā), there are three types of successive transmission: first, the presiding master hands it over to the person acting as the counterpart;
second, the person acting as the counterpart points distantly toward the donor; third, when the pure master does not know [the recipient], he returns the property to the donor.

The Master [states]: "Storing items for the sake of a designated steward (*viśuddhika*) is entirely for the purpose of eliminating the affliction of anger. This exposition of the *viśuddhi* (purification) procedure follows the ancient texts.

Regarding the phrase "those who come from outside," it refers to the fifty [rules] being reduced to three. At the beginning of the Vinaya, the occasion arose when one made a purification with a designated steward in person;

because of a dispute over an external object belonging to another, the Buddha said: "Address another person separately, merely by reciting that person's name. Later, he addressed that person [directly].

"Knowing" is the second condition. Later, once he had known [the situation], he feared that he might have committed the offense of "excess" (*dīrgha*); consequently, [the Buddha] established the rule of "not using" so that he would know [the proper procedure]. This constitutes the third condition.

Regarding the phrase "well until writing," this refers to the true *śuddhivisuddhi* (purification by declaration). The previous citation from the *Vibhaṅga* merely provides a general explanation of the underlying intent.
Next, from the section "If one performs the ritual correctly" onwards, the addition of the ritual according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* follows; these two methods apply generally to all robes.

The text within the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (or *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*) states: "Therefore, the commentary [says]... From "the second" up to "pervasive," it distinguishes and establishes their mutual non-association, as in the text.
From "the fifth" up to "belonging," it is a general indication of the teaching. Regarding the commentary's note, "always recording the donor":

because the donor is not permanent—fearing that the pure dharma (*śuddha-dharma*) might be lost due to their death or other circumstances—it is therefore recorded constantly. Regarding leather shoes being purified by declaration, as in the text. Regarding "money and treasures": [End of excerpt]

"Those who are most intelligent" refers to those who can distinguish the methods for declaring the purity (*viśuddhi*) of coins and treasures. Even though the declaration of purity is permitted for laypeople so that they may understand [the value], one must not personally possess them.
Although this is not explicitly stated in the text, by principle it follows that such items should be managed by a layperson. This is as clarified in the thirty precepts.
This refers to the two precepts concerning the window and the jewel. Regarding the phrase "five [cases] of survival and death" within the *Wuchunwang* (Five Cases of Survival and Death), it says:

"As for 'reaching five [yojanas],' if one must rely on the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (*Lunlü*), if one does not know whether they are alive or dead, one may rely on the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, which sets the limit at three *yojanas*.

If their location is known, then one follows the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, according to which they are lost when they reach another country. If it is certain that they are dead or have left the path, then one follows the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (or the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*). These two vinayas are identical in this regard."

This treatise clarifies both the meaning and the text. The remainder of the text is easily understood. Regarding the phrase "from six down to the middle," this explains the characteristics of the loss [of the *kathina*].

There are seven sections. As for the mention of "monks who have not yet reached their [full] years," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: Upāli asked the Buddha, "To whom should one perform the *śuddhi* (purification) of extra robes?
The Buddha said, "One should perform it before the five groups [of monastics]. He asked again, "At what distance should one perform the purification? The Buddha said, "Up to..."

"Within three *yojanas*, one may know of their survival or demise. He asked again, "If purification is performed in the presence of a *śrāmaṇera*, how should it be done if he has received full ordination?
The Buddha said, "One should simply address him by the name of a monk who has no seniority (*anupasaṃpanna*). He asked again, "What if he dies? The Buddha said, "He may be kept for ten days."
Regarding the purification performed before another person: the commentary critiques the ancients for the fault of "losing [the purity] through successive transmission. The ancients said:
"If one performs it by successive transmission without being face-to-face, it is not with the primary owner; therefore, it is not lost. Now, this is refuted:

we have not seen the *Ji-jing* (Suddhipravrajita-vinaya), yet since neither of these two is the actual donor, both cases result in loss. As for the phrase "if one does not know whether they are alive or dead," this refers to—

Regarding the "successive owner" (*paramparā-svāmī*): if this were a direct owner (*mukhya-svāmī*), they would always have to remain nearby, as if intending to take possession of the object immediately.
That it is now stated to be three *yojanas* away refers specifically to the case of a successive owner.

Regarding the "two kinds of precious gifts for laypeople": the first is gold and silver; the second is coins. As for being rebuked by one's teacher and thus being unable to perform the ritual of *pariśuddhi* (purification):
this refers to a donor who is a disciple that was previously rebuked by his teacher. If he later seeks to perform the purification, it constitutes a contradiction;
therefore, it is not appropriate. One must seek another person—both generally and specifically—to perform it. Regarding "the object does not enter the Saṃgha": this refers to a true donor.

They are temporarily entrusted to the presiding master; according to this, these are all instances of "provisional" offerings. An ancient person once said: "The true owner of the property is the deceased.
To claim that after death one may universally request [the property] to be passed on from one to another is an error, for it is not necessary to make such universal requests.
If the deceased were truly the legitimate owner, then subsequent property should rightfully enter the Sangha. Since it does not enter the Sangha, one knows it is merely provisional. (Commentary Note)

The term "etc. serves to reconcile the preceding text. That is to say, while it was previously stated that one must not refer to two or three people, and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* further states [that there are five groups], these appear to be contradictory.
Now, this passage reconciles them by explaining: although it generally refers to the "five groups," within those five, it is not necessary to specifically designate a single individual;
this is also consistent with the previous statement that one must not refer to two or three people. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (below) addresses this based on many taboos.

This clarifies the characteristics of the fault: regarding the cloth and the wealth, there are cases where it has been spoken of and cases where it has not; their characteristics are so closely linked that they are difficult to distinguish. Now, one must relinquish them at one time and speak of them again at another time;

that is, one may not speak of them repeatedly. Therefore, one must first relinquish [the object] and then speak of it again. If one does not relinquish the pure dharma (*viśuddhi-dharma*), one incurs an offense according to the Vinaya.

Regarding those who have accepted the two types of purification (*pariśuddhi*), this refers to the "speaking" and the "marking. Even if the assembly is harmonious, it is not accomplished [if the procedure is flawed]; this refers to taking five...
Regarding superior colors: when they are combined with one another, they do not constitute a pure combination of colors.
However, if the five primary colors and variegated patterns are combined with colors that accord with the Dharma, they then constitute a pure combination of colors.

Second is the paṃsukūla (rag-robe). Its name may be understood from its mention. Regarding the phrase "the regulation up to the confiscation," the statement that "its substance is a lowly object" is according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
As for "not associating with householders," since one does not seek robes, one will certainly not frequent villages or social gatherings.

Second, freedom from cold and heat; third, freedom from provocative stimuli; fourth, freedom from messengers sent from the four directions who seek robes through improper means—these are the four and five types of wrong livelihoods (*mithyājīva*).
The phrase "because it has arrived" distinguishes its essential nature (*tattva*). Among the ten [types of robes], the ninth, the robe for royal service, is omitted.
Xuán said: "In the Western lands, these are discarded. Here in this region, the treatment of monks and laypeople differs; that is why they do not appear [among the laity].

As for robes from within a spirit shrine, if they have been removed from their place, they are acceptable; if they have not been removed from their place, they are still entrusted to non-human beings as their guardians.

Regarding robes from among graves, these are either those wrapped around the dead or those discarded after accompanying a corpse to its burial site. As for robes sought through vows, these are those obtained by going to the abodes of spirits and deities."
Alternatively, by the water’s edge, under a tree, or by the side of a road, one should discard them immediately once the prayer has been fulfilled. Regarding those who come and go:
having wrapped a dead person and finished escorting them away, they may bring back [the discarded items] as an offering; a bhikṣu must not accept them. As for the robes of an undecomposed corpse:

according to the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, while traveling on the road, a bhikṣu saw the robes of an undecomposed corpse and immediately took them and departed. The dead person rose up and pursued him until he reached the gate of the Jetavana Monastery.

[The Buddha] fell to the ground outside [the dwelling]. Consequently, he established a rule: with the exception of the two types of ropes made of skin and hair, this is for two reasons: first, to avoid public censure; second, because they harbor many small insects.
Regarding "there was originally no prior agreement," according to the Vinaya there are two points: first, a prior agreement; second, remote occupation (the character *zhàn* is pronounced *yàn*;

it means to occupy and protect). Within the category of agreements, there are two further points: first, no prior agreement—the one who takes possession first obtains it; second, with a prior agreement—even if one has taken possession first, [it is not valid].
"It must be shared. This refers to the first phrase of the *Vinayavibhaṅga* commentary. "Remote possession" (*āśraya*) also consists of two phrases.

At one time, there was a bhikṣu who went to a cemetery to collect discarded rags (*pāṃśukūla*). As soon as he saw a garment from afar, he formed the intention of possession and said to a second bhikṣu, "This is my garment.
The second bhikṣu then ran quickly to seize it, and because of this, they fell into a quarrel. The Buddha said, "Regarding discarded rags..."

Regarding the phrase "belonging to the one who first took it," the *Chao* (Excerpts) cites this line. Regarding the next line concerning two people, although both were observing from afar and went together, even if they disputed over it, the Buddha said:
"Divide it according to its quantity. Regarding the note stating "it belongs to the one who previously moved it," the *Vinaya* says:

"If it has already been moved, even though it belongs to the one who previously moved it. Xuan says: This means that if a bhikṣu has previously moved this object, it has already become his own and is settled as such.
However, before he had yet returned, he happened to encounter another bhikṣu who was gathering and sweeping up some clothing from a distance.

Seeing it from afar—the very place where the previous person had hidden his clothes—he immediately said, "That is my robe; you must not take it. Thus, it was adjudged to belong to the one who had moved it there first, and the latter person was deemed at fault.
Regarding "avoiding the face of the presiding deity," this refers to the presiding guardian. This constitutes the third case of "ownerless" property.
Regarding "clothing": it refers to that which is hung on a tree wherever one may be, or that found by the water at the foot of a tree without a guardian or owner;
this is called "ownerless clothing. Regarding "earth-soiled clothing": it refers to that which has been discarded in a cesspool or refuse heap and is defiled by the earth.
"Third, the *dānapati* (donor): this is the formal citation of the term. Baoyun states that it is the complete Sanskrit form *dānapati*;
it is also called *dāna*, or *dānapati*. These are all corruptions or abbreviations. In this translation, it is rendered as 'shizhu' (donor).

For example, according to the Vinaya, when Jīvaka was the occasion, kings and ministers subsequently made offerings to the Saṃgha; the Buddha stated that accepting these was permitted, and so forth. This refers to the ultimate point.
This refers to the designation of "timely" (*kāla*) for the purpose of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), namely one month or five months; the opposite of this is called "untimely" (*akāla*).

This can be understood according to the text. Regarding the phrase "now, as for the specific [distinction]," the Venerable One said: "The establishment of these four types of giving is all formulated based on whether the donor’s intention is general or restricted.
That is to say, when a layperson brings goods and does not understand how to distinguish between themselves and the Sangha, one must examine [the matter closely]."
Contemplate the donor’s intention regarding the object to be given. For instance, if it is brought at an improper time, one must ask the donor:

"Is this being given to the resident monks of this monastery, or is it being given universally to all monks? If they say it is for the resident monks of the present, it is called "improper-time giving to those present" (*akāla-pratyutpanna*).
If they say it is to be given to all monks, it is called "improper-time giving acquired by the Sangha" (*akāla-saṃghalabdha*). Furthermore, regarding giving during the proper time, if the donor...

When bringing an object to be offered to the Sangha, one must likewise inquire accordingly: is it being offered to the monks who have observed the summer retreat within this specific boundary (*sīmā*), or is it being offered universally to all monks who have completed their *varṣā* (rainy season) retreat?
If it is said that it is being offered only to these specific monks, it is termed "not for those present" (*na-pratyakṣa*).

If it is said that it is being offered universally, it is designated as "obtained by the timely Sangha" (*kālika-saṃgha-labdha*). All such provisional arrangements do not exceed these four categories. As for the phrase "reaching the second": [it refers to the following].
This can be understood. Regarding the phrase "the section on the initial arrival": the "four fixed dharmas" refers precisely to this procedure of distributing voting tallies (*śalākā*).

The prohibition against receiving robes at a different location was established because of Upananda, who, having entered the rains retreat at one place, subsequently went to another place to receive his robes;

this is cited as proof for the "fixity of the previous location. The passage beginning with "until the rains retreat is not yet concluded" serves as proof for the "fixity of the previous time. This refutes [any contrary view].
Regarding "those belonging to the two groups," this is distinguished based on the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox, thereby dividing them into two parts.

As for "the three robes offered to the Buddha and others," this refers to the case where the Brahmin Vairaṇya, having invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to complete their summer retreat (*vassa*), offered these layers of cloth;

this citation serves as proof that the aforementioned rule does not necessarily require a formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*). Regarding "leaving behind food for the summer [retreat] and so forth," this refers to the surplus remaining after the donor has provided for the Saṃgha at the conclusion of the summer retreat.
The Master [Kāśyapa] wished to divide [the property]. The Buddha said: "It depends on the intention of the donor. If he does not permit it, you must not divide it.

Regarding the phrase "as for those who take [it] by two," [this refers to] that which requires a *saṃgha-karman* (formal act of the community). The Venerable [Kāśyapa] says: "This refutes the ancient masters. The ancients said:

"If they are present at the same time, one simply divides it directly; there is no need for a formal ritual (*karman*). The reason for this is that within the Vinaya according to the Dharma, there is no such *karman* [for this]."

The *Mowen* (Polishing the Text) states: "If one merely arouses the intention and forms the thought [of performing an act], one must not forcibly apply the *karmavācanā*. This is also the case for the *Shizong* (Adorning the School). Now, the difficulty is raised:

the Vinaya explains the method of mental recitation (*cittānuvartana*), which exists where there is no formal agreement or a *saṃgha*; this, by implication, shows it is for the sake of the *saṃgha*. How could there not be a *karmavācanā*?

The Master now insists that a *karmavācanā* must necessarily be performed to include [the act] within the presence of the assembly. If one were to divide [the cases] directly in this way, I fear it would contravene the teachings."

The following cites three sections of text to collectively serve as proof for the existence of this legal principle (*dharmatā*). The section beginning with "From the Vinaya says... constitutes the first section.
Furthermore, according to the text itself, there are three sub-sections. The first concerns a bhikṣu who departs before the summer robes have been distributed;

after he has left, the Saṃgha proceeds to distribute the robes, not setting aside a portion for him. When he returns, he becomes angry and reproaches them, saying: "I was here observing the rains retreat."
"It is appropriate to divide [the robes]. Wait until after I have departed, and then divide them. The bhikṣus became doubtful, not knowing whether it would constitute a valid division.
The Buddha said, "It constitutes a valid division. Secondly: At that time, a bhikṣu had not yet divided his robes when he left the boundary on some business.

He made a general assignment to another person, saying, "Accept these robes for me. That person did not accept them. The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "It constitutes a valid division, provided that..."
It is not appropriate to provide a haphazard analogy. The third case states: A bhikṣu received an assignment from someone else, but later forgot that he had accepted it on behalf of another.

He developed a doubt and questioned the Buddha. The Buddha said, "The portion is valid; however, this was merely the fault of the one who received the entrustment. Since he performed meritorious service during the summer retreat, he is entitled to receive his share.
According to these three passages, since each instance explicitly states that the portion is valid, this serves as proof for those who possess the Dharma.
This already includes the "division of shares" (as cited in the first section above). Second, from the phrase "Furthermore... onwards, it cites the second section regarding the "dharma of hearing.
In the Vinaya, there was once a bhikṣu who lived alone in a garden. At the end of the summer retreat, someone brought offerings to give him.

He resolved his mind to accept them; when other bhikṣus arrived, he did not share them with them. According to this, since that one person had already resolved his mind according to the dharma, [the others] were excluded.

This indicates that for two people, it is simply a matter of face-to-face confession (*pratimukha*), whereas for four or more, it must logically be performed through formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*).

Third, regarding the "middle period" of the time, this cites the textual passage concerning the formal procedure from the third section. The Vinaya states: "On the sixteenth day of the seventh month, someone offered goods."
The resident monks, seeing that the guests had not yet dispersed, were possessed by a mind of stinginess and envy;

they were unwilling to divide [the goods] and instead kept them until the sixteenth day of the eighth month, waiting for the guests to depart before performing a distribution of what was present at an improper time (*akāla-pratyutpanna-bhājana*).

The Buddha then punished them for their greedy hearts, decreeing instead that it be a distribution of what was acquired by the Saṃgha at an improper time (*akāla-saṃghalabdha*), to be summoned from the ten directions and divided among all. According to this principle, since the formal procedure was not performed during the proper time, [it was deemed improper].

If [the robe] is divided, it constitutes an *akāla-karman* (an improper formal act). By contrast, this implies that if it is divided during the proper time (*kāla*), it likewise conforms to the Dharma.
Regarding the "breaking of the *varṣā* due to difficult circumstances" in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it says: There was a disciple of a non-Buddhist who went forth within the Buddha-dharma.
His kinsmen said, "How can you abandon the path of an Arhat and go forth among the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas?

You must return and take it up again. He further thought, "If he learns of this, he might flee; I should go to fetch him when the rainy season retreat has ended, for then I will surely capture him without resistance.
When he heard this, he informed the Buddha. The Buddha permitted him to break the retreat and depart. Thereupon, he went from one residence to another.

Regarding the location: it is not known where the robe was kept. The Buddha said: "Take it from the place where one stayed for more days. If the number of days is equal at two locations, take half from each.

According to this principle, when encountering difficulties and moving during the summer retreat, it is permitted to receive the robe. Second, regarding the two markers during the non-seasonal period:
"those who arrive first" refers to this being equivalent to the current practice of lay families hosting assemblies and providing offerings. As for "expensive robes," they are...
Regarding items of high value that are worth a certain amount of money, one should have them cut, broken, or divided [etc., as detailed in the text].

When given according to the consensus of the Saṃgha, it is obtained by the two types of Saṃgha. This is because the donor intends the gift for the Saṃgha; therefore, it belongs to the Saṃgha. According to the Vinaya texts:
if the Saṃgha is in harmony and grants it, it is so; if they are not in harmony, half is granted. Furthermore, if permission is not granted, one-third should be granted. If not...
It should not be divided. Following this principle, one first divides it equally and then gradually reduces the portions.

Regarding the statement that "the Saṃgha obtains [it] at non-specific times," until the point where it says "as far as dividing it," this applies to all three periods and is not restricted to the summer retreat. As for the rule regarding the light belongings of a deceased person, Bao says:

"This does not mention *karmavācanā* (formal ritual); the text points to the section below on dividing the light belongings of the deceased, which is identical to this case, with only slight differences."

[End of section]. If [the property] is included among the light belongings of the deceased, it says here: "The bhikṣus residing at this place shall divide all the clothing and requisites that have been passed over;
the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* (present assembly) should divide them. If it is included among what the *saṃgha* obtains at an improper time (*akāla*), it says:

"The *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* residing at this place should divide them. The rest is identical. The reason this is not explicitly stated in the text is that the Vinaya [already covers] what the *saṃgha* obtains at an improper time. Furthermore...

There is a *karmavācanā* for light items belonging to the deceased; there is also a *karmavācanā* for this. However, although such a procedure exists among the items of the deceased, the text is not skillfully composed or superior.

Those who believe in the ritual tradition merely rely on the text concerning the "method for distributing gifts obtained by the Saṃgha at an improper time" (*akāla-saṃghalābha*) to divide the light items of the deceased.

The ancients, having personally observed that the *karmavācanā* for gifts obtained by the Saṃgha at an improper time was identical to the procedure for the items of the deceased, consequently maintained [this practice].

Regarding the property of the deceased: since it has already been divided into two categories—the heavy and the light—if the monks receive it at an improper time (*akāla*), there must likewise be two corresponding regulations (as seen in the *Xin Zhangshu*).

Now, regarding the monks receiving it at an improper time, this differs from the light property of the deceased in four ways: first, the distinction between the living and the deceased; for those who receive it at an improper time are currently living.
Second, the distinction between relinquishment and non-relinquishment; for what the monks receive at an improper time is a gift (*dāna*).

The presiding master relinquishes it himself; for the property of the deceased, another person acts as the relinquisher. Thus, the three [types of relinquishment] distinguish between the general and the specific. Regarding the "improper time" (akāla), it applies generally to all seven [categories];

regarding the property of the deceased, it applies only to five. Fourth, there is a distinction in the acquisition of merit: when the Sangha receives an offering at an improper time, according to the Sūtra, it is divided into seven portions based on those currently present.

Because it fully encompasses the five assemblies, when a person has passed away, they obtain three or four shares and one share [respectively]. Therefore, the property of the deceased is such that heavy items enter the permanent endowment (*sthavira-saṃgha*), while light items enter the current assembly (*pratyutpanna-saṃgha*).
Regarding items obtained by the Saṃgha at an improper time, if a donor has specifically directed their intention toward giving to "all monks," how could there be any restriction based on weight?
They are all equally subsumed under the same category, following the donor's original intent. Question: According to the Vinaya rules for the distribution of property, one only divides light items.
Now, regarding gifts that may consist of heavy items: is it not permissible to divide them into heavy portions? Answer:

According to the Vinaya, while it is simply not permitted to divide gold, silver, money, pearls, necklaces, and the like, there is no mention of it being forbidden to divide other items such as bedding, mosquito nets, or curtains;

therefore, we know that [division] is generally permitted (the Xiangbu school’s *liuxing* and the *chao* agree on this). As for the passage in the Vinaya beginning with "The Vinaya says, below": at the initial occasion, no person had yet been appointed, and the formal ritual had not yet been performed.

It is simply a matter of distribution. Later, when guests arrive, the novices must also share their portions, which exhausts the monks. Consequently, the formal procedure (*dharma-karman*) is established to bring them under the jurisdiction of those present;

those who do not reach the assembly may not receive a portion. Regarding the phrase "because of the two": the above explained one section (the *bhikṣu-saṃgha*), based on the discussion of monks alone.
If there is a donor, the same applies to the nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*). Now, it is said that if the gift is bestowed universally upon both sections (*ubhaya-saṃgha*):

Regarding the Sangha: if one side is lacking, the other shall stand as the formal assembly. If there are only monks and no nuns or the other three groups, then the monks constitute the formal assembly.
If there are only nuns and no monks or the other two groups, then the nuns constitute the formal assembly. As for the four types, these are:

the timely and the untimely, each being "present before" (sammukhībhūta) and "obtained by the Sangha" (sanghasammatā). Altogether, this divides into seven cases: first, although the offering is made to both divisions of the Sangha, the monks are more numerous than the nuns.
1. Few [monks], with no *mahābhikṣuṇīs*, but only the two lower assemblies (*śrāmaṇerī* and *bhikṣuṇī*). 2. No *mahābhikṣuṇīs*, but only *śikṣamāṇās*. 3. No *śikṣamāṇās*, but only *śrāmaṇerīs*. 4.

No two assemblies [of nuns], with only the *saṃgha* (monks) presiding over themselves (the *Chao* cites this fourth phrase later). 5. Few monks and many nuns. 6. No *bhikṣus*, but only *śrāmaṇeras*. 7.
Completely no *saṃgha* or two assemblies; only the *bhikṣuṇīs* act as the presiding authorities (the *Chao* cites this seventh point).

[The seven phrases]. Regarding the note on "the two assemblies receiving from one another": because this is based on the principle of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), it is generally permissible to receive from each other.

Furthermore, regarding "striking the *ghaṇṭā* while seated": this means that although the assembly has not yet dispersed, they have already been formally included in the presence [of the rite] through the performance of the ritual act.

If a guest arrives later, it is improper for them to receive a share. If one now wishes to give [a share] to them, one must strike the *ghaṇṭā* and request the assembly’s consent to grant it; if one does not so request...
[The text states: "Monk. This constitutes stealing property belonging to the *saṃgha* present before one's eyes. Regarding the phrase "if there are other offerings (*dakṣiṇā*)":
this is also from the text of the *Wǔbǎiwèn* (Five Hundred Questions). As for the phrase "one who never returns the spell to claim [the share]":

Xuán says, "This refers to a person who was among the *saṃgha* and likewise received the gift of robes, but before the items had been distributed, he immediately traveled far away. Now, his portion is left behind; since he has already gone far, he will never return."

"Come. This means that regarding this very object, one has already formed the intention to relinquish it; now, one offers this portion to others, wishing that they may find peace and security on their path—hence the term "blessing" (*parittā*).
Alternatively, it may refer to blessing the original donor, as the Vinaya states in the verse:

"If one gives for the sake of profit, one shall surely obtain such profit," and so forth. Or, if someone comes to take [the item] and incurs a *pācittiya* offense, this constitutes the misappropriation of the Sangha's property.

Regarding the death of a person: as for those who commit an offense of abandonment (*pārājika*), this is determined by comparing it to the value of the object and is settled according to the permanent property of the Saṃgha.

Now, citing this text, I shall comprehensively clarify the meaning of "donation prior to [the distribution]. The former refers to the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*): once the distribution is finished, one requests permission through a formal motion (*jñapti*). The latter refers to the portion set aside for those who are traveling; even if they do not arrive, it may be given to others who come later.
IV. On Deceased Persons: Their names are recorded as in the text. The phrase "since these matters are of the utmost gravity" establishes the underlying intent.

That which the petty person finds profit in, the Great Being (Mahāsattva) values through the Way (Dharma), whereas the petty person preserves it through wealth. As Laozi said: "If one dwells amidst the manure of the world, one will certainly not perch upon the mulberry trees;
if one possesses a mind beyond the mundane, one will certainly not discourse on fame and profit. Confucius also said: [the rest of the passage follows].

"The gentleman is attuned to righteousness; the petty person is attuned to profit. In the sublime discipline of the Śramaṇa school, one should not allow oneself to be entangled by the defilements of transient wealth.

For those who have left the household life to seek the distant goal, their ultimate aim is to rescue beings within the six destinies and four modes of birth, vowing that all may transcend the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).

Regarding "enduring toil for the sake of oceanic bliss": the ascetic practices performed over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are called "enduring toil," while the realization of the fruit of Buddhahood is "oceanic bliss."
Regarding "worldly fame is not what is sought," etc.: reputation and material gain are what the laity delight in; they are not what the Sangha aspires to.
If one maintains the mind that seeks the Way, one will not be constrained by the six sense objects. This refers to being harmonious, unified, and returning to one's fundamental nature.
If one’s disposition has not yet been harmonized and unified with the Way, then one is fundamentally not of a pure and pristine lineage, but merely covets profit.

Therefore it is so. Now, regarding those who are "superior" and "inferior": those who have attained the superior level are the various ancient virtuous masters of former times who each composed commentaries and treatises, weighing the relative importance of matters to rescue sentient beings according to their capacities.
As stated in the preface: "Among those in the world who uphold the Vinaya, there are briefly six types," and so forth.
Those who have attained the inferior level are the later students of these commentaries; although they receive and practice this Dharma, they follow their own inclinations.

However, there is a distinction. Regarding the requirement that "both must accord with two [principles]": when establishing a precept (*dharma*), it must accord with two things: first, it must accord with the substance of the reception; second, it must accord with the fundamental tenet.

This refers to the establishment of the precept according to the two types of realization (the superior and the inferior). Furthermore, the reception of the precept must also accord with two things: first, the tenet of the original reception; second, the substance and the practice of that original reception.

This refers to the reception of the precept according to the lower type of realization, which has already been explained. Therefore, the *Chao* (Commentary) uses the word "both" (*ju*) to include both the superior and the inferior cases.
It is thus that through such practice one is able to penetrate the Single Path, which is the pure conduct in accordance with the precepts.

As for the "Guiding Map," it is the name of a chariot. The *Bowuzhi* (Records of the Wide World) states: "Huang Di fought Chi You at the wilderness of Yuanlu (pronounced *che*), located north of the middle reaches of the River."

These mists were particularly thick over the hundred-li radius, causing the soldiers to lose their sense of direction and become disoriented. At that time, a wise minister constructed a south-pointing chariot (*shinan che*).
Every few li, a figure appeared atop its pole; with his hand always pointing south, he established the cardinal directions.

The drum struck once every *li* (the scripture’s mention of "once every five li" is a scribal error). Later, during the Later Han, a skilled artisan followed this original model to produce one, which remains [in use] to this day under the Sage [Emperor].

When the Emperor went forth, these two kinds of objects were always present. The current mention of the "south-pointing chariot" (*zhinan*) is intended to take up the established definitions of antiquity and manifest them;
it signifies the ultimate. The ancient masters all said that their own judgments were each definitive and ultimate teachings.

Whenever there were those who harbored doubts, Dao-yi said: "It is simply because categories of things are difficult to encompass and the various sections of the canon have mutual deficiencies. It is evident...

There are provisions for storage, though they are not fully recorded in the teachings. Relying on the texts and attaching them to specific matters, one must exercise careful scrutiny and reflection; yet the description of these matters remains vague and indistinct, as remote as the Milky Way.
As for those things that have now arrived, they are as described in the text.

The first among the ten points. Regarding the phrase "first arriving at the object": the first part is the interrogative statement; the second part, from "by means of the six lower [categories] of those who have left the household life" onwards, clarifies the reason why they do not enter the Buddha-dharma.
As for "receiving it according to one's station," the *Yi* (Ritual) states: "While alive, one receives benefits by depending on the Sangha; after death, these still reach the Sangha.
Thus, both types of offerings—the resources for communal use and those for individual consumption—bear the moisture of flowing merit. Furthermore...
He did not enter among the laity, for they were not fields of merit. Regarding Cunda and the others, the *Ji* (Zhi) states:

Due to the causes and conditions of a husband and wife from a cattle-herding family in the wilderness who had developed faith and always offered milk and curd, Cunda suddenly one day grew weary of this body.

"What benefit is there in remaining in this world? he said. Then, taking his robes and bowl, he sat beneath a tree in the forest, lay down on his right side with his head resting upon the elephant-hide mat, and entered *nirvāṇa*.
When it was time for the meal, the cowherd’s family did not see him return and grew suspicious; they went to look for him and found him beneath the tree.
Thinking he was merely asleep, they stood by his side and listened, but they heard no sound of breathing. They then felt his body with their hands.
When [the body] had grown cold, they knew he had entered parinirvāṇa. They then gathered wood and grass to perform the cremation as an act of veneration.

They collected his robes and bowl and presented them to the King. The King appraised these robes and found their value to be five coins; according to the law, he adjudicated that they should be returned to the śramaṇas (and so forth).
Regarding Upāli (Baddhananda), King Prasenajit said, "This man has no offspring; his property rightfully belongs to the state. The Buddha then dispatched a messenger to inquire about him.
"O King," and so forth, until his kinsmen and others came to dispute [the matter]. The Buddha questioned each of them individually, as detailed in the text (etcetera).

There are two different methods of division; their names may be understood from the citations. Regarding the first, "taking what is discarded as refuse" (*pāṃśukūla*), the *Vinaya* (Twenty-one [Khandhakas]) states:

A bhikṣu was swept away by water and died; his robes and bowl were hanging from the branch of a tree within the boundary. Another bhikṣu saw them and thought, "Since these have entered the boundary of the Saṃgha, they should belong to the Saṃgha.

He did not take them, but reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "They may be taken as *pāṃśukūla* (cast-off refuse). Regarding the two cases where those who regularly appear before the Saṃgha are present:
the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that when a person undergoing penance (*śikṣādattaka*) dies, the Saṃgha present at that time should divide [the property]. In the text, it follows further...
"Taking directly from one another" means that because there is no other person present at that time, they may take directly from each other.

If there are those who observe the precepts or those who are presiding over the funeral, one should take according to the agreement made with those observing the precepts, for it is appropriate for such people to take charge. Regarding "reaching the third [stage] before the distribution":
this refers to the self-division between the two factions of the heterodox and the orthodox. If one turns away from the orthodox to go toward the heterodox, or departs from here to arrive there.

Or if they are on the middle path, all are obtained by virtue of the direction toward which the mind was originally set. If a person of wrong views dies within a community of the Righteous (samyag-gaṇa), one should summon that person of wrong views to take [the property];
if no one comes, it should be treated as bedding and furniture for the Saṃgha of the four directions and must not be divided.

It is the same if a person of the Righteous dies within a community of the Wrongful (mithyā-gaṇa). The functional capacity of the "fourfold entry" (catur-āyatana) Saṃgha may be understood from this. The "fivefold entry" (pañca-āyatana) pertains to the two divisions (ubhaya-gaṇa).

"Monastics" refers to both monks and nuns. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If a monk dies at a monastic residence during a time other than the *varṣā* retreat, and there are no other monks present, the nuns should divide [the inheritance].

The same applies when a nun dies. Regarding the five groups of practitioners who arrive first and obtain [the property], according to the following text, they must take possession of it quickly to claim it as their own;
only then is it established that others cannot see it, as it has entered the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

Regarding the destination: according to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, if a bhikṣu takes his robes and bowl and travels toward a certain monastery, but dies in the interval between two boundaries before reaching it, the Buddha said that the Saṃgha of the place he was heading for shall obtain [the items]. The *Shoushu* states:
"If the destination is unknown, then whichever direction he was facing at the time of death, the Saṃgha of that monastery shall obtain them. The *Chao* agrees with this. If...

If these two [conditions] are absent, one obtains it from whichever monk is nearby. Regarding "entering the presence of the *upādhyāya*": according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, one enters directly before the *upādhyāya*, because the gravity of his nurturing and instruction is paramount.
The *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* (Chao) adopts the perspective of other schools, as they prioritize the benefits conferred by the community (*saṃgha*).

Regarding "entering the presence of those who are close": this is as stated in the text. Regarding "according to wherever one is located": the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is cited as an example; thus, it says "as" (*ru*). That...
It is said: When the bhikṣu Mūla died, his robes and bowl had been entrusted to Ānanda; three parties disputed over them, and the case was adjudicated according to the text.
The phrase "the person to whom something is entrusted" (寄人) is the current master’s [Dharmakṣema’s] terminology. Regarding "a place of entrustment where there is no person to whom it is entrusted":

suppose there is a bhikṣu who merely borrows another's room, locks his belongings himself, and does not authorize the other to take charge of them; this is called "death at a place of entrustment. Subsequently, the items follow the location where they were kept.

The Sangha receives it. As for "the top nine simply divide it," this is stated provisionally based on the initial circumstances. If it is divided later, there are ritual procedures (*vidhi*) to be followed;
as in the sixth, seventh, and ninth [cases], all require the performance of ritual procedures. Now, this is in contrast to the pure assembly below.

Therefore, it is said to be "directly so" (*zhí'ěr*). Regarding the tenth [point]: first, the term "pure assembly" (*qíng zhòng*) distinguishes between the two groups of the heterodox and the orthodox;

it distinguishes those who perform acts of censure, suspension, and formal accusation (*jiǎn bìn jǔ děng rén*). *Sōuxuán* states: "The character 'pure' (*qíng*) distinguishes those who perform censure, suspension, and accusation; the character 'assembly' (*zhòng*) distinguishes them from the single individual mentioned above" (this does not reach the level of the previous classification).
Third, regarding "among those living together": as for the phrase "taking things," there are three parts. First, it clarifies the provision of food and clothing;

if a disciple takes these by means of deception, he commits a grave offense (*pārājika*). Light items have already been discussed according to the established rules; heavy items certainly incur a grave offense.

The rest may be understood accordingly. If the teacher’s original agreement was... [the text continues]. Second, it clarifies communal living; "at one's own discretion regarding much or little" refers to this.
This refers to various types of movable property that may be disposed of according to the wishes of those in charge.

As for the robes, alms bowls, and other items used by the deceased for their own personal consumption, all such things shall be assigned to the Saṃgha. Regarding the third section, which clarifies shared property:

if one person among a group of teacher and disciples dies, the clothing and items worn on the body that are fixed as personal effects shall be assigned to the Saṃgha; the same applies to living members regarding their own personal belongings.

One may keep one’s own share as one pleases. As for any remaining communal property, half must be divided and given to the Saṃgha; the person who gave birth [to the child] shall keep the other half for themselves.

If they do not live together, this generally clarifies the characteristics of non-partnership. Regarding those who both commit an offense through the agent and the object, the determination belongs to the person who presides over the case.

This is explained by way of approximation. That which is called "the object taken" refers to what is falsely claimed. Regarding "both being light objects," this means that if the formal procedure has not been performed, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense;
once the formal procedure has been completed, if the value reaches five [units], one incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).
In the fourth section on entrustment (*anuśāsanī*), the recording of names follows the text. Regarding the explanation, the phrase "firstly" refers to following the original recipient;

that is, it follows the time of the original reception because one practices the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*). "Producing merit in a superior place" means that by entrusting wealth to another, one generates contaminated merit (*sāsrava-puṇya*) and attains a superior place, namely heaven.
As for the statement "unwholesome and inferior," the *Xuán* (Explaining) commentary says it means "intention" (*yì*); that is, it refers to a doubled intention.
Excluding the cases of entrusting [the object] to others for searching and so forth. Among the three types of non-entrusted wholesome [actions], there is none that is empty or untainted (*anāsrava*).

This is because the original aspiration of those who have left the household life is the untainted fruit of the Path; now, having been harmed, they have not yet attained it. Regarding the fourth type of non-entrusted wholesome [action], "mutual arising":

previously, one intended to relinquish [the object], which was an expansion of the mind of giving; subsequently, a mind of stinginess arises, overturning that former intention—this is what is meant by mutual arising. As it is said:
Regarding the explanation according to the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), Xuán states that this is an erroneous reference. "Loving the robe" is as explained below in the section on giving;
"loving the copper cauldron" is like the method for attending to the sick (as detailed below). As for the two distinctions, they are differentiated by contrasting the person with the object.

When both person and object are present, it is a case of receiving a beloved object and the person [who gives it]; this is the object being given, which receives the name of "entrustment" (*anuśāsanī*). Although both person and object are present...
If an object is heavy and cannot be moved, or if one moves an object to form a roll of cloth or a bundle of silk and so forth, this is merely called "entrusting" (*chu*).
As for items such as bolts of silk, clothing, jewels, or rosaries, handing them over directly is called "bestowing" (*shou*); it does not necessarily require entrustment.

Regarding the third case, where the person and the object appear in different locations: the person is in front of the sick individual, while the object is in another place; or else the object is in...

"Also by the side of the sick person. Regarding the four cases where the entrustment does not conform to the formal rule: as in the case above where one harmonious pure assembly dies, the property is divided by *karmavācanā*.
Regarding "the three [cases] within the single [category]": this refers to the statement "from three up to the elder. As for "the last person obtains it":

because the final recipient has received the entrustment and their life has ended, there is certainly no further change; therefore, the last person obtains it. Regarding "the master of the wealth commits a grave offense": that is to say...
If a patient diverts property to give it to a later person, one incurs the offense of theft with respect to the former person.

This is well-established; the following citation provides proof, as in the text. Regarding the fourth [category], it is not appropriate. As for the phrase "those who arrive at the four": a *mu* (tomb) is also called a *fen* (burial mound);

its primary characteristic is the accumulation of earth (excluding dense groves of trees). As for a *guan* (coffin), during the reign of the Emperor, Guo Zixuan wished to have his parents buried together, but the public regulations... [text ends].
The prohibition did not permit the exposure of the multitude; thus, for seven days, they wailed without ceasing. The lord of the city, moved by his filial piety, had wooden vessels fashioned for him.

Consequently, the authorities granted permission, which is why it is called "coffin wood" (*guǎnmù*). Regarding the term *guǎn*, the *Līji* (Rites of Zhou) states: "That which surrounds the corpse is called a *guǎn*. *Guǎn* carries the meaning of "appearance";
one does not wish to allow the filial son to see the decay of the physical form, and therefore the body is concealed within the outer shell (*guò*). — *Līji* (Rites of Zhou).

It is said: the outer coffin is called the *guǒ*. This means that the inner coffin (*guān*) encloses the corpse and belongs to the interior, while the outer coffin (*guǒ*) encloses the inner coffin and belongs to the exterior.
In antiquity, a single outer coffin could contain two inner coffins for joint burial. Thus, the "Text on Sacrificing at Ancient Tombs" in the *Wénxuǎn* states:

"Once the single outer coffin is opened, the double inner coffins still remain. As for the term *bēi*, it means "sorrow. It is used to record the virtues and conduct of one's ancestors, so that readers may be moved by grief and inspiration.

XIAO. When King [Qin Shi Huang] performed the Feng sacrifice on Mount Tai, he erected a stele inscribed by Li Si. Below it was a tortoise that manifested spiritual power, knowing events of a thousand years.
Its intent was to signify that [the dynasty’s] banner would not fall for a long time. Above it was a *bùláo*, which is a sea creature with variegated markings on its body.
It has two heads and four feet; it is also called a *qiulóng* (coiled dragon). Regarding the term *jié*: it means "exhausted" (*jìe*).

This refers to the practice where those of the fifth rank and above use a *bēi* (stele), while those of the sixth rank and below use a *jié*. Above, there is no captured ox head or flame; below, there is no tortoise, but rather a stone mortar.

Some say that what has been submitted for imperial approval is called a *bēi* if it has a hole, whereas what has not been submitted for approval is a *jié*; however, to claim that a *bēi* is one without a hole is incorrect. There are also [other variations].

Regarding "having passed away": this refers to cases where a memorial stone with a horizontal hole has been made, or when one has violated the king’s laws and so forth, such that the time of death is known for certain and the matter is finalized.

Regarding "hearing [the news] while previously floating about": this is similar to the previous case; one must wait until after death before requesting me to transcribe scriptures and the like, for otherwise the stone will not be established.

In the section on citations from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it states that placing [the stone] by the side of the sick person and so forth does not constitute [a valid act], because there is no corroborating evidence.
Regarding "purification by means of accomplishment": this is because there is a person present before whom one can provide testimony;

the rest of the text is easily understood. Among the five types of impoverished debts, the names are cited as in the text. As for the phrase "first with a sincere mind," this refers first to the classification according to the meaning.

"One must rely on the original object" means that if a heavy debt is repaid with a light one, the light portion enters the permanent property (*sthāvara*) of the Sangha. If one owes a light debt but receives a heavy object [as repayment], it should be used to purchase...

Regarding the taking of light portions: if one was carrying heavy items and subsequently acquires light ones before crossing the Luo River, those that differ from the property held in common with the Sangha—meaning items originally carried as heavy loads—even if they are later obtained as light items, must be entered into the permanent endowment (*sthavira*) of the monastery; they may not be treated as light goods.

This is because they were originally heavy items belonging to the collective property of the present Sangha of the ten directions; therefore, they must be entered into the permanent endowment. There is absolutely none [to be otherwise].

"Ceasing upon acquisition" means that one should permanently forfeit the light goods of a deceased person, as well as the property of impoverished spirits, when there is no one to return them and no place to seek their recovery;
thus, by letting them cease, one does not commit an offense. Regarding "ten instances of acquisition," this cites the teachings to effect a definitive judgment.
"That which should be returned" refers to returning it to the Three Jewels. The sub-commentary explains the preceding point: the judgment must be made based on the original object itself.

In the *Yue* (Vinaya of the Yueh-chih), it is stated that appropriating the permanent property of the Saṃgha, such as fields and gardens, or taking the property currently belonging to the Saṃgha from the four directions, is in all respects the same as the cases mentioned above.

In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there is a record of a bhikṣu who borrowed property belonging to the Saṃgha of the four directions for his private use; after he died, it was not known what should be done with it.
The Buddha said: "One should calculate the value of the goods and pay it to the Saṃgha of the four directions. The remainder should be divided equally among the monks present.

As for the Saṃgha of the four directions, let it be so for the time being regarding items borrowed by visiting monks. Regarding those who do not repay debts such as wine purchased on credit: at one time there was a monk who owed money for wine;
after the monk had died, [his relatives] came later to seek repayment, but the resident monks would not give it to them. They said, 'We shall bring ill repute upon you.'"

[Regarding] "the sound," the Buddha said: "One should return it. [Note: Regarding "at the appropriate time, according to circumstances," it is superior to return what is currently present and harmonious with the situation.
If no such present object exists, one shall return property held in perpetuity (*sthāvara*). Regarding "debt and interest," this refers to the debts and interest owed by a deceased person.

Regarding the case where a deceased person leaves property behind for another to manage for profit, there are many differing accounts. After death, they dispute over it, resulting in five resolutions.
The first point is found in the final section of the fifty-seventh fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:

Venerable Upananda entrusted his robes and bowl to another location while he himself died elsewhere. Both parties disputed over them. The Buddha said: "The robes and bowl belong to those present within the boundary."

The Saṃgha should divide [the property]. This means that as soon as someone dies within that boundary, the Saṃgha of this location immediately takes possession of it. Regarding the two points concerning the place of debt:
this refers to the place where interest or money is lent out. Within the boundary of the place of debt, the property should be divided, because the object owed remains within that boundary.
Once the owner has passed away and the property has no other designated recipient, it belongs to that Saṃgha. The three phrases refer to Baddhānanda:

having entrusted [the goods] to a fellow bhikṣu in another territory, he takes charge of them, maintains and preserves them, and then raises them up to give to others for the sake of profit; this is called the "place of entrustment and maintenance."
This refers to the current practice of lending money at interest on behalf of others.

When bhikṣus from various boundaries come here and take money from the place where the guarantor bhikṣu resides, that boundary where the money is taken is designated as the "place of lending at interest. After his death, three parties dispute over it.

Everyone said, "This belongs to our community. The Buddha ruled that it should go to the monks who acted as guarantors, because this object was made subject to them by virtue of those guarantors acting as its masters;
this case is also decided in the same manner as the matter concerning Ānanda (the former correct interpretation). The ancients said: "These are the guarantors on the legal contract."
This is called the "place for providing a guarantee. Searching the Profundities (*Souxuanpo*) states: "The Vinaya text [mentions] three phrases regarding the place for drafting the deed itself.

How could there not be the names of guarantors on the deed? Since it is ruled that the Sangha obtains [the property] at the place of the deed, it is clearly known that [this interpretation] is incorrect.
If there were only the deed and no guarantor, this deed would lack corroboration; upon what principle could it rely? If there were only the guarantor and no deed, it is empty..."

The Buddha ruled that the Sangha obtains the pledged object because this pledged object shares the same location as the Sangha.

If it is a light pledge and money is brought to redeem it, one should purchase light goods with it for the Sangha to divide. If it is a heavy pledge and money is brought to redeem it, it must be entered into the permanent property (sthavira-vastu). If...

The place where one dies while staying in another location is called the "place of death. When these three places dispute [the ownership], the judgment falls in favor of the monks at the "place for the half-share document.
This is because the half-share of the contract exists within this boundary; since it is in the same location as the monks, they hold this document and rely upon it.
This refers to repeatedly demanding back those items. Xuan says: "These five phrases exclude both light and heavy offenses. The following text cites the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:
