[The monks] did not know what to do. The Buddha said: "If one has received alms-food either before or after [the formal assembly], one should return to one's original location.

Regarding the boundaries: although there is no explicit textual authority in the Vinaya for this case, one must not resolve it based on two conflicting interpretations of the principle.

if the monks of both places dispute it, one follows the first rule of the *Daśabhāṇavāra*: the object belongs to the monks where it was located.
If a layperson owes a debt to a monk and the monk dies in the monastery, and the monks of both places dispute it, it likewise belongs to the monks where the debt was owed. Or...

Regarding guarantees, pledged items, and documents such as half-bills: if there is a dispute among monks from three different locations, the monks shall obtain [the property] at the location where the pledge or guarantee was made, or at the location of the document;

or they may obtain it at the location of the person previously mentioned. As for the adjudication of deposits, the method of division is as stated above. Regarding the ninth point, "obtaining according to the location":
if there is a place where a deposit was left but no person was designated as the guarantor, the monks shall obtain it; if the person was designated but no deposit was left... [text ends].

Regarding the acquisition [of property] by those residing in a location: the original text speaks in terms of the *saṃgha* boundary (*sīmā*), whereas the present discussion concerns those in lay households.
For example, if a bhikṣu entrusts an object to another bhikṣu named Zhang, who then takes it himself and further transfers it to the house of a lay donor named Li;

and if the original owner dies at the monastery where three groups of monks reside, each claiming that they rightfully deserve the property, it is then adjudicated that the monks within the boundary of the bhikṣu Zhang shall receive it.

Regarding entrusting items to a person rather than to a location: if a bhikṣu resides within the house of a deceased person and knows that the household is secure and trustworthy, he may borrow a room, lock it himself, and store his belongings there, not allowing the owner of the house to take charge of them. Should this bhikṣu die within that monastery...

In two instances where monks were disputing over property, it was acquired by the community at the place where the items had been previously deposited, because that depositing community had first selected [the claim].
Thus, the *Vinayamātṛkā* (lower volume) corroborates that the preceding Vinaya text was not definitive.

If the items are located with a layperson and have not yet been recovered upon request, one may follow the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which allows for the collection of money based on a contract (*paṇa*). The *Pañcaśata-praśna* (lower volume) clarifies that when an item is lent to another person...

When one wishes to take [an item] after death, one must inform the Saṃgha. To take it without informing them constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. If the Saṃgha knows [of the theft] and does not return the item, they commit a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).
Regarding those who commit both [offenses], "self" refers to the presiding master (*vinayadhara*) capable of adjudicating within the Saṃgha, while "others" refers to the assembly of monks;

both incur the sin of concealment and deception (the above follows the *Souxuan*, which distinguishes between self and others based on the Saṃgha). Baoyun says: "If the Saṃgha does not grant [the item] and one takes it by force..."
If one knows that the property belongs to another member of the Saṃgha and does not return it to them, both parties commit an offense (this is also one perspective).

The *Jīzhì* states: "The following text concerns the time when items belonging to a deceased person are being collected. Because there was a bhikṣu who said, 'I also have items among these,' this ruling was established.

Now, according to the case of collecting debts, the ruling is the same as this. Now, according to the case of collecting debts, the ruling is the same as this; [it is stated thus] for fear of what may happen later.
Regarding "spiritual authenticity" (*lingwei*): furthermore, if there are no virtuous persons to provide testimony, it shall not be granted.

Sixth, determining lightness or gravity: the formal record (*dian*) is as stated in the text. As for the phrase "thus reaching the offense," this determines the primary principle (*zong*). Regarding those who have not yet attained integration (*weirong*):

they are unable to harmonize the texts of the four divisions of the Vinaya, but instead judge according to their own personal sentiments; such judgments are difficult to trust. This applies regardless of where one resides separately.

Regarding the "sect" (bu): Xuán states that since the deceased no longer remembers [their past] and it is impossible to know who attended to them during their illness, one must determine the gravity or lightness of the offense based on which sect the deceased followed while alive;

The opposite of this is not [the case] (this is merely one interpretation). Now, following what was received from Tiantai, it is said that "residing according to the specific" refers to the boundary for gathering the Saṃgha.
Since it does not specify which Vinaya school the bhikṣus have received their precepts from, we shall for now simply rely on this.
Regarding the monastic community within the boundary of separate residence (*pārivāsika*), they conduct their usual affairs by adjudicating the gravity of offenses according to the Vinaya.

If one knows that another’s received *kāyabandhana* (robe-binding) fundamentally follows the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, or others, one must rely upon those texts to determine the gravity of the offense.

As for the phrase "one cannot act with a defiled mind," in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, entering a heavy object results in much gravity and little lightness, whereas in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, entering a light object results in much [gravity].

The gravity [of the offense] is light. Since the present case concerns the formal reception of the precepts according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is erroneous to cite the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* to judge a grave offense as light.
If it were indeed the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* regarding the reception of the precepts, then one should have judged it accordingly as light.

Now, to erroneously cite the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and classify it as grave—these are all instances where the internal mind has a hidden motive. It is for this reason that such a judgment is made; thus, it is said to be "erroneously raised."

This involves matters of giving and taking. Thus, the *Yi* (Ritual Code) states: "However, because human nature is narrow-minded and prone to jealousy, there are inevitably instances of obstruction and entanglement.

If the administrative official (*karmadāna*) is personally close to the resident community (*sangha*), even minor items will be treated as major and strictly collected. Conversely, if there are separate monks [acting for their own benefit], they will prioritize private gain;

even major items will be treated as minor and loosely handled," and so forth. Those who act according to this principle are said to have truly received the precepts from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*; they should embody the spirit of that Vinaya.

Within our own school, matters are conducted according to the gravity of the offense (this follows the interpretation of the Great Virtuous One). Among the various commentaries, it is all stated that "the temple" (*dàng* [in the departing tone]) refers to one's own temple;

this means that when people in charge of monastic affairs understand the situation, they intend for the temple administration to largely judge light offenses as grave and so forth (this is not the correct interpretation.

Even though the *Chao* text frequently uses the character "temple," it is a scribal error; in the *Hao* edition, it is simply the character "self," which one should recognize for oneself). This arises from poverty and other such conditions.
This refers to those who do not open up the sacred teachings to resolve their transgressions, but are merely people of limited capacity whose greedy minds remain bound by fetters.
"Now, regarding the definitive decision" establishes the heading for the section. "As listed in the introduction" refers to the six teachers of the fourth gate.
Regarding the "definitive decision at the third stage," among these six teachers, the first teacher uses only the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, while the third...
The Master first followed the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, incorporating supplementary characteristics from various schools. The fifth master generally utilized the entire *Vinaya-piṭaka*.
Now, this [work] establishes only three stages. Regarding the phrase "first, the forfeiture": this refers to the first stage established by the first master.
As for the distinction between the two categories of "heavy" and "light," the *Vinaya* section on robes states: "First, belonging to a monastery; second, belonging to the Saṃgha."
1. Garden trees and fruit-bearing trees; 2. Three separate rooms; 3. Property belonging to the separate rooms; 4. Copper cauldrons, copper jars, copper basins, axes, chisels, and lampstands;
5. Various heavy items; 6. Ropes, beds, pillows, and mattresses; 7. *Elāyanta*, *maudra*, *maumadra*, and woolen carpets (*kūṭhala*);
8. Monastery attendants; 9. Carriages and litters; 10. Water vessels, mendicant staffs, and fans.
Twelve items: iron, leather, bamboo, ceramic, and wooden vessels, and a razor. Thirteen items: robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, needle cases, and so forth.

The judgment states that the former twelve are heavy, while the latter one is considered light. Even if their weight is determined by their practical utility, all such items must be fully excluded [from the inventory].
As for the *kūṭāgāra* (a small bowl with a lid), it is used as an accessory to the alms bowl. Regarding the clothing of monastics and laypeople, etc.:

Xuán asked: "Since these are secular garments, why are they included among the light offenses? He replied: "Although these are indeed secular garments, they are dharma-robes worn by kings and ministers;

they are of the same measurement as a *qúlóu* (woolen rug) and thus fall under the light category. Furthermore, there is no second [category] to which they could belong. This master merely relied on the *Sifenlü* (Four-Part Vinaya) to reach this judgment and did not accept other views.
External schools completely reject such distinctions, hence it is said that there is no second [category] and it cannot be otherwise. This is according to the *Sifenlü*.
There is no place to express [this]. Its injunction is to employ the external school; furthermore, it cannot be taken away because it is not used—thus it is said.
"The two most serious" marks the second master (that is, the second stage). Regarding the determination of existence or non-existence:

as the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* judges that a single-layered [robe] entering a heavy [category] is [heavy], now by analogy with the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, a single-layered *kāyabandhana* (body-covering robe) should properly be included in the light [category]. (This is in reference to...)
[This refers to] a minor offense branching out from within a grave one). Furthermore, there are four types of distinctions; minor items are included in the light category.
If [an item] follows the bed or table, it must be included in the grave category (this is a minor offense branching out from within the light category). All other cases follow this principle.

Regarding the statement "first, briefly dividing into three," this is based on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* which distinguishes three categories (the *Xuanji* commentary erroneously misclassifies the original text regarding robes). From "one" up to light robes and bowls, like the two wings of a bird—these definitely enter [the category of requisites].

Regarding the light offenses, from the second to the *vinaya* rules: all of these obstruct and cause the abandonment of one’s spiritual practice (*dharma-karman*), and thus they certainly fall under the category of heavy offenses.

The explanatory note (*zhùwén*) can be understood accordingly. Regarding the third point up to "the same": this permits the possession of a single item; however, it is not fixed, as the principle of obstruction depends on the nature of the object. As for the combination of light and heavy, Xuán says:
"For those of middle capacity, the possession of one hundred articles for personal use is permitted; thus, within the context of permitted possessions, [the offense] must be considered."
Regarding items resembling precious objects, they contain both heavy and light categories. If one considers the substance of the object resembling a jewel itself, it is heavy;

however, if it has been made into prayer beads (*akṣamālā*) and the like, it is light. Some say that mosquitoes, gadflies, and so forth are heavy, while other personal belongings used for daily life are light;

this is also acceptable. As for those who judge these cases differently, various commentaries such as the *Shou-lü* and others each provide their own estimations of what constitutes heavy or light, according to the ritual protocols.

It refers to things such as those that are not "extra" (atireka). Regarding the practice of the four robes for those of superior faculties, if one possesses only three robes, it constitutes an obstruction to the path in terms of their use;

thus, they become "extra. However, for those of middling or inferior faculties, if these [fourth robes] provide relief and benefit the body in its support of the path, they are permitted within the three categories of one's own [allowable] possessions (*svabhāga*).
As for the statement "now, regarding the specific [cases]," the heading is clear. From "one" to... [the text continues].
"Those that are heavy" means that their essential nature (*svabhāva*) is heavy, as stated in the text. From "the second" down to "those that are light," it means that their essential nature is light.

The phrase "regardless of quantity" refutes the ancient [view]. The ancients said: "If many, they enter the category of the heavy, such as a hundred bolts of silk; if few, they enter the category of the light. Now it is said:
because these may support the body and facilitate the cultivation of the Path, they invariably enter the category of the light. From "the third" down to "severance," these...
"Weighty" refers to the weightiness of the object itself; because it must always be carried with one, it is categorized as light in terms of its usage.
For example, items made of cloth or silk are light in terms of their substance and thus not permitted to be kept; this is what is meant by "usage.

As for large and small canopies, the ancients stated that this constitutes the eighth chapter of the Vinaya, namely the *Nirayana*, *Maula*, and *Maulamula* sections. Thus, the *Jingzhong yi* (Rituals on Light and Heavy Matters) records the ancient tradition, beginning with: [The text continues from here.]
In that case, the *nirayanta* would not be a form of obstruction. Next, as for the various *mā-mā* [robes], are they not large and small canopies?
Since the canopy resembles a cap (*mukuta*), the Master now refutes this, saying: "To employ this—how laughable! To judge immediately upon merely hearing the sound."

I have never investigated the etymological origins of these characters; rather, I have translated them according to the spoken language and determined the nature of the objects based on their phonetic values.

This approach is bold in its categorization but clumsy in its presentation of factual reality. For instance, *elāyanta* is the name for a deer, yet the sutra clarifies that it refers to the mark on the Buddha’s shoulder-blade (*phalaka*).
It is like the haunches of the king of the *elāyanta* deer; this refers to the color of the deer’s hide.
*Mora* and *māmora* are both names for beasts, resembling the species of tigers and cubs; their hides are thick and lack softness, yet one may sit upon them.
They exist in all the countries west of Khotan, but since they are not found in this region, the Sanskrit names have been retained. The rest is not recorded in full. Now...
Regarding the terms "large and small canopies": although they are made of silk or brocade, they are included among the heavy items because they are cumbersome.

As for "pillows and fans," in the Western lands (India), these are mostly made of wool. Regarding "beds and mats," these refer to the mats used upon beds; in the Western lands, these mats are mostly made of *mṛdvīkā* (wool).

All of these are heavy items because their physical nature is derived from their practical utility. The phrase "merely based on the explanation" establishes the headings by analogy with the intermediate sections.

This is my intention. Regarding the phrase "the net of the teachings is fully comprehensive": although the various Vinaya sections are complete and sufficient in clarifying the gravity of offenses, I shall now also cite the texts to demonstrate that they are universally inclusive.
I have organized the handling of one's own property into seven categories; if one wishes to determine the gravity of an offense, one may rely on this for judgment.

As for the note regarding "applying by analogy" and so forth: in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, items such as tiles and wood are all judged based on their uneven distribution and their large or small dimensions.
This may also be applied by analogy. The first heading is as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "the four [types of bedding]":
as for sitting and sleeping mats, they are all lined internally with treated wool (*vāla*). A layer of cotton (*tūla*) is placed on the outside as a lining, and these are covered with cloth or silk.

If they are covered on only one side, they fall under the category of light woolen blankets (*kambala*). Those that resemble the *kāṣāya* (monastic robe) are still not fully understood; they should be judged according to their relative weight.

"伐" (fá) refers precisely to the *kāṣāya* (monastic robe). Because the Western lands are very cold, this is worn as clothing. As for the statement that "it is the same even when made of leather," this is because, as with the *kūla* (woolen rug), its possession is permitted;

thus it is categorized under the minor offenses (*laghu-āpatti*). Regarding heavy items such as quilts (*pī*), the ancient masters held that they were prohibited, whereas [the present rule] places them in the minor category like the *kūla*.
The Master of the present day says: "Quilts are not permitted to be kept at all; this is entirely due to worldly sentiment and is unacceptable."
For the sake of providing an illustration, the example of the *kambala-saṃghāṭī* from the *Cīvara-vastu* is cited; it is permitted to wear a woolen rug (*kambala*) as a cloak in cold regions.
Regarding bedspreads that fall under the category of heavy items, this is determined according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü).

If one follows the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Wufen lü), those of the same class as a single bedspread (*ekāstaraṇa*) are classified as light; however, thin and soft woolen rugs (*kambala*) that are suitable for clothing—such as those with five-colored patterns clearly distinguished—are all classified as heavy, regardless of their measurement in *hasta*, because they can serve as garments. As for the "king’s high-priced robe," according to the Vinaya...
Regarding the rules for robes: King Bimbisāra offered the expensive *kambala* woolen cloth he himself wore, as well as the costly woolen rugs he used.
The Buddha said, "These should be kept after being formally dedicated through the rite of *śuddha-dāna* (pure gift).

As for various fine garments, the Vinaya simply states that lay followers (*upāsakas*) sent messengers to deliver various fine robes; it does not distinguish between the names of the specific types of cloth, such as *vastra*, *aṃśuka*, or *dukūla*.
It is not clear. As for the phrase "it does not preclude including [items] such as," the Master’s current interpretation is definitive:

since these are of great value, fine garments must necessarily be very expensive; they refer to items such as *jiaoleng* (twisted-patterned silk). Furthermore, the subsequent text permits wearing "expensive, coarse garments.

Why would this exclude *ling*, *luo*, *sha*, or *gu* silks? (For now, this is the interpretation based on the Vinaya. Later, in the late spring of the second year of the Qianfeng era, the darkness was profound. A heavenly being appeared...

The Master’s discourse states: "The royal robes are categorized as worldly garments by the common eye and are thus lightly collected. Although this follows the Vinaya's ruling, it is not entirely clear.

This is likely the fault of the translators rather than the scholars. The error is like [confusing] the dimensions of a *kūrca* (rug); such items are not permitted as part of the three robes (*tricīvara*) in China.
This applies specifically to those expensive garments from cold regions. In the Western lands, many kings hold Buddhism in high esteem and govern externally..."
Regarding state affairs, he wears ordinary secular clothing; when practicing the internal path of the Dharma, he dons the robes of the Way.

As for those who are moved to wear the *saṃghāṭī*, which is identical to the monastic robes, their price is extremely high—sometimes reaching ten thousand pieces of gold. Thus, Jīvaka offered the Buddha a single robe worth one hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
Furthermore, he invited laymen and laywomen of pure faith, as well as bodhisattvas living at home, all of whom wore the three robes, even down to those of common appearance.
There are devas who likewise wear this attire. Only when the Great Master elucidated this teaching did [the Emperor] finally realize his former delusions. Thus, the Ritual Manual states:

"Now, using the immediate circumstances to apply a subtle and remote teaching," as when the Liang Gaozu personally relied upon the Buddhist teachings to receive and maintain the three robes and the mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*), and would remove his imperial robes when ascending the seat to preach. Furthermore, during the Zhenguan era, Emperor Taizong...

He presented the seven-strip robe he was wearing, valued at thirty thousand coins, to Master Zhen of Shengguang Temple. After [the Master] passed away, it was subsequently brought back into the palace.
Furthermore, in the twelfth year of the Zhenguan era, two monks from Wuzhong were presented to the Emperor: one named Daotai and the other named Huiyi.
The Emperor showed them the seven-strip robe he was wearing and commanded that they compose a poem; whichever completed it first was to be granted this robe.
When the poem was completed, he had the students evaluate its quality; they declared it to be of equal merit.

He then ordered the robe to be taken to the market, where its secular value was found to be six hundred thousand [coins]. He then returned the robe and departed, leaving behind one hundred rolls of silk and other items as prescribed by the ritual.
This is also recorded in the commentary (*śāstra*). By citing this passage as proof, it is clear that the royal robe is certainly a *dharma*-robe.
Regarding the wearing [of robes], for now I shall determine this according to the Vinaya; this is essentially the conclusion.

As for the statement that "the monk's [robes] are the lightest," this refers to their classification. Regarding the two kinds of waist-bands: first is the meditation band (*dhyāna-bandha*), which is the *śan-jo* (a type of cloth);

second is the waist-band (*kaṭi-sūtra*), which is made of *kai-gu*, *dan-dun*, or the like. *Kai-gu* is a coarse fabric made from hemp, wood-fiber, or cotton, suitable for weaving into clothing; one uses this as an undergarment against the body.

Regarding the wearing of the three robes (*tricīvara*): according to this [text], the *duanbei* (single-layered cloak) follows the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka Vinaya), where it is classified as heavy (*guru*) when entering a double-layered assembly.
Now, following the *Wufen lü* (Mahīśāsaka Vinaya), the single-layered *dunbei* may be categorized as light (*laghu*). The *Yi* (Ritual Manual) states:

"Since the *duanbei* is not the same as the *bei* (cloak) and other such items, the *man-san-yi* (sewn three robes) may follow the limit for light items. Regarding the woolen *mao-xin-jian* (wool-woven square rug), the *Yi* states: "It is made by weaving wool into cloth to form a square *zhang* mat; if its dimensions exceed the standard, [it is considered heavy]."

Regarding this, according to the *Vinaya-vidhi* (Ritual Manual): Furs are categorized as heavy or light based on their thickness; they must be systematically classified. If the thickness of the fur exceeds the measurement of the three robes (*tricīvara*), it is severed as "heavy" according to the aforementioned rule.
If it is soft and thin enough to be cut and fashioned, it is considered "light," regardless of its size or quantity. As for furs similar in kind to brocade and embroidery, the *Vinaya-vidhi* states:
"In this land [of China], these items originally did not exist; they all come from the northwest, from beyond the Great Wall. If...
When wool is gathered and woven such that the tips of the hair protrude and form patterns resembling the shapes of humans, animals, and so forth, it is called a *kūrpa* (carpet).
If the warp threads are interwoven with variegated hair to resemble the brocades of this region, it is called a *mauduka*; these are used as floor coverings, wall hangings, and the like.
Because they possess exquisite colors that are as distinct as embroidery, they are included among the "heavy" items. Even though they are small *kaśikas*, beneath them...

The *lǜmáo* (woolen) category follows [the rule for] heavy [materials]. Among the five major colors, ancient rulings classified true vermilion and the like as heavy, while yellow and white were classified as light.

The Master of the present day objects, saying: "If that were so, why does the Vinaya text classify silk cloth as light? It is because the color of silk cloth is white; therefore, it falls under the category of white and its substance.
If that were the case, although woolen carpets (*qúlù*) are also [white], the underlying intent is as follows:
If the five great colors (pañcamahāvarṇa) enter into the category of light [offenses], why is it that for woolen rugs (*kūrpa*), one judges them based on measurement alone and does not mention color?
The meaning of the response is as follows: because woolen rugs have already departed from variegated colors, they are judged based on measurement to enter the light category.

If the patterns are clearly distinct, they should be swept into the heavy category. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it can be understood that the lower [textual] evidence establishes that pure colors enter the light category. [This applies to] silk.

Regarding the meaning of "grinding" (*mò*): it is categorized as light. It is compared to wearing a thread-line. Since it is already included among the light items that are essential for the body, grinding silk is likewise comparable to grinding cotton;
thus, it should also be classified as light. If it involves a cocoon, there are insects within the grinding [vessel] (the character *shèjiāo* is pronounced *jiē*).

Inside there are bones which are placed in the heavy clothing bag. The annotation stating "reaching down to the navel, etc. refers to the range from the shoulders to the waist and navel; this means they are strung over the shoulders.

[This refers to] the practice. Therefore, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is classified as light [offense]. Regarding "a bag with joined ends": this refers to a bag whose two ends are sewn together while the middle opening remains open.

However, if the color and appearance have necessarily been changed, it is permitted to divide [the garment], because although its form differs from the norm, it is still fit to be attached to the Path; thus, it is opened [as permissible]. To alter [the color] means...
Regarding the use of a square cloth bag: it is made by joining together four squares of five colors. The bowl bag is embroidered with fine silk.

the water jar, basin, rope bed, wooden bed, water flask, sprinkling staff, fan, axe, chisel, lamp stand, and carriage—these five types of implements for work are all included among the heavy. Therefore, the Vinaya says:

The aforementioned five types are tools for creating things; as for the objects created, they vary in weight. Ancient masters included them all within the category of "heavy" (grave offenses). The commentary states:
"As for the Buddha not making a distinction," this does not mean he did not distinguish them as being included in the heavy category;

it simply means that regarding the division of iron and other materials into vessels, the Buddha said: "They should not be divided and assigned to the Sangha of the four directions. From this day forward, I permit [this practice].

The razor is classified as light (though some authorities include it among the heavy offenses). Because a razor is used constantly, it is classified as light; because money and precious gems incite greed, they are classified as heavy.

Regarding the "subsequent text": this refers to the section on the rules for robes (*cīvara-dharma*) that follows. Among the thirteen chapters, there is no specific provision for the adjudication of money.

Now, according to the section on rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*) below, it should properly be included among the heavy items. As for the phrase "from ten down to belonging": this is a classification by category. Regarding incense burners, those that are small and portable are included among the light items.
However, according to the subsequent text, those which are still considered three-fold divisions—such as hooks fixed to a wall—are [heavy], specifically those like the *ē’è* (a large hook).
"Claw" refers to a [monastic] pin. "Zen-zhen" (meditation-pin) refers to a staff used for sitting meditation, or one placed upon the crown of the head.
"Shang" (upper) refers to a spoon. "Bō-chi" (bowl-support) refers to a stand for the alms bowl when seated. "Hū-pai" (door-plaque) refers to a signboard attached above a door hook.

"As before, the small ones" refers to items such as crystal vessels; those that are small, like the aforementioned light-weight [vessels], measure *zhou-ban-ji* (half a *zhou*), which is equivalent to one *dǒu* in the Tang system.

"Chu" (舛) refers to the six heavens and six earths; "qiang" (強) means forceful. "Zhu jǔ" (竹筥)—the character for "jǔ" is pronounced as *jǔ lǚ*—refers to a large, straight-mouthed vessel called a *kuāng*;

a small, curved-mouthed vessel is called a *jǔ*. If it exceeds the standard measure, it is called a *guòliàng* (excessive measure). Regarding the "white bowl" (*bái bō*): this is not the same "bowl" (*bō*) as the *bōyú* (alms bowl).
From this point downward, the text clarifies the *bōyú*. If it exceeds three *dǒu* in capacity, it also falls under the category of heavy items, because its use is not permitted.

Regarding the *Yinjian lun* (Treatise on Introduction): as for the items such as needles and awls that should be divided [among the Sangha], they are clarified here by way of context (originally intended to clarify the needles).

As for funeral requisites that enter the heavy category, it is because they are for one's own sake. As for door-hooks, they correspond to the light category; this refers to their being light when placed aside.

Previously, it was determined that entering [the monastery] was light, but now, following the rule for entering through the inner door, it is classified as heavy. Regarding the *kalyara* vessel, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* simply calls it a small bowl or a ladle (*kañci*); nowadays, generally...

These are the *kaṭhalla* (ladle) and the *pātra* (bowl); collectively they are called *kuñjara* (translated here as "accessories for the bowl"). According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, a ladle that conforms to the prescribed measurements belongs to the category of light offenses (*laghu*).

However, if it is made of beams, ash, hemp, silk, or linen, it is heavy regardless. Regarding the three-part incense burner, it is as described in the text; as for the rosary, it is categorized separately.

Regarding the items mentioned above, there is no fixed rule; therefore, it is said that they are categorized separately as light offenses. Because the person accompanying the object is fixed, it is included among the light offenses.

However, if it is adorned with jewels, it enters the category of heavy offenses (in accordance with the *Gaoseng zhuan yiyi*, when setting up seats for preaching the Dharma and so forth, one should dismantle them and place them back according to their original locations).
Beyond these, all tools that cause harm to living beings must be destroyed and eliminated. If a man who resembles a jewel offers articles of adornment, it enters [the category of heavy offenses].

Valuable musical instruments and the like are likewise included among heavy items (*guru-dravya*). These various meanings are explained extensively in the *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* (The Inquiry of Upāli), and thus are not recounted here in full.
Regarding the phrase "the third [category] consists of those that have arrived," this refers to the first and second chapters, all of which concern heavy items; yet there remains...

"Light objects" refers to those that, after [the donor's] death, are no longer owned by him; they remain light objects that should be divided because they have been taken for oneself, and thus differ from those belonging to another.
"If there is no rule" means there is no rule for dividing a room during the three periods. If one maintains a separate room while alive, it becomes the private property [of the deceased];
thereafter, as he is no longer the owner, it is permitted that the permanent property (sthavira) of the community takes possession of the ochre-colored ground.
This refers to red earth. The rest may be understood. Regarding the "four limits" and "cutting off": "matter" refers to that which arises.

Raw hide is called *ge* (leather); tanned hide is called *wei*. Regarding ox-hide boots and slanted boots, the *Yi* (Ritual Code) states: "If the toe is flat and the boot is short, it is light and differs from the common;
thus one knows that a long boot is heavy. This is clear from various sections [of the Vinaya]. As for why they are explained here in the Sūtras and Vinaya, it is because they are made from tree bark.

Therefore, waste paper, pens, ink, and brushes are treated according to the ritual regulations. For now, a small amount is categorized as light; however, if they are sold or used to copy secular texts, they are categorized as heavy.

As for those written specifically for the sake of the Tripitaka teachings, they should be returned to the donor as originally given. Regarding the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the determination is as follows:
the ritual manual states that the vessel for bath powder may be made of copper, iron, hemp, ramie, wood, bark, or similar materials, as it is used for the constant washing of the alms bowl.

If the essential requisites are moderate in quantity, they are categorized as light; if they are substantial and difficult to maintain, they are categorized as heavy. Regarding the fifth point concerning the "five [animals]":
these refer to the keeping of six types of livestock—cattle, horses, pigs, sheep, chickens, and dogs. Once one has raised their lives, one must necessarily provide for their sustenance.
It is clear that all [these cases] fall under the "heavy" category. This concludes the sixth section. Regarding the phrase "the six arrive":

the three textual divisions, from the first part of the fourth section downward, concern the master and the slave residing within the boundary; this is the ninth chapter-gate and may be understood as follows (etc.).
That is to say, a private residence belonging to an individual is also called a *saṃghārāma*. Being a slave within such a place refers to various *saṃghārāmas*. Piṅgiya is an individual...
In the case of small temples and the like, if their master dies, all the property of the *karmadāna* (pure men) and slaves shall be subject to strict regulation;

all items belonging to the slaves shall be under the supervision and management of the original slave-owner. Second, if a slave belonging to the monastic community (*saṃgha*) dies, the clothing and belongings shall be given to their relatives.
If there are no relatives, they shall immediately enter the permanent endowment (*sthavira*) of the monastery. Third, regarding the death of a private slave...
"When the master is present and the slave has died. The principle for this is based on two categories: namely, those who live together and those who do not live together.

As stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-vibhāṣā* (the "Under-Copy"), regarding a slave who lives together [with the master], he is like one's own son. Now that the slave has died, his property remains in place;
the master shall take it himself and use it as he pleases, whether for making offerings or casting images, all of which is included within the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) for a slave. (Note)

The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "Living together" (*tóng huó*) refers to those who share in the management of affairs. From the phrase "if not living together" (*ruò bù tóng xià*) down to the end of the sub-commentary, it clarifies what it means to "not live together.
This means that the master merely provides food and clothing but does not share in the management of affairs;
one who lives together with him belongs definitively to that slave. If he dies, others may take him away, and his kinsmen will come to claim him, provided they are fully present.
There is none; this means that the object itself enters into the permanent abode (*nitya*). The commentary cites the example of the funeral rites (*mabin*) to clarify this (as detailed in the notes).
Regarding the point that "if it is supplied by the Sangha, it is different": this refers to the property of the *sangha* of the permanent abode (*chōjō*).

That which is supplied [to a deceased person] returns to the permanent abode after death (the explanations above all refer to the Dharma-treasure). However, according to the *Sōgenki*, the text of the *Kechimyaku-shō* is divided differently from the above. It says: "If..."

This is not the same as the previous case. The two phrases beginning with "directly" (*zhí'ěr*) and "the master" (*zhǔ*) are taken together as one section. The commentary explains: "This refers to those who merely provide food and clothing;
for all subsequent items such as robes and utensils, they may be directly presented [to the recipient] without any further distribution. The Venerable [Master] objects, saying:

"If that were so, it would not differ from the preceding passage concerning 'taking for oneself and distributing according to the place of residence,' and this might contradict the intent of the *Chāo* (Excerpts). Below, the *Mātṛkā-vinaya* is cited as proof, as in the text. Finally, this relies upon the *Vinaya*.

As for this: since it was already given away at the time of life, after death it is not permitted by the Vinaya to be returned to the permanent property of the monastery (*sāṃghika*), as it has already been transferred to another during one's lifetime.
If it had not been given away during life, then after death it must be entered into the permanent property according to the Vinaya.

The current phrasing should therefore be revised to: "after death, it is entered according to the Vinaya. Regarding the seventh point, from "seven" to "thus": if one follows the ritual manual (*vidhi*), it actually constitutes nine [items].

[These cases] are generally included among the light [offenses]. Now, all of these are heavy; citing the intent of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it says: "A certain bhikṣu was ill, and the Saṃgha allotted food for him at the proper time.

The attendant took it on his behalf, but the bhikṣu died immediately after receiving it. The Buddha said: "If he dies first and the food is subsequently obtained, it should be returned to its original place.

If the food was requested [for him], then later it should be divided among those who died together with him," and the commentary instructs that it should be divided in the presence of those currently present.

Regarding "entering into the heavy": this refers to one's own shared property; it should be understood by analogy with the two types of robes—those involving light and those involving heavy offenses—which are severed [from use].
Therefore, it says, "it is also thus. As for the phrase "the rest up to...": this points to what is explained in the *Samayika* (The Ritual).

That is to say, these seven examples in this *Chao* (Digest) and the ten gates judged in that *Yi* (Ritual) do not differ in their general meaning. This is intended so that later students may fully understand both; hence, it says, "a comprehensive understanding."
Regarding the statement "the third reaches the mirror": the third stage generally employs all the various teachings. As for the establishment and abolition of the formal texts (*zhengwen*):

although the *Four-Part Vinaya* (Dharmaguptaka) classifies the ritual water flask (*kamaṇḍalu*) as a grave offense, we now abolish the *Four-Part Vinaya* and instead rely on the *Ten Recitations Vinaya* (Sarvāstivāda). According to this, the formal text regarding the measurement of the vessel places it in the category of light offenses.

Because they are used as personal requisites, and furthermore because the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) excludes them, while the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Qilü) classifies their entry [into the category of offenses] as light (*laghu*).

Although the five schools are similar in this regard, the usage is as detailed in a separate fascicle, which refers to the *Lüzhong qingzhong yi* (The Rite of Light and Heavy Offenses in the Vinaya). Beyond this, there is also the *Zhuzi chao*, which is not clearly explained here.

According to the ritual procedures, it is determined that [the offering] should be collected again; this is categorized as being like a secular parasol, and thus judged to be unsuitable for almsgiving (it is understood that a light offense is incurred). "Turtle-mirror" refers to the meaning of taking up a clear mirror.
Regarding the seven methods for rewarding labor: the first section, which restates the subject, is clear. The next is the heading, as in the text. As for the phrase "initially with a sincere mind":

one who speaks untruthfully—[it is because] the caregiver originally had good intentions, but now the patient says, "He covets my robes and bowl," or "He is only capable of minor tasks," or "He should do it himself;
I will not let him suppress the caregiver's efforts. This is for the sake of [the patient].

Regarding the phrase "next comes 'increasing' (*yi*)," this clarifies that one's practice has reached fulfillment. As for "increasing oneself in wholesome dharmas," this follows the *Souxuan keju* (The Outline of Searching the Profundities).
It means that even when attending to the illnesses of others, one must not neglect one's own tasks—namely, practices such as reciting sutras and cultivating dhyāna.
If one neglects one's own tasks, then even if one accomplishes the welfare of others, one’s virtue remains incomplete. The Venerable Master [Zhiyan] took the character "self" (*ji*)...
The preceding phrase generally uses the character "yi" (以) to introduce the subsequent clause.

It states that "the body increases in wholesome qualities," which means that the benefit of growth in wholesome dharmas pertains entirely to the body of the patient and has absolutely no relation to the caregiver.

(This interpretation is superior. The phrase "there are those who reach the middle" is the conclusion. Regarding "those who have reached the ultimate," according to the text of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there were times when [the Buddha] was being cared for.

Regarding the sick: if one goes out on errands to seek medicine for a patient, or departs privately on other business, and the patient subsequently passes away, it is not known to whom the robes and bowl should be given as a reward for their labor.
The Buddha said: "They should be given to the one who brought the matter to completion. As for those of wrong livelihood mentioned in the *Jīvam̐ka*, they do not deserve a reward;
this means that from the beginning they did not intend to show compassion for others, but rather kept the robes and bowl for themselves. This constitutes an offense against the King [of the Dharma].

Regarding the Dharma: knowing that another will certainly die, it is likewise improper to bestow rewards. As for the phrase "in sequence down to the capable" (*mín*), this clarifies that the objects bestowed are received by the capable, who are those who have attained realization (*dá*).

As for the passage in the text stating "the three robes are not bestowed, nor are they adjudicated," because they are not connected with formal acceptance and maintenance (*dhāraṇa*), those who practice by dividing them up hold that since they are the same single robe, they should be rewarded together. Regarding the names and essential natures of the six requisites... [text continues]
The Vinaya traditions differ. I wish for the Vinaya Master to combine the three robes into one; the cloth for containing the robes and the inner vest into two;
the bowl as three; the bowl bag as four; the sitting mat as five; and the needle case as six (this follows the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, which excludes the water-strainer bag and adds the needle case).

The *Shizong* states: the three robes constitute one; the bowl constitutes two; the sitting mat constitutes three; the needle case constitutes four; and the cloth for containing the robes constitutes five.
The storage containers are established as six. Now, Nanshan says: "The three robes are three; the alms bowl is four; the sitting mat is five; and counting the tube makes six.
However, the container for storing robes is merely an accessory to the robe and bowl and is not one of the six; reflect upon this correctly by calculating it.

Regarding the six articles of a nun (*bhikṣuṇī*), these consist of the five robes with the addition of a needle case as the sixth. Among the four phrases, one transgresses her virtue because she lacks the requisite objects or uses money.
As for the phrase "donning [the robe] after deliberating on the matter according to the circumstances," this generally clarifies the latter three phrases;

in one phrase, a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is required, while in the other two phrases, it is sufficient to reach a consensus through verbal consultation. The phrase "to exclude those who have arrived" refers to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.
There was a bhikṣu who tended to the sick; many did not know who was entitled to receive the robes. The Buddha replied as in the text. Regarding "the labor ultimately being incomplete":
the rest of the assembly lacks the merit of massage, and laypeople lack the merit of preaching the Dharma; thus, it is incomplete.

"Based on this" and below, the present Master clarifies the meaning according to the principles. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and subsequent texts provide a miscellaneous explanation as found in the text.
Regarding the "eightfold timing," the phrase "those who arrive at eight" refers to the incident where a corpse rose up to protect its belongings. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

A certain bhikṣu from Kosala died, and while the Saṃgha was dividing his possessions in front of the corpse, the corpse rose up and said, "Do not divide my property! It was because of this that the rule was established.

(As stated above). The ninth section, "The Dharma of Enumerating Names and Establishing Ranks," can be understood [as follows]. Regarding the phrase "from 'initially' to 'the fewest': it refers to the gathering of material goods.

Next, regarding the addition of the dharma and the enumeration of names, it can be understood. Regarding the phrase "from 'initially' to 'the one who possesses the dharma': if there are five persons, one may perform [the rite]. As for the two dharmas..."
This refers to those who reward laborers and those possessing the five virtues; although they do not constitute the full number for a *saṃgha*, there must still be four persons present.

If there are only four, they may simply divide the property equally. As for what is now called "the method," it distinguishes the formal procedures and protocols of the preceding conditions; all subsequent notes should be understood according to this principle.
Those cases similar to this include the instances of ringing the bell to relinquish robes, inquiring about debts, and entrusting items; these are not "superior conditions.

This does not refer to the aforementioned closing of the door or limiting one's investigation to a specific condition; rather, it refers to the verbal formula for relinquishing robes through the spontaneous purification of one's own mind.
The Vinaya fully sets forth six conditions. Now, this *Chao* (Excerpts), following the rule for "improper time" regarding monastic gifts, states:

"Whatever exists—whether it be clothing or non-clothing, whether based on a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*)—the text is amended to read: 'whatever clothing or articles exist. Furthermore, there may be the case of death outside the monastery;
in such instances, one should name that specific residence. Or, if death occurs at one's own home, at a mill, or similar locations, one should say: 'without a fixed residence, in all cases.'"
A provisional assessment. Note: Regarding the statement that it is not strictly necessary for [the robes] to be assembled, the *Śāstra* says:

"If the six items are in another location, and if one can obtain them while attending to the sick, they must be sought out and offered as a reward. If the requirements are not met, or if there is no attendant to care for the patient, then they are distributed according to their respective portions.

Therefore, it is said that it is not strictly necessary for them to be assembled. Since it is not necessary to assemble them at the time of relinquishing the robes, one simply states generally: "The [robes]..."

Regarding the phrase "there are garments and articles; all may be decided according to the above": this has been fully explained in the three sections concerning "Living Together," "Entrusting," and "Transferring Debts" as mentioned above.
Next, regarding the determination of lightness or gravity: as asked in the sixth internal section above, if there are items to be sent in a bag, the bag is substituted for three proclamations.
As for "the reconciler returning," this refers to cases where the Vinaya does not permit it when the value exceeds five *kārsāpaṇas*. If there is a death, [the deceased] is left naked.

This invited public reproach and suspicion. They reported this to the Buddha, who consequently permitted them to cover themselves with a cloth. As for the rule that one must not expose the body, the bhikṣus did not know what material to use.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to use *saṃghāṭī* (outer robes) to cover yourselves. The bhikṣus would not take [robes] from lay donors, saying, "These belong to the Saṃgha of the ten directions.
The Buddha said, "Once you have formally assigned them to the Saṃgha, you may use them to cover your bodies. It was not otherwise.
[The text] states that one may not [do this] (this is the main body of the Five-Part Vinaya). The ancient masters followed the text in their practice, yet it seems somewhat unstable.

Now, Nanshan follows the text of the *Pañcaśata-praśna-vinaya-śāstra* (Wubai wen lun), as cited in the [relevant] excerpts (and so forth). Dongyang You said: "Although the treatise says this, one must nonetheless form the intention (*citta*) to relinquish;
if one does not form the intention to relinquish, it is likewise impermissible, just as when performing the forfeiture of an offense involving loss (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*)."

This is an example of the mind of relinquishment (this is a note from the *Shishō*). Regarding the statement, "From the five virtues to receiving [the reward]": as for "priding oneself on one's own merit," the *Book of Documents* says, "To claim credit for oneself is called 'priding' (*batsu*);
to boast of oneself is called 'being worthy' (*ken*). Now, if one stands before the assembly and claims to possess these virtues, this constitutes priding oneself on one's own merit.
If one does not possess them, one likewise cannot receive the reward. Since both cases result in an obstacle, it is entirely... [omitted].
Regarding the Sangha: the leader who upholds the Dharma may, if he so desires, decide whether or not to perform the formal act of demarcation (*sīmā-bandhana*).

In the *Caturvargika-prātimokṣa-vinaya*, it is stated that when the designated hall for the recitation of the precepts was initially small and later could no longer accommodate the large number of monks, they wished to demarcate it again. The Buddha said: "The Sangha has the autonomy to do so."

Regarding "binding" and "not binding": although the phrasing here differs from the current text, the principle remains that whether the authority to act at will is granted or not depends upon the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, it is not strictly necessary to question others before the assembly as to whether they are fully qualified or otherwise; the rest of the text may be understood accordingly.

As for the phrase "then arriving," although the names of the items listed in the *karmavācanā* differ across the four locations, the underlying intent indicates that the presence of the items is not yet fixed. However...

When the time arrives, one must also establish the procedure with precision; it must not be inconsistent. Regarding the clarification of the "method for reaching [the goal]" (*zhìfǎ*): this involves discerning right from wrong.

As for the formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) used to appoint a person according to the Vinaya regulations, there have been three different interpretations by masters throughout past and present.

The first master established three distinct procedures: first, the appointment of the person; second, the entrusting of the robe; and third, the distribution of the robe. He adhered to the scriptural text which states: "Take the robe and give it to one person."
Master Qiu commanded that the two parts be divided by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*. Now, the critique states: this textual formulation is unacceptable.
The second master retains only the first two [procedures], because within the second method for entrusting robes, the two meanings of "entrusting" (*payati*) and "dividing" (*bhajati*) are combined.

The third master retains only the single method of "entrusting and dividing," without including the appointment of a person. Now, according to the main intention of this commentary, the second master’s view is adopted. Why?
This is understood. The text states: "The Vinaya rules prescribe that a formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) shall be made to appoint a person. This refers to following the second [method].

Regarding the phrase "violating the law results in a common offense," this refutes the third master. That is to say, the Vinaya states: "One person should be appointed to divide [the property]. Since one is not appointed now, is this not a violation of the law?
As for the procedure for entrusting the robes, since the words "together" (*yukta*) and "to be divided into two" (*dvibhāga*) are used, it is also [a case of] verbal appointment.

Since it can be accomplished by combining [the two], it is said that "it is obtained through both. The *Souxuan* asks: "If one follows the second master, why does the *Chao* (the Vinaya commentary) not show the method for appointing the person?
Answer: It is because the Vinaya merely requires the appointment of a person but does not set forth the specific wording; therefore, the *Chao* omits it.
When performing the ritual now, one simply first makes the formal announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to appoint him, and thus the *karman* is successfully executed as is customary.

Regarding "first knowing" and "not possessing the requisite qualities," etc.: although the above explains that one must clearly understand the presence of virtues and the distribution of the *śikṣāpada*, at the time of performing the ritual, one must first clearly and thoroughly ascertain whether or not the virtues are present, as well as what portion of the *dharma* the *śrāmaṇera* is entitled to receive. Furthermore, one must know how much [of the portion] the *śrāmaṇera* is entitled to be given.
Quoting from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-śāstra*, it is proven that one who possesses the requisite virtues is fit to hold [the bowl], and that one may obtain [it] from a *saṃgha* in another territory.
Regarding the object: if one does not possess these virtues, one should simply provide it by harmonizing with the objects present before them. (Note:

The intent is that one must be extensively versed in the measurements of the various *śāstras* in order to harmonize with the objects present without fixed measure. As for "three cubits, five cubits, or beyond," etc.:

Regarding "measuring according to oneself": using silk cloth as a reference, one measures the length for the three robes (tricīvara) in cubits (*hasta*). Any extra material beyond this, regardless of its quantity, is to be given to a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*) who is skilled in sewing.

Regarding "inner and outer robes": these refer to the hems and the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṭhina*). As for the phrase "now it has come to being held": [it refers to the fact that] the measurement is now fixed.

According to the circumstances at that time, one should simply rely on the third master. As for the instructions in the Chinese commentary regarding not fully appointing a person to perform the ritual—specifically concerning the *vinaya* rules for rewarding labor—the sub-commentary states:
"If, within the Saṃgha, a formal act (*karmavācanā*) is performed to appoint one person to distribute [the property], the ritual for the distribution of robes and articles is no different from this;
