Item A should be returned to the Saṃgha with its name attached. Furthermore, in the previous rules for rewarding labor, after merely listing the six items, the commentary simply states:
"Clothing does not encompass everything. Now, taking the text regarding untimely offerings (*akāla-dāna*), all items are fully accounted for. The *karmavācanā* is according to the text.

Regarding the phrase "performing until midday," this refers to the method of distribution in the presence of the great Saṃgha. As for "casting lots" (*śalākā-nyāsa*), it is intended for those who cannot see [the process], so that they may record [their share].

Draw lots for each person's name one by one; collect them onto the robe according to the names. The distribution of items must not be partial. Regarding the "those who possess the Dharma" mentioned in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*:

if the distribution proceeds by breaking down the items, there is no distinction between good and bad, and thus it is unnecessary to cast lots. Those among the assembly who are "possessors of the Dharma" refer to those who consider themselves [qualified];

this means that because they have many robes and monastic requisites, they are called "possessors of the Dharma. They must divide [the items] according to the rules; it is not permissible for them to act separately.

Dedicating this as merit is the understanding of ordinary people; they certainly cannot surpass others. As for the mind of a noble one (ārya), merely relying on the Buddha’s regulations constitutes compliance with the teaching.
This can be understood from the subsequent section clarifying the distinction between those who are eligible and ineligible for the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual).

Regarding the phrase "next, reaching the middle": this refers to all four Vinayas—the *Dharmaguptaka*, the *Mahīśāsaka*, and so forth—being likewise so; it does not mean that it is restricted solely to the *Dharmaguptaka* Vinaya.

As for the phrase "even unto" (*nàizhì*), it means exceeding half [of the time], being equal to the three [periods] or the one [period] mentioned previously. Regarding the commentary in the *Shuchao*, Xuán says:

This refers to the *Zhuyi chao* (Explanatory Notes on Terms) and the *Da shu* (Great Commentary). The latter states: "Although a *jìngrén* (lay attendant) may have served the Sangha with diligence, they are nonetheless not an ordained practitioner;
therefore, their [share] is even less than that of a *śrāmaṇera*. Question: If there should be women within a monastery, is it appropriate for the *jìngrén* to receive a portion?
Answer: According to principle, it is contrary to the Dharma for a monastery to harbor women; this is discussed elsewhere in the Vinaya. Now...

This is based, for the time being, on the principle of rewarding labor; it is also appropriate that one should receive a share. Question: If one is outside the boundary acting as an agent for the Saṃgha, should one receive this object? Answer:
Although there is a distinction between being inside and outside, there is no difference in the labor performed; it is likewise appropriate that one should request a small portion from the Saṃgha.
The phrase "saying 'thus' up to 'transgressing'" is a concluding exhortation. "Thick-faced" refers to those who are unattached to worldly guests.

"Not only from beginning to end" means that at birth, which is the beginning, one does not bring a single thing with one; likewise, at death, which is the end, it is not fitting to take a single thing away.

One does not engage in such reflection. Alternatively, one may reflect at the time of receiving [the robes]: regarding the practice of the four robes, we currently possess many through greed and hoarding;
seeing that after his death the robes will be divided, I wish for each person to exercise restraint, so as to diminish my own greedy intentions.

If it comes to the point of distribution, the method is for the four people to divide them directly. The oral agreement (*mukhasaṃvāda*) says: "Venerable sirs, please bear this in mind; now I hold this..."
"O Bhikṣu, give the robe and bowl to so-and-so. The method for the distribution by the nursing bhikṣu should be understood through the threefold recitation.

Regarding the text following this procedure, it is all to be determined according to the principles of our current master. The commentary cites the Vinaya regarding "improper times" to corroborate the aforementioned principle;

that is, in the Vinaya, the Buddha ordered that [the items] be divided among one person, but as there is currently no one available, we rely on the Abhidharma-śāstra to authorize this practice. Thus, the direct method of division is carried out.

Presently, although the formal act (*karmavācanā*) has been performed, it has not yet entered into one's own possession. If someone arrives at this point, the procedure must be carried out through a process of succession.

Furthermore, because there was no one present previously, the treatise (*śāstra*) permitted it as an exception; however, since there is now someone present, one must rely on the Vinaya to perform the division again for the sake of establishing a definitive case.
For example, if two people have already completed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony and then three people together arrive within the boundary (*sīmā*), then...

This modifies the previous rule. Regarding the phrase "if there is no one present who can perform the formal act": this means that if someone arrives later, the procedure cannot be carried out because they did not hear the prior announcement.
The explanation of the *saṃgha*-dharma is hereby concluded.
Next, regarding the phrase "the two [monks] up to the attendants": "The two mouths harmonize in the distribution" means that the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) states:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! We, holding these robes and bowls of this bhikṣu, shall give them to so-and-so. The attending bhikṣu recites this three times.

The rest is as in the text. Regarding "directly handing over": it indicates that one should say, "Venerable sir, this robe, bowl, and so forth, belonging to the bhikṣu [Name], I give to you, Venerable sir.
This refers to cases such as when giving a reward for nursing the sick; it means directly handing over the object. It does not mean failing to state anything at all.

This is called "direct entrustment" (*jikkufu*). It clearly explains the three aspects of both parties. Regarding the phrase "receiving and sharing together," since the Vinaya does not provide specific wording for this, these words constitute the direct entrustment.

Now, the *Shō* (the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*) points out that the wording is as explained in the *Lun* (the *Sifenlü shanbu suishu yichao*). Later, it explains the method of mental recollection (*shinnen-hō*), saying:
Regarding the "three arrivals," Nanshan says: Having made these three statements, because one has grasped the object with the hand, subsequent people may not take it.

If one does not grasp it, and there are others later, it must then be divided. In the Vinaya, it simply says, "This is my portion" (the departing tone). The addition of the word "obtained" here is the conclusion of the *Chao*.
In the question-and-answer section, the characteristics of what is not clothing are distinguished; furthermore, this is also discussed within the section on the rules for clothing.
The bhikṣus were apprehensive and dared not give [these items] to the bhikṣuṇīs. [These included] robes, alms-bowls, bags, leather cases, and so forth.

The Buddha said: "I permit you to give them to the *vina-ho* (weaver/spinner). First, take the robes and offer them to the Saṃgha. The Buddha ordered that this be treated as an *akāla-dāna* (offering outside of the proper time), permitting the giving of non-robes and other such items to the bhikṣuṇīs.
Although these are not explicitly mentioned in the *Sūtra*, those who describe them simply state that anything which is not worn is all termed [non-robes].
It is not clothing; it does not hinder that nun. This robe is not something for the *saṃgha* to wear; both are cases where it is not yet considered clothing.

The tenth section cites the name as it appears in the text: "If it reaches completion... The commentary (*chao*) from the beginning up to "the formal regulation" concerns matters pertaining to oneself:

if there is property belonging specifically to another, it must be returned to its original temple. Private estates are easy to understand. As for "private temples," they refer to those one has built.

In places such as one's own village or private monastery (*dharma-pūjā-śālā*), as stated in the Vinaya, when a monk builds a *saṃghārāma* primarily for the sake of those with whom he is well-acquainted, this constitutes a "private temple.
Furthermore, there are many fields and gardens belonging to such a *saṃghārāma*, which constitute a "private estate.

Regarding these two types of locations, if one dies while serving as a guardian or custodian therein, heavy items revert to oneself; as for primary or light items, they are determined according to [the specific circumstances].

Regarding this distribution for the *saṃgha* present here: although this is a natural site and not a layperson’s residence, because it is managed by a person in charge, it does not compare to the homes of laypeople (*avadātavasana*).
It is not a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), yet fearing that the donor might incur sin through loss, [the distribution] is permitted for those among the five groups who arrive first.

Because it has now become different from this, it is said that one also does not receive a share of the *bhikṣuṇī* community. Regarding "heavy objects entering one's own possession" and "one's own temple":

in this region, these refer to those designated as eminent monks. Xuán says: According to principle, it should also be stated that if there is a *bhikṣu* who oversees even a single phrase [of the scriptures], then—referring to the text below—it says:
"If there is no *bhikṣu* to guard the country, it follows the household laws of laypeople. Thus we know.

This section concludes the point. Although there were monks guarding [the property], it is omitted from the text. Since there was no resident monastery, the heavy items therein were left to the discretion of the guarding monks to deliver to the permanent endowment (*sādhāraṇa*) of a nearby monastery;
for the principle of the Saṃgha is one of equality, and thus permission was granted for them to be collectively administered by that monastery.
Regarding the absence of the Sangha-dharma: there is no performance of the *poṣadha* or *karmavācanā*. Even those who know the Dharma are not permitted to hold [the ritual implements].
Thus, the Vinaya states: "If there are five masters of the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*) in a single monastery or forest, they shall receive all offerings while upholding the Vinaya.

Although the formal procedures (*vidhi*) are currently being performed, because there is no one within the monastic boundary (*sīmā*) who knows the legal codes and practices the Vinaya, the renunciants take the Dharma as their [guiding principle].
Originally, one received benefits according to the Dharma; now that the Dharma no longer exists, it is therefore improper to hold [the offerings].

If there is no bhikṣu to guard and manage them to clarify ownership, then since there was originally no fixed place of residence and these things are naturally left as they are with no one to collect or maintain them, this is the same as the *Caturvargika-vinaya*.
Regarding the five groups of practitioners who arrive first, the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "If a bhikṣu is alone in a village... [The text continues: "...he should announce [his presence]."
When a donor dies while wearing their robes, there are five classes of monastics. Whichever group arrives first from among them should be given these items.
If no one is present, they should be bestowed upon whichever group of monks is nearest to the monastery. According to this text, this is essentially similar to the customs of lay households.
As transmitted through various records, this summarizes the preceding passages; the essential meaning does not exceed this.
The fourfold classification of cases is now summarized briefly. Regarding the first point, the Great Outline of Searching for the Profundity (*Souxuan dayi*) states:

First, a person has a monastery where they originally resided, yet now separately possesses a private monastery and estates, or property located in other villages and dwellings; such a person is called a "monk who possesses [multiple sites].

Alternatively, if family members take charge of heavy items and claim them as their own, the original monastery—because it knows that the person in charge belongs to another site—[does not claim them]. Second, if...

Regarding "one's own": if there is no monastery where one originally resided, and one has established a private temple for oneself, its buildings and property—even if they are located among the various permanent endowments (*sāṃghika*) such as monasteries and estates—should also be recorded by those in charge of heavy assets.
When these items are brought into the buildings or estates, the permanent endowment shall include them according to their proximity.
If there is no monastic community (*saṃgha*) at the monastery, it is likewise not permissible to take back those who have already received [the property].

Even if there is a home temple or no fixed place of residence, should one die in a private manor temple or at a site belonging to various permanent endowments, and if there are neither bhikṣus nor family members to preside over the matter, one should immediately take the light items and assign them to the five classes of renunciants (*pañca-varga*) who arrived first by name; they shall then be sent off according to those who arrived first.
Regarding the temple: if one knows [the owner], there is a home temple (*mūla-vihāra*); it must be sent back to that other home temple.

Fourth, if heavy items are in the house of a layperson (*avadātavasana*) and many people each grasp at their own reasoning and contend together, then according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, this is treated under the fifth point and the case of five persons;

the two types of entrustment are clarified as above. The textual evidence from the lower part of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* can be understood accordingly. If there is no place of residence, then it is not [a case of entrustment].

The ritual for the boundary of the Saṃgha. "A layperson's home" refers to the residence of a worldly person; this is based on the principles set forth below in the *Nanshan* [Vinaya] as found in the text.

Regarding the statement that "one need not add the ritual for one's own school," it means that when the assembly arrives and sees [the site], they immediately grasp it with the intention that it belongs to themselves, which differs from the other case.
When two people live together and one dies, one performs the mental recitation (*cittotpāda*). "According to the distance of one's inclination" means according to where one first saw [the site].
[This refers to] the disposition of the object. It may be sent to the permanent property (*sthavira*) of the original temple, or to someone in charge at a nearby location, and so forth.

In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the section distinguishing between the same boundary (*sīmā*) and separate receipt within the rules on stealing explains that when monks who are acquaintances send gifts to one another, the monk who receives the entrustment, while traveling along the road, encounters a different monk.
This monk comes forward from ahead to inquire about [the gift], and learns that the monk to whom it was entrusted has already died. He then [receives...].

Entrusting [the robe] to another bhikṣu while remaining silent; waiting for another bhikṣu; being alone in a place beyond the range of sight or hearing and receiving it—these constitute a *vyatikrama* (transgression).
The marginal note states that these should all be directly excluded. This is because, although there is a person present, one perceives them as being absent; thus, the principle is the same.

Regarding "there is no measure of the dharma, nor vows, etc.," this serves as proof that within the same boundary (*sīmā*), separate acceptance is not established. Furthermore, it distinguishes the timing of entering the boundary. The marginal note concerns...

Regarding the "Receiving the Sangha’s Boundary": When a distant guest arrives and does not know [the rules], they must inquire as to when they entered the mountain. By verifying this, one determines whether they arrived before the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), and so forth (*et cetera*).

Now, observing the flow of the text, there appears to be a contradiction. According to the *Shanbu biqiu shi yi chao* (Commentary on the Vinaya for Bhikṣus), which can be cited here, this is a passage from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
It is essential to know the time at which the visiting bhikṣu enters the boundary, as well as the sequence of the ritual; it is not fixed that the formal act (*dharmakarma*) will be subverted.

It is established that what has already been accomplished is not [re-]accomplished. Next, citing the Vinaya, there is the case where a person is absent from the assembly; distributing robes while the group is incomplete does not constitute success, provided one measures the fourfold portion of the robes.
Should there be doubts or obstacles, how should they be resolved? To provide an illustration, consider the case of the *poṣadha* (confession ceremony):
if a bhikṣu from outside the boundary arrives for the sake of the *poṣadha*, and applies his mind single-mindedly to the ritual, it is then successfully accomplished.
If one is occupied with other matters and enters the boundary while the formal ritual is being performed, the rite will not be accomplished;
this method for the distribution of robes should be understood according to this principle. Since the logic of the communal rules is complete and sufficient, one should reflect upon it accordingly.

In the subsequent question-and-answer section: [It is asked,] "If a robe was originally within the boundary (*sīmā*), may it now be taken outside and divided? First, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, in the section on the rules for robes:

when a bhikṣu travels among the people and acquires a large amount of property belonging to the Saṃgha—whether it be easy or difficult to divide—and he does not take it with him when crossing the boundary, the Buddha said:
"One should make an announcement and bring it to a certain place to divide it. One should establish boundary markers, measure shadows, and so forth, to assemble the people."
If [the Sangha] comes in person or sends someone else, one should divide [the property] according to this text; this constitutes permission to go outside the boundary. Now, citing this precedent:
the substance of the deceased’s property extends throughout the ten directions, yet it causes the ritual procedure (*dharma*) to select it for inclusion among the *pratyutpanna* (present) Sangha.

This is just as that present Sangha obtains a substance that extends throughout the ten directions without distinction. If one were to restrict it strictly to the present [Sangha], then the property of the present [Sangha] would not properly constitute a collective assembly.

Since it has already been ordered that monks from the ten directions be summoned universally, this expresses the intention that there should be no obstruction. Regarding the instruction to "send someone to come and also give them a share":

the original request was for a distribution of goods within this boundary; now, as the goods are being taken outside the boundary, because this person has business and cannot come, it is permitted to give them a share.

This does not mean that everyone must be given a share; rather, it means that [the share] is given to all who are present. Regarding the various schools' formulations of offenses: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when the Saṃgha receives a gift...

If one goes outside the boundary, one may perform the formal act of distribution (*karmavācanā*). It should be divided into five portions with other bhikṣus, saying: "The Sangha has obtained what is to be divided;

let one bhikṣu take the robe and receive it alone upon the boundary of the *sīmā*. The Buddha said: "One must not commit an offense of transgression (*duṣkṛta*). According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the robe should be divided by the monks present before them.

If a bhikṣu takes the robe belonging to another person outside the boundary, whether by mental intention or by taking it through three verbal proclamations, the Buddha said: "This violates the Vinaya."
It is further stated that one should not say it is improper, for it can be accomplished. The commentary follows the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:

regarding the distribution of goods among the Saṃgha during the middle of the twenty-eight-day period of the rainy season retreat, the text says: "If someone comes to take a portion on behalf of another, one should ask, 'Whose portion should this person take?

If there is someone who takes it, one should question that representative, saying: 'If these two were previously in agreement and have always acted as representatives for one another, you may give it to him.'"

This refers to the summer retreat (*varṣā*). To ensure that one's efforts have not been in vain, one should receive a share from those in harmony with oneself; even if one sends a messenger to request it from a superior who has attained realization, one may still obtain a share.

Next, citing the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it says: "It is not the same as in the homes of laypeople. This is because there was concern that laypeople might use [the robes], as they are not fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*);

therefore, shares were given out beforehand. Now, however, since these are monks and nuns, they may entrust items to one another without mutual discrimination. Thus, it is ordered that one should go and retrieve the original distribution register (*pariṣaṇḍā*).
[Answer: Regarding the subsequent question and answer: Suppose a bhikṣu is in the house of a layperson (*avadātavasana*). He has an item of his own, but no one comes to take it.
He then takes it into the boundary of the Saṃgha (*sīmā*) to find a monk to whom he might entrust it. Since he does not see any monks, he brings it back to his house.
Although this object had previously entered the boundary, when the time for the distribution of robes arrives, it is still considered to belong to the five groups [of renunciants] who arrived first.
Judgment: There are further alternative interpretations, but as they are not orthodox, they are not recorded here. [The section on] "Collecting the Chapters and Combining Them" (etc.).
The above concludes the Chapter on the Two Robes. *Sifen lü chao jian zheng ji*, Scroll Fifteen.

Written by the Great Virtue Zhi-zhen, who was granted the purple robe for his mastery of the Vinaya, his lecturing at Tianchang Temple in the Wuyue Kingdom, and his presiding over ordination platforms for the promotion of merit and universal salvation.
This record was completed on such-and-such a day of such-and-such a year.

*Jianzheng-ji* (A Record of the Simplification and Rectification of the *Shifen-lü-chao*), Scroll Sixteen (concluding from the "Chapter on the Four Medicines" through the "Chapter on Various Essential Practices").
Compiled by the Great Master Jingxiao, who was granted the purple robe and lectured extensively on the Vinaya at the altar during the Wu-Yue Kingdom;

the "General Commentary on the Lower Volume" (Pingpi Tonghao) is as previously described. The table of contents is listed at the beginning of the volume, categorized under general practices for comprehensive inclusion;
these are called "general practices" because they pertain to both individual and communal monastic conduct. Furthermore, all fourteen sections of the table of contents are extant today.

This fascicle is listed at the head [of the table of contents]. Although later generations divided the four scrolls into sub-sections based on their thematic content (*zǐkē*), one must not alter the three-fascicle structural divisions (*piānkē*).

Regarding the statement from "The Two Robes" up to "Seventeen": first, the underlying intent is that while the middle fascicle has already clarified the practitioner’s own conduct (*zìxíng*), although it is logically appropriate to remain in seclusion, one must nevertheless advance in the cultivation of the path and apply oneself to its practice. This is based on the essential principles of the source texts.

The *Zi-chi* (Provisions for Sustenance) serves as a summary of essential requirements. First, one must not exceed [the limits regarding] clothing. Therefore, within the four sections on personal conduct (*xingxing*), following these are the fourteen sections on communal conduct (*gongxing*).
The first part extensively distinguishes external provisions; thus, they are presented at the outset. Regarding the two types—food and clothing—both are conditions for sustenance.
Why, then, are the two types of clothing explained first, followed by the four sections on medicinal drugs? [This is because] when one's unseemly form is exposed outwardly, clothing is always...
Food is an internal sustenance, yet it also depends upon the proper timing; therefore, with respect to its frequency, the sequence of its administration is established.

Regarding the explanation of the names: the regulations concerning what is permitted and what is prohibited are twofold. "Clothing" (*cīvara*) is the term for that which covers and protects; this is the general designation.

As for the three robes and six articles, they are distinguished because each individual item—whether it be the "one hundred and one" items, surplus property, or gifts from the laity—is unique in its specific nature. Thus, they are so named.

"Separate. The term "pian" (chapter) refers to the designation for a section or division. "Seventeen" is a word used to indicate an increased number; thus, the initial title reads "Two Robes," and so forth.
The second section, the Chapter on the Four Medicines as Internal Requisites, is divided into two parts: first, the citation of the title; second, the explanation.

The initial section covers items four through eighteen. The underlying intent here is as follows: Master Xuán stated, "The Way relies upon the body; cultivating the body depends upon conditions. To establish one's physical form, obstructions are required.

First, the two types of robes were distinguished, followed by the fact that there is no drinking of solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*). Subsequently, the four medicinal tonics (*bhaiṣajya*) are clarified; therefore, they are discussed next. Regarding the explanation of their names:

although their substances differ—such as those taken at specific times and so forth—they are all called "medicines" because they treat illness and eliminate calamities. They are received with the hands and grasped with the mind.

There are four types of receiving [the precepts]. To be free from faults and to eliminate transgressions is called "pure" (*śuddha*). That which serves as a model and standard is termed "Dharma. The sections are to be understood as explained previously (*yathāpūrvam*).
Based on this, the outline for the commentary is established (*yathāpūrvam*).
Regarding the general meaning: the phrase "the retribution reaches the recipient" distinguishes the overall intent.

Some say that the first two lines constitute the general meaning, while from the names of the medicines onwards, it explains the names of the four types of medicine. "Retribution" (pāka) refers to the ripening; it is the repayment for past causes.
Since causes may be wholesome or unwholesome, their fruits are likewise differentiated. It is also called *vipāka* (ripening), which signifies that the cause and the fruit are distinct and different.

Because it ripens at its appointed time, the cause may be either wholesome or unwholesome, while the fruit is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). "Life" (*jīvita*) refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), which has as its essence the triad of vitality, warmth, and consciousness.
This retribution and life, having been established by past causes, are capable of attracting the present fruit. To cause them to abide in the world, they must rely upon sustenance;

they are maintained, nourished, and their faculties and seeds are supported, so that the vital breath may continue to fill the void. Therefore, do not exceed the administration of medicine. (Some say: "Sustenance... [text fragment])

"Taking up and holding" refers to the limbs of the body (though this may not be correct). As for the term "medicine," it is a general designation; whatever possesses the efficacy of curing illness is collectively termed medicine.

Therefore, it is called "universal" (*sāmānya*). Because the temporal limits differ, it is said that one must divide [the mealtime] into four periods. Regarding the phrase "from *chū* (morning) to *chū* (midday)":

the *Śastraviniścaya-ṭīkā* (*Chao*), following the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, permits this. Regarding the phrase "the matter accords with the Dharma": when laypeople prepare food, if one begs for it easily and without generating censure or stinginess, the matter accords with the "middle" period;
eating before midday accords with the middle-way Dharma established by the Buddhas of the three times. This is based on...

The instruction on taking [medicines] is called "that which accords with the Dharma" (*dharmānulomika*). Regarding "at improper times" (*akāla*) and so forth: this refers to the period after midday when the light gradually fades; it is termed "improper time.

Sugarcane and other such substances are permitted to be taken after midday; this is termed "outside the proper time" (*kālabahis*). That which has not yet passed the appearance of light (*ālokanimitta*) is termed the "limiting portion" (*maryādābhāga*).

Regarding the seven-day [period], it is determined by the capacity of the practitioner; according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, if one takes them for seven days, even a chronic illness can be cured.
[The medicine] is digested. Now, regarding the efficacy of this medicine in eliminating disease, one may take it according to its instructions for a period limited to seven days;
this is because its therapeutic benefit for various ailments is profound. As for medicines to be taken for life (*yāvajjīvika*), these are all substances that are bitter and astringent;
compared to the previous three types, their potency is slight, and they can only eliminate afflictions after long-term consumption. Furthermore, the body has three [aspects].
"Planting [the seeds]" explains the term *yāvajjīva* (lifelong). "The Abhidharmakośa-śāstra" provides the scriptural proof for the meaning of *yāvajjīva*. As the text states:

within the opening chapter, it says, "Regarding its specific divisions, they may be known. First, the sub-chapters are listed. Regarding the first point, "explaining by means of the four medicines," this is the citation.
This section distinguishes the four medicines according to time. In the commentary, it says, "When the time arrives," which has two parts.
It is simply that they are not "proper" (*bhojana*). Regarding the initial "proper food," as listed in the text of the precepts, the *Śāstra* (Commentary) states:
"These five kinds are called 'food' (*āhāra*); one mouthful constitutes a sufficient portion; it is 'proper'; and all are distinct.

As for the five kinds of *khajjaka*, these are "improper food. They are also listed as in the text. The *Śāstra* states: "The opposite of the above—neither sufficient, nor proper, nor all distinct. [End of] *Saṃgha*.
Regarding the root of the *jiluoqing* (祇蘿菁): Baoyun states that when grown in the northern regions, it possesses roots shaped like those of a radish;

however, when grown in Jiang and Zhejiang, it produces only long stalks without roots and is merely called *shungcai* (菘菜). To provide an illustration, it is like the case of the *jiangjiang* (江將) and the rhizomes of ginger and taro from Huai.
In the northern regions, there are likewise only leafy vegetables and no roots. As for "powdered juice," this refers to pounded flour that has been soaked in a large amount of water.
In the north, high officials often drink this after their meals; however, it is not permissible for bhikṣus to do so after midday.

Regarding the phrase "those who speak the ultimate truth," this refers to refuting the non-prohibition of fish and meat. As for "abandoning the prior teaching": the Vinaya was established first, while the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* was established later.
The Sūtra is that which can abandon, being the latter; the Vinaya is that which is abandoned, being the former. Thus, it is said to "abandon the prior.

Regarding the instruction to "observe [meat] as being like the flesh of one's own son," the Sūtra states: for example, it is like a husband and wife who are traveling together, carrying their only son with them.
In a vast wilderness, facing perilous hardship and the exhaustion of provisions, one kills their own child to eat, consuming it while shedding tears;

yet they find no flavor therein. So it is with the bhikṣu who severs the seed of great compassion. Yuanxiu’s *Yuan* states: "The 'ground' refers to compassion itself, spoken of in terms of its gradual fulfillment;

the 'seed' refers to the stage prior to the grounds, discussed in terms of spiritual lineage (*gotra*). Only upon reaching the fruit of Buddhahood does it receive the name 'Great. Now, this includes even the initial arousal of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*), for it saves..."
To deliver sentient beings and seek the fruit of Buddhahood—those who eat meat are thus excluded from all such stages and positions.

Therefore, regarding the various Vinaya texts mentioned previously that permitted eating meat: even if one has already eaten meat based on the initial conditions, does this not constitute a transgression?
The cited commentary on the scriptural sections states: "The previous total allowance for eating meat refers not to the four types of birth, but merely to manifested transformations. It says:

This is not a case of the four modes of birth—womb, egg, moisture, or transformation—which constitute actual retributive existence; rather, it is the compassionate manifestation of Bodhisattvas to meet the capacities of sentient beings.
Because they seek to deliver ordinary and Hinayana beings, the sutra states: "To deliver sentient beings, they manifest the eating of meat;
though they manifest this, in reality they do not eat it. Regarding the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and other texts, in its eighth fascicle, that work prohibits the eating of meat.

This chapter briefly outlines ten matters. Regarding "always regarding [beings] as one's own kin": parents, brothers, sisters, and kinsmen transmigrate through the six realms of existence, being born to one another in turn;
because they do not recognize one another, one now observes that all who eat meat have been one's own relatives.

One should simply regard them as kin and refrain from killing or eating [meat]. Regarding "those born from impure elements": the father’s semen and the mother’s blood are both impure substances which combine...
"Born from a combination [of causes]" refers to what ordinary, ignorant people habitually practice; by contrast, this reveals that those of the Three Vehicles who possess wisdom do not eat it.
"Awakening to its stench" means perceiving its foul odor. "Obtaining it by taking life" means it cannot be called good.

"Perceiving the form and giving rise to consciousness" means that because one consumes meat, upon seeing the forms of deer, tigers, pigs, chickens, and so forth, one immediately gives rise to a conscious intent to slaughter them. As for the various devas...

Regarding those who discard many evil dreams: because they are not protected by devas and nāgas and are harassed by malevolent spirits, this conversely demonstrates that those who maintain the precepts and abstain from meat constantly experience auspicious dreams.
As for "tigers and wolves smelling their scent": because they possess the odor of flesh, they are frequently devoured by tigers and wolves.

Regarding the citation from the *Pañcapāda-rāja-sūtra* (The Sūtra of King Pañcapāda), among various records, it is most often cited from the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*. That text states: "In the past..."
The king of Vārāṇasī was named Māradarśaka. While he was out hunting and resting upon a mountain, a female lion, driven by desire, approached the king and had intercourse with him.
She subsequently gave birth to a son who had a human form with spotted feet. The lion presented him to the king;
once the king learned of this, he took him in and raised him, naming him Pāda-lekhita (Spotted-foot). Later, he succeeded to the royal throne. This king constantly made offerings...
He supported a rishi who would fly to the royal palace every day at mealtime. Later, because the rishi fell ill, he ceased eating and did not come.
There was a celestial being who worshipped a deity; he falsely assumed the guise of a rishi and came seeking meat, saying to the kitchen staff, "From now on, you must provide this daily.
Afterward, when the original rishi had not yet returned, they gave him the meat. How could the rishi [tolerate] this?
[The King] was reprimanded. The King said, "Yesterday you ate meat, and today you do not eat it again. How can you be so deceitful and lacking in integrity?
The Rishi replied, "I had an ailment yesterday and did not come. Who told you that I ate meat?
The Rishi then uttered a curse, saying, "For twelve years thereafter, you shall constantly eat human flesh. Having finished speaking, he departed and never returned. Subsequently, in the kitchen...
The cook prepared a meal, but lacking meat, he obtained a dead child and used it as food for the king. When the king noticed the extraordinary flavor, he questioned the kitchen staff;
they did not dare conceal the truth and fully recounted the preceding circumstances. Consequently, the king issued an edict stating that this meat must be provided daily.
Thereafter, the killings increased, and the people became resentful. The multitude desired to kill the king, but the king made a vow, saying: "It was not by my will..."

Having cultivated goodness, he has now attained the status of a king. All the merit from his offerings to the rishis, he now dedicates toward transforming his current conduct into that of a non-practitioner.
The rākṣasa speaks thus, and by this means, for twelve years he constantly eats human flesh (the origin of this account is very extensive;
here it is cited briefly, etc.). This serves as proof of the faults incurred by eating meat mentioned previously.

Regarding the statement "now, as for those who have gone far," it means that while ordinary fools mostly crave various meats (the character *shi* is pronounced lightly), this conversely reveals that the Sages possess wisdom and ultimately do not eat them.

This is the intended meaning of this precept. As for the citation from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Master Xuán says it is to bring forth the faults of those in this land who study Mahāyāna discourse yet consume wine and meat, showing how they are no different from the Mahāyāna monks of the Central Kingdom.
This refers to those in the Central Kingdom who study the Hīnayāna yet still consume fish and meat, taking wine and flesh as their practice and understanding;
such people are said not to be followers of the Mahāyāna. Not consuming wine and meat, being internally free from discrimination and attachment, constitutes the practice of the Mahāyāna.

Since they have not yet realized the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), what they speak with their mouths is merely the language of one studying the Mahāyāna; when one examines their actual practice and understanding, [it is otherwise].
They are not included among the "Great Unreclaimables" because they have not yet attained realization; they are not subsumed among the "Small Unreclaimables" because they violate the precepts.

Since they are excluded from both categories, they fall within the ranks of the butchers. As for those led by Yama, such as the *Mūrdha-śira* (Midday) Yakṣas and others who constantly consume flesh and blood and first boil great sinners—those of this present class are likewise so. This is in accordance with the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, as seen and heard in its lower sections.

One should not eat meat if there is doubt that it was killed for one's sake; that is to say, if this person habitually commits the ten unwholesome deeds, the meat from such a household must not be eaten.
If, however, they uphold the ten wholesome deeds, they certainly would not take the life of a sentient being for one's sake, and thus the meat may be eaten.

Regarding "places of great sacrifice," this refers to state ceremonies such as the grand ritual of worshipping at the suburban altars. This is a distinction made regarding the intent behind the meat: even if it was not specifically prepared for oneself, [the status of the donor determines its suitability].
Regarding the single individual: since one has now slaughtered for all beings, those who eat meat—even if they eat it themselves—are counted among those who have caused the slaughter;

therefore, it is not permitted. As for "relying on the teachings so that there is no meat to eat," this means that according to the aforementioned Vinaya teachings, one is only permitted to eat the three kinds of pure meat—those that are not seen, heard, or suspected [to have been killed specifically for oneself]. Since such meat is rare, [the practice] gradually...
Because it is prohibited and severed, this is called the "Right Abandonment of Eating Meat. Regarding its general agreement with the *Vinayamātṛkā*, that text states:

"If a person wishes to perform a sacrifice to the gods, they should form the intention: 'Whoever comes here should be given food,' maintaining a mind free of discrimination toward the sentient beings being slaughtered."

One should wait for all who come. If a bhikṣu knows that such meat should not be eaten—regarding the offense incurred by eating the remains of birds—it is clearly explained in the Vinaya that the remains of all birds and beasts may be taken if they are obtained auspiciously, provided that further expectation [of more] is not interrupted.
Only the remains of a lion may be taken without fault, because the expectation has been severed. According to this principle, one must personally witness the death before [taking it].

One may eat it because one knows with certainty that it is not the remains of birds or beasts; if one were to collect such remains, doubt would still not be avoided, as one would not know which beast’s remains they were.
As for the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, it does not even permit tasting the five pungent vegetables (*pañca-garaka*), much less consuming them.
This is an instance of using the lax to illustrate the urgent. From "In worldly custom" onwards, it uses the secular to illustrate the monastic.

Regarding the prohibition against selling wine or eating at the afternoon market (bù): the scriptures state that one who sells wine or eats at the afternoon market does not sacrifice to their ancestors.

This is because such actions show a lack of single-minded devotion to the ancestral spirits and may also bring illness upon the person. If this is so even for worldly people who merely protect their physical bodies, how much more so for those who have left the household life?
For them, the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom must certainly be protected. As for bhikṣus who eat meat, their own... [sentiment].

The failure of this approach is evident. Regarding these two paths: if one does not rely on the beauty of the oral teachings, one will greedily consume [the food], and it can be verified that this is not for curing illness;
thus, one remains utterly far removed from the path of outflow-free liberation (*anāsrava-mārga*).
The phrase "not reaching the *tīta*" distinguishes the nature of non-timely medicine (*akālabhaiṣajya*). Aside from the four exceptions, five original scriptural texts are cited;
as for the term "not cracked" (*buzhuopo*), the *Shuowen* states that *zhuo* means "high. When parching wheat, both ends rise up and swell (the character *yan* is pronounced *miao*);
one must not allow it to crack, much less when it has the aroma of a timely meal. As for "rock honey" (*śarkarā*), it is the juice of sugarcane from the Western Regions.
Pounded rice is placed inside [the vessel] and combined to form a black substance, resembling granulated sugar.
Regarding the current five types of this preparation made in various regions, such as those offered as tribute from the Yue region, there are fourteen kinds of syrups (*pāna*).

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and other texts, these are: first, *āmra*; second, *kolaka*; third, *dāḍima*; fourth, *tinduka*; fifth, *āmra* (apricot); sixth, *pārūṣaka*; seventh, *karkandhu*; eighth... [text fragment].
1. Plantain; 2. *Kāśika* (fine cloth); 3. *Tintiḍīka* (tamarind); 4. *Kharjūra* (date palm); 5. *Pūga-phala* (betel nut); 6. *Ikṣu* (sugarcane); 7.
*Harītakī* (myrobalan); 8. *Khāraparika* (alkaline juice); 9. Grape. If these are not purified by fire, their seeds are not destroyed.
If the juice is not purified by water, its flavor is not destroyed. If both are not purified, one must use fire purification rather than water purification.

[Regarding] purification: it is purified by water alone, not by fire; [in such cases], drinking is not permitted. When first purified by fire and subsequently by water, it is said that "having been purified, one may drink.

According to this principle, the application extends to all four types of medicinal substances (*catvāraḥ bhaiṣajyāḥ*). The *Yeyeshu* (Commentary on Karmas) states: "Although the text mentions 'liquids' (*pāna*), the meaning applies to all four medicines.
Just as clothing must be folded to change its color, or sandals must be worn by a lay attendant to conceal their fine appearance, so too with food and water."

It is classified as "pure" because it destroys flavor; it is the same [in this regard]. Regarding fermented grain wine (*kaṣāya*) that cannot be consumed as food or drink: this refers to the substance of the indeterminate consciousness (*avijñapti*).

Since it has transformed and lost its original nature as a received dharma (*dharmasamādāna*), it is no longer so. As for the term "wine-rain" (*surā-varṣa*) having already been formed, this is due to differences in regional colloquialisms.
This person calls "taste" *lāṅga*. If one tastes wine and it has a scent and flavor, one says there is "wine-rain.

Since the current sovereign has undergone a physical transformation and lost his sensory faculties, if he were to consume it, he would simply drink the wine; therefore, it is not appropriate [for him].

As for the molasses that has been scorched black, according to Dong Bai, it is still categorized as a "timely medicine" (*kālabhojya*). As for the *piṇḍaphala* (cluster fruit), it is common in the northern regions; its shape resembles a cherry, and its color— (Note: The source text appears to be truncated at the end.)
It is reddish-black in color and extremely sweet and delicious. Next, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* is cited to prove the permission [to consume it]:

"In the past, there was a person who wished to pay homage to the Buddha. He thought to himself, 'I must not go empty-handed. There are currently eight kinds of fermented liquors (aṣṭavidha-madya) which were drunk by the sages of old when they were about to die;

I shall take these to offer to the Buddha. When the Buddha received them, he preached the Dharma for him. Furthermore, the man intended to give them to the Saṃgha, but the monks did not dare to accept them."

Regarding "receiving": the Buddha permitted receiving [these drinks]. However, if they are capable of intoxicating a person, drinking them is strictly not allowed. The *Chao* (Excerpts) omits this. There are two types: Jambu and Bāluka;
these are excluded because they do not exist in this land. The rest is as stated in the text. The *Śāstra* (Treatise), Part II, explains them collectively.

All the aforementioned syrups must be clear and free from admixture with "timely food" (*kālabhojana*). As for the phrase "from the seventh day until drinking," this distinguishes the substance of the seven-day medicine (*saptāha-bhaiṣajya*). One should...

Regarding "medicines": according to the rules on medicines in the Vinaya, it is said that when the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, various bhikṣus fell ill during the autumn months and their complexions became haggard and withered.
The Buddha said, "I shall now permit you, O bhikṣus, to consume what kind of medicines? Thereupon, he reflected and thought:
"There are five kinds of medicines commonly used in the world that all people recognize, namely: ghee, oil, fresh butter," and so forth.
"Honey and rock honey. These are to be administered to the bhikṣus as food or as medicine, just like rice or parched rice;

they must not appear coarse. (The above is from the Vinaya text. Xuán says: "Because they have the sense of providing nourishment, they are 'food' (*āhāra*); because they have the urgency of curing ailments, [they are 'medicine']."
It is for medicinal purposes. Because one must not eat until the bowl is full, it says "like food" and so forth; because one eats only in small amounts, it says "not allowing coarseness to appear.

Regarding "molasses syrup" in the *Vinaya-mātṛkā*, this refers to sugarcane molasses. Since its inherent nature has not yet been discarded, the status of being a permitted substance (*dharmika*) is lost, and thus its consumption is not allowed.
However, if its essential nature has not been lost, its consumption is permitted. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* adds "fat."
Regarding "one kind": this refers to the allowance within the seven-day medicines for the consumption of one type, namely fat (*vasā*).

As for the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and other texts, according to the case of Śāriputra suffering from wind-disorder, the physician instructed him to consume five kinds of fat as listed in the text; yet the bhikṣus did not eat them.

He then addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha granted permission. Therefore, the text says: "One may receive [the food] at the proper time, strain it at the proper time, and cook it at the proper time according to the rules for oil and then consume it.

If one receives it at an improper time, strains it at an improper time, or cooks it at an improper time, one should not consume it. If one does consume it, one is to be dealt with according to the Dharma.

This means that meat is a food to be eaten at the proper time; if received at an improper time, it is not validly established as such. The ancient masters, having examined the Vinaya, saw that what is received at an improper time is not established as being for an improper time.

If one filters and boils [the substance], one incurs an offense. It was then stated that fat (*vasā*) is of the same category as the "time-medicine" (*kālika-bhaiṣajya*) and is not permitted to be taken for seven days.
Now, I cite the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü) as the primary text: among the "seven-day medicines," fat is added as one type.

In this passage of the *Mahāsāṃghika*, following the textual flow, it appears to serve as proof for the aforementioned seven-day medicines. Regarding the "four hundred and four diseases," the Sūtra says: "When one great element is disturbed, there are one hundred..."

First, regarding the affliction of illness: because the body is composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), there are four hundred and four types of diseases. "Miscellaneous illnesses" refers to those resulting from a combination of these three types of ailments.
"Treating with the aforementioned three medicines" means using the three medicines mentioned above in combination to treat them.

When the Buddha said that the procedure should be done in this way, it is said that Nanda saw stone honey being made; seeing rice being pounded and added into it, he became suspicious and did not dare [to eat it].

[They] prepared it as a seven-day medicine. The Buddha said: "The ritual procedure is as follows. To consume it is not an offense. Regarding those who drink it mixed with water, according to that text:
In the kingdom of Kośala, there was no place where laypeople offered water; they only offered water along with stone honey (*śarkarā*).

The group of six monks went there and ate only the stone honey, but did not drink the water. This likewise invited criticism, and they reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "From this day forward, I permit [the drinking of water]."

There are five types of people who eat stone honey (*śarkarā*). The first four are as explained in the *Śāstra* (the *Vinayavibhaṅga*). This present passage concerns the fifth type; this can be understood from the lower section of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.

Regarding the phrase "from the *Mahāsāṃghika* until it is accomplished," this is explained in terms of transformation. "Action" refers specifically to the act of kneading or forming [the mass]. This is the record of identification.
The text states: "If, within this meal-time, there is non-time [medicine] or seven-day medicine that has become pure, I shall accept it.

If one adds [the medicine] before midday but fails to perform the formal declaration (*vijñapti*), even if it subsequently transforms into clarified butter (*sarpis*), its consumption is not permitted; it is then termed impure (*aśuci*).

If one mistakenly avoids it and does not accept it—meaning that although it was previously declared, it later becomes pure, yet one avoids the clarified butter and fails to perform the acceptance (*parigraha*) in the presence of another person, nor recites the formula—it is likewise improper.
Purity is also termed impurity; thus, one should know that this refers to the post-attainment cognition (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) following the formal determination (*vijñapti*).

Regarding "the *sū* and *su* [vows] require receiving the precepts, yet receiving them at an improper time": this means that if one receives the precepts while containing food intended for daytime consumption, the reception is not valid.

Since the reception is invalid, the formal determination (*vijñapti*) is likewise not established. Regarding "both are established within the proper time": because both the reception and the formal determination are established, the character "ping" (並) is used to indicate their simultaneity. Thus it is said.
Regarding the passage beginning with "As for... (and so forth): "forcible plunder" refers to taking [honey] from bees by means of physical strength.
As for the Buddha accepting the honeycomb of a monkey that was free of bees, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (T. 1421), fascicle 28, states:

"In the past, there was a monkey who, while walking, saw a tree hollow containing ripe honey free of bees. It came to take the Buddha’s bowl; the bhikṣus blocked it and would not give it to him. He took it.
The Buddha said, "Do not prevent him; he has no ill intent. The monkey brought a bowl filled to the brim with honey to offer to the Buddha.
Knowing it was not yet pure, the Buddha did not accept it. The monkey, unable to understand the Buddha's intention, thought there were insects in it and looked around.
Seeing honey dripping from all four sides, he took it to the water's edge to wash it. The water seeped into the bowl and it became pure. Therefore—
In the future, he will serve the Buddha; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and later leave the household life to attain the path of an Arhat.
Based on this, once the taste has been destroyed by the splashing of water, greed will no longer increase. Since it is said that there are no bees, it is not an act of plundering.
Regarding the aforementioned "ripe honey without bees," there are two explanations. One says: when large bees come to eat the honey, they cause injury and damage.

Regarding this honey from bees: because the young bees fear it, they abandon it and depart. A second interpretation states that during the winter months, there may be excrement and filth within the hive;
if no one removes it, worms as large as a finger will arise and consume the honey, whereupon the bees abandon it.
Because what is taken now is of this kind, it is called "honey ripened without bees."
Regarding the phrase "four [categories] for as long as life lasts" (*yāvajjīva*) up to the mention of "food": *Gan* refers to sweet medicinal herbs such as *ren-ling* (Piper aurantiacum) and others.
According to the text in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, there are four propositions: first, all trees and the like that are unfit to be eaten are for as long as life lasts;

second, if they are fit to be eaten, they are "medicines for the time" (*kālabhaiṣajya*); third, the roots are "medicines for the time" while the stems are for as long as life lasts; fourth, the stems are "medicines for the time."
The roots are for life-long use. In the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), there is further a fourfold classification regarding raw and cooked [medicines]:
1. Both raw and cooked are "time-medicine" (*kālabhaiṣajya*), such as rice, wheat, and the like. 2. Both raw and cooked are "life-long" (*yāvajjīvika*), such as ginger, trees, and the like. 3.

Raw is "time-medicine," while cooked is "life-long," such as plums and sugarcane, and the like. 4. Raw is "life-long," while cooked is "time-medicine," such as almonds and taro, and the like. However...
Regarding the phrase "rendered fit for consumption" and so forth, this is a general explanation. All the aforementioned plants, such as roots and stalks, are innumerable and boundless;

they cannot be individually named or pointed out one by one. However, for the sake of those who eat, regardless of whether they are roots, stalks, branches, or leaves, whatever is included among the *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines taken at specific times) that is unfit [for immediate use] is subsumed under the category of *yāvajjīvika* (lifelong medicines). One should examine everything as it comes before one, rather than being restricted to only one or two items.

Regarding "determining the quantity according to the illness": this refers to the application of the rule. Although it is said that [the medicine] may be taken for seven days, if one has taken five or three [days] and the illness can be cured immediately, then because the conditions [for continued use] no longer exist, the legal status of the medicine expires;
even if the illness has not yet been fully eliminated, the medicinal drug is lost [as a permitted substance].

If there is no illness, or if one is not hungry, etc., taking even a single grain into the mouth after midday constitutes a formal offense (*sāpattika*). The same applies to oil, honey, and medicinal pastes, as explained above.

Regarding "the dosage according to the illness" and so forth: when the treatise mentions ghee and other substances, it refers to the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, which cites ghee specifically as an example of the method for preparation;

the rest should be understood by analogy. As for why lifelong medicines (*yāvajjīvika*) are not treated in this way, it is because their potency is weak, and thus they constitute a disease [in the sense that they require constant regulation].
This body possesses both body and mind; because it is subject to illness, [the rule] is permitted. Throughout one's life, these are not the same. The potency of the seven-day medicine is slight;

when the suffering of illness arises, it must be relinquished. If there is no adventitious illness—that is, no disease resulting from the disharmony of the four great elements—and furthermore, if there is neither hunger nor thirst, [it is so].
Baoyun says this is called the "primary illness," meaning it refers to chronic ailments. The Treatise states that there are two kinds of illness: first, the adventitious...

The four great elements are in harmony and free from disease. Second, regarding the primary affliction of being tormented by hunger and thirst (the *Xuánjì* notes that the fetters of the three poisons are called "old diseases"):

according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, pure *kaṣāya* (fermented grain liquor) may be drunk. This means that while the preceding [text] only distinguished between salty, bitter, pungent, and sweet, it did not clarify the sour taste;
now this is cited to clarify it. Because the taste of *kaṣāya* is sour, people do not crave it, and thus its drinking is permitted. From "As for what was said above" up to "the world."

This is a summary. Regarding the determination of its essence according to its specific function, this means it is distinguished without reference to the general categories of phenomena (*dharma*). If discussed in terms of the categories of phenomena, among the three aggregates (*skandha*), it belongs to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

It is comprised of the eight derivative objects (*bhautika*) produced by the primary elements: the four primary elements (*mahābhūta*) which act as creators, and the four derivative objects (*upādāya-rūpa*) which are created.

Among the three types of form, it is subsumed under that which is visible and possesses resistance (*sapratigha*). Among the four nutriments (*āhāra*), it is the nutriment of physical food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).

Although it is conventionally formed from the eight sensory objects (*aṣṭau viṣayāḥ*), if one takes the aspect of its meaning as providing sustenance and benefit, it is specifically identified as having the three—odor, flavor, and tangibility—as its substance;
thus, it is merely a form that is invisible yet resistant (*anidarśana-sapratigha-rūpa*). The passage beginning with "Now there is... serves to refute this.
"Fools" refers to those who are deluded regarding the teachings. "Apricot soup" and so forth refer to the substances being consumed. "Arising from within one's own mind" means [arising] from oneself.
This is one's own greedy mind. As for "vainly relying on the holy teachings," it refers to falsely relying on those scriptural records that permit [medicines] for the sick;
this is no different from eating after midday. When people see someone eating after midday has passed, they know it is certainly not the Dharma, even if it has some slight efficacy.

Now, as for these types of apricot decoctions and the like, by their very nature they are categorized as medicines to be taken for life (*yixin yao*). They are permitted when there is illness; however, since there is currently none...

To provide alcohol as an offering when the conditions for it are not met misleads later students; as this is passed down through successive generations, it violates the teachings and incurs transgressions, resulting in no possibility of liberation.
Therefore, it is said that "the stream of sin flows through long ages."

Regarding the "six flavors of determination" (*ṣaḍ-rasa-niścaya*): the opening commentary states that these are first, bitter; second, sour; third, sweet; fourth, pungent; fifth, salty; and sixth, bland.
"Determination" (*niścaya*) refers to using these six flavors to determine the dosage of the five kinds of medicinal herbs. Regarding the phrase "from clarity to the seeds":
Regarding the phrase "the five kinds of measures, up to the great allowance," this indicates the names of the five measures: first, the measure based on time (i.e., *tatkālika* medicine);

second, the measure based on the watch (i.e., *yāmika* medicine); third, the seven-day measure (i.e., *saptāhika* medicine); fourth, the measure for the duration of life (i.e., *yāvajjīvika* medicine);

and fifth, the great allowance measure (i.e., the ash, earth, and water from excrement and urine, which is categorized as a sub-division within the medicine for the duration of life). All worldly remedies that alleviate illness generally receive the name "medicine," but [only] by means of these five.

This encompasses [all things] without exception. Thus, one knows that all things are fully included. The commentary states, "There are five kinds of medicines," which refers to Paramārtha’s commentary.
These five types are as previously explained. Regarding the statement, "from sweet to those not permitted to be eaten":
licorice (*yancao*) is for life-long use; among the sour, the juice of *āmalaka* fruit is also for life-long use; among the pungent, ginger and the like are for life-long use.
The bitter taste refers to all bitter and astringent flavors; these are medicines for the duration of one's life. Question: Previously it was said there are six tastes;

why now do you say that pungent, salty, and bland are not seen? Answer: Pungent is restricted to salt alone and is only for the duration of one's life. Bland applies to all four types of medicine; therefore, it is not specifically discussed here.
The rest of the text may be understood accordingly. Regarding the phrase "all... to their use": dividing day and night each into five periods refers to the daytime.

Regarding the "five [periods] with the night five": as the watches of the day successively shift toward the later hours, from dawn until the second watch, one may take the medicine only until the end of the first watch;
