At this time, one may take [the medicine] at will, whether by day or night, as it is essential; thus, one incurs no fault by taking it oneself.
Therefore, it is said to be "greatly opened. This is something discarded by worldly people and not an object of their emotional attachment.

The note states that there will certainly be no one to provide a standard for its use, meaning that in a place where there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who makes things permissible) due to the principle of emptiness, one simply takes it oneself. Regarding the third transformation, it says: "The three reach the form."

Furthermore, speaking in terms of the substance (*dravya*): according to the perspective of its visible form, once the substance of the medicine has changed, it is no longer permissible to consume it.

Other details are as stated in the text regarding "those who arrive at the four times," which distinguishes the substances by their mutual blending. According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, among the four types of medicine, *kālika* (timely) medicine is the strongest, while *yāvajjīvika* (lifelong) medicine is the weakest.
According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, however, strength is determined by the quantity of the medicinal portion: that which is greater is strong, and that which is lesser is weak.

Weak. Now, first we shall clarify the four divisions and five phrases. First, mixing *kālika* (medicines for the proper time) with *kālika*; second, mixing *akālika* (medicines for improper times) with *kālika*; third, mixing *saptāhika* (medicines for seven days) with *kālika*;
fourth, mixing *yāvajjīvika* (medicines for life) with *kālika*. All of these are to be consumed as *kālika* medicines; this is because the *kālika* [category] is strong by virtue of its timing.

2. Non-time [medicines] combined with non-time medicines, seven-day medicines combined with non-time medicines, and lifetime medicines combined with non-time medicines—all are received as non-time medicines.
3. Seven-day medicines and lifetime medicines combined with seven-day medicines are received and consumed as seven-day medicines.
4. Lifetime medicines combined only with lifetime medicines are received and consumed as lifetime medicines. Now, the *Chao* (Excerpts) cites the *Śāstra* based on the majority of cases.

The division of various strong [medicines] relies on the mutual requirements of the medicinal portions; this must be clearly understood. The Vinaya takes the "essence" (*rasa*) as its basis, speaking in terms of taking what is above to assist what is below.

Regarding the phrase "if administered at the proper time," it first clarifies the characteristics of the seven-day [medicine]. This is explained by the fact that the harmonizing [effect] arises from administration within those seven days. The phrase "as follows" serves to manifest these characteristics.

The same applies to the analysis of medicines for the duration of life (*yāvajjīvika*); this can be understood from the text. Regarding the phrase "if for the remainder of one's life," it clarifies [the rules for long-term use].
The auxiliary medicinal substances for the *kālika* (time-medicine) category can be understood by their distinct characteristics.

If the quantities of the ingredients are equal, they are designated according to the primary substance based on similarity of potency; examples include *pr̥śniparṇī*, *vāśā*, *chāgala-śr̥ṅgī-pānaka*, *dhūmra-śyāmā*, and white-wood pills and powders, as described in the text.

The second major section concerns the purification of the site (*śuddhasthāna*). Regarding the phrase "from two up to the gate": this refers to citing the title and indicating the number [of sub-sections], which can be understood accordingly.

Regarding the phrase "from one up to 'also'": this precisely clarifies the intent behind establishing the *kappiya-kuṭi* (the pure house). "Begging for alms" (*piṇḍapāta*) refers to seeking food, as explained in the subsequent text.

As for the phrase "only opened [this practice] because of starving to death": Xuánzàng says that according to the *Bhaiṣajyavastu* (Section on Medicine) of the Vinaya, there was a bhikṣu who took medicine...
Regarding emetic medicine: because there was no pure ground (*śuci-bhūmi*) within the monastery, food was not stored therein at all.

This patient, suffering from hunger and exhaustion at night and on the verge of death, waited for the break of dawn, hoping that alms-food would arrive from outside. When the patient had already died, [the monks] reported this matter to the Buddha.

Consequently, the Buddha permitted the demarcation of separate areas within the same boundary. Since they were both inside the monastery, they shared the same boundary; thus, one may designate a quiet corner in a peripheral room as such.
This is a separate section. Various records of the past and present all ask: "By demarcating a pure area (*śuddhasthāna*), how many faults and afflictions are avoided? The answer is:

"If one does not demarcate a pure area and stays overnight within the same boundary, there is the fault of 'storing food overnight' (*antar-vasati*). Furthermore, if one cooks food within the boundary, there is the fault of 'cooking inside' (*antara-pāka*).
Now, if the demarcation is completed, these two faults are avoided. It is further asked: "Do these two faults apply only with respect to the boundary? [The text continues: "Ga..."

Regarding the monastery (*ārāma*), there is also [the issue of] "staying overnight" (*sahavāsa*) and "cooking" (*pacana*). The answer explains that this is indeterminate. One master says: "Within the boundary (*sīmā*), there is staying overnight and cooking; however, with respect to the monastery, these do not exist.

This is because the text states that one must not stay overnight or cook within the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*). A second master says: "With respect to the monastery, these exist; with respect to the boundary, they do not.
This is because the text speaks of designating a pure area (*śuddhasthāna*) within the monastery. Neither of the two explanations above constitutes the correct meaning.
Now it is said: "The *lān* boundary and the communal boundary both exist; they are neither restricted to the *lān* nor restricted to the boundary. For the Vinaya text states:

"One must not stay overnight or cook within the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*). This refers to the boundary defined by the enclosure of the courtyard, and is not restricted to that which is established through formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*).

Even if one were to perform the ritual action to establish it, if there is no physical characteristic of a courtyard, it does not constitute a place for storing provisions, and thus there is no offense. This applies even if the courtyard is fully enclosed.
Before they have been formally enclosed, the individual *saṃghārāma* is also considered "enclosed" (*sūcita*) because it can give rise to transgressions.

According to the following passage, which states that [a place] has many fences or no fences at all, food is not included [within the boundary]; thus we know that when the characteristics of the enclosure are fully established, food is indeed included.
The section beginning with the explanation of the *Vimalakīrti* is the formal explanation of the name. Regarding the phrase "karma is the cause of defilement," it is because...
To harbor greed for the same food violates the teachings. Because it is caused by the fault of "cooking overnight," it will inevitably bring about the retribution of evil fruits;
therefore, this food is designated as impure (*aśuci*). As for the statement that "this is pure from the perspective of its conditions," this is a secondary refutation of ancient errors.

The ancients claimed that "pure" was a name established in contrast to "impure. Now, however, we state that this refers to the specific conditions of this pure ground (*śucibhūmi*), which is entered through the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure).
The method of grinding is completed within [the monastery]; thereafter, one is exempt from the fault of having to cook overnight. This is called "pure" (*śuci*);

it is not a term established by contrast with "impure food" (*aśuci*). It is named "pure" because it renders things clean and bright. Second, regarding the enumeration of items, the headings are as stated in the text.

As for the phrase "first, the characteristics," the commentary states: "The kitchen quarters are like those that have courtyards. This means that although the characteristics of the monastery courtyard—

It is not enclosed; however, the kitchen building is surrounded on all four sides by a courtyard. If a bhikṣu stays overnight within this kitchen while eating, he incurs the same offense as if he were staying together [with a woman].
The same applies to walls, moats, and fences. These are what are called "such characteristics.

If a bhikṣu stays overnight inside [an enclosure] that is fully enclosed, he incurs the fault in every case; therefore it is said, "it is thus. Regarding "forming the characteristic through association," it means that—[the text continues with: not...

It is necessary that all four sides have walls and all four sides have fences; if one side has a wall and one side has a fence, or if there are fences on two sides and so forth, as long as the four boundaries are completely joined together, there is the fault of "cooking overnight," and it thus fulfills the definition of a "perimeter" (*zhou*).
Regarding the second point, "the purity of the donor": the "purity of the donor" refers to the patron (*dānapati*), as will be explained in detail in the subsequent section.
As for the phrase "food consisting of another's property," this refers specifically to food.

Since the location belongs to the Saṃgha, when a layperson brings items such as rice or flour to a monastic residence to provide for a ritual feast, and does not formally entrust them to the Saṃgha, the layperson remains the owner.

Even if one stays overnight together [with them], there is no offense; this can be understood from the citation of the Vinaya text provided below. Regarding the second point, "the location is another's property":
this phrase refers to the site itself, which belongs to a layperson (*gṛhapati*). Within it, the utensils for eating belong to the Saṃgha.

This is similar to how nowadays donors construct small private monasteries or *ārāmas* for the Saṃgha; although they intend for it to be completed for the Saṃgha, it is enclosed by a surrounding courtyard on all four sides.

"Yet it has not been decided whether [the food] has been permanently discarded; this then belongs to another. If the donor has food within [the dwelling], there is no fault for a bhikṣu to stay overnight.
Thus, the subsequent citations of scriptural evidence can be understood accordingly. "All three types of eating places are appropriate"—this phrase is easy to understand.
"These three," and so forth, is the concluding explanation. Regarding the statement "now many rely on the stomach," etc., this refutes the ancient masters. The ancients said:

A temple is constructed by laypeople; according to its origin, it belongs to others and is thus designated as "pure" (i.e., not subject to the rules of monastic property). Now, the Master raises an objection: "If that were so, then all monasteries would not belong to the Sangha.

Since there is a general designation of 'purity' regarding property belonging to others, what need is there to separately designate a pure kitchen? Therefore, we know that once something has been given to the Sangha, it immediately becomes the property of the Sangha.
The previous mention of "property belonging to others" was merely based on the state prior to the decision [of donation]; once it is given to the Sangha, the prohibition against taking it is lifted.

Furthermore, regarding the citation of scriptural evidence, the phrase "if the portion has not yet been assigned" means that although the King relinquished the use [of the rice] to the Saṃgha, he had not yet fully given the rice for the porridge to the bhikṣus;

rather, he merely entrusted its management to them. When the bhikṣus transported the rice onto the threshing floor and stayed there overnight, they feared they might commit an offense and thus raised their doubts with the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "If the portion has not yet been assigned, because it does not yet fully belong to the Saṃgha."
Because it is the property of a donor, there is no offense. Regarding "once the distribution is finished, it should not be placed [overnight]":

this means that once a certain amount of rice has been assigned to the Saṃgha, it belongs to the Saṃgha and is no longer the property of another. If one stays overnight with it on the threshing floor, one commits a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) for "storing indoors.
Regarding "the king’s passing away, etc.": this refers to when the previous gift belonged to King Bimbisāra; although it had not yet been formally assigned to him, [it was still his].
"He was the patron. Now that the King has passed away, there is no longer a patron. If bhikṣus stay overnight [in his residence], do they incur an offense? The Buddha said:

"Since King Aśoka has taken the place of King Śreṇika, he is the patron; thus there is no offense. The note states: "Based on this precedent, all other cases where [staying] would otherwise constitute an offense are to be judged accordingly."
That is to say, if one has not actually given everything away in its entirety, the Sangha incurs no offense.

However, if one has already definitively given it to the Sangha and yet falsely claims otherwise, one is merely deceiving oneself and burdening oneself with guilt. Above, rice was cited as an example; by this principle, all other types of goods are to be treated accordingly.

As for the passage concerning "the Śramaṇas of the Mahāsāṃghika school, the Brāhmaṇas, and so forth": this section of the text concerns a donor who, at night, brings food and utensils to present to the Saṃgha.
Once the donor has resolved to relinquish them, they no longer belong to the layperson and thus belong to the Saṃgha.

If one were to let them stay overnight, that would constitute *antar-vasita* (storing within); likewise, if one were to cook them in this place, it would constitute *antar-pakva* (cooking within). Therefore, it is known [that these rules apply].
When objects are situated in both [of these two places], they belong to the Saṃgha; this is identical to the legal status of the Saṃgha.
Regarding the third point, "purity in three places," the phrase "that which is divided and arrives at the three places" refers to the case of a managing bhikṣu.

This means that when a donor entrusts a bhikṣu with the responsibility for overseeing the construction of a monastery, it is called "managing. It is precisely through this that the *ārāma* (monastery) is established.
[The procedure] is concluded. One monk who knows the Dharma, or the donor, shall designate three or five adjacent dwellings as the place for preparing food at the appropriate time;
this is called the "pure kitchen" (*viśuddha-maṇḍapa*). Thus it is said that the site is designated as pure. Next, regarding the citation from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:

the preceding passage from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* merely mentions the construction of a monastery (*ārāma*), but the designation of the site is not clearly explained; if monks are already residing there, the designation is not valid.
Now, I shall cite the text of the *Cīvara-vastu*. No one has ever attained [the status of] "one who has already resided" (*vihārin*) merely by residing;

if one has already resided for a period, then the formal act of assignment (*uddeśa*) cannot be accomplished there. According to that Vinaya: At one time, a certain Brahmin householder built a monastery for the Saṃgha and instructed Upāli to first perform the formal assignment for the Saṃgha, saying, "The Saṃgha has not yet resided here.
He performed the assignment during the first watch of the night, and it was successfully established. If, however, they have already resided...

The first watch of the night is merely called the "monastic residence" (saṃgha-vihāra); it is not called "pure" (śuci). The commentary on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* regarding the "appearance of light" (*prabhāta-lakṣaṇa*) is intended to exclude ambiguity.
This means that in the *Dharmaguptaka*, both the protection of robes and the protection of food are defined by the appearance of light as the boundary for committing an offense.

Thus, the textual judgment here is limited. If one were to follow other schools such as the *Mahāsāṃghika*, the passage concerning the first watch would then become a matter belonging to another sect. This would be excessive.
Because it is urgent, one does not take [the formal act]. This commentary distinguishes this point.

Regarding the passage in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* stating "after a new dwelling has been built," this clarifies that the monks' residence according to the *Pañcavargika* is established even if the dawn has not yet appeared; however, if the dawn has already appeared, it is not permissible.
This is brought forward to show by contrast that it shares the same intent as the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, while the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is too hasty regarding the first watch of the night.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* is based on the light; since it is similar to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and can be relied upon for practice, this [passage] is cited.

Why then was the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, being too hasty and not followed, included within the *An-shi-chao* (The Extracts of An)? Answer: There are two explanations. First, according to various commentaries, it is interpreted as a distinction. Regarding the wearing of robes, that [Mahāsāṃghika] rule...

The protection is established during the first watch of the night; this is for the sake of a superior arrangement and purification. To pass beyond the first watch is urgent. Regarding the clothing and food of the first watch, there are two different conditions: the urgent and the relaxed.
Although one may not act strictly according to them, it is necessary to cite and demonstrate them. According to the interpretation from the region of Shu: [text follows].

This excerpt from the *Cīvara-vastu* contains elements of selection and omission. If one were to establish the boundaries at the beginning of the night and then fail to act accordingly, there would be no textual basis in the *Pañcavargika* for the following:
measuring the boundaries with a cord to determine "this much" space for the monks' residence and "this much" space for the pure dwelling.

For this reason, it must also be accepted; one simply changes the expression "the first watch of the night" to the phrase "the appearance of light," and that suffices (you may reflect on this as you see fit).

Next, regarding the citation from the *Vinayavibhaṅga* concerning "the time when the pillar is first erected": it says that when a monk strikes the pillar, he declares, "At this spot, a pure house shall be built for the Saṃgha.

This is stated three times. Once the procedure for one pillar is thus completed, the same applies to all other pillars. If one is unable to perform the formal assignment for each individual pillar, [the following applies].

It may also be performed by designating a single pillar. If it concerns a completed structure—that is, an existing building—it follows the same procedure as previously described for designating a site.
Regarding "village elders," these are those of advanced age among the laity; if they do not understand, the monks should instruct them.
While the designation of a site applies to all seven assemblies, the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is restricted solely to the Saṃgha.

Regarding the four *jñapti-dvitīya* (one motion and one announcement) and two *śuddha* (pure) [karmas], as for the phrase "four [types] up to the ground": this refers to not questioning the length of time one has resided there.

That is to say, regarding what is established by these *jñapti-dvitīya* [procedures], there is no distinction made as to whether monks have resided there for many years or only recently; it is sufficient that the boundary be established, and it is not the same as [the requirement for] a formal assignment (*āveśana*).

A formal assignment must necessarily be performed in a new location where people have subsequently come to reside and have passed through the summer retreat (*varṣā*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "removing the bhikṣus," the Vinaya says: "All... [and so on].

A bhikṣu thought to himself, "Should the bhikṣus' quarters be demarcated as a pure area (*śuddhasthāna*)? He addressed the Buddha, saying, "They should be so made, with the exception of the bhikṣus' [private] rooms.
The same applies to the quarters of bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and even śrāmaṇerikās. This also applies to shrines of spirits and deities.

This is also like the case of establishing a *kappiya-bhūmi* (as the Vinaya text states). Based on this, ancient masters have offered differing interpretations and judgments. The first [interpretation] states:

Once the *kappiya-bhūmi* has been established, a bhikṣu must not sleep within the clean kitchen; therefore, it says "remove" (*apakaḍḍhati*). The second states: This does not mean removing the bhikṣu.
This is a phrase used for understanding and resolving a difficulty (*paryanuyoga*), meaning that when it was previously said "remove the bhikṣu," I have already—
I do not yet know for certain. Aside from the quarters of the bhikṣus, are there other buildings—down to the shrines of spirits and deities—that may be established as *śuddhasthāna* (pure grounds)?
For now, our Master retains the initial interpretation and does not adopt the latter view, as has been extensively refuted in various commentaries;
fearing prolixity, I shall not record it here. The *Karmasūtra* asks: "Once the *śuddhasthāna* has been demarcated, bhikṣus are not permitted to stay overnight within it. And so forth.

Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Where the smoke from temple dwellings does not cease and various kinds of food are constantly prepared, these are made for the sake of human beings;
this is called impure food. A practitioner who practices according to reality should not consume such food. (Cited from Chapter [X])

*Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*, Scroll Nine). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If there is a monastery where smoke and fire are never extinguished, one who practices according to reality should not feel anger toward such food" (from Volume Four).
Regarding the *Rakṣā-śuddhi-sūtra* and other texts, they say: "The Buddha was walking with Ānanda when they encountered a pond.
To the east, west, south, and north, its depth was forty *li* throughout. Within it were tiny insects, shaped like tadpoles, their color..."

It was black as ink. The Buddha said, "These are the monks of the worlds of the ten directions who, having become angry over impure food, have fallen into this foul and filthy pool of excrement and urine.

Their subsequent retribution is as cited in the *Śāstra* (the *Shō*), etc. Regarding the mention of those in charge of administrative affairs (*karmadāna*), the *Hujing jing* (Sutra on Protecting Purity) states:
"There was a bhikṣu who had newly realized arhatship. Although he possessed a body with residual karmic bonds, he suffered from diarrhea and dysentery. [He was] in the dark..."
While using the latrine, he saw a bhikṣu groaning by its side. The arhat questioned him, and he replied, "I was originally a bhikṣu.
Because I was in charge of administrative affairs, I handled the Sangha’s pure food and gave impure food to the Sangha. Consequently, I am now born in this place for over five hundred years.
I have not heard the sound of water or broth. When I wish to go toward the latrine to take up some impurity, the ghost of that latrine strikes me so that I cannot move forward."

The Han [monks] assembled the community of monks to offer prayers and blessings; only then were they permitted to eat the food from the latrine (and so forth). Regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts, the origins of these accounts are largely the same.
In the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, it is said that various nāgas, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, attained the knowledge of past lives and became aware of their former existences.
Some had been relatives of the Saṅgha, while others, due to the conditions of hearing the Dharma, entered the monastery and ate the food of the Saṅgha; yet now they receive this evil retribution.

The *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra* and other scriptures state that those who have taken the form of a snake dwell within trees; when the tree is consumed by fire, they experience intense suffering and so forth.

Generally speaking, this refers to the precepts and exhortations of the present Master. In the lower section of the *Pañcaśata-praśna*, the general meaning of the *nidāna* (circumstantial origin) is as follows:
the character "guài" (pronounced shè lì fǎn) denotes the manner of a strange or startling collision.

Regarding the two types of protection from impurity (*pariśuddhi*): first, as for "protection from evil contact" (*pāpasaṃsarga*), this refers to the fact that eminent monks who have transcended the world do not permit manual labor.

Since they themselves do not perform such work, how could their hands even think of touching it? To touch it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; the retribution it invites is evil. Because one incurs evil through such contact, it is called "evil contact.

Furthermore, if one takes hold of something oneself without having received it [from another], this is also termed "evil contact. As for the phrase "reaching ten": [this refers to the accumulation of offenses].

First, citing the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: "It is neither a defiled touch nor an evil [offense]. This refers to giving from an impure vessel or due to an error regarding the food; it merely resembles the appearance of an evil touch.
However, because at the time of giving one gives with a single-minded focus to the other, and subsequently washes it clean and places it within a monastic vessel, there is no evil touch."
Regarding the instruction "to hand over according to this": following the above text, one should hand it over with a single-minded focus; thus, there is no principle for allowing defiling contact.

If there is leftover rice, food, or tea remaining on the bottom of the bowl beneath the vessel, and if one has not yet resolved to abandon them but still hopes to use them in the future, one must place them safely on the bed and have a *karmadāna* (attendant) take them away. If one hands them over personally, [the same care must be taken].
That is precisely what is called "an improper touch. Next, the *Pañcavargika* is cited: "This is a touch that is not improper;

if a bhikṣu receives [the item] and carries it out after having accepted it, since there was no *kappiya-kāraka* (a 'pure person') and the bhikṣu acted as the receiver himself, he touches it without committing an offense; therefore, it is not improper. Next, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is cited: "This is both improper and a touch.
This refers to when a *kappiya-kāraka* holds the item with impure hands. The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) further explains the meaning of the preceding passage.
As for the single Elder who becomes "impure": when the attendant first takes up pure food, it adheres to his hands;

because the lingering odor of the previously held defiled food remains, the Elder is called "defiled" (*duṣṭasparśa*), while the others are called "pure," as the trace of the defiled odor has been exhausted.
If the attendant lowers the food and places it into the vessel, the mixing of the pure and the impure is termed "defilement."
Regarding "shaking and selecting" (*dǒu jiǎn*) all that is impure: this refers to the aforementioned state of being unmoving. If one were to select (*jiǎn*) the center, it would remain;

however, because one now shakes and moves them, they become disordered—this is precisely what is meant by "all that is impure. According to the commentary, the various signs for selecting food that can be distinguished are as follows:
one recognizes and discerns whether something is pure or touched [by an impure hand]. If it is pure, one retains it; if it is touched, one discards it.
Remove it. If they are intermingled such that one cannot distinguish between the defiled and the pure, then replace them all at once.

As for the instruction to have someone clear away what is beneath one's feet, this is due to specific causes and conditions; it is not that contact is established through those conditions. One simply removes that spot because everything outside of it is not considered "contact.
If there are urgent difficulties and the like—meaning, for instance, being pursued by malicious people or fleeing from the threat of wild beasts—even if...

Stepping over them does not constitute an offense of contact, because there is no intentional mind [to commit it]. The subsequent point regarding "difficult circumstances" means that in all such cases, there is no transgression.
This also applies by way of circumstance when one forgets to cover food vessels and the like during rain; thus, it does not constitute an offense of impure contact.
As for the various jars of ghee and oil, these refer to pure ghee and oil, as well as the seven-day ghee and oil, which are to be kept together in one place. Regarding sugarcane, bamboo, and reeds...
Regarding those who come: when sugarcane is made into stone honey (śarkarā), bamboo and reeds are used to make containers for food; these too are placed within the clean kitchen (*śucy-āgāra*).
Setting aside for now the matter of placing sugarcane, bamboo, and reeds, let us speak briefly of the characteristics of whether butter-oil (*sarpis-taila*) becomes "touched" (*spṛṣṭa*) or not.
As for one who mistakenly brings a pure oil jar—meaning a seven-day oil jar that has already undergone the formal ritual (*adhikāra*)—it is placed inside.

Within the purified area (*pariśuddha-bhūmi*), a bhikṣu must take [the items] himself. If it is a vessel for purified oil that has not yet been consecrated (*adhivāsita*), only a lay attendant (*upāsaka*) may carry it;
it is not permissible for a bhikṣu to do so. If he grasps it, it constitutes an act of contact (*sparśana*).

Now, suppose a bhikṣu originally intended to carry a seven-day oil vessel, but by mistake, he brought a vessel of purified oil. If others see him coming and do not immediately speak out [to stop him], [it is a fault].
This means that when a bhikṣu sees [an error] but cannot speak up immediately, he says to the other person, "Why have you brought pure oil by mistake?
Having gone there and asked, if the other replies, "This is seven-day oil," the bhikṣu knows it is an error and places it on the ground. Only then does he say to them, "This is a jar of pure oil.
Regarding the phrase "one who may not utter the name": this refers to the state prior to placing it on the ground, while it is still [in the other's possession].

While it is in one's hand, one must not yet say to the other person, "This is pure oil," for that would constitute an unwholesome touch (*duṣṭa-sparśa*). Therefore, one may still receive it for seven days;

this is explained in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) itself: because it was taken by mistake, no unwholesome touch has occurred, and subsequently, by applying the formal ritual (*vidhi*), it becomes valid as a seven-day acceptance.
If a layperson does not understand how to take pure oil—meaning that since it is pure oil...

Regarding the "unconsecrated" (anadhiṣṭhita) state: one must have a lay attendant (karmadāna) take it; a bhikṣu may not hold it himself, for by holding it, he would incur the offense of physical contact (spraṣṭavya).

Now, if a layperson goes into the consecrated quarters (śucigṛha) and mistakenly brings back seven-day oil, this is also treated according to the aforementioned rule—this refers to the same ritual procedure as before.
The note regarding the loss of the oral instruction means that this seven-day oil should originally not be allowed to be held by a layperson; if they do hold it...
This constitutes contact. Since this is currently a case of confusion or error, although there is no offense despite the contact, one must not touch it again after it has been placed on the ground.
Once a bhikṣu has received it from the hands of a pure person, he must perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) again before another person, because the previous ritual has lapsed.

However, its efficacy merely continues from the preceding day. Regarding the "sugarcane, bamboo, and *veḷu* (bamboo)," these were not previously clarified; they must now be briefly explained. That is to say, sugarcane...
It resembles [the character] "zhú" (bamboo). The original intention was to have the bhikṣu go and fetch bamboo [matting], yet he has now mistakenly brought sugarcane instead.
The ritual procedure is the same as in the preceding text; although he touched the cane, because it was an error, there is no offense. As stated in the Xuánjì:

Bamboo and *zhú* (or *zhú*) may be used to make vessels for holding things. If a bhikṣu mistakenly takes one up and later makes it into a vessel, it does not constitute an offense of impure contact (*duṣṭasparśa*).

Now, examine this explanation in detail; it is greatly erroneous. Reflect upon this. As for the remaining sections below, they are explained in detail in the *Zábiàn* (Miscellaneous Discernment) and so forth. Thus it is said.
Regarding "vessels that are pure," there are five types: first, vegetables; second, plates; third, beds; fourth, boats; and fifth, carts.
As for the plate, it is defined by its circular shape; it possesses the significance of containing food. Regarding the two types, carts and boats, they lack oxen [as draft animals];

because they remain stationary on the ground, they constitute vessels. If one touches a vessel, it is equivalent to touching food. The note states that "due to specific circumstances, sitting is permitted" refers to eating while on a journey.

At that time, as there was no separate seating available, he was accommodated by curving [the space] for him to sit at the head of the assembly. Should he speak or move, it would constitute a physical contact (*sparśa*).
"Tiered platform" (*zàn*) refers to a loft; the textual characteristics are clear. Regarding the seventeen types [of vessels], their names are listed separately (*et cetera*).
As for the example of the boat not moving forward: when a boat leaves the water, it is called a "vessel"; likewise, when a cart leaves its oxen, it is also called a "vessel. (Commentary)

Regarding the statement that "one may not [touch] because the ox is present": this is said out of fear that people, seeing the ox not separated from the cart, might claim it is not a vessel and thus touch it;
now it is said that one may not, because [the ox] is not being used. Even if the ox is present, it is still called a vessel; if it moves, it immediately constitutes a violation.

Regarding the phrase "ten kinds of purity," first the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is cited, which distinguishes [purity] based on the characteristics of carrying food and its associated defilement; there is also the "life-preserving float."
[As for] "crossing water," the novice Śāmaṇera Jìngěr was [involved]. The Buddha said: "Have a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) place it upon a bag to cross.
Once they have reached the shore, do not touch it again; have the pure person take hold of it once more. If it is carried away by the current, it is permitted for a bhikṣu to take hold of it.

Regarding "that which may be eaten according to the *Mahāsāṃghika*," this refers to the same text as the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. If pure roasted flour (*piṣṭa*) is placed in an impure vessel, one may scoop it out from within.

If one obtains food, it is to be discarded in the same manner as placing it in the bowl here. Regarding items such as rice and congee, although they may be touched while assisting others, this does not constitute an offense;

for they are either pure by circumstance (*pratyaya-śuddha*) or pure by nature (*svabhāva-śuddha*). The text is very clear on this point. As for the passage from "The fourth" to "taking," it is another miscellaneous explanation.
"Evil persons" refers to bhikṣus who have broken the precepts; with an evil mind, they cause the Sangha to obtain what is impure.

It is food. Regarding "scattering seeds oneself" and so forth: because it involves movement, there is no contact. Regarding "uphill slope": the *Shuowen* states that it refers to a place of danger and peril. "Assisting by supporting or grasping" and so forth does not constitute an offense.
Regarding "taking what is pure while carrying [it]" in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: this proves that assisting by supporting or grasping is permissible in all such cases.

Regarding "touching with one's own hand is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing)": this refers to the fact that touching constitutes an offense of wrongdoing because there is no [permissible] cause. There is [a rule regarding] wearing [robes].
Regarding "medicines that exceed [the limit]": in various records, it is simply stated that they are permitted for consumption because there is an ailment;

this is to avoid public censure and the fear that others might imitate such behavior, thus requiring them to be taken in a secluded place while revealing the nature of the medicine. Some commentators claim these are substances such as expired ghee or oil, but this is incorrect.
Now, the Venerable Jing-shui states: in the text on the rules for medicine, it is permitted for a bhikṣu who is ill to consume medicines that have exceeded [their shelf life].
"Medicine" refers to leeks, garlic, scallions, and onions. One must consume them in a secluded place; furthermore, they are "defiling and conforming dharmas.

Within seven days [of consuming them], one must not go to the kitchen of the monastic community, nor enter the assembly, nor recite sutras or mantras, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "buying vermilion to await guests," this means selecting [the substance] for others and not for one's own consumption.
The sub-commentary clarifies that one must not store them for oneself. As for the phrase "from the second day onwards," etc., it means protecting against cooking for oneself. (Sub-commentary)

Regarding the reference to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and other texts: as previously stated, when a bhikṣu carries food for a śrāmaṇera and returns it to the bhikṣu, [the offense] is incurred even if there was no prior agreement;
conversely, it is not incurred otherwise. Now it is the same: if one gives with a single-minded intention and the other does not finish the food, [the offense] is incurred.
However, if there was an initial agreement that "I shall prepare this for you, and if you have any leftovers, you may give them [to me]," then it is not so.
Because there is a remainder after my meal, I do not permit eating. It is improper to light a fire over monastic vessels that have grease;
this means that if a bhikṣu burns a fire over a vessel containing the grease of food, he commits the offense of "cooking for oneself. Furthermore, one must not touch such a vessel.

Master Xuán says: Not only must one not touch the rice, but one must also not touch the fire; otherwise, it constitutes "cooking for oneself. Therefore, a *jìng-rén* (pure person) is made to boil it until it bubbles.
This clarifies that once the state of being raw has been transformed, one is permitted to warm it oneself, as this does not constitute an offense. The textual meaning is clear.

Regarding the statement "the third [case] leads to an offense," this refers to guarding against "overnight storage" (*nèi-sù*). That is to say, when a person and food are in the same place, and the dawn light (*míng-xiàng*) has already appeared.

This is called "storing food overnight" (*antar-sthāpana*). First, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* is cited regarding a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle food) bringing food to an impure area and it passing through until dawn.
Next, the *Caturvargika-vinaya* is cited regarding a bhikṣu bringing food seeking a pure area and the dawn having already broken before he could find one.

Since both of these two cases are not [the offense], they are treated as exceptions; the scriptures clearly permit them, and thus one does not commit the offense of storing food overnight. This concludes the section on "food until the fourth watch."

"Guarding against internal cooking" refers to cooking within the boundary (sīmā). Because it is cooked within the boundary, it is called "internal cooking. Regarding the phrase "originally cooked for another," this refers to a layperson or a *kappiya-kāraka* acting on behalf of others.
If one were to refer to another monk as "another," how could that other monk be expected to eat it?

Since both are monks, they would equally be guilty of the offense of internal cooking. Therefore, the text states: "If one person has committed the fault of eating [what was improperly prepared], all the śramaṇas who have received the full precepts [are affected]."
These are all instances where eating is not permitted.

Regarding the three categories of "permissible" (*tong*) and "prohibited" (*se*), the names are listed and their numbers enumerated: that which gives rise to an offense is "permissible," while that which does not give rise to an offense is "prohibited.
If one were to distinguish them by way of time, person, and medicine, it will be explained in detail according to the text below. The commentary states: "From the beginning until the main text..."

Regarding this: when there is definitely *sadyah-pāka* (food prepared on the same day) that has been kept overnight (*paryuṣita*), because it lacks the ritual method for [receiving] food at the proper time, being kept overnight is equivalent to *antaḥ-śāya* (storing within the monastery), and cooking within the boundary is equivalent to *antaḥ-pāka* (cooking within the monastery).
If one prepares it oneself, it is further combined with *svayaṃ-pāka* (self-cooking); if these transgressions are committed repeatedly, one incurs an offense.

As for the other three types of medicine—those for seven days, those for non-time, and those for life-long use—their application does not involve the aforementioned methods; they are all treated in the same manner as *sadyah-pāka*.

There are also faults such as those arising from overnight storage or boiling. If, for the sake of treating illness, there are specific or general rules regarding the addition of ingredients, then according to the nature of the medicine and its duration, if it is kept within the prescribed limits, there is no fault of overnight storage;
this is a specific rule (*niyama*). If it exceeds these limits, faults and offenses arise; this is a general rule (*sāmānya*).
Regarding non-timely medicines (*akālabhojana*), if they are consumed before the dawn has passed, they are all permissible; this is called a specific rule. Because...
Because there is no offense. Regarding "if the dawn appears," etc., various faults arise; this is called "general.
Regarding "the seven-day medicine, having completed the formal ritual, within the inner clean kitchen," etc., this is "specific," because it opens up [the allowance] so that there is no offense.

Regarding "on the eighth day, at dawn, one incurs an offense as described below," it is as explained in the following text. At times, faults such as "storing overnight," "bad contact," "transgression," or "excessive duration" arise; this is called...
This is a general rule (*sāmānya*). It must refer to those things that have no signs of being raw, such as pepper, ginger, and long pepper;
for these, cooking them over a night or cooking them oneself does not constitute an offense. Next, the *Sengqi* [Vinaya] is cited below to resolve external objections. One should raise the objection:

"If the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen) generally permits cooking for oneself, why does the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Shi) state that cooking ginger soup for oneself is also an offense? The *Chao* [the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*] resolves this by stating: "It is because [ginger] possesses the quality of being raw (*sajīva*)."

This must mean that they are cooked until thoroughly soft. Regarding "thoroughly purified": according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is permitted to cook them oneself within the boundary without offense.
This annotation follows that principle; however, it permits [the cooking] for three offenses only, while the seven-day period does not permit staying overnight together. The Vinaya says:

A bhikṣu thought to himself, "Regarding medicines to be taken for life, is it permissible to stay overnight together, to cook together, or to cook them oneself within the boundary? He then asked about this.
The Buddha said, "It is permitted. Based on this, the opening of these three [types of medicine] is because their storage for the purpose of treating illness according to one's needs is minimal;
they are not the same as the seven-day medicine or the non-timely (vikāla) medicine. If one follows the ancient masters, they permit seven-day medicine to be kept overnight.

If it were not permitted to be kept overnight, what would be the point of using the ritual formula (*vidhi*)? The present masters say that the application of the formula merely requires it to be used within the immediate time frame; it was originally not intended for overnight storage.

[The text] says: "Overnight. Because this medicinal syrup is sweet and delicious, and because of a deep attachment to storing it, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if there are various jars of ghee, oil, and so forth within a kitchen building, it is clear that seven-day medicines are kept inside a clean kitchen.

If this is so, why does the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* permit the drinking of stone-honey syrup after it has been kept overnight? The *Shuochao* explains: "This must have been permitted for a room due to difficult circumstances."
"Overnight storage" (sāṃnipātika) is not the same as ordinary seven-day medicine. Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* is cited:

since it permits the use of residual ghee or oil that has been stored overnight for nasal irrigation, it is evident that there is a fault in overnight storage and that the formal ritual (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is not applicable. As for the actual text of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Upāli asked the Buddha:
"Regarding these three kinds of medicine, if they have been kept overnight or handled improperly, may they be accepted by mouth? The Buddha said: "They may not."

He asked again: "Regarding these three medicines, may they be consumed by hand or with the mouth when one is not ill? The Buddha said: "They may not. This serves as proof that there is a fault in [keeping them] overnight.
Second, taking these four faults and clarifying them according to the *Abhidharma*: the first section can be understood through its summary.

First, it clarifies the lower [category], citing the characteristics of the faults. Regarding the phrase "From 'the first' to 'faults': as for the three types of persons," this first clarifies the prohibition against those who keep [medicines] overnight.

Furthermore, "a bhikṣu" refers to a single individual; it concerns the offense committed by sharing a lodging with oneself while providing food. Regarding the "two kinds of saṃghas," as stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:
"Having received [the invitation] today, until tomorrow, all śramaṇas and sons of the Śākya who have accepted the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) shall be impure.
This refers to the general saṃgha. As for the "śikṣamāṇa śrāmaṇera," this refers to one who confesses a grave offense as a bhikṣu. This person acts...

It is defilement because it opposes the essence [of the precept] while conforming to its outward appearance. Regarding the note stating that "in some cases there is no *śrāmaṇerī*, hence it is permitted":

this refers to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), where a *śikṣamāṇā* may take food beyond the [prescribed] time with a *bhikṣuṇī*; whereas in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong lü), a *śikṣamāṇā* is not permitted to eat or stay overnight with one.

According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, since taking food beyond the time and staying overnight are both permitted, logically there should be no offense. Yet the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* prescribes an offense; from this, one knows [the difference in interpretation].

The four parts constitute the exceptions (*kai*). It is not yet clear on what specific grounds the exception for eating another's leftovers (*para-śeṣa-bhojana*) is established; therefore, the sub-commentary provides an explanation to clarify this.
Alternatively, if there is no śrāmaṇerī present, a bhikṣuṇī may not directly take [the food] herself; thus, the exception allows her to receive it from a śikṣamāṇā.

Therefore, by implication, it is shown that if there is a *niṣadyā* (attendant), it is not permissible. Regarding "storing [food] within the precincts after demarcating a pure area (*pariśuddha-sthāna*)":
this precisely defines "storing within" (*antargrāma-śayana*). That is to say, once the pure area has been demarcated, the food should be placed only within that pure area;
if a person sleeps within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), there is no offense. Now, if one still brings the food back into the boundary and sleeps with it, this is called "storing within. (Note)
The phrase "the text does not mention 'equal' (or 'and so forth')" is intended to refute the ancient [interpretation]. The ancients said:

"Once the *śuddhasthāna* (pure ground) has been demarcated, if a bhikṣu sleeps upon that pure ground, there is no *antargrha-vāsa* (sleeping within). Now, however, it is said: "The pure ground only encompasses food; it does not encompass persons.

Thus, if one now sleeps together with someone else, it would still constitute *antargrha-vāsa*. How is this known? Therefore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* simply states: "Once the pure ground has been demarcated by the Saṃgha..."

To sleep and eat together within the monastery precincts constitutes "storing food indoors" (*antargrāma-śayana*). Where has it been stated that there is a passage exempting one from the offense of storing food indoors for a monk who is present at a *viśuddhi-sthāna* (pure ground)?
This is because a pure ground cannot possibly be devoid of people. "Cooking indoors" (*antargrāma-pāka*) is synonymous with "boiling indoors.

Regarding the phrase "once a pure ground has been demarcated," since a pure ground exists, it is logically appropriate to cook food therein; yet now [the food] is being prepared within the boundary (*sīmā*).
To boil [it] oneself constitutes an offense. To "cook for oneself" means to boil it oneself. This does not depend on whether the ground is pure or impure;
in all cases, it is improper for a bhikṣu to cook food with his own hands. Regarding the three types of people who do not eat:
these are the bhikṣu, the śikṣamāṇā, and the śrāmaṇera, as explained above; in all such cases, it becomes impure. "Improper handling" refers to improper contact. (Note)

Regarding "first receiving it as an evil grasp": this should refer to cases where, after having first received [an object], it is touched by a *kappiyakāraka* (a person who makes things permissible), whereby it becomes "previously received.
If a bhikṣu then grasps it, it constitutes an "evil grasp. Next, the three statements from the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* are cited: first, receiving but not grasping oneself;
second, grasping oneself but not receiving; third, neither receiving nor grasping. The meaning of these textual passages is very clear; one should investigate them.
This may be understood. "If another person eats, there is no offense" refers to the other group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*). Second, the distinction based on persons is as indicated in the text.
Regarding the phrase "from 'the first' up to 'as above,'" it is explained that this does not apply to other objects because they are not comprehensive; this is a distinction based on location.

Since other objects belong to laypeople, they do not constitute the characteristics of a complete monastery (*ārāma*), and thus there is no "storing overnight within" (*antar-vasati*) regarding those locations. As for the two matters of "assigning a place" and "formal announcement" (*jñapti*): [the former]...

Regarding these two locations, they must be defined by the characteristics of a courtyard (ārāma-lakṣaṇa). Even if it is a great boundary (mahā-sīmā), it must likewise possess the characteristics of an enclosure;
otherwise, the fault of "storing food overnight" (antara-śayyā-doṣa) would apply within this great boundary. This can be understood in terms of time. As for persons: regarding the three bhikṣus—
This is as explained above. "Knowing there is an offense" means being clearly aware in one's mind that there is food within the boundary and that one is staying overnight with it.
If one does not know and has no intention of violating the teaching, then even though one stays overnight with it, there is no offense.

The following passage from the Vinaya is cited to prove that when one does not know and lacks the intent to transgress, there is no offense. Regarding "the four types of nuns," three are as follows...

Above, the *śikṣāpada* is further added. Regarding those who partake of food, it is as stated in the text. As for the discussion on the four types of medicine mentioned above, it is as explained in the preceding text:
that which lasts for life (*yāvajjīvika*) does not involve "overnight storage" (*antar-śayita*), whereas the remaining three all do; this should be understood.
Regarding "cooking from the second [stage] until boiling": as for "blocking the pure ground," all four types of purification are unoffensive when used for blocking.
Regarding the timing, it applies throughout both day and night; provided that [the cooking] takes place within the boundary, it constitutes an offense regardless of whether it is day or night.

Regarding "involving persons from among the seven assemblies," this refers to being within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) surrounding the monastery (*ārāma*). If members of the seven assemblies cook for a *bhikṣu*, it is called "internal cooking" (*antaḥ-pāka*); such food must not be eaten.
The rules regarding food are as stated in the text; this can be understood in the context of the four types of medicine. Next, regarding the citation from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:

it says that a lay devotee in Śrāvastī invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha, but the Buddha did not go. Ānanda then went to invite them for a meal and returned home, where he became concerned about whether the food was raw or cold.

He then took fire and went outside the temple gate to re-boil it. At that time, the Buddha encountered him while walking and asked about it. Ānanda related the matter in detail. The Buddha said, "Well done.
From now on, if food is cold, you are permitted to re-warm it; however, if it is raw, it must be boiled again until thoroughly cooked. (This is from the Vinaya text.
I cite this here because, since he went outside the temple gate to re-warm it, it is clear that [re-heating] within the boundary (sīmā) is not permitted.

"Fearing it would constitute 'cooking within' (internal cooking). Regarding the phrase "from three [ingredients] up to combining": this distinguishes "self-cooking. It does not matter whether it is on pure ground;

if a bhikṣu transforms raw food into cooked food by himself, that is self-cooking. As for being permitted to combine pure medicinal substances oneself: this refers to those things that still possess the characteristics of raw life.

Once they have been purified by means of fire, one may combine them oneself without committing an offense. Regarding the phrase "from four [ingredients] up to cooked": the first part concerns the location. Not...
Regarding the distinction between pure and impure grounds: next, in terms of time, it does not matter whether it is day or night;

as soon as one touches it, it constitutes an improper touch, and in all such cases, an offense is committed. Concerning the various types of persons, including the Great Saṃgha, there are five propositions for analysis.

First, "touching while not having previously received [the robe]" means that although one has never before formally accepted it, one touches it directly and thus completes the act of touching. Second, "the aspect of oily potential..."

Regarding the connection: the details are explained by the commentary itself. According to the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, if one places today’s pure food upon a cloth napkin that was not thoroughly washed after yesterday’s oily and impure meal, it becomes defiled and thus constitutes a *spraṣṭavya* (contact with what is forbidden).
Third, regarding the "spontaneous loss of the vow" (*pratikṣepaṇa-saṃvara-hāni*): because the designated time has elapsed, the vow is spontaneously lost.
If one does not touch [the food], it is not an *aspraṣṭavya*; however, once the vow has been lost, to touch it again results in a transgression.

Because of the unpleasant touch, the commentary states that for the four medicines, the method of "adding" (the *adhivāsanā*) does not apply; both the midday and afternoon meals lose their status as received. Regarding the primary portion of the *kālika* (timely) medicine, it loses its status;

as for the other three medicines, since there is no oral ritual (*mukha-dharma*) for them until the end of the day, they also lose their status at midday and afternoon. If the three medicines were to have the "adding" method applied to them...
Regarding the rules for the non-timely seven-day medicine, the lifetime medicine, and the oral-administration method: each is lost according to its respective limit.
That is to say, as long as the limit has not been exceeded, the medicine is not lost; once the limit is reached, it is naturally forfeited. The seven-day medicine is forfeited on the eighth day;

the non-timely medicine is forfeited when the dawn appears; and the lifetime medicine is forfeited at the time of death. Therefore, the text states that the lifetime medicine is forfeited if one's life has not yet ended.
All bhikṣus may eat [the medicine]. If the formal acceptance (*paribhoga*) is interrupted or lost, the bhikṣus may not eat it. It is asked:

"If the seven-day limit for non-timely [medicine] has expired and the acceptance is lost, and an 'unwholesome contact' (*duṣṭa-sparśa*) arises, there is no doubt that this is so. As for this lifetime-long medicine (*yāvaj-jīvikam auṣadham*), once a bhikṣu has died, there is only the loss of acceptance;
it is as stated in the text. How then can there be 'unwholesome contact'? Master Xuán answered: "This is for the purpose of discussing the three types of medicine."

There is the fault of transgressing the limit and losing the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*). If this refers to an unwholesome touch (*duṣṭa-sparśa*), it does not exist at all for one who observes the precept for as long as life lasts.

Regarding the fourth point, "transgressing the conditions" (*pratyaya-atiyāta*) and so forth: Xuánzàng says that this was originally intended to distinguish unwholesome touch; here, however, it simply speaks of "losing the acceptance.

This means that because the acceptance is lost, subsequently grasping [the food] constitutes an unwholesome touch. Regarding the fifth point, "resolute intention" (*niścita-citta*) and so forth: this refers to forming the resolve never to eat again; subsequently, when one grasps [the food], it becomes an unwholesome touch.

It is auspicious. If one receives food while holding it without having formally accepted it, and a novice (śrāmaṇera) has touched it with oily hands, that novice must personally handle the teacher’s oily vessel;
only after that may he handle the utensils belonging to the Saṃgha. Because this constitutes contact with oiliness, it does not constitute [the fault of] "contact.

Regarding the note stating that "monastics and laypeople both grasping [the vessel] does not constitute contact": this refers to when a lay attendant (kappiya-kāraka) passes food to a bhikṣu; at that time, the bhikṣu...
If one grasps the hand of a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who makes things permissible) and has not yet released it, is this not a case of "double grasping"?
This is considered an act of receiving; therefore, it does not constitute the fault of touching [impure food]. The same applies to food already present in the bowl:

when a *kappiya-kāraka* brings food and offers it while the bottom of the bhikṣu’s bowl already contains remnants, even though they touch the remaining food inside the bowl, it does not constitute the fault of touching, because it is for the purpose of receiving. Thus it is with the bowl.
"Because it is held in the hands, the food in the bowl is likewise not lost in its status as received. This means that because the Sangha holds it in their hands, the food remains received.

Regarding the second case, "losing the status of being received due to encountering circumstances," the note stating "it is lost through contact with a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who makes things allowable)" is the formal explanation of "encountering circumstances.

As for "one must not touch it according to the Dharma," this means that since this food has already been touched by another, the rule of receiving it is lost; if a bhikṣu were to touch it, he would immediately incur an offense.
Contact also does not constitute [a violation of] receiving. Since one is now not touching this food, it is free from fault and is called "in accordance with the Dharma" (*yathādharma*).

As for washing the hands and receiving again, this is equivalent to receiving anew; thus, one must wash the hands to purify the mind. Regarding why the person who serves the food (*pariveṣaka*) need not wash their hands: because they are not subject to the fault of contact, it is unnecessary.
The three cases of violating the precepts through error and the fourth case of violating the precepts through intentional contact can be understood accordingly. Furthermore...
"Discriminating by means of three phrases" is the heading. Regarding the first phrase, "touching [food] while not being at fault," etc.:

in the previous case, because there was no intentional transgression due to forgetfulness, it is opened as being non-faulty. As for "if one sees a *śuddhakarman* (pure person), one should place it on the ground," this refers to a prior instance of confusion or error.
Now, seeing a *pariṣad* (attendant), one suddenly remembers that [the food] has not yet been formally accepted; placing it on the ground immediately constitutes no offense.

Washing the hands and accepting it again is equivalent to receiving it anew and likewise expresses the purity of the mind. Alternatively, it may be because one fears that at the time of the previous inadvertent contact, the food or fruit being held had become tainted with oily vapors;
for this reason, one washes the hands. Regarding the second case, "that which is unwholesome but not touched," this refers to those who have violated their precepts (*duḥśīla*).
If it was intentionally prepared with a malicious mind, even if virtuous bhikṣus eat it, there is no offense of contact. The Buddha said that "not touching" means it is pure;

this refers to a bhikṣu who observes the precepts, who does not touch it intentionally and thus commits no offense—this is called "pure. "Touching" means it is impure and constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing);
this refers to a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts and touches it with a malicious mind, and subsequently eats this food himself. Thus...
It constitutes an offense of improper contact and is inauspicious. This is because what has been discussed above refers to that which is both unwholesome and not merely [a matter of] meaning.
Regarding the third phrase, "both contact and unwholesome," etc.: as for the indolent person, they are negligent toward the Buddha's teachings and, being lazy and remiss, do not uphold them.

Upon finding an opportunity, they seize [food] regardless of whether it is pure or impure by contact. To seize fruit and test whether it is raw or ripe is likewise a mind of indolence; failing to comply with the precepts, they commit an intentional transgression while partaking of food.
Regarding "applying to both the raw and the cooked": "raw" refers to things such as rice and wheat, while "cooked" refers to things such as cakes and pastries.
As for the phrase "extending to the Vinaya," the section concerning "mutual concealment of a downfall" must be explained separately. First, the mutual concealment is clarified.

Next, the mutual inclusion [of impurity] is explained. First, regarding mutual covering: this refers to a tree situated on both pure and impure ground, with its branches and leaves covering both areas.
If food utensils, fruits, or the like are placed upon it, they are all determined by the location of the root. Thus, the *Yejie shu* (Commentary on the Vinaya) states:
"Purity or impurity depends on the original ground itself; it does not depend on what covers it. As for "mutual inclusion," it means:
The fruits and the tree fall upon two different grounds; this is discussed according to their distinct meanings. The Vinaya states:

There was once a tree whose roots were in an impure ground, while its branches and leaves covered a pure ground. When the fruit fell onto the pure ground, the bhikṣus did not know whether it was pure or impure.

The Buddha said: "If it falls of its own accord without being touched by anyone, it is pure. Furthermore, if it is blown down by the wind, struck down by rain, or knocked down by monkeys and various birds, it is pure."
The Buddha said: "If one does not intentionally cause [it] to fall, it is called pure. He further stated:
"If a tree stands on pure ground and its fruit falls onto impure ground," the Buddha said: (the above is from the Vinaya text). The *Shao* (Commentary) clarifies this for those who do not understand:

it asks why there would be a transgression when the aforementioned fruit from impure ground falls into pure ground, and thus subjects it to discussion. What is discussed here, however, concerns the case where the fruit falls onto impure ground.
In the middle [section], there is a bhikṣu who fears that it will constitute "storing overnight" (antarāvasita) and thus insists on discussing it.

As for what is called "falling into [the offense] through lack of attention," this refers to storing without intentional thought, where the item falls away spontaneously; it is not a fault of the object itself. Furthermore, the Vinaya text does not say "unknowingly."
Furthermore, it is not stated that the sūtra clarifies the completion of the previous stage; this is a point of lack of understanding.

Moreover, in the text, it only speaks consistently of severing the roots of the pure and the impure, and does not mention whether they have grown long or not. One who follows the sūtra’s clear indications yet fails to understand their meaning lacks comprehension.
Now, the Master says: if [the seeds] have not yet grown long and have not yet left the ground, they do not abide in rebirth, remaining within the impure.

It is not an offense. Even if the food has been stored overnight—having remained off the ground through the appearance of dawn—if one is unaware of whether it was stored overnight or not, or whether it was on pure ground or impure ground, and thus it constitutes "overnight storage" (soda) or does not constitute "overnight storage," there is likewise no offense. This is because there was no intentional hoarding, and one ate it out of ignorance.

This is the corroborating text cited from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (Wufen lü), which states that what was previously considered pure according to the four parts [of the rule] is now [treated as follows].
To cite evidence from other schools to establish that there is no overlap:

regarding the statement that "the roots of a tree are in both pure and impure ground, and the bhikṣu is likewise in both pure and impure ground," if one examines the meaning of the text, it must refer to a fruit-bearing tree that is half in pure ground and half in impure ground, with the body of the bhikṣu also being half in pure ground and half in impure ground, such that the fruit falls between them. This means:
They fell back into the realms of both the pure and the impure. As for "fruit falling therein," it means falling into both the two types of realms:
the pure and the impure. This was not something done by the bhikṣus; this is one circumstance. Seeing fruit fall onto ground that was not pure, they had a *śuddhaka* (pure person) discard the heap;
this is another circumstance. After spending the night, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Based on this, I shall establish a rule: if one does not know whether it is pure or impure..."
Regarding the permission to eat: if one knows that food may not be eaten, this is proven by the two preceding sections. Fruits and vegetables grow fully on both pure and impure ground;
the meaning of "knowing" and "not knowing" applies when monks are in the same location. Regarding the four lines at the end of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:

first, if fruit grows on impure ground but is shaded over by pure ground, and the fruit falls onto pure ground; second, if fruit grows on pure ground and remains shaded over by pure ground, the fruit... [is permitted].
"Fall upon pure ground. These two phrases concern when one may take [fruit] that has fallen without it being considered "overnight stored indoors" (*antar-śayita*).
Third, if fruit grows on pure ground but is covered by impure ground, the fruit that falls is impure.

Fourth, if fruit grows on impure ground and remains covered by impure ground, the fruit that falls on the impure ground must be taken and brought into the pure building in a timely manner. The *Chao* text merely cites these points.
These two lines explain and establish the preceding meaning. Regarding "taking at any time": since it has been placed on pure ground, there is no restriction as to the season;

one may leave it for three or five days without taking it, and in all such cases, no offense is committed. Therefore, it says "at any time" (there are those who have misinterpreted this meaning, etc.).

Regarding the requirement that [food] must be purified within the inner kitchen in a timely manner: according to the text, this should be done by the end of the first watch of the night; otherwise, it becomes impure.

Although the present *Chao* (Digest) cites a limit for this, one must follow the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya), which states that it may be placed within the inner-purified area before the appearance of the dawn light (*aruṇodaya*).
This passage is cited to explain the preceding point concerning fruits from an impure area that have fallen onto a pure area: their original status as impure remains unchanged.
As for "offenses," why is it necessary to analyze them? Furthermore, regarding "long-footed gourds" (*dīrghapāda-karkaṭī*): this refers to long-footed gourds;
it indicates that in the latter case, if they have not yet grown feet and are in an impure place, there is no offense. Regarding "transporting" and so forth:

this means if one transports grain, rice, beans, and the like in an impure place, one should determine whether an offense is incurred based on the previous rules concerning what was known or unknown. The commentary is largely identical to this Vinaya.

This means that within the *Caturvargika-vinaya*’s method for receiving the precepts, regarding the four propositions concerning whether one knows the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) has violated the precepts and so forth:

because it concerns ignorance, the attainment of the precepts is permitted; if one knows, then they cannot be attained. In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, regarding pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*), there is an offense or no offense depending on whether one knows or does not know.

Although these differ in terms of their objective circumstances, regarding the factor of knowledge, the principle is no different: if one knows, they cannot be attained; if one does not know, they can be attained. Therefore, it is said that they are largely the same.
Regarding the phrase "fifth, reaching the knower," the title can be understood as such. In the lower section of the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, it cites the *Pratītyasamutpāda* [context]:
according to the text of the *Bhaiṣajya-vastu*, it says that when the Buddha was in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a famine at that time and alms-food was difficult to obtain.

The bhikṣus placed their food on the ground by the roadside, where it was carried off by thieves. The bhikṣus then had this thought: "If the Buddha would permit us to place food within the boundary (*sīmā*)."

He was thus spared from this matter and reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "In times of scarcity, I permit staying overnight within the boundary (*sīmā*). (This is the provision for staying overnight within the boundary.

Second, I permit cooking within the boundary. Third, I permit cooking for oneself. Fourth, I permit not receiving [food formally]. These are all for the sake of those who have been carried away by the earth;
the provisions for these permissions are the same as above. Fifth, monastic food. Sixth, lay food. Seventh, aquatic fruits. Eighth, terrestrial fruits. The four items above are combined."
These are cases where the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual of "prepared food") has not been performed. Regarding fruits from water, these refer to water chestnuts, lotus roots, lotus tubers, and the like;

regarding fruits from land, these refer to varieties such as pears, chestnuts, and walnuts. For each of these four categories, there are specific allowances (*anujñā*) under certain conditions, as described at length in the Vinaya.

These were all permitted due to times of scarcity. If one were to define the transgressions (*āpatti*), there were originally only five in antiquity: namely, eating what was stored overnight (*antarāvasatha*), eating what was cooked overnight (*antarāpakva*), cooking for oneself (*svayaṃpakva*), and eating without having received a sufficient portion (*aparipūrṇa*).

Regarding the "eating" [of food]: the *Chao* (Commentary) mentions eight offenses. Our current Master says that since self-cooking is permitted, there is by implication the offense of "defiled contact" (*duṣṭa-sparśana*)—though this is not explicitly stated in the text.

Furthermore, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is permitted to take leftover food away and keep it for the next day’s meal; is this not the permission for "leftover overnight food" (*śeṣa-rātri-stha*)? [This is also not found in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*.]
Furthermore, there is the offense of destroying life. Since it is permitted to take wild fruits oneself, one may carry away the remains of food provided one informs the donor.

Xuan says: "The original purpose of an offering is to provide a single meal. Even if there is more than that, it is improper to take it home. Now, since this is a time of scarcity, taking the remains is permitted;
however, fearing the donor might be suspicious or alarmed, one should simply inform them. According to this Vinaya text, [this is the rule].
Is this not precisely the opening for "storing food overnight"? Since there is no explicit text regarding this in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is cited here.

Fourth is the method for purifying seeds that have been damaged. First, the chapter heading is presented and the names are listed as in the text. Regarding the phrase "from the enactment until the recitation," the rest is as in the precept on damaging living beings.
As above, the enactment against digging the earth serves three benefits in preventing the damage to living beings: it avoids being driven into labor by kings and ministers.

"Attaining the path of cultivation through the conditions of tranquility," etc. Regarding the phrase "the fourth [category] up to food": this clarifies the place where purification is performed and the person who performs it.

Among the four statements, the first two clarify the meaning; the latter two are derived from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. As for the note stating that when both the person and the fruit are on impure ground, they become pure and may be eaten:
this is explained by the commentary itself. Regarding the phrase "food for the other four assemblies": this refers to the *Bhikṣuṇī-vidhi* (The Rules for Bhikṣuṇīs).

[This] also excludes the śrāmaṇerī. Some commentators explain that by excluding the śrāmaṇerī and adding the one who is undergoing penance (*śikṣādattaka*), the number four is completed (as detailed according to the previous explanation).
Next, regarding "that which has been purified by fire or a knife but may not be eaten because it has become pure": this refers to when food enters the state of purity through fire;

since it has undergone internal cooking, it is the same as the second case mentioned previously. Although purification by a knife does not involve internal cooking, it nonetheless remains within the impure ground.

Because it is performed in an improper place (*asthāna*), it is likewise unfit for consumption. If the fruit is on purified ground, this constitutes purification according to the Dharma, as stated in the text.
Furthermore, one must understand that this method of purification applies to both seeds and their manifestations; if seeds are to be purified, they must necessarily be on purified ground.

If the pure characteristic (*śubha-nimitta*) also extends to impure stages, the three types of dharmas are designated as in the text. Regarding the phrase "when the Saṃgha arrives at a person's dwelling":
"the wound from a blade, the bird-purification, and the removal of seeds for eating" refers merely to the destruction of the [seed's] characteristics.

"Not fit for sowing, having been completely eaten" means that once the seed has been destroyed, there is no offense even if the seeds are eaten along with the fruit. "The skin is peeled or the bark is stripped" refers to peeling a small portion; "stripping" concerns the entirety.

"Completely removed. "Sediment" refers to the liquid settling and flowing downward; "dry" means it has become dry at times. It is also said that washing root vegetables with water constitutes purification (*śuddha*).
This is a separate passage from the latter section of the Vinaya. At one time, after the bhikṣus had washed root vegetables, they performed the purification ritual again.
The Buddha said, "There is no need for further purification; this [washing] itself is purification. Xuánzàng says: "Root vegetables..."
This refers to freshly grown plants such as celery and smartweed, which have not yet developed nodes; these are determined to be pure simply by washing.

If they do possess nodes, they must then be purified by fire.
