According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, regarding the purification of root-propagated seeds, it states that root-propagated seeds must also be purified by fire, as the textual authority differs [from other schools]. As for the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and others, there are five types [of propagation]: first, soft [propagation].

The five methods of purification according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* text are: first, cleaning; second, picking out the seeds from the eyes; third, peeling off the skin; fourth, pinching with the nails;

and fifth, purification by fire. Regarding the statement in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* that "purification by fire applies to all five types," this means that a single purification by fire suffices for all five categories—namely, root, branch, joint, covering (sheath), and seed.
Because it differs from the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika*, [it is explained] in the lower section of the *Vinayamātṛkā*.
This refers to the characteristic of clear and pure color. The *Śāstra* states: "That which is carried away by water or defiled by dust—all these are characteristics of corruption;

they do not constitute the indestructible seed. The commentary, following this principle, notes that just as sugarcane has leaves interspersed between its joints, it cannot be bundled together as pure.
Now, since the seeds of the *hǎo* (mugwort) are scattered along with their branches and leaves, separated and not adhering to one another, they do not form [a single unit].

[It is] pure; therefore, it is said that there is no further need for purification. Regarding the annotation on non-glutinous rice: one explanation states that two *shu* of unhusked rice (*tāṇḍula*) constitute one *shu* of white rice, as evidenced by the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and other texts.
It is both pure and required. Question: Above it was stated that seventeen types of grain become pure through the removal of their husks.
Since this is already rice, why is further purification necessary? Answer: If it was originally for the sake of purification that the husks were removed, then once the husks are gone, [it is pure].
It becomes pure. If one sheds its skin for the sake of purification, it is not considered pure at the moment the skin is shed, because the seed can still grow;

therefore, it must be purified again. The four characters in the commentary refer to the presence of a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who makes things allowable). A bhikṣu is not permitted to perform this himself as it would be contrary to the Dharma.
Thus, the phrase "if there is no one" refers to the case where a bhikṣu acts on his own in the absence of another person. [The text] adds: "On one's own."

Regarding "that which is prepared through action": according to that text, there are four categories of pure fruit. First, that prepared by one's own preparatory effort (*prayoga*), meaning purification by fire up to purification by the fingernails performed by oneself.
Second, that prepared by another’s preparatory effort, namely food purified for a bhikṣu by a layperson.

Third, that prepared by both one's own and another’s preparatory effort, namely when one holds the fruit oneself and purifies it together with a layperson. Fourth, that which is not... [text fragmentary]
That which is produced through the preparatory effort of oneself or others—namely, wounds from insect bites or bird pecks, up to bruises and so forth—is food obtained directly.
The present *Cāo* (Excerpts) text corresponds to the first phrase [of the verse]. Regarding the commentary in the *Shū* (Sub-commentary), it refers to the *Zhēndì Shū* (Paramārtha’s Commentary).

"Each is a *duṣkṛta*" (*jílúo*) refers to the offense of destroying the appearance [of the seed]. "Each is a *sthūlātyaya*" (*tí*) refers to the offense of destroying a living seed. Now, the fire stops [its action] upon a single contact.

"Obtaining one auspicious [fruit]" explains the aforementioned benefit. "The *Śarīputra-vinaya* states that fire [renders it] *nirvāṇa*" means that because the fruit was not touched by the superior [fire], it is [considered cooked].
"Hot ashes, fire, and charcoal" refers to hot charcoal from a recent death; these do not constitute purification.
"That which has been touched by applied fire" explains that a bhikṣu should not eat it. This single fruit, once it has been touched by fire, is considered "self-cooked."

Therefore, this does not mean that one is entirely prohibited from eating. Regarding purification by knife or nail: although there is no fault in touching such food, it must not have been cooked by oneself;

furthermore, because the location is a pure ground, eating is permitted. As for the five parts—roots and stems—that are purified by fire, this refers to the five types of root-seeds and stems, which also require purification by fire. The four parts purified by water are as previously explained.

This is an explanation. Regarding "that which is burned by a forest fire in the *Saṃghāṭi* [Vinaya]": this refers to a tree being burned; once its fruit falls to the ground, it is termed "pure" (*viśuddha*).
However, even if it is burned, if it does not fall to the ground, it does not become pure, because its roots remain in the earth. Regarding "a heap of ash and a cluster of grain":

Xuán [Zàng] says that in the kingdom of Kuḷūta, they made heaps of grain and, fearing that non-humans (*amanuṣya*) might steal them, they surrounded them with hot ashes and fire to create a sense of demarcation.
This is what is meant by "purity. Here, there must be fire within the ash; when it touches the grain, it is immediately transformed. If one acts contrary to this, it will not succeed.

The remaining text is easy to understand and need not be laboriously explained (etc.). As for the question regarding the ultimate characteristics (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*): "The seven kinds of colors of grasses and trees... [and so forth].
The colors blue, yellow, red, white, black, purple, and *piǎo* (the character for *piǎo* is glossed as *fūzhǎo*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is a yellowish-blue color.
Regarding the five types of root-seeds: roots, stems, branches, fruits, and seeds, as previously explained (*et cetera*).

Regarding the fifth section, "The Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*): To briefly extract the essential points, eight gates are established. This means that while the commentaries and sub-commentaries of old have extensively analyzed them, they were insufficient as characteristics;
therefore, the Master here has concisely extracted the essential subtleties and brought them into this work to provide an explanation and judgment via these eight gates.

Regarding the first section, "Following the Characteristics": "Following the characteristics" refers to a *bhikṣu* who observes the precept against accepting food [from improper persons]. Together with...

External conduct: such as not climbing trees to shake down fruit, and so forth. Regarding "oral acceptance" up to the limit of its duration: non-time [improper] liquids last until the appearance of dawn;
seven-day medicines last until the appearance of dawn on the eighth day; and lifetime medicines last until the illness has been cured. Furthermore, regarding the prevention of many offenses:

this prevents [the faults of] *saṃstuta* (storing overnight), *antarāla-saṃstuta* (storing within the boundary), and so on. Oral acceptance prevents only two: first, not having accepted [the gift]; second, [the fault of] storing overnight.

To grasp something without having received it constitutes an improper contact (*duṣṭa-sparśa*). As clarified below, this is explained in the section on the prevention of offenses (*āpatti-pratiṣedha*).

Regarding the phrase "from the two [types of receiving] up to obtaining with the eyes": as for whether the two types of receiving—by hand and by mouth—are common to all four medicinal substances, the answer is yes.

(Alternatively, placing the character "not" [不] in the following clause is an error in the textual division. Receiving by hand is common to all four medicinal substances in order to prevent the appearance of theft.

"Receiver" (*pratigrahaka*) refers to the meaning of receiving through the hands. "Excluding *kālāhāra* (food at the proper time)" means that for *kālāhāra*, there is only receiving by hand and no receiving by mouth;

because it is restricted to the period before noon and does not employ the method of oral reception, it is excluded. "There is also receiving by mouth, etc. is a distinction made according to specific circumstances;
this refers to cases such as when one is displeased with a śramaṇa, or when food is brought in vessels of gold or silver after a bird's nest has been burned by fire.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the mouth [method] adds three types of acceptance; this refers specifically to "acceptance by hand.

Although this is a method performed orally, it is likewise restricted to the period before noon and carries no sense of duration or proximity. Therefore, it is said to be "restricted solely to the period before noon.
The same applies to the other three medicines—those for non-time, seven-day, and life-long use—if they are accepted by hand alone without adding the oral method, they must simply reach until noon.
Before noon; after midday, the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) is lost. Because the oral method (*mukha-dharma*) pertains to the proper time (*kāla*), it is said to be "likewise.

If the oral method is added such that it applies to both proper and improper times (*akāla*), this means that when the three medicines are received by hand during the proper time, if the oral method is added, they are not restricted to the proper time but may be consumed throughout both proper and improper times.
The citation from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and other texts serves as scriptural evidence. Regarding "time periods," since fruit belongs to the proper time...

Regarding the medicinal decoction: the clear liquid is a non-time-medicine (*akālabhaiṣajya*). Now, taking the clear liquid constitutes one portion of the time-medicine (*kālabhaiṣajya*); hence it is called "a portion of the time" (*kāla-bhāga*).

This annotation reconciles the different classifications and clarifies their respective designations. As for the phrase "there must be illness, not [taking] overnight [medicines]," etc.: [Note: The provided text fragment concludes here.]
This means that the substance of this medicine must be pure; only then can it be consecrated with mantras and become effective.
If it is medicine that has already been shared with another person or has been defiled by improper contact, it cannot be consecrated, because it remains tainted by such faults.

Regarding the phrase "the three instances of what has been offered reaching [the recipient]": this distinguishes between those who have transgressed regarding medicine and those who perform the *pratimukha* (face-to-face) rite.

Regarding the "three ways of declining food": "declining" (*niṣedha*) refers to the act of refusing. This may be done by shaking the head toward both sides, or by saying with the mouth, "I do not need it," or by moving the eyes to signal that one does not want it;
in these cases, the food is not to be given. The meaning of the intermediate text is self-evident from the commentary (as indicated by "etc.").

"From 'the four ways' to 'receiving'" clarifies the method of receiving. "Receiving erroneously does not constitute [valid] reception" refers to cases such as intending to receive ghee but receiving oil instead.
"Picking up from the hand" means grasping with one's own fingers from the hands of the *śuddhika* (pure person). "Plucking" means seizing it from their hand, whether by the fingers or by the tendons;
both are termed *adharma* (unlawful). This serves to contrast with the preceding text, which indicates that only receiving by holding the palms upward (*ūrdhvahasta*) constitutes the proper method.
Regarding the division into four parts within this [section], it serves to state the number. As for the phrase "when the time comes to discuss," it is as in the precept on not accepting food:
the contrast between the food vessel and the body-mind, the contrast between the body and mind, and the single mind without a counterpart.

These three segments of text correspond to the act of giving, which is explained in the section on the gate of meditative cultivation in the lower fascicle. From the words "this merely" onwards, the discussion is based on the three medicines to establish this [point] properly.
This refers to the intention. Regarding the statement "first arriving at the dharma," this indicates the reception of non-timely medicine (*akālabhaiṣajya*). Question:

Previously it was stated that the one who bestows is the *kappiyakāraka* (the pure person), whereas now it is said that the one who bestows is also the *kappiyakāraka*. Why is it that in these two passages, the agent and the object are not fixed? Answer:
In the former case, since the recipient is a bhikṣu, the *kappiyakāraka* is the object bestowed upon. Now, it is stated that the one who bestows is the *kappiyakāraka*.

It refers specifically to the medicine one has received; therefore, it is not fixed. Regarding the phrase "from the first" and so forth: this means that the substance of the medicine is free from the eight defects, as listed in the text.

The note stating "sweet at first and sour at the end" means that it subsequently loses its original nature. The following section also clarifies the points concerning the eight defects, referring back to this passage.
Regarding the phrase "from the second" up to "come": it is as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "from the third" up to... [text ends].
"Those who [partake]" refers to the preceding classification of *pānaka* (drinks) and the differentiation of their types. "Recollection" (*saṃjñā*) is as described extensively above.

The sub-commentary (*zhùwén*) provides a detailed analysis, stating that a single list is not permitted. Regarding the phrase "from 'four' to 'days,'" it is as follows. As for the statement, "The four methods for seven-day medicine are the same as above," Xuán says:
"Since it says 'the same as above,' this should be categorized as a restatement (*dié*). It is inappropriate to call it a heading (*biāo*). Regarding the phrase:
Regarding the phrase "the initial arrival is the same as above," the change to "the eighth" signifies that there is no alteration in meaning;

it refers to the case where another bhikṣu’s possession of *saptāha-bhaiṣajya* (seven-day medicine) constitutes the eighth offense. Question: What is the difference between this and the previous fifth [offense], "keeping overnight"? Answer: The previous case concerned one's own keeping of medicine overnight.

This present case concerns that of another; it is not merely a matter of keeping overnight, but also includes offenses such as improper contact (*duṣṭa-sparśana*) and taking at an improper time (*akāla*).

This is an offense. Regarding the statement "reaching the second [category] when it is appropriate," it is as the text says. Regarding the statement "from the third down to the second," this is a restatement (*niddesa*).
The phrase "initially, there are no five faults" cites the number. Regarding the statement "from the first down to receiving," this refers to continuous possession;

that is, possessing continuously for up to seven days. Next, the text from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is cited as proof. The meaning of the question and answer is that what has been defiled by a previous medicine is called "contaminated by characteristics" (*lakṣaṇopalipta*).*
This is not an error; the textual characteristics are clear. If one obtains a different medicinal substance, it is not permitted if it is the same as the ghee (*sarpis*).

However, if it is for a different ailment and one further accepts honey or other substances, all such cases are permitted. Regarding the second point, "having stored [it] continuously," this specifically refers to the defilement caused by the passage of days.
The passing of the day acts as the defiling agent (*upakleśaka*), while the moment the item enters one's possession is what is defiled. Third, "formerly... [text fragment].
Regarding the offense of "excess" (*atireka*) when wearing other [medicines]: the medicine dyed on the seventh day is of the same flavor as the medicine currently being used;
therefore, it is not permissible to apply the formal ritual (*adhikāra*) to it. This is the position of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, cited here to demonstrate the views of other schools.

As for the fourth case, "continuous reception": because the medicine has not yet been consumed, the offense of excess is not incurred. However, to restrain a greedy mind, one must allow a one-day interval before permitting further reception.

Regarding the five types of continuous offenses (*saṃtati-āpatti*): this refers to the case where one has performed the ritual purification (*viśuddhi*) of medicinal substances and consumes them regularly.

When the eighth day arrives, although there is no offense of "excess" (*atireka*), if one continues to consume them, the subsequent acts follow upon the preceding ones, and this is termed a continuous offense. If it is a different type of medicine, however, it is permissible. The concluding text may be understood in detail.
As for the phrase "those who have reached two," this refers to applying four rules to oneself. Regarding the note on "if separated from the meal-time": [End of excerpt]

Regarding the statement "there is no need for these words": this refers to *kālāpāka* (medicines to be taken at the proper time). Fearing that one might lose the consecration after midday, it was necessary to keep track of them;
since there is none [of such concern] now, there is no need to record them. Regarding the note under the fourth point, "among those received through mutual exchange, one may also cook them oneself":

this applies when there is no *pariveṇika* (pure person) available. Regarding "having cooked in two ways": if a *pariveṇika* is present, have them cook it; if not, then cook it oneself. This does not mean...
It is boiled twice. It is not called an "unwholesome contact" because at the time of the actual boiling, the flavor has not yet changed and the original state of the mouth remains;

thus, it is not called an unwholesome contact. As soon as the flavor changes and the [original] sensation is lost, one can no longer touch it again; therefore, it is not called an unwholesome contact.
If one touches [it], it immediately becomes an unwholesome touch. The rest may be understood. Regarding the four methods of adding substances:

as for the phrase "the rest follow the counteractive measures and are to be inferred by analogy with what precedes," this text briefly cites the method of adding oil for wind disorders (*vāta-vyādhi*). Whether hot or cold, one should take medicines such as honey;

these are to be categorized according to the previous method of receiving [the precepts], differing only in the citation of the specific conditions of the illness and the names of the medicines. This concludes the four [methods] for life.

Regarding "the types": this refers to the names and enumerates the categories, which can be understood [from the context]. As for "from one up to 'explaining'": this points back to what has already been listed in the preceding text, so it is not enumerated here.
Regarding the second point, "those capable of bestowing," the commentary states that this includes medicines such as those taken at specific times; this means that among these medicines...

Alternatively, when the *xuān* (magpie) is at its head and the wheat has not yet ripened, one may consume it during the designated time; this distinguishes it from [the rules for] non-designated times (*akāla*) or the seven-day period.

Regarding the statement that "three [ingredients] must be combined to receive [the medicine]," if a single [ingredient] does not require [combination], it means that a single substance is of a uniform flavor and undergoes no transformation;

thus, there is no need to record or identify it. As for "dividing the substance," it is like a medicinal drug with a sweet taste: whatever single flavor it necessarily follows within is named a "certain pill" (*mao wan*).

This refers to the medicinal substance itself. As for the remaining factors of state (*lakṣaṇa*) and position (*avasthā*), they are called "parts of the medicine. Regarding those that arrive separately and are received separately: this refers to dividing the medicinal substance;

what arrives earlier is received earlier, and what arrives later is received later. If it arrives all at once and is received all at once, it is therefore said to be "received collectively upon total arrival.
As for the phrase "the four methods of application reach their limit," it is as previously distinguished; it is as explained above.

Within the substance [of the medicine], that which constitutes the greater portion is taken as the principal medicinal ingredient. If purchasing medicine, one must distinguish the order of priority and receive them accordingly;

this is easy to understand. Regarding the passage on the prohibitions and exhortations for purchasing at the market, such as "one must not place it on the ground," etc., this is because one fears that if it remains there even for a moment, the formal reception (*pratigraha*) will be lost.
As for the phrase "the intention of the present [text]," "suppression" (*niyama*) refers to the restraint of not following [unwholesome impulses].
The Buddha’s words are themselves a form of restraint. Now, by honoring the Dharma and following its teachings, one suppresses and curbs the greedy mind;
using medicine to sustain the body while maintaining mindfulness for the sake of the Path—this is precisely the reflection of the Great Meaning.

Regarding the statement that "the five [types of medicine] differ," this distinguishes the seven-day medicines, which must be formally purified (*śuddhi*) due to three reasons, as listed in the excerpt (etc.). This serves to guard against the fault of possessing surplus medicine when the dawn light (*ābhāsa*) is about to appear.
Because it exceeds the [proper] time, one receives it with the hand; however, as it is restricted to the middle period and lasts but a brief moment, it is said that "the time is short.

Regarding the other three [types of medicine] which do not possess [all] the requirements: the *tatkālika* (timely) medicine possesses both the initial and final meanings; the *akālika* (non-timely) medicine possesses only the latter; and the *yāvajjīvika* (lifetime) medicine possesses only the former two.

All [of these] have mutual deficiencies and do not fully possess the aforementioned meaning; thus, there is no need to perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification). The rules for purification are like those for robes:
they are cut into segments for use according to specific circumstances (*pratyaya*). (And so forth.)

Regarding the phrase "from 'it is said' up to 'six':", this clarifies the breadth or narrowness of receiving [food] by hand or by mouth. Receiving by hand is analogous to the precept against receiving food [not from a donor] and the precept regarding the seven-day medicine;
once one person has received it, it applies to all people—this is the broad sense. As for the statement that "receiving by mouth is also like this," there are two interpretations.

This is the first interpretation: it is not different from the principle of its being common to receiving by hand; therefore, it says "also like this. If, however, we rely on... [the second interpretation].

Below. The second interpretation is that it does not apply universally. Why is this so? Because the remedies are prescribed specifically for different ailments; the ailment there is not the same as the ailment here.
Furthermore, because the titles differ—the name of the bhikṣu is not the same. "Is it not so? Below, the text returns to clarify the universal meaning.
The reason for this is that the oral dharma provides the two universal remedies, as explained in the commentary itself. Namely:

The medicine has not lost its legal status; it may be taken by other bhikṣus, which constitutes a relaxation [of the rule]. Therefore, with respect to the person from whom it was received, the formal procedure (*dharma*) remains intact.

This correctly explains the meaning of "relaxation. How is this known? This is a rhetorical inquiry based on logical principle. The passage from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) below cites the Vinaya as proof.
Regarding the phrase "the rest is as explained in the *Yi-chao* and the *Shu*," the *Da-shu* refers to the *Yi-chao*. The *Da-shu* states: "As for its oral..."

Regarding the Dharma: when one receives [medicine] by calling out one's own name, as long as the medicine belonging to oneself has not been relinquished to another, one may consume it from me without losing the validity of the formal acceptance (*paribhogika*).
However, if one definitively relinquishes it to another, both forms of acceptance are lost. Thus, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"If the medicine has not yet reached the seven-day limit, but is relinquished to another, the formal acceptance is immediately lost; one should not consume it further."

Regarding the phrase "adding seven times until it is digested": the first part clarifies receiving with the hands; the repetition may be understood accordingly. As for the "method of oral [recitation]," this marks the beginning of the section.

First, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā*) is cited, which explains the repetition and rectification according to the days based on the formal procedure (*dharmavācanā*). The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* prescribes two types of cutting off."

This is the first interpretation: it does not follow the potency of the medicine. For two days, one proceeds solely according to the formal rule (*dharma*) by undertaking the seven-day rite (*saptāha-vidhi*), yet one is permitted to consume [the medicine] for two days.
To provide an illustration, this is like the seven-day rite undertaken during the summer retreat. Next, citing the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* below, it is based on their mutual connection;

according to the discussion on the potency of the medicine, that Vinaya states that medicine which has passed a night may not be consumed, and therefore one must seek it anew every day from a lay attendant (*upāsaka*).

[The bhikṣu] was weary and suffering. The Buddha asked the physician, "How many days may a bhikṣu keep medicine and yet remain in peace? He replied, "The potency of the medicine can be known to last for seven days as they overlap.
Based on this, [the Buddha] permitted keeping [medicine] for seven days. This passage is cited to prove that the preceding overlapping [of potencies] allows for a seven-day period.
Regarding "accidentally touching seven-day oil," etc., it is as described above in the section on maintaining purity (*śuci*): a lay attendant (*karmadāna*) accidentally grasped seven-day oil.

The commentary states: "According to the method of receiving [the precepts] orally, there would be an error; it is clearly understood that receiving them again is permitted. It further cites the *Abhidharma-samuccaya* (*Cheng lun*) as evidence that the seven-day period is continuous.
In the *Aṣṭaskandhaka-vinaya*, the text is cited as it appears: "As for 'Sāḍhika receives,' it refers to receiving from the mouth of a bhikṣu," etc., which is to be understood accordingly.
The treatise states: If there is a *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things allowable), one should immediately have them take charge of it and receive it from them daily;
there is no need to apply the formal ritual (*kamma*) before a *bhikkhu*. If there is absolutely no *kappiya-kāraka* to take charge of it, one must apply the oral ritual (*mukha-vāda*).

When one wishes to use it oneself, one may take it directly. Regarding the application of the oral ritual, this is again cited from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*: once the ritual has been performed, [the food] is held from the first day until the fifth day.

[If] one has already [received the medicine], and it is touched and lost, one may receive it again for seven days. If it is touched after the sixth day has passed, it is not permitted to add it again, because the period is nearly full.

Question: Regarding this section of the text, if from the first to the fifth day it is touched and lost, and one adds two more periods of reception, one again obtains the seven-day allowance for consumption.

"Although it is the same as the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, the intentions of the two masters differ. The former master, fearing that the Vinaya teachings might be applied too hastily, spoke of a seven-day continuity. The latter master..."

The intention was to respond to the occasion; it was somewhat relaxed and leisurely. The two attachments were not fixed, and the matter followed accordingly (the above briefly summarizes his main point).
The Venerable Jing-shui said: Although various commentators have explained this passage, none have understood the underlying intent of the preceding and following citations.

This was not yet understood. The current explanation states: If one loses the status of having formally accepted [the medicine] merely through physical contact, it is subsumed under the preceding section.
If, however, there is a subsequent addition, one simply takes the seven-day period from the point of that connection.

If other unaccepted medicine is added to this medicine that has already been accepted and lost its status through contact, one must distinguish between their relative strength; specifically, if the previously accepted old medicine is more abundant than the newly added unaccepted medicine.

Regarding the phrase "if [the medicine] is depleted": although one may apply the seven-day rule a second time, since it relies on the continuity of the medicinal potency, it likewise lasts for only seven days.

Alternatively, if the old portion is small and the new portion is large, one applies the formal ritual of receiving [the medicine] again; then, starting from the day the new portion was touched, one counts afresh until the full seven days are completed.
This is precisely the meaning of this text. Such an interpretation and judgment also accords with the *Śāstra* (Treatise), serving as a warning against erroneous or confused application.
