The formal restraint (*sammukhīvinaya*) does not prevent [the offense], as its meaning encompasses both [types of] unpleasant contact (*duḥsparśa*); for if one accepts without restraint, there is indeed unpleasant contact upon grasping the object. The same applies to verbal acceptance (*vācika-parigraha*).

As for those [rules] that do not prevent other [offenses], once the afternoon has passed, the [allowance] is lost; therefore, there are no two-night stays or eating at improper times (*vikāla*). Because one is currently accepting food, the two types of boiling (*dvividha-pāka*) are not prevented.

Regarding the four medicines (*catuṣ-prakāra-bhaiṣajya*), when accepted by hand, the prevention of the two offenses is likewise the same. For non-timely [food], it is verbally prevented from the two [offenses].

If one passes the midday hour by even a single instant, there is a fear that [the benefit] will be lost; thus, once the midday has passed, the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) is forfeited, and an unwholesome contact (*duṣṭa-sparśa*) arises spontaneously.

Now, the mouth can prevent this. The same principle applies to the two lower types of medicine regarding unwholesome contact. As for not preventing the other four [types of medicine], it is because one merely obtains the four clear signs (*lakṣaṇa*); therefore, there is no "two-night" period.
This is all the more so for matured medicines (*pakva-bhaiṣajya*), or those drunk raw, which do not undergo the "two-cooking" process. [These are to be kept] for seven days.

Third: The first two points are the same as before. Furthermore, it prevents the fault of keeping food overnight (*saṃnidhi*). Since this fault exists because of receiving [food] on the night [prior], the current oral rule (*karmavācanā*) is able to prevent it.

Formerly, it was said that this prevented "internal storage" (*antaḥśayana*). The *Xià dà shū* (Great Commentary on the Lower Section) states: "If one were to place [the food] back in a pure kitchen (*kalpi-kārā-śālā*), what would be the purpose of performing the formal ritual (*sīmā-bandha*)?

The *Chāo zhù* (Commentary on the *Nanhai Jīguǐ*) notes: Regarding the phrase "there is no scriptural text for this," in the section on medicinal substances (*bhaiṣajya-vastu*), Upāli questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha... [text ends].

Regarding medicinal substances that may be kept overnight or cooked indoors: the Buddha said they may be so used. Since this was not asked in reference to the seven-day limit, it is evident that the seven-day rule is not waived here.

Regarding the sixth point, "protecting against [faults] throughout one's life by means of the mouth": there may be cases where something is cooked indoors; however, if it is formed into pills or powders, there is no such fault.

If decoctions and the like are boiled or simmered within the boundary (sīmā), then there is the fault of cooking indoors; therefore, one must be able to guard against this. One must also guard against...
Regarding "cooking for oneself": because it transforms raw soup into a cooked state, it likewise constitutes a transgression.
Regarding "the arising of two offenses": this refers to the fact that after losing the status of having received [the food] due to the two types of receiving, offenses subsequently arise.

Regarding "two auspicious times having arrived": when the time-medicine (kālabhojana) arises, it loses its status of being received after noon; through improper contact and passing the night, the offense of *sāmiṣa* (storing overnight) arises.

"Bad contact" (*duṣṭa-sparśa*) is no different from what was stated previously. Oral acceptance (*mukha-paribhoga*) is the same as this. The four types of medicine accepted by hand all follow this same principle.
Regarding "non-timely" (*akāla*), three offenses arise through oral [acceptance]; "leftover overnight" (*śeṣa-rātra*) and "bad contact" are as described above, with the addition of "non-timely.

It is understandable that five offenses arise through "seven-day" (*saptāha*) oral acceptance. The meaning intended in the question and answer is that although there may be offenses for not accepting [the food], these do not arise through the method of oral [acceptance].
These exist from the very beginning; therefore, they are not mentioned [separately]. This is because they differ from various offenses that arise through the dharma of speech.

Regarding the statement "exhausted until clarity," this specifically distinguishes the six offenses arising throughout one's life: first, losing what has been received; second, improper contact; third, leftover overnight food.

Fourth, storing food overnight; fifth, cooking indoors; sixth, cooking for oneself. Furthermore, it is added that taking [medicine] while not ill brings good fortune. There are also those who hold that this meaning is not fixed;
that is to say, since dried medicine does not involve the two types of cooking, it is permissible. Regarding "the rest is as before," the precept on eating at improper times states:

"Taking [medicine] without a valid reason brings good fortune. Within the precept on refusing food, there is the loss of the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) through a firm resolve, as well as the loss [of acceptance] when encountering certain conditions.
Regarding the *śīlavipatti* (transgressions of the precepts) and so forth, the *śeṣavipatti* (residual transgressions) also clarifies the offense of residual [misconduct].

As for the six offenses mentioned above, they arise because one loses the undertaking through a definitive intention, or encounters conditions that cause one to violate the original undertaking; since the formal rite is not repeated, these offenses exist. The meaning of the second question and answer can be understood accordingly.

Third, regarding the question of the lightest offenses: taking the seven offenses concerning *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines to be taken at the proper time) as a basis, if one drinks non-time-appropriate liquid while seated, there are only five offenses and not two instances of "double-boiling.

If raw food is transformed or if one possesses *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya* (seven-day medicine) and consumes it on the eighth day, the transgressions increase by "abandonment" (*naiḥsargika*) and "handling" (*pariṣvajana*).

If the formal rite (*vidhi*) is added for *yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya* (lifetime medicine), once the illness has been cured, only one *maṅgala* (infringement) remains; however, this is not the case if the rite was not added.
This is also a medicine for the proper time. Question: Previously it was clarified that receiving [food] outside the proper time is invalid;

why is it now said that if a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) transmits the food, one avoids the offense of not receiving? Answer: The previous case concerned the observance of the precepts, wherein eating after midday is forbidden;

therefore, the reception was invalid. The present case concerns those who, due to anger or other such factors, might otherwise fail to receive; since the reception is valid here, one is exempt from the offense. (The preceding section on the Four Medicines within the "Internal Requisites" is hereby concluded.)

Now, we shall distinguish the external receptacle-world received [by sentient beings]. This section is divided into two parts; first, the topical outline is presented. Regarding the statement from "bowl-receptacles" (*pātra*) to "attached" (*fu*), the underlying intent is as follows:

Xuánzàng previously clarified that successive physical forms require concealment, and the ritual protocols have already been manifested. Next, the analysis of material food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is concluded.

This section extensively discusses the purification of the almsbowl (*pātra*). Since one has already understood the medicine to be contained within it, there must now be a vessel capable of containing it;

therefore, this is explained next. Regarding the etymology: if the full Sanskrit name *pātra* were used, it would be translated here as "appropriate vessel" (*yingqi*). Now, we simply say "bowl" (*bo*), which is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that "bowl" is a specific name for a monastic utensil, while "vessel" is a general term for anything that contains or stores things. Thus, "bowl" [is a specific instance of a vessel].

This accords with the correct practice of maintaining [the requisites]. The names of the subsequent regulations are established accordingly; the remaining cases are opened based on specific conditions, hence the addition of the title "Virtue" (*guṇa*).

The sections are as explained in the standard commentaries. Regarding the annotation: gold, wood, water, fire, and earth—these five are the fundamental materials for creating various implements used by people in their daily activities;

therefore, they are termed "action" (*kriyā*). These five encompass everything; "utensils" (*pariṣkāra*) is the general designation for these tools of production. Because they provide what is necessary to sustain the physical form, [they are called requisites].

This is called "Nurturing Life" (*yǎngshēng*). It is appended here as it emerges from the section on "Listening" (*tīngmén*). According to the commentary on the chapters, it is divided into two parts: first, the general intent; second, the detailed exposition of the chapters.

Regarding the initial statement from "nurturing" (*yǎng*) to "the latter": nurturing living beings requires no small amount of necessity; hence they are called "various requisites" (*zhòngjù*). These are abundant and flourishing.

"Also" means to gather together; it means to be numerous. "Permitted according to one's karmic retribution" means that those with superior faculties are permitted to keep one bowl, while those with middling capacity are permitted up to sixteen bowls—all such necessities are permitted according to their retribution.
The intent is that these items serve as material support for the purpose of establishing oneself on the Path.
"The conditions extend widely" means that the conditions for supporting the Path extend broadly to the later generations; this is the basis of the Dharma.
"Standard" (zhǔn) refers to the fact that the essential nature, quantity, color, and ritual application of whatever dharma is performed all rely upon the teachings of prohibition and permission;
each one has its authoritative basis. "To violate this regulation" means that if one acts in contradiction to the teaching, it is for this reason.
"This regulation and the offense shall not be pardoned if committed" means that if there is an offense committed, this transgression shall ultimately never be exempted from punishment.
This is unlike those in the secular world who, having encountered a pardon, are released; their transgressions must necessarily be washed away before they may attain purity.
As for "having mixed its physical form," this refers to confusion. Its substance was originally intended to be composed of clay and iron, yet now lacquer, wood, copper, stone, and the like are used.
Its appearance was originally intended to be like the blue-black colors of a peacock, yet now it is used as a plain white ball.

Regarding iron and so forth, is it not the case that their substance and appearance are intermingled and confused? Therefore, the purpose of establishing distinct categories is as follows: "Hence" (故) refers to the reason.

Since the preceding discussion was muddled and disordered, two streams of classification—namely, prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) and permission (*anujñā*)—are now distinguished and regulated to bring them into order.

To briefly state the intent of this section: it concludes the preceding [topic]. The specific elaboration follows below, which immediately gives rise to the two passages concerning prohibition and permission.
The meaning is as follows; it shall be clarified in the subsequent textual analysis (the above concludes the Section on the Four Fruits).
This concludes the *Commentary on the Essentials of Practice* from the *Record of the Nanshan Xingshi Chao* (concluding all miscellaneous essentials of practice).

Next follows the third section, the Chapter on Alms Bowls (*pātra*). It is divided into two parts: first, the title; second, the explanation according to the chapter. Regarding the phrase "from 'bowl' to 'attached'": first, the underlying intent.

Having previously clarified that the physical form must be subject to wear and the rules for its maintenance have been manifested, and subsequently having distinguished the completion of the section on solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), [this section now follows].
Next, the four medicinal substances are explained. Since there is food that is contained, there must logically be a vessel that contains it;

therefore, following the section on the four medicinal substances for offenses, this section on the *pātra* (alms bowl) follows. Regarding the term "releasing" (*shi*), the Sanskrit is *pātra*, which here means "vessel" or "appropriate vessel.
Both terms preserve abbreviated names. *Pātra* is a specific name for a monastic utensil, while *qi* (vessel) is a general designation for anything that holds or stores.

The *pātra* (alms bowl) is strictly subject to the rules of regulation; therefore, it is designated by the term "prohibition" (*zhi*). Other items were permitted due to subsequent circumstances; therefore, they are given the title of "allowance" (*ting*). This refers to the permissions attached to the following rules.

The details regarding the chapters and so forth may be understood accordingly. If one follows the interpretation in the *Qingzhong yi* (Protocol for Light and Heavy Matters), the *pātra* is a matter of the prohibitive teaching (*zhijiao*).
The section on vessels belongs to the Gate of Listening. As the Venerable One has described it, regarding the "five elements" (pañca-mahābhūta):

gold, wood, water, fire, and earth are the basis for creating all implements and are utilized by people in their daily activities; therefore, they are called "elements" (*xing*). These five names comprehensively explain all phenomena, and thus they are appended to the end of this chapter.

In the second section, the "Explanation of the Chapters," the initial general intent states: "Regarding 'nurturing until the end,' the necessities for sustaining the bodies of living beings are manifold;

hence they are called 'various requisites' (*saṃbhāra*). 'Abundant' (*yīngshèng*) means to gather together in great quantity; that is, when objects are amassed in great numbers, they are termed 'proliferated and complex' (*fanzá*), meaning many names.
'Permitting [their use] according to retribution' means that there are distinctions based on the superior, middling, or inferior faculties of one's karmic retribution."

As for those of superior capacity, they possess only a single alms bowl; for those of middling capacity, sixteen vessels are permitted; and for those of inferior capacity, all [utensils] are allowed to be kept.
The intent is that material requisites serve as support so that one’s realization of the Way may be established.

Although these provisions for the path are extensively provided even for the final age, whatever is undertaken must be complete in three aspects. For instance, the empowerment of ritual usage must rely upon the scriptural teachings; therefore it is said:
The Dharma has its standards by which it is based. "To establish regulations for those who transgress" means that if one violates these teachings, then regulations and punishments shall be imposed.
"If one commits an offense, there shall be no pardon" means that once a violation has occurred, there will ultimately be no time for exemption;

this is not like the common world where those who have committed offenses may escape punishment through a royal amnesty. "Since their physical appearance is made indistinguishable" refers to the confusion [of status].
Furthermore, their substance was originally earth and iron; now it is lacquer, wood, gold, silver, and so forth.

Their appearance was originally that of a peacock’s throat or a pigeon’s color—either black or blue; now it is a mixture of tin, lead, white porcelain, and tiles. How could this not be a state of confusion?
Therefore, the regulations are divided into two categories of streams to ensure their rectification. This is a brief explanation; the following text will describe them in detail.
Next, in the opening chapter, there are two parts: first, the division of chapters (as in the text); second, the citation [of the rules] (as in the text).

Regarding the phrase "from 'the beginning' to 'vessels,'" concerning the "vessels and so forth of those who have left the household life," Master Yuan says: "The *kāṣāya* has no collar; it is not the garment for court audiences. The alms bowl..."
He was without feet; he was not a vessel for the imperial court. Thus we know he was not suited for such a role. "Manifesting the Dharma-vow" (biao fazhi) means to manifest or to recognize.
Because he was known as a disciple of the Buddha, these qualities were not possessed by non-Buddhists. Regarding "having no causes for the necessities of life":

this refers to sustaining one's physical life by carrying an alms bowl to beg for food. It does not mean having shops or stalls as the cause for livelihood, nor engaging in trade as the cause for maintaining life. Therefore...
The *Jian lun* (Treatise on Views) states: "Begging for food is the practice of all virtuous people.
Having left home to study the Way and abandoned the worldly affairs of cause and karma, they beg for food because they possess no means of livelihood. They take the four seas as their home;
'home' here means to settle wherever one happens to go, without a heart of attachment. One begs for food to sustain the body and begs for the Dharma to sustain the spirit; therefore, it is so named."
[The passage concerning] the bhikṣu (and so forth).
Regarding the second [section], the "Discernment of the Substance," the phrase "the two limits" means that there are two essential requirements. Baoyun states:
According to the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga-kṣudraka-vastu*, it is permitted to keep six kinds of bowls, namely: the iron bowl, the *sumana* bowl, the *ukkala* bowl, and the *ukkasā* bowl.
The black bowl and the red bowl complete the six. Generally speaking, these do not exceed two types: first, iron; second, earthenware. Thus it is said, "In essence.

Therefore, the *Jiyesu* (Commentary on Karmas) states: "To use vessels made of various precious materials would cause confusion with householders; wooden bowls belong to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); stone bowls are used only by the Buddha.
Bhikṣus avoid all of these, using instead clay or iron, because this avoids all such confusion, simplifies matters, and makes them easy to obtain."
Regarding the Buddha’s own making of the clay for his alms bowl as a model for future generations, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
While the Buddha was in the country of Suma, he himself fashioned the clay for the bowl and had a potter fire it. He opened the kiln door and peered inside; they were all completed as golden bowls.
The potter was terrified and thought to himself, "This is the supernatural power of the śramaṇa. If the King hears of this, he will think that I possess much [wealth]."
Gold and jewels; he then buried them. (According to a record: The Buddha said, "If the King had known, thinking 'I can make a golden bowl,' he would have had the kiln-master bury it.
The details are unknown. Next, he made another crucible and fired it to produce a silver bowl; again, fearing [the King's reaction], he buried it as before.
Later, he made an iron bowl fired by heat, its color blue like the Jambu tree, and presented it to a bhikṣu. [The bhikṣu] did not dare to accept it. The Buddha said, "This is called..."

The Dharma instructs that bhikṣus shall use them; therefore, the Buddha said: "From this day forward, I permit you to keep three kinds of bowls: earthenware bowls and *sumana* bowls" (the table states:

*Sumana* is the name of a country; regarding the bowl, it refers to an iron bowl. However, because it is fired there [in that country], it is called a *sumana* bowl. It is named after its place of origin. As for those cast from metal, if they are *sumana*, they are essentially fired bowls, and thus are simply one type of bowl).
Regarding the wooden and stone bowls mentioned in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* is likewise; this is based on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-saṃyukta*.
In the *Dharmaskandha*: King Bimbisāra offered wooden bowls to the Saṃgha. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, saying, "We may not keep these; they are the practice of non-Buddhists.
If one keeps them, one must be dealt with according to the Dharma. Subsequently, he offered stone bowls to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "These are the Tathāgata’s dharma-bowls;

they should not be kept. If one keeps them, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense. Regarding bowls made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, or various other jewels, it was stated that they are likewise not permitted.
To possess [a bowl] means to possess it in accordance with the Dharma. Regarding the "fivefold wooden bowl," this refers to a sandalwood bowl.

The Buddha said that if an outsider criticizes this, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense for possessing it, provided it is capable of receiving oily food and the like. It was asked: since various bowls are not in accordance with the Dharma, they are not permitted to be possessed.
However, as for the stone bowl, since it is in accordance with the Dharma, the Buddha himself even possessed and used it, such as when it was offered by the Four Heavenly Kings. Part 4.

The alms bowls were joined together as one bowl for use. For what reason does a bhikṣu incur an offense by possessing [such a bowl]? Answer: Regarding the Buddha’s possession of a bowl, according to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, there are two reasons:
first, it was produced naturally upon the four peaks of the mountains of the Four Heavenly Kings; second, this stone is fine and smooth.
Third, when the Tathāgata was an infant, his strength was so great that he could contend with a hundred fragrant elephants without considering it a burden.

Now, if one were to permit bhikṣus to possess such an object, since it would not appear spontaneously, they would necessarily have to seek it out and manufacture it; this would obstruct and cause the neglect of their spiritual practice.

Furthermore, stone is coarse and prone to retaining grease, and those who lack the physical strength to carry it would instead give rise to weariness and distress. For these reasons, it is not permitted. Again, it is asked: at what time did the Four Heavenly Kings present [the bowl]?
Regarding the four bowls: why are they joined together as one? Answer: If one were to accept this one but not that one, it would be feared to violate the mind of equanimity.

Furthermore, if one were to accept all four bowls, since there is no need for many, one places them one upon another within the left hand and presses them down with the right hand to form a single bowl, symbolizing impartial benefit and succor. (According to the *Jian lun*, when a merchant offered roasted flour, he had no bowl.)
[This refers to] the bowl accepted [by the Buddha], which is why the Four Heavenly Kings offered it). *Hui-zhu* (spun ramie) refers to a cloth made from ramie fibers that has been lacquered.

*Gong-wa* (glazed tile) refers to tiles ground with stone on their surface and coated with earth-fat (*t'u-zhi*) so that when fired, they do not emit fumes. *Ci-bo* (porcelain bowl) refers to what are now known as porcelain or ceramic vessels.

Regarding the statement "the three colors are the same" within the *San-bian-se* (Discrimination of the Three Colors): according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are three types of color; two are as recorded in the excerpted text, and the third...
The color of the *kalaviṅka* bird is red. "Like a pigeon" refers to a grayish-blue color.

"Peacock-blue" (*mayūragrīva*) is the deep azure color on the neck of a peacock. "Plain tile" (*su-va*) refers to the earthenware vessels used today. "White iron" (*śvetāyas*) is forged and then fired;
it is tempered in the fire to make it hard and non-porous, much like the objects tempered by modern blacksmiths. However—

Regarding "merely smoothing without grinding": when making an alms bowl, one must first grind the upper surface with coarse earth, then smooth it, and only afterward place it in the steamer to fumigate it.
Now, instead of grinding first, they merely smooth it and then fumigate it. Below, in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, the number of times the fumigation is performed is clarified.

The four parts clarify the method for making the bowl: first, construct a furnace and coat it with various kinds of clay; wrap it with a paste made of apricot seeds and hemp seeds, and then cover it with ash.
Prepare the incense burner on level ground. Place the bowl (pātra) upon the burner and cover it with another bowl. Pack ash around the four sides to make it firm.
Next, pile up *guggulu* resin around the four sides and set it ablaze. Regarding the phrase "entering the cage," this refers to the bowl-cage (*pātra-kośa*).
It is made of iron; once the bowl has been placed inside, the cage is closed over it. The interior is smeared with sesame oil and then burned with a fire of cow dung. Thus it is obtained.
Regarding "internal smoke and oil" and "above the bowl":

among the four [sections on] "determining the measure," the phrase "from four to erroneous" first relies on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. As for the inclusion of additional dharma-terms within the commentary:
The *Suanjing* (Arithmetic Classic) states: Measurement begins with the *su* (grain). Six *su* make one *gui* (*Xuanyi* notes that "ten *su* make one *gui*" is likely an error).
Ten *gui* make one *chao*. Ten *chao* make one *cuo*. Ten *cuo* make one *shao*. Ten *shao* make one *he*. Ten *he* make one *chuan*.
Ten *chuan* make one *dou*. Ten *dou* make one *hu*. Thus it is called the method of incremental increase. According to the Tang *dou*, ten *chuan* constitute a large *dou*. Calculation follows this.
Giving three *dou* with a small measure is not different in meaning from giving three *dou* with a large one. As for the statement that the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) is inconsistent:
while its measures of *dou* are the same as those in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, that Vinaya further mentions the term *pātra*, yet it does not distinguish the size of the *pātra*.

Regarding the note that the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is fourfold inconsistent: Xuánzàng says, "If one calculates according to this Vinaya, the lower *pātra* appears to be large; [this refers to] excluding other edible items."

There are also six discrepancies; although these are omitted from this commentary for the sake of brevity, they are explained by citing the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (as it is stated in the *Sapariṣkāra-vyākhyāna*:
"Because there are eight discrepancies in the lower bowl, it constitutes a major offense").
Regarding the term "sāji-zao" (薩至造), it refers to the fact that those masters of the treatise had many differing interpretations and judgments.

However, within the treatise itself, one specific meaning is established as correct: it refers to a *pātra* (alms bowl) filled with fifteen *liang* of rice (Baoyun states that fifteen *liang* is the Western [Indian] scale).

This corresponds to thirty *liang* on the Qin scale (Xuan states this is the scale used during the Zhou dynasty). As for the Indian non-glutinous rice cooked in a cauldron, it resembles the "dug-in" rice (*dǎn fàn*) of the present day.
This is because it is not like the moist rice or wet gruel from the northern regions. The fifth fascicle of that treatise states: "There are three types of bowls.
The superior bowl receives three *bhojana* of rice, one *bhojana* of soup, and half a portion of other edible food.
The inferior bowl receives one *bhojana* of rice, half a *bhojana* of soup, and half a portion of other edible food. That which is between these two extremes is called the medium bowl. If...
If it exceeds that and is discarded, it is no longer called a *pātra*. As for those who discussed this among the people of the time, they were from the Western Regions (India).
Three *pātras* of food would be equivalent to two *dǔ* (pecks) of the state of Qin; this is the calculation according to the current master’s reckoning. Three *pātras* of food equal two *dǔ* of Qin.
One *pātra* of rice with soup equals half a portion of solid food, which is half a *pātra*. Thus, this constitutes one and a half *pātras*. Furthermore—
This constitutes one *dǒu*. Specifically, the upper bowl receives three *dǒu* according to the Qin measure. The Vinaya Master states that there is no other food remaining to be eaten.
The *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya-śāstra* (Duōlùn) says: "The Vinaya Master makes this determination. This means that the upper bowl receives three bowls of rice, and one bowl of others' soup;
there is nothing else remaining to be eaten. This is the space left above for the reserved food, ensuring that the finger does not touch the rice.

The middle and lower bowls may be understood by analogy. These also exclude other edible foods, but merely require that the food leave empty space so that the fingers do not touch it (Master Xuán says:

"Other edible foods" in the text likely refers to items such as vegetables). Question: Since the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* itself contains three grades of measurement, this should suffice for our own school;
why is it necessary to further cite ten [other] measures? Answer: Although our own school possesses the formal text, nevertheless...

The various schools differ regarding the size [of the measures], and ancient masters frequently cited the "universal texts" (*sāmānya-grantha*), which could be applied according to whether they were large or small.
Therefore, the Master of the present day has extensively cited the teachings on the fourteen *mātṛkās* and others to harmonize them, taking the majority as the standard limit;

all are measured at three *dōns* or one and a half *dōns*. Furthermore, this is based on the three grades of human dietary capacity, which correspond to their respective spiritual faculties (*indriya*). Thus...
It is called the "proper vessel" (*pātra*); therefore, another school is cited again. Regarding the phrase "seeing one shop, etc.," this is also from the treatise (*śāstra*).
It is as round as a pearl with one-third removed, or like a bird's egg with one-third taken away.

Those Arhats and Vinaya masters all know the origin story (*nidāna*) of this bowl, as is clear from the text. As for the term *vitti-dhara*, even if there is not so much as a single finger [of food], all...
The schools differ on this point. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, one may take three bowls of rice from another person, excluding soup and vegetables;

for the lower bowl, one may take one bowl of rice from another person, excluding soup and vegetables—this is as explained above regarding the ten *mātrā*s and so forth. As for the term "generally reduced," it refers to the statement that one should eat after measuring the portion;
thus, it applies to both increasing and decreasing. However, when discussing the actual measure of the bowl, one must rely on the authentic text; it is not a matter of arbitrary extension.
Regarding this, there is no need to perform the ritual of "purifying" (śuddhi); it is simply not to be accepted or maintained, as its possession is not permitted.
As for the statement that "five [categories] arrive," regarding the absence of a textual basis in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), the *Jiewen su* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states:

"Because the master Jue-ming transmitted the original text from the East, when it reached the frontier regions, it was transcribed as it emerged. There was no leisure to verify or cross-reference it, resulting in the formation of these distinct recensions."
He subsequently returned to the west; therefore, many parts are missing. I questioned a monk from the Kingdom of Khotan:

"Since he has extensively propagated the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, why does the *Vinayavibhaṅga* lack the ritual procedures for the various types of receiving precepts, such as the date of reception? He replied: "This is not absent; it is merely omitted. (The above is from the commentary.

The wording of the ritual for receiving precepts is as found in the text. Below, in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the mental reception (*cittasamādāna*) is clarified; the marginal note appears to compare this to the case of one living alone (*ekavihārin*).
"Qiū" (丘) means "to break with the past. The ancients said: "If it is not [the case that] there is no one [to whom to declare purity], one does not speak [of it].

Monks possessed long bowls; they would mutually receive and relinquish them according to the ritual for robes (*cīvara*). Now, this commentary simply provides for the case where no person is present to face; thus, one relinquishes the old and receives the new.

This is precisely what constitutes the constant practice of declaring purity (*śuddhi*). Question: Are there others who must further add the formal ritual? Answer: One may simply perform the mental recitation (*manasikāra*) forever.
It is established. Because of these strict regulations, they differ. The *dīrghacīvara* (extra robe) is a permitted teaching; it is allowed for ten days when a person is available.

Now, as no one is present, one may temporarily perform the mental recitation (*manasikāra*). Later, if someone is present, it must be recited again. This is a restrictive regulation (*pratikṣepa-śāsana*);

the moment one obtains [the robe] and does not maintain it, one commits an offense. Therefore, it is permitted that receiving it alone is valid. Regarding the "six losses of the method" (*ṣaḍ-vināśa-dharma*), the term "six" refers to the point of receiving.
As in the text. Furthermore, in the subsequent question-and-answer section, it is also as in the text. Moreover, according to the Commentary (*śāstra*), it asks:

"If there are two bowls, both of which have not yet had the ritual addition (*adhivāsana*) performed, which constitutes the offense of keeping an extra bowl (*atireka*)? The answer is: "The one that was brought forward first does not constitute an offense, because the regulation regarding the bowl is based on its being received [as a formal possession]."

One obtains [the robe] later because it was intended for one to accept and keep it; this is because it was combined with a long-term pure gift (*dīrgha-śuddha-dāna*). If one does not mention this now, it is termed an offense.
If one obtains it all at once, there is no offense whether it is good or bad. If there is neither good nor bad, yet one uses only one of them, it constitutes an offense of surplus (*atireka*).

The seventh is the practice of protecting the Dharma. Regarding the phrase "seven [acts] leading to offense": as for the "vessel for drinking gruel," "drinking" (chūe) refers to inhaling and exhaling air toward the food with the mouth;
the "vessel" is a shallow and wide iron or ceramic bowl. In the text, the character *ku* (苦) is pronounced in the departing tone (*qùshēng*) with the sound *kù* (meaning "to suffer" or "affliction").

Some manuscripts read *ruò* (若) in place of this character, which is incorrect. "Crouching" (*jùquán*) means to squat; one may also adopt a hunched posture, provided that one excludes standing upright and washes three times. This is done using soapberry (*zǎojiǎo*) pods.

Rinse it three times with either broth or water. According to the Vinaya, this refers to when it has become greasy. Regarding the passage from "The Four-Part [Vinaya]" down to "the color," following the *Xuánjì* (Commentary on Profundity), it is divided into two sections:
first, explaining the rules for protection; second, from "The Four-Part" onwards, variously distinguishing what is not the Dharma.

The first section is further divided into two: first, the actual explanation of protection; second, citing the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* as proof. "Sufficient to break the bowl" refers to the bowl that has been placed there.

As for the location, it is improper if it is merely broken. Regarding the breaking of a *pāṇḍulohitaka* (a bowl with stains) due to an evil intention, there is a light offense; for two people, it is a *deśanā-garhya* (confession).

As for one with a good intention, because he washed it for another and broke it by mistake, there is no offense. One must not wrap [the cloth] around all four sides. If wrapping from the mouth [of the bowl], one should leave open a space of one part;
if there are many holes, open them all so that they are spread out. When holding the bowl sideways toward the outside, [the edge] should face outward.

One interpretation says: "One must not obstruct the elbow" (this is not the correct explanation). Another says: Because a bhikṣu’s bowl was overturned with its opening facing outward on the ground, the rim of the bowl damaged his body and he broke a bone;
for this reason, it was prohibited. Regarding "placing the bowl upside down against a wall":
as in the northern regions where walls are constructed using beams, there is a protruding section at the edge of the wall about one chi long; one must not place [the bowl] in such an empty space.
Regarding the placement of the alms bowl:

because it is dangerous, two [rules] are heard and one is recited as in the text. As for the phrase "the four arrivals," it refers to sixteen types of vessels, including the two pots of various sizes.
Regarding the purification of the four types of earthenware vessels: use two jars for the upper and lower [storage]. One is kept inside the room and one is kept outside the room.
There are two lids for the cauldron and two lids for the jar. For the four items—the jar, the fourfold vessel, and the four basins—one uses each item for its specific purpose.

These sixteen locations must be declared pure before the Saṃgha. As for the "straight" storage of the *pai-nang* (the *nang* is used to catch the wind; it is what people here call a brazier), if one errs [in this practice], it is as the people of the South refer to it—a furnace.

"Vessel" (器) refers to the standard for making carts; "copper workshop" (銅作家) refers to the turning of axes and the fashioning of vessels. "Fire technique" (火術) is the general term for tools used for producing fire. Regarding the "fire-drill" (火子), the Vinaya states: "One must have a fire-drill; it is permitted to make one, etc. As for the meaning of "large bowl" (大盋):
according to the intent of the *Shō* (Commentary), if it is from one and a half *dō* up to three *dō*, it should be measured as a large bowl and its purity (*shōjō*) must be formally declared.
Since the present Vinaya states that it need not be given away as a pure gift (*fujōse*), it should refer to a bowl of more than three *dō*.

Regarding oversized alms bowls (*atimātra-pātra*): it is not permitted to keep them for personal use; they must be formally dedicated (*śuddhi*) and maintained as such. If they are of standard size, one must ensure they are not used improperly.
For fear that others might misuse them, it is necessary to give them away; thus, this [text] distinguishes them by noting that one does not formally dedicate a standard-sized bowl.
As for the phrase "from four [units] up to a scale," this refers to the vehicles used for transporting implements, which are the mounts of the Son of Heaven.
Prior to the Qin dynasty, "lǎn" (palanquin) and "jǔ" (carriage) were not distinguished and were both designated by a single name. During the Qin, Li Si divided them into two:

that which the Son of Heaven rode was called a *lǎn*, while if it was bestowed upon a monk, it could be kept as property. For instance, when Emperor Heng of the Jin dynasty bestowed one, he violated the Great Master’s [the Buddha’s] regulations;

yet it has survived to this day, etcetera. As for the "lǎnyuán" (palanquin with a shaft), this refers to a *lǎn* carried on the shoulders of men; if it has a shaft, it is drawn by people. Excluding the female oxen.
"Oxen, grass, and horses" refers here to what was said regarding bhikṣus. A leather cord causes insects to breed; this is the rule concerning hair cords.
"Torn and folded" refers to variegated silk. Regarding those who hold a fly-whisk (*cūḍāpaṭa*): it is made from the fur of the largest deer, which is called *chen*.

As for the offense of a *pāyattika* (falling down), it is because of harming the lives of insects. "Mao-tan" (the first character pronounced as *suō jiāo*) refers to the head of a whip. "Li-dao" refers to opening a wound. The use of a ladle (*tiáo*, pronounced *dú bó*) is prohibited.
On the top of the foot [of the vessel] there is a copper ring. As for the "earthen cauldron" (*tǔfù*), it is a pot with handles; Xuán says it is used for compounding medicines.

It is coated with red clay and its rim is trimmed with the hair of a red horse; it is used for compounding elixirs (*dān*). There are also three kinds of flasks, which likewise consist of copper, iron, or earthenware.
As for the *shī* (a sieve made of *luó* vines) and the glass phial (*bǐ*), because they are smooth, they can treat cataracts of the eye. [They are used for] pouring.
The nasal tube (*nāsikya-nāḍī*) is that which places medicinal substances such as clarified butter (*sarpis*) inside a tube to be poured into the nostrils.
The smoking tube (*dhūma-nāḍī*) is that which draws smoke upward from a lamp. The water-drawing tube (*pānīya-nāḍī*) is used for drawing water into jars or cauldrons.
The basin for ablution (*snāna-pātrī*) is a basin for receiving water when washing the hands or face. The rest is as stated in the text. It says, "The *Caturvarga-vinaya* has arrived."
"Those who provide for living beings" refers to those who supply iron chopsticks. "Peach-lamp staffs" are [staffs used with] lamps.

"Iron wicks" means using iron to form a ring, upon which a crow-beak is fixed to hold the lamp-wick, thereby preventing it from burning the lamp bowl. "If they are raw or spoiled" refers to blades that have not been tempered.
"Wool" refers to fine animal hair clothing. "Kappāsa" (cotton) refers to clothing made from tree flowers; it is also called clothing woven from grass flowers.

The *lāo* (pronounced with the *lì* and *dào* finals) is used for breaking through the earth; in Jiangdong it is called a *bǎ*, in Shandong it is named a *lāo*, and within the Guannei region it is called a *mò*.

Regarding the "staff held in mid-air": the Vinaya states that a bhikṣu holds an empty staff. Because non-Buddhists [accused] that a bhikṣu had hidden a sword inside [the staff] and claimed he harbored evil intent, the king investigated and executed the bhikṣu.
It was for this reason that the Buddha established this regulation. As for "salt-lid," this is the character *kuò*.

The bottom is flat like a casket. Regarding the wooden *tāng* (pronounced *tā-lǎng*), it is recorded in the *Zhōngjì*; it is written with the character *zhàng* (pronounced *tā-lǎng*, a bamboo vessel shorter than a bucket).
The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is a round vessel. It has a capacity of four *shun* and is used as a ladle. As for the phrase "increasing by one *zhi*," [it refers to this].
Citing other schools to clarify the construction of bathhouses: first, citing the *Ekottarika Āgama* to clarify the merits; next, citing the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* to clarify the location;

below that, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* clarifies the method of scrubbing and rubbing; and below the *Vinayamātṛkā*, it clarifies the method of the Elder’s admonitions, as per the text. Regarding the meditation staff (*dhyāna-yaṣṭi*):
according to the thirty-fifth [chapter] of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when various bhikṣus were sleeping while sitting in meditation, the Buddha said: "From this day forward..."

One should practice the method of the meditation staff (*dhyāna-daṇḍa*). It should be made of bamboo (*veṇu*) and eight cubits (*hasta*) in length. A junior monk (*navaka*) shall hold it and walk about the assembly.
If anyone is sleeping, one must not call out to them abruptly; rather, one should strike them with the staff to awaken them. Once they have awakened, the staff should be handed over to them.

Having received it, that person likewise holds it and walks about, following the same procedure as before. As for the meditation ball (*dhyāna-gola*), it is like a ball of wool; one hurls it from a distance at those who are sleeping.

To ensure awakening, one should follow the five methods prescribed in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: first, out of compassion; second, not to disturb others; third, for the sake of sleep; fourth, leaning the head against a wall;
fifth, stretching out the legs. Regarding the meditation support (*dhyāna-yaṣṭi*): it is like a tablet placed upon the crown of the head, with a hole drilled through it to pass a cord over the ears.
When one falls into deep sleep, it immediately drops to the ground. The Buddha said: "If it falls once, you may stretch out one leg; if it falls twice, you may stretch out both legs."

Regarding the three instances of falling [into negligence], one should rise and practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). The *Puruṣa-asthi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Skeleton) states that one should further provide a skeleton for the practitioner to contemplate.
As for "an excellent teacher and excellent instruction": one who can personally enter into the correct contemplation of phenomena is called an "excellent teacher.

One who causes such a teacher to skillfully instruct and illuminate the disciple is called "excellent instruction. Regarding the "rope, pegs (the character *qián* is pronounced *lián*; it refers to a driven stake), and railings," the term "lengthwise" is used as follows:
*Railing*: The horizontal bars are the *śūnya* (crossbars). To speak of it generally, anything constructed along the perimeter is called a railing (*vedikā*).

Regarding the phrase "increasing by one up to the dwelling," this clarifies the method for constructing a room. As for "the gift of the *cātuddisa-saṃgha* (the Saṃgha of the four quarters)," it refers to a gift made for the sake of the Saṃgha of the four quarters who come and reside there;
the donor provides for their own needs. Regarding "repairing the temple gate," that Vinaya states: "The Buddha was staying in the country of Ālavī."
The Buddha saw that a beam in a temple was damaged. He asked Ānanda, "A beam has broken; why have you not repaired it?

Ānanda replied, "The carpenter is occupied with his own work and cannot attend to the Buddha's task. The Buddha ordered Ānanda to fetch the necessary tools so that he might repair it with his own hands.

Having finished the repairs, he said to the bhikṣus, "From this day forward, I permit you to keep all kinds of woodworking tools. You yourselves may perform such repairs. (From the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Sifen lü).
Regarding "one must not do the same": in the rules for dwellings, one must not create images of men and women in union;

this is the same as the text in the *Cīvara-vastu*. Regarding "one should not use embroidery or ornamentation": this means that one must not entirely cover [the surface] with embroidery, brocade, or colorful patterns. "Variegated" refers to animal motifs.

All [images] such as dragons, snakes, mounds, and horses should be fashioned. Regarding the rule that one must not build back onto monastic land (*saṃghabhūmi*): because one is already on monastic land, if one builds a room there, when guests arrive, one must yield;

it is improper to occupy it permanently. This is because [the space] belongs to the *Saṃghika* (monastic community) property. As for the procedure of granting it by means of a formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*):
one part is granted to the *Saṃgha* to have the room repaired, while the other is given to a layperson (*avadātavasana*) to have it repaired. The intention is that first, one must...
Regarding the shared dwelling with the Saṃgha: when it is inscribed "the room of [Name]" by both parties, this is because the room was constructed for the Saṃgha by multiple donors;

therefore, it is recorded as such. One must not take one away and give it to another; rather, it should be provided according to its proper position. One must not bestow or withdraw it according to personal whim.

As for those who reside there at the same time, there is a specific period for one year; "one period" refers specifically to the four months [of the rainy season]. (The preceding consists of several sections.)
The section on "Differences" (bùtóng) concludes with the chapter on "Alms Bowls" (bòqì).

Fourth is the chapter on "Giving" (shī), which consists of two parts: first, the citation of the title; second, the explanation. Regarding the phrase "from 'Facing' (duì) up to twenty," this is the initial intent of the arrival [of the text].
When one's upper robes and food are sufficient, and one's dwelling and utensils are complete, one obtains the physical support necessary to cultivate the path and its practices. If one receives...

The practice of receiving [offerings] deviates from the proper form; it immediately leads one toward the swift current [of saṃsāra]. Therefore, one must cultivate contemplation regarding the conditions and requisites for receiving them. Thus, the following section is explained. Regarding the definition of terms:

that which is able to receive is called "receiving" (dāna), and that which is given is called "giving" (dāna). Because one cultivates contemplation based on giving, this chapter is titled "On Cultivating Discipline" (Xingzhi pian).

The sections below are as commonly explained. According to the commentary on the chapters, the first chapter provides the general intent of the introduction. The passage beginning with "Now, as for... clarifies the act of receiving.
This is the practice of giving with contentment. Regarding the statement that "merit arises from purity": the *Ratnamegha-sūtra* states that there are two kinds of fields for conditioned merit:

first, the field of compassion; second, the field of reverence. Compassion refers to sympathetic pity, such as when a state establishes infirmaries and the like (and so forth). Second is the field of reverence.
This refers to the four fruits of the śrāvaka, down to ordinary worldlings and the five groups of the ordained who strictly maintain the categories of precepts;
by making offerings with a reverent heart, one immediately generates merit, just as a fine and fertile field in the world can produce excellent crops.
This is the meaning of the "pure field" (*śukla-kṣetra*) here. Regarding those who give rise to "small desire" on the Path: practitioners, focusing their minds upon this pure field...
"Respectfully" means to bestow gifts by dedicating one's wealth. Xuan says that the sutras state that if one gives with a light heart, one will only receive the merit of a borderland.
"Only a little, only in moderation" means that the recipient, knowing the previous gift is difficult to digest, exercises self-restraint and accepts only a small amount.
"Offering much without satiety" clarifies that the cultivation of merit should be like this; [yet] one accepts little.
The term "etcetera" clarifies that the recipient of the gift ought, according to principle, to be one who accords with the teachings and practices with faith;

they should give rise to deep faith and rely upon the Buddha’s four reliances and his teaching on having few desires. Thus, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra-alaṃkāra* states: "If one can extend the hand to give, this hand is called 'excellent adornment.

If the recipient can withdraw the hand [of refusal], their excellence as an adornment surpasses the former. To say that one should merely accept what is appropriate is to lament not knowing [the proper measure].

This is a refutation of the [opponent's] position. One who skillfully responds to the Dharma guards and maintains the prohibitive precepts and constantly gives rise to the three types of wholesome conduct of speech.
When the mind accords with the pure teachings of the śramaṇa, one is able to bestow gifts and obtain merit that may be received;

one can eliminate transgressions and does not fall into the fault of failing to give. This is called being "without flaw. As for "necessarily establishing a model within affairs," "model" (gui) refers to a standard or pattern upon which things depend and rely. Internally, it is empty.

When it appears rotten and foul-smelling on the outside, those who are pure cannot digest such offerings; instead, it becomes a transgression that causes merit to flow in two directions, leaving one with nothing to rely upon.
If you can examine yourself from below, as the Vinaya says: "In eating, know moderation and do not crave flavors."

One nourishes the body without being arrogant; one does not act with pride or conceit, but merely obtains what is necessary to sustain the body so that no harm arises, thereby enabling the practice of cultivation.
Thus, suffering is extinguished and new suffering does not arise; there is neither increase nor decrease. One possesses strength but remains free from worldly affairs (as stated in the Vinaya text).
From the section on "Contentment with Food": this clarifies that power arises from [the absence of] what is not [to be had]. Below, it clarifies the absence of worldly affairs.
Regarding the establishment of the meaning of the conditions for the Path: clothing and food are the conditions for practicing the Path.

"Practice arises from these" means that once these material conditions are obtained, the practice of the three karmic paths arises therefrom. "What is it? refers to the subtle intention above. "Attachment of the emotions" refers to the state of mind.
Regarding "the attachment to pleasure": one who immediately arouses the mind to exercise self-restraint will, through such self-discipline, remain free from defiled attachment.

Regarding "not becoming deluded by flavors": it is like the case of the artemisia (chāngpú), which, though foul-smelling, was considered a delicious dish by King Zhou Wen (as recorded in the *Lüshi Chunqiu*).
Furthermore, scabs are extremely filthy, yet Liu Yong craved them. When Liu Yong served as the Magistrate of Nankang, he had more than two hundred subordinate officials. However—
The treatise states that he was faultless and without transgression, yet he was whipped daily until his sores provided the ingredients for his meals (as recorded in the *Xiyao* and the *Songshu*).

As for those who grow weary of fine delicacies, there have been no such eminent monks in antiquity; whatever food they consumed, they would add water to it, never craving its flavor—this is what is meant by growing weary of fine delicacies.
"Fangcun" is another name for the mind; whether one falls into ruin or rises to excellence depends entirely upon the mind.

Regarding "not reflecting upon the conditions of time": time consists of days and nights, comprising six hundred and thirty-eight million *kṣaṇas*. In every thought-moment (*nāman*), there is decay and passing away;

such time serves as the condition for the transformation and transmigration of the body. Why do you not reflect with discernment upon what is "slipped away" and "fallen"? "Slipped away" means to depart; "fallen" means to descend.
The teachings judge that those who enter the heavenly realms are still within a deep net—namely, receiving rebirth as domestic animals due to a greedy mind.
Such a person, when their life ends, will inevitably fall into this [state] with no prospect of escape.

As for the saying that those who receive [the results] reach this point, it is like the thirst of craving and so forth, which is like the ocean swallowing ten thousand streams; that ocean never says it is full.

"To regulate by means of the Dharma" means to measure and judge by means of the undefiled Dharma. Why worry that one will not find cessation? Regarding the "nine streams," the land of Han (China) says: [they refer to the nine schools of thought].

1. The Daoist Stream (the virtue of Chen Yao and Shun); 2. The Confucian Stream (clarifying the teachings of the Five Constant Virtues); 3. The Name Stream (rectifying the names of all things); 4. The Legalist Stream (clarifying laws such as rewards and punishments);
5. The Mohist Stream (clarifying matters such as sacrificial records); 6. The School of the Vertical and Horizontal (possessing eloquence and rhetoric);

7. The Yin-Yang Stream (clarifying the Nine Palaces and the Eight Trigrams); 8. The Agricultural Stream (farmers and the like); 9. The Miscellaneous Stream (various miscellaneous explanations of the preceding). The "Vulgar" school refers to Huang-Lao.

Huiwen, Zhuangzi, Liezi, and others were among those who even held those concerned with food and clothing in contempt. The *Book of Documents* says: "Zi-zhan did not have more than two flavors in his meals, nor did he use more than a single mat for his seat.

The *Jia Yu* says: "Yanzi wore a single fox-fur robe for thirty years until the end of his life. The *Analects*, in the "Xian Wen" chapter on shame, states: "To receive a salary when the state is well-governed is not shameful;
but to receive a salary when the state is in disorder is shameful" (*gu* here refers to official emolument). The *Yun Jing* mentions those who ate alone or drank from gourds, and so forth.
Furthermore, wearing robes made of woven hemp to cover their bodies, they do not concern themselves with the colors red and purple; using pine needles as food, they do not attend to sweet delicacies.
Even among worldly people, such is the case for those who take the vows alongside the Śākya disciples. The remaining text may be understood in detail.
The opening section of this chapter is indicated as follows in the text. Regarding the phrase "from 'initially' to 'receives':

as for 'using [the gift] by theft,' one who has broken the precepts loses both wealth and the Dharma; thus, receiving a gift in such a state is itself an act of theft. Regarding "using [the gift] while in debt":

although one may possess the precepts, if one receives a gift from another, one should first form this thought: "I receive this robe to ward off the heat and shame; I receive this food for hunger, thirst, and illness."
If one does not act [to repay], it is called being in debt. When there are those among one's kin who are in distress, this refers to the seven types of learners (*śaikṣa*) receiving offerings;

they are like a son using his father’s property, and are thus called "kinsmen and friends" (Xuanzang says: the three fruits and four stages of approach constitute the seven learners; he does not adopt the various recorded interpretations). As for "those who use [offerings as] masters," these are the Arhats;
when the afflictions of the three realms are exhausted, they are then fit to receive offerings as if they were no different from oneself, and are thus called "masters who use [them]. (2)
Both cases constitute a lapse in giving. Giving to one who has broken the precepts does not result in the recipient’s purification; instead, it causes them to fall into the evil realms.

The merit gained by the donor is meager, and they cannot escape saṃsāra, falling back into the three evil destinies. It may be understood that even if one gives to another who lacks virtue, the donor now incurs a downfall because of the object given;
thus, the donor also bears fault. If pure monks receive [the gift], they can attain the merit of Buddhahood, which is untainted (anāsrava).

This is because when one is born in an age when a Buddha exists, one does not sink into the three miserable realms (*trāya*). It is said that giving to an impure field results in diminished retribution, or perhaps no retribution at all.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are four permutations: first, the giver is pure and the recipient is impure;

second, the giver is impure and the recipient is pure; third, both are pure; fourth, both are impure (only the third permutation is called *dānapāramitā*). One should not accept [gifts] in cases where it is inappropriate.
As for this, it is as received and upheld in the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* (寶梁經), or as when a person performs prostrations and attains the eight minor dharmas, etc. (as detailed below, et cetera).

Second, the skillful means of wearying and treating [the afflictions] is set forth according to the text. Regarding the phrase "from 'great' to 'attainment,'" first the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* is cited to clarify the causes for generating weariness and ceasing desire through the practice of contemplation:
first clothing, then food, and finally dwellings, as in the text. The passage beginning with "If one can," clarifies...
"Benefit" means that by being able to contemplate that the four great elements and the five aggregates are both empty, one immediately attains the emptiness of persons and becomes an Arhat.

Although the field still possesses the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*, which have not yet been eliminated, one may rely on the contemplation of the Great Self; since the external is already empty, one can contemplate the internal mind and attain the four kinds of knowledge of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "from the four... to the approach," it refers to establishing vows and increasing cultivation to prevent the arising of future suffering as a result. This is based on [the preceding text].
The Vinaya-vibhaṅga states: The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kośala. While traveling with the bhikṣus, he encountered a great mass of fire blazing intensely.

He asked the bhikṣus, "Do you see this which must not be touched? It would be better if someone were to seize it. At that time, a woman of the kṣatriya caste and others prostrated themselves across [the path].
Regarding these two matters, which is the wholesome? The bhikṣu said, "To be able to touch a woman is wholesome. The Buddha said, "To be able to touch this fire [is wholesome];
