If one were to combine the three robes into a single patched robe, it would contradict the scriptural injunctions. Qiansu said: "Each of the three robes constitutes a patched robe;
even the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṭicīvara*) is made as a patched robe. [The interlocutor asks: "If that is so, how does this differ from the three robes mentioned below?"

Answer: The former refers to [robes] that have been cut and pieced together; this *nāṅgalīya* (pailoṭaka) robe is distinct from them. Furthermore, the former are robes given as offerings by lay donors (*dānapati*), whereas these are *pāṃsukūla* (rag-heap) robes.

(Now, I fear this may not be so; I have never seen the *nāṅgalīya* and the *pāṃsukūla* treated as separate categories. For instance, Kāśyapa possessed only a single robe; if one were to keep all three together, it would constitute a heavy burden.

Although there are such difficulties regarding the number, they are maintained out of deference to tradition). For now, I shall speak according to the previous classification: the *nāṅgalīya* belongs to this category, while the three robes (*tricīvara*) belong to the subsequent category.
Reflect upon this. The fourfold abandonment of gifts from donors is difficult to digest and was practiced by people of ten generations past.
First, regarding shame: one abandons the robes of a donor out of shame that they are difficult to digest; one wears rag-robes (pāṃsukūla) out of a sense of propriety because they require no effort.
Second, regarding the mind of detachment: one detests famous garments and dyes, for this clothing does not crave finery. Third, regarding conformity to cessation: the mind remains unmoving.
Shaking [the head] is the dharma of quiescence. Now, as for these humble items of the patched robe, one does not give rise to a mind of greed; this is precisely the non-movement of the mind.
It is not for the sake of those who are burning with passion, because one does not cling to external objects. Regarding "evil is easily seen," the *Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching* says:
"One should touch one's own head, having abandoned ornaments and wearing robes of dyed color, holding an alms bowl to sustain oneself by begging. Thus one sees for oneself.
It is so. If arrogance arises, one should swiftly extinguish it; one who practices the path with diligence does not wear this robe out of indolence.
Regarding the novice Cunda and others, the *Pāṃśukūlika-varga* (Chapter on Rag-robe Wearing) in the latter volume of that sutra states:
The Buddha told Kāśyapa, "If there is a bhikṣu who wears a rag-robe without any attachment, he is able to leave behind arrogance and is able to cast off the heavy burden."

Because he was content with what he had, the devas and nāgas always delighted in wishing to see him; Śakra, Brahmā, and the four world-protectors joined their palms in prostration, let alone the other minor deities.
The Buddha told the śrāmaṇera Cunda, "Discard these impure refuse-rags and go to Lake Anavatapta to wash them."

The devas all circumambulated him and paid homage, taking the wash-water to bathe their own bodies, thereby knowing that this person maintained the precepts, practiced meditative concentration, and possessed wisdom and majestic virtue.

(The *Biao* states: "Cūḍapanthaka was an Arhat; here he is called a śrāmaṇera. This is speaking of the cause within the context of the fruit. At the time of washing clothes, he had already received the full ordination.")

This does not refer to a śrāmaṇera (as the Arhat considered it). The brahmin Subhadra, wearing robes of fine color, was about to go to Lake Anavatapta when the devas blocked him from all four sides, not permitting him to approach the lake for fear that he would defile its waters. Therefore, Kāśyapa, who asked about this matter?
Within the Noble Dharma, one practices and trains without wavering.

Regarding the statement "from two up to conduct": as for the practitioner of subtle precepts, one does not cause this person to become a transgressor of the precepts by means of various surplus items.

The rest of the text may be understood accordingly. Regarding the statement "from three up to the Dharma": begging for alms is common to all Buddhas of the three periods of time; furthermore, one attains...
Death and hunger press upon us constantly. Furthermore, one bestows blessings and merit upon the donor while simultaneously emulating the model of the sages.

In the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Sapoduo), the lower section clarifies the faults of hastily accepting food from the monastic community; those who are uneasy do so because they observe the facial expressions of others to gauge their intentions, fearing only that the kitchen supplies might be depleted.
The section on "Accepting Donations from Laypeople" (*Tanyue*) clarifies the faults of accepting invitations from the laity, which is easily understood. Furthermore, regarding communal meals...

Below: A summary of the benefits of alms-gathering. Begging for food wherever one may be shall never come to an end (the commentary states: "For the assembly" means "for all"; it is not restricted solely to the communal meal, as it is known by the assembly).
Regarding the phrase "going to four [houses]": this indicates the manner of begging for food. "The first one" refers to the first house, continuing up to the seventh house.
Xuan says: "However, the practice of begging for food differs across various teachings. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is best if one obtains sufficient food at a single house;
if it is insufficient, one is permitted to go to other houses, but must stop once the requirement is met. This is the meaning of the present text.
In the middle [section], from the first characteristic up to the seventh characteristic, it is as if reaching the seventh house constitutes completion.

"That which was previously cooked" refers to the fact that the matured organs (the large intestine) are located below and the raw organs (the small intestine) are located above. "Not belonging to others" means that one sustains one's life by begging for oneself.
"Causing them to abide in the Three Jewels" means causing them to abide within the sphere of the Three Jewels so that they cannot be harmed by malevolent spirits or demons.

This is a delusion. One who should give rise to a heart of compassion is so called because they are able to uproot suffering and save all beings. Regarding being "easy to satisfy" and "easy to nourish": one is easy to satisfy by knowing moderation in eating;
one is easy to nourish by not discriminating between good and evil food. Regarding the "wholesome root of the invisible crown": "crown" (mūrdhan) has the meaning of the very top of the head.
Because he abandoned pride (*māna*) through the practice of begging for alms, he later attained the Way and realized the state of the invisible crown.

The *uṣṇīṣa* (crown protuberance). This mark arises from the practice of begging for alms; therefore, it is called a "root of goodness" (*kuśalamūla*). [The commentary states: For example, when the Bodhisattva Anantagātra heard that Śākyamuni was one zhang and six chi tall...

He then moved through the air to come and behold the mark of the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*). When he arrived, however, he was utterly unable to see that crown. This explanation is based on the retribution body (*vipākakāya*); the *Xuánjì* (Mysterious Record) may interpret it according to the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), but that might be too remote.
Regarding "not [associating] with men or women," this clarifies that such faults arise when accepting invitations.

As for "begging for alms" (*piṇḍapāta*): Bǎo says that in Sanskrit it is *piṇḍāya* or *piṅgala*, which means "begging for food. The current term "fēnwèi" (dividing the sustenance) refers to dividing the mouths of the multitude.

"Piṇḍa" means "portion. One portions out [alms] to protect one's own person, so that practicing the Way may be beneficial. Alternatively, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, one begs for food and then transfers it as a gift to the monks and nuns;
having thus portioned it for oneself, one portions it to protect the persons of others—hence it is called "piṇḍa.

Regarding the phrase "the monk forgets," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites the saying, "The night is long to one who cannot sleep," and so forth. The treatise states: When the Buddha attained enlightenment...
Later, his father the King ordered five hundred men to follow the Buddha and renounce the world. Upon first arriving at the city of Śrāvastī, he had Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana instruct them;
through diligent practice during both the early and late watches of the night, they all attained the fruits of the Path. Subsequently, the Buddha was about to return to his native country.

It is located fifty *li* from the city of Kapilavastu; this was formerly called the Place of Recreational Strolling. When he was practicing [austerities], he did not sleep from the first watch until the last watch of the night because he considered the night to be long.

Now, as he goes about begging for alms, he considers the road to be long. Because the Buddha preached the Dharma regarding this error, the road has become long while the night is short, due to his weariness from contemplation.
There was once a Brahmin who was deluded regarding the "Elder of Birth and Death. [Note: The term "Elder of Birth and Death" (*saṃsāra-śreṣṭhin*) refers to the cycle of rebirth.]
He arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling. The Buddha said, "In the time of Vipassī Buddha, this person once saw the Buddha.

While the Dharma was being preached, because the great assembly was so intent on hearing the teaching, he did not join them in conversation; instead, he reviled the Sangha, saying, 'These beasts have no discernment.
Due to this, for ninety-one kalpas, he fell among lions. At that time, this person should have attained the fruits of the Path, but because of his ignorance, he failed to do so."
Birth and death are far-reaching and long-lasting. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: Maudgalyāyana was seized with a staff and beaten by a brahmin.
Upon returning to the vihāra, he saw Śāriputra and recounted the preceding events in detail. Śāriputra asked, "At that time, why did you not manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to avoid it?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "I have fundamentally committed deeds that are exceedingly grave; I must inevitably undergo this seizure."
Śāriputra entered parinirvāṇa first because his illness was grave. He said to Maudgalyāyana, "I had originally intended to enter parinirvāṇa first, but Śāriputra told me, 'Wait a moment;
do not enter nirvāṇa yet. This was to follow the precedent of the past Buddhas, whose chief disciples always remained until they themselves had first attained parinirvāṇa.
Thereupon, he went to take leave of the Buddha and returned to his native village to pass away. It was there, in that house, that he entered parinirvāṇa.
"Ānanda, because the affliction of wind-disorder was so severe, the devas shed tears. [The questioner] asks: "Regarding formless sentient beings, by what cause do they have tears? Answer:

According to the Mahāyāna, although there is no coarse form (*rūpa*), there is subtle form. According to the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (or *Vibhāṣā*), although there is no form resulting from karma, there is form resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
From that concentration arises a physical body which possesses tears; however, only the general retribution (*vipāka*) has been severed.

One who cultivates the realization of suffering until reaching the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) is exempt from the collective retribution of the hells; however, Maudgalyāyana now undergoes individual retribution (*pratyeka-vipāka*).

This clarifies that begging for alms is the supreme practice of the Buddha, and one must not decline the labor. To resent it is to resent the Dharma, and such a person is identical to those who are deluded.
Regarding the statement "the four [meals] are equal," the morning meal is gruel, the midday meal is solid food, and the afternoon meal consists of leftovers.
This refers to eating from a single vessel. Horses are raised for strength; pigs are raised for meat. Now, these cases are not the same.

Regarding the "five kinds of people who eat once," the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Those who no longer eat again. The phrasing suggests that this refers to not receiving food repeatedly at the same location.
If one leaves this place and receives food again at another location, it would contradict the practice of eating in a single sitting (*ekāsana-bhojana*). According to this...
Among the ten benefits listed below, it says: "There is no seeking a second meal, which would lead to fatigue and suffering. This means that eating again at another location is also not permitted.
Furthermore, the *Sāṃkhyika* states, "One must not eat repeatedly," which serves as proof. Regarding "no seeking a second meal, which leads to fatigue and suffering":
if one eats a light meal (*khādya*), one might then seek a second meal; however, since a person stops once they have sat down [to eat], there is no such need.
This is the seeking of a second meal. There is no need for the exhaustion and suffering [associated with it].

Once one has accepted food, there is no need for the exhaustion and suffering of using eating vessels or rosaries. Regarding "no exhaustion before eating," this refers to the period before sitting down to eat;
there is no exhaustion such as the seeking of not eating, and so forth. For one who practices the subtle precepts, if they eat frequently, they would not differ from the laity.
The former is called "coarse practice," while now, ceasing after eating in a single sitting is called "subtle practice. The rest is as stated in the text.

Regarding the phrase "from six... to permission": it means that when [the food] is gathered in one place and measured to ensure sufficiency, only then does one eat until it is finished. "Twenty markers" refers to this.

"Taking what is sufficient by measure" means to take exactly as much as is needed. Regarding "extensive antidotes": wearing rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*) is the antidote for those who accept robes offered by householders; possessing only the three robes (*tricīvara*) is the antidote for those who hoard extra garments;

begging for food (*piṇḍapāta*) is the antidote for those who accept invitations from others; moderation in eating (*bhojanamātrajñatā*) is the antidote for greed and indulgence; sitting at the foot of a tree (*vṛkṣamūlika*) is the antidote for dwelling in houses and buildings; sitting in cemeteries (*śmāśānika*) is the antidote for seeking other superior locations;

and constant sitting (*naiṣadyika*) is the antidote for those prone to sleep. As for the phrase "as explained in the sūtras," Xuánzàng says: "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* itself does not cite [the specific source]."
Regarding the title of the sutra: for a person of the Qin, ten mouthfuls would correspond to what [the text] refers to as "dry pot-rice" and this as "warm rice," where half is water;
thus, those five or six [mouthfuls] should be calculated as equivalent to these ten. This citation serves to complete the preceding passage.
One should measure and take only what is sufficient, for further benefit cannot be derived.
Regarding the phrase "seven [yojanas] and so forth," this refers to an araṇya (forest hermitage). As for "if it is a thousand *li*," the *Xuánjì* states: one *gōng* consists of four *zhǔ*;
one *zhǔ* is eighteen *chí*. Four times eight is thirty-two; thus, one *gōng* equals seven feet and two inches. Ten *gōng* equal seventy-two feet. Calculating by the method of paces:
one pace is six feet; ten paces are sixty feet. Two times six is twelve. (Note: This concludes the calculation of the distance.)
Two [bow-lengths] equal one zhang and two chi. Furthermore, adding two steps, the preceding total becomes twelve steps.
Ten *gong* (bows) equal twelve steps; one hundred *gong* equal one hundred and twenty steps; five hundred *gong* equal six hundred steps, which constitutes one *li*.

Thus, it amounts to one *li* and two hundred and forty steps. (According to the calculations in the *Jì* [Record]: "One *gong* equals four *zhǒu* and seven chi and two cun; ten times ten *gong* equals three thousand six hundred chi, which together constitute six hundred [steps]").
"One pace" constitutes two *li*, and so forth. Regarding "the tiger's roar": when the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, there was a tiger that ate deer meat;
a bhikṣu picked up the remains. The tiger came seeking it and roared around the Jetavana. Consequently, [the Buddha] established the rule that one must not take the remains left by a tiger.

This is cited as proof that [the monastery] was outside the city. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Three *li* from the city, there were two *araṇya* (forest hermitages) for other monks; within the *saṃgha*-boundary, there were no [remains]."
Difficult. The *pañcayojana-cīvara-sīmā* (the five-li robe-boundary) is explained as it appears in the *Cīvara-vastu* (Precepts on Guarding Robes) according to its characteristics;

the rest is as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "reaching the fearful": for one who follows the mind of revulsion and detachment—originally weary of the world with the perception that it is not to be relished—now dwelling among the dead accords with this mind. To be separated from all loved ones refers to the six types of kin.
And so forth. Furthermore, when staying among burial mounds, one should constantly contemplate that all beings inevitably return to this state; this mind should always be maintained.

While among burial mounds, one should constantly give rise to a heart of compassion. What room is there for frivolity? Moreover, because one sees corpses with their bones and flesh scattered about, foul and loathsome, [compassion arises].
The mind should always feel weary of and detached from this impure body. Furthermore, among all things to be feared, nothing exceeds death;
if one can now dwell amidst burial mounds, what further fear could there be?
Regarding the phrase "nine [events] up to [and including]" and so forth: as for "such as when the Buddha was born," he was born beneath the Aśoka tree;

he attained enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree; he turned the wheel of Dharma beneath the Śirīṣa tree; and he entered parinirvāṇa beneath the Śāla trees. The treatise referred to is also the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
As for the ten benefits: first, housing; second, bedding; third, beloved objects; fourth, the exhaustion of sensory enjoyment.

Regarding "suffering and its accompaniments": among the four types of reliance on living under trees, this is the third. Ninth, "easy to obtain and without fault" means that [the tree] arises immediately.
Tenth, "without the clamor of crowds" means that it is not a dwelling where many people reside together.

Regarding the statement "ten [factors] up to dwelling," first, it cites the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* to clarify that practicing in the open air (*abhyavakāśa*) makes success easy; this may be understood. In the *Ekottarika-āgama*, fascicle 1, it says:
"There was once a bhikṣu who, carrying his alms bowl, went out to beg for food. A woman brought him food, and both were possessed by defiled thoughts.
When the bhikṣu received the food, his lustful mind caused him to shake the bowl violently and spill the food outside. Seeing this, the woman laughed, revealing her teeth."
Having seen this, the bhikṣu recollected the Buddha’s words regarding the various bones of the human body (as described in the text), and by means of this, he realized the fruit [of the path].
Furthermore, he preached the Dharma for a woman, and she too attained the fruit of the Way. The phrase "the discussion reached such-and-such" serves as a citation of scriptural evidence.
Regarding "few places for frivolous amusement": even beneath trees, people still gather to amuse and flirt with one another;

in the open air, it is the opposite. Regarding "not having the sound of thorns that pierce": there are many flocks of birds, and when the wind blows through the trees, they all produce sounds that damage the faculty of hearing like thorns;
now, being in the open air, this fault does not exist. Regarding "no place for bustling crowds": [this is absent here].

People travel by way of paths; this open space is not a place for traveling. As for the Great Fear Forest (*Mahābhaya-vana*), it is also called the Forest of Dread (*Bhīṣaṇa-vana*), or the Cold Forest, and is also known as the Śītavana (Cemetery) Forest. This forest is ten *li* to the northwest of the royal city, where all those who come to die are sent.

Regarding the statement "from eleven [rules] to their application," some interpret it as follows: when entering a gathering, one sits according to the seat obtained, without distinguishing between seniority based on years of ordination (*varṣāgra*).
As stated in the text below: "One sits according to the place obtained and does not cause others to rise";

and again, "one does not disturb the *sthavira* (senior) nor cause those of lower rank to feel distress. This interpretation is rejected. Both the Great and Lesser Vehicles (*mahāyāna* and *hīnayāna*)...
One should sit according to seniority by years of ordination (*śrāmaṇera-varṣa*), as prescribed in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and other texts.
If one claims that sitting does not follow this sequence and instead sits wherever one happens to be, how can this be called *dhūta* (ascetic practice)? Therefore, such a claim is untenable.

Now, we simply mean that one settles in whatever dwelling room is obtained, and uses whatever bedding materials are available for sitting and reclining, without discriminating between the fine and the coarse; this is because the subsequent text states, "one does not seek to dwell in a fine or exquisite vihāra."
And there is no exhaustion from seeking fine bedding; the phrasing and meaning are very clear (and so forth). Regarding the statement "from the twelve [vows] to 'preaching'":

*niṣadyā* (constant sitting) refers to the two feet being crossed and bound together, which is called the *paryaṅka-bandha* (full lotus posture). Regarding the statement "from the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) to 'mat'": [the text continues as follows].
Regarding the suffering of leaning against a seat: after lying down for a long time, pain arises upon turning over; now, by sitting constantly, one is free from this suffering.
Regarding not following bodily desires: one does not seek physical comfort, such as contracting or extending the limbs, or turning face up or face down.
As explained below, this is as discussed in the *Śrāmaṇera-varga* concerning the contemplation of inhalation and exhalation (*ānāpāna*).
The citations from the various schools follow the text as written. Regarding the statement "Vijñāna comes first," this has been clarified for a long time through the six versions of the *Vinaya*.
As for "eating only after [subduing] anger," this refers to disciplining one's own mind of anger. Xuanzang says: "The *kṛtānna-vidhi* (the ritual for leftover food) is not performed;

the *dhūta* practices exist only in the *Dharmaguptaka* school and are absent from the other schools. The remaining eleven points are largely the same with minor differences. Now, in the *Mātṛkā-vinaya*, there is no mention of "not performing the *kṛtānna-vidhi*."
The *Dharmapada* adds the dhūta practices to these, thus also making twelve. Regarding "not drinking liquids after midday": this is because one fears that the mind will not be single-minded;
otherwise, one would fail to contemplate the true principle and instead possess only a mind preoccupied with the desire for liquids. By not drinking now, one avoids this fault.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are no other material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), and it likewise establishes the number as twelve. The *Ratnamegha-sūtra* [also agrees].
Regarding the phrase "begging for white [food]," the *Xuánjì* states that the character "gē" (割) is pronounced as the sound of "gàizǐ" (盖子).

As for the "Ten Abodes" and so forth, that school has two forms of *dhūta* practice that differ from other sects: first, wearing garments of felt (*kṣaumika*); second, not accepting food outside of the proper mealtime after the midday meal.
Regarding "food," this refers to drinking liquids such as gruel; it refers to medicinal foods, such as ghee and the like, which may be consumed for up to seven days. — *Vimuktimārga*.
Treatise: Adding "not drinking thin gruel" is the same as the *Daśabhūmika* section of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. There is also the method for eating meals;

by further adding "begging in sequence" and "not [drinking] thin gruel," these become thirteen. Regarding the phrase "upward to the [precepts]," the upper [section] is clarified according to the various precepts of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Those twelve sūtras and śāstras are as previously analyzed. Relying on them, one shakes off [defilements] and eliminates afflictions; thus, emptiness of nature is realized.
This is right practice. Once the mental observation has been established and manifested, it is then designated as the cause of concentration and wisdom.
Regarding the four miscellaneous dharmas, as for the statement "the four lead to loss": first, providing for one's companions; and [selecting] a pure site free of grass.

According to the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*, when making an offering to hungry ghosts (*preta*), one must do so on pure ground. If giving to animals, it must be in a place where there is no grass, for fear that they might not see it.
Regarding "placing food in water without insects": if one places food in water containing insects, one fears that the water will harm or kill the insects.

As for "when a thief comes down, this is the method for providing for the thief," the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* records a case where a forest-dwelling monk (*araṇyaka-bhikṣu*) made an error in his response.

[The Buddha] distinguished it from other constellations. Because a thief stayed overnight and missed the [proper] time, he was captured; therefore, [the Buddha] decreed that [such matters] be dealt with in a secluded place.

Regarding those who use fire-jewels (*hiraṇya-maṇi*): this is because one fears the thief might suspect them of being precious objects. Below, in the *Sudarsana-vibhaṅga*, the method for rewarding labor is clarified according to the text.
(The preceding various sections, all being different [from the previous], conclude the *Dhūta-piṭaka*).

Section Six: On the Images of the Sangha. This section has two parts: first, stating the title; second, explaining the text according to its contents. Regarding the initial statement "up to the section on the Sangha," this is first the underlying intent:

having previously clarified the protocols for *dhūta* practices and the conduct of those capable of cultivation, the rules regarding the images of the Sangha have now been completed, yet the objects of instruction have not yet been manifested.
It is intended that the five classes of monastics may recognize their relative ranks, and the two classes of laypeople may understand their proper course.

[This section] is directed toward the following. Furthermore, when one wishes to construct [an image], one must rely upon a model and pattern. Since the previous [section] did not clarify this, it is explained next. Regarding the explanation of the names: "Seng" (僧) is an abbreviation;

in its original Sanskrit form, both the nature (*svabhāva*) and the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are fully present. As for "xiang" (像), it refers to a niche made of plaster over a base layer, imitating the true likeness [of the Buddha].

Because it extensively clarifies the performance of ritual offerings, it manifests the name of "paying respect. The headings of the chapters are as explained elsewhere; the annotations may be consulted in detail. Question: Regarding the image...

Question: The Saṃgha is that which relies [upon others], while the Buddha is that which is relied upon; since the Buddha is superior and the Saṃgha is inferior, why is the Saṃgha designated first? Answer:

This does not concern the relative superiority or inferiority of the supported and the supporter. Rather, the treatise takes up only the aspect of propagating and generating goodness; thus, the Saṃgha is the foremost object of faith.

As when Mañjuśrī and Maudgalyāyana first arrived, they manifested themselves in the deportment of the Saṃgha; likewise, the conversion of Aśvajit was also through the Saṃgha. This is explained in the section on "Equality."
First, the general intent; second, the detailed explanation by opening the chapters. Regarding the initial statement, "The Dharma reaches the learner":
"Dharma" refers to the teaching (*dharma*); "軌" (*gui*) refers to the ritual protocol (*vinaya*). It was established to reach and benefit the eras of the *Saddharma* and *Saddharmapratirūpaka*.

By reflecting upon the radiance of the Tathāgata and observing how sentient beings looked up to him, the teachings and protocols were thereby established. (There is an interpretation which states that the distant origin of the treatise dates back to the Zhou dynasty.)

[This refers to the] era [when he] manifested traces by appearing in this world and attaining perfect enlightenment. If one clarifies the "Image Teachings" (xiàngjiào), there is the celestial painting of the sandalwood image used as a standard. If one clarifies the proximate [period], this refers directly to Emperor Ming of the Later Han; it was through the two Venerable Ones, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna, that the Vaipulya scriptures were transmitted to this land.

(Now, regarding the fact that the auspicious signs had not yet been fully realized, the general meaning is as follows...). As for "humility," "reverence," "restraint," and "respect": humility is the difficulty of being impetuous and yielding to others, which is called respect.

Once humility and reverence are established, restraint occurs naturally; "restraint" refers to the yielding of respect. These terms—humility, reverence, and so forth—are names given to worldly persons in the nine commentaries. Herein lies respect.
The chapter on "Ritual" (*Lǐzhāng*) is one of the Five Constant Virtues. Furthermore, the *Qūlǐ* states: "There is nothing that does not involve reverence.

To humble oneself is called "yielding" (*xùn*); to apply one's wisdom is called "sincerity" (*kè*; *kě* in the rhyme). To follow established measures is called "ritual form" (*yí*). Because one humbles oneself and applies wisdom, one thereby gathers and restrains reverent ritual form.
For practitioners of the Three Vehicles, all their actions are governed by respectful decorum, as this is established at the very beginning of the tradition;
