For the sake of future bhikṣus, one fears people will say: "Because the invitations during the Buddha’s lifetime were sincere and the offerings substantial, they were established;
however, because the minds of those who invite now are light, this robe is lost. Thus, they would revile the bhikṣus, claiming their preceptual virtue is incomplete.
Therefore, it was accepted. Alternatively, it may be because one fears that future bhikṣus, by learning from the Buddha and treading upon it, might diminish their merit.
Regarding "nodding the head," this refers to nodding. When asked why he did not speak out to grant permission, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Duolun) states:

"There are three reasons for silence: first, to manifest that the habit of craving has been exhausted, and thus he does not speak; second, to stop the slander of non-Buddhists who claim, 'Gautama is full of greed'; third..."

He remained silent in order to manifest the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*). Regarding "not understanding the vow to return": this means that the vow to return was not understood; one must [recite] three times (and so forth).
As for the "eater of the sons of the Mother of Ghosts" (*Hārītī*): she is also called the "Mother of Nine Sons. This represents the King; according to the sūtra, it is said as follows.
Originally she had one hundred sons; ninety-one were in the heavens and nine were in the human world.

Their mother sought food to provide for them, yet she would swallow the flesh and blood of her small children down her throat. The Buddha, in order to transform her (and so forth), commanded his disciples as follows:
"At the time of the fast, I shall set aside one portion of food to give to you, and I will also grant you the precept against killing; thus you shall immediately attain the first fruit [of the path].

You must then make a vow to protect this community of monks. A layperson was then appointed to ensure the fulfillment of this vow. Now, if there is anyone who provides food for this mother, they may allow a bhikṣu to recite the blessing and take the food.
Because she previously vowed to protect the Sangha and because her heart naturally delights in practicing the giving of alms, it is said that "five [times] arrive."

Regarding the term "lā" (羅): if one is dissatisfied [with the rules], they commit a *pāyattika* (offense of falling). This refers to the original case where various people incur a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

If one borrows another's object with the intention of returning it by the agreed deadline, this person is one who is pure and frugal. However, for one who does not intend to repay the debt and lacks a sense of shame, even these minor matters are treated in the same way.
Baoyun says: "The *Chao* (Excerpts) was compiled at the beginning of the Tang dynasty; its sections were not yet complete. If now..."

To speak of it as such is, in fact, the terminology of a funeral announcement; this is truly unacceptable. As for not informing others before entering [the village] and falling into error: the offense is established because it causes distress to the fellow monks.
To report directly to one's fellow students is intended so that they may know one’s whereabouts. Regarding the statement "because of arriving at a good place":

when one commits an offense by eating at another location and subsequently confesses, this is a *pratideśanīya* (offense requiring confession), known as "receiving food in an araṇya" (a forest hermitage). It is because of this [rule] that...

[This] is the textual [explanation]. It should be classified as a *tishani* offense. There is an interpretation which states that because it violates the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), one must repent;

however, to claim this is a *duṣkṛta* (minor transgression) is incorrect. The reason why one incurs a *duṣkṛta* for coming uninvited is out of fear of troubling the donor. If one follows the *Pañcaśata-praśna*, [the classification is as stated above].
If one makes a sign to assemble and then departs together with the others, there is no offense. This is because the two texts may be used according to the circumstances.
Regarding the statement "from the second [case] to departing," it is as the text says.
Regarding the passage from "The Three" to the word "Request": the legal citation of the name can be understood accordingly. Regarding the passage from "If" to "Seat":
this refers to the *Qing Bintoulu Fajing* (Sūtra on the Request of Piṇḍola), two pages long, translated by An Shigao. His personal name was Piṇḍola and his family name was Bharadvāja.

Because he manifested supernatural powers before the elder Jyotiṣka to take up his alms-bowl, the Buddha prohibited [his presence] until the Parinirvāṇa, for the sake of the fourfold assembly in the three continents.

The assembly acts as a field of merit. When you wish to invite them, you should burn incense and face toward the Malaya Mountain in India, announcing your own name, clan, and so forth, and inviting them by saying: "Virtuous Pindola Bharadvaja, you who have received the Buddha’s command."

For those in the age of the Final Dharma, act as a field of merit. I pray that you accept my invitation to eat here; thereafter, one should personally explain the hidden meaning (*sandhyā-bhāṣita*) and so forth.

This should likewise be done at the time of bathing, and so on. As for what has not been seen as permissible: I have not seen anything that is permissible within the context of the Holy Teaching. Regarding the "superior conditions" (*viśiṣṭa-pratyaya*):
this refers to the two seats of the Buddha and the Saṃgha, which are considered superior. As for the term "Saṃgha": [it refers to... (text continues).
Regarding the term "zhìshì" (至士): it quotes the *Hánjīng* (含經). Its intent clarifies that the Buddha’s position is in the middle, with the monks on the left and the *śrāmaṇeras* on the right;
the meaning serves as proof that nuns should not occupy the same location.
Fourth, taking one's seat and welcoming the guests. Regarding the term "proponent of the ultimate discourse," first, the ritual for taking one's seat is clarified.

As for the eight senior nuns and so forth, this was originally a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rule for nuns; that it is extended here to the monks as a matter of courtesy is intended to bring joy to others.
One should not intentionally arrive late, for fear of causing distress to the Sangha. To laugh or depart [prematurely] is contrary to dignified decorum (*an-īryāpatha*).

The meaning is based on the following [text], which avoids censure and reproach. Regarding the phrase "the five arrivals," it refers to inviting monks who were not previously requested to serve as guests, as explained in the *Suixiang biezhong shi jie* (The Precept on Eating Separately from the Assembly According to the Characteristics) [and so forth].
When observing those who have gone forth [to the monastic life] in five-character verses, one should say to the long-lived ones, "I exhort you to give food;
to be able to sustain the lives of others is itself to obtain the fruit of long life for oneself through the gift of food. Question: The sutras do not state that this is a cause for longevity;

what then is the cause for giving food? Answer: Non-killing is the direct cause, while the giving of food is the contributing condition (*pratyaya*). It is like the two factors of birth and nourishment.
This is the parable of the mother.

The six lines of incense and the prayer for blessings are transcribed as in the text. Regarding the statement "four... up to compliant," this refers to those similar to those of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*), for fear that they might involve the essential objects of giving.
As for the snake giving gold and so forth, that is the account of the seven golden jars found in the *Saptasuvarṇakalaśa-avadāna*, which resides in the seventh [chapter]. That...
It is said: In the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a man who took great pleasure in managing his household affairs. By nature he loved to hoard gold;

having accumulated it in this manner, he obtained seven jars of gold, which he buried within his home. Later, because he had no descendants, they remained unaware of its existence. He continued to guard it with a heart of stinginess.
Thereafter, he was reborn as a snake and guarded this place for many years. Later, he suddenly thought of performing meritorious deeds.
At that time, the snake saw a man passing by the side of the road and called out to him, saying, "Come near me. The man replied, "You are a venomous snake."
"How would I dare approach? The snake said, "Even if you do not approach me, I shall still harm you. Fearing this, the man approached the place where the snake was.
The snake said to the man, "I have a jar of gold which I wish to use for making merit. Can you prepare it for me? The man replied, "I can.
He then led the man to the location of the gold, took out the gold and gave it to him. He further instructed him, "Prepare food with it."

"Tomorrow you may bring an *āśvattha* (here translated as 'grass basket') to collect me from me. When the time for the offering was set, he brought the gold to the temple and came to collect the snake.
The snake entered the basket, which he then carried before the monks. That man took his place and performed the incense offering on his behalf.
When the assembly of monks had finished eating, he preached the Dharma for the snake, who felt redoubled joy. Six jars of gold remained;

he called the *karmadāna* and went to collect them all at once, bestowing them entirely upon the Sangha. Later, the snake’s life ended, and by the power of this merit, it was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "The man who held the snake at that time was none other than myself; the snake was Śāriputra."
Pūrṇa-jaṭi was a great arhat; here [in Chinese] he is called "Fulfiller of Vows" (Mǎnyuàn). He had an elder brother named Me-na-ji who was a merchant.
Having entered the sea to gather treasures, he encountered the calamity of a venomous dragon. He then called to mind his younger brother Pūrṇa-jaṭi.

Pūrṇa-jaṭi, hearing this from afar with his divine ear, transformed himself into a garuḍa and went there. The sea dragon subsequently submerged itself, and the ship was delivered from the disaster, arriving safely.
They returned home. The younger brother converted his elder brother to the Buddha’s path and constructed a single-story sandalwood hall and pavilion for him.

Furthermore, wishing to invite the Buddha and the Sangha to partake of a meal, he and his brother each took a censer and ascended a high tower. From there, they gazed afar toward Jetavana and invited the Buddha, praying:
"We only wish that you would deign to descend to our humble kingdom tomorrow. Once their vow was completed, the incense smoke rose as they wished, ascending into the air until it reached the Buddha.
Furthermore, he washed the Buddha’s feet from afar with water; the stream was as thick as a sword-blade or a thigh, yet it reached the Buddha’s feet.

Ānanda asked the Buddha about the cause and conditions for this. The Buddha said, "In the kingdom of Fangying, Pūrṇika has converted his elder brother, who has invited me and the Saṃgha for a meal tomorrow.
Therefore, there is this auspicious sign. Consequently, he commanded the monks, including the śrāmaṇeras, each to manifest supernatural transformations and go [to the feast].

The details are as follows. On the following day, they went to receive the meal, and after it was finished, the Buddha preached the Dharma for them; all of them attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). Regarding the prohibition against standing while receiving incense:
this is from the *Three Thousand Dignified Manners* (*Sāhasrikā-vinaya-vidhi*). The origin story is as recorded in the *Vinayavibhāṣā*. It was established by command that one must sit.

Baoyun says: Now, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, because of the arising of pride, [the Buddha] instead caused him to stand and receive [the precepts]. This in the *Shuochao* (Commentary) is due to relying on the second condition;
reflect upon this. Regarding the many bhikṣus who recite hymns (*bhāṇaka*), the Vinaya says: "The Heavenly Emperor held an incense burner and led the Buddha."
Thus, they sing praises of the merits of the Buddha’s three bodies (*trikāya*). Therefore, a sutra says: "The Brahma-voice is profound and wondrous, causing people to delight in hearing it.
Furthermore, according to the *Fayuan*, the Brahma-sound in this land originated with Cao Zhi (styled Zijian), the Prince of Chen of the Wei dynasty.
He was the fourth son of Emperor Wu and was foremost in intelligence. Whenever he read Buddhist scriptures, he considered them the ultimate pinnacle of the supreme Way, and [he began to] translate...
He then established the recitation of the four tones. While traveling at Mount Yushan, he was moved by a Brahma-sound heard in the air;

reflecting on the King’s [Wang Bi’s] record of phonetic principles, he taught the various bhikṣus. Master An placed this [text] upon the "upper" section. "Brahma" (*brahman*) is a term from the Western Regions; here it is translated as "purity.
Since all conditions are stilled, it causes the mind to be pure. Regarding the words from "the four" to "to regulate," these collectively distinguish between what is correct and what is not.

One should praise the practitioner of giving (*dāna*). Giving with a mind attached to signs yields the fruits of human and celestial realms; giving without abiding in signs results in the attainment of Buddhahood and the like.

This is for the purpose of praising the dharma of the donor (*dānapati*); therefore, one explains the portion of merit, such as reverently protecting the Triple Gem and receiving the precepts of refuge and so forth.

The rest is as stated in the text (etc.). The section "Comparing the World" below distinguishes what is incorrect. "Ordinary" refers to ordinary recitation; "vertical" refers to vertical [recitation].

The "Son" is the scale of the little slave. "Praise" means to extol and manifest. As for "ascending," in the summer season nine partitions were cast [for the cauldron] to represent the nine provinces and their respective domains.
It was placed before the hall of the Son of Heaven at the formal court; within it, substances were boiled.

If one partition should cook first, it signified that this particular province would have an abundant harvest. If they all cooked simultaneously, it signified peace throughout the world. If one partition should boil first...
This represents the wild bandits. Only after this food has been bestowed upon the Three Ducal Ministers, the Nine High Ministers, and the Great Officers may they partake of it;

hence it is called "Dining from the Cauldron" (*ding-shi*). Now, the lamentation regarding poverty that exceeds this refers to the present time. The statement "reaching the middle" precisely clarifies acting according to circumstances.

Within this, there is a verse of the Middle [Period] which offers prayers for those currently practicing giving. In the lower section of the *Wufen lü* (Five-Part Vinaya), it clarifies that when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he received...

Because five hundred merchants [offered] parched flour and honey, there is this text of incantation and aspiration. As for the four kinds of unhindered eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*), they are: first, the unhindered eloquence regarding phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*);

second, the unhindered eloquence regarding meanings (*artha-pratisaṃvid*); third, the unhindered eloquence regarding language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*); and fourth, the unhindered eloquence regarding ready speech (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).

"Old man" means he is aged. The intention is that although the Buddha possesses the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), he speaks only of actual facts and merely repeats what has been said before;
moreover, it is inappropriate for an old man now to speak beyond his station. Regarding the phrase "from miscellaneous talk to formal discourse," one must know the proper time for such analysis.
As the sixth [chapter] says: In the city of Śrāvastī, there was an elder who went to sea and obtained treasures, returning to his country. At that time, the king [divided...]

He was granted a village and enfeoffed as an elder (*śreṣṭhin*). His wife gave birth to a son, who was indeed his own male heir. When a great assembly for the *pāramitās* convened, he invited the *saṃgha* to partake of a meal.

With Śāriputra serving as the presiding elder (*sthavira*), he prepared a small seat before the elder and, having sat down, offered a prayer of blessing (*svastyayana*) as recorded in the *Vinayakṣudrakavastu*.

Regarding the "Ten Powers" (*daśabala*): first, the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*); second, the power of knowing the maturation of karma (*karmavipāka-jñānabala*); third, the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-jñānabala*).

Liberation, meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*); (4) various faculties (*indriya*); (5) various inclinations (*adhimukti*); (6) various elements (*dhātu*); (7) the path leading everywhere;
(8) recollection of past lives and death-and-rebirth; (9) the divine eye-knowledge; and (10) the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*)—the detailed explanation is as in the sūtra.
At that time, Śāriputra obtained two pieces of woolen cloth. "Mahallaka" means "ignorant. Seeing that he had obtained the cloth, his mind was greatly [delighted].
He was displeased and returned to the monastery. He went to Śāriputra to request a text, but the latter would not grant it, fearing that he might not understand the proper timing.

He pressed him further, and having no other choice, Śāriputra finally bestowed it upon him. Having constantly recited and mastered it, he later arrived at a certain household and was appointed as the *upādhyāya* (preceptor).
That person died and lost his wealth; furthermore, he encountered legal trouble. Mahāla continued to harbor those original thoughts.

When the elder heard this, he became enraged and beat him, driving him out both inside and outside [the house]. He mistakenly entered the royal field and trampled the sesame seeds, further meeting with a beating from the garden keeper (this is the second instance).
Again, proceeding forward, he encountered a barley threshing floor and passed by it while circumambulating to the left, again meeting with [punishment].
He struck him. [The man] scolded him, saying, "Why do you not circumambulate to the left? He chanted the mantra, "Tuo ru" (three times). Again, proceeding forward, they encountered a burial site.
He circumambulated it to the right and offered a prayer, saying, "Tuo ru" (and so forth). Once more he was beaten. The śramaṇa felt no compassion;
seeing me being buried, he did not understand how to offer prayers. [The man] said, "From now on, never do this again! He further said, "Tuo ru. What does this mean?

He spoke thus (the fourth). Furthermore, as he proceeded forward, he encountered a man welcoming a bride. He drew near to him and offered a blessing, saying, "From now on, never do such a thing again.
Yet he was struck by the man. [The man said: "When you see my auspicious affairs, you ought to run past;

how can you walk so slowly? Thus he uttered words of ill omen (the fifth). Again, he ran wildly and encountered a person, a tree, and a wild goose, causing them to strike against his net and startle them.
The wild geese flew away, but were again captured by hunters and beaten.
"How can a śramaṇa walk with such coarse and reckless strides? You ought to approach slowly and with restraint. Thus they were rebuked, and so they crawled along until they passed through.

There they encountered a washerman who thought they had come to take his clothes; they were again struck and beaten. After passing through these seven ordeals, they finally reached Jetavana. [They] related...
The preceding circumstances are recounted. A bhikṣu reported the transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked him and established the precept (as detailed in the full text).
The seven methods for receiving food are set forth as in the original text. Regarding the "four *ra*s," there is the *Bianyi Zhangzhe jing* (Sūtra of the Householder Bianyi) in one fascicle;

it clarifies the recitation of blessings before receiving food. The *Inguo jing* (Sūtra on Cause and Effect) is likewise similar; this refers to the current practice of reciting incantations and prayers when offering food. This serves to prevent the assembly [from falling into error].
"Precepts" refers to avoiding the faults of improper contact, loss of sensory reception, and so forth. Fourth, "upright feet":
the heels touch the ground while the toes point upward. Fifth, "crossed feet": the two feet are crossed over one another rather than stepping directly on the ground.
Seventh, "tipping forward": lifting the feet to step straight forward onto empty space. "Stacking feet": pressing one foot upon the other. Stacking...
"Thighs" (bǐ) means one thigh is placed upon the other. When the feet are flat on the ground, it is specifically termed "squatting" (jùzuò).
As the sutra says: "Squatting upon a lion throne with a jeweled footstool supporting the feet. Regarding the phrase "reaching the second," this refers to the method of generation (*utpatti*).

The statement that there is no textual evidence in the sutras and śāstras means there is no text concerning the sequence of generation; it does not mean there is no text concerning generation altogether. Now...
Regarding the principle: whenever one obtains food, one must first give rise to the intention to practice giving, and only thereafter may one eat it oneself.

Furthermore, according to the *Ratnamegha Sūtra* cited in the preceding section on the dhūtas, those who eat in four portions set aside one portion for their fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*).
One portion is given to the poor and lowly beggars; the third portion is given to the various spirits and deities; and the fourth portion is for one’s own sustenance.
According to this textual sequence, it is certainly best to follow the former arrangement. As for the account in the *Chuan* (Biographies):

when the Jin-dynasty monk Shi Faming traveled to the Western Regions, he compiled the *Liguo Zhuan* (Records of Visited Countries). Regarding the practice of sending food to three places, it is said that other bhikṣus did not go out [to distribute it].
The temple of Piṇḍola; the temple of the *gāraṇa* deity (the Dharma-protecting deity); and the temple of the three *kāntāra* spirits.
According to the *Souxuan*, the *kāntāra* spirits and the Mother of Demons (*Hārītī*) are combined into one.

Now, according to the present record, the origin of the Mother of Demons is as explained in the *Hārītī-sūtra*, which has already been briefly analyzed above. As for the *kāntāra* spirits, it is as stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
The Sūtra states that these spirits also devour the sons and daughters of human families.
To convert those ghosts, when the king of the ghosts was temporarily away, the Buddha stealthily took his place upon the ghost king’s seat and manifested a massive body even larger than his own.
When the king returned from outside and saw this, he was struck with terror; he fled in panic and fell into a swoon. Out of compassion, the Buddha [acted].
He called the spirit back and restored it to its original form as a Buddha, whereupon he preached the Dharma to it.

The spirit then took refuge [in the Triple Gem] and made a vow never again to eat human men or women. Consequently, the Buddha commanded the bhikṣus to produce *piṇḍapāta* (alms-food) and give it to him.

My father once remarked that according to the Tripitaka Master’s *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions), this site where the ghost was subdued remains uniquely preserved to this day; it is located within the borders of Vārāṇasī in Central India. (Nǚzhào)

[He] returned to this country and erected a great stone pillar over twenty feet high, upon which he carved the image of a lion and inscribed the account of his subduing of the ghost, so that it might be known as authentic.
Although the origins described in the two sutras differ, both prescribe the ritual of *pārisuddhi* (confession/purification).

Nowadays, within the boundaries of the monastery (*vihāra*), there may be a temple of Hārītī; once the food has been sent [to her], the bhikṣus do not need to perform the *pārisuddhi* again. If there is none...

The Temple of the Mother of Ghosts (Harītī). There is also the temple of the Āṭavaka ghost, which is the same. If both temples are established together, an additional portion is added, making four in total.

This is logically appropriate. Regarding those who enter among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), the ancients said that those who enter the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) after death are hungry ghosts.
Now, according to the *Li han jing* (Sūtra on Separation from Containment), when the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, there was one...
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying, “I have a kinsman whom I held very dear, yet he has suddenly passed away. I now wish to offer food on his behalf;
I do not know whether he can receive it. The Buddha said, “If he has been reborn in hell or another realm, he cannot receive it, for he already possesses the sustenance required for life there.
However, within the realm of hungry ghosts (preta), there is a specific place called the ‘Entrance’ (praveśa).”
"O hungry ghost! If among your kinsmen there are those who have been born into this realm of hungry ghosts, they shall obtain [this food].
The brahmin further said, "If none of my kinsmen have been born into this realm, who then should eat the food I have offered?

The Buddha replied, "Those among your acquaintances who have been born into this realm shall also obtain this food. The brahmin further said, "If I have no acquaintances at all who have been born into this realm..."
Furthermore, how is this so? The Buddha said: "Although there is no one who is born [as that recipient], the donor himself obtains the merit. He asked again: "How does he obtain the merit himself?
The Buddha said: "If, after you have died, you should suddenly be reborn among elephants or horses, because of your past giving, you will likewise receive this karmic reward.
If you are reborn in the realms of humans or gods, you will sit and enjoy it as a result of your previous practice of giving."
As for its retribution, this is called the non-wastage of the fruit of retribution for the donor who practices giving. Having heard this, the Brahmin rejoiced and practiced accordingly;

the rest is as in the text. Regarding the phrase "the arrival of the Saṃgha," it clarifies the ritual methods for serving food and so forth. As for "washing the bowl" (*zǎobā*), one explanation says it means "to rinse the bowl.
This is like the tradition of those studying the Vinaya in the region north of the Yellow River in this land, who, when about to receive food, further [use a vessel]...
Because the vessel was rinsed with water. Some say that this refers to taking up the bowl beforehand as a means of rinsing it, fearing that it might obstruct others from receiving their food.
The *Bānguǒ Jīng* (Sūtra on Half a Fruit) states that according to the *Yùwáng Jīng* (Sūtra of King Aśoka), the king was deposed from his throne by his ministers and sons and confined within a room.
At that time, there was a high minister who had previously been on intimate terms with the king; he obtained half a *āmra* fruit and gave it to the king. The king thought to himself: "I..."

He ate it all by himself with complete mastery; yet even eating it, he could not escape death. "It would be better to offer this to the Sangha," he thought, and so he took it and presented it to the Venerable Yaśas.
The Venerable One gave it to the eight thousand *arhats* to drink together as a recitation for the king.
He ensured that not a single grain fell to the ground, fearing the suspicion of laypeople. Thus ends the fourth [chapter].

"Reaching the place" refers to the miscellaneous explanations. Regarding "pouring it out at the place where one drinks from the mouth," this means waiting for someone else to drink from the same vessel before speaking.
"Chewing and eating" refers to making noise like a pig and so forth; the rest may be understood according to the text.
8. The procedure for concluding the meal (*bhojana-paryavasāna-vidhi*);

as in the text. 9. The *dakṣiṇā*; also called the "Great *dakṣiṇā*" (*mahādakṣiṇā*); both are terms for the recitation of blessings (*adhiṣṭhāna*) over a gift. Regarding the statement "from five up to the opening," this refers to the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*).

For those living at home who practice the giving of material wealth (*āmiṣa-dāna*), according to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, by giving food one obtains physical beauty and strength; by giving clothing...

By attaining upright deportment, one gains a dwelling; by giving a house or a grove, one gains a palace of the seven treasures. By giving a well, one gains freedom from thirst; by giving a bridge, one gains carriages and horses.

For those who have left the household life and practice the gift of Dharma, explaining the Sūtras and all other virtuous words of the Tripiṭaka to benefit others—all such acts are called the gift of Dharma.
The phrase "five [senses] reaching the speaker" distinguishes the person; it refers to one whose faculties are complete.
Regarding "the feet": the Buddha said that delicious food is like a vessel filled with filth, and so forth. Regarding "half a *beǎi* (verse-chant)":

as in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, there are two verses praising the three bodies (*trikāya*). The first verse praises the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), the second verse praises the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body), and the latter half-verse extols the *dharmakāya* (dharma body).
If one recites only one body and not the whole, it is called "half a *beǎi*. Alternatively, it may refer to praising [only] two out of the three.
Whether one or two [verses] are entirely incomplete, it is also called a "half-chant" (*pāda*). Regarding the Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body:

this means that because the Buddha is fully adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, it is called "wondrous. There is no one in the world equal to him; this means that throughout the heavens above and the earth below, none can equal the Buddha. It is peerless and inconceivable:

it cannot be compared through metaphors, and it cannot be deliberated by the mind or conceived through thought. Therefore, I now pay homage (this concludes the expression of reverent salutation). Next, the half-...
This verse praises the *saṃbhogakāya*. "The form of the Tathāgata is inexhaustible" means that it is like space, pervading the *dharmadhātu* without limit.

"Wisdom is likewise so" means that the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*) are inexhaustible and their merits are likewise without end. "All phenomena are eternally abiding" means that the *dharmakāya* is neither born nor extinguished, neither departing nor arriving;

it is serenely and eternally present, pervading the *dharmadhātu*. "Therefore, I take refuge" concludes the expression of reverence. Xuán (Xuánzàng) said: "This is a *bhaiṣajyagāthā* (chant) for before a meal. If it is after a meal," [the following applies].
This refers to chanting while remaining in the world. "Chì" (pronounced chě, meaning extravagant) is as previously mentioned: "a person from a low station praising [the meal] while ascending.

In the tenth section, eight people constitute the assembly, as stated in the preceding Vinaya texts. Fearing that the time for the meal might pass, one need only have these eight people sit according to their rank, with the others sitting along with them.
Now, when departing from the house of the host, one must again have the eight senior monks (upādhyāya) lead the way.
They are arranged in mutual relation so as to manifest that the sequence of honor and subordination is not lost; the rest is as commonly explained.
The preceding many sections, in their entirety, conclude the text of the "Chapter on Invitations."
Section Eight: On the Laity and the Clergy.
This section is divided into two parts: first, the citation of the title; second, the explanation according to the commentary. Regarding the phrase "From the Honored One down to the fourth":

previously, it was clarified that after the laity have completed their material offerings (*āmiṣadāna*) by inviting [the Sangha] to receive alms, those who have left the household life—whose primary concern is benefiting others—must practice the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*). Therefore, this section follows to distinguish that. (Exegesis)

Regarding the term "name" (míng): the *Zuǒzhuan* states that to lead things so they may communicate is called "guidance" (dǎo). The *Biǎoyùn* says that when writing the character for "guidance," one places the "indicative" (shì) radical beneath the "path" (dào);

it is incorrect to place the "inch" (cùn) radical there—take note of this. As for "vulgar" (sú), it means "habituation. When the land does not naturally produce [a certain way of doing things], it is called "habituation. Once habituated, it becomes a custom (*fēng*), and thus forms a "vulgar tradition" (*sú*).

Furthermore, to be stuck in affairs and deluded regarding principle is called "extreme" (*zhōng*), referring to such things as "eternal customs" (*chángsú*) or "temporal customs" (*shísú*). As for "transforming" (huà), it means "teaching" (jiào).
To transform others by relying on the teachings is precisely what is meant by "method" (fang-fa). The details below can be understood accordingly.

Some interpret this as the character for "path" (dao), encompassing the four paths of sentient beings, which belong to those who transform others; the five groups of monastics are the objects of transformation, while the two groups of laypeople are the secular realm of those being transformed.

Now, both the subject and object are mentioned together; thus it says, "monastics and laypeople alike" (this specific phrasing is not adopted here). In the commentary, the first part provides the general intent. Regarding the phrase "the Way reaches [to others]":
the Way ultimately depends on mutual support, exceeding even the relationship between shadow and echo. This first clarifies their mutual dependence as the cause for conversion and guidance.
"Support" (*zī*) means to benefit or to rely upon. The Way relies on the wealth and goods of laypeople to support the body; the laity, in turn, rely on the Dharma of the Way.
"To provide for the spirit" means to transcend or to go beyond. As for "shadow and echo," Master Zi said: "There was a man who detested his footprints and feared his shadow; he ran to avoid them.
The more he feared the shadow and ran, the faster the shadow moved; the more he hurried to avoid the footprints, the more they multiplied."
There is much that remains unknown. One dwells in the shadow to let the image rest; one abides in stillness to cease the traces. There is a principle of occasional absence.
Now it is said that there are things that surpass shadows and echoes. Shadows depend on forms to arise; echoes depend on sounds to exist. These, then, are shadows and echoes.

Form and sound depend upon one another; yet form and sound do not depend upon shadows and echoes. Now, if the secular and the monastic were to depend upon each other in this manner, it would not be as it should be.

However, the secular relies on the monastic Dharma to nourish the spirit, while the monastic relies on the secular wealth to sustain the body. Thus, the two support one another, never for a moment parting.

Therefore, it is said that [the latter] excels [the former]. An external objection states: "The monastic and the secular differ in form, and their laws differ in four ways. How can they be like shadows and echoes?"

Regarding their kinship, the *Chao Tong* states: "Although their physical forms and so forth differ (and so on), the monastic shaves his head and donns the dyed robes, whereas the layperson returns to the opposite;
this is a distinction of form. The laity cultivates the aspect of merit through the five and eight precepts, while the Way-farer cultivates the aspect of wisdom, aspiring to seek Bodhi.
Although these starting points appear different, the ultimate destination is one and the same; for both are nothing other than seeking Bodhi and Nirvana. Thus it is said.

"Jiǎ" (假) means "provisional" or "borrowed. Regarding "yōu" (攸), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "the place where one arrives. The practice of cultivating merit without signs is called *dānapāramitā*; its meaning is "reaching the other shore.
Since *bodhi* is also the other shore, we know that the destination reached is the same.

Furthermore, what is cultivated in the mundane world is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while what is cultivated on the Path is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). It is not merely the mundane.

The conventional is identical to the ultimate; it does not differ from the ultimate while being identical to the conventional. Thus, the *Zhao lun* states: "Though their forms and robes differ, their sublime aspiration is non-dual;
therefore, the destination they reach is the same. For this reason, the following clarifies how external protection and mutual support function, as the text explains.

Therefore, it is possible to avoid forming unwholesome conditions below and instead achieve signs of benefit. If one seeks clothing and food, the mind will have no inclination to attach itself to the Dharma, and the attainment of the fruits of practice will resemble the extinction of the True Dharma.
Now, if there is external protection that provides all necessary offerings for whatever is required, and through such practice the fruits are attained, it will be just like the True Dharma.
Hence it is said: "Though hidden, it flows on again. Since the Sangha has [upheld] the Dharma...

He rescued others; those who took refuge in him were not few. He was able to lead them to leave the household life and obtain benefit, such that the monastic community, having declined, was re-established.

Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "First, there are śramaṇas who know the Dharma; second, there are lay patrons who provide external protection. Because of these, the Buddha-Dharma does not fall into ruin for a thousand years.
As for the statement regarding those who attain awakening: it refers to washing away inferior births; for inferior and limited mental consciousnesses are not uniform. Therefore—

It is said that they are indeed many. They know what is light and what is heavy; they possess the discernment to recognize the appropriate timing and measure. Those who speak from the heart harbor shallow and superficial views from their own inner minds.

Because they seek to conform to human expectations rather than the teachings, they have accumulated [errors] for the sake of converting ordinary people. They do not rely on the explanations of the holy teachings;
instead, they may act as servants to laypeople, or see those who are not disciples as being incapable of understanding the illumination of the teachings, and so forth. Thus their words are formed.

Regarding those who are deceitful and excessive: these are the aforementioned individuals. They may praise the eight impure things; or they may preach the Dharma to others for the sake of food and clothing;
or they may preach with a competitive mind, seeking out the faults of one another. This can be understood from the cited texts. As for the admonitions: [text follows].

"Zhēn" means admonition; "huì" means instruction. One who has not yet heard [the Dharma] shall now hear it, bringing radiant benefit to the teaching. (In the *Xuánjì*, the character "chàn" is used for "huì"; this section explains the numerical [correspondence] of evils.)

[I] fear this may not be the case). Second, the opening of the chapter (the division of sections, etc.). Question: All other chapters say "within it" (*jùzhōng*). Why does this chapter alone designate only the two characters "initially clarifying" (*chūmíng*)?

[The] Manifestation says: It is still directed toward the "flesh" (*ròu*). Internally, the sections are suspended and set forth; it is in the same location as the opening of the chapter-gate for the *Anju* (Sesshin/Summer Retreat) chapter.
The principle of the characteristics is no different from the principle of the commentary; it consists of six sections. For now, we take the first.

Regarding the passage from "The Great" to "is present": when the Buddha was preaching the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, the kings, ministers, and subjects of the eight classes of beings all desired to protect the Dharma so that it would not perish.
The Buddha praised them, saying, "Excellent, O donors! As for "Tiṅlizi" (亭歷子), the commentary states that he has two names; the first is...
The first is called *zhú* (the "stalk"). The second is called *tínglì* (the "stilted stalk"). The third is the leaf of the *gǒusànyǎo* plant; it is like a leaf of mustard, yet finer than sesame.
These are cited here to represent the smallest of things, by way of analogy for the vast [scale]. As for "dregs" (*zǐ*), these refer to those who are defiled within the Buddha-dharma.
As for "officials" (*diǎn*), they are not truly upright or honest. As for "phantoms" (*huàn*), they are not genuine śramaṇas.

They are called "thieves" because they steal and accept benefits for themselves; they are "drunkards" because they have lost their original nature as śramaṇas; and they are "caṇḍālas" because they sever the life-force of the Buddha’s Dharma-wisdom.
According to the sūtras, each of these types is said to be one who keeps the eight impure things and the like, and is thus termed "dregs among śramaṇas."
Regarding "the crookedness among śramaṇas" and so forth: those who now wish to give rise to arrogance in others do so by using worldly prosperity to engender thoughts of contempt.
As for the statement "from three to cessation," it is as the text says. Regarding the fourth point, "Vinaya to the middle": the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

That treatise extensively cites the three categories (*triskandha*), the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the dharma of quiescence (*śamatha*), and so forth;

these are omitted here. Regarding the meaning of the term "phrase" (*pada*) in the text, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Names (*nāman*) express intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); phrases (*pada*) express distinctions (*viśeṣa*)."
The "text" (wen) is identical to the "syllable" (zi); it serves as the basis for these two. Regarding the sounds of male and female:
for example, *upāsaka*, *upāsakā*, and *kātyāyanīputra* are all masculine sounds; whereas *upāsikā*, *upāsikā*, and *kātyāyanīputrī* are all feminine sounds.
Furthermore, "one should eliminate the mind of greed" means not seeking fame or profit.
"Not disparaging oneself" means that one thinks, "Even the Buddha’s Dharma is difficult to hear, let alone being able to explain it myself," and thus gives rise to a sense of joy and gratitude.
"Explaining the dharma of weariness" refers to feeling weary of birth, old age, sickness, death, the impurity of the body, and so forth.
"The dharma of distancing" refers to seeking liberation and attaining nirvana, delighting in transcending birth and death, and so on. The rest is as stated in the text (*etc.*).
The statement "reaching the destination of nirvana" indicates that it is not a manifestation of manifest virtue. Taking this opportunity, he explains the characteristics of three kinds of *saṃgha*:
first, the corrupt and evil *saṃgha*; second, the deluded *saṃgha*; and third, the pure *saṃgha*, as distinguished in the *Chao* [the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*] itself (*et cetera*).

Regarding the phrase "if it is not the Vinaya, it does not serve as proof": if one sees someone praising and claiming that receiving and storing the eight kinds of impure wealth is correct, this is not the precept.
The Vinaya is that which provides verification. If there are those who train in the precepts, this Vinaya is precisely what should serve as their verification.

To skillfully understand even a single character is to take the character for "Vinaya" (*lü*) as a gloss for "Dharma" (*fǎ*), because one is thereby able to fully know the distinctions between upholding and violating, permitting and prohibiting, and light and heavy [offenses].
As for "reaching the place where non-Dharma reaches," it is like the layman Vimalakīrti entering brothels, wine shops, and the like—these are places of non-Dharma; he must...
This may be done for the sake of the causes and conditions of conversion, provided that it does not cause harm or distress to oneself;

however, it is not permitted for those of the Hīnayāna who have not completely severed evil. Regarding questions concerning the end of life and so forth, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states: "Ānanda, you should only contemplate in stillness."
"In this village of Nāṭa, twelve householders have passed away. Where have they been reborn? The Buddha said, "These twelve persons have severed the five lower fetters;
at the end of their lives, they have been reborn in the heavens, where they will attain parinirvāṇa and shall not return again."

Regarding what are called the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*): first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); second, attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); third, doubt (*vicikitsā*); fourth, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*); and fifth, ill-will (*vyāpāda*). Furthermore, it was asked:
"Where are those who die [with these fetters] reborn? The Buddha said: "Those whose lust, anger, and delusion are attenuated attain the second fruit [of the path].
According to the intent of the *Chao*, when there is a question regarding the place of rebirth for one who has died, one simply examines the causes being cultivated in the present.
One knows the good and evil realms of rebirth after death; yet, because these are not seen with the ordinary eye, even if one were to answer, they would not believe or accept it.
Therefore, it is in vain to pose such questions. If you wish to transcend birth and death, simply contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

One must awaken to the fact that the cycle of saṃsāra does not cease. Regarding those who contravene the Buddha’s words and so forth, it is merely said: "Whether a bhikṣu or a layperson, [the fault] proceeds from the mouth."
"No. A bhikṣu incurs a *pārājika* offense; what about a layperson? The meaning of this passage is that laypeople do not receive the Buddha's precepts;

therefore, they do not violate what the Buddha has not prohibited. Thus, the Sūtra says that for one who has received the precepts, the offense is light. If one were to pose such a question, it would be improper to answer it.

Regarding the statement "the meaning of the three arrivals": this clarifies that entering the room and facing [the teacher] is a concise textual expression for making the meaning manifest. As for "facing toward when leaving the door," it means one faces the teacher’s representative rather than turning one's back.

The rest is as stated in the text. The *Vinayamātṛkā* (lower volume) contains a section on the method for reciting the *Poṣadha* (precepts), which is largely identical in wording to that in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Regarding the "twelvefold division of the scriptures" (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*): "twelve" indicates the number; "division" (*aṅga*) refers to categories, as there are twelve distinct classes.

The new [translation] calls them the "twelvefold teaching" (*dvādaśāṅga-śāsana*), which carries the meaning of "segmented portions. 1. *Sūtra*: This is translated as "Scripture of Accordance" (*kīng*).
It refers to all prose passages. 2. *Geya*: This is translated as "Verses to be Recited" (*ying song fen*); it is also called "Repetition" (*chóng*).
Recite. Although the matters were already explained in the preceding prose (*gadya*), fearing that later generations might not have heard them, the previous text is restated here in verse (*śloka*).

Third is the *Vyākaraṇa* (Section on Prophecy), which means "the portion of prophecy. It also refers to the bestowal of predictions; it records for the disciples the matters concerning the fruits they shall receive in the future.
Fourth is the *Gāthā* (Section on Verses), which means "the portion of chanted recitation. These arise independently, like a countenance of extraordinary beauty.

"Exquisite. Such [teachings] as "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent" constitute the five *udānas*, which here is translated as the "Section of Spontaneous Utterances" (*svayambhū-bhāṣita-varga*).

Examples include the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* and others. Question: Why does [the Buddha] speak spontaneously without waiting for a request? Answer: The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that there are two reasons for this.

First, because the multitude does not know or understand how to request [the teaching]. Second, even if they might know, they may not dare to request it rashly. If one does not speak of it oneself, there is no way for them to hear it.

The Buddha, in order to guide sentient beings according to their capacities (*jī*), speaks of it himself. Sixth is the *nidāna*, which is translated here as "Section on the Origin" (*yuánqǐfēn*) and also as "Causes and Conditions" (*yīnyuán*).

The *Xiǎnyáng lùn* states that there are three kinds of causes and conditions: first, those requested [to be taught]; second, those arising from circumstances; and third, those arising from internal necessity. Here, it refers to the first.

Second, the condition of an offense as the causal basis, such as the reason for the formulation of the precepts. Third, the condition of a specific event as the causal basis, such as the case of the six groups of monks;
or as when the Buddha spoke a verse regarding a high official in the kingdom of Śrāvastī who caught birds and then released them, beginning with "Do not disregard even a small offense," and so forth.
Seventh, the *aupamya* (analogy section), which refers to all instances where metaphors are taught within the sūtras, such as the eight hundred great [similes] in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
7. *Avadāna* (Metaphor): This refers to the seven similes and so forth found in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. 8. *Itivṛttaka* (Thus-it-was-said): This is translated as "Past Events.

It refers to the Buddha’s recounting of past lives for the sake of his disciples. 9. *Jātaka* (Birth Story): This is translated as "Previous Births. It refers to the Buddha’s own accounts of the causes and conditions of his past lives.
10. *Vaipulya* (Vast/Extensive): This is translated as "Broad and Extensive. It refers to the teachings that clarify the vast conduct of the bodhisattvas.

The *mahācarita* (Great Deeds) refers to such matters as the recording of the principles and meanings of the Mahāyāna. The eleventh is the *avadāna* (Marvelous Tales), translated here as "rare and extraordinary";

this includes such events as the jeweled tree lowering its branches, the auspicious river stilling its waves, the monkey offering honey, and the miraculous image hastening forward to welcome [the Buddha].

The twelfth is the *upadeśa* (Expository Treatises), translated here as the "Section on Discursive Analysis"; this refers to the back-and-forth of questions and answers used to investigate and exhaustively analyze the underlying principles.

This means that although the Three Piṭakas are vast and numerous, they do not exceed the twelve divisions (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), which encompass them all completely. Furthermore, among these, those that are deficient are few;

this refers precisely to the "indefinite" (*aniyata*). As for "not being at the wrong time," it may refer to the time of awakening, or to times such as when one is still immature or when one is overcome by desire.
When there is no intention to listen to the Dharma, one must not preach the Mahāyāna for them.

Master Bao, because he perceived that the time for their awakening had not yet arrived, cited the case of a layperson during the Buddha’s lifetime who, with a disrespectful mind, requested the Buddha to preach the Dharma.

The Buddha preached the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni) for him, whereupon the man said, "I have no need for this; I shall hear it elsewhere," and so forth. "Inappropriate place" refers to a location that is not a suitable setting for preaching the Dharma.
Furthermore, "a light-minded person" is one who gives rise to arrogance within themselves. "One who belittles others while praising oneself" is one who extols their own ability.

"One who treats others with contempt for their lack of understanding and so forth" refers to those who speak inappropriately in various places, causing others to lose respect [for the Dharma]. This refers to those who preach in a manner that causes the Buddha-Dharma to perish.
This refers to mutually demonstrating one's strengths and weaknesses. "The blazing worldly dharmas" refers to the mind of seeking worldly fame and profit.

"Giving with one eye" means regarding parents, teachers, elders, and others with eyes of compassion; by this one shall obtain the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), which becomes the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) upon attaining Buddhahood.
Second, regarding physical appearance: by maintaining a harmonious and joyful countenance and avoiding frowning or looking distressed, one will obtain an upright body;

upon attaining Buddhahood, one will obtain a golden-colored body. Third, regarding speech: by using virtuous words and gentle speech, one will obtain eloquence and clarity of expression in the future;

upon attaining Buddhahood, one will obtain the four types of unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*). Fourth, regarding physical conduct: by rising to welcome others, prostrating, and so forth, one will obtain longevity in the future and upon attaining Buddhahood.
It is of great fruit and retribution. Fifth, as for the gift of a mind: by giving with a virtuous and wholesome mind, one will obtain a mind free from madness and delusion in the future;
upon attaining Buddhahood, one obtains the fruit of the mind of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Sixth, as for the gift of a bed and seat: in the future, one will obtain a bed of the seven treasures;
upon attaining Buddhahood, one obtains the lion’s Dharma-seat (*siṃhāsana*). Seventh, as for the gift of a dwelling: in the future, one will obtain a natural palace; upon attaining Buddhahood...
One obtains the karmic fruit of a meditation hall as one’s dwelling. These seven types [of offerings] do not deplete one's wealth, yet they yield great fruits.

As for the phrase "the Great Assembly" and so forth, it clarifies that the Dharma has many gateways and that the manifestations for converting beings are diverse. The Four Noble Truths refer to suffering...
Regarding the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path: in the Hīnayāna, there are four aspects (*ākāra*) for each [truth] (and so forth).

In the Mahāyāna, upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one contemplates only the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Since this single [truth] is not a dharma realized in a single moment, the Buddha taught eighty thousand Dharma-gates (and so forth).
"Like the method of market trade" means desiring to receive a return. "Having no other thoughts" refers to [the mind being focused] upon the six sense objects (*ṣad-viṣaya*).

In such a state, one does not give rise to a mind of attachment. Just as fear arises in the mind when treading upon dangerous ground, at that time the Tathāgata waved his hand through the air and told the bhikṣus:
"When entering a village, you should likewise be without obstruction. The rest is as stated in the text.
Regarding the statement "ten to la": this clarifies preaching the Dharma with a compassionate mind, accepting offerings, and allowing [the audience] to listen.

"Do not engage in debate" means do not intermingle [the teaching] with worldly terminology. "One must not use worldly matters for instruction" refers to the case where the four groups of six nuns instructed laypeople;
one must not direct [one's excrement or urine] toward the sun, the moon, or shrines to deities, nor discharge them in such places. "Now is such-and-such a lunar mansion."

Regarding the prohibition against planting seeds, such as those of the *śīrṣaka* plant, for the sake of worldly gain and so forth, it may be established as a regulation. Concerning the consumption of fermented rice gruel (*tandula-juice*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 8, states:
After the summer retreat, the Buddha was traveling with the bhikṣus and arrived at a city of brahmins.

When the king learned that the Buddha was about to arrive, he thought to himself, "If he comes, who will find pleasure in me? He then established a regulation, saying: "If one gives food to the Buddha, one shall be permitted [to enter]."

Regarding the Buddha’s words: [the king] paid a fine of five hundred gold coins. Later, when the Buddha entered the city with Ānanda carrying his bowl, the people of the country each closed their doors and did not dare come out again.
At that time, there was an old woman who, carrying an earthenware vessel filled with foul-smelling dregs, went out her door intending to discard them.
Suddenly seeing the Buddha with an empty bowl, she thought to herself and said: "This man possesses such excellent marks and signs that he is fit to partake of the food of the devas."
"Why have you now lowered yourself to beg for alms? This woman is one of great compassion. If the Buddha is compassionate, I shall offer this meager food to him;
she should accept it. The Buddha then extended his bowl and received it. Having received it, he emitted light and manifested a smile. Ānanda asked the Buddha about the cause and conditions for this.
The Buddha said, "This old woman, for fifteen kalpas, has enjoyed great [happiness] among the devas and humans."
He enjoyed wealth and happiness, and later attained a male body. He left the household life and realized the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha.
At that time, there was a brahmin who, having heard this, asked: "You are the crown prince of King Śuddhodana; why do you utter such falsehoods for the sake of food?
Then the Buddha extended his tongue until it covered his face and reached up to the hairline. He said, "Is it with this tongue that you speak such falsehoods? At that time, the brahmin...
The gatekeeper thought to himself, "If a person whose tongue covers only their nose does not speak falsely, how much less so one whose tongue covers their face and reaches up to the hairline?
He then conceived faith and addressed him again, saying, "I do not understand the extent of the karmic reward for such a gift;
I pray that the Buddha will explain it to me. The Buddha asked, "Have you ever seen anything extraordinary? The Brahmin replied, "I once saw a *nigrodha* tree..."
The *lodhra* tree’s branches and leaves covered five hundred chariots. The Buddha then asked him about the size of the tree’s seed.
He replied, "It is like one-third of a mustard seed. The Buddha said to him, "Who would believe you? The brāhmaṇa said, "This is a matter of fact;
it can be verified through observation, so it is certainly not false. The Buddha then spoke, "I see the purity..."
The mind: by giving to the Buddha, one obtains a great fruit of retribution, just as this tree has many fruits from few seeds.

At that time, the brahmin’s mind was opened and his understanding clarified; he repented before the Buddha. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna. Thereupon, he raised a great cry.
He announced to all: "The gate of the Deathless (Amṛta) has opened; why do you not come forth?

Upon hearing this, everyone was moved by the desire to offer five hundred gold coins to the King to welcome the Buddha and provide for his worship. They immediately broke the restrictive regulations, and both the King and his subjects took refuge in the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they all attained pure faith. Regarding the story of Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa’s leftover soup and so forth, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
The śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa offered excellent soup to the Buddha. After the Buddha had eaten it, he passed it on to King Bimbisāra.
This demonstrates that the Buddha himself also practices giving: first, to manifest that the merit of such giving is vast; second, to reveal the non-duality between the monastic and the lay.
Regarding the phrase "from the ground up to the life-span," this clarifies that one should comfort others with a compassionate mind, thereby remaining free from censure and suspicion.

"Seeing those who have performed meritorious deeds" refers to praising those who practice giving and uphold the precepts. When one sees a person who has created merit, it is necessary to praise the blessings of their generosity and observance of the precepts, so as to cause their hearts to rejoice and prevent them from falling into despondency.
"Skillful means of using analogies to dispel [resentment]" means using metaphors to ensure that no heart of enmity arises; if it is good...
Those with good faith know that because the śramaṇas possess compassion, they do not look upon them with disrespect or lack of faith; they fear being thought fit for forced labor.

Sexual misconduct has a single characteristic, yet its specific manifestations are difficult to identify. According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, generally speaking, there are four types of sexual misconduct:

third, engaging in improper places, such as exposed areas, caityas, or locations where those practicing the holy life reside; and fourth, engaging with one’s own wife at improper times, such as when she is pregnant. Bodhi... [text continues]

it is easy to avoid, and one can attain the state of non-doing. Based on this, there are three reasons: first, [sexual misconduct] involves violating the wives of others and so forth, which constitutes a source of affliction for others.

1. Because it leads to rebirth in the miserable realms (*durgati*). 2. Because it is easy to distance oneself from [sexual misconduct]. For householders who are deeply attached to the objects of desire, it is difficult for them to abandon them entirely;

however, it is easy to abstain from sexual misconduct. 3. Regarding the third point, all noble ones (*ārya*) must certainly undertake the restraint (*saṃvara*) regarding sexual misconduct, as they cannot possibly commit it.

This applies to those noble ones who have passed through births (*jātismara*), who are endowed with natural morality (*prakṛti-śīla*), and so forth. Furthermore, the treatise asks: "What was previously received..."

it is not [obtained] universally toward the continuum [of sentient beings]. This means that one obtains the restraint based on the original vow one undertook. The original vow states: "I, regarding..."
"All sentient beings" refers to the vow to sever the transgression of sexual misconduct; it does not mean [the vow] applies to the entire mental continuum [of others].
Furthermore, one does not say "I vow" with respect to the entire continuum of all sentient beings to abstain from non-celibacy (*abrahmacarya*).

Therefore, one obtains the precept of abstaining from sexual misconduct toward sentient beings, but one does not obtain the precept of abstaining from non-celibacy. Consequently, taking a wife or concubine later does not constitute a transgression.

Regarding the prohibition [of alcohol] among the *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadyas*, the verse of the treatise states: "Among the prohibited offenses, one should abstain from alcohol alone, in order to protect the other restraints.

This means that although there are many prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadyas*), the offense of drinking alcohol is grave; it causes the mind to become greatly negligent, and one will inevitably further violate the specific restraints (*pratimokṣa-saṃvara*).

To protect all other forms of discipline (*saṃvara*), the drinking of alcohol is prohibited. Regarding the "three months": these are specifically the fifth, ninth, and [third] months. As for the revolving wheel of the karma-mirror:

Fifteen and four. This applies to both the bright and dark fortnights. The Vinaya states: the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*), and the twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth days of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣa*).

"Body. "The various faculties are difficult to complete," and so forth.

Regarding the title "One Liberated from the Worldly and Transcendental" (understanding this single title, as in the sūtras and śāstras; for the sake of convenience here, there is no need for a prolix exposition):

concerning the statement that "his merit is equal to that of one who is without outflows," the treatise says: "Even the kingly heavenly reward of one who observes the eight precepts cannot compare [to it].

Śakra spoke a verse, saying: "If a person observes the eightfold fast, their merit shall be equal to mine. The Buddha stopped him, saying: "This should be said only of one whose outflows are exhausted."
Verse: The verse says: "On the six fast days and the days of supernormal power, one who upholds the eight precepts shall obtain a retribution equal to that of ours.
Based on this, Śakra spoke the preceding verse, but the Buddha stopped him and would not allow it; thus we know that for a person who receives the eight precepts...

The merit exceeds that of the Lord of Devas and is equal to that of those who possess the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*). Regarding the rule that one may not receive [the precepts] from many but must receive them from a single person:
this is explained in reference to the Precept Master (*śīlācārya*). Among the five assemblies (*pañca-saṃgha*), one may receive them from any one individual;

it is not permitted to receive them on behalf of two or three others, for fear that the words will become confused and the explanations inconsistent. If one is able to receive them, there is no distinction as to the number [of people]. (The character "shou" [receive] is read as "shou" [bestow] in the *Baoshu*; however, the current *Jiaochao* [Commentary] fears...)

Regarding the phrase "accomplishing the eight dharmas" and so forth: according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there were certain lay followers (*upāsaka*) who, on account of some minor matter, became angry with and held a grudge against the bhikṣus.
The Buddha said: "One must not, on account of some minor matter, become angry with or reproach a bhikṣu, nor harbor a lack of respect or faith.
Only when a bhikṣu has accomplished eight dharmas should one then no longer respect or have faith in him. As for what these eight dharmas are: they are slandering the Three Jewels.
The third is [to cause] the three [refuges]. The fourth is [to cause] the four [precepts]. The fifth is to desire to render the dwellings of upāsakas unprofitable.

The sixth is to give upāsakas an evil reputation. The seventh is to desire to seize the dwellings of upāsakas. The eighth is to deceive upāsakas by taking what is not right to be right. The remainder is as in the text.

Second, regarding the inquiry on the conditions for rebirth: the names in the document are self-evident. As for the phrase "the five [cases] up to... and so forth, this refers to the *Pañcavastuka-vibhāga* (The Fivefold Method of Dividing Robes).
In that text, Piṅgiya’s parents were greedy for gain and offerings; they dared not provide for him, so he reported the matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha permitted it, as described in the *Shō* (Commentary). Regarding the incurrence of a grave offense (*gurv-āpatti*): this refers to violating the debt of nurturance, which is a form of rebellion. A father is no different from a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*). One.
"Everything may be obtained": one interpretation states that after having received the five or eight precepts, one may subsequently provide everything according to one's inclination.

(Some say this refers to bathing; because one may touch the father’s body, it is said that "everything is permitted," which conversely implies that for the mother it is not allowed. This remains unclear. "To enlighten one's parents": "qi" means to open.

This refers to following the constant laws of the Buddha, the Sangha, and the Dharma, opening the way and showing [the path] to seven generations of one's parents, causing their minds to have faith and joy, and to learn for themselves.
In this manner, he enlightened his parents and taught them for seven generations; others were likewise instructed.
Thus, the Dharma became flourishing and extensive, and he was named a "Protector of the Dharma" (*dharmapāla*). Regarding those who attain long life, the third fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

After Kāśyapa had realized that the Three Jewels are eternally abiding, he vowed to study and transform others, acting as frost and hail against those who cultivate the notion of impermanence. The Buddha then praised him accordingly.
This protection of the Dharma is not deceptive; it even leads to the increase of one’s lifespan and so forth.

Regarding Ānanda’s request to receive the precepts from Mahāprajāpatī, the causal narrative is as usual (*etc.*). As for the term "those of pure faith," this refers to those who have attained the first fruit of the Hīnayāna.
Concerning the phrase "various jewels" and so forth, in a sutra there was the son of a householder named Maitrakanyaka; his father passed away and his wealth was exhausted.
He sold firewood with his labor, earning two coins a day to support his elderly mother. As his livelihood improved, he earned four coins a day to provide for her.
Later, as his success continued to grow, he earned eight coins a day to make offerings to his mother. Subsequently, he obtained sixteen coins to present to his mother.
When the people saw his filial piety, they urged him, saying, "Your father is still alive; go gather [firewood]..."
"His profession is gathering jewels. Why do you not emulate him? Having heard this, he returned home and asked his mother.
His mother said, "Your father is still there; it is no lie that his profession is gathering jewels. The son said to his mother, "I wish to emulate my father's profession; would it be permissible?
Seeing her son’s filial devotion, and thinking he would not abandon her to go far away, she jokingly granted him permission. Believing it to be real, the son then went out.
The agreement to summon his companions was finalized. He returned home to take leave of his mother;

upon hearing this, she wailed in grief and distress, saying to her son, "Wait until after I have died, and you may go as you please. The son replied, "Mother, you have already given me your prior permission.
Now that I have made a pact with my companions, everything is settled. A person of integrity and faith must not deviate from their resolve. His mother then threw herself into his arms.
He wailed and wept. The son then pulled his hand away, whereupon he plucked out the flowers from his mother’s hair, causing them to fall.
Fearing that her son would incur guilt, the mother immediately let him go. Once the son had escaped, he entered the great ocean with his companions and reached the place of treasures.
Having obtained a vast amount of precious jewels, they wished to return home. At the time of departure, there were two routes: one by water and one by land. The crowd deliberated, saying: "The..."

They traveled by land, proceeding gradually forward. The road was infested with many bandits. According to the laws of those two lands, when bandits plundered goods, if they were able to capture the caravan leader, the goods would belong to the bandits;
if they could not capture the caravan leader, the goods would be returned to the bandits once they had already taken them.
For this reason, as the Elder Maitrakanyaka was the caravan leader, he feared being harmed by the bandits; thus, whenever he reached...
At the place where they were staying, they immediately prepared another location for lodging. When it was time to depart the following day, the caravan came to meet them and take them along;
however, during the night while they were resting, a fierce wind and rain arose. At dawn, the entire caravan set out, forgetting to go and fetch them.
Since the caravan leader, Maitrakanyaka, could not keep up with his companions and was unfamiliar with the route, he saw a great mountain in the distance.
He then proceeded to that place and again beheld a great city of deep-blue lapis lazuli. The elder, exhausted by hunger and thirst, hurried toward it.
At that time, within the city, four jade maidens came out to welcome him with songs accompanied by *lo-yi* pearls.
He entered the city and remained there for forty thousand years, experiencing pleasure and joy. Then, a sense of natural revulsion and detachment arose in his mind, and he prepared himself to depart.
He departed. The women said, "O man of Jambudvīpa, how can you be so heartless?
Having lived with us for forty thousand years, why do you abandon us and leave all at once? He continued forward and eventually saw a city made of crystal.
Within the city were eight jade maidens who, carrying eight wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi*), came to welcome him into the city.
He dwelt therein and enjoyed pleasures for eighty thousand years, after which weariness arose in his mind and he abandoned it and departed. Again he saw a city of white silver;
within the city were sixteen jade maidens who, carrying sixteen wish-fulfilling jewels, came to welcome him as before. He entered therein and stayed for one hundred and sixty thousand years.
He experienced pleasure, but later a sense of weariness arose within him, and he departed again. As he traveled on, he saw from afar a city of gold.
Inside the city were thirty-two jade maidens, each holding a *cintāmaṇi* jewel, who came out to welcome him as before.
He entered and enjoyed pleasure for three million two hundred thousand years, after which a sense of weariness arose again and he intended to leave. The women said to him:
He said, "Those who abandoned their previous abodes have since attained excellent places; if you abandon this one now, you will not attain such a place.
The elder did not believe him and continued on his way. From afar, he beheld a great iron city. The elder thought to himself, "Though its exterior is of iron..."
The women within were even more beautiful. As he gradually drew closer, he still did not see the jade maidens come out to welcome him.
The elder reflected, "Within this city, they are so intent on enjoying pleasure that they do not deign to come and welcome me.
He then continued toward the city until he saw a man wearing a wheel of fire upon his head, which the man placed upon the elder's head before departing the city. The elder asked:

The warder said, "When shall I be released from this wheel of fire? He replied, "If there were someone among the people of the world who had committed the same sins and merits as you, and they came to take your place, only then would you be spared from this matter.
The elder asked again, "I do not yet know what sins or merits I previously committed. The warder then recounted the previous events (as detailed above). Having heard this, the elder...
He questioned the wardens: "How many sinners are there in this city? The wardens replied, "We do not know their number. The elder thought to himself:

"As for my own suffering here, there is no foreseeable end to its release. It would be better if all the sinful karma of every person currently undergoing suffering within this prison were gathered together and transferred to my own body; may I suffer it in their stead so that they may all be liberated. No sooner had he...
As soon as he gave rise to this thought, the wheel of fire fell. The elder then asked the warder, "A moment ago you said this wheel would not fall;
why has it now fallen to the ground? The warder became enraged and struck him with an iron pitchfork, whereupon his life ended and he was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
The Buddha said, "Who else could that elder Maitraka have been at that time? It was none other than myself."

It is so. [The Buddha] addressed the bhikṣus: "You should know that toward one's parents, even a small unwholesome act yields great bitter fruit, while a small offering of support gains immeasurable merit.
You should single-mindedly provide for and honor your parents. Regarding the parrot who filially supported its parents, [the Buddha said]:
"In the past, within the Snowy Mountains, there was a parrot. From the *Ratnagarbha-sūtra* (or *Baozang jing*), the Buddha spoke thus: "In the past, within the Snowy Mountains, there was a parrot."
His parents were blind and ill, so he constantly gathered flowers, fruits, and other offerings to serve them.
At that time, there was a landowner who, when first sowing grain, made this vow: "The grain I sow shall be shared and eaten by all living beings.

When the parrot heard this, he would later come regularly to gather from the midst of the field once the grain had ripened. On one occasion, the landowner went out to inspect his crops and saw the sprouts.
When the crops were left in disarray, he became filled with anger and resentment. He then spread a net and captured a parrot.
The parrot said to the elder, "When you first planted [the seeds], you already possessed a virtuous mind; why do you now regret it?

It is simply because the seed is like a mother, the seed itself is like a father, truthful speech is like a son, and the field-owner is like a king who protects the field. Having spoken these words, he was the owner of that field.
He was filled with joy and asked the parrot, "For whom do you take this grain? It replied, "For my parents.
The landowner was moved by this and said to him, "From now on, you may come here to take it whenever you wish; do not hesitate or feel any doubt.
The Buddha said, "The parrot at that time was none other than myself. The landowner was Śāriputra, and the blind parents were [my parents]."
These are King Śuddhodana and Queen Māyā. Regarding those whose merit is equal to that of one in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*):

this refers to the Tuṣita Heaven, such as Maitreya, who is next in line to succeed [Śākyamuni] and attain Buddhahood in the future; currently residing in that celestial palace, he is called "one in his final birth.
Regarding the inability to repay their kindness: this means that teaching one's parents to cultivate goodness is the way to repay them, yet even such repayment cannot [fully suffice].
