It is so. Regarding the statement that the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* has arrived: before the scriptural text had yet reached this region, Master Dao’an had already altered his course [of expectation];

when the later version of the sūtra arrived, it was indeed identical to what he had previously predicted. Regarding the statement "if one reaches the essential point," [it refers to the fact that] Ānanda is impermanent; [this] increases...
One account states: In the kingdom of Vaiśālī, there was Mahāprajāpatī, who possessed the Kūṭāgāra Monastery. She was accompanied by five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, all of whom were arhats.
Upon hearing it said that after three months had passed, the Tathāgata would enter parinirvāṇa, they were overcome with grief and longing.
Unable to bear witnessing the Buddha’s entry into extinction, yet also unable to bear Ānanda’s entry into extinction, she thought, "I should first attain parinirvāṇa," and so she came.
She addressed the Buddha. The Buddha granted his silent consent. Mahāprajāpatī said again, "Today my words are rejected; I shall never again behold the countenance of the Sage.
Having spoken, she circumambulated the Buddha seven times, then circumambulated Ānanda seven times, and then circumambulated the assembly of bhikṣus.
She then withdrew by walking backward and returned to her own monastery. She spoke to the bhikṣuṇīs, saying, "I now wish to enter parinirvāṇa. The reason for this is as follows:"
"It means that the Buddha will soon enter parinirvāṇa; you should each take note of this. Upon hearing this, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs also went to the Buddha's presence and each took their leave.
The Tathāgata consented to enter nirvāṇa for all of them. Once the Buddha had granted permission, they each returned to their own quarters.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī opened the lecture hall, struck the *ghanṭā*, and spread out the seats. She then leaped into the air and performed the ten [transformations].
After eight transformations, she returned to her original seat, straightened her body, and fixed her mindfulness.

She immediately entered the first dhyāna, proceeding through the stages up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. While in that state, she reached the fourth dhyāna and attained parinirvāṇa.
At that moment, the great earth shook. Her five hundred disciples, the bhikṣuṇīs, did likewise. The Buddha said to Ānanda, "You must act quickly..."

He went to inform the general Yaśodharā, ordering him to quickly prepare five hundred couches, five hundred jars of ghee, five hundred jars of oil, five hundred bundles of *yūpa* flowers and incense, and five hundred wagonloads of firewood. Ānanda asked the Buddha, "For what purpose are these items being used?
The Buddha said, "Mahāprajāpatī and five hundred bhikṣuṇīs are entering nirvāṇa; I wish to make offerings to their śarīras. Ānanda.
Having heard this, he was overwhelmed by a mixture of sorrow and weeping, unable to restrain himself. He then went to the Great General and presented the Buddha’s instructions.

At that time, the Great General Yaśodharā explained everything in detail according to those instructions. Thereupon, the Tathāgata, together with the bhikṣus, went to the place where Mahāprajāpatī had entered parinirvāṇa.
He commanded Ānanda and Rāhula to lift Mahāprajāpatī’s body, saying, "I shall personally make offerings to her."

At that time, Śakra, the Bodhisattvas, the thirty-three gods, Brahmā, the four heavenly kings, and others came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying, "We pray only that the Tathāgata will not weary himself;
we shall provide the offerings. The Buddha said, "Stop, stop! This is not for you to do."
It is said that when a compassionate mother gives birth to a child, she provides much benefit; her grace in nurturing is profound, and her love in suckling is deep.
One must personally repay such kindness. The Buddhas of the past were also like this. At that time, the Heavenly King of the Northern Gate commanded five hundred spirits:
They went to Mount Candana to gather fragrant firewood and brought it to a peaceful, open wilderness.
At that time, the Tathāgata personally lifted one corner of the bier, while Rāhula and Ānanda each lifted a foot of the bier; they flew through the air and arrived at the cemetery.
There, the fourfold assembly lifted the corpses of five hundred bhikṣuṇīs and carried them to the site of the great cemetery, where the Buddha took up the candana sandalwood.
Each was assigned its portion; it was then entrusted to the various devas to maintain. The Buddha further placed sandalwood upon the body of Āmrapālī and spoke this verse:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; those who are born must all return to death. That which is unborn does not perish—this freedom from illness is the ultimate bliss.
At that time, humans and devas gathered like clouds. After the fire was extinguished, the Buddha commanded Mahāsthāmaprāpta to collect [the remains].
Five hundred bhikṣuṇīs erected a stūpa for Śāriputra and made offerings to it; they enjoyed happiness throughout the long night, and their merit was immeasurable.
Regarding King Śuddhodana and the others: according to the first fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, when the Buddha was in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, he was at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
While he was preaching the Dharma to the assembly, the Great King fell gravely ill in mid-air; none were able to save him.
At that time, tears fell from the King as he remembered [the Buddha], and he said to the people: "My life will not last long. It is my regret that I shall not see Siddhārtha, Nanda, and the others.
He sighed with such lamentation, saying further: "If I die without seeing my son, my life will have been in vain."
"Ji. However, because he has not yet escaped birth and death, he does not consider it suffering. When the people heard this, there was none among them who did not weep.
They then said to the king: "The Buddha is at Vulture Peak, fifty *yojanas* from here. Now Your Majesty’s exhaustion is increasing;
even if you dispatch a messenger to report this, the road is so long that his arrival would surely be late. We pray that Your Majesty will not grieve for your sons. The king then...
He replied, "My sons possess great compassion; they constantly perceive with their supernormal power and divine eye, so it will not be difficult for them to come.
At that time, the Buddha was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. With his divine ear, he heard from afar the sound of the King, his father, within the great city of Kapilavastu as he reminisced about him.
Furthermore, observing with his divine eye, he saw that the King was suffering from illness and his life was nearing its end. Thereupon, he addressed [the Bodhisattva].
Rāhula, Ānanda, and Nanda recounted in detail the matters with which their royal father was preoccupied.
Then, by means of his supernormal power, like a king of geese, he leaped into the void and suddenly vanished. Arriving at Kapilavastu, he emitted a great radiance.
The people of the kingdom saw the Tathāgata from afar; they wailed aloud with choked voices and spoke with sobbing: "The Great King’s life will soon come to an end."
"Long have we waited. We pray only that the Tathāgata would deign to go there at once. The Buddha told him:
"Impermanence and separation are the same from ancient times to the present; you should know this. Birth and death are suffering; only the Way is true.

At that time, as the Tathāgata wished to enter the royal palace, he first emitted a pure light that illuminated the king’s body, bringing peace to his afflicted pain. Knowing that the Buddha had returned, the king felt great joy.

He was so overcome with joy that he rose from his seat unconsciously. Once the Buddha had entered the palace and reached the king’s bedchamber, the king, upon seeing the Tathāgata, extended both hands with the intention of receiving His feet and addressed the Tathāgata:
“I pray that You will touch my body with Your hand to bring me peace and security.
For me, today is the last time I shall see the Buddha. The Buddha said to the king: “I only wish, Great King, that you would no longer grieve and be distressed.”
The Buddha himself extended his golden arm, which resembled a red lotus, and placed his hand upon the king’s forehead, consoling him by saying:
"Your Majesty is one who practices pure conduct; the defilements of your mind have already been removed. You should now rejoice; it is not fitting for you to be distressed."
While he was contemplating the meaning of the various sūtras and dharmas with focused attention, the king took hold of the Buddha’s hand with his own.

His heart full of devotion, he gazed upward at the Buddha, never for a moment averting his eyes from him, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "The Buddha is my son; you have received me with compassion.
While lying down, I joined my palms and mentally prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata. From this day forth, until the time of our parting and the cessation of my breath, [I shall remain thus]."
The Śākyas, crying out with great lamentation and ceaselessly reflecting upon the body, then used scented water to bathe the King’s body, wrapped it in white cotton cloth, and encoffined it.
Adorned with the seven precious gems, they placed the coffin upon a lion throne, scattering flowers and burning incense.
The Buddha and Nanda stood solemnly and respectfully before the funeral bier, while Ānanda and Rāhula [stood by].
After the funeral rites were concluded, Ānanda knelt for a long time and addressed the Buddha, saying, "The kindness with which my parents raised me was profound;
I pray that you will permit me to carry the coffin. Rāhula and Ānanda spoke in the same manner.

Fearing that people in future generations might become unfilial toward their parents, the Buddha granted his permission, so that this might be established as a ritual law for the final age. At that time, the Tathāgata himself also carried it.
The trichiliocosm shook and trembled in all directions; all the mountains rose and sank like a boat upon the water.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings transformed their bodies to become small and each took up the Buddha’s burden, which the Buddha graciously permitted.
The Buddha himself held an incense burner and walked ahead to lead the way. He further commanded one thousand arhats to go to the Great...
On the seashore, they took sandalwood fuel and piled it up; they placed the coffin upon it and set fire to it.
When the entire assembly saw the great conflagration, they wailed with grief and cried out loudly, beating their bodies with their own hands. The Buddha addressed the multitude, saying:
"The world is entirely impermanent, suffering, empty, and without solidity. You people see only this fire and take it to be [the end]."
The fires of all desires are even more intense than this. Therefore, by diligently seeking liberation from the suffering of birth and death, one attains peace and happiness.
Once that fire has been extinguished, each person gathered the *śarīra* relics, placed them in golden caskets, erected stupas, and made offerings.
At that time, the great assembly spoke with one voice, requesting: "King Śuddhodana has passed away; where will he be reborn? We pray that the Buddha [will explain]."
The Buddha spoke to the great assembly, saying: "The Pure King Śuddhodana, a person of purity, has been reborn in the Five Pure Abodes.
Upon hearing this, the great assembly was filled with joy; they paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew.

The Method for Men and Women of the Three Knowledges Entering the Monastery. The formal text is as written. Regarding the phrase "those who arrive first," and "those who have stilled their minds in silent repose":
these refer to the *ārāma* (monastery), which is originally the dwelling place of those who have stilled their minds. It is not a place where the chaotic and distracted gather;

this is because worldly people give rise to thoughts according to circumstances and are thus frequently noisy and disorderly. As for the phrase "how could those with outflows and arrogance tread upon it?": this is...

This is a place for bestowing the Dharma and providing instruction. How could one with a mind subject to outflows, deeply attached to the sentiments of pride and defiled desire, and lacking reverence in heart, tread upon this ground?
Furthermore, for those whose minds dwell beyond outward appearances, it means to settle the mind in formlessness;

for those whose physical forms differ from worldly etiquette, it means shaving the hair and donning dyed robes; and for those who take refuge and rely upon it, it means returning in devotion and offering respect.
Entrusting oneself to one’s aspiration, the principle dictates that when the Dharma is present, one should lower the head and humble the mind—this is called "bowing" (fu).

To gaze with reverence and move forward with the body—this is called "looking up" (yang). Treading upon the pure land of Vajra, one requests the Dharma from the Buddha to nourish the spirit; practicing reverence toward the Triple Gem, one hopes to be fully endowed with merit.
This is what is meant by "knowing how to tread. Next, in explaining the method for entering a temple, the text says: "Now, as for 'passing through' [the gate], it refers to Jetavana."
In the illustration, the common people emerge and enter the temple; the present transcription clarifies this according to the diagram.

Regarding the note stating that "even among the monks there are those who cannot be identified," this means that ordinary people and sages are intermingled such that they cannot be distinguished; it is not something that ordinary persons can discern.

Some may have a demeanor that is coarse and rustic, yet their minds are in accord with the ultimate principle; others may possess formal decorum, yet their thoughts are constantly preoccupied with worldly affairs; or some... [text ends]
Regarding the manifestation of the vehicle where ordinary beings and sages dwell together and perform shared activities that appear similar to secular conventions, one interpretation states:
In Confucian rites, for instance, the father sits while the son stands; in the Buddha-dharma it is not so—the preceptor and disciple both sit cross-legged in formal posture.
As for the fact that their intentions are distinct, although the positions of teacher and disciple differ, they are both fields of merit; therefore, this appearance is manifested.

Another interpretation states: When a monk sees a layperson and does not rise, it is called "having a deficiency. Examining the intent behind this explanation, it is incorrect; for one should merely subdue the pride of the *māna* (conceit) through the Way.

To manifest the mutual recognition of great beings is quite different. As for the claim that "monks take [others] as distinct," this means that to fail to follow the instructions of the Saṃgha is called "rebelliousness" (*pratyudgata*).
To examine the faults and afflictions of others is termed "taking [them] as distinct. Furthermore, another interpretation explains that it is a training in not giving rise to reverence.

To turn one's back on the Saṃgha is called "turning away. To seek out faults is called "adopting difference. This can be understood through the interpretation and judgment based on corroborating sutras.

As for "following the Buddha," it refers to circumambulating with the right side toward the object in the Western tradition as a sign of auspiciousness; constantly imagining that the Buddha is to one's right is this very act of performing circumambulation.
The head represents the mind and the ground represents the body; lowering the head to touch the ground is to contemplate the body with the mind. This is...
This is the place where one attains Buddhahood. Ego (māna) serves as its height, and the grasping of views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa) serves as its gaze.

With this haughty gaze, one scatters and wanders; to scatter and wander is to drift upon the ocean of birth and death. As for seeing a worm in the ground, it is because of faith in the Buddha’s words:

"My own self and the intrinsic nature of all beings are pure; we are all Buddhas, no different from one another. It is only because we are entangled by karmic retribution that we have not yet attained liberation. Thus it is said.
These are always causes for Buddhahood; therefore, upon seeing insects, one must not harm them. If one does not feel compassion, it becomes a cause for long life.
Regarding not spitting on monastic grounds: because the earth can produce all things, and because laypeople and children are the foundation of the Sangha, they are metaphorically called "earth.
As for "singing hymns" and so forth, this refers to chanting praises and the like to express the heart’s love and respect, as well as one's vows.

One should delight in showing respect. If the Saṃgha has faults—comparable to foul weeds, excrement, or soil—one should have no thought of perceiving them as faults, but rather remove them with one's own hands.
Regarding those whose disposition toward the Dharma and the Saṃgha is such that they would conceal faults, there is the example of Viśākhā-mātā;

for instance, upon hearing that the Saṃgha had a blemish, she was able to suppress it, and so forth. As for the phrase "if one arrives," this distinguishes the case where one has a connection [to the community] and is staying overnight at the monastery.
Regarding the *Dharmapada-sūtra*, Xuánzàng states that it is the *Ratnamudrā-sūtra*. As for the phrase "hoping to [build] a pagoda," *pò* means to strike lightly;
it is also said to mean to strike repeatedly. How could the spirit be extinguished?

If the body dies and the spirit is extinguished, then evil need not be feared, because when both body and mind perish, there is no person to undergo suffering. Although the present body dies, the consciousness remains eternally.
Since it cannot be extinguished, one undergoes bitter retribution in the evil realms; for this reason, one ought to fear it. This sutra is the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. As for "thorns" (*kaṇṭaka*):
they are common in the northern regions but do not exist in Jiangdong. When used as medicine, they have distinct prongs.
Because honoring the Sangha can bring about blessings, it is called a "fertile field"; because disparaging the Sangha can bring about transgression, it is thus likened to a thorn.

This is the "Garden. Regarding the phrase "One should know that below," the conclusion and explanation are as can be understood. As for the statement "From the pure-faith practitioner to the practitioner," those distinguished by others refer to the three types of followers.
One should not fail to show respect because their status is low; as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Though these four matters may be small..."
Yet one must not treat him with contempt. Although the Prince is young, he shall become the king; therefore, he must not be treated with contempt.

Although a snake’s cub is small, its venom can harm people; it likewise must not be treated with contempt. Although a small fire is minute, it can burn down mountains and forests; furthermore, it must not be treated with contempt.
Although a śrāmaṇera is young, having attained noble supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), he is most certainly not to be despised. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
Once there was an elder who prepared a feast and invited only the elderly and venerable, excluding the śrāmaṇeras.

At that time, all those śrāmaṇeras were arhats; they transformed their own bodies so that they all appeared as old men. When the donors saw them at their home, they joyfully invited them to sit. After they had been seated for a short while...
They then transformed back into youths. The elder was astonished and asked them in jest, "Have you finished taking the elixir of rejuvenation?
The śrāmaṇeras spoke this verse: "Do not give rise to doubt or fear; we are not human beings.
If you wish to judge the Saṃgha, such an act is truly lamentable. Out of compassion for one another, we have manifested such a transformation. You should understand this deeply."
The assembly of noble ones is immeasurable; yet you, with your worldly desires and immature years, attempt to measure these great virtuous ones.
Greatness or smallness arises from wisdom, not from age or youth. One who possesses wisdom and exerts diligent effort is "old" despite being young;
one who is indolent and lacks wisdom is "young" despite being old. For you now to pass judgment upon the Sangha is a grave error. Thus it was said below.

The concluding exhortation is easy to understand. The statement "that which is performed reaches the dung" is as written in the text. The statement "that which is reached is received" is a summary and indication.

Regarding the statement "the rest reaches the informants," those who serve as conditions for the cultivation of the Path—such as devas, nāgas, and spirits—possess the merit of providing secret protection;

humans possess the requirement of providing protection, offerings, and supplies. It is only through these means that one attains the cultivation of the Path; thus, one looks toward them as conditions, and the fourfold assembly makes offerings.

Regarding "those who provide sustenance," "those on the Path," and "those who look toward the Saṃgha as a realm for generating goodness": among these, the "manifest" refers to human beings, while the remaining three are "hidden.
This means that bhikṣus must always protect and maintain [the precepts]; if they should let them slip or lose them, even if the manifest world does not notice, [the hidden realms will].
There is nothing hidden that shall not be seen. There will surely come a time of emergence from this essential point, namely, at the time when the Tathāgata Maitreya appears in the world.
First, he shall deliver those who were disciples under the Dharma of Śākyamuni; in his first assembly, he shall deliver nine hundred and thirty million people.
In the second assembly, he delivered ninety-six billion people. In the third assembly, he delivered ninety-nine billion people.

Thus, those delivered by Maitreya in these three assemblies were all people who had planted merit during the period of the Bequeathed Dharma, or those who provided offerings when the Three Jewels flourished—such as those who burned incense, lit lamps, and performed prostrations—and yet they still attained deliverance. How much more so, then, for those who have received the precepts within their own bodies?
It is as if one has attained liberation. Regarding those who employ the Dharma in groups: two people form a companion (*bān*), and four people form a group (*chóu*).
A "group" (*chóu*) refers to a class or category. As for "transmitting and announcing," this means that having read the preceding text, one transmits it and makes it known to others.
All of these are joyful studies intended to cause [the Dharma] to circulate widely. (The various meanings above differ; this concludes the section on Monastics and Laypeople.)
○ The ninth chapter, "Host and Guest," consists of two parts:
first, the citation of the title; second, the explanation according to the text. Regarding the initial statement, "The host... up to five":

the purpose for the arrival of this chapter is that while in the preceding chapter the transformative etiquette of men and women entering the temple was observable, there are now monastics and laypeople newly arriving. It is therefore the principle for those who have resided there long-term...

One must receive [the guest]. Therefore, this is explained next. Regarding the definition of the title: the "host" refers to the established resident, while the "guest" marks the newly arrived visitor.

The host follows the protocol of honoring the guest, and the guest observes the etiquette of seeking the correct path. Since host and guest act in mutual relation, it is said that they "wait for one another.

The chapter is as explained in the usual commentaries; the four modes of deportment and their regulations are appended below (etc.). According to the textual commentary, the initial general meaning states: "When a śramaṇa arrives..."

Regarding the term "yun" (cloud): a *śramaṇa* refers to one who has left the household life; they are collectively called "Śākya," referring to the clan of the Muni, as has already been explained at length in the introduction.

"Lü" means companions. As for "guests of the three realms": these are the four classes of noble guests, namely those who have left the household life, because they seek liberation from worldly existence and do not intend to dwell there long-term.
Regarding the metaphor of the "inn": the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "ni... [the text here is incomplete].

"Zhě" (者) means "to welcome. In the region east of the Pass, it is called "nì" (逆); in the region west of the Pass, it is called "yíng" (迎). "Lǚ" (旅) refers to a traveler; it is a specific designation for a guest.
"Kuàng" (況) signifies intention or purpose. "Pō" (頗) means "capable" or "somewhat able. It is like building a lodging by the side of Luò today with the intent of waiting for guests to stay there;

since the meaning of "waiting for one another" in this chapter is no different, it is said that [this practice] "pō cún" (頗存)—meaning it exists to some extent—herein. Therefore, the Vinaya says: "Miscellaneous..."
This is the text of the *Khandhaka*. Initially, because a guest arrived and entered his room on his own, he fell to the ground; for this reason, the rule was established (and so forth).
If one considers the companions within the Three Realms, they all belong to the category of guests. Now, among these guests, those who arrive first are established as the hosts;
thus it is called a "special regulation" (*ku-zhi*). Because the methods for receiving them are few, it is called "miscellaneous practices" (*za-xing*) (and so forth).

Regarding the statement "dividing this into four," it means that within this main section, it is divided into four parts. Regarding the phrase "the first [part] up to 'etcetera,'" it is as the text states.
Regarding the phrase "the second [part] up to 'sleeping,'" "bedding and clothing" refers to the bedding laid out within the room;

it does not refer to the clothing used for the room itself. These are two types of cases where one must not sleep: suspecting others of being thieves, or because the space is cramped, and so forth. Regarding the third [part]... [text continues].
"Correctly" refers to the fourth *sthavira* (elder); this is explained in terms of the four persons who constitute a *saṃgha*. "Contemplating" means reflecting upon the words and their meaning.
"One need not prostrate" does not mean one must wait painstakingly for a single person; rather, one should simply proceed to prostrate to each individual in turn.

Regarding the phrase "the four... to the place," it indicates that those who receive the benefit together; while [some] explain this as the character "question" (*wèn*), here it is read as the character "together" (*tóng*).

Regarding the regulations for the monastic community: one must not wear the five-strip robe in places such as the capital city (and so forth). Regarding those traveling companions who have already departed:
Xuán says that one must not say to another, "Your companions have already left. This is intended as a skillful means to dismiss them, fearing they might stay;
one should instead detain them for a while and so forth. Regarding entrusting the traveling companions: this refers to having separately sought out and found other companions.
When the host departs, they entrust [the guest] to others, instructing them to treat [the guest] well and to provide medical care if illness occurs.
Regarding "local customs": this refers to the local vulgarities and corrupt speech of this region; how much more so when one is unaware of them. Regarding "avoiding what is forbidden":

this refers to the names of officials and the honorific titles of venerable elders. Regarding "certain things that may be eaten": this refers to pointing out the finest foods and urging one to eat them, thereby demonstrating a lack of stinginess.
Regarding "prohibitions," these refer to matters such as speech that is restricted within official circles. Regarding "thieves," this refers to the fear of others stealing one's robes or bowl.
Next, the rules for the four modes of deportment are distinguished. As for the passage beginning with "Now, as for... and so forth, observing the flow of the text, there are three sections.

The first two lines set forth the manifestation of the teaching based on the arousal of a virtuous mind. The next two lines explain that such an arousal must necessarily have its underlying cause and conditions. This is the reliance.

Regarding "the mind arising through the characteristics of the teaching" (*jiaoxiang xinfa*): this refers to relying upon [the teaching]. The "teaching" (*jiao*) refers to the textual expressions that can signify [the truth], namely the provisional forms of majestic deportment (*weiyi*).

These two aspects together give rise to wholesome thoughts. Regarding "establishing the cause by manifesting the fruit": commentators of old have offered many interpretations, none of which accord with the correct principle;

thus, they shall not all be recorded here. Among those currently prevalent, none precede these two explanations. The first relies on the *Souxuan* (Investigating the Profundities), based on the *Avivartika*...
When preaching the Dharma for Śāriputra, [the Buddha] did not state that the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) was the hidden cause (*mingyin*);

rather, he spoke only of the supramundane fruit, which is the manifest fruit (*xian-guo*). (This is one interpretation. Furthermore, according to the *Baoyun*: Śāriputra had planted roots of goodness in past lives; this constitutes the "hidden" (*ming*), meaning obscure or latent.
Although he himself could not recall it, he attained the illumination of the fruit in this life, which is the manifest fruit. This manifest fruit necessarily depends upon his perception.

Regarding their characteristics: it is only by hearing the Dharma that one can take this as the fundamental tenet. Therefore, it is said that "one establishes the tenet by relying on physical form and demeanor.
Thus, as for Aśvajit and Śāriputra: *Aśva* (or *Aśvaka*) in Sanskrit is translated here as Mǎshèng (馬勝, "Horse-Conqueror");
*Śāriputra* in Sanskrit is translated here as Shēnzi (身子, "Son of the Body") or Qúlùzǐ (鶖鷺子, "Child of the Crane"). According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra were comparable in their wisdom and talent; when traveling, they journeyed together, and when staying, they shared a single mind.
Later, they practiced as brahmacārins, serving the same brahmin teacher, Nāthaputra (also called Sañjayin, or alternatively Jñātiputra).
The teacher fell ill, becoming so severely prostrate that he was near death. Śāriputra stood at the head of the teacher’s bed, while Maudgalyāyana stayed by his feet.
As the teacher’s life was about to end, he smiled with joy. The two disciples addressed him together, saying, "Teacher, why do you smile?
The teacher replied, "The worldly ones lack eyesight and are beset by ignorance. I have seen the King of Kāñcanamālā die, and the multitude..."
The people cremated [the monk]. The first lady, overcome with incessant grief, threw herself into the fire, vowing to be in the same place as him;
therefore, I laughed at her. The two of them accepted my words, wishing to verify them. Later, a merchant from the kingdom of Suvarṇabhūmi arrived and inquired about it;
it was indeed just as the Master had said. He sighed in lamentation, not knowing that the Upādhyāya was a holy teacher.

Only after their deaths did they realize [the truth]. Consequently, the two made a vow, agreeing that if either should first obtain the flavor of the nectar of the Dharma, they must share it with one another (as clarified in the Vinaya).
Later, when their roots of goodness were about to ripen, they encountered the bhikṣu Ābhya preaching the Dharma.
According to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, as Ābhya was entering the city to beg for food, the Buddha foresaw this and said to him: "If you enter today..."
While begging for alms in the city, he encountered an extraordinary person along the road; he was unable to preach the Dharma extensively.

At that time, Ānanda’s deportment was perfectly composed and his appearance and attire were remarkable. Upon seeing him, Śāriputra thought to himself, "This man’s countenance and demeanor are so different;
he must surely possess an exceptionally superior teaching. He then asked, "Who is your teacher? What kind of Dharma do you preach? Ānanda then spoke.
The verse says: "All phenomena arise from causes and conditions; these phenomena cease because of conditions. My Teacher, the Honored Sage, has always spoken thus.

According to the sequence, the first line refers to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), and the second line refers to the Truths of Origination (*samudaya*) and Cessation (*nirodha*). The remaining two lines serve as a concluding indication. Question:
Among the Four Noble Truths, why are only three truths mentioned here, while the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) is not discussed? Answer: [It is said...]
Regarding the fruit realized, because there must necessarily be an antidote, it was concealed and not explicitly stated, desiring to cause others to come of their own accord to question the Buddha.
At that time, Śāriputra, having heard this, attained enlightenment. He went to where Maudgalyāyana was;
Maudgalyāyana marveled at his changed demeanor and, certain that he must have obtained a sublime Dharma, asked him about it. Śāriputra replied to him regarding what he had heard above.

Maudgalyāyana, having heard this, also attained enlightenment and went together with [the Buddha] to the place where the Buddha was. Such principles are fully contained within the sūtras of former times;
therefore, it is said that they are "fully set forth in the ancient sūtras. As for the transmission of the Dharma and its models, these are also inscribed upon tablets.

Xuánjì states: "Taking [the account of] Ānanda preaching the Dharma to Śāriputra as the model for the transmission of the Dharma" and Huáinán’s summary that Śāriputra, in turn, transmitted the aforementioned Dharma to Maudgalyāyana—these are both called 'transmission of the Dharma. However, these explanations have not yet accorded with reason.

Now, following Bǎoyún, it is said that this refers not only to how the Buddha, during his time in the Western Land, utilized the ritual of transmission to transform sentient beings; [the text] provides a full citation [of this].

The two texts, the Vinaya and the Śāstra, appear to represent the teachings that first reached this region after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; they likewise employ monastic protocols to transform sentient beings.

This is just as when Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna arrived in the Han, or Saṃghadeva came to Wu—was it not because the outward appearance and decorum of the Sangha were required to inspire faith in the people?
Thereafter, he established images and widely propagated the Buddha’s teachings. Such objects as these were among the silver of Wu;
thus it is said that they are also recorded in the "Insect-Scripture" (Tichongce). The direct narration below concludes the summary, which can be understood.

Regarding the statement "from the five [postures] down to lying down": to produce great illumination means that if one's four modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*) are not in accordance with the Dharma, there will be no benefit for illuminating the world.
Regarding "relying on the law of the king of beasts": this refers to the lion, the king of beasts, whose movements and stillness follow the Dharma.
Every morning at the first appearance of the sun, he emerges from his lair and repeatedly groans and roars; all fierce beasts...
Upon hearing this, there were none who did not submit and take refuge. It is the same for a bhikṣu:

he puts on his robes with his hands and carries his alms bowl to beg for food, always ensuring that his four modes of deportment cause other sentient beings to see them and thereby obtain benefit. As for turning the head toward the robe rack, it signifies respect for the robes.
The remaining points are as stated above: focusing the mind on the sign of light, rising quickly during the latter part of the night, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the *vīthi* (path/sequence) signs," it refers to the manner described in the section on "characteristics" (*nimitta*), such as when monastic property is spread over a covered area. Regarding the phrase "informing the assembly (*saṃgha*) and so forth," this indicates that one does not act independently.

As for the phrase "if [one has] more than ten years of seniority (*vassa*) and so forth," this means that one holds the rank of a teacher (*ācariya*); even if one is not permitted to go personally, there is no fault.

Because it is beneficial. Regarding "for the sake of those who are declining": that which is beneficial to one's own person is called "benefiting others," while that which causes harm is called "decline.
Regarding "to avoid a distracted mind": with a single-minded focus on the ground, one is freed from further攀缘 (pān-yuan—clinging to objects of perception) and does not regress.

Regarding the "characteristics of a Bodhisattva": Xuán (Xuánzàng) says this refers to those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward. Alternatively, according to the teachings found in various sutras, the Bodhisattva of the first stage is so named.
Regarding "non-retrogression in practice": from the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) onward is termed "non-retrogression through realization.
Now, it is not improper to generally designate those from the first stage onward as "non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas"—this is excellent. As for the phrase "reaching the karma of the *saṃkhyeya*":

"camel-sitting" refers to bending both knees and resting both hands upon the seat, like a camel. "Sitting in the full lotus posture" (*paryaṅka*) means crossing the left and right feet over one another.

The manner of binding [the legs] is called *paryaṅka* (full lotus posture). Regarding the "six recollections" (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Seeing) states that at the time of sleep, one must recollect the Three Jewels, as well as precepts, generosity, and the devas—these are the six.

As for the specific regulations established for each: a *bhikṣuṇī* may only kneel with both knees on the ground and is not permitted to kneel with alternating knees, because there was a transgression in the origin story (*nidāna*) that necessitated this fixed rule. For a *bhikṣu*, however, alternating knees is permitted; thus the *Yeshu* (Outline of Karma) says: "In the Vinaya..."
The body becomes weak and one may collapse to the ground while kneeling. The Buddha established a formal posture for standing that differs from that of the *saṃgha*.

Therefore, it is said: "Stand upright; do not sleep while kneeling or sitting. Crossing the two legs is contrary to the Dharma. Stand with both feet together, heels on the ground and toes pointing upward.
Place both hands behind the back, supporting the bed—this is called 'squatting backward' (*kuei-chü*). Bend the knees and place one foot on the ground. Furthermore...
Place one foot [on the ground] and rest the other upon the previously placed knee; stretching it straight is the "supporting leg," meaning one foot is positioned upon the other.

Regarding "not placing the foot up": this refers to one sitting in a squatting posture (jūza) who is treading on the ground; if the foot were raised, it would touch the robe. As for the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* stating that an elder (upādhyāya) should not rise:
the text says that if one sees them at the place where the Dharma is being taught, whether one rises on one's own initiative or because the elder instructs one to do so, [one should remain seated].
It is auspicious for both. If the Upādhyāya or Ācārya arrives, rising out of respect does not constitute an offense. However, one must not cause others to rise; to do so constitutes an offense.
Regarding "rising from one’s seat is auspicious," this refers to the offense incurred by rising on one's own initiative.
As for "exclaiming 'Dàtā' due to violating the regulations," the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as the sound of a sigh. The "original arising" is the nature of perfect luminosity, profound and tranquil.
This is truly because one has given rise to false imaginings of one's own accord. One should investigate the root cause: from what did it originally arise?

One must reflect upon and reproach oneself for this. Regarding "one who leaves their superior seat": this refers to leaving behind instructions for those remaining, so that they may keep the superior seat vacant to await the arrival of the guest.

Regarding "the hair becomes dry": the text states that when sleeping, one should rise and listen; if one falls asleep again while bathing, one should immediately form the thought in advance: "My hair will become dry."

"I shall arise" indicates that a considerable amount of time has passed. Regarding "observing the light of the stars and moon," while sleeping one should look toward the stars and moon, forming a mental resolve in advance:
"When the moon reaches such-and-such a place, or when a star reaches such-and-such a place, I shall arise.
As previously explained, this refers to the method of practice mentioned earlier; citing the scriptural passage, one should lie on the right side on the ground according to the royal lion posture.

[The preceding section on] "Lying Down" [consists of two parts, etc., concluding the chapter on the Mutual Relationship between Host and Guest]. ○ The tenth chapter, "Visiting the Sick and Attending Funerals," contains two sections:

first, stating the title; second, explaining according to the text. Regarding the first point, from "Visiting the Sick" up to the twenty-sixth [item], it is as follows: First, [the previous... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on a monastic code (Vinaya) or monastic regulations (Bhikṣu-śīla), likely from a Chinese Buddhist text such as the *Baizhang Qinggui* or similar. The translation reflects the structure and terminology typical of such commentaries.)

Master Xuan said: "The above clarifies the direct discourse between host and guest. As for a person in good health, since the sutras state that 'this body is itself the illness,' when the illness arises, one must naturally attend to it.
Furthermore, when the retribution of this Jambudvīpa life comes to an end and burial is required, one must likewise act in accordance with the proper rites."

This has not been discussed previously; therefore, it is explained next. Regarding the etymological interpretation: Sengfeng (Saṃgharakṣita) stated that attending to the sick is called "visiting the ill" (*zhānbìng*).

As for "sending off the end" (*sòngzhōng*): it refers to the rites of burial and interment performed upon the conclusion of life, hence it is called "sending off the end. The sections below are explained as usual.

Next, regarding the explanation according to the text, there are two parts: first, the enumeration of the headings; second, the explanation based on those headings, beginning with "First, attending to the sick.

Regarding the initial statement "proceeding to the specific sections," this refers to their classification by category as follows: first, attending to the sick; second, conducting funeral rites. (Note:

A detailed examination of the *Xianzheng* commentary reveals that the section for the initial enumeration of headings is missing; it has been extracted here based on the *Xuanyi* commentary. Question: All other chapters contain a general purpose (*sūtrārtha*). Why is there none for this chapter? Answer: One.

The commentary states: "The two matters mentioned in the title cannot be combined into a single meaning; therefore, they are first divided into separate sections. Second, according to the *Biāojiè* (Explanation of the Manifestation), it says:
"Because the author exercises his autonomy, he transforms the general intent into a specific restrictive intent. This does not mean that [the general intent] is entirely absent;

hence, the text below says 'up to the point of funeral rites,' which expresses the same idea as this [current] description. It does not mean that the two matters cannot be combined into a single meaning."

This is because a mere inch of water reveals no bottom. Regarding the statement "from the regulations down to the accounts": that which possesses a conditioned form refers to the karmic body (*karma-kāya*).
"Entangled in afflictions" means being bound and fettered; it refers to the chronic illness of the *kleśas* (defilements).

"The four great elements mutually reversing" refers to earth, water, fire, and wind, as they constitute its physical substance. When cold and heat are not regulated, this leads to the onset of disease. Thus it is formed.
This refers to new illnesses. Regarding the "six palaces" (*liù fǔ*): "six" is their number; "palace" (*fǔ*) refers to a place where things are gathered and stored.
The *Báihùtōng* states: first, the small intestine is the palace of the heart; second, the large intestine is the palace of the lungs; third, the stomach is the stomach-palace.
The fourth, the gallbladder, is the腑 (fu) of the liver. The fifth, the bladder, is the腑 of the kidneys. The sixth, the triple burner (sanjiao), is combined into a single腑.
As for the triple burner: from above down to the heart is the upper burner; from the heart down to the waist is the middle burner; and from the waist down to the lower part is the lower burner.
The *Nǐ'ěr yǎ* (Etymological Dictionary) states that "ní" means "near. When healthy, people are close to one another; when ill, they abandon them.

Regarding the statement, "Knowing that goodness has not yet been honored, one must surely follow evil": this refers to the fact that while nursing the sick is a virtuous act, the people of the world do not necessarily honor it;

conversely, abandoning the sick is an evil act that many emulate. Therefore, the phrase "equal [treatment] in the Vinaya" refers to the textual passage on the rules for robes (*cīvara*) in this Vinaya. The text says: At that time, there was a comparison...
"Kauṇḍinya, I have been ill for a long time, lying here amidst urine and excrement. At that time, the bhikṣus had gone out to accept invitations.
Later, the Buddha went on an inspection tour of the dwellings and saw this sick man. He then washed and cleansed the man’s clothes and body with Ānanda until they were perfectly pure.
Having perfumed them with incense, he placed him in a proper position and preached the Dharma to him. Then he asked him: 'When you were healthy...'"
"Have you ever looked after the sick? He replied, "I have never seen anyone do so. The Buddha said, "If you do not look after others, who will look after you when you are ill?

For this reason, it was established [as a rule]... [and so forth]. As for the statement that "the intent even in seeing one off at the end of life is the same as this," it means that in the world, people are close to one another while they are strong and healthy, yet after death they no longer look after each other; now, one must remain consistent from beginning to end. To provide for them is [the duty].

Because there is no difference from what preceded, it is said that the intention is the same as this exposition. Regarding the statement "from the question to the praise," this refers to the preceding scriptural text:
"If there are those who wish to make offerings to me, they should make offerings to the sick. It is from this that the present question arises. As for the meaning of the answer:

it states that one who nurses the sick is equal to the compassionate practice of the Buddha and shall likewise attain Buddhahood; therefore, it instructs them to make offerings. Furthermore, the Treatise says:

This is the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. The maternal aunt personally wove a golden-threaded *kāṣāya* with her own hands, thinking that when the Buddha returned to the palace, she would present it to him to offer her devotion.
The Buddha said: "This is a gift given out of a heart of attachment; it possesses little merit. Now, simply give it well to the Saṃgha, and you shall possess the three refuges.
Taking this as proof that one should now comply with the Buddha’s words, the Buddha commanded that it be examined.
Regarding illness: since one now provides care, this is precisely to comply with the Buddha’s words. As for the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and other texts:

at that time, there were two bhikṣus from the south who came together to pay their respects. One bhikṣu encountered illness and was unable to depart; the other could not wait and went on ahead to see the Buddha.
The Buddha, knowing this, questioned him, and he related the preceding circumstances in detail (*etc.*). The Buddha rebuked him.
"Reproach yourselves! You have all left the household life together to cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*). If you do not look after one another, who will look after you?

You should quickly return [to your duties]," and so forth. To be praised by the Buddha is to be the foremost among the eight fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). This is stated in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Xiányújīng*).

There are five kinds of giving that yield immeasurable merit: first, giving to those who have come from afar; second, giving to those traveling far away; third, giving to the sick; fourth, giving during times of famine;

and fifth, giving to those who know the Dharma. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Even if they are not noble ones (*ārya*), giving to one's parents, the sick, a Dharma teacher, or a Bodhisattva in their final birth yields immeasurable fruit.
Second, regarding the selection of persons, it says: "Second, selecting those who reach [the recipient]—this refers to opening up their robes."

Regarding the person hired to perform the cremation: it means that after death, the robes and bowl belong collectively to the Sangha of the ten directions. This provision applies when there are no *bhikṣuṇīs* present; thus, they may be included.

Now, as for the phrase "that person," it refers to the deceased individual. Fearing that the monks might exhaust themselves collecting [the items] without making a formal distribution, it is said, "if that person has nothing," thereby requiring them to relinquish [the items].
Xuán says: This is a comprehensive interpretation of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, meaning that the *bhikṣu* obtains the robe.

The ritual procedure belongs to oneself. Afterward, one may immediately hire someone; what fault is there in this? As for the other three assemblies, if one encounters them on the road, one should follow the same ritual as described above.
Next, the method of making offerings is clarified; the names [of the texts] cited can be understood from the context. Regarding the statement "the *Pañcavargika* up to the *Dharma*":
first, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* is cited based on the discourse concerning an *araṇya* (forest hermitage) where no pure attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*) is present. Next, the *Ratna*... [is cited].

Regarding the *Liang jing* (the *Liang* version of the scripture): it states that if a bhikṣu who is begging for alms is ill and has no one to look after him, such that he is unable to beg for food, he should thus subdue his mind, thinking:
"I am alone without a companion; I am solitary and single. The Dharma is my companion.
I shall now single-mindedly contemplate the Dharma, relying on the Buddha’s true teaching and reflecting well upon it myself," and so forth. Next, it cites the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

[The author] explains: There are nine modes of untimely death, as can be understood from the text. Regarding the phrase "as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*," those with a good reputation receive offerings from many people;
thus, when they go begging, they easily obtain merit and acquisitions, such that their robes and bowls become extremely numerous, and no distress arises when they go begging.

Regarding the phrase "the Buddha and the Saṃgha [committing] impurities, leftovers, overnight storage, and the *duṣkṛta* offense": an external objection states that the Saṃgha possesses leftovers and overnight storage.

[Objection: "If it is improper contact (*duṣṭa-sparśa*), how could the Buddha have it? If you admit that the Buddha has leftover food from previous days and so forth, then the Buddha would be guilty of violating the precepts.

[Response: Although this is food eaten by the Buddha, because a bhikṣu touched it, it is considered improper contact. [Objection: "If that is the case, later in the text there is mention of a bhikṣu eating the Buddha’s leftovers;
even after he has touched it, if he is able to redeem it [from the taint], why is his eating permitted? [Response: Furthermore, that case is not the same as this one.
When he was making the formal offering to the Buddha, because it belonged to the donor, he later redeemed it from the Buddha and there was no offense.
Now, however, because this food has been touched by himself, it constitutes the offense of "remaining-touched" (śeṣa-spraṣṭavya). The rest is as in the text.
Third is the Gate of Entrustment. Regarding the phrase "those who arrive," it refers to those who seek to focus their minds on the Dharma. Xuan said:
"Since the sunlight has been observed repeatedly, yet those returning are seen to be exceedingly rare, one seeks the gate of life through this;
thus, one can attain it. Therefore, one must single-mindedly contemplate impermanence and the nature of decay. As for the Buddha’s descent into the Sahā world..."
According to the Sanskrit *Sahā*, this is translated as "Mixed Evil. Furthermore, according to the Sanskrit *Saha*, this is translated as "Endurance" (*Kantshin*). Why is it called "Endurance"?
First, according to the interpretation based on the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, "Endurance" (*Rin*) is the name of the Brahmā King of this realm; it is so named because he is able to endure.
Because one does not give rise to a mind of envy or resentment toward the superior achievements of others, the name of the dwelling place is established based on the "Master" (Kṣānti).
Next, citing the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is said that the sentient beings of this world endure the three poisons and various afflictions; thus, they are called "Endurers" (*kṣānti*).

Furthermore, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states that because the Bodhisattva is truly capable of enduring while practicing for the benefit and happiness [of others], the Buddha’s own land of enjoyment is named after him.

It differs from the ordinary realm; now, for the purpose of transforming sentient beings, one simply seeks to bring them to spiritual maturity through goodness, without harboring feelings of aversion toward impurity.

Fourth is "Expounding the Dharma and Gathering the Mind. The headings of the names are as in the text. Regarding the phrase "reaching the ten," it refers to those who expound the profound Dharma. True...
The characteristic of reality is called the profound Dharma. Regarding the statement "if one arrives," as for "leaving the seat and leaving the robe":

when the Buddha saw Kāśyapa approaching, he shared half of his seat with him; afterwards, he exchanged the *saṃghāṭī* he was wearing for Kāśyapa’s rag-robe (*pāṃsukūla*), as described in the section on the dhūta practices.
Regarding the statement "if one arrives" and so forth, and the "fourfold hearing of the Truths by the Śuka bird," etc., [is found in] the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*.
The thirteenth [chapter] says: At that time, the Buddha was in Śrāvastī. The elder Sudatta revered and had faith in the Buddha’s Dharma;
he provided everything that was required. The bhikṣus came and went daily according to their needs.
In his house there were two parrots: one named Latthivana and the other named Sālavana. By nature they were silent yet wise, and were able to understand human speech.
Whenever the Saṃgha arrived at the gate, they were always instructed to deliver a message. Later, Ānanda went to the house and said to him, "I shall now teach you the sublime Dharma.
Upon hearing this, the parrot joyfully accepted it. Ānanda then bestowed upon him the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.

The Teacher commanded that the verses be collected: *Catuṣpadā* (the Truth of Suffering), *Tṛṇamukta* (the Truth of Origination), *Nirvṛta* (the Truth of Cessation), and *Mṛgā* (the Truth of the Path).
Before the gate of Sudatta’s house there was a tree. Two birds, having heard the Dharma, leaped for joy and practiced recitation;
they flew toward the tree, ascending and descending in succession seven times, chanting in unison with one voice as they received the sublime Dharma of the Four Noble Truths throughout the night.
They nested in a tree and were eaten by a wild fox. Ānanda asked the Buddha, "Where were these two birds born?
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Because you bestowed the Dharma upon them and they received and upheld it with a heart of joy, after their lives ended, they were born among the gods of the Four Great Kings.

When their celestial lifespan there was exhausted, they were born in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa; thus they proceeded through all six heavens. Having passed away from those realms, they have now been reborn here."

At the very least, they will be born among the Four Heavenly Kings; in this manner, they will be reborn seven times among the heavens of the six realms of desire, enjoying blessings at their own will and never meeting an untimely death.
Ānanda asked again, "When their lives in the six heavens come to an end, where will they be reborn?
The Buddha said, "They will be born in Jambudvīpa as human beings who leave the household life to study the Path, attaining the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha—one named Dharma and the other named Śubha."
Dharmaya. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, there is a chapter titled "The Chapter on Hearing. The thirtieth fascicle of that sūtra states:
Śakra Devānām Indra thought to himself, "If a son or daughter of good family hears the *pāramitās*, such persons have had [the teachings] enter their two ears."

Having already performed various meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and been accompanied by spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), how much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, and recite [this teaching]?
Regarding the two characters "Nirvāṇa" and "Ever-abiding": "Ever" refers to the abiding of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*). As the Sūtra says:
If there are sentient beings who hear this Nirvāṇa Sūtra— which ultimately reveals the Buddha-nature, teaches the Dharma of permanence, bliss, self, and purity as being neither born nor extinguished,
and which is the Dharma of eternal abiding— then when their lives eventually come to an end, they shall not fall into the evil realms.
Regarding the phrase "if it reaches the conditions," it is as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "if it reaches the power," this can be understood.

Regarding the phrase "that which reaches [the goal] and becomes the cause for attaining sainthood," the Sūtra says: "The emptiness of intrinsic nature is itself the inconceivable Buddha. Therefore, one should know that this refers to the practitioner of seated meditation.
This is the correct reason. Regarding the statement "if one assists [others] up to the point where it is said... and so forth:
those who are peers with the Sages—such as Trapuṣa, Kāśyapa, and others cited below—all Arhats engaged in communal affairs. This refers to Trapuṣa, who was of royal lineage;
he relinquished his Arhat body to seek the "solid dharma" (*dṛḍhadharma*). The Vinaya states that Trapuṣa himself had this thought, yet he did not know what the solid dharma was, and thus...
The *saṃgha-karmadāna* (monastic administrator) is one who is steadfast. Kāśyapa trod upon the mud to construct five vihāras. Xuán says:

according to the *Huái Sīzī Zhuàn* (Biographies of the Master and Disciples of Huái), Kāśyapa did not shrink from fatigue or hardship and constantly constructed five monasteries (*saṃghārāma*) himself.
The first was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; the second was on Mount Vairaputra; the third was on Mount Śarabhaṅga; the fourth was on Mount Tapodā; [the fifth was] on Mount Dabba...
Regarding that old mountain: five [cases] occurred in the Bamboo Grove fields; these five conditions together constitute a single rule concerning robes (*cīvara*).

There is no offense for being separated from one's robe (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). This applies up to and including matters of usage and so forth (etcetera). Furthermore, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣika* (or *Samantapāsādikā*), Kāśyapa personally managed the monastery and applied mud to the walls with his own hands.
Although he was a great Arhat, he did not seek karmic rewards; he did so only to repay his debt of gratitude and to nurture the Buddha-dharma. In contrast...

To treat ordinary persons as fields of merit of little consequence would give rise to pride; therefore, [the Buddha] subdued the disciples' hearts of arrogance and indulgence and inspired the meritorious karma of future sentient beings.

Regarding the *geya* (verses) on "splitting firewood," according to the *Saṃyuktapiṭaka*, there were two bhikṣus in South India who, having heard of that Venerable One’s reputation, came specifically to Kaśmīra to pay their respects. Upon arrival, they saw the Venerable One...
As for the one who was emaciated and thin, he was inside the kitchen by the cauldron, tending the fire. Not recognizing him, [the other] asked:
"Do you know where Śāriputra resides? He replied: "He is in the third cave. When the two bhikṣus arrived, they indeed saw the monk who had previously been tending the fire.
They questioned him with suspicion and wonder, and so forth (as detailed in the text). Regarding "Śāriputra sweeping the ground," Xuán says: "This is not yet clear."
Regarding the source [of this passage]: "Maudgalyāyana kindled [the lamp]" is stated in the *Za yao xing* (Miscellaneous Essential Practices).
As for the phrase "The foolish and ignorant do not know," the meaning is that the Saṃgha is a mass of merit; yet the foolish and ignorant do not learn this for themselves.

Therefore, the sages each abandon their own occupations to assist in communal affairs, acting as guides to lead the foolish and ignorant so that they may come to understand. (Some have provided erroneous interpretations; one should not reflect upon them. The term "note" (*zhù*) refers to... [end of fragment].
"The Heavenly Realm" refers to the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*. Regarding "recalling the merits one has cultivated," Master Kumārajīva said:
"According to the customs of foreign lands, from birth until the moment of death, all meritorious deeds performed are recorded.
When the time of death arrives, those present read them aloud for the dying person, causing their heart to rejoice so that they do not give rise to fear. Master Sengzhao said: "I fear..."
For the sake of those newly initiated bodhisattvas who are afflicted by illness and mental distraction, he exhorts them to recollect their merit in order to gladden their hearts.

Regarding "mindfulness of pure livelihood," Kumārajīva says it refers to right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*). One reflects that from birth until now, one has always practiced right livelihood and will surely proceed toward the good realms.
"What have I to fear? This tradition is likewise the original account from China. As for the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts, they cite a separate sutra from the twenty-fourth fascicle:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Those who commit evil are born in good places; those who practice goodness are born in evil places.
Ānanda asked the Buddha, "How can this be so? The Buddha said, "Regarding evil people in this life..."
Evil has not yet ripened, while wholesome karma has already ripened. By this cause and condition, although one currently commits evil, one will be born in a good realm.
The opposite is said regarding the birth of the wholesome (and so forth). As for the statement "inquiring into the essential point," this is also a self-interrogation within the treatise itself.

In the response, it is explained in terms of being fierce, sharp, and powerful. It is like a person entering a battle array who does not spare their own body or life; such a person is called a "valiant warrior" (*kṣatriya*). This is certainly [the case].
One must include the intent of admonition and exhortation. Regarding "loving clothing," it is as previously explained;
regarding "pointing to" (referring to) giving, it is as in the text. As for the phrase "its arrival": in the West, one attains rebirth through the accomplishment of ten recitations;

or, regarding the Tuṣita Heaven, one cultivates goodness according to the *Maitreya Sūtra*, such as the simultaneous cultivation of the six matters, the two causes, and the accumulation of various similar types. "Delusively generating a self" refers to this.
The Sūtra says: "Ordinary beings do not know that the internal is empty and devoid of self; they recklessly give rise to conceptual attachments, yet in reality there is no self.

That which is truly and utterly non-existent may seem to exist from the perspective of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), but it is definitively non-existent according to ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).

There is only a single, pure consciousness-mind, and no external objects can be apprehended; therefore, know that all such things are delusions. Or it is said: "There is only consciousness (vijñaptimātra) and no external objects."

"Only the deluded perceptions of sentient beings" refers to the objects of the three realms, which are transformations of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*) and lack any inherent reality. Therefore it is said: "There are no external objects;

they are merely the deluded retributions of sentient beings," arising from pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*). Regarding the "four parts" and so forth, this is a passage from the *Cīvara-vastu*.
The text states: "That sick bhikṣu thought thus: 'I shall accept these inferior three robes, for I fear [the burden upon] the caregiver.'"
Because [the donor] had obtained [them]. The Buddha said: "One should not give rise to such a thought. The text says: At that time, a patient carried his robes and bowl to offer them for support;

[the donor] feared that if he remained in a secluded place, there would be no one to nurse him later when he recovered. The Buddha said: "One should not harbor such an intention. Now, this commentary abbreviates those two points, hence it says:
"Receiving robes and bowls of poor quality, as well as giving them away to others. This is comparable to the case of King Māṇava.
Regarding the "mound" (kūṭa), both the wise and the foolish alike say that because this person, in a past life, once offered his own cloth to a Pratyekabuddha,
by virtue of this causal connection, for five hundred lifetimes he was naturally wrapped in cloth while still in the mother’s womb.
Later, at the time of his renunciation, [the jewels] were transformed into dharma robes and so forth (as detailed).
Regarding the former king who was deceived by the jewels, this is from the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra*, where he himself cites the scriptural passage: "In the past, there was a king named Nanda."

He accumulated precious jewels, intending to carry them into future lives. He thought silently to himself, "I shall now collect all the treasures within the kingdom so that there is nothing left outside.
Because of his greedy accumulation of wealth, he placed his own daughter atop a high tower and issued a decree, saying:
"If anyone brings jewels here, I shall have sexual union with your daughter. In this manner, he gathered everything from within the kingdom.
"Rare treasures are all gathered at the king's palace. At that time, there was a man who saw the king’s daughter and became so deeply infatuated with her beauty that he fell ill from his longing;
he had no treasures within his home. When his mother learned of this, she said to her son: 'All the treasures in the kingdom have been brought back to the king's place;
there is nowhere else to seek them. I recall when you were on the verge of death, there was a single gold coin in your mouth.'"
"You may go to the cemetery and retrieve it. The son followed his mother's words and indeed obtained the gold coins. He presented them to the king.
The king asked, "The treasures within my realm are completely exhausted; from where did you further obtain these coins? He then answered the king with the full truth of the matter.
The king sent men to investigate, and only when he found that the account was not false did he place his trust in him. The king then reflected to himself: "I previously accumulated..."
One accumulates all manner of wealth and treasures, hoping to take them into the next life; yet one cannot even obtain a single coin there, let alone more.
For this reason, one should dedicate it all toward the cultivation of merit. Thus, one knows that not a single thing follows oneself—how could this not be true?

As for the phrase "likewise until the sounding of the gong," it refers to those who act according to the length of their lifespan, meaning during the interval before death. Within that period, according to...
Regarding the lengthening or shortening [of the intervals] within this, it is for the purpose of providing guidance. As for striking the *muhang* (impermanence) gong, Xuán said:
"It should be struck while life has not yet ended and the faculties and consciousness have not yet perished. To do so after the breath has ceased would be of no benefit to the matter."
II. The Method for Sending Off the Deceased. The recording of the name follows the text. Regarding the phrase "thus reaching the ultimate good": this establishes the intent behind the funeral rites;

it means that once the preparatory intent is set, as previously described, one should circumambulate the remains with the aim of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*). This refers to the original aspiration of the mind: to transcend birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
In establishing all ritual procedures, one should minimize desires and distance oneself from worldly customs. "Extravagance" refers to elaborate ornamentation. As for burial in the earth...

"Burial" means interring [the body]. "Eliminating excess" means avoiding extravagance. "Not painting the coffin and being cautious on the road" refers to this. "Eliminating frugality" means not leaving the corpse exposed when departing.
Now, adopting the middle way, one should strive to ensure a favorable rebirth. As for the phrase "attaining the ultimate Dharma," it is as the text states.

Regarding the phrase "initial, middle, and final shame": in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, it says that a nun beats her breast. This refers to a case within the *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules where a nun quarrels with another;

when she is not in the right, she beats her breast and weeps, thereby inviting censure. She reports this to the Buddha, who says: "For every single blow, there is one *pāyattika*; for every single drop of tear that falls to the ground, there is also one *pāyattika*.

For the Saṃgha, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. The above constitutes the section on the restrictive conditions (*niyama-pratyaya*). In the section on the permissive conditions (*anujñā-pratyaya*), it says:

It is not otherwise, nor is it an offense. Since the sin of weeping for the deceased has not been proscribed, one knows that at present, when a teacher passes away, it is no transgression for a disciple to weep.

This, conversely, demonstrates that there is no offense according to the *Pañcaśata-praśna-vinaya*. As for the following passage, it clarifies the text concerning non-offenses due to extenuating circumstances;
thus, the text of the *Pañcavargika-saṃgīti* states: "Those who had not yet abandoned desire threw themselves to the ground, weeping with grief."
He choked with emotion for a long time before regaining consciousness... (and so forth). He secluded his mind in solitary dwelling, maintaining lofty integrity beyond the mundane world;

naturally transcending the common crowd, he was singular in his practice. That he remained as clear as a frosty sky was due to his inherent purity. When his parents died, he did not weep, for secular rites would not tolerate it;
when his two teachers died, he did not mourn, for the Vinaya rules did not permit it. Thus it is said that both the monastic and the lay communities shared in his shame.
Regarding the phrase "he goes to the place": this refers to the ritual for offering condolences. As for "grasping the hand of the disciple," this refers to the junior teacher of the deceased;

he grasps the hand because the deceased is in a state of confusion and delusion. Thereafter, they proceed to the master’s quarters and perform the rites of condolence and inquiry according to the Dharma.

If one follows secular etiquette, there is the system of the five mourning garments (*wǔfú*) and the three categories of premature death (*sānshāng*). The five garments refer to the *zhǎnsuī* (unhemmed mourning), *qísuī* (hemmed mourning), *dàgōng* (nine-month mourning), and *xiǎo...* [small mourning].

"Kong" refers to the *sī* (three-month) mourning mat. Regarding the three types of *shāng* (premature death): those from nineteen down to sixteen years of age are classified as *cháng-shāng* (long-term premature death);

from fifteen down to twelve are *zhōng-shāng* (middle-term premature death); and from eleven down to eight years of age are *xià-shāng* (short-term premature death). Those under seven years of age are included within the thirty-nine grades of mourning for the *shāng*.

As for the periods of mourning based on days and months, there are three types: first, the formal (*zhèng*); second, the derivative (*yì*); and third, the reduced (*jiàng*). All monks and nuns today [follow these].

Regarding the rites for mourning: the harmonious superiors are honored as one’s own parents; the three masters and seven witnesses follow the same precedent as the *chuanwu* (the deceased’s relatives), with no reduction in rank.

This is because the underlying sentiment is reached only by those who have transcended the mundane; they advance beyond the common world. Their mourning garments consist of five grades of coarse and fine linen.

For monks and nuns, the secular *guanjing* (ceremonial cap) is replaced by a headcloth. As for the staff used to support the weak, monks and nuns are treated the same. If the body has not yet been encoffined...

Previously, one simply remained on the straw mat at one's own station while those who came to offer condolences wept; nor were there any other words exchanged. On the third day, after the funeral rites were completed, one would then perform the formal ceremonies.

If it was a case of someone rushing back from a distance to mourn (*benshāng*), it was made clear that they had been abroad. If they needed to convey a message of grief, they would have to communicate through another person to arrange for the coffin to be moved.
Thereafter, they returned with great haste; traveling by night until the stars appeared, they halted when the stars appeared. If [the journey] was already...

Upon interring the remains, one should first go to the burial site to express one's grief. If the body has not yet been returned to the mountain, one returns directly to one’s own location to express grief;

the procedure for offering consolation is exactly as in the usual ritual. Regarding "covering the roots with robes": according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the original occasion involved a bhikṣu who went out naked and incurred public censure.

The Buddha ordered that he should cover himself with an *antarvāsaka* (inner robe). If one goes out leaving the corpse exposed, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. This refers to those present at the scene.
This is auspicious. The white canopy represents the transformation of the twin śāla trees into white. Its circumference represents the non-manifestation of form.

That four people hold it aloft represents not following heterodox paths. That incense smoke guides the way represents that wholesome karma is like fragrance. That the entire monastery accompanies the procession represents the cultivation of weariness toward impermanence and the encouragement of contemplation.
Second, the explanation of the methods of burial. The headings can be understood as they are stated. Regarding the phrase "up to that point," concerning cremation, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

A bhikṣu was concerned that there might be insects within the body; if he burned it, would he commit the offense of killing? The Buddha said: He does not commit an offense, for when a person dies, the insects also die.
They were buried and discarded in the forest. Regarding "the forest and wilds": when Zhuangzi was about to die, his disciples wished to bury him with great ceremony.
Zhuangzi said, "I shall take heaven and earth as my coffin. Liu Zhi said, "I fear he will be eaten by hawks.
Zhuangzi replied, "Above, he is eaten by crows and hawks; below, he is eaten by ants. To take from one and give to the other makes no difference."
How biased this is! When worldly people employ metaphors, even the noble ones follow suit. How could eminent monks beyond the mundane world permit elaborate funerals?

As for the passage in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* regarding "a bird pecking until the belly bursts," it says: there was a bhikṣu who was ill and possessed some money; fearing that the community of monks would obtain it, [he acted as described].
He then took it and ate it with his soup. After he died, birds came and tore open his intestines to extract the coins.

This passage is cited as evidence for the aforementioned practice of burying [the remains] in a forest. Thus, regarding the "wasted corpse" (can shi) being hired out and passed along—this refers to the method of cremation by estimation (*śar-lha*).

In this region, the application of this method is understood as follows: the doctrine of the single method of cremation is thus established; however, the master was harmed, and the master left behind...

[The term] *guǎn* (骨*宛). When a disciple views [the remains], they cannot bear to do so. If one cannot bear to view them, according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is permissible to hire someone else to perform the task in succession and teach others how to do it.

Regarding the statement "when the fourfold division arrives," as for the five assemblies being permitted to erect stupas, this refers to the six types of stupas mentioned previously in the "Section on Monastic Images.
The *Sòuxuán* cites the *Sūtra of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination*, stating that eight types of stupas possess exposed *lùpán* (dew-dish) ornaments.
The Tathāgata’s stūpa has eight exposed discs (*lu-pán*); those of a Bodhisattva have seven; those of a Pratyekabuddha, six; those of one who has attained the fruit of Arhatship, five;
