those of the third fruit (Anāgāmin), four; those of the second fruit (Sakṛdāgāmin), three; those of the first fruit (Srotāpanna), two; and those of a Wheel-Turning King, as well as of a person who has not yet attained any fruit, have one exposed disc. Now, there is a family mentioned in the records.

Regarding the phrase "from the seventh day after the Buddha’s passing" and so forth: this refers to those who have attained the fruits [of the path] as well as Wheel-Turning Kings who have not yet obtained the *lupan* (the canopy-dish).

They possess only the fire-jewel and the old leaves [as described in the scripture above]. As for "measuring the capacity and the time of decline": if it is a close relative, there is no fault in personally escorting them;

however, if they are not a close relative, one fears it might defile others, and thus it is inappropriate to do so with an impartial mind. (The preceding section, "Attending to the Sick," is hereby concluded.)
The next section, "A General Discernment of Various Essential Practices," is divided into two parts. First, regarding the title "Discerning the Names and Terms of the Twenty-Seven Reaches":

as for the intent of its inclusion, while the preceding sections have already discerned the characteristics of phenomena according to their specific matters, miscellaneous affairs are numerous and their total measure is like the sands of the Ganges.

Therefore, because it would be difficult to understand them clearly without a comprehensive explanation of their modes of activity, this section follows to discern them. As for the explanation of the name, since these matters are not uniform, [the title is given accordingly].

These are called "various trifles. Together they clarify the weighing of mixed movements. That which is indispensable is called "essential" (*yào*). Therefore, that which is relied upon for practice is called "conduct" (*xíng*).

The rest is as explained elsewhere (*yú rú cháng shuō*). There is a marginal note in one edition stating: "Regarding 'this' under the heading 'Manifesting the Name' (*xiǎnmù*), whether it is present or absent, it is acceptable in both cases.

Within the general meaning, the phrase "from the forest to consciousness" (*sēn zhì shí*) is used; "forest" (*sēn*) refers to a multitude. This is because at the time of receiving the precepts, one takes them as a collective object.

Next, the explanation according to the text. Regarding the initial statement from "The Śrāmaṇera" to "twenty-eight": first, the underlying intent.

Although those who have left the household life from the four castes are all called Śākyas, and the five grades of the monastic community are clearly set forth in both the Sūtras and Vinaya, although the preceding sections share commonalities in their subject matter, they have not yet revealed the distinct characteristics of individual practice.
Therefore, following the section on the *Mahāsāṃghika* monks, this section on the *Śrāmaṇera* has been introduced.
Regarding the explanation of the name: *śrāmaṇera* is a Sanskrit term; here it is designated as "Cessation of Affection" (*xīcí*).

Because its practices and applications differ entirely from those of the Great Sangha, it has distinct rules of conduct, as detailed in the standard texts. Regarding the commentary and so forth, the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states:

"*Śrāmaṇera* is a Western [Sanskrit] term; its original sound is *dong-xià*, translated as 'Cessation of Affection' (*xīcí*). Within that commentary, there are also two explanations; the present one refers to "ceasing worldly defilements."
The sentiment of using compassion to rescue the multitude of living beings is the second meaning of the Commentary (*śūtra*). The Commentary states:

"Some say that initially, when one has withdrawn from the mundane world, one is largely motivated by affectionate attachment (*maitrī-ānunaya*); therefore, one ceases minor acts of compassion and instead embraces great pity (*mahā-karuṇā*) to rescue and deliver all beings.
Now, it is said that the defiled sentiments of the world consist largely of affectionate attachment; this means that worldly people possess much compassion, yet they are attached to themselves.

To "rescue all living beings with compassion" means not to discriminate between the near and the distant, but to harbor pity and sympathy for all equally; this is "great compassion. This is the second meaning.
The Commentary states: Some say that ceasing evil and practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the beginning of practice—referring to the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).

Since loving-kindness is foremost among these practices at the outset, and one has now just entered the Buddha-dharma, one must immediately perform this initial practice, which is the practice of loving-kindness.
The section on "Practicing Loving-kindness" (*maitrī*) below explains the reason for this. It means that when one first enters the Buddha-dharma, one often retains worldly sentiments;

This is entirely different from the present case. According to the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang Dynasty, the new term is *śrāmaṇera*, which means "male novice" (*qínsè nán*);

This view—regarding what is not the Path as the Path—is termed "adherence to rules and rituals. It is the assertion that there is no dharma superior to this, and that nothing can surpass it.

It is not the practice of the higher realms; that is to say, while maintaining pure precepts may result in obtaining a celestial body in the desire realm produced by mundane wholesome roots (*vyavakīrṇakuśala*), birth in the higher realms must necessarily be assisted by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Attachment relies upon the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). Only when one is no longer bound to the three realms can one be said to have attained ultimate transcendence of the world.
The treatise states: "If one does not cultivate this samādhi, it is impossible to enter the lineage of the Tathāgata.

The first is form (*rūpa*); the remaining four are name (*nāman*). The twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are all not apart from name and form.
Since the two dharmas of form and mind encompass all phenomena exhaustively, the treatise states: "Among all dharmas, there are only name and form;

if one wishes to contemplate them as they truly are, one contemplates name and form. Based on this, generally speaking, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles alike rely upon name and form. Furthermore...

There is not a single dharma that exists apart from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Form is a gateway to meditation; this refers to the nine contemplations on the impurity of the white bones and so forth.
Mind is a gateway to meditation; this refers to contemplating the impermanence of the mind, which is the return to the source of its grace.

Because those of the Two Vehicles have not yet exhausted the eternally abiding true essence, they cultivate the principle of arising and ceasing. Although the Two Vehicles share the same contemplation, it lacks the [realization of] the Truths and conditions.

As for "distinction," it refers to the fact that while both [the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas] equally contemplate the arising and ceasing of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they do not distinguish between the four noble truths and the twelve links of dependent origination, as the Pratyekabuddhas do.

The *Śāstra* states: "When people of the two vehicles take the characteristics of impermanence and so forth—which are based on the false and illusory—to be True Suchness (*tathatā*), it is because their power is shallow;
they have not yet attained the nature of the original awakening of True Suchness, but merely contemplate impermanence."
The "equal characteristic" is taken as *tathatā* (suchness). Regarding the statement that "wisdom reaches identity," this means that while their meanings are distinct, their substance is identical.

This refers to the fact that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) have no separate substance; they are termed "concentration" from the perspective of immovability and "wisdom" from the perspective of illuminating function.

Both arise as empty manifestations within a single mind; thus it is said that while the phrasing is distinct, the substance is identical. To provide an analogy, it is like a mirror: the substance of the mirror is concentration, while its ability to reflect objects is wisdom.
Samādhi is the image [of wisdom], and although their names differ, their essence is non-dual. Thus, the *Huayan jing shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) states:
"That which is ever-quiescent while illuminating is called samādhi; that which is ever-illuminating while quiescent is called wisdom.

If one speaks of the Mahāyāna precepts as being divided into three categories, this refers to the Threefold Pure Precepts (*tri-saṃvara-śīla*). Therefore, the *Ye shu* (Commentary on Karma) says: "The precepts are divided into three categories; according to their meaning, they encompass all conditions."

They are not different from the various schools. How is this made clear? For example, the single precept against killing encompasses three stages: by ceasing the conditions for killing, one upholds the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint);

by constantly practicing benevolent mindfulness, one upholds the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering virtuous dharmas); and by protecting the lives of others, one upholds the *sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings).
Since this is so for this one precept, it is the same for the others. As for the statement "from restraint (*vinaya*) to the ritual" (*vidhi*), the single precept of restraint—does not...
Regarding the differences from the Śrāvakas: if one considers the first category of the rules of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), they are no different from those of the Śrāvakas.

It is not that there are no differences in the second and third categories; as the *Yeshu* (Commentary on Karma) states: "There are differences between the prohibitions and permissions regarding precious objects.

For example, if a Bodhisattva takes hold of a precious object, it is not an offense, whereas for a Śrāvaka it is an offense. If a Bodhisattva sells liquor, it is a heavy offense, whereas drinking liquor is light; for the Śrāvaka, it is the reverse. There are [such differences].
This is different. The precepts for guarding the mind that exceed ordinary standards refer to those arising from the bodhisattva’s resolve;
one commits an offense even without employing body or speech. This is what exceeds the ordinary standards of the śrāvakas.

Regarding the statement "wisdom reaches the ultimate precepts": this refers to the Bodhisattva of the first stage (*bhūmi*), who attains the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) of *tathatā* (suchness) and realizes a portion of *tathatā*.
This is what is meant by saying that the Bodhisattva dwells in the true reality (*dharmatā*). Although they have attained the true vision, they possess no mind of attainment;

therefore, it is said that they do not attain a single dharma. If this is the case, then even at the very moment of breaking a precept, there is nothing to be broken, for one does not perceive attainment.

[Question: "Does one break the precepts? [Answer: The intended meaning of the response is that because one abides in the *dharmatā* (the true nature of reality), there is nothing further to be accomplished regarding merit;

how much less could one commit further transgressions? This is because both transgression and merit are the *dharmatā*. Since nothing can be attained within the *dharmatā*, how could there be further transgression? Regarding "not performing [acts] on the level of merit," Xuánzàng says:

this does not mean that one does not perform meritorious acts; rather, it means that one does not grasp at signs (*nimitta*). Thus, although there are various causes and conditions, they do not constitute a violation.
Regarding "precepts": this means benefiting others according to their capacities; even though there are various causes and conditions, one does not violate the precepts.

As for the question, "Is it ultimate?", the intention of the questioner is as follows: The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* (*Dichijing*) exhorts one to grasp existence, meaning that one should grasp the existence of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), rather than being sent to grasp emptiness.

The *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* (*Fozangjing*) exhorts one to grasp emptiness, meaning that cessation and annihilation are emptiness, rather than being made to grasp existence. Why are these two statements [contradictory]?

Is this not contradictory? The intended meaning of the answer is as follows: The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* encourages the apprehension of emptiness in order to destroy the attachments of people of that time to existence;

it does not intend to destroy everything indiscriminately. Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "If a person were to utterly annihilate the causal conditions and the specific limits of all phenomena, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth..."
There is absolutely nothing at all. To speak in such a manner is to destroy the world for oneself. The Buddha exists for the sake of the world;
because the Dharma possesses the retribution of good and evil karma, he taught: "It would be better to give rise to the view of a self than to wrongly grasp emptiness. Why is this?
One who gives rise to the view of a self does not slander the true Dharma of all that is knowable, and therefore does not fall into the evil realms on account of it. Evil...
Those who grasp at emptiness in a distorted way destroy the faith of worldly people and deny cause and effect; for this reason, they fall into hell. What is meant by "wrongly grasping emptiness"?
It refers to the view that since both [self and phenomena] are empty, there is no benefit [to be gained from practice]. What is meant by "rightly grasping emptiness"?
It means that when one truly observes existence, it exists because it arises from conditions; when one observes emptiness, it is non-existent because the conditions have ceased.
This is called being non-perverted; it is called correctly grasping emptiness. The *Buddhagarbha-sūtra* exhorts those with views of annihilationism, stating:

"Those who cling to the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and so forth—those who grasp such views shall fall into the evil realms. If one holds the view of annihilationism..."

One will generally attain the Way quickly. Although this may not appear to be a beneficial advantage in the present, in the long run, because one clings less to things and encounters the sages to attain liberation, it is better to give rise to greed than to anger.
This means that greed is light while anger is heavy; thus it is said, "it is better to give rise [to greed].
The reason for specifically severing anger is that the Bodhisattva takes the salvation of sentient beings as his heart's purpose; if he gives rise to anger, he becomes separated from those beings.
Therefore, it is said that this "contravenes birth. Xuán (Xuánzàng) says: The ancient masters all maintain that these are bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
They must retain craving in order to moisten their births, just as a grain seed requires water to be moistened. It is the same for the bodhisattva:

by relying on the water of craving and love to moisten their births, they are able to manifest in accordance with forms within the six realms to transform sentient beings. Once they have ascended to the stages and above, they proceed spontaneously through the power of the ten vows.
They manifest through transformations throughout the worlds of the ten directions to guide the various classes of beings, yet they do not allow themselves to be moistened [by worldly attachments].

For this reason, one might wonder: "Is it permissible to give rise to this greed? If that is so, as for whether or not greed can arise—since it has been said, "It is better to give rise to greed than to give rise to anger"—should greed indeed be allowed to arise?
This refers to greed that constitutes unwholesome conduct; therefore, this question is raised. Below, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Chih-lun) provides the answer.
Just as with the various devas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), if one does not sever desire and evil, one cannot even be reborn there above, let alone attain the noble path (*āryamārga*).

When it says "one who gives rise to greed," this is said in order to rebuke those who give rise to greed; in reality, however, the meaning is as follows: [the text] speaks of "giving rise to greed" in relation to such a person.

Neither of these two [positions] can be maintained. Regarding the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇāni*), the *Abhidharmakośa* states: first, sensual desire; second, ill-will; third, sloth and torpor; fourth, restlessness and remorse; and fifth, doubt.
Since sensual desire is already present among these five, one cannot even attain rebirth in the heavens, let alone become a bodhisattva;
yet you claim that the arousal of desire is permitted. As for the statement that the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* is "inconsistent," this is an appeal to authoritative testimony (*āgama*). A bodhisattva...

One who has attained non-conceptual wisdom refers to a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). Such a person realizes the twofold emptiness of persons and phenomena and attests to the universally pervasive suchness (*sarvatraga-tathatā*).
This essence of suchness is the object realized by wisdom; in its true principle, suchness is devoid of conceptual differentiation.
Because this principle is realized through wisdom, it is designated by way of its object; thus, it is called "attaining non-conceptual wisdom" (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "all objects do not appear": "objects" (*viṣaya*) refers to external domains. This means that when a Bodhisattva attains non-conceptual wisdom, they no longer falsely cling to external objects;
their nature and characteristics are all empty, being merely transformations of the single consciousness.
Therefore, it is said that "no sensory objects (dusts) manifest. Regarding those who possess the practice of killing and so forth:
as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, when the Buddha was the King of the Kingdom of Wu, he saw five hundred Brahmins with false views;

out of compassion for them, he killed them. Furthermore, as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says, King Anantayaśas transformed people through killing and stealing, because there was prior benefit [to be gained] within.

One should practice without defilement or turbidity; to do otherwise is not permissible. Based on these points, it means that as long as one has not realized *tathatā* (suchness), because of the presence of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), there will be defilement and turbidity.
Furthermore, the *Yìzhì sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel) states:

"There are three kinds of persons who can perform transformations contrary to the ordinary course: namely, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats. These persons of the Three Vehicles are undefiled by the world."
Therefore, it is not permitted [to do so] outside of that context, nor before the path, nor during the first three fruits.

As for the statement that "Nirvana is supreme," this refers to the cessation of worldly censure; it refers to the various prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepa-śīla*). Because of the mind that guards the precepts, one would rather die than transgress them;

this is no different from the precepts of natural evil (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). The metaphor of the life-preserving bag (*uḍupa*) represents the five categories of offenses (*pañca-apatti*), while the metaphor of begging for everything represents [the complete observance of the precepts].

The first section: the analogy of begging for half [the body] corresponds to the second category of offenses (*dvitīya-varga*). Begging for one-third corresponds to the *pāyattika* (offenses requiring expiation).

One-quarter corresponds to the *pratideśanīya* (offenses requiring confession), along with the five *dukkaṭa* (or *duṣkṛta*) precepts. These are compared to the minor *rākṣasa* demons; they are likened to the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Regarding the "Immovable Ground" (*acalā-bhūmi*), Xuánzàng says it is the eighth ground (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*). This Bodhisattva relies upon the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-darśana*).
Because its characteristics and functions cannot be moved, it is named "Immovable" (*acala*); this is a name derived from its freedom from faults.

When the *Chao* (the Sub-commentary) says "from the eighth stage and above," it means that the eighth stage is named "Immovable," and "above" refers to the ninth stage and so forth—all of which are included in the phrase "and above."

Alternatively, regarding those at or above the Stage of Pure Mind (*viśuddha-citta-bhūmi*): one interpretation states that, according to the *Asaṅga-śāstra*, the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*) is the Stage of Pure Mind.

Another interpretation states that, according to the *Qinglong*, the Second Ground is the Stage of Pure Mind; this second ground is the Stainless Ground (*vimalā bhūmi*), which is so named because it is free from the stain of breaking the precepts.

"Stain" (*mala*) is what is abandoned, hence it is called "leaving" (*vi-*) [stain]. Thus, being free from stain is itself the Pure Mind. If one has not yet left the stain, then internally there is already...

Regarding "defilement": although there may be external conditions consisting of beneficial things, these are also not permitted. The *Chao* (Commentary) previously followed the principle of the first bhūmi and above, taking the first bhūmi as the state of pure mind.
This means that within this stage, the mind that perceives phenomena is pure and free from all defilements.

The preceding [explanation] regarding the scriptural text refers to being "immovable," while the following refers to the realization of the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*), in the sense of not being subject to defilement. This concerns the first bhūmi.
Thus, one obtains benefit. Furthermore, because there is no defiled or turbid mind, it is said: "If one reaches emptiness. Regarding the "small observation of the emptiness of characteristics":

the wisdom of the observing mind observes the emptiness of the characteristics of the observed object, causing the mind to become immovable, which is concentration. This refers to the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*) of a small Bodhisattva prior to the [first] ground.
During the two stages of *ūṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Summit), one observes the emptiness of the grasped object (*grāhya*). Upon reaching the stage of *kṣānti* (Patience)...
At that time, one turns back to contemplate the emptiness of the grasper (*grāhaka*). Bodhisattvas at this stage cultivate the mind while still bearing mental images;

because they have not yet attained the true nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), it is said that they "slightly contemplate the emptiness of images. Regarding the profound contemplation of consciousness-only:

the contemplating faculty is wisdom (*prajñā*), while the essence of consciousness-only is meditative concentration (*samādhi*). When Great Bodhisattvas—those from the first bhūmi upward—unify with True Suchness (*tathatā*), they attain non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*).
Wisdom is precisely the true nature of consciousness-only; therefore, it is called "profoundly contemplating consciousness-only.
Regarding the phrase "when purely perceiving emptiness, one does not differentiate form," this explains the aforementioned small bodhisattva. This small bodhisattva has dull faculties;

when perceiving emptiness, they are single-mindedly attached to emptiness and do not maintain [the presence of] form. Consequently, they speak of empty quiescence and fail to deliver sentient beings, because having attained emptiness, they do not perceive existence.

Things can be measured; therefore, it is said that one does not discriminate form (*rūpa*). Regarding "skilled knowledge of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) without discriminating emptiness (*śūnyatā*)," this explains the aforementioned great bodhisattva.
It means that this bodhisattva, having cultivated True Suchness (*tathatā*) and attained the contemplation of consciousness-only, simultaneously discards both form and emptiness;

hence, it is said that one does not discriminate emptiness. Although one enters into emptiness, one does not grasp at emptiness as a realization, because one is endowed with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
He constantly delivers sentient beings. Because he is endowed with wisdom, he is unstained by existence (*bhava*); thus, while abiding in emptiness (*śūnyatā*), he constantly transforms beings.
He traverses existence without losing his way in emptiness, never departing from the two truths (*satyadvaya*). The phrase "having reached the limit" serves as a general conclusion.

As for the "resemblance path," this refers to the various non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*), such as Udraka Rāmaputra, who attained the tranquil concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-śūnyatā-samādhi*).
It is for the sake of *nirvāṇa*. This *nirvāṇa* is like the aforementioned Path; it resembles the *nirvāṇa* within the Buddha’s teaching.
As for "resembling goodness," this refers to such things as the five heterodox methods of Devadatta, which resemble the goodness of the Buddha’s Four Reliances (*catuḥpratisaraṇa*).

Furthermore, it includes such practices as non-Buddhists throwing themselves into pits or leaping into fire, observing the precepts of chickens and dogs, or sustaining their lives by eating only rice husks; all of these are instances of resembling goodness.
Thus it is. Previously, this was discussed in terms of the external; now, it is distinguished in terms of the internal.

In the Mahāyāna, upholding the precepts means not perceiving either the one who upholds them or that which is upheld, yet constantly upholding the precepts, cultivating meditative concentration, and practicing wisdom. To blaze forth in constant contemplation, without attainment or realization—this is the truth.

If, however, one perceives both the one who upholds and that which is upheld, yet still constantly upholds the precepts, cultivates meditative concentration, and practices wisdom, [it is not the truth].

That which attains realization is called the "path resembling [the true path]. If one practices giving without dwelling on forms or sounds—even as the sutras state that not giving and so forth constitute it—this is true goodness.
If one practices giving according to worldly sentiment, or exerts effort while clinging to signs, this is called "resembling goodness."
Such matters, though difficult to learn, must be understood. To deviate from them from a young age is itself the work of Māra; this is what is called the "grove of the heterodox.

This is explained extensively in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*. The *Daśabhūmika-śāstra* sets forth the methods for Bodhisattvas to cultivate their body, precepts, mind, and wisdom.
Through extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), one attains wisdom and other virtues; this is recorded in both the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

This is the meaning of the text. For those who cannot achieve sudden realization, the intent is to first teach the observance of the precepts, and thereafter cultivate concentration and practice wisdom—just as one gradually enters deep into the great ocean.
By examining these three matters, one verifies the three paths: taking ordinary beings for oneself as the two vehicles, and including others as bodhisattvas;
by focusing solely on the three matters for the sake of others, one examines the practitioner and thereby recognizes the three paths.
This refers to the limits of the fruits [of practice]. If we discuss how the mind may diverge while the object remains the same, it is like performing a single virtuous deed;
although the deed is identical, the arising of the mind may differ in three ways. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"With inferior wisdom one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination and attains the enlightenment of a śrāvaka; with middling wisdom one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination and attains the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; with superior [wisdom...]"
The wisdom that contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination attains unsurpassed bodhi; in this regard, the objective reality is identical.

However, when viewed from the perspective of the wisdom-mind, they diverge because the fruits are distinct. Furthermore, the section beginning with "Moreover, having known" serves to summarize the essential meaning of the overall framework.
Regarding the second section, "Following the Interpretation Based on the Intent": the phrase "up to 'not yet'" is self-evident.

Regarding the phrase "from the beginning up to the main text," it states that those who do not need to go forth [into homelessness] include those who are only seven years old. The *Jì* (Skt. *Kṣudraka-vastu*) says: "Less than seven years is too young; over seventy is too old.

Even if they possess capability, none of these are permitted under any circumstances. If one has reached seven years of age and can distinguish between good and evil, one should grant them [the going forth]."

Regarding those who have left the household life: if one does not know what is wholesome or unwholesome, they should not be granted ordination. If one is over seventy and too old, ordination is not permitted.
If one has reached seventy and is healthy enough to practice various spiritual disciplines, then ordination is allowed.

If one is under seventy but incapable of performing tasks and requires assistance for rising and reclining, they likewise shall not be ordained. This is why those who are too old are not permitted [to leave the household life].

This means that perhaps due to defecating or urinating, the sense faculties are no longer restrained, one requires assistance for lying down and rising, shortness of breath is constant, and one soils the monastic grounds with mucus and saliva, thereby being rebuked by others.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also states: "In old age, there are three things lacking flavor.
According to the *Chao*, if one over seventy years of age can still cultivate wholesome deeds, their ordination is permitted. Subhadra was one hundred and twenty years old [when he attained the Way].

One may leave the household life. Once one has left the household life, one should not be expelled; this refers to the bestowing of the śrāmaṇera precepts. If the Saṃgha acts thus, they will obtain merit (śubha).
One should not be expelled for losing the characteristics of male or female; "losing the characteristics of male or female" means the loss of the sexual organs.

In the Mahāyāna, there is no reason for anyone not to be accepted, because within the Mahāyāna, one does not discriminate between old and young, or those with dual sexual organs, and so forth; it requires only that one understands the words of the Dharma Master.
They all received and attained the precepts, which are all termed "supremely pure. This clearly indicates that the Hīnayāna does not permit [such acts].
It is like dragging a crooked piece of wood through a dense forest: it is not that the forest cannot accommodate the wood; rather, because the wood itself is crooked and obstructive, it cannot enter.

Although the Mahāyāna says there is nothing that cannot be accommodated, if one's mind is perverse and crooked, it will likewise be difficult for them to harmonize with the teachings and principles. [This applies to those] who wish to burn temples and so forth.
According to the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), fascicle 17, it says: "If there is someone who wishes to seek ordination as a monk, the bhikṣu asks:
'Do your parents permit you to leave the household life? If he answers that they do not permit it, and they do not permit it, one may not grant ordination. If that person says to the bhikṣu:
'If you do not ordain me, I shall set fire to the monastery,' then if such is the case, permitting his ordination does not constitute an offense. (5)

Regarding the "Hundred Questions on Committing Grave Offenses," the *Chao* (Excerpts) commentary states: "This refers to teaching and converting others to cause them to abandon their parents or subject them to forced labor.

This corresponds to the section in the *Śāstra* beginning with "Once they have received ordination," which consists of many passages from the *Śāstra*. If [a person] was previously purchased by the master for money, it constitutes an offense because one damages another's property;
however, if one merely copies [the person] and they were not previously purchased by the master, then ordaining them does not constitute an offense. This is not found in the *Sūtra*.
Regarding the "canonical text" (*zhengwen*): this refers to what is permitted in the treatises (*lun*), whereas the sūtras (*jing*) contain no such explicit text.

According to the *Chujia gongde jing* (Sūtra on the Merit of Leaving Home), it merely states that if one grants slaves permission to leave home, the merit is vast; it does not say that one permits [the ordination of] bhikṣus and so forth. Therefore, it is said that there is no canonical text.
As for the statement that "the arrival of the Saṃgha is likewise," the previously mentioned "suffering matters" are as follows: the *Yesu* (Outline of Karma) says, "Because of the worldly net..."

It is arduous. There is much weariness with seeking pleasure; though one may initially grant permission, later there is much decline and failure. Therefore, among the sūtras and śāstras, those who experience suffering in the present but attain happiness in the future are precisely the renunciants.
Regarding "eating once" (ekāśana): the *Yejie shu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states that within the Buddha's teachings, eating once is the fundamental practice.
The allowance for two meals is based on specific conditions and is not the long-term standard. This has been constantly practiced in the Western Regions (India) down to the present day.
"1. Eating once [a day]. Regarding 'dwelling alone': one tradition says it means living in solitude; another says it means constantly remaining seated.

The *Yejie shu* (Commentary on the Monastic Precepts) states: "Sitting once in the full lotus posture, one only rises after a full cycle of time. Were it not for a profound sense of detachment, how could such a state be achieved? "2. Sleeping once":

among the three periods of the night, one remains seated during two periods and sleeps during one period, and so forth. "Moderate eating" refers to restricting the quantity of food consumed. "Excessive eating" [is the opposite].
This leads to the suffering of illness and so forth. One whose learning is extensive should always employ the wisdom of the mind and not allow it to become superficial or scattered.

Regarding the necessity of requesting [permission] to maintain a community of disciples, Xuán says: "Many do not measure themselves; therefore, when wishing to receive [disciples], one must first request permission from the resident monks for deliberation.

"Possessing virtue as prescribed in the *Pudunfa* (Method for Ordaining Others)" refers to the *Jie Jian-du* (Section on Ordination). There are three virtues required of the two masters; the first is selection (*jian*).

1. Taking the small for the large: this refers to those with ten or more years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*). 2. Distinguishing the ignorant from the wise: this refers to those who are clear and proficient in the Vinaya Piṭaka.

3. Distinguishing the indolent from the diligent: this refers to those capable of diligently providing instruction. If one does not possess these three qualities, they are not permitted [to act as a preceptor].

Some say: "A nun must beg for her own maintenance; why do the monks not see fit to prohibit this? This is because they have not read the authentic Vinaya text, which concludes by prescribing monastic offenses (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*).
Thus, we know that the requirement is the same. Regarding the name "Bird-Scaring" (Kukkuṭa): in the first *nidāna* of the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, there was a bhikṣu who ordained a young boy.
When they entered a village to beg for food, they arrived at a marketplace and would take whatever food they saw. This invited public censure and reproach. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not ordain anyone under twelve years of age" (this is the initial *nidāna*). Later, Ānanda had a donor family.

The family passed away, leaving behind only a young boy. Ānanda felt pity for him and wished to take him in as his own, but fearing he would violate the Buddha’s regulations, he did not dare to do so.
The Buddha asked, "Can this boy drive away crows? He replied, "He can. The Buddha said, "If he can drive away crows, I permit him to leave the household life and become a śrāmaṇera.
Consequently, he was named the Śrāmaṇera Crows-Driving (Kākavācana). This is what it means to be a śrāmaṇera who accords with the Dharma.
This refers to those aged fourteen to nineteen; they are precisely suited to be *śrāmaṇeras*, as they truly accord with the dharma of a *śrāmaṇera*.

As for those who are "merely nominal *śrāmaṇeras,"" since their years have already reached [the age for ordination], they ought to receive the full precepts (*upasampadā*) and thus no longer occupy the rank of a *śrāmaṇera*;

they now merely bear the title of *śrāmaṇera* in name, which is why it is called "nominal. Regarding the *Pañcaśataprśnādi* (The Five Hundred Questions, etc.), that treatise states: "When a bhikṣu was formerly a layperson..."

Regarding property hidden by one's parents or brothers: if, after one has gone forth, all the members of the household die, and the bhikṣu returns to take it for himself, he commits the offense of *pārājika*.
If there are lay relatives who are close to him, he may speak to them and have them take it to perform meritorious deeds; half of it should be given to the government.
Why is this? These items have no owner and should be surrendered to the authorities; they may not be taken in their entirety. Regarding the prohibition on "copying" (or taking by estimation):
because at the time of initial ordination one renounces everything as a whole, these are not one's own property; therefore, to take them now would be equivalent to theft.
This applies equally to debts and interests incurred prior to ordination with one's family, which are likewise judged according to this principle; hence it is said that they are "the same."

Regarding the two procedures for ordination, the titles can be understood from their names. As for the phrase "desiring to reach the second [stage]," it refers to the case of ordaining the son of a craftsman.
The *Vinaya* (Sifen lü), fascicle 34, states: At that time, there was the son of a craftsman who came seeking ordination as a bhikṣu.
The bhikṣus did not inquire carefully and ordained him. Later, his parents came to the Saṃgha and asked, "Is there such a son among you? The monks all replied, "No."
[The monks] saw that he had sought them out on his own and found them, and they consequently criticized him. They reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, if one wishes to have their hair shaved within the Saṃgha, they must inform the entire Saṃgha. If the assembly is not gathered together, they must also go from room to room to announce it;

only after this may they be ordained by shaving their hair. This is so that there may be no error in the questions and answers. The commentary states that this refers to the shaving of the hair and...
Regarding the two masters for receiving the ten precepts: they are the *upādhyāya* and *ācārya* who shave one's hair, as well as the *upādhyāya* and *ācārya* from whom one receives the ten precepts.
Xuán says: "This refers to the *upādhyāya* upon whom one relies for ordination (*pravrajyā*). Following the precedent of the ordination *upādhyāya*, the same applies to the ten-precept *upādhyāya*.
For the Mahāśramaṇera precepts, there shall be one Upādhyāya, or three, with each person acting as an Upādhyāya for one candidate; the same applies to the Ācāryas.
Regarding the ritual procedure, it is said that those who must recite the sūtras should cover the ground and sprinkle it with fragrant water.

It is indicated that the fire hall should face the eastern side of the open space, though facing the western side is also permissible, provided one does not turn one's back toward the Buddha. A perimeter of seven feet should be established, with banners suspended at the four corners.
This is explained as follows: it essentially requires only seven feet of ground. Now it is said that one should take seven feet on each side.
At each of the four corners, place a small bamboo pole, leaving twenty leaves at the top, and encircle them with colored cords.
Open up the front side so as not to obstruct people’s coming and going; all three sides are then bound with small banners attached to the cords.

Hang it up. In the center, set up a low seat for the one intending to leave the household life to sit upon. Also, provide two superior seats for the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the barber to sit upon.
First, instruct the one intending to leave the household life to prostrate before the Buddha. Having finished the prostrations, he shall descend from the hall.
A mat is spread before him where he prostrates to take leave of his parents; even if his parents are elsewhere, he must likewise do so.
One should gaze toward one’s native land and pay homage; thereafter, one recites verses and so forth, as in the text.

If one does not understand how to recite them oneself, it is permissible for someone else to instruct one (and so forth). Regarding the passage stating "having arrived at the sūtra," the treatise says:
when ordaining a śrāmaṇera, the upādhyāya should explain five kinds of dharmas—namely, hair, body hair, nails, teeth, and skin. These five, in combination, together constitute this body.
There is no substantial dharma that causes one to give rise to weary detachment.

The reason this is taught is that there are those who, having practiced this dharma in previous lives, manifest their prior karma as their hair is about to fall out and thereby attain the fruit of Arhatship.

For this reason, it was taught first, as in the case of Rāhula, who attained the fruit of Arhatship before his tonsure was even finished, and so forth. The rest is as in the text. Regarding the phrase "giving and reaching," it refers to the *cūḍā* (topknot).

Regarding this term, Xuán says it is a Sanskrit word; here it is translated as "small tuft" (*xiǎojié*) or "fetal hair" (*tāifà*). This refers to the fact that when young children have their heads shaved, they often leave a small lock of hair on the crown.

As for the "small tuft," it is like the *cūḍā*—the small remainder of hair left on the crown of the head by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) when they have severed [the defilements] of the lower realms or reached the end [of existence], yet still possess a slight residue at the summit of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). This small amount of hair left upon the crowns of these non-Buddhists is intended to signify...
This first stage may not yet be complete; now we shall follow that example as well. Shaving the hair symbolizes the absence of karma pertaining to the three realms;

if there is any remaining [karma] from the upper realms, the *upādhyāya* removes it. How great! Regarding the verse recited below, it says: "The Threefold Bestowal of the Ultimate Aspect," as in the text.
Regarding "from the beginning until the middle": as for "one person not being suitable," this means that one must have one *upādhyāya* and one *ācārya*;
it is not permitted to have only a preceptor (*śīla-ācārya*). To "remotely designate" the *upādhyāya* is what constitutes entry into the Dharma. Regarding "prostrating at the feet of the Saṃgha":

using one’s own noble crown to prostrate at the most humble feet of others expresses the utmost degree of reverence. Regarding "alternating kneeling": since the body is already held upright and inclined, [the practitioner] alternates between kneeling with the right knee on the ground and the left knee on the ground.

To express the utmost reverence, it is logically required that the right knee, the right foot, and the three wheels of the toes leave the ground; bending the upper body forward is the fundamental ritual procedure.
Joining the palms signifies a mind focused and single-minded, free from any other object of perception. As for grasping the corner of the teacher’s robe and so forth:

Xuán yún: The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that when Maudgalyāyana was about to enter meditative concentration to observe his past karma, he ascended into the air and instructed his disciple to grasp the corner of his *kāṣāya*.
Furthermore, the *Vinayamukha-śīla-sūtra* says that one who grasps the corner of the teacher’s robe has not yet attained the status of a formal successor.
If one follows the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it clarifies that Maudgalyāyana was observing his past karma with his disciple and thus had him grasp the robe. If one receives [the precepts]...
"Precepts" here refers to their non-observance. This appears to be the erroneous practice of ancient masters within the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

As for the Vinaya text appearing to be "in the presence of the Saṃgha," it is only in the Vinaya texts that receiving the ten precepts seems to be performed in the presence of the Saṃgha; this is because the Vinaya requires the assembly of the Saṃgha and the performance of the formal announcement (*jñapti*), which gives the appearance of being in the presence of the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, the *Pañcaśata-praśna* states: "It is not appropriate for a single person [to confer them]; thus, it is not 'in the presence of the Saṃgha'."

If one receives the precepts in a separate location, it is not necessary to perform the *jñapti* (single announcement). In principle, one must generate the wholesome roots of the precepts and establish the conditions for the arising of the precepts;

thus, one should inquire regarding the obstacles and impediments (*āvaraṇa*), following the same procedure as the monastic rules (*saṃghadharma*). Xuán states: "According to the bestowal of the śrāmaṇera precepts, it is essential to inquire about the obstacles and impediments.

However, among the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), it is not necessary to inquire about the crime of causing a schism in the Saṃgha; the remaining four must be inquired about. This refers to the second through the third [categories].
Regarding the speaker: in the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā*, this is divided into five parts. First, "Name-so-and-so," which states one's own name. Second, "Taking refuge in the Three Objects.
Third, "Specifically designating that which is emphasized," namely, following the renunciant. Fourth, "The immediate reliance has its source," which refers to the Upādhyāya;

through their mutual inclusion, the Dharma is entrusted and the mind is transmitted. Fifth, "As for the Tathāgata... and so forth, which serves to prevent confusion with other venerable ones, as they are not the same as those regulated by separate sections.
This refers to the master [of the craft]. The concluding passage is self-evident. Regarding the description of the characteristics, it says "reaching the limit of two [units] to manifest":

that which is eight finger-widths or more—that is, six chi or more—is called a "high bed. Generally, there are three bases for this: according to the characteristics, it is eight finger-widths or more;
according to the substance, it is images made of gold, silver, ivory, or horn; and according to the status, it refers to Buddhas, Arhats, and Pratyekabuddhas.

Regarding the Master’s statement, "Both Indic and Chinese designations are manifest": it is simply said that what is produced from color is gold (*suvarṇa*), and what resembles color is silver (*rūpya*).

Since "resembling" refers to an image, we know that "produced image" (*jōzō*) is the Indic term, while "gold and silver" is the Chinese term. Because both appear together in the text, it is called "manifested in two.
As for the phrase "from the four up to the practitioner," this refers to those who have attained the seven branches. The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "According to the treatise on karma..."

Regarding the "substance" (tǐ), it fully receives the seven branches as stated in the Vinaya texts concerning the major and minor precepts, as well as the remaining prohibitory precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-śikṣāpada*). The commentary states:

"The objects of speech are the same as those for the Saṃgha," meaning the two objects of sentient beings and non-sentient things. As for "what matters are not [instances of] upholding [the precepts]," etc., the rest may be understood from the text.

Regarding the phrase "because it arrives next": "one who cherishes and wears the Way"—here, "wearing" (*pèi*) has the sense of carrying or possessing. "One who accords with the Dharma robes"—this refers to both monastics and laypeople.
"To go astray" means to reverse one's outward form and alter one's nature. "To entrust one’s extraordinary body and life" means to prefer death over committing a transgression.
"Neither partiality nor indifference" refers to what the *Lunyu* says: "The gentleman, in relation to the world, is neither partial nor indifferent. The commentary explains: [as follows].
"Thick" refers to density; "thin" refers to sparseness. This is because when a gentleman surveys the world, he perceives neither thickness nor thinness.

The Buddha-dharma is likewise: taking the four seas as one's home, who is there to be treated with partial affection? Therefore, those who seek the Mahāyāna practice the ultimate teaching and provide universal salvation for others.
This virtue, from beginning to end, extends to the five classes of beings; all are worthy of being sustained by it, and it serves as a model for teachers of humans and devas. Thus...
Have them recite and uphold [the precepts] without negligence or laxity regarding their reception of the essence, the physical form, and the robes.
Regarding the "six recollections" that follow, they are as stated in the text. Regarding the "ten enumerations," the term "monks" refers to the listing of names.

The phrase "in accordance with these" clarifies the application of the remedies (*pratipakṣa*). As for the passage from "first" to "therefore": "First, breaking the [practice of] self-starvation heretics" refers to what was mentioned previously.
"All sentient beings abide by relying upon food and drink. By mentioning "drinking the dregs," he distinguishes the characteristics of self-starvation.
The Buddha said: "All sentient beings must rely upon food and drink to abide. Beneath the Bodhi tree, I alone awakened to this one Dharma.
When the non-Buddhists heard this, they laughed heartily and questioned the Tathāgata; it was on this account that he explained the four [nutriments] to them.
One eats food to provision the spirit, thereby attaining the fruit of sainthood. Thus, detachment from attachment is the fundamental principle.

Since you do not now recognize the source of the Way, yet take fasting as the Way, this is not the Way. It is for the sake of counteracting such non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) that the first [of the five] is established.
Second, it is to refute the non-Buddhists who hold to spontaneity (svabhāva); "pointing to the aforementioned name-and-form" refers to these types of non-Buddhists.
If one calculates that everything is entirely without cause—as the Vātsīputrīyas explain the characteristics they grasp—the Buddha says this is not so.
Both internal retribution and external retribution have fundamental causes; therefore, the second name, "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), is established. The five aggregates constitute the body.
Four aggregates—mind and mental factors—are "name," and one aggregate is "form. The mind cannot be seen; it can only be discussed as "name. Thus, it resides in...
During the period in the womb, there are thirty-eight transformations, and after nine months, one is born. Is it possible that such reliance upon the fetal matrix is spontaneous?
Regarding the third [point], those non-Buddhists who hold that the destruction of the Brahmā world is the cause, refer to the aforementioned perceptions of pain and pleasure.

As for "the sovereign Brahmā king and others," this precisely identifies the characteristics of what they conceive. The non-Buddhists maintain that at the time of the formation of the kalpa, Brahmā...

At the very beginning, when humans and beings first appeared, they immediately recognized one another by means of the "foot-measure" (the *vitasti*). Is this not because the Brahma King served as their cause? Now that there is anger and hatred, it likewise arises because of that deity.
The Buddha said, "It is not so," and thus established the perception of "pain and itch. This is based on the texts of the ancient sūtras and śāstras.

"Pain" (*duḥkha*) refers to the sensation of suffering; "itch" (*sukha*) refers to the sensation of pleasure; and "perception" (*saṃjñā*) refers to the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā*). These three are without [external] causes.
[Feeling] arises from that; it does not arise from anything above it. The first moment of mind that takes form as its object is called *vijñāna* (consciousness).
That which discerns defilement and purity is called *saṃjñā* (perception). That which experiences what is disagreeable or agreeable is called *vedanā* (feeling).

Because of the two types of perception, the three feelings arise; because of the three feelings, the three formations arise. Thus, the cycle of rebirth continues endlessly without a time of cessation. 4. Refuting the Absence of Causes.
Regarding "the fruits of non-Buddhists," this refers to the aforementioned Four Noble Truths. As for the analogy of grass and trees, the Buddha said it is not so;

for all phenomena, where there is a cause, there is a fruit. Thus, the Four Truths are taught: the two dharmas of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are mundane cause and effect, while the two truths of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are supramundane cause and effect. Ordinary beings create the causal origin and thereby invite the fruit of suffering.
The Sage cultivates the Path as the cause, thereby realizing the fruit of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). How could this fruit not exist? Question:

What distinguishes these non-Buddhists who deny causality from the aforementioned non-Buddhists who advocate spontaneity (*svabhāva*)? Answer: The former proponents of spontaneity maintain that all things are not created by any agent but exist naturally and inherently.
Those who now deny causality, however, go further by utterly repudiating the existence of both cause and effect. This is the distinction in their respective positions.

There is a distinction. Regarding the "five who refute the divine self" (ātman): this refers to the aforementioned five aggregates (*skandhas*). The passage beginning with "clinging within the body" distinguishes the characteristics of what they conceive.
They assert that there is a "Great Self" (*mahātman*) pervading space, and a "Small Self" (*aṇvātman*) within the body, as minute as a sesame seed or a grain of rice.
This [self] secretly performs all various activities; it is by means of this self that one perceives cold and heat, and knows coming, going, moving, and staying. All of these are due to that self.
The Buddha said it is not so; therefore, he established the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as the remedy for this. As the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Form (*rūpa*) is not self;
feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are likewise not self. Where then am I? Is it within form, or is it within consciousness?

When one calculates that within this body there are only the five aggregates, yet one conceives of a self, then there are five [selves]. Thus, by examining them through their combinations and separations in succession, one searches for [the self] and finds...

I could not find it, and thus I realized my false attachments and attained the principle of non-self, thereby forming a perception free from outflows (*anāsrava-saṃjñā*) that resembled that of a sage.

Regarding the "six [senses] destroying the one consciousness" of the externalist: this refers to the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). As in the passage beginning with "As in a room," this correctly analyzes the characteristics of what they conceive.
They conceive of a single consciousness pervading the six sense-faculties, like a monkey peering through and visiting six windows; yet there is no such consciousness.

Such a person claims that although there are six consciousnesses, in reality they are one; they also claim that while the sense-gates appear to be six, a single consciousness functions through them all.

The Buddha said this is not so. If there were only a single consciousness, how could it hear sounds within the scope of the eye-faculty? Now, the teaching of the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) is given as an antidote to this.

The "seventh" refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) in order to refute those non-Buddhist practitioners who do not cultivate them, thereby turning them back toward the correct path.

The following section correctly elucidates the characteristics of their speculative views. It is said that these non-Buddhists, having attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), observe the past and future in both reverse and direct order for a period of eighty thousand *kalpas* each.
Beyond these eighty thousand *kalpas*, they perceive nothing but a profound darkness; this they call "Darkness as Ultimate Truth" (*tamas-tattva*).

Regarding *nirvāṇa*, they employ the analogy of a ball of thread: all sentient beings remain with hands folded in stillness, moving spontaneously until, when the time arrives, birth and death naturally exhaust themselves.
"One might think that one realizes nirvāṇa for oneself without needing to cultivate the path. The Buddha said this is not so; one must increase one's cultivation through skillful means.

Therefore, the seven factors of enlightenment are established: from the first factor, mindfulness, up to the seventh, the factor of equanimity. These seven factors of enlightenment are explained according to the principles of correct reasoning."

It is said that one must reach [the goal]; how could one obtain the realization of the fruit without practicing? Eighth is "refuting heterodox causes and external paths," which refers to the aforementioned Eightfold Noble Path.
Regarding the phrase "or holding [the view] below," this correctly identifies what they grasp.

They see that when the retribution for chickens, dogs, oxen, and so forth is exhausted, and their distant karma is about to ripen, they will be born in those form-heaven realms; yet they do not know that others [attain birth there] through distant wholesome [karma].

The cause is as follows: [some] mistakenly believe that what they are currently practicing constitutes realization; they take such things as imitating the consumption of impure substances as their precepts, even practicing the eight worldly dhyānas and using them as *nirvāṇa*.
Such is the nature of both wrong effort and wrong wisdom. The Buddha said this is not so; therefore, he established the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
Verbal karma and the other factors serve as the causes for the Noble Path, and by providing sustenance for the spirit, one transcends the mundane world.

The ninth [point] concerns the non-Buddhists who, based on their attachment to the form and formless heavens, falsely reckon them to be *nirvāṇa*. This refers back to the previously mentioned nine abodes of sentient beings.

By means of these two realms, the text correctly analyzes the characteristics of what they falsely reckon. That is to say, the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is at the summit of the form realm, while the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is at the summit of the formless realm. In those two heavens, the cessation of the mind and mental factors is total. Since this is so...

When the mind and its mental concomitants both sink into oblivion and one is unaware of even a coarse state of mind, this is considered by some to be the Great Principle; thus they speak of these two states and call them Nirvana.
The Buddha said, "It is not so. These are merely deluded minds which outsiders do not recognize. As for true Nirvana, it is tranquil, vast, and empty; it does not belong to form or mind.
This [state you describe] is merely where sentient beings of the three realms and nine stages dwell—how can it be called the ultimate?"

Because there are existing phenomena, the nine abodes of sentient beings (*navasattvāvāsāḥ*) are taught as their antidote. (Regarding the "nine": the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments constitute eight;

adding the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti*) to the sequential attainments makes nine. The "ten" refers to those who destroy the views of outsiders regarding form and emptiness; this points back to the ten totalities (*daśakṛtsnāyatanāni*).

Below the section on "outsiders," the characteristics of what they conceive are correctly analyzed. They sever delusions through the six practices, rejoicing in the higher and loathing the lower, and rejoicing in the first [dhyāna].
Regarding meditative contemplation (*dhyāna-vipaśyanā*): one views the desire realm as a festering ulcer, a poisoned arrow, and so forth (using form to break through the existence of desire).

Furthermore, one grows weary of the four *dhyānas* and takes delight in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), regarding emptiness as the ultimate (using emptiness to break through the existence of form). The Buddha said this is not so.

Now, the establishment of the ten bases (*daśāyatana*) is merely the mutual entry of faculties and objects, involving consciousness, perception, and discrimination; it is truly not *nirvāṇa*. As for the extent of application, it is like relying on the first *dhyāna* to perform [meditation].
When practicing the contemplation of blue, one first contemplates the world as a single point of blue that gradually expands until it fills the entire world;
this is the "Samādhi of Blue Pervading All Places. The other colors are treated in the same manner. Subsequently, the visualization recedes back to its original point.

If one attains proficiency, the size [of the visualization] becomes free and spontaneous; all of this arises from the power of mental conception (as it is also the case with the three higher dhyānas). Next, one proceeds gradually toward the upper realms.

Subtle. One does not take form (*rūpa*) as the meditative object (*dhyāna-viṣaya*), such as the four formless attainments (*catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ*). Both emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and form are meditative objects; they cannot be reckoned as *nirvāṇa*.

If one perceives an objective realm (*viṣaya*), it is merely false and delusive. In reality, it is a transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*); therefore, it is said that "in truth, there is only a single consciousness.
The Buddha stated that these ten are all mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*). They are the points of entry for liberation.

Therefore, the ten totalities (daśa-kṛtsnāyatana) are taught; they do not refer to nirvāṇa. The formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is like a great ocean. Those who cannot cross it by means of breadth [are excluded].
For example, if people today wish to cross to the eastern side of the sea, this is a small sea that ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) can cross.

However, if it were the great ocean at the edge of the Iron Ring Mountains (cakravāḍa), then it could not be crossed by ordinary persons. Now, the desire and form realms are like a small sea, while the formless realm is used as a metaphor for the great ocean.
The great ocean may be known. Regarding the phrase "this reaches equality," according to the *Qishi* (Sutra on the Questions of Upāli), one should ask him:
"Who is your preceptor? Who is your teacher? How many precepts does the śrāmaṇera possess? What was his original name?

By questioning in this manner, one employs the "light of the right path" to verify whether a person is heterodox. The remaining text is self-evident. Fourth, the explanation of the characteristics of the precepts.

Regarding the statement "as for the place where the śrāmaṇeras reside," and "naturally [determined] by distance": this refers to the performance of rituals by śrāmaṇeras within the six kinds of natural boundaries (*prakṛti-sīmā*).
This is also modeled after the rules for the *bhikṣu* saṃgha; thus, it concerns the gathering of the śrāmaṇera saṃgha, whether generally or specifically.

Regarding the distinct boundaries for upāsakas as explained in the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*: as previously listed among the seventeen kinds of boundary-establishment (*sīmā-bandha*) in the section on distinguishing separate residences, "distinct" means—
There are cases where one gives to this realm but not to that realm; this is the same as giving to the *saṃgha* realm. Regarding the person to whom [the ritual] is addressed:

the ancient masters said that for a *śrāmaṇera*, the rites of declaring the purity of robes and bowls (*śuddhika*), receiving and maintaining them, the *varṣā* retreat, and so forth, are all performed in the presence of the great *bhikṣu* community.

The present master does not permit this; rather, they are performed only in the presence of other *śrāmaṇeras*. As for "neither being sufficient for both": this refers to the great *bhikṣus* and the *śrāmaṇeras*—neither [is sufficient].

[The rules] are mutually sufficient. How is the ritual procedure performed? If there is absolutely no novice (śrāmaṇera) available, one should perform it through mental recitation alone. Furthermore, this may be applied according to the circumstances; it is also a matter of understanding how to proceed or retreat.
If the senior monks (bhikṣu) are of superior status and there is no one [of equal rank], one must not seek a novice from a lower level, as that would be entirely improper.

However, if there is no one among the assembly who is a novice, and one earnestly requests the senior monks [to act as such], they should also be permitted to do so. Nevertheless, one should always seek those of superior standing.

It is untenable that the inferior [should seek] the superior; however, there is no contradiction in the inferior seeking the superior. Therefore, this explanation exists (as found in the *Pañcaśata-praśna-śāstra*, with half a line added; furthermore, it is opened up in the *Chao*, and now it is said to be "combined").

Next, the explanation of the administration of the Dharma (*dharmagrahaṇa*). Regarding the categories that apply both to the community (*saṃgha*) and to individuals: this means that the category corresponds to the Great Saṃgha;

"community" refers to communal rites (*saṃghadharma*), while "individual" refers to face-to-face procedures (*pratyekamukha*). Thus, the category applies universally. As for the phrase "those who arrive first," it refers to inviting two donors of robes; this refers to the direct and indirect [transmission].
Since within the śrāmaṇera precepts one is not permitted to hold actual [precious items] and so forth, this is exactly the same as for the monks: one must not keep them for oneself.

Furthermore, one must also invite a layperson (*avadātavasana*) to serve as the presiding master. If one commits an offense such as "excess" (*atireka*), it is the same as among the thirty offenses of the Saṃgha; all constitute an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

A *śrāmaṇera* who has not yet received the ten precepts being within the boundary does not constitute a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*). The rest is as stated in the text. Second, regarding the clarification of the communal rules (*saṃghadharma*) through both the general and specific paths:
the headings and listings are clear. As for the statement "if [the rule] applies generally until the point of departure," it is as in the text. As for "if [it is] specific... [the text follows].
