Regarding the statement "the Bhikṣuṇīs reach [the end]," the eight *pārājika* rules for Bhikṣuṇīs have their first four in common with the Bhikṣus; these are not listed again here. It refers to the precept concerning physical contact (*parāmarśana-śīla*).
[Regarding] the term: "To stroke with the hand" is called *mṛṣa-sparśana* (touching). This [rule] is for the purpose of prevention; the precept is that which cures.
Since both the subject (the curer) and the object (that which is cured) are mentioned together, it is said: "[and so forth]. As for the origin (*nidāna*):

When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, there was the nun Thullanandā who had mutual feelings of attachment toward the householder Mahāsubhadda. At the time when the householder prepared a meal and extended an invitation, the time arrived.

The nuns all departed, but the nun Nanda alone did not go. When the elder realized she had not come, he hurried to the monastery and arrived at the nuns' quarters, where he committed an offense by seizing her and feeling her with his hands.
A young novice nun guarding the room witnessed this, and the matter was reported to the Buddha.
Thus, this rule was established. The intent behind the rule is that for those who have left the household life, their conduct must naturally be pure.
Externally, one should maintain a mind free from defilement; yet now, having received a defiled mind from another, one comes into contact with a grave object.

Women are of inferior resolve, and when great evil approaches their peril, the Great Sage established prohibitions to prevent it. The root of the precept consists of six phrases: first, "if a bhikṣuṇī" (the person who commits the offense);
second, "a defiled mind" (in common with a man of defiled mind, clarifying that both possess defiled intent); third, "from below the armpits to above the knees."

The upper bodies touch one another (this clarifies the object of the offense). Fourth, whether she rubs, pulls, strokes upward, strokes downward, lifts up, lowers down, seizes, or presses (this clarifies the characteristics of the offense).

Fifth, the *bhikṣuṇī* pārājika (this clarifies the disciplinary penalty). Next, regarding the explanation in the *Śāstra*: as for the phrase "the six most serious offenses," [the first] refers to the area from the armpit to the back of the wrist;
the former distinguishes the boundaries based on the body as a whole, while the latter distinguishes them among the specific limbs.

Regarding the boundary: if one follows the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, the offense occurs from below the shoulder; this applies across all four divisions [of the Vinaya]. As for "from the wrist onwards," this takes the shoulder of the *Mahīśāsaka* as the boundary.
Why would it be restricted solely to below the armpit? The rest is as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "the nun incurs an offense":

"The Sangha does not inquire whether there was defilement or purity" means that they do not inquire about the nature of the object previously touched—specifically, whether there was a defiled mind or a non-defiled mind—but rather...

If one has a defiled mind and goes to touch [the object], one commits an offense immediately. Regarding the gravity of the offense according to the situation: if the object is grave, the offense is grave; if the object is minor, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Among the cases where there is no offense, it says that "reaching four fingers" constitutes an offense. As for the phrase "the same as in the *Bhikṣu-saṃgha*," the *Caturvargika-vinaya* states:
If one takes or gives [an object] while there is physical contact, there is no offense. If one rescues or protects [the object] due to circumstances of distress, there is no offense in any case.

Even with a defiled mind and so forth, there is no offense. It is not that there is no *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); rather, this is stated in reference to what is not proper conduct (*anācāra*). (And so forth.)
The eight matters constitute the grave precepts (*garuka-śīla*). To explain their nomenclature: the specific acts, such as grasping a robe and so forth, are designated as "eight.

The faults of base and evil conduct are termed "matters" (*vastu*). These are the things to be guarded against (and so forth). Regarding the origin story (*nidāna*): The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the nun Nanda and the householder Śālu-lukala each harbored defiled intentions toward one another. They entered a secluded place together, and even made a mutual appointment to meet.
[The Buddha] rebuked [her], and therefore established this precept. Question: Why does the previous precept constitute an offense as soon as one touches [a man] while circumambulating him?

For what reason does this precept require the completion of the eight directions to constitute an offense? Answer: The former was based on a heavy and thick defiled mind; this refers to a light defiled mind, which requires the completion of the eight directions to constitute an offense.

The root text of the precept has six phrases: (1) the person who commits the offense: "If a bhikṣuṇī... (2) clarifying the defiled mind: "...with a defiled mind... (3) clarifying the knowledge: "...knowing it is defiled... [and so forth].

*Ucchvāsaka-citta* (the four aspects of the manifestation of the offense): If one takes hold of the hand or the robe and enters a secluded place; if they stand together and converse; if they walk together; or if their bodies lean against each other;

or if they make a mutual appointment—these constitute the five points of commission (*pañca-saṃyojana-vadya*). This bhikṣuṇī commits a *pārājika* offense. (Sixth: the administration of punishment) She shall not dwell together [with the Saṅgha].

Next, the commentary (*śāstra*) explains the statement "committing the five [offenses]": this enumerates the conditions. "Committing the seven matters before repentance" means that if one has committed any of the seven [offenses]...
Regarding the matter: having completed the confession of seven *ānantarya* offenses, if one commits an eighth, one still does not incur a grave offense (*pārājika*).
However, if one has committed the previous seven and has not yet repented them, and then continues to commit one more act, the eight becomes complete and one immediately incurs a grave offense.

Regarding the phrase "reaching eight," the commentary states that what follows is the point at which it becomes grave; this refers to distinguishing the specific object. If [the act] occurs after the wrist, one commits a grave offense immediately;

in the case of the preceding precept, a single touch constitutes a grave offense without needing to reach eight. Now, when it says "grasping the hand," this refers to the light offense prior to the wrist.
The same applies to the three matters: (4) standing together in a secluded place, (5) conversing together in a secluded place, and (6) sitting together in a secluded place.
These constitute three matters. Regarding the offense of grasping the hand eight times without it constituting a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*):

this refers to the fact that each of the eight instances—whether occurring before or after—is but a single act among the eight, and thus the gravity has not yet been established. If one man commits these eight acts and so forth, there are four permutations:
the first permutation concerns the person; the second concerns one instance of time; the third concerns eight instances of time; and the fourth concerns eight persons. All of these are...
This is the first category. Regarding "not committing an offense," the statement that one does not reach the point of an offense means that according to the Vinaya:
if there is something given as a gift, or if one performs prostrations, or repents, or receives the Dharma; or if one enters a secluded place to dwell, stand, speak, or walk together with another;

or if a thief or a wild beast approaches and one bends the body to avoid it, such that they lean against each other but no evil deed is committed—in all these cases, there is no offense. If this is so, for what reason [is this said]?

Regarding the offense of *pāyattika* for entering a dark room while alone: the *Tichao* (Commentary on the Vinaya) states generally that this is because there is no purpose [for being there], and so forth.

As for the explanation of the name of the precept regarding concealing another’s grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*): it refers to knowing that another has committed a heavy offense and intentionally hiding it; this is what is prohibited, and so on.
Regarding the缘起 (nidāna): The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. Because of the nun Nanda, who knew that her sister-nun Soṇā had committed a grave offense;
fearing that outsiders might find out, she concealed it and did not report it. Later, when the sister-nun left the monastic life, [Nanda] finally spoke of it to the other nuns.

The nuns raised the matter as a transgression, and based on this, the precept was established. The intent of the establishment is that those who have left the household life cultivate pure conduct together; seeing another...
There is an offense. It is logically appropriate to bring it forth [for confession]. At first there was an intention to conceal; later one finally spoke of it. This is an extreme transgression.

Therefore, the Sage established the seven clauses of the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra: (1) the person who commits the offense; (2) "if a bhikṣuṇī"; (3) "knowing" that a bhikṣuṇī has committed a *pārājika* offense;
(4) "with a clear mind knowing" yet not revealing it herself, not telling others, and not informing the assembly; (5) "if she has an intention to conceal"; and so forth.
At another time, that bhikṣuṇī may die, or be suspended, or leave the monastic life, or join the ranks of non-Buddhists (due to the five causes, etc.).
Later, she says: "I previously knew that there was such and such an offense" (the sixth point clarifying the one who commits it).

This bhikṣuṇī is guilty of a pārājika offense (the seventh point regarding disciplinary punishment) and shall not dwell together [with the Saṃgha]. Next, the *Chao* commentary explains: "The sixth, 'committing upon reaching,' lists the conditions."

Furthermore, regarding those who have committed two of the four *pārājika* offenses: according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, if a nun conceals seven *pārājika* offenses, she incurs only a *sthūlātyaya*;

however, if she conceals the offense of sexual misconduct (*maithuna-pārājika*), she incurs a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*). This is not the case here. Regarding the phrase "forming the intention to conceal":

this refers to the mind that conceals the grave offenses of others. If one commits a grave offense oneself and conceals it oneself, there is only a *duṣkṛta*. As for the words "if it reaches... [the text continues].

As in the section on the confession of offenses (*pāpadeśanā*). As in the section on the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* [offenses]: if one has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and there is no one to whom it can be disclosed, this is not termed "concealment.
There are eight kinds that do not constitute concealment, as explained therein. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:

if a nun is subject to formal suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), etc.—this refers to a case where, having learned of another nun’s offense, she herself undergoes suspension before the offense has been confessed or concealed, or if she is insane, and so forth—all such cases are likewise [not concealment].
It does not constitute concealment, because it is insufficient to be counted as such. What is thus produced is likewise not considered an act of production.

The rest of the text is as explained there. Regarding "associated with the mind of relinquishment": this refers to the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*). One relinquishes the offenses previously committed by another;

even while further taking those offenses as an object, one does not form the intention to conceal them. By thus obtaining the relinquishment of the previous two states of mind, one who is associated in this way commits no offense.
Another interpretation is as follows: it is called "equanimity" (*upekṣā*) because one merely fears the two difficulties [of concealment and confession] and has no feelings of attachment or aversion.

Regarding the statement that "an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*) also does not constitute an offense": this means that if, with respect to another person, one does not form the intention to conceal while in an indeterminate state of mind, then there is no offense.
However, if one intends to conceal, even if one is in an indeterminate state such as sleep, it still constitutes the act of concealment; this is the description of the characteristics provided below.

Regarding the statement "if it reaches the point of regret, it is not established": this means that within the boundary (*sīmā*), there is no person who is pure. Even if one does not speak of the allowance, there is no offense;
however, this refers to one who is not pure—that is, the person against whom one confesses. If one confesses before someone who already knows [of the transgression], both parties are at fault.
The *Shoushu* (Commentary on the Essentials) states: "If one wishes to reveal [the offense], one must seek out someone whose purity is unknown and confess before them; thus it is established. If...
Regarding the "Prophetess" (Pravrajitā): both positions entail faults, as it is called *śrāvaṇī* (one who makes heard), and thus [the offense] is not established.
This characteristic is somewhat difficult to understand; I shall now explain it by citing a concrete example. Suppose the nun Zhang commits a grave offense (*pārājika*).

Then the nun Wang commits an offense identical to that of Zhang and conceals it for her, not disclosing it to others. Later, there is the nun Li, who also knows that Zhang has committed a grave offense, and she then informs the nun Wang.

Regarding the disclosure [of an offense] in the presence [of another]: it is not accomplished. For this reason, since a *pārājikā* nun who already knew beforehand that another was concealing an offense is herself a sinner, she may no longer receive the disclosure of an offense from another; both parties would possess faults, and each must disclose their own offense.

Therefore, it is not established. Regarding "the opposite of the above is not applicable": if one does not know the name of the nun who committed the offense, the category of the offense, its characteristics, and so forth, there is no offense;
hence it is said that "the opposite of the above is not applicable. Regarding "if the person ahead has already finished receiving [the confession]":

one should speak to a single person and then stop. Regarding "there is no fault of infinite regress": according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, this refers to not having the intention to disclose [the offense]. And...
One merely speaks to another, and that person in turn speaks to yet another, continuing thus infinitely; yet even by speaking, one cannot avoid concealment.
Therefore, that text states: "If a bhikṣuṇī commits a grave offense, she should confess it to others. If a co-resident disciple or a dependent disciple commits a grave offense, the teacher thinks:
'If I were to speak of this to others, the Saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs will surely expel her,' out of affection."
Therefore, by concealing another's offense, one incurs a grave offense for oneself. This nun further told other nuns that so-and-so had committed a grave offense.
Upon hearing this, those nuns thought: "If I report it, both of us will be expelled. Thus, they concealed it entirely; both committed a *pārājika* offense.
This applies even up to a hundred thousand people—all would incur a grave offense. Therefore, it is known that if one lacks the intention to confess and reveal [the fault], [the offense remains].
Although one may speak of it verbally, one cannot avoid committing an offense. Regarding those who have no fundamental fault:

for example, if a nun knows that another has committed an offense but conceals it with the intention of covering it up, she does not commit an offense herself; yet, because the original act has already been manifested, she must disclose it as soon as possible.

As for what is called "extremely grave" in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is as stated in the text. What constitutes a non-offense can be understood from this. Regarding the eight grave offenses (*aṣṭau pārājikāḥ*)—
Regarding the latter four precepts among these eight: the *Shan-chao* (Commentary) explains only the first three. As for the fourth precept, it was rarely used at that time;

therefore, it is omitted here. Nevertheless, its general meaning may be briefly stated: it concerns a *bhikṣu* who has been formally charged by the Saṃgha, and a *bhikṣuṇī* who must rely upon and comply with the Eight Rules of Respect (*gurudharma*).
This refers specifically to the case of a bhikṣu; because he has already been formally censured by the Saṃgha and yet refuses to accept the threefold admonition, he commits an offense.

It is said that there are two kinds of compliance: first, compliance regarding food; second, compliance regarding both food and clothing. Question: If one complies with a bhikṣu who has been subject to formal censure, an admonition must immediately be administered.

If one complies with a bhikṣuṇī who has been subject to formal censure, does the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha likewise administer an admonition? Answer: If one complies with a bhikṣu who has been subject to formal censure by the Great Saṃgha, an admonition is indeed required. If [one complies] with...
Regarding a nun who complies with one who has been formally charged: there is no need for admonition. If that is so, why are those who likewise comply not treated the same way? The answer is:

the Buddha ordained that nuns must show respect toward the Great Sangha (the monks). Because [in the case of the former] there is a risk of confusion, admonition is required. Since nuns are of the same class [as the monk who charged her], there is no such confusion; therefore, admonition is not required.

Regarding the phrase "among the seventeen saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses": of these seventeen precepts, nine constitute offenses upon the first commission, while eight become offenses after a third admonition.

Among the nine, the first two refer to acting as a matchmaker and the two types of slander. Among the eight, the first four are schism, assisting in a schism, corrupting families, and being of evil character;
these seven are the same as those for the monks. Furthermore, there are ten precepts that differ [from the monks]: first, speaking of a person; second, following a female thief.
Three: repeatedly engaging in sexual intercourse. Four: being alone with a woman. Five: accepting food or clothing from one with a defiled mind. Six: instructing another to accept such things. Seven:

personally associating and dwelling [with such a person]. Eight: encouraging another to associate [with them]. Nine: abandoning the Triple Gem out of anger. Ten: instigating the four types of disputes.

Of these, the first six constitute offenses upon the initial transgression; the latter four constitute offenses after three admonitions have been violated. In this text, the two regarding matchmaking and the two regarding slander are briefly indicated as being identical to those in the section for the Great Bhikṣus.
These were prevalent in the world at that time; therefore, they have been briefly pointed out. As for the four [offenses] such as schism (*saṃghabheda*), they were not practiced during that period;

thus, only their general outlines have been cited, and they have not been specifically identified. Within the latter seventeen [offenses], only the four regarding persons (*pudgala*) are explicitly clarified.

This is because these were current practices of the time, and their specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) were difficult to discern. By contrast, this highlights that the characteristics of the remaining eight types of offenses were easy to understand, and that they were likewise not practiced during that period.

This is not explained in detail. Regarding the "precepts for persons" (*pudgala-śīla*): as for the explanation of the name, because one uses the hand to record various official matters, they are called "persons.
This refers to that which is to be guarded against, and so forth. There are two origins [for this rule]. First, when the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, there was a nun residing in a certain place.
A lay devotee built a small monastery for a nun and offered it to her. Later, the nun abandoned it and departed. Subsequently, the lay devotee died. His son then began to plow this land with a spell.
When the nun returned, she forbade him from plowing it, but he would not accept her words. The nun then went to the authorities to speak on his behalf.
The officials fined the layman’s son, and his property was confiscated by the state. He was thus subjected to the ridicule and censure of the common people. (2)
Due to the junior wife of King Prasenajit, she constructed a small vihāra and offered it to the bhikṣuṇīs.
Later, the bhikṣuṇīs went on a journey through the human world and did not return for a long time. The junior wife then gave the vihāra to the daughter of a brahmin.

When the bhikṣuṇīs returned and inquired about it, the brahmin’s daughter said, "The donor gave this to me. The bhikṣuṇīs then went to the authorities to speak of the matter, and the officials questioned the bhikṣuṇīs.
He asked, "What was the matter? The nun did not understand the principle and answered falsely, saying, "The ground belongs to the King, but the site belongs to the donor.
The adjudicator said, "Since the site belongs to the donor, and the donor has already given it to her, why seek anything further now?

He then ruled that it be given to the Brahmin girl. The nuns reported this again to the Buddha. The Buddha said to the King, "It should be returned to the nuns; this was originally given as a gift to them. Later...

Regarding those who do not give [alms]: the King, relying on the Buddha’s words, instead grants [the property] back [to the recipient], punishes the judicial officer, and has the money and goods enter the royal treasury, thereby incurring public reproach;
it is for this reason that the rule was established. The intent of the rule is as follows: those who have left the household life should maintain the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).

Now, if one internally gives rise to unwholesome thoughts and goes among the laity to speak ill of others, one deeply violates compassion; it is for this reason that the rule was established. The root of the precept consists of three phrases: (1) the person who commits the offense... if...

Regarding the Bhikṣuṇī (the second clarification of the characteristics of karma): if a secular official addresses her as "householder" (*gṛhapati*), or if she addresses the son of a householder, or a slave, or a hired laborer, whether by day or by night, for even the duration of a single thought-moment, or the snapping of a finger, or a brief interval, this Bhikṣuṇī commits the first *pārājika* offense (the three dharmas of defeat).
Below [this], the *Śāstra* (Commentary) will be explained in sequence.
Regarding the statement "from the four [offenses] up to *ānantarya*": if a judicial official has prepared a preliminary draft of the verdict, *Souxuan* says:

"In the Western Regions (India), there are separate judicial officials who function similarly to the judicial officers (*sifa*) and the Grand Master of the Court of Judicial Review (*daliguan*) here in this land; they are not distinct from one another. This explanation is given according to the conventions of this region."
"Simply following the case wherever it goes through official channels" refers to documents such as written petitions and the like; "speaking orally" means not recording it in writing.

If one's property has been seized and one petitions the authorities for protection—meaning that a nun, being weak, has had her goods plundered by bandits, and the authorities personally investigate and pursue the matter until the thieves are caught and the nun’s original property is returned—then the nun does not commit an offense. This also applies if someone enters a monastery and so forth.

Regarding this, the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Views) states: "One must not seize a knife or axe, nor damage them. Even if they are damaged, one should calculate their value and return the price. If one does not return it, one commits an offense according to the amount of the calculated value.

As for "other persons," these are those who do not adjudicate legal cases; they incur only a *duṣkṛta* (light offense). Regarding the four rules concerning solitary conduct (*catur-ekākinī-śikṣāpada*):

as for the explanation of the names, there are four because of distinctions such as traveling or staying overnight. To be without a companion to provide mutual assistance is to be "solitary" (*eka*). This is...
Regarding "that which is prevented" and so forth: as for the *nidāna* (circumstantial origin), it concerns the first instance of crossing a river alone.
While the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the nun Gopā crossed a river with her robes hitched up; upon reaching the bank, she was harassed by bandits. Regarding the *nidāna* of entering a village alone:

while the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the nun Cāmā left the monastery without informing anyone; on a minor pretext, she entered a village alone and incurred public censure. Regarding the *nidāna* of staying overnight alone: [text continues].

The nun reported the transgression, and it was eventually brought to the Buddha’s attention. It was on this account that the rule was established. The intent of the regulation is as follows: nuns are women of weak constitution; entering secular society invites public censure.
To travel without a companion provides an opportunity for harassment and defilement. Because such faults are numerous, the Sage established this precept. The three phrases of the core precept are:

(1) the person who commits the offense—namely, a bhikṣuṇī; (2) the characteristics of the offense: crossing water alone, entering a village alone, staying overnight alone, or traveling behind [a man] alone.

It should be understood that for the first offense, one must relinquish [the robe] (this constitutes an offense involving three factors). Regarding the phrase "because of going alone," this distinguishes the prohibition against crossing a river alone.
Now, according to the precepts for traveling on the road, the *Dharmaguptaka Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya* merely states that one may not cross alone;

furthermore, within the conditions for the offense, it is said in both cases that it depends on the depth, such as crossing together while raising one's robes high, yet it does not specify the width, the depth, or the division by age.

The Commentary follows the *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* on the Precepts for Practicing the Path (*Daoxing jiewen*). It states that if one must walk [through water], one must lift one’s robes and remove one’s shoes and socks;
to act otherwise than the decorum prescribed for land constitutes an offense. Regarding the previous nun who entered the water hastily, according to the Vinaya text there are two stages:

first, when the previous nun enters the water herself but has not yet crossed over, she incurs only a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense); once she has just stepped onto the bank and is separated from the water by it, she incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting of the community). As for the subsequent nun who enters...
[The nun] steals [to the bank] and steps onto shore. She may take the preceding nun as her companion without offense (this is the scriptural text). Now, according to the intent of the text:

it means that the preceding nun first steps onto shore while the succeeding nun has not yet entered the water; only after the preceding nun has finished stepping onto shore does the succeeding nun enter the water.

This results in such an offense. Regarding the second section of the text: if the first nun enters the water first and the second nun has not yet entered, the first nun commits a *thullaccaya* (sthūlātyaya).
If the first nun has not yet stepped out of the water and the second nun has already entered, the second nun does not commit an offense.

If the first nun does not wait for the second nun and steps out of the water first, she commits a *thullaccaya*. If the second nun steps out of the water [afterward], she does not commit an offense (as stated in the Vinaya text). Based on this precedent...

A nun incurs two *pācittiya* offenses: namely, when she enters the water first and when she comes ashore first, because in both cases there is no interval [with another nun]. As for the case where the subsequent nun commits no offense:

this refers to when the subsequent nun obtains the preceding nun as her companion at the time of first entering the water, and again obtains the preceding nun as her companion at the time of coming ashore;
therefore, neither commits an offense, though it is only the preceding nun who has the fault. Thus the Vinaya says: "Enter the water quickly."
Upon reaching the shore, one should not wait for companions to arrive; rather, one should enter the water at the appropriate time and reach the shore all at once, so that no fault is incurred.
Regarding "lifting the robe according to the depth or shallowness [of the water]": in previous circumstances, it was precisely because the robe was lifted too high that one encountered harassment.
Now, if one adjusts the robe according to the level of the water so as not to expose the body, and puts on the undergarment upon reaching the shore, there is no offense.
Regarding the fourth case of crossing the river alone: if one violates [the rule], a question arises as to whether this might be confused with the second precedent mentioned previously.

The answer is that while they appear to be confused at first glance, upon examining the essential meaning, this is not so. In the second precedent, the intention was formed to cross alone; although he entered the water, he had not yet stepped onto the bank.
In the fourth precedent, he had already crossed the water and completed the act of stepping onto the bank. As the commentary below explains: "This refers to when the companion is separated..."

"Water" constitutes an offense immediately. Regarding the statement "entering alone incurs an offense," this distinguishes the act of entering a village alone. The initial conditions consist of two parts: first, the formal definition of the characteristics;

second, from the section on the *Caturvarga*, the distinction of traveling alone. As for the phrase "without distinguishing between within or outside the boundary," the "boundary" (*sīmā*) refers to a *kṛta-sīmā* (a boundary established by ritual action), whereas the "monastery grounds" (*ārāma*) are a *prakṛti-sīmā* (a natural boundary).
Since the Vinaya simply states "going to a village," there is a concern that people might insist it must necessarily be within a formal boundary.
Outside the monastery walls, only when one reaches a householder’s residence is it properly called a "village"; hence there is this explanation. To provide an example:
entering a village at an improper time, or quarreling within the monastery grounds, constitutes an offense (and so forth). Regarding the offense of a solitary walk within a ward (*fang*):

if we consider the local custom of this land, walking alone—separated from one's companions—within the same ward or alleyway, or within the same large household compound, constitutes only a *duṣkṛta* (light) offense.
It is a *duṣkṛta* offense. Furthermore, it is also a *duṣkṛta* offense if two nuns are together within the same household;

for instance, while one nun is sitting in front of the hall, the second nun wanders alone toward another's upper room, the lower section, the kitchen, and so forth. This is because they are within the same household.
There is no offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when one arrives at the boundary of a village or city, one must remain within arm’s reach of another person.

If one is beyond arm’s reach, passing with one foot constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), and with two feet constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If one person stands between them, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
This refers to the boundaries of two cities, or two provinces and two counties, or the boundaries of two villages east and west, or various wards.
This refers to the "street-boundary" (*vīthi-sīmā*). Citing this text as proof: if one travels alone across four quarters of a single boundary, it constitutes an obstruction within [the precincts].

Or, it may refer to the interior of a single household; if one crosses beyond this boundary, one incurs the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. "Having no cause" means having no circumstances involving the two types of hardships (the dangers of life or limb).

Alternatively, it may mean having no circumstance where one’s companion has passed away. Regarding "whenever there is a cross-road," traditionally this has mostly been interpreted in relation to that...
A transverse road constitutes a boundary. When one wishes to enter a village gate and crosses this transverse road, it is called "crossing the boundary," and for this reason, an offense is committed.

Regarding those schools that have no textual record [of this rule], the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*) rejects them as impermissible. According to the Vinaya, when traveling alone in an area without a formal boundary, an offense is incurred upon being heard or seen by others after one *gǔshēng* (a single beat of a drum) has passed since leaving one's companions.
Within this interval of one *gǔshēng*, how could there not be transverse roads? Why was an offense never prescribed for such cases? All [rules] are based on...
The village threshold serves as the boundary. If there is already a nun within the village who does not commit an offense, this is also based on being within range of sight or hearing.

If one travels alone beyond the range of sight or hearing within a single precinct, it is likewise an offense of *duṣkṛta*. Regarding the phrase "staying alone until dawn," this distinguishes the act of staying alone.
"In two places, both lay and monastic" refers to either staying in a lay residence or within one's own monastery. Arrangement [of bedding]...

Beds must not be placed side-by-side; unless there is a specific reason for illness, one must not extend one’s hand beyond the edge of the bed. Furthermore, two people are not permitted to lie on the same bed;

each person should lie according to their own side of the bedding, lifting it individually. Likewise, they are not permitted to share the same covers or bedding, nor are they permitted to join two beds together as is done with double beds in lay households.
Beds should be arranged at right angles or in a "T" shape. This applies equally to mosquito nets and curtains. There is [a rule] regarding this.
People say that one should quickly prepare a long bed, similar to those found in modern meditation halls; this is not correct.
One must tie each section of the bedding as it is laid out. If the length is insufficient, there will be a gap at every turn, and the same applies when rising and lying down again.
Regarding the phrase "going alone to a fragrant grove" (*làn*), it distinguishes the act of traveling alone. Xuán says: The *Chāo* (Commentary) cites three conditions: first, traveling on a road;
second, descending midway into a place where one is seen or heard by companions; third, descending again with companions based on the absence of such conditions.
As for "traveling alone behind," if one follows the cited conditions, traveling alone in front also constitutes an offense; this refers to traveling together on a road. Or...
Regarding "departing alone from the base": this refers to departing alone from one's place of residence, regardless of the path taken.

Furthermore, regarding "having no difficulties or adverse conditions with a companion," the Vinaya states: if a single bhikṣuṇī goes out to relieve herself of excrement or urine, or if she dies, or is carried off by bandits, or is swept away by water, there is no offense.
However, if none of these circumstances apply and she travels behind [another], she must simply...

If one departs from the range of sight or hearing, one commits an offense immediately. Next, regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: as for "not reaching the point of an offense," this refers to various miscellaneous difficulties that prevent one from keeping company.

The Vinaya states: "If there is danger from life-threatening threats, non-human beings, wild beasts, or if one is forcibly carried away, captured and bound, swept away by water, and so forth—these are the various miscellaneous difficulties.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, in places where one fears men, the rule against sleeping alone is waived.

In a place where there are many men, because there is the fear of being assailed, solitary lodging is permitted as a means of avoidance. Now, regarding the citation from the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* which clarifies that it is permitted when crossing shallow water:

this refers to cases where the water is so shallow that there is no fault of having to lift one's robes; furthermore, since the entire bank consists of nuns and there are no men to be feared, it is therefore appropriate to permit it.
As for the "four conditions" mentioned in the preceding section on the full requirements, the third is "absence [of men]."

The *nidāna* (circumstances). Now, simply reversing this constitutes non-offense. The remainder of the text may be understood in detail (*wei*). [The term] "lazy and retreating" (*xie-tui*) describes a state of accidental indolence.
Regarding the precept on spinning and weaving among the ninety single *pācittiya* rules: first, the definition of the name can be understood. As for the origin (*nidāna*):

when the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the group of six nuns spun thread themselves. Laypeople criticized and disparaged them, and so forth. The core of the precept consists of three phrases: (1) the person who commits the offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī (second, clarifying the nature of the offense) spins thread with her own hands (third, defining the offense), it is a pāyattika. [End of] one section from the *Shichao*.
As stated in the text: it is improper to wear robes that have been completed without performing the ritual of confession (*pratideśanā*), in order to sever the cause for future transgressions.

Regarding the phrase "the rest up to [the section on] oneself," this refers to the precepts from the upper category down to the lower. From the *pārājika* (defeats) down to the *thullaccaya* (grave offenses), there are no instances where they lack a specific characteristic;

however, because they were not practiced at that time, they are omitted here and not described. The *pārājika* rules are expanded according to the *bhikṣu-prātimokṣa*, while among the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meetings) and the one hundred and seven *pāyattika* (offenses requiring expiation) rules, [the same applies].
Regarding the nineteen precepts: this section clarifies only one hundred and fourteen of them. Those that follow which differ from those for the great bhikṣus are not explained here;
they are omitted because they are rarely used.
Regarding the seven points concerning the mutual inclusion of teachers and disciples within various practices:

as for the statement that a *bhikṣuṇī* who has reached the middle [of her life] ordains many who are unrighteous—this refers to women who are pregnant and give birth after receiving the precepts, or those who are female thieves and the like. In such cases, one should seek permission for half [the assembly].

If more than half [of the required number] perform the ritual, it means that when the *bhikṣuṇīs* receive the precepts, if the *bhikṣuṇī* Saṃgha is too small and cannot be obtained, one may have a pure person [perform it].

Within a group of ten people, if only five maintain the precepts, yet those exceeding five maintain pure precepts—provided that even those who slightly violate the rules of decorum (*āyatanas*) are not impure in their observance—the legal procedure may still be accomplished.
The *Chao* (the Sub-commentary) adds its own note: "Those who do not commit grave offenses (*pārājika*) may preside over the legal proceedings."

As for the remaining [offenses] that may be counted as "acceptable" (*kaku-kaku*): one may be sufficiently proficient in clarifying the characteristics of the teachings and sufficiently diligent in guarding the practice of the precepts;
hence they are called "acceptable. The reason for this is that these offenses pertain to a time before the full ordination (*mahāśramaṇa-saṃvara*) has been conferred.

Since the essence of the full ordination is obtained through the words of the Great Sangha, these cases are thus exempted. They do not constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense in the same manner as those committed by the Great Sangha. To claim otherwise would be a usurpation.
It should not be the teacher’s virtue [that is blamed]. The rest is as in the text. Regarding the sequence leading to the section on the mind (*citta*):

according to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it was in the fourteenth year after the Buddha attained enlightenment that women first began to develop the aspiration for renunciation and leave the household life.

Furthermore, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya Bhikṣuṇī-karmavācanā*, when Mahāprajāpatī requested permission to leave the household life, the Buddha refused her. At that time, Mahāprajāpatī and five hundred Śākya women then shaved their own heads.
[Her] hair [was still hanging down as she] leaned against the gate of the Jetavana. Ānanda presented her with the three requests, and so forth (*etc.*).
From afar, the Buddha proclaimed the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*). Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī heard them and received them all together with reverence and upheld them;

the five hundred Śākya women likewise accepted the Eight Rules of Respect (the above is as stated in the text). According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, however, only Mahāprajāpatī alone obtained the precepts; these were the words of the Eight Rules of Respect.

Next, the other women took Ānanda as their preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and received the full ordination through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) within the assembly of bhikṣus;
thus, eleven persons constituted the quorum for their reception. Therefore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī sought to leave the household life with the Buddha.

After Ānanda had petitioned three times, the Buddha proclaimed the Eight Weighty Rules (*gurudharma*). Mahāprajāpatī accepted them upon her head and did not dare to violate them in the slightest. Once she had obtained the precepts, then..."
She said to Ānanda, "Please speak again on my behalf to the Buddha: 'I have already accepted the eight rules; within them, I further request one boon.

I pray that you will allow bhikṣuṇīs to pay homage to bhikṣus according to the seniority of their ordination years (*varṣāgra*). How could it be right for a bhikṣuṇī who is a hundred years old [to not pay homage to a junior bhikṣu]? "
He prostrated at the feet of the newly ordained bhikṣu. Ānanda did the same for Āmrapālī. He addressed the Buddha a second time. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"It is impossible within my Dharma that nuns should be permitted to pay formal respects to monks in the prescribed order.
For this reason, it is taught that the female body has obstacles: first, one cannot become Śakra; second, one is not permitted to become a Brahmā King; third, one is not permitted to become..."
A Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) cannot become a Māra-king; fourth, he cannot become a Buddha; fifth, he may not ordain women as nuns and grant them the precepts.
The True Dharma of the Buddha shall remain in the world for a thousand years; now that she has been ordained, five hundred years have already been diminished.
It is like a household where there are few men and many women: that family will surely fall into ruin quickly. Furthermore, within my Dharma, if [this were not permitted]...
Women, after my parinirvāṇa, the upāsakas shall provide the four requisites as offerings and follow behind the bhikṣus, saying to them:
"Please accept our offerings. If a layperson sees a bhikṣu upon leaving their house, they shall take him by the arm and lead him home, saying:
"Venerable One, you have been kind to me; please deign to visit my home and sit there, so that I may find peace. If...

Once, while a bhikṣu was traveling on the road, he encountered dust and mud. A layperson untied his hair, brushed away the dust, and spread out the mud so that the bhikṣu could step upon it and pass by.
Now, having transmitted the precepts to people as described above, all such matters have been almost entirely exhausted.

Having heard this, Ānanda felt sorrow and regret at having crossed the stream [of ignorance], and said to the Buddha: "Why did you not tell me earlier? Had I known in advance, I would not have dared [to do so]."
He made his request three times. The Buddha told Ānanda, "Do not weep any longer. It was merely that Māra had corrupted your mind.

Now that he has already been delivered, has left the household life, and received the precepts, simply ensure that he follows my regulations and does not transgress them. The True Dharma shall be restored for another thousand years.

The remainder is as found in the *Jianmu lun* (Treatise on Seeing the Mother) and the *Er lun* (Two Treatises). Fearing prolixity, I shall not describe it at length here. As for the statement regarding the listing of their names, it refers to:
These are the specific names for the eight teachings. If one follows the respective sections [of the Vinaya], they are called the "Eight Unsurpassable Dharmas" (*aṣṭāv-anatikrama-dharmāḥ*).

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* calls them the "Eight Untransgressable Dharmas. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* (or *Daśabhāṇaka-vinaya*) and the *Samantapāsādikā* call them the "Eight Respectful Dharmas" (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*).

The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* calls them the "Eight Dharmas of the Teacher," while the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* calls them the "Eight Dharmas of the Venerable Teacher. The present term "Eight Reverences" (*aṣṭau gaurava-dharmāḥ*) is based on the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. Regarding this, the *Baoyun* states: "Within these..."

This is divided into two parts: first, the intention behind the precept; second, the explanation of its name. Regarding the first: in principle, there is no distinction between noble and humble; one who possesses the Way is revered.

Since the formal rules and essential protocols originate from the great *bhikṣu* community, and because the Dharma is honored and the person is respected, it is necessary to pay homage. To speak in terms of reverence, this applies to every matter.
However, these eight dharmas are particularly essential for governing *bhikṣuṇīs*, and thus they are established separately. One must examine whether one can truly practice these precepts.

This is the abiding of the pure Dharma. Therefore, the treatise states: "If nuns practice this dharma, the True Dharma shall be restored for another thousand years. Thus we know that the Dharma is propagated by relying on persons;

the meaning of this is not obscure. Regarding the explanation of the name: Baoyun says there are both general and specific [meanings]. The specific meanings are as clearly explained in the *Shan-chao* (The Vinaya Compendium).

What is here called the "Eight Respects" (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) is the general name. Although the respectful observances are numerous, when categorized according to their objects and the mental states they entail, they are distinct.
There are eight [rules] for its accomplishment. To single-mindedly offer these eight dharmas with devotion is termed "reverence" (*jing*).

Within the subsequent listing of names, they are further divided into three parts: first, the listing of names according to the *Chao* (Commentary); second, the establishment of the reasons for the eight rules;

and third, the discernment of the gravity of the offenses. Regarding the first point, "first, approaching a person": this refers to requesting that the person sit, which signifies the earnestness and gravity of the invitation. Great...
If the *saṃgha* has not yet sat down, one must now invite them to sit. Even if the *saṃgha* has already sat down, one must still invite them, so as not to contravene the regulations.
In the present day, when lay households hold vegetarian assemblies (*zhāihuì*), the monks may have already taken their seats before the nuns arrive.

If the nun understands the rules regarding seniority (*fǎshàngzuò*), she should simply reply, "The *saṃgha* is already seated," or it is also permissible for her to remain silent. (The above is the formal explanation. Alternatively, some explain that the nun...

The assembly did not dare to sit down on their own authority; therefore, they came before the *saṃgha* to request permission to sit. When the *saṃgha* then assigned them their places, saying, "Sit according to seniority," this constituted granting them permission to sit.
(Master Bao cites the analogy of a minister and his son to refute what is unreasonable. Furthermore, there is another explanation: this was the nun coming to express gratitude for the seating.
Just as in the present time, the positions of father and son are distinct in terms of honor; once the father has granted the seat, the son must immediately offer thanks.

[Regarding this treasure, it is difficult to distinguish whether they occupy the same location or different locations; the lack of principle is extreme, and so forth]. The remaining seven respects are as stated in the text. Second, explaining the reason for establishing eight: A question is asked: What is the intention?

For what reason does the number not decrease to seven, nor increase to nine, but instead clarifies only the eight respects? The answer is: It is the nature of things (*dharmatā*) that there are eight.
First, there are three respects, which follow the formal protocols for serving the Sangha (such as the case of Baizhao Temple). Next, there are two respects, which involve receiving instruction...

Regarding the request for repentance (which refers to the invitation for well-being and the *zizai* [invitation to point out faults]), within the first three [sections], the very first mark of reverence clarifies the degree of respect in bodily action (the essential meaning).

Regarding the latter two teachings, one transcends through the karma of speech (the term "du-ang" means to revile or rebuke). Furthermore, within the second category of the honored Dharma, there are two divisions:

first, clarifying the root (namely, the precepts of *śīla*); second, distinguishing the branches (that is, the confession of offenses). Moreover, the former of these two pertains to the production of goodness, while the latter pertains to the eradication of evil.

Furthermore, within the latter three forms of reverence, there are two divisions: the first two concern receiving and following [the teachings] (the fortnightly invitation of the Dharma and the half-monthly retreat); the latter...

First, the Request for Confession (which is the *pravāraṇā*). This is divided into two parts within the first two [sections]: first, the Request for the Dharma (the instruction); second, the Resolution of Doubts (the *varṣā* or rainy-season retreat).
Alternatively, it may be understood that the first concerns requesting the Dharma to seek understanding, while the second concerns initiating practice based on that understanding.

Furthermore, regarding the latter two [sections], the first prevents unarisen faults by means of diligent non-transgression (*varṣā*), while the second eliminates faults already arisen, which is to say, being able to rectify what has been transgressed.

[The term] *huǐ* (懺悔; *pravāraṇā*) refers to the invitation for admonition. This constitutes three [aspects of] respecting persons and clarifying them; respecting the Dharma establishes two. There are three ways of receiving the *huǐ*; when these distinctions are applied, they form eight [categories].
To have more than this would be redundant, while having fewer would be insufficient; neither more nor less, it is precisely these eight that are established.

Third, regarding the establishment of the offenses for violating the Eight Respects (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*), the vow states: "Violating the Eight Respects results in eight misfortunes. This indicates that...

This explanation is accepted. If one speaks according to the first condition, it is considered "yǎnrán" (unfettered) and auspicious; however, when subsequently citing [the offense] according to its specific conditions to enter it into the categories of precepts (*śīla*), one must distinguish them clearly and must not treat them as identical.

Among these eight [categories], the five—hundredfold abuse, requesting [a favor], inquiring after health, and *zì* (self-indulgence)—are strictly included within the *pāyantika* (offenses requiring expiation) category;

they definitely constitute a *pāyantika* offense. Furthermore, regarding the reception of the precepts, according to the chart, this is also a *pāyantika*; thus, it is so stated within the categories of the precepts.
Upon examination, this has not yet been seen. If the confession of a transgression does not fall within the categories of the precepts, one who violates this incurs a *duṣkṛta* (light offense).

Regarding the formal accusation (*ukkhittaka*) of a *mahābhikṣu*, there are two cases: if one obstructs the intent of the accusation, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*; if one speaks words of censure, one also incurs a *duṣkṛta*.

Furthermore, among those who revile a *mahābhikṣu*, if one reviles according to the facts, one incurs a *pāyattika* because it violates a precept; if the person is without fault and one falsely accuses them of slander, one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension).

If there were further auspicious signs according to the diagram, they would be superfluous; therefore, do not mention them. (The various masters who searched for the mysteries were not thorough, which is why I have recounted this at length.)
The preceding is a general explanation.
The phrase "as follows" below serves as the concluding indication, as per the text.

Regarding the statement "five... arrive": this refers to the requirement that three *bhikṣuṇīs* be sent into the assembly of monks to perform the *pravāraṇā*, which means requesting the Saṃgha to point out their faults.
This is what is meant. Regarding the transgression of the fifth *gurudharma*: among the eight *gurudharmas* contained within the *Madhyama Āgama*, it says:

1. Receiving the full ordination from the Saṃgha; 2. Requesting instruction every half-month; 3. Observing the rains retreat (*varṣā*) in dependence upon the Saṃgha; 4. Performing the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*) in dependence upon the Saṃgha; 5.

Not daring to question a bhikṣu regarding the meaning and principles of the Sūtras, Vinaya, or Abhidharma (the Pitakas) on one’s own initiative; if permission is granted, one may do so; 6. Not speaking ill of bhikṣus.
[The offense is] transgressed. Among the seven monks, one confesses the offense; the eight hundred summer-retreats [seniors] pay respects to the newly arrived summer-retreat [junior] elders.
These eight are to be honored; thus they are called the "Dharma of the Eight Honored Teachers. According to these eight, the fifth differs slightly from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

Since it is now not permitted to ask questions arbitrarily, because this violates the teaching, one commits the fifth offense. Regarding the offenses of truth or falsehood: if it is true, it constitutes an insult.

[If she] commits a *thullaccaya* offense; if [the accusation is] false and constitutes slander, she commits a *saṃghādisesa* offense. Therefore, in both cases it is improper. Regarding "a relative nun" and below:
with respect to a nun who has relatives and kinsmen acting as a monastic community (*saṃgha*), or if there is some other matter, one may employ skillful means and gentle speech to exhort her;
one must not speak harshly, for that would constitute reviling. The rest of the text is clear. Next, regarding the rules for the *śikṣamāṇā*, the phrase "reaching two years" refers to...
Regarding the statement that "the precepts are not obtained separately," this refutes the ancient masters. The ancients said:

"When receiving the six rules (*ṣaḍ-dharma*), one again generates and obtains the sixfold precepts upon the existing substance of the previously held śrāmaṇerī precepts. Now it is said that the *śikṣamāṇā*’s six rules constitute the substance of the training precepts (*śikṣāpada*) themselves;
they are not generated anew. This has already been clarified in the preceding introduction. The present intention is the same as theirs; therefore, it says "not [obtained separately]."

The separate attainment of the precepts refers to the intention of the Master [Daoxuan] regarding those who have previously established their resolve. This means that these six rules are to be studied for two years;
if one maintains the proper conduct without transgression, then the resolve will be established and practice perfected, at which point one is fit to receive full ordination.
Therefore, this method serves as the preliminary condition for the Great Precepts.

Regarding the statement "the four parts are as explained in the usual [texts]": for the eighteen-year-old girl who studies the precepts for two years, the vow says that if she is eighteen, she must necessarily study the Dharma for two years; if she is nineteen or twenty, she does not need to study further.
Mì (Mishan) says this is not so, because it violates established regulations; even if she is over twenty, she must still study them, for if she does not study...

Such a person will certainly not receive the Great Precepts. Question: Although one may now receive the Six Rules (ṣaḍ-dharmāḥ) without relying on the two-year period, would this not violate the teaching?

Answer: If one follows the tradition of the north of the River, it is mandatory that the two years be completed; if they are not completed, it is not permitted to confer them. However, nowadays it is not so.

If one does not accept [the vows] at all, it violates the teaching and is not established as valid. However, even if one accepts them but the duration is not fulfilled, there is no impediment to attainment, because this does not violate the teaching.
Although there is no explicit textual authority for this, when inferred through reasoning, it causes no harm. Regarding the phrase "having become weary of her former state":

this means that since she has already been married, she must have grown weary of the mundane affairs of her original life, such as the constraints of her husband and the desires of carnal passion. Regarding "being pregnant," the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
It is said: There was a householder’s wife named Līlā, who was very wealthy with abundant riches, fields, houses, and various possessions.
Later, her family estate fell apart and dispersed until she was left all alone. Because she had been pregnant for some time, she became ill and emaciated from grief, and her fetus did not grow.
She said, "I have no fetus; [the child] died," and later, mindful of the peace of a śramaṇa, she went to the vihāra to seek refuge and ordination.
After she had been ordained, she lived in peace and without trouble, and her fetus grew again. When the nuns learned of this, they expelled her, claiming she had committed adultery.
She recounted the preceding circumstances in detail, until the Buddha said: "In the future, if there is such a person, first..."
"Causing [the student] to study the Dharma for two years," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "up to two years," Xuánzàng says: "To fully learn the three dharmas" means to learn all the requested dharmas in their entirety.
The mention of "three" here refers to the stages of the dharma; thus, there are three according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. This is what is intended by the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act).
These are the bases for performing the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts) that cause one to train; this present training rule is precisely what is enacted by the *karmavācanā* masters.
"Touching with a defiled mind" refers to the preliminary stage (*prayoga*) of sexual misconduct. "Stealing four coins" is the preliminary stage of theft.
"Taking the life of an animal" is the preliminary stage of killing. "Minor false speech" is the preliminary stage of major false speech. "At an improper time... [and so forth].

"Eating [at improper times] is the fifth; not drinking alcohol is the sixth. Although the text enumerates the ten precepts—including lust, theft, killing, and lying—these fundamental acts such as lust and theft are not among the count of the six primary rules (*ṣaḍ-dharma*). Their mention within the section on the exposition of the characteristics is because they were already studied when he was a *śrāmaṇera*;
thus, they are cited here by way of reference to what preceded. The text says: "Listen attentively, [Name]. The Tathāgata, who is without..."
The Buddha, attaining perfect enlightenment, taught six rules: "One must not commit impure conduct," and so forth (as detailed).

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, these six rules consist of the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*) along with the eight matters of physical contact (*aṣṭau sparśanavastūni*). If one violates any of these six, they must undergo a probationary period of two years.
If there are violations among the other disciplinary rules, one is required to perform a formal confession of transgression (*deśanā-pāpadeśanā*). This concludes the section on the Vinaya.
"Knowing" refers to [knowing] that the food has been taken with one's own hand. "Giving food to another" refers to a *mahā-bhikṣuṇī*.

Since it is not for her own consumption and she does not need it, she receives it from a *śrāmaṇerikā*. If she were to take the food herself and eat it, she would also be subject to the offense of transgression; this is because she has already taken it herself.
One must receive [the food] before taking it. If one takes and eats it without having received it, one commits an offense.
The exception for *śrāmaṇerikās* is made on account of specific circumstances; they may take food themselves without offense. Regarding those who may give to a *bhikṣuṇī*:
this means that if there is a *śrāmaṇerikā* or a *śikṣamāṇā*, she may also pass food to a senior *bhikṣuṇī*. As for "one must receive it oneself": if there is... [text ends].
A *śrāmaṇerī* may take food for herself only if she must obtain it from another; she must not give food to others—referring here to other *bhikṣuṇīs*.
Therefore, the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* states: "A *śikṣamāṇā* should train in all the precepts, with the exception of taking food with her own hand and giving it to another.
If there is no one to receive the food, she is permitted to take it herself and eat it; if someone is present, she must have it received [by them]. To eat beyond this limit constitutes an offense.

Whether [the candidate] has a female preceptor (upādhyāyinī) or not, both cases are permissible (the above is a marginal note). Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and other texts: the thirty-eighth fascicle of that Vinaya states:
"There was a bhikṣuṇī who ordained a twelve-year-old girl and conferred upon her the full precepts (upasampadā). She was of a weak and delicate nature and was unable to endure hardships."
Regarding those who were not fully endowed with proper deportment (*īryāpatha*) and so forth, they reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, when eighteen-year-old girls wish to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*) within my Dharma, they should request from the Saṃgha two years of training in the precepts (*śikṣamāṇā*). Furthermore, the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha must be complete with a quorum of ten members;

through the formal motion (*jñapti*) and three proclamations (*karmavācanā*), it shall be accomplished. This is called 'granting the training in the precepts. During these two years, they must comply with the ten [rules]..."

Regarding the eight matters, they are as listed in the *Chao* (the *Shishi Yaolan*) as thirteen items. As for the *śikṣamāṇā*’s impure food, that which the *bhikṣuṇī*s consider pure refers to leftovers, stored food, and so forth.
Regarding "seven or eight": the seven refer to the day of the *poṣadha*, and the eight refer to the day of the *pravāraṇā*; the text of the *Chao* combines these to say "seven or eight.

Regarding the latter four *pārājika*s, they refer specifically to the eighth, the concealment [of a grave offense], and the subsequent [offenses]; these correspond to the ninth and tenth [categories].
This is the eleventh [and] twelfth. If these four precepts are transgressed again, one must again undergo two years from the beginning.

Regarding the thirteen [precepts] from the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* downward: in that Vinaya, the nuns have nineteen *saṃghāvaśeṣas*, which constitute the second category; here, they are collectively treated as one.

The number of offenses follows the specific transgression, and all are to be confessed as *pāyattika* (light offenses). "The rest is as explained there" means that there are five further precepts, according to whichever is transgressed.

Regarding the number of days: one further studies until they are completed. As for the "five," they are: first, eating at improper times; second, eating while holding food; third, handling precious objects; fourth, drinking alcohol;
and fifth, wearing perfumes and flowers. Adding these five to the previous thirteen results in eighteen.

Regarding the statement in the *Śrāmaṇerikā-dharma* that "two [acts] are not permitted": in some versions, "learning" (*xué*) is written as "staying" (*zhù*), and "precious object" (*bǎo*) is written as "going" (*wǎng*).
Jie (Jie) says: "The phrase 'vow' and 'ritual method' constitute one sentence; change the character *cha* (叉) to the character *you* (又). Bao (Bao) says: "This is quite unreasonable. Consider it.
(The preceding section, which generally explains the section on the community of nuns, is now complete.)
○ From here below begins the Section on the Separate Practices of Various Schools. The text has two parts: first, the citation of the title; second, the explanation according to the text.
Regarding the phrase "from the various [schools] up to thirty," this is the preliminary intent: it means that the preceding twenty-nine chapters all concern the specific tenets of our own school;

even when discussing external schools, it was for the purpose of establishing our own position. Now, in this chapter, we directly recount divergent doctrines to serve as a path for refining one's understanding.
To open up the thoroughfare, one first distinguishes one’s own school and subsequently describes other sects; therefore, they are distinguished in this sequence. As for the explanation of the title:

because it circumambulates and narrates the various schools, it is called "The Various Sects" (Zhubu); because it collectively presents their differences, it is called "Distinct Practices" (Biexing). The chapters are as described elsewhere (*etc.*).

Next, regarding the explanation according to the text: as for the phrase "from antiquity to the present experience," this refers to the passage of exhortation to study extensively. It states that through such study, one attains universal knowledge and is not deluded by the teachings;

thus, one encounters no obstructions in practical matters and is further able to recognize all things thoroughly. This is truly due to the richness of one's learning, as was the case with the realized masters of antiquity.
There is no contradiction or dispute. Since it is said that one is "rich in learning," one naturally assists those who are poor [in knowledge]. Furthermore, the *Lunyu* (Analects) states:
"Zixia was extensively learned and earnest in his resolve. Confucius’s commentary explains this as "broadly studying and possessing profound understanding.

If one speaks with ultimate precision, regarding the four *dharmas* (*caturvidha-dharma*) that are deficient in ritual procedure (*vastu*), it means that although one's own school (*sva-nikāya*) speaks of "delimiting the boundary" (*sīmā-bandha*), there is no distinction between what is permissible and what is impermissible.
The six characteristics [of the *ṣaḍāśraya*] concern the distinctions between the general and the specific; this constitutes a deficiency in the matter (*artha*).

Although the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* prescribes the receiving and relinquishing of the three robes (*tricīvara*), it lacks the formal liturgical formulas (*padavyañjana*) for such relinquishment and reception;

this constitutes a deficiency in the dharma (*dharma*). As for the explicit texts found in other schools, they may be distinguished according to matters such as the six characteristics for convening the Saṃgha. Relying on...
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and others are such examples. Furthermore, the practice of receiving and maintaining the three robes (*tricīvara*) is based on the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and other texts.
As for the principle that one must necessarily follow the practice: this refers to the logic that as long as the Vinaya-piṭaka has not yet been divided, it remains a single body;

therefore, one must necessarily follow and implement these practices, rather than ceasing them simply because there is no explicit textual authority. Regarding the phrase "not contradicting the two": ancient commentaries state that this means not contradicting other schools (*nikāya*), and that it is indeed so.

There are two methods for handling such matters. First, if it does not contradict the appropriate regulations and is indeed in accordance with the Dharma (this is not a correct interpretation), yet according to the *Souxuan* it states:
"Now, citing external texts that do not conflict [with our own], and taking as authoritative those passages that have not yet distinguished the fundamental oneness—this is the first method.

Second, if one recognizes the urgency or relaxation of one's own school and, without contradicting the views of the treatises, adopts the textual rules—this is the second method (this is merely a precaution against being too lax). Alternatively, one may rely on the *Baoshu* and adopt the phrasing from other texts.

The first is [to cite a text] for its own sake; the second is to adopt the meaning of another school (now, upon closer examination, this interpretation also lacks reason, as it is not yet appropriate to discuss the doctrines of other schools). My current explanation is as follows:
the passages concerning the facts and dharmas of various schools cited from within the systems of other schools serve to establish the practices of those other schools—this is the first.
When these are brought over into our own school and found to correspond with the categories of our own school—this is the second. [This involves] discarding the urgent to follow...

Regarding "relaxed" (*huǎn*): the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) contains three types of formal acts (*karmavācanā*). For instance, when performing a formal act through a motion (*jñapti*), the words at the beginning and end of the motion must be recited word-for-word;

it is not permitted to add or abbreviate them—this is "strict. Now, we abandon this strictness and instead follow the legal procedures (*dharmakarma*) of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong lü), applying its principles to the appointment of officials;

this is the "relaxed" approach of being "only much and only good. Furthermore, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, at the time of receiving the precepts, one must personally possess robes and a bowl that are in accordance with the Dharma—this is "strict."

Now, one discards this urgency and instead relies on the *Śāstra* for the borrowing of robes and bowls, which is lax when such items are lacking. Furthermore, within the four categories of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there are three grades;
the protection of the robe through the fixed period of receiving it depends solely on the appearance of dawn, which is urgent.

Now, one discards this urgency and instead relies on the texts of other schools regarding the request for days based on the completion of a task, whereby the protection of the robe takes the laxity of accepting any available garment. This is to abandon what exists and seek what does not.

For instance, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, receiving the precepts requires the presence of a preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the demarcation of a pure area (*śuddhasthāna*). Now, however, one discards these requirements.

Seeking instead from other schools, one may receive the precepts even without a preceptor and still obtain the ordination; there is no need to demarcate a pure dwelling or the like. Regarding the phrase "discarding the right and wrong of heavy and light offenses": "discarding" means to cast aside.

One casts aside the rule from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* that an offense of five coins constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), treating it as light, and adopts the rule from the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) that eighty small coins constitute a grave offense.
The *qian* offense for violating a *yī* [offense] is grave; this is thus to abandon the light in favor of the grave.

Furthermore, to discard the grave *yī* offense incurred by a second violation of the precept against sexual misconduct according to the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya), while instead adopting the *Shisong lü* (Ten-Recitation Vinaya) which treats a second violation of the first category as merely a *jí* [light offense], is to abandon the grave and turn toward the light.
Regarding what is right and wrong: to say now that one must "rely on the school" (*zong*) is to discard the fundamental, which constitutes being wrong.

Furthermore, *Souxuan* states: "Singing while reciting the precepts is correct; following the *Wufen lü* (Five-Part Vinaya) by using a direct tone is incorrect" (this contradicts the intent of the *Zigai chao*).

Those who, according to their own ignorance, engage in acceptance or rejection, are merely censuring the deluded sentiments of the ancients. "To bring shame upon oneself" means to incur it; "shame" refers to humiliation.

As for the phrase "how could the offense be categorized as something else," this means that the fault of being ignorant due to a lack of study is not something external, but is identical to the fundamental transgression of receiving the precepts.

The third section of the Separate Preface states: "Now, in judging the observance or violation [of precepts], it is based upon the substance of the reception [of ordination] and so forth. This is precisely what is meant.
If one has not yet fully entered the Dharma, they remain a śrāmaṇera. If one wishes to receive the full precepts while relying on any one of the schools (nikāya), [the following applies].
Among the five schools, one must rely on a specific school; that is, one takes the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) of that school as the essence of the ordination (*upasaṃpadā*).

Depending on this school, its practices serve as the standard for subsequent conduct. This implies, by contrast, that if the essence of the ordination belongs to the *Dharmaguptaka* school, how could it be appropriate to further rely on the texts of another?
As for the phrase "reaching the point of imitation," the matter concerns various methods; that is to say, the matters pertaining to the various schools are not few. There are...
There are myriad paths; seeking one that is difficult to return from, one finds its roots and branches so severed that it is impossible to reach [the goal].

"Reach" (jí) here means the ultimate limit. Furthermore, regarding the term "commentary" (shū): "chān" refers to a discourse that is not yet exhaustive. "Shū" takes the meaning of resolving and opening up what is obstructed.

"Essential" (*yào*) refers to the pivotal essentials. "Briefly" (*yuē*) means in summary. "To show" (*shì*) means to point out and indicate. "Rules" (*guī*) refers to regulations. "Models" (*mó*) refers to patterns and standards.

Next, within the opening chapter, regarding the phrase "from the general to the particular," it is as the text states. Within the initial section on the number of monks, from the words "first" to... [text continues].

Regarding the "intermediate" [category]: this refers to those beyond the ten [monks] headed by the *upādhyāya*. When the legal procedure (*dharmakarma*) is being performed, the name of the *upādhyāya* is recorded in the formal proclamation (*nirdeśa*), yet he is not permitted to be counted among the ten.
Because he is thus recorded but does not enter the number of the monastic assembly (*saṃgha*), he is categorized as being equivalent to the five [monks].
Regarding those who participate during the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination): this refers to the *pravāraṇā* performed by five persons, where each is selected one by one.

At the time of being selected, they do not count toward the quorum of the Saṃgha; however, once the selection is complete, when the second person is being selected, they do again count within that number. This is analogous to the time of confession (*pratideśanā*):

when seeking the Saṃgha’s permission through a formal motion (*jñapti*), they do not count toward the quorum; yet once the confession is finished and the selection is made, they again count as members of the number. Thus it is with all cases.

Regarding the "four masters for the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*": This was the practice of the ancient masters, that four masters were required for the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. Now, the *Chao* (the *Shishi Yaolan*) refutes this, stating: "The fifth [master] is the one for whom the act is performed;
since he does not enter the count of the *saṃgha*, how could [the rite] be valid? In response, they offer this defense:

"Since the *Vinaya* lists four masters among the categories of the *saṃgha*, and according to that, three matters—*pravāraṇā*, receiving ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), and the removal of offenses (*āpatti-vinodana*)—are excluded, yet it does not mention excluding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. Therefore, four [masters are required]."

A person must certainly obtain [the requisite number]. If one follows the superior interpretation of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), it would not be so; however, our Master has now determined this based on the ultimate reality.

If one follows the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* regarding the five persons required for the confession of a *pārājika* offense, the Shared Teaching is as stated above.
