When ancient masters cite the Vinaya stating that within a *saṃgha* of four persons, they do not say "therefore it may be used," this is not a correct interpretation.
Thus, the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) says: "As in the *Mahāsāṃghika*, there are five persons for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony in border regions."

Regarding the various *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses, this is the correct measure. How could there be a case where the presiding master of the confession (*pratideśaka*) is included among the four persons?
How could one possibly tolerate this? Thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "There is no such thing as performing a *karmavācanā* by oneself during the *pravāraṇā*. It further states:

"When the presiding master makes a formal motion (*jñapti*) to harmonize with the Saṃgha, it is not a matter of one's own authority; the principle requires another. Since one must rely on the Saṃgha beyond oneself, five persons are required to constitute the assembly."

Regarding "no hindrance from beginning to end," the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: Some say that if the person who presides over the ritual (*bǐng-fǎ-rén*) performs it repeatedly from start to finish, they may be included among the Saṃgha for the purpose of receiving [the precepts].
For example, in the case of receiving the precepts in frontier regions, when the Preceptor (*jiè-shī*) makes the formal announcement (*bái-hé*), he is the one being acted upon (*suǒ-wéi*);

later, when the *bái-sì* (one motion and three proclamations) rite is performed, he is the one who maintains the ritual (*néng-chí*). Now, this *Chao* (Commentary) applies this analogy to the Master of Confession (*chàn-huǐ-zhǔ*): at the initial stage, when he presides over the announcement, he is...

This is what is intended. Once the confession is completed, if there are those with whom one has karmic ties who wish to depart, the Vinaya permits it; one should then pass the robe back and grant it to them through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation).

Furthermore, regarding the person capable of presiding over the rite, from beginning to end, there is no hindrance. As for the "confession assembly" in the middle fascicle, it fully clarifies the dharma for five persons.

Regarding the statement that "the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says [one may receive] ordination even without a preceptor," the *Souxuan* (Investigating the Profundities) explains this based on having previously invited one.

It is said that although [the factors] do not arise at the time of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), this is called "non-existence" (*abhāva*), meaning they have been entirely absent from the beginning.

If they were completely non-existent, how could they be cited by name as entering into the dharma? How is this known? Next, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* is cited, which incorporates the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

Regarding the case where the Upādhyāya does not appear in person: after requesting permission for the ten precepts, if he fails to arrive at the appointed time, the disciple may then, in the presence of an Ācārya, designate that person as the Upādhyāya from afar;

in this way, one is said to have received full ordination (*upasampadā*). As for those who previously failed to receive the precepts, it refers to a slightly different circumstance regarding the ten precepts:
it means that even if the number of monks is insufficient and the Upādhyāya does not appear in person, it is still permissible, provided the conditions are met. Thus it is reversed.
This demonstrates that the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is not entirely non-existent; it is merely said to be "non-existent" because it is not currently extant. Regarding the "eunuch" (*paṇḍaka*):
one interpretation states that this refers to someone who became a eunuch after having already received the precepts, and thus their physical condition was not declared [at the time of ordination].

A second interpretation states that this refers to the time of initial reception, wherein a eunuch cannot receive the precepts, as they are counted among the thirteen "difficulties" (*antarāyika-dharma*). Now, such a person is being appointed as an upādhyāya.

One also obtains the precepts. The reason for this is that, as stated in the preceding passage, one may obtain the precepts even without a preceptor (upādhyāya); how much more so when considering a change of status after having received them?
As for the *Karmavibhaṅga* stating that a layperson may serve as a preceptor, this refers to a person who was previously a recipient of the precepts according to the Dharma.
Later, when circumstances suddenly change, one may wear white clothing; it is even permissible to act as a preceptor (*upādhyāya*) for others.

Regarding "one who receives [the precepts] while being a layperson," this refers to someone who is entirely a layperson at the time of receiving them. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Dolun) is cited below to explain:

"One who does not shave their beard and hair and lacks robes and a bowl is a layperson. The phrase "it is the same for those who are not monastics" means that this applies specifically to those who have previously received the precepts.

This refers to the account of obtaining [the precepts] through instruction; it is the same as the previous case where one dons secular clothing and white robes to serve as a *upādhyāya*. Since there is no difference in the attainment of the precepts, it is said, "it is likewise.
However, according to the lower section of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, they are distinguished at once; therefore, it is said that "none of these are permitted."
Regarding the statement that "it is also the same as in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*": when a man assumes the deportment of a woman, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra*, Upāli questioned the Buddha:
"If a man assumes the deportment of a woman, the female characteristics, the female dress, and the female form, having so fashioned himself—"
"If one follows the manner of a man, can one receive the precepts? The Buddha said, "One obtains the precepts, but the assembly of monks incurs an offense.

Again he asked, "If a woman assumes the deportment of a man, the male characteristics, male clothing, and male form, and having done so, receives [the precepts] according to the manner of a woman, can she obtain them?
The Buddha said, "She obtains the precepts, but the assembly of monks incurs an offense. This refers to the case where the two characteristics of male and female are interchanged.

This means that there are those who create obstacles for others, doing so specifically to hinder their renunciation. The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* does not recognize such individuals as having a preceptor;
this refers to those subject to the thirteen *antarāyika-dharmas*. "Those who have fundamentally violated the precepts" refers to those who have broken the heavy precepts (*gurudharma*).
"Those who were originally not in harmony" likely refers to those who, from the outset, never received the precepts at all. Most ancient records interpret it in this way.
This refers to those who have disrupted the *karmavācanā* of the Saṃgha; they are not true renunciants, for although they have received the precepts, they do not uphold them.

If a person who previously lived as a "thief-monk" (*caura-vāsika*) acts as the *upādhyāya*, and the disciple is unaware [of his status], they obtain the precepts [for themselves] but incur an offense [for the teacher]. The three lower categories below are no different from the one above; therefore, it is said that "it is likewise.
Regarding the statement "according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* up to 'fully endowed'": this refers to the successive granting of consent (*chanda*) in four locations.

When the Saṃgha in four locations within a single boundary (sīmā) simultaneously performs a legal act (dharmakarma) to confer the precepts, they may mutually grant their consent (chanda) to one another;

for example, those of the eastern courtyard may grant consent to those of the western courtyard, and those of the western courtyard may grant consent to those of the eastern courtyard, and the same applies to the south and north.
If not, it constitutes a separate assembly (*bhedasaṃgha*). Regarding "belonging to the four assemblies":
if timber is laid flat upon the ground within the four boundaries, or if it is a bed or similar object, its legs must each enter one boundary. *Souxuan* says:

for example, if a single bed has four legs, each situated in a different place, and there are three people within each boundary, each desiring to perform the ritual of reciting the precepts (*poṣadha*), while one person is at the center of the bed.

The Elder presides over the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*. Provided four places are complete, the *karmavācanā* rite is validly accomplished. According to the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*, it asks:

"Is it possible for a bhikṣu to perform the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* with people from four places? Is it also permissible with five places? The answer is: "It is permissible. This applies even up to five places and so forth.
As for the "eight persons," this refers to the requirement that at least four must be present in one place for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*; now...
There are only three [groups], which makes seven. Now, by adding one person to two locations, they become eight. Regarding the twelve people:

this refers to having five people at each of two locations for the reception of precepts; now there are only four [at one location] (making eight). One location requires four for the recitation of the *Poṣadha*;
now there are only three (added to the previous eight, making eleven). Now, by adding one person to these three locations, they are made sufficient to reach twelve. Fifteen.

Regarding "persons": this refers to two locations for receiving the precepts, each having four [members] (making eight in total). There are two locations for reciting the *Poṣadha*, each having three [members] (added to the previous, making fourteen).

Now, by adding one person, these four locations are made complete (resulting in fifteen). Regarding eighteen persons: there are two locations for receiving the precepts, each having four [members] (making eight in total).
There are three locations for reciting the *Poṣadha*, each having three [members] (added to the previous, making seventeen). Now, by adding one person...

The first five bases (āyatana) complete [the count], making eighteen. This is because each must possess its own constituent part (*bhāga*) and its respective realm (*dhātu*) in order for the number to be fulfilled;

if these are lacking, the number cannot be attained. (This follows the interpretation of Lingfeng, who maintains that the person who completes the count is included within the numbers eighty, twenty-five, and eighteen, which is highly reasonable.
According to the ancient tradition, however, the person who completes the count is said to be outside the count of eight. This is the principle.
Nor is it lost. For now, it is best to rely on the previous interpretation. Regarding a *śrāmaṇera* who commits a grave offense and is permitted to leave the household life:

this refers to being allowed to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). Regarding one who violates a *bhikṣuṇī*'s pure conduct and is not permitted [to remain]: this means he is not allowed to receive full ordination and is to be permanently expelled (*parivāsa*).

However, if he is able to reform and repent and does not commit it again, he is also permitted to receive full ordination. According to this principle, those who undergo the ritual of repentance (*kṣānti*) are admitted; as the *Souxuan* states:

The author of the *Chao* (Commentary) follows the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, which permits the practice of *śikṣādattaka* (probation for serious offenses). That Vinaya, however, strictly stipulates that it must never be granted.

Now, according to the current practice in the Song dynasty, when a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*) commits a grave offense, the *śikṣādattaka* is always permitted. By analogy, this novice (*śrāmaṇera*) who has violated a nun should likewise be permitted to undergo repentance.

Regarding the distinction between the universal and the specific within the two noble systems of law: as for the statement "from two... to loss," both the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* contain the intermediate *karma* (formal ecclesiastical act).

It is called *mā* (rubbing/smoothing). It is also termed "seeking permission" (*kṣānti-yācanā*). This means that this *karman* merely seeks permission from within the *saṃgha* to perform matters such as extending the period of the rains retreat (*varṣopagamana*) or performing the *pravāraṇā*.

Furthermore, regarding the addition of the *jñapti-karman* and so forth: this means making a formal announcement (*jñapti*) so that the assembly may hear and know; it is not fundamentally a request for the *saṃgha*’s permission.

Even if the *saṃgha* does not grant permission, once the announcement is completed, the act is established. The remaining three [types of *karman*] are the same as those in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya).
This refers to the *jñapti* (motion), the *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion with one subsequent motion), and the *jñapti-caturtha* (motion with three subsequent motions).

It is further stated that "intermediate direct *jñapti*" and the like mean that a direct *jñapti* is a *jñapti* added upon a *jñapti*. According to the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-śāstra*, there are five types of *karmas* in total:

first, the *lakṣaṇa-karma* (formal act of restriction), which refers to prohibitions such as not being permitted to enter cities for a period of one year or six months; second, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karma*; third...

Regarding the intermediate [procedures]: the fourth is a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation), and the fifth is a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations).
Among these, the first three are performed by three persons, while the remaining three are performed by four or more persons. The rest is as stated in the text.

Regarding the "triple offense" (*tri-āpatti*), the statement that "the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*) and so forth are likewise" refers to the fact that in the first section of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there is no such thing as a repeated offense;
this is based on what was taught prior to the period before one has undergone confession and purification (*deśanā-pratideśanā*). That same Vinaya, in chapter fifty-one, asks:

"Is there a case where a great bhikṣu commits an improper act yet does not incur the offense of sexual misconduct (*abrahmacarya*)? The answer is: "Yes; for example, one who has previously broken the precepts. In the second section and below, however, there are repeated offenses. Why is this?

This is known from the *Shanbu biqiu sanqian weiyi chao* (Extracts from the Three Thousand Monastic Precepts for Bhikṣus), which cites the twenty-second fascicle of that Vinaya. The text regarding the rules for the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) states:

"If a śrāmaṇerī undergoing training for repentance commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, the bhikṣus shall perform for her the six-night concealment, the *mūla-parivāsa*, and the restoration from guilt" (the above is the Vinaya text).

Xuan says: "According to the text, since it mentions the *mūla-parivāsa*, there must have been a repeated offense; thus, the six nights are both subverted by the concealment and subverted by the [repeated] offense."

Each has its own *mūlaparivāsa* (initial probation). Therefore, we know that in the lower section [of the Vinaya], according to the gravity of the offense, there are cases of repeated transgressions (*punar-āpatti*).

(The above is based on the text of the *Sòuxuánjì*). The *Biǎopò* (Refutation) states: The text of the *Chāo* (the *Vinayamātṛkā*) merely says, "Request a bhikṣu to come and grant me *mānatva* for the removal of the offense.

It is improper for the *Sòuxuán* to arbitrarily add the term "concealment" (*chǐfù*). Since the Vinaya text already states that a śrāmaṇerī undergoing training (*śikṣamāṇā*) who commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense [is subject to this], where [else] could it be found?

Furthermore, there is concealment (*pracchādana*). Because nuns are not permitted to undergo the *parivāsa* (probation), fearing they might commit an offense of contact (*sparśa*), they have only the half-month *mānatva* for purification from offenses.
As for the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offenses requiring formal meeting) committed by nuns according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is likewise improper for them to perform concealment.

(Now, examining this closely, it is not that Sōu Xuán has misinterpreted; this point is already stated within the section on the *Pārājika* and *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules. Please reflect upon this, O profound one. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is the same as the [Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya], hence it says "it is also thus."

Furthermore, regarding the fourth category of "inclusion" (*saṃgraha-vastu*), the statement "provisionally reaching the point of holding" indicates that the *Caturvargika*’s three grades are broad, whereas the *Daśabhāṇavāra* and *Mahāsāṃghika* have only two grades, which is narrow.
Moreover, the maximum duration in the *Caturvargika* is only one month, which is narrow; whereas in the *Mahāsāṃghika*, the matter concludes after thirty-nine nights.

The *Śaṃghāvaśeṣa-vastu* (Section on Matters) is thus broad. *Souxuan* states: "That which is 'intermediate' refers to a *jñapti* (motion) that has a beginning but no end. The text says: 'Venerable Saṃgha, listen! The time has come;
may the Saṃgha grant its consent,' and so forth—this is the beginning of the *jñapti*. Since the formal motion (*jñapti*) is not yet completed, there is no such thing as an end; thus it lacks an end.
Consequently, within the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual action), there may be an end or no end, but there is never a beginning, for the Saṃgha’s consent [is required from the outset]."

Because of silence, this matter is thus accepted and maintained. Furthermore, there is no objection from the venerable Saṃgha. Which elders consent? Those who consent remain silent; those who do not consent speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented and the matter for [so-and-so] is concluded; such is the meaning of the head [of the procedure]. Therefore, it is called the "intermediate *karmavācanā*.
As for the text mentioning "the rainy season retreat" (*varṣā*), the commentary states: this refers to the majority of cases during the retreat in the Western Land (India).

This is because of the rains. Yuan also explains it thus: the *varṣā* (rainy season) retreat (*anugata*) is the same as the meaning explained above. Jia Mo provides a two-part interpretation: first, the initial commencement of the retreat;
second, moving to another location due to some necessity. Because one performs the retreat in different places during the course of a single summer, these are called the "two retreats.
(This [interpretation] is highly erroneous and must not be relied upon). In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are two ways of receiving the extension of the retreat period.
This refers to the seven-night period and the thirty-nine-night period. The seven-night period is identical to the four-part [period], yet it includes the "night" (niya).

Regarding the expression "including the night," it appears to differ from the four-part period; however, in terms of its fulfillment through the appearance of light (āloka-nimitta), it is the same as the four-part period.

Speaking specifically, in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya), this extends until sunset, whereas in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), it extends until the appearance of light at dawn. This concludes [the section].

This is a mutual citation, as has already been clarified above. However, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, during a single summer retreat, one may receive only two [types of] formal acts (*dharma*);

that is, within the ninety days, one must spend half of the time practicing within one's own boundary (*svasīmā*), and it is not permitted for more than half to be spent outside. How much less so for spending the entire time outside?
Regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) performed outside, it is as stated in the text (*etc.*). As for the phrase "the *Daśabhāṇavāra* says 'once again binding'," it refers to that...
It is said: When the Buddha was staying in the city of Vaiśālī, the Licchavis prepared various kinds of exquisite meals for the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
Suddenly, clouds arose out of season, and the food and drink left in the open air were struck by wind and rain. The Licchavis said to Ānanda:
Today I have prepared offerings of food for the Buddha and the Saṃgha. As it rains in the open air, I do not know what to do.
Ānanda informed the Buddha, who instructed Ānanda to go toward a house and perform the formal ritual of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to designate the area as pure ground (*śuddha-bhūmi*).
He placed the food inside, but later it was criticized by non-Buddhists (and so forth). The Buddha then ordered that it be moved outside the monastery grounds. Furthermore...

[Regarding] "being approached by laypeople (baiyi 白衣) to beg for [food]" and so forth (as detailed): the Buddha decreed that from this time forward, none of these may be designated as *śuddhasthāna* (pure grounds).

If one does so, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. All places previously consecrated must be relinquished. As for "granary" (*cang* 倉) and so forth: the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that a "dan" (pronounced *dān*) is a small basket or container.
Based on this text, the ancient masters maintained that at present, the designation of pure grounds is entirely prohibited, even according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Granted. Nor may one rely [on that]. As it is refuted in the Introduction:

"Regarding the fifth, the object and the mind. *Souxuan* states: "The precept against sexual misconduct and intoxicants in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* is established in relation to the object; there is no allowance for lack of perception or doubt."

The *Saṃghabheda-śaṅkā-saṃyojana-mūla* (The Root of the Bondage of Doubt Regarding Schism in the Saṃgha) follows the *Vassa-hīna-śaṅkā-saṃyojana* (The Bondage of Doubt Regarding the Reduction of Age) as its standard;

it prescribes a *pācittiya* offense for the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) who eats alone. As for the other precepts involving doubt or suspicion, they are all generally exempted. Daoyao further explains that the precept against sexual misconduct and the precept regarding the reduction of age may be applied accordingly.

However, if one follows the precept against alcohol based on the mental intention (*citta*), this is the doctrine of Nanshan. In the *Fanggui*, it is stated in accordance with ancient tradition for the time being.

Now it must be distinguished. For what reason does the *Jijia* (Record of the School) list them side by side? The commentators have gone too far (consider this). Regarding those who resolve doubts concerning right and wrong:

half rely on the primary object (*mūla-viṣaya*) as correct, while half rely on a different object (*anya-viṣaya*) as incorrect. Because they vacillate between these two objects, the formal act of restraint (*saṃvara*) is established based on the primary object.
This applies equally to both prohibitions (*pratikṣepa-śīla*) and essential precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*). Therefore, the Vinaya says: "This is a woman."

Regarding the "doubt-residue" (yí cán): if one suspects there are insects in grass or wood, it is a *pāyattika* offense. If one perceives [an object] as something else but the mind does not correspond to the actual state of the object, there is no offense;

this is because the force of the decisive perception is predominant, and thus the specific nature of the object is not considered. Both prohibitive (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) and natural (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) offenses are entirely instances where the mind and the object correspond.

Regarding the formation of an offense: if it is inconsistent with the actual state, it is minor. As for the statement in the text that "there is no offense," this refers to cases where one does not commit the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*) in a specific instance;

it does not mean that there is no preparatory act (*prayoga*). Therefore, that Vinaya states: "If one kills a human being while perceiving them as a non-human, or touches a woman while perceiving her as a man."

All are *ānantarya* offenses. This is based on the transformation of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), which concludes the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the preceding mind. If one were to base it on the fundamental delusion (*mūla-moha*), there would be no offense at all;

this is as in the *Caturvarga-vinaya* regarding the precept against schism and sexual misconduct. It differs from the case of "knowing yet doubting. *Souxuan* says: "For now, let us cite the four propositions from the *Saṅghabheda-khandhaka*:

first, 'unlawful and without doubt,' which refers to speaking while breaking the Sangha unlawfully without doubt; second, 'unlawful and without doubt,' which refers to speaking [while breaking the Sangha] unlawfully without doubt."

(This phrase refers to the doubt that constitutes the root offense. Regarding the three dharmas: to break them while doubting, yet not doubting when breaking the dharma; to break the dharma while doubting, yet speak without doubting the breaking of the dharma. Regarding the four dharmas:

to doubt the breaking of the dharma, yet speak with doubt regarding the breaking of the dharma. The Vinaya text itself restricts this to three phrases, for which one falls into Avīci hell for one kalpa.

As for the fourth phrase, where there is no offense of a heinous crime (*ānantarya*), the present text states that it is "not exempted" (*akappiya*). This is explained provisionally based on the second phrase; therefore, we know that doubt is not exempted.

This refers to an offense of the mind (*citta-vajja*). The remainder is as explained elsewhere. Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika* and other schools: in their tradition, for natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*), they do not permit [the mitigation of offenses through] thought or doubt.

For example, if the actual object is a woman, yet one touches her while perceiving her as a man or a eunuch, it is all a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. However, regarding prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*), they do permit thought and doubt;

for instance, regarding living plants or grass, if one perceives them as non-living plants or grass, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (light offense) due to such thought or doubt. This excludes cases involving thought and doubt.

This means that if there was previously a preparatory mind (*pūrvopāya-citta*), and one does not abandon thoughts of doubt or thoughts of transformation regarding the fundamental delusion, these are all fundamental primary offenses (*mūlāpatti*).
Thus, that Vinaya states: "If one perceives an object with an owner as being without an owner, or harbors doubt [regarding this], it constitutes a *pārājika* offense, and so forth.

Furthermore, it cites the case of a nun concealing a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) [and so forth], and again cites the case of the offense of physical contact (*sparśana*) [and so forth]. If, however, there was no preparatory mind beforehand, then...

"Fully opening up the object before one" refers to the presence of the perceptions of "belonging to another" (*parakīya*) and "doubt" (*saṃśaya*). Depending on these, one may either commit a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) or not commit an offense at all. Thus it is said:

"If there is neither the perception that [the object] belongs to another nor the intention to steal (*steyacitta*), there is no offense. This does not mean that the five cases and three cases are not distinct;

rather, what was cited above from the *Pañcavargika*, *Daśabhāṇaka*, and other texts is merely a general summary. In fact, when compared with the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), the distinctions between the five cases and three cases are certainly not absent.

Regarding precepts such as those against sexual misconduct, all constitute a root offense regardless of whether preparatory acts were previously committed; this differs from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, prohibitory precepts (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*) allow for doubt, whereas alcohol is a prohibitory precept. In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, doubt is not permitted regarding the root offense; thus, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* does not apply the exception for doubt.

Furthermore, regarding the precept against intoxicants (*surā-meraya-virati*), when contrasted with its prohibitions, two cases of doubt (*vicikitsā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are established. Regarding the precept against sexual misconduct (*kāma-mithyācāra*), there is no such perception or doubt;

when contrasted with the five factors (*pañca-aṅga*), it is universally free of doubt, thus forming three categories. Furthermore, when both the precepts against sexual misconduct and intoxicants are contrasted with the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) in terms of the presence or absence of preparatory effort (*prayoga*), five categories are formed;

therefore, they are said to be "not the same. Looking at the *Caturvargika-vinaya* and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, they form three; looking at the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, they form five. (This is the record.)
(As explained in the *Xuánshì*).

Within the sixth section on the confession of relinquishment (*śikṣāpada*), the headings can be understood by their names. Regarding the phrase "from ten to what is required": the "two treasures" refer to the two types of stored goods.

As for "few, permanent, rare, mountainous, or abundant," one should relinquish them to a pure person (*pariśuddha-pudgala*) of like mind; or, if no such pure person is available, one should relinquish them [to the Saṃgha]. One may then receive [them back].

[These items] are to be made into bedding for the Saṃgha of the four directions. As for the remaining items that are the same: according to this Vinaya, cotton mattresses are to be torn and discarded.

Medicines kept for more than seven days, specifically those kept until the eighth day, are to be given away to the monastery attendants (*ārāmika*). Oil kept for seven days is to be discarded for use as foot ointment or for lighting lamps.

That which has been kept for six days is to be given to other bhikṣus. Regarding food, alms bowls, and so forth, these are all the same as in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. [This concludes] the first entry.

Regarding "permanent relinquishment to the Saṃgha," there are two sections. First, as for relinquishing [the object] to the Saṃgha so that it enters the Saṃgha: appointing a person to discard it in the mountains or wilderness constitutes permanent relinquishment.

Second, as for exchanging it for the clothing and food of the Saṃgha: this is "entering the Saṃgha"; the original owner may not use it, and thus it is permanent relinquishment. This refers to when the two treasures (gold and silver) are relinquished to the Saṃgha;

the Saṃgha should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement) to appoint one bhikṣu to discard them toward a place of mountain streams, rivers, or vast wilderness. If...

"Monks shall not discard [these items]," etc., as stated in the *Śāstra* (Commentary). Regarding the "five types of bedding and requisites," these refer to the five precepts from the eleventh to the fifteenth among the thirty [Naiḥsargika-pāyattika rules].
They are: first, silk from wild silkworms; second, black sheep’s wool; third, white sheep’s wool; fourth, [wool] less than six years old; and fifth, an unsewn sitting mat (*niṣīdana*).
These must be relinquished entirely to the Saṃgha; the original owner alone is not permitted to sit or lie upon them. This is the explanation.
This establishes the meaning of "entering. Regarding the third point, "entering among the lay-monks," the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"If one receives medicine on the first day and receives more on the second day, and receives more again on the seventh day, and keeps it until the dawn of the eighth day, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
It must be relinquished to the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha may then give it to a layperson or a *śrāmaṇera*. If it is used to light a lamp or to anoint the feet [it is permissible]."
The *Caturvargika-vinaya* differs [from others] in that one may return the capital to its original owner after obtaining it; in the seventh category, medicine may be given to other bhikṣus.

Regarding those items that are "similar to food," they are the same as in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*. If one begs for an alms-bowl and seizes a fine one to enter the monastic kitchen, while leaving the inferior one for the keeper, these and other such offenses require that once the object is relinquished, it is returned to the owner;
using it again thereafter incurs no fault. These constitute two types of defilement; together with the three preceding categories, they form five. This concerns inexhaustible wealth (*akṣaya-nidhi*).

"Those" refers to the wealth within the Sangha-treasure. Regarding "to subdue the greed of the original owner," this means that the interest and profits from the property may only be used for robes within the monastic quarters;
the monks themselves may not divide them. These profits must be used [for the Sangha] and are not permitted to be made into food.
If these items were divided or made into food, the original owner would receive a share and the food, thereby using it to support his own body.

This accords with one's original greedy mind; yet seeking [for more] does not cease. If one makes robes for the monastic quarters, there is no sense of them belonging to oneself, which serves as a means of subduing [the mind].
Fifth, regarding bedding and requisites (*śayanāsana*): these range from those containing mixed wild silkworm cotton down to sitting mats that have not been folded.

1. A ground-covering made of pure black silk-cotton (*tūla*) that has not been folded for six years; monks may use it. 2. A three-robe (*tricīvara*) made of white wool that fulfills the first two conditions [of being new and not folded];

among these, those of good quality are treated like the aforementioned pure black silk-cotton ground-coverings, while those of poor quality are treated like the latter [white wool] that has not been folded for six years;
monks may use them. The remainder is the same as in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*. 3. The relinquishing of seven-day medicine.

Fourth, begging for a bowl; fifth, other relinquishments (*pratyāstaraṇa*), etc., which together with the preceding make five. The rest is as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "excellent up to prohibited":
first, the "turning-cart robe" and so forth, which has two parts: first, returning it to the owner; second, entering it into the Saṃgha.

The meaning of "turning-cart" is as explained above in the section on the precept against staying overnight separated from one's robes, according to the commentary on the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*. As for that detailed account, the commentary states: "Sū... [text continues].
Regarding the two purposes [of ghee]: if a bhikṣu is ill and wishes to use ghee for his eyes, he may obtain it for three or four days.

Once the illness has subsided, he should relinquish it; if he does not relinquish it, or if he retains it for a full seven days, it becomes *niḥsargika* (an offense requiring forfeiture). He must relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
If a bhikṣu is ill and the Saṃgha provides him with more ghee, and the bhikṣu then gives that ghee to a layperson (*avadātavasana*), and the layperson subsequently...

Regarding "giving up": a bhikṣu obtains an eye. Even if the bhikṣu has no illness and does not use the eye himself, if the Saṃgha wishes to use it, they must first have it given up to a layperson (avadātavasana).
The layperson then gives it back to the Saṃgha, whereby the Saṃgha obtains the eye. This is because both the original owner, the bhikṣu, and the Saṃgha have used it;
thus, it is said there are two kinds of usage. Regarding "the dharma of receiving" and "the dharma of not receiving," this refers to the dharma of the precepts.
This does not refer to the five heterodox practices of Devadatta.

Regarding the seventh point, "following the characteristics of the precepts," where it says "from seven down to six people" and so forth, the *Xuánjì* (Commentary by Xuánzàng) groups them into three pairs:
first, those of great virtue who are senior; second, those with much shame who are gravely ill; and third, those deficient in the assembly who are not invited—all of these constitute one [category].

This is as clearly explained in the *Yiyu chao* (Commentary on the Meaning). Regarding the term "commentary by the Vinaya-son" (*lüzǐ zhù*): one interpretation states it refers to a disciple who studies the Vinaya;

another interpretation states it refers to the footnotes beneath the main text of the Vinaya. We now adopt the latter explanation. As for the phrase "extensively questioning those who uphold the Vinaya so that they may be able to resolve [doubts]":

this means that through these six [methods], offenses can be extinguished; it is not possible otherwise. The above concludes the various individual sections of the various schools (*bù*). Thus far there has been...
The third section, the "Summary" (yìwén kē), consists of thirty articles in total. This concludes the main body of the text, the *zhèngzōngfèn*.

Regarding the third part, the *liútōngfèn*, the phrase "the remainder extends to... refers to the entrustment for circulation. Although the text appears to contain an exhortation to study, it is explained from the perspective of its most prominent feature.

Written in vermilion ink: On the eighth day of the fourth month, written by the monk An of Zhenshen Temple, this concludes the seventeenth fascicle of the *Jianzheng ji* (Simplified and Corrected Record) of the *Shifen lü chao* (Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya).
Transmitted by the Vinaya Master of Zhenshen Temple in Wuyue, the śramaṇa Jing’an, during the Ding-si year, this single volume was re-edited.

The *Jianzheng ji* (Record of Rectification) in seventeen fascicles is hereby dedicated for universal circulation, with the hope that it shall endure for twelve thousand years—the lifespan of the Buddha-dharma.
Recorded on the eighth day of the fourth month. May future worthies examine this and understand my intentions.
Therefore, I have criticized it thus.
